title: With Kyiv’s air defense crews as they race to keep up with Russia’s jet-powered drones

content:
Anton, a soldier with Ukraine's 112th Separate Territorial Defense Brigade, stands beside an Oktava electronic warfare system outside Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 13, 2026. (Jakub Laichter / The Kyiv Independent)
In a cornfield north of Kyiv, pieces of blackened metal are scattered among rows of dried stalks. They are all that remains of a Russian Geran attack drone, shot down by Ukrainian fighter jets as it flew toward the capital during one of Russia's mass aerial assaults.
"Last year we had so many of them," says Halyna Prykhodko, deputy director of the Branytsia division of the agricultural company Zemlya i Volya. "We found three, four, even five in the fields."
Above Prykhodko's land is one of the routes Russian drones take to approach Kyiv. Ukrainian forces try to intercept them over the countryside before they reach the capital and crash into homes and critical infrastructure.
Since late summer, Russia has been terrorizing Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast with jet-powered drones, adding to the now-familiar threat posed by conventional Shahed-type drones and missiles. Between larger assaults, successive waves of jet-powered drones now arrive day and night.
Defending Kyiv requires a layered system of air defenses, from sophisticated missile systems and fighter jets, to mobile machine-gun and interceptor-drone units.
Over two days, the Kyiv Independent accompanied soldiers of the 112th Territorial Defense Brigade at several positions outside the capital, observing how their units hunt incoming Russian drones and adapt to Russia's evolving weapons and tactics .
Radar stations and other detection systems are the first link in a wider system coordinating Kyiv's air defenses. They track approaching Russian drones, relaying information through command posts that direct the response of individual units.
"Every unit is subordinate to its own combat command post," says Senior Sgt. Serhii, who leads a mobile fire group. His surname is withheld for security reasons. "It gathers all the information from higher commanders and other groups, and issues orders to each group."
His three-man mobile fire group is armed with a truck-mounted Browning M2HB heavy machine gun, a SkyLock targeting system, and thermal-imaging equipment.
One soldier mans the machine gun, another commands the group and operates observation equipment, and a third covers them with an assault rifle.
When a drone approaches their sector, the soldiers receive information about its direction, altitude, and distance. They must then locate it using their observation equipment, adjusting for discrepancies between the target's reported and actual positions.
The crews operate within designated firing sectors, limiting where they can engage targets to avoid endangering civilians or friendly aircraft.
The gunner must account for the target's speed, distance, and direction of travel, calculating how far ahead to fire so that the bullets and aircraft arrive at the same time at the same point.
"Firing isn't difficult. Making the calculations is."
"Firing isn't difficult. Making the calculations is," explains Volodymyr, a soldier in the mobile fire group.
Repeated practice and experience are essential, he says, until judging a target's movement and calculating the necessary lead become almost instinctive.
Weather conditions, altitude, and speed further determine whether a target can be engaged. Thermal-imaging equipment helps soldiers detect drones at night, but cloud cover can obscure them, and faster, higher-flying jet-powered drones present greater difficulties.
"Within five seconds I have to engage it as much as I possibly can," says Volodymyr.
It's his birthday when the Kyiv Independent visits the mobile fire group. He spends it at the group's position, surrounded by fields.
"Grand celebrations," he jokes when asked how he plans to mark the occasion. "I've got these wide fields. I can walk over there, walk over here. Not many options."
Other crews use shoulder-fired missiles to engage targets beyond the reach of machine guns.
"Bodya," another soldier, operates a Soviet-designed 9K38 Igla man-portable air-defense system, which uses a heat-seeking missile to pursue aerial targets. Even with a guided missile, soldiers have very little time to engage a fast-moving target.
With conventional propeller-driven Shahed-type drones, Bodya explains, the sound of the approaching engine can provide some warning. Jet-powered drones and cruise missiles, however, travel much faster, and by the time crews hear one, it can be almost on top of them. Some targets pass through his unit's engagement area in as little as 20 seconds, he says.
Ukraine primarily uses systems such as NASAMS and IRIS-T against Russian cruise missiles, aircraft, and other aerial threats, but to intercept ballistic missiles, Ukraine has to rely on its scarce arsenal of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors .
Interceptor drones have become another means of bringing down Russian targets, particularly conventional Shahed-type drones, without expending costly surface-to-air missiles.
A soldier with the call sign Gendalf shows the Kyiv Independent the Sting interceptor drones operated by his unit. Equipped with cameras, the interceptor drones transmit live video to operators who guide them toward incoming Russian drones.
But Russia's increasing use of jet-powered drones, some capable of flying at about 600 kilometers per hour, has created a problem for operators like Gendalf.
Reaching about 320 kilometers per hour at full throttle, the conventional rotary-wing interceptors available to his unit struggle to match the jet-powered drones' speed, he says.
Beyond these different means of kinetic interception, electronic warfare provides another layer of defense by targeting the signals Russian drones rely on.
At an electronic warfare unit, Maj. "Secret," the brigade's head of electronic warfare and electronic intelligence, demonstrates a sensitive spectrum analyzer developed within the brigade. The device allows soldiers to detect and analyze radio-frequency signals, including those transmitted by Russian drones.
"Here we see all the signals that are nearby," he says, pointing to a series of transmissions appearing on the screen.
"First, we have to detect the signals and understand what we need to jam," Secret explains. "What matters is that there's data exchange," he says. "I can see the flow of data in real time."
Electronic warfare can disrupt an incoming drone in two main ways. First, jamming interferes with the signals it relies on, potentially severing its connection to an operator. Second, spoofing feeds the aircraft false information, potentially misleading its navigation or diverting it from its intended course.
But disrupting a communication link does not necessarily stop an attack. Some drones can continue toward preprogrammed coordinates without further instructions, meaning electronic warfare can only complement kinetic interception.
One of the most significant developments since late summer has been Russia's growing use of jet-powered Geran drones . Some variants fly at altitudes of 5 to 6 kilometers, beyond the effective range of mobile machine-gun crews.
Soldiers defending Kyiv also describe Russian drones changing their routes and maneuvering when Ukrainian interceptors approach. Some newer Geran variants carry cameras and mesh radios that allow operators to receive a live video feed and redirect the aircraft during flight.
Ukraine is adapting its interceptors in response.
On Oct. 18, Andrii Hrytseniuk, then head of Brave1, Ukraine's government-backed defense innovation initiative, said seven types of Ukrainian interceptors had already successfully intercepted jet-powered Russian drones. Twenty-two teams joined the effort to develop high-speed systems, including models powered by miniature jet engines.
The government had ordered more than 1,000 of these new interceptors, but production is still being expanded, he said.
A similar race is playing out in electronic warfare.
The electronic warfare unit studies the wreckage of drones brought down by Ukrainian forces and examines their electronics to understand how Russia is adapting its weapons.
"We dig around in these burned-out remains, looking at how everything is configured, what electronic components they use, which antennas, which parts," Secret says.
Russian forces continually modify the communications systems carried by their drones, forcing Ukrainian units to adapt the equipment used to detect and disrupt their signals, Secret says.
"They change the signal's form, and we adapt to that form," he says.
Equipment purchased just a year earlier may no longer be as effective against modified drones. But older systems cannot simply be discarded, since Russian forces can still use the technologies those systems were designed to counter.
Secret compares the process to constantly renovating an apartment without ever being able to remove the old wallpaper.
"Every six months, every three months, the fashion changes," he says. "And without stripping off the old wallpaper, you have to glue new wallpaper over it."
"And the wallpaper is, first of all, extremely expensive and very difficult to obtain," he adds.
Russia is also changing its tactics to overwhelm Ukrainian air defenses.
"They're coming in from all directions," one air defense officer says, describing a hypothetical attack involving 15 drones.
Most might be shot down, but a handful could get through. He believes Russian forces study the results to identify routes for subsequent strikes.
"They're probing, feeling things out," he says. "Then, yes, everything's clear, a mass attack."
Meanwhile, the pace of attacks is placing a growing strain on the soldiers defending Kyiv.
"The tactic is constant exhaustion, non-stop," says Serhii.
During particularly intense periods, he says, his men have worked 20-hour shifts, leaving just four hours for sleep. And during the hours spent on alert, some targets remain beyond their reach.
One machine gunner recalls a jet-powered Russian drone passing so high overhead that he could barely make it out.
"I couldn't even see it with my eyes," he says.
But he knows how to calculate the lead needed to hit a moving drone.
"I'd tear it apart if it were lower," he says.

title: Newsletters & Email Marketing Manager
description: The Kyiv Independent, Ukraine’s main English-language publication, is looking for a Newsletters & Email Marketing Manager.
content:
The Kyiv Independent is looking to fill a Newsletters & Email Marketing Manager position within the Marketing team.
The Kyiv Independent is Ukraine's largest English-language news outlet. It was founded in November 2021 by a team of reporters and editors who were fired from the Kyiv Post for defending editorial independence. Today, the team consists of over 90 people, mostly based in Kyiv. Publishing in English, we serve as Ukraine's voice in the world and the world's window into Ukraine.
We are seeking an experienced and strategic Newsletters & Email Marketing Manager to join our growing Marketing team. In this role, you will own the growth and performance of our editorial newsletters and email marketing, from growing our contactable base to designing new formats, automated journeys, and experiments that turn readers into engaged subscribers and members. You will work closely with the editorial, reader revenue, audience, and product teams, and report to the Head of Marketing.
The ideal candidate combines a product mindset with hands-on email marketing expertise, is comfortable with data and A/B testing, and understands how newsletters can serve both great journalism and sustainable reader revenue. Within your first months, you will audit our newsletters and emails, establish baseline KPIs, and present a six-month growth roadmap to leadership.
Thanks for taking the time to apply to work with the Kyiv Independent. If you are among the qualified candidates, you will receive an email from a member of our hiring team to schedule an interview. Please note that while we would like to meet with all applicants, we may not be able to do so due to the volume of applications we receive.

title: Drone reportedly strikes business center in Russia's Voronezh as fires break out across city
description: Reports mentioned numerous explosions across the city and thick smoke rising from several locations. Some residents told ASTRA that they had not heard air raid sirens despite the ongoing attack.
content:
Editor's note: This is a developing story.
A drone reportedly struck a business center in the Russian city of Voronezh early on Oct. 26, as explosions and fires were reported across the city amid an ongoing drone attack, independent Russian media outlet ASTRA reported.
Footage published by ASTRA appears to show a drone exploding at the Chizhov Gallery business center, a 25-story building in central Voronezh.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ also published imagery of the reported attack.
ASTRA further reported fires in residential areas, having received eyewitness photographs and videos that identified locations near apartment buildings where explosions occurred.
Voronezh Oblast Governor Aleksandr Gusev confirmed that Russian air defenses responded to a drone attack over Voronezh and its surrounding areas on the morning of Oct. 26.
According to ASTRA, a drone threat was announced at approximately 3 a.m. local time, followed by a missile warning about two hours later.
Reports mentioned numerous explosions across the city and thick smoke rising from several locations. Some residents told ASTRA that they had not heard air raid sirens despite the ongoing attack.
The Kyiv Independent could not verify the extent of the damage or whether the explosions near residential buildings were caused by direct drone impacts or falling debris. There were no immediately confirmed reports of casualties.
Voronezh Oblast directly borders eastern Ukraine, with the regional capital located about 200 kilometers (nearly 120 miles) from the nearest Ukrainian-held territory in Kharkiv Oblast. The areas has repeatedly been targeted by Ukrainian long-range strikes against Russian military and industrial infrastructure.
On June 22, Ukrainian forces struck the Voronezh Semiconductor Plant, a facility producing electronic components used in Russian missile and air defense systems, according to Ukraine's General Staff.

title: Bolsonaro refuses to concede as would-be Ukraine peace mediator Lula wins Brazil election
description: Lula had expressed the view in 2024 that Brazil should remain neutral and not interfere in Russia's war against Ukraine, but in the years that followed had been engaging in diplomacy, including efforts to position Brazil as a potential mediator between Kyiv and Moscow.
content:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won reelection on Oct. 25, securing a fourth, nonconsecutive term in office, as his opponent, right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, refused to concede defeat and vowed to challenge the election results.
The election ended with Lula receiving 51.79% of votes compared with Bolsonaro's 48.21%, according to Brazil's electoral authorities.
Bolsonaro said he would seek to annul the election, calling a decision by Supreme Court Justice Cristiano Zanin to extend voting by two hours "unacceptable." The extension was introduced following transportation disruptions and severe weather that affected voting in parts of the country, according to the Associated Press. The electoral court has recognized Lula's victory, and Bolsonaro's refusal to concede does not invalidate the result. Lula had expressed the view in 2024 that Brazil should remain neutral and not interfere in Russia's war against Ukraine, but in the years that followed had been engaging in diplomacy, including efforts to position Brazil as a potential mediator between Kyiv and Moscow.
In June of this year, President Volodymyr Zelensky accepted Lula's offer to assist efforts to negotiate an end to the war, Ukrainian presidential communications adviser Dmytro Lytvyn said , according to Reuters.
The leaders held a bilateral meeting on during the G7 summit in France on June 17, discussing ways to revive stalled diplomatic negotiations, including potential outreach to permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.
While Ukraine maintains close diplomatic ties with three of the five permanent members — France, the United Kingdom and the United States — Brazil has maintained diplomatic relations with Russia and China.
Lula spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin by telephone in August, discussing the war in Ukraine and bilateral relations, CNN Brasil reported.
Brazil has maintained diplomatic and economic ties with Russia since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in February 2022, opting out of Western sanctions and expressing a wish to have a role in a negotiated settlement to the war.
Lula has also rejected suggestions that Brazil supports Russia's invasion, saying in an April interview that his government has never recognized Moscow's right to occupy Ukrainian territory.
The Brazilian president's victory comes after a closely fought campaign against Bolsonaro, the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, who is serving a prison sentence for his role in an attempted coup following his 2022 election defeat. The elder Bolsonaro also refused to concede defeat after losing to Lula in 2022. He was subsequently convicted for his role in a plot to overturn that election.
The victory makes Lula, 80, the first Brazilian president to win four terms and the first candidate since the country's return to democracy to win a presidential runoff after finishing second in the opening round.
While Bolsonaro refused to concede and asked for the vote to be annulled, election officials have expressed "absolute" confidence in the proceedings and the result, as reported by Reuters.

title: Russian-friendly Vucic concedes defeat to student protest movement in Serbian election
description: For almost two years, student-led demonstrations in Serbia rallied against Vucic's right-wing incumbent Serbian Progressive Party. Protesting against alleged corruption in the government, the movement was triggered when a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad collapsed in 2024, killing 16 people.
content:
Former Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat in parliamentary elections on Oct. 25 to the student-led protest movement that has gripped the nation for months.
“Based on a stratified sample, it is clear that we have lost this election. The student blockade list won,” Vucic said in a press briefing.
According to Vucic, the Students' List party, backed by the protest coalition, is projected to take between 135 and 140 seats in Serbia 's Parliament. Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party appears to have come in second in the elections, and will have 105 seats in Parliament.
For almost two years, student-led demonstrations in Serbia rallied against Vucic's right-wing incumbent Serbian Progressive Party. Protesting against alleged corruption in the government, the movement was triggered when a train station canopy in the city of Novi Sad collapsed in 2024, killing 16.
Vucic previously announced his resignation as Serbia's president on Sept. 27, allowing him to run as prime minister in the nation's October parliamentary elections.
Vucic, having served as either Serbia’s prime minister or president since 2014, was known as a right-wing populist leader with authoritarian tendencies and warm ties with Russia.
The elections saw Serbia's highest voter turnout, 70%, since the dissolution of Yugoslavia in 1992, according to Reuters.
The election results are being hailed as a momentous political shift for Serbia, potentially turning the Balkan country away from ties with Russia and Vladimir Putin, who endorsed Vucic.
The defeat of Serbia's right-wing government echoes recent elections in Hungary. In April, populist leader Viktor Orban, also endorsed by Putin, was defeated in a landslide election.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar drew an explicit parallel between this election and that in his country which saw him rise to power, celebrating the Serbian opposition's victory in an Oct. 25 post on X.
"In Serbia, @avucic has conceded defeat. The Students’ List has won an absolute majority in the elections. Celebrations have begun in the streets across Serbia. Sound familiar?" Magyar wrote.
The Guardian also reported that Magyar subsequently spoke with the Students' List leadership and offered Hungary's support, saying his own electoral victory in April had encouraged the Serbian movement during its struggle.

title: Zelensky details expectations for upcoming trilateral peace talks with Russia, US
description: Before a meeting between Zelensky, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and U.S. President Donald Trump can take place, technical talks among the three countries' negotiating teams must be held first, said Zelensky.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky outlined his expectations for upcoming trilateral peace negotiations, and discussed air defenses and the planned ceasefire in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in an interview on Oct. 25.
In an exclusive interview with Alla Mazur, host of "TSN The Week," Zelensky detailed Ukraine's readiness to meet with Russian and American teams for peace negotiations scheduled for early November .
Above all, Zelensky stressed the need for robust security guarantees for Ukraine in any deal aimed at ending the war.
"Our security guarantees are our guarantees, and they cannot be dictated by the Russian side," Zelensky said. "Restrictions on our army and Ukraine's neutrality are not up for discussion."
The question of NATO' s involvement in Ukrainian security will "undoubtedly" come up in the negotiations, Zelensky said. The president suggested that if Ukraine is not allowed to join NATO, European countries and the U.S. should agree to extend the body's Article 5 defensive pact to Ukraine. Ukraine would also need to maintain a strong army after a peace deal is reached. "The best, in my opinion, is NATO plus a strong Ukrainian army, as part of the alliance," Zelensky said. "If I have enough finances, I want to keep the army of 800,000 people. We decide for ourselves what our army will be. If we are in NATO, the number can be 800,000 or less. But it will be a question of who is willing to finance or co-finance with us."
Before a meeting between Zelensky, Russian President Vladimir Putin , and U.S. President Donald Trump can take place, technical talks among the three countries' negotiating teams must be held first, said Zelensky.
"The issue of territory is a red line that can only be discussed at the level of leaders," Zelensky said. "Everyone should understand: first, we are not exchanging anything for anything. We are ready to discuss. If it's a territorial issue, then at the level of leaders. Other issues can be discussed at the level of technical groups." As part of the negotiations, Zelensky said he was prepared to discuss an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, establishing a new deal to protect grain shipments in the Black Sea , and prisoner exchanges .
"Energy, grain, and people – these are the specifics," Zelensky said. "A meeting at the level of leaders is an opportunity to achieve those specifics after our trilateral meeting. That's what we are asking for and offering."
Zelensky said that by offering these points for negotiation, a refusal by the Russian team to engage on the items will help expose whether the Kremlin is serious about peace with Ukraine or not.
"We are not demanding, but rather offering this to the American side," Zelensky said. "That would demonstrate seriousness. But if it's just a political maneuver and Putin is simply saying, 'Yes, I'm ready,' because he doesn't want to escalate tensions with America before the [midterm] elections , we will very quickly see in November whether it was a trick or not."
The president also warned that loosening sanctions on Russia before the negotiations would weaken Ukraine's leverage. This follows Trump waiving sanctions on Russian oil exports in October in an attempt to ease oil prices heightened by his war with Iran.
"I don't want us to be left without tools – without sanctions, without money, or without frozen assets – at the meeting with Putin," Zelensky said. "Because then, as Mr. Trump said, we will really have very few cards in our hand." Turning his attention to the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky , Zelensky said that the planned Oct. 27 ceasefire would need to last several days and include Russian assistance.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible. "Of course, Russia will do everything it can to clear the roads in a way that encourages people to go towards Russia and stay there; they won't simply let people go," Zelensky said. "Some people will be evacuated to Ukraine – to the part that we control – in one format or another. The most important thing is to unblock the people so they can live. Ideally, they should be able to reach their destination and evacuate here, to us, to Ukraine, where they will receive everything they need and be supported."
Zelensky also detailed his conversations with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, Norway, in October that set the stage for the planned round of trilateral negotiations. In meeting with Witkoff, Zelensky said they discussed limits placed on Ukraine's Starlink military systems, restrictions on intelligence the U.S. shares with Kyiv, and air defense shortages.
While the issues plaguing Ukrainian forces' use of Starlink systems and the matter of American intelligence sharing have been resolved for now , Zelensky stressed that Kyiv still lacked key air defense assistance.
"There is progress; it's just very slow," Zelensky said. "It's not enough to simply say, 'Yes, we will give [ Patriot missiles ] to you,' and then not deliver them for a month or two. That simply doesn't work."

title: Ukraine war latest: Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
description:
Key developments on Oct. 24-25:

 * Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
 * Russian attacks kill 8, injure 51 across Ukraine over past day as drone strikes residential building in Vinnytsia
 * Moscow ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine, US after Nov. 4, Kremlin aide says
 * In less than 24 hours, Russia hits 4 hypermarkets belonging to one of Ukraine's largest retail chains
 * Massive Ukrainian drone attac
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Starlink and Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk's satellite internet system, Starlink, was working at full speed as of the morning of Oct. 24, after it had previously been limited to 161 kilometers per hour (about 100 miles per hour).
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelensky said. "I thank all Americans and all our partners who took this seriously and truly helped us. I thank members of Congress , senators, all the media, the State Department, and the President."
Ukraine's Defense Ministry told reporters on Oct. 24 that Starshield was working above speeds of 400 kilometers per hour (about 248 miles per hour) again.
"We record a speed of more than 400 kilometers per hour, the connection is stable," the ministry said.
The ministry continues to monitor and record the work of Starlink and Starshield, according to Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara.
"This is another example of direct dialogue and the persistent position of the President of Ukraine at the highest level yielding results. And this result is, above all, important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics, and communications," the ministry added.
Musk later said that Ukraine's military violated the terms of service for Starlink, adding that the "loophole" has now been closed.
Ukraine's "military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," he said in a post to X.
"Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is not a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," Musk said.
He also claimed that SpaceX has done more than any other company to help Ukraine in its fight against Russia's war.
Ukrainian activist and former Defense Ministry adviser Serhii Sternenko denied that Ukraine violated Starlink's terms of service.
"As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true. In February of this year, whitelists were introduced. Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians," he said in a post to X.
"But for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system. Otherwise, no satellite communication terminals in Ukraine would work," Sternenko added.
Using Starlink for drone missions has been "technically impossible" since all drone campaigns that require satellite communications would only work with the military Starshield service, he said.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov also denied Musk's claims, saying that all Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90 kilometers an hour and do not work on Russian territory.
"Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said in a post to Facebook. "It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."
Russian attacks killed eight people and injured 51 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Oct. 24-25.
A Russian drone struck a five-story residential building in the city of Vinnytsia overnight on Oct. 25, injuring six people, one of whom was hospitalized, Nataliia Zabolotna , head of the Vinnytsia Oblast Military Administration, said.
The strike caused structural damage between the second and third floors, completely destroying four apartments and damaging nearby parked cars, Zabolotna added.
Alongside attacks on Vinnytsia, Russia launched 153 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on Oct. 25, including 92 jet-powered drones, as well as low-cost Banderol cruise missiles, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 119 drones, including 64 jet-powered ones. As of 8 a.m., efforts to intercept the remaining drones were ongoing, with at least nine still in Ukrainian airspace.
Some drones evaded Ukrainian air defenses and struck 15 locations, while falling debris was recorded at nine other locations, according to the Air Force.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russian attacks on the Synelnykove District on Oct. 24 killed three people and injured 14 others, including an 11-year-old girl, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Five of the injured were hospitalized in serious condition.
In the Nikopol District , Russian attacks over the past day killed two women and injured five people, including a 14-year-old boy, Hanzha added.
In Kharkiv Oblast, Russian attacks killed a 45-year-old man in the town of Lozova and injured two other men, aged 43 and 26, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Kharkiv, a 39-year-old man was injured. Russian attacks also wounded three men, aged 70, 54, and 47, in the town of Derhachi, and a 45-year-old woman in the village of Mala Danylivka, Syniehubov added.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person in the village of Yarova and injured six others elsewhere in the region, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Sumy Oblast, a 31-year-old woman was killed in a Russian attack on a farm in the Buryn community, which also injured an 18-year-old man. In the Boromlia community, a Russian drone struck a car, injuring three women aged 68, 56, and 36, according to local authorities .
Russian attacks injured four people in Zaporizhzhia Oblast over the past day. Russian forces carried out 832 strikes on 52 settlements across the region using drones, artillery, aircraft, and multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), local authorities said.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks targeted 43 settlements, including the regional center of Kherson, injuring two people, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, two women suffered acoustic trauma in a Russian strike on the regional capital, Chernihiv, on Oct. 24, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
One person was injured in a Russian drone attack on Kyiv on Oct. 24, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The Kremlin is ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the U.S. after Nov. 4, when Russia celebrates National Unity Day, Russian President Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled outlet Vesti on Oct. 25.
The statement follows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky 's Oct. 23 remarks that a new round of trilateral talks is expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi a possible venue.
"The next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations," Ushakov said.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected ceasefire proposals, demanding instead that Kyiv cede the only partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Such a concession would give Moscow territory that Russian forces have been unable to capture on the battlefield. Ukraine, in contrast, has agreed to multiple ceasefire proposals put forward by the U.S.
Ushakov said he did not expect the first trilateral meeting after the pause to yield significant results, calling it a "trial run." A peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine "still needs work," he added.
On Oct. 20, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European partners, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
The following day, Witkoff held a three-hour meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, after which the Kremlin said it was ready to resume trilateral talks in November.
Witkoff said on Oct. 21 that discussions among Ukrainian, U.S., and Russian representatives would "continue at the technical level."
Putin has long avoided meeting with Zelensky. Instead, the Kremlin chief is reportedly seeking a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in China next month in an effort to secure a favorable peace deal without Ukraine's participation .
In recent weeks, Trump has also lashed out at Zelensky, unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that ultimately failed, threatened to cut off intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, and eased sanctions on Russian oil exports.
Trump has defended the sanctions relief, arguing that it could encourage Moscow to take part in peace negotiations with Kyiv.
Russian attacks hit four Epicentr hypermarkets in less than 24 hours, the company said on Oct. 25.
The latest wave of strikes highlights Russia's campaign of terror against civilians, with stores, shopping centers, and other civilian infrastructure among the targets. Epicentr, one of Ukraine's largest home improvement and retail chains, has been particularly hard hit.
In a post on Facebook , the company said Russian attacks damaged or destroyed facilities in the cities of Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Vinnytsia, and Poltava on Oct. 24-25, and described the attacks as amounting to "total destruction of the network."
The company did not specify the extent of the damage or when the affected facilities might reopen.
The Poltava Oblast Military Administration said a 52-year-old woman was injured in an attack on a hypermarket on Oct. 25. Authorities in other regions did not report any civilian casualties from attacks on Epicentr stores during the same period.
Founded in 2003, Epicentr operated 72 hypermarkets across Ukraine before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Since the start of the all-out war, ten of the company's shopping centers have been completely destroyed and another 13 have been damaged, Epicentr told the Ukrainian outlet Ekonomichna Pravda in August 2026.
Epicentr's head of public relations, Yuliia Chudnovets , said on Oct. 22 that Russian forces had struck five company sites, including one in Kyiv , in the previous 48 hours.
A massive swarm of Ukrainian drones attacked the Russian border region of Belgorod overnight on Oct. 25, according to local officials and eyewitness footage posted to social media.
The bulk of the drones have concentrated on one area in the Belgorod city center, locals report . According to the monitoring channel Exilenova-Plus, the target was the MegaGRINN shopping complex, Belgorod's largest retail and entertainment center.
MegaGRINN covers an area of more than 163,000 square meters and houses over 200 stores, as well as a supermarket, cinema, and restaurants. The facility was closed and empty of visitors during the overnight attack.
Local residents also reported a fire in the courtyard of a residential complex in the area.
The Belgorod Oblast Operational Headquarters confirmed a "massive UAV attack" against the city and said emergency services had been dispatched to the impacted areas, though they did not name any specific targets.
The attack killed one civilian and injured 14 others, authorities said. At least 30 apartment buildings, 35 vehicles, four houses, three administrative buildings, and eight commercial properties were damaged.
The Kyiv Independent could not verify these reports at the time of publication.
Videos published on social media by eyewitnesses show explosions, fires, and air defense operations over the city of Belgorod. The Operational Headquarters has warned residents to stay indoors as attacks are ongoing in the region.
The city of Belgorod lies just 34 kilometers (21 miles) from Ukraine's northeastern border with Russia and approximately 70 kilometers (43 miles) from Kharkiv. Its proximity to the front lines makes it a frequent target of Ukrainian attacks , even as Kyiv's expanding long-range capabilities allow its drones to penetrate deep in the Russian interior .
Previous Ukrainian strikes on Belgorod have targeted energy infrastructure and logistics warehouses , including facilities belonging to the Russian retail giant Ozon .
The reported drone blitz on Belgorod comes shortly after Ukraine confirmed on Oct. 24 that its Starshield system had been restored to full speed , allowing troops to more effectively coordinate drone strikes on Russian targets.
Starshield, the military application of the Starlink satellite internet system, had been operating at drastically reduced speed in Ukraine since Oct. 14. The unexplained restriction disrupted key military missions and Ukraine's ability to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones .

title: Moscow to host 2030 International Weightlifting Championships following lifting of Olympic suspensions
description: The International Weightlifting Federation will be the first Olympic organization to hold a competition in Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
content:
The International Weightlifting Federation (IWF) announced on Oct. 25 that the 2030 International Weightlifting Championships will be held in Moscow.
Recognized by the International Olympic Committee (IOC), the IWF will be the first Olympic organization to hold a competition in Russia since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
"Concerning the IWF (Senior) World Championships in 2029, it will be staged in Ahmedabad (India), and Moscow (Russia) will host the 2030 edition," the IWF said on its website .
Between its nationwide doping scandal and international outcry over its war with Ukraine, Russia has remained largely sidelined from participating in the Olympics and related competitions since 2017.
On July 7, the IOC provisionally lifted the suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee (ROC), which had been in place since October 2023. The IOC said on July 7 that the decision followed a legal review that found the ROC "no longer includes as its members any regional sports organizations in territories falling under the jurisdiction of the National Olympic Committee (NOC) of Ukraine."
In response, a group of nine European countries urged the European Commission to halt funding programs for international sports organizations allowing Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete. Ukraine's NOC subsequently appealed the IOC's decision for arbitration.
On Oct 14, Dutch authorities refused to grant visas to three Russian gymnasts, preventing them from taking part in the world gymnastics championships held in Rotterdam later that month.
Previously, Moscow hosted ⁠the World Weightlifting Championships in 1983. Since the fall of the Soviet Union, Russia has won a total of 17 medals in Olympic weightlifting competitions. In order to compete internationally, all Russian athletes will have to meet anti-doping requirements set by the IOC.
Russia's all-out war has taken a heavy toll on Ukraine, with hundreds of Ukrainian athletes and coaches killed and hundreds of sports facilities destroyed by Russian missile and drone attacks.

title: 'Putin's paranoia' — New air defenses appear around Russian president's Valdai residence, analysis shows
description: The defensive perimeter extends to the Khotilovo military base, which serves as an alternate landing site, and a secret biological laboratory on Lisiy Island, according to RFE/RL.
content:
Russia has built an additional ring of air defense towers within 50 kilometers (30 miles) of Russian President Vladimir Putin's residence in Valdai, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) and OSINT analyst Jembob reported on Oct. 25.
Valdai is a small town in Russia's northwestern Novgorod Oblast. The town had a population of around 13,600 in 2025, according to Russia's Federal State Statistics Service (Rosstat).
The defensive perimeter extends to the Khotilovo military base, which serves as an alternate landing site, and a secret biological laboratory on Lisiy Island, according to RFE/RL .
Satellite images indicate that the new perimeter encompasses both the military airfield in Khotilovo and the laboratory complex on Lisiy Island.
By October, air defense systems believed to be Pantsir or Tor units had been positioned south of Putin's residence, within the 50-kilometer (30-mile) zone.
No positions have yet been identified along the northern section of the perimeter, though additional sites could be established in the coming months, the report said.
One of the towers forming the outer defensive line was already in place by March 2026, on the grounds of the Khotilovo military air base. Putin reportedly uses the base regularly. A dedicated railway branch connects it to his Valdai residence, providing a direct train route, according to RFE/RL.
Other air defense sites have been established along the shores of the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir.
RFE/RL published an investigation into the secret laboratory on the island on Sept. 3, around the same time construction began on two new air defense towers in the area.
The Kremlin accused Ukraine of attacking Putin's residence in Valdai with more than 90 drones on Dec. 29, 2025. Russian officials claimed the drones were carrying 6-kilogram (13-pound) high-explosive warheads, but claimed that air defenses had allegedly intercepted them all, with no casualties or damage reported.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Foreign Ministry denied the allegations, calling them a "lie." Kyiv also accused Moscow of fabricating the claims to undermine Ukraine's standing with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration and derail ongoing peace efforts.
In early January 2026, the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) informed Trump that Ukraine had not targeted Putin's Valdai residence. U.S. intelligence assessed that Ukrainian forces had struck a military facility in the same region that night, but far from the Russian president's residence.

title: In less than 24 hours, Russia hits 4 hypermarkets belonging to one of Ukraine's largest retail chains
description: Russian attacks damaged or destroyed facilities in Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Vinnytsia, and Poltava on Oct. 24-25, according to a statement.
content:
Russian attacks hit four Epicentr hypermarkets in less than 24 hours, the company said on Oct. 25.
The latest wave of strikes highlights Russia's campaign of terror against civilians, with stores, shopping centers, and other civilian infrastructure among the targets. Epicentr, one of Ukraine's largest home improvement and retail chains, has been particularly hard hit.
In a post on Facebook , the company said Russian attacks damaged or destroyed facilities in the cities of Zaporizhzhia, Kharkiv, Vinnytsia, and Poltava on Oct. 24-25, and described the attacks as amounting to "total destruction of the network."
The company did not specify the extent of the damage or when the affected facilities might reopen.
The Poltava Oblast Military Administration said a 52-year-old woman was injured in an attack on a hypermarket on Oct. 25. Authorities in other regions did not report any civilian casualties from attacks on Epicentr stores during the same period.
Founded in 2003, Epicentr operated 72 hypermarkets across Ukraine before Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Since the start of the all-out war, ten of the company's shopping centers have been completely destroyed and another 13 have been damaged, Epicentr told the Ukrainian outlet Ekonomichna Pravda in August 2026.
Epicentr's head of public relations, Yuliia Chudnovets , said on Oct. 22 that Russian forces had struck five company sites, including one in Kyiv , in the previous 48 hours.

title: News from occupied Ukraine: Former Oleshky resident warns people 'won't survive this winter'
description:
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.

Key news as of Oct. 25:

 * Oleshky native warns residents may not survive winter as evacuation hopes rise
 * Russian-occupied Crimea imposes power and water restrictions after drone attack
 * Russia sentences 77-year-old Crimean activist to 18 years over alleged plot against Moscow's proxy
 * At
content:
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.
A woman who fled Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has warned that residents remaining in the town may not survive the winter, as hopes grow for a possible evacuation mission.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads and constant drone attacks make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
"If the evacuation goes ahead, it will be a lifeline for those who remain. People won't survive the winter," a woman who left Oleshky in recent months told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 24. She declined to reveal her name for security reasons.
The woman pointed to severe food shortages and a lack of fuel for heating and cooking. She said residents had already burned much of the available wood during the previous winter, leaving few options to keep their homes warm as temperatures fall.
"There is almost no chance of survival," she added.
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump mediated a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in and around Oleshky to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid, Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on Oct. 23.
Under the agreement, a ceasefire will be implemented, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky, and civilians will be allowed to leave the city freely, according to Lubinets.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 24 that Ukraine will fulfill its part of the "extremely difficult" humanitarian operation in Oleshky.
The move came amid increased attention to the worsening humanitarian crisis in the city, which over the past weeks has gained international attention, including from Pope Leo XIV .
Despite hoping the evacuation would proceed, the woman expressed concern that Russian authorities could prevent it from going ahead.
"I'd like to believe that this mission will go ahead, but you can expect anything from the Russian Federation," she said, adding that she believed civilians were being kept in the area as human shields.
Stefan Vorontsov, a volunteer coordinator with the NGO Humanity, which helps evacuate civilians from occupied territories , told the Kyiv Independent that while he hoped that people would be saved, he expects Russian provocations, blackmail, and propaganda surrounding those who manage to get out.
"God willing, we will be able to set a precedent where Russia admits what they did in the occupied territories, and we will be able to organize the first official evacuation from there, then maybe the rest of us will be able to do it too. But again, I have little faith," Vorontsov said.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help Oleshky residents leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips through Russia and Belarus. Now, they said , the risk of Russian attacks and mines has made organized evacuation impossible.
In recent months, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces. At the end of September, four people were attempting to leave the town when they stepped on a mine and were injured, while a man collecting nuts was killed by another mine.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, remained in the occupied town with severely limited access to food, drinking water, electricity, and other basic services.
Russian-installed authorities in occupied Crimea introduced electricity and water restrictions on Oct. 24 following a reported Ukrainian drone attack on energy infrastructure outside the peninsula, the Russian proxy governor of occupied Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, said.
The restrictions came after Ukrainian strikes on energy infrastructure in southern Russia on Oct. 23-24, including damage to the Taman substation in Krasnodar Krai, which supplies electricity to occupied Crimea.
Major cities, including Sevastopol and Yalta, were left without electricity following the hit on the key power station.
Aksyonov said repairs were underway while rolling power cuts were implemented.
In Sevastopol, Russian-installed governor Mikhail Razvozhaev said on Oct. 25 that renewed strain on the power grid had prompted rolling blackouts on a "three hours on, three hours off" schedule.
Razvozhaev added that electricity supply to industrial sites and shopping centers will be restricted "as much as possible" to reduce the load on the grid.
"The capacity freed up must be channeled first and foremost to residential properties. This is our top priority," Razvozhaev said.
Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported on the evening of Oct. 23 that "the entire peninsula" was without electricity.
Crimea, which was occupied and illegally annexed by Russian forces in 2014, has been hit with widespread power outages before. This summer, Ukrainian forces reportedly hit 16 power stations across Crimea in 48 hours, in an effort to hinder Moscow in its war effort.
A Russian court in Rostov-on-Don said on Oct. 22 it had sentenced 77-year-old Crimean political prisoner Volodymyr Ananiev to 18 years in prison over an alleged plot to assassinate Sergey Aksyonov, the Russian proxy governor.
"Volodymyr Ananiev is the oldest Crimean political prisoner. He suffers from vision problems and issues with his spine, muscles, kidneys, and legs, and walks with a cane," The NGO Crimean Tatar Resource Center said .
Ananiev was detained in the Russian-occupied city of Simferopol in February 2024. Russian investigators claimed Ananiev was part of a group that tracked Aksyonov's car and prepared an explosive device to blow it up.
Moscow has continued to repress Crimean Tatars and other residents, including journalists and activists, of the peninsula since its occupation in 2014. Around 300 people, including journalists and activists, were being held on politically motivated charges as of spring, more than 150 of them Crimean Tatars, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said.
Over the past week, Ukraine brought back at least 34 citizens who were forced to stay in Russian-occupied territories, including 23 children, Ukraine's human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets and the presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA said.
On Oct. 22, Lubinets said that 11 Ukrainian citizens returned to government-controlled territory. Some of those who returned faced additional challenges due to health conditions, the need for medical care, and difficulties arranging a safe way back.
Among them was a married couple whose return journey involved two attempts. The woman had previously managed to leave occupied territory, but returned after her husband became seriously ill and was admitted to intensive care. After his condition improved, she arranged for them to leave together.
Separately, Bring Kids Back UA announced on Oct. 19 that it brought home 23 more children from Russian-occupied territory.
Among the children returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory was 9-year-old Stefan, who was forced to undergo military training at a school under Russian occupation, including instruction in handling grenades and firearms, the statement said.
The Ukrainian ombudsman's office coordinates returns through the humanitarian route connecting Mokrany in Belarus with Domanove in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn Oblast . Lubinets said the office is effectively the only Ukrainian state institution systematically organizing returns from occupied territories through this route, assisting people who cannot leave independently.
The Volyn humanitarian corridor is the main working checkpoint between Ukraine and Belarus . There are currently no functioning checkpoints between Ukraine and Russia.
According to Lubinets, 24,953 people, including 2,054 children, returned to Ukraine through this humanitarian corridor between May 24, 2024, and Oct. 15, 2026. Of these, 11,815 people, including 802 children, returned in 2026 alone.
Russian security forces carried out a new round of raids across occupied Ukrainian territories in early October, targeting residents who have refused to obtain Russian passports, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) said on Oct. 22.
The raids were conducted jointly by the Russian police and the Federal Security Service ( FSB ) during the first 10 days of October as part of an operation dubbed "Illegal-2026," according to HUR.
Ukrainians without Russian passports are classified by occupation authorities as "foreign citizens" and subjected to Russian migration law.
According to the agency, residents can face pressure to obtain Russian citizenship, expulsion from occupied territory, dismissal from work, and property seizure.
Russia has pressured residents of occupied Ukrainian territories to take Russian passports since 2014, tying access to employment, social services, property rights, and other aspects of daily life to possession of Russian documents.
This is part of Moscow's long-running campaign of forced passportization. Russian President Vladimir Putin, on March 4, signed a decree that indefinitely extended the simplified process of obtaining Russian citizenship in the occupied territories.
"The goal of the decree is to passportize as many people as possible, pressuring them," Nataliia Yurlova, lawyer for the NGO Donbas SOS, told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine's reported attack on a building in the occupied city of Donetsk , Donetsk Oblast, destroyed a data center on Oct. 20, according to Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation.
Andriushchenko told the Kyiv Independent that a data center used by Ugletelecom and Elecom, a major telecom operator in occupied Donetsk Oblast, was hit at Postysheva St. 60, according to his sources.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that explosions were heard in Donetsk this morning and shared footage showing the damaged facade of the building on Postysheva St. 60.
The head of Russia's proxies in the city of Donetsk, Alexey Kulemzin, reported a Ukrainian attack on the city and shared video footage of the same damaged building on Telegram.
Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted each other’s data centers after a Russian attack damaged a Kyiv data center housing network equipment for internet provider UTELS, causing service disruptions on Sept. 23.

title: Moscow ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine, US after Nov. 4, Kremlin aide says
description: "The next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations," Yuri Ushakov said.
content:
The Kremlin is ready to resume trilateral talks with Ukraine and the U.S. after Nov. 4, when Russia celebrates National Unity Day, Russian President Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov told state-controlled outlet Vesti on Oct. 25.
The statement follows Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky 's Oct. 23 remarks that a new round of trilateral talks is expected in the first half of November, with Abu Dhabi a possible venue.
"The next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday. After that, we will be ready to resume negotiations," Ushakov said.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected ceasefire proposals, demanding instead that Kyiv cede the only partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine. Such a concession would give Moscow territory that Russian forces have been unable to capture on the battlefield. Ukraine, in contrast, has agreed to multiple ceasefire proposals put forward by the U.S.
Ushakov said he did not expect the first trilateral meeting after the pause to yield significant results, calling it a "trial run." A peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine "still needs work," he added.
On Oct. 20, U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and European partners, including Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.
The following day, Witkoff held a three-hour meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg, after which the Kremlin said it was ready to resume trilateral talks in November.
Witkoff said on Oct. 21 that discussions among Ukrainian, U.S., and Russian representatives would "continue at the technical level."
Putin has long avoided meeting with Zelensky. Instead, the Kremlin chief is reportedly seeking a meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump in China next month in an effort to secure a favorable peace deal without Ukraine's participation .
In recent weeks, Trump has also lashed out at Zelensky, unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine that ultimately failed, threatened to cut off intelligence-sharing with Kyiv, and eased sanctions on Russian oil exports.
Trump has defended the sanctions relief, arguing that it could encourage Moscow to take part in peace negotiations with Kyiv.

title: Ukraine strikes Russian titanium plant, facility producing missile, drone components, monitoring channels claim
description: Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin said at around 11 a.m. local time that 11 drones had been downed during a Ukrainian attack on the region.
content:
Editor's note: This story was updated to include details of a reported Ukrainian attack on Lipetsk Oblast.
Ukrainian forces struck Avisma, one of the world's largest titanium sponge producers in Russia's Perm Krai, and the Energiya plant in Lipetsk Oblast, which manufactures components for missile systems and drones, on Oct. 25, Ukrainian and Russian monitoring channels reported.
Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin said at around 11 a.m. local time that 11 drones had been downed during a Ukrainian attack on the region.
Makhonin added that an "industrial facility" in the northern part of the region had sustained "minor" damage but continued to operate as normal. The governor did not specify which facility had been damaged.
According to Makhonin, five employees of the facility were also injured in the Ukrainian attack.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ said the strike targeted Avisma in the town of Berezniki, located about 170 kilometers (105 miles) from the regional center of Perm. The plant is part of Russian metallurgical corporation VSMPO-AVISMA.
Located more than 1,400 kilometers (870 miles) from the Ukrainian-Russian border, Avisma has been under U.S. sanctions since 2023. The plant manufactures products used in military aircraft, nuclear submarines, armored vehicles, and missile systems.
Later in the day, Ukrainian forces also attacked the Energiya plant in the city of Yelets, in Russia's Lipetsk Oblast, more than 200 kilometers (120 miles) from the Ukrainian border, the Russian independent media outlet Astra reported, citing open-source intelligence (OSINT) data.
Lipetsk Oblast Governor Igor Artamonov said an "industrial zone" had been targeted, injuring one person. The governor did not identify the facility that came under attack.
Energiya is Russia's largest research and production enterprise specializing in electrochemical power sources. Its products are used across various sectors, including the defense industry, civil aviation, maritime transport and energy. The plant manufactures batteries for unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), power sources for air defense missile systems, and batteries for aircraft and naval vessels.
The enterprise is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the European Union, the U.K., Canada, Switzerland, Japan, Australia and Ukraine.
The plant was previously attacked in May and July 2025, as well as in January 2026 .
Ukraine had not commented on the reported strikes in Lipetsk Oblast and Perm Krai at the time of publication.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets deep within Russia and occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
Ukraine's General Staff said Ukrainian forces also struck Russian military radar stations in Belgorod Oblast overnight on Oct. 25, as well as a Russian command post in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast and a command-and-observation post in occupied Kherson Oblast.
Other targets included concentrations of Russian troops in the occupied parts of Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, the General Staff added.
Earlier, Ukrainian monitoring channels reported a fire at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in the Russian city of Omsk following a Ukrainian attack.
The overnight attack on Belgorod also damaged a local shopping and entertainment center, monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported.
Belgorod Mayor Valentin Demidov said one person was killed and 10 others were injured in the attack. Residential buildings and cars were also damaged, he added.

title: Trump wants 'business with both' Ukraine, Russia after war ends
description: "Certainly, we'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think," U.S. President Donald Trump.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 24 that he sees the U.S. doing business with both Ukraine and Russia after the war ends, despite criticism of efforts to restore commercial ties with Moscow.
The statement comes as the first tanker carrying Russian diesel is heading to New York from the Baltic port of Primorsk, set to deliver 40,000 metric tons of fuel following a supply agreement Trump announced on Oct. 9.
Soon after the announcement, Moscow partially lifted restrictions on its diesel exports, permitting the sale of 500,000 metric tons.
"Certainly, we'll do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends, I would think," Trump said.
Trump added that he wanted to "get back to life where Russia and Ukraine make a deal, and then we'd be able to do business with both."
The U.S. president also argued that Washington should have secured greater financial returns in exchange for the billions of dollars in aid provided to Kyiv during Joe Biden's presidency.
"I feel foolish because all you had to do is ask them, and they would have paid. Meaning the EU would have paid," Trump said.
Plans to import around 900,000 metric tons of Russian diesel in the coming months have drawn criticism of the Trump administration from European allies, Ukraine, and members of Congress, as the shipments would circumvent sanctions imposed on Moscow over its war against Ukraine.
The shipment would mark the first Russian diesel deliveries to the U.S. since 2022, when then-President Joe Biden banned imports of Russian oil and petroleum products in response to Russia's war against Ukraine.
The deal comes amid a growing rift between Kyiv and Washington, as Ukraine faces restrictions on Starlink access and reported delays in deliveries of Patriot air defense interceptors .
Trump has also stepped up his criticism of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, accusing him of being unwilling to end the war and calling for his replacement.
The decision to resume Russian diesel imports coincides with a challenging political landscape for Republicans ahead of the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections, with recent polls showing declining support for Trump.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll found that just 31% of Americans approve of Trump's performance, marking the lowest approval rating of either of his presidential terms.
Meanwhile, 47% of registered voters said they would vote for Democrats if congressional elections were held today, compared with 35% who favored Republicans, giving Democrats a 12-point lead — their largest of the current election cycle.

title: Russian attacks kill 8, injure 51 across Ukraine over past day as drone strikes residential building in Vinnytsia
description: Alongside attacks on Vinnytsia, Russia launched 153 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on Oct. 25, including 92 jet-powered drones, as well as low-cost Banderol cruise missiles, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
content:
Russian attacks killed eight people and injured 51 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Oct. 24-25.
A Russian drone struck a five-story residential building in the city of Vinnytsia overnight on Oct. 25, injuring six people, one of whom was hospitalized, Nataliia Zabolotna , head of the Vinnytsia Oblast Military Administration, said.
The strike caused structural damage between the second and third floors, completely destroying four apartments and damaging nearby parked cars, Zabolotna added.
Alongside attacks on Vinnytsia, Russia launched 153 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on Oct. 25, including 92 jet-powered drones, as well as low-cost Banderol cruise missiles, the Ukrainian Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses intercepted 119 drones, including 64 jet-powered ones. As of 8 a.m., efforts to intercept the remaining drones were ongoing, with at least nine still in Ukrainian airspace.
Some drones evaded Ukrainian air defenses and struck 15 locations, while falling debris was recorded at nine other locations, according to the Air Force.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , Russian attacks on the Synelnykove District on Oct. 24 killed three people and injured 14 others, including an 11-year-old girl, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Five of the injured were hospitalized in serious condition.
In the Nikopol District , Russian attacks over the past day killed two women and injured five people, including a 14-year-old boy, Hanzha added.
In Kharkiv Oblast , Russian attacks killed a 45-year-old man in the town of Lozova and injured two other men, aged 43 and 26, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Kharkiv, a 39-year-old man was injured. Russian attacks also wounded three men, aged 70, 54, and 47, in the town of Derhachi, and a 45-year-old woman in the village of Mala Danylivka, Syniehubov added.
In Donetsk Oblast , Russian attacks killed one person in the village of Yarova and injured six others elsewhere in the region, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Sumy Oblast , a 31-year-old woman was killed in a Russian attack on a farm in the Buryn community, which also injured an 18-year-old man. In the Boromlia community, a Russian drone struck a car, injuring three women aged 68, 56, and 36, according to local authorities .
Russian attacks injured four people in Zaporizhzhia Oblast over the past day. Russian forces carried out 832 strikes on 52 settlements across the region using drones, artillery, aircraft, and multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), local authorities said.
In Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks targeted 43 settlements, including the regional center of Kherson, injuring two people, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Chernihiv Oblast , two women suffered acoustic trauma in a Russian strike on the regional capital, Chernihiv, on Oct. 24, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
One person was injured in a Russian drone attack on Kyiv on Oct. 24, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,578,450 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,850 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,578,450 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 25.
The number includes 1,850 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,447 tanks, 25,605 armored combat vehicles, 166,918 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,614 artillery systems, 2,237 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,725 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,017 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Almost 283,000 Russian soldiers killed in Ukraine identified by media investigation
description: Since Mediazona last updated the figures in early October, the names of 6,880 Russian soldiers were added to the list of those killed.
content:
Russian independent media outlet Mediazona, in collaboration with the BBC Russian service, has confirmed the identities of 282,993 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine.
Since Mediazona last updated the figures in early October, the names of 6,880 Russian soldiers were added to the list of those killed. The latest count covers confirmed military deaths from Feb. 24, 2022, through Oct. 23, 2026.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reporting.
The journalists caution that the actual figures are likely significantly higher, as their findings are based on publicly available information, including obituaries, social media posts by relatives, regional news reports, and statements from local authorities.
As of Oct. 23, 2026, the deaths of 7,920 officers serving in the Russian military and other security services had been independently verified.
Officers have accounted for a shrinking share of confirmed Russian military deaths since the start of the full-scale invasion, according to Mediazona. During the initial phase of the war, when Russia relied heavily on professional contract troops, officers represented as much as 10% of those killed. By November 2024, their share had fallen to just 2–3%.
The decline reflects changes in battlefield tactics and Russia's growing reliance on recruited volunteer infantry, who face a substantially higher risk of being killed than their commanding officers.
Although estimates differ, Western intelligence assessments and independent research have generally put Russian military casualties significantly above Ukrainian losses. The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in July 2026 that Russia had suffered approximately 1.4 million casualties since the start of the full-scale invasion, compared with 525,000–625,000 for Ukraine.
"Russian fatalities in Ukraine are more than four times greater than all U.S. fatalities in all wars combined since World War II, and more than nine times greater than all Soviet and Russian fatalities in all wars combined since World War II," CSIS wrote.

title: Sanctioned Russian energy giant secretly funded US gas project, NYT reports
description: The gas project was part of an energy deal discussed by U.S. peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner during their September visit to the Kremlin, sources told the New York Times.
content:
The Russian company Novatek has been secretly funding a multibillion-dollar U.S. gas project that has been discussed in negotiations between the White House and the Kremlin over ending the war in Ukraine, the New York Times (NYT) first reported on Oct. 23.
Novatek is Russia's second-largest producer of liquefied natural gas ( LNG ) and has been subject to U.S. sanctions since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Polar LNG, an American company aiming to liquefy and export natural gas from Alaska, received secret funding from Novatek in potential violation of sanctions, the NYT reported , citing the company's former CEO and two other sources familiar with the matter.
John Riddle, former CEO of Polar LNG, resigned from the company in September after learning about the hidden ties to Novatek. Riddle said he had been told the funding came from a company in the United Arab Emirates.
"It's not only unlawful, but it's not in the U.S. interest to have Russian technology controlling the commercialization of Arctic gas in the North Slope," Riddle told the NYT.
Riddle said he notified officials in the Trump administration about the secret Russian financing and urged them to investigate the situation.
Novatek was not only channeling funds to Polar LNG — it was negotiating a deal to sell technology to the U.S. company as part of a business agreement between Washington and Moscow. U.S. peace envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed the proposal with Russian President Vladimir Putin during their visit in September , sources told the NYT.
It is not clear whether Witkoff or Kushner were aware of the financial relationship between Novatek and Polar LNG, as the deal was only broadly discussed, sources said.
The Novatek-Polar LNG proposal is reportedly one of several energy deals that U.S. President Donald Trump is looking to strike with Russia as he attempts to broker an end to the war against Ukraine. Another involves selling off parts of the Russian energy giant Lukoil to the U.S. government and other investors — including some with ties to Kushner and Wiktoff.
In a statement to the NYT, Novatek confirmed that it was looking to acquire "minority shareholder" status in the Polar LNG project.
The reported backdoor energy deals between the Kremlin and the White House have taken place against the backdrop of intensified Russian attacks on Ukraine — and a marked withdrawal of U.S. support from Kyiv.
Trump made his indifference to Russian sanctions clear when he announced a surprise deal with Putin to purchase diesel from Moscow to offset U.S. fuel prices. The first tanker of Russian diesel is reportedly now bound for the U.S.
The White House has also issued another sanctions waiver to Russia. In the last week, Witkoff has praised Putin as a "humanitarian" and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has claimed that the war in Ukraine is a narrow regional dispute that only concerns "11 percent of one part of that country."

title: Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits shopping center in Russia's Belgorod Oblast, locals say
description: The attack killed one civilian and injured 14 others, Russian authorities said.
content:
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
A massive swarm of Ukrainian drones attacked the Russian border region of Belgorod overnight on Oct. 25, according to local officials and eyewitness footage posted to social media.
The bulk of the drones have concentrated on one area in the Belgorod city center, locals report . According to the monitoring channel Exilenova-Plus, the target was the MegaGRINN shopping complex, Belgorod's largest retail and entertainment center.
MegaGRINN covers an area of more than 163,000 square meters and houses over 200 stores, as well as a supermarket, cinema, and restaurants. The facility was closed and empty of visitors during the overnight attack.
Local residents also reported a fire in the courtyard of a residential complex in the area.
The Belgorod Oblast Operational Headquarters confirmed a "massive UAV attack" against the city and said emergency services had been dispatched to the impacted areas, though they did not name any specific targets.
The attack killed one civilian and injured 14 others, authorities said. At least 30 apartment buildings, 35 vehicles, four houses, three administrative buildings, and eight commercial properties were damaged.
The Kyiv Independent could not verify these reports at the time of publication.
Videos published on social media by eyewitnesses show explosions, fires, and air defense operations over the city of Belgorod. The Operational Headquarters has warned residents to stay indoors as attacks are ongoing in the region.
The city of Belgorod lies just 34 kilometers (21 miles) from Ukraine's northeastern border with Russia and approximately 70 kilometers (43 miles) from Kharkiv. Its proximity to the front lines makes it a frequent target of Ukrainian attacks , even as Kyiv's expanding long-range capabilities allow its drones to penetrate deep in the Russian interior .
Previous Ukrainian strikes on Belgorod have targeted energy infrastructure and logistics warehouses , including facilities belonging to the Russian retail giant Ozon .
The reported drone blitz on Belgorod comes shortly after Ukraine confirmed on Oct. 24 that its Starshield system had been restored to full speed , allowing troops to more effectively coordinate drone strikes on Russian targets.
Starshield, the military application of the Starlink satellite internet system, had been operating at drastically reduced speed in Ukraine since Oct. 14. The unexplained restriction disrupted key military missions and Ukraine's ability to shoot down Russian jet-powered drones .
