content:
By the end of his pre-trial detention at Moscow's infamous Lefortovo Prison, American journalist Evan Gershkovich had developed a curious rapport with the FSB investigator tasked with proving he was a spy.
"Most people break after four months or so, but you're still holding strong — a year in," the investigator told him, and the two raised their cigarettes in a toast to "having tried to find common ground."
Gershkovich writes about many such moments in "This Cursed Beautiful Land: A Russian-American Story," his memoir of nearly 500 days in a Russian prison. His ability to capture them without artifice is one of the memoir's most distinctive qualities. It is also where the book becomes most troubling.
Read from Ukraine , these interactions raise a question that extends beyond Gershkovich's captivity: What does it mean to recognize the humanity of people who help uphold — even passively — a system of brutal repression?
Gershkovich was arrested in April 2023 while reporting in Yekaterinburg for the Wall Street Journal on Russia's military-industrial sector. The Federal Security Service (FSB) accused him of espionage, claiming he was collecting information on behalf of the American Central Intelligence Agency (CIA). The charges were baseless, and the Russian authorities provided no credible public evidence to substantiate them.
Gershkovich admits that before his arrest, he had felt "protected" and "immune" from the authoritarian system taking shape around him. He had mistaken the relative freedom afforded to a foreign correspondent for security. As with the detentions of Marine veteran Paul Whelan and basketball player Brittney Griner before Gershkovich, the Russian state demonstrated with his arrest its willingness to imprison Americans and turn their freedom into a bargaining chip in international negotiations.
After 16 months in captivity, Gershkovich was released as part of a major international prisoner exchange in the summer of 2024, which also included Russian opposition figures Ilya Yashin and Vladimir Kara-Murza. His release came shortly after the conclusion of his sham trial, which saw him sentenced to 16 years in prison for a crime he did not commit.
Much of "This Cursed Beautiful Land" details those nearly 500 days of Gershkovich waiting to regain his freedom. He learns the rules of prison conduct from cellmates; he watches momentous events, like the Wagner Mercenary Group's short-lived uprising against the Kremlin in June 2023, on television, frustrated that he cannot cover them as a journalist; he dreams and longs for his loved ones.
The relatively humane treatment he receives from his captors at the onset of his imprisonment confirms the obvious: the international attention given to his case made him a high-value hostage. At the same time, he did not have to live through the terror of being tortured for the circumstances to weigh on him.
This distinction matters. Gershkovich does not claim that his experience represents the Russian prison system as a whole, and he repeatedly refers to himself in the book as a "voyeur" among actual prisoners. He has also used his press tour for the book to draw attention to Ukrainian prisoners, including journalist Viktoria Roshchyna , who died in Russian captivity. Her body was returned to Ukraine in 2025 bearing signs of torture and evidence of mutilation, including the removal of some internal organs.
The contrast between Gershkovich's experience and that of prisoners like Roshchyna is jarring. It also exposes the limits of what the memoir can tell us about the true machinery of the Russian prison system — a system that ensnares not only those in Russia brave enough to speak out against the state, but also Ukrainians terrorized under occupation.
Yet the book is not simply an account of how an American journalist got swept up in the Kremlin's political circus. By detailing interactions with prisoners, security service officers, and prison employees, Gershkovich attempts to understand how the country descended into a state of madness. One of the reasons is that contemporary Russia, in many respects, inherited the Soviet police state — a system where widespread suspicion, political entrapment, and the presumption of guilt were instruments of power.
One of the best examples of this is the cult of personality surrounding Felix Dzerzhinsky, the founder of the Soviet secret police and an architect of the Red Terror, a period of state-sanctioned violence from 1918 to 1922 against perceived internal enemies of the Soviet Union. Gershkovich calls Dzerzhinsky an "avatar for the convulsions of modern Russian history," adding that he was "trapped in (Dzerzhinsky's) world, and so was the country."
As if to reinforce his point, in September 2023 — while Gershkovich was still in prison — Russian authorities erected a statue of the secret police chief at the headquarters of Russia's foreign intelligence service. That was more than three decades after the original monument outside the feared KGB headquarters was dismantled amid the collapse of the Soviet Union.
But the memoir's understanding of Russia becomes less convincing when it shifts its attention from the foundations of the country's authoritarianism to interactions with those who operate within it.
Gershkovich repeatedly tries to maintain a semblance of civility with the prison employees who control his life. Some, he notes, even commend his politeness despite the circumstances. Such exchanges suggest that the boundaries between captor and captive are not always expressed through open hostility. They also reveal how ordinary social conventions can survive inside a profoundly abnormal system.
At the same time, these interactions are not inherently compromising. A prisoner's willingness to converse with a guard does not amount to an endorsement of the guard's employer. Under extreme coercion, interpersonal ties can be essential to preserving one's sense of self. Gershkovich's steadiness reflects strength of character, coupled with the curiosity of a good journalist — not political endorsement.
But when kindness is presented alongside state violence, does it help us understand how repression works, or does it offer an emotional refuge from that reality?
Ukrainian writer and filmmaker Oleh Sentsov's account of his own imprisonment between 2014 and 2019 offers a useful comparison. During his hunger strike in a Russian penal colony, Sentsov also recalled moments of civility with his captors. Yet his observations are dry, sardonic, and openly contemptuous not only of the prison system but also of those who uphold it. Even a passing observation about their habits — like their listening to Russian chansons, a genre of music that glamorizes criminals — is part of a broader indictment of Russia's political and social decay.
The point is not that Sentsov was morally superior, or that Gershkovich should have responded to imprisonment by also going on a hunger strike as well. Their experiences and circumstances were radically different — Sentsov took a stand against the occupation of his native Crimea; Gershkovich was a hostage used as a bargaining chip. Rather, Sentsov's account more effectively shows that a system of brutality does not require every person within it to be sadistic — just enough people willing to perform their roles and look away from the violence and senselessness that sustain it.
The Ukrainian poet and dissident Vasyl Stus , who died in a Russian penal colony in 1985, offers another perspective. Declassified KGB records show that he cursed his captors at every opportunity he had, refused to obey basic tasks, and was so defiant that even fellow political prisoners worried that his actions would invoke collective punishment. His unyielding stance came at a great personal cost, but for him, they were the human face of the system that sought to punish him for his pro-Ukrainian stance.
Gershkovich's instinct is different. He tries to understand the people around him, including those implicated in his persecution. That instinct aligns with the work of a journalist, whose task is often to look beyond familiar categories and discover how people understand themselves — no matter how repulsive the truth might be.
This is where the memoir's emotional generosity becomes politically ambiguous. Gershkovich's encounters offer a means to distinguish individual Russians from the state that imprisoned him, preserving a connection to the country of his immigrant family's roots. That distinction is both understandable and important. Russia is not entirely reducible to its government, and Russian culture cannot be understood solely through the crimes committed in its name.
But the state's violence cannot be separated entirely from the society in which it operates. The question is how to distinguish between those who resist, those who are coerced, and those who willingly serve an authoritarian power.
Our introduction to Gershkovich's thoughts on Russia also draws on his fond memories of being raised by post-Soviet immigrants in the U.S. and of getting his footing as a young reporter in his family's homeland. There's an enduring sentimentality throughout the book, which conveys that the traumatic experience of being held hostage for over a year has not completely turned him against Russia. Indeed, he admits that the thought of never returning to Russia in his life, or at least for the foreseeable future, drives him to tears.
Even the title — portraying a country that is both beautiful and cursed — suggests a desire to see Russia in a better light. The idea of a "cursed" country evokes a dreamlike folktale: a curse, after all, can be reversed. But Russia's history, so deeply entwined with the suffering of its own people and the subjugation of its neighbors, resists such narrative neatness. To call Russia a "cursed" land is to risk sentimentalizing it.
Russia occupies an unusually privileged place in the Western cultural imagination. The insistence on its depth, including its literature and supposedly unfathomable soul, is often indistinguishable from the violence that permeates its history.
That romantic tradition can make the recognition of Russian suffering feel like a moral achievement while leaving the suffering inflicted on Russia's neighbors at the margins. It can also turn the enduring popularity of Russian culture into an argument for the country's essential goodness, as though cultural achievement were an argument against condemnation.
Gershkovich's memoir is more thoughtful than that. It is clear that he knows that the state that imprisoned him is dangerous, and he does not confuse his comparatively privileged captivity with the experience of Ukrainian prisoners. His continued attachment to Russia is not, in itself, an apology for its government. But the book enters a cultural tradition in which personal affection can too easily obscure political judgment.

title: Starshield operations restored to normal speed, Zelensky confirms as Elon Musk claims Ukraine violated Starlink terms
description: "We record a speed of more than 400 kilometers per hour, the connection is stable," the ministry said.
content:
Editor's note: This article was updated with additional comments by U.S. Billionaire Elon Musk, former Defense Ministry Adviser Serhii Sternenko, and Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov.
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Starlink and Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk's satellite internet system, Starlink, was working at full speed as of the morning of Oct. 24, after it had previously been limited to 161 kilometers per hour (about 100 miles per hour).
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Zelensky said. "I thank all Americans and all our partners who took this seriously and truly helped us. I thank members of Congress , senators, all the media, the State Department, and the President."
Ukraine's Defense Ministry told reporters on Oct. 24 that Starshield was working above speeds of 400 kilometers per hour (about 248 miles per hour) again.
"We record a speed of more than 400 kilometers per hour, the connection is stable," the ministry said.
The ministry continues to monitor and record the work of Starlink and Starshield, according to Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara.
"This is another example of direct dialogue and the persistent position of the President of Ukraine at the highest level yielding results. And this result is, above all, important for our front, for the military, the work of drones, logistics, and communications," the ministry added.
Musk later said that Ukraine's military violated the terms of service for Starlink, adding that the "loophole" has now been closed.
Ukraine's "military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week," he said in a post to X.
"Were Starlink to be turned off, the Ukrainian front line would collapse immediately. This is not a threat, it is simply a statement of fact," Musk said.
He also claimed that SpaceX has done more than any other company to help Ukraine in its fight against Russia's war.
Ukrainian activist and former Defense Ministry adviser Serhii Sternenko denied that Ukraine violated Starlink's terms of service.
"As someone who was inside the process at the Ministry of Defense, I can say with certainty that this is not true. In February of this year, whitelists were introduced. Stationary terminals could be registered by both military personnel and civilians," he said in a post to X.
"But for any satellite terminal to work while on the move, it had to be added to a special list and connected to the military Starshield system. Otherwise, no satellite communication terminals in Ukraine would work," Sternenko added.
Using Starlink for drone missions has been "technically impossible" since all drone campaigns that require satellite communications would only work with the military Starshield service, he said.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov also denied Musk's claims, saying that all Starlink terminals operating in Ukraine have a speed restriction of 70-90 kilometers an hour and do not work on Russian territory.
"Thus, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he said in a post to Facebook. "It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."
Since mid-October, Starshield had been operating at limited capacity. With speed limit caps, Kyiv's ability to defend from deadly Russian jet-powered drones and coordinate strikes against Russian targets is hindered. Despite Ukrainian and U.S. officials apparently engaging in discussions to resolve the disruptions, nobody has publicly taken credit — or blame — for making or implementing the decision. However, the Trump administration officials continue pointing fingers firmly at SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that Trump had ordered SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions, saying the president was "frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 160 kilometers (100 miles) an hour."
Trump said he had not spoken to Musk about the issue but might do so if the problems persisted.
"I have not spoken to him," Trump said. "I might have to, but I have not... I've heard it's fixed. If it's not, I will speak to him.... If there's a problem, I will get it straightened out." On Oct. 23, Zelensky confirmed that issues with Starlink continued to plague Ukrainian forces. "The speed restrictions for Starlink and Starshield are still in effect," Zelensky said. "The speed has not been restored. And the supply of interceptor missiles to protect against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed." On Oct. 23, U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal announced that he is opening a probe into the Starlink disruption. Blumenthal's investigation asks the Pentagon to clarify who ordered the restrictions and to provide information on the U.S. military's own reliance on Starlink.
UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham also brought up the issue with Trump on Oct. 23, underlining the importance for Ukraine to have full access to Starlink so they can continue to defend themselves, according to a press release from the minister's office.

title: Ukraine's Sine Engineering launches joint defense tech initiative with Finland
description: The initiative will focus on resilient communications, navigation, and onboard autonomy, as Sine Engineering specializes in producing satellite-independent navigation software, enabling drones to fly without relying on GPS.
content:
A leading Ukrainian defense tech firm, Sine Engineering, launched a new joint initiative with Finland to develop, test, and produce dual-use technologies in the Nordic country as it steps up support for Ukraine.
The initiative will focus on resilient communications, navigation, and onboard autonomy, as Sine Engineering specializes in producing satellite-independent navigation software, enabling drones to fly without relying on GPS.
The company announced the new research and development initiative at the Ukrainian-Finnish Business Forum on Oct. 22, attended by President Volodymyr Zelensky and Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo in Kyiv.
The firm expects the Ukrainian and Finnish governments to support the initiative by including it in the new Ukraine-Finland Drone Deal signed on Sept. 23. The deal lets both countries share technology and expertise, collaborate on research and innovation, and jointly develop and manufacture drone technology.
"We look forward to the support of the governments of Ukraine and Finland in including our joint R&D initiative among the projects under the Drone Deal," said Andrii Chulyk, CEO and co-founder of Sine Engineering.
"We are confident that this initiative will strengthen the technological capabilities, defense, and resilience of Ukraine and Finland, while contributing to the security of Europe and our allies."
As the Kyiv Independent first reported in March, Sine Engineering was selected as the first project under the U.S.-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund, the result of last year’s "minerals deal" discussions between Kyiv and Washington.
The defense tech company produces technology for around 200 Ukrainian drone producers, including interceptor drone manufacturers. Its technologies can also be applied for civilian use.
The new initiative is an expansion of Sine Engineering’s operations in Finland, after the company opened an office in the Nordic country last year. The company said last year that it was looking to open R&D centers abroad to attract radio engineers in Europe to help address Ukraine’s shortage of specialists.
Finland has a long history of developing radio technologies, and Sine Engineering said it hopes to expand its Finnish team to 100 people by the end of the year, 80% of whom will be engineers.
Following the business forum on Oct. 22, Kyiv and Helsinki signed seven agreements worth a total of 330 million euros (over $336 million), including support for Kyiv's energy infrastructure and greater access to Finland's satellite networks.
The Finnish tech companies ICEYE and Nokia also signed a letter of intent with Ukraine's Defense Ministry, formalizing a partnership aimed at developing Ukraine's own satellite communications system amid disruptions to Ukraine’s Starlink services.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,576,600 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,980 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,576,600 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 24.
The number includes 1,980 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,444 tanks, 25,600 armored combat vehicles, 166,501 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,565 artillery systems, 2,232 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,722 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,011 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Mass blackouts reported across occupied Crimea
description: According to satellite imagery from NASA FIRMS, the Taman substation in Russia's Krasnodar Krai — a key energy node supplying electricity to Crimea —was damaged in an overnight attack.
content:
Editor's Note: This is a developing story.
A sweeping blackout hit occupied Crimea overnight on Oct. 24 after an attack on a key electrical substation in southern Russia, according to Telegram monitoring channels.
"The entire peninsula is without electricity," the Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported on the evening of Oct. 23, citing satellite data, online monitors, and local accounts.
According to satellite imagery from NASA FIRMS, the Taman substation in Russia's Krasnodar Krai was damaged in an overnight attack. The substation supplies electricity to occupied Crimea.
Major cities, including Sevastopol and Yalta, were left without electricity following the hit on the key power station.
The online watchdog NetBlocks also reported widespread internet outages in Crimea .
Russia's proxy authorities in Crimea confirmed power outages, but then claimed they were resolved.
"As a result of an enemy attack on energy infrastructure outside of Sevastopol, our city is temporarily without power," Sevastopol's Russian-installed governor Mykhailo Razvozhaev said on Telegram.
Soon afterwards, local authorities said power had been restored in multiple cities. But according to the Crimean Wind Telegram channel, residents later said blackouts had again hit Simferopol, Yalta, and Alushta.
Another drone strike on energy infrastructure in southern Russia was also reported in Rostov Oblast overnight. Governor Yury Slyusar claimed drones damaged a transformer substation in the region's Myasnikovsky district, causing blackouts in nearly 130 homes.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the extent of the blackouts or the reported attacks at the time of publication.
The Taman substation is a key energy node, bridging the Russian energy grid to the occupied peninsula via the Kerch strait.
Crimea, which was occupied by Russian forces in 2014, has been hit with widespread power outages before. This summer, Ukrainian forces reportedly hit 16 power stations across Crimea in 48 hours, in an effort to hinder Moscow in its war effort.

title: Rubio reveals theory on Russia's war against Ukraine ahead of next US peace push
description: "People keep talking about it's a war in Ukraine. ... It's about one region of the country," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine boils down to a dispute over Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, in an interview with India Today on Oct.22.
"(P)eople keep talking about it's a war in Ukraine. That war is about Donbas. It's about one region of the country," Rubio told reporters during a state visit to India.
"At its core, (the war) is about 11 percent of one part of that country that Russia wants and cannot take militarily and that Ukraine is unwilling to give up."
Rubio's comments, framing the war as a dispute over the region, come ahead of trilateral peace talks between the U.S., Ukraine and Russia in November. In recent weeks, the Trump administration has softened its stance on Russia, waiving sanctions and moving forward with purchasing Russian diesel .
In framing Russia's full-scale invasion as a narrow regional dispute, Rubio may be revealing where the Trump administration stands going into the next round of negotiations. It also exposes a profound misunderstanding of a years-long war of conquest that has reshaped Ukrainian society.
Russian drones and missiles have struck every single region of Ukraine, including western oblasts far from the front lines. Russia has also occupied territory beyond the Donbas region, including swaths of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson oblasts and the entire Crimean peninsula .
And while taking Donbas remains a goal for Moscow, Russian President Vladimir Putin has long signaled broader ambitions. At the St. Petersburg International Economic Forum in June 2025, he said Russians and Ukrainians are "one people" and that "in that sense the whole of Ukraine is ours."
The Donbas region, made up of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, is home to a key Ukrainian fortress belt in Donetsk Oblast: four industrial cities running north to south, including Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka.
Capturing the entirety of the region has been a long-held Russian goal, but military deadlines to occupy it have repeatedly lapsed . Under the counteroffensive ' Operation Vivaldi ,' Ukrainian forces have made advances as they pushed into occupied areas of Donetsk Oblast, and Ukrainian forces have retaken more territory than Russia has captured this fall, Zelensky said on Oct. 18.
As part of the U.S.-led peace process, Russia has demanded that Ukrainian forces withdraw from Donbas entirely, rejecting a ceasefire without such concessions and effectively demanding Ukraine surrender territory that Moscow has been unable to seize militarily.
When asked by reporters about the conflict, Rubio described the war as "difficult" and conceded that Ukraine has "good reasons" not to surrender its territory, including sovereignty and long-term security.
President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters earlier this week that he would support freezing the front lines to end the fighting, a position Kyiv has held in the past and Moscow continues to reject.
While Rubio described the core of the war as a dispute "about one region of the country," Russian attacks across Ukraine have escalated dramatically in the past year.
Just one day after Rubio's interview, Russian strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure on Oct. 23 killed eight civilians and wounded 67, Ukrainian officials said, with drone impacts recorded at 19 locations.
Kyiv , roughly 500 kilometers from Donetsk Oblast, has faced increasingly heavy overnight attacks.
The impact of Russian strikes has also spilled over into neighbouring countries. A Russian jet-powered Geran drone came down near residential homes in a village in central Moldova on Oct. 23, in what Moldovan President Maia Sandu called "Russia's latest dangerous act."
Last year, during a diplomatic push to end the fighting. U.S. President Donald Trump said the " swapping " of land between Ukraine and Russia may have to take place to end the war. Various media outlets reported at the time that Moscow had suggested Ukraine hand over the entirety of unoccupied Donetsk.

title: Zelensky 'maybe not such a big humanitarian as Putin,' he quips as Ukraine's relations with Trump unravel
description: The president made the comment in an interview with ABC News two days after U.S. Envoy Steve Witkoff praised Vladimir Putin as "a humanitarian." Hours later, Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles and cluster munitions.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed his reaction to Washington's shifting allegiance in an interview with ABC News published Oct. 23.
While he maintained a calm and measured tone, avoiding getting into personal territory regarding his relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump , he did say the administration's recent actions were "not supportive" and acknowledged his frustrations.
"I'm a normal person. I'm just human. Maybe not such a big humanitarian as Putin, of course," Zelensky told ABC News.
Zelensky's remarks reference U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff's recent praise of Russian President Vladimir Putin. Following Moscow's release of an American prisoner on Oct. 21, Witkoff hailed Putin as "a humanitarian."
Hours later, Russia bombarded Kyiv's city center with ballistic missiles and cluster munitions , killing two people and injuring dozens, including children.
Zelensky didn't dwell on Witkoff's admiration of Putin, instead focusing on Ukraine's urgent military needs: namely, restored Starlink service and prompt deliveries of air defense missiles . The president confirmed that Starlink is still not working at full speed on the Ukrainian battlefield, despite claims by Trump to the contrary.
Ukraine has also received only 24 air defense missiles from its strategic partners over the last 90 days, Zelensky said.
"We are not crying and not screaming, but this is very important," he said. "I'm just trying to say that each missile is important."
While the U.S. has denied responsibility for restrictions to Ukraine's Starlink speeds and delays in Patriot shipments, Ukraine has received no explanation — and no solution. Moreover, the incidents follow a series of pro-Kremlin policy moves from the Trump administration.
These include a deal to purchase Russian diesel , a new sanctions waiver , and pressure on Kyiv to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries .
Zelensky said on Oct. 23 that trilateral peace talks among Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. will resume in November, with technical teams from each government meeting in Abu Dhabi.
The president told ABC News that Ukraine is still prepared to end the war by freezing the current battle lines.
"We are ready to stop this war as quick as possible," he said.

title: US lawmakers demand answers from Elon Musk over Ukraine Starlink restrictions
description: In a public letter, Democratic Senators and Representatives listed five questions concerning Starlink restrictions impacting Ukrainian forces, addressed to Musk. The demand comes as Ukrainian forces continue to experience severe problems operating Starlink military systems.
content:
U.S. Representative Gregory Meeks and Senator Peter Welch led four other lawmakers on Oct. 23 in demanding that Elon Musk answer questions about Ukrainian Starlink disruptions.
In a public letter , Democratic Senators and Representatives listed five questions concerning Starlink restrictions impacting Ukrainian forces, addressed to Musk. "As a publicly traded company, SpaceX has a legal obligation to disclose to shareholders and the public material events that could affect your business model," the lawmakers wrote in the letter. "The revelation that you personally wielded control over a foreign country’s military communications would require disclosure of elevated risks for corporate governance, geopolitical exposure, and potential adverse actions by foreign governments." The lawmakers gave Musk until October 31 to answer their questions.
The demand comes as Ukrainian forces continue to experience severe problems operating Starlink military systems. Since mid-October, Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk 's satellite internet system, Starlink, has been operating at limited capacity. With speed limit caps, Kyiv's ability to defend from deadly Russian jet-powered drones and coordinate strikes against Russian targets is hindered. "Just last month, more than 300 Ukrainian civilians were killed and 2,000 injured by Russian drone and missile strikes," the lawmakers wrote in their letter. "Ukraine has built an innovative network of drone systems to defend against the thousands of strikes launched each month by Russia. However, these life-saving systems often depend on Starlink’s military version, Starshield, for accurate communication and transmission of targeting data." Despite Ukrainian and U.S. officials apparently engaging in discussions to resolve the disruptions, nobody has publicly taken credit — or blame — for making or implementing the decision. However, the Trump administration officials continue pointing fingers firmly at SpaceX CEO Elon Musk. The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that Trump had ordered SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions, saying the president was "frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 160 kilometers (100 miles) an hour."
Trump said he had not spoken to Musk about the issue but might do so if the problems persisted.
"I have not spoken to him," Trump said. "I might have to, but I have not... I've heard it's fixed. If it's not, I will speak to him.... If there's a problem, I will get it straightened out." On Oct. 23, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that issues with Starlink continued to plague Ukrainian forces. "The speed restrictions for Starlink and Starshield are still in effect," Zelensky said. "The speed has not been restored. And the supply of interceptor missiles to protect against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed." On Oct. 23, U.S. Senator Richard Blumenthal, also a Democrat, announced that he is opening a probe into the Starlink disruption. Blumenthal's investigation asks the Pentagon to clarify who ordered the restrictions and to provide information on the U.S. military's own reliance on Starlink.

title: Kremlin-seized German company Metro AG transfers 1 billion rubles to Russian military without approval
description: Metro AG responded, saying it did not approve the donations. On Sept. 28, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree placing the Russian subsidiary of Metro AG under the Kremlin's control.
content:
Almost one month after being placed under the Kremlin's control, German wholesale food retailer Metro AG announced on Oct. 23 that its Russian subsidiary had donated 1 billion rubles (11.1 million euros/ $12.4 million) to support Russian forces without the company's approval.
On Sept. 28, Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree placing the Russian subsidiary of Metro AG under the Kremlin's control.
Metro AG responded on Oct. 23, saying it did not approve the donations.
"The decision by Metro Russia to donate to the Russian organization “All-Russia People's Front” was neither coordinated with Metro AG nor authorized or approved by Metro AG," the company said in a press release . "Since Metro Russia was placed under forced temporary administration as of September 28, Metro AG no longer has operational control over Metro Russia and has no influence over its operational decisions."
The Russian-controlled Metro transferred money to Russia's "People's Front. All for Victory!" fund. The funds "will be used to purchase equipment needed by soldiers on the front lines," according to a press release from the Russian company.
Metro AG is one of the world’s largest retailers, specializing in food wholesale and food distribution to restaurants and hotels. Metro AG first entered the Russian market in 2001 and operated 91 wholesale stores, employing around 9,000 employees in the country.
Moscow has seized Russian subsidiaries of Western companies throughout the war.
On Sept. 17, Putin signed a decree confiscating the assets of several international companies, including Nestle and Auchan . Other companies placed under Russian government management include Bati Logistics, FM Logistics, and Le Monlid LLC.
According to Deutsche Welle, other foreign companies taken over by the Kremlin in Russia have been used to donate to the "People's Front" fund.
In 2026, the fund received 1.5 billion rubles from Poland's Can-Pack, 1 billion rubles from the Dutch firm Akzo Nobel, and 600 million rubles from Denmark's Rockwool after all companies were placed under Russian control.

title: Trilateral peace talks with Russia, US negotiators to begin in November, Zelensky says
description: The peace discussions will begin at the technical level with negotiation teams, Zelensky said. If those efforts prove productive, then meetings between Zelensky, Russian President Vladimir Putin, and U.S. President Donald Trump will be held.
content:
Negotiation teams from Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S. will meet in Abu Dhabi in November to begin peace talks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 23.
"The plan is to meet in the first half of November and as early as possible, of course, but we are ready to meet any day, even tomorrow," Zelensky said in an address to the Hudson Institute think tank via a video call. "But it all depends on the Russians. We expected a trilateral meeting this October too, but it didn't happen because the Russians came up with another reason not to meet." The peace discussions will begin at the technical level with negotiation teams, Zelensky said. If those efforts prove productive, then meetings between Zelensky, Russian President Vladimir Putin , and U.S. President Donald Trump will be held. "We need to move from trilateral negotiations at the technical level to a meeting of leaders, because the key issues can only be resolved at that level," Zelensky said. Zelensky stressed the importance of including robust security guarantees for Ukraine in the negotiations and including Europe in the talks. Following any peace deal, a large Ukrainian army would need to be funded for at least 10 years, said Zelensky. Arriving late to the address, Zelensky said he had just finished speaking with U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff regarding the negotiations. Earlier this week, Steve Witkoff met with Zelensky in Oslo during a trip to Norway before meeting with Putin.
In the address, the president also discussed restrictions on Ukraine's Starlink military systems.
"The speed restrictions for Starlink and Starshield are still in effect," Zelensky said. "The speed has not been restored. And the supply of interceptor missiles to protect against Russian ballistic missiles is still delayed."
Since mid-October, Starshield, the militarized version of Elon Musk 's satellite internet system, Starlink, has been operating at limited capacity. With speed limit caps, Kyiv's ability to defend from deadly Russian jet-powered drones and coordinate strikes against Russian targets has been diminished.
Despite Ukrainian and U.S. officials apparently engaging in discussions to resolve the disruption to Ukrainian communications, nobody has publicly taken credit — or blame — for making or implementing the decision, which is not only politically "toxic " but also could have severe negative commercial implications for SpaceX, the operator of Starshield and Starlink.
Amid deteriorating U.S.-Ukrainian relations, Zelensky told the Hudson Institute that he hoped to strengthen the alliance between Kyiv and Washington.
"I really want our relations between Ukraine and America and with all our other partners to be just as strong as possible," Zelensky said. "Strong, truly friendly and without misunderstandings, of course. Because without America, without a strong America and America that cares about what happens in the world, the world would definitely be a worse place."
In recent weeks, Trump has lashed out at Zelensky, unilaterally imposed a failed energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, threatened to withhold aid from Kyiv, and lifted sanctions on Russian oil exports. Trump has defended his easing of Russian sanctions, saying the move could prompt Moscow to join peace negotiations with Kyiv.

title: How EU ships are still able to carry Trump's Russian diesel despite so many sanctions
description: A ship called the Agioi Fanendes, which had just left Russia's Baltic Sea port of Primorsk, was carrying 40,000 metric tons to New York and had been traveling westwards through the Baltic Sea ever since.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — When news broke on Oct. 23 that a ship was reportedly carrying a new supply of Russian diesel for U.S. President Donald Trump, one question immediately arose: How, after more than 20 rounds of EU sanctions, could European ships still be involved in facilitating that trade?
Trump's Oct. 9 deal to buy Russian diesel was part of a wider pivot towards Moscow that was met with widespread condemnation by EU leaders. The deal itself might also be illegal under U.S. sanctions policy.
However, media reports circulated on Oct. 23 that a ship called the Agioi Fanendes, which had just left Russia's Baltic Sea port of Primorsk, was carrying 40,000 metric tons to New York, and the ship has been traveling through the Baltic Sea westwards ever since.
Adding to the sense of mystery, ship-tracking website MarineTraffic noted that the Agioi Fanendes updated its status on Oct. 23 from heading to New York to, "for orders" — ship-speak for final destination unconfirmed.
That ship is owned by the Greek company Eastern Mediterranean Maritime, owned by billionaire Thanasis Martinos. It is flying under a Maltese flag. Both countries are part of the EU, so the Agioi Fanendes has to comply with the bloc's 21 sanctions packages imposed on Russia since it launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
"EU law hasn't changed," wrote Ukraine's sanctions chief Vladyslav Vlasiuk on social media.
"An EU-flagged, EU-managed ship may carry Russian diesel only if it was bought at or below the $100 a barrel price cap," Vlasiuk said.
That price refers to the G7 oil price cap, agreed in 2022 to reduce the profits Russia can make from the oil trade while still ensuring the world's energy supply.
A European Commission spokesperson confirmed to the Kyiv Independent Vlasiuk's interpretation of what is legally possible.
"EU operators are only allowed to provide maritime transport and related services for Russian crude oil and petroleum products if these are sold at or below the relevant price caps," they said.
And written guidance prepared by the Commission makes explicit that shipowners also bear some responsibility for ensuring their cargo is compliant with sanctions.
"Shipowners should obtain from their customer an attestation in which the customer confirms the Russian oil cargo transported or to be transported has been purchased at or below the price cap."
When asked to confirm the financial value of Agioi Fanendes' cargo, a spokesperson for Eastern Mediterranean Maritime instead said "kindly be advised that Agioi Fanendes is proceeding for orders as discharging port is not confirmed yet."
They had not yet replied to a follow-up question confirming receipt of the EU-required attestation by the time of publication.
To get to the U.S., the Agioi Fanendes will first have to travel through the Baltic Sea, and if it enters the territorial waters of any EU country on the way — 12 miles from their shoreline, they can also intervene to stop the ship.
The Finnish Border Guard told the Kyiv Independent when the ship was just leaving that country's territorial waters that there was no planned intercept, and no information they could share.
Sweden's coastguard, which has previously boarded several Russian shadow fleet ships, said "we are monitoring the sea traffic in the Baltic Sea 24/7 and keep an updated and thorough situational awareness."
However, they declined to comment on specific ships, adding only that they "keep track of all oil transporting ships."
In the meantime, the Agioi Fanendes has moved via international waters in the center of the Baltic Sea. But in international water, the law of the country whose flag your ship is flying is the one that applies.
"Malta is firmly committed to the rigorous implementation of European Union sanctions and expects full compliance with all applicable restrictive measures," the country's sanctions unit told the Kyiv Independent.
"Vessels flying the Maltese flag are likewise required to comply fully with the sanctions applicable to them," they said.
"We are aware of the reports concerning this particular shipment, and the relevant attestations are being sought from the vessel's owners and operators," the Maltese sanctions unit confirmed.
Only when that attestation is provided that the diesel aboard the Agioi Fanendes complies with the G7 price cap can it legally satisfy the U.S.' thirst for Russian fossil fuels.
With the buyer, seller, and the agreed price of the diesel all unknown, according to the original Reuters article on the Agioi Fanendes, the only possible way to prove that the ship is not in breach of EU sanctions would be for that attestation Malta is waiting for to be provided.

title: Inside Austria's network of Ukrainian fugitives, Russian elites, and political connections
description:
The detention of two Ukrainian journalists in Austria earlier this month while conducting an investigation has highlighted deeper systemic concerns.

Mykhailo Tkach and Yaroslav Bondarenko were investigating a former Ukrainian prosecutor general who had fled Ukraine and settled in Vienna.

Austria has increasingly come under scrutiny for providing refuge to individuals wanted in connection with corruption cases in Ukraine, as well as Russian officials and oligarchs. Meanwhile, several senior Aus
content:
Then Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl and Russian President Vladimir Putin dance during her wedding on August 18, 2018 in Gamlitz, Styria, Austria. (Roland Schlager / APA /AFP via Getty Images)
The detention of two Ukrainian journalists in Austria earlier this month while conducting an investigation has highlighted deeper systemic concerns.
Mykhailo Tkach and Yaroslav Bondarenko were investigating a former Ukrainian prosecutor general who had fled Ukraine and settled in Vienna.
Austria has increasingly come under scrutiny for providing refuge to individuals wanted in connection with corruption cases in Ukraine, as well as Russian officials and oligarchs. Meanwhile, several senior Austrian officials have maintained close ties to Russia, with some having worked for the Kremlin.
These connections, alongside concerns over Austria's approach to corruption suspects, have raised questions about the country's commitment to the rule of law.
"It is astonishing that Austria's law enforcement system seems powerless against corrupt fugitives who have sought refuge in the country, yet has acted so aggressively against investigative journalists," Daria Kaleniuk, executive director of Ukraine's Anti-Corruption Action Center, told the Kyiv Independent.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from Austrian authorities and will publish their response upon receipt.
Tkach, head of investigations at the Ukrainian media outlet Ukrainska Pravda, said on Oct. 9 that the Austrian police had brutally detained him and cameraman Bondarenko the previous day and treated them "like terrorists."
As a result of the police's actions, Bondarenko was injured as shattered glass from their car hit him in the face.
In an Oct. 12 press release, Austrian prosecutors said that the two journalists were arrested because they were mistakenly deemed conspirators of two different Ukrainian nationals currently in pretrial detention on suspicion of espionage.
" The actions of Austrian prosecutors are disgraceful," Kaleniuk told the Kyiv Independent. "Independent journalists came to Austria, only to be detained by a special police unit as if they were terrorists."
The key question is how credible the information that prompted the journalists' detention actually was, a former Ukrainian top investigator told the Kyiv Independent.
"It should be established who supplied that information, especially now that we know for certain that these people posed no threat," the ex-investigator said.
"This is where the greatest potential for abuse lies. If the reports contained specific allegations that these people were terrorists, that they were armed, and so on, then whoever made those allegations must be held accountable for providing false information."
Tkach was on an editorial assignment in Vienna to locate fugitive ex-Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko .
Ukrainska Pravda reported on Sept. 23 that Kravchenko had moved to Austria. He was fired by parliament on Sept. 15 amid a major corruption investigation.
Within the investigation, a top prosecutor described as a "confidant" of Kravchenko was charged. Publicly revealed evidence hints at Kravchenko being implicated .
He left Ukraine on Sept. 14 amid speculation that he could face charges in the same corruption case.
One possible reason for the journalists' detention in Austria was that some fugitives from Ukraine, possibly Kravchenko, could have leaked information to Austrian law enforcement agencies and manipulated them, according to Tkach.
As Kravchenko left Ukraine, he simultaneously approved charges against the head of the anti-corruption agency investigating him. The charges were later dropped as unfounded.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from Kravchenko and will publish his response once it is received.
Tetiana Shevchuk, a lawyer at the Anti-Corruption Action Center, said that "historically, Austria has welcomed Russian money and capital from other former Soviet countries."
"It has convenient banking services and a well-developed network of lawyers and luxury housing catering to wealthy people from the former Soviet Union," she told the Kyiv Independent.
Austria rarely extradites suspects in corruption cases, using the justification that former Soviet countries do not protect human rights and that there are political motives. Other European countries extradite suspects more often.
"These wealthy individuals can afford to live in luxury and effectively buy themselves justice," Shevchuk argued. "Ordinary people don't have the same access to lawyers. But if you have a lot of money, things are different. The extremely wealthy can afford to hire entire teams of lawyers."
A former Ukrainian top investigator who worked with Austria told the Kyiv Independent that "the Austrian authorities either failed to help us or responded inadequately."
"In general, they were not cooperating with Ukrainian law enforcement agencies," he said. "They were failing to act on extradition requests, requests for investigative assistance, and so on."
The former investigator argued that "it seemed like a systematic pattern of behavior," and that his "impression is that there may be some degree of political influence behind this."
One of the fugitives based in Austria, Ukrainian oligarch Dmytro Firtash , has been charged with bribery, racketeering, and money laundering by the U.S. and money laundering and organized crime by Spain .
Since 2014, he has been fighting an extradition battle with both countries. Dieter Böhmdorfer, a former Austrian justice minister, was one of Firtash's lawyers in his extradition proceedings.
Firtash's fate appeared to have been sealed in 2019, when Austria's Supreme Court ruled that Firtash could be extradited to the United States, and then Justice Minister Clemens Jabloner approved Firtash's extradition.
Surprisingly, Firtash was still able to escape justice. His lawyers filed a new appeal, and in March 2026, a Vienna court definitely rejected the U.S. extradition request.
The basis for the rejection was seen by critics as dubious: Firtash allegedly enjoyed diplomatic status as an adviser to Belarus's Permanent Mission to the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), granting him immunity from prosecution.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from Firtash and will publish his response once it is received.
Another fugitive living in Austria, Oleksandr Tupytskyi , is a former chairman of Ukraine's Constitutional Court.
In 2021, he was charged with unlawfully influencing and bribing a witness to induce false testimony, abuse of power, and illegally tampering with a government computer system.
He left Ukraine during the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Other Ukrainians who have reportedly moved to Austria include Kyrylo Shevchenko, former head of the National Bank of Ukraine; billionaire Hennadiy Boholyubov , President Volodymyr Zelensky's former Deputy Chief of Staff Rostyslav Shurma , businessman Denys Komarnytskyi, Andrii Kholodov, a lawmaker from Zelensky's party, and former pro-Russian lawmaker Yevhen Murayev.
The list of Austria-based Ukrainians also includes Viktor Tatkov, former head of Ukraine's High Commercial Court, and businessmen Oleksandr Petrovskyi and Oleh Bakhmatyuk.
Many of these fugitives are suspects in high-profile corruption cases.
The late Andriy Pornov , a former deputy chief of staff for pro-Russian ex-President Viktor Yanukovych, lived in Vienna from 2015 to 2019.
Portnov, who was widely seen as wielding immense influence over Ukraine's judiciary, was shot dead in Madrid in 2025.
Several other Yanukovych allies — Andriy Klyuyev, Serhiy Klyuyev, and Oleksii Azarov — had investments and properties in Austria.
Meanwhile, Yanukovych 's Mezhyhirya residence near Kyiv was connected to a complex ownership structure involving Austrian-registered businesses.
Austria has also been a safe haven for Russian top officials and oligarchs.
In 2023, the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) reported that Russian President Vladimir Putin's daughter, Maria Vorontsova, had frequented a 10.8 million euro chalet in Kitzbühel, Tyrol. Several local residents claimed that Putin himself had visited the property.
Funds from the Russian oligarch Arkady Rotenberg , a close Putin associate, were used to purchase the chalet, according to OCCRP.
The late Yury Luzhkov, who was mayor of Moscow from 1992 to 2010, and his billionaire wife, Yelena Baturina, maintained an extensive property portfolio in Austria, including Alpine residences and hotel investments.
Another Russian politician linked to Austria is Andrei Metelsky, secretary of the Moscow branch of Putin's United Russia party.
Metelsky associates owned four hotels in Tyrol with an estimated total value of 40 million euros in 2019, the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny 's Anti-Corruption Fund reported in 2019.
Igor Shuvalov, CEO of Russian state-owned VEB bank and former deputy prime minister, has also declared renting a residential property in Austria measuring approximately 1,480 square meters. The property was owned by Shuvalov's family, the Russian media outlet Meduza reported in 2016.
The ties run both ways, with former Austrian officials taking up positions at Russian state-owned entities.
Karin Kneissl, who was Austria's foreign minister from 2017 to 2019, triggered a scandal by inviting Putin to her wedding and dancing with him in 2018.
Kneissl was nominated to her government post by the Freedom Party of Austria, which has long maintained close ties with the Kremlin.
She also became a columnist for the Russian state propaganda outlet RT in 2020 and joined the board of Russian state-controlled oil giant Rosneft in 2021.
In 2023, she moved to Russia and started working at a think-tank promoting the Kremlin's foreign policy.
Another scandal linked to Russia took place in 2018, when Austria's Interior Ministry raided the country's domestic intelligence service.
The raid, which was later ruled to be unlawful, targeted intelligence officers investigating right-wing extremism and suspected Russian influence. Subsequent investigations raised the possibility that Russian intelligence had helped engineer the operation to weaken Austria's counterintelligence service and replace its leadership with people more accommodating to Moscow.
Vienna has earned a reputation as Europe's spy capital, where Austria's neutrality and historically lax espionage laws have reportedly helped Russian intelligence operatives establish a formidable presence.
Meanwhile, two former Austrian chancellors — Wolfgang Schüssel and Christian Kern — worked for Russian companies following their chancellorships. Another ex-chancellor, Alfred Gusenbauer, served as a supervisory board member at a Berlin-based think tank founded by Putin’s allies.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comments from the officials involved.
" Russia corrupts local elites," Shevchuk argued.
Oleg Sukhov is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent. He is a former editor and reporter at the Moscow Times. He has a master's degree in history from the Moscow State University. He moved to Ukraine in 2014 due to the crackdown on independent media in Russia and covered war, corruption, reforms and law enforcement for the Kyiv Post.

title: Ukraine war latest: Ukraine, Russia agree to local ceasefire for Russian-occupied Oleshky, mediated by Melania Trump
description:
Key developments on Oct. 23:

 * Ukraine, Russia agree on local ceasefire for Russian-occupied Oleshky, mediated by Melania Trump
 * Civilian cargo ship sinks off coast of Romania after Russian drone strike, authorities say
 * Ukraine to end automatic 100% mobilization exemptions for critical industries, Prime Minister says
 * Ukrainian drone attack triggers shut down of Moscow airports, missile reportedly strikes Oryol semiconductor plant
 * 270 Ukrainian POWs return home in latest swap with Ru
content:
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump has mediated a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in and around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid, Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on Oct. 23.
The move comes amid increased attention to the worsening humanitarian crisis in the city, which over the past weeks has gained international attention, including from Pope Leo XIV.
According to the press release from the White House press service, the First Lady "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary."
The ceasefire is scheduled to begin on Oct. 29, the press release added.
Lubinets, confirmed the agreement in a video statement on Telegram later on Oct. 23.
"I personally thank Melania Trump and her team for their efforts, leadership, and coordination between the two negotiating groups of Ukraine and the Russian Federation in reaching agreements," Lubinets said.
Under the agreement, a ceasefire will be put in place, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky, and civilians will be allowed to leave the city freely, according to Lubinets.
"The operation will take place gradually. It is extremely difficult to implement," he said. He will keep the Ukrainian public informed and show the results of the operation, he said. He also asked the public to be careful about spreading information on the mission.
Lubinets added that he had led the negotiations on the Ukrainian side and that Russia's human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, had led them on the Russian side.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also welcomed Melania Trump's role, saying she had "made a significant contribution to agreeing on the humanitarian operation" in Oleshky, Russian pro-Kremlin media outlet Ura.ru reported. Peskov said the sides are working to agree on a ceasefire in the area so that residents can be evacuated.
State-aligned Russian media RBK reported Russia's General Staff had announced a ceasefire from 04:00 a.m. local time on Oct. 27, citing Valeriy Gerasimov, Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces.
Gerasimov added that to ensure the safety of people and the delivery of vital supplies, engineering reconnaissance will be conducted.
Oleshky , located just across the Dnipro River from Kherson , has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces in the area, who prevent humanitarian aid from entering. Civilians attempting to flee via the only roads in and out of the city are frequently targeted by drones.
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," Melania Trump was quoted as saying in the press release.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."
According to the document, an "impartial American media organization" will visit the area to document the work of both sides in the area.
A civilian cargo ship sank after being struck by a Russian drone near Romania's Black Sea coast on Oct. 23, Romanian authorities reported.
The attack is the latest in a series of brazen Russian strikes on civilian shipping in the Black Sea, part of a broader escalation in Russia's economic warfare against Ukraine this year.
The ship, Khoryv, was sailing from Turkey under the flag of the Comoros and was crewed by Ukrainian and Azerbaijani nationals.
According to Romanian President Nicusor Dan, one person was confirmed dead and three others were missing from the 14-member crew.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry later confirmed that a Ukrainian crew member on board the Khoryv was killed. Four other Ukrainian nationals, including the ship's captain, were hospitalized, while two Ukrainian crew members did not require medical assistance.
The ministry said the vessel had sunk near the Romanian city of Constanta with 14 crew members on board. According to preliminary information, a drone strike may have caused the sinking.
Ukraine's Embassy in Romania is working to establish the circumstances of the incident, as well as the whereabouts and condition of the rescued Ukrainian nationals, while remaining in contact with Romanian authorities, the ministry said.
"This attack is a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine," Dan wrote on social media .
"It is time for Russia to take the peace initiatives proposed by the United States and Europe seriously, accept the ceasefire proposals and end the war."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attack , describing it as another Russian escalation in the Black Sea.
"These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law," von der Leyen wrote on X.
Romania's Interior Ministry later confirmed that nine crew members had been rescued, publishing a video showing the keel of the overturned ship barely protruding above the water's surface.
In response to a series of attacks on civilian shipping, NATO plans to increase its military presence in the Black Sea by deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones.
The announcement came after NATO's main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, met at the alliance's headquarters in Brussels on Oct. 20 to discuss security in the Black Sea.
Ukraine's government finalized changes to its military exemption system that will end automatic 100% exemptions for employees in critical industries, including defense manufacturing and energy, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi announced on Oct. 23.
Koretskyi said the changes seek to make the exemption system fairer and prevent abuses.
"The number of workers exempted from mobilization is growing by tens of thousands every month. Meanwhile, those who have been defending the country for five years must have the opportunity to return home from military service. That is why we are making difficult but necessary decisions," Koretskyi said.
Companies working in critical sectors, including defense manufacturing, energy, telecommunications, logistics, and utilities, will retain their critical status. However, the government will review the criteria used to determine which businesses qualify as critical.
Companies will still be able to request higher exemption quotas if needed to maintain operations, while the government is also developing a mechanism that would allow companies to exempt all their employees if they regularly arrange for some of their workers to voluntarily join the military, Koretskyi said.
Those joining the military would know where they would serve and for how long, while keeping their jobs and salaries, Koretskyi said.
"This will give those on the front line confidence that rotations are possible and that others will take their place. Those joining the military will also know that they are serving for a clearly defined period," he said.
Under the new rules, defense industry companies will be able to exempt up to 95% of their eligible employees from mobilization, the Defense Ministry said.
The ministry stressed that exemptions should remain available to employees directly involved in producing weapons and other equipment for Ukraine's military.
"Companies must be able to plan their operations, retain specialists, and increase production," Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said.
The Defense and Economy ministries will work out the conditions for the mechanism with businesses, with the government aiming to approve it by Dec. 1., Korestkyi said.
Civilian flights at all four of Moscow's main airports were suspended on the afternoon of Oct. 23 amid a Ukrainian drone raid on the Russian capital, local authorities reported.
Restrictions on arriving and departing flights at Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports were announced by Russian civil aviation authority Rosaviatsiya at 2:05 p.m. local time.
At Sheremetyevo, Moscow's largest airport, an air alert was sounded, and waiting passengers were advised to take shelter.
Photos later emerged on social media that allegedly showed debris from a downed drone on the tarmac at Sheremetyevo.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the photos.
Open-source flight tracker FlightRadar24 reported 85 cancelled flights and a further 229 delayed at Sheremetyevo over the day.
According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, 17 drones were shot down while heading toward the city on the afternoon of Oct. 23.
Ukraine had not commented on the reported attack as of the time of publication.
The all-clear was later sounded at Sheremetyevo Airport, Russian state news agency TASS reported at 5 p.m. local time.
An evacuation was also reported at the IQ-quarter skyscraper in the Moscow City business district, which houses offices of several Russian government ministries, including the Digital Development Ministry, Economic Development Ministry, and Industry and Trade Ministry.
Russian state news agency TASS later reported, citing emergency services, that the alarm had been false.
Meanwhile, explosions were reported in the Russian city of Oryol, approximately 350 kilometers (217 miles) southwest of Moscow, where a local industrial facility was reportedly targeted in a missile strike.
Oryol Oblast Governor Andrey Klychkov confirmed that an enterprise had been targeted, while independent Russian media outlet ASTRA, citing its open-source intelligence analysis, identified the facility as the Proton plant.
The plant manufactures semiconductor devices, LEDs, and electronic components for industrial and specialized equipment that could be used in Russian weapons systems.
Local residents reported hearing at least four explosions, ASTRA said.
As Ukrainian long-range drones have reached deeper into Russian territory, temporary airport closures across Russia have become increasingly common during Moscow's full-scale war against Ukraine.
Ukraine and Russia exchanged prisoners of war on Oct. 23, with 270 Ukrainian service members returning home, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced .
The exchange, the first in two months, also saw 270 Russian prisoners of war returned to Russia from Ukrainian captivity.
According to Zelensky, most of the Ukrainians returning home had been captured during the Siege of Mariupol in spring 2022. They included service members from the Ground Forces, Navy, and Air Assault Forces, as well as border guards and fighters from the Azov regiment, which led the city's defense.
Five of the released POWs survived the Olenivka prison massacre in July 2022, when a thermobaric munition was detonated inside a prison barracks housing Ukrainian prisoners of war.
According to Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, a "significant portion" of the released prisoners had been found guilty on sham criminal charges while in Russian captivity.
Seven Ukrainian civilians were also brought back from Russia with the help of Ukrainian authorities on Oct. 23, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said in a Facebook post. Lubinets added that another seven civilians had traveled to Russia as part of family reunification efforts supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
Zelensky, as well as the Coordination Headquarters later said that nine civilians had been released.
Lubinets called the prisoner exchange "historic," saying it brought home the largest number of convicted Ukrainian service members since 2022: 86 convicted soldiers and one person who had been facing criminal prosecution.
Ukraine, international human rights organizations, and the U.N. have described such trials in Russia as war crimes. The Third Geneva Convention grants POWs protected status under international humanitarian law and prohibits prosecuting them solely for their participation in hostilities, subject to the rules governing lawful combatant conduct.
Lubinets added that the exchange marked the return of Azov Regiment service members for the first time "in a long while."
Two of those released had been held in Russian captivity since 2018 and 2020, spending eight and six years in captivity, respectively, Lubinets said.
The youngest released POW was 24, while the oldest was 63, he added.
While intermittent U.S.-mediated "peace talks" between Russia and Ukraine have failed to secure even a partial ceasefire, prisoner exchanges remain one of the few channels of regular cooperation between Moscow and Kyiv.
The latest swap was the 11th reported prisoner exchange of 2026. The previous two exchanges took place in August.
