The prime minister said some companies had been created specifically to obtain military exemptions, turning the system into a business.
Koretskyi said the changes do not mean mobilization will intensify immediately, but warned that Ukraine must be prepared for possible developments, including increased mobilization in Russia.

title: Moldova expels Russian diplomat after Russian Geran drone falls near family homes
description: "Russia's war keeps putting Moldovan lives at risk," President Maia Sandu said, calling it Russia's "latest dangerous act."
content:
Moldova declared a member of the Russian embassy in Moldova persona non grata after a Russian drone violated Moldova's air space and fell near homes in the country's center, President Maia Sandu said on Oct. 23.
The Russian Geran drone came down near family homes and an energy facility, Sandu said .
"Russia's war keeps putting Moldovan lives at risk," she added, calling it Russia's "latest dangerous act."
Police said a local resident reported a drone found in the village of Kistelnita in Telenesti District, about 100 meters from a residential building.
Earlier that day, a drone entered Moldovan air space at 1:59 p.m. local time during a large-scale Russian attack on Ukraine, Moldova's defense ministry said. It crossed from the direction of Verkhnia Slobidka in Ukraine's Vinnytsia Oblast toward Frunzauca in Camenca District of Moldova's Russian-controlled region of Transnistria.
The drone disappeared from airspace monitoring near Pepeni in Singerei district at 2:10 p.m. and reappeared briefly before it was lost again at 2:12 p.m. near Meseni in Rezina district, the ministry said.
The incidents underscore the growing security risks posed to Moldova and the region by Russia's war against neighboring Ukraine.
Russian aerial incursions into Moldovan territory during attacks against Ukraine are becoming alarmingly routine, as a series of Russian drone incursions into Moldova's airspace was recorded during an overnight attack against Ukraine on Oct. 16.
Chisinau has repeatedly raised the alarm about these airspace violations, with Moldovan President Maia Sandu declaring that Russia's war against Ukraine is "dangerously reaching Moldova."
Moldova announced plans on Oct. 7 to build shelters at border crossings to protect border guards and people nearby in response to growing incursions.
The announcement came after the Moldovan Border Police reported on Oct. 5 that a projectile fired during a Russian attack against Ukraine ricocheted and struck a passenger bus and a border control booth at the Palanca-Maiaky-Udobne crossing, lightly injuring a border guard.

title: Inside the legal design of America's Russia sanctions U-turn
description:
The first Russian diesel tanker under the new deal between Russia and the United States is now heading for New York with a 40,000-metric-ton cargo, enough to cover barely two hours of American demand.

The deal began with a phone call, in which Russian President Vladimir Putin seems to have persuaded his U.S. counterpart, President Donald Trump, that Russian diesel could ease the energy prices he blamed on Ukraine's strikes.

And the argument appears to have landed. Within a week, Washington had
content:
Vladimir Putin (L) and U.S. President Donald Trump (R) arrive for a group photo at the G20 Summit in Osaka, Japan on June 28, 2019. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
Independent consultant on illicit finance, anti-corruption, and governance
The first Russian diesel tanker under the new deal between Russia and the United States is now heading for New York with a 40,000-metric-ton cargo, enough to cover barely two hours of American demand.
The deal began with a phone call, in which Russian President Vladimir Putin seems to have persuaded his U.S. counterpart, President Donald Trump , that Russian diesel could ease the energy prices he blamed on Ukraine's strikes.
And the argument appears to have landed. Within a week, Washington had reversed its policy, agreed to a diesel deal, issued a Treasury license opening global markets to Russian diesel, and waived the Graham Act sanctions on Russia's largest oil buyers.
Each step was presented as relief for Americans facing high fuel prices. Beyond the deal's potential electoral dividends for Trump, the legal architecture of these measures tells another story, one that deserves just as much attention.
President Trump has certified to Congress that the waiver serves the U.S. national interest, but has not publicly explained how. What both decisions do is reopen markets, revenue, and payment channels for Moscow, which has secured them without a ceasefire or any other concession to Ukraine .
The diesel deal rests on a Treasury license, General License 135 , issued on Oct. 9, which lifts U.S. sanctions on Russian diesel imposed in 2014 and 2022. Because those sanctions were set by presidential order , the president could likely lift them, though arguably only after notifying Congress.
What stands out is the license design, which does far more for Moscow than for the Americans it was meant to help. Unlike earlier licenses, which lasted 30 days and covered only cargoes already at sea, GL 135 covers Russian diesel sold anywhere in the world until April 2027, giving Russian exporters six months to supply both existing and new buyers.
Another aspect is that the license covers only diesel. That might reflect its importance to U.S. voters, but it also allows Russia an opening in one of its most valuable export markets, which has been recently targeted by Ukraine.
For American consumers, the gains are limited : the promised volumes equal less than two weeks of U.S. demand. Moreover, the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022 still bans Russian energy imports into the U.S. until Ukraine accepts the peace agreement, a condition that has not been met.
Thus, the potential U.S. diesel importers who would rely on the license risk civil penalties up to the value of their cargo and the forfeiture of their ships, which a presidential pardon cannot cancel. With so much at stake, few importers are likely to take that risk, which may explain why Trump presents the deal as supply for " the American and Global Marketplace ."
The 2022 import ban applies only to the U.S., so the diesel will go to buyers in the global markets.
There, the license lets traders, shippers and banks handle Russian diesel and take dollar payments without breaching U.S. sanctions, and the proceeds go to Russia’s oil companies.
Meanwhile, Kyiv is under pressure from Washington, which reportedly urged Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries , the same facilities that now supply the diesel its license has brought back to market.
In September, Trump signed the Lindsey Graham Act , a law targeting the five largest buyers of Russian energy and entities involved in oil sanctions evasion, which many analysts took as a sign of a tougher line on Russia.
Its main weapon was a tariff of up to 100% on goods from Russia’s biggest energy buyers: China, India and Turkey, which have bought about half, 37% and 5% of its crude exports since late 2022. However, on Oct. 16, two days before these measures were due to take effect, and only a month after signing the act, Trump waived them .
As with the license, the waiver may do little for Americans and a great deal for Russia and its biggest customers.
The sanctions package was designed to push these buyers away from Russian crude oil, which could have driven global oil prices up in the short term. Over time, however, the expectation within the G7 was that other producers would likely fill the gap, leaving Russia with fewer customers, at steeper discounts, and with less income to fund the war.
After the signed waiver, the benefit to American consumers is yet to be seen, while Moscow's revenue will be immediate.
Moreover, the benefits to Moscow extend far beyond its oil customers.
Besides tariffs, the Graham Act aimed to pressure every stage of its oil trade: the shadow fleet, the ports and insurers, state banks such as Sberbank, VTB and Gazprombank, and the Central Bank. Nearly all of this is now on hold. Existing U.S. sanctions on those banks remain, but the waiver gives up the act's reach to the foreign ports, insurers and banks Russia relies on to evade sanctions. In September 2026, Russian-flagged "shadow" tankers more than doubled year on year, carrying 36% of the shadow fleet's oil and making Russia the most common flag in the shadow fleet.
The wider cost is the loss of credibility of U.S. sanctions globally.
Washington has pressured India and China to buy less Russian oil by adding an extra 25% tariff on Indian goods , which was later withdrawn.
The Graham Act was meant to fill that gap and write these secondary tariffs into a law. The waiver shows that U.S. sanctions are less a firm commitment and can shift after a phone call.
Traders in the Gulf, Turkey and Asia, and the shadow fleet may now face lighter compliance requirements, making it cheaper for Russia to reach and sell in the global markets.
The same logic applies to banks and insurers: those that have avoided Russian business may now be more willing to reconsider, potentially allowing Russian money back into the financial system. Meanwhile, the EU, the U.K. and G7 partners still enforce their sanctions, leaving their firms barred from trade that U.S.-linked competitors can now pursue.
The past week has brought a marked shift in U.S. policy towards Russia and Ukraine.
Over the same period, there were reports of threats to U.S. intelligence sharing and disruptions to Starlink in Ukraine. The moves have drawn rare bipartisan criticism, but it is not yet clear whether that will change anything.
The law may offer firmer ground than politics. Lawmakers argue the diesel license conflicts with the 2022 import ban, which could invite a legal challenge. Some have also called for limits on the president's waiver power. Whether Congress acts will show if it is willing to defend the sanctions it wrote.
The question is whether this is a temporary detour or a new direction.
Pressure from Congress, from European allies , or from Kyiv itself could still pull Washington back towards its earlier policy of backing Ukraine against its aggressor. The deal may settle the matter on its own if it delivers neither lower prices nor progress towards peace; however, ultimately at a major cost to Ukraine and U.S. credibility.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Ieva Miyares is an independent consultant on illicit finance, anti-corruption, and governance based in Nairobi, Kenya, and a former Senior Manager in Deloitte U.K.'s Forensic and Financial Crime practice.

title: Trump vows to fix Ukraine's Starlink problems if they continue, may call Musk
description: "If there's a problem, I will get it straightened out," U.S. President Donald Trump said.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 23 that he would help resolve any remaining problems with Ukraine's military-grade Starlink service, Starshield.
The statement comes after the Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that Trump had ordered SpaceX CEO Elon Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions, saying the president was "frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 160 kilometers (100 miles) an hour."
Trump said he had not spoken to Musk about the issue but might do so if the problems persisted.
"I have not spoken to him," Trump said. "I might have to, but I have not... I've heard it's fixed. If it's not, I will speak to him.... If there's a problem, I will get it straightened out."
Ukraine uses Starshield terminals to control interceptor drones designed to counter Russia's jet-powered Geran drones, which Moscow has deployed as part of a renewed campaign of attacks targeting Ukrainian civilians and civilian infrastructure.
Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 23 that Starshield terminals were still experiencing severe problems, raising questions about whether the U.S. government controls a critical piece of national security infrastructure or whether authority ultimately rests with Musk and SpaceX .
"Overall, there's no change anywhere ," a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent when asked whether Trump's intervention had resolved the Starshield problems.
"Starshield still doesn't work," a Ukrainian intelligence official confirmed.

title: Russian daytime attack on Chernihiv civilian businesses kills 1, injures at least 25
description: Chernihiv City Council said two private businesses were targeted in the Russian attack but provided no further details.
content:
Russian forces attacked the city of Chernihiv during the day on Oct. 23, killing one man and injuring at least 25 people, local authorities said.
An air raid alert was declared in Chernihiv at around 1:40 p.m. local time due to a missile threat. Minutes later, Ukraine's Air Force reported drones and a Banderol low-cost cruise missile heading toward the city.
Chernihiv City Council said two private businesses were targeted in the Russian attack but provided no further details.
As of 4:30 p.m. local time, emergency services continued to assist the injured and deal with the aftermath of the Russian attack.
A regional police investigative team was also working at the scene, documenting the damage and collecting evidence of a Russian war crime.
Chernihiv, the regional capital, had a population of around 280,000 before Russia's full-scale invasion . Located in northern Chernihiv Oblast, which borders Belarus and Russia , the city has been repeatedly targeted by Russian forces.
Chernihiv was under Russian siege and occupation from Feb. 24 until early April 2022.

title: Exclusive: The next Russia deal Trump may be weighing after diesel

content:
U.S. President Donald Trump looks on during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on Oct. 20, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump may be considering further sanctions relief for Russia following his recent diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin, several Ukrainian and U.S. officials familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent.
The potential move would fit an approach in which the Trump administration offers Russia economic benefits in hopes of persuading Moscow to end its war against Ukraine , one U.S. government official and one Senate official said.
Trump's diesel deal with Putin has drawn bipartisan criticism in Washington and strained relations with Kyiv. President Volodymyr Zelensky called the agreement a "weak move," warning that it could pave the way for further sanctions relief.
Now, Ukrainian officials fear the administration could explore a deal involving Russia's fertilizer industry, two people familiar with the matter said.
The U.S. has not directly sanctioned Russia's fertilizer industry or banned imports of Russian fertilizers. But any potential agreement could provide sanctions relief for vessels, companies, banks, and individuals linked to the industry, one senior Ukrainian official said.
Russia has long sought an ease of restrictions affecting its agricultural exports, arguing that banking, insurance, and shipping barriers have limited its access to markets.
Moscow raised the issue repeatedly during negotiations over the Black Sea Grain Initiative (BSGI) back in 2022, but Western governments maintained that Russian food and fertilizer exports were not directly sanctioned.
"The fertilizer story is quite old, and Russians were trying to push it long ago," a Ukrainian intelligence official told the Kyiv Independent.
"Russians always lobbied for fertilizer relief in contacts with Americans and Europeans," the official added. "They actually left BSGI because of no progress on fertilizers."
Russia withdrew from the Black Sea Grain Initiative in July 2023, saying insufficient progress had been made on its demands.
Ukrainian officials now fear Washington could be prepared to offer Moscow concessions on an issue it has pursued for years.
Trump announced the diesel deal on Oct. 9, saying Russia had agreed to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel to the U.S. and international markets.
"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The announcement raised questions in Washington about the deal's legality.
"We view the Russian diesel deal as illegal as per the 2022 law that had passed both chambers and was signed into law," one Senate official said.
Congress passed the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act in 2022, banning imports of Russian-origin energy products, including diesel.
Several people familiar with the matter said Democratic officials were contacting U.S. industries involved in facilitating the deal to ensure they understood the potential legal and investigative risks.
The deal could face further scrutiny in Congress . But as questions over its legality mount, Ukrainian officials fear Washington could seek other ways to offer Russia economic concessions , with fertilizers emerging as one possible area.
"Well, they clearly have some kind of plan," one official said.
Some Senate officials also believe the Trump administration overestimates the scale of the economic deals Russia could offer Washington in return.
The potential fertilizer deal remains unclear, and the officials who spoke to the Kyiv Independent named no specific sanctions Washington might lift.
The Kyiv Independent has contacted the White House for comment and will update the story when it receives a response.
The Ukrainian president has publicly warned that the diesel deal could be the start of a broader rollback of sanctions against Russia.
"There's intuition, there's intelligence, and there are various details," Zelensky said Oct. 16. "In my view, we cannot accept these agreements. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well."
The warning shows Kyiv's concern that Washington is shifting toward economic incentives for Moscow even as Russia continues its war against Ukraine.
Before the diesel announcement, Russian officials had repeatedly argued that Moscow and Washington should expand their business ties. The Trump administration, meanwhile, had maintained that economic deals should follow an end to Russia's war.
Ukrainian officials argue that offering concessions before securing a ceasefire is unlikely to persuade Putin to stop fighting. Instead, they say, such agreements could provide Russia with additional revenue while leaving Moscow's military objectives unchanged.
The concern is especially acute because, according to Ukrainian officials, Russia offered the U.S. nothing meaningful in return for the diesel deal.
"It's clear that this only encourages Putin ," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
"He feels that he can go with a war against us, and on top of that, our allies are lifting sanctions against him and striking deals with him."
Speaking to Russian media on Oct. 22, Putin once again made his intentions clear.
Asked whether he would agree to a ceasefire allowing Ukraine to retain the territory it controls, he replied: "It's not their territory; it's the territory of historical Russia."
