title: Ukrainian forces strike Oryol electronics plant, General Staff confirms, drone attacks shut down Moscow airports
description: Restrictions were placed on incoming and outgoing flights in Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports, Russian civilian aviation authority Rosaviatsiya reported.
content:
Ukraine forces struck an electronics plant in the Russian city of Oryol, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Oct. 24, while drones disrupted airspace over Moscow's airports on Oct. 23.
The General Staff confirmed the main production building of Proton-Electrotex in the city of Orel was hit, saying "This complicates the production of components for cruise and ballistic missiles, with which the enemy hits Ukrainian cities." On Oct. 23, Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ , reported that Ukrainian missiles struck an electronics plant in Oryol, around 160 kilometers (100 miles) from the Ukrainian border. Eyewitness footage from the scene appear to show large explosions and smoke billowing into the evening sky.
Oryol Oblast Governor Andrey Klychkov confirmed that an enterprise had been targeted, while independent Russian media outlet ASTRA, citing its open-source intelligence analysis, identified the facility as the Proton plant. The plant manufactures semiconductor devices, LEDs, and electronic components for industrial and specialized equipment that could be used in Russian weapons systems. The plant reportedly supplies parts for Russia's S-71 Kover cruise missiles, the 9M723 Iskander-M ballistic missiles, and the Pantsir-S1 air defense systems.
Local residents reported hearing at least four explosions, ASTRA said.
326 kilometers (202 miles) to the north, civilian flights at all four of Moscow's main airports were suspended on the afternoon of Oct. 23 amid a Ukrainian drone raid on the Russian capital, local authorities reported.
Restrictions on arriving and departing flights at Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports were announced by Russian civil aviation authority Rosaviatsiya at 2:05 p.m. local time.
At Sheremetyevo, Moscow's largest airport, an air alert was sounded, and waiting passengers were advised to take shelter.
Photos later emerged on social media that allegedly showed debris from a downed drone on the tarmac at Sheremetyevo.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the photos.
Open-source flight tracker FlightRadar24 reported 85 cancelled flights and a further 229 delayed at Sheremetyevo over the day.
According to Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin, 17 drones were shot down while heading toward the city on the afternoon of Oct. 23.
Ukraine had not commented on the reported attack as of the time of publication.
The all-clear was later sounded at Sheremetyevo Airport, Russian state news agency TASS reported at 5 p.m. local time.
An evacuation was also reported at the IQ-quarter skyscraper in the Moscow City business district, which houses offices of several Russian government ministries, including the Digital Development Ministry, Economic Development Ministry, and Industry and Trade Ministry.
Russian state news agency TASS later reported, citing emergency services, that the alarm had been false.
As Ukrainian long-range drones have reached deeper into Russian territory, temporary airport closures across Russia have become increasingly common during Moscow's full-scale war against Ukraine.
On Sept. 1, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned airlines, insurers, and foreign governments that Russian airspace "will be de facto closed" because of Ukrainian drones. Russian President Vladimir Putin responded by accusing Kyiv of "state terrorism," despite Russia's six days of attacks on Kyiv.
Ukraine does not threaten civil aviation, but carriers flying to Moscow , St. Petersburg, and other major hubs must factor in the risk posed by drones in Russian airspace, Zelensky said in an address posted to Telegram.
"Today we want to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace , every insurer, everyone who still uses key Russian airports — Russian skies are becoming completely dangerous," he said.
"Although the Russian authorities do not report this as it should, the Russian sky will de facto be closed," he added.

title: Civilian cargo ship sinks off coast of Romania after Russian drone strike, authorities say
description: One person was confirmed dead and three others were missing from the 13-member crew, according to Romanian President Nicusor Dan.
content:
Editor's note: An earlier version of this article said the ship was sailing under the flag of the Cayman Islands. This information has since been corrected
A civilian cargo ship sank after being struck by a Russian drone near Romania's Black Sea coast on Oct. 23, Romanian authorities reported.
The attack is the latest in a series of brazen Russian strikes on civilian shipping in the Black Sea, part of a broader escalation in Russia's economic warfare against Ukraine this year.
The ship, Khoryv, was sailing from Turkey under the flag of the Comoros and was crewed by Ukrainian and Azerbaijani nationals.
According to Romanian President Nicusor Dan, one person was confirmed dead and three others were missing from the 14-member crew.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry later confirmed that a Ukrainian crew member on board the Khoryv was killed. Four other Ukrainian nationals, including the ship's captain, were hospitalized, while two Ukrainian crew members did not require medical assistance.
The ministry said the vessel had sunk near the Romanian city of Constanta with 14 crew members on board. According to preliminary information, a drone strike may have caused the sinking.
Ukraine's Embassy in Romania is working to establish the circumstances of the incident, as well as the whereabouts and condition of the rescued Ukrainian nationals, while remaining in contact with Romanian authorities, the ministry said.
"This attack is a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine," Dan wrote on social media .
"It is time for Russia to take the peace initiatives proposed by the United States and Europe seriously, accept the ceasefire proposals and end the war."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attack , describing it as another Russian escalation in the Black Sea.
"These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law," von der Leyen wrote on X.
Romania's Interior Ministry later confirmed that nine crew members had been rescued, publishing a video showing the keel of the overturned ship barely protruding above the water's surface.
In response to a series of attacks on civilian shipping, NATO plans to increase its military presence in the Black Sea by deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones.
The announcement came after NATO's main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, met at the alliance's headquarters in Brussels on Oct. 20 to discuss security in the Black Sea.

title: Ukraine confirms Oleshky ceasefire mediated by Melania Trump between Russia, Ukraine
description: The move comes amid increased attention to the worsening humanitarian crisis in the city, which over the past weeks has gained international attention, including from Pope Leo XIV.
content:
Editor's note: This story is being updated.
U.S. First Lady Melania Trump has mediated a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in and around the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast to allow the safe evacuation of civilians and delivery of humanitarian aid, Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on Oct. 23.
The move comes amid increased attention to the worsening humanitarian crisis in the city, which over the past weeks has gained international attention, including from Pope Leo XIV.
According to the press release from the White House press service, the First Lady "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary."
The ceasefire is scheduled to begin on 3:00 a.m. on October 27th, Kyiv time, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
Lubinets, confirmed the agreement in a video statement on Telegram later on Oct. 23.
"I personally thank Melania Trump and her team for their efforts, leadership, and coordination between the two negotiating groups of Ukraine and the Russian Federation in reaching agreements," Lubinets said.
Under the agreement, a ceasefire will be put in place, humanitarian cargo will be delivered to Oleshky, and civilians will be allowed to leave the city freely, according to Lubinets.
"The operation will take place gradually. It is extremely difficult to implement," he said. He will keep the Ukrainian public informed and show the results of the operation, he said. He also asked the public to be careful about spreading information on the mission.
Lubinets added that he had led the negotiations on the Ukrainian side and that Russia's human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, had led them on the Russian side.
Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 23 that Ukrainian forces would implement the decisions of the country's commander-in-chief to facilitate the humanitarian mission in Oleshky.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov also welcomed Melania Trump's role, saying she had "made a significant contribution to agreeing on the humanitarian operation" in Oleshky, Russian pro-Kremlin media outlet Ura.ru reported. Peskov said the sides are working to agree on a ceasefire in the area so that residents can be evacuated.
State-aligned Russian media RBK reported Russia's General Staff had announced a ceasefire from 04:00 a.m. local time on Oct. 27, citing Valeriy Gerasimov, Chief of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces.
Gerasimov added that to ensure the safety of people and the delivery of vital supplies, engineering reconnaissance will be conducted.
Oleshky , located just across the Dnipro River from Kherson , has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces in the area, who prevent humanitarian aid from entering. Civilians attempting to flee via the only roads in and out of the city are frequently targeted by drones.
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," Melania Trump was quoted as saying in the press release.
"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."
According to the document, an "impartial American media organization" will visit the area to document the work of both sides in the area.
Later in the day, Ukrainian lawmaker David Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People faction and close associate of President Zelensky, said that the "process of unblocking the city of Oleshky and its outskirts will begin very soon."
"To achieve this goal, a ceasefire will be achieved in the near future, as announced by the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump," Arakhamiia wrote on Telegram.
"This has been a long process, in which many people at different political levels have participated. We would like to especially note the role of the Pope and the First Lady of the United States, Melania Trump."
While several localized and temporary "ceasefires" have been announced throughout the course of the war, their implementation and enforcement on the ground has been patchy at best.
"I, like all of us, am hoping that people will be saved, preferably all who want to, and not just those who have time. But I am wary that there will be provocations, blackmail, a route through the Russian Federation (which many people will not agree to), and PR for those who manage to get out," said Stefan Vorontsov, a volunteer coordinator with the NGO Humanity, which helps evacuate civilians from occupied territories, to the Kyiv Independent.
"God willing, we will be able to set a precedent where Russia admits what they did in the occupied territories, and we will be able to organize the first official evacuation from there, then maybe the rest of us will be able to do it too. But again, I have little faith."
Even if the reported ceasefire agreement is upheld by both sides, the nature of the situation in Oleshky means actually carrying out evacuations on the ground will still be particularly challenging.
"I don't think anything (about the news), people were abandoned and no one is going to save them," said a woman from Oleshky, who declined to reveal her name for security reasons, to the Kyiv Independent.
"There is no food delivery there because all the roads are mined, the orcs (Russians) are eating our dogs because they are hungry themselves. In order to bring a bus there, all the roads need to be demined, and there is no one there to do it"
The intervention of the White House in the situation in Oleshky comes at a time of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington, after the Trump administration agreed to waive sanctions on Russia and buy Russian diesel fuel, while the artificial throttling of Starlink terminals on Ukrainian drones continues.
On Oct. 13, U.S. President Donald Trump unilaterally announced an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine, which soon turned out not to exist in practice.
Yuliia Taradiuk contributed to reporting.

title: Ukrainian media identifies Russian officers responsible for blockade, starvation of occupied Oleshky
description: Ukrainian media outlet Slidstvo.info established the presence of the 217th Guards Airborne Regiment, together with its commander, Georgy Yanchev.
content:
An investigation by Ukrainian media outlet Slidstvo.info published on Oct. 23 has uncovered the identities of Russian officers involved in the blockade of the city of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast.
The Russian-occupied city, located just across the Dnipro River from Kherson , has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces in the area, who prevent humanitarian aid from entering. Civilians attempting to flee via the only roads in and out of the city are frequently targeted by drones.
Building on a previous investigation published in late September that identified the commanders of the Russian 126th Coast Guard Brigade of the Black Sea Fleet and the 331st Guards Airborne Regiment as operating in the area, Slidstvo.info established the presence of the 217th Guards Airborne Regiment and its commander, Georgy Yanchev.
According to the Oct. 23 investigation , the 217th Regiment previously took part in the Battle of Kyiv at the outset of Russia's full-scale invasion and later fought in Chasiv Yar, one of the main hotspots of fighting in Donetsk Oblast.
Yanchev, who has served in the Russian military since 1993 and holds the rank of colonel, has three children who live in the central Russian city of Samara.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
As the humanitarian crisis in the city has grown increasingly severe this autumn, international pressure to provide assistance to the remaining residents trapped inside has mounted.
On Oct. 16, Pope Leo XIV expressed concern over the worsening situation in Oleshky during a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The pope called for a local ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the safe evacuation of civilians from the front-line city, where around 2,000 residents remain trapped amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
Ukraine and Russia are nearing an agreement on the final details of civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 18.
In the meantime, Ukrainian soldiers fighting on the western bank of the Dnipro have made repeated deliveries of food aid to the area by drone.

title: 270 Ukrainians return home from Russian captivity in latest swap
description: The exchange, the first in two months, also saw 270 Russian prisoners of war returned to Russia from Ukrainian captivity.
content:
Editor's note: The story initially reported that five people previously believed to have been killed in the 2022 Olenivka prison massacre had returned to Ukraine. However, President Volodymyr Zelensky's social media post was later edited to clarify that those who returned were survivors of the terrorist attack.
Ukraine and Russia exchanged prisoners of war on Oct. 23, with 261 Ukrainian service members and nine civilians returning home, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced .
The exchange, the first in two months, also saw 270 Russian prisoners of war returned to Russia from Ukrainian captivity.
According to Zelensky, most of the Ukrainians returning home had been captured during the Siege of Mariupol in spring 2022. They included service members from the Ground Forces, Navy, and Air Assault Forces, as well as border guards and fighters from the Azov regiment, which led the city's defense.
Five of the released POWs survived the Olenivka prison massacre in July 2022, when a thermobaric munition was detonated inside a prison barracks housing Ukrainian prisoners of war.
According to Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War, a "significant portion" of the released prisoners had been found guilty on sham criminal charges while in Russian captivity.
Seven Ukrainian civilians were also brought back from Russia with the help of Ukrainian authorities on Oct. 23, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said in a Facebook post. Lubinets added that another seven civilians had traveled to Russia as part of family reunification efforts supported by the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC).
Zelensky, as well as the Coordination Headquarters later said that nine civilians had been released.
Lubinets called the prisoner exchange "historic," saying it brought home the largest number of convicted Ukrainian service members since 2022: 86 convicted soldiers and one person who had been facing criminal prosecution.
Ukraine, international human rights organizations, and the U.N. have described such trials in Russia as war crimes. The Third Geneva Convention grants POWs protected status under international humanitarian law and prohibits prosecuting them solely for their participation in hostilities, subject to the rules governing lawful combatant conduct.
Lubinets added that the exchange marked the return of Azov Regiment service members for the first time "in a long while."
Two of those released had been held in Russian captivity since 2018 and 2020, spending eight and six years in captivity, respectively, Lubinets said.
The youngest released POW was 24, while the oldest was 63, he added.
Ukraine's Interior minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said that among the returned prisoners were a father and son, both called Volodymyr, both in Ukraine's National Border Guard, that were taken prisoner in Mariupol's Azovstal and saw each other for the first time in four years.
"Today is full of heartbreaking footage: hugs, calls to relatives and joy from the fact that you can hold the Ukrainian flag in your hands again," he said.
While intermittent U.S.-mediated "peace talks" between Russia and Ukraine have failed to secure even a partial ceasefire, prisoner exchanges remain one of the few channels of regular cooperation between Moscow and Kyiv.
The latest swap was the 11th reported prisoner exchange of 2026. The previous two exchanges took place in August.

title: Ukraine receives 50,000 rounds of ammunition for F-16 cannons from Denmark
description: First delivered to Ukraine in 2024, the U.S.-made jets have become a key part of the country's defenses against Russian attacks on its rear areas, particularly jet-powered drones.
content:
Denmark has delivered 50,000 rounds of 20 mm ammunition for the autocannons on Ukraine's F-16 fighter jets, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said on Oct. 23.
First delivered to Ukraine in 2024, the U.S.-made jets have become a key part of the country's defenses against Russian attacks on its rear areas, particularly jet-powered drones.
"Ukrainian pilots are already using them to intercept jet-powered attack drones," the ministry said on social media .
"We are grateful to Denmark for its quick and efficient response to our request for additional ammunition."
In addition to mounting points for various air-to-air and air-to-ground missiles, F-16 fighter jets are equipped with 20 mm M61 Vulcan rotary cannons designed for close-range engagements.
While missiles are often used to shoot down Russian cruise missiles during mass attacks, the cheaper autocannon ammunition is frequently used against Russian jet-powered drones, which are too fast for most Ukrainian interceptor drones to intercept.
On Sept. 30, Bloomberg reported that Kyiv was seeking to procure additional 20 mm rounds for its F-16s, with sources saying an average of 150 rounds was required per interception.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 5 that Ukraine was "scouring munitions for F-16s virtually all over the world." Zelensky also praised the jets as one of the most effective means of countering jet-powered drones.
Denmark, the Netherlands, Belgium, and Norway have collectively supplied Ukraine with around 50 F-16 fighter jets.
Intensive use in defending Ukrainian airspace means the jets require frequent maintenance, which can currently be carried out only by Kyiv's partners.

title: Analysis: Ukraine’s Starshield access is still crippled, and no one is taking the blame
description:
Eleven days after Ukraine's Starshield terminals started mysteriously malfunctioning, there is still nobody in Washington who wants to take responsibility, while Trump administration officials continue pointing fingers firmly at SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.

The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that U.S. President Donald Trump had ordered Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals, claiming Trump was "frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 100 mi
content:
Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla, SpaceX, and X, attends a press briefing held by U.S. President Donald Trump in Washington, D.C., U.S., on Sept. 29, 2026. (Finn Gomez / Getty Images)
Eleven days after Ukraine's Starshield terminals started mysteriously malfunctioning, there is still nobody in Washington who wants to take responsibility, while Trump administration officials continue pointing fingers firmly at SpaceX CEO Elon Musk.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Oct. 23 that U.S. President Donald Trump had ordered Musk on Oct. 21 to lift the restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield terminals, claiming Trump was "frustrated the system's speeds remained capped at around 100 miles an hour", another indication that the SpaceX CEO has far more control over the military version of the Starlink satellite internet service than previously believed.
In remarks to reporters, Trump refused to confirm or deny ordering Musk to restore Ukraine's service, but claimed Musk had made the change. "Whether I called or whether somebody else called, doesn’t make any difference," Trump said.
"The bottom line, he put it back," he said.
Ukraine's Starshield terminals were still experiencing severe problems on Oct. 23, multiple Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent, raising questions as to whether the U.S. government is actually in control of a piece of vital national security infrastructure, or whether, as multiple American government officials have claimed, control ultimately rests with Musk and SpaceX.
"Overall, there's no change anywhere ," a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent, when asked about whether Trump's intervention with Musk had solved the problems with Starshield.
"Starshield still doesn't work," a Ukrainian intelligence official confirmed to the Kyiv Independent. According to multiple military sources, the unpredictable "speed limit" that caps a terminal's speed at 160 kph — and in many cases, at much slower speeds — is still in place, severely hampering Ukrainian drone operations.
Ukraine uses Starshield terminals to control interceptor drones that counter Russia's jet-powered Geran drones, which Moscow has been using as part of a renewed terror-bombing campaign aimed at Ukrainian civilians and civilian infrastructure.
They are also used to control middle-range strike and logistics drones that are crucial for day-to-day operations on the front line. Despite popular misconceptions, they play no part in Ukraine's deep-strike campaign against Russian oil refineries.
"As of this morning, instances of connectivity loss at speeds of 161 km/h are still being observed. There is currently no confirmation that these restrictions have been lifted," a source in the Ukrainian Defense Ministry told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 23.
In an interview with Fox News on Oct. 21, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed he had been communicating with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio to try to fix the issues. "Regarding Starlink and Starshield: they are still restricted, but the secretary of state told me that he will work with his team to unblock this issue," Zelensky said.
Despite Ukrainian and U.S. officials apparently engaging in discussions to resolve the disruption to Ukrainian communications, nobody publicly has taken credit — or blame — for making or implementing the decision, which is not only politically "toxic " but also could have severe negative commercial implications for SpaceX, the operator of Starshield and Starlink.
Reporting in The Telegraph and the Wall Street Journal placed blame squarely on Musk's shoulders. Citing four sources familiar with the events, the Telegraph was the first to report that Musk was ultimately responsible, claiming Musk suggested restricting Ukrainian Starshield terminals to Trump, who "agreed" with the SpaceX CEO's suggestion.
Citing "U.S. officials and people familiar with the matter," the Wall Street Journal also reported that Musk ordered the slowdown, potentially after discussing it with Trump. But after the disruption became public, the White House refused a coordinated messaging strategy — leading to various figures in Washington pointing fingers at each other, as the political toxicity and potential legal consequences of helping Russia kill Ukrainian civilians by hobbling Ukrainian defenses became clear.
Musk himself attempted to shift responsibility to the Pentagon and the Trump administration for the slowdown, in a carefully crafted reply to former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov in which he didn't explicitly rule out his involvement in the affair. "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government," Musk said. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS."
Reuters reported that the order to restrict Starshield originated inside the White House and was relayed to Defense Department leaders, citing two U.S. officials and a Western official briefed on the matter.
Ukraine's embassy in Washington had attempted to get answers from both the Department of Defense and SpaceX, one Ukrainian government official told the Kyiv Independent, including high-level corporate contacts at SpaceX they had previously enjoyed a good relationship with, but were greeted with a wall of silence.
A number of sources familiar with the events previously told the Kyiv Independent they believed SpaceX and Musk were ultimately responsible for the restricting of Ukraine's Starshield, something which one source referred to as a "commercial decision."
Asked by journalists outside the White House on Oct. 19 who was responsible, Trump claimed ignorance: "I don't know who it was, but I'd like to find out," he said, appearing unconcerned about the unexplained malfunction in a critical piece of American national security infrastructure.
Other senior figures in the administration also denied responsibility and attempted to point the finger toward SpaceX, and ultimately, Musk.
Asked by journalists whether the administration was responsible for the problems with Starshield, U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth claimed the administration had not "pulled anything back." and indicated any change had come from SpaceX. "There are terms of service that ultimately need to be complied with, and that's where Starlink has the option to make those decisions," Hegseth said. "But nothing's changed from our view. We haven't made any directives or anything like that.
In a response to journalists, Rubio appeared to claim that SpaceX had the ability to modify Starshield's operation independently of the Pentagon, contradicting Musk’s claim that Starshield limits are controlled by the U.S. government.
"The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr. Musk. That's a private company," Rubio said in comments to journalists during his recent trip to India. "We don't control what a private company… how they decide their product can be used," he said.
Earlier in the week, Rubio inaccurately claimed that Ukraine had never had access to Starshield. "Starshield is a defense product, a military product," Rubio said. "It's not, at this moment, available to Ukraine, and that's under conversation," he said. "I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield. They do not have Starshield now," Rubio continued.
Despite Rubio's claims, Ukraine has operated Starshield since 2024, as contemporary reporting made clear. Ukraine was initially given access to 500 Starshield terminals under a pilot program, Bloomberg reported in 2024. By the end of 2024, two separate Pentagon contracts with SpaceX were providing 3,000 terminals of the militarized version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system.
American ambassador to NATO Matt Whitaker also attempted to shift the blame toward SpaceX and away from the administration. "They are a private company," Whitaker said in an interview with Fox News on Oct. 21. "Obviously they have terms of use that are applied to all of their customers, including the Ukrainians. I think it is more of a dispute along those lines than anybody in this administration trying to change how Starshield or Starlink is used," he said .
Rushton is a British journalist and security and foreign policy analyst based in Kyiv. He has covered Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine since February 2022, writing about every aspect of the conflict. His work has appeared in Yahoo News, New Lines Magazine, and The Telegraph, amongst others.

title: Austria expels 4 Russian diplomats, Moscow vows response
description: Three members of the Russian Embassy, as well as a Russian delegate at the OSCE responsible for military security and arms control, "carried out activities incompatible with their diplomatic status," Austria's Foreign Ministry said.
content:
Austria is expelling four Russian diplomats for security reasons, the Austrian Foreign Ministry said on Oct. 23, as reported by the DPA news agency.
Three members of the Russian Embassy, as well as a Russian delegate at the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) responsible for military security and arms control, "carried out activities incompatible with their diplomatic status," the ministry said.
Vienna hosts major international institutions like the OSCE or U.N. agencies, making it a popular target of Russian spies.
With the latest step, Austria has expelled 18 Russian diplomats since 2020. Other European countries have taken similar measures due to growing concerns about Russian espionage amid the full-scale war in Ukraine.
Russia's Foreign Ministry warned that an "inevitable" response will follow, according to the Russian state news agency TASS.
Austria previously expelled three staff members of the Russian Embassy in May over suspected signals intelligence activities in the EU country's capital.
Although neutral, Austria has joined international and EU sanctions against Russia while providing financial and humanitarian aid to Kyiv.

title: Energy facilities across Ukraine targeted as Russian attacks kill at least 8, injure 67 over past day
description: Ukrainian private energy company DTEK said one of its thermal power plants had halted generation following a Russian attack.
content:
Russian attacks killed eight civilians and wounded 67 across Ukraine over the past day, as strikes on the country's energy infrastructure triggered emergency power outages on Oct. 23, local authorities said.
Power cuts were reported in Zhytomyr, Donetsk , Khmelnytskyi, Volyn, Kharkiv, Poltava, Rivne, and Mykolaiv oblasts, state grid operator Ukrenergo said, adding that energy workers were already working to restore damaged facilities.
Ukrainian private energy company DTEK said one of its thermal power plants had halted generation following a Russian attack. The company did not disclose the plant's location.
The attacks come as Ukraine braces for what could be its most difficult winter since Russia launched its full-scale invasion, with Moscow continuing to target power generation and other critical infrastructure.
According to Ukraine's Air Force , Russia launched 176 long-range drones at Ukraine overnight, including 92 jet-powered drones. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 140 drones, including 68 jet-powered ones.
Drone impacts were recorded at 19 locations, while falling debris was reported at another 13, the Air Force said.
Elsewhere across Ukraine, a total of eight civilians were killed and another 67 wounded in Russian attacks, according to regional authorities.
In Kharkiv Oblast, three civilians were killed and a total of 46 injured, the majority coming from an attack on a market in the city of Lozova in the southeastern corner of the region, according to governor Oleh Syniehubov.
Three people were killed and one injured in attacks on Zaporizhzhia Oblast, according to regional authorities , as 940 Russian attacks of various kinds were reported in 46 settlements.
Russian attacks killed two civilians and injured nine more in front-line Donetsk Oblast, said oblast governor Vadym Filashkin.
Six people were injured in three separate Russian attacks on Sumy Oblast, including on the capital Sumy, the regional administration said.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , two people were injured in Russian attacks: a 44-year-old man in the Nikopol area, and a 26-year-old woman in the Shakhtarsk area, near the front line.
Two people were injured, including a child, in Russian attacks across the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast, regional authorities said.
A 51-year-old man was injured in a Russian attack in the Bashtanka District of Mykolaiv Oblast, Governor Heorhii Reshetilov reported .

title: First tanker with Russian diesel under Trump deal heads to US, Reuters reports
description: The tanker Agioi Fanendes is delivering the first cargo as part of a deal announced by U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 9 to purchase Russian diesel.
content:
A Malta-flagged tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of Russian diesel is en route to New York, expected to arrive early next month, Reuters reported on Oct. 23, citing LSEG data.
The tanker Agioi Fanendes is delivering the first cargo as part of a deal announced by U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 9 to purchase Russian diesel, a step he claims will help push down fuel prices.
The ship loaded its cargo in the Russian Baltic port of Primorsk on Oct. 22 and is set to arrive in the U.S. on Nov. 7, according to Reuters .
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak announced on Oct. 21 that the first tanker carrying 40,000 metric tons of diesel would soon depart for the U.S. , with additional shipments to follow.
According to Trump, Russia would "immediately supply over 300,000" metric tons of diesel fuel to U.S. and global markets, 500,000 metric tons in November, and 1 million metric tons "immediately thereafter."
Soon after the announcement, Moscow partially lifted restrictions on its diesel exports, permitting the sale of 500,000 metric tons.
The deal has been broadly lambasted by Kyiv, its European allies, and U.S. lawmakers, who argue it will provide little relief to U.S. consumers while helping to fund Moscow's war machine in Ukraine.
The agreement was followed by a sharp deterioration in Ukraine-U.S. ties, with Kyiv facing restrictions on Starlink operations and allegedly deliberate delays in shipments of Patriot interceptors.
Trump has also sharpened his rhetoric toward President Volodymyr Zelensky, claiming the Ukrainian leader is not interested in ending the war and should be replaced.

title: US Senator Blumenthal opens probe into Ukraine Starshield restrictions
description: "This decision to limit critical technology for a key ally... (puts) Ukrainian forces at risk and their people in peril," Senator Richard Blumenthal wrote in a letter addressed to U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
content:
U.S. Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal said on Oct. 22 he had launched an inquiry into sudden restrictions of Starshield satellite services in Ukraine that hampered the country's ability to intercept Russian drones.
Starshield is the militarized version of the Starlink system, operated by Elon Musk 's SpaceX company and widely used by the Ukrainian military.
Kyiv said that overnight on Oct. 14, SpaceX implemented restrictions on Starshield operations in Ukraine, capping its speed limit at 161 kilometers per hour (kph) and curbing Ukrainian interceptors' ability to down Russian jet-powered drones.
"This decision to limit critical technology for a key ally... (puts) Ukrainian forces at risk and their people in peril," Blumenthal wrote in a letter addressed to U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The move also "raises serious questions about who controls critical capabilities the U.S. government has spent billions of dollars to procure," the senator continued.
Neither Musk nor the Trump administration publicly claimed responsibility for the slowdown, but the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on Oct. 21 that the order came from the SpaceX founder.
The outlet separately wrote a day later that Trump called Musk to lift the restrictions. However, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the 161 kph limit is still in place.
Blumenthal, who sits on the Senate's Subcommittee on Investigations, asked the Pentagon to clarify who ordered the restrictions and to provide information on the U.S. military's own reliance on Starlink.
The pro-Ukraine lawmaker also stressed that the reports "raise further questions about the respective roles of (the Pentagon), the White House, and SpaceX in controlling and modifying the service."
"If the Pentagon cannot say plainly who has the authority to degrade a military communications network, our partners cannot rely on it, and our adversaries will look for ways to exploit that uncertainty."
Blumenthal asked Hegseth to provide information by Nov. 5. As the Democrats lack a majority in the Senate, they do not hold the subpoena power.
The Democratic Party aims to wrest control of both chambers of Congress from the Republicans during the upcoming midterm elections on Nov. 3.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,574,620 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,830 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,574,620 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 23.
The number includes 1,830 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,439 tanks, 25,597 armored combat vehicles, 166,088 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,501 artillery systems, 2,230 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,720 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 3,003 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Analysis: Ukraine, Russia set stage for climax of Battle of Donbas
description:
This autumn, as Russia escalated its total-war-style strike campaign against Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and economy, and relations between Kyiv and Washington hit an all-time low, the daily battles along Ukraine’s vast battlefield have faded into the background of the information space.

Despite the reduced attention in international media — often spawning misleading perceptions that both sides are bogged down in some kind of stalemate — the attritional fighting in Ukraine’s east remains
content:
Ukrainian soldiers "Mahura" and "Hrek" of the 47th Separate Mechanized Brigade return to their battalion command post after visiting forward infantry positions near the Russian border in Sumy Oblast, Ukraine, on Aug. 28, 2026. (Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images)
This autumn, as Russia escalated its total-war-style strike campaign against Ukraine’s critical infrastructure and economy, and relations between Kyiv and Washington hit an all-time low , the daily battles along Ukraine’s vast battlefield have faded into the background of the information space.
Despite the reduced attention in international media — often spawning misleading perceptions that both sides are bogged down in some kind of stalemate — the attritional fighting in Ukraine’s east remains as intense and brutal as ever, with both sides looking to establish a clear upper hand going into winter.
In simple terms of territory taken and lost, 2026 has been a year of relative success for Kyiv on the front line.
Net Russian territorial gains have largely flatlined despite consistently heavy casualties, while Ukrainian forces also managed to conduct two successful counterattacking operations, each carrying strategic importance.
Though other parts of the front line have largely stabilized, Russia’s main goal continues to be the capture of the remainder of Donetsk Oblast.
Slowly but surely, Russian forces inched closer to the gates of the last remaining Ukrainian cities in the region, largely driving out what was left of any normal civilian life in the area.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s defending forces, reorganized under a new command structure, have looked to create the conditions to grind down and stop whatever offensive power Russia can muster in its tracks.
With the Trump administration tightening the screws on Kyiv, while Moscow refuses to budge on its demand that Ukraine hand over the rest of Donetsk Oblast as a bare minimum for ceasefire discussions, the strategic and political weight of this slowly shrinking and increasingly ruined patch of land is as great as ever.
Since the full-scale invasion, the backbone of Ukraine’s defense of Donetsk Oblast has been the so-called fortress belt, made up of four industrial cities running north to south: Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka.
For about a year, all of these cities have been within range of Russian first-person-view (FPV) drones.
But over 2026, incremental advances on the ground, combined with improved technology extending the range of these drones, have made Ukrainian logistics anywhere in the area noticeably more difficult while also driving many of the remaining civilians out from their homes.
Since the Ukrainian army’s corps reform last year, the direct approach to the fortress belt has been defended by two army corps: the 11th and 19th.
Over May and June, while Ukraine was riding the high of successive positive developments in the war, Russian forces entered and overran much of Kostiantynivka , following a model of mass infiltration backed by heavy support from drones, artillery, and glide bombs that was used to take Pokrovsk last year.
Simultaneously to their frontal attacks, Russian forces have attempted to achieve a double envelopment of the fortress belt, with two large pincers pushing north and south of the fortress belt, respectively.
The northern pincer, bearing down on the liberated city of Lyman, was famously the site of Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi: a slow but ingenious series of counterattacks conducted by the country’s 3rd Army Corps under commander Andrii Biletskyi.
On the southern flank, Russia has concentrated immense offensive pressure for over a year on the mining city of Dobropillia.
After a mass infiltration of Russian soldiers in August 2025 pushed up to 20 kilometers deep behind Ukrainian lines, Kyiv redeployed the 1st Azov Corps of the National Guard, commanded by Denys Prokopenko, leader of the Mariupol garrison, to the area, where it stands to this day.
After years of brutal fighting across the front line, the defense of any area is often only as good as its weakest point.
With Russian forces learning to aggressively target potential weak links in Ukraine’s overstretched defense, raising the base level of Ukraine’s brigades has been just as important as the placement of more elite units.
While the 1st and 3rd Corps were able to gather their units in a coherent sector and lead the fight as a truly unified formation, other corps like the 11th and 19th, commanding a mixed bag of exhausted and inexperienced brigades without extra resources and assigned units, struggled.
To rectify this, in August, under new Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi, Kyiv decided to divide the defense of Donbas between two newly formed task forces, built up by Biletskyi and Prokopenko from the staff of their respective corps.
Task Force Azov would expand west, covering the frontage recently vacated by the 7th Air Assault Corps, while Biletskyi took the 11th and 19th Corps — and with them most of the fortress belt — under his wing with a new Task Force Center.
The most strategically important part of the front line was now being led directly by the military’s two most high-profile field commanders.
Operation Vivaldi was already well underway when Andrii Biletskyi was given command of the defense of the fortress belt.
His 3rd Corps was probably the best example of success in Ukraine’s corps reform , bringing up other mechanized brigades to elite standards of training and command, despite a dire manpower shortage.
Now, the general has been given the challenge of doing something similar with the brigades of the 11th and 19th Corps, some of which have been fighting high-intensity battles in their sector for years without rotation.
Over autumn, Russia’s attempts to push and probe through the hilly terrain immediately east of the fortress belt have gotten bogged down, while even Kostiantynivka — which looked likely to fall by the end of summer — is still hanging on.
The brigades fighting in this area have their work cut out for them, facing daily Russian infiltrations, a kill zone that only gets deeper and deadlier with time, and very thin, if not empty, infantry ranks.
But none of these are new problems, and over time, even with limited resources, the brigades have adapted.
All logistics to infantry positions in this area are handled by heavy bomber drones, while the revolution in unmanned ground vehicles has been key to keeping Ukrainian drone teams supplied.
Inside Kostiantynivka, the difficulty that Ukraine has had over the past year defending cities against Russian infiltrators has been turned on its head, thanks to the dogged heroism of Ukrainian infantrymen still in the city.
By now, control of one neighbourhood or another is almost impossible to accurately portray, as the positions of Ukrainian and Russian soldiers in the residential and industrial areas of Kostiantynivka heavily overlap.
While Russian forces try to push onwards towards Druzhkivka, Ukrainian troops remain entrenched in the city center of Kostiantynivka, and even on the eastern outskirts, occasionally moving around and rotating, and making it difficult for Russia to deploy its drone teams in the city.
Many of these men have been inside the city for the better part of this year and have little prospect of being evacuated if wounded.
But nonetheless, they hold on, buying Ukraine precious time to prepare the defense of the next fortress.
It is on the southwestern flank of the fortress belt, around the city of Dobropillia, where Russia’s most intense offensive continues.
Unlike the north of Donetsk Oblast, where the Siverskyi Donets River provides a natural defensive barrier, advancing in the Dobropillia area would give Russian forces a direct back door into the fortress belt.
According to Prokopenko , Russia enjoys a six to one personnel advantage in the Dobropillia area, and has deployed a third of its elite Rubicon drone unit — around 400 teams — in the narrow sector.
For the past year, the mining city of Dobropillia has provided shelter for much of the 1st Corps’ work, including many of the drone teams stopping Russian forces approaching the outskirts of the city.
But this convenience has also made Dobropillia a particular target for Russian glide bombs , launched in groups of three or four indiscriminately, but with a real chance of burying a Ukrainian drone team with every direct hit on a building.
On the ground, although a spectacular and well-coordinated attempt at a mechanized assault in summer failed, Russian forces, through sheer strength of numbers, have been slowly saturating the area around Dobropillia with small infiltration groups.
This process gained pace over autumn, and in the last few months, more videos have emerged of Russian soldiers raising flags in the city, though they are often quickly eliminated and do not indicate any certainty of territorial control.
But that nuance clearly hasn’t reached Moscow, as the Russian defense ministry claimed in October that the city had already been captured completely, a statement quickly denied by Kyiv.
A video released on October 21 by the Azov Corps argues that Russia’s increasingly outlandish claims about capturing Dobropillia are a direct result of the same culture of lies in the Russian high command chain — much the same as what helped facilitate the success of Operation Vivaldi for the Third Corps.
As well as Ukraine can organize its defense of Donbas, much in the coming half-year will depend on Russian plans and resources.
The coming weeks and autumn weather are likely to provide the last favorable conditions for Russian infiltration for the rest of the year.
If, under cover of fog and rain they can entrench themselves in and around Dobropillia before winter, Ukraine will have a lot more trouble smoking them out.
Another challenge is the looming prospect of Russian forced mobilization , which some Ukrainian commanders have argued has already started, just without a public announcement.
With a new flow of hundreds of thousands of bodies to augment those already voluntarily signing contracts, Russia could have more options, whether that means further increasing the intensity of its offensive in Donbas or attacking somewhere else and creating major strategic dilemmas for the Ukrainian defense.
Crucial could also prove to be the future of Ukraine’s ability to use Starlink , something now in the hands of Elon Musk and Donald Trump, two men who have shown consistent contempt for Ukraine’s fight for survival.
Both the 1st and 3rd Corps have made extensive use of middle-strike capabilities in offensive and defensive operations over the last year, not to mention the work of top brigades of the Unmanned Systems Forces in the area.
If Starlink is further restricted in one way or another, Ukraine’s forces and their drone-based defense could be severely hampered in their ability to spot and destroy advancing Russian troops in good time.
With that, Ukraine’s strongest card, a solid defense along the front line and a strong military uninterested in capitulation, could itself be further undermined by those who believe Ukraine has no cards.
Hi, this is Francis Farrell, the author of this piece. We are entering a new phase of the war, where once again the daily, brutal fight on the front line to hold Russia back is drowned out by geopolitical noise. Despite the difficult winter ahead of us and the effect that will have on the work of our newsroom, we will continue to report from the field wherever necessary. If you want to help us do that, please consider supporting our journalism by becoming a member.
Francis Farrell is a senior reporter at the Kyiv Independent. He is the co-author of War Notes, the Kyiv Independent's weekly newsletter about the war. For the second year in a row, the Kyiv Independent received a grant from the Charles Douglas-Home Memorial Trust to support his front-line reporting for the year 2025-2026. Francis won the Prix Bayeux Calvados-Normandy for war correspondents in the young reporter category in 2023, and was nominated for the European Press Prize in 2024. Francis speaks Ukrainian and Hungarian and is an alumnus of Leiden University in The Hague and University College London. He has previously worked as a managing editor at the online media project Lossi 36, as a freelance journalist and documentary photographer, and at the OSCE and Council of Europe field missions in Albania and Ukraine.

title: Russian drone attack injures 9 people, including 2 children
description: "Russia continues its deliberate terror against the peaceful Zhytomyr Oblast," regional Governor Vitalii Bunechko wrote on Telegram.
content:
A Russian drone struck a residential home in Zhytomyr Oblast on Oct. 22, injuring nine people, including two children, local officials said.
"Russia continues its deliberate terror against the peaceful Zhytomyr Oblast," regional Governor Vitalii Bunechko wrote on Telegram.
Two of the injured had been taken to hospital, Bunechko added. The full extent of the injuries sustained was not immediately clear.
Zhytomyr is a city in northwestern Ukraine home to over 200,000 people. The city's energy facilities have been under repeated Russian attacks in recent weeks.
While Russia has repeatedly struck Ukrainian energy facilities, it has ramped up its attacks on energy infrastructure in recent weeks ahead of the winter months. Strikes on energy facilities earlier this month left hundreds of thousands of citizens in Kyiv and front-line cities with repeated energy and water outages.
Elsewhere across Ukraine overnight into Oct. 23, explosions were heard in northwestern Ukrainian city of Lutsk, local media outlets reported. Explosions could also be heard when a drone crashed in Poltava Oblast, Vitalii Diakivnych, the head of the Poltava Oblast Military Administration, wrote on Telegram. Although the blast damaged private homes, buildings, and a power line, no people were injured according to preliminary reports.
While in Sumy Oblast, a "massive attack" of Russian drones hit civilian infrastructure facilities overnight injuring two, according to Sumy Governor Oleg Grigorov .

title: Russian disinformation campaign targets pro-Ukraine candidates ahead of midterms, lawmakers say
description: Russia is running a covert online disinformation campaign targeting U.S. politicians who support Ukraine, two Democratic lawmakers said on Oct. 21.
content:
Russia is running a covert online disinformation campaign targeting U.S. politicians who support Ukraine, two Democratic lawmakers said on Oct. 21.
Senator Mark Warner and Representative Jim Himes, two Democrats, told reporters that a recent intelligence briefing revealed Russian efforts to undermine U.S. backing for Ukraine. The misinformation campaign was particularly targeted against Democratic and Republican candidates running in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections who have expressed support for Ukraine.
The lawmakers’ comments come amid an apparent softening of the Trump administration’s stance toward Moscow. President Donald Trump recently announced that the US would allow Russia to export diesel into U.S. markets, and on Oct. 16 waived sanctions passed by bipartisan legislation aimed at countries that purchase Russian energy.
Warner and Himes said they were given a security briefing by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton. While the details of the briefing were classified, the two lawmakers said Russia was conducting a misinformation campaign targeted at Democrats running in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections, Reuters reported.
The campaign uses social media to sow distrust over the integrity of U.S. elections and generate "a sense of chaos and anarchy," the lawmakers said, according to Politico . They added that artificial intelligence has accelerated these efforts, allowing Russian operatives to more effectively target Americans online.
Senator Jon Ossoff, a Democrat running for re-election in Georgia, and James Talarico, a Democrat running for a Senate seat in Texas, are being especially targeted by AI-generated ads, Warner said.
Recent AI-generated videos targeting Talarico that emerged after early voting began in Texas were likely made by a Russian government-backed group, three teams of disinformation researchers said Oct. 22, according to NBC News .
Russian disinformation campaigns , which have also targeted France , Moldova and the United Kingdom , have become a common feature of U.S. elections .
In 2016, a grand jury indicted twelve Russian nationals for interfering with the U.S. presidential elections.
The Department of Justice said that the Russian operatives "engaged in a sustained effort" to hack into the computer networks of the Democratic National Committee, the Democratic Congressional Committee, and the Presidential campaign of Hillary Clinton, in a 2018 press release .

title: Amid Starlink crisis, Finnish tech giants announce plan to help Ukraine build its own sovereign satellite system
description: "Ukraine needs secure, sovereign, and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls," ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said in a press release announcing the deal with Kyiv.
content:
The Finnish tech companies ICEYE and Nokia signed a letter of intent with Ukraine's Defense Ministry on Oct. 22, formalizing a partnership aimed at developing Ukraine's own satellite communications system.
President Volodymyr Zelensky first announced the deal earlier in the day during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's visit to Kyiv , calling the satellite agreement "important for our defense and for the resilience of Ukraine."
The agreement with Kyiv comes a few weeks after Nokia and ICEYE announced plans to collaborate on building "broadband low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications systems for governments." These systems will support national defense, emergency response services, and border security, among other applications.
Ukraine currently relies on a different broadband LEO satellite communications system: Starlink , a service run by U.S.-based company SpaceX. Starlink has proven essential for battlefield communications, mid-range drone strikes, and air defense.
But the system has also proven vulnerable, as Ukraine learned after a week of persistent disruptions to its Starlink services. While U.S. President Donald Trump claimed that full speed and functionality had been restored to Ukraine's Starlink, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the restrictions remained in place.
The jointly developed systems that ICEYE and NOKIA want to create, however, would give nations ownership over their satellites, ground segment, and terminals, the companies said. Ukrainian forces on the front lines would therefore not lose access to mission-critical systems due to the s hifting whims of foreign governments .
"Ukraine needs secure, sovereign, and high-performance satellite communications systems that it controls," ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said in a press release announcing the deal with Kyiv.
"We have a proven track record of delivering sovereign missions at speed to help build that capability. ICEYE has proudly supported Ukraine since 2022, and we remain committed to continuing that support today."
Nokia Defense Chairman Mikko Hautala echoed the sentiment, saying the project would give Ukraine "control over the connectivity it depends on."
ICEYE describes itself as "the European leader in sovereign intelligence from space" and telecommunications giant Nokia as "a global leader in connectivity infrastructure."

title: Rosneft admits losses from Ukraine's refinery strikes becoming unsustainable, Bloomberg reports
description: Officials at Rosneft have privately voiced concerns that even a few more months of Ukraine's continued attacks could lead to lasting damage for the company.
content:
Russia's state-run oil giant Rosneft is facing mounting financial difficulties and the prospect of long-term damage as Ukraine expands its strike campaign against Russian oil refineries, Bloomberg reported on Oct. 22, citing expert analysts, insider sources, and documents reviewed by the outlet.
The news comes less than a week after the Ryazan Oil Refinery — one of Rosneft's biggest facilities — was reportedly forced to suspend operations at one of its main crude distillation units following a Ukrainian drone attack.
Officials at Rosneft have privately voiced concerns that even a few more months of Ukraine's continued attacks could lead to lasting damage for the company, according to Bloomberg.
Rosneft's 12 refineries account for approximately one third of Russia's total refining capacity. According to Bloomberg's analysis, five of 15 confirmed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries in September 2026 targeted Rosneft facilities that supply western Russia.
Documents reviewed by the outlet show that the Ryazan refinery has been shut down for more than half the time since it was hit by a Ukrainian drone blitz in May 2026. When it has been operational, the plant has run far below its actual capacity — a major blow to Russia's fourth-largest refinery, which supplies fuel to Moscow and the surrounding region.
Two other major Rosneft facilities have also suffered major disruptions over the past year. The Syzran refinery in Samara Oblast has been either completely offline or operating at below a third of its capacity for most of the past six months, data indicates.
The Syzran refinery has a processing capacity of approximately 9 million tons of crude oil per year and supplies fuel to the Russian Air Force and other military units. It also exports petroleum products via the Volga River and the Caspian Sea.
Rosneft's Tuapse refinery has been shut down since April, when Ukraine launched a sustained series of attacks against the key Black Sea export hub.
The success of Ukraine's attacks means Rosneft's profits continue to drop, despite the benefits the Iran war has channeled to the Russian oil industry.
Rosneft’s first-half net income in 2026 fell by almost 20%, to 200 billion rubles ($2.4 billion), Bloomberg reports. Its ratio of net debt to earnings also rose by 1.8 times in the first half of the year, its highest level in over five years.
Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil assets increased dramatically in the past year, with the number of confirmed hits from January to October more than doubling in 2026 compared to 2025. Ukraine has carried out at least 114 attacks on refineries in Russia, an estimate Bloomberg based on public statements from both countries.
The constant pace of repairs has led to escalating costs that Rosneft officials say are unsustainable, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke to Bloomberg. To cut costs, sources said, some refineries have deliberately stretched out repair work over several weeks.
Repairing and replacing damaged equipment is further complicated by international sanctions, which limit access to certain critical parts that would have previously been sourced from Western countries.
Rosneft said in a statement to Bloomberg that it is "taking appropriate measures to ensure the security and operation of our plants," and that "Not a single company petrol station has been closed, and consumers receive fuel in full at stable prices."
Russia has faced severe shortages of fuel in 2026, prompting sales restrictions and export bans — though U.S. President Donald Trump recently extended a lifeline to Moscow's struggling oil industry by announcing a controversial deal to buy Russian diesel.
While Ukraine briefly halted strikes on Russian oil refineries in October to honor Trump's proposed energy ceasefire , Kyiv soon resumed attacks when it became clear that Moscow had no intention of observing the truce.

title: Kyiv denies reports that Trump, Musk have restored Starlink speeds in Ukraine
description: "Overall, nothing has changed anywhere," a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 22. Starlink's speed cap of 161 kilometers per hour remains in effect, the official said.
content:
Editor's Note: This story has been updated with additional comments from U.S. President Donald Trump.
Ukraine's military Starlink service is still operating at a speed cap of 161 kilometers per hour, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 22.
The official's statement contradicts claims quoted by the Wall Street Journal (WSJ), which reported on Oct. 22 that Starlink functionality was back to normal in Ukraine following a phone call between SpaceX CEO Elon Musk and U.S. President Donald Trump.
Trump called Musk on Oct. 21 to request he lift restrictions on Ukraine's Starshield service, the military application of the Starlink program, according to the WSJ. Following the call, sources reportedly told the outlet that Starlink was functioning more normally — though some Ukrainian officials said it wasn't fully restored.
But when asked about these claims, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent they were "all false."
"Overall, nothing has changed anywhere," the official said. The 161 kph speed cap remains in place, severely limiting key military operations, including mid-range strikes and high-speed drone interceptions.
Trump was evasive about whether or not he called Musk, but also claimed that Starlink was back up and running as usual in Ukraine in comments to reporters.
"Yeah, I don't want to comment on it, whether I called, or whether somebody else called, it doesn't make a difference," Trump told a journalist when questioned about the WSJ story.
Ukraine has been trying to sort out the reasons behind the restriction — and restore service to its previous speed level — ever since Starlink was disrupted without warning on Oct. 14. While fingers have been pointed at SpaceX, the White House , and a Trump-Musk alliance, no one has claimed responsibility for the move.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that Trump had a hand in the change, saying on Oct. 18 that "no one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed."
Zelensky spoke with Rubio again on Oct. 20, as Starlink disruptions persisted. Zelensky told reporters on Oct. 22 that he was waiting for a response from Rubio as to whether Starlink communications could be restored to speeds of up to 400 kph.
Rubio promised to get back with him within 48 hours, Zelensky said, but definitive answers may take longer.
"Maybe something will become clear by morning," the official who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said.
"For now, the main interesting aspect of this is that there are absolutely no explanations for what's happening. Even though this is a top-priority system."
CORRECTION: A previous version of this story said it was reported that Musk called Trump to discuss Starlink. The WSJ reported that Trump phoned Musk. The error has been corrected.

title: In war between Russia and Ukraine, United States is first to surrender, but Americans still stand with Ukraine
description:
Got an opinion on anything you've read in the Kyiv Independent? Send it to letters@kyivindependent.com — your letter may appear in our Letters section.


Mark Cary, United States
member



I vividly remember when the Soviet Union collapsed. I was in my second year in college studying the history, ideology, and global influence of this dictatorship in an academic concentration called "Soviet and Eastern European Studies."

In 1989, the world felt joy and hope when the Berlin Wall fell. Once that
content:
Demonstrators rally in support of Ukraine in downtown Chicago, Illinois, on March 2, 2025. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
Got an opinion on anything you've read in the Kyiv Independent? Send it to letters@kyivindependent.com — your letter may appear in our Letters section.
I vividly remember when the Soviet Union collapsed. I was in my second year in college studying the history, ideology, and global influence of this dictatorship in an academic concentration called "Soviet and Eastern European Studies."
In 1989, the world felt joy and hope when the Berlin Wall fell. Once that dam broke, the end was inevitable.
Then came the horror of the murderous Soviet crackdown in Lithuania in 1991 as they tried in vain to hold on to their empire.
In December of 1991, Ukraine, Russia, and Belarus dissolved the Soviet Union, and 15 new countries were born.
The world was changed for the better, or so we thought.
Many factors contributed to this moment. All empires inevitably crack and begin to rot. The disastrous war in Afghanistan exacerbated the economic strain created by decades of military expenditures. The Soviets could no longer provide basic needs while simultaneously competing against Reagan's buildup and his willingness to challenge them at every turn.
Glasnost and Perestroika, Gorbachev's dual efforts to modernize Soviet society, backfired when the people got a taste of what could be.
In the West, we felt we "won" the Cold War. We spoke of a "peace dividend," and the United States assumed the position of the world's only superpower.
Some people called this "the end of history."
While we cheered, took a victory lap, and hoped to help guide these new emerging democracies, we failed to understand that there were those like Vladimir Putin for whom the Cold War never ended.
In 1999, a dictatorship in the fascist, imperial mold returned to Russia. Many in the United States recognized this threat; most did not.
Perhaps we weren't vigilant enough. But never in my life did I expect to see my country, led by the republican party, eagerly stand on the side of tyranny and imperialism. The party of Reagan now helps resuscitate and support an empire that we spent years, blood, and treasure trying to defeat.
What I am witnessing now in my United States is unconscionable.
Donald Trump has always had deep ties to the dark underbelly of Russia. His sons brag about the financing they receive from shady Russian oligarchs. He has selected pro-Russian politicians to cabinet positions. He has stated that he trusts the FSB over his own intelligence services.
I don't want to believe conspiracies that he was compromised by the KGB on his all-expenses-paid trip to Moscow in 1987. However, in light of his history of deference to Russian President Vladimir Putin and his now intentional switching of sides in the war between good and evil, right and wrong, democracy and tyranny, it is hard not to.
The truth is that a malignant narcissist with no values and a transactional view of policy is grasping at straws to deflect blame for his disastrous decisions.
Ukraine is an easy mark. From his shallow promise to "end the war in 24 hours" to his hatred of Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky , he sees no problem leaving Ukraine to fend for itself with only a disorganized and unprepared Europe to defend it.
Ukraine is being sacrificed at the altar of cynical political expediency.
I am sick, angry, frustrated, and tormented at this. I fear for the mental and physical health of my friends throughout Ukraine as they weather hour after hour of unrelenting attacks. We don't know what to say, how to comfort or ease both the pain of war and betrayal.
I am consumed by hatred, not only for Putin, but for the smug cabal of traitorous and ignorant Americans willing to abandon the values and principles that our country was founded on, and that we have defended throughout our history.
But I want my Ukrainian friends to know that you still have very broad and determined support in the United States.
"In the war between Russia and Ukraine, the United States is first to surrender, but Americans still stand with Ukraine" — these are the words I saw on the posters of protesters and in comments about our new embrace of Russia.
We still remember the feelings we had when we watched freedom come to Eastern Europe, and we understand that what our government is doing is objectively wrong.
Those of us who have committed to helping you will not stop. This is not only the right thing to do for Ukraine, but it is also an act of resistance by decent Americans against the creeping fascism and moral vacuousness that our leaders represent.
Stand strong, and we will always stand with you.
