title: Ukraine war latest: Ukrainian troops infiltrate Russian rear near Kupiansk through 15 kilometers of gas pipelines
description: The operation, code-named "Veles," was carried out by the 2nd Khartiia Corps together with other Ukrainian units, according to the corps.
content:
Ukrainian troops infiltrated the rear of Russian forces near Kupiansk in Kharkiv Oblast after moving about 15 kilometers (9 miles) through underground gas pipelines, Ukraine's National Guard’s 2nd Khartiia Corps said on Oct. 22.
The operation, code-named "Veles," was carried out by the 2nd Khartiia Corps together with other Ukrainian units, according to the corps.
Khartiia commander Brig. Gen. Ihor Obolienskyi said Ukrainian forces had studied how Russian troops were using underground routes and anticipated that they would try to exploit major gas pipelines running through Kharkiv Oblast.
"The Russians intended to use the gas routes to penetrate the rear of our forces. So we went underground ourselves," Obolienskyi said.
According to Khartiia, Ukrainian troops moved through the pipelines before combining the underground advance with operations above ground, including drone strikes.
The corps said more than 30 Russian soldiers were captured during the operation and that Russian forces suffered more than 100 casualties. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify those figures.
Obolienskyi said the aim was both to stop Russian troops underground and to undermine tactics they had been using on the ground and from the air.
"We anticipated the enemy's actions and mastered the tactics of conducting combat operations underground," he said.
Russian forces have used gas pipelines on several occasions to move troops covertly around the Kupiansk sector. In January, Ukrainian troops said they had stopped a Russian assault involving about 50 soldiers attempting to advance through the Soyuz gas pipeline.
More recently, Khartiia said, Russian troops retreating near Kupiansk used civilians as human shields , leading a group that included children and elderly people to the Shebelinka–Ostrogozhsk pipeline and forcing them inside the pipe toward Russian-held territory. Ukrainian troops said they did not open fire, because civilians were present
"When the battlefield became transparent, the war went underground," the corps said when it first announced the operation on Oct. 21.
Ukraine will be able to purchase weapons, ammunition, and other military equipment through NATO's centralized procurement agency, potentially giving Kyiv faster and cheaper access to defense supplies, the Financial Times reported on Oct. 22.
Ukraine is entering a partnership with the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), which handles procurement and logistical support for alliance members and partners, according to the Financial Times .
"It provides Ukraine with the ability to have a more structured framework to leverage a broad range of capabilities that we offer: procurement expertise, support services, and access to established industrial base," Jacqueline Borsboom, NSPA's director of support to operations, told the Financial Times.
The arrangement might allow Ukraine to use NATO's existing procurement system and supplier network rather than negotiating each purchase independently.
The NSPA also held an event in Kyiv last week attended by about 150 Ukrainian companies, explaining how manufacturers could register as eligible suppliers and compete for contracts, according to the Financial Times.
The new mechanism is separate from the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List ( PURL ), under which NATO allies and partners fund purchases of U.S.-made weapons and ammunition for Ukraine. More than $6 billion in military equipment has been funded through PURL since the initiative was launched in July 2025, according to NATO.
The agreement comes as Kyiv seeks to diversify and stabilize its access to military supplies amid growing uncertainty over U.S. support.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has reported disruptions to some U.S.-provided capabilities, including intelligence sharing and the Starshield satellite system used by Ukrainian forces. President Volodymyr Zelensky said after talks in Oslo this week that efforts were underway to resolve those issues.
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) announced details of a new Russian cruise missile called "Filin" and released a 3-D model of the missile alongside a list of components and electronics on its website on Oct. 22.
Russia began using the missile at the end of summer, HUR said , calling it a continuation of a Russian trend to build "inexpensive air attack means with jet propulsion and ground-based launch."
The missile is 3.5 meters long with a wingspan of 3 meters, ablte to carry either 50 kilogram or 100 kilogram warheads, HUR said. It can fly both at ultra-low altitudes and up to 6 kilometers (about 3.7 miles) high, at a top speed of 800 kilometers per hour (about 497 miles per hour), across a distance of 1,200 kilometers (about 745 miles), according to the agency.
Some parts of the missile are apparently 3-D printed, HUR said, while the electronic component base of the onboard equipment is similar to other Russian missiles, but stands out for the increased share of Chinese components. Besides Chinese components, the agency also said the "Filin" included 35 U.S.-made components.
The onboard equipment is manufactured by PLAZ LLC, which is also involved in producing the Harpiya drone, HUR said, while the engine is the Russian-made R500, produced by Reynolds LLC.
Russia uses cruise and ballistic missiles to strike at Ukraine, and increasingly at the country's energy infrastructure . On Oct. 22, Russian ballistic missiles and cluster munitions struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others.
"Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched by Russian 'humanists' on Kyiv since the evening," President Volodymyr Zelensky commented on the attack.
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Zelensky said Russia fired 21 missiles.
Agents of the Ukrainian partisan group Atesh said they disrupted Russian military communication lines around IXcellerate, one of Moscow's largest commercial data center operators, to interfere with Russian air-defense coordination and help Ukrainian drones reach their targets, the group said on Oct. 21.
"We are disabling the enemy's channels, disrupting command and control, and helping UAVs reach their targets," Atesh said .
The group claimed Russia's Defense Ministry uses infrastructure linked to IXcellerate for military communications and air-defense command systems, while concealing that traffic within civilian server networks.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim, and Atesh did not provide details on the extent or duration of the disruption. There has been no public confirmation from Russian authorities or IXcellerate that military communications were affected.
IXcellerate operates several data centers across Moscow and describes itself as a leading commercial data center operator in Russia. Its facilities host telecommunications and other digital infrastructure used by banks, retailers, and business customers.
The partisan group has previously claimed sabotage operations against Russian military and defense-linked infrastructure inside Russia, including attacks on railway and energy facilities.
Russian ballistic missiles and cluster munitions struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight on Oct. 22, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others, according to Ukrainian officials, only hours after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff visited Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office reported these numbers in the morning, saying Russia had struck across Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Pecherskyi, Svyatoshynskyi and Dnipro dsitricts in Ukraine's capital.
Among the injured are four children, one of whom has been hospitalized, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said .
"Last night, the Russians used, among others, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads against Kyiv. The peculiarity of these missiles is that they explode in the air, hitting the target, and hit everything around within a diameter of 400 meters," President Volodymyr Zelensky said .
"Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched by Russian 'humanists' on Kyiv since the evening," Zelensky commented on the attack earlier.
During a meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg, Witkoff lauded Putin — wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes in Ukraine — as a "humanitarian."
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Zelensky said Russia fired 21 missiles. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 181 drones, including 87 jet-powered ones, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 32 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight others.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that the Iskander missiles carried a K5 cluster munitions warhead.
"This warhead explodes above the ground and is specifically designed to cause maximum damage to people and equipment in an area of ​​400 by 400 meters," Beskrestnov said.
"This strike was not carried out with a military purpose. The goal was to destroy part of the old city and injure as many people as possible," he added.
Zelensky said one of the missiles struck Pechersk, in Kyiv's historic center, in an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Sviato-Vvedensky Monastery. Buildings belonging to the monastery, residential buildings, shops, cafes and other civilian infrastructure were damaged, he said.
"There was not even theoretically any military facility nearby," Zelensky said. "It was a deliberate choice of weapon, a deliberate choice of the area of use, a deliberate attempt to inflict as many casualties and as much damage on civilians as possible."
Zelensky reported two people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast as a result of the attacks.

title: Stephen Hubbard's son: 'It’s tragic when family members are torn apart' by Russian captivity

content:
Stephen Hubbard (C-L), a 74-year-old retired U.S. schoolteacher who was freed after being imprisoned in Russia following his capture in Izyum, Kharkiv Oblast, Ukraine, is seen with his family heading home in a photo shared on Oct. 21, 2026. (@SEPeaceMissions / X)
For years, Father Joseph Coleman had little ability to influence what happened to his father, Stephen Hubbard, an American retiree imprisoned in Russia after being captured in Izium, a city in Ukraine’s Kharkiv Oblast occupied by Russian forces in 2022.
Hubbard, 74, was sentenced to nearly seven years in prison after a closed trial in Russia. Russian prosecutors accused him of fighting for Ukraine as a mercenary, a charge his family has disputed. For Coleman, who lives in Cyprus and had not seen his father in years, the news of his release brought a long-awaited chance to see him "free and well."
“Two or three weeks ago, I was under the impression that all efforts were not going to be successful. Therefore, when I was told on Friday or Saturday that he would most likely be released, as they say, hope was rekindled,” Coleman said in an interview with the Kyiv Independent.
“Typically, I’m reserved until they say wheels up,” Coleman said. There had been another possibility of freedom in early 2025, he recalled, but it had fallen through. When the confirmation finally came, he said, he felt “overwhelming relief, joy.”
Coleman acknowledged that his father may have suffered mistreatment in captivity, though he said he could not be certain. “Many tragic things happen in war,” he said. “Was he mistreated? Some people say yes. I don’t know. I wasn’t there. Some evidence points to that, but I wasn’t there.”
Despite his concerns, Coleman said Hubbard appeared healthier than he had expected and was in high spirits. Still, he acknowledged that the years in Russian captivity may have left emotional scars that are less visible.
“He looks good, especially considering what he’s endured,” Coleman said. “You know, there’s always some probably emotional trauma that’s hidden that he’ll have to work out.”
For now, Coleman is not pressing his father to recount what happened behind bars. He said he had not asked Hubbard about his experiences in Russian custody and would leave it to his father to decide whether — and when — to speak about them. Hubbard has always been a reserved and private person, Coleman said, and he would not be surprised if some parts of the ordeal remained untold, even to his family.
“He'll tell me if he wants to and when he wants to,” Coleman said. “I wouldn't even be surprised if he never tells me the whole story.”
While Coleman said his father has no plans to return to Ukraine, he hopes to one day travel to both Russia and Kyiv on a religious pilgrimage. For Coleman, an Orthodox Christian, the journey would be about faith rather than politics — a chance to visit sacred sites and the relics of saints that have drawn pilgrims to the region for centuries.
“As an Orthodox Christian, it was always my hope and dream to do a pilgrimage to Russia, both to Russia and actually even Ukraine, Kyiv,” Coleman said. “But not for political reasons in any way, just strictly spiritual or religious reasons.”
Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher from Michigan, had moved to Ukraine to live with a Ukrainian woman. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, he remained in the country.
“Things kicked off, and he didn’t leave,” Coleman said. Coleman said he believed his father’s continued presence in Ukraine had made him a target. A Russian court later convicted him of being a mercenary and sentenced him to 82 months in prison.
Coleman said his understanding was that “Ukrainians put him on a list of volunteers and because of that piece of quote-unquote evidence the Russian government accused him of being a mercenary."
“Witkoff’s pathetic fawning over this KGB thug betrays American values & security.”
Coleman objected to describing Hubbard as someone who had volunteered to fight for Ukraine, saying that the characterization was misleading and could have consequences for him and his father. He knew little more about the circumstances, other than that the woman had since moved to Cyprus with her daughter.
Coleman also pushed back on reports describing his father as pro-Russian, saying that Hubbard’s connection to the Russian Orthodox tradition was religious rather than political.
“He is a part of the Orthodox Russian tradition,” Coleman said, explaining that his father had entered the Orthodox faith through that tradition and had participated in Russian-tradition Orthodox churches in both the United States and Japan. Hubbard was not officially a member of any Russian Orthodox Church , Coleman said.
Despite the uncertainty surrounding his father’s imprisonment and the negotiations that secured his release, Coleman expressed gratitude to those he believed had played a role. He named “God and Donald Trump and even President Putin .”
Asked about the Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war still held by Russia, as well as Ukrainian children taken from their families, Coleman said he believed families should be reunited.
“I think it's tragic when family members are torn apart and they should be reunited,” he said. “But beyond that, like I said, I have no political power.”
Coleman was not directly involved in the negotiations that led to his father’s release. Much of the campaigning on Hubbard’s behalf in the United States had been undertaken by his aunt, Tricia, who lives in Florida.
Coleman, meanwhile, was thousands of miles away in Cyprus, where he said he struggled with his inability to help.
“To be honest with you, in Cyprus, I felt a little helpless not being able to do anything at all,” he said. “I’m a priest, so mostly I was focused on prayer.”
He nevertheless met U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff at Witkoff’s home in Florida. Coleman said he rarely followed American political news and did not recognize Witkoff when he arrived.
“When I showed up at Steve’s house, we jumped out of the car, and there was a man with a golf club, and I didn’t even recognize him,” Coleman said.
“I told him later, I said, ‘I apologize, I didn’t recognize you,’” he recalled.
Witkoff’s role in the release drew criticism after he publicly praised Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian.”
“WTF, Steve? Look up the definition of ‘humanitarian,’” Republican U.S. Senator Thom Tillis wrote in an X post directed at the U.S. envoy. “You should go back to Ukraine and ask the families of the children Putin has kidnapped and murdered whether they agree your friend Putin is a ‘humanitarian.’”
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal also criticized Witkoff’s remarks.
“Witkoff’s pathetic fawning over this KGB thug betrays American values & security,” Blumenthal wrote. “He should cite Putin’s humanitarian greatness to the prisoners he’s tortured & killed, the children he’s kidnapped, the Ukrainians whose country he’s bombing.”
Blumenthal co-authored legislation with the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham imposing sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia and Iran. Trump signed the measure into law in September but later waived many of its provisions.
Trump denied that the United States had made concessions to secure the American’s freedom.
The U.S. “ gave nothing in exchange ” for the release, Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that “we’re getting closer” to settling the war.
Asked by a reporter how waiving of sanctions did not amount to giving Russia something in return, Trump replied, “You are a stupid person.”
The exchange took place as Trump spoke to reporters en route to a rally in South Carolina, where he was campaigning for Republican candidate Darline Graham, the late Senator Lindsey Graham’s sister. He spent two years pushing legislation to sanction Russia. Asked about his sister’s reaction to the prisoner release and the decision waive sanctions, Trump dismissed the question, saying, “You don’t know anything, fake news CNN.”
“The other important thing, very important, is that we are negotiating with Russia right now on Ukraine. We are maybe close to a deal for the first time in a long time. When you are close to a deal, you are having very delicate negotiations. You don’t put sanctions on it,” Trump told reporters.
Coleman said he did not believe sanctions are helpful.
“I think that sanctions don’t really help in the long run,” he said, adding, “I’m not really politically minded. I don’t actually even know how a sanction benefits or hurts someone, to be honest with you.”
Tanya Kozyreva is a correspondent for Suspilne based in Washington DC.

title: Ukraine strikes Russian electronic warfare station, General Staff says
description: The electronic warfare station was hit near the village of Gulevka in Russia's Bryansk Oblast. According to the General Staff, targeting Russian electronic warfare systems improves Ukraine's ability to effectively deploy drones.
content:
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian electronic warfare station in Bryansk Oblast and several military facilities in Zaporizhzhia and Luhansk oblasts on Oct. 21 and overnight on Oct. 22, Ukraine's General Staff said.
The electronic warfare station was hit near the village of Gulevka in Russia's Bryansk Oblast. According to the General Staff, targeting Russian electronic warfare systems improves Ukraine's ability to effectively deploy drones.
Ukrainian forces also struck a Russian command and observation post near Vyshneve and a drone control point near Lankove, both in Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
The General Staff said the strike on the drone control point reduces Russia's ability to launch drone attacks against Ukrainian military positions and front-line communities.
A Russian military logistics depot near Zolotarivka in Luhansk Oblast was also hit, according to the statement.
The full extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
The strikes come amid reports of further Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory. Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the city of Lipetsk and a weapons plant in Serpukhov , Moscow Oblast, overnight on Oct. 22, according to monitoring channels.

title: Russia sentences 77-year-old Crimean activist to 18 years over alleged plot against Moscow's proxy
description: "Volodymyr Ananiev is the oldest Crimean political prisoner. He suffers from vision problems and issues with his spine, muscles, kidneys, and legs, and walks with a cane," the Crimean Tatar Resource Center said.
content:
A Russian court in Rostov-on-Don said on Oct. 22 it had sentenced 77-year-old Crimean political prisoner Volodymyr Ananiev to 18 years in prison over an alleged plot to assassinate Sergey Aksyonov, the Russian proxy governor of occupied Crimea.
Moscow has continued to repress Crimean Tatars and other residents, including journalists and activists, of the peninsula since its occupation in 2014. Around 300 people, including journalists and activists, were being held on politically motivated charges as of spring, more than 150 of them Crimean Tatars, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said.
Russian investigators claim Ananiev was part of a group that tracked Aksyonov's car and prepared an explosive device to blow it up.
Ananiev was detained in the Russian-occupied city of Simferopol in February 2024. Two other people accused of involvement in the plot, Volodymyr Bodnar and Oksana Shevchenko, were previously sentenced to 13 and 10 years in prison, respectively.
Under the sentence, Ananiev will spend the first four years in prison and the remainder in a Russian maximum security penal colony. He was also fined 600,000 rubles ($7,300).
Born in western Ukraine, Ananiev later moved to Crimea, where he became an activist, worked in law and journalism, and campaigned for landowners' and Crimean Tatars' rights.
The NGO Crimean Tatar Resource Center said the man has undergone eye surgery and suffers from high blood pressure.
"Volodymyr Ananiev is the oldest Crimean political prisoner. He suffers from vision problems and issues with his spine, muscles, kidneys, and legs, and walks with a cane," the statement read .
According to the Crimean Tatar Resource Center, the Russian-installed authorities have persecuted 64 elderly Crimean political prisoners. Forty-five have been sentenced, while 19 remain in pretrial detention.
Ananiev's wife, Anna Sviatnenko, called the case against her husband "trumped-up" and told Suspilne the defense would appeal.

title: EU responds to Trump diesel deal with new Russia energy sanctions
description: A key focus of the latest proposed sanctions listings is Russia's oil processing, refining, and exporting capacity, with 31 listings spanning the breadth of Russia, from St. Petersburg to Sakhalin.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Restrictions against Russian refineries and oil export terminals loom large in a new set of EU draft sanctions listings, first presented to EU ambassadors on Oct. 21 and seen by the Kyiv Independent.
The EU's diplomatic arm, the EEAS, "proposed 117 additional listings targeting sectors which raise revenue for Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, such as the financial sector, energy sector, and the Russian shadow fleet," an Irish Council Presidency spokesperson told journalists.
The draft document lists 12 individuals and 105 entities, which, if adopted, would subject them to a transaction ban with the EU and a freeze on any assets they hold in the bloc. Being a sanctioned entity can also make it hard to do business with companies in third countries, which don't want to risk their own commercial ties with the EU.
A key focus of the latest proposed sanctions listings is Russia's oil processing, refining, and exporting capacity, with 31 listings spanning the breadth of Russia, from St. Petersburg to Sakhalin.
The EEAS' proposal of those listings is especially timely, coming barely two weeks after U.S. President Donald Trump agreed to import diesel — itself a refined oil product — from Russia.
That deal, and the U.S.' wider attitude change to Ukraine, led to widespread condemnation from EU leaders when they met in Brussels on Oct. 15-16.
"We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender," said the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas, who oversees the bloc's sanctions.
The other listings included 52 banking and financial institutions, two entities that process Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG), and a steel company operating from Russian-occupied territory in Donetsk Oblast.
The EU has also sanctioned entities in several third countries that have been helping Moscow evade sanctions, 12 in the United Arab Emirates alone, and other listings for companies based in Oman, Singapore, Hong Kong, and the Seychelles.
Also likely to be of interest are some of the 12 individuals sanctioned by the EU, which have ties to e-commerce platforms Ozon and Wildberries , which have been trading in products that help Russia's military effort, as well as Moscow's internet search engine Yandex .
All three companies have been targets of successful Ukrainian military strikes.
Finally, the EU is preparing to apply sanctions to a further 15 companies belonging to Russia's military-industrial complex, and to remove one entity in a third country because "the entity has ceased the activity which led to its inclusion in the list and has committed to refrain from any such activity in the future," reads the EU's draft legal text.
The next step is for the listings to be scrutinized by sanctions experts appointed by the 27 EU countries. After that, the list returns to ambassadors for approval, and then to ministers for a final vote.

title: What Russians are told — and not told — about Ukrainian strikes
description:
On the night of Sept. 12, Ukrainian drones attacked Taganrog. Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) reported hits on an FPV drone production facility, two drone storage sites, a Pantsir air defense system, and a radar.

content:
A woman rides on a bus as smoke rises from the area of Gazprom Neft’s Moscow oil refinery in Moscow, Russia, on Sept. 20, 2026. (AFP via Getty Images)
On the night of Sept. 12, Ukrainian drones attacked Taganrog. Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) reported hits on an FPV drone production facility, two drone storage sites, a Pantsir air defense system, and a radar.
Local authorities, as usual, listed something else: 16 commercial buildings, five cars, a football club, and a Svetofor store.
Regional social media channels summed it up in a single sentence about "drone debris" that set a store and several non-residential buildings on fire.
Under a post by a Rostov community on VKontakte, one commenter clarified: "One big-box store selling aircraft tires has been burning since 4 a.m. and is still burning."
They were referring to a military airfield where, judging by satellite imagery , fuel tanks caught fire.
Three days later, missiles struck the city.
Ukraine's General Staff reported explosions and a fire at the Atlant Aero plant, which manufactures Molniya strike drones. Russian authorities listed broken windows, a gas pipe, a grocery store, and an Ozon warehouse. The regional communities we monitor published 178 posts about the two strikes on Taganrog. Only one identified the target. Atlant Aero was not mentioned once.
The case of Taganrog offers a clear picture of how Russia's audience is structured. It is divided into segments, each seeing a different war .
Most people get their news from television and local online communities: television remains the main source of information for 61% of Russians.
Those interested in the war also read pro-war bloggers, known in Russia as Z-war bloggers. The smallest group reads independent media run by Russians abroad.
A month ago, using Novorossiysk as an example, we wrote that Russians do not see strikes on military targets. In September, we expanded our monitoring beyond 1,000 regional communities on Telegram and VKontakte to include more than 40 major nationwide channels, giving us a broader picture.
The first group gets the authorities' version.
On Sept. 9, the Ukrainian Navy said a Neptune missile had hit the Admiral Essen frigate in Novorossiysk.
Of 246 regional posts about that night, only one mentioned ships, while nearly 100 posts reported deaths: according to Russian authorities, four people were killed in the city.
Regional Russia knows about the civilian deaths, but not the frigate.
On Sept. 22, Ukraine's General Staff reported a strike on a base near the village of Tsymbulovo in Oryol Oblast, from which Russia launches jet-powered Geran drones.
Over the following month, the village's name did not appear in any of the thousand communities we monitored, including those in Oryol.
The shutdown of the Moscow oil refinery after a Sept. 20 strike, reported by Reuters, appeared in just six of 407 posts. The state-run channels in our sample, Solovyov and Komsomolskaya Pravda, simply repeated official statements in nine out of every 10 posts.
This feed creates the impression that air defenses shoot down hundreds of drones and debris falls on residential buildings.
Readers of Russian military bloggers know much more.
On Sept. 12, the Voyennyy Osvedomitel channel identified a military airfield as the likely target in Taganrog. On Sept. 18, it published a satellite image of damaged Atlant Aero workshops.
Overall, military bloggers identified the target in nine of 16 posts about Taganrog.
On the Moscow oil refinery, Z-blogger Fighterbomber wrote : "Let me remind you, this is the most heavily protected oil refinery in the country. Perhaps even in the world. I predict it will be attacked more than once."
But this knowledge is one-sided. The same channels report Russian strikes on Ukraine far more frequently and in greater detail.
Some 92% of reactions to such posts are positive. And Voyennyy Osvedomitel presented the strike on Tsymbulovo as a story of resilience: the shelters are sturdy, and the launchers are cheap to replace.
Independent media and those run from abroad provide the most comprehensive coverage of the strikes: they identified the target in 14 of 20 posts about Taganrog. Yet they have the smallest audiences.
In our sample, a typical military blogger's post about a strike on Russia receives 73,000 views, compared with 14,000 for a post by an independent media outlet.
Everything changes when a strike hits close to home.
The official account then clashes with what people heard during the night, and they start asking questions.
Under a post about Taganrog, people write : "Your Telegram channels say it wasn't just the store" and "When will they finally learn to tell the truth?"
In Oryol, a woman asked the governor about nighttime explosions during a live broadcast. She heard an explanation about a "piece of a drone" and recounted it in the comments: "Short and clear. Yes, that piece fell with such a bang that almost the whole city heard it."
The same community debunked a deepfake in which the governor supposedly admitted that the region lacked air defenses. The comments under the debunking post read: "This fake is telling the truth" and "I'd vote for the fake."
In Salekhard, the capital of the Yamalo-Nenets Autonomous Okrug, people reasoned this way after a gas plant in Novy Urengoy was hit: "How did it happen that the attack was repelled, the drone was turned into debris, and the facility it attacked is on fire? So the attack wasn't repelled, and this wasn't debris. It hit exactly what it was supposed to hit."
The numbers reflect this pattern, too. In communities based in the region that was hit, 34% of substantive comments question the effectiveness of defenses and the official figures. Another 23% describe what people saw and heard themselves or ask their neighbors about it.
They do not always find the right answers.
Novy Urengoy lies nearly 3,000 kilometers (about 1864 miles) from the Ukrainian border, and drones reached the city for the first time. The neighboring Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug banned the publication of anything about drones that same day.
The most popular comment about the strike in our databases reads: "It's been obvious for a long time that they aren't being launched from Ukraine."
Where the authorities stay silent, Russians find their own answers, and they are not always right.
Ordinary Russians in the regions know little about this war. They are told about downed drones and damaged buildings, and as long as the explosions are far away, that is enough.
Questions emerge when a strike hits their own city. In September, Yamalo-Nenets appeared on our map for the first time, and communities in 24 regions posted about the strike.
Questioning the authorities does not necessarily mean wanting the war to end. In the aftermath of the month's largest attack, the one on Moscow, 59% of substantive comments blamed the authorities and air defenses, while 16% blamed Ukraine and the West. Yet only one in 12 called for the war to end.
To sum up, here is what ordinary Russians were not told in the news in September: a strike drone factory and a military airfield in Taganrog; a frigate carrying Kalibr missiles in Novorossiysk; a launch base for jet-powered Geran drones; the shutdown of the capital's main oil refinery; and a gas plant in Yamalo-Nenets.
Russians in the regions continue to be shielded from learning by accident that the war is not going as victoriously as Putin claims. The results are rather underwhelming.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Andrii Sukharyna is Head of analytics of NGO "Join Ukraine."

title: Just hours after being bombed, we asked people in Kyiv about Witkoff's praise of Putin
description:
On Oct. 21, U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff gushingly praised Russian President Vladimir Putin for being a "humanitarian."

Just a few hours later, Kyiv once again came under a fresh barrage of devastating Russian missiles, killing at least one person and injuring over 20.

"We thought this was a war and the destruction of Ukraine, but it turns out to be an act of humanity," Nataliia Stativko, a former journalist, told the Kyiv Independent on a street devastated by one of the missiles. .

"Now
content:
Nataliia reacts as she looks at the damage inside her house following an aerial attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 22, 2026. (Diego Fedele / Getty Images)
On Oct. 21, U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff gushingly praised Russian President Vladimir Putin for being a "humanitarian."
Just a few hours later, Kyiv once again came under a fresh barrage of devastating Russian missiles , killing at least one person and injuring over 20.
"We thought this was a war and the destruction of Ukraine, but it turns out to be an act of humanity," Nataliia Stativko, a former journalist, told the Kyiv Independent on a street devastated by one of the missiles. .
"Now we will die and bury our children, knowing that this is an act of humanity."
Допис, поширений Kyiv Independent (@kyivindependent_official)
The attack hit the city's central Pecherskyi District, which, throughout Russia's full-scale invasion , had been among the capital's least frequently targeted areas and was considered safe by many residents.
"Now there is no safe place in Kyiv — death is breathing down your neck everywhere," Dasha Bilous, 25, a local resident, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Now we will die and bury our children, knowing that this is an act of humanity."
Kniaziv Ostrozkykh Street is almost entirely covered in shattered glass, and barely a single window in the surrounding buildings remains intact. A crater over a meter in diameter marks the middle of the road, where a fragment of a Russian missile lay just hours ago.
Exhausted after a sleepless night, residents are gathering pieces of plywood and plastic sheeting to cover their broken windows and keep at least some warmth inside their homes, as rain falls outside and a piercing autumn wind cuts through the streets.
While Kyiv residents pick up the pieces and try to resume their lives, they are left grappling with Witkoff's words from his Oct. 21 meeting with Putin in Saint Petersburg, in which the two discussed a " peace settlement " to Russia's war against Ukraine.
During the meeting, Moscow announced the release of 74-year-old American citizen Stephen Hubbard. Russian forces detained Hubbard during the occupation of Ukraine's Kharkiv Oblast in the early months of the full-scale invasion in 2022. In 2024, a Russian court convicted him of serving as a mercenary in the Ukrainian military, an accusation his family and lawyer disputed.
Witkoff described Putin as a " humanitarian " while commenting on Hubbard's release.
The area where Stativko lives was likely targeted overnight not only with conventional cruise and ballistic missiles, but also with cluster munitions , which scatter smaller explosive charges upon detonation, causing more widespread damage across a larger area.
Andrii Saulevych, manager of the local coffee shop Khlibna Kraina, also felt the impact of Russia's missile attack firsthand. The cafe's windows were completely blown out, but by 8 a.m. local time, it was already serving coffee to customers again.
"We put a piece of ourselves into every coffee shop," he said. "It's deeply upsetting to see everything destroyed like this."
"Humanitarians don't act this way. This is something else. This is anti-humanitarian," Saulevych added.
Another resident of the district, teacher Yaroslav Bahai, spent the morning waiting in line for humanitarian aid instead of preparing his lessons. The windows in his apartment had been blown out, and shrapnel had pierced straight through his kitchen refrigerator. His family was fortunate to survive the attack unharmed: they had taken shelter in the hallway with their children when the missiles struck.
Bahai said the war has significantly changed the way he teaches. His school cannot accommodate all its students in the bomb shelter, while the constant air raid alerts that have plagued the capital in recent months have made learning increasingly difficult, even online.
"I used to give children an assignment asking who they see themselves becoming in five years. Now they say it's hard for them to even imagine what tomorrow will look like," he said.
Bahai and his family have no plans to leave Kyiv for now, despite the approaching winter, which could be one of Ukraine's most difficult since 2022 due to continued Russian attacks and damage to the country's energy infrastructure . Bilous, however, is considering leaving the capital. Although reluctant to abandon her home, she said she can no longer cope with the constant sense of danger, which only continues to grow.
A fragment of a Russian missile landed right next to her house, shattering all the windows.
"I thought I was going to die," Bilous said.
"Such a 'gift' arrived in Kyiv after the (Witkoff-Putin) meeting. Who was it from? Putin? Witkoff? Trump?"
Kateryna Hodunova is a News Editor at the Kyiv Independent. She previously worked as a sports journalist in several Ukrainian outlets and was the deputy chief editor at Suspilne Sport. Kateryna covered the 2022 Olympics in Beijing and was included in the Special Mentions list at the AIPS Sport Media Awards. She holds a bachelor's degree in political journalism from Taras Shevchenko University and a master's degree in political science from the National University of Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.

title: Russia intensifies pressure on occupied Ukrainians without Russian passports, military intelligence says
description: Ukrainians without Russian passports are classified by Russian occupation authorities as "foreign citizens" and subjected to Russian migration law, HUR said.
content:
Russian security forces carried out a new round of raids across occupied Ukrainian territories in early October, targeting residents who have refused to obtain Russian passports, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) said on Oct. 22, as Moscow continues a long-running campaign of forced passportization.
The raids were conducted jointly by Russian police and the Federal Security Service ( FSB ) during the first 10 days of October as part of an operation dubbed "Illegal-2026," according to HUR.
Ukrainians without Russian passports are classified by occupation authorities as "foreign citizens" and subjected to Russian migration law, HUR said.
According to the agency, residents can face pressure to obtain Russian citizenship, expulsion from occupied territory, dismissal from work, and property seizure.
In occupied Luhansk Oblast , Russian authorities have also checked documents held by minors as part of the campaign, HUR said. Parents whose children do not obtain Russian passports have allegedly been threatened with fines, imprisonment, and the loss of parental rights.
HUR described the operation as another tool in Russia's broader effort to pressure Ukrainians into accepting Russian citizenship and push those who refuse out of occupied territory.
Russia has pressured residents of occupied Ukrainian territories to take Russian passports since 2014, tying access to employment, social services, property rights, and other aspects of daily life to possession of Russian documents.
Russian occupation authorities already carried out earlier phases of the "Illegal-2026" operation. In June, occupation officials said more than 300 administrative cases had been opened and more than 40 people expelled during a 10-day phase of the campaign.

title: Germany arrests Ukrainian national suspected of spying for Russia
description: The suspect allegedly collected relevant information in connection with Russia's war against Ukraine, including on the production of armored vehicles, ammunition, and explosives, as well as on military personnel and facilities on NATO's eastern flank.
content:
Germany's Federal Criminal Police arrested a Ukrainian citizen in the state of Brandenburg, surrounding Berlin, for suspected espionage on behalf of a Russian intelligence agency, Germany's Federal Prosecutor's Office said on Oct. 22.
The suspect, identified as Vadym Y., was arrested in the Oder-Spree district of Brandenburg a week after an investigating judge issued a warrant on Oct. 15, the prosecutor's office said .
Vadym Y. had been in contact with Russian intelligence through an interlocutor since at least July 2025, the prosecutor's office said. He allegedly collected relevant information in connection with Russia's war against Ukraine, including on the production of armored vehicles, ammunition, and explosives, as well as on military personnel and facilities on NATO's eastern flank.
While some of the information was publicly available, according to the prosecutor's office, the suspect allegedly also obtained details by deliberately approaching people working in the European defense industry.
The information on the suspected spy comes primarily from Germany's domestic intelligence service (BfV).
This incident comes a day after Germany's military for the first time classified Russian sabotage threats against its troops and facilities as "significant," German news outlet Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported on Oct. 21.
Reviewing internal documents from Germany's armed forces, Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported that this is the military's second-highest threat classification.
"We are noting that we face a ​significant sabotage threat overall for [Germany's armed forces]," said a defense ministry spokesperson, according to Reuters.
Germany's reclassification of Russian threats comes as experts warn Russia is testing how far it can push Europe without triggering open war — from drones crossing NATO airspace to sabotage and cyberattacks across the continent. Europe has strengthened its defenses since 2022, but key gaps remain, including in air defense, communications, intelligence, and joint command, experts say.
On Oct. 5, Martin Jaeger, head of Germany's foreign intelligence service, told lawmakers that Germany is in a "shadow war" with Russia and risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Moscow.

title: How Ukrainian researchers dissect Russian drones to uncover their next deadly upgrade
description:
In a government office, researchers of drones and electronic warfare gather around a small metal device recovered from a Russian Geran drone. Its purpose —  to measure the Earth’s magnetic field for navigation.

"This is the most recent component we found, about a week or two ago," said one of the researchers.

Outside, a Russian drone’s jet engine roared — a sound that has become almost constant in Kyiv in recent months as advances in drone technology allow Russia to strike farther, more often
content:
From a Canon camera to a magnetometer, wreckage reveals how Russian weapons keep advancing and why Ukraine’s countermeasures struggle to keep pace.
A Ukrainian soldier inspects the remains of a Russian Geran drone in a cornfield in Chernihiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 12, 2026. (Jakub Laichter / The Kyiv Independent)
In a government office, researchers of drones and electronic warfare gather around a small metal device recovered from a Russian Geran drone. Its purpose — to measure the Earth’s magnetic field for navigation.
"This is the most recent component we found, about a week or two ago," said one of the researchers.
Outside, a Russian drone’s jet engine roared — a sound that has become almost constant in Kyiv in recent months as advances in drone technology allow Russia to strike farther, more often and with greater precision. The small metal sensor on the table could make that threat even more vicious.
If it works as the researchers suspect, it could keep drones on course even when their satellite navigation is jammed, making the prospect of a winter under near-constant Russian attack even grimmer.
The researchers work at an institution under Ukraine’s Defense Ministry, and its work is rarely seen by outsiders. Here, specialists dismantle Russian weapons recovered from the battlefield or attacks to identify vulnerabilities, help develop countermeasures, and anticipate what Russian engineers might try next. The Kyiv Independent was given rare access on the condition that neither the institution nor the people inside be identified.
Their work is a race against time. The researchers estimate that developing an effective countermeasure usually takes four to six months, while Russia can introduce further modifications after two or three.
Regarding the sensor they found — in technical terms called a magnetometer — the researchers said they were still investigating its purpose and whether Russia might deploy it at scale.
But finding a new component is not the same as understanding it, and understanding it is not the same as having a way to counter it. And the Russian engineers who put the magnetometer in the drone face a similar gap. Fitting it to a handful of drones is not the same as being able to deploy it at scale.
Inside the institution, the fluorescent-lit hallways were filled with pieces of missiles, drones, fuzes, and motherboards, all neatly organized and labeled. People move in and out, some in camouflage, others in jeans and plain shirts, some carrying paperwork, others pieces of military hardware.
There is the nose of a North Korean missile , taller than a grown man, and a large section of a Russian Oreshnik missile, its cylindrical body roughly as wide as a passenger car. On the other side of the hallway were several Russian Geran drones, their triangular bodies resembling black paper airplanes enlarged to more than three meters long (9.8 feet), with wings spanning roughly three meters.
Outwardly, the Russian Gerans still resemble the Iranian drones Russia began using to terrorize Ukrainian cities in the fall of 2022. Inside, however, successive modifications had made them markedly different from those early aircraft, and even from the first Russian-made Gerans that appeared by the summer of 2023.
To trace the drones' evolution, the researchers work backward from the ones they recover. They begin by identifying and documenting each drone’s basic features, then dismantle it to map its internal systems, trace its components to their manufacturers, and reconstruct how each part contributes to the aircraft’s operation.
The researchers explained that changes inside the drones often reflected the success of Ukraine’s defenses. A navigation system that had once guided an aircraft to its target could become vulnerable to jamming, prompting Russia to try something else.
"When the Russians see that the effectiveness is decreasing, they introduce other technologies," one researcher said.
But the two sides don't take turns. Russia can introduce another modification while Ukraine is still working out how to defeat the previous one.
On one of the tables lies a Canon camera recovered from one of the first iterations of Russian drones from late 2022 used for attacks on Ukrainian cities. Still in its original casing, it looked much as it would in a shop, except that its settings had been glued in place against the vibrations of flight.
The next example they recovered a few months later, a Sony, had been stripped of its casing, leaving its lens and colorful wiring exposed. "You can already see that it’s quite a development compared to the first sample," a researcher said.
Such details helped the specialists judge how far an adaptation had progressed. You can tell a lot from the workmanship and the way it’s put together, one researcher explained. Specialists look for whether a part was improvised and attached to a drone or whether the drone was built to carry it — a sign that an experiment might be entering regular production.
Sometimes the clue is simpler. Sometimes there are letters "E" or "EE" on a drone’s tail fins, which the researchers believe stands for "experiment."
Other clues had been deliberately erased. The researchers showed antennae chips with their identifying markings scratched off, an effort, they said, to hide the supply chains bringing American and European electronics into Russian weapons despite sanctions .
"Removing markings does not make identification impossible," one researcher said. But it can turn what might have been a glance at a label into an investigation requiring specialized equipment and scarce time.
Reconstructing Russian technology can take months or even years, hampered by a lack of specialized equipment, resources, and expertise in Ukraine, and even with help from foreign partners, some electronic components remain nearly impossible to decipher without access to manufacturers’ proprietary information, which they are often unwilling to share.
Hanging in the stairwell was a completely intact Geran-3 that had reached the institution in 2025, well before this autumn’s urgent calls to accelerate production of interceptors capable of catching jet-powered drones . It had run out of fuel and landed in sand without detonating.
At its rear was a silver jet engine, roughly the size of a large melon, replacing the propeller-driven engine that gave earlier iterations of these drones their familiar moped sound. Faster flight and higher operating altitudes made jet-powered variants harder for mobile teams armed with machine guns to engage.
A message written on the black body of the drone in white marker read "greetings to Serhii from the engineers." The researchers believed it was addressed to Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to President Volodymyr Zelensky on defense technology. One researcher found a small consolation: the Russians had misspelled "engineers."
The same recovered aircraft had carried another indication of what was coming this summer beyond the jets: a camera and a mesh modem. "(That meant it was) able to send back video footage and receive control signals," a researcher said.
The researchers have a collection of the palm-sized mesh modems in their office, which they identify as Chinese-made. Mesh modems allow drones to relay video and control signals through one another, extending communications beyond an individual aircraft’s direct connection to its operator.
One researcher compared the technology to repeaters used to extend Wi-Fi coverage through a house. Here, the repeaters are other drones. This allows operators to change targets during flight and pursue even moving targets, such as trains , rather than simply sending a drone toward fixed coordinates, the researchers said.
The video feed allows the Russian operator to watch a civilian building draw closer while continuing to steer the drone toward it. He is far from the people inside but can see who he is targeting.
"If it is a civilian site, he knows what he is hitting and how," one researcher said.
The institution has possessed evidence of Russian attempts to implement jet engines and mesh relays since last year. But what a single recovered aircraft could not establish last fall was how soon or whether at all the same hardware would appear in large numbers.
Half a year later, it did. Since this summer, jet-powered drones have targeted Ukraine, particularly Kyiv, on a daily, constant basis, with the sound of explosions a regular occurrence in the capital throughout the day.
The researchers described the interval before an effective response to a modification became available as a "window of opportunity" for Russia. Once a change proved useful, Russia could concentrate resources on producing and deploying it while Ukraine was still developing a countermeasure.
"They don’t wait for us to come up with a countermeasure," one of the researchers said. The engineers attribute this problem mostly to scale. Russia likely has institutions similar to theirs, just several times larger with more resources.
The magnetometer the researchers recently recovered was still at an earlier stage of their investigation. "We can’t say for sure what it is, until we’ve completed all the necessary research," one said.
It might prove a modest refinement rather than a breakthrough. To become a widespread threat, its integration would need to be refined and its production scaled up.
But even a slight edge could be enough, helping more aircraft stay on course and tilting the balance of the war further in Russia's favor.
Jakub Laichter is a defense tech reporter at the Kyiv Independent. Before joining the Kyiv Independent, he reported from Eastern Ukraine as a freelance photojournalist since 2019.

title: Ukrainian partisans claim sabotage of military communications near major Moscow data center
description: "We are disabling the enemy's channels, disrupting command and control, and helping UAVs reach their targets," Atesh said.
content:
Agents of the Ukrainian partisan group Atesh said they disrupted Russian military communication lines around IXcellerate, one of Moscow's largest commercial data center operators, to interfere with Russian air-defense coordination and help Ukrainian drones reach their targets, the group said on Oct. 21.
"We are disabling the enemy's channels, disrupting command and control, and helping UAVs reach their targets," Atesh said .
The group claimed Russia's Defense Ministry uses infrastructure linked to IXcellerate for military communications and air-defense command systems, while concealing that traffic within civilian server networks.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim, and Atesh did not provide details on the extent or duration of the disruption. There has been no public confirmation from Russian authorities or IXcellerate that military communications were affected.
IXcellerate operates several data centers across Moscow and describes itself as a leading commercial data center operator in Russia. Its facilities host telecommunications and other digital infrastructure used by banks, retailers, and business customers.
The partisan group has previously claimed sabotage operations against Russian military and defense-linked infrastructure inside Russia, including attacks on railway and energy facilities.

title: Helsinki announces over $336 million for Ukraine to boost energy system, satellite development as Finnish PM visits Kyiv
description: "The main purpose of the visit is to show Finland's strong support for Ukraine as the war of aggression continues and the country prepares for the winter," the Finnish government said.
content:
Editor's note: This story is being updated.
Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo arrived in Kyiv on Oct. 22 to finalize a number of agreements aimed at supporting Ukraine in the coming winter.
Orpo's visit comes amid a flurry of peace diplomacy, as Russia's mass overnight strike on Ukraine's capital underscored Moscow's unwillingness to cease its attacks.
Kyiv and Helsinki signed seven agreements on Oct. 22, worth a total value of 330 euros (over $336 million), President Volodymyr Zelensky said after meeting with Orpo. The deals include support for Kyiv's energy infrastructure and greater access to Finland's satellite networks.
"We agreed to utilize more of Finland's satellite capabilities," the president said. "This is important for our defense and for the resilience of Ukraine."
The agreements involve Finnish satellite companies Nokia and ICEYE, Zelensky said.
Ukraine relies heavily on intelligence gathered via satellite networks from foreign partners to monitor Russian missile launches and prepare for Russian strikes. In a press release from ICEYE, the companies said they wanted to go even further by helping Ukraine architect its own sovereign satellite communications system .
Zelensky also said Finland would provide support for Ukraine's power grid as Moscow begins its annual winter assault on energy . Since the beginning of the full-scale war, Russia has heavily bombarded key heating and electrical facilities during the cold seasons, attempting to plunge the country into darkness and maximize civilian suffering.
"Thank you for your willingness to support our logistics and energy sectors — these are key targets for Russia, and the fact that we will have more locomotives, more energy equipment, and more resources to protect our energy infrastructure will be a significant boost," Zelensky said.
Finland's Foreign Ministry also announced on Oct. 22 that Helsinki will allocate 2 million euros ($2.2 million) in humanitarian aid to Ukraine.
"The main purpose of the visit is to show Finland's strong support for Ukraine as the war of aggression continues and the country prepares for the winter," the Finnish government said .
Orpo's agenda also included meetings with top Ukrainian officials and opportunities to "show support for the reforms needed for Ukraine's EU membership."
Orpo's visit came a day after U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21. Witkoff had met with Zelensky and European partners in Oslo a day earlier on Oct. 20 to discuss peace proposals to present to the Kremlin.
After meeting with Witkoff, Putin said Moscow was ready to resume negotiations. Zelensky later reiterated that Ukraine supported trilateral peace talks involving the U.S. and Russia.
Hours after Witkoff lavished praise on Putin during their meeting, Moscow launched several waves of ballistic missiles and drones at Kyiv, killing at least one person and injuring more than 20, according to Ukrainian officials.
Russia launched another ballistic missile attack on Kyiv in broad daylight on Oct. 22, while Orpo was visiting the capital. The Finnish prime minister visited a school damaged by a Russian drone during an earlier October attack, the Keskisuomalainen newspaper reported .
Finnish President Alexander Stubb has long called for Europe to play a bigger role in efforts to end Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine. He has said he would be ready to represent Europe in peace talks if asked.

title: Ukraine's court eases restrictions on ex-minister charged in major corruption case
description: Ukraine's High Anti-Corruption Court extended the other obligations of Herman Halushchenko, a former justice minister implicated in a major graft case, for two months.
content:
Ukraine's High Anti-Corruption Court on Oct. 22 allowed Herman Halushchenko, a former justice minister implicated in a major graft case, to remove his electronic monitoring bracelet.
The news comes months after Halushchenko was released from custody on bail of Hr 150 million ($3.4 million) in the summer. He had been held in pretrial detention since Feb. 17.
The court has not elaborated on why it allowed Halushchenko to remove his electronic monitoring bracelet.
It extended his other obligations for two months, including reporting a change of residence, not leaving Kyiv without permission, not contacting other suspects, and handing in his foreign passports.
Halushchenko was charged by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) as part of last year's probe into state nuclear energy monopoly Energoatom — the largest corruption investigation of Zelensky’s tenure.
He served as energy minister from 2021 to 2025 and was appointed justice minister in July 2025. He was dismissed as justice minister in November amid the scandal.
Halushchenko was detained on Feb. 15 while attempting to cross Ukraine's border. A prosecutor from the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) asked the court to remand him in custody, including over concerns that he might flee abroad.
The official has denied any wrongdoing and said he had no intention of fleeing Ukraine.
Halushchenko spent more than four months in pretrial detention as efforts to raise bail money continued. The fundraising later became part of another corruption scandal that hit the President's Office in August.
Iryna Mudra , then deputy head of the President's Office, and several other officials were charged with laundering Hr 150 million ($3.4 million) and transferring the funds through state-owned Sense Bank to post bail for Halushchenko.
Anti-corruption agencies asked the court to seize the Hr 150 million posted as bail for former minister Halushchenko, SAPO chief Oleksandr Klymenko said .
According to Klymenko, if the court approves the request, Halushchenko would be considered not to have paid bail and could be returned to custody.
The money could be transferred to Ukraine's Asset Recovery and Management Agency (ARMA), he added.
In a similar decision in September, the court allowed Andriy Yermak , former head of the President's Office, to remove his electronic monitoring bracelet for medical reasons.

title: Ukraine repatriates 252 bodies that Russia claims belong to Ukrainian soldiers
description: During previous repatriations, Russia at times returned the bodies of its own soldiers to Kyiv, with Ukrainian officials alleging the practice may have been aimed at avoiding compensation payments to Russian families or reflected a "negligent attitude toward their own people."
content:
Ukraine repatriated the bodies of 252 people who Russia claims were Ukrainian service members, the Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War (POWs) said on Oct. 22.
Ukrainian investigators and forensic experts will conduct examinations and identification procedures to determine the identities of the repatriated bodies, the statement read.
During previous repatriations, Russia at times returned the bodies of its own soldiers to Kyiv, with Ukrainian officials alleging the practice may have been aimed at avoiding compensation payments to Russian families or reflected a "negligent attitude toward their own people."
Kyiv thanked the International Committee of the Red Cross for facilitating the repatriation and expressed gratitude to Armed Forces personnel involved in transporting the remains to state institutions and coordinating their transfer to law enforcement authorities and forensic experts.
The return of fallen Ukrainians accelerated when peace talks resumed — but later stopped — in early 2025. Repatriation operations have become one of the few areas of continued humanitarian cooperation between Ukraine and Russia.
The latest repatriation follows a previous operation on August 13, when Ukraine brought home the bodies of 261 deceased individuals that Russia said could belong to Ukrainian service members.
While Ukraine regularly reports the number of repatriated bodies it receives from Russia, it does not publish data on the remains of Russian soldiers returned to Moscow.

title: Ukrainian military intelligence reveals new Russian cruise missile 'Filin'
description: Some parts of the missile are apparently 3-D printed, HUR said, while the electronic component stands out for the increased share of Chinese components.
content:
Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) announced details of a new Russian cruise missile called "Filin" and released a 3-D model of the missile alongside a list of components and electronics on its website on Oct. 22.
Russia began using the missile at the end of summer, HUR said , calling it a continuation of a Russian trend to build "inexpensive air attack means with jet propulsion and ground-based launch."
The missile is 3.5 meters long with a wingspan of 3 meters, ablte to carry either 50 kilogram or 100 kilogram warheads, HUR said. It can fly both at ultra-low altitudes and up to 6 kilometers (about 3.7 miles) high, at a top speed of 800 kilometers per hour (about 497 miles per hour), across a distance of 1,200 kilometers (about 745 miles), according to the agency.
Some parts of the missile are apparently 3-D printed, HUR said, while the electronic component base of the onboard equipment is similar to other Russian missiles, but stands out for the increased share of Chinese components. Besides Chinese components, the agency also said the "Filin" included 35 U.S.-made components.
The onboard equipment is manufactured by PLAZ LLC, which is also involved in producing the Harpiya drone, HUR said, while the engine is the Russian-made R500, produced by Reynolds LLC.
Russia uses cruise and ballistic missiles to strike at Ukraine, and increasingly at the country's energy infrastructure . On Oct. 22, Russian ballistic missiles and cluster munitions struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others.
"Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched by Russian 'humanists' on Kyiv since the evening," President Volodymyr Zelensky commented on the attack.
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Zelensky said Russia fired 21 missiles.

title: Ukraine to gain access to NATO procurement system for weapons, ammunition, Financial Times says
description: The arrangement might allow Ukraine to use NATO's existing procurement system and supplier network rather than negotiating each purchase independently.
content:
Ukraine will be able to purchase weapons, ammunition, and other military equipment through NATO's centralized procurement agency, potentially giving Kyiv faster and cheaper access to defense supplies, the Financial Times reported on Oct. 22.
Ukraine is entering a partnership with the NATO Support and Procurement Agency (NSPA), which handles procurement and logistical support for alliance members and partners, according to the Financial Times .
"It provides Ukraine with the ability to have a more structured framework to leverage a broad range of capabilities that we offer: procurement expertise, support services, and access to established industrial base," Jacqueline Borsboom, NSPA's director of support to operations, told the Financial Times.
The arrangement might allow Ukraine to use NATO's existing procurement system and supplier network rather than negotiating each purchase independently.
The NSPA also held an event in Kyiv last week attended by about 150 Ukrainian companies, explaining how manufacturers could register as eligible suppliers and compete for contracts, according to the Financial Times.
The new mechanism is separate from the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List ( PURL ), under which NATO allies and partners fund purchases of U.S.-made weapons and ammunition for Ukraine. More than $6 billion in military equipment has been funded through PURL since the initiative was launched in July 2025, according to NATO.
The agreement comes as Kyiv seeks to diversify and stabilize its access to military supplies amid growing uncertainty over U.S. support.
In recent weeks, Ukraine has reported disruptions to some U.S.-provided capabilities, including intelligence sharing and the Starshield satellite system used by Ukrainian forces. President Volodymyr Zelensky said after talks in Oslo this week that efforts were underway to resolve those issues.

title: Ukrainian troops infiltrate Russian rear through gas pipelines near Kupiansk, Khartiia says
description: The corps said more than 30 Russian soldiers were captured during the operation and Russian forces suffered more than 100 casualties.
content:
Ukrainian troops infiltrated the rear of Russian forces near Kupiansk in Kharkiv Oblast after moving about 15 kilometers (9 miles) through underground gas pipelines, Ukraine's National Guard’s 2nd Khartiia Corps said on Oct. 22.
The operation, code-named "Veles," was carried out by the 2nd Khartiia Corps together with other Ukrainian units, according to the corps.
Khartiia commander Brig. Gen. Ihor Obolienskyi said Ukrainian forces had studied how Russian troops were using underground routes and anticipated that they would try to exploit major gas pipelines running through Kharkiv Oblast.
"The Russians intended to use the gas routes to penetrate the rear of our forces. So we went underground ourselves," Obolienskyi said.
According to Khartiia, Ukrainian troops moved through the pipelines before combining the underground advance with operations above ground, including drone strikes.
The corps said more than 30 Russian soldiers were captured during the operation and that Russian forces suffered more than 100 casualties. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify those figures.
Obolienskyi said the aim was both to stop Russian troops underground and to undermine tactics they had been using on the ground and from the air.
"We anticipated the enemy's actions and mastered the tactics of conducting combat operations underground," he said.
Russian forces have used gas pipelines on several occasions to move troops covertly around the Kupiansk sector. In January, Ukrainian troops said they had stopped a Russian assault involving about 50 soldiers attempting to advance through the Soyuz gas pipeline.
More recently, Khartiia said, Russian troops retreating near Kupiansk used civilians as human shields , leading a group that included children and elderly people to the Shebelinka–Ostrogozhsk pipeline and forcing them inside the pipe toward Russian-held territory. Ukrainian troops said they did not open fire, because civilians were present
"When the battlefield became transparent, the war went underground," the corps said when it first announced the operation on Oct. 21.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 9, injure 57 across Ukraine as Kyiv hit by mass missile, drone attack
description: Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported.
content:
Russian attacks have killed at least nine people and injured 56 others across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia launched a mass missile and drone attack primarily targeting Kyiv, local authorities said on Oct. 22.
In Kyiv, Russian ballistic missiles struck transport and medical infrastructure in several waves overnight on Oct. 22, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others, according to city authorities.
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Kyiv was the main target of the attack. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 181 drones, including 87 jet-powered ones, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 32 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight others.
In Kharkiv Oblast , one person was killed and 15 others, including three children, were injured in Russian attacks on Kharkiv and 11 other settlements, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Sumy Oblast , one person was killed and four others injured in Russian drone attacks over the past day, the regional military administration said. Russian forces carried out nearly 60 attacks against 26 settlements across 14 communities.
In Donetsk Oblast , two people were killed, in Druzhkivka and Kramatorsk respectively, while nine others were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, local Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast , three people were killed and three others injured in Russian attacks on Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding district, local Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces launched 862 attacks against 48 settlements across the oblast over the past day.
In Chernihiv Oblast , one person was killed and another injured after Russian forces twice attacked an enterprise in Chernihiv with Banderol drones, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said. A Russian drone also struck an agricultural enterprise in Semenivka overnight, setting a warehouse and other buildings on fire.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,572,790 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 2,250 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,572,790 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 22.
The number includes 2,250 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,439 tanks, 25,594 armored combat vehicles, 165,641 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,447 artillery systems, 2,229 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,719 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,997 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: How Ukraine outmaneuvered Russian troops in Operation Vivaldi
description:
Editor's note: Most of the Ukrainian soldiers and commanders interviewed are identified by their callsigns, in accordance with military protocols.
