content:
Soldiers from the 21st Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment Kraken, who go by their callsigns "Cooper" and "Admin," prepare to launch a Darts mid-range strike drone in Kharkiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 8, 2026. (Lisa Bukreyeva / The Kyiv Independent)
Editor's note: Most of the Ukrainian soldiers and commanders interviewed are identified by their callsigns, in accordance with military protocols.
KHARKIV OBLAST — Ukrainian soldier Oleksandr had already narrowly survived crossing a mine-strewn field and a river in the crosshairs of Russian artillery when the swarm of first-person-view (FPV) drones began hunting him.
"If I'm honest, I was convinced they were going to kill us," the 37-year-old told the Kyiv Independent while chain-smoking cigarettes in the safety of his base in Kharkiv Oblast .
"I was already like, 'everyone goodbye, I love you all, everything is good,' but (the commanders were saying) on the radio, 'don't even think about it, everything will be fine.'"
Oleksandr was part of Operation Vivaldi , which lasted until mid-October and, until recently, was a top-secret counteroffensive in the Lyman sector in the northern part of Donetsk Oblast .
By pushing forward this spring, Ukrainian brigades under the Third Army Corps aimed to improve defensive positions in the area, which is critical to holding on to the remaining Ukrainian-held strongholds in the Donbas ahead of the winter, multiple commanders who took part said.
As well as liberating 277 square kilometers (107 square miles) of land and 16 villages as of Oct. 14, the operation proved something potentially even more important — that on today's drone-saturated and largely stalemated front line, it's still possible for Ukraine's infantry to advance in significant numbers.
The first task was making it through a dense minefield. Survive that, and then there was the river to cross. Survive that, and there was a chance the village of Shandryholove could be liberated from Russian forces.
The first group of three soldiers that attempted the crossing barely made it, Battalion Commander Sergii Galchenko said. Two groups that followed were forced to turn back after setting off mines.
"The enemy couldn't figure out where we were."
Those that made it needed reinforcing as soon as possible, no easy task when the few wooden bridges crossing it were destroyed, and Russian drones and artillery monitored the area constantly.
The soldiers initially waded through the water, but used wood and logs to create a makeshift crossing, according to Galchenko.
"We had a very serious problem with logistics when it came to bringing in our own reinforcements," Galchenko, who goes by his callsign "Psycho," said at his command post not far from the front.
The best way to stay alive was to keep moving, not staying in one place long enough for Russian drones and artillery to zero in on their positions.
"The enemy couldn't figure out where we were," Galchenko said.
Galchenko's battalion was assigned to enter Shandryholove from the south and move northward, clearing the central street as they went.
Two tactics proved vital — using drones wherever possible, and using a blockade tactic whereby infantry sneaked behind Russian lines to isolate Moscow's troops from the rear and block their escape.
Taking Shandryholove — a village only 0.17 square kilometers (0.066 square miles) in size — took more than a month.
"The enemy heavily mined (the area), abnormally heavily, because it understood that it couldn't stop us any other way," Galchenko said.
Anti-personnel mines were everywhere and accounted for 80% of casualties, Galchenko said, without disclosing the total number of Ukrainian casualties during the operation.
To minimize the risk to Ukrainian lives while advancing, the most important thing for the commanders was to rely on drones as much as possible, striking Russian positions ahead of the advancing troops. Soldiers on the ground would then go in to look for survivors.
"We did everything we could to prevent the infantry from encountering the enemy there," Galchenko said.
Units of the 66th Brigade advanced northward along the treeline toward heavily mined Shandryholove. The village had long been destroyed by years of heavy fighting in the area.
Oleksandr, who goes by his callsign "Marine," was in the first group of three soldiers to enter.
It was eerily quiet at first. The trio cleared a building as instructed and were approaching a church when they were spotted likely by a Russian FPV drone. A swarm soon followed.
For around four hours, the trio ran in zig-zags through the ruins of the village in a desperate attempt to avoid the drones above, while trying to stick to the concrete streets to avoid the mines below.
All three survived, but were not unscathed — one drone slammed into a door that Oleksandr had slammed shut behind him, peppering them all with shrapnel and dealing each a concussion.
The challenge in liberating Shandryholove was that Russian troops had prepared an extensive underground defensive network, primarily utilizing basements.
With the houses mostly destroyed in the village, it was difficult to assess from drone footage whether there was a basement under all the rubble, according to a company commander of the 125th Heavy Mechanized Brigade, who goes by his callsign "Ed." He estimated that there were about 50 houses in Shandryholove.
Instead of storming straight into Shandryholove, the majority of Ukraine's troops advanced along the treelines around the village to cut off the Russian troops inside, according to Ed. He said that his 125th Brigade moved roughly in parallel with other Ukrainian units, including the 66th and 60th mechanized brigades, with one advancing at a time and the others then playing catch-up.
What helped initially was that Russian troops in the village had been worn out by the cold weather when the offensive began, with some appearing to have died from exposure, Ed said.
"This really played in our favor," he added.
Shandryholove was just one of many such tiny villages that needed to be liberated for the counteroffensive to succeed. In between them, Ukrainian forces advanced along treelines, continuously changing the timing and routes of assaults to keep Russia's troops guessing.
Sometimes the soldiers would move in the dead of night, wearing anti-thermal blankets, while on other days they would switch it up to the gray hour before sunrise or daytime, according to Ed.
The pace of advance varied day to day. Galchenko said that his soldiers from the 66th could advance two kilometers (1.2 miles) in a day, while sometimes it took four days to advance 200 meters.
The vanguard of the advance was made up of soldiers sent usually in pairs to conduct the blockade maneuver, sneaking behind enemy lines to block logistics and prevent Russian infantry from being reinforced or running away to the rear, according to "Judo," a battalion commander with the 60th Mechanized Brigade.
The dense spring foliage in the forest served as a double-edged sword. This helped the infantry hide from Russian drones, but also made it difficult for friendly drones to conduct reconnaissance of the area.
It was crucial for the infantry to serve as the "ears," letting their commanders know where they heard voices and movement.
Galchenko stressed that it was important to enter the Russian positions quietly so the Russian soldiers inside wouldn't have time to warn their higher-ups that the Ukrainians were advancing.
"They knew that the quieter we entered, the more chance that the enemy would not be able to pass on (the information) to his higher-ups."
"We knew that the quieter we entered, the greater the chance the enemy would not be able to pass on (the information) to his higher-ups that we are advancing," Galchenko said.
"Then we have more chance to advance without any (potentially dangerous) moments."
As the 66th and 125th brigades were working on liberating neighboring Shandryholove in spring, the 60th was tasked to move behind the smaller village of Derylove to the south to cut it off so another unit could retake it, Judo said. When trying to infiltrate, the objective was to establish a defensive line inside Russian-held territory by carefully sending in one group after another, he explained.
The commander told his unit that they should only open fire if they were fully certain that they could kill Russian soldiers, waiting until they got as close as five meters.
"The enemy was moving through what he believed was his territory, and our group let the enemy in and completely destroyed them," Judo said.
"Their bodies were then camouflaged, in order for the enemy not to detect our group by finding the bodies of its soldiers from drones."
The soldiers would try to penetrate five kilometers (3.1 miles) into the Russian rear. He admitted that 30 to 40 percent of the time the soldiers would still be spotted by drones, then had to shoot the drones down themselves or rely on their unit to deploy countermeasures remotely.
Despite the risks, Judo said the operation went successfully, with the unit taking "minimal" casualties. He believes that there would have been many more casualties if the positional war had continued and his unit had remained on the defensive.
Russian troops responded differently to the Ukrainian offensive each day. Russia could react with an extremely heavy barrage of artillery and drone strikes, and by scattering mines, but it could also suddenly go quiet for a couple of days, according to Ed.
Stepping on a mine was the most common cause of injury, followed by FPV strikes, and then gunshot wounds, Ed said.
"On one day there could be up to two mine blasts, and then three days without any," Ed said.
Evacuation proved to be difficult, and the mines that injured advancing troops were also a threat to those that tried to rescue them. They were difficult to spot in the long grass that had appeared with the arrival of spring.
Ed recalled one incident when a soldier was dragging a wounded comrade on a stretcher when it struck a mine, killing the wounded man.
Much has been made of the rapid advances in unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) and their potential for evacuations on the battlefield, but during Operation Vivaldi, their slow speed made them prime targets for Russian drones, according to several commanders.
"If Russia sees a UGV, then I will say that there is a very high probability — 90% — that it will try to hit it," Galchenko said.
Galchenko recalled one incident when six Ukrainian soldiers were running across a field to assault a forested area when they were attacked with about 35 fiber-optic FPV drones, 12 fixed-wing Molniya drones, and heavy artillery over the course of two hours.
One appeared to have been killed outright and the other five were injured, one so severely that commanders monitoring the assault via a drone feed thought he was dead. When he regained consciousness, a UGV was sent in to bring him back without the need to send another soldier into an area already the target of so much Russian fire.
After struggling aboard, the wounded soldier made it around 1,500 meters away from the front line when a Russian drone struck, killing him.
Away from the fighting on the ground, another critical aspect of Operation Vivaldi was Ukraine's middle-strike drone capability, which hammered Russian logistics about 200 kilometers (124 miles) away.
For the 21st Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment Kraken, the targets included ammunition depots, repair bases, and fuel storage sites in occupied territories of Luhansk Oblast, according to "Dolyna," one of the unit's high-ranking commanders.
He linked the quieter days mentioned by Ed to successful strikes on Russian ammunition depots which, at least temporarily, deprived Russian artillery of shells.
Perhaps more crucially, these strikes helped deprive Russian infantry of the basic things they needed to survive — food, water, and ammunition.
"(Russian troops) were demoralized," Dolyna said at a middle-strike drone launch site in Kharkiv Oblast.
"It's hard to stay motivated when you are cold, hungry, and have nothing to keep you warm."
Operation Vivaldi had retaken 277 square kilometers (107 square miles) of territory, including 16 settlements, as of Oct. 14, according to the Third Army Corps. The unit claimed that Russian forces had suffered around 8,000 personnel losses, with over 250 soldiers captured by Ukraine as of this month. The Kyiv Independent couldn't independently verify the claimed battlefield figures.
Ukraine's casualty ratio compared to Russia's has been one to seven, with the majority of Ukrainian losses being injuries while Russia faced more fatalities, Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, the corps' commander, claimed during a briefing, as cited by Ukrainian media Hromadske.
When announcing the end of the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi, Biletskyi said, "four seasons of 'Vivaldi' are over, but the music continues."
Commanders said in early October that they believe that Ukraine has already achieved its main objective of the counteroffensive and expect the pace of the counteroffensive to gradually slow, particularly with the arrival of winter.
"(Going on the offensive) is in our blood," Judo said.
"We don't have any intention of withdrawing or retreating. Our only goal is to fight for our territory."

While reporting on an ongoing operation such as this one is difficult due to OPSEC concerns, what allows us, as local reporters, to tell their story in depth is gaining the commanders' and soldiers' trust. My goal has always been to shed light on the reality on the ground and to tell the stories as humanly as possible, because assaulting in the current drone-dominated phase of the war can be extremely deadly.
No matter how difficult the situation gets in Ukraine, we will continue to do our best to report from these front-line regions and provide a reliable window into the war. Please consider supporting our reporting , which is available without a paywall thanks to the support of our members.

title: Ukrainian forces reportedly strike Moscow Oblast weapons plant
description: Ukrainian forces struck a weapons plant in Serpukhov, Moscow Oblast, overnight on Oct. 22, monitoring channels reported.
content:
Ukrainian forces struck a weapons plant in Serpukhov, Moscow Oblast, overnight on Oct. 22, monitoring channels reported.
Eyewitnesses claimed that drones followed by missiles struck the site, known as the 75th Arsenal, according to independent Russian outlet Astra.
The site produces weapons and ammunition for the Russian army and also repairs Russian military equipment, according to the channel.
The facility has been sanctioned by Ukraine, the U.S. , and the EU for its role in Russia's war.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that 630 drones headed towards Moscow Oblast, claiming that the majority were intercepted, with 163 destroyed as they approached the city of Moscow.
In the Voronovskoye settlement, which is administratively part of Russia's capital city, two people were injured as a result of the attack, Sobyanin added.
Reports could not be immediately verified by the Kyiv Independent.
Earlier in the night, Ukrainian drones struck the Russian city of Lipetsk , according to monitoring channels.
Multiple explosions were reported in the city, and a residential building was allegedly struck, monitoring channel ExileNova Plus wrote.

title: Explosions, fires reported amid overnight Ukrainian drone attack on Lipetsk, Russia
description: Ukrainian drones struck a multi-story building in Lipetsk and caused multiple explosions around the city, according to Ukrainian monitoring channels. Eyewitness footage from the scene appears to show low-flying Ukrainian drones and fires lighting up the night sky.
content:
Ukrainian forces struck the Russian city of Lipetsk in an overnight drone attack on Oct. 22, according to monitoring channels.
Ukrainian drones struck a multi-story building in Lipetsk and caused multiple explosions around the city, according to Ukrainian monitoring channel ExileNova+.
Eyewitness footage from the scene appears to show low-flying Ukrainian drones above Lipetsk and fires lighting up the night sky.
The Kyiv Independent cannot independently verify the targets and extent of the damage of the attacks at the time of publication.
Lipetsk, 335 kilometers (208 miles) east of the Ukrainian border, has a population of around 500,000 and is home to the Novolipetsk Steel Plant. The massive plant accounts for roughly 20% of Russia's total crude steel output and is the nation's largest steel plant.
The attack damaged the windows and facades of multiple residential buildings around the city, according to Lipetsk Regional Governor Igor Artamonov. A clinic, closed at the time, was also damaged, Artamonov said.
Ukrainian forces have previously targeted Lipetsk in similar drone attacks.
On July 21 , Ukrainian drones hit the Novolipetsk Steel Plant and Lipetsk CHPP-2, a combined heat and power plant, causing fires.
As Moscow intensifies air attacks against Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure, Kyiv has responded by targeting key facilities across Russia supplying its armed forces.
On Oct. 16, Ukrainian forces struck an oil terminal, a data center, and a bridge in a large-scale overnight attack on St. Petersburg. Ukrainian drones have also disrupted air traffic in and out of Moscow in multiple operations in October.

title: Deadly Russian missile strike on Kyiv used cluster warheads, hours after Putin-Witkoff meeting
description: Among the injured people are four children, one of whom has been hospitalized, the State Emergency Service reported.
content:
The scene after a Russian ballistic missile struck Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 22, 2026. (Chris Occhicone / The Kyiv Independent)
Russian ballistic missiles and cluster munitions struck transport and medical infrastructure in Kyiv in several waves overnight on Oct. 22, killing at least one person and injuring 24 others, according to Ukrainian officials, only hours after U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff visited Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg.
The Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office reported these numbers in the morning, saying Russia had struck across Holosiivskyi, Obolonskyi, Pecherskyi, Svyatoshynskyi and Dnipro dsitricts in Ukraine's capital.
Among the injured are four children, one of whom has been hospitalized, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said .
"Last night, the Russians used, among others, three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads against Kyiv. The peculiarity of these missiles is that they explode in the air, hitting the target, and hit everything around within a diameter of 400 meters," President Volodymyr Zelensky said .
"Three waves of ballistic strikes were launched by Russian 'humanists' on Kyiv since the evening," Zelensky commented on the attack earlier.
During a meeting with Putin in St. Petersburg, Witkoff lauded Putin — wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes in Ukraine — as a "humanitarian."
Russian forces launched a mass combined attack overnight with Iskander-M, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles, as well as 210 drones of various types, including 110 jet-powered drones, the Air Force reported. Zelensky said Russia fired 21 missiles. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 181 drones, including 87 jet-powered ones, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 32 locations, while debris from intercepted targets fell at eight others.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that the Iskander missiles carried a K5 cluster munitions warhead.
"This warhead explodes above the ground and is specifically designed to cause maximum damage to people and equipment in an area of ​​400 by 400 meters," Beskrestnov said.
"This strike was not carried out with a military purpose. The goal was to destroy part of the old city and injure as many people as possible," he added.
Zelensky said one of the missiles struck Pechersk, in Kyiv's historic center, in an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra and the Sviato-Vvedensky Monastery. Buildings belonging to the monastery, residential buildings, shops, cafes and other civilian infrastructure were damaged, he said.
"There was not even theoretically any military facility nearby," Zelensky said. "It was a deliberate choice of weapon, a deliberate choice of the area of use, a deliberate attempt to inflict as many casualties and as much damage on civilians as possible."
Zelensky reported two people were killed and 34 injured, including five children, in Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast as a result of the attacks.
A source in Ukraine's energy sector speaking on condition of anonymity told the Kyiv Independent that Russia targeted energy infrastructure in the capital, particularly substations.
Zelensky said Russia had carried out more than 170 strikes on important Ukrainian energy facilities since Oct. 11, despite Ukrainian forces intercepting many of the drones and some of the missiles used in the attacks.
The capital is particularly vulnerable as it is reliant on thermal and cogeneration plants that are exposed to enemy strikes, while substations that connect it to generation sources, including nuclear plants in western Ukraine, are protected against drones but not against ballistic missiles.
DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company, announced around midday that emergency power outages were in place on the Holosiivskyi District.
Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground first reported power and Wi-Fi outages in parts of the city after a wave of ballistic missile strikes at around 3:34 a.m.
In the Dniprovskyi District, a car service station and a house were damaged late on Oct. 21 after the two sites were struck, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko .
"In the same district, debris also hit another house," he said . "There may be people trapped under the rubble."
At around 2 a.m. local time on Oct. 22, Russian attacks on Kyiv continued, filling the sky with the sounds of explosions.
In the Darnitsky District, also on the left bank of the Dnipro River that cuts through the city of 3 million, missiles hit near a transportation infrastructure facility. "I was at home, in my private house," said Vladyslav, a resident of Kyiv living near one of the strikes. "When the explosion happened, our windows were blown out. Then we saw a terrifying glow outside; we ran out and saw a house on fire, and heard people screaming.
"Fortunately, we managed to rescue a man and his wife who were inside the burning house. It's a stroke of luck that neighbors were nearby to help save these people."
Ballistic missiles again targeted Kyiv at around 3:00 a.m. local time, with at least 13 explosions rocking the city in less than eight minutes, the Kyiv Independent's Chris York said.
Following a series of explosions, the Kyiv City Military Administration said that a building housing a medical facility was damaged in the city's Pecherskyi District.
"All I see is broken windows on the floor, my neighbors are screaming, going out of their houses, and all they can do is just pray," Heorhii Rezhenko, a 26-year-old resident of Pecherskyi District, told the Kyiv Independent.
"In Europe, in the democratic world, everybody knows what happened here. The people know what happened, ... but they, for now, I think, can do nothing to stop it. Maybe all that I can say is please do something to stop it," Heorhii said.
"I am just very tired, because it was a very difficult day. But we will have more of these days."
Klitschko later confirmed that a paramedic station in the district was damaged, where six ambulances were also wrecked. Videos posted to social media suggest an Epicenter home improvement store in the Obolon District was destroyed.
The Museum of Ukrainian Diaspora, a branch of the Museum of Kyiv History, was also damaged in the attack, the museum said . Windows were blown out and the building's facade and roof were damaged. No one was injured, but the museum said it would remain closed for several days while repairs were carried out.
"In the Sviatoshynskyi District, a fire broke out inside a restaurant as a result of the enemy attack," the Kyiv City Military Administration added.
A further ballistic missile warning was issued in Kyiv around 12:30 p.m.
The latest attack comes as Russian forces continue to intensify missile and drone campaigns against Kyiv, a city the size of Berlin.
On the city's crucial Southern Bridge, transit infrastructure for the Kyiv Metro was damaged as a result of Russian strikes, Klitschko said.
The Military Administration also said that traffic in the direction from the right bank to the left bank has been restricted on the bridge.
The DSNS later reported that a monastery in the Pecherskyi District was damaged in the Russian attack as well.
The strikes on Kyiv on the night of Oct. 21 came after shows of support for trilateral peace negotiations by both President Volodymyr Zelensky and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"We hope that Russia—which has stated many times that it is ready for a meeting in one format or another—will follow through," Zelensky said.
As Kyiv was under red alert from the incoming ballistic missiles late on Oct. 21, around the world in Washington, D.C., U.S. President Donald Trump said that a deal to "settle the war" is "maybe now the closest we've been," in a roundtable conference.
Earlier on Oct. 21, a Russian drone attack on Kyiv killed at least two people and injured two others in the morning.
On Oct. 20, Russian drones repeatedly struck Kyiv, damaging a hospital in Solomianskyi District and another medical facility in Holosiivskyi District, injuring 12 people, according to local authorities. That morning, three people were killed , and four people were injured after a Russian drone struck early-morning commuter traffic.
The U.N. Human Rights Office reported in early October that an average of more than 400 civilians were killed or injured every week in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, a 55% increase from the same period in 2025.

title: German military classifies threat of Russian sabotage as 'significant' for first time, German media reports
description: Reviewing internal documents from Germany's armed forces, German media reports that this is the military's second-highest threat classification.
content:
For the first time, Germany's military now classifies Russian sabotage threats against its troops and facilities as "significant," German news outlet Sueddeutsche Zeitung reported on Oct. 21.
Reviewing internal documents from Germany's armed forces, Suddeutsche Zeitung reports that this is the military's second-highest threat classification. "We are noting that we face a ​significant sabotage threat overall for [Germany's armed forces]" said a defense ministry spokesperson, according to Reuters.
According to Suddeutsche Zeitung, the new classification was spurred by the discovery of an explosives-laden drone near the Wunstorf ⁠air base in Lower Saxony in September, as well as "sabotage incidents involving naval vessels." Previously, Germany officially accused Moscow of attempting to carry out a drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport in early August. Whereas the target of the Leipzig sabotage attempt was a Ukrainian plane, the apparent sabotage attempt at the Wunstorf ⁠air base marked the first time Germany's military was directly targeted. At German armed forces facilities, security measures will be increased under the new threat level, a defense ministry spokesman said. Germany's reclassification of Russian threats comes as experts warn Russia is testing how far it can push Europe without triggering open war — from drones crossing NATO airspace to sabotage and cyberattacks across the continent. Europe has strengthened its defenses since 2022, but key gaps remain, including in air defense, communications, intelligence, and joint command, experts say.
On Oct. 5, Martin Jaeger, head of Germany's foreign intelligence service, told lawmakers that Germany is in a "shadow war" with Russia and risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Moscow.
On Oct. 18, Lithuanian authorities thwarted an attempted arson attack on a company storing Starlink satellite communications equipment.
Denmark's intelligence service representative told Reuters on Oct. 7 that Russia has stepped up efforts to disrupt Danish companies involved in supplying weapons to Ukraine.

title: New Poland-Ukraine dispute looms as local authorities move to honor UPA military leader
description:
Warsaw has denounced Lviv Oblast authorities' plans to honor the World War II-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and its military leader, Roman Shukhevych.

The move signals a fresh rift in the already strained Kyiv-Warsaw ties just days after President Volodymyr Zelensky said the relations had finally improved.

The council of the western Ukrainian region adopted decrees on Oct. 20 symbolically declaring 2027 as the Year of the UPA, the Year of Shukhevych, and the Year of Oleh Olzhych, a Ukrain
content:
The monument to Roman Shukhevych, the military leader of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), is pictured on the 74th anniversary of his death at the Shukhevych Museum. (Anastasiia Smolienko / Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
Warsaw has denounced Lviv Oblast authorities' plans to honor the World War II-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) and its military leader, Roman Shukhevych.
The move signals a fresh rift in the already strained Kyiv-Warsaw ties just days after President Volodymyr Zelensky said the relations had finally improved.
The council of the western Ukrainian region adopted decrees on Oct. 20 symbolically declaring 2027 as the Year of the UPA , the Year of Shukhevych, and the Year of Oleh Olzhych, a Ukrainian poet and political activist.
Poland’s charge d'affaires in Kyiv, Piotr Lukasiewicz , immediately reacted by saying that "glorifying the UPA and criminal figures runs counter to European values and the strategic and neighborly relations between Ukraine and Poland." Poland’s defense and foreign ministries also decried the decision, saying it "does not build mutual trust."
The episode marks another chapter in the Ukrainian-Polish dispute over the legacy of the UPA, a resistance organization that fought for Ukrainian independence from Soviet rule.
In Poland, the group is primarily remembered for its role in the 1943-1945 Volyn massacres — killings of tens of thousands of Poles in what is today western Ukraine, then under Nazi occupation.
Thousands of Ukrainians were killed in retaliatory attacks, making the massacres one of the most painful chapters in the two nations' shared history.
Shukhevych was a Ukrainian nationalist and the supreme commander of the UPA from 1943 until his death during a gunfight with Soviet security forces near Lviv in 1950.
As Warsaw sharply denounced the Lviv Oblast authorities' decision, the government in Kyiv moved to distance itself from the step to avoid derailing the restoration of ties with its western neighbor.
"The recent decision by the Lviv Oblast Council... is counterproductive to our current efforts to further develop Ukrainian-Polish relations and resolve contentious issues amid Russia's full-scale aggression," Ukraine’s foreign ministry said in a statement shared with journalists.
Shukhevych’s legacy remains deeply contentious in Ukrainian-Polish relations, with historians in both countries offering differing views on it.
The UPA was established in 1942 as a military arm of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists — specifically, the faction led by Stepan Bandera, OUN-B. Shukhevych officially assumed the leadership of the UPA in November 1943, several months after the start of the initial wave of the Volyn massacres.
Poland's Institute of National Remembrance has named Shukhevych "an architect" of the Volyn massacres and "co-founder of collaborationist units operating alongside Germany." Shukhevych was one of the commanders of the Nachtigall Battalion — a short-lived unit staffed by Ukrainians and organized by German military intelligence — in 1941.
In 1941, as Germany invaded the Soviet Union, the OUN-B leadership hoped Berlin would tolerate a Ukrainian state and proclaimed one in Lviv. Germany rejected it, arrested Bandera and other leaders, and cracked down on the organization.
Many Ukrainian historians debate the extent of Shukhevych's personal role in the Volyn massacres and point out that under Shukhevych's command, the UPA fought both Soviet and Nazi forces.
"Some Ukrainian historians have suggested that the order of ethnic cleansing in Volyn did not come directly from Shukhevych, but was an initiative of the local UPA leadership," Myroslav Shkandrij, a historian at the University of Manitoba, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The problem, however, is that Shukhevych has become a symbol, and symbols, whether they represent heroism or villainy, are resistant to facts."
Kyiv and Warsaw also hold different perspectives on the Volyn massacres themselves.
The Polish parliament recognized the killings as a genocide against Poles committed by Ukrainian nationalists, while Kyiv views them as a two-sided tragedy.
Olesia Isaiuk, a historian at the Center for Research on the Liberation Movement, a Ukrainian research institution, frames the Volyn massacres as part of a broader Polish-Ukrainian conflict, stretching back to the Ukrainian war of independence in the wake of World War I.
"For the Ukrainian side, the Volyn event is… one of the biggest and most tragic parts of the continued Ukrainian-Polish conflict… And Roman Shukhevych is a national hero for Ukrainians because he fought against the Nazis and the Soviets," Isaiuk told the Kyiv Independent.
But as Skhandrij notes, real history often evades easy classification.
"The histories of the OUN, UPA, and Shukhevych are complex. They include both heroic and shameful episodes," he says.
"It is not easy to tell the whole truth in a simple narrative, and even more so during wartime."
The Polish envoy in Kyiv noted that while the leaders in Kyiv and Warsaw made progress on resolving historical issues, "irresponsible local officials are meanwhile undermining the relations we have worked to build."
Earlier this year, tensions erupted between the two countries when Zelensky conferred a title on a military unit in honor of the UPA.
In response, Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelensky of Poland's highest honor, the Order of the White Eagle, awarded by his predecessor.
After a period of tensions, Zelensky said on Oct. 18 that bilateral relations had finally improved. The latest episode risks reversing that progress.
"Such a decision does not build mutual trust between nations but strengthens divisions. It is necessary for the Ukrainian authorities to distance themselves from this position," Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Oct. 20.
Ukraine's foreign ministry has done just that, sharing a statement that criticized the Lviv Council decision as “counterproductive to our current efforts to further develop Ukrainian-Polish relations and resolve contentious issues.”
The ministry stressed that the decision was taken at the regional level by council members who did not consult the foreign ministry or the central government.
"At the same time, we call on the Polish side to refrain from rash steps that could undermine the normalization of our relations."
The proposals on the UPA, Shukhevych, and Olzhych were put forward by the head of the regional council's cultural committee, Sviatoslav Sheremeta.
"This is our history, our heroes, and we must duly honor their memory. I thank the councilors for their support," Sheremeta said, according to the local outlet Sokal Voice .
In response, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said on Oct. 21 that he had requested that Sheremeta be placed on Poland's list of undesirable persons, potentially barring him from the entire Schengen area for five years .
The developments also come a year before Poland's parliamentary elections, in which the coalition led by centrist Prime Minister Donald Tusk faces a growing challenge from right-wing and far-right parties.
Historical grievances play an increasingly important role in Polish public debate ahead of the elections, with right-wing forces adopting a tougher line on Ukraine.
And the dispute also arrives at a critical time for Kyiv.
"Additional foreign policy challenges are the last thing Ukraine needs today," says Sergiy Solodkyy, director of the New Europe Center think tank in Kyiv.
"At a time when Kyiv is engaged in a difficult dialogue with the United States and European support is becoming even more critical, Ukrainians have a particular interest in preserving a spirit of partnership with all EU member states," he told the Kyiv Independent.
As Ukraine's relations with neighbors were finally beginning to move in a positive direction, "opening another dispute would clearly run counter to Ukraine’s strategic interests," the expert said.
And Zelensky's deputy chief of staff, Iryna Vereshchuk, warned: "The only winner from the tension in Ukraine-Poland relations is Russia."
Martin Fornusek is an assistant editor at the Kyiv Independent. Until recently, Martin held the role of foreign affairs reporter specializing in international and regional politics, history, and disinformation. Based in Lviv, Martin often reports on international politics, focusing on developments related to Ukraine and Russia. His career in journalism began in 2021 after graduating from Masaryk University in Brno, Czechia, earning a Master's degree in Conflict and Democracy Studies. Martin has been invited to speak on Times Radio, France 24, Czech Television, and Radio Free Europe. He speaks English, Czech, and Ukrainian.

title: Ukraine war latest: Zelensky supports resuming trilateral peace talks with US, Russia after Putin claims Kremlin readiness
description:
Key developments on Oct. 21:

 * Zelensky supports resuming trilateral peace talks with US, Russia after Putin claims Kremlin readiness
 * 'Everything was in ruins' — At least 2 killed, 2 injured in Russian drone attack on Kyiv
 * Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashes in Kaliningrad Oblast during training exercises, Moscow says
 * Lockheed Martin delegation meets Ukraine's defense chiefs in Kyiv amid severe Patriot shortage
 * Denmark guarantees $113 million loan for Ukrainian defense company Fire P
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 21 that Ukraine will support trilateral peace talks with the U.S. and Russia after Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed the Kremlin is ready to resume negotiations. "We will support proposals regarding a ceasefire, ending the war , addressing the energy sector—and other sectors as well—as well as humanitarian initiatives, the return of prisoners, and the return of diplomats," Zelensky told reporters. Zelensky's statement to journalists follows Putin meeting with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff on Oct. 21. During their meeting, Putin and Witkoff discussed a "specific framework" by which the trilateral talks could take place, according to Russian state media. "We see that (U.S.) President (Donald) Trump is quite sincere and consistent in his wish to facilitate a peaceful resolution and to set everything on the path toward a peace settlement," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media.
Witkoff's visit to St. Petersburg follows his Oct. 20 meeting with Zelensky and European allies in Oslo to discuss peace proposals to pass along to the Kremlin. Witkoff described both the Oslo and St. Petersburg meetings as "constructive," but said "there is still important work left to do." Zelensky confirmed that Kyiv received briefings of the Kremlin's readiness to meet.
A Russian drone attack on Kyiv killed at least two people and injured two others on the morning of Oct. 21, local authorities said.
An air raid alert sounded in Kyiv at around 5:20 a.m. local time as drones approached the capital, which has faced an unrelenting barrage of Russian drone attacks this fall.
In the Sviatoshynskyi District, a Russian drone struck a 24-story residential building, sparking a fire on the 20th floor. At least two people were killed, and two others were hospitalized with injuries, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Nataliia, a 63-year-old resident who requested anonymity beyond her first name for security reasons, said she heard drones flying over her neighborhood throughout the night until she heard an "incredibly powerful explosion."
The whole building shook, Nataliia recalled. She only realized that her building had been hit when she checked the group chat with her neighbors, in which she was instructed to go outside because part of it had caught on fire.
"When I finally got outside, I saw the whole horror of it — everything was in ruins," Nataliia said.
In the Desnianskyi District, drone debris fell on a car, while in the Solomianskyi District, debris landed in an open area, Klitschko said.
A Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashed during a scheduled training flight in Kaliningrad Oblast, a heavily militarized Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea bordering Poland and Lithuania , the Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 21.
Moscow has not elaborated on the reason for the plane crash. The Russian Defense Ministry said the crew ejected and evacuated by a ground search-and-rescue team, without disclosing whether they were injured.
The jet crashed near the town of Chernyakhovsk, about 90 kilometers (about 56 miles) east of Kaliningrad, according to the pro-Kremlin Mash Telegram channel. It said that both pilots were injured and were taken to a military hospital.
The Su-30 is a two-seat, multirole fighter for air-to-air and air-to-ground missions. Moscow said that the jet was not carrying any weapons at the time of the crash.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara and Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi met with a delegation from the U.S. defense company Lockheed Martin, the Defense Ministry said on Oct. 21, as Ukraine faces an increasingly severe shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles.
The meeting came as Russia intensifies its ballistic missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and elsewhere across Ukraine, posing an immense challenge to Ukrainian air defenses. Lockheed Martin manufactures PAC-3 interceptors used by the Patriot air-defense system, which can engage Russian ballistic missiles, and has supported the U.S. move to grant Ukraine a Patriot production license.
The Defense Ministry said in its statement that Khmara and Drapatyi discussed "the importance of stable arms deliveries and further cooperation" with the Lockheed Martin delegation, led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics.
The meeting also included discussions to scale up the supply of PAC-3 interceptors in response to the Russian ballistic missile threat, according to the Defense Ministry.
Denmark will guarantee a 750 million Danish kroner ($113 million) loan to the Danish subsidiary of Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, the Danish government announced on Oct. 21.
The guarantee highlights Denmark's role in helping Ukraine expand defense production beyond its borders as Russian attacks threaten domestic manufacturing and supply chains.
The loan is backed by the Danish state as Russia's war against Ukraine prevents the company from borrowing on ordinary terms in Denmark. The funding will be channeled through Denmark’s Export and Investment Fund (EIFO).
"Denmark strongly supports the Ukrainians' fight for freedom," Business and Industry Minister Martin Lidegaard said. He added that hosting a Ukrainian defense company in Denmark would bring "knowledge and production, as well as partnerships" that could strengthen Ukraine, Denmark’s defense industry and a more independent Europe.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said locating Ukrainian defense production outside Ukraine would make it more resilient to Russian attacks.

title: Russia hits gas production facility in Kharkiv Oblast, critical infrastructure in Dnipro, leaving 30,000 consumers without power
description: Acting Naftogaz CEO Serhii Fedorenko said that Russia had struck the company's facilities more than 400 times since the beginning of 2026 — twice as often as during the same period last year.
content:
Russian attacks struck critical infrastructure in Dnipro, causing power outages, and a gas production facility owned by state energy giant Naftogaz in Kharkiv Oblast on Oct. 21, local authorities reported.
The latest attacks come as Ukraine heads into winter, when increased energy consumption puts additional pressure on an energy system still struggling with the damage caused by years of Russian strikes.
Russian forces attacked critical infrastructure in the regional capital of Dnipro at around 1:30 p.m. local time, leaving 30,000 consumers without power in the Synelnykove and Pavlohrad districts, as well as in the town of Samar, about 30 kilometers (20 miles) northeast of Dnipro, according to Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Governor Oleksandr Hanzha .
Hanzha did not specify which facility was targeted or the extent of the damage.
Earlier on Oct. 21, a Russian drone also struck a gas production facility operated by Naftogaz in Kharkiv Oblast .
"An enemy drone hit one of the installations at a production site," Naftogaz said . "Due to the security situation, it is currently impossible to assess the consequences of the strike."
Acting Naftogaz CEO Serhii Fedorenko said that Russia had struck the company's facilities more than 400 times since the beginning of 2026 — twice as often as during the same period last year.
The recent strikes were part of a wider Russian campaign targeting Ukraine's energy infrastructure. The Energy Ministry said facilities were targeted in Kyiv and Kyiv, Volyn, and Odesa oblasts, while more than 5,000 consumers in Volyn Oblast were left without electricity.
In Kyiv, emergency outages were introduced in parts of the Obolonskyi, Shevchenkivskyi, and Sviatoshynskyi districts following the attacks on Oct. 21, Ukraine's largest private energy company DTEK said. The company later said the situation had stabilized and Kyiv was returning to scheduled power cuts.
The New York Times reported on Oct. 2 that Ukrainian authorities had obtained what they described as a Russian Defense Ministry plan to cripple the grid in stages.

title: Stay or flee? Kyiv mothers torn on how to keep children safe as Russian attacks step up
description:
Anna Lodyhina, a mother of a 5-year-old, spent many nights on the cold floor of Kyiv's metro, driven there — like many others — by relentless Russian attacks. As her child slept, she watched over him, exhausted by the constant threat and lack of sleep.

This is just a glimpse of what Ukrainian mothers have been facing daily as Russia intensified its drone and missile campaign against Kyiv over the summer and early autumn.

Mothers are now confronted with the same question they faced almost five
content:
Nina Shkurba, a writer and mother, with her son Veniamin in the Osokorky neighborhood of Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 4, 2026. (Khrystyna Kulakovska / The Kyiv Independent)
Anna Lodyhina, a mother of a 5-year-old, spent many nights on the cold floor of Kyiv's metro, driven there — like many others — by relentless Russian attacks. As her child slept, she watched over him, exhausted by the constant threat and lack of sleep.
This is just a glimpse of what Ukrainian mothers have been facing daily as Russia intensified its drone and missile campaign against Kyiv over the summer and early autumn.
Mothers are now confronted with the same question they faced almost five years ago — to stay or to leave.
Many left for abroad at the onset of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, but returned to give their children the possibility of a childhood in their native Ukraine . But now, as Kyiv increasingly resembles cities closer to the front line, relocation has become a necessity for some.
Lodyhina, a journalist and art researcher who moved to Warsaw in March 2022 with her then-1-year-old son, said she never imagined leaving Kyiv before Russia's full-scale invasion.
"I never dreamed of emigration," she said. After two years, they returned to Kyiv.
But as Russian attacks intensified earlier this year, Lodyhina once again faced the question of whether to leave Kyiv. Living in a building without a shelter , she and her son were often forced to take refuge in the metro and sleep on its cold concrete floor amid mass strikes.
"The child slept, but I stayed awake the entire night in the metro," adds Lodyhina. With a constant lack of sleep, her health started to deteriorate, affecting her ability to focus.
She told the Kyiv Independent that she had been actively involved in volunteer work to support Ukraine's Armed Forces , but lamented that much of it stopped once the attacks intensified.
By the start of September, she had had enough. Lodyhina and her son moved to Lviv in western Ukraine to escape the never-ending terror.
"For the past three weeks, we have slept calmly. We can't get enough of it."
"For the past three weeks, we have slept calmly. We can't get enough of it; we go to bed early and still wake up late the next morning."
Despite a relative sense of tranquility in the weeks of September, reminders of war pierce any illusion of peace. While picking up her son from kindergarten, Lodyhina overheard him say he had never known life without war. His friend agreed with childlike excitement.
Her son knows the daily moment of silence — the nationwide pause at 9 a.m. to commemorate the fallen — and how to greet soldiers, she says.
As Russia continues changing its tactics, it is uncertain how long families will have to stay away from their homes in Kyiv. With winter approaching, many are also afraid of attacks on critical infrastructure that can leave the capital without heat, electricity, and water for days on end.
Lodyhina's winter preparations have been ongoing for a while now. In her new Lviv apartment, she made sure to check all the radiators and gas systems and bought a portable generator.
"I feel privileged to have a chance to relocate within the country," Lodyhina added. However, she told the Kyiv Independent that she never rules out the possibility of having to move abroad again if security and living conditions worsen in western Ukraine as well.
By October, this question is no longer theoretical, as drone attacks and air raid alerts grow more frequent in Lviv as well. Even western Ukraine is becoming less of a refuge from Russian aggression.
The turning point for Anna Ablitsova, 33, was a strike just a street away from her home. She recalls being in the kitchen while her 4-year-old son, Mykyta, was playing in the other room.
"He got really scared, started crying, ran, and put his arms around me. I got very nervous," Ablitsova told the Kyiv Independent. She notes that previous strikes, even nightly mass attacks, never affected her son this much.
When Mykyta started kindergarten, Ablitsova realized he was spending almost the entire day in an underground shelter .
"All these stories he tells me are about how (the children) were in shelters, and the teacher says, 'air raid alert, let's go to shelter,' and what kind of missile is flying their way," she says while wondering what sort of long-term repercussions such conditions will have on her son's mental health .
In August, Ablitsova and her husband began considering relocating from Kyiv amid increasingly frequent air raid alerts and drone attacks. The couple settled on Lutsk, a western city they had temporarily stayed in at the onset of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Lutsk is a five-hour drive from Kyiv, where Ablitsova and her husband work, where their family resides, and where a big part of their life remains. However, after experiencing just over a week of relative peace in Lutsk, it may prove hard to return to Kyiv .
"Now I'm a little afraid when we need to go to Kyiv. We promised to come for a birthday, but I haven't been there for a week and a half. Everything changes so quickly, and just a week ago, I lived there."
Despite having to move everything to Lutsk, at least for the next six months, Ablitsova is happy to see Mykyta no longer spending hours in the kindergarten shelter, speaking Ukrainian, and not sleeping in the hallway.
"Everyone here speaks Ukrainian. I have my child in the environment that I want him to be in, where he doesn't bring home some stupid Russian words from the kindergarten," adds Ablitsova, whose family was Russian-speaking but switched to Ukrainian on the very first day of Russia’s full-scale invasion.
But as in Lviv, the security situation in Lutsk is changing too. Weeks after the Kyiv Independent talked with Ablitsova, a Russian drone attack struck the city on Oct. 14, killing six civilians .
Leaving Kyiv amid relentless Russian attacks is not something every mother wants — or can — do.
Although many have decided to move to a safer place in Ukraine or abroad, some remain hopeful that the current difficulties will end.
"Safety is not the absence of a threat," Nina Shkurba, a 38-year-old writer, summarizes an idea developed by American psychotherapist Peter Levine.
Shkurba, along with her 9-year-old son and 16-year-old daughter, knows what it's like to be forced to leave Kyiv due to Russian aggression. Just two days after the start of the full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, she left Ukraine for the Spanish coastal city of Santander, but returned two and a half years later.
For now, she is determined to stay in Kyiv to keep the family united in their native home.
"I don't have that feeling that I need to run."
During her time in Spain, Shkurba wrote a book on the sense of belonging, which was then published in Ukraine. However, almost the entire printed supply was destroyed in August when a Russian attack struck her publisher . All that is left are the few copies in bookstores, she told the Kyiv Independent.
"I don't have that feeling that I need to run," she said, adding that going to their "dacha" — a seasonal home on the city's outskirts — helps the family recharge and find some peace.
But life in Kyiv is not the same as it was a mere few months ago. "September (was) very difficult in terms of anxiety. This is a new reality that we still have to get used to — that Kyiv feels like a front-line city ," says Shkurba.
"My son has been wanting to celebrate at the Blockbuster (shopping mall in Kyiv) all year; he was looking forward to it. But we canceled both our children's celebrations in the shopping centers because of the drone threat."
Shkurba adds that children, especially her teenage daughter, are aware of the worsening security situation.
As a precaution, Shkurba renews her and her children's Spanish documents in case they have to leave Ukraine again. It is not something she is considering now, but being prepared offers a sense of control in what seems like never-ending uncertainty about tomorrow.
No one can say for certain how long Russia's daily drone and missile campaign against Kyiv will continue. For over a month now, the air raid alert has been on for most of the day, with the city recording over 20 hours of alert on Sep. 30.
The city and its families endure, adjusting to the new alert system and avoiding places like shopping malls and train stations. Mothers who stayed in Kyiv or relocated elsewhere are victims of the same Russian terror that aims to paralyze daily life.
Despite feeling a sense of peace in Lviv, Lodyhina refuses to accept what is happening in Ukraine as the new norm.
Yevgeniya Doluda is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in journalism, politics, and history from City St. George’s University of London. Yevgeniya previously worked and volunteered with non-profit organizations in Europe and had her work published in RTL. In addition to Ukrainian, she also speaks Spanish and French.

title: Denmark guarantees $113 million loan for Ukrainian defense company Fire Point
description: The guarantee highlights Denmark’s role in helping Ukraine expand defense production beyond its borders as Russian attacks threaten domestic manufacturing and supply chains.
content:
Denmark will guarantee a 750 million Danish kroner ($113 million) loan to the Danish subsidiary of Ukrainian defense company Fire Point, the Danish government announced on Oct. 21.
The guarantee highlights Denmark’s role in helping Ukraine expand defense production beyond its borders as Russian attacks threaten domestic manufacturing and supply chains.
The loan is backed by the Danish state as Russia’s war against Ukraine prevents the company from borrowing on ordinary terms in Denmark. The funding will be channeled through Denmark’s Export and Investment Fund (EIFO).
"Denmark strongly supports the Ukrainians’ fight for freedom," Business and Industry Minister Martin Lidegaard said. He added that hosting a Ukrainian defense company in Denmark would bring "knowledge and production, as well as partnerships" that could strengthen Ukraine, Denmark’s defense industry and a more independent Europe.
Defense Minister Jeppe Bruus said locating Ukrainian defense production outside Ukraine would make it more resilient to Russian attacks.
"When Denmark supports the Ukrainian defense industry, the combat power of Ukraine’s defense increases," Bruus said. He added that production outside Ukraine would provide safer supply chains for critical defense equipment and technologies while creating opportunities for cooperation between Fire Point, Denmark’s Defense Ministry, and Danish companies.
Denmark announced in September 2025 that Fire Point would establish production of fuel for long-range missiles on Danish soil. The facility is expected to become operational by the end of 2027.
Fire Point is also expanding its European defense partnerships. In August 2026, the company signed agreements with more than a dozen European defense companies to integrate radar, guidance and other technologies into its Freyja missile defense project . The project aims to provide Ukraine with a domestic alternative to the U.S.-made Patriot air defense system .
EIFO CEO Peder Lundqvist said the fund is currently involved in almost 40 projects supporting Ukraine and cooperation between Ukrainian and Danish companies.
"The financing of Fire Point is a concrete example of how these efforts can be put into practice," Lundqvist stated.

title: Shares in one of Ukraine’s biggest farm companies fall to a two-year low
description: Trading in the company's stock was suspended on the Warsaw Stock Exchange on Oct. 20 after the price dropped 19.14% in a single day.
content:
The Ukrainian agricultural holding Astarta's shares fell to their lowest level in more than two years, raising questions about investor confidence in Ukrainian agribusiness.
Trading in the company's stock was suspended on the Warsaw Stock Exchange on Oct. 20 after the price dropped 19.14% in a single day. Financial Times market data showed Astarta shares fell a further 8% the following day.
The shares last traded at a similarly low level in September 2024, according to the Warsaw Stock Exchange .
The company's shares are now worth about half what they were in May when they topped 60 zloty ($15.45).
Other Ukrainian agricultural stocks also fell. On Oct. 20, the WIG-Ukraine index, which tracks Ukrainian stocks listed in Warsaw, declined 3.38%, while the broader WIG20 index fell 1.24%. Shares in Ukrainian milk producer IMC dropped 9.21%, while Ukrainian agro holdings Agroton, KSG Agro and Milkiland recorded smaller losses, according to Interfax-Ukraine .
The sharp drop comes as Astarta reports weaker financial results. For Astarta, whether the fall reflects a temporary reaction to a bad half-year or deeper doubts about the company’s outlook will depend on its next results and on conditions in Ukraine.
Astarta reported a net loss of 14.07 million euros ($15.8 million) in the first half of 2026, compared with a net profit of 42.27 million euros ($47.5 million) in the same period in 2025.
Revenue remained broadly unchanged at 226.5 million euros ($254 million). The loss came mainly from lower sugar and milk prices and higher logistics costs for its soybean business, which offset growth in crop production.
Astarta is a vertically integrated agricultural group with operations spanning crop production, sugar manufacturing, soybean processing and dairy farming. Listed on the Warsaw Stock Exchange since 2006, the company provides international investors with exposure to Ukraine’s agricultural sector.
Exports accounted for 62% of revenue, according to the company’s first-half 2026 financial report .

title: Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashes in Kaliningrad Oblast during training exercises, Moscow says
description: The Russian Defense Ministry said the crew was ejected and evacuated by a ground search-and-rescue team, without disclosing whether they were injured.
content:
A Russian Su-30 fighter jet crashed during a scheduled training flight in Kaliningrad Oblast, a heavily militarized Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea bordering Poland and Lithuania , the Russian Defense Ministry said on Oct. 21.
Moscow has not elaborated on the reason for the plane crash. The Russian Defense Ministry said the crew ejected and evacuated by a ground search-and-rescue team, without disclosing whether they were injured.
The jet crashed near the town of Chernyakhovsk, about 90 kilometers (about 56 miles) east of Kaliningrad, according to the pro-Kremlin Mash Telegram channel. It said that both pilots were injured and were taken to a military hospital.
The Su-30 is a two-seat, multirole fighter for air-to-air and air-to-ground missions. Moscow said that the jet was not carrying any weapons at the time of the crash.
Russia has had multiple instances of a aircraft crashing during training exercises, including ones that led to the death of crew members aboard. In September, a Russian Tu-95 aircraft crashed in Russia's Amur Oblast during training, killing six crew members and injuring one, the Kremlin-controlled Interfax news agency said on Sept. 29, citing the Russian Defense Ministry.
The crash also occurred amid escalating tensions between Russia and NATO over Kaliningrad , prompting Lithuania's Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas to call for troops to be deployed to the country's border with the Russian exclave.

title: Zelensky supports resuming trilateral peace talks with US, Russia after Putin claims Kremlin readiness
description: Zelensky's statement to journalists follows Putin meeting with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff on Oct. 21.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 21 that Ukraine will support trilateral peace talks with the U.S. and Russia after Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed the Kremlin is ready to resume negotiations. "We will support proposals regarding a ceasefire, ending the war , addressing the energy sector—and other sectors as well—as well as humanitarian initiatives, the return of prisoners, and the return of diplomats," Zelensky told reporters. Zelensky's statement to journalists follows Putin meeting with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff on Oct. 21. During their meeting, Putin and Witkoff discussed a "specific framework" by which the trilateral talks could take place, according to Russian state media. "We see that (U.S.) President (Donald) Trump is quite sincere and consistent in his wish to facilitate a peaceful resolution and to set everything on the path toward a peace settlement," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media.
Witkoff's visit to St. Petersburg follows his Oct. 20 meeting with Zelensky and European allies in Oslo to discuss peace proposals to pass along to the Kremlin. Witkoff described both the Oslo and St. Petersburg meetings as "constructive," but said "there is still important work left to do." Zelensky confirmed that Kyiv received briefings of the Kremlin's readiness to meet. "I do not yet know the final dates for this meeting," Zelensky said, though he stated talks would likely be held in November. "The agenda, naturally, is to end the war, bring peace closer, and—as I understand it—lay the groundwork for a meeting at the level of the leaders." Stressing security guarantees and reconstruction plans in peace negotiations, Zelensky said that it would be important for Ukraine's European partners to be included in the talks. While claiming the signs coming from the Kremlin were "positive," Zelensky also expressed weariness that Moscow would actually meet. "We hope that Russia—which has stated many times that it is ready for a meeting in one format or another—will follow through," Zelensky said. "In the past, things have changed or been called off. We shall see how it goes this time."
The diplomatic push comes as Russia has escalated its attacks against Ukraine and inflicted unprecedented civilian casualties.
The U.N. Human Rights Office reported in early October that an average of more than 400 civilians were killed or injured every week in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, a 55% increase from the same period in 2025.
Leading up to the Witkoff-Putin meeting in St. Petersburg, Trump on Oct. 16 issued a broad waiver of sanctions, adopted under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.
Trump lashed out online at critics of the move, claiming on Oct. 21 that doing so helped secure the release of U.S. prisoner Stephen Hubbard. After securing Hubbard's release, Witkoff praised Putin as a "humanitarian." Detailing his talks with Norway Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Oslo, Zelesnky said they discussed supporting Ukraine's drone defenses, development of air defense missiles, and communications connectivity.

title: The net gun built for civilians in Ukraine’s kill zone
description:
At a training with the Ukrainian National Guard’s Omega unit, engineers from the defense tech company BlueBird Tech describe how to use their net gun, named Chipa, to entangle an approaching drone’s propellers.

The soldiers rehearse encounters with approaching first-person-view (FPV) drones, monitoring a handheld detector as they walk. Once they spot a drone, one soldier who goes by the callsign Poliak (Ukrainian for "Pole"), pulls the safety pin and takes aim with the net gun, while the others
content:
A soldier with the call sign Poliak from the National Guard's Omega unit holds an first-person-view drone caught in a net during a training exercise in an unnamed location, Ukraine, on Oct. 20, 2026. (Jakub Laichter/The Kyiv Independent)
At a training with the Ukrainian National Guard’s Omega unit, engineers from the defense tech company BlueBird Tech describe how to use their net gun, named Chipa, to entangle an approaching drone’s propellers.
The soldiers rehearse encounters with approaching first-person-view (FPV) drones , monitoring a handheld detector as they walk. Once they spot a drone, one soldier who goes by the callsign Poliak (Ukrainian for "Pole"), pulls the safety pin and takes aim with the net gun, while the others take cover in the bushes.
With a loud boom Poliak fires, and the net spreads through the air, catching the drone and tangling in its propellers.
Chipa was originally designed for civilians living in the expanding " kill zone " on the front lines where Russian soldiers target people shopping, civilian vehicles, and even ambulances in what has become known as a " human safari ."
As the danger spreads into roads and neighborhoods behind the front, the appearance of the net gun shows just how the threats usually associated with battlefields are becoming a part of everyday civilian life in Ukraine.
"FPV drones now threaten everyone in the front line areas," says Eduard, an engineer from BlueBird Tech who asked to be identified by first name only for security reasons.
"The enemy does not distinguish between civilians and soldiers now," Poliak says.
While a drone detector can give civilians warning and time to seek cover, the net gun is intended for the moment when the drone is already close. Each launcher costs around Hr 3,000 (around $67) and can be fired only once, according to Eduard.
It was important for them that Chipa was classified as a non-firearm, which allows civilians to buy it without a firearms permit, he said.
The soldiers from the Omega unit are leaving for the front line the next day. Poliak has been fighting since 2015 and describes how the pace of change on Ukraine’s battlefields had accelerated in recent years. The dangerous part of any mission comes mostly from moving between positions.
"When you have to move out in the open, the enemy can see you from drones," he says.
In combat, Poliak’s unit carries the net guns alongside shotguns. At longer distances, he prefers the shotgun, he says. Close in, he said, the net’s wider coverage offered a better chance of stopping a drone. Eduard put its most effective range at 10 to 20 meters, depending on wind, and the drone speed.
But there is little room for error, because a drone caught in a net can still explode. Poliak said some intercepted drones had detonated, putting nearby soldiers at risk from the blast and shrapnel. A drone exploding a few meters away instead of hitting someone directly can still mean the difference between life and death.
Asked about the danger from a drone’s explosive payload, Poliak’s answer was simple: "The farther away, the better."
Jakub Laichter is a defense tech reporter at the Kyiv Independent. Before joining the Kyiv Independent, he reported from Eastern Ukraine as a freelance photojournalist since 2019.

title: Assistant to the Editor-in-Chief
description: The Kyiv Independent, Ukraine’s main English-language publication, is looking for an Assistant to the Editor-in-Chief.
content:
The Kyiv Independent is Ukraine’s leading English-language news outlet, founded in November 2021 by a team of journalists committed to editorial independence. Today, our team brings together more than 90 people, primarily based in Kyiv. As Ukraine’s voice to the world, we provide international audiences with an independent and trusted window into the country’s reality, bringing important Ukrainian reporting, perspectives, and developments to a global audience.
We are looking for a proactive, highly organized, and reliable Assistant to the Editor-in-Chief to provide day-to-day administrative and organizational support to the Editor-in-Chief while also helping coordinate the newsroom’s operations.
This is a hands-on role for someone who is comfortable managing multiple priorities, communicating with a wide range of people, and taking ownership of tasks from request to completion. We are looking for someone who can anticipate needs, follow up proactively, and find practical solutions in a fast-paced newsroom environment.
This is a full-time, Kyiv-based position with regular in-office work required.
Thank you for your interest in joining The Kyiv Independent and for taking the time to apply. Please submit your CV and a short cover letter explaining why you are interested in this role and how your previous experience would help you succeed in it.
If your application matches our current needs, a member of our hiring team will contact you to schedule an interview. We truly appreciate every application. However, due to the high volume of applications we receive, we may not be able to contact every applicant individually.

title: Lockheed Martin delegation meets Ukraine's defense chiefs in Kyiv amid severe Patriot shortage
description: The meeting came as Russia intensifies its ballistic missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and elsewhere across Ukraine, posing an immense challenge to the Ukrainian air defense.
content:
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara and Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi met with a delegation from the U.S. defense company Lockheed Martin, the Defense Ministry said on Oct. 21, as Ukraine faces an increasingly severe shortage of Patriot interceptor missiles.
The meeting came as Russia intensifies its ballistic missile and drone attacks on Kyiv and elsewhere across Ukraine, posing an immense challenge to Ukrainian air defenses. Lockheed Martin manufactures PAC-3 interceptors used by the Patriot air-defense system, which can engage Russian ballistic missiles, and has supported the U.S. move to grant Ukraine a Patriot production license.
The soaring U.S.-Ukraine tensions have put further strain on Ukrainian air defense. U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to greenlight the transfer of a significant batch of Patriot missiles for Ukraine, Ukrainian officials and military officers told the Kyiv Independent.
The Defense Ministry said in its statement that Khmara and Drapatyi discussed "the importance of stable arms deliveries and further cooperation" with the Lockheed Martin delegation, led by Orlando Sanchez Jr., president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics.
The meeting also included discussions to scale up the supply of PAC-3 interceptors in response to the Russian ballistic missile threat, according to the Defense Ministry.
"We look forward to mutually beneficial cooperation with Lockheed Martin for years to come," the Defense Ministry said on Telegram.
"Ukraine is ready to share its unique combat experience so that, together, we can make defense solutions more effective in the context of modern warfare."
Two days earlier, President Volodymyr Zelensky met with the delegation in Kyiv, where he said both sides expressed readiness to bolster cooperation, including by strengthening Ukrainian air defense.

title: Witkoff lauds Putin as 'humanitarian' as Russia releases US prisoner Stephen Hubbard
description: Russian leader Vladimir Putin announced the release of Hubbard during his meeting with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff.
content:
Editor's note: This article was updated to include comments from U.S. President Donald Trump.
Russia released U.S. political prisoner Stephen Hubbard on Oct. 21, after a visit by Washington's special envoy Steve Witkoff that took place on the same day, reports Russian state media Vesti.
Hubbard, aged 74, was sentenced two years ago by a Moscow court for allegedly serving in the Ukrainian military, in spite of his old age.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin announced the release of Hubbard during his meeting with Witkoff, adding that Hubbard had already been taken to the airport, Vesti reports.
U.S. President Donald Trump later confirmed Hubbard's release in a social media post , in which he said he asked Putin to release Hubbard in a telephone call the previous week.
And Witkoff heaped praise on Putin in return for the gesture.
"You speak so much about how my president, President Trump, is a humanitarian," Witkoff said.
"You, too, are a humanitarian, sir, and I commend you for that. I offer you my respect and thank you once again," he told the Russian leader wanted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes in Ukraine.
The remarks come just two days after Trump made similar comments , in an apparent attempt to whitewash Putin and Russia's war in Ukraine and attacks against civilians. The U.S. president said on Oct. 19 that "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," as Moscow continued to kill Ukrainian civilians .
Hubbard had reportedly been living in Ukraine since 2014. After Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, he allegedly joined a Ukrainian territorial defense unit in the town of Izium in Kharkiv Oblast , and a couple of months later was captured by Russia.
A Russian court in 2024 sentenced him to prison on charges of fighting as a mercenary — a term Moscow uses to label foreign volunteers fighting for Ukraine — with Hubbard reportedly pleading guilty to the charges.
However, his sister, Patricia Hubbard Fox, and another relative questioned Hubbard's confession in an interview with Reuters in September 2024, saying that he held pro-Russian views and was unlikely to take up arms at his age.
The U.S. State Department has designated Hubbard as wrongfully detained.
Moscow's imprisonment of Westerners for later use as political bargaining chips is a widely known and often deployed tactic.
Dmitry Medvedev, Russia's ex-president, even alluded to the policy in a Telegram post on Oct. 9, in which he said, "it is quite likely that we will have to replenish the exchange fund with European and American idiots in order to get our own people out," after Montenegro arrested the founder of the Russian war blog Rybar.
Montenegro later expelled Rybar's Mikhail Zvinchuk to Russia.
Trump wrote that the U.S. "was not required to give anything in return (for Hubbard's release) — an unprecedented situation in Russia."
However, Trump waived Russia sanctions last week, and agreed to buy diesel from Moscow earlier in October.
And there are fears that Washington is now holding back on the delivery of critical air defenses that have already been paid for by Western allies.
Witkoff is otherwise in St. Petersburg to try and spark a fresh round of peace talks, with hopes that Witkoff could get agreement for a trilateral talk between President Volodymyr Zelensky, Putin, and Trump.
However, Putin has long evaded a meeting with Zelensky. Instead, the Kremlin chief reportedly pushes to meet Trump in China next month to secure a favorable peace deal, without Ukraine at the table.
And Russian state media has made no mention of Putin committing to any trilateral talks.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 9, wound 45 across Ukraine, as yet another deadly drone attack strikes Kyiv
description: Russian troops launched attacks against Ukraine overnight with Iskander-K cruise missiles and 186 drones, including Shahed-type ones, the Air Force reported.
content:
Russian attacks have killed at least nine people and injured 45 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Oct. 21, as yet another Russian drone attack struck Kyiv while residents slept.
Russia carried out a drone attack early on Oct. 21, killing at least two people and injuring two others, the Kyiv City Military Administration said . A 24-story apartment building was hit by a Russian drone, sparking a fire on the 20th floor.
The early morning attack comes a day after Russian drones repeatedly struck Kyiv on Oct. 20, damaging a hospital in Solomyanskyi District and another medical facility in Holosiivskyi District, according to the local authorities.
Russian troops launched attacks against Ukraine overnight with Iskander-K cruise missiles and 186 drones, including Shahed-type ones, the Air Force reported . It reported downing 150 drones, 63 of which were jet-powered.
In the northeastern city of Kharkiv and its surrounding region, two people were killed and 11 others, including two children, were injured, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said .
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, four people were killed, and eight others were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said .
In the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia and its surrounding region, a person was killed, and six others were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Ivan Fedorov said .
In central-eastern Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, a person was injured by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said .
In southern Kherson Oblast, 13 people, including three children, were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said .
In southern Odesa Oblast, a Russian drone attack damaged energy facilities and a private food processing company, regional governor Oleh Kiper said . No casualties were reported.
In northern Sumy Oblast, Russian attacks injured two people, including a nine-year-old girl, over the past day, the regional military administration said .
