In northern Chernihiv Oblast, Russian missile and drone attacks injured two people, including a young woman and an 89-year-old woman, over the past day, regional governor Vyacheslav Chaus said .

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,570,540 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,820 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,570,540 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 21.
The number includes 1,820 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,436 tanks, 25,586 armored combat vehicles, 165,278 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,403 artillery systems, 2,228 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,716 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,990 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Anti-corruption agency searches Ukraine's central bank chief
description: The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) on Oct. 21 searched the premises of Andriy Pyshnyi, head of the National Bank of Ukraine, a law enforcement source told the Kyiv Independent.
content:
Editor's note: This story has been updated to include comments from the head of Ukraine's central bank.
The National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) on Oct. 21 searched the premises of Andriy Pyshnyi, head of the National Bank of Ukraine, a law enforcement source told the Kyiv Independent.
Pyshnyi confirmed the reports later that day, adding that he would continue to serve as central bank head.
The NABU said in a statement that it is "conducting searches at the National Bank of Ukraine and at the home of one of its employees."
"No one has been detained or charged," the bureau said. "No further details are being disclosed to protect the confidentiality of the pretrial investigation."
The National Bank of Ukraine confirmed the reports and said that "further explanations will be provided once the procedural actions are complete." The central bank said it "continues to operate as usual."
It is not clear in what case Pyshnyi is being investigated.
According to Pyshnyi, the investigation is unrelated to the National Bank of Ukraine or his work as its chief.
"The investigation was looking for evidence in a case involving different circumstances and individuals. The searches uncovered nothing to suggest that I or any central bank officials had committed any offenses," he wrote on Facebook.
"I respect the work of NABU and SAPO, support the independence of anti-corruption bodies, and am ready to cooperate fully with the investigation within the law."
The National Bank of Ukraine has faced criticism for failing to prevent a Hr 150 million ($3.4 million) payment through state-owned Sense Bank allegedly funded with laundered money and posted as bail for ex-Energy and Justice Minister Herman Halushchenko in June. The central bank has also been lambasted for failing to address the issue of alleged criminal schemes involving Sense Bank in general.
President Volodymyr Zelensky's ex-Deputy Chief of Staff Iryna Mudra , Sense Bank CEO Oleksiy Stupak, the bank's former supervisory board head Mykola Hladyshchenko, and other suspects were charged in August with laundering money to post bail for Halushchenko through Sense Bank.
Halushchenko was charged in February as part of last year’s probe into state nuclear power monopoly Energoatom — the largest corruption investigation of Zelensky’s tenure.
A person matching the description of Zelensky's Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov allegedly asked Mudra to launder cash to pay bail for Halushchenko, according to the leaked text of the charges against Mudra published by the media outlet Bihus.info on Sept. 15.
Furthermore, an alleged transcript of the Anti-Corruption Bureau's tapes leaked to the media outlet Hromadske in August contains multiple references to "Kyrylo," "Kyrylo Oleksiyovich," Mudra's unnamed boss, and a top official at the President's Office. There are also direct references to Budanov's last name in the transcripts.
In leaked transcripts of NABU tapes published in April and May, Vasyl Veselyi, a former aide to Sense Bank's supervisory board, and businessman Oleksandr Tsukerman mentioned influencing board appointments at the bank and talking to Zelensky's ex-Chief of Staff Andriy Yermak about the bank. Veselyi was reportedly an informal overseer of the bank on behalf of Yermak and Zelensky ally Timur Mindich, although he denied the allegation.
Sevki Acuner, former head of Sense Bank's supervisory board, said in September that Pyshnyi, head of the National Bank of Ukraine, had allegedly recommended Veselyi for a position at Sense Bank. Pyshnyi denied the allegation.
The media outlet Ekonomichna Pravda reported in September, citing its sources, that Pyshnyi and Veselyi knew each other through the late Andriy Ivanchuk, a former lawmaker who was a university classmate of Pyshnyi.
According to leaked NABU transcripts published in April, Mindich , the alleged ringleader of the Energoatom corruption scheme, and Rustem Umerov , who is now head of the Foreign Intelligence Service, mentioned plans to discuss funding for drone maker Fire Point with Pyshnyi and Sense Bank. Pyshnyi denied having discussed the issue with anyone.
In an Oct. 21 social media post, he said he would not comment on speculation, adding that all questions "should be resolved exclusively through legal channels."

title: 'Everything was in ruins' — At least 2 killed, 2 injured in Russian drone attack on Kyiv
description: An air raid alert sounded in Kyiv at around 5:20 a.m. local time on Oct. 21 as drones approached the capital, which has faced an unrelenting barrage of Russian drone attacks this fall.
content:
An emergency worker stands inside a residential building after a Russian drone struck a high-rise in Kyiv's Sviatoshynskyi district, in Kyiv, Ukraine, on the morning of Oct. 21, 2026. (Olena Zashko / The Kyiv Independent)
A Russian drone attack on Kyiv killed at least two people and injured two others on the morning of Oct. 21, local authorities said.
An air raid alert sounded in Kyiv at around 5:20 a.m. local time as drones approached the capital, which has faced an unrelenting barrage of Russian drone attacks this fall.
Допис, поширений Kyiv Independent (@kyivindependent_official)
In the Sviatoshynskyi District, a Russian drone struck a 24-story residential building, sparking a fire on the 20th floor. At least two people were killed, and two others were hospitalized with injuries, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Kateryna Dzomina, a student who lives nearby, told the Kyiv Independent that she did not hear the drone approaching, only a powerful explosion as it struck the high-rise.
"It was very scary for me because I was sleeping. One second — and immediately an explosion. Of course, there was panic," she said.
Dzomina added that this was not the first such strike in the area, saying a similar attack had occurred even closer to where she lives last year.
Nataliia, a 63-year-old resident who asked to be introduced only by her first name due to ongoing security concerns amid the ongoing war, said she heard drones fly over her neighborhood all night until "an incredibly powerful explosion."
The whole building shook, Nataliia recalls. She only realized that her building had been hit when she checked the group chat with her neighbors, in which she was instructed to go outside because part of it had caught on fire.
"When I finally got outside, I saw the whole horror of it — everything was in ruins," Nataliia said, recalling the moment when she stepped out of the building for the first time to see the damage on the 20th floor.
In the Desnianskyi District, drone debris fell on a car, while in the Solomianskyi District, debris landed in an open area, Klitschko said.
This fall, Russian forces have intensified their attacks on Ukraine using jet-powered drones , which can reach speeds of up to 600 kph and fly at higher altitudes than older propeller-driven models, making them harder for Ukraine's limited air defenses to intercept.
Russia also attacked Kyiv with drones on Oct. 20, killing one person and injuring 21 others. Twelve people were hospitalized, three of them in serious condition, Klitschko reported.
Alongside drone attacks, Russia has intensified strikes on Kyiv's energy infrastructure , leaving residents facing emergency blackouts, water disruptions and metro shutdowns caused by electricity shortages.

title: Trump envoy meets Putin in Russia, urges trilateral negotiations
description: "I hope you will consider the possibility of resuming trilateral talks," U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff told Putin.
content:
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff met Russian President Vladimir Putin in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21 for a new round of talks on ending Russia's war against Ukraine, following discussions with President Volodymyr Zelensky and European allies in Norway a day earlier.
The meeting comes amid sharply deteriorating relations between Kyiv and Washington, as Ukraine fears the U.S. is using military assistance and access to technology to pressure it to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
At the start of the meeting, Witkoff urged Putin to consider resuming trilateral talks involving Ukraine , Russia, and the U.S.
"I hope you will consider the possibility of resuming trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia , and the United States," Witkoff told Putin.
Putin thanked U.S. President Donald Trump for his attention to resolving the war and asked Witkoff about the results of the talks in Norway.
Witkoff met Zelensky and European allies in Oslo on Oct. 20 to discuss their peace proposals ahead of his visit to Russia. Zelensky said at a news conference with Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store that he hoped Witkoff would convey the proposals from Ukraine and Europe to Moscow and help arrange a meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
But Trump already brought that idea into question after reporters in Washington asked him about the prospect of a trilateral meeting.
"They don't have to be in the same room. I guess I can do it another way. It's hard for them to be in the same room. I don't care how it's done," Trump said .
And Russian leader Vladimir Putin has long evaded a meeting with Zelensky. Instead, the Kremlin chief reportedly pushes to meet Trump in China next month to secure a favorable peace deal, without Ukraine at the table.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine . Moscow is seeking territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Ukraine, by contrast, has called for a ceasefire along the current front line.

title: 'Very difficult to defeat' — How Russia uses mesh networks inside drones to precision-strike Kyiv
description:
A city stretches out beneath the lens of a Russian drone. Roads, apartment blocks, parks, and office buildings come into view as the weapon closes in on its target.

Footage like this has become all too familiar over the course of Russia's full-scale war, usually captured by small first-person-view (FPV) drones stalking anything that moves along the front line, from soldiers and vehicles in the kill zone to civilians on their way to work.

Now the camera is mounted on a long-range Russian attack
content:
A Russian drone flies over Kyiv, Ukraine, on May 24, 2026. (Genya Savilov / AFP via Getty Images)
A city stretches out beneath the lens of a Russian drone. Roads, apartment blocks, parks, and office buildings come into view as the weapon closes in on its target.
Footage like this has become all too familiar over the course of Russia's full-scale war, usually captured by small first-person-view (FPV) drones stalking anything that moves along the front line, from soldiers and vehicles in the kill zone to civilians on their way to work.
Now the camera is mounted on a long-range Russian attack drone remotely piloted far beyond the range of a conventional direct radio link, hunting civilian infrastructure inside Ukraine's capital.
"They are now operating essentially like FPV drones, " a source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry told the Kyiv Independent.
One crucial technology helping to make that possible is mesh networking, which allows drones and other radio-equipped platforms to relay communications to one another, extending a control link beyond the range of a single radio. It also allows live video footage to travel back through the network to the operator, who can see what the drone sees and adjust its flight in real time.
On Sept. 29, Russian forces released footage of a strike on the Inkom business center in Kyiv, showing an attack drone being controlled and transmitting video despite electronic warfare (EW) systems deployed throughout the city.
The footage immediately raised a question: how is that possible?
As Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov, an adviser to the Ukrainian president on the development of defense technologies, put it: "I'll say this right away: no secret satellites, no FPV drones launched from a Shahed, no Russian agents, no mysterious UAVs."
According to Beskrestnov, a Geran-5 jet-powered drone struck the business center while a second jet-powered Shahed circled above the site at an altitude of nearly three kilometers. Equipped with a mesh radio, the second drone acted as a signal relay for the Geran-5 while simultaneously filming and immediately transmitting video of the attack.
After SpaceX blocked unauthorized Starlink terminals used by Russian forces in early February, Russia has had to find other ways to maintain remote control of its drones. As it has repeatedly done throughout the war, Russia adapted.
Russian fixed-wing drones are now being fitted with mesh radios, which are proving to be an effective alternative to Starlink, albeit with limitations of their own.
Since late summer, a near-constant swarm of jet-powered Russian drones has obscured the skies over Kyiv , terrorizing residents and hunting for targets across the city.
Mesh communications are helping turn these aircraft into a formidable threat, capable of high-resolution reconnaissance and remotely operated precision strikes at unprecedented range.
A mesh network is a decentralized communications system in which nodes can connect to multiple other nodes and dynamically route data through the network rather than relying on a single fixed path.
In unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) applications, those nodes can be radios mounted on drones, vehicles, ground stations, or other platforms, each capable of relaying data across the network.
Russian drones have been documented carrying the Chinese-made XK-F358 mesh radio.
In Russian operations, those network chains begin with ground-to-air relay stations near the front line or along the borders with Russia and Belarus. Mesh-equipped drones then relay the connection from one aircraft to another, carrying it progressively farther into Ukrainian territory.
"Think of it almost like a bucket brigade for putting out a fire. Each person passes the bucket along," says Michael Bohnert, a defense researcher at RAND. "Where you have a mesh network is instead of a single line of all of these, you might have three or four lines side by side, and they can pass back and forth almost like a checkerboard."
The principle itself is not new. Bohnert compares it to commercial Wi-Fi extenders used to carry a signal into dead zones inside a building.
"It's a 15-year-old consumer technology," he says. "It's just getting it to work over long distances with everything moving that is the hard part."
Instead of traveling directly between an operator and a drone, communications can pass through several intermediate radios. Each transfer of the signal from one radio to the next is known as a "hop." Several hops can therefore carry a connection beyond the range of any single radio.
According to Mark Hay, CEO of defense company Melrose Networks, the Chinese -made XK-F358 mesh radio attached to Russian drones can support networks of up to 63 hops.
In practice, however, the number of hops a network can support depends on the amount of data it needs to transmit. Each additional relay introduces delays and reduces the available data transmission rate, potentially compromising the ability to control a drone in real time over longer chains.
In principle, each mesh modem in the chain knows which neighboring node to pass the signal to next, allowing communication to propagate across the network until it reaches the operator or the drone.
"The controller [can] communicate with the drone and vice versa," says Hay, "Through one or more hops … they are acting like relays."
Many military mesh radios also use MIMO (Multiple Input, Multiple Output), which uses multiple antennas to make individual wireless links more reliable. MIMO strengthens the connection between individual nodes, while mesh networking determines how data moves through the wider network.
Used together, they can make UAV communications more resilient and extend their practical reach. If one link is lost, the network can reroute traffic through another available path, as long as a viable connection remains.
The most immediate advantage is range. Without satellite communications, a drone controlled over a direct radio link is limited by how far that signal can reliably travel. Mesh networking extends that distance by passing communications through intermediate nodes.
"It allows you to connect over very long distances with communication systems that are relatively low power," Bohnert says.
In practice, he says, that can allow Russian forces to operate drones "two, three, maybe even four times further" than would be possible over a direct radio link.
According to an analysis published by Calibre Defence, a chain of mesh-controlled Gerans or other UAVs could maintain connectivity and live operator control up to 150–175 kilometers from the furthest ground control station, roughly twice the range reported by Beskrestnov in 2025.
Mesh networks are also more resilient. Because communications can travel through multiple paths, losing one relay does not necessarily break the connection.
"With a mesh network you can have ten transmitters attached to trees," Bohnert says. "Even if you blow up one or two where they're starting, there's another way to go along the chain."
The same flexibility can make mesh-controlled drones harder to disrupt with electronic warfare. If interference blocks one link, the network can attempt to route communications through another.
"There could potentially be multiple relay drones on the Russian side," Hay says. If electronic warfare cuts one relay off from the rest of the network, "the communications across the whole network find a way around it."
Mesh systems can rapidly switch between frequencies while keeping radios in the network synchronized, forcing electronic warfare systems to jam a broader range of frequencies to consistently disrupt the connection.
"It's a very difficult thing to defeat because it can work around your attempts to defeat it," Hay adds.
Shorter distances between individual nodes can also make the links themselves harder to jam. A jammer must generate sufficient interference at the receiving radio to disrupt the connection, a task made more difficult by the high transmission power of some Russian mesh radios.
That does not make mesh networks immune to electronic warfare. Bohnert says there is a trade-off between range and resilience: networks designed to communicate over greater distances can become easier to jam, while more resilient networks require nodes to remain closer together.
More powerful radios can partly offset that trade-off, though at a considerable cost, with some of the Chinese-made mesh radios used on Russian drones priced at over $8,000 apiece.
What mesh gives Russia is a resilient, adaptive communications network of its own, carrying control commands, telemetry, live video, and other data between operators and drones. That connection enables reconnaissance, target adjustment, and remotely operated strikes like those now seen over Kyiv.
The strike on the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) headquarters in Kyiv raised a question — how was the drone guided so precisely over the capital?
Beskrestnov believes the aircraft may have connected to a ground-based mesh relay operating inside Kyiv.
"I insist that enemy mesh radio relays are being activated in Kyiv, providing temporary, short-term control channels for Shaheds to adjust their strikes," he says. "Not many. Perhaps one to three."
At the time of the SBU strike, he adds, there were no other Shaheds in the air that could have served as airborne relays.
Hay agrees that such a setup is technically possible. A mesh radio placed on a rooftop or in an apartment could connect to the internet via fixed broadband, Wi-Fi, or a cellular network, and provide an incoming drone with a local control link during the final stage of its flight.
Airborne relays are most effective at altitude, where drones maintain a clear line of sight with one another. As they descend, buildings, terrain, and Earth's curvature begin to obstruct the radio signal. A relay inside Kyiv could carry the connection through that final stretch.
Russia's 50th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade "Varyag" has emerged as a pioneer in the use of mesh-equipped Geran and Gerbera drones for reconnaissance and long-range strikes. Part of Russia's Unmanned Systems Forces and subordinate to the Supreme High Command, the brigade targets logistics and infrastructure in Ukraine's rear.
It has been linked to attacks on bridges and data centers in Kyiv, as well as operations in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, Donetsk, Kharkiv, and Chernihiv oblasts.
Mesh gives formations like Varyag more than additional range. It allows operators to change how an attack develops after the drones are already in the air.
Bohnert describes the problem in terms of game theory. If range matters most, relay drones can be spread into a long chain, each extending the connection farther. If electronic warfare or Ukrainian interceptors pose the greater threat, the drones can fly closer together, reducing range but creating more redundant links.
The configuration can also change during an attack.
Bohnert gives the example of ten drones sent toward four possible targets. The first to arrive can show operators which targets remain reachable, allowing them to redirect the rest in flight.
"There's a lot of game theory, and it's really situational," he says. "That's why it's so dangerous."
Relay drones can also be pushed forward or replaced as they are destroyed, forcing Ukraine to keep spending interceptors while other aircraft continue toward their targets.
Russia is increasingly giving its long-range drones multiple ways to communicate. Some Geran drones have been found carrying both mesh-network equipment and cellular modems, allowing operators to use whichever connection is available at different stages of a flight.
While mesh radios transmit live video and control commands, cellular modems are used to send telemetry, including the drone's location and status.
On Sept. 14, Ukrainian officials said Russia was likely using Belarusian commercial LTE networks and radio relay stations on Belarusian territory to communicate with Shahed-type drones during mass attacks on Ukraine.
Belarusian LTE infrastructure could also serve as a gateway between the airborne mesh network and the wider internet, allowing Russian operators to communicate with drones through the mesh network without requiring each aircraft to connect directly to a cellular network.
According to Hay, a drone flying high enough to maintain mesh links could, in theory, switch to a cellular network as it descended into areas with mobile coverage, provided it could gain access to that network.
Maintaining that connection does not necessarily require an operator to manually pilot the drone throughout its flight. Computer-vision systems can also allow an operator to designate a target, leaving the aircraft to track and approach it autonomously during the final stage of an attack.
Satellite communications could eventually add another layer. In 2026, Russia began deploying Rassvet , a low Earth orbit satellite internet constellation designed as a domestic alternative to Starlink.
The program has suffered early setbacks, including the loss of one satellite and failures that left others outside their intended orbits. If the constellation becomes operational at scale, however, Russian forces would have access to a satellite communications system that Moscow controls directly.
Hay expects these systems to be used together rather than as substitutes for one another.
"They have cellular, and they have mesh network support on board them as well," he says of some Geran drones. "They will additionally have satellite, and they will use each one of these, possibly whichever one works at a given point in time during a flight."
That creates a harder problem for Ukrainian electronic warfare: disrupting one communications method does not necessarily cut the operator off if another remains available.
"It's like a game of whack-a-mole," Hay says. "You end up with a situation where one technology is used, then that no longer works, so they start using another technology."
"You hit it, you deal with that problem. It pops its head up somewhere else."
Polina Moroziuk is a junior reporter at the Kyiv Independent. She holds an MSc in Human Rights and Politics from the London School of Economics and a BSc from the University of Amsterdam. Before joining the newsroom, she worked in human rights advocacy and as a project assistant at a research and consultancy organisation, supporting projects for international organisations including UNICEF and War Child, with a focus on Ukraine and the Middle East.

title: Russian drones kill 2 in Kharkiv Oblast, strike university building in Kremenchuk
description: An 81-year-old woman and an 83-year-old man were killed when Russian drones attacked the village of Korotych, Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov reported.
content:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.
Russian drone attacks killed two elderly residents of Kharkiv Oblast and struck a university building in central Ukraine's Poltava Oblast overnight on Oct. 20–21, local authorities reported.
An 81-year-old woman and an 83-year-old man were killed when Russian drones attacked the village of Korotych, Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov reported .
Another 11 people experienced acute stress reactions, including a 2-month-old boy and an 8-year-old girl, Syniehubov said. All received medical assistance.
Emergency crews responded to the scene, and the attack damaged 13 private houses, a vehicle, and an outbuilding, which was destroyed by fire.
In Kremenchuk, Poltava Oblast, a Russian drone struck a university building late on Oct. 20, sparking a fire and injuring two people , including a 16-year-old child, according to regional Governor Vitalii Diakivnych. The child was hospitalized with a concussion and blast-related injuries, while the other injured person was in moderate condition.
Local media identified the damaged building as the fifth academic building of Kremenchuk Mykhailo Ostrohradskyi National University.
Kremenchuk Mayor Vitalii Maletskyi said students had attended classes in the building earlier that day. Emergency services responded to the fire, while authorities continued assessing the damage.
Kremenchuk has faced repeated Russian attacks in recent weeks. An Oct. 7 missile strike killed two people and injured dozens more, damaging residential buildings in the city.
Russia continues to launch day and night drone and missile attacks against Ukrainian cities, killing and wounding citizens, and damaging residences, schools, healthcare facilities, and other civilian infrastructure.

title: NATO to bolster Black Sea presence with patrol aircraft, drones after attacks on commercial ships
description: "Allies have or will send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, explosive exploitation teams, intelligence personnel, drones, and more to the Black Sea," U.S. Army Col. Martin O'Donnell, a NATO military spokesperson, said in a statement.
content:
NATO will increase its military presence in the Black Sea, deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones following a series of deadly attacks on commercial vessels in the region.
The announcement came after NATO's main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, met at the alliance's Brussels headquarters on Oct. 20 to discuss Black Sea security.
"Allies have or will send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, explosive exploitation teams, intelligence personnel, drones, and more to the Black Sea," U.S. Army Col. Martin O'Donnell, a NATO military spokesperson, said in a statement.
O'Donnell said NATO's immediate priority is improving its awareness of potential threats in the region through additional surveillance equipment and intelligence sharing.
The decision comes after a series of drone attacks on commercial vessels near the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, raising concerns about the safety and security of shipping routes used by Ukraine and other countries in the region.
On Oct. 13, drones struck two commercial vessels off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast. The Maltese-flagged, Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3 was hit by three drones near the coastal town of Byala, while the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity sank near Krapets, leaving 11 crew members missing.
Bulgarian authorities subsequently recovered suspected drone fragments from the damaged Chelsea 3 and began the process of examining them to determine the weapon's origin, The Maritime Executive reported on Oct. 20 .
Two days later, seven sailors were reported missing after the Wine Trader, a San Marino-flagged chemical tanker, caught fire near the Romanian port of Sulina amid reported drone activity.
NATO has not announced which country they think is responsible for the attacks. Military analysts have identified Russia as the likely perpetrator, although Moscow has not acknowledged responsibility.
"NATO has already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank, including with counter-drone capabilities," NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said on Oct. 20 .
"We will continue to stand united and ensure that we are ready and able to address any threat and to keep our one billion people safe."
The attacks have prompted growing concerns among NATO members about the possibility of Russia's war against Ukraine spilling over into neighbouring countries.
On Oct. 17, Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters, according to Romania's Defense Ministry. Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta said the drones were believed to be Russian-made Geran-4 models, due to their speed and other characteristics.
The Black Sea is a critical route for Ukraine's agricultural exports, but attacks on commercial shipping have raised concerns about the risks faced by civilian crews and maritime security.

title: Ukrainian forces reportedly strike energy infrastructure in occupied Donetsk Oblast, Luhansk telecom site
description: Ukrainian forces struck energy infrastructure in the city of Chystiakove in Donetsk Oblast, and blackouts were reported in Crimea amid drone fire, monitoring channels reported late on Oct. 20.
content:
Ukrainian forces struck energy infrastructure in the city of Chystiakove, Donetsk Oblast, blackouts were reported in Crimea amid drone fire, and a telecommunications site in Luhansk was hit, monitoring channels reported on the night of Oct. 20-21.
A mass drone attack targeted Chystiakove, which has been occupied by Russian forces since 2014, monitoring channel Exilenova Plus reported .
Meanwhile, in Crimea's Krasnoperekopskyi district, eyewitnesses first reported drone strikes near the local train station and the sound of Russian air defenses operating, according to pro-Ukrainian channel Crimean Wind.
Power outages then followed in the district, the channel reported late on Oct. 20.
Later, a Luhansk site previously used by Ukrainian telecom company Ukrtelecom before Russia's 2014 occupation of the city was struck, Exilenova Plus reported .
Lugacom, also known as Luhansk Communications, a Russian-installed telecom provider in occupied Luhansk Oblast, now uses the site for technical support, telecommunications services and information technology (IT).
President Volodymyr Zelensky sanctioned the company and other Russian telecom providers in June.
Ukraine regularly strikes military targets in the occupied territories and deep within Russia as Kyiv aims to reduce Russia's ability to wage its war.
On Oct. 18, Ukrainian forces struck an oil terminal, a data center , and a bridge in a large-scale overnight attack on St. Petersburg, Russian officials and media reported.
The targeted data center belonged to Russia's largest social media platform, VK, also known as VKontakte . Drones also hit the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal.

title: Zelensky confirms ballistic missile early warning systems operational after skipped alerts
description: "This is very important for our people, as we can know when a Russian ballistic missile is incoming. Therefore, this morning began with positive signals from the American side," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky on Oct. 20 confirmed that Ukraine's early warning systems for Russian ballistic missile launches are operational, after authorities previously said there were instances when Kyiv did not receive alerts from allies.
"This is very important for our people, as we can know when a Russian ballistic missile is incoming. Therefore, this morning began with positive signals from the American side," Zelensky said at a joint press conference alongside Norwegian Prime Minister Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb.
The three leaders met in Oslo alongside U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff. Zelensky said he planned to hold joint talks with all three officials, a separate bilateral meeting with Witkoff, and a trilateral meeting with Store and Stubb.
"We also have a constructive dialogue now. It was constructive because we all want peace – Ukraine, Europe, and the United States. As for what tomorrow will bring, we will see," Zelensky said at the press conference.
Ukraine has e xperienced disruptions to its early-warning systems, which rely on U.S. intelligence for incoming Russian ballistic missiles in recent days.
White House officials have attributed previous outages to "bad weather conditions," while Rubio has cited a software malfunction.
U.S. President Donald Trump has condemned Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy in recent weeks, blaming Zelensky for supposedly exacerbating the global diesel supply crisis, despite evidence that shows the U.S. war against Iran is the major driver behind the current shortage.
Ukraine has offered energy ceasefire proposals that Russia has rejected.
"(W)e offered different options. We are ready not to hit sensitive parts of Russia's energy sector if Russia stops hitting ours. Putin said no. But we're working to find a solution," Zelensky said at the Oslo press conference.

title: Ukraine war latest: Drone strikes on Yandex data centers disrupt Russian court hearings, media reports
description:
Key developments on Oct. 20:

 * Ukrainian strikes on Yandex data centers disrupt Russian court hearings, media reports
 * Ukraine's HUR claims 108 Russian soldiers killed, 29 captured in Sumy Oblast operation
 * Power outages in half of Ukraine's oblasts after Russian assault on power plants
 * Fire at oil pumping station in Russia’s Tambov Oblast after drone attack, monitoring channels say
 * Poland has no Patriot missiles left for Ukraine, Sikorski says
 * Russian drones strike Kyiv hospital,
content:
Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian tech giant Yandex's data centers disrupted dozens of court hearings across Russia, independent Russian media outlet Verstka reported on Oct. 16.
The disruptions come as Moscow and Kyiv increasingly target each other's data centers .
Russian courts began canceling hearings on Oct. 8, following a Ukrainian strike on one of Yandex's largest data centers in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast. PravoTech, the company responsible for maintaining Russia's electronic arbitration court system, subsequently reported a major outage at a Yandex Cloud data center.
The disruptions affected courts across several Russian regions, including Sverdlovsk, Smolensk, Tula, Kostroma, Ivanovo, and Yaroslavl oblasts. Courts were unable to hold online hearings, record audio and video, or access documents through the electronic court system, the Moscow Times reported .
Russia intensified its attacks on Ukraine's digital infrastructure in September. On Sept. 23, a Russian strike damaged a Kyiv data center, disrupting internet access for around 100,000 households and affecting cloud services.
Ukraine responded with strikes on three Yandex data centers, a Sberbank facility under construction, and a data center operated by Russian social media giant VK between Oct. 8 and 18. Most recently, on Oct. 20, Ukrainian forces reportedly destroyed another data center in Donetsk Oblast .
Ukrainian special forces killed 108 Russian soldiers, captured another 29, and struck more than 1,100 Russian targets during a seven-week operation in Sumy Oblast, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) reported on Oct. 20.
According to HUR's Active Operations Department, the operation was carried out by its Group 10 special forces unit, which reportedly thwarted Russian offensive plans and prevented Russian troops from cutting off Ukrainian logistical routes in the region.
Over the course of seven weeks, Ukrainian operatives cleared Russian troops from more than 600 hectares of forest before handing over the positions to Ukraine's Defense Forces, the intelligence agency said.
HUR did not specify the exact location of the operation or when it took place.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claims.
Ukraine's defensive operations reduced the pace of Russia's territorial advances by more than half in the first six months of 2026, then-Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi said on July 10.
Separately, on Sept. 28, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps reported further territorial gains in northern Donetsk Oblast as part of Operation Vivaldi , a counteroffensive that had reclaimed a total of 176 square kilometers. According to the corps, the latest phase of the operation inflicted more than 2,000 Russian casualties and resulted in the capture of over 250 Russian soldiers.
Due to Russian attacks, Ukraine's state-owned electricity operator reported power outages in twelve of Ukraine's oblasts on Oct. 20.
"There are new power outages in the Kirovohrad, Zhytomyr, Lviv, Odesa, Rivne, Ternopil, Khmelnytskyi, Zaporizhia, Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Chernihiv oblasts in the morning," Ukrenergo said .
To avoid overloading previously damaged equipment, power limitation schedules for industry will be applied across all of Ukraine, as well as hourly outage schedules in some oblasts, according to the operator.
Russia continues to "systematically and purposefully attack" Ukraine's energy sector, Ukrainian First Deputy Minister of Energy of Artem Nekrasov said in a briefing on Oct. 20.
"At night and in the morning, Russia attacked energy facilities in Kirovohrad, Zhytomyr, Lviv, Odessa, Rivne, Ternopil and Khmelnytsky Oblasts," Nekrasov said , adding that due to the Russian strikes some consumers were left without power supply.
The strikes come as Russia intensifies its drone and missile campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure as the country approaches its fifth winter since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
The day before, another wave of Russian missile and drone strikes had hit 28 electrical substations and other critical energy facilities across Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 19.
16 ballistic missiles and over 200 drones were used in what Zelensky described as a " targeted attack on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast ."
A fire reportedly broke out at an oil pumping station near the Russian city of Michurinsk in Tambov Oblast after an overnight drone attack on Oct. 20, according to Telegram monitoring channels.
Tambov Oblast governor Yevgeny Pervyshov said that a Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire "on the territory of one of the enterprises" in Michurinsky District but did not specify at which facility. He claimed that four drones in total were shot down overnight and in the morning of Oct. 20, mainly by mobile fire groups. He reported no casualties.
On video footage of the reported attack published by monitoring channel Exilenova+ , a fire and dark smoke can be seen at what residents supposedly identified as a diesel fuel tank.
Independent Russian outlet ASTRA said the fire likely started at the Nikolskoye-1 linear production and dispatch station near the village of Novonikolskoye.
The Nikolskoye linear production and dispatch station is a major oil and petroleum facility, operated by Transneft as part of the Druzhba oil pipeline network. The station is located about 350 to 400 kilometers (about 220 to 250 miles) from the frontline in Ukraine.
Ukrainian authorities did not yet confirm an attack. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify a fire at the station.
Ukraine attacked the station previously on Aug. 18, 2025 . Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, who heads Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, then confirmed that drones of the 14th Regiment of the Unmanned Systems Unit attacked the Nikolskoye oil pumping station, which halted the operation of the Russian Druzhba oil pipeline.
The Druzhba pipeline , part of which crosses Ukraine, remains a key route for supplying Russian crude to Hungary and Slovakia under an exemption from European Union sanctions imposed over Moscow's war in Ukraine.
Poland is not in a position to provide Ukraine with U.S.-made Patriot missiles, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) in an interview published on Oct. 19, as Kyiv struggles to intercept Russian missile strikes.
Sikorski said that the shortage of interceptor missiles had worsened after the attacks on Iran, and that Russia now produces more missiles.
“This is a genuine problem,” Sikorski said.
At the same time Sikorski added that other NATO countries still could transfer such resources to Ukraine, but did not specify which countries he was referring to.
For now, Sikorski said, Poland can only join in the appeals to other countries to help supply Ukraine with the much needed missiles.
The comments come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian ballistic missile attacks and increasingly severe shortages of the interceptors needed to defend against them.
Patriot systems are among Ukraine's most important defenses against Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to intercept using other systems.
On Oct. 15, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Polish aid helped Ukraine defend Kyiv during recent attacks, having provided ammunition used by Ukraine's anti-aircraft guns. Zelensky also hinted at other, more sensitive Polish support which would have to remain confidential; "sometimes it should remain between the two of us," he said.
On Oct. 18, Zelensky said that Washington has approved only some of the missiles purchased through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which allows NATO allies to finance the purchase of U.S.-made weapons for Ukraine, according to Bloomberg .
"The American side approved the delivery of only some of them, but not the rest. And this is not a technical issue," Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president said the U.S. is currently supplying just 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, approximately one-quarter of the number provided under former President Joe Biden's administration.
Russian drones repeatedly struck Kyiv on Oct. 20, damaging a hospital in Solomyanskyi District and another medical facility in Holosiivskyi District, injuring five people, according to local authorities.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Russia struck the operating room of the Strazheska Institute of the National Academy of Medical Sciences in Kyiv, injuring one patient.
"This is the second time. Last year, the attack hit the fourth floor of the institute, and now it is on the sixth floor, where the operating room is located," Koretskyi said.
The medical facility in Holosiivskyi was damaged by debris from a Russian drone, Kyiv city mayor Vitali Klitschko said in the afternoon.
While Klitschko initially reported two people injured, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMCA) later raised the total number of injured people to five.
Debris also fell on railway tracks in Solomyansyki District but did not lead to a fire, the mayor said. Several other buildings in Holosiivskyi area was also seemingly struck in the attack, according to Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground.
A large-scale fire also broke out in Kyiv's Desnianskyi District, close to the Northern Bridge, KMCA spokesperson Kateryna Pop told RBC Ukraine . Initial reports on social media that the Northern Bridge was hit were not correct.
The Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) also said that the Northern bridge was not hit, but that traffic on the bridge may be disrupted due to inspections of the consequences of the nearby attack.
In the Obolon District, debris from a drone fell on a market, KMCA said . The consequences of the incident were still under investigation.
Following another attack in the afternoon, Klitschko said that an energy facility was hit in Shevchenkivskyi District, as emergency services were on their way.
Earlier this morning, at least three people were killed and four people injured after a Russian drone struck early morning commuter traffic in the Holosiivskyi District of Kyiv.
Ukraine's State emergency service reported the victims of Russia's drone strike, saying "The enemy is once again cynically attacking civilians. Behind each such blow are human lives, pain, and ruined destinies."
The Russian drone crashed near a gas station in the Holosiivskyi District close to the administrative border with Kyiv Oblast, Kyiv city mayor Vitali Klitschko said .
Images shared by the Kyiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office showed multiple cars ablaze at the scene of the attack near the Kyiv-Odesa highway.

title: As Trump turns toward Russia, Zelensky drops his restraint
description:
President Volodymyr Zelensky has spent much of the past two years trying to win over Donald Trump. Flattery, constant meetings, and carefully calibrated concessions have become hallmarks of his dealings with the U.S. president.

But the strategy has failed, prompting Zelensky to change course and adopt a more confrontational tone.

"Frankly, Trump has crossed the Rubicon," a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent, summing up the mood in Kyiv following Washington's latest deals with Moscow
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky in Brussels, Belgium, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Nicolas Economou / NurPhoto via Getty Images)
President Volodymyr Zelensky has spent much of the past two years trying to win over Donald Trump. Flattery, constant meetings, and carefully calibrated concessions have become hallmarks of his dealings with the U.S. president.
But the strategy has failed, prompting Zelensky to change course and adopt a more confrontational tone.
"Frankly, Trump has crossed the Rubicon," a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent, summing up the mood in Kyiv following Washington's latest deals with Moscow and its obstruction of Ukraine's ability to defend itself .
Since the February 2025 Oval Office clash , Zelensky and his team have pursued a carefully calibrated diplomatic strategy aimed at avoiding friction with Washington and preventing the U.S. from pulling back its support. They have closely managed their public messaging, repeatedly thanking Trump and his administration, at times almost as a matter of routine.
Yet months have passed with little progress in U.S.-mediated peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow. Each new round has followed much the same pattern: Washington holds talks with both sides, then presents a proposal largely aligned with Moscow's demands. Kyiv pushes to renegotiate the terms in pursuit of a fairer deal, only for the negotiations to collapse once again.
According to officials and experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent, Trump's recent dealings with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin , as well as Washington's obstruction of Ukraine's ability to defend itself, went too far, leaving Zelensky with little room to maneuver.
"It's a pity that we're losing a strong partner," Zelensky said in an interview aired on Oct. 14, responding to Trump lifting sanctions on Russian oil. "When President Trump chooses one side, not our side. If you're in the middle, you have to stay in the middle, not on the wrong side… I don't know who pushed (Trump), but this is not the right side of history."
"The masks have been taken off. Trump doesn't want Ukraine to win."
Oleksandr Merezhko, chair of Ukraine's parliamentary foreign affairs committee, says Zelensky has focused his criticism on Trump's actions rather than making the dispute personal, taking care "not to wound his ego."
"Zelensky is delicate but firm," Merezhko told the Kyiv Independent. "The president can't stay silent when Trump has effectively struck a deal with Putin. The masks have been taken off. Trump doesn't want Ukraine to win."
Describing Zelensky's comments as "quite provocative" and "emotional," Oleksandr Kraiev, head of the North America program at the Ukrainian Prism think-tank, says Ukraine is right to push back against Trump's actions. According to Kraiev, Kyiv's silence could encourage European countries to follow Trump's business-driven approach.
"This is not about personal attitudes, but about seeing reality as it is. Trump's view of reality is distorted," he continues.
The looming U.S. midterm elections in early November are seen as a key factor behind Trump's hostile rhetoric and actions toward Kyiv.
Ukrainian officials had long expected relations with Washington to come under strain, as Trump's eight-month-long war with Iran had caused a global spike in fuel prices and was expected to severely damage his party's chances at the ballot box.
At an EU summit in Brussels last week, Zelensky was asked whether Trump was using him as a scapegoat for his troubles at home and abroad. Zelensky responded with a smile.
Merezhko argues that Ukraine should focus not on appealing to Trump, but on appealing to "forces that can limit his mistakes."
"We must avoid giving the impression that we are taking sides in the election campaign by backing the Democrats. Many Republicans criticize Trump's actions," he says. "It is crucial for us that Ukraine's friends win. And we have friends in both camps — Republicans and Democrats."
As Zelensky pushes back against what he sees as Trump's tilt toward Russia, his increasingly firm defense of Ukraine's interests has boosted his domestic support.
In Ukraine, many see Trump's pressure on the president as pressure on the country itself, prompting Ukrainians to rally around Zelensky. The Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) has described this as a "rally-round-the-flag" effect.
After the Oval Office clash, Zelensky's approval rating jumped from 57% to 68%. Following the latest dispute, Zelensky received a similar boost. Around 43% of Ukrainians trusted Zelensky between Oct. 8 and 9, while 52% did not. Between Oct. 10 and 16, his trust rating rose to 57%, while the share of those who distrusted him fell to 39%, according to a KIIS poll published on Oct. 20.
Zelensky, whose standing has been battered over the past year by corruption scandals involving members of his inner circle, appears to understand this correlation well.
Asked whether he would run for re- election if a presidential vote were held during the war, Zelensky said he was ready to do so, calling it his "responsibility." He had previously largely evaded the question of whether he would seek another term.
"Even in moves that are entirely focused on foreign policy, Zelensky clearly has domestic political calculations in mind," Kraiev says. "His ratings are rising, and he has come to embody a Ukraine united against both Russia and an unpredictable America."
"When (else) should he start thinking about domestic politics?"
