Kateryna began her career in journalism in 2020 and holds a bachelor's degree in journalism from Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv. She also studied at journalism schools in the Czech Republic and Germany.

title: Witkoff to visit St. Petersburg after Zelensky talks
description: U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian officials in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21 to discuss European and U.S. proposals for peace in Ukraine, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said.
content:
U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff will meet Russian officials in St. Petersburg on Oct. 21 to discuss European and U.S. proposals for peace in Ukraine, Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store said.
This will "possibly pave the way for a meeting at leaders' level," Store said at a press conference in Oslo on Oct. 20 after talks with Witkoff and President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The officials, as well as Finnish President Alexander Stubb, met in Norway in a precarious moment for Ukraine, with Russia escalating attacks against energy infrastructure.
Meanwhile, Kyiv's ties with Washington are sharply deteriorating amid concerns that the U.S. could be withholding the delivery of Patriot air-defense missiles funded by Ukraine's allies, as well as other support.
"We have some clear ideas on how to get to peace. And we are united with our European partners in this effort, and we want the Americans to take these ideas to the Russians," Zelensky said at the press conference.
"One of the important ideas is to move to a trilateral meeting of the leaders, to address the issues that only the leaders can do."
Witkoff will also present to the Russian side proposals on Article 5-like post-war security guarantees for Ukraine, which were discussed in Oslo, Zelensky said.
Russian President Vladimir Putin has long evaded a meeting with Zelensky. Instead, the Kremlin chief reportedly pushes to meet U.S. President Donald Trump in China next month to secure a favorable peace deal, without Ukraine at the table.
"We discussed and found key elements on security, and we discussed and found key elements on the economy," Stubb commented on the latest talks, saying that proposals have been developed by European, Ukrainian, and U.S. officials.
The Finnish president remarked that despite "a lot of noise in the public space," negotiations are advancing well "on the technical level."
Jared Kushner joined the talks in Oslo online, and officials are also expected to hold discussions with national security advisors from European countries.
Witkoff was not present at the final press conference. When asked about his absence by a reporter, Store said, "This is a press conference among political leaders."
The New York Times reported earlier that Witkoff would meet Putin while in Russia, possibly to discuss the release of Stephen Hubbard , a 74-year-old American citizen who was reportedly serving with a Ukrainian territorial defense unit in Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, when Russian forces detained him in 2022.
More than a year and a half of U.S.-led peace efforts have failed to make headway as Moscow continues to demand that Ukraine cede Donbas, a strategically vital region in Ukraine's east that Russian forces were unable to take fully by force.
The peace push has now been further hampered by a sharp deterioration in Ukraine-U.S. relations, following the unexpected announcement of a U.S.-Russia diesel deal on Oct. 9.
Since then, Zelensky and Trump have exchanged sharp public criticism. Trump said his Ukrainian counterpart "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
Trump has also refused to condemn the Kremlin over its escalating attacks on Ukraine, including strikes on the country's already vulnerable energy infrastructure.
Zelensky, meanwhile, warned in an interview with NBC News that siding with Putin would be a "historic mistake."

title: Russian occupation official exposed in Kyiv Independent documentary charged with war crimes
description: According to the SBU, Sharlai heads the department responsible for religious organizations within Russia's occupation administration in Zaporizhzhia Oblast. He also served as Russian President Vladimir Putin's trusted representative in occupied Melitopol during Russia's 2024 presidential election.
content:
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said on Oct. 20 that it had notified Artem Sharlai, a Russian occupation official previously investigated by the Kyiv Independent, of suspicion of war crimes in absentia over his alleged involvement in the persecution of religious communities in occupied Melitopol.
According to the SBU , Sharlai heads the department responsible for religious organizations within Russia's occupation administration in Zaporizhzhia Oblast. He also served as Russian President Vladimir Putin's authorized representative in occupied Melitopol during Russia's 2024 presidential election.
Investigators allege that Sharlai helped organize widespread repression against religious communities that resisted Russian occupation or refused to join the Russian Orthodox Church.
The Kyiv Independent previously investigated Sharlai's involvement in religious persecution in its documentary No God But Theirs , released in May 2025.
The investigation documented the systematic persecution of Christian communities in occupied Melitopol, including the closure of churches, confiscation of religious property, and detention and forced expulsion of clergy.
In the documentary, Ukrainian Greek Catholic priest Oleksandr Bohomaz identified Sharlai as one of the officials personally involved in searches of religious properties, including inspections of religious literature.
The Kyiv Independent's undercover journalists also contacted Sharlai while posing as representatives of the Russian Orthodox Church .
During the recorded conversation, Sharlai discussed efforts to suppress religious groups he described as "sects" and identified two associates — Andrii Zinchenko and Viacheslav Lytvynenko — involved in his department's activities.
According to the SBU, Sharlai compiled lists of pro-Ukrainian parishioners for Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB), which were subsequently used to carry out raids against clergy and worshippers.
During these raids, Russian forces allegedly abducted people from their homes or the streets and detained them in occupation-run prisons, where they were subjected to torture, including beatings and suffocation with plastic bags, the SBU said.
Sharlai was notified of suspicion under Part 1 of Article 438 of Ukraine's Criminal Code, which concerns violations of the laws and customs of war.
The SBU said the investigation remains ongoing under the supervision of Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office.

title: Almost 46,000 foreigners have signed contracts with Russian army since 2022, Ukraine says
description: This year, the Kremlin has significantly increased its recruitment of foreigners into its army, with 16,168 individuals already identified in the first nine months of 2026, according to Ukraine.
content:
A total of 45,959 foreigners have signed contracts with the Russian Armed Forces since the beginning of the full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War reported on Oct. 20.
These foreigners came from 151 countries and unrecognized territories, according to the Ukrainian state agency.
Russia has been recruiting foreigners to join its armed forces by luring individuals into signing a contract in exchange for Russian citizenship and monetary compensation. Many have been sent to the front lines in Ukraine, facing death or capture.
This year, the Kremlin has significantly increased its recruitment of foreigners into its army, with 16,168 individuals already identified in the first nine months of 2026.
This surpasses the total number of foreign recruits in 2025, according to the Coordination Headquarters.
The agency estimates that Russia aims to recruit up to 18,500 foreigners by the end of the year. With the current pace, the number of new soldiers could reach about 21,500.
The report revealed that most recruits come from Russia-friendly countries like Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, and Belarus.
Other recruits come from Africa and Latin American countries: 1,449 citizens of Colombia, 699 of Burundi, 530 of Zimbabwe, and 503 of Peru signed contracts as of Oct. 1, 2026.
Further survey findings revealed that 46.7% of recruits signed the contract to obtain Russian citizenship, while 28% were unaware they would be sent into combat.
Almost half, 48.8%, were taken prisoner by Ukraine's Armed Forces after being wounded, while 79% want to return to Russia during a prisoner exchange.
Data was gathered by a project within the Coordination Headquarters, " I Want to Live," intended for Russian soldiers who wish to surrender.

title: Things Russia has done to Ukraine that Trump thinks are 'fine'
description: From the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion, Russian forces have inflicted countless atrocities against Ukraine.
content:
A wounded resident sits at the site of a Russian missile strike on an apartment building in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 14, 2026. (Genya Savilov / AFP via Getty Images)
"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," U.S. President Donald Trump remarked to a group of journalists outside the White House on Oct. 19.
The comments came as tensions between Kyiv and Washington are rising after reports that the U.S. stopped warning Kyiv of incoming Russian ballistic missiles and limited the use of Starshield , a military version of Elon Musk's Starlink, for Ukraine, making it difficult to intercept Russian attacks on Ukraine.
While Russia wages its war with no regard for civilian lives or human dignity, these are just some of the things that Trump seemingly considers "fine."
The U.S. president spoke only hours after Russia had launched another deadly attack on the people of Ukraine a few hours before he made his comments. A Russian drone struck a park in the town of Nova Vodolaha, Kharkiv Oblast, killing six and injuring at least 15 others.
Inna Mariukhna, a 28-year-old teacher at a local school, was one of those killed in the attack. She was pushing her 1-year-old daughter, Anhelina, in a stroller when the Russian jet-powered drone struck them both. Anhelina was killed instantly, while Inna succumbed to her injuries in hospital.
Pictures showing Anhelina's bloodied and lifeless body, still strapped in her stroller, her small shoes still perfectly tied, were posted on social media by many including President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Arina Koval, an 8-year-old girl, was also killed in the drone strike, as were 34-year-old Yulia Spichak, 36-year-old Marianna Tsymbal, and a sixth victim who has not been named.
Zelensky described the attack as an "absolute atrocity." Trump thinks this is "fine."
In the morning hours of Oct. 20, at least three people were killed and four people injured after a Russian drone struck early morning commuter traffic in the Holosiivskyi District of Kyiv.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported Russia's drone strike, saying: "The enemy is once again cynically attacking civilians. Behind each such blow are human lives, pain, and ruined destinies."
This was but one of hundreds of continuous Russian strikes on Ukraine's capital and dozens of other cities and communities across the country, as the Kremlin is pursuing another theory of victory — attempting to bomb Ukrainian cities into submission.
"328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in September 2026."
According to the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine , at least 328 civilians were killed and 2,105 injured in September 2026, an 85% increase from September 2025. The deadly trend is continuing into October, according to the mission. "The first two weeks of October were among the deadliest periods for civilians in years," Danielle Bell, head of the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine, said.
Recent U.S. actions have increased the threat for Ukrainian civilians. Ukraine's Starshield satellite internet terminals, which Ukraine uses to control anti-drone interceptors, have been impeded, while deliveries of vital Patriot interceptors have been deliberately delayed by the Pentagon, Zelensky said on Oct. 18, an allegation corroborated by reporting in the Kyiv Independent and the Washington Post.
The New York Times, meanwhile, reported a Russian plan, presented to the publication by Ukrainian authorities, to destroy Ukraine's beleaguered energy system once and for all. While Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy system have been ongoing throughout the year at a low level, Moscow has recently ramped up mass attacks to wipe out power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure for its fifth winter offensive during the full-scale invasion.
At a recent official event of Russia's International People's Unity Club in Moscow, Russian Lt. Col. Alexey Selivano said : "Wherever Russian troops arrive, Ukrainians cease to exist."
From the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion, Russian forces have inflicted countless atrocities against Ukraine.
In March 2022, Russian forces carried out a massacre of Ukrainian civilians and prisoners of war in Bucha, a suburb to the west of Kyiv, after their failed attempt to take the Ukrainian capital. Liberating Ukrainian forces found the bodies of victims, some with their hands tied, lying in the streets. The bodies of 458 people were eventually recovered from Bucha. The majority of them had been shot, tortured or bludgeoned.
From the opening days of Russia's full-scale invasion, the people of Mariupol suffered horrifically during the 86-day Russian siege. To this day, the exact number of Ukrainian civilians killed in Russia's assault on the city is unknown. According to preliminary estimates by Ukraine's Center for the Study of Occupation, at least 22,000 civilians were killed during the siege. The true figure might never be known, as Russia has deliberately destroyed graves and cremated bodies in an attempt to conceal the true death toll in Mariupol. Some estimates put the actual figure as high as 87,000.
A Russian airstrike on March 16, 2022, likely killed 300 to 900 people hiding inside the Mariupol Drama Theater, according to different estimates, including an Associated Press investigation and figures by exiled local authorities. They were awaiting evacuation from the then-besieged Mariupol amid heavy Russian bombardment. Footage of the theater shows that the word "Children" in Russian was written in large letters on the square in front of the theater. Russia bombed the building regardless.
Across Ukraine's occupied territories, Russia has been kidnapping Ukrainian children. Russia's forcible transfer of children constitutes crimes against humanity, according to a probe by an U.N.-mandated independent commission.
"Based on new evidence, the Commission has now concluded that the Russian authorities committed two types of crimes against humanity: deportation and forcible transfer of children, as well as their enforced disappearance," Erik Mose, chair of the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine, said in a statement on March 12.
This was an issue the White House at least appeared to care about previously, with the U.S. State Department allocating $25 million in funding in March 2026 to help trace and rehabilitate Ukrainian children abducted by Russia.
In May, the United Nations also blacklisted Russian armed and security forces for carrying out systematic sexual assaults , rape, and widespread torture of Ukrainian prisoners. Despite Russia's refusal to grant access to U.N. human rights investigators, they were still able to independently verify 310 cases of conflict-related sexual violence in Russia and Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory. The victims were prisoners of war and civilian detainees, the vast majority of them men.

title: Death is a master from Russia
description:
At the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, while in my hometown of Kyiv, I wrote an essay in German for a German website titled "Russia Dehumanizes the World."

The Ukrainian translation of this text, published under the title "The Dehumanization of the World," was included in my new book, "Сплески" ("Splashes"). The essay ends as follows:

"War. The Russians are near. Death is near. Death is a master from Russia.
We are still here.
We, Ukrainians. We, human beings.
We,
content:
Empty graves are seen after the exhumation of bodies from mass burial sites in Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Nov. 4, 2022, following the city's liberation from Russian occupation. (Dimitar Dilkoff/AFP via Getty Images)
At the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, while in my hometown of Kyiv, I wrote an essay in German for a German website titled "Russia Dehumanizes the World."
The Ukrainian translation of this text, published under the title "The Dehumanization of the World," was included in my new book, "Сплески" ("Splashes"). The essay ends as follows:
"War. The Russians are near. Death is near. Death is a master from Russia. We are still here. We, Ukrainians. We, human beings. We, Ukrainians. We, human beings."
This passage paraphrases a line from Paul Celan's haunting surrealist poem "Death Fugue": "Tod – Meister aus Deutschland" ("Death is a master from Germany").
Paul Celan survived World War II and the Holocaust, in which the German Nazis murdered almost all his loved ones. But he could not survive the trauma of violence and loss. At the height of his fame and success, he took his own life by throwing himself from a Parisian bridge into the Seine. He drowned, drowning his inexhaustible pain…
At the beginning of the Russian invasion, my greatest fear was the occupation of Kyiv . We did not yet know what would happen in Bucha and many other Ukrainian cities. We had not yet seen the horrific photographs of Ukrainian men and women tortured and murdered by the Russians. But I knew that the Russian occupation brought torture and death.
It has always been this way, going back to time immemorial. History repeats itself.
The first attempt to establish a state on the territory of present-day Russia began in the 12th century with Andrei Bogolyubsky's sacking of Kyiv in 1169. This happened before the Mongol invasion.
Ever since, waves of violence have rolled relentlessly over our lands from the east. And since the Tsardom of Muscovy established its dominion on the blood of the peoples it conquered and subjugated, this threat has never disappeared.
The attempt to establish the Hetmanate, the first modern state on the territory of present-day Ukraine, ended with the Russian destruction of its Cossack capital, Baturyn, and the mass murder of its inhabitants in 1708.
At the beginning of the 20th century, the Russian Bolsheviks drowned Kyiv in blood when Kyiv briefly became the capital of the Ukrainian People's Republic. Our ancestors then lost their struggle for our freedom and independence to the Russian Bolshevik Empire, and our lands once again fell under Russian occupation, bringing enslavement and death.
The Russian Bolsheviks inflicted the Holodomor , carried out mass repression, and persecuted the Ukrainian language and culture.
After the collapse of yet another incarnation of the Russian empire, the Soviet Union , Ukraine finally gained independence.
It seemed that we might free ourselves from Russia's destructive imperial influence peacefully and build our own independent democratic republic.
But when, in 2013, the Ukrainian people rose up against President Viktor Yanukovych's criminal gang, directed from the Kremlin, to secure a European future for our country, the Russians attacked us once again.
In 2014, they seized Crimea and the southeastern part of our country, and in 2022, they tried to subjugate all of Ukraine. We repelled the Russian invaders, and so far, they have failed.
Now they have adopted a different tactic. The Russians are destroying our cities with drone and missile attacks , trying to make normal life in them impossible, killing civilians and sowing fear and death. They are intensifying the shelling of peaceful Ukrainian cities. Every day, dozens of Russian missiles and hundreds of drones attack Ukrainian residential buildings, hospitals, railway stations, and other civilian targets.
As we fall asleep at night, we do not know which of us will wake up alive, and which of us will be killed by the Russians. The Russian missile genocide continues.
Tonight, like most Kyiv residents, I barely slept. The Russians bombarded Kyiv with missiles and drones. The noise was deafening.
This morning, there is no water or electricity. The Russians have once again struck critical infrastructure. I washed myself with the few drops left in the tap and went downstairs to the coffee shop in my building. It has a power generator, so there is electricity: I can wash my hands with hot water, drink a good cup of coffee, and work.
Finishing this text here, I hope that in a few hours, Kyiv's heroic electricity workers, risking their lives under Russian bombardment, will restore power, allowing me to conduct my philosophical anthropology seminars remotely from home for students at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv.
Not all my students can connect: the electricity and internet connection keep cutting out.
As soon as an air raid alert sounds, I must interrupt the seminar and let everyone go to a shelter.
And I have begun to worry about a question: Is what I am doing appropriate at a time like this? Does it make sense to discuss the nature of the human being, human freedom and dignity, the value of human life and life itself with my students when Russian shelling could cut short any one of our lives?
Yet this is exactly what the Russians are trying to achieve by shelling Ukraine's peaceful cities.
They are trying to make ordinary, peaceful life in our cities impossible, hoping that this will force us to capitulate. But I know all too well what it means to live under Russian rule: repression, torture, death.
So we have no choice. Our military must continue to resist on the front line, while civilians must sustain ordinary life in the rear, as far as possible. Through extraordinary effort and at the cost of the lives of so many Ukrainian heroes and heroines, Ukraine's Armed Forces managed to drive the Russian onslaught back from Kyiv.
The Russian missile terror continues. But I believe it will not force us to surrender, because defeat would mean either forced emigration or captivity and death for us. Victory, by contrast, will make a free and dignified life in Ukraine possible.
An independent, democratic, prosperous Ukraine is the guarantee of a peaceful and free life for all the peoples of Europe . If we succeed in stopping the Russian imperial onslaught here, Russian imperialism will no longer threaten other peoples in Europe and around the world.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Vakhtang Kebuladze is a philosopher, publicist, and translator, a professor at Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv and an associate professor at Kyiv-Mohyla Academy.

title: Ukraine's HUR claims 108 Russian soldiers killed, 29 captured in Sumy Oblast operation
description: According to HUR's Active Operations Department, the operation was carried out by its Group 10 special forces unit, which reportedly thwarted Russian offensive plans and prevented Russian troops from cutting off Ukrainian logistical routes in the region.
content:
Ukrainian special forces killed 108 Russian soldiers, captured another 29, and struck more than 1,100 Russian targets during a seven-week operation in Sumy Oblast, Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) reported on Oct. 20.
According to HUR's Active Operations Department, the operation was carried out by its Group 10 special forces unit, which reportedly thwarted Russian offensive plans and prevented Russian troops from cutting off Ukrainian logistical routes in the region.
Over the course of seven weeks, Ukrainian operatives cleared Russian troops from more than 600 hectares of forest before handing over the positions to Ukraine's Defense Forces, the intelligence agency said.
HUR did not specify the exact location of the operation or when it took place.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify these claims.
Ukraine's defensive operations reduced the pace of Russia's territorial advances by more than half in the first six months of 2026, then-Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi said on July 10.
Separately, on Sept. 28, Ukraine's 3rd Army Corps reported further territorial gains in northern Donetsk Oblast as part of Operation Vivaldi , a counteroffensive that had reclaimed a total of 176 square kilometers. According to the corps, the latest phase of the operation inflicted more than 2,000 Russian casualties and resulted in the capture of over 250 Russian soldiers.

title: Rubio says delays in US air defense shipments to Ukraine not deliberate
description: "I think the important takeaway for you is that there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine," Rubio said, acknowledging possible delays in interceptor shipments.
content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Oct. 20 acknowledged a possible delay in a shipment of missile interceptors to Ukraine, but denied that this would be a deliberate decision to harm Kyiv.
"Every country in the world would like interceptors... It's probably the most in-demand product right now in the defense field," Rubio told reporters during his trip to India.
"So when a country doesn't get interceptors from the United States , it's not because we're denying. We have our own needs, too."
The Kyiv Independent reported on Oct. 19 that U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is holding up supplies of Patriot missiles , which Ukraine relies on to intercept Russian ballistic missiles, as ties between Ukraine and the U.S. sour.
"Hegseth has the contracts for Patriot missiles on his desk. He is not signing off on them," one Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent, referring to a shipment already paid for by Kyiv's allies.
Rubio acknowledged that a batch of interceptors may have been held up as the U.S. weighs its strategic priorities, but claimed that "there has not been some deliberate political directive to go out and harm Ukraine."
Patriot interceptors have been in short supply worldwide as the U.S. and its allies burned through their stockpiles during the war with Iran. Ukraine has been receiving limited amounts of Patriot missiles paid for by NATO allies under the PURL initiative, among other channels.
Rubio said he held a 45-minute phone call with President Volodymyr Zelensky earlier on Oct. 20 to discuss recent tensions in U.S.-Ukraine relations.
The rift emerged following the unexpected announcement of a U.S.-Russia diesel deal on Oct. 9.
Since then, Zelensky and U.S. President Donald Trump have exchanged sharp public criticism. Trump accused his Ukrainian counterpart of not wanting to end the war and suggested Zelensky should be replaced as Ukraine's leader.
Kyiv, in turn, accused Washington of pressuring it to halt strikes against Russian refineries by threatening to cut off arms shipments and intelligence support.

title: Poland to demand explanation from Ukraine over drone incident in Lithuania
description: Lithuania said the drone entered its airspace from the Polish side before exploding on its territory on Oct. 18. Ukraine linked the incident to Russian jamming.
content:
Poland will seek an explanation from Ukraine on a drone that allegedly entered Polish territory over the weekend before exploding in Lithuania, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Oct. 20.
Lithuania said the drone entered its airspace from the Polish side before exploding on Oct. 18, damaging a moving car. No injuries were reported.
Ukraine offered its apology and explained the incident as another possible case of Russian jamming diverting Ukrainian drones from their intended targets in Russia.
"We will investigate all circumstances. I count on the full cooperation of the Ukrainian side so that we can precisely explain what happened," Tusk said at a government meeting, as reported by RMF24 . "Without emotion, without ill intentions."
Polish authorities have been unable to confirm whether the drone entered Poland's airspace before flying into Lithuania.
Vilnius has echoed Kyiv's explanation, saying that the drone was likely part of a Ukrainian attack against St. Petersburg but was diverted by Russian electronic warfare.
The Polish prime minister said he would discuss the incident with Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda, whom he is hosting in Warsaw.
"We will cooperate very closely with Lithuania and will certainly clarify this drone incident," Tusk noted.
Poland and the Baltic countries are among the NATO members most affected by drone incursions spilling over from Russia's war against Ukraine.
Both Poland and Lithuania border Russia's fortified exclave of Kaliningrad and Moscow's key ally, Belarus.
Stray Ukrainian drones diverted by Russian jamming, as well as Russian drones and missiles launched against targets in Ukraine, have repeatedly entered NATO airspace, prompting local governments to ramp up security measures.
"I want to make it absolutely clear that Poland does not allow operations to be conducted on or over our territory without the explicit consent of the Polish state," Tusk said.
"That will not change, no matter who might be conducting those operations."
Kyiv has previously refuted that it would be using NATO airspace for its attacks against Russian targets.
Poland has backed Ukraine's resistance against Russia throughout the full-scale war, but their ties took a hit earlier this year after Kyiv named one of its military units after the World War II-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army.
After a period of tensions, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 18 that "our relations with Poland have indeed improved."

title: Russian drones strike Kyiv hospital, injure 12 across the city
description: Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Russia struck the operating room of the Strazheska Institute of the National Academy of Medical Sciences in Kyiv, injuring one patient.
content:
Russian drones repeatedly struck Kyiv on Oct. 20, damaging a hospital in Solomyanskyi District and another medical facility in Holosiivskyi District, injuring 12 people, according to local authorities.
Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Russia struck the operating room of the Strazheska Institute of the National Academy of Medical Sciences in Kyiv, injuring one patient.
"This is the second time. Last year, the attack hit the fourth floor of the institute, and now it is on the sixth floor, where the operating room is located," Koretskyi said.
The medical facility in Holosiivskyi was damaged by debris from a Russian drone, Kyiv city mayor Vitali Klitschko said in the afternoon.
While Klitschko initially reported two people injured, the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMCA) later raised the total number of injured people to five.
Ukraine's National Police later reported that a total of 12 people were injured in the city, according to the State Emergency Service (DSNS).
Debris also fell on railway tracks in Solomyansyki District but did not lead to a fire, the mayor said. Several other buildings in the Holosiivskyi area were also seemingly struck in the attack, according to Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground.
DSNS later said that an administrative building in the Holosiivskyi district was damaged. First responders rescued four people from upper floors after a fire broke out.
A large-scale fire also broke out in Kyiv's Desnianskyi District, close to the Northern Bridge, KMCA spokesperson Kateryna Pop told RBC Ukraine . Initial reports on social media that the Northern Bridge was hit were not correct.
The Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) also said that the Northern Bridge was not hit, but that traffic on the bridge may be disrupted due to inspections of the consequences of the nearby attack.
DSNS later reported that a fire broke out at a community garage in the Desnianskyi District.
In the Obolon District, debris from a drone fell on a market, KMCA said . The consequences of the incident were still under investigation.
Following another attack in the afternoon, Klitschko said that an energy facility was hit in Shevchenkivskyi District, as emergency services were on their way.
Earlier this morning, at least three people were killed and four people injured after a Russian drone struck early morning commuter traffic in the Holosiivskyi District of Kyiv.
DSNS reported the victims of Russia's drone strike, saying, "The enemy is once again cynically attacking civilians. Behind each such blow are human lives, pain, and ruined destinies."
The Russian drone crashed near a gas station in the Holosiivskyi District close to the administrative border with Kyiv Oblast, Kyiv city mayor Vitali Klitschko said .
Images shared by the Kyiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office showed multiple cars ablaze at the scene of the attack near the Kyiv-Odesa highway.

title: Zelensky meets Trump envoy Witkoff in Norway as US-Ukraine ties sour
description: Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb are also taking part in the talks.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky met U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo for talks on Oct. 20, amid deteriorating ties between their two countries.
The Kyiv-Washington relations have soured as Ukraine accuses the U.S. of using military assistance and access to technology to pressure it to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store and Finnish President Alexander Stubb took part in the talks.
While Witkoff attended the meeting in person, U.S. envoy Jared Kushner was scheduled to join remotely due to an alleged illness, Reuters reported on Oct. 19, citing a source familiar with the matter.
"President Volodymyr Zelensky has asked Norway and Finland to organize a meeting as part of the ongoing diplomatic efforts, in a critical time for Ukraine," Store said in a statement .
"Together with President Alexander Stubb, I'm glad to be able to host this meeting in Oslo."
Zelensky said he would hold a separate bilateral meeting with Witkoff, a trilateral meeting with Store and Stubb, and joint talks with all three officials.
Other European officials — reportedly including representatives of the U.K., Germany, France, and Poland — were also expected to join the discussions.
The EU would be represented by Bjoern Seibert, head of the cabinet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a senior Commission official told the Kyiv Independent. Seibert, regarded as von der Leyen's "right-hand man," previously took part in an earlier round of peace talks on Oct. 9.
Lorenz Meyer-Minnemann, the deputy chief of staff in the Office of the Secretary General at NATO, will also take part in the talks, a NATO official told the Kyiv Independent.
"We are maintaining all contacts that can help bring peace. We will also discuss strengthening our air defense and joint production," said Zelensky on social media upon his arrival in Norway.
The Kyiv-Washington ties plummeted following the unexpected announcement of a U.S.-Russia diesel deal on Oct. 9.
Since then, Zelensky and U.S. President Donald Trump have exchanged sharp public criticism. Trump said his Ukrainian counterpart "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
Trump has also refused to condemn the Kremlin over its escalating attacks on Ukraine, including strikes on the country's already vulnerable energy infrastructure.
Zelensky, meanwhile, warned in an interview with NBC News that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake."
His remarks came amid concerns in Kyiv that Washington could be withholding the delivery of Patriot air defense missiles funded by Ukraine's allies and cutting off crucial intelligence about Russian missile attacks.
Witkoff is also reportedly expected to meet Putin in Russia to discuss the possible release of Stephen Hubbard , a 72-year-old American citizen who was reportedly serving with a Ukrainian territorial defense unit in Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, when Russian forces detained him in 2022.

title: Data center in occupied Donetsk destroyed, expert says
description: Ukraine has increasingly used long-range strikes and strikes against data centers to weaken Russia's ability to sustain the war.
content:
An overnight attack on a building in occupied Donetsk, in Donetsk Oblast, destroyed a data center of Ugletelecom and Elecom, the main telecom operator in the occupied Donetsk region, on Oct. 20, according to Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation.
Andriushchenko confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that the data center was hit on the premises of Postysheva St. 60, in occupied Donetsk, according to his sources.
Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ reported that explosions were heard in Donetsk this morning and shared footage showing the damaged facade of the building on Postysheva St. 60.
The head of Russia's proxies in the city of Donetsk, Alexey Kulemzin, reported a Ukrainian attack on the city this morning and shared video footage of the same damaged building on Telegram.
Ukrainian officials did not confirm the attack.
Moscow and Kyiv increasingly strike at each other's data centers after a Russian attack damaged a Kyiv data center housing network equipment for internet provider UTELS, causing service disruptions on Sept. 23.
Ukraine, which has increasingly used long-range strikes to weaken Russia's ability to sustain the war, retaliated. Between Oct. 8 and Oct. 18, Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers, a Sberbank facility under construction, and a data center belonging to social media giant VK.
The consequences of Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centers could extend far beyond disrupted banking and online services, potentially setting back the country's AI development and affecting military technology.
73% of Donetsk Oblast are currently occupied by Russia , while the city of Donetsk has been under Russian occupation since 2014. Occupied Donetsk Oblast has been facing one of the most severe water crises among Ukraine's occupied territories. Residents of the occupied city of Donetsk have reported going entire days without running water.
Beyond the water crisis, municipal services have deteriorated, with garbage collection among the problems affecting cities such as Donetsk and Mariupol.

title: EU to bolster tracking of Russian shadow fleet and hybrid attacks with new Arctic Strategy
description: "When we see Russia rebuilding its Arctic military footprint, pursuing hybrid strategies against its neighbors, and reshaping the security of the Arctic, it impacts the EU as a whole," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The EU unveiled its new Arctic Strategy on Oct. 20, a strategic pivot to confront the threat Russia poses to Europe's northern flank and Moscow's use of the region to avoid sanctions.
"When we see Russia rebuilding its Arctic military footprint, pursuing hybrid strategies against its neighbors, and reshaping the security of the Arctic, it impacts the EU as a whole," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
"The merger of Russia's Baltic Sea and Arctic fleets shows Moscow considers the two regions to be interconnected. We need to do so too," a senior EU official told journalists ahead of the announcement by von der Leyen.
The strategy foresees bolstering Europe's icebreaker fleet — a longtime demand of Finland — increasing protection of critical infrastructure in the region, and monitoring for potential acts of sabotage and the movement of Russia's shadow fleet through the region.
Moscow's shadow fleet, composed mostly of old, dilapidated ships, is helping Russia circumvent sanctions and has been increasingly intercepted by European navies and coast guards.
The Arctic Strategy would expand the scope of tracking beyond the Mediterranean and Baltic Seas to also cover the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans, with the establishment of a Maritime Security Hub.
However, the Maritime Security Hub does not come to life immediately following a proposal by the European Commission.
The senior EU official explained that the idea first needs to be discussed with EU member states to see who is willing to contribute what to the initiative.
The idea also mentions working closely with NATO and its member countries, but it is not yet confirmed which non-EU countries will participate.
And the precise geographical scope of the new measures also remains unclear.
Alongside the Maritime Security Hub, the press release announcing the new Arctic Strategy also mentions an Arctic Cable Club for protecting subsea infrastructure.
But senior European Commission officials repeatedly said they "have not drawn lines on the map for where will be covered."
Ireland recognized in its new National Maritime Security Strategy that it is particularly vulnerable to undersea sabotage by vessels of the Russian shadow fleet, but EU officials would not comment on whether the seas around Ireland fall within the scope of the new strategy.
And Irish diplomats could not give an opinion on the EU's new Arctic Strategy, given that it has yet to be presented to them.
However, Ireland already participates in a range of EU security and defense initiatives, and there is no reason to expect it would not wish to benefit from the proposed Maritime Security Hub.

title: Poland has no Patriot missiles left for Ukraine, Sikorski says
description: Sikorski said that the shortage of missiles had worsened after the attacks on Iran.
content:
Poland is not in a position to provide Ukraine with U.S.-made Patriot missiles, Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) in an interview published on Oct. 19, as Kyiv struggles to intercept Russian missile strikes.
Sikorski said that the shortage of interceptor missiles had worsened after the attacks on Iran, and that Russia now produces more missiles.
“This is a genuine problem,” Sikorski said.
At the same time Sikorski added that other NATO countries still could transfer such resources to Ukraine, but did not specify which countries he was referring to.
For now, Sikorski said, Poland can only join in the appeals to other countries to help supply Ukraine with the much needed missiles.
The comments come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian ballistic missile attacks and increasingly severe shortages of the interceptors needed to defend against them.
Patriot systems are among Ukraine's most important defenses against Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to intercept using other systems.
On Oct. 15, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Polish aid helped Ukraine defend Kyiv during recent attacks, having provided ammunition used by Ukraine's anti-aircraft guns. Zelensky also hinted at other, more sensitive Polish support which would have to remain confidential; "sometimes it should remain between the two of us," he said.
On Oct. 18, Zelensky said that Washington has approved only some of the missiles purchased through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which allows NATO allies to finance the purchase of U.S.-made weapons for Ukraine, according to Bloomberg .
"The American side approved the delivery of only some of them, but not the rest. And this is not a technical issue," Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president said the U.S. is currently supplying just 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, approximately one-quarter of the number provided under former President Joe Biden's administration.

title: South Korea to withdraw some diplomatic staff from Ukraine amid POW dispute
description: "This measure was taken because ​we judged it necessary to facilitate an amicable resolution of the ‌issue ⁠and restore trust between the two countries," said Park Doo-soon, a spokesperson for South Korea's Foreign Ministry, according to Yonhap.
content:
Seoul will withdraw some diplomatic personnel from Ukraine amid deteriorating relations with Kyiv following the disclosure of a transfer of North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to South Korea, Yonhap news agency reported on Oct. 20, citing the South Korean Foreign Ministry.
The decision follows South Korea's earlier decision to recall its ambassador to Ukraine on Oct. 8, to which Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi responded that "diplomacy should prevail over emotions."
Relations between the two countries have plummeted after President Volodymyr Zelensky disclosed the transfer of two North Korean POWs to South Korea during his speech at the U.N. General Assembly on Sept. 23. Seoul claims the announcement violated a confidentiality agreement.
"This measure was taken because ​we judged it necessary to facilitate an amicable resolution of the ‌issue ⁠and restore trust between the two countries," Park Doo-soon, a spokesperson for Seoul's Foreign Ministry, said during a press briefing, according to Yonhap.
He did not disclose how many diplomats will be leaving Ukraine.
Nonetheless, a charge d'affaires is set to remain in Kyiv to ​represent South Korean nationals in Ukraine and to maintain diplomatic communications between the countries, Park added.
Seoul also justified the decision by the growing threat of Russian air strikes , which make it difficult to ensure the safety of its staff.
The move marks another episode in the deteriorating Ukrainian-South Korean ties sparked by Zelensky's revelation of the POW transfer.
Despite Seoul's anger , Ukraine's Presidential Office said it would have been "strange" to keep the entire transfer secret and initially claimed there was no confidentiality agreement.
Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha later described the spat as a "diplomatic misunderstanding."
Seoul rebuffed Kyiv's claims about an alleged lack of a confidentiality agreement and only sharpened its rhetoric after Ukraine's denial.
"If you (Ukraine) continue to refuse to acknowledge the facts and to issue a public apology, we will take additional measures," said South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Oct. 2.
"As this is a matter concerning the honor of the Republic of Korea's people and nation, we cannot overlook it," he added in a social media post .
South Korea said on Oct. 6 it received an apology from Ukraine that differed "from the level we expect," adding it would "take firm measures" if no further explanation or apology is provided.
Ukraine announced the capture of two North Korean soldiers in early 2025 as an estimated 11,000 North Korean troops were deployed to Russia's Kursk Oblast .

title: Hungary blocks next step in EU membership bids of Ukraine, Moldova, no explanation given
description: Colleagues asked their Hungarian counterparts to explain their position, but they did not, one diplomat said.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Hungary blocked the next step in the EU membership process for Moldova and Ukraine, even though their previous demands had been met, national and EU diplomats told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 20.
Ukraine and Moldova are proceeding together in their EU membership process until all six enlargement clusters — to-do lists of reforms to align with EU law — are unlocked.
The two countries unlocked another two of those clusters on Oct. 13 in Luxembourg, leaving two more that it is hoped will open by the end of the year.
Technical experts from the 27 EU countries met on Oct. 20 with a view to agreeing to take a procedural step, that would start the process of unlocking the final two clusters, which cover agriculture, environment, and transport.
However, Hungary blocked the move, leaving 26 other countries disappointed in its wake, three diplomats told the Kyiv Independent.
Colleagues even asked their Hungarian counterparts to explain their position but they did not, one diplomat said.
Instead, Hungary apparently said their position is the same as before.
Hungary's Permanent Representation to the EU was asked to comment for this story, but failed to do so before publication.
One thing Hungary's position cannot be based on: education rights for Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking minority, which Kyiv passed a law about on Oct. 12.
Instead, the block is expected to be temporary, so that the Hungarian government is not seen by the opposition as being "soft" on Ukraine.
The discussion will come up at every subsequent enlargement working party meeting in Brussels, until the deadlock is broken, as advancing the membership bids of Ukraine and Moldova is a priority of the Irish EU Council Presidency, which chairs the meetings until the end of the year.
Senior EU and national officials told the Kyiv Independent they predict the final two clusters to formally open in December.

title: Zelensky's trust rating surges amid Trump's pressure campaign, poll finds
description: U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized Zelensky, saying Ukraine should consider finding someone else to negotiate on its behalf.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky's trust rating rose by 14 percentage points after U.S. President Donald Trump began his pressure campaign against Ukraine, according to a poll published by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) on Oct. 20.
The findings come amid worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington, as Ukraine accuses the U.S. of using military assistance and access to technology to pressure it to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries. Trump has repeatedly criticized Zelensky, saying Ukraine should consider finding someone else to negotiate on its behalf.
According to the KIIS poll , 43% of Ukrainians trusted Zelensky between Oct. 8 and 9, while 52% did not. Between Oct. 10 and 16, his trust rating rose to 57%, while the share distrusting him fell to 39%.
Across the full survey period, from Oct. 8 to 16, 54% of respondents said they trusted Zelensky. Of those, 22% said they trusted him completely, while 32% somewhat trusted him.
At the same time, 41% said they did not trust the Ukrainian president . Of those, 24% said they did not trust him at all, while 17% somewhat distrusted him.
Trump has shifted toward Moscow in what appears to be an effort to lower domestic fuel prices. On Oct. 9, he announced a plan to purchase Russian diesel despite years of U.S. sanctions on Russian energy products. He also ordered Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries.
The overall figures were identical to those recorded in late August and early September, suggesting that confidence in Zelensky has remained virtually unchanged over the past month.
"There are indeed many Ukrainians who criticize President Zelensky for the various problems facing Ukraine and Ukrainians," KIIS Executive Director Anton Hrushetskyi said.
"While Ukrainians may be genuinely outraged by instances of corruption among members of the president's team or by poor personnel decisions, the voices of critics are significantly quieter when it comes to relations with other countries, securing support for the country in the defense sector, and, in general, defending Ukraine's interests on the international stage ."
Before Trump's criticism, Zelensky's rating was tested by major corruption scandals .
The latest survey was conducted through computer-assisted telephone interviews using a random sample of cell phone numbers across all regions of Ukraine under government control.
KIIS surveyed 1,031 Ukrainian citizens aged 18 and older.
A similar shift in public support occurred in 2025. Zelensky's approval rating rose to 68% following his heated exchange with Trump in the Oval Office. Before the diplomatic dispute, a February 2025 survey found that 57% of Ukrainians trusted the president.

title: At least 16 killed, 69 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over past day as Russian drone kills 2 children in park
description: On the night of Oct. 20, Russia attacked Ukraine with 165 Shahed-type and other drones, 105 of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force said.
content:
Editor's note: The story was updated to include the latest casualty figures from Russian attacks in Kyiv.
At least 16 people were killed and 69 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia killed at least two children in a drone strike on a park in Kharkiv Oblast, regional authorities said on Oct. 19 to 20.
Six people, including two children, were killed in a Russian drone strike on a park in Nova Vodolaha, Kharkiv Oblas t. A one-year-old girl called Anhelina was killed instantly in her stroller. Her mother, Inna Mariukhna, died of her injuries in hospital. Images of the little girl, lying dead in her push-chair, circulated on Ukrainian social media, sparking outrage after President Donald Trump told reporters at almost the same time that, "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine."
President Volodymyr Zelensky called the attack an "absolute atrocity," and called on his allies to support Ukraine with more air defenses. He also explicitly warned against striking deals with Russia and easing sanctions at this moment.
Another person was injured in the town of Chuhuyiv in north-eastern Kharkiv Oblast over the past day, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said, bringing the total to six killed and 16 injured in the Oblast. Russia also struck residential buildings and powerlines with missiles and drones, the governor added.
On the night of Oct. 20, Russia attacked Ukraine with 165 Shahed-type and other drones, 105 of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force said. The Air Force said it shot down or suppressed 115 Russian Shahed-type and other drones, 73 of them jet-powered, across 30 locations.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , one person was killed while eight others were injured in Russian attacks on the front-line cities of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, as well as in the villages of Ocheretyne and Dmytro-Daryivka over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said. While Russian attacks damaged private houses, cars, and administrative buildings, a strike on the village of Starovarvarivka also damaged the local church, the governor added.
In Kyiv , at least three people were killed and four people injured after a Russian drone struck early morning commuter traffic in the Holosiivskyi District, according to Ukraine's state emergency service .
In Kyiv Oblast , Russian attacks on Obukhiv District killed three people and injured six, according to Tymur Tkachenko , head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast , over the past day, Russia carried out 848 attacks on 52 settlements of the region, killing one and injuring five people in the attacks, regional governor Ivan Fedorov said. The attacks were carried out by Russian artillery, UAVs, MLRS, and air strikes, the governor reported.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , a Russian attack on an industrial enterprise in Kryvyi Rih on Oct. 19 killed two people and injured eight others, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said. Another attack on a warehouse in Dnipro injured four people on the morning of Oct. 20, the governor added .
In southern Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks injured 18 people, including a child, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Russian forces targeted 36 settlements across the region with artillery fire, drones, and air strikes, he said.
Due to Russian attacks, Ukraine's state-owned electricity operator reported power outages in twelve of Ukraine's regions on Oct. 20.
"There are new power outages in the Kirovohrad, Zhytomyr, Lviv, Odesa, Rivne, Ternopil, Khmelnytskyi, Zaporizhia, Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Chernihiv regions in the morning," Ukrenergo said .
Vinnytsia Oblast Governor Nataliia Zabolotna said on Oct. 20 that Russia continues its mass attack on energy infrastructure. She added that energy workers were trying to restore light to people's homes.
In northwestern Zhytomyr Oblast , for three days running, the Russian forces continued their attempts to destroy energy facilities and railway infrastructure, regional governor Vitalii Bunechko said.
In northwestern Volyn Oblast , Russian drone attacks left several settlements without electricity, regional governor Roman Romaniuk said. The cities of Kovel and Lutsk were hit hardest, with damage reported to critical and civilian infrastructure.
Ukrenergo , Ukraine's state grid operator, reported that as a result of the attack, power outages occurred in 12 regions.

title: Power outages in half of Ukraine's oblasts after Russian assault on power plants
description: To avoid overloading previously damaged equipment, power limitation schedules for industry will be applied across all of Ukraine, as well as hourly outage schedules in some regions, Ukrenergo announced.
content:
Due to Russian attacks, Ukraine's state-owned electricity operator reported power outages in twelve of Ukraine's oblasts on Oct. 20.
"There are new power outages in the Kirovohrad, Zhytomyr, Lviv, Odesa, Rivne, Ternopil, Khmelnytskyi, Zaporizhia, Donetsk, Kharkiv, Sumy and Chernihiv oblasts in the morning," Ukrenergo said .
To avoid overloading previously damaged equipment, power limitation schedules for industry will be applied across all of Ukraine, as well as hourly outage schedules in some oblasts, according to the operator.
Russia continues to "systematically and purposefully attack" Ukraine's energy sector, Ukrainian First Deputy Minister of Energy of Artem Nekrasov said in a briefing on Oct. 20.
"At night and in the morning, Russia attacked energy facilities in Kirovohrad, Zhytomyr, Lviv, Odessa, Rivne, Ternopil and Khmelnytsky Oblasts," Nekrasov said , adding that due to the Russian strikes some consumers were left without power supply.
The strikes come as Russia intensifies its drone and missile campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure as the country approaches its fifth winter since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
The day before, another wave of Russian missile and drone strikes had hit 28 electrical substations and other critical energy facilities across Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 19.
16 ballistic missiles and over 200 drones were used in what Zelensky described as a " targeted attack on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast ."

title: Russian drone attack on Kyiv rush-hour traffic kills at least 3, injures 4
description: The Russian drone crashed near a gas station in the Holosiivskyi District near the administrative border with Kyiv Oblast, according to Kyiv city mayor Vitali Klitschko.
content:
At least three people were killed and four people were injured after a Russian drone struck early morning commuter traffic in the Holosiivskyi District of Kyiv on Oct. 20, according to local authorities.
Ukraine's State emergency service reported the victims of Russia's drone strike, saying "The enemy is once again cynically attacking civilians. Behind each such blow are human lives, pain, and ruined destinies."
The Russian drone crashed near a gas station in the Holosiivskyi District close to the administrative border with Kyiv Oblast, Kyiv city mayor Vitali Klitschko said .
Images shared by the Kyiv Oblast Prosecutor's Office showed multiple cars ablaze at the scene of the attack near the Kyiv-Odesa highway.
A pre-trial investigation has been initiated into the violation of the laws and customs of war, the Prosecutor's Office announced.
Earlier the same morning, three people were killed and at least six others injured as a result of a Russian attack on a production and warehouse building in the city of Obukhiv, just to the south of the Ukrainian capital, Ukrainian emergency services reported .
Kyiv Oblast governor Tymur Tkachenko identified the victims of the Russian strike as two women and one man, and added that the fire had been extinguished
On the night of Oct. 20, Russia attacked Ukraine with 165 Shahed-type and other drones, 105 of them jet-powered, Ukraine's Air Force said. The Air Force said it shot down or suppressed 115 Russian Shahed-type and other drones, 73 of them jet-powered, across 30 locations.
Kyiv and other cities are frequently attacked by jet-powered drones, which weren’t widespread last winter. They are faster and fly higher than Russia's older propeller-powered drones, making them harder for Ukraine’s limited air defenses to shoot down.

title: Fire at oil pumping station in Russia’s Tambov Oblast after drone attack, monitoring channels say
description: Tambov Oblast governor Yevgeny Pervyshov said that a Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire 'on the territory of one of the enterprises' in Michurinsky district but did not specify at which facility.
content:
A fire reportedly broke out at an oil pumping station near the Russian city of Michurinsk in Tambov Oblast after an overnight drone attack on Oct. 20, according to Telegram monitoring channels.
Tambov Oblast governor Yevgeny Pervyshov said that a Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire "on the territory of one of the enterprises" in Michurinsky District but did not specify at which facility. He claimed that four drones in total were shot down overnight and in the morning of Oct. 20, mainly by mobile fire groups. He reported no casualties.
On video footage of the reported attack published by monitoring channel Exilenova+ , a fire and dark smoke can be seen at what residents supposedly identified as a diesel fuel tank.
Independent Russian outlet ASTRA said the fire likely started at the Nikolskoye-1 linear production and dispatch station near the village of Novonikolskoye.
The Nikolskoye linear production and dispatch station is a major oil and petroleum facility, operated by Transneft as part of the Druzhba oil pipeline network. The station is located about 350 to 400 kilometers (about 220 to 250 miles) from the frontline in Ukraine.
Ukrainian authorities did not yet confirm an attack. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify a fire at the station.
Ukraine attacked the station previously on Aug. 18, 2025 . Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, who heads Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, then confirmed that drones of the 14th Regiment of the Unmanned Systems Unit attacked the Nikolskoye oil pumping station, which halted the operation of the Russian Druzhba oil pipeline.
The Druzhba pipeline , part of which crosses Ukraine, remains a key route for supplying Russian crude to Hungary and Slovakia under an exemption from European Union sanctions imposed over Moscow's war in Ukraine.

title: Zelensky, Rubio discuss critical military systems amid US-Ukraine tensions
description: "I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position," President Volodymyr Zelensky said after the conversation.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed tensions in U.S.-Ukraine relations with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio during a phone call on Oct. 20, the Ukrainian president said.
The conversation comes as Kyiv accuses Washington of using military aid and access to technology as leverage to pressure Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
"It was a substantive conversation — focused on the issues that matter," the Ukrainian president said . "I am grateful for his readiness to help and his clear position."
The two discussed ballistic missile interceptors, early warning of Russian ballistic missile attacks, and the situation with Starlink and Starshield, Zelensky said.
Ukraine has recently experienced disruptions to its early-warning systems for incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which rely on U.S. intelligence. American officials have attributed previous outages to "bad weather conditions," while Rubio has cited a software malfunction.
Ukraine has also experienced disruptions to Starlink and Starshield services, which have severely hampered Ukrainian drone operations, including the use of interceptor drones to counter Russian jet-powered attack drones on Ukrainian cities.
Alongside the disruptions to intelligence and satellite services, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to approve the transfer of a significant batch of Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine, Ukrainian officials and military officers told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian officials have described the alleged delay as another example of political pressure from Washington, warning that it could put civilian lives at risk.
The tensions come as U.S. President Donald Trump has criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries while Washington seeks to address rising global fuel prices driven by his war in Iran.
Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 9, allowing Russia to supply millions of tons of diesel to U.S. and international markets despite sanctions imposed over Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,568,720 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,560 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,568,720 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 20.
The number includes 1,560 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,425 tanks, 25,570 armored combat vehicles, 164,871 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,359 artillery systems, 2,227 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,714 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,986 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: The political calculus of peace in Ukraine
