For years, Ukraine's leadership framed victory, not compromise, a
content:
In Ukraine, calls for peace are testing both public opinion and political ambition.
Emergency services deal with the aftermath of a massive Russian missile and drone attack in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 8, 2026. (Kostiantyn Liberov / Libkos / Getty Images)
In Ukraine, few words carry as much weight — or as much political risk — as peace.
In early October, several prominent Ukrainian politicians publicly called for an end to Russia's war on terms many considered to be closer to the Kremlin's desires. Their proposals differed, but the public reaction revealed a deep-seated fear: that calls for peace could be a prelude to concessions to Moscow rather than a path to a just settlement.
For years, Ukraine's leadership framed victory, not compromise, as the ultimate goal of the war. But Donald Trump 's return to the White House last year changed the political landscape, increasing pressure on Kyiv to negotiate an end to the war while insisting that any settlement must not come on Moscow’s terms.
Now, increasing Russian drone attacks on Kyiv, renewed tensions with Washington and stalled negotiations with Moscow have created fresh uncertainty over how — and on what terms — the war might end.
In these recent statements, critics see more than a desire to stop the fighting. They suspect political maneuvering: populist appeals, and politicians' attempts to position themselves for a future contest for power, or efforts to test how much compromise the public might tolerate.
"The main goal of all these statements is to see how society would react to such a scenario," said Olha Vasylevska-Smahliuk, a lawmaker from the ruling party. "The first is a peace deal with Russia, the second is the removal of the president, and the third is holding elections."
"Of course, we need peace," she added. "The question is under what conditions."
As Ukrainian officials prepared for another round of talks with Washington, Oleksiy Goncharenko, then a lawmaker with the opposition European Solidarity, laid out his own plan for ending Russia's war.
In an Oct. 4 op-ed in one of Ukraine's leading publications, Goncharenko called for seeking an agreement with Moscow, arguing that this wouldn't be synonymous with surrender. He proposed a number of agreements mediated by third countries, with both sides making concessions and with the issue of the eastern Donbas region — the main territorial sticking point — addressed last. His plan also called for Russian to receive the same status as other minority languages in Ukraine and for the Moscow-affiliated Ukrainian Orthodox Church to be allowed to operate.
"Can we destroy Russia right now? No, we can’t. If we accept this objective reality, we can't fight until we cease to exist. We must know when to stop and preserve our state," Goncharenko said.
Critics argued that the proposals came too close to capitulation to Russia , a characterisation the lawmaker rejected.
Mykola Kniazhytskyi, a lawmaker from the same European Solidarity party, said peace depended first and foremost on Russian President Vladimir Putin . Russia has shown no willingness to make concessions or abandon its goal of seizing Donbas.
"Any calls for peace directed at Ukraine, and any accusations against the Ukrainian side in this regard, are clearly playing into Putin's hands and those politicians who seek to portray the victim as the guilty party and absolve the aggressor of responsibility," Kniazhytskyi told the Kyiv Independent.
For Kyiv, accepting a freeze along the current front line would already be a "huge concession," argues Olexiy Haran, politics professor at the Kyiv Mohyla Academy and research advisor at the Democratic Initiatives Foundation.
"Putin has no interest in negotiations or compromise. He wants it all."
"Twenty percent of our territory remains under occupation, where every day brings terror and the destruction of everything Ukrainian," he adds. "These are speculations. Putin has no interest in negotiations or compromise. He wants it all."
Goncharenko has long been a conspicuous figure in Ukrainian politics. One of parliament’s most recognisable lawmakers, he has amassed more than 200,000 Telegram followers.
Before joining former President Petro Poroshenko 's team in 2014, he was part of the now banned Party of Regions and promoted pro-Russian narratives, including calls to make Russian Ukraine's second official language.
Since 2025, he has distinguished himself by voting against extending the mobilization in Ukraine, the only lawmaker to do so, and regularly criticized the country's draft policies . His positions have repeatedly put him at odds with his party, prompting questions about why he remained a member.
Several European Solidarity lawmakers told the Kyiv Independent that Goncharenko's views had been debated within the faction before, but expulsion had never been considered. The earlier disagreements concerned his rhetoric rather than the substance of his positions, they said. His peace proposal exposed a deeper ideological divide.
On Oct. 5, the party expelled him from its parliamentary faction.
For months, lawmaker Danylo Hetmantsev has drawn a line between what he describes as Ukraine's "peace party" and "war party" — a framing critics say risks depicting those who support the country's defense as those who oppose peace itself.
More cautious in his rhetoric, Hetmantsev, a member of President Volodymyr Zelensky 's Servant of the People party and chair of the parliament’s finance, tax and customs policy committee, places himself in the "peace party," which he says is "led by Zelensky."
Hetmantsev hasn't named people he considers part of the "war party." According to him, they "benefit from war" and "want to fight to the last Ukrainian."
Lawmaker Oleksandr Merezhko calls this narrative pro-Russian, arguing that it creates the false impression that Kyiv wants the war to continue. He traces the framing to the Kremlin, which used the term "war party" early after the full-scale invasion to describe Russian officials and businessmen advocating escalation.
Multiple lawmakers from Zelensky's party told the Kyiv Independent that they don’t share Hetmantsev's views. The Servant of the People’s 229 lawmakers hold different positions, they said, and Hetmantsev's viewpoint is not a common position within the party.
Another politician who surprisingly entered the debate was Ihor Terekhov, mayor of Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city. Responding to an op-ed by Valerii Zaluzhnyi , Ukraine's ambassador to the U.K. and former commander-in-chief, Terekhov interpreted it as suggesting that war was Ukraine's inevitable future. Zaluzhnyi's article didn't explicitly say that, arguing instead that ending Russia's war couldn't be treated as a business deal.
"Our ability to endure the war should not be seen as consent to living through it. We strive for peace and prosperity," Terekhov wrote on social media in response.
Terekhov is among the handful of regional politicians regularly featured in nationwide polls. Pollsters have grouped Terekhov and Hetmantsev as potential participants in a joint political project. A spring survey conducted by the Socis sociology center suggested that this hypothetical party could outperform the ruling Servant of the People party.
Terekhov, 59, is among the Ukrainian mayors who reinvented themselves after Russia's full-scale invasion. He has faced criticism for his shifting positions on language and culture, though his public image since 2022 has largely revolved around leading the city battered by Moscow's relentless attacks.
One of Ukraine's best-known mayors, Terekhov is seen as loyal to the central government and has become a familiar face in Kyiv's power circles. During the recent government reshuffle , Terekhov was one of the candidates for the prime minister's post, pro-government lawmakers told the Kyiv Independent.
"(The politicians) are playing to certain sentiments in society, saying what part of the electorate wants to hear," Merezhko says. "That's the problem. We need to put populism aside and stop looking at everything through the lens of the next election. We don't know when a ceasefire will come."
Some see the recent flurry of peace proposals as an attempt to see how far public opinion has shifted, as they grapple with intensified Russian attacks and brace for another difficult winter.
"I wouldn’t rule out the possibility that the authorities are testing the waters to see how society reacts," Haran says.
Recent polls showed that despite the hardships that Ukrainians face, public views on ending the war and the means of achieving peace have changed little over the past year.
The latest KIIS poll published Oct. 19 showed around 64% of respondents blamed Russia for stalling peace negotiations and rejected the idea that Ukraine’s government should be more willing to compromise.
The same poll found that around 62% of Ukrainians are prepared to endure the war for as long as necessary.
For those who spoke to the Kyiv Independent, calls for peace overlook a basic obstacle — Putin has shown no willingness to compromise. His demand that Ukraine withdraw from Donbas comes with no guarantee that Russian forces would not advance into neighbouring regions.
"Russia's terms are well known," says Mykyta Poturaiev, a lawmaker from Zelensky's party. "Calling for peace on Moscow's terms is tantamount to calling for the destruction of the Ukrainian state. A country has an electorate, Russian-occupied territories don't."
Hello! I’m Kateryna Denisova, the author of this article.
As Russia’s attacks on Ukraine intensify, the end of the war remains out of sight. My colleagues and I are working around the clock to tell you about the latest developments on the battlefield and behind the scenes of Ukrainian politics.
If you found this article valuable, consider joining our community to support independent journalism from Ukraine.
Kateryna Denisova is the reporter for the Kyiv Independent, specializing in Ukrainian politics. Based in Kyiv, she focuses on domestic affairs, parliament, social and war-related issues. Kateryna began her career in journalism in 2020 and holds a bachelor's degree in journalism from Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv. She also studied at journalism schools in the Czech Republic and Germany.

title: Zelensky arrives in Norway for talks with Trump envoy as US-Ukraine tensions deepen
description: "We are maintaining all contacts that can help bring peace," Zelensky said upon arrival.
content:
Editor's note: This story has been updated to include the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Oslo on Oct. 20 for talks with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store, Zelensky announced on social media.
"Important meetings are scheduled," including a bilateral meeting with Witkoff, Zelensky said.
The president will also hold a trilateral meeting with Store and Stubb, as well as a meeting with all three officials. The talks will touch upon "Russia's illegal war of aggression against Ukraine and the ⁠overall security ​situation in Europe," said Stubb.
"We are maintaining all contacts that can help bring peace. We will also discuss strengthening our air defense and joint production," said Zelensky on social media.
The planned meetings come amid rising tensions between Kyiv and Washington, as Ukraine accuses the U.S. of using military assistance and access to technology to pressure it to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Witkoff will attend the meeting in person, while Jared Kushner is expected to join remotely due to an alleged illness, Reuters reported on Oct. 19, citing a source familiar with the matter.
"President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has asked Norway and Finland to organize a meeting as part of the ongoing diplomatic efforts, in a critical time for Ukraine," Store said in a statement .
"Together with President Alexander Stubb, I'm glad to be able to host this meeting in Oslo."
Zelensky met with the Finnish and Norwegian leaders shortly after his arrival, as well as with Norway's King Haakon VIII, with whom the president discussed efforts to rescue Ukrainian children abducted by Russia.
"We discussed what steps we can take to make this happen," Zelensky said on X.
"We are also doing everything we can to help our people in Oleshky, which is under Russian occupation. The situation there is simply horrific," he said, describing a dire situation in a Russian-occupied town in Kherson Oblast.
Other European officials — reportedly including representatives of the U.K., Germany, France, and Poland — are also expected to join the discussions in Oslo.
The EU would be represented by Bjoern Seibert, head of the cabinet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, a senior Commission official told the Kyiv Independent. Seibert, regarded as von der Leyen's "right-hand man," previously took part in an earlier round of peace talks on Oct. 9.
Lorenz Meyer-Minnemann, the deputy chief of staff in the Office of the Secretary General at NATO, will also take part in the talks, a NATO official told the Kyiv Independent.
The new round of talks comes amid worsening relations between Kyiv and Washington following the announcement of an unexpected U.S.-Russia diesel deal on Oct. 9.
Since then, Zelensky and U.S. President Donald Trump have exchanged sharp public criticism. Trump accused his Ukrainian counterpart of not wanting to end the war, saying he "doesn't want to end this war, and probably never did."
Trump has also refused to condemn the Kremlin over its escalating attacks on Ukraine, including strikes on the country's already vulnerable energy infrastructure.
Zelensky, meanwhile, warned in an interview with NBC News that siding with Russian President Vladimir Putin would be a "historic mistake." His remarks came amid concerns in Kyiv that Washington could be withholding the delivery of Patriot air defense missiles funded by Ukraine's allies and cutting off crucial intelligence about Russian missile attacks.
Witkoff is also reportedly expected to meet Putin in Moscow to discuss the possible release of Stephen Hubbard , a 72-year-old American citizen who was reportedly serving with a Ukrainian territorial defense unit in Izium, Kharkiv Oblast, when Russian forces detained him in 2022.

title: Moldova denies sending protest note to Ukraine over border guards' Dniester crossing
description: The two Ukrainian border guards had entered Moldova in a motorboat on Oct. 15 while attempting to detain a Ukrainian man crossing the Dniester River near Holosnita, along the Vinnytsia Oblast border.
content:
Moldova's Foreign Ministry denied sending a diplomatic protest to Ukraine over an incident involving two Ukrainian border guards, contradicting an earlier statement by a senior Moldovan lawmaker.
On Oct. 19 , the chair of Moldova's parliamentary national security committee, Lilian Carp, said protest notes had been sent to Ukraine's embassy and authorities after Ukrainian border guards crossed into Moldova. Moldova's Foreign Ministry subsequently denied issuing a protest note and indicated that the matter was being addressed through established channels between the two countries' authorities.
The two Ukrainian border guards had entered Moldova in a motorboat on Oct. 15 while attempting to detain a Ukrainian man crossing the Dniester River near Holosnita, along the Vinnytsia Oblast border. Moldova's Border Police detained the officers, and prosecutors opened criminal proceedings over the alleged illegal crossing, an offense under Article 362 of Moldova's Criminal Code.
Ukraine's State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko said the man resisted detention and evaded capture, and that low water levels and an engine failure caused the border guards' boat to drift onto the Moldovan bank.
The two guards were returned to Ukraine after discussions between authorities. Ukraine's border service said an internal investigation remained underway. The man they were pursuing remained in Moldova.
The Ukrainian man, a 49-year-old from Kyiv, told Moldovan media that he was trying to reunite with family members who had left Ukraine for Bulgaria because of the war. According to PRO TV Chișinău , he has remained in hospital, and is requesting asylum.
The incident happened during a time of heightened security concerns in Moldova related to Russia's war against Ukraine.
On the night of Oct. 15–16 , four Russian drones violated Moldovan airspace before returning to Ukraine, prompting condemnation from Moldova's Foreign Ministry.

title: Ukraine appoints new commander of Third Army Corps as Biletskyi takes charge of Center forces
description: Rohoziuk previously commanded the 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade, which participated in the operation that Ukrainian forces say reclaimed 277 square kilometers (107 square miles) and liberated 16 settlements in the Lyman sector.
content:
Dmytro "Rohoz" Rohoziuk has been appointed commander of Ukraine's Third Army Corps, replacing Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi, who now leads the Ukrainian military's Center grouping of forces.
Biletskyi announced the appointment during a press conference on Oct. 19 outlining the results of Operation Vivaldi , the Ukrainian counteroffensive operation in Donetsk Oblast.
Rohoziuk previously commanded the 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade, which participated in the operation that Ukrainian forces say reclaimed 277 square kilometers (107 square miles) and liberated 16 settlements in the Lyman sector.
Biletskyi personally selected Rohoziuk to lead the corps, according to Ukrainian media outlet Grunt .
Rohoziuk began his military service during Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, defending Kyiv as part of the Azov Regiment.
He later served with the Third Separate Assault Brigade near Bakhmut, commanded a company in its First Assault Battalion, and held operational planning positions before becoming deputy chief of staff after the Third Army Corps was established.
In October 2025, Biletskyi appointed Rohoziuk commander of the 60th Separate Mechanized Brigade. Under his leadership, the brigade strengthened its drone and reconnaissance capabilities and stabilized its positions on the front, according to Grunt.
The brigade subsequently became one of the key formations involved in Operation Vivaldi.
On Oct. 14, the Third Army Corps announced that Ukrainian forces had recaptured another 101 square kilometers in the Lyman sector as part of the operation.
Biletskyi will now move on to assume responsibility for the Center grouping of forces, which oversees a substantial section of Ukraine's eastern front.

title: Zelensky appeals to US lawmakers for answers as White House turns on Kyiv
description: "We want to understand what is happening, why it's happening, and where all this is heading," Zelensky told a bipartisan group of U.S. senators and representatives.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky met with members of the U.S. Congress via videoconference on Oct. 19 to discuss recent changes in American policy that have left Ukrainians baffled, anxious, and more vulnerable to Russian attacks.
The meeting, which included Democrats and Republicans from both the Senate and the House of Representatives, was organized by Senators Richard Blumenthal and Thom Tillis.
Zelensky briefed the legislators on Ukraine's current challenges, namely delayed deliveries of Patriot interceptors , ongoing restrictions to Starlink access for Ukrainian soldiers, and an abrupt end to warnings about Russian missile launches.
The president described the current predicament — which appears to stem from U.S. President Donald Trump's latest pro-Russian pivot — as "the most difficult situation since the very beginning of this war."
Zelensky highlighted Ukrainian forces' progress on the front lines , including the successes of the Operation Vivaldi counteroffensive in Donetsk Oblast. But then he described a cascade of disasters that "stand in sharp contrast to what we are achieving on the battlefield."
Ukraine's Starlink/Starshield service is still operating under a speed cap that has disrupted the military's ability to launch mid-range drone strikes and intercept Russia's deadly, high-speed jet drones.
"(You) need to understand how serious this is. ... Russia's attacks have become even more vicious and dirty," Zelensky told the assembled lawmakers.
"There is hardly an hour when Russia isn't attacking somewhere or hitting something. And this happens every single day."
Zelensky also stressed the lack of early warnings from U.S. partners regarding Russian missile strikes , saying that there had been three separate attacks in recent days where Ukraine received no advance notice — and "no explanation" after the fact.
The Pentagon is also refusing to approve the transfer of Patriot missiles from Europe to Ukraine, even though these weapons have already been paid for through the U.S.-NATO PURL program, Zelensky said.
Ukraine desperately needs to replenish its supply of U.S.-made Patriots, the only interceptors that can reliably shoot down Russian ballistic missiles. But Zelensky said Washington was withholding approval without explanation.
The president also shared that Ukraine had proposed a 30-day moratorium on Russian refinery attacks in exchange for Patriot supplies. Neither the U.S. nor Russia showed any interest, he said.
"All of this suggests that some political decision has been made to slow down support for us. ... We want to understand what is happening, why it's happening, and where all of this is heading," he said.
In the weeks leading up to the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, U.S. President Donald Trump has made a hard turn on Ukraine — after months of ignoring the Kyiv-Moscow peace process while busy in the Middle East, Trump decided to focus on Ukraine again.
But instead of condemning Russia's assault on energy infrastructure or relentless ballistic missile attacks on civilian targets, Trump decided to blame Ukraine — and Zelensky — for rising fuel prices.
Trump on Oct. 9 announced a deal to purchase Russian diesel , kicking off the series of blows to Ukraine that Zelensky detailed to lawmakers. The diesel announcement was followed by pressure on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil assets, a sanctions waiver for Russia, and the restriction on Starlink.
The White House has denied ordering restrictions on Starshield or deliberately withholding information about Russian missile strikes. The administration has also defended the diesel deal despite widespread bipartisan backlash.
Speaking to reporters on Oct. 19, Trump said that Russia "hasn't been doing very much" in Ukraine lately.
"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," he said.

title: What Russia's doing to Ukraine is 'fine,' Trump says
description: "Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," Trump said, hours after a Russian drone strike in a public park killed six people, including two children.
content:
Editor's Note: This story is being updated.
According to U.S. President Donald Trump, Russia "has been fine on Ukraine" and "hasn't been doing much" to the country it has been attempting to violently conquer for over a decade.
"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven't been doing much," Trump told reporters on Oct. 19.
The president's remarks came the same day that a Russian daytime drone strike in a public park killed six people, including two children. The night before, Russia attacked Kyiv with over a dozen ballistic missiles and targeted nearly 30 critical energy facilities across the country.
But Trump had nothing to say about any of that, choosing instead to praise Russian President Vladimir Putin for his restraint in both Ukraine and Iran.
When asked if he was open to a trilateral meeting with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping, Trump said he was, but that such a meeting wouldn't be for Ukraine's sake — since Russia, apparently, "has been fine on Ukraine." He said the main purpose of the meeting would be to discuss nuclear disarmament.
The president was questioned about the three-way summit after the Wall Street Journal reported that Putin wants to use the meeting — which would exclude President Volodymyr Zelensky — to secure a peace deal favorable to Moscow.
Trump then said he would be willing to talk to Xi about Ukraine, saying "he's been very fair with Ukraine. He hasn't been much involved, and same with Russia."
"They haven't been nearly what they could have been, and I appreciate that."
It's not clear whether Trump was referring to China's support for Russia, or Russia's aggression in Ukraine.
Trump defended his recent deals with Putin and sanctions waivers for Russia , saying the U.S. was negotiating with the Kremlin regarding the release of a high-profile hostage. He also said Russia was "very well-behaved on Iran."
"We also have a very good situation with respect to Iran. (Putin's) laying off Iran," Trump said.
"It's nice because we're hitting Iran very hard, as you know, economically as well as militarily, and Russia's done nothing there that we can see, and I think that's a very positive."
Russia is Iran's close ally and has pledged to assist Tehran in its war with the U.S. Multiple media outlets have reported on Russia shipping weapons to Iran, aiding in missile development , and providing intelligence to help Iran attack U.S. bases in the Middle East.
Even U.S. General Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, confirmed on April 30 that Russia was supporting Iran in the war with the U.S.
While Ukraine sent its experts to help shoot down Iranian drones attacking Gulf states, Putin pledged to supply Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian with all "the necessary goods" and support the country during the war.
But in his remarks to the media on Oct. 19, Trump seemed convinced that Putin, not Zelensky, was his true ally.
"Russia could have done a lot more to help Iran. Russia's done very little for Iran," Trump insisted.
The U.S. president again lashed out at Zelensky , saying Ukraine should consider getting someone new to negotiate on their behalf.
"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given nothing to us."
Ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, Trump has taken a hard turn toward Moscow in an apparent bid to lower domestic fuel prices: On Oct. 9, he announced a plan to purchase Russian diesel , despite years of U.S. sanctions on Russian energy products. He also ordered Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries .
Lawmakers and critics from both political parties pointed out that the war in Iran was the main driver of the surge in global oil prices, and condemned the deal for rewarding Moscow even as it continued pummeling Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure.

title: Pope Leo, Zelensky discuss hopes for ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky
description: The conversation with Zelensky comes three days after the pope spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin to call for a ceasefire to evacuate civilians from the front-line town.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky updated Pope Leo XIV on Russia's war against Ukraine, including the ongoing crisis in occupied Oleshky, during a phone call on Oct. 19.
The call comes three days after the pope spoke with Russian President Vladimir Putin to propose a ceasefire in Oleshky , a front-line town in Kherson Oblast where around 2,000 residents remain trapped without sufficient supplies of food or medicine.
Zelensky said he and the pope discussed the humanitarian emergency unfolding in Oleshky, including the Vatican's diplomatic efforts with Russia .
"We are working to help our people there and are preparing solutions," Zelensky said . "His Holiness informed me about his contacts with the Russian side regarding this issue."
Pope Leo's call for a ceasefire on Oct. 16 was his second known phone conversation with the Putin since becoming pope in 2025. The Russian president blamed Ukraine for the crisis in Oleshky, according to the Kremlin's account of the call.
Ukraine and Russia are currently discussing a ceasefire proposal and are nearing an agreement to evacuate residents from Oleshky , Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 18.
The sides are negotiating a local ceasefire to allow residents to be evacuated directly to Ukrainian-controlled territory, rather than having to travel first through Russian-occupied areas and then through Russia and Belarus, Lubinets said.
No final agreement has been publicly announced, and it remains unclear when an evacuation could begin. It is not clear to what extent Pope Leo's intervention impacted the agreement.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
Despite the escalating emergency, Russian forces have been preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing occupied regions to provide aid.
Zelensky said he also spoke with Pope Leo about Russia's intensifying attacks — and the failure of Kyiv's partners to provide advance warning of missile launches.
"Of course, we also discussed all the security challenges and threats we are currently facing, including the recent instances where we did not receive advance warning from our partners about Russian ballistic missile attacks, which has happened three times recently," he said.
The night before, Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing at least one person and injuring eight others. Ukrainian officials said they received no warning from the U.S. or other partners until after the first missiles struck.

title: 'We will fight' — We asked Ukrainian soldiers about Trump's latest outburst
description:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 18 claimed his approach to ending the war in Ukraine is "very simple."

In a post on Truth Social, Trump explained that his decision to ease sanctions on Russia while simultaneously piling pressure on Ukraine was to avoid "foolishly (driving) Russia away from the bargaining table."

For many of Trump’s critics in Ukraine, his recent decisions are viewed in similarly simple terms — Trump is helping Russia win the war.

Trump also doubled down on his criticism o
content:
A soldier from a separate task force rifle battalion of the National Police of Ukraine in Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Dmytro Smolienko / Ukrinform / Future Publishing via Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 18 claimed his approach to ending the war in Ukraine is "very simple."
In a post on Truth Social , Trump explained that his decision to ease sanctions on Russia while simultaneously piling pressure on Ukraine was to avoid "foolishly (driving) Russia away from the bargaining table."
For many of Trump’s critics in Ukraine, his recent decisions are viewed in similarly simple terms — Trump is helping Russia win the war.
Trump also doubled down on his criticism of President Volodymyr Zelensky, and appeared to suggest that Ukraine's position in the war was untenable.
"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead. I WANT THIS WAR END!"
But as Russia escalates its aerial bombardment of Ukraine's cities, its forces remain largely stuck on the front lines.
And as Operation Vivaldi has shown, in some sectors Moscow's troops are actually going backwards.
The Kyiv Independent asked Ukrainian soldiers what they thought about Trump's latest outburst.
Some soldiers asked to be identified by callsign or first name only for security reasons.
The enemy has not achieved any successes that would suggest a victory on their part. Civilians are the most susceptible to a decline in morale — especially lately, as Russia has been launching mass strikes against civilian infrastructure.
I wouldn't take Trump's words seriously.
He is a media-focused, overly talkative, choleric, elderly, and unwell man.
Honestly, this is more than just another Trump outburst. He’s repeating Russian talking points and blaming Ukraine and Zelensky for the consequences of Russia’s invasion. Yes, Ukraine has suffered terrible losses. But Russia has suffered losses just as significant, and it will suffer even more — Ukrainian ballistic missiles will see to that. Yet Trump talks only about Ukraine’s losses, as if they were a reason to force the victim of aggression to surrender, while demanding almost nothing from Putin, who started this war. And the claim that Ukraine has "lost its seas" is simply absurd. I want this war to end too. But a just peace starts with Russia ending its invasion, not with Ukraine being forced to surrender. Ask Ukrainians if we’re going to capitulate. No. Why would we? Nothing has changed for us, even if Trump stops helping. We won’t surrender. We had no choice before, and we still don’t.
In my opinion, Trump is seeking to bring the fighting in Ukraine to an end by any means necessary, including through Ukraine’s capitulation. He confidently declared to the entire world that he would stop the war in Ukraine, yet year after year he has failed to do so. People no longer believe these claims, and consequently, his slogan that "this war would never have happened under my presidency" is also raising more and more doubts.
It is absolutely clear to me that he is concerned primarily with his own image and approval ratings. That is why he has repeatedly threatened Ukraine — a country that is defending itself against aggression and fighting for its own land. I do not think Trump is genuinely interested in the actual situation on the battlefield. He can easily take Putin’s claims at face value when Putin says that Russia controls certain Ukrainian towns and cities that Russian forces have been unable to reach for years.
I never thought I would see the day when the Russian population, living under the constant influence of propaganda, would be more skeptical of Putin’s claims than the American president.
As for morale at the front, we are not giving up. By now, we have grown accustomed to Trump’s statements and his constantly shifting attitude — from threats against Putin one day to threats against Zelenskyy the next. But when it came to the situation with Starlink , for example, most of us were stunned.
Any restrictions affecting the main communication tool we rely on at the front are not a way of forcing us into a ceasefire at any cost. They are a shove in the back of every one of us, putting our lives at risk. When our hands are tied and we are prevented from defending our own lives and the lives of our loved ones, it hits us hard psychologically. It is not merely a slap in our faces; it is a slap in the face of the entire civilized world.
I hope Trump abandons the idea of using our lives as leverage and understands that we will continue fighting to the end regardless. Otherwise, he risks going down in history as the president who betrayed the entire civilized world.
Returning to the situation on the battlefield, Russia has clearly become bogged down along the front line and is retreating in some sectors. And, as if by some cruel law of nature, every time Russia begins to lose the initiative on the battlefield, those whom we thought were our allies start putting obstacles in our way.
It is especially painful to watch this happen at a time when Putin, faced with the hopelessness of Russia’s situation on the battlefield, has shifted almost entirely toward a strategy of terror against Ukrainian civilians. He is no longer betting on victory at the front — having realized that he cannot defeat the Ukrainian army — but instead on breaking and defeating our civilian population.
But President Trump, and the international community as a whole, must understand one thing — in February 2022, I picked up a weapon and went out to defend Kyiv without even having a helmet or proper body armor. All I had was a Kalashnikov light machine gun, while massive columns of the Russian army were advancing toward our district of the capital. There were many of us like that.
Back then, there was no talk of Starlink or Tomahawks. We went into battle fully aware of how slim our chances were, prepared to fight off an enormous enemy army with little more than our bare hands.
Today, we have a massive army of our own, our own weapons and strike capabilities, and technologies that many countries around the world cannot replicate.
Even if the entire world turns its back on us, we will still stand and fight for our country — because we are Ukrainians.
In my opinion, the best option is to achieve peace along the current line of contact. The main priority is to stop the bloodshed and save lives.
Those who have been fighting since the very beginning are exhausted, and few have any desire to continue. Especially when faced with such injustice.
Trump acts in his own country's interests; for them, it is better if this war ends, as it yields nothing positive. In this situation, neither side — neither us nor Russia — will win, so it is difficult to discuss any clear outcome.
As for why he is pressuring us rather than Russia — I suspect it is simply because we are the weaker party.

title: Shooting at Kyiv draft office injures 6 as mobilization tensions rise
description: Three military personnel and three personnel were injured and are receiving treatment. The gunman has been detained and investigation is underway.
content:
An individual opened fire at a recruitment center in Kyiv the evening of Oct. 19, injuring three police officers and three military personnel, according to local authorities.
The incident marks yet another violent eruption amid Ukraine's deepening mobilization crisis .
The shooting occurred at around 7 p.m. local time at a Territorial Recruitment Center (TCC) in Kyiv's Pechersk district, city police and draft officials reported . A man suspected of draft evasion had been brought to the center by police.
The man then produced a weapon and opened fire on police and service members at the draft office, wounding three police officers and three military personnel. All victims were transported from the scene by ambulance and are receiving medical care, authorities said.
The shooter has been detained and an investigation into the incident is underway.
Forced mobilization — a reality of Ukrainian life under martial law — remains one of the greatest sources of social and political tension in Ukraine, frequently leading to violent clashes between recruiters and civilians.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, dozens of attacks on enlistment officers have been reported across the country, with incidents rising in 2026.
In August, a draft officer in Lviv was stabbed to death while conducting a document check and four recruiters in Odesa were injured in a shooting on the job. In September, an explosion at a Lviv recruitment center sparked a terrorism investigation.
Many of the targeted draft officers are former front-line soldiers reassigned to recruitment duties after being wounded in combat.
Presidential Office Head Kyrylo Budanov said on Aug. 28 that Ukraine needs to mobilize at least 30,000 people per month in order to maintain the country's defense against Russia. But with increasing manpower problems on the front lines and fewer people volunteering to fight, draft efforts have become more aggressive.
Reports of recruitment officers forcibly detaining men on the streets are also on the rise, with such claims getting additional amplification thanks to Russian disinformation campaigns .

title: Ukraine war latest: Ukraine evacuates wounded soldier from front line by drone for first time, military says
description:
Key developments on Oct. 19:

 * Ukraine evacuates wounded soldier from front line by drone for first time, military says
 * Ukraine brings home 23 children from Russian occupation
 * Ukraine, Russia nearing agreement on evacuation of civilians from occupied Oleshky, ombudsman says
 * 3 waves of Russian missiles slam Kyiv overnight, killing at least 1, injuring 8
 * 'Absolute atrocity' — Russian drone strike on park in Kharkiv Oblast kills children
 * Russia strikes 28 critical energy facilities
content:
Ukrainian forces have carried out what they describe as a "first-of-its-kind" aerial evacuation of a wounded soldier directly from a front-line position by drone, the Ukrainian military and defense company Gurzuf Defense announced on Oct. 19.
The operation involved Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade , 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade, and 10th Army Corps, along with Ukrainian drone manufacturer Gurzuf Defense .
The Ukrainian military did not disclose the date of the operation or the section of the front line where it took place.
The wounded soldier, serving with the 30th Brigade, had spent nearly 500 days at a front-line position "under constant threat of death." His fellow soldiers maintained contact with him and delivered food, water, ammunition, and medicine by drone, Gurzuf Defense said .
After the soldier suffered a severe injury, evacuating him by ground became impossible because of Russian drone activity in the area and mined terrain. Attempting to reach him on foot or with a ground robotic vehicle , the usual way of evacuating the wounded, would have put the rescue team at risk.
Ukrainian troops used a heavy-lift hexacopter drone, the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6.
The team first delivered special equipment with carabiners to the wounded soldier, then sent the drone equipped with a winch. Guided remotely by fellow soldiers who remained in contact with him, the soldier secured himself to the evacuation system, Gurzuf Defense said, calling the operation an "unprecedented mission."
The drone then transported him to a safer position, where other soldiers met him and arranged further evacuation to a hospital. The mission lasted 1 hour, 14 minutes, and 36 seconds, covering a distance of 62 kilometers (39 miles).
The company said the operation required close monitoring of the airspace and electronic warfare protection throughout the flight. The soldier is now receiving treatment and rehabilitation, and his life is no longer in danger, according to the 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade.
"An extremely complex operation, but a successful one. This is a historic event," "Napalm," a 92nd Brigade programmer who was involved in preparing the operation, said .
"It marks the next stage in the evacuation of the wounded, which we will all eventually reach. Now the serious, systematic work begins to ensure that such missions take place on a regular basis," Napalm added.
Gurzuf Defense co-founder Pavlo Feldblium warned that aerial evacuation should not be treated as a routine practice, citing the risks to wounded soldiers during flight. Each mission would need to be planned individually for the specific circumstances and location, he said.
"Air rescue is a last resort when there is no other way to save a person," Feldblium said.
According to the Ukrainian outlet Ukrainka Pravda, the hexacopter Heavy Shot Ayudag-6's platform has a flight range of up to 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) and an operational altitude of 150–300 meters (500 to 1,000 feet), while the aircraft itself weighs about 98 kilograms (215 pounds) and can carry 70–90 kilograms (150 to 200 pounds).

title: Ukraine's EU integration chief slams proposal to pick chief prosecutor in open contest
description: The EU has demanded a reform of Ukraine's notoriously corrupt and politicized prosecution service and called for making the procedure for picking the prosecutor general less political and more merit-based. Meanwhile, anti-corruption activists and pro-reform lawmakers have accused the Ukrainian authorities of sabotaging rule of law reforms and resisting the demand for depoliticizing the Prosecutor General's Office.
content:
Vsevolod Chentsov, Ukraine's deputy prime minister for European integration, spoke out in an Oct. 19 interview against the idea of an open contest for prosecutor general.
The EU has demanded a reform of Ukraine's notoriously corrupt and politicized prosecution service and called for making the procedure for picking the prosecutor general less political and more merit-based. Meanwhile, anti-corruption activists and pro-reform lawmakers have accused the Ukrainian authorities of sabotaging rule of law reforms and resisting the demand for depoliticizing the Prosecutor General's Office .
"I see experts arguing that there should be an open competition for the position of prosecutor general," Chentsov told the Ukrainian media outlet Yevropeiska Pravda. "But that is not something the EU requires, nor is it standard practice in Europe."
He argued that recommendations by Council of Europe experts "clearly emphasize the need to comply with Ukraine’s Constitution, which sets out the roles of the president and parliament in the appointment process."
"How to ensure transparency and select candidates based on their professional qualifications remains open for discussion," Chentsov said. "But personally, I see neither the need nor the possibility of holding an open competition for the position. A balance must be struck between political independence and professional competence."
According to a plan approved in December by Taras Kachka, Ukraine's former deputy prosecutor general for European integration, and EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos, Ukraine should "conduct a comprehensive review of the selection and dismissal procedure of the prosecutor general , with a view to aligning it with European best practice." The plan also envisages reinstating transparent contests for other top prosecutor jobs.
According to Ukraine's interim benchmarks for EU accession, Kyiv "needs to depoliticize the position of the prosecutor general, including by making the selection and dismissal procedures more objective, transparent and merit-based, taking into account European standards."
An EU official who spoke on condition of anonymity told the Kyiv Independent that the EU accession benchmarks "are not calling for it to be an elected position but the process should still change."
"For the EU, the gold standard is to have the involvement of independent, international vetters," the official said. "Separately, the EU and Ukraine launched a task force last week to implement Kachka-Kos and the EU's Rule of Law benchmarks. It serves to identify deficiencies in the current set-up, which would also include the prosecutor general's selection process."
In June, Anastasia Radina, head of parliament's anti-corruption committee from President Volodymyr Zelensky's party, submitted to parliament a bill seeking to select the prosecutor general in a transparent contest with the participation of international experts.
Radina's opponents argue that the Kachka-Kos plan does not envisage a contest involving international experts and that a contest for the prosecutor general's job contradicts Ukraine's Constitution.
Radina has denied the claim that it contradicts the Constitution.
"There may be different interpretations of the benchmark, but I'm not aware of anyone having proposed an alternative approach so far," she told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine's prosecutor generals are appointed by the president with parliament's approval and have been seen as closely aligned to whoever is in power. Radina's bill seeks to depoliticize the prosecutor general's appointment.
The debate on selecting the prosecutor general intensified under the previous occupant of the job, Ruslan Kravchenko.
Kravchenko faced scrutiny due to his role in the crackdown on the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) in 2025.
He was fired by parliament on Sept. 15 amid a major corruption investigation.
Within the investigation, a top prosecutor described as a “confidant” of Kravchenko was charged. Publicly revealed evidence hints at Kravchenko being implicated .
He left Ukraine on Sept. 14, under the pretext of an official trip to a conference in Paris. But the organizers told the Kyiv Independent that they had not expected him to attend, strengthening the suspicions that the trip was a fig leaf for fleeing Ukraine to avoid potential charges.
As Kravchenko left Ukraine, he simultaneously approved charges against the head of the anti-corruption agency investigating him. The charges were later dropped as unfounded.
Kravchenko later moved to Austria , the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda reported on Sept. 23.

title: Why Russia's war on Ukraine's data centers could backfire on Moscow

Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers could backfire, experts have told the Kyiv Independent, as Kyiv's retaliatory attacks have exposed vulnerabilities in how Moscow has organized IT infrastructure.

content:
People use their mobile phones as they walk past the Moscow City business center in Moscow, Russia, on April 15, 2026. (Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images)
Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers could backfire, experts have told the Kyiv Independent, as Kyiv's retaliatory attacks have exposed vulnerabilities in how Moscow has organized IT infrastructure.
On Sept. 23, a Russian attack damaged a Kyiv data center housing network equipment for internet provider UTELS, causing service disruptions. The attack also affected cloud service Fex.net and disrupted internet access for around 100,000 households in Kyiv. Since then, Russia has increasingly targeted Ukraine's digital infrastructure.
Moscow is expanding its targets to find new ways to pressure Ukraine as its battlefield offensives in 2026 have failed to achieve their objectives, Tetiana Trach, a Russia researcher at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW), told the Kyiv Independent. The strikes on data centers fit into Russia's broader campaign to damage Ukraine's economy and make civilian life harder.
Ukraine, which has increasingly used long-range strikes to weaken Russia's ability to sustain the war, retaliated. Between Oct. 8 and Oct. 18, Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers, a Sberbank facility under construction, and a data center belonging to social media giant VK.
But while Ukraine suffers from daily Russian drone and missile barrages, Russia faces a different problem. Serhiy Petrenko, former Yandex Ukraine head, estimated that around 80% of Russia's data centers are concentrated in Moscow and the surrounding region — within reach of Ukrainian long-range drones.
Russia's centralized digital infrastructure leaves Moscow facing two challenges: inflicting comparable damage on Ukraine and protecting its own data centers from further strikes. Experts say neither will be easy.
"Russian data centers appear more vulnerable than Ukrainian ones. Russia appears willing to accept this risk," Trach said.
The Russian pro-war milblogger 'Art Jockey' said that attacks on data centers had previously been treated as an informal red line between the two countries, and that Moscow's decision to target Ukrainian facilities had opened the door to retaliation.
"With no end in sight to the war he started nearly five years ago, Putin opted for another round of escalation," they wrote. "It's not that no one had thought of attacking data centers before. Putin simply decided to make the first move now, effectively removing the restraints on Ukraine as well."
Russia's war against Ukraine in 2026 can be seen as a contest between two strategies of long-range attacks, with both sides seeking to increase pressure beyond the battlefield, a July analysis by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) concluded. The recent strikes on data centers fit that pattern.
Following a meeting with military leaders on Sept. 25, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that the Ukrainian government had decided to strengthen the protection of data centers and other critical communications infrastructure.
Despite the recent damage, knocking out internet access across Ukraine would be extremely difficult, Anatolii Frolenkov, a representative of the 1-IX internet exchange point, told the Kyiv Independent in September.
"Russian strikes would have to be continuous and happen at a hundred different sites to be effective."
"The internet will not disappear completely," Frolenkov said. "There will be outages, there will be problems. It won't work as smoothly or as quickly, things may glitch, and operators may go down for a couple of hours because the infrastructure is being physically destroyed."
Samuel Bendett, an expert on Russian military technology at the Center for a New American Security (CNAS) and the Center for Naval Analyses (CNA), told the Kyiv Independent that "Russian strikes would have to be continuous and happen at a hundred different sites to be effective."
Trach agreed that Russia could continue causing temporary internet outages in Ukraine but said a nationwide shutdown was unlikely given the country's decentralized infrastructure.
On Oct. 8, outages occurred in many segments of the Russian internet at about 4 p.m. local time, especially in Moscow and St. Petersburg, after Ukraine struck a Yandex data center , the Moscow Times said. Several banking services, Google, RuTube, the website of the Russian Railways, and many retail websites were unreachable.
"We certainly are capable," Zelensky commented on the attack. "We always respond in kind."
Subsequent Ukrainian strikes on Yandex data centers in October disrupted payments, banking, and online services in Russia, while parts of the infrastructure were still recovering more than a week later.
"This is the first serious problem with potentially major consequences for Russia's financial system, and the campaign against data centers has only been going on for a few days," the milblogger Art Jockey said on Oct. 12.
He warned that if Ukraine disabled the main services of Sberbank, Russia's largest lender, it could trigger panic among depositors and mass withdrawals.
Two days later, Ukrainian drones struck a Sberbank data center under construction in Balakovo. The bank confirmed the attack but said its services were operating normally.
"You didn't think it would end with Yandex, did you?" Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point said the same day on social media platform Threads.
On Oct. 18, VK confirmed an attack on its data center in Leningrad Oblast but said its services remained operational. Users, however, reported disruptions across the social network and its affiliated platforms, according to Downdetector, a service that tracks online outages.
The consequences of Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centers could extend far beyond disrupted banking and online services, potentially setting back the country's AI development and affecting military technology.
"The Russians, I think, didn't think it would get that far, that fast."
"Yandex and other data centers that were hit are going to set Russian AI development back significantly," Bendett said.
Yandex and Sberbank are both major players in Russia's AI development, while the state plays a central role in the sector. Russia also recently announced plans to share drone attack data with developers to train neural networks and algorithms, according to Bendett.
While Russia's military AI programs have traditionally operated separately from commercial developers, they still depend on some of the same computing resources, advanced chips, and civilian specialists. Western sanctions also complicate replacing damaged equipment.
"The dependence could be quite substantial. And if civilian specialists are raising the alarm about these attacks, then Russian military AI could be impacted," Bendett added.
"Is there any hope for air defenses?" a Art Jockey asked, answering his own question with "there isn't much hope."
"Sooner or later, if Ukraine decides to strike this facility, its drones will get through — if not on the first attempt, then on the second or third," he said.
On Oct. 12, Russian Digital Development Minister Maksut Shadayev said his ministry was discussing data center protection with the Defense Ministry, according to Russian news agency Interfax.
Two days later, President Vladimir Putin convened senior officials for a cybersecurity meeting, although the Kremlin denied any connection to Ukrainian drone strikes.
Besides government ministers and top security officials, the meeting included Sberbank chief executive Herman Gref and central bank governor Elvira Nabiullina, according to Reuters .
On Oct. 16, Kemerovo Oblast governor Ilya Seredyuk proposed housing data centers inside depleted open-pit mines and quarries, given their natural protection from aerial bombardment.
"The Russians, I think, didn't think it would get that far, that fast," Bendett said.
"Now they're scrambling for solutions, like putting data centers underground or farther away. But what's done is done."
Tania Myronyshena is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent. She has written for outlets such as United24 Media, Ukrainer, Wonderzine, as well as for PEN Ukraine, a Ukrainian non-governmental organization. Before joining the Kyiv Independent, she worked as a freelance journalist with a focus on cultural narratives and human stories. Tania holds a B.A. in publishing and editing from Borys Hrinchenko Kyiv University.

title: Russian captain charged with stealing Ukrainian grain from occupied territories
description: The captain was charged with violating the procedure for entering and exiting Ukraine's temporarily occupied territory with intent to harm the interests of the state, and violating the laws and customs of war.
content:
The captain of a Russian cargo ship has been charged in absentia in connection with illegally transporting over 54,000 metric tons of stolen grain from Ukraine's occupied territories, the Prosecutor General's Office and the Security Service (SBU) said on Oct. 19.
This marks the first time such action will be considered a war crime by Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office.
The captain was charged with violating the procedure for entering and exiting occupied territories with intent to harm the interests of the state, and violating the laws and customs of war.
According to the investigation, the vessel, "Matros Pozynich," made two shipments between 2022 and 2023, when Russian forces seized grain from Ukrainian farmers in Crimea .
Acting Prosecutor General Anton Kovalskyi said that "a legal framework has been established and applied in practice that allows for the captain's participation in the removal of grain – illegally seized in the occupied territory – to be classified as a war crime."
The shipments, totaling roughly 27,000 metric tons each, departed from the temporarily occupied city of Sevastopol for the port of Latakia in Syria.
According to the SBU's statement , the vessel's captain was taking orders from top Russian officials that violate parts of the Geneva Convention, specifically the prohibition of looting property from occupied territories.
Safe and reliable grain export in the Black Sea has been one of the key topics of discussion, as constant Russian attacks on Ukraine's ports put around 32 million tons of agricultural products worth approximately $10 billion at risk, according to Ukraine's Agriculture Ministry.
"We are making maximum use of alternative routes — the Danube, rail, and road transport. But they cannot fully replace maritime exports. Without the restoration of stable shipping through the Black Sea, production will begin to decline in the long term," on Oct. 14 Taras Vysotskyi, Agriculture Minister, said in conversation with Turkish Ambassador to Ukraine Fatma Ceren Yazgan.

title: Ukraine to compensate damaged cargo ships, as Russia rejects Black Sea proposal
description: Under a mechanism developed by Ukraine’s Infrastructure Ministry, Kyiv will compensate shipowners, operators, and charterers whose vessels fly under the Ukrainian or a foreign flag for up to 80% of the assessed damage if insurers don’t cover the risks.
content:
Ukraine’s government will partially compensate civilian vessels damaged by Russian strikes in the Black Sea as Kyiv and foreign partners discuss stabilizing shipping routes amid Russian attacks on both foreign and Ukrainian ships.
Under a mechanism developed by Ukraine’s Infrastructure Ministry, Kyiv will compensate shipowners, operators, and charterers whose vessels fly under the Ukrainian or a foreign flag for up to 80% of the assessed damage if insurers don’t cover the risks.
The mechanism will cover damage to or destruction of ships, loss of or damage to cargo, and emergency and rescue operation costs.
"This decision is intended to reduce financial risks for participants in maritime shipping and to support the continuity of Ukraine’s export and import logistics," the Infrastructure Ministry wrote in a public statement.
"Despite the constant threats, Ukraine’s maritime logistics keeps operating. Our task is to ensure its stability and to create additional guarantees for shipowners carrying cargo to Ukrainian ports."
With the hostilities in the Black Sea threatening global food supplies, Turkey, India, and Egypt offered to transport food from both Ukrainian and Russian ports under their respective flags, but Moscow declined to guarantee them safe passage, President Volodymyr Zelensky told Bloomberg on Oct. 19.
Some in the logistics sector are skeptical that talks between foreign partners and Russia will yield results anytime soon.
Russia stepped up attacks on cargo ships in the Black Sea over the summer, hitting 52 vessels in just six weeks in July and August. While ships are now largely avoiding Ukrainian ports, Russia hasn’t stopped its attacks, with Romania accusing Moscow of hitting four merchant ships in 24 hours on Oct. 15, killing eight people.
As a result, insurance rates in the Black Sea are through the roof, with London’s marine insurance market expanding its high-risk zone beyond the coastal waters of Ukraine and Russia on Sept. 18, Reuters reported.
Russia's attacks on vessels, as well as port facilities, have effectively halted Ukraine’s agricultural exports, putting around 32 million metric tons of agricultural products worth approximately $10 billion at risk, Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry said last week. Alternative routes, such as the Danube River ports and railways, cannot handle enough cargo.

title: How Russia exploits echoes of war fatigue in Ukraine

content:
Firefighters recover the body of an elderly woman from the rubble of a residential building hit by a Russian airstrike in Sloviansk, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 17, 2026. (Diego Herrera Carcedo/Anadolu via Getty Images)
On the night of Oct. 2, Russian drones struck Kyiv's Southern Bridge once again. The city closed it and Paton Bridge, restricted traffic on Metro Bridge, and was gridlocked by multi-kilometer traffic jams by morning.
On the same day, Oleksii Honcharenko, a member of parliament from the opposition European Solidarity party, wrote that "we are losing the war" and need to "negotiate about everything under the sun."
He proposed discussing a neutral status instead of NATO membership, making concessions on the Russian language and the Moscow Patriarchate church , and taking the initiative to propose a phased lifting of sanctions on Russian energy in exchange for an end to long-range strikes.
The apparent idea was that Ukrainians, exhausted by constant terror, would take up his call and demand that the government make concessions to Moscow.
Honcharenko's statement came as a surprise even to his fellow party members. It was not the first time he had made remarks that ran counter to the opposition's line. But this time, he outdid himself, and it didn't take long for him to pay the price: expulsion from the parliamentary faction.
Komsomolskaya Pravda war correspondent Alexander Kots published an analysis under the headline "The Odesa Strangler Honcharenko: 'We Are Losing the War.'"
Russian propagandist Vladimir Solovyov's channel, with 1.1 million subscribers, published extensive quotes about neutrality. It had to add a note that the author is listed as a terrorist and extremist in Russia : in December last year, a Moscow court sentenced Honcharenko in absentia to 18 years in prison.
In Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky called the lawmaker's remarks "abnormal messages," and Honcharenko's parliamentary faction expelled him on Oct. 5, as the ideas expressed remain deeply unpopular with opposition parties too.
Political analysts see this as the beginning of Honcharenko's own campaign under the banner of a "peace party."
There is fertile ground for such a campaign, but it is important not to mistake exhaustion for a willingness to surrender.
According to Gallup , 66% of Ukrainians want the war to end through negotiations as soon as possible, up from 22% in 2022. The figure reflects a profound weariness with a war that has consumed lives, destroyed cities, and placed an intolerable burden on society; it does not, in itself, signify support for capitulation, abandoning Ukraine's sovereignty, or accepting Moscow's demands.
Yet this state of affairs has prompted savvy politicians, eager to capitalize on public sentiment, to exploit this exhaustion for political gain. Russia, too, is exploiting the renewed discussion of peace negotiations, but to pursue its own objectives.
What Russia made of his words interests us a lot. At Join Ukraine, we monitor around 1,000 Russian regional communities on Telegram and VKontakte, as well as 45 major nationwide Russian channels, every day.
"None of the posts about Honcharenko suggested that Russians were pleased by the prospect of negotiations."
From Oct. 2 to 6, seven pro-war and state-run channels in our sample mentioned Honcharenko 15 times.
Regional communities ignored the story, with just two mentions among 74,000 posts. The Russian provinces do not care about a Ukrainian lawmaker, but propagandists do — a lot.
Three brief conclusions can be drawn from what was said about Honcharenko in Russia.
First, Russians are becoming convinced that terrorizing cities works. Russian journalist behind the popular Telegram Channel Voenkor Kotenok juxtaposed Honcharenko's posts from 2022 with his current remarks: "This is what 'Geran' (drone) does when it brings life. The preventive measures should have started four years ago, instead of whining."
Second, there will be no concessions in return. Boris Rozhin , who has 755,000 followers, wrote: "It would be a big mistake to consider [him] a representative of 'Ukraine that wants peace.' Peace in Ukraine has nothing to do with Nazis."
None of the posts about Honcharenko suggested that Russians were pleased by the prospect of negotiations.
The third conclusion is the shortest: Russians find Honcharenko ridiculous. More than half of the reactions to these posts were laughing emojis .
Ukraine, meanwhile, is not refusing to talk to Russia. On Oct. 7, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry outlined five ceasefire formats that Kyiv is ready to discuss. The difference is that in Moscow, the phrase "we are losing" is interpreted exclusively as a sign that the terror is working.
According to estimates by the DeepState project, the Russian army captured 341 square kilometers (131,6 square miles) between July and September, less than 0.06% of Ukraine's territory.
The actual situation may differ: recent Ukrainian advances have not been marked on the map for operational security reasons. The Ukrainian army has held this front for a fifth year, and the Armed Forces of Ukraine are probably the only ones who can say whether we are losing.
The Kremlin is now betting less on military victory than on political victory.
The Institute for the Study of War believes that Putin expects to force Ukraine to capitulate by spring 2027 through mass strikes using jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles.
Such a plan requires a society that decides for itself that it has lost. Russia is working toward this goal far from the front lines, carrying out dozens of acts of sabotage in European countries to reduce support for Ukraine .
Inside Ukraine itself, it is conducting large-scale information operations. One such operation unfolded alongside the Honcharenko story.
Starting in mid-September, a network of accounts called on Ukrainians to attend a "Maidan for Peace" on Oct. 3. Its demands included peace on any terms, open borders, and immediate presidential elections. Journalists at Texty found that the profile spreading the calls listed Russia as its location.
"The narrative that Ukraine is an aggressive actor that supposedly does not want reconciliation and therefore does not want the war to stop is a Russian political campaign."
Eventually, only a few dozen people showed up in the square.
Russian channels, though, told a different story. SHOT reported that "Ukrainians took to the Maidan," while WarGonzo claimed there were 4,000 participants.
Five channels in our sample garnered around 780,000 views on this story, while Gazeta.ru ironically illustrated the peace protest with a photo from a 2019 rally against concessions to Putin.
During our monitoring, we managed to even capture some humiliation from their own audience. "At least they came out, while we're like mice, afraid to stick our noses out," wrote a commenter under such a post in a Perm regional community.
The demand for immediate elections in this list is no accident. Putin has called Zelensky illegitimate since 2024.
Elections are prohibited by law under martial law. Millions of voters are abroad, and hundreds of thousands are on the front lines. No security conditions for holding elections have been established. An election campaign under these circumstances would give Russia several months during which politicians would compete to improve their own chances and tear apart any social consensus.
The debate over a war party and a peace party in Ukraine is absurd. In a country bombed day and night, there can be no war party by definition. Instead, there is a debate about how to end the war without losing the state.
“Russia, taking strikes and enduring deprivation, will achieve the complete exhaustion and destruction of Ukraine as a space fit for human life.”
The narrative that Ukraine is an aggressive actor that supposedly does not want reconciliation and therefore does not want the war to stop is a Russian political campaign.
Inside Ukraine, it is aimed at dividing society; abroad, at depriving Ukraine of support from its Western partners.
Judging by recent decisions on imports of Russian diesel and U.S. President Donald Trump 's statements about strikes on energy infrastructure, this campaign has been successful internationally.
It will result in more money flowing into Russian state coffers and, consequently, greater funding for the war against Ukraine — meaning more civilians killed and tortured.
As for domestic Ukrainian discourse, despite their psychological and physical exhaustion, Ukrainians have not shown support for a campaign advocating peace on Russia's terms.
The so-called "peace" protest in central Kyiv failed: only a small group of people attended, including some known for their pro-Russian views.
Six days after Honcharenko's post, Z-war correspondent Kotenok described what Russia is offering in return: "Russia, taking strikes and enduring deprivation, will achieve the complete exhaustion and destruction of Ukraine as a space fit for human life."
The quote speaks for itself. It shows what really lies behind Russian calls for peace.
When Ukrainian politicians voice positions that echo the Kremlin's and destabilize society from within, they send Moscow a clear signal to continue terrorizing Ukraine.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Liubov Tsybulska is a strategic communications expert and a leading authority on hybrid threats in Ukraine. As the founder and current director of NGO "Join Ukraine," she leverages her extensive expertise to address critical national security challenges. Previously, she served as the inaugural Head of the Centre for Strategic Communication and Information Security under Ukraine's Ministry of Culture and Information Policy.

title: Ukraine, Russia nearing agreement on evacuation of civilians from occupied Oleshky, ombudsman says
description: The two sides are discussing a local ceasefire to allow residents to be evacuated directly to Ukrainian-controlled territory, Lubinets said on Oct. 18.
content:
Ukraine and Russia are nearing an agreement on the final details of civilian evacuation from the front-line town of Oleshky and nearby settlements in the Russian-occupied part of Kherson Oblast, Ukrainian Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 18.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
The two sides are discussing a local ceasefire to allow residents to be evacuated directly to Ukrainian-controlled territory, rather than having to travel first through Russian-occupied areas and then through Russia and Belarus, Lubinets said in an interview with Ukrainian broadcaster Espreso.
"We are making as much progress as possible. We are now moving toward agreeing on the final details to ensure a ceasefire and evacuate everyone ... directly to territory controlled by the Ukrainian government," Lubinets said.
Lubinets did not specify what direct evacuation to Ukrainian territory entails, but one possible option is to transfer civilians across the Dnipro River to the Ukrainian-controlled western bank.
He added that Kyiv has been holding daily negotiations to unblock the humanitarian evacuation and that Moscow has begun considering a proposal Kyiv put forward long ago.
"We still have some difficult issues to resolve, but I hope that in the near future we will all see concrete results from these negotiations," Lubinets said.
No final agreement has been publicly announced, and it remains unclear when an evacuation could begin.
Lubinets said on Sept. 16 that more than 6,000 people possibly remain in Oleshky and the surrounding area, including about 200 children. His office said it had verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave safely.
While Russian troops occupy Oleshky and the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, the Ukrainian military controls the western bank. Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Russian forces have been preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
In September, 12 people from Oleshky reached Ukrainian-controlled territory, Tetiana Hasanenko, the exiled head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 6.
In spring, evacuation volunteers still managed to help people from Oleshky leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukrainian-controlled areas in exhausting multiday trips through Russia and Belarus. Now, they said , the risk of Russian attacks and mines has made organized evacuation impossible.
In recent weeks, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky alone or in pairs to the neighboring village of Radensk on roads mined by Russian forces.

title: Russian attacks cost Ukrainian businesses $7.7 billion in 2026, prime minister says
description: More than 1 million square meters of real estate, particularly warehouse and logistics facilities, have been destroyed or significantly damaged this year, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi in an interview with BBC Ukraine.
content:
Russian attacks have caused an estimated $7.7 billion in losses to Ukrainian businesses since the beginning of 2026, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in an interview with BBC News Ukraine published on Oct. 19.
More than 1 million square meters of real estate, particularly warehouse and logistics facilities, have been destroyed or significantly damaged this year, Koretskyi said. The $7.7 billion estimate includes damage to business premises, manufacturing facilities and goods stored in warehouses.
"This is a very large figure that continues to grow," Koretskyi said.
The damage comes as Ukrainian businesses face mounting operational disruptions and weaker production as a result of Russian attacks and the ongoing invasion, now in its fifth year.
A monthly survey of 467 companies by the Kyiv-based Institute for Economic Research and Policy Consulting found that fewer businesses were operating at full capacity, while the share of companies reporting lower production volumes rose to its highest level in months.
The share of companies operating close to full capacity also fell for a second consecutive month, from 55% to 47%, according to the survey. Meanwhile, the proportion of businesses reporting lower production volumes rose from 15.6% to 22.6%.
The survey also found that 47.5% of companies said they could not forecast what their business would look like in two years, up from 40% in August.
Operational disruptions remain widespread. The survey found that 58.7% of companies lost working time because of air raid alerts, while 49.5% had to halt production during alerts.
Against this backdrop of mounting pressure on businesses, the government is considering measures to address wartime risks.
Koretskyi said in the interview that the government had proposed raising value-added tax (VAT) by one percentage point to establish a special fund to compensate businesses for insurance against war-related risks. The proposal was discussed at an online meeting with large companies several days earlier.
Discussions with businesses on other proposed policy changes have been more limited. Koretskyi said there had been no extensive consultations on changes to the rules for exempting employees from mobilization .

title: Ukraine brings home 23 children from Russian occupation
description: Among the children returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory is 9-year-old Stefan, who was forced to undergo military training at a school under Russian occupation, according to Bring Kids Back UA.
content:
Ukraine has brought home 23 more children from Russian-occupied territory over the past week, the presidential initiative Bring Kids Back UA announced on Oct. 19.
The rescued children are now receiving psychological support and assistance in restoring their Ukrainian documents, Bring Kids Back UA said.
Among the children returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory is 9-year-old Stefan, who was forced to undergo military training at a school under Russian occupation, including instruction in handling grenades and firearms, the statement said.
Another child returned to Ukraine was 13-year-old Polina, who survived a Russian combat drone strike near her home and was later afraid to go outside, the statement said.
Russian troops also raided her home and destroyed communication devices to limit access to information, according to Bring Kids Back UA.
As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation and forced transfer of Ukrainian children to Russia. Ukrainian human rights groups estimate that hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian children are under Russian control, including those who have been deported or forcibly transferred and those who remain in occupied territories and are at risk of deportation.
