Ukrainian officials estimate the real figure of abducted children could be far higher. Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets puts the number at up to 150,000 , while Presidential Commissioner for Children's Rights Daria Herasymchuk has given a range of 200,000–300,000 . In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Russian President Vladimir Putin and Russia's Commissioner for Children's Rights Maria Lvova-Belova for their role in state-sanctioned child abductions.

title: 'It's significant': Ukraine fears US is withholding allied-funded air defense supplies to pressure Kyiv
description:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to approve the transfer of a significant batch of Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine, Ukrainian officials and military officers told the Kyiv Independent, raising suspicions in Kyiv that Washington is deliberately withholding the weapons to pressure Ukraine.

President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 19 that there are delays in providing "certain types of vital supplies," pointing a finger at the U.S. Department of Defense.

"There are political
content:
Ukrainian officials described the alleged delay as another example of political pressure that could put civilian lives at risk.
U.S. President Donald Trump (L) speaks as U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (R) looks on during a meeting in the Cabinet Room of the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., on Dec. 2, 2025. (Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images)
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has yet to approve the transfer of a significant batch of Patriot interceptor missiles for Ukraine, Ukrainian officials and military officers told the Kyiv Independent, raising suspicions in Kyiv that Washington is deliberately withholding the weapons to pressure Ukraine.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 19 that there are delays in providing "certain types of vital supplies," pointing a finger at the U.S. Department of Defense.
"There are political agreements that have not been implemented at the working level," he added.
One senior Ukrainian official and two Ukrainian military officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, say Hegseth is holding up supplies of Patriot missiles , which Ukraine relies on to intercept ballistic missiles.
"Hegseth has the contracts for Patriot missiles on his desk. He is not signing off on them," one Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
The official added that the missiles had already been paid for by Ukraine's allies.
The delay comes as Russia launches near-daily ballistic missile attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure, leaving Kyiv dependent on its limited supplies of interceptors.
"Hegseth has the contracts for Patriot missiles on his desk. He is not signing off on them."
It also builds on the latest strain in relations between Ukraine and the Trump administration, which the U.S. president criticizing Kyiv's strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Ukraine has also recently experienced repeated disruptions to its early-warning systems for incoming Russian ballistic missiles, which rely on U.S. intelligence. American officials have attributed the outages, which have occurred several times in the past, to “bad weather conditions,” while U.S. State Secretary Marco Rubio has cited a software malfunction.
Ukaine has also experienced disruptions to Starshield and Starlink services , which have severely hampered Ukrainian drone operations, including the interceptor drones Ukraine uses to counter Russian jet-powered attack drones.
Ukrainian officials described the alleged delay as another example of political pressure that could put civilian lives at risk.
Patriot systems are among Ukraine's most important defenses against Russian ballistic missiles , which are particularly difficult to intercept. Any delay could seriously undermine Ukraine's defense of its cities and critical infrastructure.
Ukraine obtains Patriot interceptors through several channels, one senior Ukrainian military official said. One of the main mechanisms is NATO's Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), through which Kyiv's allies fund weapons purchases from the U.S.
Zelensky said the U.S. delivers only 12 Patriot interceptors to Ukraine each month.
Kyiv also seeks missiles directly from countries that may have them in stock. Ukrainian embassies contact governments to identify available supplies.
Ukrainian officials declined to disclose the country's current interceptor stocks, citing operational security.
"(Ukraine) never discloses the quantity of weapons we have on hand so that the enemy remains unaware of the situation," one Ukrainian defense official said.
Another senior Ukrainian official described the batch allegedly awaiting Hegseth's approval as "significant."
"It's hard to call this a 'monthly supply,' because there's no set amount of how much you need for a month," the official said. "But it's significant."
The status of the broader supply program remains less clear. A NATO official said PURL deliveries were continuing, including shipments of air defense equipment.
"Support to Ukraine through PURL continues to flow. This includes air defense," the official said.
Another NATO official acknowledged that some shipments could face delays but said political reasons were unlikely to explain them.
Ukrainian officials, however, believe the hold-up is a political decision rather than a routine logistical delay.
"It looks like this is a political refusal to sign," one Ukrainian official said.
"First, it was missile early warnings. Now this. It's clear what they're doing."
The Kyiv Independent contacted the Pentagon for comment, but had not received a response. A U.S. government official disputed Ukraine's claims, calling them "not true."
As of the morning of Oct. 19, a Ukrainian defense official said there had been no change in the supply situation, and Hegseth had still not approved the transfer.
The dispute over Patriot interceptors comes amid mounting tensions over Ukraine's campaign against Russian energy infrastructure.
Trump has criticized Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries as his administration seeks to address rising global fuel prices, driven by his war in Iran .
On Oct. 9, Trump announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin allowing Russia to supply millions of tons of diesel to U.S. and international markets despite sanctions imposed over Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia subsequently partially lifted its ban on diesel exports, allowing additional supplies to reach foreign markets.
With fuel prices putting pressure on U.S. consumers, Trump has increasingly blamed Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, while denying responsibility for the situation at the gas pumps.
One senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the administration's approach was driven by domestic politics.
"He can't admit he was wrong about the war in Iran, so — purely for campaign purposes — he's fallen back on the old narrative of accusations against Ukraine," the official said.

title: Over 100,000 Ukrainians safe from deportation as US is set to extend protection status
description: Temporary Protection Status was granted to Ukraine’s citizens on March 3, 2022, just over a week after Russia begun its full-scale war against Ukraine.
content:
The U.S. is expected to extend Temporary Protected Status (TPS) for 100,000 Ukrainian refugees beyond its current expiration date of Oct. 19, CNN reported on Oct. 18.
CNN cited a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.
The spokesperson said that an official statement will be made “at the appropriate time,” but those under TPS are safe to remain in the country.
Under TPS, Ukrainians are allowed to legally stay in the U.S., apply for an Employment Authorization Document (EAD) and enroll in educational institutions, including higher education programs.
TPS for Sudanese refugees will also be extended, CNN reported. Two other countries retaining their Temporary Protected Status are El Salvador and Lebanon.
TPS was granted to Ukraine’s citizens on March 3, 2022, just over a week after Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine.
It is usually granted to countries for anywhere from six to eighteen months. Previously, Ukraine’s status was renewed on Jan. 17, 2025 and came into effect in April that year for another 18 months.
However, U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has terminated the status for multiple countries since March 2025, affecting about one million people across 13 countries, including Afghanistan, Haiti, and Syria.
The pending review from the U.S. comes at a time when President Volodymyr Zelensky and Trump’s relationship has been rather rocky following an unexpected announcement of a diesel deal between Washington and Moscow.
On Oct. 16, the U.S. also waived sanctions against Russia envisaged by the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on Oct. 16.
"He (Zelensky) could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead. I WANT THIS WAR END!,” Trump wrote on Oct. 18 on his social media platform, Truth Social.
In response, Zelensky has called such easing of sanctions “wrong” and told British host Piers Morgan in an interview on Oct. 14 that he laments the recent course of events.
"It's painful when President Trump chooses one ‌side, not our ⁠side," he added.

title: Ukrainian forces evacuate injured soldier from front-line position by drone in 'first-of-its-kind' mission, video shows
description: The operation involved Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade, 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade, and 10th Army Corps, along with Ukrainian drone manufacturer Gurzuf Defense.
content:
Ukrainian forces have carried out what they describe as a "first-of-its-kind" aerial evacuation of a wounded soldier directly from a front-line position by drone, the Ukrainian military and defense company Gurzuf Defense announced on Oct. 19.
The operation involved Ukraine's 92nd Separate Assault Brigade , 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade, and 10th Army Corps, along with Ukrainian drone manufacturer Gurzuf Defense .
The Ukrainian military did not disclose the date of the operation or the section of the front line where it took place.
The wounded soldier, serving with the 30th Brigade, had spent nearly 500 days at a front-line position "under constant threat of death." His fellow soldiers maintained contact with him and delivered food, water, ammunition, and medicine by drone, Gurzuf Defense said .
After the soldier suffered a severe injury, evacuating him by ground became impossible because of Russian drone activity in the area and mined terrain. Attempting to reach him on foot or with a ground robotic vehicle , the usual way of evacuating the wounded, would have put the rescue team at risk.
Ukrainian troops used a heavy-lift hexacopter drone, the Heavy Shot Ayudag-6.
The team first delivered special equipment with carabiners to the wounded soldier, then sent the drone equipped with a winch. Guided remotely by fellow soldiers who remained in contact with him, the soldier secured himself to the evacuation system, Gurzuf Defense said, calling the operation an "unprecedented mission."
The drone then transported him to a safer position, where other soldiers met him and arranged further evacuation to a hospital. The mission lasted 1 hour, 14 minutes, and 36 seconds, covering a distance of 62 kilometers (39 miles).
Drone operator of the 30th Mechanized Brigade, callsign "Chornyi" ("Black" in Ukrainian), said he is "very pleased" that everything went well.
The company said the operation required close monitoring of the airspace and electronic warfare protection throughout the flight. The soldier is now receiving treatment and rehabilitation, and his life is no longer in danger, according to the 30th Separate Mechanized Brigade.
"An extremely complex operation, but a successful one. This is a historic event," "Napalm," a 92nd Brigade programmer who was involved in preparing the operation, said .
"It marks the next stage in the evacuation of the wounded, which we will all eventually reach. Now the serious, systematic work begins to ensure that such missions take place on a regular basis," Napalm added.
Gurzuf Defense co-founder Pavlo Feldblium warned that aerial evacuation should not be treated as a routine practice, citing the risks to wounded soldiers during flight. Each mission would need to be planned individually for the specific circumstances and location, he said.
"Air rescue is a last resort when there is no other way to save a person," Feldblium said.
According to the Ukrainian outlet Ukrainka Pravda, the hexacopter Heavy Shot Ayudag-6's platform has a flight range of up to 25 kilometers (15.5 miles) and an operational altitude of 150–300 meters (500 to 1,000 feet), while the aircraft itself weighs about 98 kilograms (215 pounds) and can carry 70–90 kilograms (150 to 200 pounds).
It is named after its six motors and Mount Ayudag near Gurzuf, a resort town in Russian-occupied Crimea .
Heavy drones have primarily been used to deliver ammunition and other supplies to front-line positions.

title: 'Extremely unpleasant experience' — Why Kyiv faces growing risk of sewage crisis this winter
description:
As regular Russian strikes on energy facilities leave parts of Kyiv without running water, fears are mounting that further power outages could spark a serious humanitarian and public health crisis in a city whose water and sewage system depends entirely on electricity.

Kyiv’s water system is one of the city’s biggest power consumers, requiring huge amounts of electricity to draw water from the Dnipro river and pump around 700 million liters of clean water daily to households and businesses.

It
content:
A man fishes from the shore of the Dnipro River as smoke rises over a residential area following Russian strikes in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 8, 2026. (Viktor Fridshon / Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
As regular Russian strikes on energy facilities leave parts of Kyiv without running water, fears are mounting that further power outages could spark a serious humanitarian and public health crisis in a city whose water and sewage system depends entirely on electricity.
Kyiv’s water system is one of the city’s biggest power consumers, requiring huge amounts of electricity to draw water from the Dnipro river and pump around 700 million liters of clean water daily to households and businesses.
It is also extremely reliant on the central energy grid, making it vulnerable to Russia’s bombing campaign targeting energy facilities.
While some residents have stockpiles of clean water in their homes, water industry experts warn that the main threat comes from the failure of the wastewater system, which needs electricity to transport sewage to wastewater plants.
If left untreated, sewage could flood the city and pose a serious health and environmental hazard.
"Transporting and treating wastewater is a major challenge for utility companies. Equipment is aging, and a lack of electricity for pumping can have serious consequences," Oleksandr Skhin, director of Ukraine’s Association of Water Utilities, told the Kyiv Independent.
While Ukraine’s government has said the country is well prepared for the winter, Kyiv’s residents are growing increasingly skeptical, particularly after Moscow launched one its biggest ever attacks on the capital’s substations on Oct. 14, leaving many households without water and power.
As the Kyiv Independent previously reported, the capital has not prepared sufficiently for the heating season, leaving the city without enough backup power generation. Consequently, recent attacks have not only caused emergency blackouts in the city, but forced the capital to return to scheduled power outages, which haven’t been imposed since the spring.
With the constant voltage fluctuations, Kyiv’s aged electric water utility system simply "burns out," Serhii Horkutsenko, deputy head of Kyivvodokanal, the capital's state-owned water supply company, told Ukrainian media Ekonomichna Pravda in an interview published on Oct. 12.
Moreover, Russia has increased the intensity of its attacks on Ukraine’s energy system fivefold since 2024, Olena Pavlenko, head of the Kyiv-based energy think tank Dixi Group, told the Kyiv Independent. As a result, Kyiv’s energy system is in a more critical state than in previous years, while Russia continues to escalate attacks and deploy new tactics .
A weaker, worn-out energy grid also puts the water system at greater risk because it makes it harder to meet the electricity demands of pumping stations, Oleksii Andriiashchenko, sales manager at Grundfos Ukraine, a major water pump producer, told the Kyiv Independent.
He expects that parts of Kyiv will be left without electricity and water for weeks this winter. In the worst-case scenario, the water system could collapse, leading to overflowing sewage tanks that flood the city.
At the same time, Russia has also directly targeted Kyiv’s only sewage plant — the Bortnychi plant — with drones and missiles on several occasions, Mykhailo Yatsuk, director of the Institute of Water Problems and Land Reclamation, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The destruction of the Bortnychi plant poses the greatest threat. Furthermore, there is a risk of damage to sewage pumping stations. This could create problems for the integrated system and cause significant environmental damage," Yatsuk said.
According to Yatsuk, Kyiv’s authorities are much better prepared than previous years and have emergency plans for different scenarios, despite the public perception that the city is not ready.
Authorities have also stockpiled equipment and materials needed to repair damaged water infrastructure, he added.
Ahead of the winter, Kyivvodokanal is already operating 103 generators across its network and is expecting the delivery of more high-capacity generator systems currently being manufactured abroad, Kyiv’s mayor Vitalii Klitschko said on Oct.13. But generators cannot replace the main energy grid, nor can they work continuously, Klitschko said.
What's more, generators can only power smaller pumping stations, not larger, more critical ones, said Andriiashchenko. And Kyiv still needs to construct new high-capacity power generation facilities, like co-generation plants, to fully back up the main water system, Petro Panteleev, first deputy head of the Kyiv City State Administration, said in a public statement.
At the same time, Horkutsenko said that Kyivvodokanal is struggling with staffing and funding shortages. One person is doing the work of four, he stressed. Nonetheless, he promised that the agency would deliver drinking water to residents by truck during severe outages.
But even then, trucking in water deliveries won’t be enough to cover the city’s sanitation and hygiene needs, since the average household consumes 100 liters of water per person per day, according to Skhin.
The lack of water for hygiene and cleaning has been a problem for several Ukrainian cities throughout the war, said Skhin. In Chernihiv, the director of the local water utility could only distribute enough water for drinking to residents from his tractor during a monthlong outage at the start of the full-scale war, he said.
"People had to find their own ways to meet sanitation and hygiene needs, including collecting water from rivers or melting snow," Skhin said.
"It was an extremely unpleasant experience."
Dominic is the business reporter for the Kyiv Independent, reporting on Ukrainian companies, investment, energy, corruption, and reforms. Based in Kyiv, Dominic joined the Kyiv Independent team in 2023, having previously worked as a freelancer. He has written articles for a number of publications, including the Financial Times, bne IntelliNews, Radio Free Europe/Liberty, Euronews and New Eastern Europe. Previously, Dominic worked with StopFake as a disinformation expert, debunking Russian fake news in Europe.

title: US reacts to Kyiv's claim it received no advance notice of Russian ballistic missile launches
description: In the Oct. 19 attack on Kyiv, at least one person was killed, and eight others were injured as Russian missiles struck Kyiv in multiple waves overnight.
content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he could not confirm reports that Ukraine received no advance warning before Russia's ballistic missile attack on Kyiv on Oct. 19, citing a lack of information, as he spoke to reporters during a visit to Samarkand, Uzbekistan.
Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty journalist Alex Raufoglu asked Rubio during a press briefing to comment on Kyiv's statements that it had received no advance warning of Russian missile launches.
"I don't know. I mean, where did it happen last night? I don't know exactly," Rubio told reporters on Oct. 19.
In the Oct. 19 attack on Kyiv, at least one person was killed, and eight others were injured as Russian missiles struck Kyiv in multiple waves overnight. Explosions were reported shortly before 11 p.m., followed by further attacks around 3 a.m. and 7 a.m. local time.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on X on Oct. 19 that Ukraine had not received early warning from its partner countries, including the U.S., ahead of the attack. He added that Russia launched 16 ballistic missiles, with Kyiv and the surrounding region as the primary targets.
Later in the day, Ukraine's Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on national television that Ukraine received no advance warning from its partners before the first wave of ballistic missile attacks at around 11 p.m., but that information about the second wave, at around 3 a.m., was provided.
He added that a similar situation had occurred during previous attacks, including the one overnight on Oct. 14.
Alerts did sound before the overnight strikes overnight on Oct. 19, though the warnings were unusually short. The first explosions were simultaneous with the blaring of air raid sirens, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
The U.S. provides Ukraine with intelligence to help its military detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
Rubio said on Oct. 19 that "a few nights ago" there was a software problem involving the Ukrainian early warning system.
"I know that EUCOM (U.S. European Command) had been involved in looking at, and that's the report they gave us back. I can't comment on what happened last night," he said.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent that the first overnight wave followed a similar pattern.
"The 'warning' about a ballistic threat came through only after the strike had already happened," the official said. "They're up to something again."
It can be common for Russia's high-speed ballistic missiles to hit with very little advance warning .
The attack came just hours after Zelensky said the U.S. had resumed intelligence sharing with Ukraine about Russian missile launches.
The president's announcement came as a relief after Kyiv endured "massive explosions" on Oct. 12, when five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The Oct. 12 attack came after the U.S. threatened to withhold intelligence from Ukraine unless Kyiv stopped attacking Russian refineries, sources told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukrainian officials have previously explained that satellite surveillance of launch sites can be vulnerable to transmission delays. Bad weather may also cause interference with the Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) satellites, a surveillance network U.S. forces use to monitor Russian launch sites.
But the senior official who spoke to the Kyiv Independent said although bad weather had affected warnings before, this number of strikes with little to no warning "has never happened before." "Now we're seeing 'bad weather' three times in a row," the official said. "When nothing comes through on any channel... well, we get it."

title: Russian court jails pro-war blogger critical of Kremlin
description: Tetiana Montian, a Ukrainian-born blogger, has supported Russia's aggression against Ukraine but at the same time accused the Russian authorities of incompetence and corruption.
content:
A Russian occupation court in Ukraine's Donetsk on Oct. 19 sentenced a Russian pro-war blogger critical of the Kremlin to one and a half years in jail for alleged "extremism."
Tetiana Montian, a Ukrainian-born blogger, has supported Russia's aggression against Ukraine but at the same time accused the Russian authorities of incompetence and corruption.
The court also banned her from managing Internet sites for two years.
She was convicted for "extremism" based on her statement in a 2022 video stream in which she called for "taking down" the Russian regime's propagandists "without the slightest regret."
The Russian verb used in the phrase can mean to kill someone but Montian argued that she had meant banning hostile accounts, not physical violence.
Montian was born in the Ukrainian city of Kerch in 1972 and became a lawyer and activist.
Starting from 2014, Montian supported Russia and its proxies during Moscow's invasion of the Donbas.
She moved to Russia in 2021 and acquired Russian citizenship.
On Feb. 17, 2022, a week before Russia's full-scale invasion, she addressed a meeting of the United Nations Security Council at Russia's invitation.
She described Ukraine as a colony of the West and accused Kyiv of killing civilians in the Donbas. These accusations reflected the Russian government's justification for military intervention.
Later she supported Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
However, Montian's support for Russia's military objectives did not translate into unconditional loyalty to the Kremlin.
She has criticized Russian President Vladimir Putin , the Russian authorities, and Kremlin propagandists, accusing them of mistakes, incompetence, and corruption.
She has lambasted Putin largely for not conducting the war against Ukraine more effectively, rather than for launching it.
In 2023 Montian attacked Putin for his decision to annex Crimea in 2014, arguing that Russia could have controlled its military facilities in Sevastopol without formally annexing the peninsula.
"If Putin weren't such a stupid f**khead, none of this would have happened," she said .
The same year, Montian also called Kremlin propagandist Vladmir Solovyov a fascist and traitor.
In February 2026, she also said that "there is absolutely unrestrained terror " in Russian-occupied parts of the Donbas, and people are terrified of criticizing the authorities.
Montian is not the first pro-war activist critical of the Kremlin jailed in Russia.
Other pro-war activists jailed during the full-scale invasion include Igor Girkin , Andrei Kurshin, and Sergei Udaltsov.

title: 4 killed, 55 injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over past day as 550,000 households lose power
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russian forces targeted energy facilities in 11 oblasts across Ukraine.
content:
Editor's note: The story was updated to include the latest casualty figures from Russian attacks in Kyiv Oblast.
At least four people were killed and 55 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia continued to target energy infrastructure across the country, regional authorities said on Oct. 18-19.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that, overnight and on the morning of Oct. 19, Russia attacked energy facilities in Vinnytsia, Volyn, Kirovohrad, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Kharkiv, Ternopil, Odesa, and Rivne oblasts.
"In this one night alone, more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, and the lights went out for at least 550,000 families. Repair crews are working at the sites," Zelensky said.
Russian forces launched Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and Iskander-K cruise missiles, 269 Shahed-type attack drones, including 59 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, and S-8000 Banderol missiles overnight on Oct. 19, Ukraine's Air Force said .
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 243 drones and four Iskander-K cruise missiles, while strikes were recorded at 25 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at eight locations, the Air Force said.
The Air Force did not specify how many Russian ballistic missiles were launched or how many were shot down.
Zelensky said Russian forces launched 16 ballistic missiles , with Kyiv and the surrounding region being the main targets of the attack.
Ukrenergo , Ukraine's state grid operator, reported that as a result of the attack, power outages occurred in 10 regions.
"Where safety conditions currently permit, emergency repair work is already underway. Power company staff are doing everything they can to restore power to all affected customers," Ukrenergo said .
Vinnytsia Oblast Governor Nataliia Zabolotna said on Oct. 19 that Russia continues its mass attack on energy infrastructure. She added that parts of Vinnytsia Oblast and the regional capital were left without electricity and water after the attacks.
In northwestern Zhytomyr Oblast , for two days running, the Russian forces continued their attempts to "destroy critical infrastructure," including energy facilities, regional governor Vitalii Bunechko said.
In northwestern Volyn Oblast , Russian drone attacks caused power supply disruptions, regional governor Roman Romaniuk said. The cities of Kovel, Manevychi, and Lutsk were hit hardest, with damage reported to critical and civilian infrastructure.
Russia continues to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure despite the so-called energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, which was announced by U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 11. Since then, Russia has attacked Ukrainian energy and oil and gas facilities 76 times, Zelensky said on Oct. 18.
Ukraine has targeted Russian energy facilities and export infrastructure to disrupt a key source of funding for Moscow's war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukrainian power plants and substations, seeking to deprive civilians of electricity and heating.
Beyond damage to energy infrastructure, Russian attacks caused civilian casualties in several regions. In eastern Donetsk Oblast , two people were killed while two others were injured in Russian attacks on the front-line cities of Kramatorsk and Druzhkivka over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In the city of Kyiv , after multiple waves of Russian missile attacks, one person was killed, and eight others were injured, city authorities said .
In Kyiv Oblast's Irpin , about 20 kilometers (12 miles) northwest of the capital, one woman was killed and 19 people were injured, including nine children.
At around 9 a.m. local time, Tymur Tkachenko , head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration, said that three people were missing. Search operations are ongoing, he added.
In north-eastern Kharkiv Oblast over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and 17 settlements in the surrounding region, injuring 11 people, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In northeastern Sumy Oblast , as a result of a Russian drone strike on a civilian car, an 11-year-old boy, a 39-year-old man, and a 32-year-old woman sustained injuries, regional authorities said .
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast , over the past day, Russia carried out 738 attacks on 56 settlements of the region — three people were injured in the attacks, regional authorities said .
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , two people, including an 84-year-old woman, were injured in Russian attacks across the region, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on Oct. 18 and Oct. 19 .
In northern Chernihiv Oblast , Russian troops launched a Banderol missile strike on the city of Chernihiv. A secondary school was damaged, while two people were injured in the attack.
In northwestern Rivne Oblast , two women were injured, regional governor Oleksandr Koval said.
In southern Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks injured one person, a child, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Russian forces targeted 24 settlements across the region.
In western Lviv Oblast , six houses and vehicles were damaged in Russian attacks on the region, Governor Maksym Kozytskyi said.

title: Russian attacks hit Ukrainian water filtration, plastics factories overnight
description: The overnight assault also damaged a data center in Kyiv and infrastructure in Volyn Region, where around 66,000 electricity metering points were left without power, regional officials said.
content:
Editor's note: This article was updated to reflect additional information about an attack on a pharmaceutical distributer.
Russian attacks heavily damaged industrial facilities and critical infrastructure across Ukraine overnight on Oct. 19, hitting factories in the Kyiv suburb of Irpin, a data center in Kyiv, infrastructure in Volyn Region, and a pharmaceutical distributor in Rivne, according to local officials and company statements.
The overnight assault also damaged a data center in Kyiv and infrastructure in Volyn Region, where around 66,000 electricity metering points were left without power, regional officials said.
Russian attacks on Ukrainian businesses and critical infrastructure in the Kyiv area have significantly increased in recent months and weeks, as Moscow looks to cripple Ukraine's economy, as well as its energy and water systems ahead of winter.
Irpin Mayor Oleksandr Markushyn said one of the city’s largest enterprises had suffered serious damage and caught fire in the overnight attack, without specifying the name of the company. The blast wave also shattered windows in nearby apartment buildings, he said.
Local reports indicated that Ecosoft, a Ukrainian manufacturer of water filtration and purification systems, sustained damage in the overnight attack on Irpin, though it remains unclear whether this was the enterprise referenced by the mayor.
The company lost a factory in Irpin in 2022 at the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, with courts assessing the direct damage to the facility back then at around 13.1 million euros. It partially resumed operations in Ukraine's western city of Ternopil in March 2022 before reopening in Irpin in June of the same year. It closed its Ternopil operations in April 2023.
Another company in the area, Planet Plastic — which produces polyethylene products, including industrial and agricultural films, packaging materials and pipes used in water supply and gas distribution — confirmed that missiles struck its production facilities directly, causing significant destruction.
After its factory was nearly destroyed at the start of the invasion in 2022, Planet Plastic resumed operations in Irpin in 2025, but says it was forced to suspend them indefinitely in August due to intensified Russian air attacks on the region.
In Kyiv, telecommunications operator DataGroup reported that a Russian strike destroyed the infrastructure and equipment at its data center. The company said the facility could not be restored, but services were continuing through backup infrastructure. No employees were injured, it added.
The overnight attack on Kyiv killed one person and injured eight, according to local authorities. A metro station, medical facilities, educational institutions, residential buildings and other sites were also damaged.
Ukraine's western Volyn Oblast was also targeted overnight and into the morning of Oct. 19. Around 15 Russian drones were directed at the region, with Kovel, Manevychi and Lutsk among the areas most heavily affected, the Volyn Regional Military Administration said .
Strikes and falling drone debris damaged critical and civilian infrastructure. Around 66,000 electricity metering points remained without power as of the administration’s 9:30 a.m. update. Officials reported no deaths or injuries in the region at that time.
In Rivne, a Russian drone reportedly struck a warehouse belonging to pharmaceutical distributor BaDM during the overnight attack, according to Ekonomichna Pravda, which cited participants in Ukraine’s pharmaceutical market.
BaDM is one of Ukraine’s largest pharmaceutical distributors, supplying medicines and medical products to pharmacies and healthcare providers across the country. The Rivne Regional Military Administration confirmed that the western region was targeted overnight.
The reported strike is the latest in a series of attacks on pharmaceutical storage facilities in Ukraine. A BaDM warehouse was also reportedly hit on Sept. 14, while a 43,000-square-meter distribution center belonging to the company was completely destroyed in a Russian missile and drone attack in December 2025.

title: US-Russia-China summit would only 'encourage Putin to continue this war,' Ukraine says
description: "A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia could help end the war sooner," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said. "A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war."
content:
Kyiv on Oct. 19 lambasted proposals for a three-way summit of the U.S., Russian, and Chinese presidents on ending the war in Ukraine, amid reports that the Kremlin is pushing for such a meeting.
"A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine , the U.S. , and Russia could help end the war sooner," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.
"A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China , and the U.S. would do only the opposite: encourage (Russian President Vladimir) Putin to continue this war."
The comments follow reporting by the Wall Street Journal that Putin wants to use the potential summit with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping—without President Volodymyr Zelensky present—to secure a peace deal favorable to Moscow, capitalizing on the warming U.S.-Russia ties.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told the Wall Street Journal that discussions about the summit were taking place, even though there "is no clear understanding yet regarding the meeting itself or its potential agenda."
The Kremlin proposed holding the summit on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting, held in Shenzhen, China, between Nov. 18 and 19, according to the outlet's sources.
Commenting on the news, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters that "there's been talks of a meeting," without giving further details.
"I don't know whether it's been finalized, but the ⁠president has been clear. He'd like the war in Ukraine and ​Russia to end."
Sybiha commented that "inviting Putin to such a meeting would feed his appetite for self-aggrandizement and give him a stature he does not deserve."
"He is not a global leader; he is a war criminal. And Russia is not a global power; it is a global problem."
Zelensky has repeatedly expressed readiness for a trilateral summit with Trump and Putin on neutral ground to negotiate an end to the war. The Kremlin responded that Putin would meet Zelensky only in Moscow, effectively turning down the proposal.
"By any pragmatic or moral measure, Putin has no place at the table with presidents Trump and Xi," Ukraine's chief diplomat added, noting that rather than accepting a ceasefire, Russia is escalating its attacks against Ukrainian civilians.
The news comes as U.S.-Ukraine ties plummet and Trump warms to the Kremlin, announcing a major deal on the purchase of Russian diesel and delaying the long-awaited Russia sanctions package.
The pivot was accompanied by unexpected restrictions on Starlink terminals used by the Ukrainian military and alleged delays in shipments of already paid-for Patriot interceptors, which are crucial for defending the Ukrainian skies against Russian ballistic missiles.
Trump has also declined to denounce Russia for disregarding his unilaterally declared "energy truce" by continued attacks against the Ukrainian energy grid, while blasting Zelensky for allegedly not wanting "to end the war."
Zelensky said that Trump siding with Russia would put him on the "wrong side of history," but added that the U.S. and Ukraine are in "constant communication" and are preparing their "next steps in diplomacy."

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,567,160 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 2,100 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,567,160 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 19.
The number includes 2,100 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,416 tanks, 25,565 armored combat vehicles, 164,578 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,317 artillery systems, 2,224 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,714 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,974 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: US delaying Patriot missiles already paid for under NATO initiative, Zelensky says
description: Zelensky has appealed to Washington repeatedly, making the case for additional Patriot missiles as Russia intensifies strikes against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.
content:
The United States is delaying the delivery of Patriot interceptor missiles already paid for under a NATO-coordinated weapons purchasing initiative, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with Bloomberg on Oct. 18.
Washington has approved only some of the missiles purchased through the Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) initiative, which allows NATO allies to finance the purchase of U.S.-made weapons for Ukraine, Zelensky said, according to Bloomberg .
"The American side approved the delivery of only some of them, but not the rest. And this is not a technical issue," Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian president said the U.S. is currently supplying just 12 Patriot interceptor missiles per month, approximately one-quarter of the number provided under former President Joe Biden's administration.
Unlike the military aid provided under Biden, Ukraine must now purchase the missiles, Zelensky said.
The accusations come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian ballistic missile attacks and increasingly severe shortages of the interceptors needed to defend against them.
Ukraine's Patriot interceptor stocks had again reached critically low levels by mid-October, with a Ukrainian official telling the Washington Post that only a handful remained. CNN separately reported that Kyiv's available missiles had been exhausted.
Patriot systems are among Ukraine's most important defenses against Russian ballistic missiles, which are particularly difficult to intercept using other systems.
Russia launched ballistic missile attacks against Kyiv on consecutive nights, Oct. 18 and 19 , killing at least one person in the first attack and damaging residential buildings and infrastructure.
Zelensky also told Bloomberg that he had proposed suspending Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure in exchange for additional Patriot missiles.
"My latest model was: We don't target Russian diesel, you give us missiles for Patriot systems to protect our facilities. But they just want us to stop attacking diesel," Zelensky said.
The proposal comes at a time of growing tensions between Kyiv and Washington over U.S. President Donald Trump's demands that Ukraine halt its strikes on Russian oil refineries.
The Trump administration has threatened to restrict military and intelligence support unless Ukraine ends the campaign, even as Russia continues targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Trump previously appeared to support expanding Ukraine's access to Patriot missiles. On July 8 , he told Zelensky that Ukraine could produce the missiles domestically.
But Trump walked back that promise on July 31 , saying Washington had not agreed to grant the licenses and describing the technology as difficult to share.
In September , Zelensky said Trump had made a final decision to grant Ukraine licenses to manufacture Patriot missiles, although domestic production has yet to begin.
Zelensky has appealed to Washington repeatedly, making the case for additional Patriot missiles as Russia intensifies strikes against Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure.
The U.S. government has not publicly confirmed Zelensky's latest figures or explained the reported delays in approving deliveries.

title: Ukraine has retaken more territory than Russia captured this fall, Zelensky says
description: "The trend this year continues," Zelensky said, "Since the start of fall, our warriors have liberated more territory than the Russians have managed to capture. The same was true at other points this year."
content:
Ukrainian forces have recaptured more territory than Russian forces have seized this fall, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an Oct. 18 post on social media.
"We are seeing results on the front," Zelensky said, in his evening video message.
The Ukrainian Armed Forces are destroying Russian attempts to launch assaults in Dobropillia, a city in the Donetsk region, while defending their positions in Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia, he highlighted, adding that the "front is strong."
"The trend this year continues," Zelensky said, "Since the start of fall, our warriors have liberated more territory than the Russians have managed to capture. The same was true at other points this year."
Under ‘Operation Vivaldi’ Ukrainian forces have made advances as they pushed into occupied areas of Donetsk Oblast. Ukraine's Third Army Corps unveiled on Oct. 14 , that it had retaken another 101 square kilometers in the Lyman sector in Donetsk Oblast.
In total, Operation Vivaldi saw the liberation and return of 16 settlements and 277 square kilometers (106 square miles) to Ukraine, corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said in a recent announcement.
At the same time, Russian high-ranking military officials continue to present "greatly exaggerated claims of Russian frontline advances that do not correspond to battlefield realities" according to an Oct. 17 post on social media sharing findings from a report published by the Institute for the Study of War, an independent conflict monitor based in the U.S.
Russian forces have lost on average seven kilometers daily thus far in October 2026, the ISW reports, contrary to Putin’s false claim of continued Russian advances.
According to the ISW, the Russian forces make these false claims to present a narrative of military success, "such that Ukraine and its Western partners should capitulate to Russia’s negotiation demands."

title: US Treasury Secretary downplays Russia sanctions waiver, warns Zelensky to 'be careful'
description: Trump appointee Scott Bessent insisted that no sanctions against Russia had been lifted — they had merely been waived.
content:
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent denied accusations that Washington’s recent actions were tipping the scales in Russia's favor and warned President Volodymyr Zelensky to "be careful," in an Oct. 18 interview with NBC News.
The comments came two days after U.S. President Donald Trump waived most of the sanctions and tariffs introduced in a bipartisan Russia sanctions bill he signed last month. They also follow Zelensky's claim that the recent decision to slow down Ukrainian Starlink access came from inside the American government.
"President Zelensky should be very careful about making statements like this that aren't true," Bessent said when asked by NBC host Kristen Welker about Zelensky's comments.
When SpaceX abruptly implemented a speed cap on Ukraine's Starshield services earlier this week, a blame game ensued. It was not immediately clear if the restrictions came from SpaceX, the U.S. government, or outside sabotage. The Ukrainian Armed Forces relies on Starshield services to conduct military operations.
In what seemed a remarkable coincidence, the restrictions followed a threat from the U.S. government to withhold intelligence support should Ukraine continue to bomb Russian oil refineries. The Telegraph reported on Oct. 16 that Elon Musk, SpaceX CEO, proposed the speed cap to Trump — and Trump "agreed," citing multiple sources familiar with the matter.
Zelensky appeared earlier on Welker’s "Meet the Press," where he said Ukrainian intelligence reports show the decision to curb Starlink access came from the U.S. government.
"It was a message from the American government to limit this feed," Zelensky said, "and technically SpaceX did it."
Both Trump and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio have "categorically" denied the accusation, Bessent said, adding that it was "reckless" of Zelensky to make such a charge.
Bessent also commented on the Trump administration’s decision to waive sanctions included in the recently passed Graham Act.
When asked what concessions Russian President Vladimir Putin had made to earn sanctions relief, Bessent claimed that "the only thing that has been lifted is the diesel embargo" and said "no one has been tougher" on sanctioning Russia than Trump.
The U.S. president, in an effort to lower diesel prices before the U.S. midterm elections, has sought to strike a diesel deal with Russia, despite the rising cost of diesel having been widely attributed to the U.S. war with Iran.
Pressed by Welker about the executive order waiving the sanctions in the recently passed Graham Act, Bessent repeated that "no sanctions have been lifted."
The new sanctions, which never went into effect, were waived rather than lifted.

title: 'I want this war end' — Trump defends pro-Russian policies in scathing diatribe against Zelensky
description: "His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead."
content:
Editor's Note: This is a developing story.
U.S. President Donald Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social on Oct. 18 to defend his recent decisions regarding Russia — including the waiving of sanctions, a deal to buy diesel, and intense pressure on Ukraine to stop targeting oil refineries.
The pro-Kremlin moves have sparked outrage and alarm in both Ukraine and the U.S., as Russia continues battering Ukrainian cities and makes no concessions towards a peace agreement in exchange for Trump's sanctions relief.
The Trump administration has gone beyond public criticism of Kyiv. The Kyiv Independent reported on Oct. 12 , citing two Ukrainian officials, that Washington threatened to suspend intelligence sharing and weapons deliveries in an effort to compel Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian energy facilities.
But this is all part of Trump's diplomatic plan, the U.S. president claimed in his post.
"My decision on Russia is a very simple one," he wrote on Truth Social.
"I am in the process of negotiating Peace in the war between Russia and Ukraine, and don't want to do anything that will drive, foolishly, Russia away from the bargaining table. Great progress is being made, and that includes current hostage negotiations!"
Trump defended his diesel deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin by saying that Moscow is not helping Iran in the war with U.S., but is rather helping the international community by "sending, at a low price, millions of barrels of diesel to the World."
"Russia is doing very little, if anything, to help the Islamic Republic of Iran, compared to what they could be doing, and I want to keep it that way, and will, unless stupid people get in the way," he wrote.
The U.S. president announced a deal with Putin on Oct. 9 allowing Russia to supply millions of tons of diesel to American and international markets despite sanctions imposed over Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Russia subsequently partially lifted its diesel export ban, allowing additional supplies to reach foreign markets.
With the war in Iran driving up global fuel prices, including for U.S. consumers, Trump has sought to pin the blame on another target as midterm elections approach. His choice was Ukraine — specifically, the country's increasingly successful strike campaign on Russian oil refineries.
The diesel deal has also raised questions about whether easing restrictions on Russian energy exports will provide Moscow with additional revenue to finance its war. A Kyiv Independent analysis published Oct. 14 examined the limited economic benefits of the agreement and its potential political advantages for the Kremlin.
"Zelensky is using Diesel Refineries in Russia as a target, knowing that these attacks are seriously hurting the world diesel markets, including those in the United States," Trump said in his post, despite evidence that the war in Iran is the primary driver of the price surge.
Zelensky said on Oct. 18 that Russia had attacked Ukrainian energy and oil and gas facilities 76 times since Trump announced an energy ceasefire on Oct. 11, leaving tens of thousands of families without electricity. Ukraine initially paused strikes on Russian refineries following Trump's announcement, but resumed the campaign on Oct. 15 after Moscow continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Trump then doubled down on criticism of President Volodymyr Zelensky, accusing the Ukrainian leader of not wanting to end the war at all.
"He could have made a better deal two years ago than he can now. His country is in shambles, a large portion of his land is lost, his oceans and seas are gone, and his male population is low, wounded, and/or dead. I WANT THIS WAR END!"

title: NATO jets scramble as drone explodes in Lithuanian airspace
description: A flying object, likely a drone, entered Lithuanian airspace and exploded on Oct. 18, sending residents to shelters and damaging a civilian vehicle, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said.
content:
An unidentified object, likely a drone, entered Lithuanian airspace and exploded on Oct. 18, sending residents to shelters and damaging a civilian vehicle, according to Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda.
The incident is the latest in a string of drone incursions along NATO's eastern flank , stoking concern that Russia's war in Ukraine is spilling over into NATO territory.
NATO fighter jets were scrambled in response to the incident, Nauseda said on social media. The jets were unable to identify the object because of cloudy weather and did not attempt to shoot it down.
"Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the eastern flank of NATO and EU," the Lithuanian president said.
The object later disappeared from radar, possibly after exploding, and local officials investigated what appeared to be drone debris near the village of Juodzionys in northern Lithuania . There were no casualties.
Heorhii Tykhyi, spokesperson for the Ukrainian Foreign Ministry, said in a statement on social media that the incident may have been caused by Russian electronic warfare diverting Ukrainian drones from their intended targets.
"We apologize for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused," Tykhyi said.
"We sincerely thank Lithuania, our ally, for supporting Ukraine in countering Russian aggression, which is the root cause of the security threats in our region," he added.
Lithuanian Defense Minister Robertas Kaunas said the drone flew in from Poland, but the Polish Defense Ministry said its radar did not confirm the object crossing the border, according to Reuters.
There have been several similar incursions along NATO’s eastern flank in recent months. The previous day, Romanian fighter jets on Oct. 17 shot down two drones in Romanian national airspace.
The two drones were jet-powered, belonging to the Geran family of Shahed-style attack drones frequently used by Russia to attack targets in Ukraine, according to Romania's Defense Ministry. The ministry did not specify which nation the drones belonged to.
Earlier on Oct. 18, Lithuanian authorities thwarted an attempted arson attack on a company storing Starlink satellite communications equipment overnight, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said.
An investigation is underway to identify the perpetrator, and Sinkevicius said he believed Russian actors commissioned the attack.
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said both these security incidents represent "a direct consequence of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and its wider repercussions for European security."
"Hybrid attacks, sabotage, and airspace incursions threaten critical infrastructure, spread fear, and seek to undermine European support for Ukraine," he added.

title: News from occupied Ukraine: 11 Ukrainians, including 96-year-old woman, evacuated from Russian occupation
description:
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.

Key news as of Oct. 17:

 * Eleven Ukrainians, including 96-year-old woman, return from Russian-occupied territories, ombudsman says
 * Russia sends terrorism case against 6 teenagers in occupied Luhansk Oblast to court
 * Ukrainian troops struck Russian drone sites, ammunition depots in occupied
content:
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.
Eleven Ukrainian citizens have returned to Ukrainian-controlled territory from Russian-occupied areas, including a 96-year-old woman and her son, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 16.
One of those evacuated was a man who had remained in occupied Luhansk after his wife died in 2018. His relatives had already left and were waiting for him in Ukrainian-controlled territory, but he had struggled to leave his home. After suffering three heart attacks and developing problems with blood pressure and mobility, he needed specialized transport to make the journey, Lubinets said.
Another case involved a 96-year-old woman and her son from the Russian-occupied village of Tavriiske in Kherson Oblast . The son had been caring for his mother when he was wounded in a Russian air attack in September. He sustained severe injuries, lost an eye, and was hospitalized.
Both needed assistance to return to Ukrainian-controlled territory, as the son was recovering from his injuries and his elderly mother could not travel independently. They returned together on Oct. 15, according to Lubinets.
Separately, Save Ukraine, a Ukrainian humanitarian NGO, said on Oct. 11 that 33 children were returned to Ukraine from the Russian-occupied territories over the past week.
The Volyn humanitarian corridor in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn Oblast is usually used for such evacuations, as it is the only working checkpoint between Ukraine and Belarus . There are currently no functioning checkpoints between Ukraine and Russia.
Given that the territory of Belarus was used by Russia to launch its full-scale invasion, the area around the crossing is heavily fortified with mines and anti-tank hedgehogs.
The last direct route from Russia to Ukraine through a checkpoint in Sumy Oblast was closed in August 2024 amid escalating Russian attacks in the oblast.
The fate of thousands of Ukrainians currently in captivity, as well as those living under occupation , remains uncertain. Between 3.5 million and 5 million Ukrainians remain in Russian-occupied territories and in Russia itself, according to an estimate cited by Lubinets in July.
Many Ukrainians cannot leave for various reasons, such as age, illness, disability, financial constraints, family responsibilities, and the threat of property expropriation by the occupation authorities.
Russian occupation authorities have sent a criminal case against six teenagers accused of carrying out arson attacks on infrastructure in occupied Luhansk Oblast to court, Russia's Investigative Committee branch in the occupied region claimed on Oct. 6.
According to the statement on Telegram, the teenagers allegedly carried out 20 arson attacks between May and September 2025, targeting electrical substations, gas infrastructure, mobile phone towers, and vehicles in the occupied town of Sverdlovsk and its surrounding area.
The alleged damage exceeded 2.5 million rubles ($32,000), the agency said. The teenagers face charges including terrorism, incitement to commit a terrorist act, and intentional property destruction.
The claims cannot be independently verified.
The case comes amid broader repression in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories. The UN Human Rights Office said in a September 2025 report that Russian authorities have used arbitrary detention and criminal prosecutions against Ukrainian civilians, with frequent violations of procedural safeguards.
Ukraine's military struck Russian drone launch sites, military supply and ammunition depots, troop concentrations, and communications infrastructure in Russian-occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Crimea between Oct. 11 and Oct. 16, Ukraine's General Staff said.
Near the occupied city of Donetsk, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian site used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones overnight on Oct. 14. Military supply depots and Russian troop concentrations near several settlements were also targeted, according to the General Staff's Oct. 14 report .
Ukrainian forces struck a fuel and lubricants depot near Dovzhansk and an ammunition depot near Rubizhne on Oct. 12 and overnight into Oct. 13. Russian troop concentrations near Kuzemivka were also targeted, the General Staff said in its Oct. 13 report .
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian troop concentration near Naberezhne on Oct. 12 and overnight into Oct. 13. They also hit a concentration of personnel from the Russian military's Rubikon drone unit near Novokostiantynivka on Oct. 14 and overnight into Oct. 15, according to the General Staff's Oct. 13 and Oct. 15 reports .
Ukrainian forces struck four storage facilities for Russian attack drones near occupied Hvardiiske. Damage was confirmed in the General Staff's Oct. 15 report . On Oct. 15 and overnight into Oct. 16, Ukrainian forces also struck two telecommunications towers equipped with antenna systems near Olenivka, according to the General Staff's Oct. 16 report .
Coal mining equipment in Russian-occupied parts of Donbas has deteriorated by 80–90% after 12 years without modernization, Alexander Klimenko, chairman of the board of directors of the Rodina industrial group, said, according to the Russian-backed Luhansk Information Center on Oct. 15.
Rodina, an investor in the coal industry in occupied Luhansk Oblast, has purchased one of only two new mining complexes acquired in Russia this year, the company said. It did not specify where the equipment would be installed or when it would enter operation.
The admission comes amid a wider decline in the region's coal industry. Coal production in occupied Luhansk Oblast fell from 6.7 million metric tons in 2018 to 1.34 million metric tons in 2024, while 68 mines were undergoing liquidation as of July 2026, according to figures cited by Ukrainian media Realna Gazeta .
Donbas was historically central to Ukraine's coal industry, supplying fuel for thermal power plants and coking coal for steel production. The deterioration of mines threatens an industrial sector that once supported regional employment, steelmaking, and energy production.
The 80–90% wear estimate was provided by Rodina's chairman and was not independently verified. The Russian-backed report did not identify the mines assessed or explain how the figure was calculated.
While the humanitarian crisis in the Russian-occupied front-line city of Oleshky recently garnered media attention, all regions of occupied Ukraine face worsening humanitarian issues at the hands of Russia's occupation authorities, the Kyiv Independent reported on Oct. 15.
Across all occupied territories, civilians face failing water and electricity systems, shortages of qualified doctors, deteriorating municipal services, and mass depopulation, while specific problems differ from one occupied region to another.
Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation, told the Kyiv Independent that the problems are driven by the failure of Russian occupation authorities to maintain basic services, as well as wartime destruction, proximity to the front line, and a lack of qualified personnel.
Russia currently occupies all of Crimea, 99% of Luhansk Oblast, 73% of Donetsk Oblast, 65% of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, and 57% of Kherson Oblast, according to geolocation estimates from the open-source intelligence project DeepState . Crimea, as well as parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, have been under occupation since 2014, while parts of Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts have been under occupation since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.

title: Ukraine war latest: St. Petersburg slammed by drones in mass Ukrainian attack
description:
Key developments on Oct. 17-18

 * Massive Ukrainian drone attack hits oil facility, bridge, and data center in St. Petersburg
 * US resumes intel sharing on Russian missile launches with Ukraine, Zelensky says
 * Ukraine hits Russian drone manufacturing plant in Rostov Oblast
 * 'Planned operation' — Zelensky confirms Ukraine's Starlink access not fully restored
 * Russia launches 'one of its largest attacks' on Ukraine's energy grid

Ukrainian forces struck an oil terminal, a data center, and
content:
Ukrainian forces struck an oil terminal, a data center, and a bridge in a large-scale overnight attack on St. Petersburg on Oct. 18, Russian officials and media reported.
Ukrainian drones hit the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal and a data center belonging to Russia's largest social media platform VK, formerly known as VKontakte .
VK confirmed that a drone had attacked its data center, saying its services remained operational. However, users reported disruptions across the social network and its affiliated platforms, according to Downdetector, a service that tracks online outages.
Russian e-commerce giant Ozon reported a drone attack on one of its logistics centers.
Ozon said some orders may be canceled as deliveries are rerouted to other logistics centers. The company is one of Russia's largest e-commerce platforms and a major rival of Wildberries, often dubbed "Russia's Amazon."
Aleksandr Drozdenko, governor of Leningrad Oblast, said 127 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the region. Drone debris damaged four cars in a parking lot, while fires were reported at several locations.
St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed the attack, reporting fires at the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky District. According to Beglov, one person was killed and five others injured, while 12 apartment buildings and two houses were damaged.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the targets or the extent of the damage at the time of publication.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ reported that the "massive" drone attack began at 2:50 a.m. local time.
Eyewitness footage shared by St. Petersburg residents appeared to show Ukrainian drones flying over the city as Russian air defense systems operated.
Large explosions lit up the night sky in the city of 5.6 million people, located 850 kilometers (530 miles) north of the Ukrainian border.
Numerous videos appeared to show the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal engulfed in flames. Located in the city's port, the facility is one of Russia's largest fuel storage and export facilities.
It receives and ships petroleum products by river, rail, and road, with a reported annual throughput of 12.5 million tons.
The United States has resumed sharing intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missiles with Ukraine after a pause lasting several days, President Volodymyr Zelensky told NBC News' "Meet the Press" in an interview published on Oct. 18.
"Only the United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky said .
The U.S. provides Ukraine with intelligence to help its military detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats. Zelensky said the issue had since been resolved and thanked Washington for restoring intelligence sharing.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Now it works."
Zelensky also expressed hope that talks with the U.S. could take place next week, despite the ongoing difficulties between Kyiv and Washington.
"I'm very open to this, even with all the difficult circumstances," he said, estimating that a meeting could take place on Oct. 20-21.
The resumption of intelligence sharing follows a Russian missile attack on Kyiv on Oct. 12, when five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital, causing "massive explosions." Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
A senior Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent that Ukraine's military leadership contacted its U.S. counterparts after the strike to clarify what had happened.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either," the official said. "The Americans said they just didn't see (the launch)... That's a weak excuse."
Ukraine's General Staff reported on Oct. 17 that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian military drone manufacturing plant in Rostov Oblast the day before.
According to the report , the strike targeted a production and storage facility belonging to Roboavia, a company that develops and manufactures drones for the Russian military, near the settlement of Lenina in Rostov Oblast.
Among the drones it produces are the Sarych , which uses video and thermal imaging equipment for surveillance, and the Klin , a loitering munition designed to strike targets, according to Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
Roboavia is linked to Russia's Era Military Innovation Complex, a Defense Ministry project focused on developing military technology. The General Staff said the strike was intended to interfere with drone production and deliveries to Russian forces. The extent of the damage and its result on operations remains unconfirmed.
The military also reported that Ukrainian forces struck a logistics warehouse used by a Russian missile brigade near Latyshi in Bryansk Oblast on Oct. 12.
The Ukrainian military said the strikes were aimed at aimed at disrupting UAV production and supply to Russian forces.
Speed caps on Starlink operations in Ukraine remain in place, hindering efforts to counter Russian jet-powered drones, President Zelensky said on Oct. 17.
Ukraine first experienced malfunctions with Starshield terminals — the militarized version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system — on Oct. 14, when they began losing connectivity as they approached a certain speed.
While Ukraine reported that connectivity was restored by the next day, Zelensky now confirmed that a speed limit of 161 kilometers per hour remains in place.
"Some of our interceptor drones use Starlink to intercept the enemy's fast-moving jet-powered drones," Zelensky said.
But with the current speed cap, Ukrainian interceptor drones cannot down Russian jet-powered drones, the president said, adding that Ukraine "thankfully" also uses other anti-drone air defenses.
The disruptions also complicate other military operations, as some drones rely on Starlink to deliver food, water, and other equipment to soldiers in front-line positions, he added.
The unexpected throttling of Starlink systems sparked a debate about who made the decision, with media reports linking it to SpaceX owner Elon Musk or the White House.
The move came as Ukraine-U.S. ties plummeted with Trump concluding a diesel deal with Russia and publicly lambasting Zelensky.
The Ukrainian president confirmed that Kyiv received no warning about the restrictions and has been trying to clarify the issue with U.S. authorities and SpaceX.
Ukraine has either received no response from U.S. channels or has been told the problems stem from "technical issues," Zelensky said, dismissing that explanation.
He called the restrictions a "planned operation" targeting Ukraine, noting that the speed limits remain in effect in Ukraine but not in EU countries.
Kyiv sent several vehicles equipped with its Starlink devices to the EU for testing, where they exceeded the speed limit in place in Ukraine, he explained. The president added that European partners are already working on a possible alternative to Starlink.
Russian attacks against Ukraine killed seven people and injured around 90 over the past day, regional authorities said on Oct. 17, with the country reporting one of the heaviest Russian attacks against energy infrastructure so far.
Ukrainian forces downed 289 out of the 332 drones, including jet-powered attack drones, launched by Russia overnight, the Air Force reported . Russian drones and ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M or the North Korean KN-23 model struck 22 different locations, and debris fell in three areas, according to the statement.
The attacks came as Russia continued its campaign against Ukraine's energy grid ahead of winter. Attacks on energy facilities across the country overnight and on the morning of Oct. 17 left some homes without power, the Energy Ministry said .
President Zelensky described Russia's latest attack as "one of the largest strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure." Russian forces targeted more than 15 key power generation and transmission facilities across Ukraine, he said.
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelensky said on social media, calling on Washington to pressure Moscow through a "sanctions blackout."
"Financial rewards for (Russian President Vladimir) Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground."

title: 'A great deal depends on America's position' — Zelensky holds call with Trump's peace envoys as US pivots to Moscow's side
description: According to the president, the U.S. and Ukraine are in "constant communication" and are preparing their "next steps in diplomacy."
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky held a phone conversation on Oct. 18 with U.S. President Donald Trump's special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, who have been tasked with leading peace talks between Kyiv and Moscow.
The call comes as Ukraine faces severe challenges in its relationship with Washington, once its strongest partner in defense against Russia's full-scale invasion. But in recent days, Trump has waived sanctions on Russia , demanded Ukraine halt attacks on oil refineries , and reportedly ordered restrictions on Ukrainian forces' access to vital Starlink services on the front lines.
Zelensky said his conversation with Kushner and Witkoff on Oct. 18 focused mainly on the results of their teams' latest diplomatic talks in Miami.
According to the president, the U.S. and Ukraine are in "constant communication" and are preparing their "next steps in diplomacy."
"We are constantly informing our partners about the real situation with the ongoing Russian shelling, which does not stop for a minute, and the issue of air defense," Zelensky said.
"A great deal depends on America's position here. Ukraine remains ready to work constructively, honestly, and for real results."
Later in his evening address on Oct. 18, Zelensky said the call also included discussion of Patriot air defense systems, critical for intercepting Russian ballistic missiles.
In an interview with NBC's "Meet the Press" published Oct. 18, Zelensky said he hoped Ukraine would be able to hold talks with the U.S. as early as next week. He also said Washington had resumed sharing intelligenc e with Kyiv regarding Russian missile launches.
The pause in missile warnings was just one of multiple blows to U.S. support for Ukraine the White House has dealt in the days since Trump abruptly announced a plan to purchase diesel from Russia to offset domestic fuel prices.
Trump on Oct. 9 said he'd made a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin , shocking not only Ukraine but also many U.S. lawmakers from both parties. When questioned about helping fund Russia's ongoing war, Trump doubled down, saying Zelensky was making problems for the world by attacking refineries and that Ukraine should get a new president.
Then, on Oct. 11, Trump unilaterally declared an "energy ceasefire" between Ukraine and Russia. The truce appeared to be a surprise to both Kyiv and the Kremlin, but Zelensky said Ukraine was prepared to suspend attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow stopped battering Ukraine's power grid.
The Kyiv Independent reported on Oct. 12 that the Trump administration had threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials in a push to protect Russian oil refineries. The U.S. warned it would suspend intelligence sharing and weapons support through NATO's PURL program if Ukraine refused to comply.
While Ukraine paused strikes on refineries, Russia made no such concessions. Zelensky revealed on Oct. 18 that Russia has attacked Ukrainian oil and gas facilities 76 times since Trump's energy ceasefire announcement the week before.
Trump has refused to blame Russia for breaking the truce, and Kyiv has resumed strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Troubles mounted for Ukraine on Oct. 14, when the sudden introduction of a speed cap on Starlink systems disrupted multiple battlefield operations, including mid-range drone strikes and air defense.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk reportedly proposed the restriction to Trump, who agreed with the plan — though both have dodged responsibility for the move.
Zelensky has confirmed that the speed limit remains in place, hindering the efficacy of Ukraine's middle-strike campaign and the ability of interceptors to stop Russian high-speed jet drones.
A week after announcing the diesel deal with Putin, Trump issued a broad waiver of sanctions against Moscow under the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on Oct. 16.
Despite the devastating turn in U.S. policy, Zelensky said on Oct. 18 that Ukraine was still working with Washington to bring about an end to the war.
"Peace comes only through strength and cooperation built on trust," the president said.
