"We are doing everything on our part to make this happen, and to ensure that America's position is strong and helps bring peace closer."

title: US resumes intel sharing on Russian missile launches with Ukraine, Zelensky says
description: "We are very thankful for this... Now it works," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
content:
The United States has resumed sharing intelligence about incoming Russian ballistic missiles with Ukraine after a pause lasting several days, President Volodymyr Zelensky told NBC News' "Meet the Press" in an interview published on Oct. 18.
"Only the United States has this unique intelligence to tell our side when Russia uses ballistic missiles. We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky said .
The U.S. provides Ukraine with intelligence to help its military detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats. Zelensky said the issue had since been resolved and thanked Washington for restoring intelligence sharing.
"We are very thankful for this," he said. "Now it works."
At the same time, he said Ukraine was still experiencing an ongoing speed restriction on its use of Starshield — the militarized version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system
Asked whether U.S. President Donald Trump or SpaceX CEO Elon Musk had personally ordered the restrictions, Zelensky said he did not know but believed "both" were involved. He added that if Trump decided to lift the restrictions, the service would return to its previous state.
The resumption of intelligence sharing follows a Russian missile attack on Kyiv on Oct. 12, when five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital, causing "massive explosions." Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
A senior Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent that Ukraine's military leadership contacted its U.S. counterparts after the strike to clarify what had happened.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either," the official said. "The Americans said they just didn't see (the launch)... That's a weak excuse."
The incident came amid broader tensions over U.S. support for Ukraine. The Kyiv Independent earlier learned that the Trump administration had threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials in a push to protect Russian oil refineries.
Zelensky also told NBC that if thet U.S. chooses to support Russia over Kyiv, consequences would be dire — for both the Ukraine and the United States.
Such a move would be a "historic mistake" for Washington, Zelensky said. A U.S-Russia alliance would also destroy Ukraine's chances of defending itself against the full-scale invasion.
"“If these two countries will be together ... we will not prevail, and we will not be able to stand," Zelensky warned.
But the president also expressed hope that talks with the U.S. could take place next week, despite the ongoing difficulties between Kyiv and Washington.
"I'm very open to this, even with all the difficult circumstances," he said, estimating that a meeting could take place on Oct. 20-21.
Zelensky also denounced Kremlin narratives — sometimes repeated by Trump — that he opposes democratic elections in Ukraine.
If the U.S. and Russia believe Ukraine must hold elections during wartime, Moscow must grant Kyiv an unconditional ceasefire for 60 days, he said. The president said he made it clear that a minimum of 60 days was necessary for Ukraine to change its laws, prepare election infrastructure, and guarantee soldiers the opportunity to vote.
"If you think that I don't want elections, it's not true, and it's not fair," he said.
Zelensky said he would run for office again if elections were held during wartime, citing a responsibility to continue defending his country.

title: Lithuania foils arson attack on Starlink equipment, suspects Russian involvement
description: The attackers attempted to set fire to satellite antennas and a control unit, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said.
content:
Lithuanian authorities thwarted an attempted arson attack on a company storing Starlink satellite communications equipment overnight on Oct. 18, Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius said.
The attackers attempted to set fire to satellite antennas and a control unit. Investigators found incendiary liquids and containers with capacities ranging from three to 10 liters at the scene, Sinkevicius told Lithuania's national broadcaster LRT Radio .
"The authorities had warned the company of possible attacks, security had been stepped up, and the attempt failed," he later wrote in a Facebook post.
Sinkevicius described the incident as part of Russia's hybrid warfare campaign, pointing to similar suspected sabotage incidents across Europe , including in Poland and Bulgaria.
"We will learn more about who ordered it, how everything happened, and who was behind it. It is likely that it is already clear who commissioned it — the Russian side," he added.
A similar incident was reported in Poland on Sept. 23, when a fire broke out at a Starlink ground station in what may have been an attempt to disrupt its operations.
The suspected sabotage attempt in Lithuania came as a drone crashed and exploded in the country's north near the Latvian border on Oct. 18, damaging a passing car, Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center, told LRT Radio.
Authorities have yet to determine whether the drone carried explosives or what caused the blast, Sinkevicius told the broadcaster.
It remains unclear who the drone belonged to. Ukraine launched a large-scale attack on the Russian city of St. Petersburg overnight on Oct. 18, and similar drone incidents in the Baltic states have occurred during Ukrainian attacks on the city.
Sinkevicius said Lithuania's warning system had been activated but had not functioned perfectly, with reports received only from the Kaunas district.
The prime minister said he would convene the National Security Commission on Oct. 19 to discuss both incidents.

title: Russian drones hit western Ukraine as nationwide attacks kill 10, injure 73
description: Russian strikes hit 20 locations, while falling debris was reported at four other sites.
content:
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least 10 civilians and injured 73 others over the past day, regional authorities reported on Oct. 18.
Russia launched an Iskander-M ballistic missile, 180 Shahed drones, including 26 jet-powered Shaheds, as well as S-8000 and Banderol loitering munitions, also known as Dan-T, and Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force reported.
Ukrainian forces intercepted 152 drones, including 16 jet-powered drones. Russian strikes hit 20 locations, while falling debris was reported at four other sites.
Three western Ukrainian oblasts came under Russian attack on the morning of Oct. 18, continuing Moscow's recent pattern of targeting critical infrastructure across multiple regions.
In Volyn Oblast, in northwestern Ukraine, Russian drones attacked an industrial facility in the town of Manevychi, sparking a large fire, acting regional Governor Roman Romaniuk said .
Warehouses and production facilities caught fire, with the blaze covering a large area and generating heavy smoke. No casualties or injuries had been reported as of the latest update.
The attack marked the second strike on an industrial facility in Manevychi in three days. An earlier Russian attack on the Agrofrukt LTD facility on Oct. 16 killed one person and injured eight others, Manevychi Mayor Oleksandr Havryliuk said .
In western Ternopil Oblast, Russian drones attacked an energy infrastructure facility near the settlement of Staryi Vyshnivets, Governor Taras Pastukh said . The strike left some consumers without electricity. No casualties had been reported at the time of his statement.
Russian forces also launched a large-scale drone attack on Rivne, in northwestern Ukraine, targeting civilian infrastructure, regional Governor Oleksandr Koval said . The strikes sparked fires at the impact sites. No casualties had been reported as of the latest update.
In Odesa, Russian forces struck the roof of a multistory residential building on the morning of Oct. 18, injuring two people, including a 14-year-old girl, regional Governor Oleh Kiper said .
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed seven people and injured 14 others, Governor Vadym Filashkin said . Most of the casualties were reported in Sloviansk, where multiple houses were damaged.
Russian attacks in Kherson Oblast injured 32 people, including one child, regional Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said . Russian forces targeted critical infrastructure, social infrastructure, and residential areas across the region.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured four others, regional Governor Ivan Fedorov said . Russian forces launched 10 missiles at the city of Zaporizhzhia. Over the past 24 hours, they carried out 808 strikes on 53 settlements across the region.
In Sumy Oblast, Russian attacks killed two people and injured five over the past 24 hours, according to the regional military administration. Russian forces carried out nearly 50 attacks across the region, damaging or destroying civilian infrastructure.
In Kharkiv Oblast, 12 people were injured in Russian attacks, regional Governor Oleh Syniehubov said . Russian forces struck Kharkiv and nine other settlements using ballistic missiles, drones, glide bombs, known as KABs, and a multiple-launch rocket system.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, three people were injured in Russian attacks, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said . Russian forces attacked three districts more than 10 times using drones and artillery.
Russian forces again targeted critical infrastructure in the city of Dnipro on the morning of Oct. 18. Information about possible casualties was still being clarified, Hanzha said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, one person was injured when a Russian Geran drone struck a residential yard, regional Governor Viacheslav Chaus said .

title: Zelensky reveals how many Russian attacks have followed Trump's energy ceasefire
description: "Tens of thousands of families are without power," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
content:
Russia has attacked Ukrainian energy and oil and gas facilities 76 times since U.S. President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between the two countries, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 18.
The attacks have continued despite Trump's announcement, as the U.S. president has so far avoided confronting Russian President Vladimir Putin over the violations while pressuring Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities, claiming they are driving up global oil prices.
"Tens of thousands of families are without power," Zelensky said .
"The Russians are trying to cause a blackout... And the U.S. needs to see that Russia is not making any concessions in response to the lifting of sanctions or agreements."
"It is Russia that must face pressure to give peace a chance," he added.
Trump unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11 without specifying its scope, taking Ukrainian officials by surprise.
Zelensky has said Ukraine is ready to adhere to a comprehensive energy truce, provided Russia does the same. He also noted that Ukrainian forces had refrained from attacking Russian refineries for several consecutive days following Trump's announcement.
Russian attacks on Ukraine's power grid have nevertheless continued, while the Kremlin has declined to make any commitments to the proposed truce.
Despite the continued strikes, Trump has declined to blame Moscow for violating the ceasefire while increasing pressure on Kyiv. His administration has threatened to cut off intelligence sharing and military aid unless Ukraine halts its attacks.
Ukraine has targeted Russian energy facilities and export infrastructure to disrupt a key source of funding for Moscow's war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has attacked Ukrainian power plants and substations, seeking to deprive civilians of electricity and heating.
The Kremlin said Oct. 14 the scope of Trump's energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine had not been specified, as Russian attacks on Ukraine's power grid continued.

title: Hungary ready to allow Ukrainian grain transit to Western Europe, prime minister says
description: "If it just passes through the country, then obviously there is no obstacle to it," Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar said.
content:
Hungary is ready to allow Ukrainian grain to transit through its territory to Western Europe, Prime Minister Peter Magyar told Hungarian TV channel RTL in an interview published Oct. 17.
The announcement followed a request from President Volodymyr Zelensky at an EU summit in Brussels on Oct. 16, as Kyiv sought to secure European support amid deteriorating ties with the U.S.
Zelensky said grain shipments across the Black Sea were currently not possible due to Russian attacks and urged Poland, Romania, Slovakia, and Hungary to allow Ukrainian grain to transit through their territory to Western countries, as they had done at the beginning of Russia's full-scale invasion.
During their first bilateral meeting, Zelensky also told Magyar that transporting Ukrainian grain to Western Europe in sealed rail cars would be a great help.
"I said that if it just passes through the country, then obviously there is no obstacle to it," Magyar said.
The Hungarian prime minister said a well-established transit procedure had been in place three to four years earlier, but was later discontinued.
Under the previous government led by Viktor Orban, Hungary declared a state of emergency and introduced a ban on Ukrainian agricultural products.
Concerns about the strength of Ukraine's agricultural sector have also complicated its relations with other European countries. Poland is blocking progress on one part of Ukraine's EU membership talks over concerns that Ukraine's accession would hurt Polish farmers.
The meeting between Zelensky and Magyar took place the same week the Ukrainian president signed a law on the educational rights of Ukraine's national minorities, a step Hungary had demanded before allowing Kyiv's EU accession talks to proceed.
"We see the Ukrainian parliament's adoption of the minority education law and the immediate start of its implementation as a first step towards rebuilding mutual trust," Magyar said after the meeting.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,565,060 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 2,090 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,565,060 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 18.
The number includes 2,090 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,416 tanks, 25,561 armored combat vehicles, 164,246 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,293 artillery systems, 2,224 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,711 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,968 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Marco Rubio says Trump's Russian oil sanctions waiver is a '60-day pause,' denies restricting Starlink access
description: "I think the President wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," said Rubio.
content:
Speaking with reporters on Oct. 18, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio detailed U.S. President Donald Trump waiving sanctions on the sale of Russian oil and addressed issues surrounding Ukraine's access to Starlink services.
When asked to respond to criticisms of Trump waiving sanctions that restrict the sale of Russian oil , Rubio said the waiver was a temporary measure to study the policy's impact on the global economy.
"I think the President wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyze what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the U.S. economy," said Rubio.
Noting high energy prices around the world as a result of the U.S's war with Iran and the global need for oil, Rubio said that "we need that period of time to sort of study all this and figure out what the right combination is."
The Secretary's comments come following widespread outcries that Trump's move will create a windfall for Moscow, helping it continue attacking and killing Ukrainians.
"Unfortunately, I don't think this is a way to stop (Russian President Vladimir) Putin. On the contrary, he feels joy that he has such support," President Volodymyr Zelensky said about Trump's actions amid a falling out between the two leaders .
Rubio also addressed rumors that the U.S. had a role in limiting Ukrainian access to vital Starlink systems.
"No one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet or slow down speed so that certain drones couldn’t use it," Rubio said.
Ukraine relies heavily on Starlink, a satellite internet network operated by SpaceX, for battlefield communications and drone operations, including its campaign against Russian forces and logistics, and interceptor drones used against Russian long-range attack drones.
Ukraine first experienced malfunctions with Starlink systems on Oct. 14, when they began losing connectivity as they approached a certain speed.
While Ukraine reported that connectivity was restored by the next day, Zelensky claimed that a speed limit of 161 kilometers per hour remains in place.
"Some of our interceptor drones use Starlink to intercept the enemy's fast-moving jet-powered drones," Zelensky said.
Multiple media reports have alleged that the issues with Starlink stem from U.S. leadership.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk approached U.S. President Donald Trump with the idea of restricting Starlink speeds for Ukrainian forces, the Telegraph reported on Oct. 16, citing four sources familiar with the matter.
Conflicting reports about the reason for the cutoff — and who was responsible — have left Ukraine with questions even after Starlink service stabilized on the front lines.
"I don’t know what their theory is, but nothing to do with the White House," said Rubio. "I saw a report on that the other day. It’s just categorically false."
When asked to respond to Zelensky's comments, Rubio pushed back.
"I don’t know what Zelenskyy said," said Rubio. "I’m not sure Zelenskyy knows what he’s talking about, but it wasn’t deliberate. We have nothing to do with that."

title: Massive Ukrainian drone attack hit oil facility, bridge, and data center in St. Petersburg
description: St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed the attack, reporting fires at the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky District.
content:
Editor's note: This story has been updated to include additional details.
Ukrainian forces struck an oil terminal, a data center, and a bridge in a large-scale overnight attack on St. Petersburg on Oct. 18, Russian officials and media reported.
Ukrainian drones hit the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal and a data center belonging to Russia's largest social media platform VK, formerly known as VKontakte .
VK confirmed that a drone had attacked its data center, saying its services remained operational. However, users reported disruptions across the social network and its affiliated platforms, according to Downdetector, a service that tracks online outages.
Russian e-commerce giant Ozon reported a drone attack on one of its logistics centers.
"We evacuated all employees, and no one was injured. A fire broke out, and emergency services are working at the scene," the company wrote on Telegram.
Ozon said some orders may be canceled as deliveries are rerouted to other logistics centers. The company is one of Russia's largest e-commerce platforms and a major rival of Wildberries, often dubbed "Russia's Amazon."
Aleksandr Drozdenko, governor of Leningrad Oblast, said 127 Ukrainian drones were shot down over the region. Drone debris damaged four cars in a parking lot, while fires were reported at several locations.
St. Petersburg Governor Alexander Beglov confirmed the attack, reporting fires at the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal, the Ruchyi oil depot, and industrial warehouses in the Kolpinsky District. According to Beglov, one person was killed and five others injured, while 12 apartment buildings and two houses were damaged.
Russian state media later reported that the number of injured has risen to 10 people, citing the Leningrad Oblast Health Committee.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the targets or the extent of the damage at the time of publication.
Ukrainian monitoring channels Exilenova+ and Supernova+ reported that the "massive" drone attack began at 2:50 a.m. local time.
Eyewitness footage shared by St. Petersburg residents appeared to show Ukrainian drones flying over the city as Russian air defense systems operated.
Large explosions lit up the night sky in the city of 5.6 million people, located 850 kilometers (530 miles) north of the Ukrainian border.
Numerous videos appeared to show the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal engulfed in flames. Located in the city's port, the facility is one of Russia's largest fuel storage and export facilities.
It receives and ships petroleum products by river, rail, and road, with a reported annual throughput of 12.5 million tons.
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point claimed that its FP-1 attack drone was used to strike the terminal.
The strike comes after U.S. President Donald Trump's attempted energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine failed to prevent attacks on energy infrastructure.
Russian independent media outlet Astra also reported that a power substation was hit during the attack. Blackouts and low water pressure were reported in the region, and an apartment building was damaged, according to the outlet.
The strike on VKontakte's data center marks the latest attack on Russian internet infrastructure. Ukrainian forces have struck multiple Yandex data centers in recent weeks, following President Volodymyr Zelensky's promise that Ukraine would "respond in kind" to Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted St. Petersburg, Russia's second-largest city, several times during the full-scale war. On July 4, Ukrainian forces struck and damaged the St. Petersburg Oil Terminal in an overnight attack.
Asked about Ukraine's latest attacks on St. Petersburg, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov sought to downplay their impact, telling reporters that Ukrainian strikes on Russia were incapable of "changing the course of events."
As Moscow intensifies its attacks on Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure, Kyiv has continued to hit sites deep in Russia . Swarm attacks by Ukrainian drones have disrupted air traffic around Moscow and damaged data centers in the capital region in recent days.

title: Kromberg and Schubert electrical wiring plant in Lutsk halts operations following Russian attack
description: The Lutsk facility in northwestern Ukraine, which manufactures wiring systems for BMW, Audi, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, and Skoda vehicles, was attacked by Russian drones on Oct. 16.
content:
A Kromberg & Schubert electrical wiring plant in the city of Lutsk halted operations due to Russian attacks on the facility, the company announced on Oct. 17.
"The business has stopped!" said the company's Ukrainian division in a social media post. "Our absolute priority is the safety, life and health of each of the employees. We are currently assessing the current circumstances and coordinating all further steps."
The Lutsk facility in northwestern Ukraine, which manufactures wiring systems for BMW, Audi, Mercedes-Benz, Porsche, and Skoda vehicles, was attacked by Russian drones on Oct. 16.
Kromberg & Schubert, a German-owned corporation, established its Ukrainian division in 2005 and had 5,500 workers at its Lutsk plant as of May 2025, according to its website .
The company said it will notify employees when they can return to work, though it did not give an estimate of how long that may take.
Though far from the front lines, Lutsk has been a target for Russian strikes since the full-scale invasion began in 2022.
On Oct. 14, Russian drones killed six people and injured 10 others in Lutsk. A large-scale fire broke out in the 'Eurogroup' warehouse as a result of the Russian attack, killing five people at the scene and injuring a sixth person so severely that they succumbed in hospital, regional governor Roman Romaniuk said .
Throughout the war, Moscow has struck foreign-owned businesses operating in Ukraine. On Sept. 3, a Coca-Cola facility outside of Kyiv was damaged in Russian attacks, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky claimed was "a clear Russian signal to America."

title: Romanian F-16s down two jet-powered drones after airspace incursion
description: The two drones were jet-powered, belonging to the Geran-family of attack drones frequently used by Russia to attack targets in Ukraine, according to Romania's Defense Ministry. The Ministry did not specify which nation the drones belonged to.
content:
Two Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones flying in Romanian national airspace, the country's Defense Ministry announced on Oct. 17.
The two drones were jet-powered, belonging to the Geran-family of attack drones frequently used by Russia to attack targets in Ukraine, according to Romania's Defense Ministry. The Ministry did not specify which nation the drones belonged to.
Initially, Romania's radar system detected a group of aerial targets flying around 120 kilometers (75 miles) east of Snake Island in the Black Sea . Romania then scrambled two F-16 fighter jets from its Borcea Air Base at 5:43 p.m. local time.
Two drones were shot down between 6:01 p.m. and 6:05 p.m. local time over Romanian national waters. The drones spent a total of five minutes maneuvering in the nation's airspace.
Geran drones are among some of the latest drones deployed by Russian forces in attacks on Ukraine. They are particularly difficult to engage , flying significantly higher and faster than any of Russia's older drone models, with a maximum speed of 600 km/h (370 mph).
Amid Ukraine's shortage of air-to-air missiles, F-16 jets are increasingly being used to shoot down Geran drones. Ukrainian warplanes are responsible for the downing of about 55-60% of all jet-powered drones launched by Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists on Oct. 17.
In recent months, Russian drones have flown into Romanian airspace multiple times, raising tension between Moscow and the NATO member state.
On Oct. 15, seven sailors were reported missing from one of two tanker ships that caught fire in Romania's Black Sea following drone incursions into the country's airspace.
Ten days prior, a cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast after a Russian drone strike , killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
On Sept. 24, suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova overnight amid a sustained mass drone and missile attack on Ukraine.

title: Zelensky warns Russia may expand missile threats from Belarus against western Ukraine
description: Ukraine's State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko has separately reported that equipment based in Belarus helps relay or amplify signals for Russian Shahed and Geran drones heading toward western Ukraine and Poland's border region.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned Russia may use Belarus to intensify missile and drone attacks on western Ukraine, putting the region under a growing threat.
Speaking to journalists on Oct. 17 , Zelensky said Russia was already using drone signal repeaters in Belarus and that he believed Russian President Vladimir Putin needed the support of Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko to station additional ballistic missiles in the country.
“But this is a direct involvement of Belarus in this war, and [that] is, in my opinion, very dangerous. And, of course, for Belarus too,” Zelensky said.
Ukraine's State Border Guard Service spokesperson Andrii Demchenko has separately reported that equipment based in Belarus helps relay or amplify signals for Russian Shahed and Geran drones heading toward western Ukraine and Poland's border region.
In September, Ukraine's military intelligence chief Oleh Ivashchenko said that units of Russia's 101st Missile Brigade, equipped with the Oreshnik intermediate-range ballistic missile system, had been deployed to Belarus.
A series of Russian attacks has struck cities and communities across western Ukraine in recent days, including in Volyn, Rivne and Lviv oblasts, resulting in deaths and injuries, damaged infrastructure and widespread power outages .
Zelensky also said Ukraine would increase air defenses across the country, distribute them according to the level of threat, and expand production of defensive turrets.

title: Ukraine hits Russian drone manufacturing plant in Rostov Oblast
description: Among the drones it produces are the Sarych, which uses video and thermal imaging equipment for surveillance, and the Klin, a loitering munition designed to strike targets, according to Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
content:
Ukraine's General Staff reported on Oct. 17 that Ukrainian forces struck a Russian military drone manufacturing plant in Rostov Oblast the day before.
According to the report , the strike targeted a production and storage facility belonging to Roboavia, a company that develops and manufactures drones for the Russian military, near the settlement of Lenina in Rostov Oblast.
Among the drones it produces are the Sarych, which uses video and thermal imaging equipment for surveillance, and the Klin , a loitering munition designed to strike targets, according to Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
Roboavia is linked to Russia's Era Military Innovation Complex, a Defense Ministry project focused on developing military technology. The General Staff said the strike was intended to interfere with drone production and deliveries to Russian forces. The extent of the damage and its result on operations remains unconfirmed.
The military also reported that Ukrainian forces struck a logistics warehouse used by a Russian missile brigade near Latyshi in Bryansk Oblast on Oct. 12.
The Ukrainian military said the strikes were aimed at aimed at disrupting UAV production and supply to Russian forces.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted facilities supporting Russia's war effort, including defense manufacturing plants and military supply infrastructure.

title: Russian troops executed Ukrainian POWs in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, military says
description: The Russian soldiers are believed to belong to the 38th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade, which is operating in the area. Kravchuk alleged that orders of this nature within the brigade are issued at the initiative of its commander, Colonel Valery Kazak.
content:
Russian forces are accused of executing Ukrainian prisoners of war (POWs) on the Huliaipole front in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, a Ukrainian military spokesperson told Ukrainska Pravda on Oct. 17.
Ukrainian forces intercepted radio communications between Russian soldiers as the alleged executions took place, according to Maksym Kravchuk, spokesperson for Ukraine's Southern Forces Group.
Kravchuk said Russian troops received orders to kill wounded Ukrainian soldiers, including instructions to "take them out immediately." The Russian soldiers reportedly carried out the orders, killing what Ukrainian officials believe were two unarmed POWs.
The incident occurred several days before the allegations were made public, although the exact date and location of the reported executions have not been disclosed.
The Russian soldiers are believed to belong to the 38th Separate Motorized Rifle Brigade, which is operating in the area. Kravchuk alleged that orders of this nature within the brigade are issued at the initiative of its commander, Colonel Valery Kazak.
The Ukrainian military said the intercepted communications and other relevant materials had been handed over to law enforcement authorities.
The execution of prisoners of war is prohibited under the Geneva Conventions and constitutes a war crime.
Russian forces have previously been accused of executing Ukrainian POWs in the Huliaipole sector. In November 2025 , five Ukrainian soldiers were reportedly captured and executed near the village of Zelenyi Hai, according to the Ukrainian battlefield monitoring group DeepState. Ukraine's Prosecutor General's Office subsequently confirmed that five POWs had been shot by Russian forces.
According to figures released by Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets in August 2026, Russian forces have executed at least 345 Ukrainian soldiers who surrendered since the beginning of the full-scale invasion.

title: Russia may seek to get back immobilized assets through Ukraine's partners, Zelensky says
description: "Today, this is fully under Europe's control. That means (Russian assets) are safe for now," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
content:
Russia could try to reclaim some of its immobilized assets through Ukraine's partners, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed to reporters on Oct. 17, without naming specific countries.
"We have this information, but we have discussed the details with European partners. Today, this is fully under Europe's control. That means it is safe for now," Zelensky said.
During talks with European counterparts on Oct. 9, U.S. officials floated the idea of releasing some of the 200 billion euros ($227 billion) in Russian assets held in the EU to Washington as a bargaining chip in peace talks, according to media reports.
The proposal resurfaced as EU leaders gathered in Brussels for a summit on Oct. 15-16, where they firmly rejected handing the assets to the U.S.
Zelensky met with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever on the sidelines of the summit on Oct. 15. The talks apparently failed to yield a breakthrough on the fate of funds in Russian assets that have been immobilized by Euroclear under Belgian jurisdiction since 2022.
As part of Kyiv's broader push for Europe to use the Russian funds to support Ukraine, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described the direct use of the assets as "a fair approach" and said that "the aggressor must pay."
However, little progress has been made since four EU countries sought to revive the debate in August. The European Commission has been reluctant to put forward a concrete proposal until all 27 member states agree on how to proceed.

title: Over half of Russian jet-powered drones downed by Ukraine's aircraft, Zelensky says
description: Ukraine has secured contracts and assurances from partners on additional supplies of F-16 ammunition, Zelensky noted, adding that the current deliveries were at a "satisfactory level."
content:
Ukrainian warplanes are responsible for the downing of about 55-60% of all jet-powered drones launched by Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists on Oct. 17.
Efforts are underway to increase the supply of 20 mm rounds for Ukraine's F-16 fleet, Zelensky added.
The news follows reports that Ukraine's F-16s have been grappling with air-to-air missile shortages, hampering the Air Force's ability to counter the newer, faster drones attacking the energy grid .
Ukraine has secured contracts and assurances from partners on additional supplies of F-16 ammunition, the president noted, adding that the current deliveries were at a "satisfactory level."
According to the president, Ukraine is deploying new, cheaper missiles — both domestically produced and others to be supplied by partners — to counter Russian jet-powered drones.
Ukraine is also producing dozens of anti-drone turrets and aims to scale up production, Zelensky added.
At the same time, Ukrainian interceptor drones — another key tool in the counter-drone arsenal — are constrained by Starlink restrictions now in place in the country, according to the president.
While Ukraine is quickly developing and obtaining weapons to counter Russian drone attacks, anti-ballistic missile defenses remain its most critical gap.
"Yesterday... I spent the whole day, and also the day before, discussing possible European air defense packages, including PAC-2 and PAC-3 Patriot missiles," Zelensky said, referring to the talks he held at the EU summit in Brussels earlier this week.
"There will be news, there will be results," he said, without providing further details.

title: 'Putin feels joy' — Zelensky calls Trump's waiving of key Russia sanctions 'wrong'
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky said on oct. 17 U.S. President Donald Trump was "wrong" to further "block" sanctions against Russia, while expressing hope that he would do "everything possible" to stop the full-scale war.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 17 that U.S. President Donald Trump was "wrong" to further "block" sanctions against Russia, while expressing hope that the U.S. leader would do "everything possible" to stop the war.
Zelensky's comments came after Trump issued a broad waiver of sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on Oct. 16.
"Unfortunately, I don't think this is a way to stop (Russian President Vladimir) Putin. On the contrary, he feels joy that he has such support," Zelensky told reporters.
He described bipartisan support for the Russia sanction bill in September as "a major victory," calling the decision to "scrap" it "wrong."
The bill, which Trump signed weeks earlier, allows the U.S. president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five buyers of Russian oil and gas, among other measures. Trump said he would use these powers if necessary to help end Russia's war against Ukraine
Zelensky said it is likely that Washington will continue to ease sanctions on Moscow, adding that the diesel deal was "only the first step" and that further moves could follow.
"We very much hope, and I personally hope, that the U.S. president will do everything possible to make Putin stop the killing, stop attacks on our energy infrastructure, and end this war," he added. "But once again, this can't be achieved by restricting Ukraine's response to Russia for killing our people."
"This certainly does not stop the war," the president added.
Trump's move came amid growing U.S. pressure on Ukraine to halt the attacks on Russian oil refineries. Washington has reportedly threatened to cut intelligence sharing and weapons support, while blaming the strikes for rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by energy experts.

title: 'Planned operation' — Zelensky confirms Ukraine's Starlink access not fully restored
description: Zelensky called the restrictions a "planned operation" targeting Ukraine, noting that Starlink speed limits remain in effect in Ukraine but not in EU countries.
content:
Speed caps on Starlink operations in Ukraine remain in place, hindering efforts to counter Russian jet-powered drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 17.
Ukraine first experienced malfunctions with Starshield terminals — the militarized version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system — on Oct. 14, when they began losing connectivity as they approached a certain speed.
While Ukraine reported that connectivity was restored by the next day, Zelensky now confirmed that a speed limit of 161 kilometers per hour remains in place.
"Some of our interceptor drones use Starlink to intercept the enemy's fast-moving jet-powered drones," Zelensky said.
But with the current speed cap, Ukrainian interceptor drones cannot down Russian jet-powered drones, the president said, adding that Ukraine "thankfully" also uses other anti-drone air defenses.
The disruptions also complicate other military operations, as some drones rely on Starlink to deliver food, water, and other equipment to soldiers in front-line positions, he added.
The unexpected throttling of Starlink systems sparked a debate about who made the decision, with media reports linking it to SpaceX owner Elon Musk or the White House.
The move came as Ukraine-U.S. ties plummeted with U.S. President Donald Trump concluding a diesel deal with Russia and publicly lambasting Zelensky.
The Ukrainian president confirmed that Kyiv received no warning about the restrictions and has been trying to clarify the issue with U.S. authorities and SpaceX.
Ukraine has either received no response from U.S. channels or has been told the problems stem from "technical issues," Zelensky said, dismissing that explanation.
He called the restrictions a "planned operation" targeting Ukraine, noting that the speed limits remain in effect in Ukraine but not in EU countries.
Kyiv sent several vehicles equipped with its Starlink devices to the EU for testing, where they exceeded the speed limit in place in Ukraine, he explained. The president added that European partners are already working on a possible alternative to Starlink.

title: Russian Ryazan oil refinery halts operations of one main unit after drone attack, Reuters reports
description: Since President Volodymyr Zelensky announced the resumption of strikes  on Oct. 15, Kyiv has not reported any new attacks on Russian oil refineries or confirmed reports of such strikes.
content:
Russia's Ryazan oil refinery suspended operations at one of its main crude distillation units, CDU-6, following a drone attack on Oct. 15, Reuters reported a day later, citing unnamed industry sources.
The news comes amid a dispute between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil and energy infrastructure.
U.S. President Donald Trump has pressured Ukraine to halt the attacks , reportedly threatening to cut intelligence sharing and weapons support, while blaming the strikes for rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by energy experts.
After Trump unilaterally announced an "energy ceasefire" between Moscow and Kyiv on Oct. 11, Ukraine initially paused refinery strikes. However, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 15 that Kyiv had lifted the pause due to Moscow's continued attacks against Ukraine's energy grid.
The same unit of the Ryazan oil refinery had already been shut down following a drone strike in September. The refinery's three other primary crude distillation units — CDU-1, CDU-3, and CDU-4 — reportedly continue to operate.
The oil refinery has been targeted repeatedly in recent months. It was struck on Sept. 6 and May 15, with repairs after the May attack lasting until around mid-July. A further attack on July 29 halted operations for several weeks.
Since Zelensky announced the resumption of strikes earlier this week, Kyiv has not reported any new attacks on Russian oil refineries or confirmed reports of such strikes.
Throughout the week, Moscow continued its near-constant drone attacks on Ukraine and launched a large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv overnight on Oct. 13–14, damaging a residential neighborhood and targeting several energy facilities.
On Oct. 16, Russia launched one of its largest attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, targeting more than 15 key energy facilities across the country, Zelensky said. The attack came as Trump waived sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act.

title: Anger over Kyiv's winter preparations fuels calls for Mayor Klitschko to resign
description:
Local residents gathered on Oct. 17 in front of the city council to demand that Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko step down from the post he has occupied for over 12 years.

"Kyiv without Klitschko," hundreds of protesters chanted as they took to the streets in central Kyiv, according to Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground. The rally lasted over two hours.

Kyiv's failure to prepare for the coming winter amid Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, coupled with broader mismanagement, were the
content:
Local residents gathered on Oct. 17 in front of the city council to demand that Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko step down from the post he has occupied for over 12 years.
"Kyiv without Klitschko," hundreds of protesters chanted as they took to the streets in central Kyiv, according to Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground. The rally lasted over two hours.
Kyiv's failure to prepare for the coming winter amid Russian attacks on critical infrastructure, coupled with broader mismanagement, were the main factors that brought people to protest.
The protest comes as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure and Kyiv struggles to ensure reliable access to basic utilities and adequate shelter.
The cardboard signs read "Where are the shelters?" "Resign" and "12 years of irresponsibility." Others mockingly called on Klitschko to "leave Kyiv," turning his recent advice that residents consider relocating ahead of a difficult winter back on the mayor himself.
"We believe Klitschko's resignation could send a positive signal not only in Kyiv but across Ukraine, showing that city leaders must fulfill their duties," Oleksii Hromov, an activist with the NGO Social Movement, which co-organized the protest, told the Kyiv Independent.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has criticized Kyiv's preparations for winter, saying other cities are significantly better prepared. But despite growing public frustration, Klitschko's removal remains unlikely, as the city's complex governance structure limits the options for dismissing him during wartime.
The dispute also raises a broader question: who is ultimately responsible for ensuring Kyiv can withstand another winter?
Zelensky said on Oct. 13 that "In almost all regions of Ukraine, including border and front-line areas, resilience plans have been implemented more effectively than in the capital."
Emergency power and water outages, triggering the hum of generators on almost every street, returned to Kyiv as Russia renewed its campaign against energy infrastructure as early as Sept. 30.
Power outages are not new to Kyiv, but near-daily water loss is unprecedented.
Serhii Gorkutsenko, deputy head of Kyivvodokanal, the capital's city-owned water supply company, explained the problem in an interview with Ukrainska Pravda.
"The entire electrical water utility system dates back to the 1970s. With such (voltage) fluctuations, it simply can't hold up — it burns out," he said.
This year's issue is not merely about restoring water supply but also about the sewage system, without which Gorkutsenko said there will be "an epidemiological disaster in three days, because no one will stop using the sewers."
Besides the lack of basic amenities, Kyiv also suffers from a deficiency in safety infrastructure, despite the full-scale war continuing for over 4.5 years.
The lack of shelters and the state of existing ones has been an echoing concern for months, if not years.
Klitschko told reporters on Sept. 11 that mobile shelters have been purchased and "within a month, the first batch — about 40 or 50 of them, as far as I recall — will be installed at public transit stops where there are no permanent shelters."
That promised number suddenly diminished . The Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) told the media outlet Slidstvo.info on Oct. 6 that far fewer will arrive over a much longer timescale.
The first and so far the only new public mobile shelter appeared on Oct. 15, more than a month after Klitschko's claims.
Yelyzaveta Semko, a PR manager and copywriter who has lived in Kyiv for nearly 10 years, said the city authorities' handling of preparations for winter was the final straw that brought her to the protest.
"I’m tired of our city authorities' inaction," she told the Kyiv Independent.
According to Semko, the only shelter available in her residential building during Russian attacks is its basement. Nearly five years into the all-out war, she said, no proper shelters have been built nearby.
"Instead, the authorities are spending budget money on unnecessary things during wartime, like glass bus stops, relaying paving stones, and so on," she continued.
The overarching message of the Oct. 17 protest was simple — Klitschko should resign.
However, the issues outlined by the organizers were plentiful. They addressed everything from safety to public transport issues, and the neglect of cultural heritage sites.
Corruption and the city's financial mismanagement was also on the list of protestors' grievances.
Klitschko has been in power since 2014 and was decisively reelected as Kyiv's Mayor twice, in 2015 and 2020.
During these terms, Klitschko has been widely criticized for failing to address the city's urgent needs, instead focusing on building developments that demolish "cultural heritage, green zones, and public spaces," wrote activist and veteran Dmytro Koziatynskyi on social media prior to the protest.
Not all the protesters were calling for Klitschko's resignation. Several held placards in support of the mayor, while those who spoke to the Kyiv Independent also blamed the central government for Kyiv's poor preparations for winter.
Artem, 43, defended Klitschko's record, pointing to the "renovation of many roads and parks."
But 21-year-old student Pavlo took a different view, arguing that green spaces were disappearing as more residential complexes continued to spring up across Kyiv.
"I think Klitschko may be a good boxer, but politics isn’t for him," he added.
This is the second time in October that a protest has been held at the City State Administration's doorstep. In the evening of Oct. 7, people gathered in protest of the mass felling of trees during the construction of a heating pipeline in Teremky, a district fiercely targeted by Russian attacks.
"I just go around all week and tell people at work, and my foreign friends, and everyone about how Kyiv is an incredibly uncomfortable place to live," Kyiv resident Nadiia told the Kyiv Independent during the Oct. 7 protest.
Klitschko's ousting remains unlikely, however.
Kyiv is run in a convoluted manner, with numerous administrative bodies whose duties either overlap or omit certain areas entirely.
Klitschko is currently Kyiv's mayor and, due to the city's special status as the country's capital, is also the head of the Kyiv City State Administration, a post equivalent to a regional governor. According to the law, the elected mayor is usually appointed as the head of the city administration.
The city is also governed by the Kyiv City Military Administration (KMVA), a structure created by Zelensky following the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. Andrii Tkachov currently leads it and is responsible for "preparing the city for defense, maintaining public order and ensuring the safety of the civilian population, enforcing the legal framework of martial law, and ensuring the city's essential functions," as written on its website .
Only the heads of KMDA and KMVA can be appointed by the president, while the mayor is elected by popular vote.
Considering this, Klitschko cannot be fully dismissed by Zelensky , but can only resign on his own will. What Ukraine's president can do is strip Klitschko of his title as head of the administration, thus limiting his power over decisions in Kyiv.
Hromov said he’s under no illusions about Klitschko's possible resignation and expects that, if he steps down, the President’s Office could install a loyal official in his place
"It doesn't matter who holds this position," he said. "What matters is that they fulfill their duties."
Following Zelensky's latest criticism, the city's mayor had five minutes in Ukraine's parliament to address the growing issues.
"We, as the city government, are doing everything in our power to ensure the city's functioning, despite the setbacks the central government is constantly trying to inflict on us; unfortunately, this is what their so-called 'cooperation' looks like," he said on Oct. 14.
He also revealed that, so far this year, Kyiv's power grid has been struck nearly 50 times by missiles and unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), an increase since last year.
"Where is the capital's air defense? Where is the protection for Ukrenergo's (energy operator) facilities? Where are the billions you allocated for this?" Klitschko appealed, pointing the finger at the government.
In 2026, Kyiv was allocated over $2.3 billion for winter preparation, but only 51.1% had been used as of Sept. 1, according to the Finance Ministry.
The Kyiv Independent reached out to the Kyiv City State Administration and Klitschko with a request for comment, but has not received a response at the time of publication.

title: Slovakia, Hungary won't join 70 billion euro EU package sought by Ukraine, Fico says
description: Zelensky asked EU leaders for an additional 70 billion euros to help cover Ukraine's defense and "resilience" needs in 2027, as Kyiv grapples with a budget shortfall amid escalating Russian attacks.
content:
Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico said on Oct. 16 his country would not take part in a 70-billion-euro ($79 billion) support package requested by President Volodymyr Zelensky at an EU leaders' summit in Brussels.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar took a similar stance, Fico said , according to the Slovak news agency TASR.
Zelensky asked EU leaders on Oct. 16 for an additional 70 billion euros to help cover Ukraine 's defense and "resilience" needs in 2027, as Kyiv grapples with a budget shortfall amid escalating Russian attacks.
The request came only six months after the European bloc approved a 90 billion euro ($101 billion) loan to help Ukraine until the end of 2027. But while this loan is being disbursed, Kyiv still faces a shortfall, as non-EU partners — apart from Norway — have failed to help bridge the gap.
Like Slovakia and Hungary, Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis also signaled that his country would not join an additional financing package for Ukraine.
The three countries opted not to join the 90-billion-euro package as well, though they did not block its approval.
Fico said Bratislava would continue to help Kyiv through other means, citing educational projects, logistics, and energy cooperation as examples.
The Slovak and Czech leaders have stepped back from their countries' direct military assistance after taking office, while Hungary has not supplied weapons to Ukraine throughout the full-scale war.
Kyiv's EU partners have acknowledged the need to cover Ukraine's shortfall for next year, though no consensus has been reached on the 70 billion euros yet. French President Emmanuel Macron said Ukraine's allies would analyze the request.
"We will indeed be looking at the funding. The funding that will be provided by the G7 countries, by our partners and, of course, by the Europeans," Macron said.

title: Russia launches 'one of its largest attacks' on Ukraine's energy grid as US 'disregards' Graham's sanctions, Zelensky says
description: Ukrainian forces downed 289 out of the 332 drones, including jet-powered attack drones, launched by Russia overnight, the Air Force reported. Russian drones and ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M or the North Korean KN-23 model struck 22 different locations, and debris fell in three areas.
content:
Editor's note: The story has been updated to include comments from President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Russian attacks against Ukraine killed seven people and injured around 90 over the past day, regional authorities said on Oct. 17, with the country reporting one of the heaviest Russian attacks against energy infrastructure so far.
Ukrainian forces downed 289 out of the 332 drones, including jet-powered attack drones, launched by Russia overnight, the Air Force reported . Russian drones and ballistic missiles of the Iskander-M or the North Korean KN-23 model struck 22 different locations, and debris fell in three areas, according to the statement.
The attacks came as Russia continued its campaign against Ukraine's energy grid ahead of winter. Attacks on energy facilities across the country overnight and on the morning of Oct. 17 left some homes without power, the Energy Ministry said .
President Volodymyr Zelensky described Russia's latest attack as "one of the largest strikes on Ukraine's energy infrastructure." Russian forces targeted more than 15 key power generation and transmission facilities across Ukraine, he said.
"At a time when the Russians have carried out such a massive attack on our energy sector, a decision was unfortunately made in America to completely disregard the Lindsey Graham Act, which was supposed to impose truly effective pressure on Russia to bring this war to an end," Zelensky said on social media, calling on Washington to pressure Moscow through a "sanctions blackout."
"Financial rewards for (Russian President Vladimir) Putin — all of this only encourages him to keep attacking. We must not give up ground."
In Kharkiv Oblast , Russian attacks killed a man and a woman, aged 58 and 71. Another 41 people were injured or suffered from stress, including three children, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said .
Four women and three men were injured in Sumy Oblast in Russian drone attacks, local authorities reported .
Russian attacks near the city of Nikopol in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed a 74-year-old woman and injured two men over the past day, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said . One more man was killed in Dnipro, the regional center, after Russian forces targeted an industrial facility.
Russia launched one of its largest attacks on central Vinnytsia Oblast since the start of the full-scale invasion, targeting civilian and critical infrastructure with drones and injuring six people, Governor Natalia Zabolotna said .
Russian forces targeted civilian infrastructure in Odesa Oblast , injuring at least four people, Governor Oleh Kiper said .
Two people were killed in Kramatorsk in Donetsk Oblast , Governor Vadym Filashkin said . Fifteen more people were injured in the region over the past day.
Russian troops also attacked Zaporizhzhia Oblast , injuring six people, said Ivan Fedorov, head of the Zaporizhzhia Oblast Defense Council.
In Kherson Oblast , Russian forces targeted 31 towns and villages, including the regional center of Kherson. One person was killed, and at least 19 others were injured, including children, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin reported .

title: Exclusive: Watchdog lists ships carrying Russian gas, blasts Trump sanctions waiver
description: "Republicans and Democrats passed this law in Lindsey Graham's name to squeeze Russia's war revenues. Trump has now hollowed it out before its main sanctions could bite," said Alexander Kirk, a sanctions campaigner at Urgewald.
content:
The NGO Urgewald has identified what it says are all the 134 vessels involved in Russian gas trade since 2022, which have carried over 150 million metric tons of cargo since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, according to data shared with the Kyiv Independent.
As of Oct. 15, around 1.5 million metric tons more were in transit.
The news comes as U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 16 issued a broad waiver of Russia sanctions that were set to take effect two days later under a law championed by the late U.S. Senator Lindsey Graham.
The law authorized the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five countries buying Russian gas and oil, and also provided for extensive sanctions against Russian officials, banks, and the energy sector, including ships involved in the Russian liquefied natural gas ( LNG ) trade.
"Republicans and Democrats passed this law in Lindsey Graham's name to squeeze Russia's war revenues. Trump has now hollowed it out before its main sanctions could bite," said Alexander Kirk, a sanctions campaigner at Urgewald, on Oct. 17.
"That is a betrayal of the bipartisan effort behind this law and a lifeline to (Russian President Vladimir) Putin."
Between the law's signing on Sept. 18 and Oct. 15, 42 tankers had transported Russian gas, according to the analysis.
These include Boris Davydov, an Arc7 tanker that departed Russia's Yamal terminal on Oct. 6; Konstantin Posiet, which departed Arctic LNG 2 on Sept. 21; and Clean Horizon, which left Yamal the same day with a cargo later delivered to the French port of Dunkerque.
U.S. lawmakers from both parties have urged the White House to impose sanctions under Graham's law in order to pressure Moscow toward ending the war in Ukraine. For LNG tankers, this would enable Washington to target those ships and restrict their access to international shipping services.
Instead, Trump has taken increasingly accommodating steps toward Russia, announcing a deal earlier in October to purchase Russian diesel.
"Congress must challenge this retreat and demand that the administration explain whose interests are served by shielding Russia's energy trade from the pressure this law was designed to impose. Ukraine should not have to pay the price for Washington's unwillingness to act," Kirk said.
The list of 134 ships carrying Russian gas between Feb. 24, 2022, and Oct. 15, 2026, includes 17 Arc7-class LNG carriers, an advanced tanker type designed to export product from the Russian Yamal LNG terminal in the Arctic.
The EU paid 7.88 billion euros (about $8.9 billion) worth of gas from the Arctic project in the first nine months of 2026, Urgewald reported earlier.
While the U.S. has never been a major buyer of Russian fossil fuels and banned all imports in 2022, the EU remains the leading buyer of Russian LNG , followed by China, Japan, and South Korea, according to the CREA think tank.
But the EU has been phasing out Russian LNG imports, with a full import ban to take effect in January 2027.
Urgewald's latest findings underscore how much Russian LNG trade continues to rely on Western services.
Of more than 2700 voyages undertaken since February 2022, about a third were taken by ships owned by either the Greek shipping company Dynagas or the U.K.-based, U.S.-owned company Seapeak, according to data.
Both account for roughly 17% of the voyages each, with the Dutch Anthony Veder gas shipping company coming in third.
Greece has secured a sanctions exemption for Dynagas , allowing the company to continue shipping Russian LNG to non-EU countries even after the EU ban takes effect.
Other operators include Russian companies such as Gazprom and Novatek, as well as China's Cosco.
LNG trade has faced weaker sanctions pressure than Russia's oil exports, which have been constrained by an EU- and G7-imposed price cap, forcing the country to rely increasingly on its shadow fleet to ship its oil.
"Europe must now act with urgency. Sanction the tankers, cut off the services that keep them operating, and close the loopholes sustaining Russia's LNG exports," Kirk said.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,562,970 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,950 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,562,970 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 17.
The number includes 1,950 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,415 tanks, 25,554 armored combat vehicles, 163,883 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,266 artillery systems, 2,221 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,710 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,962 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Trump waives latest Russia sanctions amid growing Ukraine-US tensions
description: U.S. President Donald Trump issued a broad waiver of sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on Oct. 16.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump issued a broad waiver of sanctions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act on Oct. 16.
The law was the latest U.S. effort to intensify economic pressure on Russia as it continues to wage its war, granting Trump broad authority to impose or waive sanctions and tariffs under the act.
The Executive Order increases the duty on goods from Russia by 500% and by 100% on goods from the top five importers of crude oil and natural gas that originated in Russia. The same order largely waives these measures.
The decision to issue widespread waivers within the Graham Act sparked immediate criticism.
"Trump just waived all of the sanctions on Russia provided for in the Lindsey Graham Sanctioning Russia Act, just as I and others warned he would," Democratic Representative Don Beyer said in a post to X.
He called for the U.S. Congress to "fix" the "flawed" law and condemned Trump for "surrendering" to Russian President Vladimir Putin by defying the congressional intent of the Graham Act.
"Trump has proven he will twist this law and abuse the powers it conferred on him, and while he has let the tariff powers lie for the moment, the law as written also empowers Trump to weaponize new trade authorities against our allies and trading partners," Beyer added.
Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, a co-author of the law, said that Trump "confirms again that he stands on the side of a bloodthirsty thug and the enablers of Russia's war machine and against the majority of Americans, their representatives in both houses of Congress, and our European allies."
"These waivers have nothing to do with our national security, and everything to do with sucking up to Vladimir Putin. I hope my Republican colleagues will join me in condemning this craven, cowardly action," the senator said in a press statement.
Meanwhile, Russia has hailed Trump's sanctions waiver as a "historic moment."
"The suspension of some of the provisions of the Graham Act marks an important and truly historic moment," Kirill Dmitriev, Russia's economic negotiator, said on X.
"The U.S.-Russia economic dialogue and peacemaking efforts will continue," he said.
On Oct. 13, a bipartisan group of U.S. senators called on Trump to rescind his deal to buy Russian diesel, joining other colleagues in Congress who lambasted the controversial agreement.
Meanwhile, President Volodymyr Zelensky warned on Oct. 16 that Trump's diesel deal with Russia risks paving the way for further sanctions relief for Moscow.
"In my view, we cannot accept these agreements. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well," he said.
On Oct. 10, Trump lashed out at Zelensky, demanding he halt attacks on Russian refineries and suggesting the Ukrainian people replace him as their leader if they want an end to the war.
Trump also lambasted Zelensky for supposedly exacerbating the global diesel supply crisis, despite evidence that shows the U.S. war against Iran is the major culprit behind the current shortage.
"We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries, because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump claimed.
Trump said on Oct. 9 that Russia had agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets following a call with Putin.

title: Russian attacks put millions of Ukrainians at risk of displacement this winter, UN Migration says
description: Where heating is available, many cannot afford to adequately heat their homes. Only 32% of households reported being able to do so during the last heating season, a figure that dropped to just 1% in frontline regions.
content:
Millions of Ukrainians who returned home are at risk of displacement this winter as Russia continues its attacks on civilian infrastructure, the International Organization for Migration (IOM), also known as U.N. Migration, reported Oct. 16.
The agency estimates that around 1.56 million Ukrainians who returned home as of June 2026 now live in frontline districts where three in four people need materials to repair damaged walls while nearly two in four need insulation and roofing materials.
A total of 4.1 million returnees have moved back to Ukraine in a figure that does not include Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs), the report found .
"For millions of Ukrainians, the challenge is no longer simply whether they can return home. It is whether they can remain there safely, and right now the conditions are making it difficult," Arthur Erken, IOM Regional Director for Europe and Central Asia, said .
Where heating is available, many cannot afford to adequately heat their homes. Only 32% of households reported being able to do so during the last heating season, a figure that dropped to just 1% in frontline regions.
Six in 10 households have also reduced heating consumption, U.N. Migration says.
Russia regularly attacks energy infrastructure and residential buildings in fatal strikes that leave many without power.
Russia launched a large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv overnight Oct. 13-14, wreaking destruction in a residential neighborhood and targeting several energy facilities in Kyiv.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that all three of the city's combined heat and power stations were attacked, as well as critical infrastructure in the Kyiv Oblast that provides power to Kyiv and central regions.
The attack killed five and injured 25 in total, with many casualties coming from a strike on a Kyiv residential building.
At least three women were killed, and another 25 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of the Russian strike on the residential building, Kyiv Police said .

title: Sky closed over Moscow multiple nights in row as Ukraine resumes refinery strikes
description: Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency announced restrictions at three of Moscow's four major airports, while the Transportation Ministry said the region's aviation operations were under "special monitoring."
content:
Flights over the city of Moscow were restricted for the sixth night in a row on Oct. 16-17, according to flight-tracking data and updates from Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency (Rosaviatsiya).
The latest restrictions coincide with President Volodymyr Zelensky's announcement on Oct. 15 that Ukraine would no longer hold back from attacking Russian oil refineries. That same night, flights were grounded in both Moscow and St. Petersburg.
Rosaviatsiya announced late in the evening of Oct. 16 that three of Moscow's four major airports — Vnukovo, Domodedovo, and Zhukovksy — were suspending operations due to security risks.
"Temporary restrictions have been introduced on the arrival and departure of aircraft," the agency said. "These restrictions are necessary to ensure flight safety."
Earlier in the day, Russia's Transportation Ministry said that civil aviation operations in Moscow Oblast had been placed under "special monitoring" by the ministry and Rosaviatsiya. The previous evening, Rosaviatsiya announced that flights were grounded at all four of Moscow's airports as well as at Pulkovo Airport in St. Petersburg.
While the agency did not at first announce restrictions at Moscow's Sheremetyevo Airport the night of Oct. 16-17, independent flight-tracking data indicated that the facility was also experiencing disruptions and delays.
According to aviation monitor Flightradar24 , Sheremetyevo Airport is currently the fifth-most disrupted airport in the world and is experiencing "major problems."
Rosaviatsiya then announced temporary restrictions at Sheremetyevo Airport at around 2 a.m. local time.
Meanwhile, Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported that nearly 30 drones bound for the capital have been intercepted as of 1:30 a.m. local time on Oct. 17.
The latest closure marks the sixth consecutive night that restrictions have been imposed on air travel over Moscow, leading to long passenger queues and hundreds of flight delays. Russia's Transportation Ministry said it was deploying additional staff to the capital's airports in response to the situation.
Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin claimed that Ukraine fired nearly 500 drones at the region overnight on Oct. 13-15, all of which he said were intercepted by Russian air defense units. The following night, he claimed nearly 100 Ukrainian drones were shot down over Moscow.
Ukraine had refrained from strikes on Russia's refineries for three days to accommodate demands from U.S. President Donald Trump, who unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow.
Trump has claimed that Ukraine's refinery strikes are driving up oil and diesel prices worldwide, despite evidence that the U.S. war in Iran is in fact the primary culprit.
While Zelensky attempted to accommodate Trump — who threatened to withhold intelligence from Ukraine and struck a deal with Russian President Donald Trump to buy diesel from Moscow — Russia hammered Ukrainian cities and energy infastructure in large-scale attacks.
On Oct. 15, Zelensky said Ukraine's refinery attack pause was over.

title: US lawmaker introduces bill blocking Trump's Russian diesel deal
description: "This deal won't lower costs for the American people, who are already paying for Trump's failed war of choice in Iran. It will hand Putin millions of dollars to continue slaughtering Ukrainian civilians with impunity."
content:
U.S. Representative Gregory Meeks, a Democrat and ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, introduced a bill on Oct. 16 that would block the Trump administration's plan to import Russian diesel.
The move comes a week after U.S. President Donald Trump shocked both Ukraine and the United States by announcing a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to buy millions of tons of diesel from Moscow — a deal Trump claimed would lower gas prices for Americans.
Meeks' new legislation , titled the Prohibit Corrupt Russia Oil Deals Act, bans the U.S International Development Finance Corporation (DFC) from investing in Russian energy products and mandates the White House impose sanctions on Russian fuel. It also nullifies the general licenses issued by the Treasury Department and prohibits any future licenses.
"This deal won't lower costs for the American people, who are already paying for Trump's failed war of choice in Iran," Meeks said.
"It will hand Putin millions of dollars to continue slaughtering Ukrainian civilians with impunity. At a time when the United States should be increasing pressure on the Kremlin, Donald Trump is cozying up to Putin and striking self-enriching deals instead of standing with Ukraine."
Meeks called on all his fellow congressmembers to support the legislation. The bill thus far has 17 co-sponsors in the House — all Democrats, with the exception of Republican Rep. Don Bacon.
Trump's diesel deal drew vocal bipartisan outrage from lawmakers after it was announced on Oct. 9. Members of Congress from both sides of the aisle argued the move would undermine recently enacted sanctions against Russia, potentially provide Moscow with billions of dollars to grow its war chest, and contradict U.S. efforts to pressure Putin into peace talks.
Republicans currently control both chambers of the U.S. Congress — but that could change with the upcoming midterm elections in November. Trump's approval rating has dipped drastically, with even conservative voters dissatisfied with his handling of key issues such as inflation, the economy, tariffs, and foreign policy.
Trump has chosen to blame Ukraine for the skyrocketing gasoline and diesel costs in the U.S., saying Kyiv's attacks on Russian oil refineries have caused the price hike. The claim is heavily disputed by experts , who point to the U.S. war in Iran and closure of the Strait of Hormuz.
