content:
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev in Sofia, Bulgaria, on Oct. 6, 2026. (Nikolay Doychinov / AFP via Getty Images)
The balancing act of Bulgaria's Moscow-friendly leader stands on shaky ground.
Since taking office in May, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has taken a harsh line on Ukraine while adopting steps his critics say are accommodating to Moscow .
Radev's course has now come under scrutiny as Bulgaria, a southeastern NATO member state, feels first-hand the spillover of Russia's war against Ukraine.
Four merchant vessels were hit by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast in October. Two of the vessels sank and several sailors are reported dead or missing.
Under fire from opposition, Radev, a former military officer and Bulgaria's ex-president, only cautiously hints at Moscow's complicity — stopping short of a direct accusation.
"Radev’s balancing act between the West and Moscow would eventually catch up with him."
With Russian drone incursions and Moscow-backed hybrid operations on NATO territory growing ever more brazen and frequent , Bulgaria has no guarantee that the strikes in its waters will come to an end.
Radev's room to maneuver between Bulgaria's NATO membership and a thaw in ties with Moscow is shrinking, observers say.
"I have argued for some time that Radev's balancing act between the West and Moscow would eventually catch up with him," Dimitar Keranov, an analyst at the German Marshall Fund's European Resilience program, told the Kyiv Independent.
Two Turkish-managed ships were hit by naval and aerial drones about 70 nautical miles (130 kilometers) east of the Bulgarian town of Byala on Oct. 6, inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
The Alfa Watan, flying a Togo flag, sank, with 10 crew members — including nine Syrian nationals — presumed dead.
Two more vessels were hit by drones near the Bulgarian Black Sea coast on Oct. 13, including the Ukrainian-owned, Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, hit east of Byala. Its crew, including seven Ukrainians, was rescued.
The second ship, the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity, was hit by drones east of the Bulgarian village of Krapets and sank, with 11 sailors reported missing.
The attacks came amid escalating hostilities in the Black Sea, with Moscow attempting to impose a blockade on Ukrainian trade by attacking ports and merchant ships.
Several commercial ships were also hit in and around Romanian waters over the past weeks.
While Ukraine has blamed Russia, Radev was initially hesitant to name the origin of the drones, saying only "they were clearly either Russian or Ukrainian."
Both Russian and Ukrainian drone incursions have been recorded along NATO's eastern flank over the past months, with the latter being a result of Russian jamming diverting Ukrainian unmanned vehicles.
But Radev's hesitation has provided an opening to the country's opposition.
On Oct. 6, lawmakers from the GERB–SDS, a center-right opposition coalition, blasted Radev for failing to properly identify the culprit.
The coalition's junior partner, the SDS (Union of Democratic Forces), even called the attack "an act of aggression by the Russian Federation in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone."
Finally, after the second attack, Radev acknowledged that Russia was the one to benefit from the attacks, and Sofia summoned the Russian envoy.
Nevertheless, Radev has not formally accused Moscow, citing a lack of decisive evidence.
Keranov summarizes this position as a "convenient deflection."
"Formal attribution takes time, but once a government concludes that the logic points to Moscow, it does not need a final forensic report to act on that assessment."
But Ruslan Stefanov, a program director and chief economist at the Center for the Study of Democracy, a Sofia-based European public policy institute, says waiting for proof is reasonable.
On the other hand, "continued failure to identify Russia as the main driver of instability and unsafe navigation in the Black Sea does not reflect operational reality and is widely seen as part of a broader pattern of unnecessary and harmful caution toward Moscow," he said.
"Moscow is testing Bulgaria because it sees it as the weak link on NATO’s southern flank."
The maritime attacks are not the only security-related incidents hitting Bulgaria in recent weeks and months.
Earlier in October, two masked men were said to have set fire to 11 out of 17 Starlink antennas at a facility near Sofia.
Ivaylo Mirchev, one of the leaders of the opposition Democratic Bulgaria (DB), hinted at connections to "Russian-style sabotage."
Yet Radev has remained tight-lipped about who was behind the arson, even though Poland blamed Moscow for a similar attack against a Starlink station on Polish territory in September.
Ukraine widely uses Starlink network services , operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, for both civilian purposes and to support military operations.
And in August and September, explosions hit two arms facilities of the EMCO company, which supplies weapons to Ukraine.
The company called the September incident sabotage, while the Bulgarian Interior Ministry did not rule out either foreign interference or company neglect.
As Bulgaria's president, Radev was ranked among the most Ukraine-skeptical voices in the EU — often compared to former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Since assuming the premier office, he has pulled Bulgaria out of the U.K.- and French-led Coalition of the Willing and halted arms supplies to Ukraine from Bulgarian army stocks.
He has also lambasted Western military aid for Kyiv, claiming it prolongs the war, and instead urged a diplomatic resolution.
At the EU level, Radev's government has blocked the inclusion of Moscow Patriarch Kirill in the 21st sanctions package and pushed to water down the EU's language on Ukraine's accession.
In light of these steps, drone strikes off the Bulgarian coast put Radev in an "uncomfortable position," Stefanov said.
"He built his campaign on the claim that there can be no military victory over Russia and that Bulgaria's interest lies in de-escalation," the expert noted.
"Those choices now raise the obvious question of why Bulgaria has not been spared."
Keranov believes that "Moscow is testing Bulgaria because it sees it as the weak link on NATO's southern flank."
Most NATO members along the alliance's frontier — from Romania to the Baltics — have already toughened their response to Russian provocations, with allied jets repeatedly downing invading drones.
Their leadership is also less reluctant to openly blame Moscow for the incursions.
While Radev's hesitation has provided ammunition to his domestic opponents, the prime minister's political position remains strong, Keranov said, adding that his popularity at home is not the real question.
"It is whether Bulgaria acts like a strong NATO member or keeps signaling indecision."

title: Ukraine war latest: Drone attack sparks fire at industrial facility in Russia's Surgut district
description:
Key developments on Oct. 16:

 * Drone attack sparks fire at industrial facility in Russia's Surgut district, governor says
 * Pope Leo urges Putin to allow humanitarian aid, evacuations from Russian-occupied Oleshky
 * Ukrainian military strikes million-dollar Russian radar in Krasnodar Krai, General Staff claim
 * Zelensky's ask: 300 Patriot missiles, 70 billion euros, and Russian assets
 * Emergency blackouts in Kyiv, as Klitschko announces start of heating season

A fire broke out at an indu
content:
A fire broke out at an industrial facility in Russia's Khanty-Mansi Autonomous District following a drone attack, regional governor Ruslan Kukharuk said on Oct. 16, while Ukrainian activist Serhii Sternenko said the facility was the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant.
"As a result of a drone attack on an industrial facility in the Surgut district, a fire broke out. Emergency services are working at the scene," Kukharuk said .
He added that specialists were assessing the scale and nature of the damage. Kukharuk did not identify the facility or say who was responsible for the attack.
"The Defense Forces struck the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant," Serhii Sternenko, a Ukrainian activist and volunteer who previously served as an adviser to then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, said . The facility is located more than 2,400 kilometers (1,490 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
In videos shared by Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova , a large fire and thick dark smoke can be seen on the territory of an industrial facility.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify that the facility reportedly hit was the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant. Ukrainian officials have not publicly claimed responsibility for the attack.
The Surgut plant processes gas condensate and produces petroleum products, including motor and aviation fuel. Its designed processing capacity reaches 12 million metric tons of raw materials per year, Sternenko said.
The reported strike comes amid a dispute between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil and energy infrastructure.
U.S. President Donald Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for rising global fuel prices, a claim disputed by energy experts . His administration also threatened to cut intelligence sharing and weapons support unless Kyiv stopped targeting Russian energy facilities, according to Ukrainian and European officials.
On Oct. 9, Trump announced a deal allowing Russia to supply diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets despite sanctions imposed following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia subsequently eased restrictions on diesel exports.
Two days later, Trump announced what he described as an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine. Ukrainian officials said Kyiv had not been informed of the agreement in advance.
Ukraine initially halted strikes on Russian refineries following the announcement, while Russia continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. On Oct. 15, Zelensky said that Kyiv had lifted the pause due to Moscow's continued attacks.
"The block is out. We're done," Zelensky said.
Pope Leo expressed concern over the worsening humanitarian crisis in Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson Oblast during a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 16, the Vatican said.
The pope called for a local ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the safe evacuation of civilians from the front-line city, where around 2,000 residents remain trapped amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
Despite Russia's failure to cooperate with evacuation efforts, Putin blamed Ukraine for the crisis in Oleshky.
"Putin provided the pope with detailed explanations of the Kyiv regime's responsibility for the humanitarian situation in Oleshky," Russian state news agency TASS reported.
Oleshky is an occupied front-line city on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, where civilians live amid a Russian military presence and attacks from both Ukrainian and Russian forces.
The humanitarian situation has worsened since the summer, as evacuation efforts have come to a halt. Continued attacks have made it increasingly difficult to deliver essential food and medicine.
Ukraine had prepared an evacuation mission, with the International Committee of the Red Cross ready to participate and Ukrainian forces preparing to observe a ceasefire, according to Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets. Russia, however, had not confirmed its willingness to proceed, he said.
The call came as Leo remains hospitalized in Rome after undergoing surgery for lung cancer on Oct. 13. It was his second known phone conversation with Putin since becoming pope in 2025.
The Ukrainian military struck a Russian Nebo-U radar near the settlement of Magri, in Krasnodar Krai, on the night of Oct. 16, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.
"The Nebo-U is a long-range, three-coordinate radar designed to detect and track aerial assets, including aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles," the General Staff said in a statement .
"Striking such systems reduces the enemy's ability to monitor airspace and detect aerial assets in time. The estimated cost of the radar station is about US $100 million," they said.
The General Staff did not give details about what Ukrainian munition was used to carry out the strike.
A day prior, an overnight attack on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia's Voronezh region carried out with the Neptune coastal missile system hit six Su-34M bomber jets, destroying four and damaging two, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 15.
On Aug. 23, Ukrainian drones struck two Russian fighter jets, a large missile-carrying drone, high-value radars, and other air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said then.
Krasnodar Krai, a strategic region along Russia's Black Sea coast, has increasingly come under Ukrainian drone attacks as Kyiv extends the range of its strikes deep into Russian territory.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky used his appearance at the Oct. 16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels to list the main things Kyiv needs to survive the winter and beyond, but those asks won't come cheap.
"I am grateful for your support for Ukraine," Zelensky told EU leaders.
"Without a determined European Union capable of making strong decisions Putin would have gone much further by now," Zelensky said.
But with Russia ramping up its use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones to pummel Kyiv, and the U.S. taking steps to undermine Russia sanctions and Ukrainian security, Zelensky also came to the bloc with new requests for help.
"We need a winter package... 300 Patriot interceptors specifically against ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
The U.S.-made Patriot are considered the only technology currently capable of consistently taking down Russian ballistic missiles, and several European countries still hold stocks of them, such as Spain and Greece.
But for Spain, European diplomats have told the Kyiv Independent that there is a real fear that Madrid will not receive any more Patriot missiles in the future because of U.S. President Donald Trump's personal dislike for Spain's center-left Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez.
Greece on the other hand has a visceral fear that depleting its own supplies of Patriots might be perceived as a sign of weakness by neighboring Turkey, which Athens fears Ankara would act upon by annexing Greek islands near the Turkish coast.
Likewise, Ukraine's demand to "deal with the frozen assets," unsettles several countries around the table.
Using the 200 billion euros ($227 billion) of Russian assets immobilized within the EU to support Ukraine came up in late 2025, but consensus on the idea was out of reach.
"We need something like a special EU-controlled custodian to reduce the risk of them being unfrozen and divided up among those who clearly do not want what is best for Europe or an end to this war," Zelensky said.

"My personal view is that if you have immobilized assets, like in every war, even the Second World War, they were never touched. But at the end of a conflict, there's always a peace deal. And part of this peace deal is the use of immobilized assets," De Wever told journalists at a press conference during the night of Oct. 15.
"Are there people on this planet who maybe dream of doing it differently this time and operationalizing those assets earlier? ... Yes, there are ... Do I want to talk about it? No, I don't," De Wever said.
And the risk of Russia's assets being returned, despite some wishful thinking from the U.S. that Europe would hand them over, is nonexistent. The EU bound itself in December 2025, so that any vote to unfreeze the Russian immobilized assets must be unanimous.
"Nobody could ever dream of operationalizing those immobilized assets without unanimity here around the table," De Wever said.

"The war will cost 155 billion euros ($174.5 billion) next year. And we need at least 70 billion euros ($78.8 billion) more from you," Zelensky said.
"This is a realistic amount and I ask you to find this support. It will help us hold Russia back," he added.
But the request for 70 billion euros comes only six months after the bloc approved a 90 billion euro loan to help Ukraine until the end of 2027. The idea was always that third countries would step in to help bridge the remaining gap, but so far only Norway has done so.
And the government has been notoriously unclear at communicating its financial needs, as noted earlier that day by Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker.
However, Zelensky's estimate of a 70 billion euro shortfall does match the estimated shortfall figure that a senior EU official familiar with Ukraine's financial situation shared with the Kyiv Independent.
On all three requests, even if they land on sympathetic ears, a decision would still not be expected the same day.
And because there is nonetheless a European consensus to support Ukraine, the demands are very likely to dominate discussions in Brussels over the next weeks.
Emergency blackouts were implemented across Kyiv due to Russian attacks on the city's energy infrastructure, Ukraine's biggest private energy firm DTEK said on Oct. 16, as Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko announced the start of the city's heating season.
"We remind you that during emergency shutdowns, schedules are not valid," DTEK said . Kyiv already operates under scheduled power outages , allowing residents to plan their days around them, but Russian attacks on the city's energy infrastructure led to additional emergency power outages over the past weeks.
On the same day, Klitschko announced that Kyiv's centralised heating system will be turned on, starting with social institutions such as schools, hospitals, and kindergartens. The decision was sparked by "extreme conditions" created by constant bombardment, Klitschko said.
Two areas of the city, the Dniprovskyi and Darnytskyi districts, would not have their centralised heating switched on due to "significant damage" to a power facility in the area, Klitschko said, while repair efforts were ongoing.
Kyiv, a city the size of Berlin, is home to over 3 million people, with average temperatures of -4.6 degrees Celsius to -1 degrees Celsius (23.7 degrees Fahrenheit to 30 degrees Fahrenheit) in the winter months.
In Kyiv Oblast, Buchanan, Obukhiv, and Fastiv districts were also experiencing emergency blackouts, DTEK said .
In Western Ukraine, the city of Lutsk was left without power, Andriy Razumovsky, secretary of Lutsk City Council, announced on social media.
"Due to an attack by enemy drones, the city was left without electricity. Utilities are operating on backup power sources," Razumovsky said .
Overnight on Oct. 13 to 14, Russia launched a large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv, wreaking destruction in a residential neighborhood and targeting several energy facilities in Kyiv.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that all three of the city's combined heat and power stations were attacked, as well as critical infrastructure in the Kyiv Oblast that provide power to Kyiv and central regions.
"The targets of Russian ballistic missiles were power system facilities in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and the region," he said.
"Overnight, the Russians deployed 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media on Oct.14, adding that 600,000 people were left without power.

title: 'They were both in on it' — Musk suggested Trump restrict Ukraine's Starlink service, Telegraph reports
description: Four sources familiar with the discussion said that Elon Musk approached U.S. President Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Ukraine's Starlink service on the battlefield.
content:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk approached U.S. President Donald Trump with the idea of restricting Starlink speeds for Ukrainian forces, the Telegraph reported on Oct. 16, citing four sources familiar with the matter.
The news comes after SpaceX abruptly implemented a speed cap on Ukraine's vital Starshield service on Oct. 14, with no warning to Kyiv in advance. The sudden restriction disrupted multiple battlefield operations, including mid-range drone strikes and air defense.
Conflicting reports about the reason for the cutoff — and who was responsible — have left Ukraine with questions even after Starlink service stabilized on the front lines.
But the Telegraph on Oct. 16 reported that it was Musk who proposed the speed cap to Trump — and Trump "agreed," one source said.
The claim contradicts Musk's own comments on the matter. Following the Oct. 14 disruption, Musk wrote on his social media platform X that any Starlink restrictions applicable to the military were the ultimate decision of the White House.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government," he said. "Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president)."
Musk neglected to mention his own role in the change.
A senior source told the Telegraph that after the chaos and violence that followed the restriction, Musk was concerned about negative consumer reactions in Europe.
"He tweeted out that he was innocent and that it was the U.S. administration that did it," the source reportedly said. "The reality is that they were both in it."
This account was confirmed by two Ukrainian sources and a high-ranking European official, according to the Telegraph.
Ukraine relies heavily on Starlink for battlefield communications and drone operations, including its "middle strike" campaign against Russian forces and logistics in occupied Ukrainian territory and interceptor drones used against Russian long-range attack drones.
The impact of the Starlink restriction in Ukraine was immediate, and carried high stakes for both soldiers and civilians. President Volodymyr Zelensky highlighted the deadly consequences in comments to reporters on the sidelines of an EU leaders' summit in Brussels Oct. 16.
"We use Starlink to intercept jet-powered Shaheds that strike our civilians and kill our families," Zelensky said .
According to Zelensky, interceptor drones relying on Starlink operate at high speeds, but the restrictions had reduced connectivity for some Ukrainian systems to around 70 kilometers per hour (43 mph).
"When the speed was reduced, we were unable to intercept some of the jet-powered Shaheds. We were unable to use a tool to protect civilians," he said.
The restrictions also affected deliveries of food and water to troops operating in areas under constant Russian drone surveillance, the president said. Zelensky stressed that Ukrainian forces do not use Starlink for deep strikes inside Russia.
The Starlink incident came amid heightened tensions between Kyiv and the White House, with Trump demanding that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian oil refineries and making a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import diesel from Russia.
The White House threatened to halt intelligence sharing if Ukraine refused to comply — even as Russia continued to pound Ukraine's energy grid night after night and attack civilians with ballistic missiles.
But Trump has also dodged responsibility for the decision to restrict Starlink.
Reuters reported on Oct. 15 that the order to restrict Starshield came from within the White House, citing two U.S. officials and a Western official. The officials did not identify who issued the order, while a senior U.S. official denied that Trump personally requested the restriction.
In remarks at the White House on Oct. 16, Trump said he did not think either he or Musk was responsible for the slowdown.
The Pentagon has given no public explanation regarding the restriction.
The future of Ukraine's Starlink service also remains murky. Zelensky said on Oct. 16 that Starlink is not yet operating at its former speed, but that speed is in the process of being restored.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15 that connectivity had "been restored and remains operational," but military personnel in Ukraine's drone sector have continued to report uneven performance.

title: Pope Leo calls for ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky during call with Putin
description: The pope called for a local ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the safe evacuation of civilians from the front-line city, where around 2,000 residents remain trapped amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
content:
Pope Leo expressed concern over the worsening humanitarian crisis in Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson Oblast during a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 16, the Vatican said.
The pope called for a local ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the safe evacuation of civilians from the front-line city, where around 2,000 residents remain trapped amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
Despite Russia's failure to cooperate with evacuation efforts, Putin blamed Ukraine for the crisis in Oleshky.
"Putin provided the pope with detailed explanations of the Kyiv regime's responsibility for the humanitarian situation in Oleshky," Russian state news agency TASS reported.
Oleshky is an occupied front-line city on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, where civilians live amid a Russian military presence and attacks from both Ukrainian and Russian forces.
The humanitarian situation has worsened since the summer, as evacuation efforts have come to a halt. Continued attacks have made it increasingly difficult to deliver essential food and medicine.
Ukraine had prepared an evacuation mission, with the International Committee of the Red Cross ready to participate and Ukrainian forces preparing to observe a ceasefire, according to Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets. Russia, however, had not confirmed its willingness to proceed, he said.
The call came as Leo remains hospitalized in Rome after undergoing surgery for lung cancer on Oct. 13. It was his second known phone conversation with Putin since becoming pope in 2025.

title: Ukraine, Turkey discuss securing Black Sea shipping as $10 billion in exports at risk
description: Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi raised the issue during a meeting with Turkish Ambassador to Ukraine Fatma Ceren Yazgan earlier this week.
content:
Ukraine has asked Turkey to help restore safe and stable Black Sea shipping, warning that restrictions on port operations caused by Russian attacks put around 32 million tons of agricultural products worth approximately $10 billion at risk, Ukraine’s Agriculture Ministry said.
Russia’s attacks on commercial vessels and Ukrainian port operations have disrupted the country’s Black Sea shipping routes, threatening agricultural exports that are a major source of revenue for Ukraine’s economy.
With alternative routes unable to handle the full volume of maritime shipments, prolonged disruption could reduce farmers’ incomes, constrain investment in the next planting season and deepen the economic impact of the war.
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi raised the issue during a meeting with Turkish Ambassador to Ukraine Fatma Ceren Yazgan earlier this week. He said alternative export routes via the Danube, railways and roads cannot fully replace maritime shipments.
"Without the restoration of stable shipping through the Black Sea, production will begin to decline in the long term," Vysotskyi said, adding that farmers need greater certainty ahead of the spring sowing season.
He warned that lower export revenues could leave farmers with fewer resources to purchase seeds, fertilizers and crop protection products, potentially leading to reduced planting areas and affecting rural communities.
Yazgan said Turkey was ready to help find practical solutions and raise the issue with international partners. The two sides also discussed cooperation on irrigation projects and the potential involvement of Turkish businesses.
Separately, Turkey has been discussing a temporary, partial ceasefire with Ukraine and Russia to protect merchant vessels carrying civilian cargo, according to Turkey’s permanent representative to NATO, Basat Ozturk. Ankara hopes to draw on its experience with the Black Sea Grain Initiative to develop a new maritime security mechanism.
Restoring reliable Black Sea shipping is critical to Ukraine’s agricultural export revenues and future production. The economic impact of any truce would depend on effective protection for commercial vessels and sustained access to Ukrainian ports.

title: There is nothing apolitical about the scientists behind Russian weapons
description:

content:
Two men attempt to escape from the National Academy of Sciences building after it was hit by a Russian drone and caught fire in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 28, 2026. (Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
Physicist at the French National Center for Scientific Research
A lunchtime drone attack on the head office of Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv's downtown on Sept. 28, 2026, might have come as a shock to scientists based outside the country.
Unfortunately, for Ukrainian scientists, those who can be seen climbing down the ladders from the burning building , such attacks are part of the daily routine.
As documented in the UNESCO report from 2024, over 30% of Ukraine's research infrastructure has been damaged by the Russian attacks, and its institutions were forced to move , some multiple times, to safer areas which remain under Ukrainian control.
Occupied Ukrainian scientific institutions undamaged by the war, such as Crimean Astrophysical Observatory, the Marine Hydrophysical Institute, the Institute of Biology of the Southern Seas, the Nikitsky Botanical Garden, Askania Nova Biosphere Reserve, V. I. Vernadsky Taurida National University, and universities in Donetsk, Luhansk, Kerch, and Mariupol, not only saw their facilities appropriated by the Russian scientific community but also had their institutional identities usurped .
Some Ukrainian scientific facilities, such as the RT-70 radio telescope in Yevpatoria in occupied Crimea, have even been repurposed for military use.
While the Russian scientific community benefits greatly from the seizure and repurposing of Ukrainian research facilities, Russian scientists are simultaneously portrayed as victims of the war because of the sanctions and supposed international isolation brought by it.
The physical expropriation extends to a broader ideological appropriation of Ukrainian scientific heritage.
Portraying Nobel laureate Elie Metchnikoff, a pioneer of cellular immunity born near Kharkiv, George Gamow, a pioneer of Big Bang theory born in Odesa, or Serhii Koroliov, a chief designer of the Soviet space program born in Zhytomyr and the driving force behind the launch of the world's first artificial satellite Sputnik 1 in 1957, as Russian scientists symbolically incorporates their Ukrainian birthplaces into an imagined Russian scientific and cultural geography, only reinforcing claims to Ukrainian territory and legitimizing the seizure of its scientific infrastructure and resources.
By appropriating Ukrainian scientific achievements, Russia enhances the prestige of its own scientific establishment — a legacy apparently too valuable to tarnish with sanctions — while marginalizing Ukraine's contribution to global scientific progress.
The victim narrative also obscures the important role played by the Russian scientific establishment in supporting the ongoing war effort, not only through direct involvement in weapons research and development but also through knowledge and technology transfer and personnel training.
These activities are facilitated by the longstanding and close collaboration between the Russian scientific community and its military-industrial complex.
A prominent example of such cooperation is the Dubna military-industrial hub , infamously known for the Kh-101 and S8000 Banderol missile production and the development of glide bombs, which are eventually used by Russian soldiers to terrorize Ukrainian civilians.
Dubna also hosts the Space Communications Center, which supports intelligence collection and the coordination of Russian occupation forces operating in Ukraine.
For decades, international sources such as Encyclopedia Britannica have presented Dubna as a ‘science city’ centered on the Joint Institute for Nuclear Research (JINR). Such descriptions omitted the existence in Dubna of the missile design bureau Raduga and its production plant, both of which, alongside JINR, are " city-forming enterprises of Dubna ."
Collaboration between JINR and Raduga was crucial for the establishment of the university in Dubna in 1994 , the Dubna Special Economic Zone in 2005, and the construction of numerous housing complexes for their employees.
University students, taught by JINR scientists, are subsequently recruited by enterprises in Dubna , many of which are subject to international sanctions. JINR scientists themselves either founded or work in some of these companies.
In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, scientists from Dubna continue to be prominently represented in global organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in Vienna, UNESCO in Paris, the International Union of Pure and Applied Physics (IUPAP) in Trieste and Geneva, and the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) in Geneva, to name a few.
Participation in these organizations reinforces the visibility of JINR and lends credibility to its self-presentation as an "apolitical" institution.
In 2016, the IAEA funded a JINR project with the Institute of Biology of the Southern Seas in occupied Sevastopol, facilitating the integration of Crimea into the Russian scientific sphere.
The Global Conference of the International Decade of Sciences for Sustainable Development, organized by UNESCO in July 2026 in Paris, France, included a session dedicated to JINR .
That same month, JINR was featured at the IUPAP-organized International Conference on High Energy Physics 2026 in Natal, Brazil. Over 240 JINR scientists currently have in-person access to the CERN site, which allows them and their families to live in Switzerland and France and to freely travel within the Schengen area.
On Aug. 8, 2025, Ukraine imposed sanctions on JINR, making it the only country to have done so.
This oversight perpetuates a self-reinforcing cycle in which participation in international scientific activities allows Russian researchers to maintain access to global research networks, which can be used both to legitimize Russia's occupation of Ukrainian territories and to acquire knowledge and technologies that strengthen the Russian military-industrial complex and increase its capacity to attack Ukrainian civil and scientific infrastructure.
The examples discussed here represent only a fraction of a broader, systematic pattern that challenges the portrayal of Russian science as an apolitical enterprise and Russian scientists primarily as victims of sanctions and international isolation.
Therefore, it is time to finally put under scrutiny how scientific cooperation, institutional prestige, and continued participation in international scientific organizations can coexist with, and potentially facilitate, military production and the legitimization of occupation, while scientists in Ukraine face the physical destruction of their institutions.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Tetiana Hryn'ova is a physicist at the French National Center for Scientific Research.

title: EU doubles down on helping Ukraine's rule of law with new task force
description: "This step shows our commitment to supporting Ukraine's path to EU membership," the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Ukraine and the EU are launching a new task force composed of Ukrainian and EU officials that will begin meeting regularly to drive progress on key rule-of-law reforms, the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos announced on Oct. 16.
"Following the opening of two more negotiating clusters this week, I discussed the next steps with Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi," Kos posted on social media.
"We agreed to launch a joint Task Force to accelerate progress on the interim benchmarks and advance essential rule of law and anti-corruption reforms. This step shows our commitment to supporting Ukraine's path to EU membership," she added.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also mentioned in his address to EU leaders that the task force had been established the day before.
"Our goal is to get a positive assessment ... as soon as possible," Zelensky said, with "a team that can work on joint decisions and concrete steps to move things forward."
The task force will involve regular meetings between Ukrainian and European Commission officials, who will work through rule-of-law reforms pragmatically, with documents on the table.
Those reforms also come under so-called " interim benchmarks ," which, after Ukraine opens all six negotiating clusters — expected by the end of 2026 — will be the next thing to do on its EU membership to-do list.
"Ukraine will continue to actively pursue reforms," Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said .

title: Zelensky calls on EU to keep Moldova's membership bid shackled to Ukraine
description: "It would be simply wrong to split us apart on our way into the EU — I hope not. Morally wrong," President Volodymyr Zelensky told EU leaders.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky called on the EU to keep the membership processes of Ukraine and Moldova tied together on Oct. 15, risking holding back Moldova for years as Kyiv struggles to pass reforms.
Ukraine and Moldova are two of the EU's frontrunner countries for future membership in the bloc, and earlier that week, they took another step forward in their integration process.
The two countries have had their EU bids tied together thus far, an informal political decision made by EU leaders that was expected to end once both countries have opened all six enlargement clusters — to-do lists of reforms to fully align with the bloc.
"When Ukraine and Moldova are moving so closely together — that's great — when we are doing so much to support Moldova and create the conditions it needs, it would be simply wrong to split us apart on our way into the EU. I hope not. Morally wrong," Zelensky told EU leaders.
Zelensky's argument for keeping Moldova bound together with Ukraine on the membership process rests on Kyiv "protecting Moldova from Russia's attempts to cause trouble through Transnistria," a Russian-occupied territory of Moldova that borders Ukraine.
"This takes serious work from our security services and intelligence. We even have to pull some of our military forces away from other tasks," Zelensky said.
There has been no public reaction from Moldova to the idea of keeping the bids tied together, but the most senior EU officials working on the bloc's enlargement have told the Kyiv Independent that Moldova is surging ahead with integration, far ahead of Ukraine.
"Moldova is adopting EU laws faster than any country since Hungary in 2002, and the body of laws to adopt is far bigger now," one senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent earlier.
In comments to Moldovan media, French President Emmanuel Macron also backed the idea that the pace of accession should match the pace of reforms.
"Our goal is to move forward according to the approach we have established, based on each country's own merits," Macron told the regional outlet TVR Moldova.
"No one can ignore all the progress made by the Republic of Moldova."
EU leaders overnight adopted conclusions on enlargement that appeared to move toward separating the Moldovan and Ukrainian accession bids.
"The European Council recalls that the accession process is merit-based and that each candidate country advances in its accession negotiations on the basis of its individual progress," read the conclusions .
In any case, for now, the next step for both countries is to unlock the remaining two enlargement clusters, which are expected to happen before the end of the year.

title: Belgium promises to deliver 10 F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year
description: De Wever said that Ukraine urgently needed the fighter jets, as they were one of the few weapons capable to strike Russian jet-powered drones.
content:
Belgium will deliver ten F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine this year, Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said at a press conference attended by the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15.
“Ukraine urgently needs operational fighter jets and we can make our contribution,” De Wever said following a meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of the European Council meeting in Brussels.
"We will supply 10 this year. We have fallen a little behind because of delays with the F-35s, but those are now starting to arrive, which will enable us to send F-16s to Ukraine," the prime minister said. As Belgium is modernizing its air force with U.S.-made F-35 fighter jets, the country said it would transfer some of its F-16 fighter jets to Ukraine.
On Sept. 29, Zelensky said that Belgium will provide Ukraine with three U.S.-made F-16 fighter jets by the end of the year.
De Wever said that Ukraine urgently needed the fighter jets, as they were one of the weapons capable of defending Ukraine from "Russian jet-powered drones."
The Geran-5 jet-powered drone is Russia's latest attempt to force Ukraine to capitulate. Small, and with a tubular fuselage reminiscent of a missile rather than a drone, the Geran-5 flies higher, faster, and is significantly more difficult to shoot down. Russia's jet drones target civilian infrastructure such as supermarkets , schools , shopping malls , telecommunications infrastructure , data centers , gas stations , and medical facilities .
Zelensky and De Wever also discussed the possibility of supplying Ukraine with ammunition for the F-16s.
F-16s are used in both offensive and defensive operations. The aircraft have been used for intercepting Russian missiles and drones during aerial strikes against Ukraine. They can also be deployed to launch missiles at Russian positions along the front line.

title: Ukraine’s plan to tighten military exemptions draws fire from lawmakers, businesses
description: On Oct. 16, 63 lawmakers registered a draft resolution calling on the government to reverse its changes, consult with businesses, and reconsider a proposed "coordination center" overseeing the exemption system.
content:
Ukraine's government is facing mounting criticism over proposed changes to military exemption rules, with lawmakers and businesses warning that the measures could deprive critical industries of workers needed to sustain wartime operations.
The Cabinet of Ministers approved changes to the military exemption system on Oct. 13, though the final rules have yet to be adopted and published. The proposed changes reportedly include lowering exemption quotas for defense-industrial and energy companies from 100% to 85%, and for housing and utility companies from 75% to 60%.
On Oct. 16, 63 lawmakers registered a draft resolution calling on the government to reverse its changes, consult with businesses, and reconsider a proposed "coordination center" overseeing the exemption system.
The dispute highlights a difficult balance for Ukraine as it tries to mobilize more troops while keeping critical industries staffed during the war. Businesses fear the revised rules could deprive them of workers essential to production, energy infrastructure, and defense manufacturing, at a time when companies are already facing labor shortages and disruptions caused by the war.
During a question-and-answer session in Parliament on Oct. 16, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi defended the need to reform the system but sought to reassure critical businesses that they should not expect sweeping changes.
"The regulation is still being worked on. It will be finalized, adopted and published. There is no betrayal there," Koretskyi said.
He said genuinely critical companies, particularly those in the defense and energy sectors, had no reason to worry.
"I can say with confidence that there will be no radical changes for these people and these industries," Koretskyi said.
At the same time, Koretskyi acknowledged that the current system has been abused. He said some companies with a 100% exemption quota exploit the system by employing people who do not perform critical functions.
During his comments in parliament, Koretskyi cited an energy company's contractor with 100 employees, only 20 of whom worked directly for the company, while all 100 received military exemptions. He also said abuses continued on a large scale, prompting the government to consider changes to the system.
"The mobilization and exemption system needs to be improved — that is an indisputable fact," Koretskyi said, adding that the General Staff needs additional soldiers to fight Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion, now in its fifth year.
But he said it was too early to criticize the final rules because the government had not yet completed and published the revised regulation.
In their resolution, the lawmakers also questioned a proposed "coordination center," calling for business representatives to be included if the government decides to establish it.
Ukrspecsystems, a Ukrainian defense company that develops unmanned aircraft systems for the Defense Forces, warned that the proposed cut from 100% to 85% would hit the industry’s output.
"For production, the consequences would be immediate: delays in defense orders and an outflow of candidates who will avoid working in the defense industry because of unpredictable rules," the company said in a post on Facebook on Oct. 16.
"We expect this provision to be dropped for defense industry enterprises and the reservation rules to remain stable for the long term."

title: Russian industrial facility reportedly on fire after drone attack in Surgut region
description: Ukrainian activist and volunteer Serhii Sternenko claimed the facility was the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant, which processes gas condensate and produces petroleum products.
content:
A fire broke out at an industrial facility in Russia's Khanty-Mansi Autonomous District following a drone attack, regional governor Ruslan Kukharuk said on Oct. 16, while Ukrainian activist Serhii Sternenko said the facility was the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant.
"As a result of a drone attack on an industrial facility in the Surgut district, a fire broke out. Emergency services are working at the scene," Kukharuk said .
He added that specialists were assessing the scale and nature of the damage. Kukharuk did not identify the facility or say who was responsible for the attack.
"The Defense Forces struck the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant," Serhii Sternenko, a Ukrainian activist and volunteer who previously served as an adviser to then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, said . The facility is located more than 2,400 kilometers (1,490 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
In videos shared by Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova , a large fire and thick dark smoke can be seen on the territory of an industrial facility.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify that the facility reportedly hit was the Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant. Ukrainian officials have not publicly claimed responsibility for the attack.
The Surgut plant processes gas condensate and produces petroleum products, including motor and aviation fuel. Its designed processing capacity reaches 12 million metric tons of raw materials per year, Sternenko said.
The reported strike comes amid a dispute between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil and energy infrastructure.
U.S. President Donald Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for rising global fuel prices, a claim disputed by energy experts . His administration also threatened to cut intelligence sharing and weapons support unless Kyiv stopped targeting Russian energy facilities, according to Ukrainian and European officials.
On Oct. 9, Trump announced a deal allowing Russia to supply diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets despite sanctions imposed following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russia subsequently eased restrictions on diesel exports.
Two days later, Trump announced what he described as an "energy ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine. Ukrainian officials said Kyiv had not been informed of the agreement in advance.
Ukraine initially halted strikes on Russian refineries following the announcement, while Russia continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure. On Oct. 15, Zelensky said that Kyiv had lifted the pause due to Moscow's continued attacks.
"The block is out. We're done," Zelensky said.

title: Amid Trump tensions, Zelensky says Ukraine will stand its ground — with Europe's support
description: "I am standing up for Ukraine's interests solely and the people of Ukraine. We were attacked, we were occupied, our people were killed," Zelensky said when asked to comment on Trump's latest attacks against him.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked Washington for its support for Ukraine during an Oct. 16 press conference in Brussels, but made clear that the U.S. is one country among many, and he will stand up to it if he has to.
"I am standing up for Ukraine's interests solely and the people of Ukraine. We were attacked, we were occupied, our people were killed," Zelensky said when asked to comment on U.S. President Donald Trump's latest attacks against him.
"Yesterday, there were a thousand drones in Ukraine. A thousand. But the American side said that it's 'difficult to speak with Zelensky. It's less difficult to manage with (Russian President Vladimir) Putin.' Of course," Zelensky retorted.
Zelensky also challenged Trump's broader approach to Russia over the past few days, saying "we cannot proceed with these diesel deals, " because it will be followed by the lifting of further sanctions on gas, banks, individuals, and Russian assets.
"If I don't stand up to this, if I don't defend against it, who else will do this?" Zelensky asked.
But Zelensky mostly spent as much time talking about the other supporters he can count on, and especially Europe.
"I feel full support from Europe now. Especially over this past month. Europe is very united," Zelensky said.
Those comments follow a wave of European condemnations of Trump's recent policy shift toward Moscow.
"We're grateful to Europe, America, and other countries. Japan has been helpful, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, everybody," Zelensky said.
The Ukrainian leader underscored the role that countries besides the U.S. play in providing military support to the war-ravaged country.
On PAC2 and PAC3 Patriot interceptor missiles, Zelensky said, "We are receiving them not only from the U.S. We are working with Europe; we are working with other countries in the world."
Along with being "grateful" to the White House and to the U.S., Zelensky thanked NATO and "the Europeans, who are financing all of this."
And on intelligence sharing, Zelensky said that "many countries are sharing their intel with us. We are talking about dozens of countries."
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot mentioned the day before that intelligence from his country accounts for two-thirds of the total going to Ukraine.
And "together with the Europeans we will produce our anti-ballistic system Freyja," Zelensky said, emphasizing that Ukraine is working to be "as independent as possible."
The Freyja project "involves tens of countries... we will break through this barrier, and we will produce our own anti-ballistic system that is quicker to produce, cheaper to produce," Zelensky said.
Even on the diplomatic front, Zelensky suggested Europe was coming into its own, noting that European allies are taking steps to create a new format for engaging with Russia and to facilitate dialogue with the U.S.
For Zelensky, Europe's united backing "does help. It does influence the relationship with America."
"Our European colleagues support and only support," Zelensky said.

title: 'Gas deals will follow' — Zelensky warns Trump could ease more sanctions on Russia
description: "It will all come down to the banking system, individual people, and the chemical industry," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump's diesel deal with Russia risks paving the way for further sanctions relief for Moscow, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 16.
Zelensky warned that easing sanctions could eventually lead to the normalization of relations with Moscow, despite Russia showing no readiness to agree to even a ceasefire in Ukraine .
"There's intuition, there's intelligence, and there are various details," Zelensky told reporters in Brussels.
"In my view, we cannot accept these agreements. Because gas deals will follow. And I am absolutely certain of this. After gas, they will lift sanctions on other things as well."
"It will all come down to the banking system, individual people, and the chemical industry."
Zelensky said his main concern was the fate of frozen Russian assets. European diplomats previously told the Kyiv Independent that Moscow was seeking their release from the United States in exchange for agreeing to an energy ceasefire with Ukraine.
"What I consider to be risks are frozen assets," he said. "If I don't defend them, who will do it?"
The deal has strained Ukraine-U.S. relations after Washington unexpectedly announced an arrangement allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed over Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zelensky criticized the decision on Oct. 9, warning that allowing Russia to export diesel would provide Moscow with additional revenue to sustain its war.
"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the moment when we are talking about peace, the U.S. is allowing Russia to export diesel."
Tensions had already escalated after Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for rising global fuel prices, a claim disputed by experts . His administration also threatened to cut off intelligence support and arms shipments unless Kyiv halted the attacks.
The latest rift follows months of failed attempts to negotiate an end to Russia's war against Ukraine. As diplomatic efforts have stalled, Russia has continued to attack Ukrainian energy infrastructure ahead of the coming winter.
Russia offered the United States nothing in return for sanctions relief on diesel.

title: Europe's far right has a Putin problem
description:
Europe's far-right parties grow increasingly divided on something that once united them — sympathies for Vladimir Putin's Russia.

As nationalists and right-wing populists across Western Europe move closer to power, many are seeking to distance themselves from their past admiration for a country waging Europe's largest war since 1945 while conducting hybrid attacks against much of the continent.

Despite finding common ground on dislike of liberalism, NATO, and the EU, Europe's far right is bein
content:
Rassemblement National (RN) candidate Marine Le Pen in Paris, France, on Sept. 28, 2026. (Anne-Christine Poujoulat / AFP via Getty Images)
Europe's far-right parties grow increasingly divided on something that once united them — sympathies for Vladimir Putin's Russia.
As nationalists and right-wing populists across Western Europe move closer to power, many are seeking to distance themselves from their past admiration for a country waging Europe's largest war since 1945 while conducting hybrid attacks against much of the continent.
Despite finding common ground on dislike of liberalism, NATO, and the EU, Europe's far right is being forced to rethink its relationship with Moscow — much like it had to do with U.S. President Donald Trump.
France 's National Rally (RN) and the U.K.'s Nigel Farage now harden rhetoric on Russia while signaling a more conditional, rather than simply hostile, approach to Ukraine, as part of a strategy to cast a wider net of voters.
But the Alternative for Germany (AfD), which has emerged as Europe's largest and most extreme nationalist party, is moving in the opposite direction.
The split comes at a critical moment. The National Rally's Marine Le Pen is a frontrunner for the French presidential election next April, the AfD is leading the German polls, and Farage's Reform party was, until very recently, a favorite to win the next elections in Britain.
Experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent explain the reasons behind this divide and what the coming string of European elections could mean for Ukraine.
For years, far-right leaders have been ranked among the most Moscow-friendly voices in European politics.
In 2014, Farage, the man who later led a campaign to push the U.K. out of the EU and whose Reform party now polls second at 22%, expressed his admiration for Putin as an "operator."
As recently as 2024, while Russia’s full-scale invasion had already been raging for two years, he suggested that the eastward expansion of the EU and NATO provoked the war.
Comments like these have made it easy for his opponents to blast him as a Putin fan.
Now, Farage seems intent on proving he is no such thing.
"Russia in general and Putin in particular are extremely unpopular with Brits, so why would they want to convey the impression that they have any sympathy with them?"
Last year, the Reform leader called the Russian dictator a "very bad dude" and said NATO should shoot down Russian jets intruding into its airspace.
On Ukraine, he has cautiously affirmed support for Ukraine — even backing the idea of using frozen Russian assets for Kyiv's benefit.
And while he criticized plans for a post-war " reassurance " force in Ukraine as outlined by the Labor government, Farage backed sending British troops to the country, if on a temporary basis and as part of a U.N. peacekeeping mission.
Reports have emerged that Farage is even considering a trip to Ukraine as part of his quest to brush off his Russia-friendly image.
A similar shift is taking place across the English Channel.
Prior to 2022, Le Pen said that the Russian occupation of Crimea was not illegal, and her party took out a loan from a Russian bank.
But after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, she backpedaled.
Now, the three-time failed presidential candidate sees she has a real chance to win, with a court clearing a path to her candidacy despite last year's embezzlement conviction.
As the vote nears, she is treading cautiously on foreign policy.
Le Pen has condemned Russian aggression and has backed continued military assistance to Ukraine, even as she wants Paris to cut financial aid — citing France's own budget constraints — opposes Kyiv's EU membership , and is skeptical about future EU aid if it burdens France.
She also said she would be happy to visit Ukraine for talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The RN's younger co-leader, Jordan Bardella, has taken a tougher stance on Russia, naming the country a threat — something that Le Pen avoided in a recent interview with the Financial Times .
Both party chiefs also blasted Moscow in September over its seizure of European business assets in the country and denounced Russian interference and destabilization efforts.
Elsewhere in Europe, far-right parties have proved they can tone down their views on Russia and Ukraine in exchange for government seats.
Matteo Salvini, head of Italy's League party, remembered for once sporting a T-shirt with Putin's likeness, has largely fallen in line behind Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni's firmly pro-Western, pro-Ukraine course, save for some symbolic resistance.
And the former Dutch government also maintained its support for Kyiv, even though Geert Wilders's far-right Party for Freedom (PVV) was the strongest party in a short-lived coalition.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, a right-wing populist, while expressing his disdain for EU plans to earmark billions of euros of support for Ukraine, echoed Zelensky's take on a set of recent pro-Russian moves made by the U.S.
"Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin, and we have to do something," Babis said on Oct. 16.
This shift is far from uniform, however.
As Meloni, Italy's right-wing, anti-immigration prime minister, prepares for the 2027 elections, she faces a new pro-Kremlin challenger.
Roberto Vannacci, a retired army general, left the League in February to found his own nationalist party, National Future.
Vannacci, a former military attaché in Moscow, has famously said he prefers Putin over Zelensky.
With support reaching as high as 8% in recent polls, National Future has already surpassed Meloni's junior coalition partners.
But the most striking example is the AfD, currently the strongest opposition party in Germany, nearing 30% in polls.
The AfD was seen as so extreme that the far-right European Parliament group expelled it at the RN's urging in 2024, prompting the AfD to form a new ultranationalist coalition, Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN).
The party campaigns on a halt to military and financial aid to Ukraine, the lifting of sanctions against Russia, and the resumption of Russian energy purchases.
Given the AfD's particular brand of extremism and Berlin's role as the leading military donor to Ukraine, this is an especially worrying signal for Kyiv and Europe.
Like in the U.K., the next German parliamentary elections are expected no later than 2029.
With Russia's full-scale war nearing its fifth anniversary, many countries have seen the public's support for Ukraine cool — but not collapse.
Politicians vying for victory in upcoming elections have to take this into account, with the U.K. being a prime example.
Farage's party certainly has a reputation to fix, after its former leader in Wales, Nathan Gill, was sentenced to prison for taking bribes from pro-Russian Ukrainian politicians.
"Russia in general and Putin in particular are extremely unpopular with Brits, so why would they want to convey the impression that they have any sympathy with them?" Tim Bale, a professor of politics at Queen Mary University of London, comments on Reform's strategy.
A poll from last fall shows that 59% of Brits support continued assistance to Ukraine, and slightly over half back sanctions even at the cost of paying more for energy and food.
The support is somewhat cooler in France, where 47% favor continued arms deliveries to Ukraine, down from 65% in 2022.
Yet this is not an insignificant number, and the majority of French people — including a little over half of RN voters — see Russia as an enemy , according to polls.
Anton Shekhovtsov, a visiting senior fellow at Central European University in Vienna, notes that Le Pen likely remembers well the "reputational nightmare" her Russian loan has caused.
"Everybody just pointed to that loan and said, 'you're all Russian Trojan horses in France,'" Shekhovtsov said in comments for the Kyiv Independent.
Now, Le Pen likely sees an example in Meloni — a politician who emerged from a similar far-right background but maintained a pro-Western course, the expert notes. Meloni's government has been Italy's longest-serving since World War II.
But the AfD has doubled down on its pro-Russian course, despite the majority of Germans continuing to support Ukraine. It does not seem to be hindering its rise.
Jakub Wondreys, a researcher at the Hannah Arendt Institute for the Research on Totalitarianism in Dresden, offers an explanation.
"The key factor is the party's internal division, which we don't see elsewhere. It is specific to German politics, and to the AfD itself," Wondreys tells the Kyiv Independent.
While all parties have different wings, the AfD is notably decentralized, with the former border between West and East Germany surviving as a key divide.
The AfD's extremist, more Moscow-friendly wing is rooted in East Germany, a former Soviet satellite state. The "moderates" are stronger in the west, the researcher explains.
The AfD is growing nationwide, but the east remains its main stronghold — as evidenced by its recent victories in regional elections there. This means that the more extreme wing of the party is also its loudest and most influential one.
This split was laid bare when the AfD's two leaders, Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla, disagreed over a trip by a group of their colleagues to Sochi last November.
Weidel, who hails from what was West Germany, criticized the visit, while Chrupalla, himself born in socialist East Germany, downplayed it, adding that he does not consider Russia a threat.
Recent polls show that 54% of Germans from what was East Germany think aid to Ukraine has gone too far, compared to 39% in the west. Eastern Germans are also less likely to see Russia as a threat.
Yet even an RN or Reform victory would not bode well for Ukraine, regardless of their change of rhetoric, experts warn.
As Bale points out, no matter its public posturing, a Reform government "might try to spend less money on defense aid behind everyone's back."
Just on Oct. 12, Farage pledged to take a "keen look" at whether British aid to Ukraine is being swallowed up by corruption there and signaled that London's support cannot be limitless.
The RN's victory might not end military support for Ukraine, but it will likely curtail the financial assistance and weaken the European sanctions push against Moscow.
And Shekhovtsov warns that even if Le Pen does not adopt overtly pro-Russian positions after the elections, her victory could be such an upset for France and Europe that it might shift political attention away from supporting Ukraine.
The coming election season has the potential to shake the European pro-Ukraine coalition to its core.
I hope you enjoyed this article. In our team, we believe fact-based reporting should be available to all – that's why we don't use any paywall.
If you'd like to help us provide you with more in-depth coverage of Ukraine's struggle against Russian aggression, European politics, and other topics, please consider joining the Kyiv Independent community .
Martin Fornusek is an assistant editor at the Kyiv Independent. Until recently, Martin held the role of foreign affairs reporter specializing in international and regional politics, history, and disinformation. Based in Lviv, Martin often reports on international politics, focusing on developments related to Ukraine and Russia. His career in journalism began in 2021 after graduating from Masaryk University in Brno, Czechia, earning a Master's degree in Conflict and Democracy Studies. Martin has been invited to speak on Times Radio, France 24, Czech Television, and Radio Free Europe. He speaks English, Czech, and Ukrainian.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 3, injure 53 across Ukraine, as Moscow hammers energy infrastructure
description: Ukraine's Air Force said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 149 Shahed-type drones, 108 of them jet-powered.
content:
At least three people were killed and 52 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russian attacks targeted energy infrastructure in several oblasts, regional authorities said on Oct. 16.
In western Volyn Oblast , Russian attacks injured two people and left 370,000 people without electricity, regional governor Roman Romaniuk said. Russian attacks with jet-powered Shahed-type drones across 20 locations destroyed civilian and critical infrastructure, the governor added.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 149 Shahed-type drones, 108 of them jet-powered. The Air Force said it neutralized 114 of the Russian drones, 108 of them jet-powered, across 24 locations.
In Kyiv , a Russian drone crashed in Kyiv's Pechersk District on Oct. 15, injuring seven people and causing damage to a residential building, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Three of the injured people were hospitalized, Klitschko said . The Russian drone crashed near a five-story residential building, damaging the facades of nearby buildings, as well as setting a car on fire, he added.
In Kyiv Oblast , two people were injured over the past day, according to regional governor Tymur Tkachenko . One person was injured during a morning attack in the Fastiv District that also damaged eight residential buildings on Oct. 14, while another person was injured after a Russian attack in the Buchan District on the morning of Oct. 15.
In Kharkiv Oblast , three people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Among the three injured was a 105-year-old woman, Syniehubov said. Russia attacked the oblast with glide bombs, missiles, and FPV-drones across four settlements, the governor added.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , Russian attacks over the past day killed one person and injured six others, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin . One person was killed and three injured in Kramatorsk, while three others were injured in Sloviansk, Filashkin said. Russian attacks also damaged private houses, infrastructure, shops, and cars.
In Cherkasy Oblast , Russian attacks on the city of Uman injured five people, regional governor Ihor Taburets said. Three injured people were hospitalized, and a Russian attack elsewhere led to a fire in a warehouse, the governor said.
In southern Kherson Oblast , two people were killed and six others injured over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Russia struck the oblast with artillery fire and drones, Prokudin said, damaging residential areas and social infrastructure.
In Rivne Oblast , seven people sought medical help after a Russian attack on civilian infrastructure, including residential buildings, according to regional governor Oleksandr Koval . None of the seven injured had to be hospitalized, Koval said.
A Russian attack on Ternopil Oblast , injured five people on Oct. 15, as Russia attacked the city twice, setting fire to a business building, according to regional governor Taras Pastukh .
In northeastern Sumy Oblast, six people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, the Sumy military administration said. Russian troops carried out 70 attacks on 38 settlements, using artillery, mortars, FPV-drones, UAVs, and glide bombs, the administration said.
In southern Odesa Oblast , four people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, according to regional governor Oleh Kiper . Russia struck private houses, a manufacturing enterprise, as well as energy infrastructure, the governor added.

title: Zelensky, Hungary's Magyar hold first 'one-on-one' talks at EU summit
description: "We see the Ukrainian parliament's adoption of the minority education law and the immediate start of its implementation as a first step towards rebuilding mutual trust," Magyar said on X after the meeting.
content:
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky and Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar met for their first bilateral talks in Brussels on Oct. 16, as their countries seek to open a "new chapter" in relations.
Both leaders are in Brussels for a two-day EU summit, where Kyiv seeks to drum up European support amid deteriorating ties with the U.S.
The meeting comes the same week Zelensky signed a law on the educational rights of Ukraine's national minorities, a step Hungary had demanded before allowing Kyiv's EU accession talks to proceed.
"We see the Ukrainian parliament's adoption of the minority education law and the immediate start of its implementation as a first step towards rebuilding mutual trust," Magyar said on X after the meeting.
The Hungarian prime minister also said that both countries would continue talks at the ministerial level, focusing on the situation of national minorities.
Magyar underscored that both countries agreed on the need "to build a new foundation for our political and economic relations" and expressed solidarity with Ukraine in the face of "Russia's brutal aggression."
After Ukraine passed the minorities bill, Hungary lifted its veto on the opening of two more negotiation clusters for Ukraine, allowing their official launch on Oct. 13.
The law gives Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking minority and other EU-language minorities more room to use their native language in education.
Ukrainian officials have said it would formalize existing education rights for national minorities rather than bring major practical changes.
Roughly 80,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine's westernmost Zakarpattia Oblast.
Zelensky said the meeting focused on Ukraine's EU accession efforts, as well as opportunities for bilateral cooperation, trade, and agricultural issues.
"We also discussed diplomacy and efforts to end Russia's war," the president said, adding that the leaders agreed to exchange visits.
"We're moving on our relationship with Hungary; we had a very good meeting," Zelensky said later at a press conference in Brussels. He did not rule out traveling to Budapest.
"I hope that we will get to the point where a new chapter opens (in Hungarian-Ukrainian relations)," Magyar said about his meeting with Zelensky a day prior, saying the two could then meet again in Berehove, a Zakarpattia Oblast town considered the heart of the Hungarian-speaking community in Ukraine.
Magyar has floated a meeting in Berehove since the spring, but no firm date has been set so far. The two held brief conversations in June in Brussels, and then again in July at the NATO summit in Ankara.

title: Ukrainian military strikes million-dollar Russian radar in Krasnodar Krai, General Staff claim
description: 'Striking such systems reduces the enemy's ability to monitor airspace and detect aerial assets in time. The estimated cost of the radar station is about US $100 million,' the General Staff said.
content:
The Ukrainian military struck a Russian Nebo-U radar near the settlement of Magri, in Krasnodar Krai, on the night of Oct. 16, according to the Ukrainian General Staff.
"The Nebo-U is a long-range, three-coordinate radar designed to detect and track aerial assets, including aircraft, cruise missiles and ballistic missiles," the General Staff said in a statement .
"Striking such systems reduces the enemy's ability to monitor airspace and detect aerial assets in time. The estimated cost of the radar station is about US $100 million," they said.
The General Staff did not give details about what Ukrainian munition was used to carry out the strike.
A day prior, an overnight attack on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia's Voronezh region carried out with the Neptune coastal missile system hit six Su-34M bomber jets, destroying four and damaging two, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 15.
On Aug. 23, Ukrainian drones struck two Russian fighter jets, a large missile-carrying drone, high-value radars, and other air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said then.
Krasnodar Krai, a strategic region along Russia's Black Sea coast, has increasingly come under Ukrainian drone attacks as Kyiv extends the range of its strikes deep into Russian territory.

title: Emergency blackouts in Kyiv, as Klitschko announces start of heating season
description: Kyiv's centralised heating systems will be turned on, starting with social institutions such as schools, hospitals, and kindergartens. The decision was sparked by "extreme conditions" created by constant bombardment, Klitschko said.
content:
Emergency blackouts were implemented across Kyiv due to Russian attacks on the city's energy infrastructure, Ukraine's biggest private energy firm DTEK said on Oct. 16, as Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko announced the start of the city's heating season.
"We remind you that during emergency shutdowns, schedules are not valid," DTEK said . Kyiv already operates under scheduled power outages , allowing residents to plan their days around them, but Russian attacks on the city's energy infrastructure led to additional emergency power outages over the past weeks.
On the same day, Klitschko announced that Kyiv's centralised heating system will be turned on, starting with social institutions such as schools, hospitals, and kindergartens. The decision was sparked by "extreme conditions" created by constant bombardment, Klitschko said.
Two areas of the city, the Dniprovskyi and Darnytskyi districts, would not have their centralised heating switched on due to "significant damage" to a power facility in the area, Klitschko said, while repair efforts were ongoing.
Kyiv, a city the size of Berlin, is home to over 3 million people, with average temperatures of -4.6 degrees Celsius to -1 degrees Celsius (23.7 degrees Fahrenheit to 30 degrees Fahrenheit) in the winter months.
In Kyiv Oblast, Buchanan, Obukhiv, and Fastiv districts were also experiencing emergency blackouts, DTEK said .
In Western Ukraine, the city of Lutsk was left without power, Andriy Razumovsky, secretary of Lutsk City Council, announced on social media.
"Due to an attack by enemy drones, the city was left without electricity. Utilities are operating on backup power sources," Razumovsky said .
Overnight on Oct. 13 to 14, Russia launched a large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv, wreaking destruction in a residential neighborhood and targeting several energy facilities in Kyiv.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that all three of the city's combined heat and power stations were attacked, as well as critical infrastructure in the Kyiv Oblast that provide power to Kyiv and central regions.
"The targets of Russian ballistic missiles were power system facilities in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and the region," he said.
"Overnight, the Russians deployed 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media on Oct.14, adding that 600,000 people were left without power.

title: Austria slams Ukraine's opaque finances, with 'so many numbers swirling around'
description: "We have to classify so that we know how we can shape the support and solidarity with Ukraine in the future," Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker said.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker criticized the lack of transparency in Ukraine's finances, as President Volodmyr Zelensky attends the Oct. 16 EU leaders' summit to lobby for more financial support.
"So many numbers are swirling around that you have to put them in order... you have to make it transparent, where this (budget) hole comes from," Stocker told journalists.
Zelensky is asking EU allies for increased budgetary support, with Kyiv foreseeing a sizeable budget gap for 2027, though the exact size remains difficult to determine.
However, Stocker was not against providing financial support for Ukraine, as his Czech counterpart, Andrej Babis, seems to be .
"We have to classify so that we know how we can shape the support and solidarity with Ukraine in the future," Stocker said.
The Kyiv Independent reviewed the draft budget in Ukraine's parliament, which, as of Oct. 7 , contained a Hr 1.66 trillion ($40 billion) budget shortfall for 2027.
