But then Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi wrote on social media on Oct. 14 that Ukraine's needs for 2027 "top $52 billion." He also said the "military's off-budget requirement is estimated at $45 billion."
Adding to the confusion is that officials either refer to a single budget hole or spin out the country's defense needs as a separate financial gap.
A senior EU official familiar with Ukraine's 2027 financial planning strategy told the Kyiv Independent that the numbers Koretskyi posted are "again new numbers."
The estimates the EU had received amounted to approximately 70 billion euros ($78.8 billion), the official said.
Stocker said he is ready to believe Ukraine about rising costs "due to these intensified and massive attacks by Russia... but the fact that this is immediately reflected in a budget gap is something you will have to talk about."

title: 4 Russian drones violate Moldovan airspace during overnight attack against Ukraine
description: The incidents underscore the growing security risks posed to Moldova and the region by Russia's war against neighboring Ukraine.
content:
Yet another series of Russian drone incursions into Moldova's airspace was recorded during the latest overnight attack against Ukraine, Moldova's Defense Ministry reported on Oct. 16.
Between 11:02 p.m. on Oct. 15 and 3:46 a.m. local time on Oct. 16, Moldova's Defense Ministry s aid three Russian drones crossed into the country's territory before returning to Ukraine's airspace.
A fourth drone entered at 5:59 a.m. and reentered again at 6:09 a.m. before turning back to Ukraine.
The incidents underscore the growing security risks posed to Moldova and the region by Russia's war against neighboring Ukraine.
Russian aerial incursions into Moldovan territory during attacks against Ukraine are becoming alarmingly routine, with five Russian drones and missiles exploding on Moldova's territory on Oct. 3 alone.
Chisinau has repeatedly raised the alarm about these airspace violations, with Moldovan President Maia Sandu declaring that Russia's war against Ukraine is "dangerously reaching Moldova."
Moldova announced plans on Oct. 7 to build shelters at border crossings to protect border guards and people nearby in response to growing incursions.
The announcement came after the Moldovan Border Police reported on Oct. 5 that a projectile fired during a Russian attack against Ukraine ricocheted and struck a passenger bus and a border control booth at the Palanca-Maiaky-Udobne crossing, lightly injuring a border guard.
Russia also struck border crossings between Ukraine and nearby Romania in early September.

title: Czech Prime Minister Babis rails against EU budget support for Ukraine
description: "I don't like that there are 100 billion euros ($112 billion) from the European budget for Ukraine, that this money should be borrowed," said Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis.
content:
Editor's note: The story has been expanded with additional comments made by Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis expressed his disdain for EU plans to earmark billions of euros of support for Ukraine in its next seven-year budget, in comments made to journalists at the Oct. 16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels.
The EU operates on a seven-year budget cycle that needs to be unanimously agreed upon, and leaders hope to reach consensus on the 2028-2034 budget before the end of the year, as 2027 will be a bumper year for elections across the bloc.
While consensus on the budget as a whole remains out of reach, support for Ukraine seemed like a consensus issue until Babis' latest comments.
"I don't like that there are 100 billion euros ($112 billion) from the European budget for Ukraine, that this money should be borrowed," Babis said.
"It should not be in the multi-year financial framework, where member states don't have enough money," he added.
The 100 billion euros figure is already outdated, reflecting the amount initially proposed for the budget by the European Commission earlier in the year.
That figure was reduced to 89 billion euros ($100 billion) in June as part of a first compromise proposal, and it remained unchanged in the second and latest compromise , published Oct. 10.
"In any case, Czechia will not guarantee for it," Babis added.
Surprising in the other direction was Babis' criticism of U.S. President Donald Trump, after portraying himself as aligned with Trump for several years. "Trump effectively betrayed us by concluding the business deal with Putin , and we have to do something," Babis said, echoing President Volodymyr Zelensky's take on a set of recent pro-Russian moves made by the U.S. against Ukraine. Babis said the day before that Europe needs to agree on how to proceed with issues such as peace talks, given that at the moment, "we are completely out." His turn on Trump brings Babis closer to the European mainstream, with many EU leaders not holding back in condemning the U.S. president for his latest overtures towards Moscow.

title: Poland provided aid to defend Kyiv, Zelensky says
description: Zelensky said Poland had provided ammunition used by Ukraine's anti-aircraft guns, but also hinted at other support which would have to remain confidential.
content:
Polish aid helped Ukraine defend Kyiv during recent attacks, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on the sidelines of the European Council summit in Brussels where he met with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk on Oct. 15.
Zelensky said Poland had provided ammunition used by Ukraine's anti-aircraft guns. Zelensky also hinted at other, more sensitive Polish support which would have to remain confidential; "sometimes it should remain between the two of us," he said.
Tusk gave Ukraine message of solidarity - "you are not alone."
"I would like to assure you, as I have already stated publicly here: Ukraine, your people and you personally – you are not alone… you can count on me personally, on Poland, and also on the EU. After my talks here in Brussels with all the leaders, it is absolutely clear that anything that could help Putin and Russia in this war is unacceptable for Europe and Poland," the Polish Prime Minister said .
In response, Zelensky thanked Tusk for Poland's help for Ukraine as it faces an upsurge in Russian attacks.
"We are very grateful to the Prime Minister, his team, the government, and the entire Polish people for standing with us in this absolutely barbaric war waged by Russia against Ukraine. Thank you for your support and for maintaining close contact throughout these extremely difficult months. These are very hard times. It is no longer just about days and nights – they are attacking us 24/7,” Zelensky said .
The meeting comes as tensions between Kyiv and Washington D.C. show no sign of easing, amid an American push to strong-arm Ukraine into ceasing drone attacks on Russian oil refineries. President Donald Trump has recently falsely blamed Ukraine for record high diesel prices sparked by America's faltering war with Iran.
Polish and Ukrainian relations have also been strained in recent months. In May, a decision by Ukraine to name a military unit in honor of the Ukrainian Insurgent Army led to Polish President Karol Nawrotski stripping Zelensky of Poland's "Order of the White Eagle".
Yet, Poland remains an important strategic partner for Ukraine, as well as a critical source of military materiel.
The same day, in Warsaw, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced that Ukraine expects to purchase an additional 125 million euros (about $1.484 million) worth of Polish weaponry by the end of 2026, financed by a loan from the Polish government.
"We are currently discussing how to finalize this agreement. I hope this will happen in the near future—by the end of the year—since there is political will for it, and funds have been allocated in Poland’s budget,” Sybiha said.
Ukraine is Poland's biggest arms-export customer, taking two thirds of Polish armaments production in 2025, spending 1.68 billion euros (about $1.90 billion) on Polish arms. Besides supplying armaments on a commercial basisPoland has also donated significant amounts of military materiel to Ukraine, including tanks, fighter jets, and artillery systems.

title: Zelensky thanks EU's 'real leaders' for their continued support as bloc confirms new sanctions package on the way
description: "We supported Trump's energy ceasefire but we see Russia did not respect it, and so we have to increase the pressure," von der Leyen told journalists, before announcing that the EU is working on a new 22nd package of sanctions against Russia.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived for the second day of an EU leaders' summit on Oct. 16, ready to discuss support for Ukraine's energy grid, 2027 budget, and EU membership bid.
Zelensky's visit comes as the U.S. government pivots in a decidedly pro-Russian direction, leading Kyiv and Brussels to condemn Washington's betrayal of Ukraine and emphasize their close ties.
"Our message to President Zelensky is very simple. The support of the EU to Ukraine remains as strong as ever. This is no time to withdraw support... no time to relieve Russia sanctions. It is time to increase our support, increase our pressure," European Council President Antonio Costa said.
"I cannot count the many times you were here, and it shows the closeness that we have," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen added.
"I'm so thankful that we have such huge support from EU leaders, real leaders," Zelensky said ahead of the EU leaders meeting, accompanied by Costa and von der Leyen.
"I am thankful the EU stands with us," Zelensky said.
"We supported Trump's energy ceasefire, but we see Russia did not respect it, and so we have to increase the pressure," von der Leyen told journalists, before announcing that the EU is working on a new 22nd package of sanctions against Russia.
"Dear Volodymyr, you can count on us not only to support you in war but most importantly for your future as a member of the EU," Costa said.
Costa and von der Leyen both congratulated Zelensky and Ukraine's parliament for passing key reforms that allowed Kyiv's EU membership bid to proceed earlier in the week.
"The goal is toward the end of the year to open the final two clusters," von der Leyen said, in reference to the to-do lists of reforms Ukraine is partway through unlocking.
Zelensky then headed to a meeting with Costa and von der Leyen, after which they are expected to announce a new dedicated EU task force to help Ukraine advance the rule of law, which is essential for the country to unlock EU support funds and become a member of the bloc.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,561,020 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,790 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,561,020 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 16.
The number includes 1,790 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,414 tanks, 25,552 armored combat vehicles, 163,554 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,242 artillery systems, 2,217 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,708 air defense systems, 449 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,958 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Investigation: The romance scam tricking men into ‘rescuing’ Ukrainian women from Russian occupation
description:
Stefan, a 48-year-old Austrian national whose name has been changed at his request, had been looking for a Ukrainian partner. Having previously dated a Ukrainian woman, he said he was drawn to what he viewed as the importance of family in Ukrainian culture.

He met "Alona Panchenko," who claimed to be from the Russian-occupied city of Enerhodar in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, on the international dating website Christian Cupid. Soon after they matched, she suggested moving their conversation to email.
content:
The Kyiv Independent uncovers how scammers on dating sites pose as women trapped in Russian-occupied Ukraine, using fake identities to talk foreign men into sending them money. (Daria Filippova / The Kyiv Independent)
Stefan, a 48-year-old Austrian national whose name has been changed at his request, had been looking for a Ukrainian partner. Having previously dated a Ukrainian woman, he said he was drawn to what he viewed as the importance of family in Ukrainian culture.
He met "Alona Panchenko," who claimed to be from the Russian-occupied city of Enerhodar in Zaporizhzhia Oblast, on the international dating website Christian Cupid. Soon after they matched, she suggested moving their conversation to email.
As their relationship continued, however, he began noticing that something was off.
Over the next three months, they exchanged lengthy emails but never spoke by phone or video. "Alona" said she had no mobile phone and could only communicate via an old tablet connected to public Wi-Fi due to conditions in occupied Enerhodar.
Her story grew increasingly desperate. She said she was unemployed, had run out of money, and had even been hospitalized with "severe exhaustion" after going two days without food. Eventually, she told Stefan the only way they could meet was if he helped her escape the occupied territory.
To support her story, "Alona" regularly sent photos that supposedly showed herself and life in Enerhodar.
The evidence she provided was fabricated. The Kyiv Independent traced her portraits to another person, found that photos she claimed she had taken in Enerhodar came from a local media outlet, and identified signs of AI manipulation in some images and videos. The ID she shared also contained an invalid number and an AI-edited portrait.
The request for money revealed another inconsistency. "Alona" instructed Stefan to list Ukraine as the recipient's country of residence when making the transfer through Western Union. That contradicted her claim that she was living in Russia-occupied Enerhodar, where Western Union does not operate.
Stefan says he never sent the money. But other men interviewed by the Kyiv Independent did.
Since 2022, the non-profit Helping to Leave has received thousands of requests to rescue people from Russian-occupied territories. Some of those requests were to rescue women who may have never existed at all.
The charity has helped thousands of people flee occupied areas , and its team was used to urgent pleas for evacuation. But over time, a different kind of request began arriving.
Foreign men started writing to Helping to Leave asking to rescue Ukrainian women they had met online, women they believed were trapped in Russian-occupied territories .
Some asked the charity to arrange an evacuation. Others had already sent money, believing they were paying for the woman's escape and that they would finally meet once she reached safety. They never did.
Over the past four years, the non-profit says it has received around 200 such requests, which now arrive up to four times a week, according to Nataliia, the project's communications specialist, who asked to be identified only by her first name due to the sensitive nature of her work with people in Russian-occupied territories.
Ukrainian and international media have long documented romance scams in which foreign men send money or travel to Ukraine to meet women who turn out to be fake. But the war has given scammers a new way to exploit the sympathy of unsuspecting foreigners.
An investigation by the Kyiv Independent into 58 cases referred by Helping to Leave found evidence that many of the women were not under Russian occupation at all.
Instead, scammers appeared to be using stolen photos, fake identities, forged documents, and, in some cases, AI-manipulated images and videos to convince men to send money.
The Kyiv Independent spoke to two foreign men who had online relationships with women claiming to be trapped in Russian-occupied territories. Their stories followed a pattern: no video calls, escalating crises, and urgent requests for money.
Karsten R., a German citizen, described a similar experience to that of Stefan with a woman calling herself "Viktoriia Kremenchutska." She claimed to be trapped in Russian-occupied territory, avoided video calls, and asked for money to escape.
After Karsten agreed to send money, she said she had begun her journey. But as she supposedly made her way out, she repeatedly asked for more funds — first to cross the checkpoint between occupied and Ukrainian-controlled territories, then to pay off an alleged debt she said was preventing her from leaving.
The documents and images she sent were also fake. Her passport copy was forged — the photo was photoshopped, the surname had a typo, and the font was inconsistent with a Ukrainian passport, the Kyiv Independent found. The photos, supposedly of her, turned out to be images of another woman — a woman from Russia . Other photos showed signs of AI manipulation.
"I told her, 'I want to see your suitcases. I want to see you holding a piece of paper with my name and the date on it," Karsten told the Kyiv Independent. He received the photo he demanded — but the Kyiv Independent confirmed it was AI-edited.
Even after discovering the fake documents and images, Karsten struggled to let go. At one point, he considered driving to a Ukrainian border crossing when "Viktoria" said she was trapped there trying to leave. Eventually, he became convinced he was talking to scammers.
The Kyiv Independent examined 58 cases referred by Helping to Leave, using available photos and contact details to trace the identities behind the profiles.
The relationships mostly started on dating websites, including UkraineDate, Christian Cupid, and International Cupid. In several instances, the women contacted men directly through Instagram or X. Some cases could not be verified because the available information, such as photos or contact details, was insufficient.
Using facial recognition tools and open-source research, the Kyiv Independent matched 22 profile photos to real women. Two more profiles appeared to rely on AI-generated identities. The remaining cases could not be verified, as they did not include any photos of the women they believed to be communicating with.
Out of the 22 profiles that used real photos, only seven used names that matched the women pictured. In some cases, the women even joined video calls to confirm their identity. But they lied about their whereabouts: the women identified were either living in Ukrainian-controlled territory or had moved abroad. None were in the Russian-occupied territories.
Not all accounts that used real women's photos actually belonged to them. In the remaining 15 cases, the names and surnames did not match the women whose photos appeared on the profiles. Ten of the 15 women were popular Instagram bloggers from Russia, Moldova, Ukraine, Germany , Denmark , and Latvia .
Dozens of women's photos were repeatedly reused across several dating profiles under different identities, often with the accounts presenting themselves as Russian women, the Kyiv Independent found.
This was the case with the images used by "Alona" and "Viktoriia," which were found across multiple profiles. The Kyiv Independent traced the photos used by "Alona" to Natalia Cernisova, a woman from Chisinau, Moldova, and those used by "Viktoriia" to Anna Kolesnyak from Russia. Both women run popular Instagram blogs.
In addition to stolen photos, the accounts used by both "Alona" and "Viktoriia" also sent images and videos that appeared to be AI-manipulated.
The profiles used by "Alona" and "Viktoriia," along with several others reviewed by the Kyiv Independent, are listed in the Ukrainian Dating Scammer Blacklist maintained by Ukrainian Passport, a platform that helps foreigners verify women from Ukraine and Russia.
An investigator with Ukrainian Passport, who asked to not be identified for safety reasons, said some scammers use content from popular Instagram influencers to create fake profiles, and in some cases may even be working with the influencers.
"If necessary, the influencer will even record a video to make the profile seem authentic, while being careful not to reveal too much. Later, she can always say it was for an audition or so. We've seen that happen before," he told the Kyiv Independent.
Anna Bauer, founder of the Kyiv-based Grace Family dating agency, described another way real women's identities can unintentionally enter the online dating ecosystem.
She said scouts sometimes recruit women for professional photo shoots, after which their photographs may be sold between dating agencies. This creates a risk that legitimate images can later be misused by fraudulent operators.
The Kyiv Independent received a response from one Ukrainian Instagram blogger, Anastasiia Mazur-Palamarchuk, whose photos were used in one of the scam profiles. She said her images were used without her consent.
"I'm not registered on any online dating website," she said.
The Kyiv Independent is listing several common lies used by scammers, based on the conversation with Nataliia from Helping to Leave and its own expertise.
Scammers often invent stories about crossing directly from occupied territories into Ukrainian-controlled areas through the front line, sometimes fabricating tales of "special drivers" or secret humanitarian corridors.
Civilians cannot cross active front lines because of ongoing fighting and the constant air attacks in front-line areas.
There is currently only one existing humanitarian corridor, located in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn Oblast. The crossing point, which is located on the Ukraine - Belarus border, is used almost exclusively by people fleeing the occupied territories.
People leaving occupied territories have to first go to Russia, then to Belarus, before reaching Ukraine or neighboring EU countries. The journey is usually made by bus or train, while specialized transportation is needed only in specific cases, such as for people with disabilities. Some also leave Russia by air, for example by flying to Georgia, though this route is less common.
While living under Russian occupation is indeed dangerous and harrowing, scammers often exaggerate the severity of their own living conditions to explain why they cannot communicate frequently, and to build sympathy with the men.
Helping to Leave gave an example of a woman who said she lived in Donetsk. She claimed she was living in her basement because of constant shelling, had almost no internet connection, and thus couldn't do a video call.
But the city of Donetsk isn't being shelled. Although Ukraine conducts drone strikes on occupied territories, it says they target military facilities. While this can't be independently verified, the reported death toll from such strikes is typically much lower than that of Russian attacks on Ukrainian civilian areas. There is no evidence that Donetsk is under such threat that residents would live in basements.
Scammers use these claims to extort more money from victims, saying the women cannot pass security checks unless bribes are paid to border guards and officials.
While before the full-scale war, bribes might have been an option for some to travel between the occupied parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts and Ukraine-held territories, this practice doesn't exist anymore as there are no checkpoints between these territories.
People who fled occupation with the help from Helping to Leave have not reported being asked to pay bribes along the way, the organization told the Kyiv Independent.
Some scammers claim they can't use phones or messaging apps or make video calls because everything is blocked under occupation.
Many popular messaging apps continue to work in occupied territories, often with the help of VPN services. Limiting communication to email allows scammers to hide their identity and manage multiple victims simultaneously without having to do voice or video calls.
Scammers claim they can't travel through Russia because they only hold Ukrainian documents. They also use this to appeal to the victim's political sympathies.
In reality, taking a Russian passport in the occupied territories is not a political choice but a matter of survival: It is nearly impossible to access healthcare without Russian documents. This is part of Russia’s policy of forced passportization in occupied Ukraine, which means many people living under occupation have likely been forced to obtain Russian documents.
Scammers also request exorbitant travel expenses, far exceeding the actual cost of public or private transportation.
According to Helping to Leave, women in these cases typically ask for around 800 euros or $800 — roughly twice the actual cost of the journey from the Russia-occupied territories to the government-controlled part of Ukraine through Belarus.
A review of emails and messages shared with Helping to Leave and the Kyiv Independent revealed recurring elements in how women claiming to be trapped in Russian-occupied territories describe their situations.
The women presented themselves as trapped and abandoned, with no help available from Ukrainian authorities or humanitarian organizations. In some cases, they suggested that evacuation assistance did not exist, leaving the men to believe they were the only ones who could help.
"Natalia (from Helping to Leave) won't help me get out of here. How can you not understand that?" "Alona" wrote to Stefan.
In reality, when women from the cases reviewed by the Kyiv Independent were referred to the non-profit, they either never contacted it or did not cooperate when coordinators tried to understand what assistance they needed.
When it came to appearing live on a video call with the men, the women similarly said it was impossible, claiming unstable internet in occupied territories, outdated devices, or blocked messaging services.
None of them shared personal social media accounts, either. But in many cases, the Kyiv Independent found that the women whose photos were used in the dating profiles were active on Instagram, where their lives looked nothing like the stories the men were being told. It is unclear whether the real women knew their images were being used.
After matching on dating websites, conversations usually moved to email, Telegram, or WhatsApp. Telegram accounts often hid phone numbers, while WhatsApp accounts were typically registered with Ukrainian numbers.
Some women also sent WhatsApp live locations that appeared to show them in occupied territories. But such data can be manipulated using GPS spoofing tools, making it unreliable as proof of someone's whereabouts. This can be done using specialized apps. The Kyiv Independent was able to share a live location in Paris while physically in Ukraine in just 10 minutes.
When the Kyiv Independent contacted the phone numbers and Telegram accounts provided by the women to the men who believed they were dating, none answered. Most phone numbers were invalid or no longer active, suggesting they may have been temporary numbers used only as burner numbers for the scam and later discarded.
When text messages and excuses failed to persuade men to send money, the people behind the profiles turned to documents to try and back up their claims.
Many women sent what they claimed were Ukrainian passports, but all except one contained signs of digital manipulation, including altered personal details, edited photographs, or invalid passport numbers, the Kyiv Independent found.
Some also sent fake travel tickets or documents that appeared to show fines or penalties allegedly preventing them from crossing the border. They claimed these payments were necessary before they could continue their journey.
Once trust had been established, requests for money followed.
Most of the women suggested cash pickup services such as Western Union, RIA, or MoneyGram. Some also requested PayPal transfers. These methods allowed money to be collected without directly revealing bank account details.
Karsten, who believed he was helping "Viktoriia" escape the city of Donetsk , received a copy of what she said was her ticket for a direct taxi ride from Russian-occupied Donetsk to Kyiv . But the route itself should have been a warning sign: That journey is impossible as it would require crossing an active front line.
He covered the 280-euro "ride." The document he was sent was a crudely photoshopped Ukrainian railway ticket.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion, civilians leaving occupied Donetsk for Ukrainian-controlled territory have generally had to travel through Russia before entering Ukraine through a third country.
Determining who was behind the scheme was one of the most difficult parts of the investigation.
In some cases, the women whose images were used in the profiles took part in the conversations themselves. The Kyiv Independent found four cases in which the women agreed to video calls with the men, confirming that the person in the photos matched the person on the call.
Many profiles never moved beyond text messages. It was much harder to determine who was actually operating the account when the photos had been taken from unrelated women and there was no live contact.
But money transfers provided some clues.
Some women asking for cash pickup through Western Union, RIA, or MoneyGram instructed the men to use the names listed on their dating profiles and to select Ukraine as the recipient's country of residence. Because cash-pickup services require recipients to show identification matching the transfer details, whoever collected the money was likely using the same identity the victim had been shown.
The instructions also contradicted their stories: Despite claiming to live under Russian occupation, the women asked men to list Ukraine as their place of residence when sending money.
While Ukraine and most of the international community recognize the occupied territories as part of Ukraine, in practice they are controlled by Russian authorities and cut off from Ukraine's financial system.
Western Union does not operate in Russian-occupied areas, a customer service representative told the Kyiv Independent. This means any money sent to Ukraine could only have been collected in Ukrainian-controlled territory, not in the occupied areas where the women claimed to live.
The Kyiv Independent also identified at least two cases with apparent links to Russia. In one, the "woman" asked the victim to pay a travel agency she said was helping her leave the country. The bank details she sent named the recipient as Vladislav Gafarov, a Russian national, with an account at a Russian bank.
The phone number the "woman" used to message the victim belongs to Gafarov, according to a leaked 2023 database of clients of Russian microfinance organizations. The same database lists him as an employee of the S.M. Budyonny Military Academy of Communications in St. Petersburg.
Another possibility is that some accounts may be managed by multiple people.
Karsten, who believed he was in a relationship with "Viktoriia," also came to suspect he had not been talking to just one person. Looking back, he noticed that the writing style would sometimes change dramatically — with some messages feeling as though they had been written by a woman, while others seemed to come from a man.
By the time he stopped sending money, Karsten had transferred 2,500 euros. Some victims sent even more: One man who contacted Helping to Leave had transferred around 9,000 euros.
The use of Ukrainian women's identities in online romance scams is nothing new.
Over the years, Ukrainian and international media have documented cases in which foreign men were persuaded to send money or travel to Ukraine to meet women they believed they had formed relationships with, only to discover the relationships were not genuine.
Some traveled across the world only to be stood up, while others realized the dates were part of a business model designed to keep them paying for restaurants, messages, translators, and other services.
Similar scams have also been reported in Russia, Belarus , Kazakhstan , Ghana, and Nigeria, among other countries.
While there are legitimate matchmaking services, past investigations have found cases in which agencies relied on fictitious profiles or paid chat operators to prolong conversations and keep foreign clients spending money.
In 2023, Ukraine's largest job-search platform Work.ua listed matchmaking agencies among common fraud operations that it blocks from its platform.
A video call should be one of the first steps when building a relationship with someone met online, according to Anna Bauer-Zuieva, owner of Grace Family, a long-running Ukrainian dating agency.
"It’s not about sending videos back and forth — it's about a real face-to-face (call)," Bauer-Zuieva told the Kyiv Independent. She said asking a person to show their surroundings during a live call can verify their story.
Scammers often rely on emotional pressure, presenting themselves as vulnerable and in urgent need of help. People looking for a genuine relationship, she said, usually do not begin by presenting themselves as someone who needs to be rescued.
For those who have already fallen victim, recovering money can be much harder. Once money has been collected by a scammer, it is generally not possible to recover it through services such as Western Union and Ria. The companies encourage customers to report suspected fraud, while PayPal advises users to contact customer support if they believe they have been targeted.
Victims can also report suspected fraud to Ukrainian police. According to Ukrainian Passport, people who are outside Ukraine can submit an application, appoint a lawyer in Ukraine to represent their interests, and provide testimony via video call.
For those who want to help people living in occupied territories, Nataliia from Helping to Leave said the safest way is to support verified humanitarian organizations rather than send money directly to someone they have only met online.
Yuliia Taradiuk and Natálie Zehnalová have contributed to this piece.
Linda is a Ukrainian junior reporter investigating Russia’s global influence and disinformation. She has over two years of experience writing news and feature stories for Ukrainian media outlets. She holds an Erasmus Mundus M.A. in Journalism, Media, and Globalisation from Aarhus University and the University of Amsterdam, where she trained in data journalism and communication studies.

title: Order limiting Starlink access for Ukraine's military came from within White House, Reuters reports
description: Starlink, implemented speed restrictions on Oct. 14 without warning, limiting speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour). The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike and interceptor drones.
content:
An order to implement speed restrictions on Starlink systems for the Ukrainian military came from within the White House, Reuters reported on Oct. 15, citing U.S. and Western officials.
Starlink, implemented speed restrictions on Oct. 14 without warning , limiting speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour). The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike and interceptor drones.
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones. It is restricted from using it inside Russia itself.
Pentagon officials received notice from within the White House that the Starshield service — Starlink's military package — needed to be slowed down, two U.S. officials, and another Western official, told Reuters on the condition of anonymity. Officials did not state who was responsible for issuing the order.
The speed restrictions were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from multiple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
Presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said that "several" military missions severely disrupting amid the restrictions.
Connectivity for Starlink systems used by the Ukrainian military have "been restored and remains operational," a source in the Defense Ministry told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15.
But a source in Ukraine's drone industry who requested anonymity due to the nature of their work told the Kyiv Independent that "in some cases, it works perfectly, in some places it does not."
While the source of the disruption has yet been publicly confirmed, Ukrainian officials as well as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have pointed towards Kyiv's deteriorating relationship with the White House.
A post on X from Musk said only U.S. President Donald Trump had the power to determine the speed restrictions for Starshield systems.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action," he said .
According to Reuters, a senior U.S. official denied that the request came from U.S. President Donald Trump.
The restrictions came as Ukraine continues to come under significant and sustained pressure from the Trump administration to cease attacks on Russian oil refineries, something Kyiv views as an essential part of its defense against Russia's invasion.
The Ukraine-U.S. relations continue to hit a low point after Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries for the rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts — and his team threatened to cut off intelligence support and arms shipments unless Kyiv halts the attacks.
Washington then unexpectedly unveiled a deal allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed due to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A few days later, on Oct. 11, Trump unilaterally announced an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, taking Ukrainian officials by surprise — as Russia continued to strike Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
Personal tensions between Trump and President Volodymyr Zelensky appeared to unravel in the days following. When asked whether he felt betrayed by Trump for the diesel export decision, the Ukrainian leader answered: "Really, ‌yes... but it's a ​little bit more complicated than ​just my ​emotions or my feelings."
In response, Trump described the Ukrainian president on Oct. 15 as "not a good guy for (the U.S.) to deal with," adding that he was "not a big fan of Zelensky."

title: Ukraine's Patriot interceptor stocks again reach critically low levels, media reports
description: Ukraine's supply of Patriot interceptor missiles has reached a critical low, multiple media outlets reported on Oct. 15 citing Ukrainian officials, as Russia intensifies attacks on energy infrastructure ahead of the upcoming winter months.
content:
Ukraine's supply of Patriot interceptor missiles has reached a critical low, multiple media outlets reported on Oct. 15 citing Ukrainian officials, as Russia intensifies attacks on energy infrastructure ahead of the upcoming winter months.
A Ukrainian official told the Washington Post that "only a couple" of Patriot missiles remain, after its Oct. 7 supply of ten missiles was depleted in Russian attacks on Kyiv. While CNN reported , citing a source familiar with the situation, that Kyiv's supply of missiles has completely run dry.
The Kyiv Independent was not immediately able to verify the number of interceptor missiles remaining.
While varying reports cite differing figures on the number of interceptor missiles remaining, Kyiv's critical shortage of air defense munitions , particularly of Patriots — the only weapons capable of reliably intercepting Russian ballistic missiles — appears evident amid the uptick of Russian strikes on the Ukrainian capital.
Days prior on Oct. 13-14, Russia launched yet another large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv targeting all three of the city's combined heat and power stations, as well as critical infrastructure in the Kyiv Oblast that provide power to Kyiv and central regions, with 39 ballistic missiles. The attack killed three women and injured another 25 people.
The source told CNN that nearly all of the Russian missiles slipped through Ukrainian air defenses amid a lack of Patriot interceptor missiles.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly called on allies to supply more of the U.S.-made Patriot missiles to Kyiv amid Russia's unrelenting attacks.
Zelensky said in August amid initial appeals during the shortage that Ukraine could destroy all Russian ballistic missiles if the United States were to sell Kyiv 10% of its Patriot interceptor missile stockpile.
Optimism grew in Kyiv in September amid Zelensky's announcement that U.S. President Donald Trump had approved granting Ukraine licenses to produce Patriot air defense missiles.
In recent weeks, however, tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have continued to grow, leading to uncertainty in future relations between Kyiv and Washington.
Trump harshly criticized Zelensky in an interview on Oct. 15 describing the Ukrainian president as "not a good guy for (the U.S.) to deal with."
The comments come as Ukraine-U.S. relations hit a low point after Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries for the rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts — and his team threatened to cut off intelligence support and arms shipments unless Kyiv halts the attacks.
Washington then unexpectedly unveiled a deal allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed due to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A few days later, on Oct. 11, Trump unilaterally announced an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, taking Ukrainian officials by surprise.
Even as Kyiv backed the truce and said it had paused its strikes against Russian refineries since the announcement, Moscow has continued attacking the Ukrainian power grid, meeting no criticism from Trump.
"I think Trump's advisers are wrong. I don't know who is pushing him to the wrong side," Zelensky said.

title: 'I'm not a big fan of Zelensky,' Trump says as US-Ukraine tensions deepen
description: U.S. President Donald Trump criticized President Volodymyr Zelensky in an interview with Newsmax published on Oct. 15, describing the Ukrainian president as "not a good guy for (the U.S.) to deal with."
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump criticized President Volodymyr Zelensky in an interview with Newsmax published on Oct. 15, describing the Ukrainian president as "not a good guy for (the U.S.) to deal with."
"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump said, claiming that the Ukrainian president does not want to help bring an end to the Russia-Ukraine war.
"He says he wants to settle, but he doesn't. I'm not a big fan of Zelensky. They've destroyed that country," the U.S. president said , criticizing the Obama and Biden administrations for their handling of the war, including the 2014 Russian annexation of Crimea.
Trump's comments came in response to a question on whether Trump asked Zelensky to halt Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Earlier in the day on Oct. 15, Zelensky lifted restrictions on Ukraine's strikes against Russian oil refineries after Russia continued to strike Ukraine's energy infrastructure over the past days.
The latest comments from Trump come amid deepening tensions between the two leaders.
The Ukraine-U.S. relations hit a low point after Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries for the rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts — and his team threatened to cut off intelligence support and arms shipments unless Kyiv halts the attacks.
Washington then unexpectedly unveiled a deal allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed due to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A few days later, on Oct. 11, Trump unilaterally announced an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, taking Ukrainian officials by surprise.
Even as Kyiv backed the truce and said it had paused its strikes against Russian refineries since the announcement, Moscow has continued attacking the Ukrainian power grid, meeting no criticism from Trump.
"I think Trump's advisers are wrong. I don't know who is pushing him to the wrong side," Zelensky said.
When asked whether he felt betrayed by Trump, the Ukrainian leader answered: "Really, ‌yes... but it's a ​little bit more complicated than ​just my ​emotions or my feelings."
Ukraine's president has not yet responded to Trump's latest comments.
The latest rift follows months of repeatedly failed attempts to negotiate a peace deal between Russia and Ukraine. Amid yet another halt in negotiations, Russia continues to pummel Ukrainian energy infrastructure ahead of the upcoming winter months.

title: Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Yandex data center, warehouses in overnight attack on Russia
description: According to monitoring channels ExileNova+ and SuperNova+, Russian technology giant Yandex's data center in Vladimir Oblast, around 500 kilometers (310 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was targeted in the overnight operation.
content:
Ukrainian forces appeared to strike multiple targets across Russia's Moscow, Rostov, and Vladimir regions in a widespread drone attack overnight on Oct. 16. The Kyiv Independent can not independently verify attack targets or damage at this time.
According to monitoring channels ExileNova+ and SuperNova+ , Russian technology giant Yandex's data center in Vladimir Oblast, around 500 kilometers (310 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was targeted in the overnight operation.
Footage from residents at the scene shows large explosions and air defense systems operating around residential buildings.
Following strikes on the same Yandex site on Oct. 11, the company announced operations at the data center had been completely shut down. That strike marked the third near-consecutive day of attacks on Yandex data centers in Russia, following confirmed strikes in Ryazan and Kaluga oblasts on Oct. 8 and 9.
The string of attacks on Russian data centers follows President Volodymyr Zelensky's statement that Ukraine would retaliate in kind to Russian strikes on Ukrainian internet infrastructure.
Earlier in the night around Moscow, Ukrainian drones shut down airspace above multiple airports. According to Russian opposition news channel Astra, plane departures and arrivals to the Vnukovo, Domodedovo, Zhukovsky, and Sheremetyevo airports were canceled overnight.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that over 59 Ukrainian drones were destroyed by the capital's air defense system throughout the night.
The closure of Moscow's airspace partially realizes threats made by Zelensky in September when he promised that Russian skies would soon be "de facto closed."
"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," said Zelensky.
It is currently unclear what, if any, targets were hit around Moscow . Eyewitness footage from city residents shows what appears to be flames illuminating the night sky, accompanied by the sounds of drones overhead and loud explosions.
Previously, several Moscow airports temporarily suspended flights on Oct. 9, as suspected Ukrainian drones and balloons entered airspace around the Russian capital.
Over 950 kilometers (590 miles) southeast of Moscow, Ukrainian drones attacked targets in the Rostov Oblast.
According to regional Governor Yuri Slusar, production and storage facilities were damaged, and a fire broke out as a result of the drone attack in the town of Aksay. The Chertkovsky district and the city of Bataysk in the region were also targeted, Slusar said.

title: G7 countries pledge 260 million euros to repair Chornobyl safety infrastructure damaged in Russian attack
description: The confinement structure, located about 130 kilometers (80 miles) north of Kyiv, was severely damaged in February 2025 after being struck by a Russian drone.
content:
Group of Seven (G7) nations will provide 260 million euros ($292 million) to help repair safety infrastructure at the Chornobyl Nuclear Plant damaged in a Russian attack, the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) announced on Oct. 15.
"The G7 (Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States) expressed grave concern over the nuclear safety risks caused by the strike and pledged to mobilize funding to repair the New Safe Confinement," the EBRD said in a statement.
The New Safe Confinement is a massive, arching steel structure that was erected in 2016 to cover the remains of the reactor unit that exploded during the 1986 Chornobyl nuclear disaster . The structure encloses the original sarcophagus that was built shortly after the disaster to prevent the release of nuclear contamination.
The confinement structure, located about 130 kilometers (80 miles) north of Kyiv, was severely damaged in February 2025 after being struck by a Russian drone .
"This is a terrorist threat to the entire world," President Volodymyr Zelensky said at the time. "The only country in the world that attacks such sites, occupies nuclear power plants, and wages war without any regard for the consequences is today's Russia."
The attack breached the structure’s inner and outer protective structures, damaged critical systems, and "severely compromised its two primary functions: containing radioactive material and enabling the safe dismantling of the unstable original sarcophagus over Reactor Four," according to the EBRD.
The EBRD estimates that 500 million euros ($561 million) is needed to repair the structure, and the work must be completed by 2030 to limit the risk of corrosion and safeguard the structure’s 100-year design life.
Previously, the site was briefly occupied by Russian forces in the early days of the full-scale invasion. Russian troops held the station's staff hostage, creating significant risks to nuclear safety. On Mar. 31, 2022, Russian troops withdrew from the station. During the occupation, increased radiation levels were recorded due to the movement of heavy machinery that stirred up contaminated dust.

title: Zelensky meets Belgian Prime Minister De Wever, but silence reigns on Russian assets
description: The talks apparently failed to yield a breakthrough on the fate of €200 billion ($227 billion) in Russian assets frozen by Euroclear under Belgian jurisdiction.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky met with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever on the sidelines of the EU leaders’ summit in Brussels on Oct. 15.
However, the talks apparently failed to yield a breakthrough on the fate of €200 billion ($227 billion) in Russian assets immobilized by Euroclear under Belgian jurisdiction.
Zelensky's Telegram post following the 20-minute evening meeting makes no mention of assets at all, and focused instead on Russia's attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure and cooperation with Belgium to source fighter jets and ammunition to tackle Moscow's jet-powered Shahed drones.
De Wever's chief of staff for foreign affairs and security, Pascal Heyman, likewise posted a picture of the meeting on social media, saying the two exchanged views on "Russia's war in Ukraine and Belgium's steadfast assistance to the country," but also making no mention of Russian assets.
Zelensky had been expected to raise the question of the EU using Russian immobilized assets to finance Ukraine's needs, as the Belgian prime minister was the most prominent opponent of the move the last time it was discussed, in December 2025.
Ukrainian politicians have also begun calling for Europe to use the assets , and Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha penned an opinion piece in Politico to that end.
Instead, the only reference to Russian assets was a social media post from Zelensky published after the meeting with De Wever, but about his earlier meeting with Belgian King Philippe.
It is "important that frozen Russian assets remain immobilized," Zelensky wrote.
"As long as the war continues, Russia must not receive anything it could invest in further killings and destabilization in Europe," Zelensky said.
U.S. diplomats raised the idea of transferring the assets immobilized in Europe to their jurisdiction for them to be used in negotiations with Russia.
However, this idea was not likely to ever be taken seriously in European circles, and was roundly criticized at the Oct. 15 summit.

title: Russian drone strikes leave portions of Kyiv without power, fires burning
description: Damage to energy facilities in the Kyiv region has also reduced water pressure in areas of the capital on the Dnipro River's right bank. Emergency specialists are switching power supplies to water pumping stations, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
content:
After Russian strikes on critical energy infrastructure late on Oct. 15, portions of Kyiv were left without power.
"Widespread power outages have occurred in certain areas of Kyiv and the surrounding region," said Ukrainian state energy operator Ukrenergo. An assessment of the damage and emergency repair work will follow after air raid alerts are lifted, said Ukrenergo .
Kyiv Independent journalists reported hearing loud blasts from air defense systems at work over the city's Podil district shortly before power outages were reported. It remains unclear what attack precisely caused the outages around Kyiv , a city the size of Berlin.
Damage to energy facilities in the Kyiv region has also reduced water pressure in areas of the capital on the Dnipro River's right bank. Emergency specialists are switching power supplies to water pumping stations, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
According to Klitschko, debris from a downed Russian drone fell into a courtyard of a private residence, and a fire broke out in a residential building in the city's Shevchenkivskyi district.
Russian attacks also caused widespread power outages in the city of Lutsk in northwestern Ukraine on Oct. 15.
The latest attack comes as Moscow increases strikes on energy sites, leaving the capital's three million residents without reliable access to power. Across the nation, Moscow has recently ramped up mass attacks to wipe out power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure for its fifth winter offensive during the full-scale invasion.
Despite U.S. President Donald Trump unilaterally declaring a halt on energy strikes between Ukraine and Russia, Moscow has continued to target Ukrainian electricity infrastructure.
On Oct. 14, Moscow's forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones against energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv, Zelensky said, calling it " ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."

title: UK to resupply Ukraine with more Storm Shadow missiles to strike Russia, Bloomberg reports
description: In a meeting in London on Oct. 14, President Volodymyr Zelensky and U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed on a new shipment of missiles, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. No official public announcement of this resupply has been made.
content:
The U.K. will send Ukraine more long-range Storm Shadow missiles to strike targets deep in Russia, Bloomberg reported on Oct. 15.
In a meeting in London on Oct. 14, President Volodymyr Zelensky and U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham agreed on a new shipment of the missiles, Bloomberg reported , citing people familiar with the matter. No official public announcement of this resupply has been made.
Following U.S. President Donald Trump lifting sanctions on the sale of Russian oil in the U.S., European leaders have moved to increase support for Ukraine as Russian forces continue to attack energy and civilian infrastructure around the country.
In response to Moscow's escalating attacks, the U.K. considers Kyiv's use of Storm Shadow missiles to strike Russian military targets as a defensive action, according to Bloomberg. The new stock of missiles will help Ukrainian forces strike targets up to 250 kilometers (155 miles) inside Russia.
The added missiles may also shore up Ukraine's own domestically produced long-range FP-7 missiles to hit Russian energy sites. On Oct. 15, Zelensky said operations against Russian oil refineries would continue following Moscow's disregard of Trump's unilaterally imposed energy ceasefire.
Ukraine has utilized the Storm Shadow missiles since 2023 and started targeting sites deep in Russia in 2024.
Russian authorities said that the U.K.-made missiles were used in a Ukrainian strike on Russian army command posts in Donetsk on Aug. 26 that allegedly killed more Russian officers than in any other single attack during the war.
On Aug. 25, Zelensky announced that the U.K. and France granted Kyiv permission to produce its own Storm Shadow and SCALP missiles.

title: Russian soldier faces life in prison over alleged killing of 5 Ukrainian troops, civilian in Kharkiv Oblast
description: The suspect was identified as 36-year-old Leonid Ryzhikov, a Russian citizen from St. Petersburg who served in the 2nd Battalion of Russia's 1009th Motorized Rifle Regiment.
content:
A Russian soldier suspected of killing five unarmed Ukrainian service members and a civilian in Kharkiv Oblast on Oct. 13 has been charged with war crimes, Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) reported on Oct. 15.
The suspect was identified as 36-year-old Leonid Ryzhikov , a Russian citizen from St. Petersburg who served in the 2nd Battalion of Russia's 1009th Motorized Rifle Regiment.
According to the SBU, Ryzhikov was mobilized into the Russian army in late July after serving eight years in prison for causing grievous bodily harm and theft. He was subsequently deployed to Russian-occupied territory in Kharkiv Oblast .
On Oct. 5-6, Ryzhikov came under Ukrainian fire near the village of Starytsia and fled his position, the SBU said. Armed with an AK-74 rifle, he began moving toward Kharkiv on foot, hiding in wooded areas. Along the way, he allegedly stole civilian clothes from an abandoned house.
On Oct. 13, Ryzhikov allegedly shot and killed a 60-year-old local resident who was fishing at a pond near the village of Mykhailivka. He then pushed the man's body into the water, according to investigators.
Later that day, the suspect entered a private house in the village of Momotove, where five Ukrainian service members were temporarily staying.
The soldiers were unarmed, dressed in civilian clothes, and were not participating in combat at the time, the SBU said. Ryzhikov allegedly shot all five, some of whom were asleep.
After the killings, he reportedly hid his rifle at a nearby property and continued toward Kharkiv, where he was arrested in the city's Saltivskyi district on Oct. 14.
Law enforcement officers also recovered the AK-74 rifle allegedly used in the killings.
Ryzhikov has been charged with war crimes resulting in deaths under Article 438 of Ukraine's Criminal Code. He faces life imprisonment if convicted.
Investigators are seeking to place him in pretrial detention, while the investigation remains ongoing.
Earlier ,Ukrainian media reports had described the suspect as an escaped Russian prisoner of war. The SBU's later account instead said he fled his Russian position after coming under Ukrainian fire.
The 72nd Separate Mechanized Brigade confirmed on Oct. 14 that five of its service members had been killed in the incident.

content:
Nearly 48 hours after Ukraine's Starshield terminals started mysteriously malfunctioning, nobody in Washington, nor at SpaceX, has taken responsibility for the apparent decision to hobble Ukrainian military communications.
Starshield terminals — the militarized version of SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet system — began losing connectivity as they approached a certain speed, causing havoc among Ukrainian drone units.
The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike drones, as well as the interceptor drones Ukraine uses to help protect cities from Russia's ongoing aerial bombardment.
"The fact that nobody in Washington wants to own up to helping Russia kill Ukrainians shows how politically toxic this decision was," American journalist and commentator Michael Weiss told the Kyiv Independent.
The restrictions came as Ukraine continues to come under significant and sustained pressure from the Trump administration to cease attacks on Russian oil refineries, something Kyiv views as an essential part of its defense against Russia's invasion.
Ukraine has repeatedly offered to observe an "energy ceasefire" which would see both sides cease attacks on energy infrastructure such as power plants, oil refineries, and oil terminals, something Russia has repeatedly refused to accept.
Ukrainian activist Serhii Sternenko, a former adviser to ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, was one of the first to raise the alarm about the restrictions on Oct. 14, saying that a "number of critical missions were disrupted."
"The restriction came without any warning," Junior Sergeant Dimko Zhluktenko of the 413th Unmanned Systems Regiment, told the Kyiv Independent. "In my estimate, that has already cost Ukraine tens of millions of dollars in losses."
As the scale of the problem became clearer over the course of the day, the question of who had actually ordered the restrictions grew louder, but there is still no definitive answer.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk shifted responsibility to the Pentagon and the Trump administration for the slowdown, saying on Oct. 14 that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government."
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately POTUS," he said in a reply to Fedorov on social media.
Axios, citing "U.S. officials," reported the restrictions were the result of a "technical malfunction in the system," though no further evidence of this has emerged.
According to Axios, the White House denied any role in imposing the restrictions and said it planned to contact SpaceX to determine what had happened. The Pentagon has not publicly explained the restrictions.
The move has sparked bipartisan anger in Washington, as a historically unpopular President Trump approaches midterm elections that the Republican Party is predicted to badly lose.
"I’m not holding my breath for Defense Secretary Hegseth to offer transparency, so we’ll be asking the DOD Inspector General to initiate an investigation and report back to Congress and the American People," Republican Senator Thom Tillis said on social media .
"At best, this was an unacceptable error or lapse, and at worst a conscious decision to clear the field for a Russian attack," Tillis said.
"Reports of Starlink failing in Ukraine are deeply alarming — potentially crippling air defense against Russia’s murderous missiles & drones. Trump & Musk must be held accountable," Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, who co-sponsored the Lindsey Graham Sanctions Act with the late senator from South Carolina, said on social media .
By the following day, Starshield was operating more reliably in Ukraine , but the new 160 km/h speed cap remained in place.
"We have now confirmed that Starshield works at 160 km/h, so those glitches have been fixed. But the cap itself is the problem. 160 km/h is not enough, and it limits how we can defend ourselves against the Russians," Zhluktenko told the Kyiv Independent.
"As of now, Starshield's operation has resumed and continues, as we have confirmed through reports from units," a source in the defense ministry told the Kyiv Independent.
"The Ministry of Defense is also continuing communication to clarify all the reasons and circumstances of yesterday's restriction," they added.
Other Ukrainian military units were still apparently experiencing intermittent problems, another Ukrainian military source said, speaking to the Kyiv Independent on condition of anonymity. “In some cases, it works perfectly, in some places it does not," they said.
Neither SpaceX nor the Pentagon responded to requests for comment from the Kyiv Independent.

title: The EU loophole Russia is using to free its oligarchs from sanctions
description: Russia has exploited an EU sanctions loophole to unfreeze $3 billion worth of assets held by Belgium's Euroclear, according to a Flemish media report, and Austria's Raiffeisen Bank could be about to execute the same maneuver.
content:
Russia has exploited an EU sanctions loophole to unfreeze $3 billion worth of assets held by Belgium's Euroclear, according to a Flemish media report, and Austria's Raiffeisen Bank could be about to execute the same maneuver.
Belgian media outlet Apache reported on Oct. 15 that in April 2025, Euroclear compensated $3 billion from its holdings of Russian investors' assets, which were frozen in place by Western sanctions.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin has responded to EU sanctions being imposed against those helping him carry out his war in Ukraine by seizing European assets and sometimes using them to compensate individuals whose money held in Europe has been frozen by the EU's restrictions.
In 2024, Russia’s National Settlement Depository (NSD), the Russian counterpart to Euroclear, compensated several Russian investors in Europe by seizing $3 billion from the Russian bank accounts of European nationals, following an order from Putin, Apache reports.
Among the beneficiaries according to Apache, Putin-aligned politician Efim Malkin, as well as MTS Bank, PJSC Rosbank, and Leader Asset Management CJSC.
Euroclear told Apache that Belgium authorized them to "debit an equivalent amount of the sanctioned Russian accounts to compensate customers whose cash had been purchased in Russia," in line with EU regulation 269/2014 .
That regulation is the legal underpinning for the EU's sanctions against those helping Russia wage its war on Ukraine, but its Article 5 allows EU countries to unfreeze assets in certain circumstances.
On Sept. 22, Austria's Raiffeisen Bank won a court case in Vienna that paves the way for a similar move, which essentially rewards the bank for continuing to do business in Russia for years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
Russia expropriated 2.1 billion euros ($2.4 billion) of Raiffeisen's assets in January 2026, and then awarded it to a Russian investment company called Rasperia, which has ties to the sanctioned Russian oligarch Oleg Deripaska.
With the Austrian court ruling, Rasperia has four weeks to appeal, at which point Raiffeisen can ask Austria to refund Raiffeisen using Rasperia's assets frozen in the EU.
Raiffeisen's corporate spokesperson Christof Danz previously told the Kyiv Independent that the bank's "priorities are supporting Ukraine and exiting Russia. Solving the current legal dispute rapidly facilitates attaining both objectives."
A European Commission spokesperson confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that "once the judgment of the Vienna court is final and enforceable, Raiffeisen may request authorization from the national competent authority to release the frozen assets."
The spokesperson mentioned that this is possible thanks to the same Article 5 that arose in the Belgian situation reported by Apache.
Raiffeisen's maneuver "will all but legitimize Deripaska’s attempts to trade his Austrian assets for Russian ones, signaling to oligarchs everywhere that there is a surefire route to avoiding European sanctions," said Max Hammer, human rights campaigner at the civil society organization Bank Track.
Bank Track has since called for the European Commission and Austrian authorities to step in and investigate new allegations that Raiffeisen's Russian operation has been helping sanctioned entities evade Western restrictions.
With the start of such an investigation, Bank Track also would expect Austria "not (to) authorize the unfreezing of sanctioned shares while those investigations are ongoing."
The European Commission spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent that they are aware of the allegations made against Raiffeisen, and that Raiffeisen denies the allegations.
"We are in contact with Member State authorities who are competent to investigate such allegations," the spokesperson said.
The date at which Raiffeisen can request Austria to unfreeze the assets is expected to be Oct. 20.
