content:
Yulia Latynina in an unnamed location, on Feb. 9, 2013. (Wikimedia Commons)
Correction: Leonid Ragozin's travel data has been corrected.
Latvia's decision last week to declare Russian-born journalist and blogger Leonid Ragozin persona non grata has drawn attention to a broader trend: Russians who once presented themselves as opponents of Vladimir Putin are now accused of echoing Kremlin narratives.
Some now live in Europe, taking advantage of the freedom and security that their adopted countries provide to broadcast their views.
Ironically, some of them blame the European Union for Russia’s war against Ukraine and most of the world's other problems while enjoying the liberties and safety provided by EU member states.
"Why are people who support Russia’s war or provide a justification for their country's actions welcomed in Europe?"
They span a wide spectrum, from self-styled impartial commentators who insist on hearing "both sides" to outspoken supporters of Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from Ragozin and will publish his response once it is received.
One of these commentators, Ragozin, has worked as a journalist for various English-language and Russian-language publications, including BBC, Newsweek Russia, Al-Jazeera, Bloomberg, the Guardian, Politico, the New Republic, Time, and the Washington Post.
According to data from a leaked database obtained by the Kyiv Independent, Ragozin regularly visited Russia between 2014 and 2022. He went to Russia on Feb. 17, 2022 – before the full-scale invasion began on Feb. 24 – and again left Russia on March 3, 2022.
Latvia's Foreign Ministry announced on Oct. 6 that it had declared a Russian citizen persona non grata, without naming the individual. On Oct. 14, Ragozin confirmed that Latvia had referred to him and said that he had been notified of his expulsion from Latvia.
Ragozin said he was facing "political persecution" and argued that this was "revenge by far-right politicians for my investigation into their links to Russian neo-Nazis who found refuge in Kyiv" and "a punishment for my commentary on the Russian aggression in Ukraine."
Unlike some other critics of Ukraine, Ragozin has taken a more nuanced and subtle approach. He has never explicitly supported Russian President Vladimir Putin .
However, he has been repeatedly accused of promoting Kremlin-friendly narratives. Ragozin has written mostly in English and targeted an important audience — right-wing and left-wing commentators in the West, as well as the "Global South."
In 2021, Ragozin effectively blamed Ukraine for "provoking" an escalation with Russia by seeking NATO membership. He argued that Russia’s troop buildup around Ukraine's borders was reactive rather than aggressive .
Instead of criticizing the Kremlin, Ragozin has focused on lambasting nationalists and "neo-Nazis" in Ukraine.
Ragozin has effectively blamed the West for the war, arguing that it pushed Kyiv into an unwinnable conflict.
He also argued that "the war can only end on Moscow's terms " and accused Ukraine and Europe of sabotaging peace talks by seeking a compromise.
In a September interview , Ragozin said that he doesn't "think Russia has a deliberate policy of targeting civilians, but that can change." Over the past week, at least 150 Ukrainian civilians were killed by Russia, with the Kremlin targeting public transport in Kramatorsk , and apartment buildings in Pryluky and Zaporizhzhia .
Russia executed civilians in Bucha in 2022 and has deliberately destroyed cities in Ukraine's east — Avdiivka, Bakhmut, Siverskodonetsk, Pokrovsk, and Druzhkivka — to name a few.
Konstantin Eggert, who headed the BBC Russian Service's Moscow bureau in the 2000s and was part of the board that selected Ragozin for the position of producer, commented on him for the Kyiv Independent.
Eggert said that several times he "heard the opinion that Ragozin is de facto equating the aggressor (Russia) with the victim of aggression (Ukraine), denying or downplaying atrocities committed by the Russian forces and portraying the Baltic States to his audience as irresponsible warmongers."
"I agree with this critical assessment of Ragozin's views," he added. "I believe that Ragozin or anyone else is perfectly entitled to hold and broadcast such views. But they should not be surprised if others describe such positions as chiming in with the Kremlin narratives ."
InformNapalm, a Ukrainian open-source intelligence outfit, told the Kyiv Independent that "his recurring arguments effectively reinforce the Kremlin's preferred narrative about the causes of the war and the terms on which it could end, particularly among Western audiences."
Ragozin denied the accusations against him on X on Oct. 14.
"My stance on the war in Ukraine remains unchanged," he said. "I condemn the Russian aggression and support Ukraine's sovereignty over occupied territories…. But I'll continue to criticize Western countries for mishandling this conflict and not acting in the best interests of the Ukrainian people."
Yulia Latynina, a blogger, columnist, and writer, has gone much farther than Ragozin in the evolution of her views on Ukraine.
She used to be one of Russia’s most prominent anti-Kremlin liberal opinion leaders and called herself a "libertarian."
Latynina left Russia in 2017 following several attacks on her, as well as on her house and her car, that she blamed on people linked to the late Yevgeniy Prigozhin , then a trusted confidant of Putin.
According to media reports, since 2017 Latynina has been based alternately in Cyprus and Estonia . Her phone number is Cypriot, and several organizations founded by Latynina are based in Estonia.
Between 2014 and 2023, Latynina fully supported Ukraine and opposed Russia’s war.
But starting from 2024, she changed her views dramatically, turning into a harsh critic of Ukraine and the West. As Donald Trump was re-elected president of the U.S. in 2024, she increasingly aligned her views with the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of Trump and his allies.
Now, Latynina fully supports Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine.
"If the project of Ukraine as an 'anti-Russia' cannot be destroyed completely, then it should be weakened as much as possible."
Latynina believes that Ukraine represents a "strategic threat" to Russia and that Russia had a right to invade Ukraine to defend its "strategic interests." Her views on foreign policy are now similar to those of Russian imperialists Alexander Dugin , Alexander Prokhanov, and Eduard Limonov.
Latynina has argued that it is in Russia’s strategic interest to ensure that the boundary between the Russian and Ukrainian languages is "as far west as possible."
" If the project of Ukraine as an 'anti-Russia' cannot be destroyed completely, then it should be weakened as much as possible," Latynina said in a 2026 interview .
When asked in 2026 about the war’s negative impact on Russians' living standards, she said that strategic interests should override their concerns, and average Russians "will always live like shit" regardless of the war.
Asked why she has shed her libertarian credentials and embraced something resembling Dugin's Eurasianism, Latynina told the Kyiv Independent that she had not read Dugin and had been influenced by U.S. foreign-policy realists George Kennan, Pat Buchanan, and Jeffrey Sachs.
" Russia could not allow a territory that had taken shape as a result of the Russian Empire's and the Soviet Union's westward expansion... to suddenly turn into Halychyna stretching from the river to the sea," she said in a reference to Halychyna (Galicia), a historic region in western Ukraine that, according to Russian propaganda, is the core base of Ukrainian nationalism.
She has opposed ending the war on terms that she thinks are "unfavorable" to Russia — such as freezing the front line.
In her attempts to justify Russia’s war, Latynina has gone as far as to claim that states "have a right to aggression."
Asked how this reconciles with the libertarian principle of the non-initiation of force, Latynina cited the Roman historian Livy in a comment for the Kyiv Independent, saying that "war is just for those for whom it is necessary."
In 2025, Latynina also shocked the audience by publishing an article trying to justify Russia’s actions by drawing parallels with Nazi Germany. She argued that Nazi Germany's expansionism was a result of the mistreatment of ethnic Germans abroad — similarly to alleged violations of Russian speakers' rights in Ukraine.
Like Ragozin, Latynina has also blamed Ukraine and Europe for the lack of progress in peace negotiations and accused them of perpetuating the war. She has repeatedly criticized what she sees as a stagnant European bureaucracy mired in a deep crisis.
Asked why she lives in the EU despite hating it, Latynina told the Kyiv Independent that "it's up to the bots and the nationalist decolonization advocates to explain why Latynina should be persecuted in a free country for refusing to toe the party line."
She now presents the Russian opposition as puppets of the West, saying that they will sell out Russia’s interests if they come to power.
Latynina's increasingly pro-Kremlin and pro-war narratives have prompted speculation that she is either working for the Kremlin or contemplating a return to Russia.
She has denied working for the Kremlin. Latynina said in a 2026 interview that the status of a foreign agent was impeding the publication of her books in Russia, and that she was thinking of the possibility of being stripped of that status.
However, she told the Kyiv Independent she had not contacted the Russian authorities about the issue so far.
Some other notable Russian commentators occupy a middle ground between Latynina and Ragozin.
Oleg Kashin, who had long been an independent journalist critical of the Kremlin, acknowledged that Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014 was illegal.
Despite this, he supported the annexation, arguing that it was a "restoration of historical justice."
" There is no doubt that it was annexed in violation of international law," Kashin, who is based in the U.K., told the Kyiv Independent. "But I don't believe that international law is taken seriously at all. There are simply no major players in world politics that genuinely abide by it… My Russian heart won't let me say that we should have made sure Crimea remained part of Ukraine."
Kashin also condemned the use of Russian troops in the Donbas in 2014. However, he blamed Ukraine for allegedly fueling tensions leading up to Russia’s invasion of eastern Ukraine.
On the eve of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, Kashin wished "Russian soldiers good luck and strength" in a future military conflict in Ukraine.
However, he eventually became a critic of Russia’s full-scale invasion, saying that it was at odds with Russia’s national interests.
He attributed his initial support for Russian soldiers in 2022 to his belief that Russia would only invade the Donbas , not the whole of Ukraine, and replace Russian proxies with Moscow's direct control.
" When I realized that what was actually happening was an insane and suicidal march on Kyiv, I naturally spoke out against it immediately," he told the Kyiv Independent.
He said, however, that he believes that a limited Russian invasion of the Donbas in 2022 "would have been far more beneficial than the criminal regimes that had been established in the Donbas with Russia’s support" in 2014.
For Ukraine and its supporters, the question that arises is clear — why are people who support Russia’s war or provide a justification for their country's actions welcomed in Europe?
"When assessing information influence, what matters is not just how someone describes themselves — as an opposition figure or a critic of Putin — but also the specific narratives they consistently promote to their audience," InformNapalm said.
Oleg Sukhov is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent. He is a former editor and reporter at the Moscow Times. He has a master's degree in history from the Moscow State University. He moved to Ukraine in 2014 due to the crackdown on independent media in Russia and covered war, corruption, reforms and law enforcement for the Kyiv Post.

title: Russia builds massive new launch base for jet-powered attack drones in six weeks, satellite images show
description: Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) group Absolutely Reliable Source reported the construction on Oct. 13, citing satellite imagery. The analysts identified eight launch positions and 32 areas for preparing drones for takeoff.
content:
Russia has nearly completed construction of a major new facility for launching jet-powered attack drones near the Millerovo military airbase in Rostov Oblast in just six weeks, satellite imagery shows, with experts saying it could become operational within weeks.
Ukrainian open-source intelligence (OSINT) group Absolutely Reliable Source reported the construction on Oct. 13, citing satellite imagery. The analysts identified eight launch positions and 32 areas for preparing drones for takeoff.
According to the group, the facility is intended for launching Russia's Geran-5 jet-powered attack drones. Satellite images show that the site was an empty field on Sept. 1, while the first section of the complex was nearing completion by Oct. 12.
The analysts also reported that satellite imagery from Oct. 12 appeared to show drones being unloaded at the facility.
The group suggested that construction had been accelerated to expand Russia's drone attack capabilities following strikes on Kyiv in September. It also noted similarities between the new facility and Russia's existing Tsymbulova drone base in Oryol Oblast.
Later, on Oct. 15, Reuters published an investigation , revealing that the facility covers approximately 0.9 square kilometers and is located about 3.5 kilometers from Millerovo airbase.
Reuters' analysis found that two of the eight launch platforms already had launch rails installed, while rails were under construction on two others.
Mike Monnik, founder and CEO of the private intelligence company DroneSec, told Reuters that the facility could become fully operational within weeks, potentially sooner. He estimated that it could launch 100 or more jet-powered drones within 24 hours, depending on available supplies and operational needs.
Russia has significantly increased its use of jet-powered attack drones against Ukraine in recent months, with Kyiv and the surrounding region among the main targets.
Unlike older, propeller-driven models, Russia's newer jet-powered drones can reach speeds of up to 600 kilometers per hour, making them more difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
Ukraine has been developing new interceptor drones to counter the threat. On Oct. 12, former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov announced that a new Ukrainian interceptor had shot down two Russian Geran-5 drones during its first week of deployment.

title: Open letter to Trump from ex-Ukrainian President Yushchenko: Ukraine's desire for peace is not willingness to surrender
description:
Mr. President,

I write these words without diplomatic formulas or ceremonial language. I write simply, from one human being to another, and from one president to another — two men who understand that there are moments in history when decisions determine not only the fate of nations, but the fate of freedom itself.

For Ukrainians, freedom is not an abstraction. It is not a slogan written into a political declaration. Freedom is in our blood. It comes to us through generations — from our Cossack
content:
A woman holding a child cries next to a residential building damaged following a Russian air attack on the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv, Ukraine, on July 2, 2026. (Roman Pilipey / AFP via Getty Images)
I write these words without diplomatic formulas or ceremonial language. I write simply, from one human being to another, and from one president to another — two men who understand that there are moments in history when decisions determine not only the fate of nations, but the fate of freedom itself.
For Ukrainians, freedom is not an abstraction. It is not a slogan written into a political declaration. Freedom is in our blood. It comes to us through generations — from our Cossack forefathers, from ancestors who valued above all else their liberty, their dignity, and the land God gave them.
We are a nation rooted in the soil. Our identity grew from love of our home, our field, our village, our city, our church, our family, and the sky above us. Ukrainians have never sought what belongs to another nation. But neither have we ever willingly surrendered what is ours.
Mr. President, look at what is happening in Ukraine right now, at this very moment. Every day and night, our cities shudder under Russian ballistic missiles, Iranian Shahed drones, and aerial bombs.
Russia strikes ordinary residential buildings in ancient Kyiv, sleeping neighborhoods in Zaporizhzhia, Odesa, Dnipro, Kharkiv, and towns across our country. Families are killed in their homes. Millions live under the threat of another siren, another explosion, another night wondering whether their children will still be alive in the morning.
And when there is talk of "concessions" or deals with Putin, the Kremlin's answer is more missiles, more drones, and more bloodshed. Ukrainian families pay the price.
Behind every statistic is a human life. A mother buries her child. A child stands beside the grave of a father. A family returns to what was once its home and finds only broken concrete and photographs scattered through the ruins.
This is not a distant "conflict." This is the daily reality of millions of Ukrainians.
And against this reality, Ukrainians hear calls that Ukraine should stop. That Ukraine should restrain its strikes against the infrastructure that finances and sustains Russia's war. That trade in Russian energy can somehow be separated from the missiles and drones Russia sends against Ukrainian families. It cannot.
Money paid for Russian fuel is not an abstraction called "commerce." It finances an economy geared toward total war. Russia needs resources to wage this unjust war, and Ukraine is fighting to deprive Russia of those resources.
There is a profound moral difference between the aggressor and the nation defending itself.
Mr. President, America knows this distinction better than most nations. It knows how dangerous it is to believe that trade can tame an aggressor or make the threat disappear. History taught us that lesson at a terrible price.
Before the United States entered World War II, America traded extensively with Imperial Japan, including in strategically important materials. Washington hoped for years to avoid a wider war in the Pacific. Ultimately, economic pressure and diplomacy could not prevent catastrophe, and on Dec. 7, 1941, Pearl Harbor was attacked.
History may not repeat itself exactly, but it does raise the same questions again. What price do free nations pay when aggression is rewarded rather than stopped?
Ukraine once placed extraordinary faith in the international order led by the United States. When the Soviet Union collapsed, Ukraine inherited one of the largest nuclear arsenals in the world. In negotiations with our allies, we agreed to give it up. We did so because we believed that a world governed by agreements was safer than a world governed by nuclear weapons.
In 1994, the United States of America, along with its partners, signed the Budapest Memorandum , providing Ukraine with official assurances of security, sovereignty, and the inviolability of our borders.
They pledged not to threaten or use force against Ukraine. America assumed a moral responsibility toward Ukraine. So how can anyone today, when a treacherous enemy has attacked us, forget America's signature on this document?
Ukraine kept its word. Russia broke its word.
That history matters today. Because when a nation gives up the most powerful weapons on Earth in return for international commitments, and is later invaded by one of the very states that made those commitments, the consequences extend far beyond Ukraine.
Every nation in the world is watching and asking whether agreements with great powers mean anything. They are asking whether giving up nuclear weapons makes a country safer — or more vulnerable. And they are watching America.
One does not negotiate with tyrants — one stops them.
Mr. President, our nations are connected by more than treaties and diplomacy. We have stood together many times before. One of the six Marines who raised the American flag at Iwo Jima was Sergeant Michael Strank, whose family came from Lemkivshchyna and who gave his life fighting for the United States.
When American and Soviet forces met at the Elbe in April 1945, American Lieutenant William Robertson was first embraced by a Ukrainian boy from the Cherkasy region — Oleksandr Silvashko.
Ukrainian soldiers served alongside American forces in Iraq and Afghanistan, and, today, Ukraine continues to share its hard-won military experience with its American partners, including expertise in countering Iranian-designed drones. Ukrainians and Americans have shed blood together in defense of freedom against tyranny.
Mr. President, above all, there is one thing I want you — and the world — to understand.
The Ukrainian spirit cannot and will not be broken.
Do not mistake the Ukrainian desire for peace for a willingness to surrender. The Ukrainian spirit cannot and will not be broken.
No people wants peace more than a people whose children are being killed. But peace cannot come by asking the victim to pay the price for the aggressor's crimes. We cannot agree to a peace that will later cause the deaths of many more of our children and grandchildren.
We are a people with deep roots, bound to our land by love, labor, and the spirit of freedom. We will never yield our land willingly to anyone. This is our home, given to us by God. We were here, we are here, and we will always be here. We cannot be intimidated by missiles, and we cannot be forced to surrender.
Ukrainian identity has been forged through centuries of attempts to erase it. The Russian Empire tried to silence our language, destroy our culture, starve our people, imprison our leaders, and rewrite our history. And still Ukraine survived. We survived because our roots are deep, and because the blood of a free people flows in our veins.
Russia can destroy our buildings. It can terrorize our cities. It can kill our people. But it cannot destroy who we are. It cannot compel Ukrainians to cease being Ukrainian.
Mr. President, America's greatness was not built by accommodating tyranny, but by understanding, at decisive moments of its history, that freedom must be defended before the price of defending it becomes immeasurably greater.
Ukraine is defending that principle today with the lives of our people.
Today, the free world faces questions larger than Ukraine itself: whether borders may be changed by force; whether agreements between nations still have meaning; whether aggression will be rewarded; and whether the free world will stand beside those who choose freedom.
One does not negotiate with tyrants — one stops them.
Mr. President, I believe America understands this.
With faith in truth, freedom, and the honor of the free world,
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Viktor Yushchenko is the third president of Ukraine, serving from 2005 to 2010. He previously served as prime minister of Ukraine from 1999 to 2001 and governor of the National Bank of Ukraine from 1993 to 1999.

title: Europe shuts US out of Russian assets conversation
description: "These are frozen Russian assets held in Europe, belonging to Russians who are destroying Ukraine and killing people there every day... the idea of releasing these assets is completely out of the question," said Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Multiple EU leaders on Oct. 15 firmly rebuffed the idea that the 200 billion euros ($227 billion) of immobilized Russian assets held in the bloc would be handed to the U.S. as a bargaining chip in peace talks.
The idea was floated by U.S. officials when they met with European counterparts on Oct. 9, and was first reported on the next day by the New York Times.
The proposal surfaced in the media again as EU leaders meet for a two-day summit in Brussels, where several countries are set to raise the issue of using Russian assets to support Ukraine.
"It cannot be viewed positively in any way. Absolutely not," said Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, in response to questions from journalists.
"These are frozen Russian assets held in Europe, belonging to Russians who are destroying Ukraine and killing people there every day... the idea of releasing these assets is completely out of the question," Orpo said.
"On the contrary, a proposal will be put forward today to continue exploring ways to ensure that these frozen assets are used to support Ukraine," he added.
Likewise, Austrian Prime Minister Christian Stocker said he is "not convinced of the idea of imprisoning these assets under U.S. control in view of the volatility in U.S. policy and how quickly things are changing there."
"The assets are frozen in Europe, and they shall remain frozen in Europe. That is a matter for us, and we will decide it," German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told reporters.
"All these things that they (Russia) are interested in, the frozen assets, the lifting of sanctions, it is up to Europeans to decide," said the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas.
The EU's draft conclusions for the summit were also updated on Oct. 14 to say that leaders "will revert to the issue (of financing Ukraine) in a timely manner," supporting Orpo's comment that the bloc will continue working on possible ways to use Russia's immobilized assets to support Ukraine.
Even if some EU leaders might have supported placing Russian assets under U.S. jurisdiction — and none have said so — the idea was a non-starter, given that the bloc would need unanimous agreement.
The chances of that happening have never been slimmer, after recent U.S. moves against Ukraine have provoked widespread condemnation from European leaders.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 17, injure 67 across Ukraine,   as drone waves wreak havoc in central, western oblasts
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Russia used a total of 850 Shahed-type drones since 09:00 a.m. on Oct. 14.
content:
At least 10 people were killed and 66 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as hundreds of Russian drones struck targets across the full width of the country, regional authorities said on Oct. 15.
Kirovohrad Oblast experienced the most massive attack the oblast has seen since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion overnight, as Russia killed three people and injured six others, said regional governor Andrii Raikovych . The casualties are the result of Russian attacks on Kropyvnytskyi, he added.
Russia struck critical infrastructure, transport enterprises, logistics facilities, and residential buildings with almost 360 drones across 26 locations, Raikovych said.
"It is obvious that Russia deliberately escalated the attacks, having received a relaxation of sanctions and seeing attempts to put pressure on Ukraine. Russia uses every such moment and must be responsible for what it does," President Volodymyr Zelensky said, referring to the attack.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight from 06:00 p.m. with 580 Shahed-type and other drones, as well as with two Kh-59 guided aircraft missiles. The Air Force said it neutralized 536 of the Russian drones across 31 locations.
Zelensky said that Russia used a total of 850 Shahed-type drones during the day since 09:00 a.m. on Oct. 14.
"There were constant waves, and our sky was not clear of them for a single hour," he said.
Russian attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, killed three people and injured three more, authorities said. Regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported two people died in Novooleksandrivka and two others injured. A third person was injured in a Russian strike on a private house in Pavlohrad, Hanzha added. Zelensky raised the number of people killed in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast to three.
In western Volyn Oblast , wreckage of a Russian drone fell on the city of Lutsk , killing six people and injuring 12 others, regional governor Roman Romaniuk said. A large-scale fire broke out in the 'Eurogroup' warehouse as a result of the Russian attack, killing five people at the scene, and injuring a sixth person so heavily they succumbed in hospital, Romaniuk said.
In Rivne Oblast , a Russian drone crashed into the city during the day on Oct. 14, injuring eight people, including a child born in 2012, according to regional governor Oleksandr Koval . The oblast also experienced several attack waves overnight, but no people were injured, he said .
In Kyiv Oblast , Russian attacks over the past day injured four people across Bucha, Obukhiv, and Fastiv districts, the regional military administration said. In total, Russia struck across 26 locations in the oblast, damaging private houses, infrastructure, warehouses, and cars.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , three people were killed and eight others injured in Russian attacks over the past day, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin .
In Kharkiv Oblast , Russian attacks injured nine people, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. The explosion of an unknown object in the village of Spodobivka also killed one man and injured a 15-year-old boy, the governor added. Russian attacks damaged private and commercial buildings, as well as parts of the power grid, Syniehubov said.
In southern Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks killed one person and injured five other people over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said. Many settlements in the oblast, including the city of Kherson, were under Russian artillery, drone, and air attacks throughout the day, he added.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast , seven people were injured as Russia attacked over the past day, with almost 200 artillery strikes, 734 drones of varying types, and two missiles, according to regional governor Ivan Fedorov .
A Russian attack on Ternopil Oblast injured five people, as a Russian drone struck a manufacturing enterprise in Chortkiv, according to regional governor Taras Pastukh and Ukraine's interior ministry .
In northeastern Sumy Oblast , Russian attacks did not lead to casualties or injuries but damaged a numer of private houses and civil infrastructure, as the air raid alert lasted for more than 18 combined hours, the Sumy military administration said.

title: Ukrainian special unit destroys Russian drone operator training center, military intelligence says
description: The operation also destroyed the residenceof the Russian officer corps, in particular of those training the sabotage groups of the 18th Army.
content:
Ukrainian units destroyed a Russian training center for drone operators in Khorly, in occupied Kherson Oblast, Ukraine's military intelligence agency (HUR) said on Oct. 15.
Service members of the HUR special unit "Shamanbat," together with the 426th Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment, conducted an operation overngiht on Oct. 11 to destroy the training center for drone operators of Russia's 18th Combined Arms Army, HUR said .
The operation also destroyed the residence of the Russian officer corps, in particular of those training the sabotage groups of the 18th Army, HUR added.
The intelligence agency said that its operation completely destroyed the training center. In a video released together with the statement, details of the operation and its aftermath can be seen, showing several drone strikes on the training facility.
The Russian 18th Combined Arms Army was formed in August 2022 “to free up more experienced units to fight on key axes" in Ukraine, according to the U.K. defense ministry. The formation is likely "an amalgamation and uplift" of other units operating in Kherson Oblast, including the 22nd Army Corps, which normally forms the Russian garrison in occupied Crimea, the ministry said.

title: Zelensky arrives in Belgium, prepares to meet Prime Minister De Wever
description: "All of us in Europe want this war to end. And for that to happen, strong signals are needed — more real pressure on Russia and more defense support for Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media upon arrival.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in Belgium on Oct. 15, where he plans to meet Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever to discuss finances before taking part in an EU leaders' summit.
"All of us in Europe want this war to end. And for that to happen, strong signals are needed — more real pressure on Russia and more defense support for Ukraine," Zelensky wrote on social media upon arrival.
The social media post mentions a meeting with the Belgian prime minister, plans for which the Flemish newspaper De Morgen first reported on Oct. 13.
That meeting was likewise confirmed by a Ukrainian diplomat, who told the Kyiv Independent it is expected to take place at 8 p.m. local time.
On top of the agenda for Zelensky is building consensus for the use of some 200 billion euros ($227 billion) of Russian assets immobilized in Europe, the lion's share of which is held in Belgium's Euroclear.
Ukraine upped its advocacy efforts this week to try and get EU countries to back the idea, previously shot down in December, with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha publishing an opinion piece with Politico — the news outlet that claimed in December 2025 that De Wever was "Russia's most valuable asset," which provoked a strong response from the Belgian leader.
The topic is expected to come up during the ongoing European Council summit, but with no definitive conclusion this time, no matter how positively a De Wever-Zelensky meeting might go.
Zelensky will attend the summit only on the morning of Oct. 16 and, on the sidelines, is expected to meet with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar.
The Magyar meeting is significant as the first bilateral between the two leaders and comes days after Ukraine adopted a long-awaited law to bolster the rights of Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking minority , which was also required to advance its EU membership bid.

title: 7 sailors missing as two ships off Romanian Black Sea coast catch fire amid drone incursion
description: Romanian authorities opened an investigation into the possibility of a drone strike on one of the tankers, after drones violated the country's airspace overnight.
content:
Seven sailors are missing from one of two tanker ships that caught fire in Romania's Black Sea overnight amid drone incursions into the country's airspace, Romanian officials said on Oct. 15.
The San Marino-flagged "Wine Trader," a chemical tanker, reported a fire aboard and eight people missing at 07:00 a.m. local time near the Romanian city of Sulina, a press release by Romania's naval authority said . The authority has since updated the numbers to seven missing.
Search and rescue operations were continuing, it added.
On the evening of Oct. 14, Romanian defense minister Radu Miruta said the country's authorities were also investigating a reported drone attack on an chemical tanker, the "Yara J," Romanian media Digi24 reported.
The Romanian Agency for the Rescue of Human Life on the Sea (ARSVOM) received a call for a rescue mission for the Comoros-flagged ship after it had caught fire.
The sailors from Syria, India, and Iran were all safe aboard, but said the ship was hit by a drone at about 08:25 p.m. local time, Digi24 said.
The leader of the Romanian Seafarers' Free Union, Adrian Mihalcioiu, considered the incident an intentional attack of a ship in Romanian territorial waters en route to Ukraine, Digi24 said.
Miruta said that no drone was seen approaching the ship on the defense ministry's radars, but at the same time pointed toward two drones that entered Romania's airspace at 10:26 p.m. local time, according to Digi24.
"Whether it was struck by a drone or not, an investigation is currently underway," he said. "It is a matter of significant gravity, as long as such incidents occur in Romanian territorial waters."
On Oct. 13, two cargo ships were struck by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast overnight, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
Radev called the attacks " absolutely unacceptable " and said Bulgaria had informed its permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union. Sofia is seeking assistance to strengthen surveillance of the air and maritime domains and improve its response capabilities.
Attacks by Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea intensified over the summer.
In July, Ukraine launched Operation Molochka, a campaign targeting Russia's shadow fleet in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in an effort to tighten the noose around Russian-occupied Crimea .
Turkey called on Moscow and Kyiv in August to impose a moratorium on attacks against vessels, following a series of strikes in the region that involved Turkish-flagged ships.
While Kyiv has said it is ready to accept a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, Moscow has shown no interest in de-escalating the situation.
Ukraine established its own Black Sea maritime corridor in August 2023, after Russia withdrew from a U.N.- and Turkey-brokered grain deal. Since then, Russia has regularly targeted ports and civilian shipping.

title: From Oleshky to Mariupol, crises across Russian-occupied Ukraine deepen
description:
While the humanitarian crisis in the Russian-occupied front-line city of Oleshky recently garnered media attention, all regions of occupied Ukraine face worsening humanitarian issues at the hands of Russia's occupation authorities.

Across all occupied territories, civilians face failing water and electricity systems, shortages of qualified doctors, deteriorating municipal services, and mass depopulation, while specific problems differ from one occupied region to another.

Petro Andriushchenko,
content:
Fire at an electrical substation caused by a drone strike in Melitopol, Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukraine, on April 14, 2026. ( Militarnyi / Exilenova+)
While the humanitarian crisis in the Russian-occupied front-line city of Oleshky recently garnered media attention, all regions of occupied Ukraine face worsening humanitarian issues at the hands of Russia's occupation authorities.
Across all occupied territories, civilians face failing water and electricity systems, shortages of qualified doctors, deteriorating municipal services, and mass depopulation, while specific problems differ from one occupied region to another.
Petro Andriushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation, told the Kyiv Independent that the problems are driven by the failure of Russian occupation authorities to maintain basic services, as well as wartime destruction, proximity to the front line, and a lack of qualified personnel.
Russia currently occupies all of Crimea, 99% of Luhansk Oblast, 73% of Donetsk Oblast, 65% of Zaporizhzhia Oblast, and 57% of Kherson Oblast, according to geolocation estimates from the open source intelligence project DeepState . Crimea, as well as parts of Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, have been under occupation since 2014, while Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts are under occupation since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.
Between 3.5 million and 5 million Ukrainians remain in Russian-occupied territories and in Russia itself, according to an estimate cited by Ukrainian Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets in July.
Many Ukrainians cannot leave for various reasons, such as age, illness, disability, financial constraints, family responsibilities, and the threat of property expropriation by the occupation authorities.
The occupied parts of Kherson Oblast face some of the most severe humanitarian conditions among the territories under Moscow's grip.
Russian troops continue to use towns and villages on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast to launch attacks on the Ukrainian-held side.
Settlements along the Dnipro River, including Oleshky and Hola Prystan, are exposed to the threats of active warfare, including constant drone attacks, while mined roads and a lack of safe evacuation routes leave civilians with almost no way out.
"It's coming at us, it's coming from us. Russia isn't carrying out any evacuations and ( Volodymyr Saldo , Russian proxy head of occupied Kherson Oblast) isn't doing anything there at all," Andriushchenko said about the predicament of settlements caught near the front line.
Oleshky residents have reported that the town is running critically low on food due to a lack of supplies, while only a few residents have managed to evacuate. Russian forces are preventing international humanitarian organizations and Ukraine from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
More than 6,000 people may remain in Oleshky and the surrounding area, including about 200 children, Lubinets said on Sept. 16. His office said it had verified 358 people who urgently need assistance to leave the city safely.
Russia's destruction of the Kakhovka Dam in June 2023 also compounded water shortages across the region, and the impact is still evident today.
Serhii Danylov, deputy head of the Association of Middle East Studies, who focuses on Kherson Oblast, told the Kyiv Independent that the Kakhovka Reservoir was a crucial source of water in the area. Due to its destruction, the entire system of the North Crimean Canal has dried up, he said.
"Even if we imagine that water will appear now, it is impossible to restore the canals — they need to be built from scratch," Danylov said.
Electricity disruptions have further affected water supplies, while damaged infrastructure and shortages of medical workers have made it harder for residents to access essential services.
In an Oct. 1 report , Ukraine's National Resistance Center said the occupation administration lacked enough functioning water trucks to supply affected communities.
Some settlements received electricity for only 20 to 30 minutes before outages resumed for an indefinite period, the center said in a separate Oct. 6 report .
In occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast, unstable electricity supply is one of the most pressing problems. It is partially connected to Ukraine's strikes against Russian military targets in occupied Ukraine.
Ukraine targets energy infrastructure in occupied territories to disrupt Russian military operations, as electricity is essential to sustaining its forces and logistics.
Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, known by his callsign "Madyar," said that 240 energy facilities were hit in occupied Ukraine between 1 July and 13 August.
"We've been putting up with it for a year now – they (the Russians) can't fix it, because they're such clueless idiots that they're incapable of doing it," Andriushchenko said.
Some areas experience such prolonged electricity outages that availability is the exception rather than the norm. On the Kyrylivska Spit, electricity is reportedly available for only a few hours a week. Enerhodar, Melitopol and Berdiansk have also faced unstable power supplies.
Residents of Melitopol complained about voltage fluctuations reaching 280 to 300 volts, which had damaged household appliances, Ukrainian media outlet Akzent , which focuses on Zaporizhzhia Oblast, reported on Oct. 5. When asked what they lacked most , they replied that it was electricity and water, according to a video published Oct. 7 on Telegram.
The Russian occupation authorities in Berdiansk district also acknowledged systematic electricity outages and water supply disruptions lasting more than eight hours, urging residents to boil water and use filters due to the risk of acute intestinal infections.
The National Resistance Center also reported electricity and water-supply problems elsewhere in occupied Zaporizhzhia Oblast. In a July 26 report on Enerhodar , it said residents had gone months without reliable electricity and water, as the unstable power affected water pumping equipment.
Andriushchenko attributed the ongoing problems to repeated damage to energy infrastructure and the inability of the occupation administration, led by Yevgeny Balytsky, to restore it.
Additionally, Russian-installed gas operator Zaporizhzhia Gas announced scheduled gas supply cuts in occupied Melitopol and parts of Melitopol and Pryazovske districts on Oct. 12–13, citing the need to protect gas distribution infrastructure from potential Ukrainian drone attacks. Gas restoration at some addresses was scheduled to take place gradually through Nov. 4.
The electricity, water, and gas crisis is accompanied by yet another major problem — a severe shortage of doctors. The issue is particularly acute in rural areas, where medical care can be virtually unavailable.
Many Ukrainian medical professionals left the occupied territories after Russia's full-scale invasion, while attempts to bring in doctors from Russia have failed to close the gap, Andriushchenko said.
"Nobody wants to go to the occupied territory, whatever the salary they're offered, and the doctors who are left there are the worst of the worst, because the decent ones have actually all been evacuated," he said.
Occupied Donetsk Oblast has been facing one of the most severe water crises among Ukraine's occupied territories. Residents of the occupied city of Donetsk have reported going entire days without running water.
"The problem with water is so severe, it's all you can think about from morning till night," a female member of the Zla Mavka partisan group who lives in the city of Donetsk told the Kyiv Independent.
Farther north, where the region's Soviet-era water system depended heavily on infrastructure connected to the Dnipro River and the Siverskyi Donets, the problem is particularly acute.
Wartime destruction of key infrastructure has severely disrupted that system, while a new water route from the Don River cannot provide enough water to meet the region's needs, according to Andriushchenko.
To provide occupied Donetsk Oblast with water, Russia would need access to the Dnipro River in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, or at least proper access to the Siverskyi Donets in Kharkiv Oblast, which are both controlled by Ukraine, Andriushchenko said. Otherwise, Donetsk Oblast "will simply die out sooner or later," he added.
In Mariupol , residents have also reported severe water shortages, even having to register and wait to collect water. Russia's siege of the city devastated its water infrastructure, and under occupation, Mariupol has struggled to recover.
The National Resistance Center reported problems with utility services in both Mariupol and Donetsk. In a July 20 report , it said residents in occupied Donetsk Oblast were receiving bills for utilities that were not being provided or not even connected to their homes.
Beyond the water crisis, municipal services have deteriorated, with garbage collection among the problems affecting cities such as Donetsk and Mariupol. Telegram channel Mariupol Seichas regularly posts footage showing streets filled with uncollected garbage.
Andriushchenko said this problem exists because there are neither enough resources to run public utilities nor enough staff to operate them.
The medical system in Donetsk Oblast is facing a similar crisis. Despite the construction of housing for young doctors and new diagnostic centers in Mariupol, some facilities remain effectively empty because there are not enough medical workers willing to work near the front line, Andriushchenko said.
"They built several huge diagnostic centers in Mariupol, and they are building new ones, but they are (just) standing there. There is simply nobody to work there," he said. "The medical collapse is a constant story. People die from whatever they are treated for, unfortunately."
The situation in occupied Luhansk Oblast is comparatively stable, particularly in the regional capital, Luhansk. The city is farther from the front line, meaning its infrastructure can function more consistently than in many other occupied areas.
But outside the city, conditions are considerably worse. Cities such as Sievierodonetsk have been heavily affected by destruction and population loss.
In April, Ukraine's Luhansk Oblast Military Administration said that the occupied part of Luhansk Oblast had been facing a shortage of specialists in several fields.
"There is an acute shortage of doctors, teachers, and civil servants," the administration said.
Water problems have also persisted. Previous Kyiv Independent reporting found that years of neglect and wartime damage had left parts of the water network in occupied Luhansk Oblast barely functioning, with residents reporting that tap water was unsafe to drink.
A woman from Luhansk told the Kyiv Independent that it was impossible to drink tap water because of its quality, describing it as "poison." She said she had heard rumors that it might come from flooded mines.
The National Resistance Center said in a Nov. 15, 2025, report that residents in some areas went days or weeks without water and that some had resorted to draining water from heating systems for household use.
Occupied Crimea remains significantly better supplied than other occupied territories, according to Andriushchenko.
"If the other occupied territories generally have no direct importance for Putin, Crimea is the pearl of his imperial ambitions, and that is why they take special care of it," Andriushchenko said.
Crimea's occupation in 2014 did not involve the level of ground fighting and destruction later seen in Kherson, Zaporizhzhia, Donetsk, and Luhansk oblasts. Moscow then began integrating the peninsula into its system and invested significant resources in maintaining infrastructure on the peninsula, Andriushchenko said.
According to him, earlier problems with water and electricity supply were addressed after the occupation, as the Kremlin treats Crimea as a strategically and politically important territory.
Yet the peninsula also experienced electricity shortages, and water supply remains vulnerable due to droughts, infrastructure problems, and wartime disruptions.
Crimea has also faced shortages of qualified medical workers, said Andriushchenko, and Sevastopol, in particular, has struggled to retain doctors since the occupation. He said that Russia at times had to bring medical workers from other occupied Ukrainian territories.
A local resident who lived in Crimea after its occupation and worked in the medical sphere also told the Kyiv Independent that the availability of certain medical services has fallen significantly since the occupation.
As winter draws closer, the humanitarian situation across the occupied territories remains dire.
In occupied Oleshky, residents are increasingly worried about how they will survive the winter without regular food deliveries, medicine, electricity, or reliable transport, Tetiana Hasanenko, exiled head of the Ukrainian Oleshky City Military Administration, said.
"People's moods are very panicked and depressed," Hasanenko said. "They understand that the summer has passed and no evacuation has been organized."
Yuliia Taradiuk is a Ukrainian reporter at the Kyiv Independent. She has been working with Lutsk-based misto.media, telling stories of Ukrainian fighters for the "All are gone to the front" project. She has experience as a freelance culture reporter, and a background in urbanism and activism, working for multiple Ukrainian NGOs. Yuliia holds B.A. degree in English language and literature from Lesya Ukrainka Volyn National University, she studied in Germany and Lithuania.

title: 'Incoherent,' 'deeply problematic,' and 'bad,' Europe reacts to Trump's recent pro-Russian turn
description: "Every step now to help the Russians increase their financing of the war is a bad sign. We very much stick to Volodymyr Zelensky's view on this," Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The most recent pro-Russian turn of the U.S. Trump administration has not gone unnoticed in Europe, with EU leaders lining up at an Oct. 15 summit in Brussels to criticize the moves, even as they hold out hope for the future of the transatlantic alliance.
U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 9 a deal to buy Russian diesel , and called for President Volodymyr Zelensky to be replaced. Ukraine's military use of Starlink was restricted days later without warning, and the U.S. might have also limited intelligence sharing, which would put Ukrainian civilians at even more risk of being killed in Russian aerial attacks.
"This is not the right side of history," Zelensky said in an Oct. 14 interview in which he considered the latest moves from the U.S. to be a betrayal of Ukraine.
"We very much regret this agreement on diesel ... the U.S. makes such an agreement, which basically is not at all about Ukraine, but rather about American politics basically," said outgoing Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson.
"Every step now to help the Russians increase their financing of the war is a bad sign. We very much stick to Volodymyr Zelensky's view on this," Kristersson said.
The agreement with Russia "will not solve the fuel price problem," said Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro, who said the move was not "coherent."
"It is also not coherent because it gives a wrong signal in relation to support for Russia's aggression against Ukraine," Montenegro added.
The EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said Europe and the U.S "definitely have different approaches to this war."
"We see that we have to pressure the aggressor to stop the war, not the victim to surrender," Kallas said.
She also emphasized Europe's role as a "strong player," saying the U.S. policy shift on Russia "has been going on for over a year already, and Europe has stood by Ukraine. That is why Russia has not achieved their goals."
"I think the American president overestimates that you can eventually get Putin to peace by being very friendly with him," said Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten,
"It's really a very bad choice by Trump ... (the U.S.) is more often an unpredictable ally than we have been used to," Jetten said.
The news about unilateral restrictions being placed on the use of Starlink over Ukraine, without prior warning, faced criticism, too.
"There is only one word to describe it, it is deeply problematic. And yet another example of how the tech giants have gained all too much power and influence," said Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen.
Her Austrian counterpart Christian Stocker said it was "a bad sign for the security of Ukraine, for the security of Europe."
"It shows once again that it is very dangerous when information is not in one's own hands, not in the hands of Europe," Stocker said.
The moves from the U.S. led Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha to say Europe needs to " take its future in its own hands, " at an Oct. 12 meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers, a sentiment echoed by several EU leaders since.
"Trump's and Putin's agreement is very dangerous, and for all these reasons Europe must once again take its role," said Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo.
When asked if there was a European consensus, Orpo replied "I haven't noticed any discrepancy in this matter. All the discussions I've had have been very consistent."
Even so, there was a similarly clear will not to lose contact with the U.S. entirely.
"We will continue our discussions with the U.S., even if there are some decisions that we do not support," said Luxembourgish Prime Minister Luc Frieden.
We have to continue our engagement with the U.S. because we've had moments in the past when there were challenges and difficulties ... and it was retrieved by good outreach and engagement," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin.
"And I've no doubt that will continue," Martin added.
"I have long ago chosen not to respond to every tweet and every statement from the American government, but really to focus on the common interests and to appeal to them that we have been their best friends for 250 years," said Dutch Prime Minister Jetten.
"My appeal is we are all friends. We are all on this side of history and we know very well who is on the other side," said Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda.
Nauseda implored the U.S. to "please stay united in our family because Russia is challenging our way of life, our rules, our rule of law, democratic rules, human rights, everything."

title: ECHR opens proceedings against Hungary over detention, 'torture' of Ukrainian bank staff
description: "The fact that the ECHR has accepted the complaint and opened proceedings indicates that there are reasonable legal grounds for the case, that it has legal merit, and that the court intends to examine it on its merits," the Ukrainian state-owned Oschadbank said.
content:
The European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has opened proceedings in six cases against Hungary over the alleged torture and unlawful detention of Ukrainian Oschadbank employees in spring, the state-owned bank said on Oct. 15.
The cases stem from a March incident that took place during Hungary 's election campaign, when Viktor Orban was still prime minister. Hungarian authorities detained seven Oschadbank employees on suspicion of money laundering as they traveled from Austria to Ukraine through Hungary in two bank vehicles carrying $40 million, 35 million euros, and 9 kilograms of gold.
The employees were released the day after their detention, while the cash and gold were returned to Ukraine in May.
The cases were brought by six staff members of a state-owned Ukrainian bank who say they were tortured and illegally detained. A similar case is expected to be filed on behalf of a seventh worker.
Kyiv previously condemned the incident, calling it "hostage-taking" and "state terrorism." Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said the staff were subjected to "physical and psychological pressure."
"The fact that the ECHR has accepted the complaint and opened proceedings indicates that there are reasonable legal grounds for the case, that it has legal merit, and that the court intends to examine it on its merits," the bank's statement read .
The bank staff applications cite Articles 3 and 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which prohibit torture and protect the right to liberty and security.

title: Russian drone strikes Kyiv, injures 7, sets car ablaze
description: The Russian drone crashed near a 5-story residential building, damaging the facades of nearby buildings, as well as setting a car on fire.
content:
The aftermath of a Russian drone attack in a residential area in the Pechersk District of Kyiv, Ukraine on Oct. 15, 2026. (Serhii Korovayny/The Kyiv Independent)
A Russian drone crashed in Kyiv's Pechersk District, injuring seven people and causing damage to a residential building on Oct. 15, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Three of the injured people were hospitalied, Klitschko said . The Russian drone crashed near a five-story residential building, damaging the facades of nearby buildings, as well as setting a car on fire, he added .
"The blast wave blew the kitchen door off its hinges, and glass rained down. A neighbor was standing in the middle of the kitchen; she was knocked down by the blast and fell, sustaining injuries. We looked around — we hadn't even had time to react to it all — and everything was covered in glass," Inna Kozub, a local resident, said about the attack.
"I started shaking all over, and tears began to flow ... I was just overcome by panic," she said.
"We live here, my wife called and said that it (the drone) flew here, I was at work. And I sped home quickly. The children were at home, upstairs, just slightly injured," said Ruslan, another resident.
"They heard that the attack was coming, they jumped out into the corridor. The older one carried them out of the room. And then the windows flew out. He threw the little one to the ground and covered them," Ruslan added.
"There are a lot of these attacks now and they say that this is a matter of the Americans stopping helping us," he said.
Another Russian drone attack in the afternoon struck a warehouse in Sviatoshynskyi District, leading to a fire breaking out, Klitschko said .
Kyiv has come under continuous Russian attacks over the last weeks that saw strikes on civilians, as well as the capital's transport and energy infrastructure.
Ukraine's Air Force said Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 580 Shahed-type and other drones, of which it neutralized 536 across 31 locations.
Overnight on Oct. 13-14, Russia launched a large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv, wreaking destruction in a residential neighborhood and targeting several energy facilities in Kyiv.

title: Ukraine destroys 4 Russian Su-34 bomber jets, damages 2 with Neptune missile, Zelensky says
description: The attack was carried out with the Neptune coastal missile system, Ukraine's naval forces said.
content:
An overnight attack on the Borisoglebsk military airfield in Russia's Voronezh region hit six Su-34M bomber jets, destroying four and damaging two, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 15.
"The Russians used them (the Su-34Ms) to terrorize our people. These aircraft were ready for new strikes on Ukraine and were equipped with aerial bombs," Zelensky said .
"Russia is dragging out the war, therefore, our long-range operations will continue," he added.
The attack was carried out with the Neptune coastal missile system, Ukraine's naval forces said on Telegram . Ukraine's General Staff said that explosions and a fire were recorded on the airfield territory.
Voronezh Oblast Governor Alexander Gusev warned several times of a drone attack. Online footage of the attack filmed by local residents showed explosions and a large fire at the airfield. The Borisoglebsk military airfield is about 370 kilometers (about 230 miles) from the front line.
Neptune is Ukraine's ground-launched, domestically produced anti-ship cruise missile with a maximum range of several hundred kilometers which it used in April 2022 to sink Russia's Black Sea flagship, the Moskva.
In 2025, Ukraine unveiled an upgraded version of the missile, which had already demonstrated a range of 1,000 kilometers (620 miles). In March 2025, President Volodymyr Zelensky said the system had successfully completed testing and would be deployed for combat use.
The Su-34M is a heavily modernized, upgraded variant of the baseline Su-34 fighter-bomber. The Russian Su-34 is a Russian medium-range fighter-bomber. Ukrainian forces have targeted the warplanes in attacks on Russian military airfields and have reported downing the jets on several occasions.

title: Integrating Ukraine into EU a powerful response to Russia's attacks, says Irish PM
description: What Russia is doing is "appalling and... horrific, and it illustrates that Putin is not interested in peace. That's why we must manifest our support for Ukraine in the practical ways that we can," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Ireland's Prime Minister Micheal Martin doubled down on his country's push to move forward Ukraine's EU accession bid as much as possible by the end of the year, in comments made at the Oct. 15 EU leaders' summit in Brussels.
Ireland is chairing the EU's Council Presidency until the end of 2026, meaning it is responsible for the bloc's agenda during that period. One of Dublin's oft-stated priorities is to unblock and make serious progress on EU enlargement.
"Now is the time to be ambitious over the next months to open all clusters in respect of Ukraine and Moldova," Martin said, referring to the six to-do lists of reforms that Kyiv is partway through unlocking.
"The people of Ukraine need that as a very strong signal given the extraordinary pressure they are under from Russian attacks on civilians and civil infrastructure," Martin said, reiterating that he aims to have all six clusters open by the end of the year.
Russia has upped its attacks across Ukraine with extensive use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones against civilian targets.
The draft conclusions for the EU leaders' summit refer to these developments, but lack new concrete measures to help Ukraine fend off Russian attacks.
What Russia is doing is "appalling and... horrific, and it illustrates that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin is not interested in peace. That's why we must manifest our support for Ukraine in the practical ways that we can," Martin said.
For him, advancing Ukraine's EU membership bid is one of those things.
Ukraine unlocked a third and fourth of the six enlargement clusters on Oct. 13, leaving two still to go.
Despite Hungary and Bulgaria attacking ambitious words on enlargement in the draft conclusions for the ongoing leaders' meeting, it seems there are no public objections to Ukraine being able to open the remaining two.
Lithuania's President Gitanas Nauseda said he "does not see any big obstacles to opening the remaining two clusters" and echoed Martin's message that "Ukraine has to receive some positive signals."
"One of the strongest signals is the chance and the light at the end of the tunnel regarding the integration of Ukraine into the EU," Nauseda added.

title: Ukrainian parliament passes key bill on international parcel taxes
description: The bill's passage is a condition for unlocking an approximately $700 million IMF tranche and 3.7 billion euros ($4.1 billion) in EU macro-financial assistance.
content:
Editor's note: The story has been updated to include comments from Ukrainian officials.
Ukraine's parliament passed a bill on taxing e-commerce and international parcels on Oct. 15, meeting a condition linked to international financial assistance after missing earlier deadlines.
The bill passed its final vote with 252 lawmakers in favour after facing criticism from some lawmakers. Parliament had previously failed to advance the bill and sent it back for revision.
Its adoption is linked to Ukraine receiving the International Monetary Fund's ( IMF ) tranche of around $700 million and the EU tranche of 3.7 billion euros ($4.1 billion) in macro-financial assistance.
The legislation introduces the value-added tax (VAT) on international parcels worth up to 150 euros ($168), which are currently tax-exempt. Lawmakers also backed new customs regulations for international mail and express shipments.
The changes could take effect on July 1, 2027, but only after a separate government decision.
Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko said the tranches would be disbursed to Ukraine’s state budget "in the coming weeks."
"The adopted bills will ensure a level playing field for Ukrainian businesses and allow the state budget to raise an additional Hr 10 billion ($222 million) annually to fund the Armed Forces," he added.
The parliament repeatedly failed to pass some of the conditions set by Ukraine's partners throughout 2026, amid widespread unpopularity of the changes. Most toxic was a package of new taxes, including a tax on small imported parcels, and a tax on income received from digital platforms, such as Uber.
In recent days, lawmakers have advanced several key bills tied to Western aid, with $29.5 billion in funding at stake if parliament and the government fail to meet the required conditions.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said on Oct. 15 he hoped lawmakers would maintain the pace of passing bills.
"The results of this plenary week give us all reason to be optimistic, but there is still a lot of work ahead," Koretskyi wrote on social media.
"We count on the same constructive cooperation in the coming plenary weeks to ensure that all necessary decisions are adopted on time and Ukraine receives the full amount of international financial aid."

title: Slovakia to hold talks with Ukraine, revive economic meetings with Russia
description: The Slovak-Ukrainian talks will be held in Lviv on Nov. 5 and focus on expanding border crossings, providing humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, and establishing a school for Ukrainian children in Bratislava.
content:
Slovakia's Prime Minister Robert Fico announced on Oct. 14 that the Slovak and the Ukrainian governments will hold their next round of talks in the western Ukrainian city of Lviv on Nov. 5.
Separately, Fico also confirmed talks with Russia on Nov. 25 under the framework of a joint economic commission, a format that was suspended after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Slovakia 's populist, Moscow-friendly leader framed this outreach as part of Bratislava's foreign "policy toward all four cardinal directions."
Fico noted that the upcoming Slovak-Ukrainian talks will be the fourth meeting of this format, with the last one held in the eastern Slovak city of Kosice last October.
The negotiations are to focus on expanding border crossings, providing humanitarian assistance to Ukraine, and establishing a school for Ukrainian children in Bratislava.
Fico last visited Ukraine in September 2025 for talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky. He was also scheduled to attend the inaugural Carpathian summit on Sept. 18 in Ukraine's Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast, but ultimately skipped the event for health reasons.
Speaking to Slovak lawmakers before his departure for the European Council, Fico said that EU leaders are set to hold talks on a potential next loan for Ukraine and said Bratislava would not take part.
Fico's government has declined to participate in the EU's 90-billion-euro ($101 billion) loan for Kyiv adopted in April, but has not blocked it either and has voiced support for Ukraine's accession talks.
At the same time, the Slovak leader has consistently criticized energy sanctions against Russia and military aid to Ukraine, cutting off arms deliveries from Slovak army stocks. He was the only EU leader to visit the Russian capital for the May 9 Victory Day celebrations in 2025 and this year, meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Fico agreed with Putin on restarting the intergovernmental commission during the May celebrations in 2025, the Slovak newspaper Sme reported .
The last meeting of the commission, focused on economic and scientific cooperation between the two countries, was held in November 2021, months before the start of the all-out war in Ukraine.
The Slovak leader did not provide further details about the upcoming talks with the Russian side.

title: Starlink service in Ukraine 'restored,' Defense Ministry source says
description: SpaceX, the owner of Starlink, implemented speed restrictions on Oct. 14 without warning.
content:
Connectivity for Starlink systems used by the Ukrainian military have "been restored and remains operational," a source in the Defense Ministry told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 15.
SpaceX, the owner of Starlink, implemented speed restrictions on Oct. 14 without warning , limiting speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour). The unexpected restriction disrupted active military operations, including the use of mid-range strike and interceptor drones.
" As of now, (Starlink military package) Starshield service while on the move has been restored and remains operational. We have confirmed this through reports from our units," the source said.
"The Defense Ministry is also continuing its engagement to clarify all the reasons and circumstances surrounding yesterday’s restrictions."
The source did not say if all restrictions had been lifted or if some speed restrictions still applied.
Serhii Sternenko , an activist and former advisor to Fedorov who was one of the first to report the restrictions, also said on Oct. 15 that "Starlink (Starshield) service has been restored."
But a source in Ukraine's drone industry who requested anonymity due to the nature of their work told the Kyiv Independent that "in some cases, it works perfectly, in some places it does not."
The source of the disruption has yet to be confirmed, but Ukrainian officials as well as SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have pointed towards Kyiv's deteriorating relationship with the White House.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Oct. 14.
A post on X from Musk said only U.S. President Donald Trump had the power to determine the speed restrictions for Starshield systems.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action," he said .
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones. It is restricted from using it inside Russia itself.
The speed restrictions that were put in place on Oct. 14 were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from multiple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry told journalists that the actual speeds available during the day were even lower than the 160 kph limit.
A soldier working on mid-range strike drone operations, who requested anonymity, confirmed that "certain issues are being observed" but declined to elaborate, citing operational security.
Two other commanders — both from elite drone units working on the eastern and southern front lines — reported issues with Starlink terminals on "middle strike" drones flying at higher speeds.
Both likewise requested to remain anonymous, and declined to describe the problems in more detail, so as to not assist the enemy.

title: Zelensky lifts pause on Ukraine's strikes against Russian oil refineries
description: Ukraine had refrained from strikes on Russia's refineries for three days, President Volodymyr Zelensky said, while Russia resumed its attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky lifted restrictions on Ukraine's strikes against Russian oil refineries after Russia continued to strike Ukraine's energy infrastructure over the past days, Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times on Oct. 15.
"The block (on attacking refineries) is out. We’re done," Zelensky said .
U.S. President Donald Trump unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, causing confusion in Kyiv. According to a senior Ukrainian official, Ukraine had no prior information about an energy ceasefire.
On Oct. 14, the Kremlin said that the extent of Trump's proposed energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine was not specified, as Russian attacks against Ukraine's power grid and civilians continued.
Ukraine had refrained from strikes on Russia's refineries for three days to accommodate the U.S. request, Zelensky said, while Russia resumed its attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Russia launched a large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv overnight on Oct. 13-14, wreaking destruction in a residential neighborhood and targeting several energy facilities in Kyiv.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that all three of the city's combined heat and power stations were attacked, as well as critical infrastructure in Kyiv Oblast that provide power to Kyiv and central regions.
"Overnight, the Russians deployed 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media , adding 600,000 people were without power.
Zelensky said that Ukraine could only agree to halt strikes on Russia's energy infrastructure if Ukraine were to receive more U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles, calling it the "minimum."
Yet, ceasing strikes on Russian energy might also encourage further deals between Washington and Moscow, benefitting Putin's war machine, Zelensky told the Financial Times.
"The question will be when will the next deal be? Maybe it will be gas. Definitely it will be gas."
Kaja Kallas, the EU high representative for foreign affairs and security policy, expressed her support for the resumption of strikes on Russian oil refineries.
"The majority of Russia's funding for the war comes from oil revenues. So clearly Ukraine wants this war to stop, and that's why cutting off the funding for the war is the way to do it," Kallas said before a European Council meeting on Oct. 15.
"We should squeeze Russia, not Ukraine, to surrender, to end this war," Kallas added.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,559,230 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,880 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,559,230 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 15.
The number includes 1,880 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,414 tanks, 25,537 armored combat vehicles, 163,324 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,233 artillery systems, 2,216 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,707 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,955 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.
