content:
Employees work at a power plant of Ukrainian energy provider DTEK, which was damaged by constant Russian air attacks, at an undisclosed location in Ukraine, on Nov. 13, 2025. (Roman Pilipey / AFP via Getty Images)
Volleys of explosions deafened Kyiv in the early hours of Oct. 14, as Russia targeted multiple energy facilities powering the embattled capital amid a new campaign to isolate and disconnect the city following a brutal summer of relentless strikes on businesses and critical infrastructure.
While Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy system have been ongoing throughout the year at a low level, Moscow has recently ramped up mass attacks to wipe out power plants, substations, and gas infrastructure for its fifth winter offensive during the full-scale invasion.
The latest attack on Oct. 14 alone targeted 26 power facilities, President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on social media.
There’s also been a recent uptick in Russian drones and missiles flying near nuclear plants , one energy official with knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent under the condition of anonymity.
The drones are likely monitoring the plants and their infrastructure, with the official warning that Russia may be preparing to strike them — something Moscow has largely refrained from throughout its invasion.
Ukraine is in a vulnerable position. In just the week of Oct. 5-11, there were around 200 hits on power sector facilities and 17 on the oil and gas sector, the Energy Ministry’s press department told the Kyiv Independent. And Ukraine lacks critical air defense against Moscow’s expanding arsenal, energy specialists told the Kyiv Independent.
As the winter draws closer, Russia will likely expand its campaign to other major cities to sow panic.
Meanwhile, Russia’s tactics and weapons technology have changed since last winter. In addition to ballistic missiles, Moscow overwhelms Ukraine’s air defense by launching jet-powered drones and AI-powered loitering munitions en masse, attacking during the day as well as at night, and hitting infrastructure that power plants rely on, like railways for coal deliveries, energy experts said.
The recent attacks have already left hundreds of thousands of citizens in Kyiv and front-line regions suffering power and water outages. The situation has deteriorated so much in Kyiv that power to the metro was even temporarily cut off following attacks on Oct. 8 and 14. "The overall pattern is systematic: the strikes damage the network, force emergency restrictions, and slow down repairs, especially when crews cannot work safely during air-raid alerts," Viktoria Gryb, a lawmaker and head of the parliament’s subcommittee on energy security, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The methods and targets can change, so I would not call this a simple repeat of last winter. But the goal remains the same: to destabilize the energy system."
The first few weeks of Russia’s latest campaign have primarily targeted Kyiv , continuing Russia’s months-long offensive on the capital’s economic centers that has made life in the city increasingly harder and more dangerous.
For now, Moscow is picking up where it left off last winter — focusing on disconnecting Kyiv by targeting power plants in and around the capital, as well as key substations, Olena Pavlenko, president of the Kyiv-based energy-focused think tank DiXi Group, told the Kyiv Independent.
The capital is particularly vulnerable as it is reliant on thermal and cogeneration plants that are exposed to enemy strikes, while substations that connect it to generation sources, including nuclear plants in western Ukraine, are protected against drones but not against ballistic missiles.
Meanwhile, the city hasn’t prepared enough backup generation supplies for when its power plants are inevitably taken offline. Despite experiencing a humanitarian crisis last winter when residents lacked heating and power in minus 25 degrees Celsius, political infighting and funding shortages mean the city will likely experience the same difficulties again.
Kyiv and other cities are also frequently attacked by jet-powered drones, which weren’t widespread last winter. They are faster and more precise than the older propeller-powered drones, making them harder for Ukraine’s limited air defenses to shoot down.
"Jet-powered drones changed the game to some extent. They are cheaper than missiles and can destroy more distributed generation infrastructure," Pavlenko said.
"It’s easier for jet-powered drones to attack transformers, smaller transformers, and infrastructure for cities. This has a huge impact on cities in terms of heating supply, water supply, and sewage."
In addition to striking power plants and substations, Russia has also increasingly hit power lines around big cities over the last few weeks to cut power supplies to consumers. While not a new target, Russia’s tactics have improved, including attaching a new type of warhead to a jet-powered drone designed to destroy high-voltage electricity pylons.
Ukraine’s three operational nuclear power plants, which generate around 60% of the country’s electricity, will likely be the country’s lifeline again once other power plants are taken offline.
Unlike substations, which are largely protected against jet-powered drones via massive concrete fortifications, power lines and pylons are more exposed since they can’t be easily shielded. But damaged power lines can be restored in 24 hours, in contrast to substations, which require complex repairs, the anonymous energy official said.
The problem with pylons could surface in the long run, as Ukraine’s steel industry has shut down amid debilitating strikes on factories. Stockpiles of products to reconstruct pylons will gradually deplete until steel firms can safely resume production, the press service of Metinvest, Ukraine’s largest steel company, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The situation regarding future supplies is becoming critical," Metinvest’s press service wrote in a statement to the Kyiv Independent.
After the last autumn and winter period, which saw Russia wipe out more than half of Ukraine’s gas production and 9 gigawatts of energy generation, the energy sector expects the same challenges again this year.
There’s little else that Russia can target, said Volodymyr Kudritsky, former head of Ukraine's state-grid operator Ukrenergo and co-founder of energy firm Nedzhen.
"We’ve already seen 95% of the menu. The Russians have left themselves with very little room to surprise us more," Kudritskyi told the Kyiv Independent.
The key issue for the energy sector is the air defense situation, as Ukraine struggles to down the jet-powered drones, said Kudritskyi. In recent months, Ukraine has developed interceptors that are showing increasingly positive results , but more time is needed to scale production.
At the same time, Ukraine continues to upgrade and reinforce protection at its energy facilities, including concrete fortifications, electronic warfare, early threat detection systems, and critical equipment reserves, the Energy Ministry said.
As the winter draws closer, Russia will likely expand its campaign to other major cities to sow panic, said Pavlenko. While attacks so far this autumn have largely impacted cities like Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Zaporizhzhia, Russian drones and ballistic missiles can reach deep into western Ukraine.
There’s also a heightened threat to nuclear infrastructure, like substations, this winter, said Pavlenko. Ukraine’s three operational nuclear power plants, which generate around 60% of the country’s electricity, will likely be the country’s lifeline again once other power plants are taken offline.
The risks to nuclear plants were majorly tested last winter, as Moscow targeted substations connected to the plants. One of the worst Russian attacks in February halved the output of nuclear plants, with Ukraine stabilizing the situation before it could worsen.
In a worst-case scenario, a big attack on substations could disconnect nuclear plants from the grid, forcing the plants to shut down, said the anonymous energy official. The consequences would be "extremely serious," they added.
Dominic is the business reporter for the Kyiv Independent, reporting on Ukrainian companies, investment, energy, corruption, and reforms. Based in Kyiv, Dominic joined the Kyiv Independent team in 2023, having previously worked as a freelancer. He has written articles for a number of publications, including the Financial Times, bne IntelliNews, Radio Free Europe/Liberty, Euronews and New Eastern Europe. Previously, Dominic worked with StopFake as a disinformation expert, debunking Russian fake news in Europe.

title: Russian attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast kill 2, spark residential fires

content:
In Dnipro district, two people were killed when a private house was destroyed in the Novooleksandrivka community.
Several private houses also caught fire in Pavlohrad, where emergency crews were working. Authorities were still assessing whether anyone had been injured or killed.
Regional authorities did not immediately specify what weapons were used in the attacks.

title: 'Intense' Russian aerial assault on Kropyvnytskyi kills 3, injures 6
description: The city and surrounding region were targeted in an "intense" Russian attack that began late on Oct. 14, Governor Andrii Raikovych reported. The strike targeted local logistics, transportation, and industrial enterprises.
content:
Russia launched a mass aerial assault against the central Ukrainian city of Kropyvnytskyi overnight on Oct. 14-15, killing at least three people and injuring six.
Kropyvnytskyi is the regional center of Ukraine's Kirovohrad Oblast and has a population of approximately 220,000.
The city and surrounding region were targeted in an "intense" Russian attack that began late on Oct. 14, Governor Andrii Raikovych reported. The strike targeted local logistics, transportation, and industrial enterprises.
The attack has killed at least three people and injured another six, Raikovych said. Five of the wounded victims have been hospitalized.
The governor did not specify which targets in the city were hit. Attacks against the city are ongoing, and the full extent of the damage is not yet clear.
Shortly before Raikovych's report, Ukraine's Air Force issued a "red alert" for Kropyvnytskyi due to the threat of Russian jet-powered, high-speed drones in the region.
The mass attack on Kropyvnytskyi shows that Russia has not slowed its large-scale bombardment of Ukrainian cities, despite the so-called "energy truce" in place between Russia and Ukraine.
U.S. President Donald Trump made an unexpected and unilateral announcement of the truce on Oct. 11, claiming that both Kyiv and Moscow agreed to halt attacks against each other's energy infrastructure.
While Kyiv said it had halted attacks against Russian oil refineries since then, Russia immediately broke Trump's ceasefire by continuing to attack Ukraine's power grid and civilian infrastructure. Trump declined to blame the Kremlin for breaking the truce when asked about the matter on Oct. 13.

title: Hungary’s Magyar to meet Zelensky for first time at upcoming EU summit
description: Magyar's announcement comes two days after Zelensky signed a law strengthening the educational rights of Ukraine's national minorities, a step Hungary had demanded before allowing Kyiv's EU accession talks to move forward.
content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar announced on Oct. 14 that he would hold his first official meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky on the sidelines of an EU summit in Brussels on Oct. 16.
Magyar shared the announcement in a post about his upcoming trip to Brussels, where EU leaders will convene on Oct. 15-16 for talks expected to focus heavily on Ukraine .
"On Friday morning, I will hold, for the first time, an official bilateral meeting with the President of Ukraine," he said.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that while Kyiv is ready for such a meeting, they have not yet agreed on a time and place. Zelensky has yet to confirm the meeting.
Magyar's announcement comes two days after Zelensky signed a law strengthening the educational rights of Ukraine's national minorities, a step Hungary had demanded before allowing Kyiv's EU accession talks to move forward.
The law gives Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking minority and other EU-language minorities more room to use their native language in education. Ukrainian officials have said it would formalize existing education rights for national minorities rather than bring major practical changes.
Roughly 80,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine's westernmost Zakarpattia Oblast.
Hungary's former prime minister, the Kremlin-friendly Viktor Orban, frequently invoked the issue when blocking Ukraine's EU accession process.
Magyar's election win and his pro-European Tisza party have brought more constructive dialogue with Kyiv, but he has made clear that cooperation is conditional .
This summer, Hungarian and Ukrainian officials announced an agreement on the educational, linguistic, and cultural rights of Ukraine’s Hungarian minority, and Hungary lifted its veto on Ukraine’s EU accession talks. That allowed the launch of the first negotiating clusters, the thematic groups of reforms Ukraine must complete for EU membership.
But Budapest later blocked the launch of additional clusters, pending Ukrainian progress on the terms of the agreement, starting with education.
The new legislation cleared the way for more clusters to be opened, and the EU shared two more reform clusters with Ukraine on Oct. 13, allowing the accession process to move forward.
The Foreign Ministry said on Oct. 14 that the passage of the new language law should lead to "cooperation in all areas" between Hungary and Ukraine ahead of the Brussels summit and Magyar-Zelensky meeting.
"Our peoples deserve good neighborly relations," Sybiha said.

content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Ukraine's EU membership bid does not need to advance "as soon as possible" anymore, according to the latest draft conclusions of the Oct. 15-16 summit of EU leaders in Brussels, due to pressure from Bulgaria and Hungary.
Ahead of each summit, common conclusions are prepared in advance by the 27 EU countries, and can keep changing until the end of the gathering.
In the draft conclusions dated Oct. 13 , the text read "The European Council ... looks forward to the opening of all the other clusters as soon as possible, in line with the merit-based approach," read the draft conclusions.
The EU just unlocked an additional two enlargement clusters — to-do lists of reforms that Ukraine must complete to join the bloc — on Oct. 13, and it is expected that the remaining two will be opened in December.
But the draft conclusions as they stand on Oct. 14 no longer contain the words "as soon as possible."
Three national diplomats have confirmed that Bulgaria and Hungary were the countries to push for the removal of this wording, with the main justification being to keep it the same as in June.
June was when EU leaders last met, and Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar led a successful push to scrap the reference to advancing Ukraine's EU membership bid "as soon as possible" then too.
But the latest move is nonetheless surprising as Hungary's bilateral issue with Ukraine over minority rights has been resolved , and there are no publicly known objections to Kyiv opening the remaining two clusters.
The change was also made to the part of the draft conclusions concerning Moldova, whose EU accession process leaders handcuffed to Ukraine for the opening of the enlargement clusters.
There were at least three other smaller changes to the draft conclusions concerning Ukraine: a reference to "member-state vessels" being attacked in the Black Sea , stronger wording on the return of children — describing them now as "unlawfully deported," and a reference to Ukraine's financing.
Now the draft conclusions read that leaders "will revert to the issue in a timely manner," which could be interpreted as setting the stage for a serious exchange over Russian immobilized assets, that some think could dominate discussion at the December summit.

title: Ukraine war latest: Operation Vivaldi liberates another 101 square kilometers in Donetsk Oblast
description:
Key developments on Oct. 14:

 * Ukraine retakes another 101 square kilometers in Donetsk Oblast's Lyman sector, Third Army Corps says
 * Zelensky arrives in UK as London vows to speed up anti-drone missile deliveries for Ukraine
 * 'Ostentatious disrespect' — Zelensky says Russia defied Trump's energy ceasefire with latest missile strike
 * Germany puts Ukrainian on trial over Nord Stream sabotage
 * SBU detains 18-year-old suspected FSB agent in Kyiv over attempt to activate 148 Starlink termi
content:
Ukraine's Third Army Corps, together with its attached units, has retaken another 101 square kilometers during the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman sector in Donetsk Oblast, the corps announced on Oct. 14.
Ukraine liberated the villages of Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi, while Russia lost about 3,000 of its soldiers in the fourth stage of the operation, the corps reported on Telegram .
"The enemy was unable to cut the key logistics artery of our group in the Donbas. We thwarted the offensive of the group 'Zapad' and forced it to transfer part of the units of the 1st Tank Army, which weakened the pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi," corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said.
In total, Operation Vivaldi saw the liberation and return of 16 settlements and 277 square kilometers (106 square miles) to Ukraine, the corps said. "Four seasons of 'Vivaldi' are over, but the music continues."
On Sept. 15, Biletskyi confirmed that Ukrainian forces under the command of the 3rd Army Corps were conducting a series of counterattacks north of the front-line city of Lyman in Donetsk Oblast.
The operation dealt "a heavy blow to the combat capabilities of Russia's 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies," Biletskyi said then, adding that Ukrainian drone strikes had pushed Russian supply hubs across the state border.
The fight for the heart of the so-called Donbas fortress belt — Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka — is crucial going into the winter months, when Russia will look to maximize its foothold in urban areas to prepare for a 2027 offensive campaign.
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in the U.K. on Oct. 14 to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III, as London pledges missiles to help Ukraine counter Russia's jet-powered drones.
The visit comes at a tense moment for Ukraine, with U.S. President Donald Trump 's administration pressuring Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil refineries and threatening to cut off intelligence sharing and arms shipments.
Ahead of Zelensky's visit, Burnham vowed that the U.K.'s support for Ukraine remains "rock-solid."
The Ukrainian president was first welcomed by King Charles at Buckingham Palace before meeting Burnham.
"I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience. It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine," Zelensky said on X.
The British prime minister then welcomed Zelensky at 10 Downing Street in the company of a military ceremonial guard, the first such honor granted to a foreign leader, according to the BBC .
The British government has announced an air defense missile package worth 45 million pounds (around $60 million) for Ukraine, as the country faces an intensifying onslaught of Russian missiles and drones.
"The U.K. will accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), which have proven extremely effective against jet-powered drones that are being used to strike far beyond the front lines in Ukraine, including Kyiv and beyond," the British government said in a press release on Oct. 13.
Russia has been increasingly deploying jet-powered drones that are faster and more difficult to intercept than older Shahed models, posing a new threat as Ukraine braces for massive strikes against energy infrastructure in winter.
Of the 45-million-pound package, the U.K. will expedite the delivery of 10 million pounds ($13 million) worth of LMMs to meet the most urgent winter needs.
"I’m announcing that we're accelerating the delivery of British-made air defenses for (Ukraine)," Burnham told the press while meeting Zelensky. The British leader also said he would seek to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the U.S.
Burnham's office said earlier that he had instructed his cabinet to prepare additional military and financial assistance packages for Ukraine, as well as fresh sanctions against Russia.
The U.K. further reiterated that it stands by its plans to ban maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
London said last year it would implement the phased ban over 2026 "in lockstep with our European partners."
The EU plans to ban Russian LNG imports by January 2027 but has failed to agree on a full ban on maritime services, with Greece securing a carve-out for Russian LNG exports to non-EU countries.
Russia demonstrated its disregard for U.S. President Donald Trump's proposed energy ceasefire by launching drones and missiles against Ukraine's power grid overnight, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 14.
Moscow's forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones against energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv, Zelensky said , calling it "ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
At least three people were killed, and another 22 were injured as a result of the Russian strike that hit a residential building in the Desnianskyi district and power plants elsewhere in the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Russia has ramped up aerial strikes against Ukrainian energy sites as winter nears, despite Trump's unexpected and unilateral announcement on Oct. 11 that both Kyiv and Moscow agreed to halt attacks against each other's energy infrastructure.
Even as Kyiv said it had halted attacks against Russian oil refineries since Trump's ceasefire announcement, Trump declined to blame the Kremlin for breaking the truce when asked by a reporter on Oct. 13.
"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale," Zelensky noted, adding that at least 600,000 people are without power and reporting damage to 26 power facilities, as well as four oil and gas sites.
"Russia does not consider the American President 's statements strong," the Ukrainian leader added.
The comments come as Washington piles on pressure on Kyiv to halt its aerial campaign against Russian refineries, which he linked to rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts.
The Kyiv Independent has previously learned that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials with cutting intelligence sharing and arms sales unless it stopped attacking Russian refineries.
While Ukrainian and U.S. sources told the Kyiv Independent earlier this week that Washington has not yet stopped intelligence support, questions about the early warning provided by partners are mounting as strikes now hit Kyiv even before the alarm sounds.
Presidential Advisor Serhii " Flash " Beskretnov and Serhii Sternenko , an activist and former advisor to ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, claimed on Oct. 14 that Elon Musk's SpaceX has limited the speed of Starlink terminals in Ukraine, causing disruption to "a number of critical missions."
"The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor," Zelensky noted, urging Washington to impose sanctions on Russia under late Senator Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill and calling for additional supplies of Patriot interceptors.
Ukrainian citizen Serhii Kuznetsov went to trial in Hamburg on Oct. 14 on suspicion of involvement in the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines.
A series of explosions rocked the controversial Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines in September 2022, destroying three out of four key gas pipelines linking Russia and Germany via the Baltic Sea.
Kuznetsov, a former soldier, was accused of leading the sabotage group, involving six other people. German investigators claim that he commanded the yacht "Andromeda," from which a team of divers allegedly carried out the attack against the pipelines.
On the first day of the trial, prosecutors accused Kuznetsov of being an accomplice to war crimes by committing an attack against civilian infrastructure.
Kuznetsov and Kyiv have denied any involvement in the sabotage.
The trial — the first held in connection with the Nord Stream sabotage — is expected to run until February.
Kuznietsov was arrested in August 2025 near the Italian town of Rimini under a European arrest warrant before being extradited to Germany.
Another Ukrainian suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravliov, was detained in Croatia in August 2026 and awaits extradition. Zhuravliov was first detained in Poland in September 2025, but a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany and instead released him a month later.
The Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never became operational, had long been a flashpoint in European energy politics.
Even before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine , critics said it deepened Germany's dependence on Russian gas and undermined European energy security.
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has detained an 18-year-old man in Kyiv suspected of working for Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). According to investigators, he attempted to register 148 Starlink terminals for use by Russian forces.
The SBU reported that the terminals were intended to support the planning of Russian military operations in the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. Ukrainian security officers say they prevented the devices from being activated.
According to the investigation, the suspect is a former student at a Kyiv college, where he trained to become a welder. After completing his studies, he began looking for ways to earn quick money through Telegram channels.
He was allegedly contacted by an FSB officer who offered him money in exchange for cooperation.
Within days of being recruited, the suspect registered 15 Starlink terminals using the passport details of relatives and acquaintances. He then prepared personal information belonging to other individuals to register another 133 devices.
SBU officers detained the suspect near a post office, where he allegedly planned to activate another batch of terminals.
The 15 previously registered Starlink terminals, whose details had already been sent to his Russian handler via a messaging app, were also blocked.
The suspect remains in custody without the possibility of bail. If convicted, he faces life imprisonment and confiscation of property.
The case adds to a growing number of incidents in which Russia allegedly recruits Ukrainians to carry out assignments on Moscow's behalf, including a recent case on Oct. 12, when Ukrainian authorities detained a 19-year-old suspected of plotting a bomb attack on a bus carrying soldiers in Rivne.
According to the SBU, the suspect had also been recruited through Telegram channels offering quick money.
On Oct. 6, the SBU reported arresting a suspected collaborator in Kyiv who allegedly helped Russia establish repeater stations for its drones and gather intelligence on targets in the capital.
In August, the SBU detained a suspected Russian agent in Kharkiv Oblast who allegedly registered 27 Starlink terminals for Russian forces.

title: Editorial: Donald Trump is helping Russia win the war
description:
It's already been said many times that the U.S., under President Donald Trump, was turning its back on Ukraine.

But the past few days show something worse than abandonment: Trump is now actively helping Russia win the war.

Many media and commentators have been far too careful in their phrasing, saying that Trump is "squeezing Ukraine" or putting pressure on it. We all need to do the responsible thing and call it what it is, as ugly as it sounds: Trump is not trying to reach a deal — he is tryi
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 13, 2026. (Samuel Corum / Sipa / Bloomberg via Getty Images)
It's already been said many times that the U.S., under President Donald Trump, was turning its back on Ukraine.
But the past few days show something worse than abandonment: Trump is now actively helping Russia win the war.
Many media and commentators have been far too careful in their phrasing, saying that Trump is "squeezing Ukraine" or putting pressure on it. We all need to do the responsible thing and call it what it is, as ugly as it sounds: Trump is not trying to reach a deal — he is trying to "end the war" by simply helping Russia win.
Since last week, the Trump administration has been in a downward spiral of betraying Ukraine and embarrassing the U.S.
It started when Trump announced that he had reached a deal with Vladimir Putin to buy diesel from Russia. By doing so, he went against the sanctions bill he himself had signed less than a month ago, which sought to penalize countries buying energy from Russia.
The deal is not going to help bring down fuel prices for regular Americans, but it sends a tremendously harmful signal: That it's alright to make deals that pump cash into Russia, despite its brutal ongoing invasion of Ukraine.
That move was followed by Trump announcing a surprise energy ceasefire that Kyiv didn't know about. When Russia ignored it and continued to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure, Trump said nothing about it.
It only got worse from there. For the past two nights, Russia has hit Ukrainian cities with ballistic missiles that came without any warning. That is, the early warning alerts that Ukraine typically receives about missile and drone launches from its partners — chiefly, the U.S. While there is no confirmation yet, there is a strong possibility that the U.S. has limited some intelligence data sharing .
If true, it would mean more Ukrainians killed. No warning means there is no time to get to the shelter. At least three people were killed in such an attack in Kyiv last night — civilians in their homes.
No warning means there is no time to get to the shelter.
Finally, this morning, we learned that Ukraine's military use of Starlink had been restricted without warning, undermining Ukraine's middle-strike capabilities that are critical for its front-line operations against Russia. In the rear, it hurts Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian drones targeting civilians.
This betrayal comes after one of the deadliest weeks for Ukrainian civilians. Last week, Russia killed more than 150 civilians in Ukraine. Just one of the strikes, on a bus stop in Kramatorsk, killed 33 people. In another Russian attack, in Pryluky, three one-year-old children were among the dead.
Most strikingly, Trump has repeatedly condemned Ukraine's strikes on Russian oil refineries — Moscow's largest source of revenue to fund its war effort — but remained silent on Russia's slaughter of Ukrainian children.
The most recent time we found Trump publicly condemning Russian strikes on Ukrainian civilians was in 2025.
While Trump has shown his disdain for Ukraine on many occasions (you will remember the Oval Office episode , surely), his latest cynicism should shock even his most ardent supporters.
But what may come as a surprise to the American president is that giving a boost to Russia’s war effort, while a big help, cannot force Ukrainians to stop fighting. That is not up to the U.S. What is up to it, and to its president, is whether it wants to uphold the values of democracy by supporting a country under siege from its aggressive neighbor that wants to determine its future.
Because helping Russia to win the war won't stop it. It will simply give it the ability to cause more death and more destruction. In other words, it will help prolong the war.
And the danger isn't confined to Ukraine — the rest of Europe is at risk. U.S. intelligence last month warned that Russia could launch a limited attack on a NATO country as early as this fall.
An emboldened Putin makes that more likely. Trump is endangering the security of the entire European continent in an attempt to score short-term political points. It's difficult to name a time when a U.S. president has acted so recklessly on the international stage.
We all need to start calling it what it is:
Trump indeed wants the war to end quickly. He’s just choosing to end it with a Russian victory.
The Kyiv Independent is an award-winning English-language media outlet that offers on-the-ground reporting from Ukraine. The publication has received international recognition for its coverage of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

title: Zelensky says he feels betrayed over Trump-Russia deal
description: "It's painful when President Trump chooses one ‌side, not our ⁠side," Zelensky said in an interview with British host Piers Morgan.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 14 that Ukraine is "losing a strong partner" as the U.S. eases sanctions on Russia while ramping up pressure on Kyiv.
Asked by British host Piers Morgan in an interview whether he feels that Ukraine is losing the U.S., Zelensky said, "Yeah, but not because of us. We can't be weak."
"It's painful when President Trump chooses one ‌side, not our ⁠side," he noted.
The comments come after Trump announced a deal to purchase diesel from Russia on Oct. 9, while saying that Zelensky should be replaced as Ukraine's leader.
When asked whether he felt betrayed by Trump, the Ukrainian leader answered: "Really, ‌yes... but it's a ​little bit more complicated than ​just my ​emotions or my feelings."
Zelensky also said that the apparent decision to throttle Ukraine's Starlink service, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, is a "big mistake." Ukraine confirmed on Oct. 14 that its access to Starlink terminals has been severely restricted, hampering combat operations.
The president said that Kyiv has asked for the restoration of Starlink operations, warning that "people will die" otherwise.
The Ukraine-U.S. relations hit a low point after Trump blamed Ukrainian strikes against Russian refineries for the rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts — and his team threatened to cut off intelligence support and arms shipments unless Kyiv halts the attacks.
Washington then unexpectedly unveiled a deal allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed due to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
A few days later, on Oct. 11, Trump unilaterally announced an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine, taking Ukrainian officials by surprise.
Even as Kyiv backed the truce and said it had paused its strikes against Russian refineries since the announcement, Moscow has continued attacking the Ukrainian power grid, meeting no criticism from Trump.
"I think Trump's advisers are wrong. I don't know who is pushing him to the wrong side," Zelensky said.
"This is not the right side of history."

title: SBU detains 18-year-old suspected FSB agent in Kyiv over attempt to activate 148 Starlink terminals for Russia
description: The SBU reported that the terminals were intended to support the planning of Russian military operations in the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. Ukrainian security officers say they prevented the devices from being activated.
content:
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has detained an 18-year-old man in Kyiv suspected of working for Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). According to investigators, he attempted to register 148 Starlink terminals for use by Russian forces.
The SBU reported that the terminals were intended to support the planning of Russian military operations in the Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia regions. Ukrainian security officers say they prevented the devices from being activated.
According to the investigation, the suspect is a former student at a Kyiv college, where he trained to become a welder. After completing his studies, he began looking for ways to earn quick money through Telegram channels.
He was allegedly contacted by an FSB officer who offered him money in exchange for cooperation.
Within days of being recruited, the suspect registered 15 Starlink terminals using the passport details of relatives and acquaintances. He then prepared personal information belonging to other individuals to register another 133 devices.
SBU officers detained the suspect near a post office, where he allegedly planned to activate another batch of terminals.
The 15 previously registered Starlink terminals, whose details had already been sent to his Russian handler via a messaging app, were also blocked.
The suspect remains in custody without the possibility of bail. If convicted, he faces life imprisonment and confiscation of property.
The case adds to a growing number of incidents in which Russia allegedly recruits Ukrainians to carry out assignments on Moscow's behalf, including a recent case on Oct. 12, when Ukrainian authorities detained a 19-year-old suspected of plotting a bomb attack on a bus carrying soldiers in Rivne.
According to the SBU, the suspect had also been recruited through Telegram channels offering quick money.
On Oct. 6, the SBU reported arresting a suspected collaborator in Kyiv who allegedly helped Russia establish repeater stations for its drones and gather intelligence on targets in the capital.
In August, the SBU detained a suspected Russian agent in Kharkiv Oblast who allegedly registered 27 Starlink terminals for Russian forces.

title: Draft EU summit conclusions reveal what leaders will and will not say on Ukraine

BRUSSELS, Belgium — Leaders of the EU's 27 member states have a Ukraine-packed agenda when they meet in Brussels Oct. 15-16, according to the latest draft conclusions of the upcoming meeting seen by the Kyiv Independent.

The 25-page document contains six-and-a-half pages of comments specifically on Uk
content:
A red carpet and European Union (EU) flags in the Europa building ahead of a European Council meeting in Brussels, Belgium, on Thursday, Oct. 23, 2025. (Simon Wohlfahrt/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Editor's Note: Following publication, the Kyiv Independent received the revised draft conclusions, which set out a less ambitious position on Ukraine's bid for EU membership. Read the story here .
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Leaders of the EU's 27 member states have a Ukraine-packed agenda when they meet in Brussels Oct. 15-16, according to the latest draft conclusions of the upcoming meeting seen by the Kyiv Independent.
The 25-page document contains six-and-a-half pages of comments specifically on Ukraine, three-and-a-half pages on defense and security, where Ukraine features prominently, and a page on the future of enlargement.
Those hoping for a long list of decisions from the European Council will be left disappointed, as the document mostly consists of leaders noting developments since they last met in June and issuing calls for what should happen next.
But some of those calls can lead to concrete outcomes further down the line.
For example, the draft conclusions say that the European Council "calls for the swift and effective implementation of the measures concerning Russian ex-combatants, and for further (sanctions) measures."
A visa ban for Russian soldiers was pushed for in the bloc's previous sanctions package, but ultimately fell through after France and Italy railed against it.
Since Russia's drone attack on Leipzig , Germany, the conversation has shifted, and EU diplomats from three countries said France had begun to budge when foreign ministers met in Luxembourg on Oct. 12.
Finland also upped the pressure by issuing a letter arguing against issuing visas to Russians and outlining five key demands.
The draft conclusions signal that concrete action is due to land soon.
In a similar vein, the Council conclusions state that it "underlines the EU's readiness to step up its engagement" on "diplomatic efforts to bring Russia's war of aggression to an end."
The week before, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's right-hand man discussed peace with the U.S., NATO, and Ukraine.
But those talks were overshadowed by U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement of a likely-illegal diesel deal with Russia — a development that the conclusions note with "regret."
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told journalists on Oct. 12 that the U.S.' approach shows that "Europe should take its future in its own hands, speak with one voice, and restore peace," and the conclusions' readiness to do so suggests that the EU agrees.
On other topics, the draft conclusions expose the EU's seeming inability to tackle Ukraine's most pressing issues.
With Kyiv being pummeled by ever more jet-powered drones and ballistic missiles, the call for "further intensified efforts and coordination to strengthen Ukraine's air and missile defense capabilities, the resilience of its critical infrastructure, and its energy system," rings especially hollow.
Similarly, the call for "immediate restoration of safe passage for grain cargo ships in the Black Sea," after weeks of Russian blockade, and the sinking of ships — which has also led to the loss of life — reads as weak in the absence of any accompanying measures.
However, the European Council "stresses the need to prevent grain stolen by Russia from temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories from being exported via the EU," read the conclusions, which suggests support may be gathering for a Russian grain transit ban , as proposed by Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania the week before.
Likewise, support may be brewing for future EU action to prevent Russia's re-entry into international sports and cultural events, which the conclusions say should not be allowed to happen, three days after EU Sports Commissioner Glenn Micallef met with EU foreign ministers for the first time to discuss the issue.
The result of Micallef's meeting was the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, announcing that her team "will put forward proposals on how to sustain Russia's isolation in global sports."
And in the meantime, some countries take unilateral action, such as the Netherlands, which has denied visas to Russians due to compete at an international gymnastics event in Rotterdam, even as the world body for gymnastics has again allowed Russian and Belarusian athletes to compete under their own flag.
Other mentions in the conclusions can be seen as messages to other allies of Ukraine, in Europe and beyond.
That the EU "strongly condemns the deployment of North Korean military forces in the war against Ukraine" is a useful reminder to South Korea of what is at stake for them, just as relations between Kyiv and Seoul reach a new low .
And the renewed call for "international partners to swiftly step up their support to help meet Ukraine's pressing financing and military needs," likewise points to the fact that since the EU adopted its 90 billion euro loan ($100 billion) for Ukraine in April, third countries appear to have slowed down on their own contributions to Kyiv.
One word missing from the draft conclusions: "assets." This is despite a renewed push from various directions to revive discussions about how to use 200 billion euros ($224 billion) of immobilized Russian wealth to directly support Ukraine.
Four EU countries reopened the topic with an open letter in August, and it came up prominently during the Oct. 12 meeting of foreign ministers.
Sybiha spoke about the idea to journalists, published an opinion piece the same day with news website Politico , and had strong support from his Swedish colleague Maria Stenergard, who even brought along visual aids for the discussion.
But the lack of a mention is because the EU is still by no means united on what approach to take.
Belgian newspaper De Morgen reported on Oct. 13 that President Volodymyr Zelensky wants to meet with Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever bilaterally around the EU leaders' summit, which he will also attend on Oct. 16.
De Wever led resistance to the use of Russian assets in December 2025, the last time it was seriously discussed, and as the vast majority of immobilized Russian government assets are in Belgium, a solution that does not work for De Wever will go nowhere.
In response to a question from the Kyiv Independent about the Russian assets, Kallas said "I think this discussion will continue because eventually it is about sharing the risks between member states."
"It is important that it is not off the table. We are thinking about different tools to fill that financing gap," Kallas said.
Alternative options do exist: Russian assets could be invested more profitably to create new funds for Ukraine, as suggested by a plan called the Windfall Optimization Loan Framework, or the EU could simply agree to create new loans.
What is clear is that the topic is not set to disappear just yet, with one senior EU official telling the Kyiv Independent they expect it to dominate EU leaders' December meeting.
The October meeting of EU leaders was supposed to have the future of EU enlargement as a main topic, to which end the European Commission issued proposals for consideration on Oct. 6.
Instead, with a new multi-year budget to discuss, energy prices, migration issues, the Middle East, and all the other Ukraine topics on the agenda, enlargement risks being overshadowed, and it only accounts for one page in the 25-page Council conclusions draft.
Even so, that one page contains a potentially big shift, if the conclusions are adopted as written.
"The European Council ... looks forward to the opening of all the other clusters as soon as possible, in line with the merit-based approach," read the draft conclusions.
What looks like an innocuous enough sentence takes on new meaning when one has in mind the last leaders' meeting in July, in which Hungary lobbied hard to remove the words "as soon as possible" because it wanted Ukraine to pass a law bolstering the rights of its Hungarian-speaking minority first.
Ukraine passed that law on Oct. 12, unlocked two further enlargement clusters on Oct. 13, and may have no further obstacles to overcome.
France and Poland were expected in some quarters to make it difficult to unlock the remaining cluster covering agriculture due to fears of Ukrainian competition, but they publicly ruled this out on Oct. 13.
A high-ranking EU official and a European minister told the Kyiv Independent that they expect the last two clusters to open in December 2026, as several EU countries must follow their own political procedures at home to give a formal green light.
For example, Slovenia needs to vote on the decision through its parliament, even if the vote itself is not expected to cause any problems, and has never done so for Ukraine so far.
But that does not mean Ukraine has nothing still to do.
Both for the EU's financial support to be greenlighted, and for Ukraine to join the bloc one day, the Council conclusions "recall the importance of Ukraine continuing its reform efforts and upholding the rule of law."
Chris Powers is the Brussels Correspondent with the Kyiv Independent. He reports on EU news and policy developments relevant to Ukraine, bridging the gap between Brussels and Kyiv. He was formerly the Defense and Tech Editor at the EU media outlet Euractiv. Chris holds a BA in History from the University of Cambridge and an MA in European Studies from the College of Europe.

title: Germany puts Ukrainian on trial over Nord Stream sabotage
description: On the first day of the trial, prosecutors accused Serhii Kuznetsov of being an accomplice to war crimes by committing an attack against civilian infrastructure. Kuznetsov has denied any involvement.
content:
Ukrainian citizen Serhii Kuznetsov went to trial in Hamburg on Oct. 14 on suspicion of involvement in the sabotage of the Nord Stream pipelines.
A series of explosions rocked the controversial Nord Stream 1 and 2 pipelines in September 2022, destroying three out of four key gas pipelines linking Russia and Germany via the Baltic Sea.
Kuznetsov, a former soldier, was accused of leading the sabotage group, involving six other people. German investigators claim that he commanded the yacht "Andromeda," from which a team of divers allegedly carried out the attack against the pipelines.
On the first day of the trial, prosecutors accused Kuznetsov of being an accomplice to war crimes by committing an attack against civilian infrastructure.
Kuznetsov and Kyiv have denied any involvement in the sabotage.
The trial — the first held in Germany in connection with the Nord Stream sabotage — is expected to run until February.
Kuznietsov was arrested in August 2025 near the Italian town of Rimini under a European arrest warrant before being extradited to Germany.
Another Ukrainian suspect, Volodymyr Zhuravliov, was detained in Croatia in August 2026 and awaits extradition. Zhuravliov was first detained in Poland in September 2025, but a Polish court refused to extradite him to Germany and instead released him a month later.
The Nord Stream 2 pipeline, which never became operational, had long been a flashpoint in European energy politics.
Even before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine , critics said it deepened Germany's dependence on Russian gas and undermined European energy security.

title: Trump's diesel deal 'legitimizes Moscow' while it bombs Ukraine, Italy's Meloni says
description: Speaking to the Italian Senate, Meloni noted that "the surge in fuel prices is due primarily to the war in Iran, not the conflict in Ukraine," the Italian Ansa news agency reported.
content:
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Oct. 14 that the U.S. deal to buy Russian diesel is "very risky," joining other European voices criticizing the deal.
Speaking to the Italian Senate, Meloni noted that "the surge in fuel prices is due primarily to the war in Iran, not the conflict in Ukraine," the Italian Ansa news agency reported .
The news follows a deal announced Oct. 9 between Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Donald Trump, allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed due to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The U.S. Treasury Department said that, following Trump's direction, "the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
In response to the deal, the Russian government partially lifted the diesel export ban, permitting the sale of 500,000 metric tons of diesel to foreign markets, effective Oct. 10.
Meloni said that the "outcome of this move is questionable, while the risks are clear: legitimizing Moscow while its bombs continue to fall on Ukrainian cities, generating new revenue to finance the war, and implicitly weakening the leverage of sanctions."
The step goes against the longstanding Western strategy of pressuring Putin to begin earnest negotiations to end the war, she noted.
Meloni, Italy's right-wing prime minister, had long been counted among Trump's ideological allies in Europe, but their relationship has sharply deteriorated over the spring and summer.
President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked the Italian prime minister for her "support and a clear, unequivocal, principled stance."
"Thank you for understanding who the aggressor is and what it means to build a dignified and lasting peace. This is possible only through strength and joint efforts for our security," Zelensky said on X.

title: Moscow says scope of Trump's energy truce unclear after launching new attack on Ukraine
description: The comments come hours after Russia launched another deadly aerial attack targeting Ukrainian cities and power plants, in what Zelensky called a show of disregard for the Trump-backed truce.
content:
The Kremlin said on Oct. 14 that the extent of U.S. President Donald Trump's proposed energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine was not specified, as Russian attacks against Ukraine's power grid continue.
"What is the outline of the energy ceasefire, and what does it mean? Has it been specified?" Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told journalists, adding that "work in this direction continues."
The comments come hours after Russia launched another deadly aerial attack targeting Ukrainian cities and power plants, in what President Volodymyr Zelensky called a show of disregard for the Trump-backed truce.
The U.S. president unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11 without outlining its scope, taking the Ukrainian leadership by surprise.
An undisclosed White House official told Axios that Trump's announcement concerned only oil refineries and that a broader ceasefire covering the energy grid could come next, though no party has publicly confirmed this framework.
Such a deal would heavily favor Russia , as it operates a vast network of oil refineries, while Ukraine has only one refinery and is concerned mainly about its power grid, heavily battered by Russian missiles and drones.
Zelensky has said Ukraine is ready to adhere to a full, comprehensive energy truce — provided Russia does the same — and noted that Ukrainian forces have not attacked Russian refineries since Trump's announcement.
But Russian strikes against the Ukrainian power grid have continued unabated, and the Kremlin has declined to make any commitments to the truce.
In spite of this, Trump has declined to blame Moscow for breaking the truce while ramping up pressure on Ukraine, with his administration threatening to cut off intelligence and military aid.
Ukraine confirmed on Oct. 14 that its access to Starlink terminals, operated by Elon Musk's SpaceX, has been severely restricted, hampering combat operations.

title: Ukrainian drones reportedly hit Sberbank data center in Russia
description: Ukrainian defense company Fire Point commented in a social media post on Wednesday morning, saying 'You didn’t think it would stop with just Yandex, did you?'
content:
A Ukrainian overnight attack reportedly targeted a data center under construction belonging to Russian state lender Sberbank in Balakovo in Saratov Oblast, deputy chief executive Alexander Vedyakhin said on Oct. 14.
Saratov regional governor Roman Busargin said that Ukrainian drones had attacked the region on the morning of Oct. 14, according to Russian state news agency TASS.
Vedyakhin confirmed the attack to TASS, saying that all systems and services of the bank continued operating, and that no employees were injured in the attack. Busargin also said that "all infrastructure facilities" operated normally.
Nonetheless, Russian users reported disruptions to the online services of Sberbank, including its AI service GigaChat, the independent Moscow Times said.
Russian authorities announced construction of the facility in 2020, expecting it to cover about 60,000 square meters (about 645,800 square feet), while Russian state-aligned media Vedomosti said it will house a new supercomputer worth 500 billion rubles.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point commented in a social media post on Wednesday morning, saying "You didn’t think it would stop with just Yandex, did you?" after it trolled Russian tech giant Yandex on Oct. 12, following reported damage to another of its data centers, disrupting access to its financial services.
Yandex's data center in Vladimir Oblast completely shut down following a reported drone attack on Oct. 11, Russian state news agency TASS said on Oct. 11, citing the company.
The strike marked the third attack on a Yandex data center in four days, following confirmed strikes in Ryazan and Kaluga oblasts on Oct. 8 and 9.
On Oct. 11, Yandex Cloud reported power disruptions in an availability zone identified as being located at the company's data center in Vladimir.
Sberbank remains heavily isolated under Western sanctions , having been entirely cut off from the SWIFT international payment messaging network.
Ukrainian authorities did not comment on the strike.

title: Behind the scenes: Kyiv Independent's September digest
description: In September, we gave our travel series a home of its own, launched a new way to reach readers, saw our community's support translate into practical help for journalists on the front line, and met our community at events in Brazil and the Netherlands.
content:
Welcome to the Kyiv Independent's monthly digest, where we share company updates, milestones, and the stories behind our work.
In September, we gave our travel series a home of its own, launched a new way to reach readers, saw our community's support translate into practical help for journalists on the front line, and met our community at events in Brazil and the Netherlands.
On Sep. 11, the Kyiv Independent War Crimes Investigation Unit presented its latest investigative documentary, Last Seen in Crimea , which investigates a system of secret prisons in Russian-occupied Crimea where Ukrainian civilians have been held without contact with the outside world, often without formal charges, and subjected to torture and other forms of abuse.
Olesia Bida , the film author, shared that the main goal of the investigation was to identify those, who are directly responsible for these unlawful detentions. “Systems like this do not operate on their own — they depend on those who run them and those who carry out their orders,” she says.
The documentary is available to watch on the Kyiv Independent Youtube channel .
Our travel series, Dare to Ukraine , now has its own YouTube channel . The series explores Ukraine beyond the headlines, from its culture and history to its landscapes and, above all, its people. All 11 episodes from both seasons are now available in one place. As our deputy chief editor, Toma Istomina , put it, the series "captures the heart and soul of Ukraine." We hope the new channel will help even more people discover it.
We've also launched a WhatsApp channel , giving readers another way to follow our work. It brings our field reports, investigations , analysis , and long-form stories straight to your phone, alongside a weekly recap of the most important developments in Ukraine.
We also have an update on a project made possible by our community . In May, ahead of World Press Freedom Day, we launched our No News is Bad News collection to help protect journalists reporting near the front line. Through sales of the collection, plus additional donations, our community raised more than $24,000 .
The funds enabled the Institute of Mass Information to purchase 26 Vydun 7.5 FPV drone detectors for independent regional journalists working near the front line, exceeding our original goal of funding 20 detectors. The Institute had been seeking funding for the equipment for months, as many potential donors were unable to support purchases of equipment suitable for military use. The detectors provide early warnings of approaching drones, giving journalists crucial time to seek cover.
Our editor-in-chief, Olga Rudenko , spent part of September meeting audiences and fellow journalists abroad.
First, she traveled to São Paulo for the Festival piauí de Jornalismo , held under the theme "In the eye of the hurricane: editors-in-chief in times of turmoil." Joining newsroom leaders from eight countries, Olga spoke about what it takes to lead an independent newsroom in a country under attack.
Later in the month, she traveled to Deventer to speak at the Nederlands Journalistiek Festival . In a session titled "The Kyiv Independent: building independent journalism in wartime," she joined Wendelmoet Boersema, the editor-in-chief of Dutch newspaper Trouw and a former correspondent in the post-Soviet countries.
Their conversation explored the challenges of journalism under fire, the importance of holding those in power to account, and why independent reporting is particularly vital when a country is fighting for its future.
In the meantime, Francis Farrell and Olena Zashko travelled to Bucharest, Romania for a screening of Can You Hear Me? The Invisible Battles of Ukrainian Military Medics , the Kyiv Independent documentary co-authored by them. The film follows a group of Ukrainian military medics as they travel from the front-line in Ukraine to the quiet forests of Sweden, for a short mental health retreat.
September also brought opportunities to share our journalists' experiences and perspectives with international audiences.
Our deputy chief editor, Toma Istomina , spoke to Canadian Affairs about daily life in Kyiv under the threat of Russian aerial attacks. The city is now under round-the-clock air-raid alerts, forcing residents to weigh the risks of carrying on with their lives against the need to seek shelter. Toma also shared her mother's experience of receiving a cancer diagnosis and undergoing treatment during the war, explaining how interrupted sleep and the constant stress of attacks make recovery even harder.
Olga's visit to Brazil also drew interest from local media. In an interview with Marie Claire Brasil , she discussed leading an independent newsroom in wartime. She also spoke to Poder360 about the debate over holding elections in Ukraine during wartime.
For a deeper look at the issue, you can also watch Olga Rudenko and our deputy chief editor, Oleksiy Sorokin, discuss wartime elections on the Kyiv Independent's YouTube channel .
Meanwhile, Helsingin Sanomat , Finland's largest daily newspaper, featured Kyiv in a story exploring how younger Ukrainians view President Volodymyr Zelensky. Its reporters traveled to the Ukrainian capital to hear their perspectives firsthand.
September also brought us two awards that recognized not only our journalism, but also the work that makes it possible to keep that journalism free to read.
Our chief operating officer, Zakhar Protsiuk , was named among INMA's 2026 30 Under 30 honorees . The International News Media Association's awards recognize young professionals making an impact on the news industry. INMA highlighted Zakhar's role in growing the Kyiv Independent's membership from 6,000 to more than 35,000 members, with reader revenue now covering more than 70% of our budget.
We also received the 2026 Online Journalism Award for Innovation in Revenue Strategy from the Online News Association, in the Medium Newsroom category. This marks our second consecutive win in the category. The judges praised our "authentic and transparent membership model" and its central principle: keeping independent journalism freely accessible during wartime.
Neither milestone would have been possible without the people who choose to support us. Consider joining our community of members today .

title: Russian drone debris damages artwork of famous contemporary artist at museum in northwestern Ukraine
description: Petro Antyp's polyptych "Cosmogony," a Ukrainian interpretation of the world's origin, spans thousands of square meters. The museum’s founder, Viktor Korsak, described the damage inflicted upon the panel "The Future" as a "symbolic and at the same time terrifying coincidence."
content:
Debris from a Russian drone damaged artwork by one of Ukraine's most prolific contemporary artists at the Korsak Art Museum in Lutsk, a northwestern Ukrainian city, the museum staff reported on Oct. 14.
Petro Antyp's polyptych "Cosmogony," a Ukrainian interpretation of the world's origin, spans thousands of square meters. The museum's founder, Viktor Korsak, described the damage inflicted upon the panel "The Future" as a "symbolic and at the same time terrifying coincidence."
The museum was damaged in a fire caused by a Russian drone attack against Lutsk on Oct. 13, the staff said. "Now the war itself has intervened in a work about the future. And I wonder: perhaps we should not fully restore the damaged section? Perhaps these traces of war should remain as a historical artifact and a warning to future generations? But the most important thing is that we continue to create!" Korsak wrote. Established in 2018, the Korsak Museum is the country's largest museum of contemporary Ukrainian art. The museum has received international recognition for its curatorial work, including a Special Commendation at the 2025 European Museum of the Year Awards. Although the Oct. 13 attack damaged part of the collection, Roman Korsak, Viktor's son and the museum's owner, told the Kyiv Independent that the museum continues to operate. "We know the collection remains at risk. But we believe the greater loss would be to hide art away from people and close our doors at such a difficult time," Korsak said. Ukraine's cultural heritage has long been a target of Russian aggression. The Culture Ministry reported that, as of September 2026, Russia has damaged or destroyed at least 2,161 cultural heritage sites and 2,665 cultural institutions since the start of the full-scale war.
Tens of thousands of artworks are also estimated to have been looted by Russia from Ukraine's museums in the occupied territories and active combat zones.
Russia attacked Ukraine's northwest again on Oct. 14, exacting a deadly toll : at least six people were killed and 20 injured in Volyn Oblast, including Lutsk, and in neighboring Rivne Oblast.

title: Trump's Russian diesel deal isn't about economic relief
description:
When U.S. President Donald Trump announced Oct. 9 that Washington had agreed to buy millions of tons of Russian fuel, he pledged that the deal would mean lower gas prices for ordinary Americans.
