"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announc
content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin delivers a speech during the 23rd Annual Meeting of the Valdai Discussion Club in Moscow, Russia, on Oct. 1, 2026. (Sefa Karacan / Anadolu via Getty Images)
When U.S. President Donald Trump announced Oct. 9 that Washington had agreed to buy millions of tons of Russian fuel, he pledged that the deal would mean lower gas prices for ordinary Americans.
"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" he said.
The statement is far from reality, experts warn. The initial shipments, as announced by Trump, are small and unlikely to significantly lower prices in the long term.
Although Trump is hoping for a midterm boost, the only winner is the Kremlin.
The deal is putting new strain on Kyiv-Washington relations, as Ukraine is forced to press pause on one of its most successful war tactics.
Meanwhile, Moscow is buoyed by the prospect of weakened sanctions, which could boost its economy, its war chest, and its global image.
Global diesel prices are soaring. In its most recent report on Oct. 5, the U.S. Energy Information Administration put the cost of U.S. diesel at $6.20 per gallon — a rise of $2.49 in just 12 months.
The main factor driving those soaring prices is the U.S.-Iran war. The conflict has not only disrupted the flow of oil tankers passing through the Strait of Hormuz but has also driven up security costs for those ships making the journey.
A study by Ukraine's KSE Institute, shared with the Financial Times, assessed that the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran had a far bigger impact on global diesel and gasoil supplies than Ukrainian drone strikes, estimating that exports from the Persian Gulf fell by 152 million barrels between March and August, compared with a 68 million-barrel drop in Russian exports over the same period.
But Ukrainian drone strikes against Russia’s oil refineries have also made their mark.
In a report published in September, the International Energy Agency said that the amount of crude oil moving through Russia’s refineries had fallen to a 20-year low, with diesel production down by nearly 30%.
Global energy markets operate on a razor-thin balance between supply and demand, meaning any drop in output will affect prices, says Jeff Krimmel, founder of consulting firm Krimmel Strategy.
He says that Trump's deal could trigger a small drop in diesel prices, but that those changes are unlikely to last.
While the numbers in Trump's announcement are impressive at first glance, they are a small drop in the global energy market.
In October 2026, the U.S. Energy Information Administration reported that the country was using 493,000 tons of distillate fuel oil — a category that includes diesel and certain heating oils — in a single day. If that rate continues, the total of Russia’s first two deliveries, or 800,000 tons, would supply U.S. needs for less than 48 hours alone.
Real change would need a much wider shift, says Krimmel.
"The U.S. administration wants some visible demonstration that they're responding to this diesel supply crunch and the price rise that comes with that crunch," he says.
"(But) there is no single deal that the U.S. president can make with any foreign leader to change the shape of diesel markets in the near term."
Meanwhile, the planned diesel shipments place increasing pressure on Ukraine.
Kyiv's long-distance drone strikes against Russia’s oil infrastructure have become one of Ukraine's most effective weapons, slowly eating away at the Russian economy. Russia was plagued by fuel shortages throughout the summer, with some regions suspending civilian sales. Notably for world leaders such as Trump, the shortages also led the Russian government to place a temporary ban on diesel exports in July.
A lack of available data from Russia means that it's difficult to know how quickly the country has been able to repair its drone-damaged refineries. But the fall in Russia’s refinery output has been great enough for experts to express doubt that Moscow would be willing or able to fulfill the export numbers outlined by the U.S. president.
However, with his eyes now focused on U.S. opinion polls rather than global affairs, Trump has started to intensify his criticism of Ukraine for carrying out such strikes.
"The relationship with the U.S. (and Ukraine) is right now probably as bad as it was on Feb. 28, 2025, when we had this massive bust-up between Trump and Zelensky in the Oval Office," says Stefan Wolff, professor of international security at the U.K.'s University of Birmingham.
Shortly after the diesel deal was announced, Kyiv halted strikes on Russian refineries, following the terms of a unilateral, U.S.-led "energy ceasefire." Moscow has continued its attacks.
Even so, Trump threatened Kyiv with the withholding of intelligence and other assistance in a bid to protect Russian oil refineries, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent.
President Volodymyr Zelensky later shared that several missile strikes on Ukraine took place with "no early warning from our partners" — a suggestion that the U.S.-Ukraine intelligence sharing had been, at least partly, disrupted.
Ukraine's Starlink access was also restricted without warning on Oct. 14, severely disrupting "several" military missions, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," Beskrestnov said.
Ukraine could keep exerting pressure on Russia’s energy infrastructure without targeting refineries, says Wolff. In particular, oil tankers in Russia’s shadow fleet are among the potential targets.
But Kyiv will be pressured to keep Washington onside to keep receiving vital aid, such as air defenses, to protect civilians under Russian bombardment.
“Air defences are clearly depleted,” says Wolff. “There's not a lot that the Europeans can put in to backfill what the Ukrainians have used. So, I mean, in that sense, they still very much depend on the U.S., as do the Europeans.”
While Russia won't make large amounts of money from the small shipments outlined by Trump, the shift signals new possibilities for further sales down the line — greater revenues to fund Russia’s war machine.
But the real win for Russia is not only the breathing space to bring its refineries back online, but the outsized political statement that Trump's deal sends.
The U.S. Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until April 7 to make Trump's deal happen. That decision from a powerful global player such as the United States — a country that has, until recently, publicly pledged to support Ukraine — may prompt other countries to rethink their own stance on sanctions.
It could also open the door for countries buying Russian oil products at lower prices to start paying more, says Daniel Spiro, a professor at Uppsala University specializing in resource and political economics.
"The fact that Trump is now saying it's okay to buy from Russia, that could mean that those buying that oil and diesel are going to think, now it's safe, so we can pay full price for it," he says.
While Russia won't make large amounts of money from the small shipments outlined by Trump, the shift signals new possibilities for further sales down the line — greater revenues to fund Russia’s war machine.
"From Russia's perspective, it's symbolic. It shows that Russia can negotiate with others. It gives a green light; it shows that the world is reliant on Russia," says Spiro. "I do think it's mainly symbolic. But, sometimes, symbolism matters."
Katie Marie Davies is a freelance journalist who has worked in Russia and the UK. She has previously worked as a news editor at The Moscow Times and features editor at The Calvert Journal.

title: Netherlands denies visas to 3 Russian athletes, barring them from world championships
description: Angelina Melnikova, Viktoria Listunova, and Anna Kalmykova were denied entry as "one or more Schengen area member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations," the Russian Gymnastics Federation said.
content:
Dutch authorities refused to grant visas to three Russian gymnasts, preventing them from taking part in world gymnastics championships held in Rotterdam later this month, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said on Oct. 13.
Angelina Melnikova, Viktoria Listunova, and Anna Kalmykova were denied entry as "one or more Schengen area member states consider the athletes a threat to their international relations," the federation said on its Telegram channel.
Participation of Russian athletes in international competitions remains controversial and, in some sports, restricted due to Russia's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine .
At the same time, Dutch authorities approved visas for five other gymnasts, the Russian Gymnastics Federation said later on Oct. 13, noting that 47 of the 61 members of the Russian delegation had been granted entry so far.
Listunova publicly expressed support for Russian aggression in Ukraine and was previously denied visas for a gymnastics competition in Croatia in August.
Melnikova has also voiced backing for Russian President Vladimir Putin and even ran as a candidate for the ruling United Russia party in local election primaries last year.
Both Melnikova and Listunova are Olympic gold medalists.
Kalmykova, in turn, holds a sports contract with the Russian National Guard, according to Kyiv .
The Russian Gymnastics Federation denounced the decision and said it would appeal to the International Olympic Committee and World Gymnastics.
Rotterdam will host the World Artistic Gymnastics Championships from Oct. 17 to 25, serving as the first stage of team qualification for the 2028 Olympics in Los Angeles.
World Gymnastics imposed sanctions on Russian and Belarusian gymnasts at the outbreak of the full-scale war in 2022, but allowed them to compete as "neutral athletes" two years later.
The international association finally lifted its ban in May 2026, allowing Russian and Belarusian gymnasts to compete under their national flags, as part of a broader loosening of restrictions on Russian athletes.
Kyiv continues to urge global sports organizations to maintain sanctions against Russian and Belarusian athletes.
Russia's all-out war has taken a heavy toll on Ukraine, with hundreds of Ukrainian athletes and coaches killed and hundreds of sports facilities destroyed by Russian missile and drone attacks.

title: Russian drone attack on western Ukraine kills 6, injures 20 in Lutsk, Rivne
description: Wreckage from a drone damaged damaged several buildings in Lutsk, while a drone crashed into Rivne.
content:
Russian drone attacks on cities in Ukraine's western Volyn and Rivne oblasts killed three people and injured 20 others on the morning of Oct. 14, regional authorities said.
Wreckage of a Russian drone fell on the western city of Lutsk in Volyn Oblast, killing six people and injuring 10 others, regional governor Roman Romaniuk said .
As a result of the wreckage falling, a large-scale fire broke out in the 'Eurogroup' warehouse, killing five people at the scene, and injuring a sixth person so heavily they succumbed in hospital, Romaniuk said. Ten more people were injured in the incident, he added.
Elsewhere in the city, wreckage damaged a nine-story residential building, injuring two people including a child.
In Rivne, a Russian drone crashed into the city, injuring 8 people, including a child born in 2012, according to the regional military administration . The attack also damaged the roofs of two residential buildings, several windows, and four cars, the administration added.
Since midnight, air raid alerts had been issued six times in Volyn Oblast, as Russia hammered Ukraine with ballistic missiles and drones.
In total, Zelensky said Russia struck Ukraine with 39 missiles including Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles from Kursk, Bryansk, Voronezh, and Rostov regions in Russia, as well as with 128 Shahed-type UAVs, including 77 jet-powered ones.
Ukraine's Air Force said it neutralized four ballistic missiles and 115 Russian drones overnight.
Russian attacks have struck several locations in western Ukraine, distant from the front line, over the past day.
On Oct. 13, a Russian drone struck a university building in the northwestern city of Rivne, in neighboring Rivne Oblast, injuring 25 people, Rivne's National Police branch said on Oct. 13.
In Lviv Oblast, Russian drone attacks injured three people over the past day, said regional governor Maksym Kozytskyi.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 10, injure 91 across Ukraine over past day as ballistic missiles strike Kyiv for second straight night
description: In total, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia struck Ukraine with 39 missiles including Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles.
content:
At least 10 people were killed and 91 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia struck Ukraine with 39 missiles and 128 Shahed-type drones, regional authorities said on Oct. 14.
In Kyiv , at least four people were killed and 25 others injured in overnight missile strikes on the capital, the Kyiv City Prosecutor's Office said . At least three women were killed, and another 24 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of a Russian strike on a nine-story residential building in the city's Desnianskyi District. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that at least one additional victim from Kyiv's Darnytskyi District was hospitalized, and another person killed in the city's Holosiivskyi District.
"Overnight, the Russians deployed 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media , adding 600,000 people were without power.
In total, Zelensky said Russia struck Ukraine with 39 missiles including Iskander-M, KN-23, S-400, Zircon, and Onyx missiles from Kursk, Bryansk, Voronezh, and Rostov regions in Russia, as well as with 128 Shahed-type UAVs, including 77 jet-powered ones.
Ukraine's Air Force said it neutralized four ballistic missiles and 115 Russian drones overnight.
In Kyiv Oblast , one person was injured over the past day by Russian strikes, regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said. Civilian facilities, energy infrastructure, homes, warehouses and production facilities, and commercial establishments were hit in Russia's attacks on the oblast.
In Rivne Oblast , a Russian drone strike on a university building in the northwestern city of Rivne, injuring 25 people over the past day, Rivne's National Police branch said. Of the 25 injured, two were in critical condition, while three others are under medical examination, the police said .
In Kharkiv Oblast , over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and settlements in the surrounding region, injuring nine people, including a child, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Russia targeted the region with eight ballistic missiles, as well as multiple drones, Syniehubov said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , three people were killed and 17 injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, according to regional governor Vadym Filashkin .
In northeastern Sumy Oblast , one person was injured by Russian mortar shelling, the Sumy military administration said. Russian forces attacked with a wide arsenal of artillery, mortars, glide bombs, and UAVs. In total, air alert in the oblast lasted 18 hours and 36 minutes during the day.
In southern Kherson Oblast , two people were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, said regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin . Russia attacked multiple settlements in the oblast with air, drone, and artillery fire, damaging critical and social infrastructure, as well as residential areas.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast , one person was killed and three injured over the past day, according to regional governor Ivan Fedorov . In total, during the day, Russia launched 1,030 strikes on 56 settlements of Zaporizhia region using artillery, UAVs, and rocket launchers, he said.
In western Lviv Oblast , Russian drone attacks injured three people over the past day, said regional governor Maksym Kozytskyi.
Russian attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast killed two people and injured five others, including a child, over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
Chernihiv Oblast suffered several Russian strikes on a school and administrative building, but no casualties were reported over the past day, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.

title: Zelensky arrives in UK as London vows to speed up anti-drone missile deliveries for Ukraine
description: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham also said he would strive to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the U.S.
content:
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky arrived in the U.K. on Oct. 14 to meet British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and King Charles III, as London pledges missiles to help Ukraine counter Russia's jet-powered drones.
The visit comes at a tense moment for Ukraine, with U.S. President Donald Trump 's administration pressuring Kyiv to halt strikes against Russian oil refineries and threatening to cut off intelligence sharing and arms shipments.
Ahead of Zelensky's visit, Burnham vowed that the U.K.'s support for Ukraine remains "rock-solid."
The Ukrainian president was first welcomed by King Charles at Buckingham Palace before meeting Burnham.
"I thank His Majesty King Charles III for the audience. It is important for me to have the opportunity to personally thank him for his unwavering support for Ukraine," Zelensky said on X.
The British prime minister then welcomed Zelensky at 10 Downing Street in the company of a military ceremonial guard, the first such honor granted to a foreign leader, according to the BBC .
The British government has announced an air defense missile package worth 45 million pounds (around $60 million) for Ukraine, as the country faces an intensifying onslaught of Russian missiles and drones.
"The U.K. will accelerate deliveries of British Lightweight Multirole Missiles (LMMs), which have proven extremely effective against jet-powered drones that are being used to strike far beyond the front lines in Ukraine, including Kyiv and beyond," the British government said in a press release on Oct. 13.
Russia has been increasingly deploying jet-powered drones that are faster and more difficult to intercept than older Shahed models, posing a new threat as Ukraine braces for massive strikes against energy infrastructure in winter.
Of the 45-million-pound package, the U.K. will expedite the delivery of 10 million pounds ($13 million) worth of LMMs to meet the most urgent winter needs.
"I’m announcing that we're accelerating the delivery of British-made air defenses for (Ukraine)," Burnham told the press while meeting Zelensky. The British leader also said he would seek to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the U.S.
Burnham's office said earlier that he had instructed his cabinet to prepare additional military and financial assistance packages for Ukraine, as well as fresh sanctions against Russia.
The U.K. further reiterated that it stands by its plans to ban maritime services for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports.
London said last year it would implement the phased ban over 2026 "in lockstep with our European partners."
The EU plans to ban Russian LNG imports by January 2027 but has failed to agree on a full ban on maritime services, with Greece securing a carve-out for Russian LNG exports to non-EU countries.

title: Update: Russian soldier arrested, suspected of killing 5 Ukrainian soldiers, 1 civilian in Kharkiv Oblast
description: The Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office said that an unknown person killed five service members of Ukraine's armed forces in Kharkiv Oblast on Oct. 13
content:
Editor's Note: This story has been updated to include the most recent developments.
A Russian soldier suspected of killing five Ukrainian soldiers and one civilian was arrested in Kharkiv on Oct. 14, the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office reported.
Previously, Ukrainian media reported that a Russian prisoner of war (POW) escaped from captivity and killed five Ukrainian service members in Kharkiv Oblast on Oct. 13. Prosecutors confirmed that an investigation was underway and authorities were searching for the attacker.
The detained suspect is a 36-year-old Russian citizen from St. Petersburg serving in the Second Battalion of Russia's 1009th motorized rifle regiment, the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office said after the arrest.
According to the prosecutor's office, investigators believe the suspect may have been involved in Russian sabotage and reconnaissance operations. The report did not identify the individual as a POW, but said he was wearing civilian clothes at the time of his capture.
Investigators also believe the man may have shot and killed a civilian in addition to the murders of five Ukrainian soldiers.
The suspect is alleged to have seen a man fishing in the village of Tsyrkuny, some 16 kilometers (10 miles) from the Russian border, and shot him for fear of exposure. An autopsy revealed a gunshot wound to the head, the prosecutor's office said.
The gunman then made his way to the village of Momotove, outside the regional capital, where he allegedly shot and killed five members of the Ukrainian military. The suspect was eventually arrested in Kharkiv.
Earlier on Oct. 14, multiple media outlets reported that five Ukrainian military personnel had been murdered in Kharkiv Oblast the previous day.
Around 4:00 p.m., a man in civilian clothing approached a building housing members of the 72nd Separate Mechanized Brigade, opened fire, and first killed one Ukrainian service member, before entering the house and killing four others, according to Glavkom .
A source in the military command in the Kharkiv region told BBC Ukraine that the suspected attacker was a Russian prisoner of war.
The Regional Prosecutor's Office confirmed an investigation was underway, but did not identify any suspects as Russian POWs.
The prosecutor's office said investigators were examining several possible motives, including whether the attacker may have been linked to a Russian sabotage and reconnaissance group.
The brigade shared a statement , saying that "On October 13, a tragic event occurred in the territory of Kharkiv region, as a result of which servicemen of the 72nd separate mechanized brigade named after the Black Zaporozhians died."
"According to preliminary information, persons who are likely citizens of the Russian Federation may have been involved in the incident," it added.
In total, the shooting lasted for about two hours, Glavkom said, while BBC Ukraine added that residents called the local police station at 04:20 p.m. about the incident. Another service member was injured in a neighboring village, according to Glavkom.
Glavkom said that two servicemen of the Russian armed forces fled captivity in Kharkiv Oblast.
During the search for the suspect, BBC Ukraine reported that the attacker was a man with a height of 160-170 cm, a lean physique, with dark hair and a unkempt beard, wearing dark blue jeans, a long-sleeved black jacket, and a grey backpack, and carrying a machine gun.
On Oct. 6, Ukraine's Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said that Ukraine took 858 more Russian servicemen into captivity than Ukrainians were taken into Russian captivity, an average 107 per month.
Since mid-2023, the group said, Ukraine has taken more prisoners than Russia . The Ukrainian military provides bonuses for taking Russian soldiers as prisoners, as each Russian soldier might be an opportunity to exchange Ukrainian service members or civilians in Russian captivity, it added.
Ukraine and Russia exchange prisoners of war , one of the few remaining areas of direct humanitarian cooperation between the two countries amid Russia's full-scale invasion.
Ukraine and Russia have also continued repatriating the bodies of fallen soldiers despite a broader diplomatic process that has largely stalled.

title: Operation Vivaldi's 'Fourth Season' — Ukraine retakes another 101 square kilometers on Lyman front, Biletskyi says
description: Ukraine liberated the villages of Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi, while Russia lost about 3,000 of its soldiers in the fourth stage of the operation, Ukraine's Third Army Corps reported on Telegram.
content:
Ukraine's Third Army Corps, together with its attached units, has retaken another 101 square kilometers during the fourth stage of Operation Vivaldi on the Lyman sector in Donetsk Oblast, the corps announced on Oct. 14.
Ukraine liberated the villages of Zelena Dolyna, Lypove, and Kolodiazi, while Russia lost about 3,000 of its soldiers in the fourth stage of the operation, the corps reported on Telegram .
"The enemy was unable to cut the key logistics artery of our group in the Donbas. We thwarted the offensive of the group 'Zapad' and forced it to transfer part of the units of the 1st Tank Army, which weakened the pressure on Kupiansk-Vuzlovyi," corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi said.
In total, Operation Vivaldi saw the liberation and return of 16 settlements and 277 square kilometers (106 square miles) to Ukraine, the corps said. "Four seasons of 'Vivaldi' are over, but the music continues."
On Sept. 15, Biletskyi confirmed that Ukrainian forces under the command of the 3rd Army Corps were conducting a series of counterattacks north of the front-line city of Lyman in Donetsk Oblast.
The operation dealt "a heavy blow to the combat capabilities of Russia's 20th and 25th Combined Arms Armies," Biletskyi said then, adding that Ukrainian drone strikes had pushed Russian supply hubs across the state border.
The fight for the heart of the so-called Donbas fortress belt — Sloviansk, Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, and Kostiantynivka — is crucial going into the winter months, when Russia will look to maximize its foothold in urban areas to prepare for a 2027 offensive campaign.

title: EU disburses close to 3 billion euros of defense money to Ukraine ahead of leaders summit
description: The funding will go towards drones, air defense systems, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition, reads a European Commission press statement.
content:
The EU disbursed 2.86 billion euros ($3.2 billion) in military support to Ukraine on Oct. 14 as part of the bloc's 90 billion-euro ($100 billion) support loan for Kyiv.
"With today's 2.86 billion euro disbursement, we keep addressing Ukraine's most urgent operational needs," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
The funding will go towards drones, air defense systems, missiles, radars, electronic warfare systems, and ammunition, reads a European Commission press statement.
"As Russia stalls on the front lines, it continues to escalate its aerial attacks — cruelly targeting Ukrainian civilians and infrastructure. Europe's steadfast support matters more than ever to help Ukraine protect its skies," von der Leyen said.
The disbursement lands one day before EU leaders are set to meet for a two-day summit, which President Volodymyr Zelensky is also expected to attend.
"Ukraine will be front and center at this week's European Council," von der Leyen said after an Oct. 11 call with Zelensky.
The latest disbursement was also previewed as a result of that call, with Zelensky thanking von der Leyen for the payment in a Telegram post .
"These funds will strengthen us," Zelensky said.
The latest announcement follows a previous disbursement of 1.24 billion euros ($1.4 billion) in defense support on Oct. 7, and further disbursements from the EU are expected until the end of the year.
Within the EU's 90 billion euro loan, 28.3 billion euros ($31.7 billion) were earmarked for Ukraine's defense needs in 2026, of which 18.26 billion euros ($20.44 billion) have now been disbursed.
Ukraine's plans for how to spend the remaining 10 billion euros ($11.2 billion) have already been approved by the EU; all that is required is for Kyiv to send the receipts for sign-off by Brussels.

title: US senators urge Trump to drop Russian diesel deal, use Graham's sanctions law
description: "This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," reads the letter signed by six Democratic and six Republican senators.
content:
A bipartisan group of U.S. senators on Oct. 13 called on U.S. President Donald Trump to rescind his deal to buy Russian diesel, joining other colleagues in Congress who lambasted the controversial agreement.
"This deal is a gift to our adversary and a betrayal of our Allies; it should be rescinded," says the letter signed by six Democratic and six Republican senators, including Democrat Richard Blumenthal and Republican Mitch McConnell, and shared with the Kyiv Independent.
The lawmakers instead urged Trump to deploy sanctions under the late Republican Senator Lindsey Graham 's law , which was passed in September and authorizes the president to impose up to a 100% tariff on the top five countries buying Russian gas and oil, among other measures.
"These authorities require you to apply economic pressure on Russia and the chief enablers of its war, in particular China," the senators wrote.
The news follows a deal announced Oct. 9 between Russian President Vladimir Putin and Trump, allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed due to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
The U.S. Treasury Department said that, following Trump's direction, "the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
In response to the deal, the Russian government partially lifted the diesel export ban, permitting the sale of 500,000 metric tons of diesel to foreign markets, effective Oct. 10.
"Granting Moscow the ability to sell Russian diesel freely in global markets damages American security interests and is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine, who continue to defend themselves from Putin's murderous, illegal war," the letter read.
The agreement was announced as Trump ramps up pressure on Kyiv to halt attacks against Russian refineries as part of his unilaterally announced energy truce, with his administration threatening to cut off intelligence and arms shipments to Ukraine.
Ukraine has said it had paused attacks against Russian refineries, despite Russia continuing to strike the Ukrainian power grid, most recently overnight on Oct. 14.
In the letter, the senators said they recognize the need to lower energy costs for U.S. families, but warned that the Russian diesel deal will have a "negligible impact on fuel prices" while filling the Kremlin's war chest.
Earlier, on Oct. 11, seven bipartisan members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee released a statement condemning the decision, urging the White House to "immediately reverse course."

title: 'This cannot be a coincidence' — Ukraine's Starlink access restricted without warning, Zelensky adviser says
description: Ukraine relies on Starlink to operate its mid-strike drones in Russian-occupied Ukraine. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that only the U.S. president has the right to determine speed and usage restrictions for Starlink military systems.
content:
Ukraine's Starlink access has been restricted without warning, severely disrupting "several" military missions, presidential adviser Serhii "Flash" Beskrestnov said on Oct. 14.
The speed restrictions were accompanied by signal disruptions and instability, even at lower speeds. Military personnel from mulitple units reported serious issues with Starlink throughout the day.
"I confirm that (Starlink owner) SpaceX implemented speed restrictions on Starlink terminals while in motion last night. Currently, the restriction applies to the Starshield 'military service package' and limits speed to 100 miles per hour (160 kilometers per hour)," Beskrestnov said in a post on social media.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry later told journalists that the actual speeds available during the day were even lower than the 160 kph limit. By the end of the day, service was reportedly stabilized, but the restriction remained in place.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said only U.S. President Donald Trump had the power to determine the speed restrictions for Starshield systems.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action," he said .
Ukraine relies on Starlink for several military applications including operating its "middle strike" campaign in Russian-occupied Ukraine, as well as interceptor drones that defend against Russia's new jet-powered attack drones.
This mid-range strike campaign this year has allowed Ukraine to strangle Russian logistics , hampering its ability to fight on the front lines.
A source in Ukraine's Defense Ministry confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that speed limitations had been discovered and the cause was being investigated.
"This complicates drone missions —specifically those involving interceptors and mid-range strike drones — and hampers capabilities for frontline logistics, reconnaissance, and signal relay," the source added.
A soldier working on mid-range strike drone operations, who requested anonymity, confirmed that "certain issues are being observed" but declined to elaborate, citing operational security.
Two other commanders — both from elite drone units working on the eastern and southern front lines — reported issues with Starlink terminals on "middle strike" drones flying at higher speeds over the last 24 hours.
Both likewise requested to remain anonymous, and declined to describe the problems in more detail, so as to not assist the enemy.
During the day, Ukraine's 7th Air Assault Corps said on social media that it was experiencing a "throttling" of its Starlink connectivity.
"The consequences are already being felt in the field. Since the start of the day alone, a drone unit operating within the 7th Corps' area of ​​responsibility in the Huliaipole sector has had to cancel a number of missions due to these connectivity issues," the corps said.
Later in the evening of Oct. 14, ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov — who famously negotiated with Musk to cut off Russian forces from Starlink while in office — announced that service was being restored, with the speed limit in place.
"Attack drones and interceptor drones should be operational again," he wrote. "Now, the focus should be on completely removing the speed limit for Starshield."
Fedorov, who no longer holds a position in the Ukrainian government after being dismissed by President Volodymyr Zelensky in July, did not provide evidence for his claims or explain where he got his information, though he thanked Musk in his post on X.
The Defense Ministry confirmed that service had been stabilized at a speed of 160 kilometers per hour.
"SpaceX continues to maintain the 161 km/h limit. Throughout the day, the actual limits were significantly lower. However, as of now, we observe that connection quality has improved at speeds up to 160 km/h," the ministry said in a comment to reporters.
The Defense Ministry is currently negotiating with partners and with SpaceX "regarding stable service conditions and the prevention of sudden restrictions."
But Musk's response was not encouraging — particularly for Ukraine's middle-strike campaign.
"Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government," he wrote in response to Fedorov.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately (the president). .... Usage of Starlink is limited to civilian or defensive activities and cannot be used for offensive military action, as doing so would be inappropriate for a commercial company."
Musk comments point to a link between the Starlink disruption and Kyiv's deteriorating relationship with the White House — a fear voiced earlier in the day by Beskrestnov.
"Obviously, this action cannot be a coincidence and is associated with the current political situation," he said.
As reported by the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 12, U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened Ukraine with the withholding of intelligence and other assistance in a bid to protect Russian oil refineries.
Beskrestnov did not provide evidence that the Starlink restriction was connected to U.S. pressure on Ukraine, and the White House has not commented on the issue.
Serhii Sternenko , an activist and former advisor to Fedorov, also reported the restriction of access, saying "SpaceX likely took these measures at the request of the Trump administration."
The development comes after Ukraine worked with SpaceX earlier this year to deactivate unauthorized Starlink terminals being used by Russian forces. Starlink has played a critical role in Ukrainian military communications throughout the full-scale war.
The threats came after a confusing 48 hours during whichTrump announced a controversial "deal" with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, followed by repeated demands that Ukraine replace Zelensky as president, followed by Trump announcing a unilateral " energy ceasefire " between Russia and Ukraine, which blindsided both Moscow and Kyiv.
Ukraine has since refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries but Russia has continued its blitz on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, most recently overnight on Oct. 14 when "several" power plants in Kyiv were hit. Trump has refused to accuse Russia of breaking the ceasefire.
The reported Starlink restrictions come as questions have been raised about U.S. intelligence sharing in relation to Russian ballistic missile launches, following two straight nights of attack on Kyiv with little to no warning.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Despite the failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 13.
But later that day, around 10:30 p.m. another wave of ballistic missiles hit Kyiv, again without the usual warning.
At least three women were killed, and another 24 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of a hit on a residential building in the Desnianskyi District. Three more waves of ballistic missiles struck Kyiv throughout the night.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat told Ukrainian TV that Ukraine received no warnings from its partners about the first wave, though it did for the following three.
"Ukraine did not attack Russian oil refineries, yet Trump has already begun imposing sanctions on my country. Meanwhile, sanctions against Russia have been eased," Sternenko said.

title: 'Ostentatious disrespect' — Zelensky says Russia defied Trump's energy ceasefire with latest missile strike
description: "The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale," President Volodymyr Zelensky said, adding that "Russia does not consider the American President's statements strong."
content:
Russia demonstrated its disregard for U.S. President Donald Trump's proposed energy ceasefire by launching drones and missiles against Ukraine's power grid overnight, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 14.
Moscow's forces deployed 39 ballistic missiles and over 120 drones against energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv, Zelensky said , calling it "ostentatious disrespect toward the United States."
At least three people were killed, and another 22 were injured as a result of the Russian strike that hit a residential building in the Desnianskyi district and power plants elsewhere in the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
Russia has ramped up aerial strikes against Ukrainian energy sites as winter nears, despite Trump's unexpected and unilateral announcement on Oct. 11 that both Kyiv and Moscow agreed to halt attacks against each other's energy infrastructure.
Even as Kyiv said it had halted attacks against Russian oil refineries since Trump's ceasefire announcement, Trump declined to blame the Kremlin for breaking the truce when asked by a reporter on Oct. 13.
"The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale," Zelensky noted, adding that at least 600,000 people are without power and reporting damage to 26 power facilities, as well as four oil and gas sites.
"Russia does not consider the American President 's statements strong," the Ukrainian leader added.
The comments come as Washington piles on pressure on Kyiv to halt its aerial campaign against Russian refineries, which he linked to rising global fuel prices — a claim disputed by experts.
The Kyiv Independent has previously learned that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials with cutting intelligence sharing and arms sales unless it stopped attacking Russian refineries.
While Ukrainian and U.S. sources told the Kyiv Independent earlier this week that Washington has not yet stopped intelligence support, questions about the early warning provided by partners are mounting as strikes now hit Kyiv even before the alarm sounds.
Presidential Advisor Serhii " Flash " Beskretnov and Serhii Sternenko , an activist and former advisor to ex-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, claimed on Oct. 14 that Elon Musk's SpaceX has limited the speed of Starlink terminals in Ukraine, causing disruption to "a number of critical missions."
"The American President has all the effective and necessary tools to bring peace closer through strength, justice, and pressure on the aggressor," Zelensky noted, urging Washington to impose sanctions on Russia under late Senator Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill and calling for additional supplies of Patriot interceptors.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,557,350 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,650 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,557,350 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 14.
The number includes 1,650 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,414 tanks, 25,535 armored combat vehicles, 162,789 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,195 artillery systems, 2,212 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,704 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,951 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: 'Blown out of proportion' — Domestic politics at the core of South Korea's rift with Ukraine
description:
Seoul's diplomatic spat with Kyiv continues to deepen, but experts say it is less about Ukraine than about South Korea's own politics.

The East Asian country, traditionally counted among Ukraine's partners in the region, announced on Oct. 8 that it is recalling its ambassador from Kyiv amid a dispute over North Korean prisoners of war (POWs).

The rift started on Sept. 23 with President Volodymyr Zelensky telling the U.N. General Assembly that Kyiv had transferred two North Korean POWs, capture
content:
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung listens to a journalist during a news conference at the presidential Blue House in Seoul, South Korea, on Sept. 18, 2026. (SeongJoon Cho/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Seoul's diplomatic spat with Kyiv continues to deepen, but experts say it is less about Ukraine than about South Korea's own politics.
The East Asian country, traditionally counted among Ukraine 's partners in the region, announced on Oct. 8 that it is recalling its ambassador from Kyiv amid a dispute over North Korean prisoners of war (POWs).
The rift started on Sept. 23 with President Volodymyr Zelensky telling the U.N. General Assembly that Kyiv had transferred two North Korean POWs, captured while fighting on Russia's side, to Seoul.
The move angered South Korean President Lee Jae Myung, who accused Ukraine of violating a confidentiality agreement. Ukraine initially claimed that there was no such deal, with Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha later downplaying the situation as a "diplomatic misunderstanding."
In a matter of days, the row turned into a never-ending tit-for-tat war of words: on Oct. 6, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said that Ukraine had privately apologized for the incident but that the apology was, apparently, "insufficient."
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry responded that Sybiha had merely expressed regret that the situation had escalated to this level, noting that diplomatic correspondence should remain confidential.
While there is no end in sight to the diplomatic stand-off, experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent argued that none of this was likely to affect the strategic side of relations between Ukraine and South Korea.
“Even now, (South Korea’s) Foreign Ministry says cooperation with Ukraine will continue, so hopefully a cooling-down period will come, and both countries can get back to what is really important.”
Instead, the feud says more about the politically tense situation of President Lee — and about South Korea's piling geopolitical challenges.
After the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, South Korea has officially joined Western-led anti-Russian sanctions, notably by restricting strategic exports and helping cut Moscow off from the international financial system.
In practice, the sanctions regime is not fully respected. For instance, the Guardian has found that Seoul is now exporting diesel by sea to Russia , after heavy Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries caused shortages across the country.
"South Korea joined the sanctions, but is partially circumventing them, and is not ready to openly supply Ukraine with weapons," explained Leonid Petrov, a Korea researcher at the Australian National University.
Seoul maintains this ambivalent approach because authorities want to be able to normalize ties with Moscow if the war in Ukraine ends, said Sydney Seiler, a researcher and former U.S. national intelligence officer for North Korea.
On the other hand, South Korea remains a donor — albeit a relatively minor one — of humanitarian and non-lethal military aid to Ukraine, with commitments totaling approximately $627 million since 2022, according to the Kiel Institute.
"And when it comes to arms deliveries, South Korea doesn't support Ukraine openly, but it can do this indirectly, for instance, by selling arms to (an intermediary like) Poland," explained Chun In-Bum, a retired South Korean lieutenant general and expert affiliated with the Institute for Security and Development Policy, a Stockholm-based think tank.
Another issue is intelligence cooperation, where South Korea is seriously interested in learning from Ukraine's wartime experience, Chun said.
"Even now, (South Korea's) Foreign Ministry says cooperation with Ukraine will continue, so hopefully a cooling-down period will come, and both countries can get back to what is really important," he added.
Ultimately, the Ukraine-South Korea feud was mainly about Kyiv's announcement seemingly getting in the way of potential talks between Seoul and Pyongyang, according to Seiler.
"Lee is interested in warming up relations with North Korea and ultimately in holding a summit with (North Korean dictator) Kim Jong Un," noted Fyodor Tertitskiy, an international relations scholar at Korea University in Seoul.
On the North Korean side, though, there is absolutely no interest in rapprochement with Seoul, experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent agreed. In any case, Seiler doubts the POW transfer would have much bearing on whether Kim decides to engage.
But since Lee cares deeply about this initiative, his administration is particularly sensitive to it, Chun explained.
On top of the diplomatic issues, Zelensky's announcement also raised some worry about the security of the transferred North Korean soldiers.
"It's quite well-known that South Korea is full of North Korean spies, many of whom disguise (themselves) as people who defected from the North," Petrov explained. "So, it makes sense that these kinds of exchanges should be done quietly."
But Chun believes that Zelensky's announcement at the U.N. General Assembly did not change much in terms of the soldiers' safety, as North Korea would have found out about the exchange anyway.
The development came at a particularly sensitive time for Lee, whose ratings fell for a second week in a row to 35.2%, an Oct. 12 poll showed .
According to Petrov, these ratings were also one of the reasons why Zelensky's move became "a scandal deliberately blown out of proportion" by Seoul.
Finally, South Korea's changing geopolitical situation also plays a role. With China, Russia, and North Korea in the immediate vicinity, authorities in Seoul are increasingly wary of the strengthening alliance of the three countries.
"Lee Jae Myung is mainly just trying not to irritate any of these countries," Petrov said.
But Lee's administration might not be "fully comprehending" the geopolitical shifts going on in the region, Seiler said, by insisting on attempts to appease North Korea, which "aren’t working," rather than prioritizing cooperation with partners like Ukraine and the U.S.
"In any case, Zelensky did the right thing" by transferring the North Korean soldiers to Seoul, Chun said.
"This was a courageous move, especially (since) they could have just sent them back to Russia — as a Korean, I am just personally thankful to Ukraine that they did not."
Karol Łuczka is a freelance journalist focused on Ukraine and Russia. He also works as Eastern Europe Advocacy Lead at the Vienna-based International Press Institute (IPI). Karol holds an MA in International Security from Sciences Po Paris.

title: Fire breaks out near Russian metallurgical plant after reported drone attack
description: Footage shows an explosion and subsequent fire after a reported drone strike near a large metallurgical plant in Balakovo, located in the Saratov region, according to reports by the Exilenova+ Telegram channel.
content:
A fire has broken out in the Russian industrial city of Balakovo following reports of Ukrainian drone strikes on Oct. 14, according to Telegram monitoring channels.
Footage shows an explosion and subsequent fire after a reported drone strike near a large metallurgical plant in Balakovo, located in the Saratov region, according to reports by the Exilenova+ Telegram channel. The region experienced widespread power outages as a result of the attack, the channel reported.
Balakovo, a city on the east bank of the Volga River, is home to a large steel mill with a stated capacity of over 1 million tons per year, according to the Balakovo Metallurgical Plant’s website. It was not immediately clear as to whether the plant was damaged in the attack.
Saratov’s regional governor claimed that the drone attack damaged several buildings and killed one person in a statement on Telegram.
Elsewhere in Russia, a fire at an oil-loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don was reported to be burning for a fourth day following drone strikes on Oct. 10.
A reported drone strike over the weekend hit the oil terminal, which is located in the city’s industrial Zheleznodorozhny district. The terminal handles petroleum products for export, including shipments from the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery.
Rostov Oblast Regional Governor Yuriy Slyusar claimed that over 100 drones had been struck down that night in a statement on Telegram.
Footage published on the Exilenova+ Telegram channel shows rising flames and a thick cloud of smoke. The fire, which has burned for three days, had died down to a smolder before flaring up again, Exilenova+ reported.
As of Oct. 13, at least eight of the Novoshakhtinsk terminal’s 12 tanks have been put out of service, according to an OSINT analysis by the independent Russian outlet Astra . The facility, which can receive and load an estimated 2.5 to 3.5 million tons of oil products a year, handles exports and also supplies the Russian armed forces, the outlet said.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reports. No information was immediately available on the extent of the damage for either attack.
While Ukrainian officials have not yet commented on the reported attack on the terminal, Ukrainian forces have repeatedly targeted Russian energy facilities in recent months.
Last week, U.S. President Donald Trump declared an energy ceasefire, and demanded that Ukraine stop targeting Russian oil facilities. He claimed that these attacks contributed to heightened oil prices, widely attributed to the US war in Iran.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he would be willing to agree to an energy ceasefire if Russian forces stop targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure.

title: Russia detains Japanese journalist on espionage charges
description: Russia's Security Service (FSB) said that a Japanese citizen working for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was arrested in the country's far east near islands disputed by Russia and Japan before being taken to Moscow.
content:
Japanese journalist Yuki Imai was arrested on charges of espionage on Oct. 13, according to Russian court records.
Russia's Security Service (FSB) said that a Japanese citizen working for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was arrested in the country's far east near islands disputed by Russia and Japan before being taken to Moscow.
The outlet has a dedicated team covering Japan-Russia relations, territorial disputes between the two countries, and Russia's war against Ukraine.
FSB footage circulated by Russian state media appears to show the journalist pinned to the ground as Imai is handcuffed before being forced to power on his laptop in front of officers.
Russia's FSB claims the suspect collected data on the number of mobilized soldiers and volunteers in Russia's war against Ukraine for Japanese intelligence among residents living on the disputed islands controlled by Moscow.
Russia regularly brings politically motivated charges against opposition figures, journalists, and foreign citizens.
Russia has banned independent media outlets and is currently detaining dozens of journalists and media workers, according to Reporters Without Borders.
On Oct. 4, Moscow police detained about 60 people at an authorized Communist Party rally after demonstrators began chanting anti-Kremlin slogans, according to the party and Russian rights group OVD-Info.

title: Large-scale Russian missile attack on Kyiv strikes power plants, residential buildings, killing 5, injuring 25
description: Russia launched yet another large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv overnight on Oct. 13-14, wreaking destruction in a residential neighborhood and targeting several energy facilities in Kyiv.
content:
The aftermath of a Russian missile strike on a Kyiv residential building late on Oct. 13, 2026. (Serhii Korovayny/The Kyiv Independent)
Russia launched yet another large-scale ballistic missile attack on Kyiv overnight on Oct. 13-14, wreaking destruction in a residential neighborhood and targeting several energy facilities in Kyiv.
Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said that all three of the city's combined heat and power stations were attacked, as well as critical infrastructure in the Kyiv Oblast that provide power to Kyiv and central regions.
"The targets of Russian ballistic missiles were power system facilities in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and the region," he said.
"Overnight, the Russians deployed 39 ballistic missiles and more than 120 strike drones and loitering munitions against our energy and critical infrastructure in Kyiv, Kyiv Oblast, and Kharkiv," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media , adding 600,000 people were currently without power.
"This was a targeted Russian ballistic strike specifically against the energy sector — an area regarding which the U.S. President had called for a ceasefire. The strike was entirely deliberate and demonstrative in its scale. Russia has never before shown such blatant disrespect toward America," he added.
Explosions were first heard in the capital beginning in the late evening hours of Oct. 13 when a Russian missile , with little warning, struck a nine-story residential building in the city's Desnyanskyi district, igniting a large-scale fire, Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko reported .
Ukraine received no warning from its partners about the first wave of Russian missile strikes, but did receive warnings during the subsequent three strike waves, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said during a national telethon, according to Ukrinform .
At least three women were killed, and another 25 people, including a 7-year-old girl, were injured as a result of the Russian strike on the residential building, Kyiv Police said . Among those injured, 16 people were hospitalized, and four are in serious condition, Klitschko reported.
Over a dozen explosions were again heard in the capital between 4:45 a.m. - 6:45 a.m. local time, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground, amid subsequent waves of missiles attacks. Kyiv Independent journalists reported brief power outages and flickering lights around 5:30 a.m.
Due to the Russian attacks, one of the capital's water pumping stations has been cut off, leading to a reduction in water pressure in the Pechersk district, the Kyiv City State administration (KMDA) said .
In the morning, all three of Kyiv's metro lines temporarily stopped working, according to Kyiv Independent reporters on the ground.
Klitschko reported that another person was killed in the city's Holosiivskyi district following the latest waves of attacks. Kyiv Police later raised the number of people killed in Holosiivskyi district to two.
Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported that an unspecified "non-residential" building, a home, and a vacant building were also damaged across the city.
Ukraine's Air Force said it neutralized four ballistic missiles and 115 Russian drones overnight.
The latest Russian attacks on energy infrastructure come just days after U.S. President Donald Trump declared an energy ceasefire, and demanded that Ukraine stop targeting Russian oil facilities. He claimed that these attacks contributed to heightened oil prices, widely attributed to the US war in Iran.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said he would be willing to agree to an energy ceasefire if Russian forces stop targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Zelensky said earlier in the day that "Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for the two days since the American president announced an energy ceasefire."
In the aftermath of the attack, presidential adviser Dmytro Lytvyn told reporters that allies had not provided early warning of the launches for the second day in a row. Ukraine's Air Force also said no alerts had been received on either day.
Afterwards, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that no early warning was provided to Ukraine, adding that a Kyiv thermal power plant and residential building were targeted.
"Our system detected these missiles almost as they were approaching Kyiv," Zelensky said.
Local resident Maksym told the Kyiv Independent that he and his partner had to evacuate to their building's corridor before heading to a shelter after windows were shattered in a nearby explosion.
"Everything was very fast. We didn't even understand anything," he said.
Russian missile threats also triggered air raid alerts in parts of Lviv, Volyn, and Ivano Frankivsk oblasts in western Ukraine, far from the front lines.
Ukraine did not receive any advance warning of the attack from allies, which is unusual, presidential advisor Lytvyn said when asked by reporters.
Ukraine's Air Force confirmed that Russia had launched ballistic missiles at Kyiv, saying that "no information from partners regarding missile launches from enemy territory has been received," either on Oct. 12 or 13.
In the Russian attack on Oct. 12, at least 12 people were injured, including a 17-year-old, according to the Kyiv City State Administration's Health Department.
Just a day earlier, sources told the Kyiv Independent that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials, warning of plans to withdraw support from Ukraine in a push to protect Russian oil refineries.
"They called all the top military officials with threats," one Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent. "They're telling everyone that they're going to turn off both the intelligence sharing and PURL."

title: Trump refuses to accuse Russia of breaking energy ceasefire, says Ukraine 'hit sites the day before'
description: According to President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Kremlin attacked six energy facilities on Oct. 11, injuring 33 people across the country.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 13 did not directly accuse the Kremlin of violating his energy ceasefire, saying Ukraine also previously struck Russian energy sites in response to reporters' questions.
Trump unexpectedly announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia on Oct. 11, taking Kyiv by surprise , adding that there was a ceasefire in place " because I said they agreed ."
When asked by reporters whether he thinks Russia violated the ceasefire, he briefly answered , "I'll let you know about that later."
"Well, Ukraine hit many sites the day before," Trump responded to another question.
Just hours after Trump's announcement, Russia violated the ceasefire by striking Kharkiv's CHP-5 power plant.
According to President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Kremlin attacked six energy facilities on Oct. 11, injuring 33 people across the country.
Following the attack, Zelensky disclosed that over the past week, Russia has carried out over 200 strikes on Ukraine's electricity and transmission facilities, in addition to 17 strikes on gas and oil facilities.
Nonetheless, Ukraine has refrained from attacking Russia's oil refineries for the past two days.
"We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same," Zelensky said on Oct. 12, noting that a ceasefire focused only on oil refineries makes no sense since Ukraine has a single "badly damaged" refinery previously attacked by Russia.
Russia has yet to formally respond to the ceasefire, stating Putin is not interested in a ceasefire.
"We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it," said Kremlin's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov on Oct. 12, without providing further details on what "long-term peace" entails.
"We are working with them (Ukraine) and Russia on getting the war to end," said Trump.

title: Ukraine war latest: Russian missiles slam central Kyiv before air raid alert sounds
description:
Key developments on Oct. 13:

 * Kyiv under 'particularly vile' missile attack before air raid alert issued
 * French Navy intercepts Russian shadow fleet tanker in Indian Ocean
 * Trump says Ukraine, Russia agree to energy strike ceasefire 'because I said they agreed'
 * 'Absolutely unacceptable' — 11 crew members lost at sea after commercial ships hit by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast
 * Russian forces use group of civilians as 'human shields' near Kupiansk, fire at them afterwards, Uk
content:
Kyiv came under missile attack shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, with powerful explosions reported before an air raid alert was issued in the Ukrainian capital, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Kyiv Independent staff reported powerful blasts in central Kyiv, with air raid sirens and mobile notifications sounding only afterward. At 11:09 p.m., Kyiv Independent journalists reported further explosions in the capital as the attack continued. The cause of the latest blasts was not immediately confirmed.
Ukraine's Air Force later reported that Russian forces had attacked Kyiv with what appeared to be six ballistic missiles at approximately 10:10 p.m. President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 13 that it was five ballistic missiles that hit civilian infrastructure.
Zelensky called the strike "particularly vile," adding that there was no early warning from Ukraine's partners about missiles coming.
"Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
The Air Force said radar systems detected the incoming missiles during the attack, but that it had received no information about launches from Russian territory. It added that it was investigating why it had received no information about the launches.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed during the national news telethon that the alarm had been sounded only during the missile attack, but said that this had occurred previously, according to Ukrainska Pravda .
The delayed air raid alert prompted speculation on Ukrainian social media about whether the lack of advance warning was connected to reported U.S. threats to withdraw intelligence-sharing support for Ukraine.
Ukraine receives intelligence from the United States to help detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
The Kyiv Independent reported earlier on Oct. 12 , citing two Ukrainian officials, that Washington had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian energy infrastructure.
Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said that intelligence sharing between the U.S. and Ukraine was ongoing and had not been stopped, during a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum on Oct. 13.
“You probably ask if we receive intelligence from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation," he said.
The French Navy intercepted and boarded a tanker suspected of flying under a false flag as part of Russia's shadow fleet on Oct. 12, French President Emmanuel Macron announced.
The tanker, DF Peak, was allegedly transporting sanctioned Russian fuel and was halted by the French Navy 450 nautical miles (833 kilometers) south of the French territory of Reunion in the Indian Ocean.
"France is determined to combat the ghost fleet, wherever it may be in the world," Macron wrote on X . "This action, carried out in accordance with international maritime law, demonstrates our determination to uphold the rule of law and combat all illicit trafficking, wherever it occurs."
The tanker DF Peak, previously named Kaliningrad, has falsely sailed under the flag of Benin, according to the Ukrainian Defense Intelligence's War and Sanctions portal . The crude oil tanker is sanctioned by the U.S, EU, Switzerland, Canada, and Japan.
The vessel is currently under escort by the French Navy, France's Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said on X .
"International law is not optional," wrote Vautrin. "Our armed forces are fully mobilized to enforce it and combat illicit activities at sea."
Russian state media TASS said the Russian embassy in Paris told them that "France is violating international law by detaining merchant vessels on the high seas and is attempting to cover up piracy by invoking the provisions of the UN Convention."
The DF Peak is just one tanker of Russia's "shadow fleet" — a group of aging, poorly insured tankers used by Moscow to ship out its oil in violation of international sanctions. Western governments have also accused Moscow of using the fleet to support its hybrid war against Europe.
Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn on Oct. 12, U.S. President Donald Trump once again said that Ukraine and Russia agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure, despite the confusion around the alleged ceasefire.
"They agreed," said Trump after a reporter pointed out that neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed they would refrain from strikes on energy sites. "Do you know why? Because I said they agreed. That's why. They agreed because I said they agreed. And that thing has to get settled."
The U.S. president's comments came after he unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, causing confusion in Kyiv. According to a senior Ukrainian official, Ukraine had no prior information about an energy ceasefire.
In a short interview after Trump' s announcement, President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios, "If President Trump negotiated it with (Vladimir) Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it."
Russia has nothing to say yet about an energy ceasefire with Ukraine announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, the Kremlin's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Oct. 12.
When asked by a reporter about his response to Russia continuing to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure after his announcement, Trump said there had been violations by both sides, without pointing to any evidence.
Hours after Trump's announcement on Oct. 11, Russia struck Kharkiv’s CHP-5 power plant . In Overnight attacks on Oct. 11-12, at least 10 people were killed and 69 others injured across Ukraine as Russia continued to target residential buildings and energy infrastructure across the country.
Ukraine will halt its strikes against Russian refineries only if Moscow ceases its attacks against the Ukrainian power grid, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 12, signaling that a refinery-only truce makes little sense for a country with a single, badly damaged refinery .
Two cargo ships were struck by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast overnight on Oct. 13, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
According to Radev , the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, registered in Odesa and owned by a Ukrainian company, was hit by three aerial drones about 18 nautical miles east of the coastal town of Byala in Bulgaria .
All 15 crew members, seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijani nationals, were evacuated to the port of Varna, and five received medical assistance, Radev said.
He added that another vessel was struck 17 nautical miles east of Krapets, a Bulgarian village, as he was told at an extraordinary meeting of the Security Council under the Council of Ministers.
The vessel sank, and five crew members were rescued, while 11 crew members were still missing at sea, according to Bulgarian officials, reported Reuters . Reuters further said that Bulgarian media had identified the ship as the ⁠cargo ship Azov Concord.
Radev called the attacks " absolutely unacceptable " and said Bulgaria had informed its permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union. Sofia is seeking assistance to strengthen surveillance of the air and maritime domains and improve its response capabilities.
Bulgarian authorities have not established who was responsible for the attacks. Radev said there was no clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either the Ukrainian or Russian side, but argued that "the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation." Radev said he would summon Russia's ambassador for a meeting on Oct. 13.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attacks, saying the Black Sea had become "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine."
Russian forces led a group of civilians toward a gas pipeline, using them as human shields, and afterwards opened fire at them near the front-line city of Kupiansk in Ukraine's Kharkiv Oblast on Oct. 13, the Ukrainian military said, providing alleged drone footage of the incident.
The group included two women, a child, and several men who were being led toward the Shebelinka–Ostrogozhsk gas pipeline, according to Ukraine's 13th Khartia Corps. The group came under repeated mortar and artillery fire as it moved.
Drone footage recorded by Ukrainian reconnaissance units showed casualties among the civilians, Khartia said, adding that Ukrainian troops had not opened fire. Based on the impact patterns, the strike originated from the eastern bank of the Oskil River, where Russian forces are positioned, the corps said.
Khartia called the strike a "deliberate provocation" and warned that Russian media could use footage from the incident to falsely accuse Ukraine of attacking civilians. The corps said it would hand over the materials for a war crimes investigation.
"Civilians are used as human shields by the Russians, and then become their target for disinformation campaigns," Khartia wrote.
Ukraine's Joint Forces grouping separately said on Oct. 13 that Russian forces had struck a column of civilians leaving Kupiansk during what it described as a forced evacuation. The military said it was still establishing the number of casualties.
According to the Joint Forces grouping, Russian troops had conducted similar operations in recent weeks, using civilians as human shields to cover the withdrawal of some of their soldiers.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
A Russian drone struck a university building in the northwestern city of Rivne , injuring 25 people, Rivne's National Police branch said on Oct. 13.
Of the 25 injured, two were in critical condition, while three others are under medical examination, the police said .
Ukraine's Education and Science Minister Andrii Butenko said that a fire broke out in a building of Rivne State Humanitarian University as a result of the Russian drone strike. The Faculty of Music building was almost completely gutted by the fire, while neighboring teaching facilities had windows smashed, he added.
Oleksandr Koval, head of Rivne Oblast Military Administration, said on Oct. 13 that the drone strike damaged the second floor of the building. The fire in the building had been contained, and emergency services were on site.
"All victims are receiving medical assistance. Rescuers, police, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and municipal services are working at the scene," Koval said .
According to the university, all students were in shelters at the moment of the attack. There were casualties amongst the university's administrative staff.
At around 10:35 a.m., Ukraine's air force had reported a jet-powered drone flying over Rivne. The air alert was issued in the city at 10:10 a.m.

title: 'Even isolated Shahed strikes cause power and water outages' — Zelensky criticizes Kyiv's preparedness for Russian attacks
description: Zelensky said he had begun consultations on urgent security and administrative measures to address the situation and accelerate the implementation of Kyiv's resilience plan.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized Kyiv's preparedness for Russian attacks on Oct. 13, saying the capital is staying behind other Ukrainian regions in implementing resilience plans aimed at keeping essential services running during the heating season.
"As of mid-October, virtually across the entire country — even in border and frontline regions — the implementation of resilience plans is further advanced than in Kyiv," Zelensky said in a statement following a meeting of the Staff of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief on Oct. 12.
"And Kyiv residents certainly feel it — when even isolated hits by Shaheds cause electricity and water outages across large parts of the capital," he added.
Zelensky said he had begun consultations on urgent security and administrative measures to address the situation and accelerate the implementation of Kyiv's resilience plan.
The proposed measures include strengthening the protection of energy facilities and critical infrastructure, coordinating efforts with the government and military, and introducing changes to Kyiv's governance procedures.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko rejected accusations that the city's authorities had failed to prepare for the heating season.
"Unfounded accusations are being made about an alleged failure of the heating season, spread by outlets linked to the central government," Klitschko wrote on Telegram on Oct. 13.
The mayor also accused the central authorities of attempting to undermine local self-government by removing community leaders on what he described as fabricated grounds.
"The people elected me, and I am working, doing everything possible under extremely difficult conditions to justify the trust of Kyiv residents and keep the city functioning amid constant devastating enemy attacks," Klitschko said.
Russian strikes have repeatedly disrupted essential services in the capital in recent days.
On Oct. 8, Russian attacks left much of Kyiv without electricity and water, disrupting metro services. The city faced further power and water outages on Oct. 11 as Russia continued targeting Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Ukraine introduced nationwide energy resilience plans in March to protect critical infrastructure, repair damaged facilities, and install backup power and heating systems ahead of winter.

title: No, Ukraine's strikes on Yandex data centers didn't cripple Russian influence ops
description:
Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian data centers sparked viral claims about a sudden drop in Russian influence operations on social media — even as experts see no evidence to support this.

Kyiv struck data centers run by Yandex — Russia's "answer to Google" — in three different regions between Oct. 9 and 11, a response to Russian strikes against similar facilities in Ukraine.
