content:
Ukrainian drone strikes against Russian data centers sparked viral claims about a sudden drop in Russian influence operations on social media — even as experts see no evidence to support this.
Kyiv struck data centers run by Yandex — Russia's "answer to Google" — in three different regions between Oct. 9 and 11, a response to Russian strikes against similar facilities in Ukraine.
Yandex acknowledged the attacks, noting that its data center in Vladimir Oblast had to be shut down due to damage and reported disruptions to various online services within Russia.
Soon after, commentators on social media began reporting an alleged decrease in activity by "Russian bots" online, linking this to Ukrainian strikes on Yandex.
President Volodymyr Zelensky even alluded to this in his address to the Warsaw Security Forum, saying it is "a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms."
Yet beyond anecdotal examples circulating online, there is no data showing that the attacks on Yandex disrupted Moscow-backed disinformation and influence operations.
At least some of the claims appear to stem from a simple confusion of terms.
The source of this confusion is a chart from the internet company Cloudflare showing that bot activity from Yandex's network dropped to 54.7% after a Ukrainian strike on a data center in Ryazan Oblast.
The rate then plummeted to 0.3% after the third data center was hit in Vladimir Oblast .
But the chart simply shows automated web page requests from Yandex's own infrastructure, primarily its search crawlers — bots that browse and index web content.
It has nothing to do with activity by what is commonly referred to as Russian bots or trolls on social media.
"No reliable graph can consolidate bot and troll activity across multiple social media platforms without their internal data that measures telemetry, traffic, and behavior," Roman Osadchuk, the director of Threat Intelligence at the LetsData tech company, tells the Kyiv Independent.
Osadchuk acknowledges a moderate dip in social media comments and posts, both by bots and real users, over the weekend, but regards it as a coincidence.
This decrease "could be explained by tech complications on the side of companies that run influence operations like SDA or Structura, or it could simply be lower output from the weekend shift on the troll/bot farm, or a general fluctuation in comments."
No major fact-checking or disinformation-monitoring organizations reported a radical drop in Russian disinformation activity on social media, though some European officials echoed the claims.
In Poland, Tomasz Siemoniak, a minister coordinating the work of special services, claimed he had received exclusive information from the country's internal security service, the ABW, about a "radical decline in Russian bot activity online" due to the strikes.
But no such data has been published, and local disinformation monitors report no drop in Moscow-backed influence operations.
The Disinformation Analysis Center at Poland's state-run Research and Academic Computer Network (NASK) recorded no significant decrease in activity by disinformation accounts between Sept. 30 and Oct. 11.
"Only isolated cases of individual accounts becoming inactive were observed, but there is no basis for conclusively linking these instances to the attacks in question," the center's Daria Tomczuk told the Kyiv Independent.
Nor is there convincing evidence in other European countries.
Czech Member of the European Parliament Tomas Zdechovsky shared a graph purportedly linking the Ukrainian attacks to a drop in online activity around the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
But the German technology website Rohtext disputed this, noting that the graph does not list a source or explain a methodology. Rohtext reported no links between AfD activity and Yandex centers.
Another theory that appeared online is that damage to Yandex data centers may have disrupted the infrastructure supporting Moscow's influence operations.
However, Russian disinformation is believed to heavily rely on decentralized networks of proxies abroad, which would not be disrupted by strikes against Russian data centers.
"There's a lot of documented evidence that these troll operations operate in other countries like North Macedonia or the Philippines," Dave Troy, a disinformation researcher and investigative journalist, told the Kyiv Independent.
Given the blockade on the Russian internet imposed by the outside world and heavy domestic restrictions, it simply makes more sense to run disinformation operations from abroad, he adds.
This proxy strategy also makes it hard to pinpoint a drop in activity that is decisively Russian.
One commentator pointed to a drop in impressions under posts linked to Storm-1516, a Kremlin-backed disinformation group.
But Bot Blocker , a group monitoring Russian disinformation, countered that the bot network used by Storm-1516 is most likely a neutral commercial engagement-for-hire provider, not affiliated with a particular state.
"This engagement amplifying network is quite unlikely to be run from Yandex data centers," Bot Blocker told the Kyiv Independent.
Troy warns that misstating the impact of Ukrainian strikes on Russian data centers could pose a strategic risk by itself.
"The danger is thinking a specific victory has been achieved, but in reality the threat lies elsewhere and must still be assessed and fought," he adds.

title: Ukraine advances EU membership bid with 4 of 6 integration to-do lists unlocked
description: The move was made possible the day after Ukraine's parliament passed a law bolstering the rights of the country's Hungarian-speaking minority — a demand that Hungary had said must be fulfilled before it would allow further progress.
content:
Editor's note: this article was updated with comments made at a press conference following the opening of the two enlargement clusters.
LUXEMBOURG — Ukraine celebrated the opening of two more EU enlargement clusters at a ceremony in Luxembourg on Oct. 13, a key milestone in the process to eventually become a member state.
Ukraine and Moldova have been advancing their EU membership bids in tandem and are currently trying to open all six of the bloc's enlargement clusters — to-do lists of reforms that must be completed to join the bloc.
"We welcome the continued momentum on Ukraine's candidacy, now the majority of clusters are open, following a prolonged period without movement," said Thomas Byrne, Ireland's Europe Minister, who is chairing enlargement discussions until the end of 2026
On Oct. 13, Ukraine and Moldova unlocked clusters 2 and 3, titled "internal market" and "competitiveness" respectively. They are the two largest clusters by number of policy files.
"Behind these technical names will be real benefits for Ukrainians," said the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos .
Among the benefits Kos mentioned: more support for businesses, better working conditions, better consumer protection, and more investments and jobs.
"Ukraine is fully committed to the reforms required for membership and intends to move through this work as quickly as possible," said Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration Vsevolod Chentsov.
The move was made possible the day after the Verkhovna Rada, Ukraine's parliament, passed a law bolstering the rights of the country's Hungarian-speaking minority — a demand that Hungary had said must be fulfilled before it would allow further progress.
In June, Kyiv and Chisinau opened the first cluster , on the rule of law, followed by another on external relations in July.
That leaves only two clusters remaining to be opened, which the European Commission and the Irish Council Presidency of the EU hope to be done with by the end of 2026.
The two remaining clusters risk being harder to get through, as they encompass sectors of the economy such as agriculture and transport, where Ukraine has a competitive edge, and some EU countries fear losing out.
However, two potential opponents, France and Poland, reiterated their support on Oct. 13 for opening all six clusters.
On Oct. 6, the European Commission issued a set of proposals on the future of EU enlargement , which also suggested that Ukraine's agricultural sector would require special treatment, to be handled during the enlargement process rather than used as a block on progress.
Kos told the Kyiv Independent ahead of the opening of the clusters that "once Ukraine will be so far that we will think of what will go in the accession treaty, we will put down the solutions for both sides."
Kos was clear that the process needs to both protect European farmers and help Ukraine export to feed the world, all while Kyiv adopts EU standards.
But Kos' mention of the accession treaty, which is only being drafted near the very end of the EU enlargement process, indicates that she does not expect the strength of Ukraine's agricultural sector to be used as a reason to block progress at this stage.

title: How the Russian army is learning from Ukraine and NATO
description:
The Russian army entered its full-scale war against Ukraine with a reputation as one of the strongest in the world, but the first weeks of the invasion showed that this assessment was wrong. The reasons were sought in logistics, equipment, training, and motivation, but most of the failures stemmed from an inability to make sound decisions on the battlefield.

The Russian army found itself in a war in which commanders had to operate in situations where orders from above were either absent or no l
content:
British army soldiers work at a command post during the Allied Spirit 25 military exercise at the U.S. Army’s Hohenfels training area in Hohenfels, Germany, on March 12, 2025. (Alex Kraus/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The Russian army entered its full-scale war against Ukraine with a reputation as one of the strongest in the world, but the first weeks of the invasion showed that this assessment was wrong. The reasons were sought in logistics, equipment, training, and motivation, but most of the failures stemmed from an inability to make sound decisions on the battlefield.
The Russian army found itself in a war in which commanders had to operate in situations where orders from above were either absent or no longer reflected battlefield conditions.
This was when the fundamental problems with Russian military education became clear. For decades, it had trained officers to carry out tactical tasks and work with staff documents, but not to think and act independently.
In this respect, Russian and Western ( NATO ) military training systems differ in ways that go far beyond methods and training procedures. They reflect different command cultures and, consequently, different views of a commander's role in modern warfare, and we saw this firsthand in our study.
One of the core ideas of NATO's military doctrine is mission command, a command philosophy built on trust, a shared understanding of the mission, and disciplined initiative by commanders at every level.
A senior commander defines the objective, intent, and key constraints but does not attempt to prescribe every step their subordinates must take, leaving them free to choose how to accomplish the mission in response to the situation.
This allows decisions to be made at the level with the clearest understanding of conditions on the ground, without depending on constant instructions from above.
The Ukrainian Defense Forces have recently been moving more decisively toward this kind of command culture. This is clearly reflected in the Leadership Principles recently issued by Ukraine's Commander-in-Chief.
The principles identify an understanding of the commander's intent, initiative, responsibility, the development of subordinates, and the ability to learn and adapt as key leadership requirements.
Essentially, the goal is to build a culture in which a lower-level commander does not wait for detailed instructions at every step but acts on a clear understanding of the mission and takes responsibility for the outcome.
The Russian military tradition, by contrast, has historically followed the opposite logic: rigid centralized control inherited from the Soviet military school and rooted in the state's broader autocratic culture of governance.
Western researchers call this a top-down command system and argue that it leaves lower-level commanders with virtually no ability to make decisions independently. Its weaknesses were evident early in the full-scale war, including during the battle for Hostomel Airport, the crossing of the Siverskyi Donets River, and the deployment of Russian equipment at the Chornobaivka airfield.
Waiting for orders from above, units lost time or repeated actions that were clearly doomed to fail.
No command philosophy can work without institutions to support it. For mission command, that institution is the professional non-commissioned officer (NCO) corps.
In NATO armies, NCOs serve as the backbone connecting officers with enlisted personnel. They train subordinates, pass on practical experience, maintain discipline, and carry out much of the day-to-day leadership.
NCOs also build the trust that mission command requires, which is why particular attention is paid to their training and expanded authority. The Russian army is far less suited to this model.
Duties assigned to NCOs in NATO armies have traditionally been performed in the Russian military by junior officers, primarily lieutenants commanding platoons. In this system, sergeants have little scope for leadership or mentorship. Their job is to follow orders and handle organizational matters.
This creates a problem for the Russian army when it comes to delegating initiative to lower levels: sergeants and junior commanders are not trusted to act independently in complex situations. This is particularly paralyzing for combat units when conditions change rapidly.
The differences between NATO and Russian military training models are also evident in how they approach learning from mistakes. NATO places greater emphasis on critical thinking, operating amid uncertainty, and analyzing outcomes.
The main methodology is the After Action Review (AAR), a structured review conducted after a training exercise or operation. It revolves around four questions: "What was planned?", "What happened?", "What worked and what didn't?", and "What should change?" The essential condition for this approach is the ability to discuss mistakes honestly without fear of punishment, so that lessons can be learned and improvements identified.
The Russian system also has mechanisms for analyzing combat experience. Its biggest problem, however, lies in the logic of its top-down management system, which tends to punish "failures." This is why there is so much lying and embellishment in reports sent up the chain of command: admitting a mistake means facing punishment.
The result is distorted information reaching senior leadership, an unwillingness to take initiative at lower levels, and a growing fear of deviating from instructions — all of which directly contradict mission command.
Russian officers themselves acknowledge this problem. In 2023, the journal Military Thought (Voennaya Mysl) published the results of a survey of more than 100 artillery officers, most of them at the tactical level. About 81% had combat experience. Only 12% of respondents favored a policy of "intelligent initiative."
Among the obstacles, 40% cited "excessive micromanagement and commanders' distrust of subordinates," while only 30% supported a ban on punishing unsuccessful initiatives. The researchers also identified a problem with military education: the concept of "initiative" is absent even from the document governing educational activities at Russian Defense Ministry universities.
It would be convenient to reduce the differences in military training to the formula "flexible NATO vs. inflexible Russia," but the war in Ukraine has shown that reality is more complex.
The Russian armed forces are capable of learning and adapting their tactics fairly quickly under pressure. Even in Russia's public discourse, military analysts have openly reflected on the Russian military's key mistakes.
After suffering losses in 2022, Russian forces restructured their logistics in response to HIMARS strikes, changed how they used armored vehicles in response to the threat posed by FPV drones, integrated commercial (unmanned aerial vehicles) UAVs into reconnaissance on a massive scale, shortened the "detect-to-strike" cycle, and began using small assault groups more extensively.
These groups have created considerable problems for Ukrainian commanders by infiltrating the rear of Ukrainian forces.
Adaptation has also become visible at the personnel level. There have been more cases of junior commanders identifying the most experienced and motivated soldiers among their subordinates and informally transferring some responsibility to them.
Some principles resembling mission command are being absorbed less through doctrine than through the pressures of war itself.
The fastest changes are taking place in technology and specific combat procedures. Russia is developing command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance systems (C4ISR), training UAV operators, and transferring front-line experience into its higher education system.
Military educational institutions — including the Mikhailovskaya Military Artillery Academy, the Military Academy of Air Defense, the Military Academy of Communications, and the Military University of Radioelectronics — are adjusting their curricula, testing new equipment, and maintaining contact with graduates who have combat experience.
Particularly telling is that military education in Russia is no longer limited to professional military training but is increasingly penetrating the general education system. At the same time, its ideological and propagandistic component is spreading even into preschool education.
Of course, these "cosmetic changes" do not mean that the Russian army will become like Western armies. Its most fundamental difference remains its attitude toward service members. The value placed on their lives and expertise remains low.
The Soviet model continues to serve as the benchmark for a victorious army.
The Soviet command sacrificed 27 million people in the war against Nazism. The principle of "we won't spare any expense" — a Russian expression meaning that no price is too high — makes the system even more dangerous.
Russia could build an even harsher model of military training adapted to modern warfare, combining new technologies, total control, and a generation of ideologically conditioned soldiers whom it will readily throw into new wars.

Liubov Tsybulska is a strategic communications expert and a leading authority on hybrid threats in Ukraine. As the founder and current director of NGO "Join Ukraine," she leverages her extensive expertise to address critical national security challenges. Previously, she served as the inaugural Head of the Centre for Strategic Communication and Information Security under Ukraine's Ministry of Culture and Information Policy.

title: Massive fire at industrial plant in Russia's Rostov Oblast spreads to 9,000 square meters
description: The Aksaykardandetal plant manufactures drive shafts and metal components for agricultural and specialized machinery, and has metalworking capabilities which could potentially be used to manufacture military equipment components.
content:
A massive fire broke out at an industrial plant that produces parts for specialized vehicles in Russia's Rostov Oblast on Oct. 13, spreading across 9,000 square meters, Russia's Emergency Situations Ministry reported.
The blaze erupted at warehouses on the premises of the Aksaykardandetal plant in the town of Aksay, near Rostov-on-Don . A warehouse wall collapsed as the fire spread, according to Russian state-controlled news agency Interfax.
The Aksaykardandetal plant manufactures drive shafts and metal components for agricultural and specialized machinery. The facility also has metalworking capabilities, including stamping and heat treatment, which could potentially be used to manufacture components for military equipment .
The ministry said firefighters received a report of a fire at a warehouse storing plastic products at 4:10 p.m. local time. Personnel were evacuated from the premises.
According to the ministry, 98 emergency personnel and 36 vehicles were deployed to combat the blaze. Strong winds and large quantities of flammable materials complicated firefighting efforts.
Footage shared by the Telegram channel Exilenova+ showed thick columns of black smoke rising above the area. Another video showed local residents lining up at a gas station as smoke from the fire filled the sky in the background.
The cause of the fire remains unclear. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.

title: Luxembourg's excuse for de-listing Russian oligarch Mikhail Fridman fails to convince
description: Luxembourg's move to delist Mikhail Fridman has "set a dangerous precedent," as other Russian oligarchs may push to get the same treatment, lawmaker Franz Fayot told the Kyiv Independent.
content:
LUXEMBOURG — Luxembourg's prime minister defended his government's September push to delist Mikhail Fridman from EU sanctions in the country's parliament on Oct. 12, primarily by showing a lack of awareness of EU rules.
In September, the EU took the controversial decision to delist two Russian oligarchs, Mikhail Fridman and Alisher Usmanov , after a threat by France, Luxembourg, and Slovakia to otherwise let all 3,000 of the bloc's Russia sanctions expire.
The sanctions were due for renewal, and that required unanimity to proceed, allowing the three countries to plausibly make this threat.
In Luxembourg's foreign affairs committee, whose meetings are not made publicly accessible, Prime Minister Luc Frieden justified the move in terms of national interest, two lawmakers, Franz Fayot from the social democrats and Sam Tanson from the green party, told the Kyiv Independent.
Frieden said that the national interest was to try and make an arbitration case initiated by Fridman for $16 billion go away, "given the exceptionally high amount of his claim relative to Luxembourg's national budget," Tanson explained.
With Slovakia pushing for the delisting of Usmanov and Fridman, and France doubling down specifically over Usmanov, Frieden explained to lawmakers that he made the "opportunistic" calculation that getting Fridman delisted now might cause him to drop the arbitration and thus benefit Luxembourg in the long run, Fayot said.
However, as Fayot and Tanson explained and Luxembourg's leading newspaper the Luxemburger Wort also reported, there was no contact between the Luxembourgish government with Fridman or his legal team, and so far, that arbitration proceeding has not been withdrawn.
"Luxembourg appears willing to weaken the EU sanctions regime in response to a potentially enormous financial liability without having established that delisting would eliminate it," Tanson said.
The move might even have weakened Luxembourg's case in any eventual arbitration proceeding, Fayot added.
This could be interpreted as an "admission that Luxembourg had a say ... contrary to what was pretended," Fayot said.
Frieden's fears also do not hold ground, given the EU clarifying with every sanctions package that countries do not have to abide by any legal ruling to compensate sanctioned Russian companies or individuals if sanctions are the reason a deal or contract could not be carried out.
A European Commission spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent that the EU's sanctions regulations include a "no-claims clause" to that effect, adding that the latest sanctions packages included a range of additional safeguards to allow those who uphold sanctions to recover damages incurred in doing so.
However, that did not stop Frieden from saying there was "no solidarity at EU level for any damage," Fayot said.
Tanson told the Kyiv Independent that the solidarity question was not discussed in detail, but that it appears to be "the government's general position ... that Luxembourg would have to bear the financial burden alone if it were ordered to pay compensation."
Tanson explicitly asked Frieden about EU rules that would protect Luxembourg from having to compensate Fridman after a future court ruling, to which he replied "he was not aware of such a rule," an exchange also confirmed by Fayot.
The Kyiv Independent asked Prime Minister Frieden's head of communications about these comments and asked for a reaction but had not received any response at the time of publication.
The Luxemburger Wort also reported that Luxembourg's Bilateral Investment Treaty (BIT) with Russia was cited as a basis for having to respect the ruling of an arbitration in Fridman's favor.
In comments made separately to the Luxemburger Wort, Tanson said she asked if it would not make sense to terminate the treaty, but that Foreign Minister Xavier Bettel opposes this.
In the EU, there have been some conversations about a coordinated ending of the bloc's BITs with Russia , of which 17 still exist, but even so the comments made by the EU about an obligation to not comply with legal rulings that undermine sanctions also extends to these treaties.
Instead, Fayot told the Kyiv Independent that he fears Luxembourg has "set a dangerous precedent," as other Russian oligarchs may push to get the same treatment.
The move "weakens the position of smaller countries," and risks creating a "regulatory chill" Fayot warned.
"If a single (small) member state can be put under sufficient financial pressure through judicial or arbitration proceedings to push for an individual's delisting, this risks undermining the entire sanctions system," Tanson said.
Tanson added that the sanctions delistings send the "wrong signal to both Russia and Ukraine."
For her, the move tells Moscow that EU unity is fragile, and for Ukraine, "it raises serious questions about the reliability of European support."
Fayot also said "he's sure the Ukrainians aren't crazy about this," a fact confirmed shortly after the committee meeting.
That same morning, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha met with Prime Minister Frieden , then immediately headed for a meeting of EU foreign ministers, where he told journalists "our position is that the delisting of the two Russian oligarchs was a wrong step, it was a wrong decision."
"That's why we will propose to impose sanctions on an additional 10 Russian oligarchs. It was a wrong step," Sybiha repeated.

title: Russia responsible for Starlink sabotage, says Poland
description: Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that German Police had arrested two suspects on behalf of Polish services and called the attack “another act of hybrid warfare” in a post on X.
content:
Polish authorities on Oct. 12 blamed Russian intelligence services for an arson attack on a Starlink ground station in Poland on Sept. 23, and said two Turkish citizens had been detained as suspects in Germany.
The two suspects had been arrested on behalf of Polish services on Oct. 10 under suspicion of having set fire to the station in Wola Krobowska, in Poland's Masovian Voivodeship, said Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in a post on X . He called the attack “another act of hybrid warfare.”
Tomasz Siemoniak, the minister coordinating Polish special services, made Russia responsible for the attack, reported AP .
“We have no doubt that Russian intelligence services are behind this act of sabotage,” he said, according to AP.
He also said that "​It is worth adding that Russian services are increasingly turning ​to individuals linked ‌to the criminal underworld," according to Deutsche Welle .
On Sept. 24, Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski told reporters that a fire at a Starlink ground station in Poland may have been a deliberate attempt to disrupt internet access used by Ukrainian forces at the front.
The station is operated by the state-owned telecommunications company Exatel and serves as an internet hub that carries traffic through Poland , including to Ukraine, Gawkowski said.
He suggested Russia could be behind the incident, describing it as potentially part of Moscow's hybrid warfare .
Polish authorities are also investigating an alleged assassination plot targeting Tusk and his deputy, Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, Jacek Dobrzynski, a spokesperson for Polish intelligence agencies, said on Oct. 11.
Police received numerous reports of a possible assassination attempt, after which a meeting was called between representatives of the Interior and Administration Ministry, the State Protection Service, and the Internal Security Agency.
"We are taking this matter very seriously," Kosiniak-Kamysz said at a press briefing on Oct. 11.

title: Less than half of EU citizens support Ukraine's quick accession, poll shows
description: Support for Ukraine's EU accession varied across the bloc, reaching 69% in Sweden, the highest share among the countries surveyed. Romania recorded the lowest level of support, at 40%.
content:
A survey published by eupinions on Oct. 13 found a significant gap between Ukrainians and EU citizens in support for Ukraine’s accelerated EU accession and their views on Kyiv’s role in defending Europe against Russian aggression.
The survey, conducted by Nira Data across all 27 EU member states and Ukrainian government-controlled territories and published by the Bertelsmann Stiftung’s eupinions project, found that 47% of EU citizens believe Ukraine should join the bloc in the coming years, compared with 83% of Ukrainian respondents.
Support for Ukraine's EU accession varied across the bloc, reaching 69% in Sweden, the highest share among the countries surveyed. Romania recorded the lowest level of support, at 40%.
Economic costs of Ukraine's accession appeared to be a key driver among respondents in most EU countries.
"Ukraine's precarious financial situation poses a challenge to the EU as a whole, as stability in our large European neighbor is a matter of shared interest. The estimated financing needs for reconstruction alone now exceed 500 billion euros ($560 billion)," said Miriam Kosmehl, the organization's expert on Eastern Europe.
Twenty-eight percent of EU respondents consider increased financial burden as the main challenge if Ukraine joins the Union.
The question of security was also raised in the report.
Over half, or 58% of Ukrainians, believe that their country is making a greater contribution to protecting the EU from possible Russian aggression. On the other hand, only 16% of EU citizens agree with the statement.
Besides Ukraine, Germany, France, and the Netherlands had the highest percentage of citizens who believe Ukraine does more to protect Europe from Russia.
However, a mere 14% of EU citizens believe that Ukraine's membership has the possibility of making the Union "stronger and more influential on the global stage."
Kosmehl noted that Ukraine's defense of its sovereignty and independence directly impacts the future of democracy and security in Europe.
“Russia seeks to exploit internal divisions to weaken EU consensus and solidarity. Open societies face particular challenges in addressing targeted influence operations,” she adds.

title: Last Seen in Crimea: Kyiv Independent documentary investigates Russia's secret detention system for Ukrainian civilians
description: The Kyiv Independent's War Crimes Investigations Unit has released Last Seen in Crimea, a new documentary investigating a system of detention in Russian-occupied Crimea where Ukrainian civilians have been held without contact with the outside world, often without formal charges, and subjected to torture and other forms of abuse.
content:
The Kyiv Independent's War Crimes Investigations Unit has released Last Seen in Crimea, a new documentary investigating a system of detention in Russian-occupied Crimea where Ukrainian civilians have been held without contact with the outside world, often without formal charges, and subjected to torture and other forms of abuse.
The documentary was released online on Sept. 11, on the Kyiv Independent's YouTube channel and website . An in-person screening was held in Kyiv on the same day at the National Museum of the History of Ukraine in the Second World War, followed by an audience Q&A with the Kyiv Independent team.
The investigation traces how Russia's system of political repression in Crimea , built up since the 2014 occupation, has expanded to include civilians taken from territories occupied after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
At the center of the film are two detention facilities in Crimea's capital of Simferopol — SIZO No. 2 and the more secretive SIZO No. 8 — as well as the officials and structures behind them.
The Kyiv Independent's reporting found evidence that SIZO No. 2, formally operated by Russia's Federal Penitentiary Service, has been used to hold Ukrainian civilians under conditions that former detainees describe as abusive and coercive, with Federal Security Service ( FSB ) personnel having particular access to the facility.
SIZO No. 8, meanwhile, was formally transferred under FSB control in 2026 and has remained largely closed to public scrutiny. The investigation also identified Anton Panin, a former FSB investigator involved in the politically motivated case against Crimean Tatar activist Nariman Dzhelyal and his co-defendants, as the apparent head of SIZO No. 8 shortly before the facility came under FSB control.
"For us, one of the key goals of this investigation was to identify the individuals directly responsible for the unlawful detention, ill-treatment, and torture of Ukrainian civilian detainees in the occupied territories," says film author Olesia Bida.
"Systems like this do not operate on their own — they depend on those who run them and those who carry out their orders."
One of the survivors featured in the film, Anatolii, a businessman from Kherson Oblast, was abducted from his home after helping wounded Ukrainian soldiers escape Russian-occupied territory. He spent years being moved between makeshift detention sites and prisons before being taken to SIZO No. 2 in Simferopol, where he was tortured and held in abusive conditions. His family did not know whether he was alive for months.
The documentary also follows Dzhelyal, a Crimean Tatar activist who spent five months in SIZO No. 2 after being detained in 2021 and accused of sabotage. He was later sentenced to 17 years in prison before being released in a prisoner exchange and is now Ukraine's ambassador to Turkey.
A third story follows Tetiana Zelena, whose brother Serhii Lykhomanov was detained in Crimea in December 2023. His family spent two months trying to establish where he was being held before learning that he was in SIZO No. 8. His lawyer was denied access to him even after a court authorized a visit.
Together, the stories show how the system operates across different stages of detention: people can disappear without their families knowing where they are, be held without meaningful access to legal representation, and in some cases remain outside any formal legal process altogether.
Human rights experts interviewed for the film describe this status as incommunicado detention — people held without charges, court decisions, or contact with the outside world.
For the investigation, the Kyiv Independent interviewed 13 former detainees of SIZO No. 2 and obtained testimony from three additional former detainees through their lawyers. The team also spoke with around two dozen relatives of Ukrainian civilians who remain in detention. Because many of those still held are unable to speak publicly, some relatives requested anonymity for the safety of the detainees.
The investigators also cross-referenced leaked Russian databases , procurement records, court and other documents, and social media activity to identify people involved in the detention system. This reporting helped the team trace the career of Panin, who had previously worked as an FSB investigator and was later linked to the administration of SIZO No. 8.
The scale of the system extends far beyond the people featured in the film. According to Ukraine's Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets, Russia is holding roughly 16,000 Ukrainian civilians across some 200 detention sites in Russia and occupied Ukrainian territories.
Only around 450 had been returned home at the time of the film's release. Unlike prisoners of war, Ukrainian civilian detainees do not have a functioning exchange mechanism. The U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has also documented deaths of Ukrainian civilians in Russian captivity.
The documentary can be watched on the Kyiv Independent's YouTube channel and website , alongside the full written investigation, Inside Russia's FSB prison system in occupied Crimea , by Bida, a War Crimes Investigations Unit reporter and the film''s author.
Last Seen in Crimea is the latest documentary from the Kyiv Independent's War Crimes Investigations Unit , founded in 2023 to document Russian atrocities against Ukrainian civilians. Over three years, the unit has produced more than a dozen documentaries, held more than 90 screenings worldwide, and received multiple journalism awards, including an IRE Award.

title: Ukraine's parliament supports several bills tied to Western funding, with dozens remaining ahead
description: On Oct. 13, lawmakers supported three bills in the first reading linked to funding from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the EU under the Ukraine Facility — an EU financial assistance program launched in 2024.
content:
Ukraine's parliament has voted for several bills on Oct. 13 linked to Western funding, as the government seeks to secure billions in financial assistance.
Delays in fulfilling international commitments put 29.5 billion euros ($33 billion) in funding at risk , prompting the government to suspend non-essential spending. Parliament must pass around 30 bills by year's end to secure the funds, with votes on some of them expected this week.
On Oct. 13, lawmakers supported three bills in the first reading linked to funding from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the EU under the Ukraine Facility — an EU financial assistance program launched in 2024.
These include bills to cap borrowing costs, restrict courts' access to bank secrecy, and simplify value-added tax (VAT) administration for businesses.
A long-debated bill on the Single Euro Payments Area (SEPA), aimed at aligning Ukraine’s financial monitoring rules with European Union standards, was also due to be considered. Some lawmakers from the ruling Servant of the People party who spoke to the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 12 were optimistic about its chances of passing.
However, the bill was ultimately pulled from the agenda for a first-reading vote after it became clear it lacked sufficient support, according to several lawmakers.
"I think it's absolute nonsense (not to vote for the bill). It's a European directive in every detail," pro-government lawmaker Mykyta Poturaiev told the Kyiv Independent.
Lawmakers are expected to continue voting on other key bills on Oct. 14.
Months of slow progress on legislation and reforms linked to Western funding has pushed the government to step up its engagement with lawmakers.
Since taking office this summer, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi has held several discussions with lawmakers on the issue. On Oct. 12, he met with members of President Volodymyr Zelensky 's Servant of the People party alongside Finance Minister Serhii Marchenko.
Yet securing support for some of the required reforms remains uncertain.
Some lawmakers who spoke with the Kyiv Independent doubted the anti-corruption strategy, which lays out Ukraine's vision anti-corruption policy for 2026–2030, would garner enough support.
Other rule-of-law reforms have also stalled in parliament.

title: Fact check: Russia turns to AI to push fakes about 'women's draft' in Ukraine
description:
Russian disinformation yet again targets the sensitive topic of mobilization in Ukraine — this time, pushing falsehoods about an alleged forced draft of women.

Pro-Kremlin social media accounts and Russian media have spread AI-generated images alleging that Ukrainian women are being lured to join the Armed Forces by targeted recruitment posters, while others claim they are being outright called up for military service.

But though tens of thousands of Ukrainian women enlisted in the army as vol
content:
Servicewomen of the “Fighting Witches” mobile group of Ukraine’s Air Defense Forces practice shooting at a base in Kyiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Nov. 2, 2024. (Yevhenii Vasyliev/Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
Russian disinformation yet again targets the sensitive topic of mobilization in Ukraine — this time, pushing falsehoods about an alleged forced draft of women.
Pro-Kremlin social media accounts and Russian media have spread AI-generated images alleging that Ukrainian women are being lured to join the Armed Forces by targeted recruitment posters, while others claim they are being outright called up for military service.
But though tens of thousands of Ukrainian women enlisted in the army as volunteers, these claims are false — there is no mandatory draft of women in place, nor is it being prepared.
Telegram channels have once again proven to be fertile ground for such fabricated stories, with both Ukrainian- and Russian-language channels involved in spreading them.
One fake post from Sept. 15 alleged that posters featuring women in military uniforms had appeared around Odesa, a city in southern Ukraine. Other channels reposted identical photographs but claimed they had been seen around Lutsk, in western Ukraine.
The banners' message was intended to show how domestic chores hardly differ from tasks at the front, reading, "You figured out the washing machine — you'll figure out FPVs (first-person-view drones) too."
"There were no such banners, and an AI verification tool indicates they were AI-generated," Roman Osadchuk, the director of Threat Intelligence at the LetsData tech company, told the Kyiv Independent.
LetsData spotted the campaign in mid-September as it began circulating on social media.
A similar fake image was posted on the Telegram channel of Russian state TV presenter Olesya Loseva on Sept. 29. The post featured a bogus advertisement she claimed had been displayed in one of Kyiv's shopping centers.
The image features a young woman standing over a baby and a gun, with the Ukrainian-language caption reading: "A real Ukrainian woman can do these things in 40 seconds!"
When the Kyiv Independent ran this image through Hive Moderation, a platform that detects AI-generated or synthetic content, it returned a near-certain verdict — 99.9% likely to be AI-generated.
"This narrative is recurring and gets amplified from time to time, meaning that it comes and goes, sometimes using 'new tools' like AI-generated imagery," adds Osadchuk.
While disinformation and propaganda have long been central to Moscow's arsenal, Russia is now harnessing AI to spread falsehoods faster and more widely.
"Russia-linked actors have mostly used AI tools to amplify existing tactics, such as producing inauthentic content at scale and spreading content to reach broader audiences and fuel polarization," the European Center of Excellence for Countering Hybrid Threats reported in March.
Besides Telegram, the narrative has also appeared on X, where a post by Donbass Segodnya, a pro-Russian news outlet, featured images of a woman apparently holding summons papers, implying that a mass call-up of women has begun.
Women can indeed receive summonses, but only if they are in the military register, which is mandatory only for women with relevant medical or pharmaceutical education.
Even then, this does not mean they can be mobilized against their will. The women are simply added to the register and can be summoned to update their personal data or undergo a medical examination.
Since 2022, Ukraine has been carrying out a large-scale draft of military-age men to boost its army's ranks and resist Russian aggression — a topic repeatedly targeted by Russian disinformation and propaganda .
Women have also joined the military as volunteers, with about 76,000 being part of Ukraine's Armed Forces, including 57,000 serving in military roles. However, Ukraine has not instituted a mandatory draft for women.
"There are no decisions to mobilize women in Ukraine," said Ukraine's Center for Countering Disinformation, a body at the country's National Security and Defense Council, on Aug. 26.
"The parliamentary committee on national security, defense, and intelligence officially stated that there are no legislative initiatives, draft laws, or internal discussions concerning the introduction of such mobilization.
Moscow launched this latest disinformation campaign just as rumors of women's conscription circulated in Ukraine.
Former Defense Minister Oleksii Reznikov raised the issue in an interview with Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL) on Aug. 20, arguing that requiring women to serve in the military would "immediately double the mobilization pool."
Separately, former U.S. Special Envoy for Ukraine Keith Kellogg said on Aug. 24 that he believed women should be mobilized to help Ukraine's manpower problem since "they (women) fight no worse than men."
The Ukrainian parliament reacted by saying that the comments "do not reflect the actual legislative work."
With no draft law on the table, the mobilization of women remains confined to AI-generated content.
Yevgeniya Doluda is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in journalism, politics, and history from City St. George’s University of London. Yevgeniya previously worked and volunteered with non-profit organizations in Europe and had her work published in RTL. In addition to Ukrainian, she also speaks Spanish and French.

title: Russian forces use group of civilians as 'human shields' near Kupiansk, fire at them afterwards, Ukraine's military says
description: The group included two women, a child, and several men who were being led toward the Shebelinka–Ostrogozhsk gas pipeline by Russian forces, according to Ukraine's 13th Khartia Corps.
content:
Russian forces led a group of civilians toward a gas pipeline, using them as human shields, and afterwards opened fire at them near the front-line city of Kupiansk in Ukraine's Kharkiv Oblast on Oct. 13, the Ukrainian military said, providing alleged drone footage of the incident.
The group included two women, a child, and several men who were being led toward the Shebelinka–Ostrogozhsk gas pipeline, according to Ukraine's 13th Khartia Corps. The group came under repeated mortar and artillery fire as it moved.
Drone footage recorded by Ukrainian reconnaissance units showed casualties among the civilians, Khartia said, adding that Ukrainian troops had not opened fire. Based on the impact patterns, the strike originated from the eastern bank of the Oskil River, where Russian forces are positioned, the corps said.
Khartia called the strike a "deliberate provocation" and warned that Russian media could use footage from the incident to falsely accuse Ukraine of attacking civilians. The corps said it would hand over the materials for a war crimes investigation.
"Civilians are used as human shields by the Russians, and then become their target for disinformation campaigns," Khartia wrote.
Ukraine's Joint Forces grouping separately said on Oct. 13 that Russian forces had struck a column of civilians leaving Kupiansk during what it described as a forced evacuation. The military said it was still establishing the number of casualties.
According to the Joint Forces grouping, Russian troops had conducted similar operations in recent weeks, using civilians as human shields to cover the withdrawal of some of their soldiers.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claim.
Throughout the full-scale war , the Russian military has regularly breached international warfare conventions, including through indiscriminate attacks on civilian areas and the abduction of civilians from occupied territories.
On Sept. 29, Khartiia Corps said Russian troops use civilians , including children and elderly people, as human shields to flee via a gas pipeline in northeastern Kharkiv Oblast amid the Ukrainian push in the Kupiansk sector.
Khartiia Corps said the group of civilians would have to walk more than 10 kilometers (about six miles) through the pipeline before exiting into a forest, where they would likely be transported to Russian-occupied territory.

title: Letters to the editor: Readers question Trump's Russian diesel deal and US sanctions policy
description:
This week's letters come from readers questioning the Trump administration's decision to purchase Russian diesel fuel amid rising prices in the United States. An American reader argues the deal benefits Russian President Vladimir Putin at Ukraine's expense, a scholar questions whether a U.S. sanctions bill will meaningfully pressure Moscow, and a British reader raises concerns about Washington's turn to Russian oil.

Got an opinion on anything you've read in the Kyiv Independent? Send it to lett
content:
President Donald Trump (R) walks toward Russian President Vladimir Putin (L) to shake hands during a joint press conference at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson in Anchorage, Alaska, U.S. on Aug. 15, 2025. (Jae C. Hong / AP)
This week's letters come from readers questioning the Trump administration's decision to purchase Russian diesel fuel amid rising prices in the United States. An American reader argues the deal benefits Russian President Vladimir Putin at Ukraine's expense, a scholar questions whether a U.S. sanctions bill will meaningfully pressure Moscow, and a British reader raises concerns about Washington's turn to Russian oil.
Got an opinion on anything you've read in the Kyiv Independent? Send it to letters@kyivindependent.com — your letter may appear in our Letters section.
U.S. President Donald Trump's MAGA Republican Party is projected to lose the midterm elections in a few weeks, and much of his power and support within the government could evaporate.
Trump needs a scapegoat for the crippling rise in diesel prices in the United States . He has now decided that scapegoat will be Ukraine and President Volodymyr Zelensky .
The diesel "deal" Trump announced a few days ago is nothing but a calculated act of gaslighting aimed at Americans and a wholesale admission that he has always been on Team Russia.
Trump says the deal will give the United States 1.8 million tons, or 14 million barrels, of diesel over the next 90 days, with another 3 million tons next year if Russia can supply it.
This figure is so minor in real terms that it would keep American trucks and industry running on diesel for a mere six days. Donald Trump has simultaneously destroyed American credibility, sided with the enemy, and sold out Ukraine for a pittance.
Karl Frost, United States / Germany member
The Lindsey Graham bill in the US, passed by Congress on Sept. 16, was celebrated internationally as a landmark Russian sanctions bill. Ukraine supporters who cheered this seem not to have fully appreciated that most Democrats voted against it.
Despite appearances, legally, the bill does not mandate Russia-related sanctions. The legally consequential aspect of the bill is authorizing discretionary tariff powers for the president with no meaningful oversight.
The bill identifies two categories of tariff targets: the top five importers of Russian oil and the top five facilitators of Russian sanctions evasion.
There is language in the bill "mandating" these tariffs. However, the bill gives the president arbitrary, discretionary powers to make exceptions. In other words, the president is not actually mandated to impose these tariffs.
Trump already had the power to sanction Russia, which he was not using, so there is no reason to think this further permission to tariff Russian oil consumers will be used, especially in light of his announcement that the U.S. would buy diesel fuel from Russia to offset fuel price increases caused by his war with Iran.
Unlike the "importer" tariffs, which do have relatively objective criteria, the "facilitator" tariffs are based on presidential interpretation. The Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed, for example in Dalton v. Specter , that where a statute grants such pure executive discretion as spelled out in the bill, courts will decline to review the factual basis behind the president's determination. The president could theoretically designate any nation currently locked in a trade dispute with the U.S., including allies of Ukraine , as a "facilitator of sanction evasions," slap them with 100% tariffs, and face zero judicial review.
This is the central concern raised by Democrats. As U.S. Representative Don Beyer stated , "This bill would do more harm than good for America and for Ukraine . Giving (Trump) this power when he has shown us over and over again what he will do with it would be an incredible mistake."
Mostly no, at least not directly, except for dropping illusions. This matters because the bill is being presented as a tool to pressure Russia and support Ukraine. Trump already declines to use his existing sanctions powers, so there is little reason to expect this one to pressure Russia, and it could actually backfire on Ukraine.
I am a U.K. citizen living in the South West of England. I have a 23-year-old diesel car and am now paying 2 pounds per liter ($2.65).
I am appalled by the descent of the U.S. to the level of barbarism shown by its leaders: resorting to shouting down opposition when they have no reasoned argument and using personal insults against journalists who ask pertinent questions. But back to diesel.
Several weeks ago, Mr. Trump was castigating Ukraine for attacking Russian oil and petrochemical facilities. In the current circumstances, these are appropriate targets, in contrast with Russia's attacks on homes and civilian infrastructure. His "argument" was that Ukraine was causing a global diesel shortage through this strategy, while failing to acknowledge the sanctions he had imposed on Russia.
Ordinary Russians queuing for fuel learned more about their leaders' war from these shortages than from any other source. Mr. Trump had conveniently forgotten that he had contributed to the shortage by attacking Iran, which discovered it could hold the whole world to ransom by closing the Strait of Hormuz, creating shortages of all fuels and many other oil-based products.
Suddenly, Mr. Putin is America's savior, agreeing to export "millions of barrels" of oil to the US! Where has this oil appeared from? Is it the result of lifting sanctions on the shadow fleet? Is Ukraine no longer attacking Russian oil facilities? Maybe these are magic oil wells?
Any story that will last long enough for Mr. Trump to tell it to voters ahead of the midterm elections appears on his antisocial media sites.
