title: As Russian missiles slip through Kyiv's air defenses without warning, officials say US intelligence sharing remains intact. For now
description:
Despite the recent failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent.

Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.

The attack came as Washington had threatened to susp
content:
A police officer photographs the engine of a Shahed drone in front of a multistory residential building damaged in a Russian drone strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Oct. 12, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
Despite the recent failure of Kyiv's early warning system and threats to halt U.S. intelligence sharing with Ukraine, Washington made no such decision, Ukrainian and American sources told the Kyiv Independent.
Five Russian S-400 missiles struck the Ukrainian capital shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, causing "massive explosions," Kyiv Independent journalists reported. Air raid sirens and mobile alerts sounded only after the attack.
The attack came as Washington had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian energy infrastructure, the Kyiv Independent has learned.
Ukraine receives intelligence from the U.S. to help detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
Zelensky described the strike as "particularly vile," saying Kyiv "received no early warning from our partners about this strike." His remarks raised questions about whether Washington had suspended intelligence assistance to Ukraine.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, in turn, publicly said that intelligence sharing with the Americans continued, saying on Oct. 13, "Yes, we continue this cooperation."
Multiple sources told the Kyiv Independent that there was no decision to cut intelligence sharing. The incident instead appears to have involved a failure to detect or communicate the missile launch in time to warn Kyiv.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either."
The S-400 is a Russian air defense system with secondary ground-attack capabilities. Since 2022, Russia has repeatedly used the system, as well as its older version, the S-300, to strike Ukrainian cities.
One senior Ukrainian official familiar with the matter said Ukraine's military leadership contacted its U.S. counterparts after the strike to clarify what had happened.
"They say they didn't cut it off, but they didn't warn us (about the attack) either," the official said.
"The Americans said they just didn't see (the launch)... That's a weak excuse."
The official alleged that the incident might have been "a game" to test Ukraine's reaction. Ukraine's military leadership also warned senior officials that if similar incidents became a pattern, they could indicate that Washington was using intelligence assistance to pressure Kyiv.
There is, however, no evidence in the information provided that the incident resulted from a deliberate decision to withhold intelligence.
Detection of ballistic missile launches is largely carried out by a network of sophisticated infrared detecting spy satellites, which identify the thermal spikes caused by the launch of ballistic missiles , Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent.
The system is generally extremely reliable but not infallible, Hoffmann said, explaining that certain environmental conditions, such as dense, unusually high cloud coverage, could impair its functioning.
Like any system, Hoffmann said, it was susceptible to "human or technical failure" or "extraordinary circumstances" that could impair its functioning.
Missile attacks on Kyiv , which precede air raid warnings, are uncommon but have occurred several times since 2022. In almost all cases, it was the ballistic missiles, which fly at extremely high speeds, that escaped detection by radar.
"Friends, this is not the first time that the intelligence services of our partners have not recorded the launch of the S-400," Zelensky's advisor, Sergey Beskrestnov, said on Oct. 12. "You should not draw conclusions prematurely."

title: Ukraine hits Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile maintenance base, General Staff says
description: The Iskander-M is one of Russia's principal ballistic weapons. Since the beginning of 2026, Moscow has launched more than 500 ballistic missiles against Ukraine.
content:
Ukrainian forces struck an Iskander-M repair base, a radar station, logistics depots, and Russian troop concentrations, the General Staff said on Oct. 13.
The Iskander -M repair base islocated near Kondrinka in Russia's Kursk Oblast , according to the General Staff . The facility is used to repair self-propelled launchers and transporter-loader vehicles of the Iskander-M operational-tactical missile system
The Iskander-M is one of Russia's principal ballistic weapons. Since the beginning of 2026, Moscow has launched more than 500 ballistic missiles against Ukraine.
Kyiv's military intelligence estimates that Russia can produce more than 200 cruise and ballistic missiles of various types each month, with Iskander-M missiles among its production priorities.
In addition, a radar station was struck in Bryansk Oblast , the General Staff said.
Across Russian-occupied territories, Ukrainian troops also struck Russian troop concentrations. In the occupied Luhansk Oblast, a fuel and lubricants depot, an ammunition depot, and a logistics facility belonging to Russian units were struck.
The strikes are part of a series of attacks on Russian military infrastructure in Russia and occupied Ukrainian territories.

title: Kyiv stopped attacking Russia's oil refineries, Moscow continues pounding Ukraine's energy grid, Zelensky says
description: "Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for the two days since the American president announced an energy ceasefire. But Russia did not heed," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
content:
Since U.S. President Donald Trump's sudden announcement of an energy truce between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, Ukraine has not targeted Russia’s oil refineries or energy infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct 13.
Russia ignored the ceasefire, Zelensky added.
"Ukraine has not carried out strikes on Russian oil refineries or the energy sector in general for the two days since the American president announced an energy ceasefire. But Russia did not heed," Zelensky said on social media.
Trump made it very clear that the U.S. can influence both sides when responding to reporters' questions on why he announced a ceasefire without consulting either side.
"They agreed because I said they agreed . And that thing has to get settled."
The announcement of yet another ceasefire was news to Kyiv , but Zelensky expressed Ukraine's willingness to uphold it in an interview with Axios .
"If President Trump negotiated it with (Vladimir) Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it."
Russia soon violated the energy ceasefire by attacking Kharkiv's CHP-5 power plant in the evening of Oct.11.
Following the attack, Zelensky disclosed that over the past week, Russia has carried out over 200 strikes on Ukraine's electricity and transmission facilities, in addition to 17 strikes on gas and oil facilities.
"They have killed more than 150 of our people, and more than 700 people have been wounded," he wrote.
On Oct. 12, Russia seemingly rejected the idea of a ceasefire. "We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said in turn.
The truce also makes little sense for Ukraine if it only addresses oil refineries. Zelensky said Ukraine is "ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same," but it must go beyond just oil refineries to include energy infrastructure.
"In Ukraine, we have just one oil refinery. And it was badly damaged by Russian strikes long, long ago," Zelensky said on Oct. 12 in a video address to the Warsaw Security Forum.
As Russia continues to pound Ukraine's energy grid, Kyiv — a city with over three million residents, comparable in population and size to Berlin — endures hour-long power outages , with some districts also being deprived of water.
"It was clear that Putin does not read Truth Social, and his 'Shahed' drones follow a different set of instructions," Zelensky said.

title: France, Poland, Spain, do not see agriculture as blocking further EU progress for Ukraine
description: Spain's European Affairs Minister Fernando Sampedro told the Kyiv Independent that "we really hope that in the case of Ukraine and Moldova we will be able to open all clusters as soon as possible."
content:
LUXEMBOURG — Three of the EU's largest member states, France, Poland, and Spain, said on Oct. 13 they want Ukraine's EU accession process to continue and that Kyiv's strong farming sector should not be used to slow membership talks.
Ukraine is partway through unlocking the six to-do lists of reforms it must complete to join the EU, but one of the as-yet unopened lists covers agriculture.
The sheer size of Kyiv's agricultural sector raises concerns among EU farmers, who are less competitive and heavily dependent on subsidies, and who fear that Ukraine joining the EU will drive them out of business.
French far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen has already leaned on farmers' fears about Ukraine as the French elections near.
"There are member states that have a lot of doubts," said Poland's European Affairs Minister Ignacy Niemczycki, ahead of a meeting of European affairs ministers in Luxembourg, though he did not name specific countries.
But France, Poland, and Spain all said they support Ukraine being able to advance its EU membership bid.
Spain's European Affairs Minister Fernando Sampedro told the Kyiv Independent that "we really hope that in the case of Ukraine and Moldova we will be able to open all clusters as soon as possible."
"The earlier the better, so that we can accompany the strong efforts that both governments are doing," Sampedro said.
French European Affairs Minister Benjamin Haddad commended Ukraine for passing a bill on minorities the day before, which persuaded Hungary to lift its block on membership talks.
"We support the opening of all negotiation clusters with Ukraine and Moldova... I think now it is time to move forward," Haddad said.
Later on Oct. 13, Ukraine will unlock clusters two and three, which cover a wide range of economic reforms. It had already opened clusters addressing the rule of law and external relations earlier in the year.
When asked by the Kyiv Independent if Ukraine is ready to open the final two, Haddad replied, "I support that."
Niemczycki told journalists that "opening a cluster does not mean closing it," and explained that opening clusters is required for negotiations to take place.
"This is a very good moment, because we can tell our friends from Ukraine to enter the EU. To get closer, you have to do this, this, and this," Niemczycki said.
He also said that Polish business is "open to competition, but they want Ukraine to follow the same rules," which, for him, means Ukraine aligning with the EU.
Other countries likewise spoke in favor of progressing Ukraine's EU membership bid, such as Germany and Finland, which, like Poland, see Ukraine's joining as a geopolitical asset.
"We are absolutely not afraid of Ukrainian agriculture," Finnish European Affairs Minister Joakim Strand told the Kyiv Independent.
"We think that Ukraine is doing an excellent job when it comes to defending Europe today, and we hope and believe that the future of Ukraine is within the European Union," Strand said.

title: Russian drone strikes university building in Rivne, injures 25
description: Ukraine's Education and Science Minister Andrii Butenko said that a fire broke out in a building of Rivne State Humanitarian University as a result of the Russian drone strike.
content:
A Russian drone struck a university building in the northwestern city of Rivne, injuring 25 people, Rivne's National Police branch said on Oct. 13.
Of the 25 injured, two were in critical condition, while three others are under medical examination, the police said .
Ukraine's Education and Science Minister Andrii Butenko said that a fire broke out in a building of Rivne State Humanitarian University as a result of the Russian drone strike. The Faculty of Music building was almost completely gutted by the fire, while neighboring teaching facilities had windows smashed, he added.
Oleksandr Koval, head of Rivne Oblast Military Administration, said on Oct. 13 that the drone strike damaged the second floor of the building. The fire in the building had been contained, and emergency services were on site.
"All victims are receiving medical assistance. Rescuers, police, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and municipal services are working at the scene," Koval said .
According to the university, all students were in shelters at the moment of the attack. There were casualties amongst the university's administrative staff.
At around 10:35 a.m., Ukraine's air force had reported a jet-powered drone flying over Rivne. The air alert was issued in the city at 10:10 a.m.
On Oct. 12, the air alert was issued several times in Rivne Oblast .
The city of Rivne came under Russian drone attack at around 9 p.m. local time, Koval said. A non-residential building was damaged, while no one was injured. Later, at 11 p.m., air defenses were active in the city.
Separately, the Sarny District of Rivne Oblast came under attack late in the evening of October 12, Koval added. Сivilian infrastructure, non-operational facilities, dormitories, and residential buildings were damaged as a result of the attack.
Overall, Russian attacks across Ukraine killed 10 people and injured 80 over the past day, regional authorities said on Oct. 13.
Overnight on Oct. 13, Russian forces launched five ballistic missiles, 108 Shahed-type attack drones, including 74 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, and nine Banderol missiles, Ukraine's Air Force said .
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 88 drones, while strikes were recorded at 17 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at seven locations, the Air Force said.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 10, injure 80 across Ukraine over past day as Moscow hits homes, railway infrastructure
description: Overnight on Oct. 13, Russian forces launched five ballistic missiles, 108 Shahed-type attack drones, including 74 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, and nine Banderol missiles, Ukraine's Air Force said.
content:
At least 10 people were killed and 80 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia continued to target residential buildings in cities including Kyiv, regional authorities said on Oct. 13.
In Kharkiv Oblast over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and settlements in the surrounding region, killing four people and injuring 36, including four children, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said. President Volodymyr Zelensky later raised the number of injured in a missile strike on Kharkiv, meaning that 42 people were injured in the Oblast in total.
All four deaths occurred in residential buildings.
In Kyiv , at least two people were killed and 14 others injured in drone attacks throughout the day, including a strike on a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi District.
Kyiv also came under ballistic missile attack shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, with powerful explosions reported before an air raid alert was issued in the Ukrainian capital. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a warehouse and railway infrastructure had been damaged.
In Vinnytsia Oblast , Russia struck a production complex belonging to Ukrainian confectionery company Roshen , the company said.
"Thanks to the timely activation of the warning system and the prompt evacuation, the lives of employees were saved," Roshen said in a statement .
Overnight on Oct. 13, Russian forces launched five ballistic missiles, 108 Shahed-type attack drones, including 74 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, and nine Banderol missiles, Ukraine's Air Force said .
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 88 drones, while strikes were recorded at 17 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at seven locations, the Air Force said.
Air defenses were active in the far-western Lviv Oblast overnight as Russian drones "struck villages and private homes," Lviv Mayor Andrii Sadovyi said , though he reported no casualties.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , four people were killed and 11 others were injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In northeastern Sumy Oblast , two people were injured in Russian strikes, regional authorities said .
In southern Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks injured six people, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast , over the past day, Russia carried out 910 attacks against 58 settlements in the region — five people were injured in the attacks, regional authorities said .
Dnipropetrovsk and Chernihiv oblasts also came under Russian attacks, but no injuries were reported.

title: 'Absolutely unacceptable' — 11 crew members lost at sea after commercial ships hit by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast
description: Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev called the attacks "absolutely unacceptable" and said Bulgaria had informed its permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union.
content:
Two cargo ships were struck by drones near Bulgaria's Black Sea coast overnight on Oct. 13, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
According to Radev , the Maltese-flagged Chelsea 3, registered in Odesa and owned by a Ukrainian company, was hit by three aerial drones about 18 nautical miles east of the coastal town of Byala in Bulgaria .
All 15 crew members, seven Ukrainians and eight Azerbaijani nationals, were evacuated to the port of Varna, and five received medical assistance, Radev said.
He added that another vessel was struck 17 nautical miles east of Krapets, a Bulgarian village, as he was told at an extraordinary meeting of the Security Council under the Council of Ministers.
The vessel sank, and five crew members were rescued, while 11 crew members were still missing at sea, according to Bulgarian officials, reported Reuters . Reuters further said that Bulgarian media had identified the ship as the ⁠cargo ship Azov Concord.
Radev called the attacks " absolutely unacceptable " and said Bulgaria had informed its permanent representatives to NATO and the European Union. Sofia is seeking assistance to strengthen surveillance of the air and maritime domains and improve its response capabilities.
Bulgarian authorities have not established who was responsible for the attacks. Radev said there was no clear and conclusive evidence to attribute responsibility to either the Ukrainian or Russian side, but argued that "the logic suggests that the outcome benefits the Russian Federation." Radev said he would summon Russia's ambassador for a meeting on Oct. 13.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned the attacks, saying the Black Sea had become "another front of escalation of the Russian war in Ukraine."
"Putting the lives of the crew in grave danger and threatening security in the Black Sea. We stand with Bulgaria and thank its rescuers for their swift response."
Ukraine's Infrastructure Ministry said Russia has repeatedly targeted Ukrainian ports, port infrastructure, and civilian commercial vessels in the Black Sea, posing a threat to international shipping and logistics routes.
Attacks by Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea intensified over the summer.
In July, Ukraine launched Operation Molochka, a campaign targeting Russia's shadow fleet in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in an effort to tighten the noose around Russian-occupied Crimea .
Turkey called on Moscow and Kyiv in August to impose a moratorium on attacks against vessels, following a series of strikes in the region that involved Turkish-flagged ships.
While Kyiv has said it is ready to accept a moratorium on attacks in the Black Sea, Moscow has shown no interest in de-escalating the situation.
On Aug. 6, drones reportedly struck several merchant vessels in the Black Sea, including two ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. A Russian strike on a separate civilian vessel that day killed at least one crew member and injured several others.
Ukraine established its own Black Sea maritime corridor in August 2023, after Russia withdrew from a U.N.- and Turkey-brokered grain deal. Since then, Russia has regularly targeted ports and civilian shipping.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,555,700 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,390 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,555,700 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 13.
The number includes 1,390 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,412 tanks, 25,534 armored combat vehicles, 162,418 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,141 artillery systems, 2,211 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,704 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,942 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Trump says Ukraine, Russia agree to energy strike ceasefire 'because I said they agreed'
description: The U.S. president's comments came after he unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, causing confusion in Kyiv. According to a senior Ukrainian official, Ukraine had no prior information about an energy ceasefire.
content:
Speaking to reporters on the White House lawn on Oct. 12, U.S. President Donald Trump once again said that Ukraine and Russia agreed to halt strikes on energy infrastructure, despite the confusion around the alleged ceasefire.
"They agreed," said Trump after a reporter pointed out that neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirmed they would refrain from strikes on energy sites. "Do you know why? Because I said they agreed. That's why. They agreed because I said they agreed. And that thing has to get settled."
The U.S. president's comments came after he unilaterally announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine on Oct. 11, causing confusion in Kyiv. According to a senior Ukrainian official, Ukraine had no prior information about an energy ceasefire.
In a short interview after Trump' s announcement, President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios, "If President Trump negotiated it with (Vladimir) Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it."
Russia has nothing to say yet about an energy ceasefire with Ukraine announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, the Kremlin's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Oct. 12.
When asked by a reporter about his response to Russia continuing to attack Ukraine's energy infrastructure after his announcement, Trump said there had been violations by both sides, without pointing to any evidence.
Hours after Trump's announcement on Oct. 11, Russia struck Kharkiv’s CHP-5 power plant . In Overnight attacks on Oct. 11-12, at least 10 people were killed and 69 others injured across Ukraine as Russia continued to target residential buildings and energy infrastructure across the country.
Ukraine will halt its strikes against Russian refineries only if Moscow ceases its attacks against the Ukrainian power grid, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 12, signaling that a refinery-only truce makes little sense for a country with a single, badly damaged refinery .
Trump's energy ceasefire announcement followed his lifting of sanctions on Russian oil on Oct. 9, a move that could help Moscow earn a substantial boost in its war funding and blindsided Kyiv. By removing the sanctions, Trump could try to reduce high oil prices caused by his war with Iran ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November.
On Oct. 12, the Kyiv Independent learned that the Trump administration threatened to cut intel sharing and weapons shipments to Ukraine if more Russian oil refineries were targeted in attacks.
"We're going to see what happens," said Trump to reporters on Oct. 12 about ending the war. "We'll get it done"

title: French Navy intercepts Russian shadow fleet tanker in Indian Ocean
description: The tanker DF Peak, previously named Kaliningrad, has falsely sailed under the flag of Benin and is sanctioned by the U.S, EU, Switzerland, Canada, and Japan.
content:
The French Navy intercepted and boarded a tanker suspected of flying under a false flag as part of Russia's shadow fleet on Oct. 12, French President Emmanuel Macron announced.
The tanker, DF Peak, was allegedly transporting sanctioned Russian fuel and was halted by the French Navy 450 nautical miles (833 kilometers) south of the French territory of Reunion in the Indian Ocean.
"France is determined to combat the ghost fleet, wherever it may be in the world," Macron wrote on X . "This action, carried out in accordance with international maritime law, demonstrates our determination to uphold the rule of law and combat all illicit trafficking, wherever it occurs."
The tanker DF Peak, previously named Kaliningrad, has falsely sailed under the flag of Benin, according to the Ukrainian Defense Intelligence's War and Sanctions portal . The crude oil tanker is sanctioned by the U.S, EU, Switzerland, Canada, and Japan.
The vessel is currently under escort by the French Navy, France's Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said on X .
"International law is not optional," wrote Vautrin. "Our armed forces are fully mobilized to enforce it and combat illicit activities at sea."
Russian state media TASS said the Russian embassy in Paris told them that "France is violating international law by detaining merchant vessels on the high seas and is attempting to cover up piracy by invoking the provisions of the UN Convention."
The DF Peak is just one tanker of Russia's "shadow fleet" — a group of aging, poorly insured tankers used by Moscow to ship out its oil in violation of international sanctions. Western governments have also accused Moscow of using the fleet to support its hybrid war against Europe.
Throughout Russia's war on Ukraine, European powers have intercepted shadow fleet vessels in an attempt to stop Moscow from reaping the windfall of illegal fuel sales.
Detentions have helped cut the number of ships in Moscow's shadow fleet flying a false flag to less than half between last October and June 2026, according to a report by the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA) think tank published on Sept. 25.

title: UK sanctions Dutch businessman exposed by Kyiv Independent for shipping EU machinery to Russian missile suppliers
description:
The U.K. has sanctioned Alexander Tattersall, a Dutch national, and Redwing Metal, the Turkish company he co-owns, nearly four months after a Kyiv Independent investigation revealed the firm had funneled EU-made industrial machinery to Russian metallurgical plants that supply the country's missile and fighter jet manufacturers.

Tattersall and Redwing Metal were blacklisted as part of a package of 38 designations announced by the U.K. Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) on Oct. 8
content:
The U.K. has sanctioned Alexander Tattersall, a Dutch national, and Redwing Metal, the Turkish company he co-owns, nearly four months after a Kyiv Independent investigation revealed the firm had funneled EU-made industrial machinery to Russian metallurgical plants that supply the country's missile and fighter jet manufacturers.
Tattersall and Redwing Metal were blacklisted as part of a package of 38 designations announced by the U.K. Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO) on Oct. 8, targeting Russian oil companies, shadow fleet tankers, crypto exchanges, and suppliers of goods critical to Russia's military.
In its announcement , the U.K. government said the package included a European national designated over his association with a third-country entity exporting machine tools to Russia , adding that such trade gives Moscow "material benefits on the battlefield."
U.K. sanctions freeze any assets the designated individuals and companies hold under British jurisdiction and bar British citizens and businesses from dealing with them.
They may also have wider effects, according to Roman Steblivskyi, director of policy and advocacy at the Economic Security Council of Ukraine (ESCU). The designation means that the supply chain through Redwing Metal to Russia has most likely been closed, he told the Kyiv Independent.
Although the EU has yet to sanction Redwing Metal, Steblivskyi said the U.K. sanctions would effectively cut Redwing Metal off from European partners as well.
"I do not think that EU companies or banks would approve transactions with Redwing Metal after the U.K. sanctions were imposed. It is too risky," he said.
The same may apply to Redwing Metal's Turkish counterparts, Steblivskyi added. "This company is sanctioned, so it is already a red flag at least."
The Russian beneficiaries of the supply chain, however, remain partially outside the scope of Western sanctions .
The Kyiv Independent's investigation , published in collaboration with Italy's IrpiMedia and the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP), revealed the role of a Turkish company co-owned by Alexander Tattersall in supplying machinery to the Russian defense industry.
Russian customs records showed that Redwing Metal, set up in Turkey shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, shipped $5 million worth of European equipment in 2023 and 2024 to two Russian metallurgical plants: Aluminum Metallurg Rus (AMR) and Stupino Metallurgical Company (SMK).
The shipments included CNC lathes, metal heat-treatment furnaces, hydraulic presses, and other machinery produced by Italian, German, Spanish, and Czech manufacturers — equipment that EU export controls bar from being sold to Russia.
Both plants are controlled by Russian businessman Nikolay Timokhin, the son-in-law of Igor Zavyalov, who has served as deputy head of Russia's state-owned defense conglomerate Rostec since 2007.
The plants use such equipment to produce metal alloys for Russia's defense industry. An analysis of financial documents by the Kyiv Independent showed that AMR and SMK have supplied more than 40 Russian defense manufacturers since the start of the full-scale war, including producers of Kh-101 and Kh-59 missiles, missiles for S-300 and S-400 air defense systems, and fighter jets . Many of these companies are part of Rostec.
Customs data also showed Redwing Metal shipped a further $1.3 million worth of EU-made shipbuilding equipment — including anchors, mooring winches, and ventilation fans — to another company in Timokhin's group, SMS (formerly SMK-Snab), for installation on two Russian Navy ships under construction.
According to Turkish corporate records, Tattersall, who resides in Switzerland, owns 40% of Redwing Metal. The remaining stake is held by a local lawyer, Veysel Cengiz Soylemezoglu.
Tattersall's ties to Timokhin's business predate the full-scale war. For years, he ran a network of AMR trading companies in Switzerland, Germany, and the U.S. that sold AMR's aluminum products on Western markets. In 2019, he was photographed inside the AMR plant in Russia at celebrations marking the factory's 65th anniversary.
When approached by the Kyiv Independent ahead of the investigation's release, Tattersall confirmed he co-owned Redwing Metal but described himself as a part-time consultant with limited knowledge of its operations. He said that, to his knowledge, the company had never been involved in any "schemes" to ship sanctioned goods to Russia.
Soylemezoglu declined to comment on the shipments at the time, citing privacy obligations. Timokhin, AMR, and SMK did not respond to requests for comment.
On July 23, the EU sanctioned AMR , one of the two Russian metallurgical plants that received prohibited EU-made machinery through the Turkish company Redwing Metal.
But the second plant, SMK, and the company that received the shipbuilding equipment, SMS, have not been sanctioned by the EU. Neither has Timokhin, whose business group includes all three companies.
Redwing Metal and Tattersall are also absent from the EU sanctions list.
Sanctions experts interviewed for the investigation said that routing banned EU-made equipment to Russia through Turkey amounts to circumvention of EU sanctions.
EU nationals found to have knowingly helped bypass export restrictions through a third-country intermediary could face both financial penalties and criminal charges under national law, they said.

title: Russian missile attack on Kharkiv kills 4, injures at least 41 including rescuer
description: A State Emergency Service rescuer was also injured while responding to the attack and was hospitalized, RBC-Ukraine reported, citing the emergency service. His condition was not immediately confirmed.
content:
Russian forces launched a large-scale missile attack on Kharkiv on Oct. 12, killing four and injuring at least 41 people, including an emergency responder, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Hours after the strikes, three bodies were pulled from the rubble, said Ihor Terekhov, the city's mayor . Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov later reported a fourth victim found under the rubble. Ukraine's State Emergency Service said that 41 people were injured, while four people were rescued from the rubble.
Three other people trapped beneath the rubble were rescued earlier, UNIAN reported , citing Ukraine's State Emergency Service.
Syniehubov said Russian forces had used 10 Banderol-type missiles in the attack, targeting civilian infrastructure.
"From the evening until now, the Russians have attacked Ukraine with more than a hundred different means of attack: jet drones, loitering munitions and ballistic missiles," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in the morning of Oct. 13.
In the city's Kholodnohirskyi district, a strike hit a four-story residential building, destroying an entire section. At least 10 nearby houses were also damaged, Syniehubov said.
In the Shevchenkivskyi district, another strike hit a five-story residential building. A bank on the ground floor and six vehicles caught fire, while three nearby apartment buildings sustained window damage.
Among the injured were two people in serious condition, including a 19-year-old man admitted to a burn unit and another man undergoing surgery, according to Syniehubov.
A State Emergency Service rescuer was also injured while responding to the attack and was hospitalized, RBC-Ukraine reported , citing the emergency service. His condition was not immediately confirmed.
Rescue workers from Ukraine's State Emergency Service, emergency medical teams, and the National Police were working at the impact sites. Police officers were also conducting door-to-door checks to identify residents requiring medical assistance.
Kharkiv, Ukraine's second-largest city, lies roughly 30 kilometers (19 miles) from the Russian border and has been subjected to repeated Russian attacks throughout the full-scale invasion.
A Russian air strike on Kharkiv on Oct. 11 killed at least one person and injured eight others .

title: Ukrainska Pravda demands investigation into Austrian police conduct after journalists' detention
description: Tkach is known in Ukraine for his investigations of high-level corruption. He alleged that the arrest could have been retaliation from subjects of his investigations, who could have manipulated Austrian authorities by filing a fake report.
content:
Ukrainian news outlet Ukrainska Pravda is calling for an independent investigation into the detention of two of its journalists in Vienna, saying Austrian law enforcement officers used excessive force, and questioning the justification for their arrests.
Investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko were arrested on Oct. 8 while carrying out an editorial assignment, and held in custody for 12 and 24 hours, respectively. They described the arrest as "brutal" and said they were treated "like terrorists."
Tkach is known in Ukraine for his investigations of high-level corruption. He alleged that the arrest could have been retaliation from subjects of his investigations, who could have manipulated Austrian authorities by filing a fake report.
In an Oct. 12 statement, editor-in-chief Sevgil Musayeva criticized the Vienna prosecutor's office for defending the actions of officers.
"The right to investigate suspicions does not mean the right to use any means," Musayeva wrote, arguing that the measures taken against the journalists were unjustified and disproportionate.
In an Oct. 12 press release, Vienna prosecutors said that the two journalists were arrested because they were mistakenly deemed conspirators of two different Ukrainian nationals currently in pretrial detention on suspicion of espionage.
The connection was alleged because of "witness statements" that claimed both groups were observed surveilling a certain property, and on the fact that "surveillance was carried out during the same period and in the same manner."
The prosecutor's office maintained that the arrests were justified by the information available at the time and were unrelated to the journalists' professional activities. The prosecutors claimed that at the time of the arrest, "it was not known that the accused were a Ukrainian investigative journalist and a cameraman."
The statement also claimed that the arrest originally targeted only one of the two journalists, and the police arrested the second one "on their own initiative." However, a detailed account of the arrest and questioning, shared by Ukrainska Pravda on Oct. 9, appears to contradict that claim. Both reporters were treated as subjects of an investigation and presented with accusations during their questioning.
Musayeva questioned how investigators had verified the witness accounts, and challenged the prosecutors' explanation that authorities were unaware of the men's profession, saying their identities could have been quickly verified through publicly available information or by contacting Ukrainska Pravda.
Musayeva demanded explanations for the force used during the arrests, the length of the journalists' detention, the seizure of their communications equipment and damage to or loss of their property.
Bondarenko said in an Oct. 10 account that officers smashed the windows of the journalists' vehicle and forced him face down onto broken glass. He said three glass fragments were subsequently removed from beneath his eye during a hospital procedure while he remained handcuffed. Tkach previously described being dragged from the vehicle by armed, masked officers and restrained with a knee against his neck despite repeatedly identifying himself as a journalist.
The journalists had been investigating the whereabouts of former Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko, who is believed to be in Vienna.
Musayeva said the outlet would work with lawyers to seek an independent investigation, establish responsibility for any violations and obtain compensation for damages.
"The release of our colleagues does not close this story," she wrote. The International Press Institute (IPI) has also expressed concern over the journalists' detention and the force reportedly used during their arrests, calling on Austrian authorities to clarify the legal grounds for their detention and investigate the circumstances of the incident.

title: Kyiv under 'particularly vile' missile attack before air raid alert issued
description: Kyiv Independent staff reported powerful blasts in central Kyiv, with air raid sirens and mobile notifications sounding only afterward.
content:
Editor's note: This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.
Kyiv came under missile attack shortly after 10 p.m. local time on Oct. 12, with powerful explosions reported before an air raid alert was issued in the Ukrainian capital, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Kyiv Independent staff reported powerful blasts in central Kyiv, with air raid sirens and mobile notifications sounding only afterward. At 11:09 p.m., Kyiv Independent journalists reported further explosions in the capital as the attack continued. The cause of the latest blasts was not immediately confirmed.
Ukraine's Air Force later reported that Russian forces had attacked Kyiv with what appeared to be six ballistic missiles at approximately 10:10 p.m. President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 13 that it was five ballistic missiles that hit civilian infrastructure.
Zelensky called the strike "particularly vile," adding that there was no early warning from Ukraine's partners about missiles coming.
"Intelligence on Russian ballistic missile launches helps save lives, and this is one of the most critical issues. This is precisely what helps prevent people from being killed – when there is an early warning about ballistic missiles," Zelensky said.
The Air Force said radar systems detected the incoming missiles during the attack, but that it had received no information about launches from Russian territory. It added that it was investigating why it had received no information about the launches.
Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat confirmed during the national news telethon that the alarm had been sounded only during the missile attack, but said that this had occurred previously, according to Ukrainska Pravda .
He also noted that not only the U.S. shares its intelligence with Ukraine, but other NATO countries do as well, covering strategic aviation, ship movements, and ballistic missile launches.
"There are moments when this information fails to arrive. This is not the first case... If there were certain technical issues this time, I believe the intelligence can sort them out. And they will resolve this problem together with our partners," Ihnat said.
At least 12 people were injured in Russian attacks on Kyiv on Oct. 12, including a 17-year-old, according to the Kyiv City State Administration's Health Department.
As of 10:15 p.m. local time, four people had been hospitalized in moderate condition, while eight others, including the teenager, received medical assistance at the scene.
The delayed air raid alert prompted speculation on Ukrainian social media about whether the lack of advance warning was connected to reported U.S. threats to withdraw intelligence-sharing support for Ukraine.
Ukraine receives intelligence from the United States to help detect and track Russian missile launches and other aerial threats.
The Kyiv Independent reported earlier on Oct. 12 , citing two Ukrainian officials, that Washington had threatened to suspend intelligence sharing unless Kyiv stopped striking Russian energy infrastructure.
Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said that intelligence sharing between the U.S. and Ukraine was ongoing and had not been stopped, during a speech at the Warsaw Security Forum on Oct. 13.
“You probably ask if we receive intelligence from the American side. Yes, we continue this cooperation," he said.
The Kyiv Independent has reached out to Ukrainian and U.S. officials for comment.
A Russian drone attack on a private residential building in the Darnytskyi district in the morning injured one woman, the city's military administration said .

title: Ukraine war latest: Russian drones strike Kyiv morning and evening, kills 2, injures 14
description:
Key developments on Oct. 12:

 * Russian drone attacks throughout the day strike Kyiv apartment block, kills two people, injures 14
 * Russia strikes Roshen confectionery factory in Vinnytsia
 * New interceptor drone destroys two Russian Geran-5 drones in first week, Fedorov says
 * SBU detains 19-year-old suspected of plotting bomb attack on bus full of soldiers
 * Fire Point trolls Russia's Yandex after drone attack on data center
 * Russia-led military bloc launches joint military drills in B
content:
Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv twice on Oct. 12, killing one person and injuring at least 14 others, city authorities said.
During an evening attack, a Russian drone struck a 25-story residential building in Kyiv's Darnytskyi District, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration.
A woman was killed in the strike, while 11 people were injured, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Earlier in the day, Russia launched a drone attack on Kyiv, injuring three people, including an elderly woman.
Klitschko first said at 11:32 a.m. local time that air defenses were operating in the city.
Drone debris fell in an open area near residential buildings in the Solomyanskyi District of Kyiv and on a house in Darnytskyi District , while in the Pecherskyi District , a fire caused by wreckage of a drone that had crashed near a building was brought under control, Klitschko said.
Yuliia Sheremet, 38, the owner of the house that was damaged in Darnytskyi District, told the Kyiv Independent that her elderly, disabled father was at home when the attack occurred.
Sheremet was working not far away at the time, so she "immediately ran" to her house when she heard explosions and saw the smoke rise.
"And I saw there was no home anymore..."
Her father was injured but survived. Neighbors helped her to get him out. "It's nothing short of a miracle that Dad didn't die today," Sheremet said.
"I'm in shock... It's impossible to live like that, and I don't know how to carry on. We're all exhausted. We need help so that we can defend Ukraine."
Kyiv resident Yana Mohal, 25, woke up to a "horrible and loud" sound in Darnytskyi District, she told the Kyiv Independent. She went outside to see whether she could help Sheremet's father, an "elderly man with a dog," who was trapped in a damaged house.
Mohal added that it was the first time that the Russian attack had struck so close to her.
Russia is regularly attacking Kyiv and other cities across Ukraine. At least 16 people were killed and more than 100 others injured in Kyiv and the surrounding region between Sept. 25 and Oct. 2, according to a Kyiv Independent count based on official reports.
Russia struck a production complex belonging to Ukrainian confectionery company Roshen in Vinnytsia on Oct. 12, the company said.
"Thanks to the timely activation of the warning system and the prompt evacuation, the lives of employees were saved," Roshen said in a statement .
Vinnytsia Oblast authorities earlier reported that a Russian attack had hit a civilian infrastructure facility in the city and caused a fire. More than 50 rescuers and 13 pieces of emergency equipment were deployed to the site, while explosive ordnance specialists inspected the surrounding area. No injuries were reported.
Roshen later confirmed that its Vinnytsia production complex had been hit.
The company rejected claims circulating in Russian media that its facilities were being used to manufacture drones.
"The corporation's enterprises produce confectionery products and do not manufacture drones or other products for military purposes. The production complex in Vinnytsia is a civilian facility," the company said.
The company did not immediately disclose the extent of the damage to the plant.
"Strikes on food industry facilities endanger the lives of civilian workers, destroy production capacity and jobs, and disrupt the supply of goods," Roshen added.
A new model of interceptor drone developed by former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has been tested successfully, Fedorov himself claimed on social media, posting video footage of the drone successfully intercepting two Russian Geran-5 drones.
"Our new interceptor is already taking down jet-powered Shaheds over Kyiv. Two Geran-5s down in its first week," Fedorov said .
The development time from conception to the first successful tests was just one month, Fedorov claimed, while the new interceptor was deployed by "Lasar's Group," a special forces unit within the 27th Separate Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard.
The successful test comes as Ukrainian cities are under repeated assault from Russia's new generation of jet-powered drones, especially the Geran-5, which blurs the line between a drone and a cruise missile, according to experts.
"The Geran-5 much more resembles a low-cost cruise missile than a long-range drone like the original Shahed derivatives," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent .
The Geran-5 is particularly difficult to engage, flying significantly higher and faster than any of Russia's older drone models, with a maximum speed of 600 km/h (370 mph).
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has foiled an alleged Russian plot to bomb a bus carrying Ukrainian soldiers in the northwestern city of Rivne, detaining a 19-year-old student suspected of preparing the attack, the SBU and Rivne Regional Prosecutor's Office said on Oct. 12.
According to the SBU , the suspect planted an improvised explosive device under a bus transporting "an entire unit" of Ukrainian soldiers and installed a remotely accessible camera disguised in a juice box opposite the parking area to monitor the vehicle.
Russian intelligence operatives planned to detonate the bomb once the soldiers boarded the bus and were moving to their permanent deployment location, the SBU said.
The suspect acted in exchange for money after being recruited by Russian intelligence services through Telegram channels offering quick earnings, according to the SBU.
After arriving in Rivne , he allegedly collected the explosives from a hiding place designated by his Russian handler and planted the device under the military vehicle. The explosive device was reinforced with two glass bottles containing flammable liquid, the SBU said.
SBU officers discovered the plot, neutralized the explosives, and detained the suspect at the city's bus station when he attempted to leave for Kyiv . Investigators also seized his phone, which the SBU said he had used to report the planted device to his Russian handler.
The Rivne Regional Prosecutor's Office said the suspect had been formally notified of suspicion of an attempted terrorist attack. A court ordered his detention without bail. If convicted, he faces up to eight years in prison and possible confiscation of property.
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point trolled Russian tech giant Yandex on Oct. 12, after the company reported damage to another of its data centers, disrupting access to its financial services.
"Today, another Yandex data center was damaged," Dima Pirogov, head of Yandex's fintech division, wrote on X on Oct. 11.
Pirogov said the disruption had left many users unable to check their balances, pay for purchases, or transfer money.
"Dima, have you tried turning it off and on again?" Fire Point replied.
The incident follows a series of reported drone strikes on Russian data centers that have disrupted Yandex services.
Yandex's data center in Russia's Vladimir Oblast was completely shut down on Oct. 11 following a reported drone attack, Russian state news agency TASS said, citing the company.
Russia and four other members of the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) have begun joint military exercises in Belarus on Oct. 12, the organization said.
The drills will run from Oct. 12 until Oct. 16 at two training grounds on Belarusian territory, involving more than 1,500 military personnel, over 300 pieces of military equipment, and around 80 drones, according to the CSTO .
Military contingents from Belarus , Russia , Kazakhstan , Kyrgyzstan , and Tajikistan are participating in the exercises.
The drills focus on training CSTO "peacekeeping forces" and involve exercises to respond to biological threats, the organization said.
CSTO Deputy Secretary-General Mirlan Turgunbekov said in an Oct. 11 statement that the exercise is "particularly relevant given the escalating military and political situation."
The CSTO, which was established in 2002, includes Russia, Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. Russia is by far the most powerful member of the alliance. Armenia is not particpating in the drills.
Belarus has supported Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine by allowing Moscow to use its territory as a staging ground for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

title: Ukraine moves to speed up privatization of state-owned assets
description: If passed, the bill could help alleviate bottlenecks the State Property Fund has repeatedly faced when trying to sell state-owned assets and help shore up funds for the state budget.
content:
Ukraine’s privatization agency could see a major boost in the near future after parliament approved the first reading of a bill on Oct. 12 to streamline the auction of thousands of state-owned assets.
If passed, the bill could help alleviate bottlenecks the State Property Fund has repeatedly faced when trying to sell state-owned assets and help shore up funds for the state budget. Privatization is also key condition set by Western partners such as the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank for continued financial support to Ukraine.
Under the current rules, the fund can only privatize assets after other state bodies, such as ministries and local authorities, transfer them. There is also no deadline for those transfers, so assets can sit on the books of government bodies indefinitely with no clear path to privatization.
One of the bill's key amendments would give state bodies a strict 20-day deadline to transfer assets to the fund. Until now, such transfers have sometimes taken months or even years, Dmytro Natalukha, chairman of the State Property Fund, told the Kyiv Independent. While some state bodies are happy to transfer "rubbish" assets, they are reluctant to hand over assets that provide benefits or incentives, he said. But if the bill passes, and an agency misses the deadline, the fund would be able to take over the assets itself, he added.
"This will allow us to improve the efficiency of the privatization process and generate additional revenue for the state budget," Natalukha said.
"This draft legislation was prepared to speed up property transfer procedures, accelerate the preparation of assets for auction, and relieve the state budget of preparation expenses."
Additionally, the bill proposes creating a state-owned consulting firm managed by the fund that would employ specialists to prepare assets for privatization . It would act like a sales department, Natalukha said, and receive 5% of an asset’s sale price if the sale is successful. The buyer would cover the fee, he added.
The bill’s second reading could take place in the near future, and it could be adopted by early December, Natalukha said.
"Strengthening the institutional capacity of the fund should create better conditions for attracting investments, developing enterprises, and making more efficient use of state property," the parliament wrote in a press release.
Parliament also approved the first reading of several other bills on Oct. 12, including a proposal to direct more money to the military. Revenue from processing and issuing documents related to state export controls on military and dual-use goods would go to the state budget and then be allocated to the Defense Ministry.
Of those funds, 50% would go toward the procurement, modernization, and repair of weapons and military equipment, while the remaining 50% would be used to pay allowances to Armed Forces personnel, Ukraine’s Parliament wrote on Telegram.
As Ukraine faces a severe budget shortfall , it is looking for ways to boost funding. The government has positioned privatization as a relatively straightforward and secure way to invest in Ukraine, with the goal of raising $295 million by the end of 2026.
But the State Property Fund has been plagued by problems, including staffing shortages and low salaries. As the Kyiv Independent previously reported , these issues are discouraging foreign investors. Experts told the Kyiv Independent that poor government communication about viable projects and the risks posed by the ongoing war are also major roadblocks.
Meanwhile, the assets often come saddled with debt, are in poor condition or — if confiscated — in the firing line of potential lawsuits.
In total, the government’s portfolio includes about 3,000 assets, ranging from factories to bakeries. Kyiv has previously said it wants to whittle that number down to just 100 key enterprises. Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion, 1,200 assets have been added to the State Property Fund’s portfolio, with about 200 more expected by the end of the year.

content:
U.S. President Donald Trump in the Brady Briefing Room of the White House on April 22, 2020, in Washington, DC. (Mandel Ngan/AFP via Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump had a busy weekend, undermining sanctions on Russia, blaming Ukraine for the war Russia started — again — and insisting that Russian refineries become drone-free zones.
"We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries , because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump said on Oct. 10.
"And (President Volodymyr Zelensky) wants to make problems for the world, he wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel. ... We have a world problem, and the problem is caused by the lack of refineries for diesel fuel. So what does he do? He goes and hits the refineries," he added.
Trump failed to mention the considerable evidence that shows the U.S. war against Iran that he started and cannot finish is the major culprit behind the current shortage of diesel.
The Kyiv Independent has since learned that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials in a push to protect Russian oil refineries, despite Moscow's continuing bombing of Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Trump's latest pressure on Ukraine to end the war Russia started and refuses to stop has angered people both home and abroad, even sparking a bipartisan backlash in the U.S. Congress at his decision to ease sanctions on Russian diesel.
Across social media, some people wondered how they could help Ukraine continue to hit Russia.
There are several ways people can help fund Ukraine's drones, and even a few options when it comes to what they hit.
Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces (USF), Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and military intelligence (HUR) have all carried out long-range strikes against targets in Russia, including oil infrastructure.
USF does not have a dedicated fundraiser but is supported by donations from United24 and the Come Back Alive foundation. But there is one specific branch of the USF that one can donate directly to.
The 1st Separate Center of Unmanned Aerial Systems was Ukraine's first experimental unmanned aerial systems (UAS) unit, founded in 2022, originally as the 14th Separate UAS Regiment. Since then, it has become the largest UAS unit, specializing in long-range strikes on Russia.
"We are the ones who toss the war over to enemy territory," by striking Russia's military-industrial complex, oil industry, and logistics facilities, the unit says on its website . Over the years, it has struck several Russian airfields, artillery arsenals, and ammunition depots. In 2025, the unit carried out more than 50 successful operations against Russia’s oil infrastructure, such as strikes on oil refineries in Ryazan, Volgograd, and Saratov, inflicting a 38% loss on Russia’s oil refining capacity, the unit says .
Outside of long-range drone strikes on Russian territory, there are several organisations that support mid-range strikes on Russian targets in occupied Ukraine, as well as first-person-view (FPV) drones for use on the front lines.
Founded by Dimko and Iryna Zhluktenko and named after their now legendary dog, Dzyga’s Paw is a Ukrainian charity that equips frontline soldiers with the technology and equipment they need to keep up the fight day in, day out.
Since February 2022, they've raised over $6 million from thousands of donors across 70+ countries, and delivered drones, Starlinks, night vision, and other hi-tech gear directly to 100+ military units.
Come Back Alive is an independent foundation that started equipping Ukrainian soldiers with bulletproof vests in 2014, writing "come back alive" on each of their vests. Today, it is one of the largest providers of equipment for Ukrainian service members all across the front lines, having supplied the military with more than 157,000 FPV drones, over 14,000 units of thermal imaging optics, more than 5,400 units of infantry weapons, 2,400 pickup trucks, over 100 unmanned reconnaissance systems, a Bayraktar TB2 strike UAV complex, and more, according to its website .
Besides supplying equipment, the organization's instructors also train highly qualified military specialists, including sappers, snipers, divers, electronic-warfare specialists, and UAV and UGV operators.
As part of these efforts, Come Back Alive currently raises funds for the Yatagan UAV Operators School , which it launched in partnership with PrivatBank in 2024 within the structures of the Ground Forces. Over the last two years, the school has trained thousands of Ukrainian service members already.
The Sternenko Community Foundation is the charitable organization of well-known Ukrainian activist Serhii Sternenko and has become the largest non-governmental provider of FPV-drones to the Ukrainian military. According to its website , the foundation has purchased almost 300,000 FPV-drones for the Ukrainian military by mid-October.
In its current "Rusoriz Digital" fundraiser, the foundation seeks to scale FPV-drones using a digital link, allowing them to operate at ranges above 50 kilometers (31 miles) and more resistant to electronic warfare measures. As of today, the foundation has already supplied more than 50 units with the technology and already procured over 10,000 of these drones, for use against Russian logistics behind the front lines.
Unite with Ukraine is led by the Ukrainian World Congress , an NGO established in 1967 and recognized by the UN and the Council of Europe to represent Ukrainian diaspora communities globally.
Together with its partner organizations "Saint Javelin" and "The Last Capitalist," it raises funds for fixed-wing mid-range strike UAVs in support of the several brigades.
The International Unity Movement is a Ukrainian charitable foundation established in 2022, aiming to raise funds across the spectrum of security challenges that Ukrainians face throughout Russia's war.
As part of their work, they support the 423rd Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment "Scythian Griffins," which carries out combat operations and mid-range drone strikes on the Zaporizhzhia sector. Since its founding in 2024, the unit has destroyed hundreds of Russian vehicles , UAVs, and artillery systems, as well as dozens of tanks and warehouses.
United24 is Ukraine's official government fundraising platform, set up by Zelensky shortly after the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Donors can support a wide range of areas including drones, defense, medical aid, demining, reconstruction, education, and sports.
The Serhiy Prytula Charity Foundation was founded in 2020 and shifted much of its work toward supporting the military after Russia’s full-scale invasion.
It supplies frontline units with drones, vehicles, communications equipment, electronic warfare systems, optics, and medical supplies, while also running humanitarian programs for civilians affected by the war.

title: Russia strikes Roshen confectionery factory in Vinnytsia
description: "The corporation's enterprises produce confectionery products and do not manufacture drones or other products for military purposes. The production complex in Vinnytsia is a civilian facility," the company said.
content:
Russia struck a production complex belonging to Ukrainian confectionery company Roshen in Vinnytsia on Oct. 12, the company said.
"Thanks to the timely activation of the warning system and the prompt evacuation, the lives of employees were saved," Roshen said in a statement .
Vinnytsia Oblast authorities earlier reported that a Russian attack had hit a civilian infrastructure facility in the city and caused a fire. More than 50 rescuers and 13 pieces of emergency equipment were deployed to the site, while explosive ordnance specialists inspected the surrounding area. No injuries were reported.
Roshen later confirmed that its Vinnytsia production complex had been hit.
The company rejected claims circulating in Russian media that its facilities were being used to manufacture drones.
"The corporation's enterprises produce confectionery products and do not manufacture drones or other products for military purposes. The production complex in Vinnytsia is a civilian facility," the company said.
The company did not immediately disclose the extent of the damage to the plant.
"Strikes on food industry facilities endanger the lives of civilian workers, destroy production capacity and jobs, and disrupt the supply of goods," Roshen added.
The Oct. 12 strike is not the first Russian attack to damage Roshen facilities during the full-scale war.
On Aug. 27, a Russian attack destroyed a Roshen logistics center in Chubynske in Kyiv Oblast's Boryspil district. Earlier, on Jan. 24, Russian forces struck a Roshen confectionery factory in Kyiv's Holosiivskyi district.
Russia has also intensified attacks on other civilian infrastructure and Ukraine's energy sector in recent weeks. President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 11 that Russian forces had carried out more than 200 strikes on electricity generation and transmission facilities over the previous week, as well as 17 strikes on gas and oil facilities. Russian attacks killed more than 150 people and wounded more than 700 during that period, he added.
