content:
The release from custody of Iryna Mudra, a former deputy head of the President’s Office, last week followed an unusual development.
While Ukrainians had been previously accustomed to corruption suspects easily escaping justice, now the trend was the opposite. Mudra had the money to pay the bail but banks refused to process payments for posting it, fearing that they could be accused of taking part in money laundering.
Furthermore, decreasing political protection for corruption suspects may motivate suspects to testify on other participants of criminal schemes.
One of the crucial questions is whether Mudra's former boss, President Volodymyr Zelensky's Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov , is involved in her alleged corruption scheme .
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from the President's Office and will publish its response once it is received.
In August, Mudra , lawmaker Maksym Mykytas, and Viktor Dubovyk, head of the legal policy department at the President's Office, were charged with laundering Hr 150 million ($3.4 million) and transferring the funds through Sense Bank to post bail for ex-Energy and Justice Minister Herman Halushchenko .
Halushchenko was charged by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) in February as part of last year’s probe into state nuclear energy monopoly Energoatom — the largest corruption investigation of Zelensky’s tenure.
Mudra, Mykytas and lawmaker Vadym Stolar were also charged in August with illegally seizing real estate by hacking the corporate register, forging documents, influencing the Justice Ministry and bribing judges and prosecutors.
On Aug. 25, the High Anti-Corruption Court placed Mudra in custody for two months and set bail at Hr 20 million ($448,000).
However, for a long time banks refused to process payments for Mudra’s bail.
Mudra’s lawyers accused the banks of blocking payments without justification and in violation of the law.
"The accusations against her involved money laundering through bail payments," Tetiana Shevchuk, a lawyer at the Anti-Corruption Action Center, told the Kyiv Independent. "The case attracted a great deal of attention, which made banks cautious about processing those payments."
She said that "this became a sensitive issue because a bank could process a payment today, only for a journalistic investigation to come out tomorrow, prompting the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) to step in and accuse it of violating financial monitoring rules."
Roman Verbovskyi, another expert at the Anti-Corruption Action Center, argued that "banks simply decided not to process any payments in this case, even if there was documentation showing that the funds were legitimate, because they feared the money might have come from illegal sources."
In September, the High Anti-Corruption Court ordered the National Bank to investigate banks' decisions to block payments for Mudra's bail.
As a result, the bail was paid, and Mudra was released on Oct. 8.
However, the bail payments were not entirely transparent, according to an Oct. 8 investigation by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL )' s Schemes project.
The bail was paid by Mudra herself, her common-law husband, a singer, a private company engaged in wholesale meat trading, a cleaning woman convicted of stealing gaming devices, a person who had previously posted bail in a different corruption case, and a man who had been sued by an energy company over unpaid debts, Schemes reported.
In some cases it was not clear where the individuals and entities got the money or what they have to do with Mudra. Some of them declined to comment on their motives.
"The investigation by Schemes reveals that the source of the money wasn't entirely transparent," Shevchuk said. "So there may have been legitimate grounds for blocking the payments, and the banks may have been justified in doing so."
Masi Nayyem, founder of the law firm Miller, told the Kyiv Independent that they "can only respond to what has actually happened."
"We don't know the people who made the payments," he said. "If they broke the law, everyone responsible should be held accountable."
Miller represents Mudra's interests in court.
The difficulties with Mudra's bail were similar to those faced by ex-Justice and Energy Minister Halushchenko .
The court set Hr 150 million ($3.3 million) bail for him in February, but he struggled to raise the money. He spent several months in a detention facility, and the bail was posted only in June.
According to Shevchuk, keeping Halushchenko out of jail was important for his accomplices because he could have tried to cut a deal with the Anti-Corruption Bureau and testify against them. The same applies to Mudra, she believes.
"When someone is held in pretrial detention, they may become more willing to cooperate with investigators or seek revenge against their accomplices," Shevchuk added. "So getting someone out of pretrial detention is the first priority if you want to ensure they remain loyal."
One of those against whom Mudra could potentially testify is her former boss, President's Office Head Kyrylo Budanov.
A person matching Budanov's description allegedly asked Mudra to launder cash to pay bail for Halushchenko, according to the leaked text of the charges against Mudra published by the media outlet Bihus.info on Sept. 15.
The official then supervised Mudra's actions in the alleged money laundering scheme uncovered by the NABU, according to the text.
The leaked text does not identify Budanov by name. However, the charges identify the person as an official of the President's Office and Mudra's boss, saying that she was trying to curry favor with that person, Bihus.info reported.
Mudra has only one boss at the President's Office — Budanov.
Furthermore, an alleged transcript of the Anti-Corruption Bureau's tapes leaked to the media outlet Hromadske in August contains multiple references to "Kyrylo," "Kyrylo Oleksiyovich," Mudra's unnamed boss, and a top official at the President's Office. There are also direct references to Budanov's last name in the transcripts.
Budanov's name and patronymic match those mentioned in the tapes shared with Hromadske.
The transcripts also involve Timur Mindich, a Zelensky associate who fled to Israel before being charged in the Energoatom case in 2025. He had informal control over state-owned Sense Bank, according to the NABU tapes.
Apparently looking for political cover while he was abroad, Mindich asked "Kyrylo" — an apparent reference to Budanov — to take control of the bank, according to a June statement by Mudra in the transcripts leaked to Hromadske.
In June, Mykytas also said that Mindich had delivered cash for Halushchenko's bail to "Kyrylo Oleksiyovych" — an apparent reference to Budanov, according to the alleged transcripts.
When asked about alleged references to him in the tapes, Budanov told Hromadske in August: "Let the court sort it out. You know, (my name) comes up in a lot of places."

title: Poland investigates alleged plot to kill prime minister, his deputy
description: "We are taking this matter very seriously," National Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said at a press briefing on Oct. 11.
content:
Polish authorities are investigating an alleged assassination plot targeting Prime Minister Donald Tusk and his deputy, Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, Jacek Dobrzynski, a spokesperson for Polish intelligence agencies, said on Oct. 11.
Police received numerous reports of a possible assassination attempt, after which a meeting was called between representatives of the Interior and Administration Ministry, the State Protection Service, and the Internal Security Agency.
"We are taking this matter very seriously," Kosiniak-Kamysz said at a press briefing on Oct. 11.
"Month after month, year after year, the police, the State Protection Service, and the intelligence services face an increasing number of threats and acts of intimidation targeting Poland and its people. Right now, we're talking about threats directed at the most important figures in the country, threats to the safety of the prime minister and the deputy prime minister."
Karolina Galecka, spokesperson for the Interior and Administration Ministry, noted that threats were directed to the police via the State Protection Service, emphasizing that they were sent the very same day as the meeting.
Dobrzynski noted that the threats appeared credible, and it was determined that the information be made public so it "doesn't spread like a snowball, so that there is no speculation."
"We are talking about a high probability that these threats will be carried out," Dobrzynski added.
TVN24 , a Polish news channel, obtained the contents of the report that was sent to the Secret Services.
"The informant contacted a radical organization via social media, seeking volunteers to carry out a gun attack. The informant also reported meeting a man named Krzysztof, with whom they discussed guns, hatred of the government, and a planned mass murder," the report read.
Some details about the informant are known, although more cannot yet be disclosed, according to TVN24.
Tusk briefly disclosed on social media that the man behind the attack's threats was detained.
"The man who threatened to commit an attack was detained. I thank the police for their quick and decisive action," Tusk wrote.
News of another detainee were disclosed on Oct. 13 by Adam Szlapka, spokesperson for the Polish government.
"Yesterday in Oborniki, the police detained a 46-year-old man suspected of publicly inciting on the internet the murder of representatives of Polish authorities, including the prime minister and the Marshal of the Sejm," Szlapka said on social media .
However, not all reactions displayed concern. Former Polish President Andrzej Duda called such threats "everyday business" and accused Tusk of using this as an opportunity "to cover up the problems" his government is dealing with.
On the other hand, Andrzej Derlatka, former head of Poland's Foreign Intelligence Agency, pointed the finger at the Kremlin .
"I won't hide it: From Putin's perspective, Poland is Russia's biggest enemy," he told TVP Info.
Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis and Foreign Minister Petr Macinka also commented on the matter.
"Our intelligence services remain in contact with the Polish ones and cooperate constantly. If the Polish side asks for support and assistance, we will certainly meet their needs," Babisz told the Denik N newspaper.

title: New interceptor drone destroys two Russian Geran-5 drones in first week, Fedorov says
description: The successful test comes as Ukrainian cities are under repeated assault from Russia's new generation of jet-powered drones.
content:
A new model of interceptor drone developed by former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov has been tested successfully, Fedorov himself claimed on social media, posting video footage of the drone successfully intercepting two Russian Geran-5 drones.
"Our new interceptor is already taking down jet-powered Shaheds over Kyiv. Two Geran-5s down in its first week," Fedorov said .
The development time from conception to the first successful tests was just one month, Fedorov claimed, while the new interceptor was deployed by "Lasar's Group," a special forces unit within the 27th Separate Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard.
The successful test comes as Ukrainian cities are under repeated assault from Russia's new generation of jet-powered drones, especially the Geran-5, which blurs the line between a drone and a cruise missile, according to experts.
"The Geran-5 much more resembles a low-cost cruise missile than a long-range drone like the original Shahed derivatives," Fabian Hoffmann, a senior research fellow at the Norwegian Institute for Defence Studies, told the Kyiv Independent .
The Geran-5 is particularly difficult to engage, flying significantly higher and faster than any of Russia's older drone models, with a maximum speed of 600 km/h (370 mph).
Multiple Ukrainian and Western defense companies are scrambling to build new models of interceptor drones to combat Russia's newer, faster jet-powered munitions.
"The Geran-5 is a significantly more difficult target to intercept than the Geran-4, or any of the previous generation of Russian drones," one senior engineer working for a defense contractor told the Kyiv Independent, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the work's sensitive nature.
Only 57% of jet-powered drones are currently shot down by Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky acknowledged in his evening address on Sept. 28, a figure he described as "much less than necessary."

title: SBU detains 19-year-old suspected of plotting bomb attack on bus full of soldiers
description: The SBU said it had foiled a series of alleged terrorist plots prepared by Russian intelligence services in Rivne this year. Previous alleged plots targeted a park area and administrative buildings in the city center.
content:
Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) has foiled an alleged Russian plot to bomb a bus carrying Ukrainian soldiers in the northwestern city of Rivne, detaining a 19-year-old student suspected of preparing the attack, the SBU and Rivne Regional Prosecutor's Office said on Oct. 12.
According to the SBU , the suspect planted an improvised explosive device under a bus transporting "an entire unit" of Ukrainian soldiers and installed a remotely accessible camera disguised in a juice box opposite the parking area to monitor the vehicle.
Russian intelligence operatives planned to detonate the bomb once the soldiers boarded the bus and were moving to their permanent deployment location, the SBU said.
The suspect acted in exchange for money after being recruited by Russian intelligence services through Telegram channels offering quick earnings, according to the SBU.
After arriving in Rivne , he allegedly collected the explosives from a hiding place designated by his Russian handler and planted the device under the military vehicle. The explosive device was reinforced with two glass bottles containing flammable liquid, the SBU said.
SBU officers discovered the plot, neutralized the explosives, and detained the suspect at the city's bus station when he attempted to leave for Kyiv . Investigators also seized his phone, which the SBU said he had used to report the planted device to his Russian handler.
The Rivne Regional Prosecutor's Office said the suspect had been formally notified of suspicion of an attempted terrorist attack. A court ordered his detention without bail. If convicted, he faces up to eight years in prison and possible confiscation of property.
The SBU said it had foiled a series of alleged terrorist plots prepared by Russian intelligence services in Rivne this year. Previous alleged plots targeted a park area and administrative buildings in the city center.

content:

title: 'A miracle that Dad didn't die today' — Russian drone attacks throughout day strike Kyiv, kill 2, injure 14
description: "I'm in shock... I don't know how to carry on. We're all exhausted," Kyiv resident Yuliia Sheremet told the Kyiv Independent as the Russian strike on Ukraine's capital injured her father and severely damaged her house.
content:
An emergency worker at the site of a Russian attack in Kyiv's Darnytskyi District on Oct. 12, 2026. (Chris Occhicone / The Kyiv Independent)
Russian drone attacks hit Kyiv twice on Oct. 12, killing two people and injuring at least 14 others, city authorities said.
During an evening attack, a Russian drone struck a 25-story residential building in Kyiv's Darnytskyi District, according to the Kyiv City Military Administration.
A woman was killed in the strike, while 11 people were injured, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. Earlier in the day, Russia launched a drone attack on Kyiv, injuring three people, including an elderly woman.
Klitschko first said at 11:32 a.m. local time that air defenses were operating in the city.
Drone debris fell in an open area near residential buildings in the Solomyanskyi District of Kyiv and on a house in Darnytskyi District , while in the Pecherskyi District , a fire caused by wreckage of a drone that had crashed near a building was brought under control, Klitschko said.
Допис, поширений Kyiv Independent (@kyivindependent_official)
Yuliia Sheremet, 38, the owner of the house that was damaged in Darnytskyi District, told the Kyiv Independent that her elderly, disabled father was at home when the attack occurred.
Sheremet was working not far away at the time, so she "immediately ran" to her house when she heard explosions and saw the smoke rise.
"And I saw there was no home anymore..."
Her father was injured but survived. Neighbors helped her to get him out. "It's nothing short of a miracle that Dad didn't die today," Sheremet said.
"I'm in shock... It's impossible to live like that, and I don't know how to carry on. We're all exhausted. We need help so that we can defend Ukraine."
Kyiv resident Yana Mohal, 25, woke up to a "horrible and loud" sound in Darnytskyi District, she told the Kyiv Independent. She went outside to see whether she could help Sheremet's father, an "elderly man with a dog," who was trapped in a damaged house.
Mohal added that it was the first time that the Russian attack had struck so close to her.
Russia is regularly attacking Kyiv and other cities across Ukraine. At least 16 people were killed and more than 100 others injured in Kyiv and the surrounding region between Sept. 25 and Oct. 2, according to a Kyiv Independent count based on official reports.
Ahead of winter, Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure .
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 11 that Russia had carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine's electricity generation and transmission facilities over the past week, as well as 17 strikes on gas and oil facilities. Russian attacks killed more than 150 people and wounded more than 700 during that period, he added.
Yuliia Taradiuk is a Ukrainian reporter at the Kyiv Independent. She has been working with Lutsk-based misto.media, telling stories of Ukrainian fighters for the "All are gone to the front" project. She has experience as a freelance culture reporter, and a background in urbanism and activism, working for multiple Ukrainian NGOs. Yuliia holds B.A. degree in English language and literature from Lesya Ukrainka Volyn National University, she studied in Germany and Lithuania.

title: Fire Point trolls Russia's Yandex after drone attack on data center
description: The incident follows a series of reported drone strikes on Russian data centers that have disrupted Yandex services.
content:
Ukrainian defense company Fire Point trolled Russian tech giant Yandex on Oct. 12, after the company reported damage to another of its data centers, disrupting access to its financial services.
"Today, another Yandex data center was damaged," Dima Pirogov, head of Yandex's fintech division, wrote on X on Oct. 11.
Pirogov said the disruption had left many users unable to check their balances, pay for purchases, or transfer money.
"Dima, have you tried turning it off and on again?" Fire Point replied.
The incident follows a series of reported drone strikes on Russian data centers that have disrupted Yandex services.
Yandex's data center in Russia's Vladimir Oblast was completely shut down on Oct. 11 following a reported drone attack, Russian state news agency TASS said, citing the company.
An Oct. 9 strike damaged the company's data center in Kaluga , disabling several modules and potentially disrupting services. Yandex described its data centers as critical infrastructure for its services and said employees were working around the clock to restore operations.
Another drone attack on Oct. 8 caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo , Ryazan Oblast, forcing it to suspend operations completely.
Yandex even updated its user agreement on Oct. 10 to include drone and missile attacks among circumstances of force majeure that could exempt the company from contractual obligations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that Ukraine was responding to Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. "We always respond in kind," he told journalists, adding that Russia "has been and still is striking our data centers."
The attacks came amid an expanding campaign of Ukrainian long-range strikes against infrastructure inside Russia.
The Ukrainian defense company Fire Point , founded in 2022, is one of the country's leading weapons manufacturers, specializing in drones and missiles.
Fire Point plans to complete development of its FP-9 ballistic missile by the end of autumn, with a stated range of up to 850 kilometers (530 miles). It is also finalizing work on the FP-7 ballistic missile, which has a range of up to 300 kilometers (185 miles).
One of the biggest winners of Ukraine's wartime defense spending, Fire Point's history is not without controversy . The company has faced intense scrutiny amid a major corruption investigation into Timur Mindich, a former business associate of President Volodymyr Zelensky.

title: Kremlin has nothing to say on Trump's energy ceasefire, rejects Zelensky's truce proposal
description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Oct. 12 reiterated his readiness to adhere to the energy truce — provided that Russia follows suit.
content:
Russia has nothing to say yet about an energy ceasefire with Ukraine announced by U.S. President Donald Trump, the Kremlin's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Oct. 12.
“Contacts are ongoing. As soon as we have anything to say on the matter, we will be sure to let you know,” Peskov said, the Russian state news agency TASS reported.
The news comes shortly after Trump claimed on his Truth Social platform on Oct. 11 that both Kyiv and Moscow had agreed to an energy truce — an announcement that took Ukrainian officials by surprise.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky on Oct. 12 reiterated his readiness to adhere to the energy truce — provided that Russia follows suit.
Ukraine will halt its strikes against Russian refineries only if Moscow ceases its attacks against the Ukrainian power grid, Zelensky said on Oct. 12, signaling that a refinery-only truce makes little sense for a country with a single, badly damaged refinery.
However, Russia has broken the energy truce shortly after Trump's announcement by first striking Kharkiv's power plant in the evening of Oct. 11, and continuing to target Ukraine's energy infrastructure across multiple regions.
On Oct. 12, Peskov also rejected Zelensky's proposal of a 60-day ceasefire to hold elections, saying it wants a peace deal instead.
Peskov said that "both President Putin and officials at other levels have repeatedly stated that we do not want a ceasefire."
"We want long-term peace and are prepared to do everything possible to achieve it," he added.
However, Peskov stated that Putin would be willing to "issue an order not to launch strikes against Ukraine on election day, if Kyiv decides to hold the election."
"The 60 days that Zelensky is demanding are not needed to hold the election, but rather to regroup, heal their wounds, and continue the war," the Kremlin spokesman added.
Russia's Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said on Oct. 12 "I don't think he's (Zelensky) earned a break, and I don't think we'll buy into assurances and promises again."
Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine's Foreign Minister, responded to Lavrov remark by calling him a "war criminal," adding Lavrov "has already earned a front-row seat at the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression."
Trump announced, following a call with Putin on Oct. 9, that Russia had agreed to supply diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets.
While responding to reporters' questions on Oct. 10, Trump said: "I suggest they (Ukrainians) get a new leader who can make a deal."
"Zelensky could have settled this war many times, many, many times, and he chooses not to," Trump claimed.

title: US threatens to cut intel sharing, arms shipments to Ukraine to protect Russian oil refineries, sources confirm
