content:
The Kyiv Independent has learned that the Trump administration threatened senior Ukrainian military and government officials in a push to protect Russian oil refineries.
Two Ukrainian officials said their U.S. counterparts had made clear that Washington would hold Kyiv responsible if Russian energy infrastructure were struck during the recently announced ceasefire.
"They called all the top military officials with threats," one Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent. "They're telling everyone that they're going to turn off both the intelligence sharing and PURL."
The threats come after a confusing 48 hours during which U.S. President Donald Trump announced a controversial "deal" with Russian President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel, followed by repeated demands that Ukraine replace Volodymyr Zelensky as president, followed by Trump announcing a unilateral " energy ceasefire " between Russia and Ukraine, which blindsided both Moscow and Kyiv.
Multiple senior Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that Kyiv had not been informed in advance of Trump's Oct. 11 ceasefire announcement. After the announcement, Ukrainian officials reportedly came under pressure to abide by the ceasefire and refrain from striking Russian oil refineries.
Russia continued to attack Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with the Kharkiv thermal power plant being hit just hours after Trump's announcement.
According to another official, President's Office Deputy Head Pavlo Palisa, in charge of military affairs, and Mykhailo Drapatyi, commander-in-chief of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, had received calls from the American side.
PURL — which stands for "Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List" — is a Europe-led initiative that aims to provide Ukraine with critical U.S. weaponry, financed primarily by NATO members. In the first year of the initiative, $6.7 billion worth of weaponry was provided through the scheme.
Although direct U.S. military aid has been suspended since Trump's inauguration, intelligence sharing has continued.
Speaking to the Russian news agency TASS, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov declined to comment on the reported energy truce but said Russia was "ready to do everything possible" to achieve "long-term peace."
Nonetheless, the Ukrainian president signaled Kyiv's willingness to abide by the terms of the ceasefire, while adding they would need more information about the exact proposal.
Ukrainians remain skeptical that the one-sided energy ceasefire will hold.
"Immediately after (Trump's ceasefire) post, Russia launched a targeted strike on a power plant in Kharkiv, causing further damage to our energy system," Zelensky said during an event attended by Kyiv Independent journalists at the Warsaw Security Forum.
"It was clear that Putin does not read TruthSocial."
"We agreed to an energy ceasefire. The American team knows very well what this means for us. We do not have major oil reserves, large oil export capacity, or dozens of oil refineries," Zelensky said.
He repeated Ukraine's willingness to agree to a mutual energy ceasefire, but reiterated it would have to include energy infrastructure, not just refineries, as Ukraine does not have any functional oil refining infrastructure.
"In Ukraine, we have just one oil refinery. And it was badly damaged by Russian strikes long, long ago. So importing oil products is simply our reality," Zelensky said.
"And that is why our offer is honest and clear. We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same. We agree if they agree," he continued.
"And we have already shown that we mean it. Last night, Russian oil refineries were not burned. But at midnight, a Russian jet-powered Shahed struck a gas production facility in Ukraine."
Editor's note: An earlier version of this story stated that Deputy Head of the President's Office Pavlo Palisa had confirmed the information to the FT. Palisa later publicly denied confirming the information to the publication, and the Kyiv Independent removed the relevant paragraph.

title: Russian assets are only leverage if Europe uses them, says Ukraine's FM Sybiha
description: "Europe can no longer stay immobilized on Russia's immobilized assets. The leverage is not in holding the money, but in using it for defense," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
content:
LUXEMBOURG — Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha told journalists that Europe using Russia's frozen assets to help Ukraine is how it shows its strength in a world where it cannot depend in the U.S.
"Europe can no longer stay immobilized on Russia's immobilized assets. The leverage is not in holding the money, but in using it for defense," Sybiha said.
"We hear reservations and we are ready to address them: shared responsibility, not Belgium's burden," he added.
He later described making direct use of the 200 billion euros ($224 billion) of Russian assets immobilized in the EU since 2022 as "a fair approach," and that "the aggressor must pay."
But since four EU countries tried to reopen the topic in August, there has been no further progress on the issue, with the European Commission unwilling to make a concrete proposal until the 27 member states can agree on what they want.
Sybiha's comments came as part of a wider call for Europe to show it has leverage against Russia and to use it, naming sanctions and integrating Ukraine as other forms of leverage, in addition to using Russian assets.
"My message to European colleagues is simple: the era of dependence is over. Europe should take its future in its own hands, speak with one voice and restore peace," he said.
Sybiha's message came after several days of what he called "puzzling moves."
Those moves included U.S. President Donald Trump's likely illegal deal to buy Russian diesel; Trump's declaring that Ukraine should hold elections to remove President Volodymyr Zelensky; and Trump's unilateral announcement of an " energy ceasefire ," without telling Ukraine or Russia, and which Russia has not kept.

title: Update: Zelensky signs minority schools bill to appease Hungary, advance EU talks
description: The vote paves the way for the EU to formally open two more accession clusters with Ukraine and Moldova at a meeting in Luxembourg on Oct. 13.
content:
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky on Oct. 12 signed into law a bill reinforcing the educational rights of Ukraine's national minorities, a step that Hungary demanded before allowing Kyiv's EU talks to move forward.
The bill was passed by parliament earlier the same day.
The vote paves the way for the EU to formally open two more accession clusters with Ukraine and Moldova at a meeting in Luxembourg on Oct. 13.
The bill passed with the support of 266 lawmakers, according to lawmaker Yaroslav Zhelezniak. It still requires a presidential signature to become law.
The law would give Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking community and other EU-language national minorities more room to use their language in education. Roughly 80,000 ethnic Hungarians live in Ukraine's westernmost Zakarpattia Oblast.
According to the new legislation, schools where more than 50% of pupils study in the relevant minority language may be granted special status, and the head or deputy head of such a school must be proficient in that language, among other measures outlined in the bill.
"We welcome today’s important step by the Ukrainian Parliament on minority education rights. A positive result of months of joint work and constructive dialogue," Hungary's Foreign Minister Anita Orban said on X.
"Thank you to our Ukrainian partners. Let's keep this momentum going!" Orban added after the vote, as she met her Ukrainian counterpart, Andrii Sybiha, on the sidelines of an EU foreign ministers' meeting in Luxembourg on Oct. 12.
The bill covers official EU languages and languages of recognized indigenous peoples but not Russian, reflecting Kyiv's ongoing push to remove Russian from official and public spaces and counter decades of Moscow-imposed Russification.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar also commented on the bill's passage, noting it "will make it significantly easier for Hungarian children in Transcarpathia (Zakarpattia Oblast) to use their mother tongue."
Ukrainian officials, in turn, have said the legislation does not bring major practical changes but rather formalizes the education rights for national minorities.
"It brings our legislation into line with EU principles," Ukrainian lawmaker Mykyta Poturaiev told the Kyiv Independent.
"There is nothing in it that we don't already provide for, in principle."
Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former Prime Minister Viktor Orban spent years blocking Ukraine's EU accession talks, claiming Kyiv failed to protect the rights of its Hungarian minority.
The victory of Magyar 's pro-European Tisza party in the Hungarian parliamentary elections in April provided new impetus to resolve the issue.
In early summer, Kyiv and Budapest announced an agreement on the educational, linguistic, and cultural rights of Ukraine's Hungarian minority.
Hungary then lifted its veto on Kyiv's EU accession talks, allowing the launch of clusters one and six — lists of reforms focused on democratic institutions and the rule of law, and on external relations, respectively — in June and July.
The agreement also allowed Moldova's accession talks to move forward, as the EU has politically linked the membership bids of Kyiv and Chisinau.
But Budapest later blocked the launch of additional clusters until Kyiv begins implementing changes under the agreement, starting with educational rights.
Ukraine expects that the passage of the law will help unblock two more clusters, addressing internal market and competitiveness — a step that was preliminarily cleared by EU envoys on Oct. 7.
"I will never tire of repeating: there is no better way to guarantee the rights and security of the Hungarian national minority in Ukraine than to ensure Ukraine's accession to the EU as soon as possible," Sybiha said.
While meeting his Hungarian counterpart in Luxembourg, Ukraine's chief diplomat "thanked the Hungarian side for its constructive position" on accession talks.
All 27 EU member countries have agreed in principle to open the next two accession clusters with Ukraine and Moldova, the Irish EU Presidency confirmed after the bill was passed.
This clears the way for the formal opening of the clusters at the Intergovernmental Conference on Oct. 13.
"(I am grateful) to Ukrainian MPs for adopting (the) European integration bill, safeguarding the educational rights of Indigenous peoples and national minorities in Ukraine," Ukraine's Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration Vsevolod Chentsov said on X.
"An important step towards securing human rights and advancing (Ukraine's) EU accession."
Kyiv aims to have all six accession clusters open by the end of the year.

title: Russia-led military bloc launches joint military drills in Belarus
description: The drills involve more than 1,500 military personnel, over 300 pieces of military equipment, and around 80 drones, according to the Collective Security Treaty Organization.
content:
Russia and four other members of the Russian-led Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) have begun joint military exercises in Belarus on Oct. 12, the organization said.
The drills will run from Oct. 12 until Oct. 16 at two training grounds on Belarusian territory, involving more than 1,500 military personnel, over 300 pieces of military equipment, and around 80 drones, according to the CSTO .
Military contingents from Belarus , Russia , Kazakhstan , Kyrgyzstan , and Tajikistan are participating in the exercises.
The drills focus on training CSTO "peacekeeping forces" and involve exercises to respond to biological threats, the organization said.
CSTO Deputy Secretary-General Mirlan Turgunbekov said in an Oct. 11 statement that the exercise is "particularly relevant given the escalating military and political situation."
The CSTO, which was established in 2002, includes Russia, Armenia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Tajikistan, and Kyrgyzstan. Russia is by far the most powerful member of the alliance. Armenia is not particpating in the drills.
Belarus has supported Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine by allowing Moscow to use its territory as a staging ground for the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Although Belarus has not officially deployed its own troops to fight in Ukraine, Minsk has continued military cooperation with Moscow and provided support for Russia's war effort.
Ukrainian officials said on Sept. 14 that Russia is using Belarusian infrastructure, including LTE networks and repeater stations, to help maintain stable signals for Shahed-type drones during attacks on Ukraine.
Belarus held military exercises near its borders with Poland and Lithuania from Sept. 15 to 18, the Belarusian Defense Ministry said on Sept. 15.
Belarus has also been building new railway infrastructure in the country's southern Gomel Oblast that will be capable of receiving military trains carrying personnel and heavy equipment, the Belarusian Railway Workers' Community reported on Aug. 24.
In May 2026, Belarus and Russia held nuclear weapons exercises, amid Ukrainian concerns about deeper military cooperation between the two countries.

title: Exclusive: Finland pushes to all but eliminate Russian travel in EU
description: "The Kremlin must see that continued aggression will deepen its isolation. I ask you to take these proposals forward as an urgent priority," writes Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen in a letter seen by the Kyiv Independent.
content:
LUXEMBOURG — Finland's Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen has made five requests to the EU that would drastically curtail Russian citizens' ability to travel into and around the bloc, in a letter dated Oct. 12 and seen by the Kyiv Independent.
"The Kremlin must see that continued aggression will deepen its isolation. I ask you to take these proposals forward as an urgent priority," writes Valtonen, as EU foreign ministers meet in Luxembourg.
The first demand is to "stop issuing Schengen visas to Russian nationals for non-essential travel, including tourism." Finland has placed national restrictions since 2022, she said, but several countries — notably France, Spain, and Italy — have opposed attempts to ban Russian tourist visas.
Valtonen writes that she would support a German proposal "for visas with limited territorial validity," but only as an interim measure.
Second, Valtonen calls for a binding visa ban as a sanctions measure against Russian President Vladimir Putin's inner circle and any people or entities sanctioned by the EU.
And third, Finland wants to refuse visas to "Russian athletes and sports team members with close ties to the Russian government."
The reentry of Russian athletes at world sporting events has caused considerable anger in EU political circles, and the EU's Sports Commissioner, Glenn Micallef, is attending the Oct. 12 foreign ministers' meeting — for the first time — to discuss what actions can be taken.
Valtonen also reissued the call for a visa ban on Russian ex-combatants from entering the EU, which was previously proposed in the EU's 21st sanctions package from July, but was watered down as countries could not agree on the mechanism for enforcement.
The ex-combatants ban was also mentioned ahead of the foreign ministers' meeting by Valtonen's Estonian counterpart, Margus Tsahkna, who warned of the risk their entry to the EU represents , with "many of them supported by the Russian secret services."
And finally, Finland has asked the European Commission "to submit a robust amendment to the visa code," that would "enable the (European) Union to impose binding visa restrictions swiftly and consistently when its political or security relations with a third country deteriorate severely."
The European Commission is expected to propose a new visa law in January that will take a much tougher approach toward countries that threaten the EU, such as Russia.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 10, injure 69 across Ukraine as Moscow targets energy infrastructure in several oblasts
description: Overnight on Oct. 12, Russian forces launched 121 Shahed-type attack drones, including 76 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
content:
At least 10 people were killed and 69 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia continued to target residential buildings and energy infrastructure across the country, regional authorities said on Oct. 11-12.
Russia struck Kharkiv's CHP-5 power plant on Oct. 11, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. Ukraine's Presidential Office confirmed that the attack occurred after U.S. President Donald Trump announced a so-called energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.
In Kharkiv Oblast over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and settlements in the surrounding region, killing five people and injuring 42, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
Separately, in western Zhytomyr Oblast , an energy facility was under Russian attack overnight on Oct. 12, regional governor Vitalii Bunechko said. No casualties were reported.
In Kyiv , a high-voltage power line was damaged on Oct. 11 as a result of Russian attacks, Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said. Large parts of the city were without running water. Ukrainian energy company DTEK also reported short power outages in different parts of the Ukrainian capital.
Overnight on Oct. 12, Russian forces launched 121 Shahed-type attack drones, including 76 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force said .
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 89 drones, while strikes were recorded at 15 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at four locations, the Air Force said.
In western Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast , a Russian attack killed three Ukrainian service members and injured three others on the evening of Oct. 11, Mayor Ruslan Martsinkiv said.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , one person was killed and 18 others were injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said. The city of Sloviansk suffered the heaviest losses, with one person killed and 10 injured.
In northeastern Sumy Oblast , as a result of a Russian drone strike on a civilian car, a 39-year-old man was killed, while three other people, including two ambulance workers, were injured, regional authorities said .
In southern Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks injured two people, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast , over the past day, Russia carried out 817 attacks on 57 settlements of the region — one person was injured in the attacks, regional authorities said .
Dnipropetrovsk and Chernihiv oblasts also came under Russian attacks, but no casualties were reported.
Russia regularly strikes Ukraine's energy infrastructure, especially ahead of winter.
Trump announced the energy ceasefire in a Truth Social post , writing: "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed."
Ukraine had no information about the energy ceasefire announced by Trump, a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
In an interview following the announcement, Zelensky told Axios that if "President Trump negotiated it with (Vladimir) Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it."
Zelensky said Russia had carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine's electricity generation and transmission facilities over the past week, as well as 17 strikes on gas and oil facilities. Russian attacks killed more than 150 people and wounded more than 700 during that period, he added.

title: 'We have one refinery' — Zelensky says energy ceasefire must cover power grid, not just oil, as Russia strikes energy facilities across Ukraine
description: Ukraine will halt its strikes against Russian refineries only if Moscow ceases its attacks against the Ukrainian power grid, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 12, signaling that a refinery-only truce makes little sense for a country with a single, badly damaged refinery.
content:
Ukraine will halt its strikes against Russian refineries only if Moscow ceases its attacks against the Ukrainian power grid, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 12, signaling that a refinery-only truce makes little sense for a country with a single, badly damaged refinery.
"In Ukraine, we have just one oil refinery. And it was badly damaged by Russian strikes long, long ago," Zelensky said in a video address to the Warsaw Security Forum.
The news comes shortly after U.S. President Donald Trump claimed on his Truth Social platform that both Kyiv and Moscow agreed to an energy truce — an announcement that took Ukrainian officials by surprise.
The Ukrainian president confirmed that Kyiv learned of the supposed truce only from media reports, but reiterated his readiness to adhere to it — provided that Russia follows suit.
"We are ready to respect an energy ceasefire if Russia is ready to do the same," Zelensky added in his speech, noting that Ukraine did not attack any Russian refineries overnight, while Moscow struck a Ukrainian gas production facility.
"Last night, we did not attack any energy facilities on Russia, because President Trump said there would be an energy truce between Ukraine and Russia. We did not attack while Russia hit our gas stations, energy infrastructure and other facilities," Zelensky said in a separate message later that day.
In total, Russian forces had struck six Ukrainian energy facilities on oct. 12 alone, injuring 33 people, Zelensky said .
"It is increasingly clear that Russia does not want to accept the energy ceasefire proposed by the United States and intends to continue its terrorist air attacks against our people and communities," he said.
Russian forces also struck a power plant in Kharkiv on Oct. 11 shortly after Trump's announcement, and the Kremlin has not confirmed adherence to any truce.
"It was clear that (Russian President Vladimir) Putin does not read Truth Social, and his 'Shahed' drones follow a different set of instructions," Zelensky remarked. "But this post is actually about something that affects the lives of millions of people — and that makes it very important."
Adding to the confusion, an undisclosed White House official told Axios that Trump's announcement concerns only oil refineries and that a broader ceasefire covering the energy grid could come next.
Russia is one of the world's largest oil refiners, boasting a wide network of refineries whose production helps fund Moscow's war machine in Ukraine.
Ukraine effectively has only one oil refinery, in Kremenchuk in central Poltava Oblast, which has faced heavy attacks since the start of Russia's all-out invasion.
While Ukrainian drones have been targeting Russian refineries throughout the war to undercut the Kremlin's wartime revenues, Moscow has been attacking the Ukrainian energy grid and other critical infrastructure sites, leading to large-scale outages of electricity, water, and heat.
Ukrainian officials warn that Russia is preparing another massive campaign against energy infrastructure this winter.
"This winter, if Russia does not agree to an energy ceasefire, we will respond," Zelensky warned.
The last few days saw Trump ramp up pressure on Kyiv, demanding that Ukraine halt attacks on Russian refineries and suggesting that the Ukrainian people replace Zelensky if they want an end to the war.
Trump also announced a deal to buy Russian diesel and blamed Ukrainian attacks for the global diesel supply crisis, despite evidence that the U.S. war against Iran is the primary cause of the current shortage.
Kyiv's European allies have already expressed skepticism about the alleged energy truce.
"We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it," said Kaja Kallas, the EU's chief diplomat. "Of course, personally, I would also welcome that the ceasefire would include people not being killed."
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said that while the announcement is a "good thing... the Russians have continued to attack energy infrastructures at the gates of winter in Ukraine, especially in Kharkiv, and so things must be followed up effectively."

title: EU passes sanctions against Russia's illegal election in occupied Ukrainian territories
description: Of the 77 sanctioned individuals, 74 ran as candidates in the sham elections, while the remaining three were newly elected members of Russia's central electoral commission.
content:
LUXEMBOURG — EU foreign ministers unanimously approved 77 new sanctions listings on Oct. 12, targeting people who ran in and helped set up Russia's September sham election on illegally occupied Ukrainian territory, the Irish EU Presidency confirmed for the Kyiv Independent.
Russia held its State Duma elections from Sept. 18 to 20, while voting in occupied Ukrainian territories began in late August.
Of the 77 sanctioned individuals, 74 ran as candidates, while the remaining three were newly elected members of Russia's electoral commission. Most election organizers and 24 candidates were already subject to EU sanctions.
Ukraine already sanctioned over 40 people involved in those elections on Sept. 26, and the EU had previously passed election-related sanctions after Moscow banned the only remaining anti-war party, Yabloko (Apple), from competing.
The Russian State Duma elections were the first elections for Russia's lower house of parliament to be held in the occupied Ukrainian territories after Russia had issued Russian passports en masse to Ukrainians there, requiring them to renounce their Ukrainian citizenship.
However, the State Duma elections were not the first Russian-organized votes held in the occupied territories.
In September 2022, Russian occupation authorities held sham referendums in the occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts.
Russia organized so-called regional elections in the occupied territories in 2023 and held presidential elections there in 2024, in which Russian President Vladimir Putin was again declared the winner.
Also on Oct. 12, the EU passed almost 1,600 sanctions listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex.

title: EU votes through largest ever Russia sanctions list
description: "This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war," chief EU diplomat Kaja Kallas said, adding that more than half of the roughly 1600 listings "are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."
content:
LUXEMBOURG — EU foreign ministers voted through almost 1,600 new restrictions targeting Russia's military-industrial complex on Oct. 12, the largest single addition to the sanctions lists ever.
The new listings target industry players ranging from shipyards and aviation companies to electronics manufacturers, armored vehicle repair facilities, and aerospace companies, and were first reported on by the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 21.
"This is the single largest expansion of our sanctions list since Russia started its war," chief EU diplomat Kaja Kallas said, adding that more than half of the listings "are connected to the production chain for ballistic missiles."
"We are making it significantly harder, slower, and more expensive for Russia to produce the weapons it uses to kill Ukrainians."
The new additions take the total number of Russia sanctions passed by the EU from around 3,000 to over 4,500.
The new listings appear to have been compiled using a rather general criterion, namely, their entitlement to subsidies from the Russian government and their designation by the Russian state as part of the military-industrial complex.
EU sanctions entail freezing assets owned by these entities but held within the bloc and banning transactions with sanctioned entities.
It is unclear whether any of these entities did business with EU countries or held assets in the EU.
However, a senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent that the impact of the sanctions on the newly targeted entities' ability to do business with third countries should not be underestimated.
Southeast Asian countries, in particular, the official said, are unwilling to risk hurting relations with the EU by doing business with companies sanctioned by the bloc.
Ultimately, the aim of the sanctions is to hamper and make more expensive the running of Russia's war machine. Anything that complicates its ability to source western components, the EU official explained, is surely a good thing.

title: Lithuania calls on EU to designate Russia's foreign intelligence agency a terrorist organization
description: "Only when we increase our sanctions, when we show that we are serious, will we deny Russia the possibility to raise havoc in our capitals," Budrys said.
content:
Russia will not stop its hybrid attacks against Europe until the EU shows it is serious, and calls Moscow's foreign military intelligence agency a terrorist organization, Lithuania's Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys told journalists ahead of an Oct. 12 meeting of EU foreign ministers.
"We have to review GRU , Russia's military intelligence (agency), which in their operations is already acting as a terrorist organization," Budrys said.
"That is why it is for the EU to designate this organization as a terrorist organization and everyone who is related to them," he added.
GRU has been linked to a series of hybrid attacks across Europe: including a recent arson attack in Munich and the Leipzig airport drone attack in August.
And Budrys is particularly familiar with GRU's work, having worked most of his career for Lithuania's State Security Department — the country's civilian intelligence and security agency which assesses and eliminates threats to national security.
"Only when we increase our sanctions, when we show that we are serious, will we deny Russia the possibility to raise havoc in our capitals," Budrys said.
For Budrys, the EU did the opposite in September, when it bowed to pressure from France, Slovakia, and Luxembourg, and delisted two oligarchs.
"When we projected our weakness by delisting two prominent oligarchs from our sanctions, we saw how Russia reacted to it. They escalated, escalated both in Ukraine and now they're escalating in Europe, in our countries," Budrys said.
The EU maintains a terrorist list that includes both individuals and entities and functions similarly to the EU's Russia sanctions.
However, no Russian entity has yet been filed on the EU terrorist list, which only contains Islamists such as Hamas, Islamic State, and the perpetrators of the 9/11 attack against the U.S.

title: EU should 'hold a mirror to itself' on Russia sanctions before criticizing others — Latvian minister on Trump diesel deal
description: "Let's look at ourselves. The EU first took out two big Russian oligarchs, the biggest ever supporters of Putin's regime, from the sanctions," Latvia's Foreign Minister Baiba Braze said when asked to comment on a U.S. deal to buy Russian diesel.
content:
Editor's note: This article was updated to include comments from Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot.
LUXEMBOURG — The EU should first consider its own track record on applying sanctions before criticizing others, Latvia's Foreign Minister Baiba Braze said on Oct. 12 when asked to comment on a U.S. deal to buy Russian diesel.
"Let's look at ourselves. The EU first took out two big Russian oligarchs, the biggest ever supporters of (Russian President Vladimir) Putin's regime, from the sanctions ," Braze said ahead of a meeting of EU foreign ministers in Luxembourg.
Braze was referring to the Sept. 21 decision to delist Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman from EU sanctions, which was pushed for by Slovakia, Luxembourg, and France.
"Before we criticize the others, obviously we should hold a mirror to the EU itself," Braze said.
The Latvian minister and representatives of other 26 EU countries are expected to vote on two new sanctions packages, one against people who ran in Russia's September election on illegally occupied Ukrainian territory, and another 1,600 listings against Moscow's military-industrial complex — the largest ever single list of new additions.
"Obviously, our position has not changed. Pressure on Russia, sanctions, support to Ukraine. Russia's isolation is the way to peace. We all want peace," Braze said.
Her Lithuanian counterpart, Kestutis Budrys, likewise reiterated his criticism of the EU's previous decision to delist the two oligarchs.
"When we projected our weakness by delisting two prominent oligarchs from our sanctions, we saw how Russia reacted to it. They escalated, both in Ukraine and now in Europe, in our countries," Budrys said.
Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot also said Belgium regrets the withdrawal of the two names.
"Belgium thinks that, on the contrary, we must intensify them to continue to have an impact," Prevot said.
Belgium, Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania are the only countries known by the Kyiv Independent to have abstained from the vote to delist the two oligarchs, after being among the strongest opponents to the move.
On U.S. President Donald Trump's diesel deal more widely, Estonia's Foreign Minister, Margus Tsahkna, played down the impact.
"I don't think that in real life this diesel deal is actually going to change anything... it is much more connected to the domestic situation in the U.S., with the midterms coming," Tsahkna said.
"We have had this kind of turbulence from President Trump's side to Ukraine before. We need to focus on what we can do, and it is obvious that Europe must do more to support Ukraine," Tsahkna said, echoing his Latvian colleague's position.
Germany's European Affairs Minister Gunther Krichbaum described the Trump deal with Russia as "not our way."
"I would wish that everyone contributes to putting further pressure on Russia... every euro, every dollar that flows from energy purchases here into Putin's cash register helps Russia produce and use new weapons against Ukraine," Krichbaum warned.
And the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas called on the U.S. to "put sanctions in place so that we can actually finish this war."
Then, "all these effects of attacks on refineries would not be there, would not be necessary if the war is over," Kallas added.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,554,310 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,470 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,554,310 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 12.
The number includes 1,470 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,410 tanks, 25,527 armored combat vehicles, 162,056 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,090 artillery systems, 2,209 multiple-launch rocket systems, 1,703 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,927 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Russia lost over 50,000 soldiers in September, Bloomberg reports
description: Inflicting heavy personnel losses has become a stated strategic objective of Ukraine. In January, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Ukraine aimed to "kill 50,000 Russians per month," arguing that losses on that scale could undermine Moscow's ability to sustain the war.
content:
Russian forces suffered over 50,000 personnel losses in September, including upwards of 28,000 Russian soldiers killed on the battlefield, a NATO official told Bloomberg on Oct. 11.
The September figure, the highest monthly total in 2026, aligns closely with official estimates released by Ukraine's General Staff estimating 46,230 Russian personnel losses in September 2026. The General Staff did not distinguish how many of the losses were fatal.
According to the unnamed NATO official, Ukraine's Armed Forces suffered 5,000 casualties over the course of the month. The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the figure as Ukrainian officials rarely comment on the number of losses sustained on the battlefield.
According to the General Staff, Russian personnel losses have risen from 31,710 in January to 46,230 in September — an increase of nearly 46%.
Inflicting heavy personnel losses has become a stated strategic objective of Ukraine. In January, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said Ukraine aimed to " kill 50,000 Russians per month ," arguing that losses on that scale could undermine Moscow's ability to sustain the war.
The increase also comes as Russia faces growing pressure to replace troops while sustaining offensive operations along the front.
Ukrainian intelligence has also said Russia's General Staff is prepared to mobilize around 300,000 people in 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027 if needed.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in July that Russia has lost more than 1.5 million troops killed or wounded since the beginning of the full-scale invasion. The figures cannot be independently verified, and Moscow does not publish comprehensive casualty data.
As of Oct. 11, Ukraine's General Staff reported that Russia suffered 1,552,840 personnel losses since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. The figure is presumed to include those soldiers killed, wounded, captured, and missing.

title: 3 killed, 25 injured in Russian strike near Kharkiv
description: Among those killed were a 16-year-old boy, as well as a 19-year-old woman, and a 51-year-old woman, authorities said, in a strike that landed near a grocery store as well as several residential buildings.
content:
At least three people have been killed and 25 others injured in a Russian missile strike on a residential area in the community of Pisochyn, located just outside Kharkiv, Ukraine's National Police reported on Oct. 11.
Among those killed were a 16-year-old boy, as well as a 19-year-old woman, and a 51-year-old woman, authorities said , in a strike that landed near a grocery store as well as several residential buildings.
The injured victims, which included two girls aged 13 and 9, suffered a multitude of injuries and are receiving medical care. The extent of the injuries sustained was not immediately disclosed.
The attack comes amid a deadly day in Ukraine's second-largest city, Kharkiv. Earlier in the day on Oct. 11, two glide bombs struck the Nemyshlyanskyi district of the city, killing one and injuring at least eight others.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said "this week alone, the Russians have launched around 1,450 aerial bombs, 75 missiles of various types and over 1,640 attack drones, around 60% of which are jet-powered."
Russia regularly conducts fatal strikes on civilian infrastructure in cities across Ukraine as it continues to wage its war. Kharkiv also serves as a regular target of given its proximity to the front line.

title: EU to provide Ukraine with 3 billion euro tranche of military funding this week
description: The European Union is set to disburse approximately 3 billion euros ($4.8 billion) of defense support to Ukraine this week as part of the bloc's 90 billion euro support loan ($100 billion) for Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 11.
content:
The European Union is set to disburse approximately 3 billion euros ($4.8 billion) of defense support to Ukraine this week as part of the bloc's 90 billion euro support loan ($100 billion) for Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 11.
"We deeply appreciate every concrete step taken to support our defense and our people," Zelensky said following a phone call with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Oct. 11.
The phone call came hours after U.S. President Donald Trump's announced an energy ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia. Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that Kyiv had no information about the energy ceasefire, although Zelensky clarified that Ukraine would "accept it."
In a post on X following the call, von der Leyen said the European Commission "fully supported" Zelensky's calls for a ceasefire, adding that the EU would provide the funding this week "to strengthen Ukraine’s defences and protect its skies."
The EU's 90 billion euro loan to Ukraine, approved in April 2026, was intended to provide two-thirds of Kyiv's financial and defense needs until the end of 2027.
In 2026, 28.3 billion euros ($31.7 billion) was earmarked for defense, and Ukraine's plans for how to spend that money have all been submitted and approved by Brussels.
The EU most recently disbursed a 1.24 billion euro ($1.4 billion) tranche of support on Oct. 7. With the most recent disbursement, 15.4 billion euros ($17.2 billion) of the 28.3 billion euros remain to be paid out, pending Kyiv's submission of receipts, which Brussels then needs to cross-check.
In addition to the defense funding that remains to be disbursed, the sum also includes 17.1 billion euros ($19.1 billion) of budgetary support that Kyiv will receive in exchange for carrying out political and economic reforms.
Even after accounting for support from the EU's 90 billion euro ($100.9 billion) loan, Ukraine still anticipates a $42 billion hole in its 2027 budget .

title: Russian drone strike kills 3 service members in Ivano-Frankivsk, wounds 3 others
description: The attack was the latest in a series targeting the western Ukrainian city, with strikes reported on three days within a four-day period.
content:
A Russian drone strike on western Ukraine's Ivano-Frankivsk killed three Ukrainian service members and wounded three others on the evening of Oct. 11, Mayor Ruslan Martsinkiv said.
The wounded sustained injuries that were not life-threatening, Martsinkiv said in a video address. No civilians were injured.
The attack was the latest in a series targeting the western Ukrainian city, with strikes reported on three days within a four-day period.
Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast Governor Svitlana Onyshchuk initially reported two deaths and one injury. She later said the injured person had died in hospital, bringing the death toll to three. Martsinkiv subsequently confirmed that all three people killed were military personnel and reported three additional injuries.
The strike damaged a building and civilian infrastructure, according to local authorities. The full extent of the damage was still being assessed as of 11 p.m. local time.
Ukraine’s Air Force had warned that a jet-powered drone was approaching Ivano-Frankivsk before the strike.
Russian forces attacked Ivano-Frankivsk five times overnight on Oct. 9. A day earlier, falling drone debris sparked a fire in the city during another Russian attack. A man born in 1959 was killed in the Oct. 8 strike, according to regional authorities.

title: US threatens to halt weapons procurement for Ukraine over strikes on Russian energy sites, FT reports
description: The reported pressure preceded President Donald Trump’s announcement on Oct. 11 that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to stop attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure.
content:
The Trump administration has threatened to suspend a mechanism used to buy U.S. weapons for Ukraine unless Kyiv stops striking Russian energy infrastructure, the Financial Times (FT) reported on Oct. 11, citing unnamed European officials.
U.S. officials conveyed the warnings in calls to Kyiv and European capitals on Oct. 10 and 11, according to officials who participated in the conversations or were briefed afterward. Washington also threatened to stop sharing intelligence, the outlet reported .
The weapons procurement mechanism, known as the Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL), allows U.S. weapons to be purchased for Ukraine.
The reported pressure preceded President Donald Trump’s announcement on Oct. 11 that Moscow and Kyiv had agreed to stop attacks on each other’s energy infrastructure.
“Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
Zelensky’s office said it had no knowledge of an agreement. Russia also struck Kharkiv's power plant following Trump's announcement.
A senior Ukrainian official close to Zelensky that crews were still working to restore power and water in Kyiv following Russian strikes when Trump made his announcement. "Nobody has heard [of the ceasefire]," the official said.
Earlier, Zelensky had expressed support for a halt to energy infrastructure attacks in an interview with ABC News.
The White House declined to confirm or comment on the calls described by the European officials.

title: 'To keep oil prices from rising' — Russian lawmaker questions Trump’s energy ceasefire claim
description: "We all know that Trump often says things to keep oil prices from rising," Igor Ananskikh, first deputy chair of the committee, told Russian outlet Ostorozhno Novosti.
content:
A senior member of Russia’s State Duma energy committee said he had no information about an energy ceasefire with Ukraine announced by U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 11, suggesting Trump could be trying to influence oil prices.
"We all know that Trump often says things to keep oil prices from rising," Igor Ananskikh, first deputy chair of the committee, told Russian outlet Ostorozhno Novosti. "I don’t know how closely this reflects reality."
Dmitry Novikov, first deputy chair of the Duma’s international affairs committee, said he had not attended the negotiations and referred the outlet to Trump’s press service.
Trump announced that an energy ceasefire was effective immediately and that both sides had agreed. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the announcement was news to him.
Russia struck Kharkiv’s CHP-5 power plant that day, Zelensky said. Ukraine’s Presidential Office confirmed that the attack occurred after Trump’s announcement.
“Just now, there was a strike on CHP-5 in Kharkiv — on Kharkiv’s energy infrastructure,” Zelensky said at around 8 p.m. local time.

title: Russia struck Kharkiv's power plant shortly after Trump announced 'energy ceasefire'
description: Ukraine's Presidential Office confirmed that the attack occurred after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.
content:
Russia struck Kharkiv’s CHP-5 power plant on Oct. 11, President Volodymyr Zelensky said. Ukraine’s Presidential Office confirmed that the attack occurred after U.S. President Donald Trump announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine.
"Just now, there was a strike on CHP-5 in Kharkiv — on Kharkiv’s energy infrastructure," Zelensky said at around 8 p.m. local time.
Following the strike on the power plant, a Russian missile strike hit a grocery store in the suburbs of Kharkiv, killing three people and injuring at least 22, including two children, Kharkiv Oblast Governor Oleh Syniehubov said .
Ukraine had no information about the energy ceasefire announced by Trump, a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
Trump announced the ceasefire in a Truth Social post , writing: “Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed.”
In an interview following the announcement, Zelensky told Axios that if "President Trump negotiated it with (Vladimir) Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it."
Zelensky said Russia had carried out more than 200 strikes on Ukraine’s electricity generation and transmission facilities over the past week, as well as 17 strikes on gas and oil facilities. Russian attacks killed more than 150 people and wounded more than 700 during that period, he added.
Trump’s announcement came less than an hour after Zelensky’s interview with ABC News, in which he said a two-month ceasefire arranged by Trump and Putin would allow him to prepare Ukraine for a new presidential election.
Ukraine has been under martial law since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022. Ukrainian law prohibits elections while martial law is in effect.

title: Ukraine war latest: Russia pounds Kyiv's energy infrastructure as Trump’s energy ceasefire claim catches Ukraine off guard
description:
Key developments on Oct. 10-11:

 * Russia besieges Kyiv's energy infrastructure as Trump calls for an energy ceasefire
 * Ukraine's drone production jumps 370% in 2026, says defense ministry
 * Russian attacks kill at least 2, injure 25 across Ukraine as Moscow targets energy infrastructure around Kyiv
 * Third Yandex data center in Russia shut down following reported drone attack
 * Russian guided bombs hit Zaporizhzhia residential neighborhood, killing at least 20, injuring 32

Kyiv's electri
content:
Kyiv's electricity and water grids came under renewed strain on Oct. 11, as Russia continued its attacks on civilian infrastructure despite U.S. President Donald Trump's call for an "energy ceasefire."
"The enemy continues to attack energy infrastructure," warned Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko on the afternoon of Oct. 11, hours before Trump said an energy ceasefire was reached between Ukraine and Russia.
A senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent Ukraine had no information about an energy ceasefire that Trump announced.
Mayor Klitschko mentioned damage to a high-voltage power line. "Emergency crews are already working," he said. Large parts of the city have been without running water.
Throughout the day, journalists from the Kyiv Independent heard explosions in both downtown Kyiv and further out.
Ukrainian energy company DTEK also reported short power outages in different parts of the Ukrainian capital.
The day before, Trump tried to pin the blame for the continuation of the war on President Volodymyr Zelensky, calling on him to stop attacking Russian oil refineries after he had signed a potentially illegal deal with Moscow to import diesel .
But Zelensky made clear that these attacks, which have reduced Russian refining capacity by 45%, would only be called off once Moscow stops attacking Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
Attacks on Kyiv already plunged the city into near-total darkness on Oct. 8, and the expectation is that Ukrainians will have to brace for more of the same over the winter months.
Ukraine's defense ministry announced on Oct. 11 that it has ordered and received significantly more drones so far in 2026 than it had done for the whole of the previous year.
A press release from the defense ministry notes that its procurement agency has contracted for 5.5 times as many drones as in the same period of 2025, and that the volume of deliveries has increased by almost 3.7 times.
"The task of the Ministry of Defense is to give the army drones to work effectively at every level," said Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara in a press statement.
"Technology and the availability of sufficient means increase combat effectiveness and at the same time reduce risks for our soldiers," Khmara said.
"Such indicators became possible thanks to the direction of support from international partners and the scaling of the capabilities of the Ukrainian defense industry," reads the press statement.
An increasing number of deals between Ukraine and other European countries are helping bolster drone procurement across the continent, whether it is the announcement of support packages from Germany , the U.K. signing a battlefield data deal with Kyiv to develop AI drone swarms, or the EU-Ukraine drone alliance beginning work in September.
More EU money to help Ukraine procure drones is also expected to arrive by the end of 2026.
The bloc disbursed 1.2 billion euros ($1.4 billion) on Oct. 7 and is expected to make another payment to Ukraine ahead of the Oct. 14 summit of EU leaders, two EU officials told the Kyiv Independent.
Of the EU defense support available to Kyiv by the end of 2026 alone, 15.4 billion euros ($17.2 billion) remains unused.
At least two people were killed and 25 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia continues to target residential buildings and energy infrastructure across the country.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , one child was killed and a further five people injured, of which two are children, said Serhii Lysak, head of the oblast's military administration.
Following that announcement, Russia attacked a residential building, injuring at least four people, along which two eight-year-old girls, Lysak said , taking the total injured in the region to at least nine.
One person was killed and four injured in Donetsk Oblast, reported Governor Vadym Filashkin.
Kyiv Oblast 's military administration reports four people injured, with Russian drone strikes targeting "civilian facilities, housing, and energy infrastructure."
While in Kharkiv Oblast, six people were injured, of which one child, Governor Oleh Syniehubov posted on Telegram.
One person was also injured in Kherson Oblast , noted Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration, while three people were evacuated from liberated communities in the region.
Sumy Oblast military administration noted that two men were injured as a result of drone attacks.
Chernihiv Oblast , Khmelnytskyi Oblast, Kirovohrad Oblast, Mykolaiv Oblast , Odesa Oblast, and Rivne Oblast were also attacked but no casualties or significant damage was reported.
Russian technology giant Yandex's data center in Vladimir Oblast has been completely shut down following a reported drone attack, Russian state news agency TASS said on Oct. 11, citing the company.
The reported strike marks the third near-consecutive day of attacks on Yandex data centers in Russia, following confirmed strikes in Ryazan and Kaluga oblasts on Oct. 8 and 9.
Earlier on Oct. 11, Yandex Cloud reported power disruptions in an availability zone identified as being located at the company's data center in Vladimir.
"There are power interruptions in the ru-central1-a availability zone. The team is working to resolve the issue," the company said in a statement published on its official Telegram channel.
Yandex Go users across Russia reported being unable to order taxis on Oct. 11, with similar disruptions reported in Serbia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia, according to Russian independent media outlet Ostorozhno Novosti..
The outlet also reported that Yandex Pro, an application used by taxi drivers and couriers, was unavailable, while employees experienced problems accessing internal support systems. Users also reported disruptions to Yandex's smart home services.
Russian independent media outlet ASTRA reported that Yandex Cloud experienced power disruptions at its Vladimir data center following warnings of a drone attack in the region. Ukrainian monitoring channels also circulated images purportedly showing a fire near the facility.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the images or the extent of damage at the facility or to any of the Yandex apps or services.
The latest incident follows two drone strikes that Yandex has publicly acknowledged.
On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo , Ryazan Oblast, forcing it to suspend operations completely. Yandex said it could not yet determine when the facility's equipment could be restored.
A second strike on Oct. 9 damaged the company's data center in Kaluga , disabling several modules and potentially disrupting services.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that Ukraine was responding to Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. "We always respond in kind," he told journalists, adding that Russia "has been and still is striking our data centers."
In a statement on Oct. 9, Yandex described its data centers as critical infrastructure for its services and said employees were working around the clock to restore operations.
On Oct. 10, Yandex updated its user agreement to include drone and missile attacks among circumstances of force majeure that could exempt the company from contractual obligations.
Russian forces struck a residential neighborhood in Zaporizhzhia with guided aerial bombs early on Oct. 10, killing 20 people, including three children, and injuring 32, reported Zaporizhzhia Oblast's regional administration reported amid ongoing search-and-rescue operations.
The injured victims also include three children, the State Emergency Service said .
Russia attacked the neighborhood with five guided aerial bombs , nearly destroying parts of residential buildings and trapping civilians underneath the rubble, according to authorities.
One strike partially destroyed a section of an apartment building, causing parts of the building to collapse to the second floor, according to Mykhailo Semikin , acting governor of Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
A woman was pulled out from underneath the collapsed building after being trapped for eight hours. Rescue workers continue searching for people, as several individuals remain unreachable, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said said in the afternoon.
The State Emergency Service reported that three people had been rescued as of 6:15 p.m. local time.
Ukraine's Air Force warned at around 5 a.m. that Russian tactical aircraft had launched guided aerial bombs toward Zaporizhzhia.
Vyhivskyi said that despite the threat of a double-tap strike, Ukraine's first responders were trying to clear the rubble from the buildings as quickly as possible.
The attack was "against ordinary homes, against families with children," Vyhivskyi noted.
The attack came a day after Russian guided aerial bombs struck residential areas of Zaporizhzhia on Oct. 9, killing at least one person and injuring seven others, including a child, according to regional officials.
Russian forces have repeatedly targeted Zaporizhzhia, a southeastern Ukrainian city near the front line, with guided aerial bombs, drones, and missiles.
Russia has occupied parts of Zaporizhzhia Oblast since the beginning of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, while the regional capital of Zaporizhzhia remains under Ukrainian control.

title: Trump's Russia-Ukraine energy ceasefire claim is news to Kyiv
description: Ukraine has no information about an energy ceasefire that U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11, a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
content:
Editor's note: This story has been updated with comments from President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Ukraine had no information about an energy ceasefire that U.S. President Donald Trump announced on Oct. 11, a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
Trump announced the ceasefire in a post on Truth Social, writing that "Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed."
In a short interview after Trump's announcement, President Volodymyr Zelensky told Axios, "If President Trump negotiated it with (Vladimir) Putin, please tell us when the ceasefire begins. We are ready, and we will accept it."
The Ukrainian official also expressed doubt that Russia had been informed of the ceasefire.
Following news of Trump's announcement, Zelensky said he discussed the proposed energy ceasefire with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney, Finnish Presindent Alexander Stubb, and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, noting that Kyiv was "awaiting details from the American side" on the ceasefire proposal.
"For our part, Ukraine has always FULLY supported steps toward de-escalation, the protection of lives, and the decisions necessary to end the war and ensure lasting peace," Zelensky said .
This is not the first time Trump has announced a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, but a tangible agreement has remained out of reach so far.
Trump's announcement comes less than an hour after Zelensky was interviewed by ABC News, in which he said if Trump can arrange a two-month ceasefire with Putin, he can prepare Ukraine to hold a new presidential election.
Ukraine introduced martial law when Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, but elections cannot be held when martial law is in effect.
Trump and his allies have said Ukraine should elect a different president , and have accused Zelensky of prolonging the war.
But over that same time, Russia has continued to attack civilian targets across Ukraine, including Kyiv's energy infrastructure.

title: Zelensky says if Trump, Putin want elections in Ukraine, a two-month ceasefire is needed
description: Zelensky said he told Trump's team, "please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections."
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky pushed back against criticism from U.S. President Donald Trump in an Oct. 11 interview with ABC News, where he said if they want him out of office, he will hold an election, provided there is a ceasefire.
"With all respect to President Trump, it's up to our society, up to our people to choose one or another leader," Zelensky said in an interview with ABC News.
Ukrainian law forbids elections during martial law, which was declared when Russian launched its full-scale invasion.
But after Trump reached a likely illegal deal with Moscow to import Russian diesel, he defended his position by lashing out against Zelensky.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal. Because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Trump said.
"I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," he added.
Trump has previously called for elections in Ukraine , amplifying Kremlin propaganda narratives about Zelensky's lack of legitimacy — often shortly after meetings with Russian delegates.
Zelensky said he told Trump's team, "please tell Putin, give us two months, 60 days off. Total ceasefire, 60 days, and we will organize elections."
"Of course, we will be ready for any choice of our people," Zelensky said.
When asked why Zelensky thought Trump and others such as tech oligarch Elon Musk are blaming him for the continuation of the war, he did not hold back.
"Because these people can't find the key how to stop Putin. Because it's more difficult to stop Putin than to pressure others," Zelensky said.
Zelensky also attacked Trump's claim that Ukraine is to blame for rising fuel prices in the U.S. and across the world.
"Everybody in the world understands the prices are rising because of the war in the Middle East, because of the blocking of Hormuz," Zelensky said.
"People have to hear reality. Don't play games with people," he added.
Even so, Zelensky expressed hope that Europe, the U.S., and Ukraine would keep working together to stop Putin.
"We count on American support... but in any way we will defend ourselves because otherwise we will lose our life and homes, our freedom, independence, Ukraine," Zelensky said.

title: Russian air strike on Kharkiv kills at least 1, injures 8

"Today we will continue to coordinate with our partners — there will be discussions with European leaders," Zelensky added, with a view to securing air defense systems and ammunition for combat aircraft.

title: Russia behind Britain's Brexit vote, UK prime minister admits for first time
description: "These things are important now to put clearly on the record and, I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," media reports Burnham saying.
content:
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed Kremlin involvement in his country's 2016 referendum on leaving the European Union, the Observer newspaper reported on Oct. 11.
Burnham asked about Kremlin involvement when he became prime minister in July, reports the Observer, where he said he was given "the clear answer that, yes, there was."
The Observer reports that Burnham made his comments on one of the U.K.'s biggest politics podcasts, The Rest is Politics , with the episode set to come out Oct. 12.
It would mark the first public acknowledgment by a British prime minister of Russia's role in the country's divisive Brexit campaign, in which the country decided to leave the EU with 52% in favor and 48% wanting to remain part of the bloc.
Russia has long been suspected of driving euroscepticism in the U.K. and other European countries, and of working to bolster the country's "Leave" campaign more than ten years ago.
Burnham's comments were made days after he visited German counterpart Friedrich Merz in Berlin.
In Germany, the pro-Russian Alternative for Germany party is enjoying record levels of support, and won elections in the eastern regions of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg West Pomerania in September.
"These things are important now to put clearly on the record and, I believe, help voters in Germany and France understand that some of this politics is instigated via our enemies, namely Russia," the Observer reports Burnham saying.
The comments also emerge as Burnham works to deepen ties with the EU, a process that began under his predecessors Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer , and which has been helped by a shared commitment to support Ukraine.

title: Ukraine will only stop attacking Russian oil as part of an energy ceasefire, Zelensky says
description: "The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia, and Russia alone. It is already possible today to halt the attacks on our energy sector, but Putin does not want to do so," Zelensky said.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky pushed back against pressure from the U.S. to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, writing on social media on Oct. 11 that Moscow first needs to stop targeting Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
"The real cause of the war in Europe is Russia, and Russia alone. It is already possible today to halt the attacks on our energy sector, but (Vladimir) Putin does not want to do so," Zelensky said.
"Ukraine will be prepared to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries if Russia ceases its attacks on our energy infrastructure," he wrote.
As recently as Oct. 8, Kyiv was plunged into near-total darkness due to Russian attacks on the energy grid, and attacks have continued unabated since then.
Zelensky's comments follow U.S President Donald Trump saying "he better damn well stop" attacking Russian refineries, on Oct. 10, shifting the blame for Russia's war on Ukraine.
That remark, in turn, came one day after Washington announced a deal with Moscow to import diesel, despite such a move being illegal under U.S. law.
But that deal has also provoked strong backlash in the U.S., and there is a new bipartisan push in Congress to prevent the import of Russian diesel.
"Any de-escalation measures must be reciprocal and backed by genuine guarantees," Zelensky added, given that Russia has repeatedly not honored ceasefires in the past.
The pressure being applied to Zelensky also alludes to how effective Ukraine's attacks on Russia have been, with Ukraine's General Staff estimating in September that 45% of Moscow's refining capacity had been taken offline.

title: At least seven injured in Russian aerial bombing of Sloviansk
description: "There may be people trapped under the rubble," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a social media post.
content:
A Russian air attack on a residential area of the city of Sloviansk, Donetsk Oblast, on Oct. 11 has caused at least seven casualties.
Russia attacked the city at around 10:00 Kyiv time, dropping three FAB-250 bombs on a residential area, Sloviansk's Mayor, Vadym Lyakh, wrote on Facebook.
Shortly after, President Volodymyr Zelensky said "the Russians struck a five-storey block of flats in Sloviansk – the entrance hall there has been completely destroyed, and there may be people trapped under the rubble," in a Telegram post.
"This is happening constantly," Zelensky said.
"In total, this week alone, the Russians have launched around 1,450 aerial bombs, 75 missiles of various types and over 1,640 attack drones, around 60% of which are jet-powered," he added.
Lyakh said that seven people are known to have been injured, three of which have been hospitalized.
And another person was wounded by shelling in a separate residential area, Lyakh said.
"Take care of yourselves. Let’s stay strong. We’re in this together!" Lyakh wrote.

title: Ukraine welcomes Baltic push to ban Russian grain transit through EU
description: "It is important to see this initiative now being advanced at the EU level," wrote Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi.
content:
Ukraine's Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi thanked the prime ministers of Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia on Oct. 11 for launching an EU push to ban Russia from transporting its grain through the bloc.
"It is important to see this initiative now being advanced at the EU level," Vysotskyi wrote on X.
"Thank you to our Baltic partners for their consistent and strong support of Ukraine," he said.
Lithuania's Prime Minister Mindauga Sinkevicius called for the EU to impose sanctions on Russian grain, and to ban transit, on Oct. 8, which was followed the day after by a joint letter from the three Baltic prime ministers to put it on the EU agenda.
That letter calls on the bloc to do more to prevent grain stolen from occupied territory from being exported via the EU, to ban Russian grain from transiting EU territory, and to further bolster EU-Ukraine Solidarity Lanes, to help Kyiv get more grain out to markets.
A Russian-imposed blockade of the Black Sea is hurting Ukraine's ability to collect tax revenue from agricultural exports, causing global grain prices to rise , and putting at risk countries in North Africa and the Middle East, which are highly dependent on Ukrainian exports.
"The EU must not become a channel through which Russia compensates for the economic consequences of its own aggression," the letter reads.
When such a ban could be agreed on and implemented remains unknown, but the three Prime Ministers will attend a summit of EU leaders in Brussels on Oct. 14, where President Volodymyr Zelensky is also expected to attend.
And on Oct. 26, Vysotskyi is expected to attend a meeting of EU agriculture ministers in Luxembourg.

title: Inside Ukraine's world of naive art — and the Gunia aesthetic it inspired
description:
A cat's fur for a brush, crushed petals for paint, and an eye for beauty — as it turns out, that's all some Ukrainian artists needed to make some of the most distinctive paintings of the 20th century.

"Naive My Love," a new coffee table book by French publisher Assouline in collaboration with Ukrainian fashion and design brand Gunia Project, celebrates the bold colors, imaginative motifs, and deeply personal visual language of Ukrainian naive and folk art.

The book's visuals stand on their own
content:
A cat's fur for a brush, crushed petals for paint, and an eye for beauty — as it turns out, that's all some Ukrainian artists needed to make some of the most distinctive paintings of the 20th century.
"Naive My Love," a new coffee table book by French publisher Assouline in collaboration with Ukrainian fashion and design brand Gunia Project, celebrates the bold colors, imaginative motifs, and deeply personal visual language of Ukrainian naive and folk art.
The book's visuals stand on their own, but they are accompanied by texts that trace the origins of naive and folk art, along with short biographies of about 40 self-taught Ukrainian painters and sculptors, featuring examples of their painting, embroidery, carving, and other decorative arts.
While naive and folk art overlap in themes, they differ in motivation and technique — folk art is rooted in communal traditions passed down through generations, while naive art is typically created by self-taught artists expressing a highly personal, individual vision.
As "Naive My Love" points out, these works — created by Ukrainians for their own enjoyment — stood in quiet defiance of socialist realism, the only form of art officially sanctioned in the Soviet Union for those hoping to build a career. Their personal, heartfelt creations offered an alternative to the state-prescribed aesthetic, expressing individuality and resistance through art.
The most famous of all the Ukrainian naive artists is Maria Prymachenko (1909-1997), whose storied life in Kyiv Oblast inspired much of her work: she walked with a cane after contracting polio as a child, survived the Holodomor, raised her son alone after his father died fighting in World War II, and lived through the Chornobyl nuclear disaster.
Her art is most memorable for its saturated colors and fantastical beasts. The book includes paintings such as "The Beast of War," a massive, snarling brown beast that takes up most of the canvas. However, beneath the beast is a red flower hiding in plain sight — a reminder that even when terrible events seem to dominate day-to-day life, beauty still finds a way to exist in the world.
Artist Polina Raiko's (1928-2004) work, which became more widely known through Russia’s full-scale war against Ukraine, is also featured in the book. At 69, Raiko began painting the walls inside her home in Oleshky to cope with a series of family hardships — the colorful doves and angels that adorned her walls represented her desire for inner peace.
"I was working in my garden, got tired, painted a dove, and rested. It was joyful. It was like I wasn't alone. I looked and looked at it — could I have really done that? No. But I did. I couldn't believe myself. And I was so, so joyful in my soul," Raiko said of her work, as quoted in the book.
The house soon attracted the attention of locals and people from across Ukraine, and it was eventually designated a national heritage site. However, Raiko's one-of-a-kind house was almost completely destroyed in the summer of 2023 after Russia blew up the Kakhovka Hydroelectric Power Plant dam , flooding Kherson Oblast and neighboring southern regions.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food , water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make it almost impossible to evacuate safely.
It was only a matter of time before Gunia, as a brand, released a book about art. As they describe in the book, objects such as a rushnyk — a traditional embroidered cloth that is personalized in every home — can shape and inspire new directions in product development. That's why expeditions are crucial for the brand's designers: they help them better understand and reinterpret Ukrainian folk art, giving age-old traditions a fresh, contemporary twist.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 2, injure 25 across Ukraine as Moscow targets energy infrastructure around Kyiv
description: In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russia killed one child and injured nine other people in attacks on civilian targets.
content:
Editor's note: this article was updated as further Ukrainian oblasts provided updates on attacks over the last 24 hours.
At least two people were killed and 25 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia continues to target residential buildings and energy infrastructure across the country.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , one child was killed and a further five people injured, of which two are children, said Serhii Lysak, head of the oblast's military administration.
Following that announcement, Russia attacked a residential building, injuring at least four people, along which two eight-year-old girls, Lysak said , taking the total injured in the region to at least nine.
One person was killed and four injured in Donetsk Oblast, reported Governor Vadym Filashkin.
Kyiv Oblast 's military administration reports four people injured, with Russian drone strikes targeting "civilian facilities, housing, and energy infrastructure."
While in Kharkiv Oblast, six people were injured, of which one child, Governor Oleh Syniehubov posted on Telegram.
One person was also injured in Kherson Oblast , noted Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson regional military administration, while three people were evacuated from liberated communities in the region.
Sumy Oblast military administration noted that two men were injured as a result of drone attacks.
Chernihiv Oblast , Khmelnytskyi Oblast, Kirovohrad Oblast, Mykolaiv Oblast , Odesa Oblast, and Rivne Oblast were also attacked but no casualties or significant damage was reported.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,552,840 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,930 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,552,840 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 11.
The number includes 1,930 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,408 tanks, 25,521 armored combat vehicles, 161,503 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,039 artillery systems, 2,205 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,701 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,924 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Third Yandex data center in Russia shut down following reported drone attack
description: On Oct. 10, Yandex updated its user agreement to include drone and missile attacks among circumstances of force majeure that could exempt the company from contractual obligations.
content:
Russian technology giant Yandex's data center in Vladimir Oblast has been completely shut down following a reported drone attack, Russian state news agency TASS said on Oct. 11, citing the company.
