The reported strike marks the third near-consecutive day of attacks on Yandex data centers in Russia, following confirmed strikes in Ryazan and Kaluga oblasts on Oct. 8 and 9.
Earlier on Oct. 11, Yandex Cloud reported power disruptions in an availability zone identified as being located at the company's data center in Vladimir.
"There are power interruptions in the ru-central1-a availability zone. The team is working to resolve the issue," the company said in a statement published on its official Telegram channel.
Yandex Go users across Russia reported being unable to order taxis on Oct. 11, with similar disruptions reported in Serbia, Kazakhstan, Belarus and Armenia, according to Russian independent media outlet Ostorozhno Novosti..
The outlet also reported that Yandex Pro, an application used by taxi drivers and couriers, was unavailable, while employees experienced problems accessing internal support systems. Users also reported disruptions to Yandex's smart home services.
Russian independent media outlet ASTRA reported that Yandex Cloud experienced power disruptions at its Vladimir data center following warnings of a drone attack in the region. Ukrainian monitoring channels also circulated images purportedly showing a fire near the facility.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the images or the extent of damage at the facility or to any of the Yandex apps or services.
The latest incident follows two drone strikes that Yandex has publicly acknowledged.
On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at the company's data center in Sasovo , Ryazan Oblast, forcing it to suspend operations completely. Yandex said it could not yet determine when the facility's equipment could be restored.
A second strike on Oct. 9 damaged the company's data center in Kaluga , disabling several modules and potentially disrupting services.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that Ukraine was responding to Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centers. "We always respond in kind," he told journalists, adding that Russia "has been and still is striking our data centers."
In a statement on Oct. 9, Yandex described its data centers as critical infrastructure for its services and said employees were working around the clock to restore operations.
On Oct. 10, Yandex updated its user agreement to include drone and missile attacks among circumstances of force majeure that could exempt the company from contractual obligations.
The reported attacks come amid an expanding campaign of Ukrainian long-range strikes against infrastructure inside Russia.

title: Civilians evacuated from Russian-occupied territories, including Chornobyl disaster responder
description: Ukraine continues to quietly coordinate evacuations from temporarily Russian-occupied territories, where residents’ quality of life is severely diminished, particularly those who are elderly, disabled or require medical treatment.
content:
Sixteen Ukrainian civilians have been evacuated from Russian-occupied territories to government-controlled Ukraine, Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets announced on Oct. 10.
The evacuees crossed through the Novi Yarylovychi checkpoint on Ukraine's border with Belarus, Lubinets said , describing the complicated arrangements required to help people leave Russian-occupied areas.
Among those returned was an elderly man with a disability who helped respond to the 1986 Chornobyl nuclear disaster. He had been living with his wife in occupied Luhansk Oblast, where the couple struggled to leave because of her deteriorating health.
The woman had suffered a severe stroke in April and required constant care, and her husband also needed medical treatment and could no longer care for her, Lubinets said.
With their daughter was waiting in Kyiv, arrangements were being made to bring both parents to safety. Unfortunately, the woman died before the evacuation could take place, and only her husband was able to return.
"The daughter was waiting for both parents, but met only one," Lubinets said.
Another evacuee, a woman with severely limited mobility who had been living alone under occupation, required specialized transportation, medical assistance and a carefully planned route.
Lubinets said preparations had to be carried out discreetly to avoid attracting the attention of Russian occupation authorities and putting the woman at further risk.
The return of Ukrainian citizens was organized by Ukrainian agricultural company MHP and its founder and CEO Yuriy Kosyuk, according to Lubinets.
He also thanked Charitable Foundation Caritas Ukraine, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and others, for helping those who returned to receive immediate medical care, temporary housing, financial assistance, psychological support and transportation onwards.
"Crossing the border is only the beginning of a return to a safe life," Lubinets said.
Ukraine continues to quietly coordinate evacuations from temporarily Russian-occupied territories, where residents’ quality of life is severely diminished, particularly those who are elderly, disabled or require medical treatment.
On Sept. 19 , Ukraine returned 15 civilians from Russian-occupied territories, while a further 41 civilians returned through a Volyn Oblast border crossing during August and September, according to previous announcements by the ombudsman's office.
Lubinets said his office continues to process requests, assess security risks and coordinate routes for Ukrainians still seeking to leave occupied territory.

title: 11-year-old boy killed, five injured by Russian drone attack in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
description: The latest attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast follow several days of deadly Russian strikes across Ukraine, hitting residential buildings and critical civilian infrastructure, killing civilians, disrupting power and water supplies, and damaging bridges and other infrastructure.
content:
One child was killed, and five other people were injured, including two children, in Russian drone and missile attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast on Oct. 10, regional authorities reported.
The boy was killed when Russian forces dropped a munition from a drone on the Pokrovske community in Nikopol district, according to regional officials.
A 10-year-old girl and a 12-year-old boy were among the injured, and have been hospitalized. A 47-year-old man and two women, aged 49 and 61, were also injured.
Russian forces attacked Dnipropetrovsk Oblast more than 30 times throughout the day with drones and artillery, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported.
In Nikopol district, the attacks damaged residential buildings, a gas station and an ambulance. Russian strikes also hit the Zelenodolsk community in Kryvyi Rih district, damaging private homes and infrastructure.
In the Mykolaiv community of Dnipro district, vehicles and agricultural machinery were damaged.
Nikopol , located across the Dnipro River from the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant , has faced frequent Russian artillery and drone attacks throughout the full-scale invasion.
The latest attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast follow several days of deadly Russian strikes across Ukraine , hitting residential buildings and critical civilian infrastructure, killing civilians, disrupting power and water supplies, and damaging bridges and other infrastructure.
Zaporizhzhia has faced three consecutive days of deadly attacks. Russian strikes killed one person on Oct. 8 and another on Oct. 9, before guided aerial bombs struck a five-story apartment building on Oct. 10 , killing at least 20 people, including three children, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service.
Russian attacks on Kyiv's energy infrastructure on Oct. 8 also caused widespread power outages, disrupting public transportation and water supplies across the capital. Four people were killed and at least 19 injured in the attacks.

title: 'Will only lead to more slaughter' — Bipartisan backlash erupts in US over Trump-Russia diesel deal
description: Lawmakers from both major parties argued the move would undermine recently enacted sanctions against Russia, potentially provide Moscow with billions of dollars in revenue, and contradict Congress's efforts to pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine.
content:
Editor's Note: This story has been updated with a joint bipartisan statement from members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee.
U.S. President Donald Trump's deal allowing Russian diesel exports to American and global markets drew sharp criticism on Oct. 10 from both Democrats and Republicans in Congress, who warned the move could help fund Russia's war against Ukraine.
Trump on Oct. 9 shocked Ukrainians and many in the U.S. when he announced that he would ease sanctions against Moscow by opening up global markets to Russian diesel. He claimed this would alleviate a worldwide diesel shortage, which he attributes to Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries rather than his own decision to attack Iran.
Lawmakers from both major parties argued the move would undermine recently enacted sanctions against Russia, potentially provide Moscow with billions of dollars in revenue, and contradict Congress's efforts to pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the war in Ukraine.
Some lawmakers questioned whether the plan would meaningfully lower fuel prices for Americans, which have increased dramatically across the country since the start of the U.S. war with Iran.
Others pointed out that Trump's deal with Putin may even be illegal. In 2022, then-President Joe Biden signed a law prohibiting American imports of Russian energy products, with conditions for lifting the ban tied to an agreement by Russia to withdraw its troops from Ukraine.
"Congress banned Russian energy imports in 2022. (The president) cannot simply ignore that law to buy diesel from Putin," Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, said after the deal was announced.
On Oct. 11, seven bipartisan members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee released a statement condemning the decision, urging the White House to "immediately reverse course."
"President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law," the statement reads .
"Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: the U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies."
"The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians," the statement concludes.
Trump also recently signed another bill on Sept 18, which paved the way for further sanctions on Russia. Lawmakers claim the new agreement allowing for Russian diesel imports undermines that legislation.
"A few weeks ago, Congress overwhelmingly passed legislation to increase sanctions and tariffs on Russia," Senator Lisa Murkowski, a Republican, wrote on social media, referring to the recent sanctions bill.
"The president should be using those authorities instead of allowing Russia to export diesel, rake in revenues and continue its catastrophic war in Ukraine."
The sanctions bill, named for the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham , a staunch supporter of U.S. aid to Ukraine and sanctions against Russia , allows the president to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from foreign countries that meet specified criteria within 30 days of the law’s enactment.
The newly announced diesel deal directly contradicts the provisions made in the legislation, Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, said in a statement on social media.
Trump's deal "will lead to the slaughter of more innocents in Ukraine," he added.
"This agreement with a murdering dictator is a stain on our nation's character, an insult to Lindsey Graham's memory, and directly contrary to Congress's intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill," Blumenthal said.
Congresswoman Gluesenkamp Perez, a Democrat, also criticized the deal, writing on social media that it "undermined" decisions made by Congress.
"It won't actually bring down prices," she said, adding that "we're now funding the war against Ukraine."
"Whose side is Trump on?" Senator Mark Kelly, a Democrat, asked on social media. "The entire goal was to choke off Putin's money for the war by punishing countries who were evading the sanctions and buying Russian oil. Does that mean we're sanctioning ourselves now?"
Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick promised that bipartisan legislation blocking all purchases of Russian oil would be introduced in the coming days.
"We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. ... It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly," he wrote .
Critics of the proposed deal include Congressman Don Bacon, a Republican, who, in a lengthy post on social media stated that although Americans want lower diesel prices, "buying Russian fuel is the wrong answer."
"Now is the time to use those sanctions to squeeze Putin’s war machine," he said. "Not reward a dictator by putting more money in his hands while he continues targeting and killing Ukrainian civilians."
Trump has framed the proposed diesel deal with Russia as a way to lower costs for Americans ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. The midterm elections, which will determine which party controls Congress, are set to take place on Nov. 3, and voters are critical of rising oil prices and a general increase in cost of living tied to the war in Iran.
But support for Ukraine remains popular among Americans. A recent Economist/YouGov poll found that 61% of Americans sympathize more with Ukraine, compared to only 3% who sympathize more with Russia.
Before Trump's diesel announcement, U.S. lawmakers had been putting pressure on the administration to enforce the sanctions outlined in the recent legislation before the Oct. 18 deadline.
In a letter shared with the Kyiv Independent and later made public, Shaheen and Republican Senator Roger Wicker argued that Russia's intensified missile strikes targeting Ukraine's civilian population and energy infrastructure, along with new North Korean troop deployments, make immediate economic pressure necessary.

title: News from occupied Ukraine: Russia prepares Oleshky disinformation campaign, budgets for occupation for next three years
description:
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.

Key news as of Oct. 10:

 * Russia prepared series of Oleshky disinformation operations, SBU says
 * Russia's new three-year federal budget maintains funding for occupied Ukraine
 * Ukrainian troops struck Russian drone sites, command posts in occupied territories
 * Residents in occupied Luhansk
content:
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.
Russia prepares a disinformation campaign involving staged interviews with residents of the Russian-occupied front-line town of Oleshky, Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) said on Oct. 7.
According to the SBU, Russian forces ordered one of their units to produce a series of videos featuring residents of the occupied city. The operation is planned for October and early November.
The interviews are intended to blame Ukrainian forces for air attacks and blockading Oleshky , discredit Ukraine's leadership, and portray Russian troops positively, the agency said.
"(Russia) is failing on the battlefield and is therefore attempting by any means possible to undermine the psychological and emotional well-being of Ukrainians and destabilize the situation within our country," the SBU said.
Oleshky in the occupied part of Kherson Oblast has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, remained in the occupied town.
Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make it almost impossible to evacuate safely.
While Russian troops occupy Oleshky and the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, the Ukrainian military controls the western bank. Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Russian forces are preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
In September, only 12 people reached Ukraine-controlled territory from Oleshky, the local military administration head told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 6.
Russia plans to allocate more than 865 billion rubles ($10 billion) to a state program covering Russian-occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts over the next three years, according to the draft federal budget.
The Russian government submitted its proposed 2027-2029 budget to the State Duma on Sept. 30, Russian news agency Prime reported, citing the explanatory note accompanying the draft.
The proposed allocation totals 293.8 billion rubles ($3.4 billion) for 2027, 290.1 billion rubles ($3.4 billion) for 2028, and 281.7 billion rubles ($3.3 billion) for 2029. The figures were also published by the Russian-installed administration of occupied Kherson Oblast in its Oct. 6 report.
Moscow says the funding is intended to restore infrastructure and support socioeconomic development in the four occupied regions. The state program was established to oversee their reconstruction and development under Russian control.
"The relatively stable federal budget allocations... suggest that Russia continues to view investment in the occupation as a lucrative and necessary federal priority because it facilitates the forced integration of occupied territories into Russia," the Institute for the Study of War said on Oct. 8.
Ukraine's military struck Russian drone launch sites, command posts, communications infrastructure, and supply depots in Russian-occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson oblasts between Oct. 4 and Oct. 8, Ukraine's General Staff reported.
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian site near occupied Donetsk used to store, prepare, and launch attack drones on Oct. 7 and overnight on Oct. 8. They also hit a telecommunications hub near the regional capital of Donetsk, command and observation posts, command posts, and military supply depots elsewhere. Russian troop concentrations near Burlatske were also targeted, according to the General Staff's Oct. 8 , Oct. 7 , and Oct. 6 reports.
The strikes targeted Russian command posts near Prydorozhnie, a drone depot near Siverskodonetsk, and an ammunition depot near Khrustalnyi. Ukrainian forces also hit a military supply depot and a fuel and lubricants depot, and targeted Russian troop concentrations, the General Staff said in its Oct. 5 , Oct. 6 , and Oct. 7 reports.
Ukrainian forces struck Russian command posts near Bilotserkivka and Kamianka, a drone depot and command post near the city of Berdiansk, and a military repair unit and Russian troop concentrations elsewhere, according to Oct. 5 and Oct. 7 reports.
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian command post near Shchaslyvtseve in occupied Kherson Oblast on Oct. 5 and overnight into Oct. 6, the General Staff said in its Oct. 6 report.
The strikes are part of a series of attacks on Russian military infrastructure in occupied Ukrainian territories.
At least 64 people over the age of 60 have been subjected to political persecution in Russian-occupied Crimea, including 49 men and 15 women, the Crimean Tatar Resource Center said in a report published on Oct. 8.
The report documents cases of older people targeted by Russian occupation authorities. According to the organization, 44 of those documented have been sentenced, while 20 others are being held in pretrial detention.
The charges include alleged treason, espionage, sabotage, and links to religious or political groups banned in Russia. Some people have also been accused of financing Ukraine's military or involvement in the Noman Celebicihan Crimean Tatar volunteer battalion.
The oldest man documented is 77-year-old Volodymyr Ananiev, for whom Russian prosecutors are seeking a 22-year prison sentence. The oldest woman is 71-year-old Halyna Dovhopola, the group said.
The Kyiv Independent's September 2026 investigation showed that Russia turned the system of political persecution it had been building in Crimea since 2014 into a hub for the unlawful detention of Ukrainian civilians, primarily from Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, after its full-scale invasion.
Russian occupation authorities in Siverskodonetsk, Luhansk Oblast, have set deadlines for residents of two apartment buildings to remove their belongings before the buildings are demolished.
According to notices published by the occupation administration in October, residents of a building at 30 Soviet Avenue must clear their apartments by Oct. 15, while those at 17 Budivelnykiv Highway have until Oct. 20, 2026.
Both buildings, which were damaged during fighting, have been included in the occupation authorities' demolition program.
A September 2026 investigation published by ZMINA found a surge in building demolitions in the city, as by 2026 Russia had demolished only a few high-rise buildings there. But this summer, at least 79 buildings were added to the demolition plan.
The demolition of apartment buildings in occupied Siverskodonetsk reflects a broader Russian policy across occupied Ukrainian territories, including Mariupol , where authorities have designated residential buildings for demolition, often declaring them unsafe.
ZMINA concluded that the practice can deprive Ukrainians of their property and make it harder for displaced residents to reclaim their homes.
Some properties are declared "ownerless" if residents cannot meet the Russian occupation authorities' requirements, allowing the authorities to take control of them. The demolitions and property seizures can also facilitate the redevelopment of occupied cities and strengthen Russia's control over these territories, ZMINA reported.
Ukraine has evacuated a teenager from Russian-occupied territory who was detained by Russian forces over his pro-Ukrainian views and suspected of "terrorism," Ukrainian Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 7.
Lubinets didn't specify when and from which region the teenager was rescued.
The teenager was evacuated using the Volyn humanitarian corridor at the border between Belarus and Ukraine. Lubinets said this corridor was established as part of negotiations with Russia and has been operational since 2025. Borders with Russia and Belarus in other areas are closed.
He added that leaving occupied territories remains extremely difficult for many residents.
Over the past week, Ukraine also brought back 25 children and teenagers from Russian-occupied territories to areas under its control, according to Save Ukraine, a Ukrainian humanitarian NGO, Oct. 2 statement .
Lubinets said on Sept. 25 that around 1.6 million Ukrainian children may still be living in the occupied territories.
"They are issued with Russian documents, placed with Russian families, subjected to propaganda, and stripped of their Ukrainian identity. They are forcibly displaced," Lubinets said.
Russia is forcibly militarizing childhood , as in schools, Ukrainian children are forced to undergo military training, while thousands of young Ukrainians are being conscripted into the Russian army.
"The Russian leadership has a single aim: to continue the war against Ukraine using others' hands. To train a new generation of soldiers," Lubinets said.

title: Russia partially lifts ban on diesel exports after Trump-Putin deal
description: Effective Oct. 10, the Russian government will permit the sale of 500,000 tons of diesel to foreign markets. Moscow previously banned diesel exports in July in response to Ukrainian strikes.
content:
The Russian government has partially lifted its ban on diesel exports, the Russian state news outlet TASS reported on Oct. 10, citing a government statement.
The move follows a deal announced Oct. 9 between Russian President Vladimir Putin and U.S. President Trump, allowing Moscow to export diesel fuel to the U.S. and other markets despite sanctions imposed to due to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
In response to the deal, the Russian government partially lifted the diesel export ban, permitting the sale of 500,000 tons of diesel to foreign markets, TASS reported. The decision takes immediate effect on Oct. 10.
Russian oil companies will also immediately begin contracting for the sale of diesel fuel to foreign markets, the Kremlin reportedly told TASS.
Russia first announced an export ban on diesel fuel in July 2026, after a series of successful Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities crippled the country's fuel supply . Moscow was forced to restrict fuel sales, import supplies from India for the first time, and permit production of lower-grade gasoline at its refineries, among other measures.
Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak claimed that the easing of the export ban would not affect consumers in Russia.
Diesel production volumes in Russia are "sufficient" the meet the demands of the both domestic and global markets, he said.
The U.S. has not imported Russian fuel products since March 2022, shortly after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion in late February.
The Trump administration has, however, previously eased sanctions against Russian oil. In March 2026, after the U.S. and Israel launched their war against Iran, Washington issued a temporary sanctions waiver allowing for the sale of Russian oil stranded at sea. The waiver was renewed twice .
The U.S. has multiple times turned to Russia for oil relief during the war with Iran, even as Russia ships weapons to Tehran and assists with attacks against U.S. targets in the Middle East.

title: US Democrats call on FBI Director Kash Patel to cancel upcoming trip to Russia
description: In the letter, Rep. Jamie Raskin and Rep. Jim Himes urged the FBI director to cancel the visit, citing “urgent national security concerns,” including the FSB's history of conducting espionage operations against American officials.
content:
Two top House Democrats are urging FBI Director Kash Patel to cancel a reported trip to Russia, warning in an Oct. 9 letter that the visit could pose security risks.
Politico first reported in July that Patel was planning a fall visit to Russia , where he will be hosted by Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). He is allegedly set to visit both Moscow and St. Petersburg during the trip, which is tentatively scheduled for Oct. 14.
In the letter , Rep. Jamie Raskin and Rep. Jim Himes urged the FBI director to cancel the trip, citing “urgent national security concerns,” including the FSB's history of conducting espionage operations against American officials.
Rep. Jamie Raskin is a Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee and Rep. Himes is a Ranking Member of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence.
The Democrats refer to Russia as a "hostile foreign power" and question why the FBI Director would visit a country that "has been committing war crimes, conducting influence operations against U.S. elections, conducting malicious cyberattacks against our critical infrastructure, and helping our adversaries target and kill American soldiers?"
The letter described the visit as part of the FBI’s expanded cooperation with Russian and Chinese law enforcement agencies, citing Reuters reports that Patel has forged new partnerships with agencies in both countries.
In their letter to Patel, officials also question the timing of the FBI director's visit, citing the sanctions bill signed by President Trump which targets Russia's economy over its war against Ukraine.
Yet, on the same day the letter was published, Trump announced that Russia would supply U.S. and global markets with millions of tons of Russian diesel.
"This is why I voted against the Russia sanctions bill," Rep. Himes wrote on social media on Oct. 9. "Trump was never going to sanction Russia. He's going to refill Putin’s coffers and get an oil deal done to enrich his cronies."
The FBI has not replied to the letter or confirmed Patel's travel plans.
Since taking over the bureau in February 2025, Patel has sought closer ties with Moscow. This has raised concerns within the FBI, given the Kremlin's history of aggressive intelligence operations against the United States, according to an Oct. 9 investigation by The Atlantic .
Patel has previously called on Congress to investigate how U.S. aid to Ukraine is being used, and has criticized the amount of aid being sent.
The Trump appointee has also taken money from pro-Kremlin operatives in the past, according to the Washington Post. Patel received $25,000 in 2024 from a film company run by pro-Kremlin filmmaker Igor Lopatonok, the WP reported in Feb. 2025.
While the role of FBI director has traditionally been considered independent from government influence, U.S. national security expert Evelyn Farkas has described Patel as one of Trump's "yes men."

title: 'He better damn well stop' — Trump slams Zelensky for attacking Russian refineries, says Ukraine should get 'new president'
description: "I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president," U.S. President Donald Trump said when questioned about his deal to ease sanctions against Russia in exchange for diesel.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump lashed out at President Volodymyr Zelensky on Oct. 10, demanding he halt attacks on Russian refineries and suggesting the Ukrainian people replace him if they want an end to the war.
The comments came in response to questions from reporters about his recent deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to ease sanctions on Moscow by opening up global markets to Russian diesel supplies .
When asked if such a deal would prolong Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine, Trump told reporters he sees the situation "differently."
"Zelensky could have settled this war many times, many many times, and he chooses not to," Trump claimed.
Trump then lambasted Zelensky for exacerbating the global diesel supply crisis, despite evidence that shows the U.S. war against Iran is the major culprit behind the current shortage.
"We said you could do whatever you want to Russia, don't hit the refineries, because that's a world problem that's caused," Trump said.
"And he wants to make problems for the world, he wants to make problems for our farmers, our ranchers, with diesel fuel. ... We have a world problem, and the problem is caused by the lack of refinereis for diesel fuel. So what does he do? He goes and hits the refineries."
Trump made no mention of his war against Iran, the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, or Russia's relentless attacks against Ukrainian energy infrastructure and civilian neighborhoods. Instead, he framed the failure of the U.S. peace push as a result of Zelensky's stubbornness.
"And he's not going to affect our farmers, he's not going to affect our ranchers, and he's not going to affect the rest of the world," Trump said. "So he better damn well stop."
When asked about the daily suffering of Ukrainians under Russia's intensifying attacks, Trump had nothing to say about accountability for Moscow — and one main suggestion for the people of Ukraine.
"You know what I suggest? I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal. Because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does," Trump said.
"I think it's time for Ukraine to get a new president."
Trump has previously called for elections in Ukraine , amplifying Kremlin propaganda narratives about Zelensky's lack of legitimacy — often shortly after meetings with Russian delegates.
The tactic of blaming Zelensky has also allowed Trump to sidestep questions about Washington's warming relations with Russia amid mass attacks on Ukrainian cities.
Trump's diesel deal with Putin came as a shock to Ukrainian officials, who felt they had been invited to diplomatic talks with U.S. officials in Miami on Oct. 9-10 as part of "a trap."
Officials involved in the negotiations told the Kyiv Independent that they believed they would be discussing the terms of an energy ceasefire with Russia — one that would place equal demands on both sides.
Instead, the U.S. struck an economic deal with Moscow while pressuring Kyiv to halt refinery attacks, without any reciprocal demand for Russia to suspend strikes.
The deal seemed to be a way for Trump to dodge consequences — including skyrocketing gas prices and a steep drop in approval ratings — from his decision to wage war in Iran.
But Russian diesel may not provide relief at the pump or the polls, according to Seton Hall University Professor Margarita Balmaceda, an expert in the political economy of energy and associate at the Harvard Ukrainian Research Institute (HURI).
"As I see it, this deal has the potential to do much to help Russia — and to help Russia pursue its war against Ukraine — but not so much to help ease the diesel and gasoline crunch, the causes of which lie largely in the continued tensions around the Strait of Hormuz," Balmaceda said.
Zelensky has said repeatedly that Ukraine is ready to pause attacks against Russian energy infrastructure — as long as Russia agrees to the same terms. Thus far, Russia has shown no interest in de-escalating attacks.
Ukraine has long considered Russian oil refineries valid military targets, as Russian oil exports fund the Kremlin's war chest and refineries produce fuel for the armed forces. According to the Defense Ministry, Ukrainian attacks have disabled over 51% of Russia's total refining capacity.
When Trump announced the deal on Oct. 9, Zelensky said it was "a weak decision by our strong partners" that would allow Putin to prolong the war against Ukraine.
The next day, Kyiv was greeted by Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered strike drones in yet another daytime attack against the city's power grid. Residents were left without power and water.
"The consequences of allowing Russia to sell oil products were most clearly felt in Kyiv today, when, following numerous attacks with jet-powered Shahed drones against energy facilities, a ballistic missile attack began as well," Zelensky said in a message published on Telegram following the attack.
The money Russia earns from diesel exports will fund further destruction in Ukraine, the president warned.
"Every additional billion dollars Russia manages to earn from exports will be spent precisely on this: finding and importing critical components, equipment for weapons production, upgrading Shahed drones, manufacturing missiles, and recruiting additional mercenaries for the front," he said.
Elsewhere in Ukraine, a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia targeted a residential building, killing 20 civilians, including three children.

title: Exclusive: 'It felt like a trap.' How Ukraine was blindsided by Trump's Putin pivot
description:
When U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner told Ukraine's delegation on Oct. 9 that President Donald Trump was preparing to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, the Ukrainians struggled to believe what they were hearing.

The delegation had traveled to the United States to discuss a possible energy ceasefire with Russia. Instead, Kyiv's negotiators found themselves blindsided by a decision they feared would hand Moscow fresh revenue to finance its war against Ukraine while undermining
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump and Russia's President Vladimir Putin arrive for a press conference at Joint Base Elmendorf- Richardson, Aug. 15, 2025, in Anchorage, Alaska. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)
When U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner told Ukraine's delegation on Oct. 9 that President Donald Trump was preparing to lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, the Ukrainians struggled to believe what they were hearing.
The delegation had traveled to the United States to discuss a possible energy ceasefire with Russia. Instead, Kyiv's negotiators found themselves blindsided by a decision they feared would hand Moscow fresh revenue to finance its war against Ukraine while undermining Kyiv's leverage in negotiations.
"It was not just our delegation there, but a European one as well," one senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent. "It's just that everyone was sitting there like fools."
Washington was asking Ukraine to restrain its attacks on Russian energy while giving Moscow an economic reprieve — all as Trump faced consequences from the war against Iran.
"And yet he's the one who got everyone dragged into a war in Iran — a war with no way out — and is selling us out… Just to get a temporary, deceptive reprieve a few weeks before the election," the official said.
The Kyiv Independent spoke with several Ukrainian officials involved in or close to the negotiations. All of them were granted anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.
For Ukraine, the key question was why Kyiv should surrender a major means of pressuring Moscow if Russia faced no obligation to stop attacking Ukraine's energy system .
President Volodymyr Zelensky had sent a Ukrainian delegation to the United States for talks scheduled for Oct. 9-10. The agenda included a possible energy ceasefire with Moscow and a separate arrangement to halt attacks in the Black Sea.
Instead, the talks were derailed after Trump announced that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Kyiv had not been informed of the decision in advance. Although Zelensky publicly acknowledged that Washington was considering a deal with Moscow, Ukrainian officials said they had not known the details before the announcement that evening.
For the delegation, the revelation raised questions about whether Washington had already negotiated terms with Moscow while Ukrainian and European officials were still trying to establish the parameters of an energy truce.
"It felt like a trap," the senior Ukrainian official said.
"To be honest, everyone was shocked as f*ck."
The timing of the U.S. decision only deepened the suspicion.
Following Trump's direction, the U.S. Treasury Department announced that its Office of Foreign Assets Control was "immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
One Ukrainian official pointed to April 7, the date on which the waiver was set to expire, as evidence that Washington had planned the measure around a specific timetable.
"They lifted the sanctions until April 7... So they were preparing this for Oct. 7. It's a birthday present for Putin . They're counting the six months," the official said.
The dispute had been building for weeks.
Trump had previously pressed Zelensky to stop Ukrainian attacks on Russian energy facilities, arguing that Kyiv should stop disrupting Russia's fuel production.
"Mr. Zelensky has to do one thing. He has to stop knocking out diesel fuel in Russia," Trump told Zelensky on Sept. 13.
Kyiv rejected the premise that Ukraine should halt its strikes unilaterally. Ukrainian officials said Zelensky had repeatedly made clear that any energy ceasefire would have to apply to both sides, with Russia also stopping its attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
That distinction is central to Kyiv. Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, terminals, and other energy facilities aim to disrupt a major source of funding for Moscow's war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has systematically targeted Ukrainian power plants and substations, seeking to deprive civilians of electricity and heating.
A ceasefire that stopped only Ukrainian attacks would therefore leave Russia's campaign against Ukraine's energy system intact while protecting infrastructure that helps sustain the Russian war machine.
Yet, Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent that U.S. negotiators presented the issue differently during the talks, framing Zelensky as responsible for the impasse because he had refused to halt attacks on Russian refineries .
The Ukrainians were also told that Washington would cut off intelligence sharing that has helped Kyiv identify and strike targets inside Russia, one person present at the talks told the Kyiv Independent.
U.S. intelligence has played an important role in Ukrainian attacks , and restricting access to it would weaken Kyiv's ability to conduct strikes deep inside Russian territory.
One senior Ukrainian official involved in the talks responded with bitter humor.
"I hope the Americans don't give them Patriot (air defense systems) to protect their oil refineries," the official said.
The remark, however, captured a broader fear in Kyiv.
Washington already ended up helping Moscow shield the infrastructure that finances its war while pressuring Ukraine to surrender a means of striking back.
Another senior Ukrainian official said Ukraine had not agreed to stop attacking Russian refineries and would not commit to doing so without reciprocal Russian action.
For Kyiv, the principle remained unchanged. An energy truce could work only if both countries accepted the same restrictions.
"It was just f**king stupid to bury the idea of an energy truce with that move," one official said, suggesting that Washington was trying to strip Ukraine of its greatest source of leverage in the negotiations.
Events on the ground showed how little the announcement had changed.
Just hours after Trump's announcement, Ukrainian drones struck an oil loading terminal in Russia's Rostov-on-Don. The terminal handles petroleum products for export and supplies fuel to Russia's military.
Russia, meanwhile, launched a drone attack followed by a missile strike on Kyiv on Oct. 10, also targeting Ukrainian energy facilities.
Neither side had agreed to stop striking energy infrastructure, and the U.S. announcement had done little to bridge the gap between their positions.
Zelensky addressed the decision in a voice message to reporters late on Oct. 9, warning that allowing Russia to export diesel would just give Moscow additional revenue to sustain its war.
"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the moment when we are talking about peace, the U.S. is allowing Russia to export diesel."
He also questioned the purpose of sending a Ukrainian delegation to negotiations under those circumstances.
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. This is certainly not honest, and it is certainly not how partners should act," Zelensky said, calling the decision "a weak decision by our strong partners."
Ukraine was being asked to make concessions on the battlefield even as Moscow continued to attack its cities and energy infrastructure.
For one senior Ukrainian official, the explanation for Washington's move was straightforward: Trump was trying to deflect blame for the consequences of his own foreign policy.
"Clearly, Trump doesn't want to admit that it was his war against Iran that caused so many problems for Americans," the official said.
Tim Zadorozhnyy is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent covering foreign policy, U.S.-Ukraine relations, and political developments across Europe and Russia. He studied International Relations and European Studies at Lazarski University and Coventry University. Tim began his journalism career in Odesa in 2022 as a reporter for a local television channel. He later spent a year and a half at the Belarusian independent media outlet NEXTA, first as a news anchor and later as a managing editor. He is fluent in English, Ukrainian, and Russian.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 24, injure 47 across Ukraine as rescue operations continue in Zaporizhzhia
description: Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 160 drones, including 110 jet-powered drones and Gerbera drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
content:
At least 24 people were killed and 47 others injured across Ukraine over the past day, as Russia heavily targeted Zaporizhzhia where people remain trapped under rubble for over eight hours.
In Zaporizhzhia, at least 20 people were killed, including three children as Russia attacked the city with guided aerial bombs. Eighteen were injured, including three children, Ukraine's State Emergency Service reported amid ongoing search-and-rescue operations.
The death toll continued to rise as emergency workers conducted search-and-rescue efforts throughout the day. One woman was trapped beneath the rubble of a collapsed building for eight hours. In total, 26 residential buildings were damaged.
In Kyiv , Russia launched a series of missiles at the city following a morning drone attack on energy infrastructure. The afternoon attack had injured at least seven people in the city’s northern Obolon district by 5 p.m., Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. Five were hospitalized, three of them in serious condition.
In Kherson and Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks killed two people and injured another nine over the past day, the regional military administration said.
The city and its oblast were subjected to Russian airstrikes, drone attacks, and artillery shelling. Critical and social infrastructure were targeted, as well as residential neighborhoods where six private homes received damage.
In Sumy Oblast , the regional military administration reported injuries, without disclosing the exact number of people affected. Russia launched up to 30 attacks on 19 settlements in 12 regional communities, using artillery, first-person view (FPV) drones, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAV), guided artillery bombs and mortars across the region.
The regional administration reported damage and destruction of civilian infrastructure.
In Kharkiv Oblast , a 65-year-old man was killed and at least six people were injured as Russia launched 107 UAV drones, four missiles, nine guided aerial bombs and two FPV type drones overnight, said Governor Oleh Syniehubov . The attack hit nine settlements, targeting civilian infrastructure.
In the village of Martove, a farm and its five outbuildings were damaged, including agricultural equipment. Seven cows were killed during the attack.
In Kharkiv , a medical facility was hit during a daytime attack, injuring four women and causing fire in the building, said Governor Oleh Syniehubov.
In Donetsk Oblast, one person was killed and 11 people were injured, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Kramatorsk, four people received injuries while five were injured in Sloviansk. In the Pokrovsk district, a high-rise building, two private homes and an education facility were destroyed. A church was damaged in the village of Ocheretyne.
Russian forced attacked settlements in the region 26 times over the past day.
In Chernihiv Oblast , the small city of Semenivka was attacked with twoGerbera-type drones around 5:25 a.m., said Oleksandr Seliverstov , head of the Novgorod-Siverskyi Regional State Administration.
A fire broke out in a utility building on the grounds of a private residence, as information about casualties and injuries are yet to be revealed.
In Ivano-Frankivsk, the city was attacked five times said regional Governor Svitlana Onyshchuk .
In Dnipropetrovsk, Russia attacked the city and nearby regions over ten times with artillery and drones, according to the regional military administration . In Kryvyi Rih, infrastructure was also targeted.

title: 'Every extra billion will be spent on this' — Zelensky warns as missiles hit Kyiv after Russia sanctions relief
description: Loud explosions rang out in Kyiv around 2 p.m. on Oct. 10, according to Kyiv Independent journalists in the city, as Russia launched a series of missiles at the city following a morning drone attack on energy infrastructure.
content:
This is a developing story and is being updated.
Loud explosions rang out in Kyiv around 2 p.m. on Oct. 10, according to Kyiv Independent journalists in the city, as Russia launched a series of missiles at the city following a morning drone attack on energy infrastructure.
The afternoon missile attack on Kyiv had injured at least seven people in the city’s northern Obolon district by 5 p.m., Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. Five were hospitalized, three of them in serious condition.
"The consequences of allowing Russia to sell oil products were most clearly felt in Kyiv today, when, following numerous attacks with jet-powered Shahed drones against energy facilities, a ballistic missile attack began as well," President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a message published on Telegram following the attack.
President Donald Trump said on Oct. 9 that he had agreed with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel onto global markets , a move that drew sharp criticism from Ukraine and its allies for providing sanctions relief to Moscow.
Instead of facing further sanctions for its ongoing invasion of Ukraine, "yesterday, unfortunately, there were entirely different signals sent to Russia — signals suggesting that further attacks are somehow permissible," Zelensky said in his statement.
"Every additional billion dollars Russia manages to earn from exports will be spent precisely on this: finding and importing critical components, equipment for weapons production, upgrading Shahed drones, manufacturing missiles, and recruiting additional mercenaries for the front," he said.
According to the president, only "some of the missiles were intercepted," implying that others may have hit targets.
During the missile attack, the Obolon district was hit, where missile debris fell on the grounds of a residential building, Klitschko reported in a statement posted to his official Telegram channel.
A strike in the Obolon area caused a fire of over 200 square meters, Pavlo Petrov, spokesperson for the State Emergency Service told Ukrainian news outlet Novyny , adding that five people had been injured in the area and were currently receiving medical assistance.
The site of the strike was a boating station near the Obolon neighborhood's popular Natalka park, according to the station's manager Valery Hudnik.
"Our boatman was covered in an explosion wave. He was taken in the ambulance. I hope everything will be okay with him," Hudnik told Novyny.
The fire was extinguished, and rescue workers had begun dismantling and dousing the structures, Petrov said, adding that a single-story building and the courtyards of residential high-rises in the area were also damaged in the strike.
Just an hour earlier, parts of Kyiv were left without electricity after Russian strikes damaged energy infrastructure on Oct. 10, Klitschko said earlier. Kyiv Independent journalists reported power outages in the city's Pechersk and Borshchahivka districts around 12:50 p.m.
"Due to damage to a power facility in the Kyiv region, the capital's power supply situation has deteriorated. The city is also experiencing water supply disruptions," the mayor said.
Sudden voltage drops halted Kyiv Metro train services and escalator operations, the Kyiv City State Administration said. As of around 2:30 p.m., the metro had since resumed service with longer intervals between trains, the administration said.
The Bucha district in Kyiv Oblast also lost power, according to DTEK, Ukraine's largest private energy company.
"Utility workers are already on the ground, working to restore power to all homes as quickly as possible," said DTEK in a social media statement.
Russian attacks on Oct. 8 plunged the capital into near-total darkness, causing chaos on public transportation and leaving millions without water supply.
Since Oct. 1, Russia has been ramping up its attacks on Ukraine's energy grid, causing emergency power outages and forcing the city to introduce power outage schedules.
"Russia's choice is war," the president wrote in his statement published on Telegram.
"Strong signals are needed from the United States, Europe, and other partners: signals in support of Ukraine and aimed at limiting Russia’s ability to wage war and terrorize people."

title: New compromise EU budget maintains Ukraine support, but trims help for EU integration
description: "Our commitment to Ukraine is central to our overall ambitions," reads a text explaining the EU's latest compromise budget proposal.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — A new compromise proposal for the EU's 2028-2034 budget published Oct. 10 has been forced to cut costs, including for EU candidate countries, but support for Ukraine emerges relatively unscathed.
The bloc operates on a seven-year budget cycle, and countries hope to finalize the next budget by the end of 2026, before France, Poland, Italy, and many more countries hold elections in 2027.
The budget is also important for Ukraine, both because it supports countries working to integrate into the bloc and because the EU is Kyiv's leading financial backer.
The latest proposal includes dedicated Ukraine support of 88.87 billion euros ($99.55 billion).
The amount is unchanged from the last attempt at compromise, published in June, but remains below the 100 billion euros ($112 billion) initially proposed by the European Commission.
"Our commitment to Ukraine is central to our overall ambitions," reads the proposal put forth by the Irish Council Presidency of the EU, which leads negotiations on the budget.
But the budget requires unanimity of the 27 EU countries in order to pass, and several countries, often described as 'the frugals', have pushed for wide-ranging cuts.
That has led to a reduction in the size of the "Global Europe" pot, which finances the EU's development budget, humanitarian aid, and support for countries working to integrate with the EU — including Ukraine.
The latest proposal has reduced the Global Europe pot by just over 20 billion euros ($22.4 billion), from 169.5 billion euros ($189.9 billion) down to 149 billion euros ($167 billion).
Within that, support earmarked for EU candidate countries has fallen by almost four billion euros ($4.5 billion), down from 36.5 billion ($40.9 billion) to 32.6 billion ($36.5 billion) — just over 10%.
Realistically, Ukraine is not the most at risk of suffering from that 10% cut, with the proposal stating that "additional funding for Ukraine may be prioritized from the Enlargement and Europe and Global pillars."
Rather, the two big financial questions for Ukraine remain outside the scope of these budget negotiations.
Ukraine anticipates a $42 billion hole in its 2027 budget , even after accounting for support from the EU's 90 billion euro ($100.9 billion) loan.
Given that the loan is unable to single-handedly cover two years of support for wartime Ukraine, it is unclear how the EU will continue to find new money to help Kyiv if the war rages well beyond 2028.
In a briefing with journalists on the future of enlargement , a senior EU official said of the long-term funding of Ukraine due to the war, "there is a massive uncertainty, no one is pussyfooting about that."

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,550,910 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,420 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost 1,550,910 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 10.
The number includes 1,420 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,406 tanks, 25,515 armored combat vehicles, 160,946 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,000 artillery systems, 2,201 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,699 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,917 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Russian guided bombs hit Zaporizhzhia residential neighborhood, killing at least 20, injuring 32
description: Three children were among those killed by a Russian airstrike in the early hours of Oct. 10. Some victims were trapped for hours beneath the rubble as rescuers searched for survivors.
content:
Editor's note: This story was updated to include the most recent casualty numbers.
Russian forces struck a residential neighborhood in Zaporizhzhia with guided aerial bombs early on Oct. 10, killing 20 people, including three children, and injuring 32, reported Zaporizhzhia Oblast's regional administration reported amid ongoing search-and-rescue operations.
The injured victims also include three children, the State Emergency Service said .
Russia attacked the neighborhood with five guided aerial bombs , nearly destroying parts of residential buildings and trapping civilians underneath the rubble, according to authorities.
One strike partially destroyed a section of an apartment building, causing parts of the building to collapse to the second floor, according to Mykhailo Semikin , acting governor of Zaporizhzhia Oblast.
A woman was pulled out from underneath the collapsed building after being trapped for eight hours. Rescue workers continue searching for people, as several individuals remain unreachable, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said said in the afternoon.
The State Emergency Service reported that three people had been rescued as of 6:15 p.m. local time.
Ukraine's Air Force warned at around 5 a.m. that Russian tactical aircraft had launched guided aerial bombs toward Zaporizhzhia.
Vyhivskyi said that despite the threat of a double-tap strike, Ukraine's first responders were trying to clear the rubble from the buildings as quickly as possible.
The attack was "against ordinary homes, against families with children," Vyhivskyi noted.
The attack came a day after Russian guided aerial bombs struck residential areas of Zaporizhzhia on Oct. 9, killing at least one person and injuring seven others, including a child, according to regional officials.
Russian forces have repeatedly targeted Zaporizhzhia, a southeastern Ukrainian city near the front line, with guided aerial bombs, drones, and missiles.
Russia has occupied parts of Zaporizhzhia Oblast since the beginning of its full-scale invasion in February 2022, while the regional capital of Zaporizhzhia remains under Ukrainian control.

title: Major fire reported at oil terminal linked to Russia's Novoshakhtinsk refinery after suspected drone strike
description: ASTRA also reported damage to a residential building in Rostov-on-Don's Donskaya Sloboda complex, identifying its location through footage posted by residents. It remained unclear what struck the building amid reports of continued drone activity and Russian air defense operations.
content:
A large fire broke out at an oil-loading terminal in Russia's Rostov-on-Don overnight on Oct. 9–10 amid a reported drone attack, according to footage published by the Exilenova+ monitoring channel.
An OSINT analyst with the independent Russian outlet ASTRA identified the burning facility as the Yug Rusi oil-loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don's Zheleznodorozhny district, based on footage supplied by local residents.
The terminal handles petroleum products for export, including shipments from the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery, which belongs to the Yug Rusi group of companies.
Videos circulating on multiple accounts on Telegram appeared to show large flames and thick smoke rising from the site. Exilenova+ later reported that the terminal was still burning.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the footage or determine the extent of the damage. Russian regional authorities acknowledged a fire and reported that air defenses were operating, but did not confirm damage to the terminal, and Ukrainian military officials had not claimed responsibility for the reported attack.
ASTRA also reported damage to a residential building in Rostov-on-Don's Donskaya Sloboda complex, identifying its location through footage posted by residents. It remained unclear what struck the building amid reports of continued drone activity and Russian air defense operations.
The Yug Rusi oil-loading terminal is separate from the Novoshakhtinsk refinery's main processing facilities. According to the refinery's published specifications, its Rostov-on-Don terminal has an annual capacity of 3.5 million metric tons for receiving and shipping petroleum products.
The reported attack follows a Ukrainian strike on the Novoshakhtinsk refinery on Sept. 25 , which sparked a fire at the facility, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, storage depots and fuel infrastructure in recent months in an effort to disrupt fuel supplies to the Russian military and reduce Moscow's energy revenues.
U.S. President Donald Trump has urged Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities, arguing that the attacks contribute to rising global diesel prices.
Zelensky has said Ukraine is prepared to stop targeting Russian energy facilities if Moscow agrees to halt its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, insisting that any pause must be reciprocal.

title: US, Ukrainian, European officials discuss ending Russia's war at Miami meeting
description: The meeting coincided with U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel to the United States and global markets following a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
content:
U.S., Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami on Oct. 9 to discuss efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine ahead of winter, on the same day Washington moved to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports.
Discussions were described by U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff as “constructive”, and covered preparations for winter, including protecting Ukraine's energy infrastructure and maintaining grain exports, as well as security guarantees and longer-term arrangements aimed at preventing future conflict. The topics of Ukraine's postwar reconstruction, economic recovery and potential accession to the European Union were also reportedly covered.
In addition to the United States, representatives from the E3 group of France, Germany and the United Kingdom, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO took part.
Ukraine's delegation included Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov, Foreign Intelligence Service chief Rustem Umerov, presidential adviser Sergiy Kyslytsia and lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a negotiating team that has traveled to the U.S. and engaged in such discussions in the past.
Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that the negotiations were expected to last two days, Oct. 9–10, and that he anticipated a briefing from the delegation upon its return to Kyiv on Monday, Oct. 12.
In a post on X, Witkoff said that the talks helped identify areas for further consideration ahead of Washington's next engagement with Russia, but announced no concrete agreements. His statement did not indicate whether further meetings would take place on Oct. 10.
Ukrainian representatives had not publicly released their own account of the meeting at the time of publication.
The meeting coincided with U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel to the United States and global markets following a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The U.S. Treasury Department subsequently issued a temporary authorization permitting purchases of Russian diesel, drawing criticism from Kyiv and European officials over the potential financial benefit to Moscow.
The Kyiv Independent reported earlier on Oct. 9 that Russia was seeking sanctions relief as part of negotiations over a possible halt to attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Moscow also wants to link a potential energy truce to ceasefire arrangements in the Black Sea.
The discussions come as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine's energy facilities ahead of winter, threatening electricity and heating supplies across the country.

title: Zelensky appoints former European integration minister Kachka as EU ambassador
description: During Kachka’s tenure overseeing EU integration, Ukraine opened its first two accession negotiation clusters — groups of policy areas in which candidates must meet EU requirements.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky appointed Taras Kachka, Ukraine’s former deputy prime minister for European and Euro-Atlantic integration, as the country’s representative to the European Union and the European Atomic Energy Community, according to a decree published on Oct. 9.
Kachka served as deputy prime minister from July 17, 2025, to July 14, 2026. His move to Brussels was announced during a July government reshuffle, when Zelensky said Kachka would swap roles with Ukraine’s then-ambassador to the EU, Vsevolod Chentsov.
During Kachka’s tenure overseeing EU integration, Ukraine opened its first two accession negotiation clusters — groups of policy areas in which candidates must meet EU requirements. These covered fundamental reforms , including the rule of law, and external relations .
In December 2025, Kachka and EU enlargement chief Marta Kos co-signed a letter identifying the 10 most pressing rule-of-law reforms Ukraine should complete by the end of 2026.
He also worked with the European Commission to agree on the timing and content of reforms tied to installments of the EU’s 90-billion-euro loan for Ukraine, finalized in April.
Speaking at the Bruegel think tank’s annual conference in Brussels on Sept. 2, Kachka sought to reassure European partners that Ukraine would maintain its reform efforts despite the war.
“The voices and questions of member states and different stakeholders are not ‘blah, blah, blah,’” he said when asked by the Kyiv Independent how he would reassure Brussels. “The scale of this mutual undertaking on deterring Russia is so huge that it requires enormous trust between all of us.”
“Rule of law, anti-corruption, is really the cornerstone of this trust,” he added.
His appointment comes amid parliamentary delays in passing EU-backed legislation, which have put installments worth 2.1 billion euros and 3.7 billion euros at risk.
Zelensky has called on the EU to bring forward some loan installments scheduled for 2027. Kachka said the request reflected unfulfilled promises of additional financing from other allies.
He praised the EU’s decision to borrow jointly to support Ukraine’s wartime needs, calling it “a really revolutionary thing,” and said he remained optimistic that partners including the U.K., Canada, and Japan would provide further support.

title: Trump allows Russia to supply millions of tons of diesel to US, global markets
description: "Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," U.S. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Oct. 9 that Russia had agreed to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the U.S. and global markets following a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote on Truth Social.
"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" he added.
The U.S. Treasury Department said that, following Trump’s direction, "the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) is immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
"We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need, so we are happy to get it," Trump told reporters.
"I want to thank President Putin, to be honest with you," he added, but nonetheless called Washington Ukraine's "strong partner."
Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Chuck Schumer, and Elizabeth Warren condemned the six-month authorization for global purchases of Russian diesel, calling it "a total betrayal of Ukraine, our European allies and American national security."
In a joint statement, they accused Trump of funding Russia’s war effort to offset fuel price increases caused by the U.S. war with Iran. They also said the decision undermined bipartisan legislation passed weeks earlier to curb Russian energy revenues.
"Putin only responds to strength, which means cracking down on Russia and the enablers of its war against Ukraine," they said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also criticized the decision , saying it would provide Russia with additional revenue to finance its war against Ukraine.
"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the very moment when we are talking about peace, America is allowing Russia to export diesel."
Zelensky said Ukraine’s negotiating team is currently in Florida for two days of talks with U.S. officials on ending the war, or at least securing a ceasefire that could begin with a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.
"I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. This is certainly not honest, and it is certainly not how partners should act," he told reporters, calling the move "a weak decision by our strong partners."
Zelensky added that Ukraine was ready to reciprocate any Russian steps toward de-escalation, a position already known to U.S. negotiators. He said Ukraine would halt strikes on Russian refineries and other oil facilities if Moscow stopped attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, describing Ukraine’s strikes as a response to years of Russian attacks on its power system. Kyiv has proposed such an agreement to Washington, he added, and believes the U.S. has enough influence to secure it.
A European diplomat questioned whether the deal would lower diesel prices, telling the Kyiv Independent: "This is very unlikely to have a real impact on prices but the symbolism will have a real impact."
European Commission chief spokesperson Paula Pinho told the Kyiv Independent that "the EU is reducing its dependence on Russian fossil fuels and will resolutely continue to do so."
"Europe knows too well the hidden costs linked to over reliance on Russian hydrocarbons — and Europe does not wish to fuel Russia’s war against Ukraine," Pinho said.
Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, also responded to the deal by saying "EU Foreign Ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war," she wrote on X .
"This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t," she added.
Ukrainian sanctions official Vladyslav Vlasiuk called the deal "economically pointless" in his social media post .
"The U.S. consumes 3.5 million tons of diesel weekly and produces 4.9 million. Russia’s proposed 300,000 tons cover just 15 hours of U.S. demand, or 1.5 days of U.S. diesel exports. Economically pointless," Vlasiuk wrote.
The Kremlin said Russia had confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to U.S. and global markets during the call.
The move comes as Russia is seeking relief from U.S. sanctions in talks over a potential halt to attacks on energy infrastructure in its war with Ukraine, the Kyiv Independent reported on Oct. 9, citing American and Ukrainian officials with knowledge of the negotiations. Moscow also wants to link the proposed energy truce to ceasefire arrangements in the Black Sea.
Those talks follow intensified Russian strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. A senior Ukrainian defense official told reporters that Moscow aims to strengthen its negotiating position by causing as much damage as possible to the country’s power system.
Russia may also seek the release of frozen Russian assets, a European diplomat familiar with the discussions told the Kyiv Independent.
Russia’s government on Sept. 30 extended a ban on diesel exports by fuel producers through Oct. 31 amid problems in the domestic fuel market. Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Oct. 2 that domestic diesel supplies were sufficient and that Moscow could partially reopen exports if production exceeded demand, according to state media.
Putin said on Oct. 1 that Russia had enough diesel but that sanctions prevented it from supplying global markets. Speaking at the Valdai Discussion Club, he dismissed as "absurd" a proposal to halt Russian strikes on Ukrainian ships in exchange for Ukraine stopping attacks on Russian oil refineries, arguing that sanctions would still prevent additional Russian diesel from reaching international buyers.

title: Ukraine war latest: Drones strike another Yandex data center in Russia
description:
Key developments on October 09:

 * Second Russian Yandex data center damaged by drone attack in two days, company says
 * Twenty Russian officers killed in Ukrainian strikes on Donetsk, independent monitors claim
 * Russia forcibly removes 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, ombudsman says
 * Russian airports closed amid alleged Ukrainian balloon and drone raid
 * Ukraine confirms strikes on Russian cruise missile fuel plant, missile facilities

A drone att
content:
A drone attack damaged a Yandex data center in Russia's Kaluga Oblast overnight on Oct. 9, disabling several modules at the facility and threatening further disruptions to the company's services.
Several modules of the data center were completely disabled, Yandex said in a statement carried by pro-government Russian newspaper Vedomosti.
"Some Yandex services may experience disruptions as a result," the company said, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Yandex reported no injuries at the facility.
The attack came as drones struck other parts of Kaluga Oblast overnight, injuring nine people, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said. He also reported damage to houses in two districts of the oblast. Russian authorities claimed to have shot down 26 drones over the region.
Ukraine has not publicly confirmed responsibility for the attack on the Kaluga data center.
The strike marks the second reported attack on a Yandex data center in Russia in two days.
On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at a major Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, forcing the facility to suspend operations and disrupting parts of Yandex's cloud infrastructure.
The Sasovo facility houses tens of thousands of servers and two of the company's three supercomputers used to develop artificial intelligence models. Yandex said it was still assessing whether damaged equipment could be restored.
The attack coincided with reports of widespread internet disruptions across Russia, affecting banking services, transport websites, and online platforms.
Responding to questions about the Sasovo strike on Oct. 8, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine would continue retaliating against Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers.
"We certainly are capable," Zelensky said. "We always respond in kind. Regarding data centers, as you all know, they have been and still are striking our data centers."
"We responded to them," he added. "I cannot share all the details."
Russian forces struck several Ukrainian internet providers and data centers in Kyiv in late September, disrupting internet access for approximately 100,000 households, according to Ukrainian officials.
Ukrainian missile strikes on Russian army command posts in Donetsk on Aug. 26 killed more Russian officers than in any other single attack during the war, independent monitors claim.
Mediazona , an independent Russian outlet that tracks Russian military deaths in collaboration with the BBC Russian Service, identified 20 officers killed in the attack.
Each of the dead Russian officers was identified by name, age, and rank by Mediazona. Seven colonels, six lieutenant colonels, five majors, one captain, and one senior lieutenant were killed in the strikes, which hit the headquarters of the Central Military District and the 41st Combined Arms Army in occupied Donetsk .
According to Mediazona, 18 of the Russian officers died immediately in the missile strike, while two succumbed to their injuries.
Denis Pushilin , the head of the Russian illegal occupation administration in Donetsk Oblast, confirmed in a post on Telegram that Ukraine had launched an attack on targets in Donetsk on Aug. 26, claiming that Anglo-French "Storm Shadow" air-launched cruise missiles were used, and that eight civilians were injured.
Mediazona also identified two other instances of "mass casualties" amongst staff officers of the 41st Combined Arms Army, according to their research, eight officers were killed on Aug. 4, with an additional four killed on Sept 8, 2025.
At least 276,113 Russian soldiers have been killed in Ukraine since 2022, according to Mediazona, which tracks individuals killed by searching through obituaries, posts on Russian social media networks, and leaked Russian databases.
Russian forces forcibly removed 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territory in Kharkiv Oblast to an unknown destination, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 9.
The civilians, including children, young people, and elderly residents, were taken from an area of the oblast where active fighting continues. Their current whereabouts and the conditions in which they are being held remain unknown, Lubinets said .
"Russia calls this an 'evacuation.' But when people are taken away against their will, intimidated, and left with no choice, it is not a rescue. It is coercion," Lubinets said.
The ombudsman did not specify which settlement the civilians were taken from or where they had been transported.
According to Lubinets, Russian forces published footage of what they described as a rescue operation on their Telegram channels. He said the footage showed signs of intimidation and pressure on civilians who had not consented to being relocated.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the circumstances of the reported removals.
Lubinets also warned that Russian occupation authorities had created a Telegram bot to collect personal information under the pretext of evacuation, potentially putting civilians and their relatives at risk.
