Forcible transfers and deportations of civilians from occupied territory are prohibited under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention.
Lubinets said he had appealed to Russia's human rights commissioner, demanding information about the 25 civilians, their whereabouts and conditions, and measures to secure their return to Ukraine.
He also appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross , the United Nations , and other international organizations for assistance.
Russia has repeatedly forcibly transferred and deported Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territories since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
In March 2026, a United Nations commission concluded that Russia's deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children amounted to crimes against humanity.
Several Moscow airports temporarily suspended flights on Oct. 9, as suspected Ukrainian drones and balloons entered airspace around the Russian capital.
Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports all halted operations during the alleged Ukrainian raid, disrupting flights and causing long delays.
According to FlightRadar24 , an open-source air traffic monitoring website, multiple Russian government aircraft from the Rossiya Special Flight Detachment, which transports top-level Russian government officials, were scheduled to fly into Moscow's airports on Oct. 9.
At least one of the aircraft, an Ilyushin Il-96-300PU flying from Türkmenbaşy in Turkmenistan to Vnukovo Airport in Moscow, was reportedly forced to divert to St. Petersburg, according to FlightRadar24.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed "the Ministry of Defense's air defense forces repelled an attack by 15 UAVs" on the Russian government's messaging app, MAX.
A number of unknown balloons, which both Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels claimed were launched by the Ukrainian military, were also seen in the Russian skies .
Local Russian Telegram channels showed mysterious balloons in the skies near Moscow, and air defense activity.
Russian outlet BAZA claimed that, "reconnaissance balloons launched from Ukraine," were shot down over Yaroslavl Oblast, a region of Russia north of Moscow.
By 5:42 p.m. Moscow time, Russian wire service RIA Novosti reported that Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports had reopened.
On Sept. 1, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced a plan to close Russia's skies.
"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said, as he warned "every airline that uses Russian airspace" against flying over the country.
"The Russian sky will be de facto closed, " he added.
In the weeks following the announcement, Ukrainian drone raids have caused severe disruption to Russian air travel, but the result has fallen short of the complete closure Zelensky promised.
Ukraine's military launched an attack on several Russian regions overnight on Oct. 9, striking three Russian facilities involved in missile launches and fuel production, including a factory that manufactures fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed.
The attacks targeted facilities in Tver and Nizhny Novgorod oblasts, while Russian and Ukrainian monitoring channels separately reported strikes on oil infrastructure in other regions.
In Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Ukrainian forces struck a facility belonging to the V.P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes near Dalneye Konstantinovo-5, the General Staff said .
The institute is part of Russia's Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure (TsENKI), which develops, maintains, and operates rocket launch complexes, fueling equipment, and missile control systems.
Another strike targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near Surovatikha, also in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast. According to the General Staff, the attack was intended to weaken Russia's capacity to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
In Tver Oblast, the General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant, where Telegram monitoring channel Exilenova+ , citing resident accounts, had earlier reported flashes of explosions and smoke.
The plant, which produces components of Decilin-M rocket fuel, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, was previously struck in a Ukrainian attack in February 2026. The attack destroyed around 6,000 FPV (first-person-view) drones and their components, the General Staff said .
The plant is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the U.K., and several other countries.
Russia routinely uses Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, including during recent mass missile strikes on Kyiv.
Elsewhere in Russia, a Ukrainian attack reportedly led to a fire at an oil depot located north of the city of Belgorod, according to NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) monitoring platform.
The extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
In Russia's Komi Republic, Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Lukoil-owned Ukhta oil refinery on the morning of Oct. 9, with footage showing black smoke rising from the facility, independent Russian outlet The Moscow Times reported.
Independent Russian media outlet Astra geolocated eyewitness footage showing smoke rising from the refinery, while Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ reported explosions and drone activity in Ukhta.
The refinery processed approximately 3 million metric tons of oil in 2025, accounting for around 1.1% of Russia's total oil refining output. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, and vacuum gas oil.
Russian aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights at Ukhta airport amid the attack. Local authorities also declared a drone alert, while the city's mayor, Marina Meteleva, described the situation as under control.
The refinery, located approximately 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in February 2026 and August 2025.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
While the weaponry used in the reported attack was not immediately clear, Ukraine has often used long-range drones to strike facilities and oil infrastructure that directly support Russia's war in Ukraine.

title: US sanctions court that seeks to arrest Putin, prompts backlash
description: In 2023, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and another Russian official, Maria Lvova-Belova, for "unlawful transfer of population (children) from occupied areas of Ukraine to the Russian Federation."
content:
The U.S. on Oct. 9 imposed severe financial sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), which issued an arrest warrant for Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2023.
The new sanctions would prohibit transactions with the court after a grace period of six months. Any companies doing business with the court afterward can be punished by the U.S. government.
The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and the U.K. issued a joint statement in support of the ICC on Oct. 9.
"We... reaffirm our continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC," they said. "As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the court by the United States."
The ministers said that they appreciate "the work undertaken by the court to prepare for such measures so that the Court can continue to fulfil its mandate under the Rome Statute and we underline our unwavering support in enabling the court in doing so."
"Nevertheless, if put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the court’s work, its dedicated staff and their families," they said. ".... We remain both united in our support for the ICC and committed to engaging in constructive and inclusive dialogue with non-States Parties as we prepare for the Assembly of States Parties in December 2026. We will continue to work together to support the court’s vital work, uphold the rules-based international system, and advance accountability."
In 2023, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Putin and another Russian official, Maria Lvova-Belova, for "unlawful transfer of population (children) from occupied areas of Ukraine to the Russian Federation."
Previously, U.S. President Donald Trump's administration had also sanctioned many of the court's judges individually.
Trump has criticized the ICC's attempts to investigate alleged crimes committed by U.S. military personnel and its actions against Israel.
In 2024, the court issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Yoav Gallant, then Israel's defense minister, as part of an investigation into alleged war crimes in Gaza.
The court, set up in 2002 and based at The Hague in the Netherlands, investigates genocide, war crimes, and other offenses.

title: Why have EU sanctions missed the company behind Russia’s tank industry?
description:
With more than four years of full-scale war and 12 years since Russia first invaded Ukraine, it seems the European Union has developed an extensive arsenal of tools to sanction Moscow, but one problem appears to persist: the visibility problem.

Consider two companies that share a name.

The first is Research and Production Corporation Uralvagonzavod in Nizhny Tagil, Russia's only tank manufacturer. It has been under EU sanctions since March 2022 for supplying the T-72B3 tanks used against Ukrai
content:
Russian tanks move during the "Zapad-2025" (West-2025) joint Russian-Belarusian military drills at a training ground near Borisov, Belarus, on Sept. 15, 2025. (Olesya Kurpyayeva / AFP via Getty Images)
Executive director of the B4Ukraine Coalition
With more than four years of full-scale war and 12 years since Russia first invaded Ukraine, it seems the European Union has developed an extensive arsenal of tools to sanction Moscow, but one problem appears to persist: the visibility problem.
Consider two companies that share a name.
The first is Research and Production Corporation Uralvagonzavod in Nizhny Tagil, Russia's only tank manufacturer. It has been under EU sanctions since March 2022 for supplying the T-72B3 tanks used against Ukraine . Its EU entry names its owner: Rostec, Russia's state defense conglomerate.
The second is Moscow-registered Concern Uralvagonzavod. Since 2020, Russia 's company register has listed it as the tank plant's sole executive body, or basically the entity running it. Its chief executive, Aleksandr Potapov, is on the EU sanctions list. Its Moscow address appears in the EU's export-control entry for the plant. When listing a Rostec executive in June 2026, the Council of the EU itself described the Concern as "subject to Union restrictive measures."
Yet the Concern is not named on any EU sanctions list.
"At that pace, the gap would probably close by year 2030 — a remarkably leisurely timetable for a sanctions regime meant to constrain a war already underway."
That matters because of how EU sanctions reach beyond the names on the page. A listing does two things: it freezes a company's assets in the EU and, more importantly for a Russian arms maker with little to freeze in Europe , it bars anyone in the EU from making funds or economic resources available to it: no payments, no supplies, no contracts.
It has long been the law that these prohibitions also cover entities owned or controlled by a listed person. The Council's Best Practices clarified that a stake of 50% or more counts as ownership and that holdings of several listed shareholders are added together.
In March 2026, in EM System (C-84/24), the Court of Justice confirmed that such a stake creates a presumption of ownership or control. One that can be rebutted, but that is the starting point.
The rule, however, is built to reach downwards — to the companies a sanctioned entity owns or controls, yet whether it reaches the company that runs a sanctioned factory is not clear.
The Concern may still be off-limits through a different and less visible route.
Rostec itself is not under an EU asset freeze. It sits instead on a separate list, Annex XIX of Regulation 833/2014, whose ban on transactions extends to companies Rostec owns by more than 50%. Whether that ban covers the Concern, or any other Rostec subsidiary, depends on ownership percentages that nobody outside Russia can check.
Uralvagonzavod's own latest available annual report, dated Aug. 20, 2020, declines to disclose its shareholders, citing a 2019 Russian government resolution that allows companies to withhold such information.
A European supplier is therefore asked to apply an ownership test to data Moscow has made secret — and, if it gets the answer wrong, it has a ready defense: there was no way to know.
The stakes extend beyond one tank maker.
Ukraine's military intelligence service maintains a structure map tracking 553 entities affiliated with Rostec. Of those, 145 (26%) are subject to some form of EU restrictive measure.
Seven of Rostec's eight top-level holding companies — including Russian Helicopters, the Kalashnikov Concern, Technodinamika, High Precision Systems, United Aircraft Corporation, and United Engine Corporation — are individually sanctioned.
An independent investigation by the Independent Anti-Corruption Commission (NAKO), working from a separate dataset of 482 Rostec-linked entities, reached a similar figure: 23%.
The Uralvagonzavod group shows that gap up close. Ukrainian intelligence attributes 32 subsidiaries to it, with 21 not being named on any EU list.
Many are support businesses — catering, workwear, and a hotel, but the unnamed include Chelyabinsk Tractor Plant–Uraltrak, which Ukrainian intelligence identifies as the main producer of engines for T-72, T-90M, and T-14 tanks; a research institute for tracked military vehicles; an armored-vehicle repair plant working under defense ministry contracts; and the design bureau behind the flatcars that carry T-90M tanks.
The EU has added four of the group's companies since 2024. At that pace, the gap would probably close by year 2030 — a remarkably leisurely timetable for a sanctions regime meant to constrain a war already underway.
Each new sanctions package is a negotiated political act, yet ownership rules require no negotiation: they are already the law. They only work, however, if those expected to apply them can see what they are applying them to.
For a workable alternative, Europeans can simply look across the Atlantic. The U.S. Commerce Department's Entity List lets officials add dozens of Rostec-linked companies to an export-control regime without the political weight of a full sanctions designation — a faster instrument used precisely because full designations are slow.
The EU has comparable tools, but it does not use them visibly enough to be trusted by outside observers.
First, publish what the authorities already know: where the Commission or national competent authorities have assessed that an unlisted entity is owned or controlled by a sanctioned Rostec company, say so — and where Russia withholds the ownership data needed to make that call, treat the secrecy itself as a reason to list the entity by name.
Second, name the companies that run sanctioned plants: management companies such as Concern Uralvagonzavod sit above the factories they control, where the ownership rule offers no transparency, and should be designated directly.
Third, when the next package is drafted, prioritize the defense-critical subsidiaries still missing from the list — starting with the plant that builds Russia's tank engines.
By doing so, the EU can address the contradiction of sanctioning the factory that builds Russia’s tanks while forgetting about the one that actually runs it.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Nezir Sinani is the executive director of the B4Ukraine Coalition, an alliance of more than 100 civil society organizations pressing companies and financial institutions to stop enabling Russia’s war against Ukraine. Nezir has experience in environmental and social policy research, strategic communications, and civil society advocacy.

title: Russian airports closed amid alleged Ukrainian balloon and drone raid
description: Local Russian Telegram channels showed mysterious balloons in the skies near Moscow, and air defense activity.
content:
Several Moscow airports temporarily suspended flights on Oct. 9, as suspected Ukrainian drones and balloons entered airspace around the Russian capital.
Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports all halted operations during the alleged Ukrainian raid, disrupting flights and causing long delays.
According to FlightRadar24 , an open-source air traffic monitoring website, multiple Russian government aircraft from the Rossiya Special Flight Detachment, which transports top-level Russian government officials, were scheduled to fly into Moscow's airports on Oct. 9.
At least one of the aircraft, an Ilyushin Il-96-300PU flying from Türkmenbaşy in Turkmenistan to Vnukovo Airport in Moscow, was reportedly forced to divert to St. Petersburg, according to FlightRadar24.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed "the Ministry of Defense's air defense forces repelled an attack by 15 UAVs" on the Russian government's messaging app, MAX.
A number of unknown balloons, which both Russian and Ukrainian Telegram channels claimed were launched by the Ukrainian military, were also seen in the Russian skies .
Local Russian Telegram channels showed mysterious balloons in the skies near Moscow, and air defense activity.
Russian outlet BAZA claimed that, "reconnaissance balloons launched from Ukraine," were shot down over Yaroslavl Oblast, a region of Russia north of Moscow.
By 5:42 p.m. Moscow time, Russian wire service RIA Novosti reported that Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports had reopened.
On Sept. 1, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced a plan to close Russia's skies.
"There will simply be drones in Russia's skies on a scale that has to be taken into account," he said, as he warned "every airline that uses Russian airspace" against flying over the country.
"The Russian sky will be de facto closed, " he added.
In the weeks following the announcement, Ukrainian drone raids have caused severe disruption to Russian air travel, but the result has fallen short of the complete closure Zelensky promised.

title: EU represented by von der Leyen's right-hand at Ukraine peace talks, sources say
description: Two EU officials confirmed that Bjoern Seibert would be representing the European Commission at those talks, alongside the National Security Advisers of the E3 countries: France, Germany, and the U.K.
content:
Editor's note: This story has been updated to clarify that European, NATO, U.S. and Ukrainian officials are taking part in peace negotiations.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The European Commission is representing the EU at the latest round of Ukraine peace talks on Oct. 9, with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's chief of staff, Bjoern Seibert representing the bloc, diplomatic sources confirmed to the Kyiv Independent.
The question of who represents the EU at peace talks , or if it is even represented at all, has roiled the bloc repeatedly, even as Brussels is clear that Russia is not serious about ending its war of aggression.
President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists on Oct. 8 that the peace talks would include U.S. officials as well as Europeans and NATO.
Two EU officials said Seibert would be representing the European Commission at those talks, alongside the National Security Advisers of the E3 countries: France, Germany, and the U.K.
For the Commission, the talks are simply another part of the "constant work with Ukraine to strengthen their position while also trying to secure peace," a senior EU official familiar with the peace talks told the Kyiv Independent.
That's "even more important right now as we are seeing Russia's increasing attacks," the official added.
But the EU has never been able to agree on who has the right to represent it in peace negotiations.
Earlier in 2026, the idea of a dedicated EU peace envoy dominated discussions in Brussels, driven by speculative reporting from the EU's main media outlets.
There was a debate over whether the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas , should take on the role or for EU countries to pick a specific representative.
Then it transpired that Pedro Lourtie, the chief of staff of European Council President Antonio Costa, had opened a diplomatic backchannel to Moscow without first telling all EU countries, to which several countries have told the Kyiv Independent they took offense.
And then some EU countries objected strongly to the idea that the E3 countries could represent the bloc in peace talks, partly because France and Germany were too lax with Russia in the past, and partly because the U.K. is not even a member country of the bloc.
Seibert, representing the EU, might similarly receive some blowback from national capitals.
Diplomats from three EU countries confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that they were unaware of Seibert's role as a representative.
And the idea of von der Leyen and her chief of staff concentrating power around themselves is an oft-repeated topic on the Brussels media scene, and beyond .
However, the senior EU official aware of the peace talks notes that "there is no set way this works, it's rather ad hoc how these things happen both with Ukraine and the U.S."
And Seibert "frequently debriefs to ambassadors," they added.
Separately, another high-ranking EU official described a format that is "a little bit established" for peace talks during a briefing with journalists.
"That's now being, again, replicated in Miami as we speak," they said.
And at least one national diplomat does not see Seibert participating in the talks as a problem at all, believing that U.S. President Donald Trump has a positive view of von der Leyen.
"Kallas has done a great job being vocal about the right things, and she is doing a great job, but in difficult negotiations, you have to choose your negotiator to match the other side," the diplomat told the Kyiv Independent.

title: Russia forcibly removes 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, ombudsman says
description: "Russia calls this an 'evacuation.' But when people are taken away against their will, intimidated, and left with no choice, it is not a rescue. It is coercion," Dmytro Lubinets said.
content:
Russian forces forcibly removed 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territory in Kharkiv Oblast to an unknown destination, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 9.
The civilians, including children, young people, and elderly residents, were taken from an area of the oblast where active fighting continues. Their current whereabouts and the conditions in which they are being held remain unknown, Lubinets said .
"Russia calls this an 'evacuation.' But when people are taken away against their will, intimidated, and left with no choice, it is not a rescue. It is coercion," Lubinets said.
The ombudsman did not specify which settlement the civilians were taken from or where they had been transported.
According to Lubinets, Russian forces published footage of what they described as a rescue operation on their Telegram channels. He said the footage showed signs of intimidation and pressure on civilians who had not consented to being relocated.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the circumstances of the reported removals.
Lubinets also warned that Russian occupation authorities had created a Telegram bot to collect personal information under the pretext of evacuation, potentially putting civilians and their relatives at risk.
Forcible transfers and deportations of civilians from occupied territory are prohibited under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention.
Lubinets said he had appealed to Russia's human rights commissioner, demanding information about the 25 civilians, their whereabouts and conditions, and measures to secure their return to Ukraine.
He also appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross , the United Nations , and other international organizations for assistance.
Russia has repeatedly forcibly transferred and deported Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territories since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
In March 2026, a United Nations commission concluded that Russia's deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children amounted to crimes against humanity.

title: Exclusive: Putin puts a price on Trump's Ukraine energy truce — Kyiv fears the cost
description:
Russia has demanded sanctions relief from the U.S. as part of talks over a possible energy ceasefire with Ukraine, while also seeking to link the initiative to a ceasefire in the Black Sea, U.S. and Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks told the Kyiv Independent.

The demands come as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, with one senior Ukrainian defense official saying Moscow is trying to inflict as much damage as possible to gain leverage before potential negotia
content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin leaves the podium after holding a press conference with U.S. President Donald Trump at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on Aug. 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
Russia has demanded sanctions relief from the U.S. as part of talks over a possible energy ceasefire with Ukraine, while also seeking to link the initiative to a ceasefire in the Black Sea, U.S. and Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks told the Kyiv Independent.
The demands come as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure, with one senior Ukrainian defense official saying Moscow is trying to inflict as much damage as possible to gain leverage before potential negotiations.
Kyiv is already facing daily blackouts amid Russian attacks. A Russian assault on Oct. 8 caused widespread power outages across the capital, a city of more than three million people.
Publicly, Moscow has shown little willingness to commit to an energy ceasefire. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Oct. 8 that Russia saw no point in negotiating a sectoral ceasefire.
"Kyiv is not currently proposing a long-term settlement, but rather a ceasefire in an area that is its Achilles' heel — the energy sector," Peskov said.
Privately, however, Russian officials have signaled that Moscow is willing to consider the initiative, two Ukrainian officials and one U.S. official told the Kyiv Independent.
But Russia is tying a possible agreement to other demands, including sanctions relief, three people familiar with the negotiations said.
The U.S. has been pressing both Kyiv and Moscow to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure, making an energy ceasefire one of the main issues in peace talks.
President Donald Trump is also seeking to demonstrate progress on Ukraine before the U.S. midterm elections, several Ukrainian officials told the Kyiv Independent.
After their latest trip to Russia , Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner returned with the impression that an energy ceasefire was possible.
Russian Envoy Kirill Dmitriev visited the U.S. twice in September for meetings with Witkoff and Kushner, where they discussed a possible halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.
During those meetings, Dmitriev told the U.S. envoys that Russia wanted sanctions relief as part of a deal, according to Ukrainian and U.S. officials briefed on the discussions.
It remains unclear which sanctions Moscow wants lifted.
One European diplomat briefed on the matter told the Kyiv Independent that Russia could be seeking the release of frozen Russian funds as part of the deal.
"If they get sanctioned funds released … the likelihood that these will be used to escalate (war) is almost guaranteed," the diplomat said.
"No one really thinks they are genuinely seeking to adhere to a ceasefire ."
Ukrainian officials familiar with the talks confirmed that Russia was demanding sanctions relief but said they did not know which restrictions Moscow wanted removed.
The issue is expected to feature in discussions between Kyiv and Washington.
A Ukrainian delegation is due to meet with Trump's envoys in the U.S. on Oct. 9 to discuss proposals for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire.
The Ukrainian team is expected to receive a briefing on the U.S. talks with Russia and seek clarification about Moscow's demand for sanctions relief.
Asked about economic deals between the U.S. and Russia, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that Ukraine "knows a lot" but was not ready to discuss the matter publicly.
"I'm not ready to talk about it publicly or in detail," Zelensky told reporters.
For Kyiv, Moscow's demands raise the question of whether Russia is genuinely interested in halting attacks or is using negotiations to secure additional concessions while continuing its military campaign.
"Every time negotiations begin, they come up with more and more demands," one Ukrainian official briefed on the talks told the Kyiv Independent.
"Now this lifting of sanctions has come up."
Ukraine objects to the prospect of Russia receiving economic benefits in exchange for an energy truce. Kyiv's position is that any halt to attacks on energy infrastructure must be reciprocal, with both sides stopping strikes, rather than Russia receiving additional concessions for agreeing to the pause.
The dispute comes as broader peace talks remain stalled because of Russian territorial demands , which Kyiv considers unconstructive.
Washington is now pursuing a narrower agreement on energy infrastructure and Black Sea shipping that could demonstrate progress without resolving the larger questions at the heart of Russia's war against Ukraine.
Kyiv still hopes that the discussions will lead to a trilateral meeting with Russian representatives.
When Zelensky met German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv on Oct. 4, Witkoff texted the Ukrainian president that Washington wanted to hold such a meeting in late October. Zelensky replied that Ukraine would support it.
Before Kyiv can assess the prospects for a deal, Ukrainian officials want to understand what Moscow is asking for — and whether the Kremlin is prepared to stop its attacks without securing additional benefits in return.

title: Montenegro to expel founder of Russian war blog Rybar, citing security reasons
description: "Today, employees of the Police Department, together with the National Security Agency and with the support of international partners, conducted a targeted and coordinated operation aimed at preventing, detecting, and neutralizing illegal activities on the territory of Montenegro," Montenegro's police said.
content:
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
Montenegrin authorities decided to expel Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the pro-Kremlin war blog Rybar, and four other Russian citizens for national security reasons, the local newspaper Vijesti reported on Oct. 9.
The blogger, his wife Valeria Zvinchuk, and three other associates — reported to be Sergei Belous, Pavel Lekatorchuk, and Kira Doroshenko — were detained earlier on Oct. 9 by Montenegrin law enforcement and security authorities in the town of Risan.
Zvinchuk is the founder of Rybar, one of Russia 's most popular pro-war blogs, with over 1.5 million followers on Telegram. It focuses on battlefield developments in Ukraine while promoting pro-Russian propaganda about the war.
The channel's staff has been subject to U.K. and EU sanctions, and the U.S. announced a $10 million reward in 2024 for information on Rybar's activities.
"Today, employees of the Police Department, together with the National Security Agency and with the support of international partners, conducted a targeted and coordinated operation aimed at preventing, detecting, and neutralizing illegal activities on the territory of Montenegro," the Balkan country's police said.
The swift response prevented "potentially harmful actions" by the group on Montenegrin territory, according to the law enforcement agency.
The group was said to have arrived in the country less than two days ago. During the investigation, the Montenegrin police seized sophisticated digital equipment, including a drone, cameras, and several phones.
"Following the results of the criminal, operational, and intelligence investigation, it was established that these individuals cannot continue to stay in Montenegro, and in accordance with the Law on Foreigners, a decision was made to expel them for reasons of national and internal security," the police said.
Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajic previously confirmed Zvinchuk's detention, without disclosing further details about the operation.
"Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future," Spajic said on X.
Montenegro, a small nation in the Western Balkans , joined NATO in 2017 and is currently leading talks to join the EU.
Russia's Embassy has requested that Montenegro's authorities clarify the reasons for the detention of Zvinchuk and other Russian citizens, Russian state news agency TASS reported earlier on Oct. 9.
Separately, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said that Russian diplomats will work to protect Zvinchuk's rights.
Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia's security council and former president known for his inflammatory rhetoric, issued threats against the West over the propagandist's detention.
"Now we will quite likely have to replenish our exchange pool with European and American morons to get our own people out," Medvedev said on his Telegram channel.

title: Second Russian Yandex data center damaged by drone attack in two days, company says
description: Several modules of the data center were completely knocked out of operation, Yandex said in a statement.
content:
A drone attack damaged a Yandex data center in Russia's Kaluga Oblast overnight on Oct. 9, disabling several modules at the facility and threatening further disruptions to the company's services.
Several modules of the data center were completely disabled, Yandex said in a statement carried by pro-government Russian newspaper Vedomosti.
"Some Yandex services may experience disruptions as a result," the company said, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed.
Yandex reported no injuries at the facility.
The attack came as drones struck other parts of Kaluga Oblast overnight, injuring nine people, regional Governor Vladislav Shapsha said. He also reported damage to houses in two districts of the oblast. Russian authorities claimed to have shot down 26 drones over the region.
Ukraine has not publicly confirmed responsibility for the attack on the Kaluga data center.
The strike marks the second reported attack on a Yandex data center in Russia in two days.
On Oct. 8, a drone attack caused a fire at a major Yandex data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Oblast, forcing the facility to suspend operations and disrupting parts of Yandex's cloud infrastructure.
The Sasovo facility houses tens of thousands of servers and two of the company's three supercomputers used to develop artificial intelligence models. Yandex said it was still assessing whether damaged equipment could be restored.
The attack coincided with reports of widespread internet disruptions across Russia, affecting banking services, transport websites, and online platforms.
Responding to questions about the Sasovo strike on Oct. 8, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine would continue retaliating against Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers.
"We certainly are capable," Zelensky said. "We always respond in kind. Regarding data centers, as you all know, they have been and still are striking our data centers."
"We responded to them," he added. "I cannot share all the details."
Russian forces struck several Ukrainian internet providers and data centers in Kyiv in late September, disrupting internet access for approximately 100,000 households, according to Ukrainian officials.

title: Food court flop? Kyiv’s historic market empties after million-dollar makeover

But by the end of 2025, the maze of vendors had shru
content:
A man walks past a closed bar at the Bessarabskyi Market in Kyiv, Ukraine on Oct. 6, 2026. (Danylo Antoniuk/ The Kyiv Independent)
Bessarabskyi Market has stood in Kyiv for 114 years. Its upscale makeover lasted less than one.
Less than a year after the late-2025 reopening, most of the restaurants are gone, and the hall is quieter than before the renovation.
Before the makeover, Bessarabskyi was a labyrinth of produce stalls, offering everything from churchkhela — a sweet from the Caucasus — and watermelons from southern Ukraine to pigs' feet and sauerkraut craft beer.
But by the end of 2025, the maze of vendors had shrunk and been partly replaced by a cocktail bar, a performance stage, and 17 new food and drink stalls ranging from a sushi bar to an Indian restaurant.
Today, Bessarabskyi has one eatery left — a fast food chain called Big Mama. The stall sits in a row of identical tiled stalls with wooden countertops, freshly built and all but one shuttered.
The project — which looked to replicate the success of the popular Kyiv Food Market — is nothing short of a failure. In early June 2026, Natalia Dzhulai left her post as manager of the $3.5 million project , and 15 of the new eateries have closed, leaving only a coffee shop and a fast food chain still standing. Natalia Dzhulai refused to provide a comment to the Kyiv Independent as she is no longer part of the project.
Bessarabskyi’s transformation is part of a wider trend. Across Europe, developers have sought to turn grocery markets into profitable food courts. But in wartime Ukraine, the reality of changing a historic market and piece of Kyiv’s heritage into a trendy food court proved more difficult than developers expected.
Ihor Kravets, an architectural researcher who has been vocal about Bessarabskyi’s renovation, believes that the food court may have been successful had it been launched in 2019.
"Were it not for the blackouts caused by constant attacks, the general emotional exhaustion of the public, and the growing financial constraints facing consumers — the food court could have continued operating despite the other disadvantages."
The wider economy is also strained. Mobilization and the 3 million people who have fled Ukraine have created a shortage of 2.5 million workers in Ukraine’s economy, according to the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development . In March 2026 alone, 300 Kyiv food and drink establishments closed, according to Olga Nasonova , who runs a restaurant consulting business in Ukraine.
But Bessarabskyi’s renovation faced obstacles beyond its wartime circumstances.
Before the opening, the renovation was met with heavy criticism for its lack of transparency. As a municipal enterprise, the renovation needed to be a city-led project, but the public was not shown what the food court would look like. The developers and project managers sought no input from the community, and even to this day it is still unclear who the architect behind the food court actually is.
"The criticism (of the project) started before the opening, and after it the outcry only got stronger, so the operator started from a minus," said Pavlo Peker, an architect who pioneered the project to protect Kyiv’s historic Zhytnyi Market from a similar food court renovation.
Peker attributes the failure of the food court at least in part to the lack of public involvement: "The failure…could’ve been predicted…People don’t like that…Kyivans were just not a part of the process…so the people behind the Bessarabskyi project didn’t really know what the project needed," he said.
The lack of research meant the renovation ended up replicating what already existed nearby, but at higher prices and lower quality. Kravets said. "This was particularly off-putting given the venue's environment: unbearably stuffy in the summer and plagued by icy drafts in the winter."
"Kyivans were just not a part of the process…so the people behind the Bessarabskyi project didn’t really know what the project needed."
In the winter of 2025, Kyiv endured record-breaking cold and blackouts brought on by Russian attacks so severe that Mayor Vitali Klitschko urged those who could to leave the capital.
Some of Bessarabskyi’s new tenants felt that the impossible task of heating Bessarabskyi, a vast brick building with high ceilings, multiple entrances and a heritage status that restricts structural modifications, was the reason the food court lost customers.
"The winter started and it’s impossible to warm a place like Bessarabskyi, so customers stopped coming, and gradually stalls started to close," said Ruslan Kravchenko, the owner of Big Mama. Kravchenko would likely have also had to close up shop, had Big Mama not had a branch nearby with which it could share resources.
Kravchenko’s stall is surrounded by empty seating for the few and far between customers and a new stage added during the renovation.
While Kravchenko was speaking about the lack of customers, a shirtless man holding a plastic beer bottle clambered onto the stage added during the renovation, which after the reopening hosted live music and even a Q&A with former Foreign Minister Dmytro Kuleba but has not held a performance in months. The man’s shouts echoed across the empty building as he was removed from the building by police.
Above the stall, a slideshow of photographs of old Kyiv play on a 2x2 meter screen: Khreshchatyk as a dusty road for carts and horses, Kyiv’s center made up of two-story buildings — and, of course, Bessarabskyi bustling with customers.
Bessarabskyi today couldn't be further away from the one in the photographs.
Even without competitors, Big Mama may soon have to close. "When there were other restaurants, customers would bring their friends, and that would drive business, but now it’s difficult," said Kravchenko.
Although the eateries at Bessarabskyi have proved to be short-lived, more of the produce vendors have remained.
Natalia Vorovyoba is one of two remaining fresh fruit vendors at Bessarabskyi and, like many of the remaining produce vendors, has worked at Bessarabskyi for almost three decades. The renovation, which many hoped would drive profits, made Bessarabskyi unrecognizable, she said.
"The bar in the middle of the market…makes no sense for a grocery market,."
Vorovyoba has managed to remain at Bessarabskyi despite business declining over the years. She now fears that the renovation may have dealt the fatal blow and that she may soon have to leave.
"When I first started working at Bessarabskyi, there were so many people there was barely anywhere to stand. I could sell 60 kilograms of strawberries at once, but there are days now when I don’t get any customers," Vorovyoba explained.
While Natalia Dzhulai, the manager of the food court project, promised that 50 grocery vendors would stay at the market — 90% of the number pre-renovation — now only a handful remain.
"They didn’t tell us what it was going to look like — they said only half of it would be taken by the food market, but you can see it’s clearly more than half," Vorovyoba said.
The future of Kyiv’s grocery markets is uncertain. Some, like Peker, are optimistic that this is just another chapter in Bessarabskyi's history, while others, like Kravets, are less so.
"It’s a very worrying situation. Potential investors have been scared off. The priceless historic building has fallen into neglect, and it’s unclear who will fund its upkeep," Kravets said.
But in some ways Bessarabskyi’s produce vendors are lucky to have survived the market's development at all. Other projects to turn markets into more profitable venues threaten to change the site altogether.
Demiivskyi Market in Kyiv is set to be torn down completely and will be the site of a new 30-story building which will be built by Manhattan Invest.
Other markets in Kyiv have become the sites of Russian attacks. In Kyiv in 2026 alone, Russia destroyed both the Lukianivskyi Market and the massive book and flea market on Pochaina in two separate and direct strikes.
Alessandra Hay is a freelance journalist covering Ukraine and Iran. She holds a BA in Russian and Persian from the University of Oxford and an MA in Political Sociology from UCL’s School of Slavonic and Eastern European Studies. Her writing has appeared in the Kyiv Independent, the London Review of Books, and the Counteroffensive.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 41, injure 67 across Ukraine as glide bombs strike Zaporizhzhia
description: Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 136 drones, including 93 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
content:
At least 41 people were killed and 67 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Russian glide bombs struck Zaporizhzhia, local authorities said on Oct. 9.
In Zaporizhzhia , Russian glide bombs destroyed and damaged residential buildings, killing one person and injuring seven others, including a child, Ivan Fedorov , co-chair of the Zaporizhzhia Oblast Defense Council, reported.
Across the whole of Zaporizhzhia Oblast , two people were killed and 18 injured in Russian attacks over the past day, Fedorov added . Russian forces launched 1,039 strikes against 51 settlements in the oblast.
Russia attacked Ukraine overnight with 136 drones, including 93 jet-powered Shahed-type drones, Ukraine's Air Force said. Air defenses shot down or suppressed 114 drones, including 77 jet-powered Shaheds. The Air Force reported drone strikes at eight locations, while debris from intercepted drones fell at seven locations.
In Donetsk Oblast , Russian attacks killed 35 people and injured another 24 over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said. Of those killed, 32 were in Kramatorsk and three in Bilenke.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , two people were killed and three others injured, the regional military administration said. Russian forces launched more than 60 attacks on districts of the oblast using drones, artillery, and aerial bombs.
In Sumy Oblast , one person was killed and 14 others injured, including two children, the l ocal authorities said. Two 12-year-old boys were injured in a drone attack. Russian forces launched nearly 40 attacks against 21 settlements in the oblast over the past day.
In Kherson Oblast , four people were injured, including a child, the regional military administration said. Russian forces targeted critical and social infrastructure as well as residential neighborhoods, damaging 12 private houses, gas pipelines, and vehicles.
In Kharkiv Oblast , three people were injured in Russian attacks on 17 settlements, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. Two men aged 51 and 53 were injured in Zolochiv, while a 72-year-old woman was injured in Khotimlia. Russian forces used aerial bombs, multiple-launch rocket systems, and drones, including FPV drones, in the attacks.
In Chernihiv Oblast , an elderly man was injured after a Russian drone struck a courtyard in a village in the Liubech community, the regional military administration said. Overnight, a Russian Geran-type drone also struck a hypermarket on the outskirts of Chernihiv, causing a fire.
In Ivano-Frankivsk Oblast , a 67-year-old man was killed in a Russian attack on the city of Ivano-Frankivsk, regional Governor Svitlana Onyshchuk said.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,549,490 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,710 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,549,490troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 9.
The number includes 1,710 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,402 tanks, 25,509 armored combat vehicles, 160,412 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,950 artillery systems, 2,199 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,693 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,908 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Ukraine confirms strikes on Russian cruise missile fuel plant, missile facilities
description: Ukraine's military launched an attack on Russia's Tver Oblast overnight on Oct. 9, reportedly targeting a Russian factory that manufactures fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
content:
Ukraine's military launched an attack on several Russian regions overnight on Oct. 9, striking three Russian facilities involved in missile launches and fuel production, including a factory that manufactures fuel components for Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed.
The attacks targeted facilities in Tver and Nizhny Novgorod oblasts, while Russian and Ukrainian monitoring channels separately reported strikes on oil infrastructure in other regions.
In Nizhny Novgorod Oblast, Ukrainian forces struck a facility belonging to the V.P. Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes near Dalneye Konstantinovo-5, the General Staff said .
The institute is part of Russia's Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure (TsENKI), which develops, maintains, and operates rocket launch complexes, fueling equipment, and missile control systems.
Another strike targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near Surovatikha, also in Nizhny Novgorod Oblast. According to the General Staff, the attack was intended to weaken Russia's capacity to produce explosives and rocket fuel.
In Tver Oblast, the General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant, where Telegram monitoring channel Exilenova+ , citing resident accounts, had earlier reported flashes of explosions and smoke.
The plant, which produces components of Decilin-M rocket fuel, as well as fuel additives for diesel and aviation kerosene, was previously struck in a Ukrainian attack in February 2026. The attack destroyed around 6,000 FPV (first-person-view) drones and their components, the General Staff said .
The plant is under sanctions imposed by the U.S., the U.K., and several other countries.
Russia routinely uses Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles missiles to attack Ukrainian cities, including during recent mass missile strikes on Kyiv.
Elsewhere in Russia, a Ukrainian attack reportedly led to a fire at an oil depot located north of the city of Belgorod, according to NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS) monitoring platform.
The extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
In Russia's Komi Republic, Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Lukoil-owned Ukhta oil refinery on the morning of Oct. 9, with footage showing black smoke rising from the facility, independent Russian outlet The Moscow Times reported.
Independent Russian media outlet Astra geolocated eyewitness footage showing smoke rising from the refinery, while Ukrainian monitoring channel Supernova+ reported explosions and drone activity in Ukhta.
The refinery processed approximately 3 million metric tons of oil in 2025, accounting for around 1.1% of Russia's total oil refining output. It produces gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, and vacuum gas oil.
Russian aviation authorities temporarily suspended flights at Ukhta airport amid the attack. Local authorities also declared a drone alert, while the city's mayor, Marina Meteleva, described the situation as under control.
The refinery, located approximately 1,700 kilometers (1,056 miles) from the Ukrainian border, was previously targeted by Ukrainian drones in February 2026 and August 2025.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
While the weaponry used in the reported attack was not immediately clear, Ukraine has often used long-range drones to strike facilities and oil infrastructure that directly support Russia's war in Ukraine.

title: UK to provide $71 million winter aid package to Ukraine
description: The latest announcement comes as Kyiv experienced widespread power outages on Oct. 8 following a Russian attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Over 3 million residents in the capital lost power in what officials described as "an attack on one of the energy facilities important for the city of Kyiv."
content:
The United Kingdom will provide Ukraine with 54 million pounds ($71 million) in humanitarian and energy funding ahead of Ukraine's fifth winter under Russian attack, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced on Oct. 8.
The latest aid package, announced during Miliband's first trip to Ukraine as Foreign Secretary, includes 20 million pounds ($26 million) in funding for emergency repairs to Ukraine's energy grids, as well funding for back-up generators and solar power sources. Another 34 million pounds ($45 million) will support be invested in "securing heating, and maintaining water infrastructure" in anticipation of the winter months, according to a government press release .
The latest announcement comes as Kyiv experienced widespread power outages on Oct. 8 following a Russian attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Over 3 million residents in the capital lost power in what officials described as "an attack on one of the energy facilities important for the city of Kyiv."
Residents across Ukraine are preparing for another harsh winter, with additional Russian attacks expected on energy infrastructure across the country, as Moscow continues to test the resolve of Ukrainians.
Speaking in Kyiv, Miliband said that the latest funding sends a clear message to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
"You cannot wait us out. Until you choose the path of peace, the U.K. will not relent in its support for Ukraine, our values, or our national security. You will remain a pariah," Miliband said.
Earlier in the day, the U.K. published 38 new sanctions listings targeting ships helping Russia evade existing sanctions and a range of companies in Moscow's military-industrial complex, energy, and cryptocurrency sectors.
A staunch ally of Ukraine, London also announced last month that it will provide Ukraine with a £100 million ($135 million) air defense package, including funding for Patriot missiles, as Kyiv prepares for renewed Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure.
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, the U.K. has provided Ukraine with over 1 billion pounds ($1.3 billion) in humanitarian and energy support.

title: UK service member charged with spying for Russia makes first court appearance
description: Under the U.K.'s National Security Act 2023, junior intelligence specialist Teddy Young, 24, was charged with two offenses for allegedly trying to pass protected information to a foreign power between November 2024 and May 2025.
content:
A Royal Navy sailor charged with passing military secrets to Russia appeared in court in London on Oct. 8.
Under the U.K. 's National Security Act 2023, junior intelligence specialist Teddy Young, 24, was charged with two offenses for allegedly trying to pass protected information to a foreign power between November 2024 and May 2025.
"These are very serious charges against a serving member of the armed forces," Commander Helen Flanagan, head of London's Counter Terrorism Policing unit, said . "We have worked extremely closely with relevant operational colleagues within the Ministry of Defense as our investigation has progressed to ensure appropriate measures could be taken to mitigate any potential risks linked to this matter."
Young allegedly used his security clearance to access sensitive defense and intelligence information while deployed aboard a Royal Navy warship. Young subsequently attempted to pass information to Russian authorities using the dark web, according to the Associated Press.
While Young is the first member of the British armed forces to be charged under the National Security Act 2023, he is not the first foreign national to attempt to pass on sensitive information to Russia during its war on Ukraine.
Australian authorities charged a dual Russian-Australian citizen after he allegedly joined Ukraine’s military and tried to pass on information about Ukrainian forces to people linked with Russian intelligence, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said on Aug. 21.
In September 2025, British police arrested three people on suspicion of espionage for Russia.

title: Two trains collide in Lviv, injuring 8
description: The railway operator initially reported that the passenger train's driver suffered a leg injury and four passengers required medical attention. The crew of the electric locomotive was unharmed.
content:
Eight people were injured when a passenger train collided with an electric locomotive at a railway station in Lviv on Oct. 8, Ukrainian authorities and local media reported.
The diesel-powered passenger train, traveling from Lviv to Sokal, collided with the locomotive while departing Pidzamche station, Ukrainian state railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia said .
The railway operator initially reported that the passenger train's driver suffered a leg injury and four passengers required medical attention. The crew of the electric locomotive was unharmed.
The number of injured later rose to eight, according to Tetiana Andreieva, spokesperson for the Lviv Regional Emergency Medical Care Center, who spoke to Suspilne. Five people were hospitalized, while three received treatment at the scene.
Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said emergency crews were working to free the passenger train's driver, who had become trapped inside the cab following the collision.
Emergency responders were also assisting injured passengers at the scene.
Ukrzaliznytsia said railway specialists and emergency services were investigating the circumstances of the collision.
The cause of the crash has not yet been established.

title: 'We were being arrested like terrorists'— Ukrainian journalist says his detention in Austria was brutal
description: The acclaimed journalist was reportedly on an editorial assignment in Vienna with his colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko when he was detained by Austrian authorities.
content:
Editor's note: This story is being updated.
Ukrainian investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach said on Oct. 9 that the Austrian police had brutally detained him and his colleague the previous day and treated them "like terrorists."
He argued that there was no evidence whatsoever for the accusation that they face — spying for Ukrainian military intelligence.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comment from Austria's Interior Ministry and will publish its response once it is received.
The two Ukrainian journalists detained in Austria on Oct. 8 are suspected of espionage, Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said at a press conference on Oct. 9.
Tkach, head of the media outlet Ukrainska Pravda's investigations team, has been released, while cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko is still in custody, Karner said , as cited by the Ausrian newspaper Kleine Zeitung. The Austrian newspaper Der Standard reported that two alleged Ukrainian military intelligence employees had also been detained in Austria.
The International Press Institute (IPI) and Ukrainian media and civil society organizations, including the Institute of Mass Information and the Media Movement, called on Austrian authorities to transparently investigate the detention of Ukrainska Pravda journalist Mykhailo Tkach and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko in Vienna.
"Austrian authorities must clarify the reason for their arrests, including the legal grounds for the seizure of their reporting equipment," IPI Executive Director Scott Griffen said in a statement.
After being released, Tkach said on Oct. 9 that "suddenly, out of nowhere, about seven armed men wearing masks appeared and immediately smashed the windows of our car."
As a result of the armed men's actions, Bondarenko was injured as shattered glass from the car hit him in the face, he added.
"They pointed their guns at us and started shouting something in German," he said. "I immediately raised my hands and told them we were journalists. They quickly dragged Yaroslav and me out of the car and threw us face down onto the road."
He said that he kept repeating that he was a journalist but one of the armed men put his knee on his neck and shouted at him to shut up.
"Then they dragged me into a nearby archway, pushed me up against a wall with my face toward it and told me to keep quiet," Tkach said. "For the first 30 minutes, I had no idea who these people were. My first thought was that someone might have ordered our kidnapping."
He added that "no one had shown us any identification, asked us any questions or offered any explanation, and I hadn't noticed any police markings."
“It felt like we were being arrested as terrorists," Tkach said. "They didn't speak to us at all. They just kept shouting at us, pointing their guns at us. There was absolutely no communication.”
"At 4 a.m. on Oct. 9, Mykhailo Tkach was released after being detained for more than 12 hours in Vienna," Sevhil Musayeva, Ukrainska Pravda's chief editor, wrote on Facebook earlier on Oct. 9. "However, his communication devices have still not been returned, so the editorial team is currently unable to contact him directly. Our colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko was injured during the detention and was hospitalized. Police did not begin questioning him until the early hours of the morning."
She added that the legal status of both journalists is unclear.
"The allegations made against our colleagues while they were detained are unlike anything our editorial team has encountered before and raise serious questions," Musayeva added. “We expect Austrian law enforcement authorities to explain the circumstances surrounding our colleagues’ detention, Yaroslav’s injury, and the reasons why both were held for so long. We also expect clarification of their legal status and the return of their communication devices.”
Musayeva said that Tkach had previously been detained in other countries and released within an hour to an hour and a half once the circumstances had been clarified.
"This is the first time they have been held for more than 12 hours," she argued. "The length of their detention, the nature of the allegations made against our colleagues, Yaroslav’s injury, and our inability to contact Mykhailo directly are all causes of serious concern.”
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said on Oct. 9 that "Ukrainian diplomats and consular officials at the Ukrainian Embassy in Austria have been working with their Austrian counterparts to resolve the situation."
He said that Ukraine's Foreign Ministry is investigating the circumstances of Tkach's detention and trying to establish if Bondarenko has also been released.
Ukrainska Pravda criticized Tkach's detention the previous day. "The editorial office considers this detention illegal and demands his immediate release and an official explanation for the actions of the Austrian law enforcement officers," Musayeva wrote in an announcement .
The acclaimed journalist was reportedly on an editorial assignment in Vienna to locate fugitive Ukrainian Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko when he was detained by Austrian authorities.
Ukrainska Pravda reported on Sept. 23 that Kravchenko had moved to Austria.
Kravchenko was fired by parliament on Sept. 15 amid a major corruption investigation.
He left Ukraine on Sept. 14, under the pretext of an official trip to a conference in Paris. But the organizers told the Kyiv Independent that they had not expected him to attend, strengthening the suspicions that the trip was a fig leaf for fleeing Ukraine to avoid potential charges.
As Kravchenko left Ukraine, he simultaneously approved charges against the head of the anti-corruption agency investigating him. The charges were later dropped as unfounded.
As one of Ukraine's most prominent investigative journalists, Tkach has helped expose corruption and money laundering inside President Volodymyr Zelensky's inner circle.
On Sept. 29, Tkach received a Free Media Award 2026 in Oslo "for his dauntless and consistent investigative wartime journalism."
This is not the first time Tkach has encountered difficulties in his reporting, including being assaulted multiple times throughout his career. Tkach and Bondarenko were previously detained by Polish authorities while reporting on the transit of goods between Poland, Russia, and Belarus in February 2024.

title: 'We always respond in kind' — Zelensky addresses Ukrainian attacks on Russian data center
description: "We certainly are capable," Zelensky said about striking Russian data centers. "We always respond in kind. Regarding data centers, as you all know, they have been and still are striking our data centers."
content:
Responding to journalists' questions in a press pool chat on Oct. 8, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine will continue to retaliate against Russia for strikes on Ukrainian data centers.
"We certainly are capable," Zelensky said about striking Russian data centers. "We always respond in kind. Regarding data centers, as you all know, they have been and still are striking our data centers."
The President's comments follow Ukrainian strikes on a Yandex data center in Russia's Ryazan Oblast on Oct. 8. The attack caused internet disruptions for several banking services, as well as for Google, RuTube, and the website of Russian Railways.
Yandex Cloud later acknowledged an "incident" and power supply problems, warning that the outage could affect other parts of its cloud network and advising customers to move some services elsewhere while engineers worked to restore operations.
"We responded to them," Zelensky told reporters when asked about the Yandex attack. "I cannot share all the details."
The attack came after Russian forces struck Ukrainian data centers and internet providers in late September. Officials said the strikes disrupted service for around 100,000 households as Moscow expands its attacks on Ukraine's internet infrastructure.
"As Russia is not achieving its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said about the attacks.
Zelensky clarified to reporters that Kyiv's retaliation against Russia will not match Moscow's targeting of children after Russian strikes killed dozens across Ukraine, including multiple minors, on Oct. 8.
"Let me tell you frankly: Ukraine certainly, most certainly, does not retaliate against children," Zelensky said. "It does not. And it never will. But certain adults will soon receive a response."

title: Zelensky sends delegation to meet Trump envoys as he hints at secret US-Russia economic talks
description: "Meetings are expected to take place over two days... we are counting on a European team to join our negotiating group," President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
content:
A Ukrainian delegation will meet with U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in the United States on Oct. 9 to discuss proposals for an energy and Black Sea ceasefire, President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters on Oct. 8.
The talks come amid growing uncertainty over Trump's latest push to end Russia's war against Ukraine, with officials in both Washington and Moscow casting doubt on the prospects for progress.
"Meetings are expected to take place over two days," Zelensky said. "And we are counting on a European team to join our negotiating group and the American negotiating group."
The Ukrainian delegation will include Foreign Intelligence Service Chief Rustem Umerov , Zelensky's Chief of Staff Kyrylo Budanov , and other senior officials, the president said.
The meeting follows comments by U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said on Oct. 8 that ending Russia's war against Ukraine through negotiations was currently unattainable.
Rubio said that the goal remained out of reach because Russia insists on gaining full control over Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast without fighting, a demand Kyiv has rejected.
The latest rounds of peace negotiations have stalled over Moscow's territorial demands. The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the partially occupied Donbas , a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine . Moscow is effectively seeking territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Ukraine has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
Responding to Rubio, Zelensky said that Washington could not simultaneously discuss future economic projects with Russia while describing diplomacy as being at an impasse.
Asked what kind of economic deals Washington and Moscow might be discussing, Zelensky told reporters that Ukraine "knows a lot" but was not ready to discuss the matter publicly.
"I'm simply not ready to talk about it publicly or in detail," the president said.
The latest diplomatic effort began in early September, when Trump's envoys traveled to Kyiv and Moscow seeking progress before the U.S. midterm elections.
The visits produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
A month later, however, even that meeting remains uncertain.
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said on Oct. 7 that there were currently no plans for U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine.

title: Russia lifts quarantine in Irkutsk region, where lab worker allegedly died of plague
description: Initial reports raised concerns that 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who worked at the Anti-Plague Institute, might have died of pneumonic plague after a laboratory accident.
content:
Quarantine has been lifted in Russia's Irkutsk region, where a lab technician at the Anti-Plague Institute of Eastern Siberia and the Far East died on Oct. 2, Russian state media reported on Oct. 8.
Initial reports raised concerns that 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, who worked at the institute, might have died of pneumonic plague after a laboratory accident.
Citing a source close to law enforcement agencies, the independent Siberian news outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal) wrote on Oct. 2 that FSB officers, Russia's security services, had escorted ambulances transporting people who had been in contact with Shipilova for medical examinations.
RFE/RL's Siberia.Realities also reported on Oct. 5, citing a relative of an institute employee who spoke on condition of anonymity, that more than 60 staff members had been confined to the facility as a precautionary measure.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify this information.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's federal public health agency, publicly acknowledged that "anti-epidemic measures" were linked to the illness of an institute employee. However, the Russian state media and local authorities have claimed that it was "pneumonia of unknown etiology."
Although he didn't name Shipilova, Irkutsk Oblast Governor Igor Kobzev said in his Oct. 8 Telegram address that "the patient" had been vaccinated against dangerous infections she worked with at the institute and that proper safety controls when working with pathogenic microorganisms had been "confirmed."
He also said that "nearly 5,000 laboratory tests" found no dangerous pathogenic microorganisms.

title: Open letter to the US administration: The G20 invitation to Putin should come with conditions
description:
The Trump administration recently announced that it has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to December's G20 summit in Miami.

This invitation erodes the well-deserved isolation of Putin for his brutal and unprovoked invasion of Ukraine. Putin last appeared on U.S. soil for a bilateral meeting with President Donald Trump in Anchorage, Alaska, in August 2025. That meeting produced no progress toward ending the war that Putin started against Ukraine.

If anything, the Russian bombardment of
content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin arrives for his inauguration ceremony at the Grand Kremlin Palace in Moscow, Russia, on May 7, 2024. (Sergei Bobylyov/Pool/AFP/Getty Images)
Former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Ukraine, Russia, Belarus, and Moldova
The Trump administration recently announced that it has invited Russian President Vladimir Putin to December's G20 summit in Miami.
This invitation erodes the well-deserved isolation of Putin for his brutal and unprovoked invasion of Ukraine . Putin last appeared on U.S. soil for a bilateral meeting with President Donald Trump in Anchorage, Alaska, in August 2025. That meeting produced no progress toward ending the war that Putin started against Ukraine.
If anything, the Russian bombardment of Ukraine has only increased over the past year.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky , not Putin, is the leader who should be invited to the G20 gathering. Zelensky leads a country of incredibly brave and determined people whose fight for their freedom should inspire us all.
"The only issue on which G20 leaders should engage Putin is ending his war against Ukraine."
If the invitation to Putin is not rescinded, as a bipartisan group of U.S. Senators urged , it should be made conditional on the following two points:
First, Putin should announce and observe an immediate, unconditional, and full ceasefire to the war he started, not simply one restricted to energy facilities, as proposed by President Trump, but rejected by Putin . He should not be allowed to set foot on U.S. soil again as long as his forces continue to attack Ukraine.
Second, Putin should commit to meeting face-to-face at the G20 with President Zelensky, along with President Trump and leaders from the European Union , to negotiate a permanent end to the war.
European nations have borne the brunt of assistance to Ukraine after direct aid from the United States ended last year, and they deserve a seat at the table. Any negotiation should ensure the full sovereignty and territorial integrity of Ukraine, the return of Ukrainian prisoners of war and kidnapped children, the right for Ukraine to determine its own future, and reparations for the damage Russia has caused.
Putin started the war against Ukraine in 2014, not just in 2022, and bears responsibility for the deaths and injuries of hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians, to say nothing of more than 1.5 million Russian soldiers.
Putin has been indicted by the International Criminal Court for war crimes, specifically for directing the targeted abduction of tens of thousands of Ukraine's children and their transport into Russia. He created the worst security crisis on the European continent since World War II , and it is he who refuses to end the fighting.
President Zelensky and Ukraine, by contrast, have repeatedly demonstrated flexibility and willingness to end the war, though not on the condition of Ukraine's capitulation to Russia.
At last month's United Nations gathering, 51 countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement , urging the Kremlin to agree to a full ceasefire and enter meaningful negotiations. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov countered that Russia would not pause its "special military operation" even during negotiations, once again illustrating that Russia, not Ukraine, is responsible for prolonging this war.
As the group of bipartisan Senators noted, allowing Putin to participate in a G20 Summit in the United States "raises serious concerns about legitimizing and normalizing a government that continues to attack Ukrainian civilian targets every day."
President Zelensky stated that the invitation for Putin to attend the G20 meeting could be “one of the best opportunities proposed by the U.S. side. I believe this is an opportunity for a trilateral meeting that could yield results."
When Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the invitation to Putin, he described it as "an opportunity for him (Putin) to engage not just with the (American) president but with other world leaders." The only issue on which G20 leaders should engage Putin is ending his war against Ukraine.
If Putin agrees to that, then the Trump administration will deserve credit for helping end the war Putin started. However, in the more likely scenario that Putin doesn't agree, he should stay in Moscow, while the West ramps up assistance for Ukraine and tightens sanctions on Russia to help Ukraine achieve victory.
We welcome others to join in this call. Ian Brzezinski, Former Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Europe and Policy
Michael Carpenter, Former U.S. Ambassador to the OSCE, Former NSC Senior Director for Europe
Kim Davis, Founding Partner, Charlesbank Capital Partners

David J. Kramer, Former Deputy Assistant Secretary of State for Ukraine, Russia, Belarus, and Moldova
Nadia McConnell, President, U.S.-Ukraine Foundation
Robert McConnell, co-founder, U.S.-Ukraine Foundation
William Taylor, Former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine

David J. Kramer is executive director of the George W. Bush Institute and vice president of the George W. Bush Presidential Center.

title: Ukraine war latest: Russian glide bomb strikes in Kramatorsk kill at least 33
description:
Key developments on Oct. 8:

 * At least 33 dead after Russian glide bomb strikes Kramatorsk buses
 * Russian drone barrage on Kyiv kills 4, injures 19, disrupts electricity, water supplies
 * Polish SIM cards found in Russian drones downed in Poland
 * US, Russia confirm Trump's latest Ukraine peace push is falling apart
 * Ukraine strikes Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Siberia, General Staff confirms
 * UK ramps up sanctions against Russian shadow fleet, crypto industry, big oil

A Russian glid
content:
A Russian glide bomb strike on two minibuses in Kramatorsk killed 33 people on the morning of Oct. 8, Ukraine's emergency service (DSNS) said.
Twenty-two more people were injured in the Russian attack, Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin said . Fire broke out in at least two busses following the Russian strikes, according to DSNS .
"Russia comes to the Ukrainian land with death. She hits our cities, kills our people and multiplies her crimes every day," Filashkin said .
