President Volodymyr Zelensky said that doctors were still fighting for the lives of some of the injured people and warned that the number of dead may still increase. Two dead people could not yet be identified due to the severity of their injuries, he added.
"This strike will not go without our response. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this," Zelensky said.
The Kramatorsk and Sloviansk military administrations ordered the stop of all public transport.
"The Russians are targeting civilians. For them, a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one hit can kill as many people as possible," Filashkin said.
Across Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast, four more people had been killed and six injured by Russian attacks as of the morning of Oct. 8, prior to the Kramatorsk strike, according to the governor .
In total, Russian forces shelled settlements in the Donetsk region 31 times over the last day, and 256 people, including 32 children, were evacuated from the front line, according to the Donetsk governor.
Russian drone strikes on Oct. 8 have killed four people and injured at least 19 in Kyiv, the city's authorities said.
A Russian drone struck a four-story commercial building in Solomyanskyi district, killing two and injuring two, and leading to a fire, while the wreckage of another fell on the Holosiivskyi district, Klitschko said .
Prior to that strike, Klitschko said that Russian attacks on the capital this morning had killed one person and injured 11 others.
A fourth person died of their injuries in hospital, the Kyiv city military administration (KMDA) said in the afternoon.
Klitschko raised the number of injured to 19, 13 of which were hospitalized, in an update on 07:21 p.m. local time.
At 10:00 a.m. local time, Ukraine’s biggest private energy firm DTEK announced emergency energy shutdowns in Brovary, Buchanskyi, Vyshgorod, and Boryspil districts of the oblast.
Shortly after, KMDA announced that the right bank of Kyiv may experience interruptions in water supply, as the power decrease in the electricity grid also meant a decrease in pressure of the water supply network. This applied especially to the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomyanskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
The drop in voltage from external power supply centers also temporarily halted Kyiv Metro train services and escalator operations, the KMDA said .
DSNS also said that a fire broke out at a logistics facility in the Buchanskyi district in Kyiv Oblast following a Russian drone strike.
In Sviatopetrivske in Buchanskyi district, a school-kindergarten and a nearby playground in a residential complex were damaged in the attack, Kyiv Oblast Governor Tymur Tkachenko said . In another settlement in the district, a woman was injured and hospitalized, he added.
Overnight, Russian drone strikes on Kyiv had already killed four people and injured 21 across four districts, KMDA said .
Polish military prosecutors found Polish SIM cards in some of the Russian drones downed during a Russian mass drone incursion into the country on the night of Sept. 9 to Sept. 10, 2025, RMF24 reported on Oct. 8.
Polish authorities didn't disclose whether three Polish SIM cards had been stolen or obtained illegaly, according to RMF24 . The investigation was discontinued after it did not lead to the identification of the specific people responsible for the Russian incursion.
"The investigation was discontinued because the perpetrator of the crime of violating Polish airspace and thus posing a threat to public safety was not identified," Marcin Kozak, spokesman of the District Prosecutor’s Office in Lublin, said.
On Sept. 9, 2025, more than 30 Gerbera-type drones breached Polish airspace, some of which were shot down by the Polish military, RMF24 reported .
Ending Russia's war against Ukraine through negotiations is currently unattainable , U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Greek media outlet Kathimerini on Oct. 8, casting further doubt on President Donald Trump's latest push to broker peace.
The comments confirm earlier Kyiv Independent reporting that Washington's latest effort to advance negotiations faces growing uncertainty.
At this point, there appears to be no prospect of a negotiated settlement, Rubio said . He added that the goal remains out of reach because Russia insists on gaining full control over Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast without fighting, a demand Kyiv has rejected.
The latest rounds of peace negotiations have also stalled over Moscow's territorial demands.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine . Moscow is effectively seeking territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Ukraine has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
The diplomatic effort now faces another obstacle: Moscow has given little indication that it intends to take part in further talks. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said on Oct. 7 that there were currently no plans for U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine.
"There are currently no plans to hold talks in this format," Ryabkov told reporters.
The latest effort began in early September, when Trump's envoys traveled to Kyiv and Moscow seeking progress before the U.S. midterm elections. The trips produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
A month later, however, even the trilateral meeting remains uncertain.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Oct. 8 that Ukrainian negotiators will meet with Trump's envoys in the U.S. later this week to discuss the prospects for peace talks with Russia.
Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that its forces struck Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Russia's Omsk Oblast on Oct. 8.
"The destruction of such facilities is the exercise by Ukraine of its inalienable right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," the General Staff said .
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point had previously reported an attack on the refinery, saying that the refinery was hit with its own long-range FP-1 attack drones.
Videos and images from local residents, shared by Ukrainian monitoring channels , show explosions, fire, and smoke rising from the area surrounding the oil refinery.
Omsk Oblast Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed that there was a drone attack on the region. Ukrainian authorities have not yet confirm a strike on the refinery.
Omsk is located in southwestern Siberia, north of the Kazakh border. The city of more than 1 million people is some 2,500 kilometers (about 1,550 miles) east of Ukraine controlled territory.
The Omsk oil refinery is owned by Russia's state-owned energy giant Gazprom. It's the country's largest refinery by refining capacity, processing more than 21 million metric tons of crude oil per year.
The plant produces a wide range of fuels, lubricants, and petrochemical products and is involved in supplying the Russian military, Ukraine's General Staff said after Ukraine struck the refinery on July 6. According to the military , the facility has a refining depth of about 99%, one of the highest rates in Russia.
Earlier, an overnight Ukrainian strike on the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery in Russia's Bashkortostan region caused a large blaze at the plant, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Oct. 8.
The U.K. published 38 new sanctions listings on Oct. 8, targeting ships helping Russia evade existing sanctions and a range of companies in Moscow's military-industrial complex, energy, and cryptocurrency sectors.
"The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences," reads a U.K. government press release.
Among the businesses in the new sanctions listings are three cryptocurrency exchanges and two payment platforms.
Xeltox Enterprises, one of those listed entities has "been involved in obtaining a benefit from or supporting the government of Russia by carrying on business in a sector of strategic significance (...) the financial services sector," reads the U.K. government's sanctions listing .
Russia has increasingly sought to use cryptocurrency , which is hard to track, to circumvent global sanctions, and the new U.K. sanctions target the "A7" network, which is at the heart of Moscow's attempts to evade financial sanctions.
That has prompted the U.K., the U.S ., the EU , and Ukraine to target crypto schemes in recent sanctions packages.
Also featuring on the listings are two further oil companies: Zarubezhneft and INK Capital.
"The U.K. was the first country in the G7 to sanction the top four Russian oil companies," reads the press statement.
The U.K. has also added 12 ships to its list of sanctioned vessels accused of being part of Russia's shadow fleet — dilapidated vessels suspected of helping Moscow evade price caps and bans on its trade in oil and gas.
That takes the number of ships sanctioned by the U.K. to 645 and the total number of Russia sanctions to 3,537.

title: Russian attacks plunge Kyiv into near-total darkness, disrupt power, metro, water supply
description: The drop in voltage temporarily halted Kyiv Metro train services and escalator operations, the Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) said. Other parts of the capital's public transport network were also affected.
content:
Residential buildings are seen without power during widespread outages following Russian attacks on Kyiv, Ukraine on Oct. 8, 2026. (Olga Rudenko / The Kyiv Independent)
The Russian attack on Ukrainian energy infrastructure on Oct. 8 has caused widespread power outages across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, home to over 3 million people.
"There was an attack on one of the energy facilities important for the city of Kyiv," Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said . "Energy workers are doing everything possible to restore electricity as quickly as possible." Throughout the day, the city experienced power outages in most neighborhoods, with the city metro shut down due to lack of electricity. Without power, many residents also reported a lack of running water. As of 12:30 a.m. local time on Oct. 9, areas of the city to the left of the Dnipro river still remained without power, while electricity has been restored in parts of the right bank. Ukraine's state electrical operator, Ukrenergo, announced that limits to electricity consumption will be placed on certain regions of the country on Oct. 9 due to the attack.
DTEK subsequently announced that emergency power cuts had been introduced on Kyiv's right bank and in the Bucha and Vyshhorod districts of Kyiv Oblast on Ukrenergo's orders.
Допис, поширений Kyiv Independent (@kyivindependent_official)
Kyiv Independent reporters across the city on Oct. 8 observed power cuts in Podil, Pechersk, Solomianskyi districts, and the left bank. Ahead of winter, the sound of generators returned to Kyiv throughout affected neighborhoods, as businesses sought to keep operating. In the dark of the evening, buskers continued to perform on the capital's main street of Khreshchatyk.
The drop in voltage temporarily halted Kyiv Metro train services and escalator operations, the Kyiv City State Administration (KMDA) said . Other parts of the capital's public transport network were also affected.
The city administration said that some services had been temporarily suspended because of the drop in voltage, while authorities were working to replace part of the Borshchahivka high-speed tram line with buses.
Kyiv Independent reporters described heavy traffic, people hailing taxis, and streets filling with people, as commuters sought alternative transportation.
The power disruption also affected Kyiv's water network. The city administration warned that residents on the right bank could experience interruptions in water supply because lower voltage had reduced pressure in the system, particularly in the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi, and Shevchenkivskyi districts. By 9 p.m. local time, pumping equipment was reactivated, though the city said it would take "some time" to fully restore normal water pressure throughout the entire network.
Earlier on Oct. 8, Ukraine's largest private energy company, DTEK, announced emergency power shutdowns in parts of Kyiv Oblast, including the Brovary, Bucha, Vyshhorod, and Boryspil districts.
The Kyiv Oblast Military Administration said Russia had significantly intensified attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure in recent weeks, targeting power lines and transformers and disrupting electricity transmission to consumers.
Energy workers are operating around the clock to repair damaged equipment and stabilize the grid, the administration said.
The disruptions followed a morning of repeated Russian drone strikes on Kyiv and the surrounding region that killed and injured civilians and damaged buildings and infrastructure.
Russian drone strikes on Oct. 8 killed four people and injured at least 19 in Kyiv, the city's Mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said .
Polina Moroziuk is a junior reporter at the Kyiv Independent. She holds an MSc in Human Rights and Politics from the London School of Economics and a BSc from the University of Amsterdam. Before joining the newsroom, she worked in human rights advocacy and as a project assistant at a research and consultancy organisation, supporting projects for international organisations including UNICEF and War Child, with a focus on Ukraine and the Middle East.

title: Moldova ready to take in more Ukrainian refugees come winter, Sandu says
description: "If this winter in Ukraine is as difficult as the whole world expects, we are ready to receive as many people as need safety," Moldovan President Maia Sandu said at the Moldova Security Forum in Chisinau on Oct. 8.
content:
Moldova is ready to take in more Ukrainian refugees this winter if Russia inflicts another humanitarian crisis upon the country through its targeted mass attacks, President Maia Sandu said on Oct. 8.
"Since 2022, more than one million Ukrainians fleeing the war have arrived in Moldova, and around 100,000 have found a home here. If this winter in Ukraine is as difficult as the whole world expects, we are ready to receive as many people as need safety," Sandu said at the Moldova Security Forum in Chisinau, as reported by Moldovan media outlet Newsmaker.
Russia's targeting of Ukraine's energy infrastructure last winter led to prolonged blackouts and heating outages across the country during sub-zero temperatures.
Speaking about preparations for the coming winter, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Ukraine is better prepared than last year, but warned that Russia has strengthened its own capabilities by stockpiling jet-powered drones and missiles.
At the Moldova Security Forum, former Moldovan Prime Minister and current Presidential Special Envoy Dorin Recean also said that Moldova is preparing for the coming winter logistics-wise, as Ukraine and Moldova's energy grids are interconnected.
Moldova has dealt with repeated violations of its airspace during Russia's attacks against Ukraine.
After five Russian Banderol missiles and drones, exploded on the country's territory during the overnight attack against Ukraine on Oct. 3, Sandu warned that "(Russia's) war is dangerously reaching Moldova."
In response to the growing threat, Moldova announced on Oct. 7 that it plans to build protective shelters at border crossings with Ukraine where border guards and people in nearby areas can take cover during drone incursions.

title: Ukraine strikes Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Siberia, General Staff confirms
description: Videos and images from local residents, shared by Ukrainian monitoring channels, show explosions, fire, and smoke rising from the area surrounding the oil refinery.
content:
Ukraine's General Staff confirmed that its forces struck Russia's Omsk oil refinery in Russia's Omsk Oblast on Oct. 8.
"The destruction of such facilities is the exercise by Ukraine of its inalienable right to self-defense in accordance with Article 51 of the UN Charter and is aimed at reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," the General Staff said .
Ukrainian drone manufacturer Fire Point had previously reported an attack on the refinery, saying that the refinery was hit with its own long-range FP-1 attack drones.
Videos and images from local residents, shared by Ukrainian monitoring channels , show explosions, fire, and smoke rising from the area surrounding the oil refinery.
Omsk Oblast Governor Vitaly Khotsenko confirmed that there was a drone attack on the region. Ukrainian authorities have not yet confirm a strike on the refinery.
Omsk is located in southwestern Siberia, north of the Kazakh border. The city of more than 1 million people is some 2,500 kilometers (about 1,550 miles) east of Ukraine controlled territory.
The Omsk oil refinery is owned by Russia's state-owned energy giant Gazprom. It's the country's largest refinery by refining capacity, processing more than 21 million metric tons of crude oil per year.
The plant produces a wide range of fuels, lubricants, and petrochemical products and is involved in supplying the Russian military, Ukraine's General Staff said after Ukraine struck the refinery on July 6. According to the military , the facility has a refining depth of about 99%, one of the highest rates in Russia.
Earlier, an overnight Ukrainian strike on the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery in Russia's Bashkortostan region caused a large blaze at the plant, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Oct. 8.
Several images and videos show the moment the plant was struck, as well as thick smoke and fire coming from the grounds of the refinery.
"(The facility) is one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical complexes," the General Staff said in a post on social media. "The facility has a processing capacity of up to 10 million (metric) tons of hydrocarbon feedstock per year and produces automotive gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, bitumen, polyethylene, and other oil refining and petrochemical products."

title: Polish SIM cards found in Russian drones downed in Poland
description: An investigation on a mass Russian drone incursion into Polish air space on Sept. 9 concluded on Oct. 8.
content:
Polish military prosecutors found Polish SIM cards in some of the Russian drones downed during a Russian mass drone incursion into the country on the night of Sept. 9 to Sept. 10, 2025, RMF24 reported on Oct. 8.
Polish authorities didn't disclose whether three Polish SIM cards had been stolen or obtained illegaly, according to RMF24 . The investigation was discontinued after it did not lead to the identification of the specific people responsible for the Russian incursion.
"The investigation was discontinued because the perpetrator of the crime of violating Polish airspace and thus posing a threat to public safety was not identified," Marcin Kozak, spokesman of the District Prosecutor’s Office in Lublin, said.
On Sept. 9, 2025, more than 30 Gerbera-type drones breached Polish airspace, some of which were shot down by the Polish military, RMF24 reported .
In attacks on Ukraine from the territory of Belarus , Russia likely used Belarusian Long-Term Evolution (LTE) networks, as well as a network of repeater stations on Belarusian territory, to help provide stable signals to Russian Shahed-type drones used in mass attacks on Ukraine, two Ukrainian officials said on Sept. 14, 2026.
The revelation came two days after Russia sent hundreds of drones, hugging Ukraine's northern border, in a rare a mass attack targeting regions in western Ukraine on Sept. 12. Speaking on a Radio NV livestream, Presidential Advisor Serhii "Flash" Beskretnov said the flight path of the drones used in the attack suggested the use of Belarusian mobile networks for the cross-border attacks.
Lacking access to technology like SpaceX's Starlink, Russia consistently uses a mix of innovative radio technology to maintain connection with Shahed-type drones during mass attacks on Ukraine.
On Sept. 13 , 2026, Tusk warned that Russian escalation could intensify in the upcoming months, following Russian strikes on a Polish-Ukrainian border crossing and a passenger train. "The escalation of actions of the Russian Federation is becoming a fact and its examples are getting closer and closer to our borders," Tusk said in a briefing with defense officials . "What can be expected is that the next weeks and months will be a period of very intensive actions from the Russian side. Unfortunately, we cannot rule out that this escalation will also concern our territory."
Poland will change procedures for military aircraft and helicopters that engage objects entering from the direction of Russia, Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said on Sept. 28, 2026. Under the current peacetime procedure, Polish pilots must fly close enough to visually confirm a target in Polish airspace before firing at it.
The new procedures will replace this visual identification with so-called positive identification, meaning the radar reading alone will be enough for the pilot or the operational commander to authorize shooting down the object, Polish broadcaster RMF24 reported.
This procedure would allow Polish forces to shoot down missiles or drones entering Polish airspace from the direction of Russia faster than previously.

title: Drones above, robots below — inside Operation Vivaldi, Ukraine’s push to recapture territory in Donetsk Oblast
description:
DONETSK OBLAST — On a screen, live footage from a reconnaissance drone shows two men in Ukrainian pixel camouflage dashing in short bursts through the ruins of apartment buildings. Then they vanish into a basement.

It is late summer, and the 3rd Army Corps and attached units are fully engaged in a counteroffensive in the Lyman sector called Operation Vivaldi. Russian forces are trying to recapture Lyman, a city in Donetsk Oblast that Russian officials have claimed their forces control. Ukrainia
content:
Tsyhan and Kalash, combat wing operators of the Darts crew of the NAFO, the 66th Mechanized Brigade, set the drone up for launch in the Lyman sector, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Aug. 11, 2026. (Diana Delyurman / The Kyiv Independent)
DONETSK OBLAST — On a screen, live footage from a reconnaissance drone shows two men in Ukrainian pixel camouflage dashing in short bursts through the ruins of apartment buildings. Then they vanish into a basement.
It is late summer, and the 3rd Army Corps and attached units are fully engaged in a counteroffensive in the Lyman sector called Operation Vivaldi . Russian forces are trying to recapture Lyman, a city in Donetsk Oblast that Russian officials have claimed their forces control. Ukrainian infantry on the ground tell a different story.
For weeks, the operation ran under a news blackout until 3rd Army Corps commander Brig. Gen. Andrii Biletskyi made it public on Sept. 15 . By late September, the corps said it had retaken 176 square kilometers using closely coordinated infantry, air defense, electronic warfare, aerial drone units, and unmanned ground vehicles.
Watching the video feed are drone operators from the 66th Mechanized Brigade, subordinate to the 3rd Army Corps. They are waiting for a batch of Darts, fixed-wing strike drones, to join the fight for Lyman .
Their commander, call sign Deputat, is rushing to bring the drones. His car races down a road beneath tunnels of anti-drone netting, pine forests on either side, a landscape typical of northern Donetsk Oblast. Out of the darkness, a roadside coffee stand appears, glowing faintly. The car speeds past, then turns off onto rough ground.
"Turn on the electronic warfare device," Deputat orders a soldier in the car.
After some time, Deputat stops, quickly unloads the cargo, shakes hands with the soldiers, and drives off. The crew carries the drones into the dugout. They moved into this position only recently, after pushing closer to the front line. The gray zone is less than 10 kilometers away.
Four men live, sleep, and work in the cramped shelter. Crews usually rotate every couple of weeks, but heavy Russian shelling near the positions can delay a rotation.
In one corner is a workstation: a desk with several screens, one showing a video call with other units, another a live map of Donetsk Oblast. The areas marked gray or occupied are different from the picture Russian commanders paint. The soldiers listen to the call as they prepare to join a combined strike.
For hours, units attached to the 3rd Army Corps have been striking a Russian artillery position with HIMARS rockets and drones. According to the 3rd Army Corps, such missions play a crucial role in the operation by pushing Russian mortar and artillery crews out of the area and clearing the way for the infantry.
On the call, someone says, "If I were in their shoes, I'd hop on a motorcycle and get the hell out of there." The soldiers in the dugout laugh. The Ukrainians say the Russian crew won't abandon its howitzer because its soldiers are more afraid of their own commanders.
The strike is delayed. As the wait drags on, the young men grow restless and step out into the dugout's corridor to smoke. Kalash, a soldier with light stubble, is the oldest in the crew. The others jokingly call him Mom. As he cooks breakfast on a camping stove, the smell of scrambled eggs and sausage fills the damp air.
Finally, the duty officer on the call says, "Let's start the mission."
"This is the NAFO crew. We want to join the strike on the howitzer," replies a soldier with the call sign Intelihent, who is piloting today. Every member of the crew can do every job: assemble the drone, prepare it for launch, navigate for the pilot, and fly the strike.
Tsyhan, tall and tanned, assembles a Dart. It reminds him of building Lego as a kid, he says. He and Kalash carry the drone out into the field, set it up for launch, and talk over the radio with the men in the dugout.
"Get out of there," comes the voice over the radio.
The drone must fly several dozen kilometers. Intelihent works the controls while Bratok, a dark-haired soldier, helps him navigate. Back in the dugout, all four stare at the screen, fidgeting nervously on the wooden bench.
"NAFO, locking on target," Intelihent says.
The drone strikes. Direct hit. The men cheer and clink cans of energy drink.
On the reconnaissance drone's feed, a stand of trees bursts into flames. Russian soldiers run out of a dugout and try to put out the fire. Then the feed cuts out. Pleased, the men post screenshots to the platoon's group chat. But someone on the call reports that the smoke is clearing and the target has survived. They must strike again.
"Don't worry, we've got plenty of planes," Kalash tells the others.
But the threat of retaliatory strikes looms over the dugout. Drone operators are among Russia's top targets.
"I think it'll be a few days before they come after us," Tsyhan says.
Eventually, several Ukrainian units working together destroy the Russian artillery position. The 3rd Army Corps said coordination between neighboring units played a key role in the operation.
The men finish the breakfast Kalash made. Some stretch out on camping mats on the wooden benches and sleep fully dressed. Another strike request could come at any moment.
Bratok is on duty, keeping an eye on the screens. To pass the time, he flips through live feeds from reconnaissance drones and unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs). On the screens, the war plays out in real time across the Lyman sector. The video feed from a ground robot catches his eye: a dirt road, and in the corner a tiny call sign that reads Kuzya.
Elsewhere in the Lyman sector, Kuzya himself is watching the same feed. The young redhead was one of the first UGV operators in the 66th Brigade's tank battalion. He used to be a driver, risking his life to bring food, medicine, and ammunition to the infantry. He still delivers supplies, but at far less risk. His UGVs can carry half a metric ton of cargo and keep going even after hitting a mine.
The battalion began building up its UGV capabilities in early 2026. They learned how to use ground drones from the 3rd Army Corps. Now, the 66th Brigade ranks among the top five units for UGV use, according to the Delta system's June 2026 rating. According to the team, its 20 operators now cover most of the battalion's logistics, running 100 to 150 missions a month and rarely taking a day off.
At first, the battalion's commanders were skeptical of the robots, until a heavily mined road left them unable to resupply a group of Mavic operators. Today, UGVs play an important role in Operation Vivaldi. The 96th Separate Support Battalion’s robots move ahead of the infantry and clear mines. Some are carried behind Russian lines by drones and launch an assault. But less visible work, logistics, matters just as much.
"Soldiers win battles, but logistics wins wars," says Aibolit, a burly man whose long beard gives him a Viking look. At the UGV hub, he decides which cargo goes on which vehicle.
The increased use of UGVs for logistics in the 3rd Army Corps and its attached units means infantry can reach the front line in armored vehicles or on foot, carrying only light backpacks. Reliable logistics also lets support teams deliver small comforts to the front, lifting the morale of infantrymen who may hold the same position for a month.
Orders come in every day. A soldier can order something in the morning and be drinking a soda in the gray zone by midnight. "It's like ordering pizza," Aibolit says.
As evening falls, the men prepare two vehicles, open platforms on massive wheels, for a mission. They load packs of bottled water, fuel canisters, a generator, and sealed boxes of food the soldiers ordered. It takes them only minutes.
"Is the sky clear?" Aibolit asks over the radio.
"Negative. Lancet threat," comes the reply.
"We're holding all movement," Aibolit says.
A drone icon flashes on their screens. It seems to be heading straight for the hub. "Maybe it'll come here, maybe somewhere else," one of them says, and shrugs. The soldiers play it down, saying their town is quiet, yet not a day goes by without a Russian strike. To disrupt Ukrainian logistics, Russian forces freely use guided bombs, including against targets with no apparent military value.
Once the threat has passed, the men drive the vehicles out into the yard. A few minutes later, the robots roll off into the darkness.
Kuzya usually takes the vehicles into the gray zone, where the ground is heavily mined. He knows every pothole and bush on the route. His screen is almost entirely black, except for a stretch of cratered road lit by the robot's headlight.
Along the way, he passes wrecked cars marked with a white "Z." Stray dogs run up and bark at the strange visitor. Before long, they get used to it and trot alongside until they lose interest. Kuzya smiles.
Eventually, the robot stops. Soldiers in camouflage appear on the black-and-white screen and quickly unload the cargo. One walks up to the camera and gives Kuzya a thumbs-up before they disappear into the woods.
Kuzya turns the robot around to reload for the next mission. On a narrow dirt road, it meets another robot, and the two little vehicles circle each other as if they were dancing.
That evening, Deputat drives back from another delivery to his soldiers, beneath the netting, stars peeking through the mesh. A burned-out SUV, recently hit by a Russian Lancet, lies by the roadside.
"When you're coming back from the positions and you see the coffee stand, you know you're safe," he says.
Diana Deliurman is a Ukrainian independent journalist and photographer. Born in Odesa, Ukraine, in 2000, she earned a degree in History of Art from Taras Shevchenko National University of Kyiv. During her studies, she began her journalism career, taking part in various training programs and fellowships, including an internship at the Kyiv bureau of Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty. Since then, her reporting and photography have been published by outlets including The Kyiv Independent, The Telegraph, The Conversationalist, Frontliner, and LB.ua. She is also a contributor to Getty Images.

title: Ukrainian actor Serhii Strelnikov enlists in Unmanned Systems Forces
description: Strelnikov has starred in several critically acclaimed films in recent years, including the 2026 action-thriller "Killhouse," where he played a special forces commander.
content:
Ukrainian actor Serhii Strelnikov announced on Oct. 8 that he had enlisted in the Unmanned Systems Forces, calling it "an honor to be among these people."
"I am committed to learning, adapting to new conditions, and conscientiously fulfilling the duties entrusted to me," he wrote in an Instagram post.
According to Strelnikov, he has joined the Ferro-6 Unmanned Systems Battalion of the 9th Separate Unmanned Systems Brigade, which he described as "consisting at its core of soldiers with infantry combat experience who now locate and destroy the enemy from the air."
Strelnikov has starred in several critically acclaimed films in recent years, including the lead in the historical drama "Dovbush" (2023). The film is based on Oleksa Dovbush, a legendary 18th-century Ukrainian outlaw who became a folk hero in the Carpathian Mountains during the time of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth.
He also played Special Forces Commander "Sova" in the 2026 action thriller " Killhouse ," based on a real-life rescue mission conducted by Ukraine's special forces. The Ukrainian Oscar Committee shortlisted the film as a potential submission for the country at the 2027 Academy Awards.
Many prominent figures from Ukraine's cultural sphere have enlisted in the Armed Forces of Ukraine since the start of the full-scale war to help defend the country against Russian aggression. Strelnikov's "Killhouse" co-star, Denys Kapustin, enlisted in the 3rd Assault Brigade after filming of the action thriller wrapped.

title: US, Russia confirm Trump's latest Ukraine peace push is falling apart
description: At this point, there appears to be no prospect of a negotiated settlement, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
content:
Editor's note: This story has been updated to include President Volodymyr Zelensky's remarks.
Ending Russia's war against Ukraine through negotiations is currently unattainable, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Greek media outlet Kathimerini on Oct. 8, casting further doubt on President Donald Trump's latest push to broker peace.
The comments confirm earlier Kyiv Independent reporting that Washington's latest effort to advance negotiations faces growing uncertainty.
At this point, there appears to be no prospect of a negotiated settlement, Rubio said . He added that the goal remains out of reach because Russia insists on gaining full control over Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast without fighting, a demand Kyiv has rejected.
The latest rounds of peace negotiations have also stalled over Moscow's territorial demands.
The Kremlin has repeatedly rejected a ceasefire and demanded that Kyiv surrender the partially occupied Donbas, a strategically important region in eastern Ukraine . Moscow is effectively seeking territory that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Ukraine has instead called for a ceasefire along the current front line.
The diplomatic effort now faces another obstacle: Moscow has given little indication that it intends to take part in further talks. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said on Oct. 7 that there were currently no plans for U.S.-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine.
"There are currently no plans to hold talks in this format," Ryabkov told reporters.
The latest effort began in early September, when Trump's envoys traveled to Kyiv and Moscow seeking progress before the U.S. midterm elections. The trips produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, Russia, and the U.S.
A month later, however, even the trilateral meeting remains uncertain.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Oct. 8 that Ukrainian negotiators will meet with Trump's envoys in the U.S. later this week to discuss the prospects for peace talks with Russia.
"You can't, on the one hand, negotiate with Russia about future economic projects, and on the other, talk about a diplomatic impasse," the Ukrainian president responded to Rubio.
"We are not in a diplomatic impasse. Shut down (Russia's) entire economy. Silence Russia. Don't feed them with your sales; impose sanctions on their weapons," he added.

title: Russian strikes kill at least 10, injure 45 across Ukraine over past day
description: Russia attacked across Ukraine with 142 Shahed-type drones, 82 of which were jet-powered overnight on Oct. 8, Ukraine's Air Force said.
content:
At least 10 people were killed and 45 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Oct. 8.
In Donetsk Oblast , four people were killed and six others injured, Governor Vadym Filashkin said .
Two of those people died in Zelenye. In Sloviansk, one person died and three were injured, while a high-rise building, an administrative building, a shop, a service station, a gas station, a car, and a bus were damaged. In Veselia Hora, Novodonetska community, one person died, and a private house was damaged. One person was injured in Zolote Prudy, and a private house, a car, and a truck were damaged. In Druzhkivka, a person was injured.
Russia attacked across Ukraine with 142 Shahed-type drones, 82 of which were jet-powered overnight on Oct. 8, Ukraine's Air Force said . The Air Force said it shot down or suppressed 126 drones.
In Ukraine's capital city Kyiv , four people were killed and 21 others injured, including four children, the Kyiv city military administration (KMDA) said .
In Solomianskyi district, a UAV fell on the roof of a five-story residential building, causing a fire, while elsewhere in the district falling debris injured one person. In Desnianskyi district, falling drone debris also caused a fire in a 12-story residential building.
In the wider Kyiv Oblast , three people were injured overnight, regional governor Tymur Tkachenko said . Two people were injured in Bucha district and one person in Brovary district. Three warehouses, an infrastructure object, a private house, and four vehicles were also damaged across the oblast.
In Sumy Oblast , two children, fourteen-year-old boys, died from the detonation of an explosive object, while four people were injured from Russian drone strikes, according to the Sumy military state administration. In the city of Sumy, a 46-year-old woman and men aged 69 and 49 were injured by Russian drones, while a 62-year-old man was injured in Velykypysarivska.
In Kharkiv Oblast , three people were injured overnight, said regional governor Oleh Syniehubov. In the city of Kharkiv, a 67-year-old woman was injured, while a 62-year-old man was injured in the city of Dergachi, and a 70-year-old woman was injured in the village of Dobrenka.
In Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks injured five people, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said . Russian forces also struck critical and social infrastructure, residential areas, in particular, a high-rise building and four private houses, as well as private cars.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast , three people were injured by Russian attacks over the last day, regional governor Ivan Fedorov said . He said he knew of 84 reports of damage to housing, cars, and infrastructure in the oblast.
In Odesa Oblast , the Russian attack damaged the territory of a parking lot, damaging several cars, and an animal shelter, killing one of the animals inside, regional governor Oleh Kiper said . Damage to civilian enterprise, settlements, and a bus were also reported in Dnipropetrovsk and Rivne oblasts.

title: UK ramps up sanctions against Russian shadow fleet, crypto industry, big oil
description: The U.K., the EU, and Ukraine have all targeted crypto schemes in recent sanctions packages as Russia uses the technology to evade existing sanctions.
content:
Editor's note: this article was updated with further details provided in a U.K. government press statement released after this article was first published.
The U.K. published 38 new sanctions listings on Oct. 8, targeting ships helping Russia evade existing sanctions and a range of companies in Moscow's military-industrial complex, energy, and cryptocurrency sectors.
"The message is simple: if you help Russia fund or equip this war, you will face the consequences," reads a U.K. government press release.
Among the businesses in the new sanctions listings are three cryptocurrency exchanges and two payment platforms.
Xeltox Enterprises, one of those listed entities has "been involved in obtaining a benefit from or supporting the government of Russia by carrying on business in a sector of strategic significance (...) the financial services sector," reads the U.K. government's sanctions listing .
Russia has increasingly sought to use cryptocurrency , which is hard to track, to circumvent global sanctions, and the new U.K. sanctions target the "A7" network, which is at the heart of Moscow's attempts to evade financial sanctions.
That has prompted the U.K., the U.S ., the EU , and Ukraine to target crypto schemes in recent sanctions packages.
Also featuring on the listings are two further oil companies: Zarubezhneft and INK Capital.
"The U.K. was the first country in the G7 to sanction the top four Russian oil companies," reads the press statement.
The U.K. has also added 12 ships to its list of sanctioned vessels accused of being part of Russia's shadow fleet — dilapidated vessels suspected of helping Moscow evade price caps and bans on its trade in oil and gas.
That takes the number of ships sanctioned by the U.K. to 645 and the total number of Russia sanctions to 3,537.

title: South Korea to recall Ukraine envoy amid North Korean POWs dispute
description: "The government looks forward to the smooth resolution of all pending issues between the two countries and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to this end," the South Korean Foreign Ministry said in a press release.
content:
Editor's note: This article has been updated to include a comment from Ukraine's Foreign Ministry. South Korea decided to recall its ambassador from Ukraine, the South Korean Foreign Ministry announced on Oct. 8, amid ongoing deterioration in Kyiv-Seoul relations.
The decision to summon Ambassador Park Hee-chang home comes after Seoul demanded an apology from Kyiv over the disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to South Korea.
Seoul claims that President Volodymyr Zelensky broke a confidentiality agreement when he announced the transfer during his U.N. speech on Sept. 23.
The dispute escalated further when Zelensky's office claimed that no such agreement existed, prompting South Korean President Lee Jae Myung to threaten retaliatory measures.
"The government looks forward to the smooth resolution of all pending issues between the two countries and will continue consultations with the Ukrainian side to this end," the South Korean Ministry said in a press release .
Ukraine invited South Korea’s ambassador to the Foreign Ministry to “seek constructive solutions” to the ongoing diplomatic issue, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi told journalists on Oct. 8. “We are convinced that diplomacy should prevail over emotions. Despite Seoul’s decision to recall the ambassador (in Ukraine), Ukraine remains open to resuming constructive dialogue — even if it takes time.”
His South Korean counterpart, Cho Hyun , claimed on Oct. 6 that he had received an apology from Sybiha but said it was not on "the level we expect, so we intend to take firm measures."
Ukrainian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi later clarified that Sybiha merely expressed regret over the escalation in the diplomatic dispute.
Kyiv announced in January 2025 that it had captured two North Korean soldiers during battles in Russia's western Kursk Oblast.
The two were among the many thousands dispatched by North Korean dictator Kim Jong Un in 2024 to bolster Russian forces in the border region, making North Korea the only country to send its serving forces to fight on Moscow’s side to date.

title: Russian drone barrage on Kyiv kills 4, injures 19, disrupts electricity, water supplies
description: At 10:00 a.m. local time, Ukraine’s biggest private energy firm DTEK announced emergency energy shutdowns in Brovary, Buchanskyi, Vyshgorod, and Boryspil districts of the capital.
content:
Russian drone strikes on Oct. 8 have killed four people and injured at least 19 in Kyiv, the city's authorities said.
A Russian drone struck a four-story commercial building in Solomyanskyi district, killing two and injuring two, and leading to a fire, while the wreckage of another fell on the Holosiivskyi district, Klitschko said .
Prior to that strike, Klitschko said that Russian attacks on the capital this morning had killed one person and injured 11 others.
A fourth person died of their injuries in hospital, the Kyiv city military administration (KMDA) said in the afternoon.
Klitschko raised the number of injured to 19, 13 of which were hospitalized, in an update on 07:21 p.m. local time.
At 10:00 a.m. local time, Ukraine’s biggest private energy firm DTEK announced emergency energy shutdowns in Brovary, Buchanskyi, Vyshgorod, and Boryspil districts of the oblast.
Shortly after, KMDA announced that the right bank of Kyiv may experience interruptions in water supply, as the power decrease in the electricity grid also meant a decrease in pressure of the water supply network. This applied especially to the Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomyanskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts.
The drop in voltage from external power supply centers also temporarily halted Kyiv Metro train services and escalator operations, the KMDA said .
DSNS also said that a fire broke out at a logistics facility in the Buchanskyi district in Kyiv Oblast following a Russian drone strike.
In Sviatopetrivske in Buchanskyi district, a school-kindergarten and a nearby playground in a residential complex were damaged in the attack, Kyiv Oblast Governor Tymur Tkachenko said . In another settlement in the district, a woman was injured and hospitalized, he added.
Overnight, Russian drone strikes on Kyiv had already killed four people and injured 21 across four districts, KMDA said .
In Solomyanskyi district, a UAV fell on the roof of a 5-storey residential building, causing a fire, while elsewhere in the district falling debris injured one person.
In Desnyanskyi district, falling drone debris also caused a fire in a 12-storey residential building.
At the time of writing, Klitschko said there had been a further strike on Shevchenko district, emergency services were dispatched.
Russia attacked across Ukraine with 142 Shahed-type drones, 82 of them jet-powered, on the night of Oct. 8, Ukraine's air force said . The Air Force said that air defense shot down or suppressed 126 of these drones.

title: Ukrainian agriculture urges EU to talk details, not panic, in future membership negotiations
description: We need "a substantive discussion about adaptation periods, the volumes of market access, and safeguard mechanisms," said Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi.
content:
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi and the sector's main lobby organization in Brussels doubled down on their commitment to integrating Kyiv's geopolitically powerful farming sector into the EU system on Oct. 7.
Their respective interventions came one day after the European Commission published a view on how the future of enlargement could work.
Ukraine's agricultural might could mean that the EU needs "targeted arrangements to significantly limit financial support and market access for sensitive agricultural products," the document argues.
However, Vysotskyi said permanent restrictions on access to the EU's single market are a non-starter, in written comments first shared with Politico and seen by the Kyiv Independent.
"Ukraine cannot agree to such an approach," the Ukrainian minister said.
Likewise, the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB) put out a press statement saying, "Ukrainian agricultural producers cannot be expected to bear the full economic cost of alignment with EU standards while being denied the corresponding perspective of full participation in the EU Single Market."
For both Vysotskyi and UCAB, part of the solution relies on baking transition periods into the enlargement process, just as was the case in previous rounds of EU expansion, which would give the bloc and Ukraine time to adapt to one another and stretch out disruption over a longer period of time.
"Transitional periods are a normal part of EU enlargement, and Ukraine is ready for them," Vysotskyi said.
But "transition should facilitate integration, not become a mechanism for permanently excluding Ukrainian agriculture from the internal market," UCAB notes.
Ukraine's farming sector has already begun complying with EU rules, a process that is expensive, essentially irreversible, and undertaken only because it comes with the promise of a level playing field in the EU market.
It is market access rather than financial support that matters most for Ukraine, Vysotskyi said, as the sector already operates with little state support.
But that has not stopped French far-right leader Marine Le Pen already playing to the fears of French farmers that Ukrainian counterparts would take away their share of EU subsidies.
EU farms are typically small-scale, uncompetitive, and dependent on the bloc's Common Agricultural Policy for generous subsidies that keep them operational.
Ukraine's farming sector, by contrast, is a giant capable of competing on the world stage, and with that size comes geopolitical leverage.
Because of that, the European Commission is clear that while Ukraine should gain market access as part of EU membership, Ukrainian agriculture needs to remain competitive on the world stage.
"Our budget can never compensate for gains that Ukraine's very competitive — the only real competitive agriculture sector in Europe — can gain in the world," a senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent, ahead of the publication of the Commission's new plans.
To overcome that obstacle, highly technical negotiations need to take place.
Vysotskyi seems to mirror the European Commission's thinking that for each specific product, there should be "a substantive discussion about adaptation periods, the volumes of market access, and safeguard mechanisms."
That could mean one rule for Ukrainian chicken, another for wheat, another for plant proteins, and so on.
Decisions "must take into account the situation in each specific sector and must not turn into permanent restrictions for the entire Ukrainian agricultural sector," Vysotskyi said.
And UCAB says that "the Ukrainian agricultural sector is ready to contribute constructively to this work."
UCAB calls for agricultural businesses, associations representing the sector, and EU agricultural organizations to all be included in a dialogue on Ukraine's agricultural integration.
"Ukraine is preparing to become part of the European Union. Its agricultural sector should not merely be accommodated within the future European agricultural model. It should be involved in designing it," reads the UCAB press statement.

title: At least 33 dead after Russian glide bomb strikes Kramatorsk buses
description: "Russia comes to the Ukrainian land with death," Donetsk Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
content:
Firefighters perform cooling and search operations on the burnt shell of a passenger bus following a Russian missile and aerial bomb strike in Kramatorsk, Donetsk Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 8, 2026. (State Emergency Service of Ukraine)
A Russian glide bomb strike on two minibuses in Kramatorsk killed 33 people on the morning of Oct. 8, Ukraine's emergency service (DSNS) said.
Twenty-two more people were injured in the Russian attack, Donetsk regional governor Vadym Filashkin said . Fire broke out in at least two busses following the Russian strikes, according to DSNS .
"Russia comes to the Ukrainian land with death. She hits our cities, kills our people and multiplies her crimes every day," Filashkin said .
Допис, поширений Kyiv Independent (@kyivindependent_official)
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that doctors were still fighting for the lives of some of the injured people and warned that the number of dead may still increase. Two dead people could not yet be identified due to the severity of their injuries, he added.
"This strike will not go without our response. Russia is trying to destroy all life in Donbas, and the world needs to react to this," Zelensky said.
The Kramatorsk and Sloviansk military administrations ordered the stop of all public transport.
"The Russians are targeting civilians. For them, a bus with passengers is an attractive target precisely because one hit can kill as many people as possible," Filashkin said.
Across Ukraine's Donetsk Oblast, four more people had been killed and six injured by Russian attacks as of the morning of Oct. 8, prior to the Kramatorsk strike, according to the governor .
In total, Russian forces shelled settlements in the Donetsk region 31 times over the last day, and 256 people, including 32 children, were evacuated from the front line, according to the Donetsk governor.
Russia attacked across Ukraine with 142 Shahed-type drones, 82 of them jet-powered, on the night of Oct. 8, Ukraine's air force said . The air force said that air defense shot down or suppressed 126 of these drones.
On Oct. 2 , Russian forces struck a passenger bus with a first-person-view ( FPV ) drone in the front-line city of Kramatorsk , Donetsk Oblast, at around 7:08 a.m., injuring two people, the Kramatorsk City Council said.
The bus was already operating on its route and carrying passengers when the attack occurred, according to the statement.
Jonas Heins is Assistant Editor at the Kyiv Independent. Before joining, Jonas worked in several think tanks and research institutions across Central and Eastern Europe. He grew up in Germany and holds an MA in European Studies from the University of Padova. Currently he is pursuing an MA in Central and East European, Russian, and Eurasian Studies from the Universities of Glasgow and Tartu.

title: Lithuania calls for EU sanctions against Russian grain
description: Russia being able to trade grain while it blockades Ukraine from doing likewise "is an unacceptable situation," said Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius.
content:
Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius renewed calls for the EU to impose sanctions on Russian grain in a social media post on Oct. 8.
" Lithuania will propose not only banning such transit (of Russian grain through the EU), but also adding individual oligarchs from the Russian agricultural sector who are supporting the war to the list of sanctioned persons," Sinkevicius wrote on Facebook.
The comments were made in response to Russia's ongoing Black Sea blockade, which is slashing Ukraine's income from food exports but also putting importer countries in the Middle East and North Africa in a precarious situation.
And Kyiv accused Russia of striking cargo ships off the Black Sea coast of Romania and Bulgaria on Oct. 5 and 6, leading to civilians being killed.
"At the same time, Russia is using ports and infrastructure in Europe, including the Baltic States, to export its own grain," Sinkevicius said.
"This is an unacceptable situation, which has so far been tolerated on the grounds that EU sanctions do not apply to food products," he noted.
In an interview with the Kyiv Independent, the EU's sanctions envoy David O'Sullivan said the bloc has not pushed sanctions on agricultural goods "because it doesn't really affect the war machine."
O'Sullivan also noted that sanctions had already slashed EU trade with Russia by 75%, and a total decoupling is not necessarily the objective of the EU's sanctions policy.
Absent a change of EU policy, Sinkevicius said he has already ordered "stricter controls on the origin of grain to ensure that grain stolen from Ukraine or mixed with other grain is not transported through Lithuania."
"We will not allow the Russian war machine to profit by using our infrastructure as a gateway to global markets," Sinkevicius said.

title: Russian oil refinery in Salavat hit by Ukraine, General Staff confirms
description: The Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat facility is one of Russia’s largest oil refining and petrochemical plants, located some 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) from the front line in Ukraine.
content:
An overnight Ukrainian strike on the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat oil refinery in Russia's Bashkortostan region caused a large blaze at the plant, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed on Oct. 8.
Several images and videos show the moment the plant was struck, as well as thick smoke and fire coming from the grounds of the refinery.
"(The facility) is one of Russia's largest oil refining and petrochemical complexes," the General Staff said in a post on social media. "The facility has a processing capacity of up to 10 million tons of hydrocarbon feedstock per year and produces automotive gasoline, diesel fuel, fuel oil, bitumen, polyethylene, and other oil refining and petrochemical products."
The Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat facility is located some 1,300 kilometers (800 miles) from the front line in Ukraine.
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) drones previously hit the Gazprom Neftekhim Salavat plant in September, a source in the agency told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 24.
A fire broke out at the plant following several drone strikes, the source said. Local authorities have also confirmed the attack.

title: France's Le Pen opposes Ukraine EU membership over farming fears
description: The EU's Enlargement Commissioner, Marta Kos, had already said, "We have to protect the farmers in the EU, and we are already discussing this subject with Ukraine."
content:
French far-right politician Marine Le Pen spoke against EU membership for Ukraine on Oct. 7 by whipping up fears that Kyiv's agricultural sector would destroy France's.
Le Pen is leading the polls for France's April 2027 presidential election, and her stance on Ukraine and Russia has already become a key campaign issue for her and her competitors .
"If Ukraine were to enter the European Union, we would be the first to suffer," Le Pen claimed in a video posted to social media.
"We would be the losers, not only in terms of competition with a large agricultural country like Ukraine, but also in the sharing out of Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) (subsidies), because the CAP is a shrinking cake," Le Pen said.
The CAP is an EU program established in 1962 that subsidizes the EU's farming sector, allowing small and uncompetitive farms to continue to exist.
It is also at risk of being reduced already, as Brussels haggles over the bloc's 2028-2034 budget. The fear is that adding a large agricultural country such as Ukraine would exacerbate that situation further.
Le Pen's comments came one day after the European Commission published a communication on the future of enlargement , which noted that the bloc needs to seriously address how to integrate Ukraine's farming sector into the EU smoothly.
Ukraine "will and can become a member of the CAP. Under which conditions, this will be discussed," said the EU's Enlargement Commissioner, Marta Kos , at a press conference on Oct. 6.
"We also have to protect the farmers in the EU, and we are already discussing this subject with Ukraine," Kos added.
Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotskyi said, "We understand the sensitivity of certain segments for European farmers," in written comments shared with the Kyiv Independent.
However, he thinks there are also many opportunities for the EU that come with bringing in Ukraine's farming sector, even for European farmers.
"We do not share the approach under which Ukraine's integration is viewed exclusively as a threat to European farmers," Vysotskyi said.
And Kyiv's lobby for agriculture in Brussels, the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB), said that while it understands the concerns of European farmers, it is "increasingly concerned by an excessively protectionist approach towards the integration of Ukrainian agriculture," in an Oct. 7 press statement .
For UCAB, part of the answer lies in communication.
"UCAB has consistently advocated an open and structured dialogue with European farmers, EU institutions, and member states to jointly develop a model for the future enlarged European agricultural market."

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,547,780 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,880 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,547,780 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 8.
The number includes 1,880 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,399 tanks, 25,4502 armored combat vehicles, 159,795 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,883 artillery systems, 2,194 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,692 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,890 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Massive internet outage in Russia after Ukraine reportedly hits largest Yandex data center in drone attack
description: The Sasovo data center is located on the grounds of the Sasta machine-tool plant, a manufacturer of metal-cutting and high-precision CNC metalworking machines used across Russian industry, including the defense-industrial, aerospace, oil and gas, and heavy machinery sectors.
content:
Outages occured in many segments of the Russian internet at about 16:00 p.m. local time on Oct. 8, especially in Moscow and St. Petersburg, after Ukraine struck a Yandex data center, the Moscow Times said.
Several banking services, as well as Google, RuTube, the website of the Russian Railways, as well as many retail websites were not reachable, according to the Moscow Times .
A major Yandex data center in Russia's Ryazan Oblast was reportedly damaged in an overnight drone attack, with a large fire reported at the industrial site.
OSINT groups Exilenova+ and ASTRA identified the site as Yandex DC Sasovo, located in the city of Sasovo. Yandex describes the facility as its largest data center, supporting the company's services and cloud infrastructure.
Yandex Cloud later acknowledged an "incident" and power-supply problems in its “ru-central1-b availability zone”. According to company updates, disruptions began at around 1:31 a.m., and roughly 40 minutes later the situation had not yet stabilized.
Yandex warned that the outage could affect other parts of its cloud network and advised customers to move some services elsewhere while engineers worked to restore operations.
The company did not publicly link the incident to the reported drone attack.
Exilenova+ also reported disruptions affecting some Yandex services following the strike. Public outage monitors, however, did not show evidence of a widespread outage across Yandex's main consumer services. The Sasovo data center is located on the grounds of the Sasta machine-tool plant, a manufacturer of metal-cutting and high-precision CNC metalworking machines used across Russian industry, including the defense-industrial, aerospace, oil and gas, and heavy machinery sectors.
Sasta says its production complex includes machining and assembly workshops, a foundry, and research and development facilities, and that its equipment is used by enterprises in Russia's defense industry.
The plant has been under U.K. sanctions since 2024 over its role in Russia's defense sector.
It remains unclear whether the Yandex data center, the Sasta plant, or both were the intended targets of the reported attack.
In 2022, Ryazan Governor Pavel Malkov described the Sasovo complex as a high-tech facility housing tens of thousands of servers used to rapidly process requests across Yandex services.
Neither regional authorities nor Ukraine's military had publicly confirmed the reported strike at the time of publication. Yandex acknowledged the infrastructure incident and power problems but did not say what caused them.

title: US senators urge Trump administration to enforce new Russia sanctions law ahead of Oct. 18 deadline
description: The senators called for tougher action against Russia's oil revenues and sanctions-evasion networks, urging the administration to match European and U.K. designations of shadow-fleet vessels.
content:
U.S. Senators Jeanne Shaheen and Roger Wicker are pressing the Trump administration to begin implementing the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act as soon as possible. While most of the law's provisions take effect on Oct. 18, the bipartisan senators urged the administration not to wait until the deadline.
In a letter shared with the Kyiv Independent and later made public, Shaheen and Wicker argued that Russia's intensified missile strikes targeting Ukraine's civilian population and energy infrastructure, along with new North Korean troop deployments, make immediate economic pressure necessary.
The senators called for tougher action against Russia's oil revenues and sanctions-evasion networks, urging the administration to match European and U.K. designations of shadow-fleet vessels. The EU and U.K. have designated more than 600 vessels, compared to 216 by the United States, most of them in early 2025.
Shaheen and Wicker warned that the gap leaves hundreds of tankers able to continue transporting oil and ultimately feeding the Russian war machine while avoiding U.S. restrictions. They urged Washington to match allied shadow-fleet designations one-for-one, arguing that U.S. sanctions have added impact by cutting vessels off from the global dollar system and Western maritime services.
In the letter, Shaheen and Wicker acknowledged the administration's sanctions against Lukoil and Rosneft in 2025, saying they dealt a significant blow to a major source of Moscow's revenues. They noted, however, that Russia has since bypassed those sanctions, routing transactions through intermediaries concentrated in the UAE and Hong Kong, and called on the administration to target those networks.
The senators also urged Washington to impose secondary sanctions on third-country suppliers in China, the UAE and Türkiye that provide advanced machine tools, microelectronics, and other dual-use components used in Russian ammunition production and jet-powered drones.
The letter further called for sanctions against companies supporting Russia's Rassvet low-Earth-orbit satellite network, including Bureau 1440, 5C Group and Eltex. The senators warned that a fully deployed constellation could strengthen Russian battlefield communications and targeting capabilities.
Shaheen and Wicker also pointed to recent reports of a possible multi-billion-dollar deal involving Lukoil's international assets , arguing that the Treasury Department should make clear that financing Russian state-linked businesses would violate the law's investment restrictions.
Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18.
Most provisions take effect Oct. 18, marking the first major deadline for the administration to demonstrate how aggressively it intends to wield the new sanctions authority.

title: Moldova to build drone shelters near Ukrainian border amid escalating Russian attacks
description: In addition to the new structures, some Moldovan border guards currently stationed on the Ukrainian side of the border will be transferred to the Moldovan side.
content:
Moldova plans to build protective shelters at border crossings with Ukraine where border guards and people in nearby areas can take cover during drone incursions, Moldovan Interior Minister Daniella Misail-Nichitin said on Oct. 7.
The announcement followed an increase in drones violating Moldovan airspace in recent weeks.
The protective structures would provide a place of refuge in the event of incoming drone strikes, and will be placed at checkpoints along the country's border with Ukraine , Misail-Nichitin told Moldovan media outlet NewsMaker.
In addition to the new structures, some Moldovan border guards currently stationed on the Ukrainian side of the border, at "Kryva" and "Palanka" stations, will be moved to the Moldovan side, she said.
Ukrainian officials are also in talks with neighboring countries about restructuring border operations to improve security and make border crossing easier as drone incursions increase, Heorhiiy Tykhyi, a spokesperson for the Foreign Ministry, said on Oct. 7.
Drones have crashed into Moldovan territory throughout Russia's full-scale war, with multiple incidents occurring in the past two weeks.
A projectile fired during a Russian attack on Ukraine on Oct. 5 ricocheted and struck a passenger bus and a border control booth at the Palanca-Maiaky-Udobne crossing, lightly injuring a border guard, Moldova's Border Police said.
"The security environment around Moldova has become more difficult," Moldovan Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said during a press conference in Brussels on Oct. 5. "Russian drones and missiles pose a serious risk to our population and infrastructure."
During another Russian overnight attack against Ukraine on Oct. 3, five Russian air attack weapons, including Banderol missiles and drones, violated Moldova's airspace and exploded on the country's territory, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said.
Sandu condemned the attacks in a post on social media on Oct. 3.
"(Russia's) war is dangerously reaching Moldova," she said, adding that "Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped."
Drones also invaded Moldova's airspace three separate times on Sept. 30, as Russia launched a day-long attack against Ukraine overnight and into the following afternoon.

title: Lithuania to deploy troops along border with Russia's Kaliningrad after Latvia incident
description: The move is a preventative measure in response to signals that Russia may announce mobilization, Lithuanian Interior Minister Martians Katelynas said.
content:
Lithuania's Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas called for troops to be deployed to the country's border with Kaliningrad, a Russian exclave, in a statement on Oct. 7.
The request came in response to an incident in neighboring Latvia the day prior, as well as the overall security situation in the region amid escalating tensions between Russia and NATO regarding Kaliningrad .
"I have appealed to the Defense Minister, Robertas Kaunas, to have Lithuanian Armed Forces units deployed to help border guards protect the border with the Kaliningrad region," Katelynas said in a statement on social media.
The move is a preventative measure in response to signals that Russia may announce mobilization, he said.
The requested deployment follows two security breaches at the Latvian border on Oct. 6. First, armed guards escorted groups of illegal migrants across Latvia's border with Belarus . Shortly after, masked individuals once again crossed the Latvia-Belarus border, stealing equipment before returning.
The Lithuanian minister said that there was no reason to panic and that the situation at the border is calm.
"Deploying soldiers is a preventive decision, so that we are prepared and can stop similar incidents," he said.
The move comes a day after Lithuania's parliament took the first step toward lifting the country's ban on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory.
The measure would repeal Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution, which currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory.
NATO has expanded its presence in the Baltics in recent months, with a German military brigade permanently stationed in Lithuania, as security concerns over Russian provocations have grown in the region.
Kaliningrad, officially part of Russia, is an exclave on the Baltic Sea, sandwiched between Poland and Lithuania . The region has become a flashpoint between Russia and NATO.
In a warning to NATO in September, Russia claimed that it was "ready to use the entire arsenal of ​forces and capabilities at its disposal, including nuclear weapons, in order to defend its territory should NATO countries undertake any attempt aimed at ​isolating the Kaliningrad Region from the rest of the country."
Russian President Vladimir Putin invoked the threat of nuclear force again in remarks the following day.
"Can we be sure this weapon will never be used? Of course not," Putin said about nuclear weapons in a speech on Oct. 1. "We're all familiar with the saying: If a gun is hanging somewhere on the stage at the beginning of a performance, on the wall, it's bound to go off eventually."

title: Russia hits another Kyiv apartment building after day of deadly strikes, injuring 4
description: The strike caused a fire and partial structural damage at a 12-story building, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service. Four people were injured,  including two children.
content:
Editor's Note: This is a developing story.
Russia launched another drone strike against Kyiv on the evening of Oct. 7, hitting a 12-story apartment building and injuring four people, including children.
The strike followed a large-scale attack that began overnight on Oct. 7 and killed nearly 30 people across Ukraine, including four victims in Kyiv.
While rescuers were still clearing the rubble from the mass strike, Russian drones continued to menace the capital into the evening. At 10:23 p.m. local time, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported that a drone hit the 10th floor of a 12-story residential building in the city's Darnytskyi district.
The strike caused a fire on the upper floors and partial structural damage, according to Ukraine's State Emergency Service. Four people were injured, including two children.
First responders rescued another 22 people from the burning building, including eight children, the State Emergency Service said. The fire has been extinguished, and emergency services continue to work at the scene.
Residential buildings in Ukraine's Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Poltava, and Dnipro oblasts were targeted by Russian drones and missiles on Oct. 7. The date coincides with Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday.
In Pryluky , Chernihiv Oblast, a Russian cruise missile destroyed a five-story building, killing 20 people and injuring 55 more. Five children were among those killed in the attack.
Russia also targeted critical infrastructure, leaving a significant number of Kyiv residents without access to electricty or water.

title: 56 Ukrainians still missing as Nepal ends flash flood search-and-rescue operation
description: "Unfortunately, despite weeks of efforts by diplomats, consuls, and rescuers, (the missing Ukrainians) have still not been found among either the dead or the injured," Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
content:
Fifty-six Ukrainians remain missing after Nepal ended its search-and-rescue operation following August's deadly floods, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said on Oct. 6.
Devastating flash floods ravaged Nepal after a glacier collapsed in the Himalayas on Aug. 26, drowning villages in mud and debris. At least 1,455 people were killed in the floods, and over 5,200 people were unaccounted for.
While active rescue operations have been suspended, the search and identification of remains continue, the ministry said.
"Unfortunately, despite weeks of efforts by diplomats, consuls, and rescuers, (the missing Ukrainians ) have still not been found among either the dead or the injured," the Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Out of the missing Ukrainian citizens, 46 were traveling together in a tour group . Contact with the group was lost when the flash flooding began. Rescue efforts have been ongoing for over 40 days, but none of the missing Ukrainians have been identified.
While there have been no official reports of Ukrainians killed, Nepalese officials said they were considering commencing the legal process of declaring missing persons as dead.
"We are initiating due processes to complete ‌required ⁠legal formalities," Phanindra Paudel, chief of the National Emergency ​Operation Centre, told Reuters.
These formalities would allow families of the missing individuals to complete relevant administrative tasks, such as filing life insurance claims, in their home countries.
The Ukrainian embassy in India has contacted relevant authorities concerning procedures for official documentation, the ministry said.
The Ukrainian National Police is also working to finalize a database of DNA profiles of those missing in the floods to share with Nepalese authorities.

title: Explosive device in field kills 2 boys in Sumy Oblast
description: Two 14-year-old boys in the Konotop district were killed after the device detonated, Governor Oleh Hryhorov said. The prevalence of unexploded ordnance and landmines poses severe risk to Ukrainian civilians in front-line regions.
content:
Two 14-year-old boys in Sumy Oblast's Konotop district were killed on Oct. 7 after encountering an explosive device, Governor Oleh Hryhorov reported.
The boys found the explosive device in a local field, Hryhorov said . The device detonated, killing both children. The victims died at the scene of the explosion from "severe injuries," according to the governor.
Konotop, in Ukraine's northeastern Sumy Oblast , lies about 65 kilometers (40 miles) from the Russian border. The front-line region endures daily attacks , which continue posing risks to civilians after the air raid sirens stop.
"In addition to constant enemy attacks, there is a serious danger of encountering explosive devices. Such discoveries often pose a deadly threat," Hryhorov warned. He reminded civilians to be extremely cautious and avoid approaching, touching, or attempting to move any suspicious objects.
While Hryhorov did not specify the type of device that caused the teenagers' deaths, landmines and unexploded ordnance represent a severe and widespread danger in Ukraine .
Five years of Russia's full-scale invasion has transformed the country into the world's largest minefield, with up to a quarter of Ukrainian territory contaminated by mines.
