Hundreds of civilians have been killed by unexploded ordnance since February 2022, though the true figure is believed to be much higher.

title: Amid the rubble of a Ukrainian apartment building, locals have one wish for Putin’s birthday
description:
PRYLUKY, Chernihiv Oblast – Families stand outside the ruins of a five-story apartment building, watching rescuers dig through what remains of their homes.

Some sit wrapped in blankets, staring at the rescue operation, waiting to see who is pulled from the rubble next. Five bodies so far are those of children, three of them only one year old.

They were among at least 20 people killed by a Russian cruise missile that struck a five-story residential building in Pryluky as part of a mass salvo th
content:
Local residents hug as they look at a multi-floor residential building destroyed following a Russian aerial strike in Pryluky, Chernihiv Oblast, on Oct. 7, 2026. (Genya Savilov / AFP via Getty Images)
PRYLUKY, Chernihiv Oblast – Families stand outside the ruins of a five-story apartment building, watching rescuers dig through what remains of their homes.
Some sit wrapped in blankets, staring at the rescue operation, waiting to see who is pulled from the rubble next. Five bodies so far are those of children, three of them only one year old.
They were among at least 20 people killed by a Russian cruise missile that struck a five-story residential building in Pryluky as part of a mass salvo that struck cities across Ukraine overnight on Oct. 7.
A date which also happens to be Russian President Vladimir Putin's birthday.
"As a Christian, you cannot wish death on someone," Olga, a 41-year-old resident of Pryluky, who asked that her surname not be published, tells the Kyiv Independent.
"But I wish that he could feel even the tiniest fraction of what our people and our children are feeling," she says. "I wish he could feel it, and that the people around him could feel what our children are feeling.”
"Let him feel what every person and every child in our country is feeling."
"I hope he drops dead soon," says 75-year-old Volodymyr Ivashchenko.
As the search and rescue operation continues, people rush between buildings with relatives and neighbors, covering shattered windows and salvaging what they can from damaged apartments.
The roar of excavators fills the courtyard as emergency workers lift slabs of concrete from what had been apartments only hours earlier. Rescue workers standing on the exposed floors throw smaller pieces of wreckage below, stripping away ruined walls, furniture, and fragments of the lives that had been inside.
There is little to distinguish the neighborhood from countless other residential districts across Ukraine. Apartment blocks surround courtyards and children's playgrounds. Grocery stores and small businesses line the surrounding streets. Across the road stands the Children and Youth Creativity Center, one of the city's oldest institutions, where generations of children have gone to sing, dance, do gymnastics, and prepare for school.
Ivashchenko had woken at around 6 a.m. Before the explosions, the first thing he noticed was a humming noise outside.
"I said to my wife, 'Maybe the wind has picked up,'" he recalls.
"The windows flew open, and the whole house shook. It shook very badly," Ivashchenko says.
He remembers several explosions in quick succession and a deafening sound overhead that made him think an aircraft was passing above his roof.
Hours later, his hands and legs are still shaking.
"I feel so sorry for those innocent people, especially those tiny children," he says. "A tiny child, one year old. A young mother who had her whole life ahead of her."
At 75, Ivashchenko says, he had already had the chance to live a long life. The children killed in the building had not.
"It's the 21st century. Is there really no one who can stop this one clown, or whatever you want to call him?" he says.
"How many more deaths can there be? How much more destruction?"
For Olga, the sight of the destroyed building is inseparable from the children who filled the courtyards around it.
"There are actually so many children in our courtyard," she says.
On the morning of the attack, Olga and her family were asleep. Her children were in one room, she was in another, and her husband was sleeping in the living room.
After the first explosion, they rushed into the corridor and sheltered between two walls. A second explosion followed, and then, several minutes later, another.
When they eventually went outside, the neighboring building where her 7-year-old son regularly played with other children was partly destroyed.
The blast had blown out every window in Olga's apartment facing the courtyard. Her husband had been in the living room when a balcony door was thrown toward him, but he escaped serious injury.
"You can repair everything," she says of the damage to their home. "You can't bring back the lives of the people who lived there."
Tetiana Pinchuk, 69, has lived in the district since 1974. She had taken her dog outside early that morning and returned home to rest when the explosions began.
"There were several explosions. Bang, bang, bang," she said.
Every window in her apartment was blown out.
"All of them, literally every one," Pinchuk says.
Doors inside the apartment were damaged as well, including those leading to the kitchen and bedroom. Pinchuk was unhurt, but hours later, her dog was still terrified.
Looking at the damage around her, she keeps returning to the same question.
"I just can't understand why you would bomb ordinary people. Why?" she says.
It is not the first time she has seen strikes damage her part of Pryluky. She recalls previous attacks near the local Epicentr home-improvement store, the Nova Poshta delivery company, and elsewhere in the district.
"But none of the previous attacks were like this morning," she says.
When asked what she wished for Putin's birthday, Pinchuk does not hesitate.
Earlier in the war, she says, she had opposed strikes on homes inside Russia because she believed ordinary people should not be held responsible for the actions of their government.
"I thought you should only hit what needs to be hit, because I felt sorry for ordinary people," she says.
"Now I don't feel sorry for them anymore."
Pryluky, like many cities across Ukraine, has become home to families displaced from front-line regions. Pinchuk said some of those families had children who were playing in these same courtyards after already fleeing the war once.
"I wasn't born here, but I consider it my hometown," she says. "That's why this hurts so much."
Fifty-eight-year-old Ludmila was preparing for work at around 6:30 a.m. when she heard the explosions. Her mother lives directly opposite her, and Ludmila immediately began calling her before contacting her husband, who works in Kyiv .
"My old classmate was killed, her daughter, and her daughter's child," Ludmila says.
She tries to describe some of the others she knew who died, but can't get the words out. Instead, she looks back toward the destroyed building.
"Seeing the bodies, especially the bodies of children," she sighs. "That's very hard."
Polina Moroziuk is a junior reporter at the Kyiv Independent. She holds an MSc in Human Rights and Politics from the London School of Economics and a BSc from the University of Amsterdam. Before joining the newsroom, she worked in human rights advocacy and as a project assistant at a research and consultancy organisation, supporting projects for international organisations including UNICEF and War Child, with a focus on Ukraine and the Middle East.

title: Ukraine war latest: Russian attack on Pryluky kills at least 20, including 5 children
description:
Key developments on Oct. 7:

 * Russia slams Ukraine with missiles, drones on Putin's 74th birthday, at least 26 dead including 5 children
 * Huge blaze breaks out at Russian oil facility in Samara Oblast
 * EU provides Ukraine 1.2 billion euros for drones and missiles
 * Russia carried out sabotage against Danish defense firms, intelligence says
 * Erdogan raises Black Sea safety in call with Putin

At least 26 people have been killed in yet another Russian overnight mass missile and drone atta
content:
At least 26 people have been killed in yet another Russian overnight mass missile and drone attack on Ukrainian cities on Oct. 7, coinciding with Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday.
In the city of Pryluky, in Chernihiv Oblast, a Russian cruise missile hit a residential building, killing at least 20 people, including five children, and wounding at least 55, including seven children.
Three of the dead children, named Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhiy, were only one year old, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media. The other child was an eight-year-old named Maksym, he added.
A fifth child was killed by the Russian strike, as Ukraine's state emergency service (DSNS) said as of 7:13 p.m. local time.
"Today, as a 'birthday gift' to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region," Zelensky said .
"It was an ordinary five-story apartment block. There may still be people under the rubble. First responders are working nonstop at the site – doing everything possible to find every person," he added.
Chernihiv Oblast Governor Viacheslav Chaus said that on Putin's birthday, he hopes "the Russian dictator ends up in custody in The Hague or in hell."
Pryluky resident Halyna Osovyk, 55, woke up, and soon after, her flat was shaken by an explosion, she told the Kyiv Independent. Then came more strikes, smoke, and shattered windows. Across the road, two entrances of a neighboring apartment building were destroyed, and rescuers were searching the rubble for people.
The woman herself was still shaking as she spoke. Her hands and legs trembled.
"It was just sheer horror. And the sound of the missiles — you simply cannot put it into words," Osovyk said.
She knew some of those affected. One family was trapped under the debris – the mother, grandmother, and one child were killed, while another child was rescued and taken to the hospital. Another woman and her child were also pulled from the rubble and hospitalized, Osovyk said. As rescuers continued clearing the ruins, people waited for news of relatives who were still missing.
Pryluky had experienced Russian attacks before, she added, but never a morning like this. Asked what she would wish for Putin on his birthday, she replied: "I wish he could have what we are going through now."
Large fires have broken out at a major oil pipeline and storage facility in Russia's Samara Oblast , according to footage shared on social media and NASA satellite monitoring.
Footage posted to social media showed large fires and clouds of black smoke above the facility, which is a major node in Russia's network of oil pipelines.
NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which uses satellite data to detect thermal anomalies and fires, detected multiple hotspots at the facility.
The facility, which is located near the village of Prosvet, in Samara Oblast, includes pumping stations, tank farms, and blending stations. It has been a repeated target during Ukraine's campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil infrastructure.
Earlier that day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky alluded to a Ukrainian strike on oil facilities in Samara Oblast, without specifying which facility had been hit.
The European Commission announced the disbursement of 1.24 billion euros ($1.4 billion) of defense support to Ukraine on Oct. 7, part of the bloc's 90 billion euro support loan ($100 billion) for Kyiv.
"Today's disbursement will help strengthen Ukraine's defense industry. And Ukraine's ability to defend itself. To protect people and infrastructure," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in a press statement .
"The money will be spent on drones, drone interceptors, drone ammunition, and missiles manufactured by Ukrainian entities," reads the press release.
The EU's 90 billion euro loan to Ukraine, approved in April 2026, was intended to provide two-thirds of Kyiv's financial and defense needs until the end of 2027.
In 2026, 28.3 billion euros ($31.7 billion) was earmarked for defense, and Ukraine's plans for how to spend that money have all been submitted and approved by Brussels.
Russia has stepped up efforts to disrupt Danish companies involved in supplying weapons to Ukraine, Denmark's intelligence service representative told Reuters on Oct. 7.
Josefine Christensen, an analyst at the Danish national security and intelligence service (PET), said Russia was increasingly focusing on targets directly connected to Western military support for Ukraine.
According to Christensen, Russia planned a lot of operations in spring but ​carried out "very little," while in early summer they started ⁠to carry out "a lot more."
She added that Russia's operational boldness is growing as it is now trying to hit targets that have a direct impact on the front line , meaning weapons production.
Russia is relying on individuals recruited online to conduct such operations. Some are first tasked with gathering information or photographing potential targets before being offered more serious assignments.
European drone manufacturers and suppliers have attracted particular attention. Christensen cited a list released by Russia's Defense Ministry in April that included European companies involved in producing drones and related components.
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan called Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 7, telling him Turkey is ready to contribute to efforts for direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, and stressing the importance of the safety of navigation in the Black Sea, according to Erdogan's office.
The two Presidents discussed bilateral relations, as well as regional and global issues, Turkey's Directorate of Communications said.
Erdogan also congratulated Putin on his birthday and his party's success in the latest Russian parliamentary elections, the office said.
The security situation for Black Sea shipping has worsened over the past weeks.
On Oct. 5, a cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.

Its previous assessment , published in February 2025, estimated that under certain conditions Russia could become capable of fighting a local war against a neighboring country within about six months, a regional war involving several Baltic-area states within roughly two years, and a large-scale European war within around five years.

title: War in Ukraine spreads across 3 different dimensions
description:
Any war is not that simple and has many angles, but Russia's war in Ukraine is becoming more difficult each day. And not only because of its constant intensity, but because of its complexity.

In the next few months, we will see three concrete, distinctive tracks of Russia's war in Ukraine developing separately and very differently from each other.

You will see a lot of different, mixed news that will be hard to put together into one picture, but we need to accept that the war is changing, and
content:
Recruits, supervised by instructors, cover a distance on Day Zero of Basic Military Training at the 118th Separate Mechanized Brigade of the Ukrainian Armed Forces, April 5, 2026. (Dmytro Smolienko/ Ukrinform/Future Publishing via Getty Images)
Any war is not that simple and has many angles, but Russia's war in Ukraine is becoming more difficult each day. And not only because of its constant intensity, but because of its complexity.
In the next few months, we will see three concrete, distinctive tracks of Russia's war in Ukraine developing separately and very differently from each other.
You will see a lot of different, mixed news that will be hard to put together into one picture, but we need to accept that the war is changing, and our perception and understanding of it should change as well.
Russia's war will unfold in three main dimensions: civilian cities, the front-line battlefield, and diplomatic negotiations.
First, we will see more disturbing and cold-blooded attacks on civilian cities, their infrastructure, and energy facilities.
Alongside the now-routine campaign to plunge millions of Ukrainians into darkness, Russia has revived a tactic of destroying bridges with a long and particularly violent history.
After Ukraine's brief period of independence in 1917–1921, the Soviet army set about demolishing the bridges connecting the two banks of the Dnipro, which cleaves Kyiv in two, seeking to sever one of the capital's most vital arteries and render movement across the city perilous or impossible.
The crossings on the river were blown up and destroyed several times during the retreats of different armies, but the most extensive destruction, which completely cut off the left bank, took place in June 1920.
This was a sad and unfortunate chapter of Ukrainian history, followed by the forced incorporation into the USSR , the artificial famine, or the Holodomor as we know it today, as well as the persecution of the Ukrainian people, language, and culture, until Ukraine once again regained its independence in 1991.
Unfortunately, Moscow has evolved little in either strategy or geopolitical goals. We are therefore likely to see another attempt to cut Kyiv off from its connections across the Dnipro River.
This track is especially important to the Kremlin because it is one of the main reasons why the Ukrainian government is calling for immediate anti-ballistic support, as well as licenses to manufacture such systems domestically.
The main goal of the Russians is to kill the morale of the Ukrainian people and destroy their resistance.
Yet, no matter how terrible it sounds, for the most part, destroying historical sites and attacking civilians is an act of agony and desperation from Russian President Vladimir Putin . Because while he still has the capacity to show his power against civilian women and children, the situation on the battlefield is completely different.
And this is how we come to the second dimension of this war: the front-line battlefield.
On the front line, despite intense fighting, Putin is struggling to show significant gains, while Ukraine is introducing new technologies that are changing how the war is fought. For the first time since 2023, Russian forces are actively losing ground.
These days, we are seeing major Ukrainian achievements on the battlefield and new military innovations.
One example is the NC13 Unit's new "Gryphon" tactic, which combines heavy bomber drones with unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs), essentially ground robots. Since January 2026, the unit has carried out more than 100 successful missions, deploying kamikaze UGVs deep behind Russian lines to strike personnel, logistics, and staging areas.
The technology has become an important part of Operation Vivaldi , a headline-grabbing Ukrainian counteroffensive that has liberated more than 176 square kilometers (68 square miles) of territory.
According to the Presidential Office, Russian forces suffered more than 5,000 casualties during the first three stages of the operation. The Third Army Corps separately reported 2,000 Russian personnel casualties during the latest stage.
UGVs also carried out approximately 80% of logistics operations and 90% of wounded evacuations for Ukrainian troops during the operation.
Ukraine has also introduced and deployed its domestically produced FP-7 ballistic missile in combat for the first time. With a range of 200-250 km (155 to 250 miles) and a weight of 150-200 kg (330-440 pounds), it is designed for counterattacks against Russian missile launchers and military-industrial sites in occupied territories or near the border.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also recently stated that Ukraine is working on a satellite system similar to Starlink.
And this is not to mention the regular, almost routine Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, which are actively crippling Russia's economy and demonstrating the remarkable capabilities of Ukrainian technology, with drones and missiles able to reach targets across vast distances of Russian territory, from Moscow to Siberia.
The so-called third dimension of the war is perhaps the most confusing, as it is becoming increasingly difficult to understand what motivates the participants in this branch of the conflict.
From a moral perspective, from the standpoint of technological development, and based on basic democratic alignment, the Western world should have provided Ukraine with more military aid, greater intelligence sharing so Kyiv could strike the launch sites of Russian ballistic missiles, and more support of every kind a long time ago.
But at this point, Putin appears to be convincing at least the American administration that he will somehow win a war he has been unable to win since 2014, while also presenting himself as holding the stronger hand in negotiations.
For Europe , meanwhile, horrific attacks on civilians and open threats of further aggression against the Baltic states, for some reason, do not seem to be working as an alarm or a call to action, but rather as intimidation that causes fear.
Although we are seeing more action and something of a wake-up call across the European continent, European countries are also confronting another reality: after relying heavily on the United States for their security since World War II and giving up much of their own defense capacity and leverage, they now find themselves unable to manufacture enough military capabilities to ensure their own security and fully support a neighboring country that is under invasion.
Meanwhile, it is the U.S. that is currently leading and managing negotiations between Ukraine and Russia.
Unfortunately, the White House has not shown much decisiveness in response to Russian threats and appears instead to be emboldening Putin, first by inviting him to Alaska and now to Miami for the G20 summit.
The facts on the ground also demonstrate that the Kremlin has intensified its attacks on Ukraine since the beginning of the Trump administration.
Despite promises to end the war in one day, over the past 2 years, the war has grown more dangerous and aggressive, with incidents increasingly affecting neighboring NATO countries on land and at sea. Yet the world appears to have gradually become accustomed to this reality without a proportionate response.
The logic seems to be that if a strike was not deliberately aimed at Moldova or Poland, or if a civilian vessel in neutral waters carrying corn and owned by Turkey was struck, killing the captain and damaging the ship, then somehow it does not count because Russia supposedly did not do it on purpose.
At the same time, at least judging by public statements from the American side, it appears that Ukraine is being pressured to surrender despite all the evidence of how Ukrainian forces and society are prevailing in this war.
When President Donald Trump calls for "both sides to stop the war" and attributes the conflict partly to the negative personal relationship between Putin and Zelensky , we risk losing sight of the basic realities of this war: Russia is the aggressor, the war began in 2014, when Zelensky was not even president, and it was certainly not caused by the personalities of the two leaders.
Putin has publicly expressed ambitions to restore the USSR and regain control over former Soviet territories, and his interests extend beyond Ukraine to countries such as Poland and the Baltic states.
We will see major Ukrainian achievements on the battlefield and deep inside Russian territory. We will see terrible losses among Ukrainian civilians because of Russian strikes, and we will see the inability of negotiations to stop the aggressor.
As so many times before, it will all come down to the indecisiveness of Ukraine's allies and their willingness to actually pressure Russia and provide Ukraine with the military support it needs.
Demands that Ukraine surrender territory, including some of its most heavily fortified positions in Donbas, contrast sharply with the situation on the battlefield. One conclusion we can draw is that the Kremlin has somehow managed to convince the White House of its claimed achievements despite the facts on the ground.
It looks like Moscow is essentially threatening that if Ukraine does not give up on the battlefield, Russia will destroy its civilian cities and kill as many civilians as possible.
This also appears to be part of Putin's argument with Trump: "If you do not pressure them to surrender, I will kill as many civilians as possible." And it seems that this manipulation and blackmail are working, at least in the U.S.
As a result, Ukraine is not receiving all of the military aid and anti-ballistic systems it needs to protect its people. President Trump has repeatedly presented himself as someone who does not want to bet on the losing side, yet the current approach appears to underestimate Ukraine's ability to continue resisting Russia.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Kateryna Lisunova is a Ukrainian journalist based in Washington, D.C., and a Media Advisor at Razom for Ukraine. She is a former Voice of America Congressional correspondent and a freelance contributor for the BBC. She currently contributes to Ukrainska Pravda and Times Radio. Originally from Kyiv, she has worked as a multimedia journalist for over 14 years, specializing in U.S.–Ukraine relations.

title: Erdogan raises Black Sea safety in call with Putin
description: The two Presidents discussed regional issues and the safety of navigation on the Black Sea, Erdogan's office said.
content:
Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan called Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 7, telling him Turkey is ready to contribute to efforts for direct talks between Russia and Ukraine, and stressing the importance of safety of navigation in the Black Sea, according to Erdogan's office.
The two Presidents discussed bilateral relations, as well as regional and gloabl issues, Turkey's Directorate of Communications said.
Erdogan also congratulated Putin on his birthday and his party's success in the latest Russian parliamentary elections, the office said.
The security situation for Black Sea shipping has worsened over the past weeks.
Drones reportedly struck several merchant vessels in the Black Sea on Oct. 6 , including two ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. A Russian strike on a separate civilian vessel killed at least one crew member and injured several others.
One crew member, a steward, was killed, and seven others were injured when a Russian drone struck a merchant vessel flying the Marshall Islands flag in the Black Sea, according to Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper . The vessel was carrying rapeseed oil and was damaged in the strike, with a fire breaking out in the superstructure.
Separately, two merchant ships, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able, were hit by drones of unknown origin about 112 kilometers (70 miles) off Bulgaria's coast on Oct. 6, according to Bulgarian broadcaster Nova . The incident is believed to be the first reported drone attack on commercial shipping inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
On Oct. 5, a cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.
On Oct. 3, Russian forces attacked a civilian cargo ship sailing under the Liberian flag at a port near Odesa in the Black Sea, killing one.
The sailor killed was a motor engineer, and three other crew members were injured in the strike, according to the Ukrainian Sea Ports ​Authority. 13 other crew members were evacuated from the vessel.
"This is yet another deliberate attack by Russia on civilian shipping," said the Sea Ports Authority. "Russia continues to terrorize the peaceful merchant fleet and sailors who risk their lives every day to ensure the operation of Ukrainian maritime routes."
Fifty-one countries backed Ukraine in a joint statement condemning Russia and calling for Black Sea passage as the U.N. Security Council met, the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said on Sept. 23, against the backdrop of the U.N. General Assembly.
"As the Security Council meets to discuss the situation in Ukraine, we reaffirm our shared commitment to the principles of the U.N. Charter and peace. We stand in solidarity with Ukraine as it continues to face Russia's war of aggression," Kallas said .

title: Huge blaze breaks out at Russian oil facility in Samara Oblast
description: NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which uses satellite data to detect thermal anomalies and fires, detected multiple hotspots at the facility.
content:
Large fires have broken out at a major oil pipeline and storage facility in Russia’s Samara Oblast, according to footage shared on social media and NASA satellite monitoring.
Footage posted to social media showed large fires and clouds of black smoke above the facility, which is a major node in Russia's network of oil pipelines.
NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), which uses satellite data to detect thermal anomalies and fires, detected multiple hotspots at the facility.
The facility, which is located near the village of Prosvet, in Samara Oblast, includes pumping stations, tank farms, and blending stations. It has been a repeated target during Ukraine's campaign of deep strikes against Russian oil infrastructure.
Earlier that day, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky alluded to a Ukrainian strike on oil facilities in Samara Oblast, without specifying which facility had been hit.
While the cause of the current fire has yet to be officially stated, earlier on Oct. 7 Ukraine's General Staff confirmed damage caused to the facility in a previous Ukrainian drone strike on Oct. 2.
"As a result of the October 2, 2026 strike on the LVDS "Samara" in Prosveta, Samara Oblast of the Russian Federation, damage to eleven RVS-20000 tanks, three RVS-50000 tanks, sections of pipelines, and an automated oil production station was confirmed," the General Staff said in a statement.
The strikes on Russian oil infrastructure are aimed at "reducing the military-economic potential of the Russian Federation," they said.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 28, injure more than 138 over past day, rescue efforts continue in Pryluky
description: Fourteen of those killed died when a Russian cruise missile hit a residential building in Pryluky, in Chernihiv Oblast.
content:
At least 30 people were killed and at least 138 were injured in Russian attacks against Ukraine in the past 24 hours, according to Ukrainian authorities.
Nineteen of those killed died when a Russian cruise missile hit a residential building in Pryluky, in Chernihiv Oblast, during Russia's latest mass attack on Ukrainian cities.
At least five children were among the dead in Pryluky. 55 more people were injured, including seven children. Rescue efforts were continuing at the time of publication.
The Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, was also heavily targeted by Russian missiles and drones. Two people were killed when a Russian munition impacted a garage cooperative in the Darnytskyi district of the city, according to Kyiv Mayor, Vitaliy Klitschko. A third person, a woman, was killed later in the day, Klitschko said , as well as 8 people injured .
According to the Ukrainian Air Force , Russian forces used a variety of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles, and drones in the overnight attack.
Out of an unspecified number of ballistic missiles launched at Ukraine, five were shot down or suppressed by electronic warfare, according to the Air Force.
Thirty-nine of 48 cruise missiles were confirmed shot down or suppressed as of 10 a.m. Kyiv time, while 117 Russian attack drones were shot down or suppressed out of 130 launched.
Hits by enemy missiles and drones were recorded at 18 locations, according to the Air Force.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, seven people were injured as a result of a Russian attack on a medical facility in Kryvyi Rih, according to regional authorities. An additional two people were injured in Russian attacks in the Nikopol region.
In Donetsk Oblast, 12 people were injured in various Russian attacks over the past 24 hours, according to regional authorities.
In Kharkiv Oblast, two people were injured in Russian attacks over the past 24 hours, according to regional authorities.
In Kirovohrad Oblast, two people were killed in Russia's overnight attacks, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian attacks killed one person and injured 11 more, including one child, according to regional authorities.
In Poltava Oblast, two people were killed in Russia's overnight attacks in the city of Kremenchuk, according to President Volodymyr Zelensky. An additional 40 were injured.
In Sumy Oblast, two people were killed in Russian attacks over the past 24 hours, according to regional authorities. Twelve people were injured.
In Zaporizhia Oblast, one man was killed and six more people were injured as a result of Russian attacks on the city of Zaporizhia and the surrounding district according to regional authorities.

title: EU ambassadors wave through largest-ever list of Russia sanctions
description: The list targets a wide range of defense industry players, from shipyards and aviation companies to electronics manufacturers, armored vehicle repair facilities, and aerospace companies.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — EU ambassadors unanimously approved nearly 1,600 sanctions targeting Russia's military-industrial complex on Oct. 7, paving the way for them to be formally adopted by EU foreign ministers on Oct. 12 in Luxembourg.
The list, previously seen and reported by the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 21, targets a wide range of defense industry players, from shipyards and aviation companies to electronics manufacturers, armored vehicle repair facilities, and aerospace companies.
It is the largest single list of new sanctions put forward for EU consideration, with the total list of entities and individuals sanctioned as a result of Russia's war on Ukraine currently standing at roughly 3,000.
Once adopted, the EU intends to move towards a more agile approach of adopting smaller lists of sanctions on a rolling basis rather than bundling them into a single package.
In practice, that change has already taken effect, with separate decisions taken in recent weeks to sanction Russian citizens involved in barring the opposition Yabloko party from parliamentary elections, abducting Ukrainian children, and spreading propaganda in Europe.
Another list of sanctions against those who rigged Russia's September election, and against candidates who ran in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territory, is also being prepared.

title: In Kyiv district battered by Russian strikes, a protest to save trees turns ugly
description:
In one of Kyiv's hardest-hit districts, a heating pipeline meant to help residents weather Russian attacks this winter has instead pitted them against their own city's administration.

Residents of Teremky, a neighborhood in southwestern Kyiv, say that while they are not against the pipeline itself, they oppose what they see as an unnecessary destruction of greenery to build it.

But after a violent pushback by municipal security guards injured several demonstrators, including women, the protest
content:
Demonstrators gather on the steps of the Kyiv City State Administration building during a protest in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 23, 2026. (Yevgeniya Doluda/The Kyiv Independent)
In one of Kyiv's hardest-hit districts, a heating pipeline meant to help residents weather Russian attacks this winter has instead pitted them against their own city's administration.
Residents of Teremky, a neighborhood in southwestern Kyiv , say that while they are not against the pipeline itself, they oppose what they see as an unnecessary destruction of greenery to build it.
But after a violent pushback by municipal security guards injured several demonstrators, including women, the protests grew beyond an effort to save a century-old forest strip.
The community now wants to tackle not only ecological issues and winter preparations but also a broader problem with what they see as poor management by the city administration.
Following a series of protests, the demonstrators took to the stairs of the Kyiv City State Administration building on Sept. 23.
Aliona, a 34-year-old Kyiv resident, stood there with a clear message: "We are ready to fight. Not just with the enemy abroad. We are ready to fight injustice."
The heating pipeline project in Teremky was presented as a way to help the capital through yet another harsh winter of relentless Russian attacks on the energy grid and other critical infrastructure.
The city administration says the project aims to provide backup heating to over 200 buildings, primarily residential, in a district heavily impacted by Russian strikes.
However, initial construction plans foresaw cutting down hundreds of trees, some of which have stood for over a hundred years, according to residents. The project, implemented by the municipal energy enterprise Kyivteploenergo, has faced criticism for allegedly exploiting local green areas for commercial gain.
"Kyivteploenergo is a very well-known company that, frankly, pursues a very socially irresponsible policy. Their legitimacy is under great question, and they make decisions that are beneficial to a minority of people," said Vitalii Dudin, a co-founder of Social Movement, a left-wing group campaigning for social justice.
"It's very easy to neglect the interests of the community," he told the Kyiv Independent.
Following close to a dozen protests, a two-week moratorium was announced on Aug. 12 to devise an alternative plan. Petro Panteleiev, the first deputy head of the Kyiv City State Administration, said the process "involved scientists and experts."
Panteleiev confirmed that the community's request to lower the number of trees to be felled had been granted and that construction should resume. The new plan supposedly reduced the number of trees to be cut down from 200 to about 10, but protesters remain skeptical of this promise.
Pipeline work resumed on Sept. 21, with heavy machinery appearing just a week prior. Although the city administration said that no trees were cut down that day, locals and protesters remained skeptical.
With temperatures already dropping in Kyiv, Panteleiev stressed the critical need to complete the pipeline project after a nearly two-month delay.
"Last winter, there were serious problems with heating in Teremky; after massive attacks, people remained without heating for a long time," the city official said in a Sept. 22 press release.
But protesters say they are not against the heating pipeline project itself, but rather the way it is being handled.
"I want to save my city, to see it green, and of course, I want warmth for all citizens. I don't want children and other people to be cold in the winter," said Kyiv resident Yuliia, 30, during the Sept. 23 protest.
"But we want this done properly and correctly," she added in comments for the Kyiv Independent.
"We have repeatedly proven (that alternatives exist) and found engineers who have proposed alternative routes, but the authorities ignore all this and do not communicate properly," said Tania, 36, a Teremky resident and protest participant.
The standoff entered a new phase when the rallies were met with force.
During a peaceful protest at the entrance to the construction site on Sept. 22, Tania said she was "roughly dragged through mud" by municipal guards, a local service tasked with maintaining public order and enforcing city regulations.
"I asked them to let me go, but they kept going and going, and they were really having fun doing it," Tania told the Kyiv Independent.
"They didn't let me go until the very end, when I was already starting to lose consciousness from the pain."
Despite multiple finger fractures on her left hand, she managed to attend the protest.
Videos of violent incidents involving Tania and others quickly circulated on social media, sparking outrage. Protesters called these events a "travesty" and demanded that the city administration issue a response.
In response to the Kyiv Independent's request for comment, the Kyiv City State Administration said that "the city is open to dialogue with residents," and "there have been repeated public meetings, during which residents' comments and suggestions were discussed."
The administration added that construction of the heating pipeline will continue according to updated plans despite repeated protests, but separately pledged to investigate the violent incidents.
"We will conduct a thorough and comprehensive investigation of the (municipal guard) employees' actions," Oleh Kuiavskyi, a deputy head of the city administration, said on Sept. 24 in a statement published on the administration's website.
However, since then, the violence has only escalated. On Oct. 6, Liubomyr Dmytryshyn, 24, a veteran who participated in the protests against the mass removal of trees, was arrested following a police search of his home.
According to a statement from Semiyarusna Hora, an urbanistic youth organization that Dmytryshyn leads, "law enforcement officers used physical force against Liubomyr without justification, resulting in bodily injury."
The organization also said the police seized his wife's phone and laptop, although she did not participate in any protest activities.
Dmytryshyn's sister, Yaroslava, said she is pained to see this happen to her brother, adding that "Liubomyr was detained without a proper explanation, and force was used against him during the search."
"People who defend their cities and their country should feel the support of the state, not face persecution from it," she added in a comment for the Kyiv Independent.
The Kyiv police confirmed they had launched a criminal investigation against a 24-year-old native of Lutsk, citing "a gross violation of public order… involving resistance to a representative of authorities maintaining public order."
The law enforcement body claimed that during an otherwise peaceful Sept. 27 rally, several participants provoked conflicts with police officers, using physical force and pyrotechnics, resulting in an injury to a policewoman.
The 24-year-old detainee "organized and coordinated the actions of the participants during the conflict with the police," according to the statement.
The police added that the investigation is ongoing, while Dmytryshyn's attorneys said he is currently being held in a temporary detention facility.
For many, these violent clashes marked a turning point at which the destruction of greenery was no longer the only problem.
The fact that the fight had grown beyond the trees was evident from dozens of cardboard signs during the evening protest on Sept. 23.
The messages varied from "Stop cutting down trees, find an alternative," and "Heating pipeline, yes; cutting down trees, no" to a poster with multiple pictures of civilians being assaulted by authorities with a statement: "This is not a dialogue."
Nadiia, 26, a photographer and copywriter, attributes the conflict to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko's shortcomings.
"Unfortunately, he (Klitschko) has been in power for what, 10 years; I haven't seen any steps towards ecology," she said.
Nadiia's pensioner mother, Slavna, agrees, adding: "We only see corruption."
The protests over the destruction of greenery grew into broader discontent with how Kyiv is being run.
"I just go around all week and tell people at work, and to my foreign friends, and to everyone about how Kyiv is an incredibly uncomfortable place to live," said Nadiia.
Residents are also frustrated with what they see as a lack of communication, transparency, and dialogue between their communities and the city administration. "This is not about a specific project, but about trust in the authorities," said Dudin.
Numerous protesters told the Kyiv Independent that they feel they are "being lied to" about the true intention behind the construction of the heating pipeline. Many believe there are undisclosed details about financing and the real beneficiaries.
"This is a blatant lie on the part of the Kyiv City State Administration," believes Tania.
There have been no reports or official investigations suggesting wrongdoing in connection with the project.
As of now, there are no plans to halt the pipeline construction, nor is it clear whether the city administration will adhere to its promise to remove only 10 trees.
However, some protesters still hope the city administration will listen to them and understand their demands.
Despite her injury, Tania is motivated to keep protesting.
"We want to be heard, for people to understand that they are being lied to," she said.
For others, there is simply no alternative, as Teremky has been and will continue to be their home.
"I walked through that forest park area every day to kindergarten," Tamila, 50, told the Kyiv Independent.
She awaits her husband's return from the army and hopes that he will come home to a familiar green neighborhood rather than a construction site. Yet for her, this fight goes beyond the people who stood on the steps of the Kyiv City Administration building.
"We want to preserve the forest park zone not only for us, but for future generations," she said.
Yevgeniya Doluda is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent. She holds a Bachelor of Arts in journalism, politics, and history from City St. George’s University of London. Yevgeniya previously worked and volunteered with non-profit organizations in Europe and had her work published in RTL. In addition to Ukrainian, she also speaks Spanish and French.

title: EU provides Ukraine 1.2 billion euros for drones and missiles
description: "The money will be spent on drones, drone interceptors, drone ammunition, and missiles manufactured by Ukrainian entities," reads a European Commission press release.
content:
The European Commission announced the disbursement of 1.24 billion euros ($1.4 billion) of defense support to Ukraine on Oct. 7, part of the bloc's 90 billion euro support loan ($100 billion) for Kyiv.
"Today's disbursement will help strengthen Ukraine's defense industry. And Ukraine's ability to defend itself. To protect people and infrastructure," said European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in a press statement .
"The money will be spent on drones, drone interceptors, drone ammunition, and missiles manufactured by Ukrainian entities," reads the press release.
The EU's 90 billion euro loan to Ukraine, approved in April 2026, was intended to provide two-thirds of Kyiv's financial and defense needs until the end of 2027.
In 2026, 28.3 billion euros ($31.7 billion) was earmarked for defense, and Ukraine's plans for how to spend that money have all been submitted and approved by Brussels.
With the Oct. 7 disbursement, 15.4 billion euros ($17.2 billion) of the 28.3 billion euros remain to be paid out, pending Kyiv's submission of receipts, which Brussels then needs to cross-check.
For example, Kyiv has yet to submit receipts for the purchase of Patriot PAC-3 ballistic missile interceptors, an EU official told the Kyiv Independent.
The EU gave permission for Ukraine to buy U.S. made Patriot interceptor missiles in September.
"For the rest of 2026, Ukraine still has 32.5 billion euros ($36.4 billion) available in financial support," reads the EU's press release.
In addition to the defense funding that remains to be disbursed, the sum also includes 17.1 billion euros ($19.1 billion) of budgetary support that Kyiv will receive in exchange for carrying out political and economic reforms.

title: EU ambassadors clear path for Ukraine to open two new accession clusters
description: Assuming all goes as planned, opening the two clusters could help Ukraine benefit from the European Commission's new "gradual integration" idea.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — EU ambassadors on Oct. 7 took the next step in advancing Ukraine and Moldova's push for membership, paving the way for the opening of two so-called enlargement clusters next week.
Candidate countries for EU membership have to align with the bloc by completing reforms, split into six so-called clusters .
Ambassadors agreed on Oct. 7 to take the next step on the two largest clusters, internal market and competitiveness, which address broad parts of the economy.
The decision also applied to Moldova because the EU politically linked the two countries' accession efforts.
In practice, that means Chisinau has had to wait as Hungary stalled Ukraine's EU bid until the country strengthens the rights of its Hungarian-speaking minority.
Budapest and Kyiv reached a political deal on minority rights in early summer, which led to the opening of the first two clusters in June and July , on the rule of law and external relations, respectively.
But progress stalled again as Hungary demanded that Ukraine adopt a law implementing changes to education for national minorities as outlined in the summer agreement.
The bill was submitted to the parliament on Oct. 2, which was enough to allow EU ambassadors to proceed, but between then and now, much remains to be done.
Ukraine first needs to submit a written negotiating position to the EU, which is understood to be already ready.
Then an EU working group of technical experts from the 27 countries needs to agree on the bloc's common position, which must, in turn, be adopted by ambassadors and ministers from the 27 EU countries.
And if Ukraine's parliament fails to pass the minorities law on Oct. 12, then the formal meeting to open the clusters the day after will not be allowed to take place.
But assuming all goes as planned, the EU should open the next two negotiation clusters with Ukraine and Moldova at the Intergovernmental Conference in Luxembourg on Oct. 13.
The amount of bureaucracy involved has prompted the European Commission to propose paring back some of that paperwork.
"Based on the treaties, we need two unanimity decisions, giving candidate status, and finishing," said the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos in a discussion with European Parliament members on Oct. 7.
"But now, in between, we have 150 steps also for sending a letter to a candidate country," the commissioner fumed.
Assuming all goes as planned, opening the two clusters could help Ukraine benefit from the European Commission's new "gradual integration" idea pitched on Oct. 6.
This would mean that as Ukraine completes reforms, it should already begin to enjoy some EU benefits, and a senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent that progress on the internal market cluster is critical because it addresses "economic security and critical infrastructure."

title: Norway's 2027 budget includes almost $9 billion in new Ukraine support
description: The money would be funneled into Norway's Nansen Support Program, named after humanitarian Fridtjof Nansen, who led famine relief efforts in Ukraine in the early 1920s.
content:
The Norwegian government proposed its new defense budget for 2027 on Oct. 7, in which Oslo has earmarked 85 billion Norwegian kroner ($8.89 billion) in support for Ukraine.
The contribution comes as Ukraine and the EU increasingly pressure third countries to increase their financial contributions to Kyiv, which faces a 1.66 trillion hryvnias ($40 billion) budget shortfall for 2027.
The 85 billion kroner, first reported by Reuters in August, would be funneled into the Nansen Support Program, named after Norwegian humanitarian Fridtjof Nansen, who led famine relief efforts in Ukraine in the early 1920s.
The program provides both military and financial support to Kyiv, and the latest pledge from Oslo would increase its overall size to 344 billion Norwegian kroner ($36 billion).
Norway also recently contributed 90 million euros ($100 million) to the EU's Ukraine Facility, which disburses funds to Ukraine in return for it passing key reforms.
Since the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, Norway has been the ninth-largest donor to Ukraine by total allocations, according to data from the Kiel Institute think tank's Ukraine Support Tracker.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,544,260 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,690 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,545,950 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 7.
The number includes 1,690 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,396 tanks, 25,498 armored combat vehicles, 159,128 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,836 artillery systems, 2,192 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,690 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,878 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action. While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Russia slams Ukraine with missiles, drones on Putin's 74th birthday, at least 30 dead including 5 children
description: Chernihiv Oblast Governor Viacheslav Chaus said that on Putin's birthday, he hopes "the Russian dictator ends up in custody in The Hague or in hell."
content:
Locals and rescuers carry an injured man from a residential building destroyed in a Russian missile strike in Pryluky, Chernihiv Oblast, Ukraine, on Oct. 7, 2026. (Evgeniy Maloletka / AP)
At least 30 people have been killed and over 100 injured in yet another Russian overnight mass missile and drone attack on Ukrainian cities on Oct. 7, coinciding with Russian President Vladimir Putin's 74th birthday.
In the city of Pryluky, in Chernihiv Oblast, a Russian cruise missile hit a residential building, killing at least 22 people, including five children, and wounding at least 54, including seven children, according to Ukraine's state emergency service (DSNS).
Three of the dead children, named Oleksandr, Kyrylo, and Serhiy, were only one year old, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media. The other child was an eight-year-old named Maksym, he added.
A fifth child was also killed by the Russian strike, DSNS said as of 7:13 p.m. local time.
"Today, as a 'birthday gift' to Putin, the Russian army destroyed a residential building in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region," Zelensky said .
"It was an ordinary five-story apartment block. There may still be people under the rubble. First responders are working nonstop at the site – doing everything possible to find every person," he added.
Chernihiv Oblast Governor Viacheslav Chaus said that on Putin's birthday, he hopes "the Russian dictator ends up in custody in The Hague or in hell."
Pryluky resident Halyna Osovyk, 55, woke up, and soon after, her flat was shaken by an explosion, she told the Kyiv Independent. Then came more strikes, smoke, and shattered windows. Across the road, two entrances of a neighboring apartment building were destroyed, and rescuers were searching the rubble for people.
The woman herself was still shaking as she spoke. Her hands and legs trembled.
"It was just sheer horror. And the sound of the missiles — you simply cannot put it into words," Osovyk said.
She knew some of those affected. One family was trapped under the debris – the mother, grandmother, and one child were killed, while another child was rescued and taken to the hospital. Another woman and her child were also pulled from the rubble and hospitalized, Osovyk said. As rescuers continued clearing the ruins, people waited for news of relatives who were still missing.
Pryluky had experienced Russian attacks before, she added, but never a morning like this. Asked what she would wish for Putin on his birthday, she replied: "I wish he could have what we are going through now."
Beyond the devastating attack in the northeastern town of Pryluky, the overnight assault targeted residential neighborhoods and civilian infrastructure in the country's central and southern regions.
Russian missile strikes damaged five apartment buildings in Dnipro and four high-rise buildings in Kremenchuk, Poltava Oblast, Zelensky confirmed in a statement.
The ballistic and cruise missile strikes in Kremenchuk claimed two more lives.
Poltava Regional Prosecutor's Office reported that the people killed in Kremenchuk were a 72-year-old woman and a 40-year-old man. 47 civilians were injured in the city, said Vitalii Diakivnych , head of Poltava Oblast Military Administration.
Strikes also damaged a city community center, authorities said.
The city of Oleksandriya in Kirovohrad Oblast was also attacked in the early hours of Oct. 7. Regional Governor Andrii Raykovich reported that two people were killed and three injured, with one man remaining missing.
The Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, was also heavily targeted, as was southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia , where transport infrastructure was damaged amid the large-scale attack, officials reported.
Russia's barrage on the capital killed at least four people and injured 13, while also causing massive disruptions to the city water supply.
The first deaths were reported in the Darnytskyi district, where city authorities said that two people were killed.
More casualties were reported in the following night and day as drones and missiles continued to strike the city.
Multiple explosions were first heard in Kyiv at around 3:15 a.m. local time, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground. Ukraine's Air Force previously warned of several Russian Tu-95 bombers approaching the border.
"The missiles are falling one after another. At least 10-12 explosions from what I can count. It's pretty loud in the city center," the Kyiv Independent's Tim Zadorozhnyy reported.
Other Kyiv Independent journalists described strikes around Kyiv's Podil district, with flames and smoke seen in the capital.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said a strike was reported at an unspecified "non-residential area" in the Obolon District, while warehouse facilities were hit in the Podil District .
Explosions were again heard two hours later at 5:15 a.m. amid a second wave of missile attacks.
Earlier, drones headed toward Ukraine's capital at 9 p.m. local time, Ukraine's Air Force reported, and an air raid alert was announced in the city shortly after, lasting from 9:09 p.m. until 9:58 p.m.
Drone attacks in the capital continued through the day on Oct. 7, injuring at least 13 people in the Obolon and Solomianskyi districts, Klitschko said . Six injured medical personnel have been hospitalized, including one woman in serious condition.
According to the Kyiv City Military Administration, a fire broke out on the first to third floors of a five-story residential building in the Solomianskyi district as a result of the drone attack. Firefighters rescued 12 people from the upper floors.
At 5:43 p.m. local time, Klitschko reported fallen debris on the roof of an administrative building in the Sviatoshynskyi district.
A woman's body was found at the site of the Russian attack in Obolonsky District. Klitschko said at 7:42 p.m. local time that in the district, a car near a residential building was on fire as a result of fallen drone debris.
The Kyiv City Military Administrationa also said that one man was also killed in the attack, without specifying the district.
Klitschko later added that after the attack, which disrupted the electricity supply in Kyiv, some water pumping stations lost power, and there were interruptions to the water supply on the western bank of the city.
According to the Ukrainian Air Force, Russian forces used a variety of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles, and drones in the overnight attack.
Out of an unspecified number of ballistic missiles launched at Ukraine, five were shot down or suppressed by electronic warfare, according to the Air Force.
Thirty-nine of 48 cruise missiles were confirmed shot down or suppressed as of 10 a.m. Kyiv time, 117 Russian attack drones were shot down or suppressed out of 130 launched.
Hits by Russian missiles and drones were recorded at 18 locations, according to the Air Force.
President Volodymyr Zelensky, in his Oct. 7 evening address, said that it is important that world leaders do not remain silent "in the face of what happened."
"...Russia intends to continue down this path: towards escalation, killings and attacks. Putin does not feel that this is causing him any problems. Real problems," he said.
Zelensky earlier in the day urged citizens to take air raid alerts seriously and warned that Russia is preparing a large-scale attack on Ukraine, citing recent intelligence.
"Please, please, take care of yourself. Please respond to signals of missile danger," he said.
The latest large-scale attack comes as Putin turns 74 years old on Oct. 7. The average male life expectancy in Russia is 68 years as of 2024, according to the World Bank Group.
Russia attacked Kyiv the previous night, damaging cars , and has targeted the city's key bridges in recent days.

title: Armed individuals from Belarus threaten Latvian soldiers at border, followed by another breach
description: "The escorts of the illegal migrants, who were located on the Belarusian side, were armed, issued threats to (Latvian) soldiers, and also actively urged and drove the migrant group toward Latvia," Latvian Interior Minister Janis Dombrava said.
content:
Armed individuals who escorted 20 migrants and attempted to help them illegally cross into Latvia from Belarus threatened Latvian soldiers before another group briefly crossed into the country, Latvian Interior Minister Janis Dombrava said Oct. 6.
"The escorts of the illegal migrants, who were located on the Belarusian side, were armed, issued threats to (Latvian) soldiers, and also actively urged and drove the migrant group toward Latvia," he said in a post to X.
Shortly after, a group of masked individuals illegally crossed into Latvia , stealing equipment before returning to Belarus.
"Several hours after this conflict, people dressed in masks entered Latvian territory, damaged a distribution cabinet, and stole cameras before the border guard's assignment could arrive, after which the individuals returned to Belarusian territory," Dombrava said.
The Latvian Minister warned Belarusian authorities that border incidents like these could lead to "serious consequences" for Minsk.
Similar incidents have taken place in the past, and the EU sanctioned the country in 2021 for its instrumentalisation of migrants.
Acts of hybrid warfare against Europe from Moscow and Belarus have intensified in recent months as Russia continues its war against Ukraine.
Overnight on Sept. 15, NATO forces shot down a drone that flew into Lithuanian airspace from Belarus, Lithuanian authorities said.
The drone entered Lithuanian airspace from neighboring Belarus , flying over Lentvaris near the capital, Vilnius, before being shot down near the major city of Kaunas, head of the country's National Crisis Management Center Vilmantas Vitkauskas told public broadcaster LRT.

title: Zelensky warns Russia preparing mass strike
description: Zelensky called on Ukraine's allies, particular in Europe and the U.S., to transfer any means of protection to the country if they can.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky warned on Oct. 6 that Russia is preparing a large-scale attack on Ukraine and urged citizens to take air raid alerts seriously, citing recent intelligence.
"Please, please, take care of yourself. Please respond to signals of missile danger," Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
The president said Ukraine's emergency services and air force were ready to respond to the Russian attack "to the extent that our means of protection allow."
Zelensky called on Ukraine's allies, particularly in Europe and the U.S., to transfer any means of protection to the country if they can.
"The world is bigger than Russian evil, and protecting life must be a common cause. I thank everyone who is really helping," he said.
He did not specify when the attacks were expected to take place.
At least 13 people were killed and 104 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day as a Russian air strike damaged a hospital in Kryvyi Rih, local authorities said on Oct. 6.
In recent weeks, Russia has increasingly launched jet-powered attack drones toward the capital around the clock, bringing air raid alerts, air defense fire, and explosions into the middle of workdays, commutes, and afternoons in the city.
At least 16 people were killed and more than 100 others injured in Kyiv and the surrounding region between Sept. 25 and Oct. 2, according to a Kyiv Independent count based on official reports. The highest number of injuries came on Sept. 25, when at least 59 people were wounded as drones caught residents in the middle of the working day.
Some 62% of Ukrainians are ready to endure Russia's war for as long as necessary, according to a Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) poll published Oct. 6.
The share has remained largely unchanged since late July and early August, despite the beginning of intensified Russian attacks using jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure during the survey period. KIIS said the results show that the attacks had not led to a decline in Ukrainians' willingness to endure the war as of Sept. 21.

title: Ukraine war latest: Russia strikes civilian vessels in Black Sea off Bulgaria's coast
description:
Key developments on Oct. 6:

 * Drones strike merchant vessels in Black Sea off Bulgaria and Ukraine, killing at least one
 * Russian losses to Ukrainian drones surge in early October, Madyar says
 * Despite intensified Russian attacks, 62% of Ukrainians ready to endure war as long as needed, poll finds
 * Shadow fleet tanker reportedly ablaze near Russian port city Sochi
 * Klitschko's promise of 50 mobile shelters for Kyiv set to fall far short
 * Poland to deploy Patriots near Ukrainian borde
content:
Drones struck several merchant vessels in the Black Sea on Oct. 6, including two ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. A Russian strike on a separate civilian vessel killed at least one crew member and injured several others.
One crew member, a steward, was killed, and seven others were injured when a Russian drone struck a merchant vessel flying the Marshall Islands flag in the Black Sea, according to Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper . The vessel was carrying rapeseed oil and was damaged in the strike, with a fire breaking out in the superstructure.
"By deliberately targeting civilian shipping and port infrastructure, Russia is grossly violating the norms of international law, thereby posing a threat to global food security," Kiper said.
Separately, two merchant ships, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able, were hit by drones of unknown origin about 112 kilometers (70 miles) off Bulgaria's coast on Oct. 6, according to Bulgarian broadcaster Nova . The incident is believed to be the first reported drone attack on commercial shipping inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in the evening that Ukrainian forces did not conduct operations in this area of the Black Sea. He said that Ukraine verified the details with Bulgaria and concluded it was a Russian attack, calling it a combined attack with sea and air drones.
The Togo-flagged vessel suffered severe structural damage and sank. The fate of its crew remains unknown, with the search for survivors continuing. NOVA reported that life jackets had been spotted near the vessel, but no people had been found.
The second vessel caught fire following the attack. All 18 crew members were rescued by a Bulgarian ferry. Two sailors were seriously injured, one with severe burns, the other with a head injury. The crew members are Indian and Turkish nationals, according to Nova.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev convened an emergency meeting with representatives of state institutions following the attacks. He described the attacks as a "gross violation of international law" and warned that such attacks pose growing risks to Black Sea shipping, increase insurance costs, and further complicate maritime transport.
Russian casualties attributed to Ukrainian drone strikes rose sharply during the first five days of October compared with the same period in August and September, Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, known by his callsign "Madyar," said on Oct. 6.
Between Oct. 1 and Oct. 5, Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces recorded 2,699 Russian troops killed or wounded, compared with 1,931 during the same period in September, Brovdi said in a Telegram post. The figure represents a 39.7% increase, according to Brovdi.
Compared with the first five days of August, the reported number of Russian casualties was 76.5% higher, rising from 1,529 to 2,699.
