title: Europe is learning the wrong lesson from Russia's drone war
description:
European governments are preparing for a form of confrontation that their current investments do not fully match.

While Russian-linked sabotage usually uses drones, logistics networks, criminal intermediaries, and deniable proxies against European cities, official policies and national strategies remain focused on detecting and intercepting each incident as it arises.

This approach treats only the instrument of attack, leaving the vulnerability it exploits mainly overlooked.

That vulnerabilit
content:
A sign reading "No drone zone" at Brussels Airport in Zaventem, Belgium, on Nov. 5, 2025. (Nicolas Tucat/AFP via Getty Images)
Founder and Director of the Strategic Security Initiative
European governments are preparing for a form of confrontation that their current investments do not fully match.
While Russian-linked sabotage usually uses drones, logistics networks, criminal intermediaries, and deniable proxies against European cities, official policies and national strategies remain focused on detecting and intercepting each incident as it arises.
This approach treats only the instrument of attack, leaving the vulnerability it exploits mainly overlooked.
That vulnerability is clear: Europe's security architecture remains slow, fragmented, and expensive to mobilize across agencies and national boundaries.
In this environment, drone incursions become just separate incidents, while the problem of long, inefficient responses remains unaddressed. The incident at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 4 with a quadcopter carrying plastic explosives that went unnoticed by security systems and landed near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft without detonating, belongs to a wider pattern of Russian sabotage activities against European cities, especially those targeting the major airports across the continent.
Each case, whether or not an attack was intended or completed, leaves the same residue of uncertainty, and that uncertainty is what makes cheap, deniable activity so effective against institutions that are otherwise highly capable.
A drone flying near or above an airport can disrupt the normal performance of critical civilian infrastructure by forcing the immediate closure of airports, overloading the work of police and intelligence services, and occupying resources even if no attack follows.
Democratic governments have legitimate reasons to take ambiguous threats seriously, but that very prudence can hand Moscow and its proxies an operational advantage, since an attacker capable of creating enough doubt to interrupt normal activity has no need to defeat an air-defense system at all.
Thus, the strategic value of such operations is their ability to force the defender to spend time, resources, and political capital determining whether an attack is actually taking place.
Under these conditions, Europe may win individual tactical engagements while losing the broader struggle over resources, resilience, and tempo.
More importantly, Europe's reading of Russia's drone campaign in Ukraine has focused attention on counter-drone technology, sensors, and interception systems, all of which are necessary for protecting infrastructure but cannot compensate for the institutional fragmentation that an adversary is actively exploiting.
In fact, Ukraine's experience demonstrates the importance of an organizational approach.
Against years-long Russian drone attacks, Ukraine has progressively connected battlefield reporting, air-surveillance data, acoustic and other sensor inputs, drone feeds, and intelligence into increasingly integrated situational-awareness and command systems, including the DELTA platform, allowing information from different sources to be brought together and distributed to those responsible for action.
It has also adapted its response architecture by combining centralized information with distributed defensive capabilities, enabling units and mobile teams to respond to threats without waiting for every decision to move through a complicated process of hierarchy.
As a result , Ukraine streamlined the process of detection, identification, decision, and action. This is a useful model that Europe should explore.
Attribution is another problem, because deniable sabotage is designed to take advantage of the interval between an incident and a verdict.
When investigators need weeks to establish responsibility, as it was during the Leipzig incident , where German authorities took around four weeks to publicly assign responsibility to Russia, attribution becomes a retrospective exercise and no longer functions as an indispensable aspect of deterrence and defense.
Indeed, public attribution requires credible evidence, and obtaining one might take a long time before authorities establish rock-solid data. .
However, when a citizen is suddenly stranded at an airport due to a drone-related disruption, the consequences of delayed decision-making are immediate and tangible.
To effectively address these challenges, Europe needs to organize counter-sabotage efforts that would incorporate connections, allowing aviation authorities, law enforcement, intelligence services, and armed forces to share information across institutional and national boundaries before an incident becomes a crisis.
In this process, applying lessons from the Ukrainian experience is essential because Ukraine has been forced to solve the problem Europe now faces, and it has learned to turn fragmented information into a usable operational picture and then convert that picture into action before an adversary can weaponize the gap.
Intercepting a drone can prevent an incident, but it cannot address the broader system behind it, leaving the entire process supporting a single drone operation largely intact.
Herewith, success should not be measured by the number of intercepted drones, as it reflects little about the capabilities of the entire system.
The decisive advantage is ensuring that Russia , not Europe, is forced to react, robbed of initiative, denied the ability to dictate the tempo, and made to confront operational costs and risks. Because only by reclaiming the initiative can Europe shift from a posture of reaction to one of control and force its adversaries onto the defensive.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Megi Benia is Founder and Director of the Strategic Security Initiative (SSI), an independent policy research initiative focused on international security. A former Georgian diplomat, she specializes in Russia's influence operations, NATO's collective defense posture, cybersecurity, and transatlantic affairs.

title: Russian losses to Ukrainian drones surge in early October, Madyar says
description: Between Oct. 1 and Oct. 5, Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces recorded 2,699 Russian troops killed or wounded, compared with 1,931 during the same period in September, Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, said.
content:
Russian casualties attributed to Ukrainian drone strikes rose sharply during the first five days of October compared with the same period in August and September, Robert Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, known by his callsign "Madyar," said on Oct. 6.
Between Oct. 1 and Oct. 5, Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces recorded 2,699 Russian troops killed or wounded, compared with 1,931 during the same period in September, Brovdi said in a Telegram post. The figure represents a 39.7% increase, according to Brovdi.
Compared with the first five days of August, the reported number of Russian casualties was 76.5% higher, rising from 1,529 to 2,699.
The largest increase was recorded in the area of responsibility of the Ukrainian National Guard's 1st "Azov" Corps, covering the Dobropillia-Pokrovsk sector in Donetsk Oblast , according to Brovdi.
Ukrainian drone operators recorded 1,268 Russian troops killed or wounded in that area during the first five days of October, compared with 884 in the same period in September — a 43% increase. The figure was almost twice as high as the 664 casualties recorded during the first five days of August, representing a 91% increase, Brovdi said.
The figures cited by Brovdi cover only casualties attributed to Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces and do not include casualties from other Ukrainian military units.
Ukraine's General Staff said on Oct. 1 that Russian forces suffered an estimated 46,230 personnel losses in September, the highest monthly figure recorded by Ukraine so far in 2026.
Ukraine has increasingly relied on drones to inflict casualties and disrupt Russian operations along the front line.
Oleksiy Melnyk, co-director of the Kyiv-based Razumkov Center and a former Ukrainian Defense Ministry official, told the Kyiv Independent in May that drones now account for 70% to 80% of Russian casualties. FPV drones often carry enough explosives to kill a soldier outright, he said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in July that Russia has lost more than 1.5 million troops killed or wounded since the beginning of the full-scale invasion. The figures cannot be independently verified, and Moscow does not publish comprehensive casualty data.
Russia has so far avoided announcing another nationwide mobilization , instead relying on an increasingly coercive recruitment system to replenish its forces.
Moscow uses financial incentives, regional recruitment quotas, pressure on businesses and public institutions, recruitment of students and reservists, as well as the enlistment of foreign nationals and residents of occupied Ukrainian territories to sustain its military manpower.
Ukrainian intelligence has also said Russia's General Staff is prepared to mobilize around 300,000 people in 2026 and another 300,000 in 2027 if needed.

title: Everything you need to know about EU's first step to making Ukraine's membership real
description: "As enlargement countries advance on their path of reform, the EU must be ready to welcome them," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press release.
content:
European Council President António Costa (L) speaks with journalists alongside President Volodymyr Zelensky, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the EU summit, the meeting of the heads of state and government of the European Union, in Brussels on June 18, 2026. (Michael Kappeler/picture alliance via Getty Images)
Editor's note: this article was updated with comments made at a press conference given by the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The European Commission published a document on Oct. 6 about the future of EU enlargement, a first step toward making Ukraine's eventual accession feel real, but also laying bare some of the work the bloc needs to do to be ready.
"As enlargement countries advance on their path of reform, the EU must be ready to welcome them," Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in a press release.
The Commission was also asked by EU countries to propose ideas on how enlargement should work in the future, primarily in order to prevent backsliding on the rule of law by future EU members.
The 25-page communication is a first attempt to address both of these questions and to make enlargement feel like a real prospect for which the current 27 EU member states need to prepare.
It will be accompanied in October by a set of progress reports on how Ukraine and other candidate countries are faring with the reforms required of them, as well as concrete roadmaps for the four most advanced countries.
Those roadmaps will lay out specific milestones, with dates, between today and the eventual completion of the work required for Albania, Moldova, Montenegro, and Ukraine to become EU members.
The Commission's decision to focus on four countries is also considered an important "political signal," four different EU officials have told the Kyiv Independent.
"These countries have shown significant progress in terms of readiness over the last years," said Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos at a press conference to launch the document.
For Ukraine, that message is especially important, as its pace of reform has slowed in recent months, and given that it is much larger than the other three, its entry into the EU raises more challenging questions.
That decision to include Ukraine has also been coupled with a forceful defense by Kos of the reform work done so far, on the one hand, and a similarly strong push for Kyiv to keep passing reforms on the other.
Just the financial cost of the EU's relationship with Ukraine puts it in a different league than the other three countries being discussed.
"For Montenegro, the bill is one euro per person, per year, so it was extremely cheap," a senior EU official told journalists ahead of the document's publication.
"Most of the accession candidates are very small countries, so we expect this enlargement grant to be relatively affordable … Ukraine is a very different animal," they said.
In the next EU budget, which spans 2028-2034, funding for candidate countries is set to come from a pot of money called "Global Europe," which the original Commission proposal for the budget set at 200 billion euros ($225 billion).
That proposal mentioned 15 billion euros ($17 billion) to be available for all candidate countries — not just the four most advanced — and a 100 billion euro ($113 billion) reserve for Ukraine, intended to address reconstruction.
But the cost of Ukraine's reconstruction was already estimated at $588 billion by the World Bank in February 2026.
"If you look at what has happened with funding of Ukraine, it's been completely driven by the war," the senior EU official explained in answer to a question from the Kyiv Independent.
"There is a massive uncertainty, no one is pussyfooting about that," they said.
The EU's farmers have jealously guarded their subsidy program, the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), since its introduction in 1962.
In exchange for complying with EU rules, EU funding enables the bloc's farmers to continue operating in a food landscape where they would otherwise be unable to compete on price.
But the sheer size of Ukraine's agricultural sector puts it in a different league, prompting the Commission document to argue that "targeted arrangements should significantly limit financial support and market access for sensitive agricultural products."
The farming sectors of Montenegro, Moldova, and Albania are "a small stone you put in a pond, it doesn't create a lot of shocks and waves," a second EU official explained.
They explained that forcing Ukraine to fully integrate with all EU rules in the sector would raise their costs to the point that it could price them out of world food markets.
"Our budget can never compensate for gains that Ukraine's very competitive — the only real competitive agriculture sector in Europe — can gain in the world," a third EU official explained.
But equally, exempting Ukraine's agricultural sector from EU standards risks breaking the bloc's single market, which relies on all member countries' businesses operating on a level playing field.
Ukraine "will and can become a member of the CAP. Under which conditions, this will be discussed," Kos said.
"We also have to protect the farmers in the EU, and we are already discussing this subject with Ukraine," she added.
The Commission's document does not lay out a specific plan for addressing this already, arguing that it needs to be properly negotiated between Ukraine and EU countries.
However, two senior EU officials told journalists that they could see the discussion becoming very detailed, distinguishing between agricultural products. One rule for chickens, another for sunflower seeds, another for plant proteins, another for wheat, and so on.
More clear for them is that the EU needs to open the fifth enlargement cluster with Ukraine, and soon, where these questions can be fully grappled with.
The document commits the Commission to helping prepare the draft agreement for cluster five, to "reflect the targeted arrangements for Ukraine in the area of agriculture … at an appropriate moment."
Ukraine already unlocked two of the EU's six enlargement clusters in June and July , to-do lists of reforms required by the bloc in order for Kyiv to become fully aligned.
Another two are set to open on Oct. 13, if Kyiv passes a law expanding protections for the country's Hungarian-speaking minority the day before.
But the remaining two clusters cover sectoral issues such as agriculture and the trucking industry, where Ukraine has a competitive advantage, which intimidates some EU countries.
For the Commission, opening those two remaining clusters is important to do soon.
With a sweep of elections due to take place in EU countries in 2027, "if we do not make a step now politically, the discussion is going to get pretty complex," one EU official warned.
To help make the prospect of Ukraine joining the EU more palatable over time, the Commission also makes several proposals on "gradual integration" of candidate countries into the EU.
Essentially, the plan would be to reward alignment with the EU by already unlocking some of the benefits that come with membership.
The idea is not entirely new, with Ukraine already included in the bloc's mobile roaming area, and Ukrainians being able to participate in the Erasmus youth exchange program.
But now the Commission wants to map every EU policy area, institution, agency, and program, for what could be offered to candidate countries, and when.
What gradual integration is not, however, is an alternative to EU enlargement, the document notes.
Likewise, the Commission is not proposing that new EU countries have fewer veto rights than existing members, except for a small voluntary commitment for countries not to use bilateral issues to stop other countries from joining.
And the plan to introduce safeguards to curtail voting rights if a country backslides on rule of law "will only be in place if there are breaches," Kos said.
Some other ideas pitched to include candidate countries more in the EU, such as observer seats in the European Parliament and Commission, as proposed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz , did not make it into the document.
"We don't want to open a new policy or political discussion," one senior EU official explained.
Instead, the plan is to show what is possible with the EU's existing framework, but if countries agree on other specific ideas, they can formally propose them.
One opportunity for EU countries to weigh such ideas will be when leaders are set to discuss the Commission's document as a whole on Oct. 15 in Brussels.
And it is expected that President Volodymyr Zelensky will be there with them.
Chris Powers is the Brussels Correspondent with the Kyiv Independent. He reports on EU news and policy developments relevant to Ukraine, bridging the gap between Brussels and Kyiv. He was formerly the Defense and Tech Editor at the EU media outlet Euractiv. Chris holds a BA in History from the University of Cambridge and an MA in European Studies from the College of Europe.

title: Rubio presses Russia for answers over suspected plague death in Siberia
description: "We're watching it very closely, hour by hour," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
content:
Russia should provide more information about the death of an employee at a plague research laboratory in Siberia, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Oct. 6.
"I think it's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world," Rubio told reporters in Iceland. "We're watching it very closely, hour by hour."
The comments came after the death of Darya Shipilova, a laboratory technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov, sparked concern over a possible case of pneumonic plague and prompted quarantine and other measures in Irkutsk Oblast.
Independent Russian media reported that she may have accidentally broken a test tube containing bacteria that cause pneumonic plague while working at the institute on Sept. 25. Russian authorities have not publicly confirmed that account.
Russian officials have been evasive about the cause of Shipilova's death and have sought to reassure the public. Irkutsk Oblast Governor Igor Kobzev said on Oct. 5 that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the region was stable.
U.S. President Donald Trump said Oct. 5 that Washington would help Russia manage its plague scare.

Nestlé now says it is "assess
content:
Seagull walks on a logo of Raiffeisen bank atop a building behind a monument of Soviet country founder Vladimir Ulyanov, also known as Lenin in Moscow on April 12, 2022. (Kirill Kudryavtev /AFP via Getty Images)
When Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, most global businesses rushed for the exit.
Swiss food and drink firm Nestlé was not among them. The company hunkered down, a decision it framed as ensuring local people's "right to food."
It made little difference to the Kremlin. On Sept. 17, the Russian government placed Nestlé Russia under temporary external administration, a move that could lead to the company's ultimate confiscation or nationalization .
Nestlé now says it is "assessing the situation and its options." It is not alone. In recent weeks, French supermarket chain Auchan and German food wholesaler Metro have been among those who have also seen their assets placed under external control.
Auchan told Russian news outlet RBC that it was continuing operations and had sought further clarification from the government. Metro said that the effects of the decision were "currently being analyzed."
But there seems to be little prospect of returning to business as usual, with the Kremlin tying its decision to geopolitics and its war on Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov told reporters that the companies were from "unfriendly countries" that were "actively involved in military actions against our nation, and involved in strikes carried out by Kyiv," he said.
When foreign businesses moved into Russia after the collapse of the Soviet Union , they found a market with both high risks and high rewards.
Multinational companies made phenomenal returns in Russia throughout the 1990s and early 2000s, says Charles Hecker, the author of Zero Sum: The Arc of International Business in Russia.
But they also made assumptions about how Russia would develop economically and politically .
"Companies failed to keep pace with the political change in the country," Hecker says. "They were making life-changing sums of money in Russia. And I think that that distracted us from some of the political and geopolitical realities."
Today, the Russian market is as risky as that of the 1990s, but offers little in the way of returns. While leaving is still an option, companies that do so face steep penalties. Foreign firms from so-called "unfriendly countries" must sell assets at an eye-watering 60% discount, while also paying a "contribution" to Russia’s state budget equal to 35% of those assets' market value.
Some companies paid up. Others hoped they would benefit from playing the long game, says Christopher Hartwell, a professor of international business policy at the ZHAW School of Management and Law.
"You think, maybe if I just keep my head down, it'll blow over. You think, if I'm going to come back in 10 years, after (Russian President Vladimir) Putin dies and this war is over, it's going to be very difficult to get back into the market because you have competitors who are using all of your assets. So maybe we need to stay here in terms of, you know, just keeping our foot in the door," he says.
Moscow also signaled goodwill toward such firms. In March 2025, Putin told a congress of Russian industrialists that Western companies that left but kept their staff and technology, with Russians running them under a different brand, had "made an independent and responsible choice."
Yet there had already been grave warnings of what was to come. Even if companies in 2022 could not have imagined their assets being expropriated by the Russian state, their calculations would have quickly changed when the Russian subsidiaries of companies such as Danone and Carlsberg were similarly placed under external administration in 2023.
Russian state news agency TASS reported on Sept. 29 that 135 companies linked to foreign firms had been placed under such controls.
"Anybody could have seen this coming from a mile away," says Hartwell.
A transnational corporation such as Nestlé is a greater prize for the Kremlin, and its assets are likely to be used to buy the loyalty of groups on which the Kremlin relies, says geopolitical analyst Alexander Kokcharov.
Danone and Carlsberg are good examples of what is yet to come.
In 2023, Yakub Zakriev, reportedly a relative of Chechen leader Ramzan Kadyrov, was named head of Danone's Russian subsidiary, before it was sold on to another firm linked to a former Chechen official. Another Putin ally, Taimuraz Bolloev, was also named head of Baltika, the Russian brewer formerly owned by Carlsberg, before it too was sold on.
Many of these groups would usually receive money of some kind from Russia’s state budget, says Kokcharov. But as Russia’s economy continues to struggle and resources are instead pushed toward the war, gifting business assets can make up the shortfall.
As Moscow's war on Ukraine consumes Russian society, buying that loyalty and shoring up budgets have become more important than maintaining business relationships, says Kokcharov. Meanwhile, Nestlé's case suggests that the Kremlin is giving up on the idea of returning to "business as usual."
"My understanding was that the Kremlin saw war in Ukraine as temporary. The sanctions are temporary. The disruption of business relationships is temporary. And once Russia achieves what it wants in Ukraine, there would be some sort of a thaw, some sort of a reset," Kokcharov says. "My guess is that now they realize that this is not happening. "
This shift in outlook means it's unlikely that Nestlé, Auchan, or Metro will be the last Western companies to face their assets being taken out of their control.
"If you're a Western company still trying to do business in Russia, you are playing with fire," says Kokcharov. "The entire political system is concentrated on the war, and it doesn't care about Western businesses or reputations, for that matter."
For those companies that have chosen to shelter in place in the Russian market, it is another stark warning to add to an increasingly long list.
"You can have a good run if you get in bed with authoritarians, but at some point you're going to wake up and realize that your wallet and your kidneys are gone," says Hartwell. "And was it really worth it?"
Katie Marie Davies is a freelance journalist who has worked in Russia and the UK. She has previously worked as a news editor at The Moscow Times and features editor at The Calvert Journal.

title: Despite intensified Russian attacks, 62% of Ukrainians ready to endure war as long as needed, poll finds
description: The share has remained largely unchanged since late July and early August, despite the beginning of intensified Russian attacks using jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure.
content:
Some 62% of Ukrainians are ready to endure Russia's war for as long as necessary, according to a Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) poll published Oct. 6.
The share has remained largely unchanged since late July and early August, despite the beginning of intensified Russian attacks using jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure during the survey period. KIIS said the results show that the attacks had not led to a decline in Ukrainians' willingness to endure the war as of Sept. 21.
Another 4% of respondents said they were ready to endure the war for about a year, while 23% said they could continue for only several months or up to six months.
"Despite the intensification of Russian terror against the civilian population — and the fact that our Western partners' response has not always been sufficiently decisive or backed by concrete actions — Ukrainians are prepared to continue bearing the burden of war until an acceptable peace is achieved," KIIS Executive Director Anton Grushetskyi said.
The survey was conducted from Sept. 12-21, when Russia had begun a new campaign of attacks involving jet-powered drones and strikes on civilian infrastructure. KIIS noted that the survey was completed before subsequent attacks on bridges across the Dnipro River.
The findings also show that 79% of Ukrainians believe Ukraine will ultimately win the war, including 47% who are certain of victory and 32% who said they rather believe Ukraine will prevail. Only 7% believe Russia will win, while 14% were undecided.
However, confidence in an eventual Ukrainian victory has declined since late July. At that time, 85% said they believed Ukraine would win, including 60% who were certain of it.
By September, the share who were certain of victory had fallen to 47%.
At the same time, 69% said they would support an immediate ceasefire along the current front line if Ukraine did not legally recognize occupied territories as Russian, continued strengthening its military, and maintained its path toward the European Union and NATO.
The poll was conducted through computer-assisted telephone interviews with 1,002 adults across all regions of Ukraine controlled by the government.
Residents of Ukrainian territories not controlled by Kyiv and Ukrainian citizens who left the country after Feb. 24, 2022, were not included.

title: Drones strike merchant vessels in Black Sea off Bulgaria, Ukraine, killing at least 1
description: A Russian drone struck a merchant vessel flying the Marshall Islands flag in the Black Sea. Separately, two merchant ships were hit by drones around 112 kilometers (70 miles) off Bulgaria's coast on Oct. 6.
content:
Drones reportedly struck several merchant vessels in the Black Sea on Oct. 6, including two ships in Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone. A Russian strike on a separate civilian vessel killed at least one crew member and injured several others.
One crew member, a steward, was killed, and seven others were injured when a Russian drone struck a merchant vessel flying the Marshall Islands flag in the Black Sea, according to Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper . The vessel was carrying rapeseed oil and was damaged in the strike, with a fire breaking out in the superstructure.
"By deliberately targeting civilian shipping and port infrastructure, Russia is grossly violating the norms of international law, thereby posing a threat to global food security," Kiper said.
Separately, two merchant ships, the Togo-flagged Alfa Watan and the Palau-flagged Able, were hit by drones of unknown origin about 112 kilometers (70 miles) off Bulgaria's coast on Oct. 6, according to Bulgarian broadcaster Nova . The incident is believed to be the first reported drone attack on commercial shipping inside Bulgaria's exclusive economic zone.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in the evening that Ukrainian forces did not conduct operations in this area of the Black Sea. He said that Ukraine verified the details with Bulgaria and concluded it was a Russian attack, calling it a combined attack with sea and air drones.
The Togo-flagged vessel suffered severe structural damage and sank. The fate of its crew remains unknown, with the search for survivors continuing. NOVA reported that life jackets had been spotted near the vessel, but no people had been found.
The second vessel caught fire following the attack. All 18 crew members were rescued by a Bulgarian ferry. Two sailors were seriously injured, one with severe burns, the other with a head injury. The crew members are Indian and Turkish nationals, according to Nova.
Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev convened an emergency meeting with representatives of state institutions following the attacks. He described the attacks as a "gross violation of international law" and warned that such attacks pose growing risks to Black Sea shipping, increase insurance costs, and further complicate maritime transport.
The incidents come amid a growing number of attacks and incidents involving civilian shipping in the Black Sea, raising concerns over the security of one of the region's key trade routes.
A day earlier, on Oct. 5, a cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast after a Russian drone strike killed two people and injured at least 11 others, prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.

title: Escape from Oleshky — 12 people reached Ukraine-controlled territory in September, official says
description: In recent weeks, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces.
content:
Twelve people reached Ukraine-controlled territory from the Russian-occupied front-line city of Oleshky in September, the local military administration head told the Kyiv Independent on Oct. 6.
Oleshky in the occupied part of Kherson Oblast has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make it almost impossible to evacuate safely.
In spring 2026, evacuation volunteers still managed to help people from Oleshky leave for other occupied settlements in Kherson Oblast or Ukraine-controlled areas in exhausting multi-day trips through Russia and Belarus. Now, they said , the risk of Russian attacks and mines has made organized evacuation impossible.
In recent weeks, some residents have started walking out of Oleshky to the neighboring village of Radensk alone or in pairs, on roads mined by Russian forces.
Tetiana Hasanenko, exiled head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said that while over 60 people left the city of Oleshky in September this year, only twelve managed to reach Ukraine-controlled territory.
The others either left for the neighboring settlement of Radensk, approximately 15 kilometers (10 miles) away to find food and return, or stayed in other occupied towns in Kherson Oblast .
"Most (of those who left the city in September) are still in the occupied territory. Some people have no documents, and most of them were forced to return to Oleshky because they have relatives there who cannot get about on their own, or they have children whom they simply cannot lead through a minefield," Hasanenko said.
While Russian troops occupy Oleshky and the eastern bank of the Dnipro River in Kherson Oblast , the Ukrainian military controls the western bank. Russian troops use towns and villages on the eastern bank to launch attacks across the river, including on the liberated city of Kherson.
Russian forces have placed guns, mortars, and mines in and around residential neighborhoods due to the city's proximity to Ukrainian-controlled territory, Oleksandr Tolokonnikov, deputy head of the Kherson Regional Military Administration, told the Kyiv Independent.
Hasanenko previously told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 30 that four people were attempting to leave the town when they stepped on a mine and were injured, while a man collecting nuts was killed by another mine. The incidents occurred along routes used by civilians to leave the occupied town.
"These people left Oleshky at 6 a.m. and must have failed to spot something before stepping on a landmine. One woman suffered a back injury and injuries to her limbs. She was taken to the hospital on a bicycle. The others were transported in garden trolleys," Hasanenko said.
The local hospital, which is operating without basic medical supplies, electricity, or running water, is also struggling to function, Hasanenko said. Four doctors, all elderly former hospital staff, continue to work there, she said.
"But there are absolutely no medical supplies. The only thing they can do is stop the bleeding. There are no medicines," Hasanenko said.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, remained in the occupied town with severely limited access to food, drinking water, electricity, and other basic services.
Russian forces are preventing Ukraine and international humanitarian organizations from accessing the occupied territories to provide aid.
Oleshky lies on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, less than 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) from the regional center of Kherson.

title: South Korea says it received 'insufficient' apology from Ukraine over North Korean POWs, mulls envoy recall
description: The South Korean government is considering several measures in response to the dispute, including a potential recall of South Korea's Ambassador to Ukraine, according to South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun.
content:
South Korea has received an apology from Kyiv over the disclosure of the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war (POWs), but the message fell short of Seoul's expectations, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun said on Oct. 6, Yonhap News Agency reported.
Cho said the apology was among the messages he received from Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
"But there is a difference from the level we expect, so we intend to take firm measures," the South Korean chief diplomat said, according to Yonhap.
The minister noted that the South Korean government is considering several options, including a potential recall of South Korea's Ambassador to Ukraine, an idea proposed by a lawmaker.
President Volodymyr Zelensky angered Seoul by disclosing information on two North Korean POWs transferred to South Korea during his speech on Sept. 23 at the U.N. General Assembly in New York.
South Korea claimed this breached a non-disclosure agreement and demanded an apology. In response, the Ukrainian Presidential Office said no such agreement existed, calling it "strange" to keep the transfer a secret.
The disagreement escalated on Oct. 2 when South Korean President Lee Jae Myung wrote on social media that Kyiv's denial of the agreement's existence was "branding the head of state of the other country a liar," warning of "additional measures" if Kyiv does not apologize.
"This is a matter concerning the dignity of the Republic of Korea's citizens and the nation, we cannot overlook it," he wrote on X.
During a parliamentary audit on Oct. 6, Cho emphasized that the arrangement was meant to keep North Korean soldiers and their families safe, noting that the Ukrainian side was the first to introduce the non-disclosure idea.
Sybiha has previously dubbed the incident a "diplomatic misunderstanding," adding that he hopes the situation is resolved promptly as South Korea is an important ally.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry has not commented on whether Kyiv issued an apology to Seoul.
Ukraine announced the capture of two North Korean soldiers in early 2025 as an estimated 11,000 North Korean troops were deployed to Russia's Kursk Oblast.
Ukrainian military intelligence (HUR) revealed in June that there were over 7,000 North Korean casualties , both killed and injured, during Ukraine’s incursion into Russia’s Kursk Oblast from August 2024 to March 2025.

title: Russia testing Europe's defenses below threshold of open war, experts say
description: What may look like a string of hybrid incidents increasingly resembles a sub-threshold war against Europe, says Olena Davlikanova, a security policy expert.
content:
Russia is testing how far it can push Europe without triggering open war — from drones crossing NATO airspace to sabotage and cyberattacks across the continent. Experts warn that Europe has strengthened its defenses since 2022, but key gaps remain, including in air defense, communications, intelligence, and joint command.
Russia is testing the limits of Europe's security without formally crossing into open war. Its attacks on Ukrainian cities have intensified in recent months, including strikes on civilian infrastructure. Russian drones entering NATO airspace have also become a recurring occurrence, while Western officials have raised the alarm over a rise in Moscow's hybrid operations across Europe.
In September, Germany accused Russia of orchestrating an attempted drone attack at Leipzig Airport in early August. The incidents are raising a broader question: how far Moscow can escalate its pressure on European countries without prompting a direct military response.
The Kyiv Independent spoke with participants of the Ukraine Recovery Lab, sponsored by Erste Foundation and organized as part of the European Forum Alpbach in Austria, held Aug. 24-Sept 4.
What may look like a string of hybrid incidents increasingly resembles a sub-threshold war against Europe, says Olena Davlikanova, a security policy expert.
The Everywhere War Tracker records a sustained campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks, military provocations, and airspace violations, which has grown more intensive and audacious since 2024 as Moscow has tested how far it can push Europe without triggering open conflict.
"Russia is waging a war against the European model of freedom, equality, and solidarity, and against the institutions that sustain it, especially the EU. This is a war fought in small steps," says Leopold Schmertzing, а strategic foresight and security and defense policy expert.
"I struggle to see it ending without a fundamental change in either the current Russian model or the European one."
Schmertzing argues that, despite Europe contributing far more to Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine than it did to earlier conflicts, most Europeans still experience it as a war happening somewhere else.
"My fear is that we will only fully wake up when our own capitals are attacked and our citizens are killed. By then, it will be too late to prepare," he added.
Experts believe Europe is better prepared for a potential confrontation with Russia than it was in 2022, but important gaps remain. Air defense, drones, communications, intelligence and joint command remain weak points, they say, while European militaries have yet to fully adapt to the realities of modern warfare.
Ukraine's experience shows that unmanned systems can have an outsized impact, but European defense spending has yet to reflect that lesson.
More than 80% of Russian targets destroyed on the battlefield are hit by drones, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in January.
"That is how the modern war looks like," says Kateryna Mykhalko, managing director of the German-Ukrainian defense industry consortium New Age Defense.
"At the same time, the technology delivering 80% of battlefield results receives only roughly 2% of European defense budgets," she adds.
The EU and Ukraine have sought to deepen cooperation in the sector. The EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance aims to accelerate the development and production of drones and counter-drone systems, combining Ukraine’s battlefield experience with Europe’s industrial capacity.
For Europe, the challenge is therefore twofold: closing military capability gaps while developing a response to forms of Russian aggression that experts believe are already unfolding across the continent.
"Russia is a hard nut to crack because it is deeply vulnerable in some respects and remarkably insulated in others," Schmertzing says. "We have a great deal to learn from Ukraine about where pressure works and where it doesn't."

title: SBU arrests collaborator suspected of setting up repeater stations for Russian drones in Kyiv
description: The man was suspected of "collecting data on defense facilities and critical infrastructure to adjust massive attacks on Kyiv from September 21 to 24 this year," the SBU said on Oct. 5.
content:
The Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), together with the National Police, detained a Russian collaborator, allegedly hired by the Federal Security Service (FSB) to help direct long-range mass attacks on the Ukrainian capital.
The man was suspected of "collecting data on defense facilities and critical infrastructure to adjust massive attacks on Kyiv from September 21 to 24 this year," the SBU said on Telegram on Oct. 5.
According to the case materials, the attacker tracked potential "targets" for four days in order to direct Geran-5 type jet drones and ballistic missiles at the capital.
Since the beginning of the full-scale invasion, Russian collaborators helping Moscow's war effort inside Ukraine have been a consistent focus of the work of Ukrainian counterintelligence.
In recent weeks, Russia’s daytime jet-powered drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital have become notorious not only for their difficulty to intercept, but also for their precision, highlighted by the targeting of bridges across the Dnipro River.
This has been enabled by the use of mesh radio networks, built around a decentralized network of radio repeaters that allows both airborne drones and ground-based repeaters to constantly share radio and control signals between them in real time.
On October 3, presidential advisor Serhii "Flash" Beskretnov asserted that the increased precision of Russian strikes on central Kyiv must have been enabled by the existence of mesh radio repeaters located inside the Ukrainian capital, something that suggested the presence of well-resourced collaborators assisting the Russian strikes.
The news comes after Russian jet-powered drones hit two of the most important bridges across the Dnipro River in Kyiv, the southern and northern bridges, several days in a row.

title: Russian strikes kill 13, injure 104 across Ukraine, damage Kryvyi Rih hospital
description: Regional Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that four people were injured in the Kryvyi Rih attack, including two medical workers.
content:
At least 13 people were killed and 104 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day as a Russian air strike damaged a hospital in Kryvyi Rih, local authorities said on Oct. 6.
In the city of Kryvyi Rih , Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, Russia attacked the hospital with Banderol missiles, chair of the City Defense Council, Oleksandr Vilkul, reported . The Banderol missile is a cheap Russian cruise missile that is often used to target front-line cities.
Regional Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said that four people were injured in the attack, including two medical workers.
Elsewhere in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , Russian attacks killed one person and injured three others over the past day, Hanzha said on Oct. 5 and Oct. 6 .
Overall, overnight on Oct. 6, Russian forces launched 137 Shahed-type attack drones, including 49 jet-powered versions, as well as Gerbera and Parodiya decoy drones, Ukraine's Air Force said .
Ukrainian air defenses shot down or suppressed 114 drones, while strikes were recorded at 17 locations. Debris from downed drones fell at four locations, the Air Force said.
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast , over the past day, Russia attacked the city of Kharkiv and settlements in the surrounding region, killing seven people and injuring 70 people, including children, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
Kharkiv suffered the most, with dozens of people being injured in a Russian Oct. 5 glide bomb attack .
"The enemy attacked Kharkiv with at least three glide bombs (KABs), with strikes recorded in the Slobidskyi district," Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in a post on Telegram .
In eastern Donetsk Oblast , three people were killed and 11 were injured in Russian attacks across the region over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In the northeastern Sumy Oblast , as a result of Russian drone strikes, a 49-year-old man was killed and four people were injured, regional authorities said .
In southern Kherson Oblast , Russian attacks in the region killed one person and injured four others, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast , over the past day, Russia carried out 955 attacks on 58 settlements of the region — eight people were injured in the attacks, regional authorities said .

title: Lithuania takes 1st step to lift nuclear weapons ban amid Russian threat
description: Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said removing the constitutional ban would strengthen Lithuania's resilience and deterrence.
content:
Lithuania's parliament voted on Oct. 6 to advance a constitutional change that would remove the country's ban on deploying nuclear weapons on its territory.
The move comes as Vilnius seeks to strengthen its deterrence amid growing security concerns in the region because of Russia's aggressive posture .
The parliament approved the proposal in its first reading by 106 votes to 18, with six lawmakers abstaining. The measure would repeal Article 137 of Lithuania's constitution, which currently prohibits weapons of mass destruction and foreign military bases on Lithuanian territory.
The proposal comes as Lithuania expands its defense cooperation with NATO allies, including the permanent deployment of a German military brigade, and as France considers expanding its nuclear deterrence role in Europe .
The amendment now faces a second and final vote, which cannot take place for at least three months. It would require the support of at least 94 of the 141 lawmakers to pass.
Parliament Speaker Juozas Olekas said before the vote that removing the constitutional ban would strengthen Lithuania's resilience and deterrence.
"This would mean that we secure the strongest possible support," he said .
Olekas said the final vote could take place on Jan. 12.
Lithuania has significantly increased its defense spending in recent years. The country also hosts a NATO multinational force, with Germany permanently expanding its military presence there.
Lithuania's security concerns are also shaped by its location between Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast and Belarus . Both countries host Russian military capabilities, while Kaliningrad borders NATO members Poland and Lithuania.
The proposed repeal would remove the constitutional provision itself rather than directly authorize a specific nuclear deployment.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,544,260 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,540 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,544,260 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 6.
The number includes 1,540 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,396 tanks, 25,494 armored combat vehicles, 158,551 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,785 artillery systems, 2,184 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,688 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,866 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA). While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Russian drone strikes Zaporizhzhia bridge in overnight attack
description: The bridge has been closed, and traffic rerouted, according to the Zaporizhzhia City Council. The strike follows multiple attacks on bridges in central Kyiv in the past week.
content:
A Russian drone struck one of the bridges over the Dnipro River in Zaporizhzhia during an overnight attack on Oct. 6.
The bridge has been closed, and traffic rerouted, according to the Zaporizhzhia City Council. Photos from the scene show damage to the bridge's road surface. The exact bridge struck was not disclosed by the city council.
During the overnight attack, five people in the region, including two members of the Red Cross, were also injured and were reported to be receiving medical help.
The strike follows multiple attacks on bridges in central Kyiv in the past week.
From Oct. 1 to Oct. 4, Kyiv's Southern and Northern bridges were targeted in multiple Russian drone strikes amid an intensifying campaign against infrastructure in the capital.
As his war against Ukraine stretches on, and as Ukrainian forces pummel Russian energy infrastructure , Russian President Vladimir Putin has sought to increase strikes against Ukrainian civilians.
On Oct. 3, President Zelensky said that Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents revealing that Putin issued a "new doctrine" allowing Russian forces to launch broader strikes against Ukrainian civilian target s this upcoming winter.
Under the new policy, roads, schools, and hospitals around Ukraine will be targeted by Russian forces in an attempt to force civilians to flee cities, Zelensky said.

title: South Korea shipped fuel to Russia via sanctioned vessels, media reports
description: Potentially undermining sanctions, over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, from South Korean ports were loaded onto sanctioned Russian tankers, based on analysis of port records and ship-tracking data.
content:
In several instances in July and August 2026, fuel was shipped from South Korea to Russia, according to the Guardian on Oct. 6.
Potentially undermining sanctions, over 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mostly diesel, from South Korean ports were loaded onto sanctioned Russian tankers, the Guardian reported . The findings were based on an analysis of port records and ship-tracking data.
Seven Russian tankers, including three sanctioned by the UK and EU, made 14 voyages from the nation's far-eastern ports to South Korean ports, where they were loaded with fuel before returning. In one instance, fuel was loaded onto a Russian tanker via ship-to-ship transfer, avoiding South Korean ports.
The transfer of fuel does not appear to violate South Korean law, the Guardian reported, despite involving vessels sanctioned by Seoul's western partners. South Korean export controls against Russia currently focus on electronics, machinery, and vehicles.
While Moscow is known to use its shadow fleet of aging, poorly insured tankers to ship out its oil in violation of international sanctions, Ukrainian attacks on Russia's oil infrastructure have sent it scrambling for fuel.
Ukraine has systematically targeted Russia's oil and gas infrastructure in long-range strikes, dramatically increasing its campaign against oil refineries in the past two years. Kyiv considers refineries valid military targets, as they supply both fuel and funds to the Russian armed forces.
On Oct. 4, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said that over 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity has been disabled by Ukrainian attacks.
Since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, South Korea has stood as an ally to Ukraine, sending ​630 million euros ($706 million) in bilateral aid as of February 2026, according to the Kiel Institute for the World Economy.
However, in recent weeks, relations between Seoul and Kyiv have been strained.
President Volodymyr Zelensky angered Seoul after providing details of a transfer of North Korean prisoners of war (POWs) to South Korea during a Sept. 23 U.N. General Assembly speech. South Korean President Lee Jae Myung on Oct. 2 warned of "additional measures" against Ukraine if its government refuses to take responsibility for a downward spiral in Kyiv-Seoul relations.
While the South Korean foreign ministry did not comment on the findings directly, it told the Guardian in a statement that as “a responsible member of the international community, the [South Korean] government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”

title: Largest oil facility in Moscow region erupts in flames following massive Ukrainian drone attack
description: Ukraine's drone struck the Volodarsk Linear Production and Dispatch Center near the village of Konstantinovo, according to monitoring channels.
content:
Ukrainian drones targeted a large oil facility in the Moscow Oblast during a mass attack, monitoring channels reported overnight on Oct. 6. Ukraine's drone struck the Volodarsk Linear Production and Dispatch Center near the village of Konstantinovo, according to Telegram channel Exilenova Plus. The Kyiv Independent was not able to immediately verify the reports.
According to Russian state media, the overnight attack was the largest drone attack the region has seen in the past two years.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said that at least 650 Ukrainian drones flew towards the capital during the overnight attack, with Russian air defenses downing 105. 650 drones flew towards the Moscow region. The majority of them were destroyed by air defense forces at a distance. 105 drones were destroyed as they approached Moscow. Eyewittness footage from Konstantinovo, located around 40 kilometers (25 miles) from downtown Moscow, appear to show flames erupting from the Volodarsk facility as smoke billows. The site is around 450 kilometers (280 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Creating 3 million tons of petroleum products each year the Volodarsk facility is the largest oil depot in the Moscow region, reported Astra , an independent Russian outlet. Pipelines connect the Volodarsk site to major airports in the Moscow region.
Ukraine regularly strikes military infrastructure deep within Russia and the occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
As Ukrainian forces work to return the war to Russian soil, the Defense Ministry on Oct. 4 reported that over 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity has been disabled by Ukrainian attacks.
Meanwhile, Russia continues attacks on Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure.
Russia targeted Kyiv late on Oct. 5, with drone debris falling into a residential area in the city's Pecherskyi district after air defenses shot it down, a reporter on the ground said.

title: Trump says US will 'help' Russia deal with plague
description: "I hate to see them having it; it's a rough disease," U.S. President Donald Trump said. "We'll help anybody that has that kind of problem, were willing to help."
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Oct. 5 said that Washington will help Russia manage its plague scare as the country faces reported quarantines.
When asked by reporters about the plague in Russia, Trump confirmed he's aware of the situation and said that the U.S. will "help them."
"I hate to see them having it; it's a rough disease," he added. "We'll help anybody that has that kind of problem, were willing to help."
On Oct. 4, Russian officials and media reported that an aluminum factory and multiple hospitals in Russia's Irkutsk Oblast have instituted preventative safety measures, including quarantines and mask mandates , following a laboratory worker's recent death by the plague.
Darya Shipilova, a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov, is alleged to have accidentally broken a test tube containing the pathogen that causes pneumonic plague while collecting samples a week earlier. She died after reportedly contracting the disease on Oct. 2.
Trump's remarks come as Russia continues deadly strikes on Ukrainian cities and as Ukraine alongside its allies continue to call for stronger sanctions.
The U.S. leader on Sept. 29 faced bipartisan pushback over possible Russia sanctions relief amid reports that his administration is considering the move in exchange for the release of political prisoners.

title: US not removing diplomats from Kyiv amid Russian threats, Rubio says
description: "(I)f a threat arises that we feel needs to be addressed by a change in posture, we'll do so.  We haven't done that up to this point," U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said.
content:
Washington does not currently plan to remove its diplomats from Kyiv as Russia continues attacks and warns foreign diplomats to leave, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters on Oct. 5.
"Look, we have an embassy presence there, and we'll make the determination about whether it's safe for them to be there or not," Rubio said at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland. "(I)f a threat arises that we feel needs to be addressed by a change in posture, we'll do so. We haven't done that up to this point there."
Days earlier, on Oct. 2, Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that no foreign diplomatic missions have notified Kyiv of plans to relocate.
"If any diplomatic missions are planning to relocate, they inform us; that is the established procedure," Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said.
Rubio also noted that Russia has issued the same warning to diplomats for months and that attacks against Kyiv are not a new threat to foreign missions.
"They've been warning diplomats to leave for months, and I don't think it's a surprise to anyone that Kyiv is under attack. I think that's well understood... we analyze every single day the safety of every diplomatic mission in the world," he said.
Russia has continued fatal attacks against Kyiv and cities across Ukraine as it continues to wage its war.
On the morning of Oct. 4, Russia also struck the roadway of Kyiv's Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River with a drone, injuring two people, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The strike was the fourth day in a row of Russian attacks on Kyiv that targeted key bridges, including the Southern Bridge .
Russia again targeted Kyiv late on Oct. 5, with drone debris falling into a residential area in the city's Pecherskyi district after air defenses shot it down, a reporter on the ground said.
