title: Ukraine war latest: Kharkiv devastated by Russian glide bombs, children among victims
description:
Key developments on Oct. 5:

 * Children among dozens injured as Russian glide bombs hit Kharkiv, 5 dead
 * New automatic gun turrets successfully down first Russian jet-powered drones, Air Force says
 * Russian drones strike cargo ship in Black Sea, kill captain, Zelensky says
 * Ukrainian pilots to soon start training on French Rafale jets, Zelensky says
 * Estonia moves troops closer to Russian border amid shift in strategic thinking

At least five people have been killed, and 53 others, incl
content:
At least five people have been killed, and 53 others, including children, injured after Russian forces struck Kharkiv with glide bombs on Oct. 5.
"The enemy attacked Kharkiv with at least three glide bombs (KABs), with strikes recorded in the Slobidskyi district," Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in a post on Telegram .
"As a result of the strikes… warehouse buildings are on fire, and residential buildings have been damaged. There may be people under the rubble of a residential building that was hit in the attack. A search and rescue operation is underway," he added.
Russian glide bombs , often called KABs (Kerovana Aviabomba) in Ukraine, are repurposed aerial bombs equipped with wings and precision guidance systems such as GPS, laser, or infrared targeting.
Automated machine gun turrets using artificial intelligence to aim have downed their first Russian jet-powered drones over Ukraine, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Oct. 5.
A day prior, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that twelve such turrets had been installed where Russian jet-powered drones have been particularly active, including around Kyiv.
"There are already cases of shooting down even jet UAVs, even 'Geran-5' from the those very turrets," Ihnat said on national television.
"The use of innovative technologies — artificial intelligence — has eliminated human error. Machine vision is used in the shooting down. Artificial intelligence allows you to target even jet-powered drones."
Since Russia started using jet-powered drones en masse against Kyiv toward the end of summer this year, they, especially the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models, have presented an air defense problem for which Ukraine has not yet found a single solution.
A cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast on Oct. 5 after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.
At the time of the attack, the ship was sailing outside Romania's territorial waters but within the country's exclusive economic zone, about 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers) from the Romanian coast and roughly 9 nautical miles (16.6 kilometers) southeast of the Pescarus offshore oil platform operated by OMV Petrom, according to Romanian media outlet Digi24.ro. First reports had placed the incident near the Neptun Deep gas development.
Estonia's 1st Brigade, the main combat-ready element of the country's land forces, will be moving to a newly expanded base less than 50 kilometers from the Russian border, placed to better meet a possible Russian attack.
The move, revealed in comments by the unit's commander, Tarmo Kundla, published in the Financial Times on Oct. 5, comes amid increased awareness of Russian military designs on the Baltic country .
The 1st Brigade will relocate from its previous base in Tapa to the town of Johvi, just west of the city of Narva on the Russian border.
Narva is often seen as a potential flashpoint of hybrid or kinetic attacks not only due to its location, but because the majority of its population is Russian-speaking, a common tool of Russian propaganda to justify aggression.
According to Kundla, the brigade's move is connected to a shift in strategic thinking for the Estonian military, which relies on the airpower of NATO forces based in the region — as well as on the deterrent of the alliance's Article 5 — to protect against an attack from its much larger neighbor.
President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed further European assistance in phone calls with the French and Polish leaders on Oct. 5, as Ukraine braces for a new wave of Russian attacks while U.S.-led peace talks fail to make headway.
Zelensky revealed after his call with French President Emmanuel Macron that France is preparing fresh defense assistance for Ukraine amid relentless Russian strikes, with a new support package expected "soon."
"Ukrainian pilots will soon begin training on French Rafale aircraft in France. This is a significant step forward for Ukraine's combat aviation," he added.
Kyiv announced in 2025 that it aims to purchase 100 Rafale jets to bolster its growing fleet of Western-made aircraft. The Rafale is a 4.5-generation multirole fighter, considered one of the most advanced among European jets.
France is Ukraine's staunch ally in its war against Russian aggression and has provided Kyiv with long-range missiles and intelligence support, among other assistance.
Zelensky said that both sides are also "continuing to work on localizing the production of French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine."

title: Putin allows Italy's UniCredit banking group to reorganize, sell Russian subsidiary
description: UniCredit, one of the few European banks still active in Russia, announced in May that it plans to sell most of its Russian subsidiary — UniCredit Bank Russia — to a private investor from the United Arab Emirates, while retaining control over its payments arm.
content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin allowed the Italian banking group UniCredit to reorganize its Russian subsidiary and sell the new unit, according to an official decree published on Oct. 5.
Moscow has barred companies from countries it has labeled as "unfriendly" — including Italy — from selling or transferring their shares in Russian businesses without approval from the authorities.
UniCredit, one of the few European banks still active in Russia , announced in May that it plans to sell most of its Russian subsidiary — UniCredit Bank Russia — to a private investor from the United Arab Emirates, while retaining control over its payments arm.
Putin's approval paves the way for the reorganization and sale, which UniCredit aims to complete by the first half of 2027.
Banks like UniCredit and Austria's Raiffeisen Bank have faced mounting pressure from European capitals to exit the Russian market since the outbreak of Russia's full-scale war in 2022 and the subsequent sanctions.
At the same time, Western companies face the risk of Moscow seizing or confiscating their assets in Russia as a form of pressure against Western governments.
Only last month, Putin signed a decree on the confiscation of the assets of the Swiss food company Nestle and the French supermarket chain Auchan, and the Kremlin seized control over the Russian subsidiary of Germany's wholesale food retailer Metro AG.

title: He fled Maduro's Venezuela. Now he leads Ukraine's South American battalion.
description: The Bolivar Battalion consists of about 250 soldiers, most of them from Colombia, Chile, and Veneuzela.
content:
Colonel Jose David Chaparro takes part in a routine infantry training session in Mykolaiv Oblast, Ukraine, in May 2026. (Nastassia Kantorowicz Torres/ The Kyiv Independent)
At a military training site in Mykolaiv Oblast, Col. Jose David Chaparro, call sign "Katana," does one-arm push-ups with his team. The 59-year-old Venezuelan commands the Bolivar Battalion, a drone unit within the Security Service of Ukraine’s Special Operations Center "A" (Alpha).
"Remember, if you control your breathing, you control it all," he tells the soldiers who struggle to hold a plank position.
He quizzes them on drones. "Apart from pornography, you can also review drone tactics online," he says, and the group laughs.
After training, three recruits are formally inducted into the battalion. Chaparro taps each new member on the shoulder with a katana, the traditional Japanese sword that is also his call sign.
Three years after its founding, the Bolivar Battalion has grown to about 250 soldiers. Most are Colombian, along with a few Chileans, Venezuelans, Italians, Germans, and Portuguese. As Ukraine intensifies recruitment of foreign volunteers , many from Latin America, Chaparro has become more critical of the approach. His unit offers a window into Ukraine's growing reliance on foreign volunteers, and the challenges that come with the recruitment push.
Chaparro was born and raised in San Cristobal, Venezuela. He came to Kyiv in 1989 for a postgraduate law degree and lived through the collapse of the Soviet Union before returning to Venezuela in the late 1990s, where he eventually worked in the government.
From 2001 to 2005, he served as acting consul in Moscow . During that time, he says, the gap between the government's ideology and his own democratic values widened so far that he resigned and returned to Venezuela once again.
In 2013, Chaparro joined students and other protesters who took to the streets and built barricades in San Cristobal, tired of injustices, political repression, food shortages, inflation, and insecurity. By early 2014, the social uprising, known as guarimbas, had spread across Venezuela, and the government of Nicolas Maduro violently cracked down on the protesters. Chaparro's opposition to the regime forced him to flee to Ukraine with his family between 2013 and 2014, he says.
Once in Kyiv, Chaparro joined the barricades once again at Ukraine's EuroMaidan Revolution. Venezuela and Ukraine, he says, "share a mutual enemy: Russia." Moscow backed the governments of Hugo Chavez and Maduro as they repressed dissent in Venezuela.
When Russia's full-scale invasion started in 2022, Chaparro volunteered in the Territorial Defense Forces .
In 2023, he founded the Bolivar Battalion, named after Simon Bolivar, who led Venezuela, Colombia, and Ecuador in their fight for independence from Spanish colonial rule. In 2025, the battalion was integrated into the SBU .
"The first rule I heard from the colonel: stay alive," says a Colombian soldier with the call sign "Billy," who has served under Chaparro for more than a year. He transferred from another battalion, where he says he felt he was being sent on combat missions to die. He knew Chaparro recruited differently and required soldiers to train for a couple of months before signing a contract, unpaid but with living costs covered.
Lt. Col. Kostiantyn Milevskyi, head of the Ground Forces department that coordinates foreigners' military service, says that pre-contract training for soldiers is unusual and probably specific to special operations units, yet he cannot confirm it.
For Chaparro, training ensures his soldiers are committed to the cause and able to fight. Billy says that Chaparro looks after every one of his soldiers. They trust him, Billy says, because they know he will not send them on a mission he would not take on himself. Chaparro is not required to accompany his soldiers to the front line, but he does.
The battalion now operates a range of drones, from first-person-view (FPV) strike drones to fixed-wing reconnaissance drones. It fights in Donetsk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts. Chaparro says that no soldier has been killed in action since the battalion switched to drone warfare 15 months ago.
Chaparro says Ukrainians have welcomed him with open arms and see him as "just another Ukrainian." But within the military, he says, he has at times faced hostility because he is Latino.
A soldier with the call sign "Aries" recalls a racist remark a senior Ukrainian officer made to Chaparro, telling him to "get out of the house and take your Indians with you." Aries says Chaparro defended his soldiers and nearly got into trouble himself. "Not everyone will stand up for you like that," Aries says.
Military analyst Viktor Kevliuk from the Centre for Defence Strategies estimates that between 10,000 and 16,000 foreign volunteers serve across Ukraine's armed forces. South Americans make up 40%, the largest regional group, he says.
"For Ukrainian society, all of them, they are heroes and will be heroes up to the end of their days."
Kevliuk says foreign volunteers have proven especially valuable amid Ukraine's mobilization problems and an estimated 200,000 absent-without-leave cases as of early 2026, which he attributes partly to combat exhaustion and resistance to conscription among Ukrainians who did not volunteer.
"While foreign fighters help partially alleviate manpower shortages," he says, "they do not offer a systemic solution to Ukraine's broader personnel crisis."
Ukraine's approach to recruiting foreigners has changed considerably since 2022, when it waived visa entry requirements for foreign volunteers. Once in Ukraine, however, many foreign volunteers faced bureaucratic uncertainty over residency, documentation, and their long-term legal status.
In late 2025, the government announced several reforms to change the situation for foreign volunteers. Some, such as pay raises for infantry and noncombat roles, affect every service member, but others were specific to foreign volunteers.
Among the reforms was the formalization of combatant status, so a foreign national can obtain veteran status on the same terms as a Ukrainian. Combined with a residency permit introduced this year, that status opens a path to Ukrainian citizenship .
Since January, Ukraine also permits multiple citizenship for nationals of a government-approved list of countries, meaning some foreigners can see military service as a path to migration without giving up their original citizenship.
"Many, he says, "come looking for a future, or for money, or for opportunities," but have no military experience."
On June 12, then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov wrote that reforms aimed at filling 30% to 50% of assault and infantry positions with foreigners would begin rolling out.
Milevskyi says the recruitment process has been deliberately streamlined. The biggest change is financial: Ukraine now covers recruits' travel costs to the country. "No one is giving them money. Ukraine is just paying for tickets, or renting the plane," he says. Once enough recruits sign up to fill a plane, flights are chartered from cities such as Bogota, Colombia, according to him.
Chaparro does not believe the Defense Ministry's recent reforms solve the problem of recruiting qualified soldiers. The challenge, he says, is attracting professional soldiers and retaining them. The South Americans now arriving in Ukraine "are in the most part, frauds," he says.
"They say they can operate a drone, throw a grenade with three hands, yet deliver nothing," he says. Many, he says, "come looking for a future, or for money, or for opportunities," but have no military experience.
Chaparro says the volunteers he fought alongside in 2022 were experienced professionals, and the gap between them and the new arrivals is "like the difference between the moon and the earth."
Milevskyi sees it differently. He says recruits must submit documents "which prove they served in the police, that they were in touch with the army." Asked whether inexperienced recruits were being sent to the front within days, he called it "rumors."
Colombians make up a large share of foreign volunteers, he says, "because of the lifestyle in Colombia and because the salary in the Ukrainian army is double, triple, four times more than they can imagine in Colombia."
Billy says money was not his reason to come and fight for Ukraine. "Money was never the driving factor for me. As a professional soldier I always knew I would come one day," he says. He sees it as his military duty.
Aries, like Billy, was a professional soldier in Colombia. He followed the war and saw TikTok videos saying Ukraine's armed forces needed more troops. Bored with working odd jobs in Spain, he traveled to Ukraine and enlisted. "I like the military life," he says.
A soldier with the call sign "Valera," one of the few women in the battalion, says she came to Ukraine "to fight for what is right and be part of the change." She says money is a secondary motivator.
Chaparro sits at a table, laughing, drinking an espresso, and sharing chicken nuggets with his soldiers. He treats them to food and drinks at a gas station in Mykolaiv Oblast to celebrate the three new members.
"For Ukrainian society, all of them, they are heroes and will be heroes up to the end of their days," Milevskyi says of foreign volunteers.
Nastassia Kantorowicz Torres (she/her) is a photojournalist and non-fiction storyteller. She is a contributor for Sipa Press (France) and freelancer. Nastassia covers war, migration, water, post-conflict solutions and gender-based perspectives. Her work was exhibited in Camera meets ICP, A living Archive group show, and published in Le Parisien, El Pais America and others. She was an International Women’s Media Foundation (IWMF) 2025 Women on the Ground: Reporting from Ukraine’s Unseen Frontlines, IWMF’s 2019 Adelante Fellow (Colombia/ Venezuela Border) and a National Geographic COVID-19 Emergency Fund for Journalists 2020 recipient. She received the 2018 Documentary Essay Prize of the Center for Documentary Studies at Duke University. She is a member of Women Photograph. She completed a postgraduate certificate in Documentary Practice and Visual Journalism from the International Center of Photography in 2017. Nastassia worked in development projects in Colombia and in humanitarian aid with Doctors without Borders in Eastern African countries. She holds a master’s degree in Public Affairs from the Institute des Sciences-Politiques Paris. She is from Colombia with dual citizenship from the United States. Nastassia lives in Kyiv, Ukraine since fall 2024.

title: Ukrainian pilots to soon start training on French Rafale jets, Zelensky says
description: France is preparing fresh defense assistance for Ukraine amid relentless Russian aerial attacks, with a new support package expected "soon," Zelensky revealed after his call with French President Emmanuel Macron.
content:
Editor's note: The story has been updated with the latest details.
President Volodymyr Zelensky discussed further European assistance in phone calls with the French and Polish leaders on Oct. 5, as Ukraine braces for a new wave of Russian attacks while U.S.-led peace talks fail to make headway.
Zelensky revealed after his call with French President Emmanuel Macron that France is preparing fresh defense assistance for Ukraine amid relentless Russian strikes, with a new support package expected "soon."
"Ukrainian pilots will soon begin training on French Rafale aircraft in France. This is a significant step forward for Ukraine's combat aviation," he added.
Kyiv announced in 2025 that it aims to purchase 100 Rafale jets to bolster its growing fleet of Western-made aircraft. The Rafale is a 4.5-generation multirole fighter, considered one of the most advanced among European jets.
France is Ukraine's staunch ally in its war against Russian aggression and has provided Kyiv with long-range missiles and intelligence support, among other assistance.
Zelensky said that both sides are also "continuing to work on localizing the production of French missiles and aerial bombs in Ukraine."
The Ukrainian president underscored France's commitment to Freyja , a joint European anti-ballistic missile defense project led by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point.
Zelensky added that he and Macron would discuss the details further during an in-person meeting, without giving a specific date.
In a separate call with Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, Zelensky briefed the Polish leader about ongoing preparations for trilateral talks between Ukraine, the U.S., and Russia.
"There are no obstacles on our part, but it is important that the U.S. side prepares on its end and ensures Russia's readiness," said Zelensky.
The president said on Oct. 4 that Washington is pushing for Ukraine and Russia to hold technical-level negotiations before the end of the month.
Another topic of discussion between the two was Ukraine's winter preparations, as Russia has already begun targeting energy infrastructure ahead of what is expected to be another brutal winter.
Zelensky noted that "not everything can be discussed in detail over the phone," and the two leaders agreed to meet in the near future.
Tusk and Zelensky last met at the Carpathian 8 Summit on Sept. 18, where the countries of the Carpathian region discussed economic, cultural, and security cooperation.
The president also held a phone call with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten later that day to discuss ways to strengthen Ukraine's air defenses and the status of peace talks.
"A significant share of (Russian) drones are shot down specifically by the F-16s that the Netherlands transferred to Ukraine, and there are opportunities to support their operation with the necessary means," Zelensky said.

title: Trump's Ukraine-Russia peace gambit begins to unravel. Again
description:
U.S. President Donald Trump's latest push for peace between Ukraine and Russia is facing growing uncertainty, with few in Kyiv believing it can deliver a breakthrough — or even bring the three sides together for talks, the Kyiv Independent can reveal.

The latest effort began in early September, when Trump's envoys traveled to Kyiv and Moscow seeking progress before the U.S. midterm elections.

The trips produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a trilateral meeting betwee
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump speaks during a visit to the Fort Bragg U.S. Army base on Feb. 13, 2026, in Fort Bragg, (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
U.S. President Donald Trump's latest push for peace between Ukraine and Russia is facing growing uncertainty, with few in Kyiv believing it can deliver a breakthrough — or even bring the three sides together for talks, the Kyiv Independent can reveal.
The latest effort began in early September, when Trump's envoys traveled to Kyiv and Moscow seeking progress before the U.S. midterm elections.
The trips produced one tangible outcome: an agreement in principle to hold a trilateral meeting between Ukraine, Russia , and the U.S. The sides were expected to discuss proposals for an energy ceasefire, a possible reopening of the Black Sea grain corridor, and humanitarian issues such as prisoner-of-war exchanges.
Kyiv never expected the talks to produce a full ceasefire by spring 2027, according to a senior Ukrainian official. Still, Kyiv agreed to participate.
A month later, even the trilateral meeting itself remains uncertain. Moscow has shown little urgency to commit to the talks, people familiar with the negotiations said.
"The U.S. wants to organize meetings. I think we will support it. But it is very important that not only Ukraine but also the Russian side support these meetings," President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters during a side gaggle on Oct. 4.
The latest sign that Washington is still trying to move the process forward came on Oct. 4, as Zelensky was meeting German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Kyiv.
Zelensky's phone buzzed with a message from Trump's peace envoy Steve Witkoff . He told the Ukrainian president that Washington wanted to hold the trilateral meeting in late October. Zelensky texted back that Ukraine would support it.
But the proposed timing represents a significant delay. The meeting was initially expected to take place in early October in the UAE, where the sides were expected to discuss the energy initiative and a possible reopening of the Black Sea grain corridor.
People close to the negotiations attributed the delay to Russia's position.
Ukrainian and U.S. officials have already shared their vision for the next steps with Moscow , people familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent.
The effort has also continued through Kirill Dmitriev, Putin's envoy, who visited the U.S. twice in September for meetings with Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.
It remains unclear why the trilateral meeting was pushed back by almost a month.
One major issue expected to be discussed is an energy ceasefire . Ukraine and Russia have repeatedly targeted each other's energy infrastructure throughout the war.
Ukraine has struck Russian energy facilities and exports to disrupt a key source of funding for Moscow's war effort. Russia, meanwhile, has repeatedly attacked Ukrainian power plants and substations, seeking to leave civilians without electricity and heating.
The urgency of the issue has grown as winter approaches.
Russia struck Kyiv's energy infrastructure overnight and throughout the day on Sept. 30 in a renewed campaign to push Ukraine into the dark, and reviving fears of another winter of attacks on the electricity grid.
One senior Ukrainian official said Russia could have little incentive to rush into talks while it can still inflict damage on Ukraine's energy system. The official suggested Moscow may be seeking to destroy as much Ukrainian energy infrastructure as possible before negotiations , potentially giving Russia greater leverage at the talks.
Since late August, Russia has also intensified attacks on Kyiv. The Ukrainian president said Moscow had effectively removed restrictions on its targets, including schools, energy infrastructure, and civilian sites.
"Russia is deliberately escalating things as much as possible to provoke a response from Ukraine, so that it can continue the escalation and keep raising the stakes as much as possible before any talks with the Americans," Zelensky said.
The uncertainty surrounding the trilateral meeting raises a broader question: after months of failed attempts to broker a ceasefire, can another round of U.S.-led diplomacy produce a different result?
Trump has sought to broker an end to Russia's war against Ukraine since returning to office in January 2025. So far, his efforts have failed to deliver.
Washington is not the only outside power that has tried to find a way forward.
India has proposed a ceasefire plan combining a halt to attacks on energy infrastructure with measures to protect shipping in the Black Sea. India's proposal incorporates elements of initiatives put forward by other countries, including Turkey , Egypt, and the United States, according to a Ukrainian official familiar with the matter.
Russia has rejected the proposal, the official said.
The rejection is significant for Kyiv because it suggests that the problem is not simply finding another intermediary or drafting another proposal. Moscow has also resisted initiatives from countries it maintains close relations with.
For now, Washington continues to pursue the same track, even as Kyiv grows increasingly doubtful about what it can achieve.
"Putin doesn't seem afraid. He feels he can do whatever he wants. There's no pressure from the U.S. … but he's afraid of Trump, no matter what," Zelensky said.
Tim Zadorozhnyy is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent covering foreign policy, U.S.-Ukraine relations, and political developments across Europe and Russia. He studied International Relations and European Studies at Lazarski University and Coventry University. Tim began his journalism career in Odesa in 2022 as a reporter for a local television channel. He later spent a year and a half at the Belarusian independent media outlet NEXTA, first as a news anchor and later as a managing editor. He is fluent in English, Ukrainian, and Russian.

title: What does Russia's rising military budget say about its plans for the war?
description:
The Russian government began the month by submitting a three-year budget plan to parliament, proposing yet another increase in funding for its war against Ukraine.

On the surface, the planned increase looks substantial. Russia's overall military budget is set to rise to around 17 trillion rubles (approximately $200 billion) in 2027, up from 12 trillion rubles in 2026 — a 27% increase in nominal spending.

When combined with spending on law enforcement, another heavy budget line, expenditures on
content:
Russia's President Vladimir Putin (C) looks on as he visits an observation post during the "Center-2026" strategic command-and-staff exercise at the Chebarkulsky training ground in Chelyabinsk on Oct. 2, 2026. (Alexander Kazakov / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)
The Russian government began the month by submitting a three-year budget plan to parliament, proposing yet another increase in funding for its war against Ukraine.
On the surface, the planned increase looks substantial. Russia's overall military budget is set to rise to around 17 trillion rubles (approximately $200 billion) in 2027, up from 12 trillion rubles in 2026 — a 27% increase in nominal spending.
When combined with spending on law enforcement, another heavy budget line, expenditures on the military and security forces account for 43% of the total government spending.
The figures are striking, but experts who spoke to the Kyiv Independent cautioned that they can be misleading.
Rather than pointing to a sudden surge in military spending, the latest budget figures suggest that Russia is continuing to gradually build up and sustain its military capacity, signaling a readiness for a prolonged war.
Next year, Russia's military and security forces will get more money than any other sector — only 21% of the 2027 budget is allocated to healthcare, education, and social payments combined. That is generally similar to what is directly funneled to the military, but only half of the number when allocations to security forces are added.
Russia's high military budget would also be maintained in 2028 and 2029, according to the three-year budget plan.
"It's difficult to speculate, but the planned budget hike suggests that (the Kremlin) may intend to recruit more people (into the army) under contract in 2027," said Michael Kofman, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Guesses on the actual purpose of the increases can only be speculative, argued in turn Pavel Luzin, a researcher with the Center for European Policy Analysis.
On top of the already high military budget, the Russian government can additionally increase funding throughout the year without parliamentary approval, said Sergey Aleksashenko, an exiled Russian economist and former deputy finance minister.
"Basically, the numbers we are seeing, this is what the Kremlin wants us to see," he said. "Around May (this year), the Defense Ministry requested additional funding from Vladimir Putin, and this request was granted."
While Russia does not publish detailed data on military spending, Luzin agreed that the figures for 2026 were likely higher than what was settled in the Russian government's initial budget: "approximately 16-17 trillion rubles, in my assessment," the researcher told the Kyiv Independent.
As for funding on healthcare, education, and social payments, these are set to decrease next year , Russian economist Alexandra Prokopenko found in a recent study.
The 27% army budget increase may sound significant, but this number is a bit misleading, Aleksashenko said.
"Russian military expenditures are growing step by step, but not as dramatically as (this figure) would suggest, because that number was calculated on the wrong basis," the Russian economist added.
According to him, instead of basing the increase on Russia's initial plans for 2026, these should be compared to what Russia actually spent throughout the year: in that case, the increase would be much lower.
"It's not extraordinary that the government admitted that it will spend at least 17 trillion rubles on the military in 2027," Luzin agreed.
The bulk of the on-paper increase is linked to inflation, specifically cost-push inflation in the military industry, but also salaries and payments to wounded and families of killed Russian soldiers, the researcher added.
"At the same time, the Russian government is also beginning a new round of investments, trying to modernize the sector, because Russia's military industry cannot produce more than it did (at its peak) in 2024," he added.
In fact, Russia's upcoming budget says more about how the government wants to raise money for the war, Prokopenko explained — more than it does about how much money will be spent and on what.
"Officially, Russia's budget deficit is to be cut to 2.2% in 2027, but since the start of the full-scale invasion, the government never managed to stick to the original budget deficit plans," Prokopenko said. "For instance, for 2026, the plan was to keep the deficit to 1,6%, as opposed to 2,6% in 2025, but in the end the projection for this year is 3,2%."
Russia fills its deficit either through taking out money from its National Wealth Fund or by borrowing on the internal market, Prokopenko said.
However, the Russian government is having trouble attracting private businesses and citizens to invest in bonds — as a result, when Russia's Central Bank conducted its most recent bond auction, major state-owned banks bought around 84% of the total sum, Prokopenko said.
To raise money for the war in Ukraine, Russia also raised taxes , for instance by hiking VAT rates to 22% in 2026, by overall increasing income tax the previous year, and by introducing a planned tax on dividends and yields on bonds starting in 2027.
While Russia is clearly looking for money for the war, and the prime role of state-owned banks in financing debt can look awkward, this says little about the actual state of the Russian economy, Aleksashenko said.
"I don't see any problems on the financial or the economic side which would make Putin stop the war," the Russian economist argued.
"He is generally conservative with expenditures, so I don't think we'll be seeing a sudden boost in boots on the ground. As for the cost of this war (to the Russian economy), unfortunately, while it might not be sustainable in the long run, Putin sees the price to pay as acceptable."
Karol Łuczka is a freelance journalist focused on Ukraine and Russia. He also works as Eastern Europe Advocacy Lead at the Vienna-based International Press Institute (IPI). Karol holds an MA in International Security from Sciences Po Paris.

title: Russian drones strike cargo ship in Black Sea, kill captain, Zelensky says
description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
content:
A cargo ship caught fire in the Black Sea off the Romanian coast on Oct. 5 after a Russian drone strike, killing two, injuring at least 11 more, and prompting a large search-and-rescue operation.
After Romanian media and authorities initially reported a fire on the grain ship Royad Mammadov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that a civilian ship was attacked by two Russian drones, adding that it was a Turkish-owned ship transporting corn.
According to Zelensky, the ship was crewed by citizens of Azerbaijan and India. While the Russian strike killed the vessel's captain, Zelensky said. Romania's interior ministry said that two people were killed in the attack.
At the time of the attack, the ship was sailing outside Romania's territorial waters but within the country's exclusive economic zone, about 20 nautical miles (37 kilometers) from the Romanian coast and roughly 9 nautical miles (16.6 kilometers) southeast of the Pescarus offshore oil platform operated by OMV Petrom, according to Romanian media outlet Digi24.ro. First reports had placed the incident near the Neptun Deep gas development.
"Ukraine has repeatedly proposed concrete steps to de-escalate and guarantee security in the Black Sea. There have also been corresponding proposals from third countries," Zelensky said.
"But Russia consistently chooses terror and sinking civilian ships instead of normal navigation. Pressure is needed to restore global food security. And everyone who is truly interested in this should help."
Romania's Interior Ministry later said 11 crew members had been rescued. The vessel was sinking, while injured survivors were evacuated for emergency medical treatment. Romanian authorities had not provided details about the cause of the fire.
The incident is the latest in a string of Russian attacks that has crippled civilian and commercial shipping in the Black Sea.
Ukraine's maritime corridor, opened in 2023 after Russia withdrew from the U.N.-backed grain deal, has been largely closed again after a spate of Russian attacks, both on port infrastructure and ships themselves, over summer 2026.
The International Maritime Organization has warned that the war poses a "serious and immediate threat" to crews and vessels operating in the Black Sea and Sea of Azov.
The latest incident comes two days after a Russian strike on a Liberian-flagged cargo ship in Ukraine's Odesa region killed one person and injured three, according to Ukrainian port authorities cited by Reuters.

title: NATO drafts strategy on repelling Russian attack against eastern flank
description: The plan is intended to clarify how NATO would respond to a potential incursion into its territory and reassure the public of the alliance's readiness, according to Bloomberg.
content:
NATO is preparing a plan to defend against a possible Russian attack on its eastern flank while integrating drones and AI into its defenses, Bloomberg reported on Oct. 5, citing the plan's draft and undisclosed official sources.
Supreme Allied Commander Europe, U.S. General Alexus Grynkewich, is set to present the strategy, called Theory of Victory, in Poland on Oct. 12, according to Bloomberg .
A NATO official confirmed the plan's existence to the Kyiv Independent.
While allied officials have said that a conventional Russian attack against NATO is not imminent, they have warned that Moscow might attempt to test the alliance's eastern flank by hybrid attacks or drone incursions.
Grynkewich's plan is intended to clarify how NATO would respond to a potential incursion into its territory and reassure the public of the alliance's readiness, according to Bloomberg.
According to the outlet's sources, it would outline how to integrate traditional military capabilities with new technologies that emerged after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. The alliance plans to repel a potential Russian incursion through a combination of land forces and other assets, including drones and AI-powered targeting.
Subsequently, allied forces would seek to destroy Russian command and control to deliver a quick and decisive victory.
At the same time, the plan said NATO would avoid any provocations on its part while working to counter Russian hybrid attacks.
NATO has not publicly commented on the contents of the plan.
Tensions between Russia and the alliance have surged since the outbreak of the full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022, with Moscow repeatedly issuing threats to NATO members and countries backing Kyiv.
The concerns are further fueled by escalating Russian hybrid attacks and provocations on NATO soil, from drone incursions in Poland and Romania to alleged Moscow-backed sabotage operations in Estonia and Germany.
The Baltic Sea region is often cited as the most likely flashpoint in a Russia-NATO confrontation, but local governments have said they do not see signs that Moscow is planning a conventional attack in the near future.
Nevertheless, Estonian officials recently told the Financial Times that Tallinn is moving the core of its forces to a newly expanded base less than 50 kilometers (30 miles) from the Russian border to better meet a potential Russian attack.

title: Children among dozens injured as Russian glide bombs hit Kharkiv, 5 dead
description: People are reportedly trapped under the rubble of a residential building in the city.
content:
At least five people have been killed, and 53 others, including children, injured after Russian forces struck Kharkiv with glide bombs on Oct. 5.
"The enemy attacked Kharkiv with at least three glide bombs (KABs), with strikes recorded in the Slobidskyi district," Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov said in a post on Telegram .
"As a result of the strikes… warehouse buildings are on fire, and residential buildings have been damaged. There may be people under the rubble of a residential building that was hit in the attack. A search and rescue operation is underway," he added.
Russian glide bombs , often called KABs (Kerovana Aviabomba) in Ukraine, are repurposed aerial bombs equipped with wings and precision guidance systems such as GPS, laser, or infrared targeting.
Unlike traditional free-fall bombs, KABs can glide tens of kilometers before impact, allowing Russian aircraft — typically the Su-34 — to release them from a distance, safe from the operating range of Ukrainian air defense missiles or fighters.
Warhead sizes vary by model, ranging from about 300 kilograms to 3 metric tons , enough to destroy multistory buildings with a direct hit.
Russian forces use glide bombs against important, hardened, or entrenched targets, such as bridges, command posts, or drone teams spotted by reconnaissance assets.
Russia regularly launches fatal strikes on civilian infrastructure in cities across Ukraine as it continues to wage its war. Kharkiv is a frequent target given its proximity to the front line.

title: Zelensky could celebrate fresh EU accession breakthrough in Brussels next week, source says
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky will attend a summit of the EU's 27 national leaders on Oct. 15 if Kyiv is able to unlock the next step in its EU accession process, a Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
content:
European Council President Antonio Costa, President Volodymyr Zelensky, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen at the June 2026 European Council Summit in Brussels. (Benoit Doppagne / Belga / AFP via Getty Images)
President Volodymyr Zelensky will attend a summit of the EU's 27 national leaders on Oct. 15 if Kyiv is able to unlock the next step in its EU accession process before then, a Ukrainian official confirmed to the Kyiv Independent.
The Ukrainian parliament is expected to pass a law on Oct. 12 that will bolster the rights of Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking minority, which Hungary has required of Kyiv in order for it to drop its veto on advancing Ukraine's EU accession process.
If that happens, and the EU therefore unlocks the next two so-called enlargement clusters, then Zelensky will attend the European Council summit, a Ukrainian official familiar with the president's agenda told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine has opened two of six enlargement clusters so far, listing the reforms that Kyiv must implement to be fully aligned with EU rules and thus able to join the bloc.
The first two clusters opened in June and July , respectively, but further progress has been held back after months of Ukraine failing to pass the ethnic minorities reform, despite agreeing with Budapest in July to do so.
"It is possible that we would open the next two clusters ... next week," the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said at an Oct. 5 press conference in Brussels.
"Of course, the member states will have to speed up the procedure," Kos said.
The steps taken between the passage of the law and the holding of an intergovernmental conference (IGC), which marks the opening of an enlargement cluster, are essentially just formalities, but they take some time.
Normally, IGCs are held on the margins of a meeting of European ministers called the General Affairs Council. The next one of those is scheduled to take place in Luxembourg on Oct. 13.
However, that would mean the bloc has to carry out the formalities overnight, so it could be that the IGCs instead take place on Oct. 14, one day before EU leaders are set to meet.
If all goes smoothly, Ukraine is expected to open clusters two and three, broad areas of economic reform.
That would leave still to open clusters four and five, which cover more sectoral areas of the economy where some countries still have reservations, for example, due to the size and competitiveness of Ukraine's agricultural and transport sectors.
But Kos remained hopeful that all six clusters would be unlocked by the end of the year.
If Zelensky attends the Oct. 15 European Council, he will have several topics to weigh in on.
The Summit is expected to discuss the future of EU enlargement, with a key set of proposals to be published on Oct. 6, as well as Ukraine's war effort, and wider European defense and security.
It will also touch on negotiations over the EU's 2028-2034 budget, which includes a separate line for Ukraine support, currently set at 89 billion euros ($100 billion).
Chris Powers is the Brussels Correspondent with the Kyiv Independent. He reports on EU news and policy developments relevant to Ukraine, bridging the gap between Brussels and Kyiv. He was formerly the Defense and Tech Editor at the EU media outlet Euractiv. Chris holds a BA in History from the University of Cambridge and an MA in European Studies from the College of Europe.

title: More than half of Ukrainians say Zelensky should not run for president again, poll says
description: The KIIS survey also revealed that 45% of Ukrainians believe their country's affairs are moving in the wrong direction, while 40% think the opposite.
content:
Some 53% of Ukrainians think President Volodymyr Zelensky should not run for a second term, according to a poll published by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) on Oct. 5.
In turn, 42% think Zelensky should participate in Ukraine's next presidential election, while 5% were undecided, according to the latest poll.
Ukraine's constitution does not allow elections under martial law, which was declared when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The survey shows a steady decline in support for Zelensky's second term. In December 2023, 59% of respondents said the incumbent president should run again, and only 45% shared this view in December 2025.
The study comes as the president faces growing scrutiny over corruption scandals implicating figures from his inner circle and unexpected personnel decisions, including the firing of popular Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Nevertheless, recent polls continue to show Zelensky among the leading candidates in future elections, alongside Fedorov and Valerii Zaluzhnyi, the former military chief and current ambassador to the U.K.
A little over a year ago, Zelensky told Axios that he would not seek re-election once the war with the Kremlin ends.
"If we finish (the) war with (the) Russians, I'm ready not to go for the second term because it's not my goal — elections," Zelensky said in September 2025.
The same survey found that a vast majority of Ukrainians — 71% — oppose holding presidential elections during wartime.
The possibility of holding elections during wartime was briefly raised in August by Fedorov, whose sudden dismissal sparked nationwide protests .
However, the Ukrainian public did not respond favorably to Fedorov's call for elections due to the many logistical constraints faced by military personnel, millions of Ukrainians abroad, and those living near the front line.
The KIIS survey also revealed that 45% of Ukrainians believe their country's affairs are moving in the wrong direction, while 40% think the opposite.
Furthermore, 44% said they "mostly feel disappointment" about Zelensky's current government , and 33% said they feel shame. Both markers have increased since the KIIS's last survey in December 2025.
"There is a significant demand in Ukrainian society for the renewal of political elites, and it has only intensified in recent years," commented Anton Hrushetskyi, executive director of KIIS, in a press release.
The poll was conducted between Sept. 12 and 21, with the participation of 1,002 respondents living in government-controlled territories.

title: New automatic gun turrets successfully down first Russian jet-powered drones, Air Force says
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky previously announced that twelve such turrets had been installed where Russian jet-powered drones have been particularly active, including around Kyiv.
content:
Automated machine gun turrets using artificial intelligence to aim have downed their first Russian jet-powered drones over Ukraine, Air Force spokesperson Yurii Ihnat said on Oct. 5.
A day prior, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that twelve such turrets had been installed where Russian jet-powered drones have been particularly active, including around Kyiv.
"There are already cases of shooting down even jet UAVs, even 'Geran-5' from the those very turrets," Ihnat said on national television.
"The use of innovative technologies — artificial intelligence — has eliminated human error. Machine vision is used in the shooting down. Artificial intelligence allows you to target even jet-powered drones."
Since Russia started using jet-powered drones en masse against Kyiv toward the end of summer this year, they, especially the Geran-4 and Geran-5 models, have presented an air defense problem for which Ukraine has not yet found a single solution.
Most existing interceptor drones , which were responsible for downing the majority of Russia’s Shahed-type attack drones until recently, are not fast enough to intercept jet-powered drones.
Jet-powered interceptors are actively in development, but producing them at the scale required to contain the jet-powered drone threat is likely impossible due to the lack of supply chains for cheap jet engines in the West.
In the meantime, advances in artificial intelligence technology have led to better automatic aiming systems, allowing small arms like U.S.-made Browning heavy machine guns to add to Ukraine's anti-drone air defense network.

title: No country is delivering more on reforms than Ukraine right now, says EU enlargement chief
description: "We should never forget the country is fighting for its survival," the EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos told journalists when asked to comment on the pace of Ukraine's reforms.
content:
The EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos praised Ukraine's reform work during an Oct. 5 press conference on EU-Moldova relations, stressing that Kyiv is delivering despite difficult wartime circumstances.
The comments come only a day before the EU is expected to unveil proposals for the future of EU enlargement , including work on membership roadmaps for Ukraine, Moldova, Albania, and Montenegro — the four most promising candidates.
Kos was asked by a Ukrainian journalist to give her view on how Ukraine's reform rate compares with Moldova, broadly seen as the fastest reformer among the candidates.
"Both countries are delivering under very difficult circumstances," Kos said.
"And both countries are in the frontrunner group of four," she added.
Ukraine's parliament has faced scrutiny over delays in passing reforms needed for EU membership and to secure foreign aid.
But Kos went on to highlight that Ukraine's circumstances place it in a different category altogether.
"We should never forget the country is fighting for its survival. The country is in the accession process. And the country has to deliver reforms to get additional money for the budget and the military," Kos explained.
"There is no other country in the world who is delivering more than Ukraine at this moment," Kos said.
In September, Kos co-signed a letter to the Verkhovna Rada, Ukraine's parliament, identifying the reforms it has to complete by the end of the year in order to unlock over 20 billion euros ($23 billion) of financial support, even providing a concrete list of laws to be enacted and their current state of play.
One key law that the parliament needs to pass, concerning the rights of Ukraine's Hungarian-speaking minority, is expected to be put to a vote on Oct. 12. Budapest has blocked the opening of additional clusters for Ukraine until the bill is adopted.
"We hope that the law will pass the (Verkhovna) Rada," Kos said.
"Once this will happen... it is possible that we would open the next two clusters for Moldova and Ukraine next week," she added.
Ukraine and Moldova have had their membership bids linked and have so far unlocked two of the six to-do lists of reforms, known as enlargement clusters .
The first two clusters opened in June and July , respectively. If the law on minorities passes on Oct. 12, Kyiv and Chisinau are expected to be able to open clusters two and three on economic topics.
That would leave only clusters four and five, which address sectoral issues, and where fears over the size and competitiveness of parts of Ukraine's economy, notably the agricultural and transport sectors, risk holding up progress.

title: Moldova aims to complete EU technical talks by 2028, join bloc by 2030
description: Moldova has "taken major strides towards membership," the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said at the end of the 10th EU-Moldova Association Council meeting in Brussels.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Moldova hopes to have completed all the technical work required to join the EU by the start of 2028, with full membership by 2030, the country's Prime Minister Vasile Tofan said at a press conference on Oct. 5.
Moldova has "taken major strides towards membership," the EU's top diplomat Kaja Kallas said at the end of the 10th EU-Moldova Association Council meeting in Brussels. The country's "reform pace is very strong," Kallas said.
Tofan said he hopes Moldova can open the remaining four of six enlargement clusters — to-do lists of reforms the country needs to complete to be fully aligned with the EU — by the end of 2026.
The opening of clusters for Moldova and Ukraine has been politically coupled together by EU countries, and in June and July, Chisinau and Kyiv opened the first two of those six clusters.
However, political concerns over Ukraine have hindered progress for both countries.
A dispute with Budapest over Ukraine's Hungarian minority has prevented the opening of two clusters on macroeconomic topics.
Kyiv hopes to resolve this matter once its parliament adopts a relevant law addressing Hungary's concerns. The bill is expected to be put to a vote on Oct. 12.
Likewise, fears about Ukraine's large agricultural and transport sectors are sparking sectoral concerns, holding up the remaining two clusters.
Tofan said his country is "not afraid of ambitious timelines" and "not asking for shortcuts," but rather believes that Chisinau will have enacted all the reforms by early 2028. He voiced hope that Moldova will be part of the bloc by 2030.
"European integration is truly our national project," Tofan said.
The EU's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos signaled that this timetable could be possible and emphasized the " impressive pace " of Moldova's reform agenda.
EU accession "could happen during your mandate," Kos told Tofan during the press conference.
Moldova's parliamentary term is four years long, and the last election was held in September 2025.
Kos also signaled that she believes Ukraine will be able to pass its minorities bill on time, so that "it is possible we will open the next two clusters next week."
"This really is the autumn of enlargement," Kos said.

title: German intelligence chief warns of 'violent conflict with Russia'
description: Russia is conducting a "shadow war," head of Germany's foreign intelligence service (BND), Martin Jaeger, said.
content:
Germany is in a "shadow war" with Russia and risks being drawn into a violent conflict with Moscow, Martin Jaeger, head of the foreign intelligence service (BND), told lawmakers during a Parliamentary Control Committee hearing on Oct. 5.
"No other country currently poses such a direct, comprehensive, and concrete threat to Germany," Jaeger said during the public hearing , in reference to the attempted Russian drone attack at Leipzig airport on July 31.
"Russia is waging a shadow war against us," Jaeger said further, meaning an undeclared war that cannot be grasped by conventional military or judicial understandings of the term.
Jaeger warned of further sabotage and nuclear intimidation by Moscow to ensure that no measures against Russia would be taken in Berlin or other European capitals, and to halt support and arms deliveries for Ukraine.
Calling the Russian intelligence services "highly professional and reckless," Jaeger also said that the threat of Russian attacks on targets in Germany remains "real and present."
Jaeger said the BND does not currently see signs of a large-scale Russian attack on NATO territory, but warned of low-level Russian military activity, especially in the Baltic region.
Sinan Selen, head of the internal federal intelligence service (BfV), also said that Russia was willing to carry out sabotage and assassinations.
Martina Rosenberg, head of the military intelligence service (MAD), added that the German military was facing enemies from outside, as well as from within.
All three intelligence chiefs called for reforms of their agencies, allowing them to operate in more offensive capacities, such as against cyberattacks or to sabotage adversarial weapons programs.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Oct. 4 for a visit aimed at reaffirming Berlin's support for Ukraine, the German news agency dpa reported.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said he welcomed Merz to Kyiv on Sunday morning and that the chancellor would hold talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky on bilateral relations, European affairs, and international issues.

title: Luke Harding's 'Betrayal' charts the collapse of the rules-based order — and who is to blame
description:
Luke Harding's “Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest" begins with a turning point in the full-scale war most people probably haven't spent enough time coming to terms with: North Korean soldiers getting ready to join the biggest land war in Europe since 1945.

content:
Luke Harding's “Betrayal: Trump, Putin and the New Age of Conquest" begins with a turning point in the full-scale war most people probably haven't spent enough time coming to terms with: North Korean soldiers getting ready to join the biggest land war in Europe since 1945.
"Soon they would be stumbling through alien woods and fields, sent by one dictator to help out another. It was a sign of a world turned upside down. The rules-based international order — the post-1945 understanding that states didn't invade each other or change borders by force — seemed broken," Harding writes.
At the start of the full-scale war, the idea of North Korean soldiers fighting in Europe would have seemed implausible to most. Today, it is just one more sign of a world reverting to Great Power politics, the betrayal at the heart of Harding's book. The U.S., Russia, and China pursue their "strategic interests," and as a result, millions of people are left hostage to a system that should have died with the last century.
Who is to blame for the collapse of the post-1945 order? As the title suggests, Harding doesn't pin it on a singular country or individual. But Harding reserves some of his most acerbic digs for U.S. President Donald Trump , whom he calls, among other things, "the prostrator-in-chief when it comes to Russia." In his second term, Harding argues, Trump has emboldened authoritarian leaders like Russia's Vladimir Putin and China's Xi Jinping to act with unprecedented impunity.
One of the most telling examples is the so-called Alaska summit in August 2025, when Trump invited Putin for his first visit to the U.S. in nearly a decade. Before the summit, as Harding reminds the reader, Trump warned that Russia would face "severe consequences" if it didn't agree to a ceasefire with Ukraine .
Although the Alaska summit was presented as a chance for the U.S. to press Russia for peace, it opened with pomp and ceremony : Trump applauded as Putin walked toward him along a red carpet, and the two stood side by side as a B-2 stealth bomber and F-35 fighter jets flew overhead. The talks ended without any hope of ending the war , and the visuals were disturbing — including Putin casually brushing off a journalist's question about civilian deaths.
As Harding writes, "Putin could be seen grinning (during the summit), smirking even, an international outlaw no longer. The invitation was a rare honor, granted to few statesmen. It was a sign of Trump's esteem for his visitor, and a scene that might have been scripted by the Kremlin's own talented dramaturgs."
Trump's praise of Putin over the years has fueled endless speculation about his motives, most famously including the theory that he is some " compromised asset ." Harding acknowledges that the Czechoslovak security services kept files on Trump and his first wife, Ivana, in cooperation with the Soviet counterparts, and that the couple visited the USSR in July 1987. Two months later, Trump ran full-page newspaper ads criticizing U.S. foreign policy, which Harding describes as "an unusual move for a non-politician."
However, the record is suggestive rather than conclusive, and it raises as many questions as it answers. Harding wonders whether it is indifference, fear, the prospect of lucrative business deals, or a genuine wish not to imperil peace talks that drives Trump's actions – or lack thereof – toward Russia. Whatever the answer, he argues, Trump's inaction has been seen as "a moral choice of sorts" that "ignored the Kremlin had a long and outrageous history of lying," and the Kremlin, in turn, has interpreted his behavior as a sign of approval.
Perhaps most importantly, "Betrayal" ties this high-level state intrigue to Harding's on-the-ground reporting from Ukraine , introducing readers to Ukrainians still living in front-line cities who no longer fear the sounds of explosions, as well as the soldiers defending against Russian advances. These Ukrainians are reminders that there is no sense to Russia's talk of "defending" its so-called "sphere of influence," and that Ukrainians alone have the right to decide what's best for their country.
However, the book also looks beyond Ukraine to the aftershocks of the collapsing post-1945 order, like Trump repeatedly entertaining the idea of the U.S. taking Greenland — by force, if necessary. Putin, when asked about it, called it "an issue that concerns two specific nations and has nothing to do with (Russia)." According to Harding, the reasoning behind Putin's words was obvious: "if the Americans took Greenland, Putin's war in Ukraine looked like less of an aberration."
The U.S., long the world's leading power, still stands for a sense of order, even if that feeling is increasingly nostalgic. Leaders like President Volodymyr Zelensky , Harding notes, have no choice but to push on through Trump's erraticism — "self-appointed world peacemaker one day, warmonger the next" — for a greater cause.
If the book has any setback, it is one of scale: the events Harding describes are so vast, from the front line in Ukraine to covert Russian agents trying to influence U.K. politicians, that it is sometimes easy to get lost in the urgency of the book's underlying message. Yet the book earns its place in an argument that is only beginning, and it leaves the reader with a question that no one in power seems eager to answer: what sort of world do we want to inhabit, and whom do we want to lead it?
Hi, this is Kate Tsurkan, thanks for reading this article. There is an ever-increasing amount of books about or related to Ukraine, Russia, and Russia's ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine available to English-language readers, and I hope my recommendations prove useful when it comes to your next trip to the bookstore.
If you like reading about this sort of thing, p lease consider supporting The Kyiv Independent.

title: 'It was humiliating' — Ex-US Army Secretary says Washington lags behind Ukraine in war innovations
description: "When you would see what Ukraine's budget was and how small it was relative to ours and how, despite that, they had better weapons of war, it was a wake-up call," former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll told Rolling Stone.
content:
Former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll sees significant shortcomings in the U.S. military's ability to adapt to modern warfare compared with Ukraine's rapid innovations, he said in an interview with Rolling Stone magazine published on Oct. 4.
"When you would see what Ukraine 's budget was and how small it was relative to ours and how, despite that, they had better weapons of war, it was a wake-up call," said Driscoll in his first-ever interview following his resignation on Aug. 31, after alleged friction with U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
"In some ways, it was humiliating seeing how quickly a nation could change when it needed to," added Driscoll, who has long praised Ukraine's advances in drone technology and visited the country in 2025 as part of Washington-led peace talks.
During his time at the White House, Driscoll was a strong advocate for modernizing the U.S. Army through investments in counter-drone systems and the creation of the Unmanned Assault Battalion, a "drones-first" 600-soldier unit that cooperated with Ukrainian advisers.
However, Driscoll's ambitious modernization plans allegedly faced opposition from Hegseth.
"Once he (Hegseth) makes a decision, there's nothing I can do about it," said Driscoll.
The two officials promoted different visions for strengthening the U.S. Army. While Driscoll focused on adjusting to the new realities of modern warfare, Hegseth has promoted a "warrior culture" centered on more traditional methods, such as soldiers' physical fitness.
After Driscoll's departure from the White House, the U.S. Army ordered the Unmanned Assault Battalion to return to being a standard airborne infantry unit.
"President Trump came into his second term with a military that had been very poorl­y prepared for modern war," said Driscoll.
"I viewed my role as to advocate as hard as I could for leaders who I thought were good," he added.

title: Estonia moves troops closer to Russian border amid shift in strategic thinking
description: The country's 1st Brigade will relocate from their previous base in Tapa to the town of Johvi, just west of the city of city of Narva on the Russian border.
content:
Estonia's 1st Brigade, the main combat-ready element of the country's land forces, will be moving to a newly expanded base less than 50 kilometers from the Russian border, placed to better meet a possible Russian attack.
The move, revealed in comments by the unit's commander, Tarmo Kundla, published in the Financial Times on Oct. 5, comes amid increased awareness of Russian military designs on the Baltic country .
The 1st Brigade will relocate from its previous base in Tapa to the town of Johvi, just west of the city of Narva on the Russian border.
Narva is often seen as a potential flashpoint of hybrid or kinetic attacks not only due to its location, but because the majority of its population is Russian-speaking, a common tool of Russian propaganda to justify aggression.
According to Kundla, the brigade's move is connected to a shift in strategic thinking for the Estonian military, which relies on the airpower of NATO forces based in the region — as well as on the deterrent of the alliance's Article 5 — to protect against an attack from its much larger neighbor.
“We have to start from the border and win from the first battles,” Kundla said, explaining that the move will help the army to fight with a posture of "active defense," allowing immediate return strikes on targets deeper in Russian territory in the event of an invasion.
Although Moscow has failed to achieve any of its strategic aims in almost five years of full-scale war against Ukraine, Russia's war has led many countries on NATO's eastern flank to amp up defense spending and reassess military doctrine, as the nature of warfare itself has undergone a paradigm shift.
In recent years, the Trump administration's open questioning both of the United States' status as Europe's security guarantor, and of Article 5 itself, has unnerved NATO members on the eastern flank.
In 2026, Estonia announced a record 42% increase in defense spending, reaching 2.4 billion euro ($2.69 billion), or around 5.4% of the small country's GDP.
With the extra spending also came procurement of new weapons systems, including U.S.- and South Korean-built rocket systems that could strike St. Petersburg.
“We are in the process of changing everything,” said a military policy official at Estonia’s defense ministry quoted by the Financial Times.
“The reality is that the [Estonian defense planning] has been the same for the last 10 years. But Russia is already planning to double its forces across our border.”

title: Projectile injures border guard at Moldova-Ukraine border, hits bus
description: The incident occured as Russia carried out attacks against Ukraine, Moldova's border police said.
content:
A projectile that fell on the grounds of the Palanca-Mayaky-Udobne border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova ricoched from the ground, struck a passenger bus and a control booth, and lightly injured a Moldovan border guard on Oct. 5, Moldova's Border Police said.
The incident occured at 9:38 a.m. local time, as Russia carried out attacks against Ukrainian infrastructure, the border police said, according to Moldovan media NewsMaker and Zairul de Garda .
Moldova's General Police Inspectorate said it closed the border crossing for the duration of its investigations and urged drivers to avoid the area, NewsMaker reported.
Overnight, Russia launched 205 attack drones of various types, including 49 jet-powered drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down 172 drones, including Shahed-type, Gerbera, and other drones, as well as two Banderol loitering munitions, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at three others.
"The security environment around Moldova has become more difficult," Moldovan PM Vasile Tofan said during a press conference in Brussels on Oct. 5. "Russian drones and missiles pose a serious risk to our population and infrastructure."
Kaja Kallas, the EU's High representative for Foreign Affairs, also condemned Russian violations of Moldovas airspace with missiles and drones.
"This is completely unacceptable. The Kremlin is putting lives at risk across the continent. Moscow's aim behind these actions is to create fear and paralyze our decision making," Kallas said.
Palanca borders Ukraine's Odesa Oblast , which Russia regularly attacks with drones and missiles. Russia's attacks on Ukraine frequently lead to violations of Moldova 's airspace and explosions on the country's territory.
On Oct. 3, five Russian air attack weapons , including Banderol missiles and drones, violated Moldova's airspace and exploded on the country's territory during Russia's latest overnight attack against Ukraine, Moldovan President Maia Sandu said.
"(Russia's) war is dangerously reaching Moldova," Sandu wrote in a post on X on Oct. 3, condemning the attack. "Moscow is putting lives at risk across Europe and must be stopped."
Drones invaded Moldova's airspace three separate times on Sept. 30, as Russia launched a day-long attack against Ukraine overnight and into the following afternoon.
On Sept. 24 , suspected Russian drones crashed in Romania and Moldova overnight, amid a sustained mass drone and missile attack on Ukraine.
On Aug. 16, NATO fighter jets shot down a suspected Russian drone that violated Romanian airspace near the Moldovan border, Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta confirmed.
A day later, on Aug. 17, a Russian S-8000 Banderol cruise missile entered Moldovan airspace during a Russian attack on Odesa, before crashing in a cornfield approximately 3 kilometers (1.8 miles) outside of the village of Talmaz, in the Stefan Voda district of Moldova.

title: Kharkiv targeted in deadly Banderol strike as Russia kills 5, injures 61 across Ukraine over past day
description: Overnight, Russia launched 205 attack drones of various types, including 49 jet-powered drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
content:
Russian forces struck the northeastern city of Kharkiv on the evening of Oct. 4, killing a 42-year-old man and injuring eight more people, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
The strike was carried out with Banderol missiles, a cheap Russian cruise missile that is often used to target front-line cities, as well as the Black Sea port of Odesa.
Four more people were injured in Kharkiv Oblast over the previous 24 hours, bringing the total number of civilian casualties country-wide to five killed and 61 injured.
Overnight, Russia launched 205 attack drones of various types, including 49 jet-powered drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down 172 drones, including Shahed-type, Gerbera, and other drones, as well as two Banderol loitering munitions, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at 13 locations, while debris from downed targets fell at three others.
Russian first-person view (FPV) drones killed two civilians in two separate attacks outside the city of Zaporizhzhia, regional authorities said, with each attack injuring one more person respectively.
In Sumy Oblast, one person was killed and a total of 29 injured by Russian attacks across the border, with most of the wounded coming from a glide bomb strike on the regional capital.
One person was killed and three other injured in the city of Nikopol in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, while another man was injured in the city of Pavlohrad, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha reported.
Five people — including a ten-year-old boy were injured in Russian drone attacks on Chernihiv Oblast, regional governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
In Kherson Oblast, daily Russian attacks on settlements on the Ukrainian-controlled side of the Dnipro River injured six people, according to regional authorities.
Two people were injured — one of whom hospitalized — after Russia's drone attack on the Northern Bridge in Kyiv, city mayor Vitalii Klitschko said.
One person was injured in the front-line city of Kramatorsk in Donetsk Oblast, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said.

title: Pro-Russian Dodik claims party victory in Bosnian elections
description: "If it had not been for (U.S. President) Donald Trump's magnificent victory, we would probably be political corpses today," Milorad Dodik told his supporters, while also thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin.
content:
Pro-Russian Serb nationalist politician Milorad Dodik declared his party the winner in Bosnia and Herzegovina's elections held on Oct. 4.
Dodik was not on the ballot, but Zeljka Cvijanovic from his Alliance of Independent Social Democrats (SNSD) party is poised to retain her seat in the country's tripartite presidency, according to preliminary results.
The Balkan country held elections for the presidency, shared among the Croat, Serb, and Bosniak ethnic groups, as well as for regional and cantonal governments, under a complex political system established after the 1992-1995 Bosnian War.
"If it had not been for (U.S. President) Donald Trump 's magnificent victory, we would probably be political corpses today," Dodik told his supporters , while also thanking Russian President Vladimir Putin , who voiced support for the SNSD before the elections.
Dodik, known for his separatist and pro-Moscow views, served as the president of Republika Srpska — Bosnia's Serb-dominated entity — between 2022 and 2025.
In 2025, he was stripped of office and barred from running for six years for defying the country's international envoy.
With over 95% of the votes counted, Denis Becirovic of the Social Democratic Party (SDP BiH ) is set to retain his Bosniak seat in the presidency, and Bosnian Croat nationalist candidate Darijana Filipovic has claimed victory in the race for the Croat seat.
Dodik's SNSD is also expected to retain power in the Republika Srpska local parliament and presidency.
The vote was marked by a relatively low turnout, with 42% of voters casting ballots, down almost 10% from the 2022 elections.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,542,720 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 2,020 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,542,720 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 5.
The number includes 2,020 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,393 tanks, 25,487 armored combat vehicles, 157,985 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,733 artillery systems, 2,182 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,688 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,859 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA). While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Dozens detained at authorized Russian Communist Party rally after chants of 'Down with the Tsar'
description: The event had been authorized by Moscow authorities, but detentions reportedly intensified as the rally was ending and participants shifted toward more directly anti-Kremlin slogans.
content:
Moscow police detained about 60 people at an authorized Communist Party rally on Oct. 4 after participants began chanting anti-Kremlin slogans, according to the party and Russian rights group OVD-Info.
The rally marked the anniversary of Russia's 1993 constitutional crisis, when a standoff between President Boris Yeltsin and hard-line lawmakers culminated in the military shelling the parliament building in Moscow. Authorities said 123 people were killed, while unofficial estimates put the toll in the hundreds.
The Communist Party has organized annual events as a symbol of resistance to Yeltsin-era reforms, but this year's authorized rally took a turn as participants chanted slogans including "Freedom for political prisoners," "For fair elections," and "Down with the Tsar."
OVD-Info says participants also chanted “No to political repression,” “Down with Roskomnadzor,” and “Down with the party of crooks and thieves.”
