The event had been authorized by Moscow authorities, but detentions reportedly intensified as the rally was ending and participants shifted toward more directly anti-Kremlin slogans.
According to OVD-Info, around 20 people were initially taken to Moscow's Krasnopresnenskiy police station before the reported total rose to about 60. The detainees were not all Communist Party supporters: 26 were Communist Party participants, 30 were members of the liberal Yabloko party, and several others were activists.
The Communist Party, Russia's main parliamentary opposition, generally aligns with the Kremlin on major national security and foreign policy issues, including support for Russia's war against Ukraine. It occasionally criticizes domestic policy but does not directly challenge President Vladimir Putin's rule.
Russia has pushed harder against political opposition and anti-war activism in recent years. In August, Russia's Supreme Court banned the Yabloko party from participating in upcoming parliamentary elections taking place Sept. 18-20. In September, authorities arrested members of the banned pro-peace Yabloko party, Anna Shatunovskaya-Byurno and Grigory Grishin, among others, as part of a broader crackdown on dissent and political organizing.

title: Russian double-tap Banderol strikes hit Kharkiv, killing 1, injuring 6
description: Kharkiv has also faced repeated attacks with other Russian aerial weapons in recent days. On Oct. 2, Russian glide bombs struck the city’s Slobidskyi and Nemyshlianskyi districts, killing two women and injuring 36 people, including three children.
content:
One person was killed and six injured, as Russian forces carried out a double-tap strike using Banderol missiles in Kharkiv’s industrial district.
Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov confirmed the death and casualties, reporting that an administrative building and vehicles were burning. At least 10 multi-story residential buildings were damaged in the attack, and search and rescue operations are ongoing.
Banderol missiles have been a part of Russia's increasing use of jet-powered loitering munitions, combining features of a cruise missile and a jet-powered drone. Its speed, maneuverability, and low-altitude flight profile can make the Banderol difficult for Ukrainian air defenses to intercept.
After a July 8 Banderol missile struck Kharkiv, Spartak Borysenko, head of the department for combating crimes committed in the context of armed conflict at the Kharkiv Regional Prosecutor's Office, told Suspilne Kharkiv that the munition can reach speeds of up to 800 kilometers (500 miles) per hour and carry around 300–400 kilograms (660–880 pounds) of explosives.
"It has a guidance system and numerous control surfaces, and it can change its direction and altitude while in flight," Borysenko said.
On Sept. 24, three Russian S-8000 Banderol missiles struck a farm in Kharkiv Oblast, killing 6 and injuring 14.
Kharkiv has also faced repeated attacks with other Russian aerial weapons in recent days. On Oct. 2, Russian glide bombs struck the city’s Slobidskyi and Nemyshlianskyi districts, killing two women and injuring 36 people, including three children.
The latest strike is evidence of Russia’s increasing use of fast, maneuverable jet-powered munitions against targets in Ukraine, adding further strain to air defenses already contending with drones, glide bombs, and missiles.

title: Russian drone strike hits energy facility in Poltava Oblast, leaves 22,000 without power
description: The strike comes just two days after another Russian drone hit an energy facility in the region’s Lubny district, leaving around 6,000 consumers without electricity.
content:
A Russian drone struck an energy infrastructure facility in Poltava Oblast on Oct. 4, leaving around 22,000 consumers without electricity, regional authorities said.
Poltava Oblast Governor Vitalii Diakyvnych said crews from Poltavaoblenergo were working to restore power.
No casualties were reported in the initial assessment.
The strike comes just two days after another Russian drone hit an energy facility in the region’s Lubny district, leaving around 6,000 consumers without electricity.
Poltava Oblast , one of Ukraine’s key gas-producing regions, has repeatedly come under Russian attack. In March, Russian strikes hit Naftogaz facilities in the region for three consecutive days , killing one employee.
Russia has intensified attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure ahead of winter, repeatedly targeting power generation, transmission and gas facilities across the country.
The renewed attacks on energy infrastructure echo Russia's campaign against Ukraine's power grid last winter, which caused widespread rolling outages and heating disruptions. This fall, however, Moscow appears to be expanding the scope and scale of its infrastructure campaign, repeatedly targeting Kyiv's bridges alongside energy facilities.

title: US proposes trilateral talks with Russia, Ukraine by end of October, Zelensky says
description: "The American side is currently in contact with Ukraine and Russia and is proposing to hold some kind of meeting at the technical level in a trilateral format by the end of October," the president said.
content:
The United States is pushing for Ukraine and Russia to hold negotiations at the technical level before the end of the month, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 4.
The president's remarks come amid a renewed diplomatic push from Washington to restart peace talks, following a v isit by U.S. envoys to Kyiv and Moscow in early September.
"The American side is currently in contact with Ukraine and Russia and is proposing to hold some kind of meeting at the technical level in a trilateral format by the end of October," Zelensky told reporters at a press conference alongside German Chancellor Friedrich Merz .
Zelensky said he spoke directly with the U.S. negotiating team on Oct. 3, but could not disclose all the details of the ongoing preparations. The president confirmed that Ukraine is ready and willing to participate in trilateral talks.
"We're open to the UAE or any other country proposed by the U.S. side," Zelensky said. "I know they'll propose this to the Russian side as well — or may have already done so, I'm not sure of the sequence of events. And we'll wait for a response."
Following the latest visits by Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump began pushing Russia and Ukraine to halt attacks on each other's energy facilities. Ukraine has said it will agree to an energy ceasefire only if Russia also suspends attacks.
Moscow has shown no signals of pausing its assault on Ukraine's power grid, and sources familiar with the matter have told the Kyiv Independent that Trump privately doubts Russian President Vladimir Putin will agree to an energy truce before winter.
The energy initiative, along with a possible reopening of the Black Sea grain corridor , is expected to be on the agenda at the coming trilateral meeting, which could take place in the United Arab Emirates.
Amid the peace push, Russia has continued escalating strikes against Ukraine, launching relentless days-long attacks on Kyiv and other cities. Zelensky said on Oct. 3 that Putin had issued a "new doctrine" allowing Russia to deliberately target Ukrainian civilians in the coming months.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them (to) attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelensky said.

title: Ukraine's deep strikes have wrecked over half of Russia's oil refining capacity, Defense Ministry says
description: "Fifty-one percent of the damaged oil refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy's economy, to its ability to wage aggression, and to supply its military formations," Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said Oct. 4.
content:
Over 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity has been disabled by Ukrainian attacks, the Defense Ministry reported on Oct. 4.
Ukraine has systematically targeted Russia's oil and gas infrastructure in long-range strikes, dramatically increasing its campaign against oil refineries in the past two years. Kyiv considers refineries valid military targets, as they supply both fuel and funds to the Russian armed forces.
Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara reported on the consequences of Ukraine's strategy in an update on Oct. 4. Citing analysts from Ukraine's intelligence services, Defense Ministry, and General Staff, Khmara said that over 51% of Russia's oil refining capacity has been disabled.
"This is the result of carefully planned, systematic, and comprehensive actions aimed at crippling the Russian war machine and destroying its military-economic potential," Khmara said.
"Fifty-one percent of the damaged oil refining capacity is a significant blow to the enemy's economy, to its ability to wage aggression, and to supply its military formations."
The Defense Ministry listed recent attacks at Russia's Moscow , Yaroslavl , Kirishi , Perm , Ilsky , Saratov , and Syzran refineries in its report.
The ministry's assessment marks an increase from the 45% drop in Russian refining capacity reported by Ukraine's General Staff on Sept. 21.
It also follows a decree from Russian President Vladimir Putin, signed Sept. 28, restricting access to data on the country's oil refineries and energy exports amid Ukraine's escalating deep strikes.
Ukraine's long-range strike drones and missiles have proved capable of regularly reaching targets more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory. The military reported a new record on Sept. 9, after a Fire Point FP-1 drone struck a Russian gas facility 3,200 kilometers (1,988 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The Defense Ministry reported on Oct. 4 that Ukraine tripled its production and procurement of long-range strike drones in 2026 — and that it hopes to keep growing.
"This is not the limit," the ministry said. "We will continue to scale up our long-range strike capabilities."

title: Plague death triggers quarantine, mask mandates in Russia's Irkutsk region in Siberia
description: The measures come after Darya Shipilova, a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov, died after reportedly contracting plague on Oct. 2.
content:
An aluminum factory and multiple hospitals in Russia's Irkutsk Oblast have instituted preventative measures, including quarantines and mask mandates, following a laboratory worker's recent death by plague, Russian officials and media reported on Oct. 4.
The measures come after Darya Shipilova, a lab technician at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Shelekhov, died after reportedly contracting plague on Oct. 2. A week earlier, Shipolova is alleged to have accidentally broken a test tube containing the pathogen that causes pneumonic plague while collecting samples.
Several hospitals in the city of Irkutsk have reportedly also closed for a three-week quarantine, according to the Russian outlet Lyudi Baikala (People of Baikal). These include city hospitals No. 1, 3, and 10, as well as the Ivanovo-Matreninsk Children's Clinical Hospital.
A source in the healthcare sector has told the outlet that Irkutsk doctors are "openly talking about plague," though the disease is not mentioned in official documents.
The Kyiv Independent could not verify the Russian outlet's claims at the time of publication.
The director of the Irkutsk Aluminum Plant (IrkAZ) in Shelekhov, Artem Fominykh, announced a mask mandate for factory employees on Oct. 2 "due to the current situtation in our region." He urged employees to seek immediate medical attention if they experienced any symptoms of illness.
Fominykh later said on Oct. 4 that the mask mandate was a routine response to seasonal respiratory illness.
Russian officials have been evasive about the cause of Shipilova's death and the possible risk of plague infection in Irkutsk Oblast.
Authorities in Baykalsk urged residents on Oct. 3 to temporarily avoid traveling to Shelekhov and nearby settlements due to the reported plague case — then deleted the warning less than two hours later.
"Due to unofficial information about a confirmed case of plague in a person in the city of Shelekhov, we ask you to limit visits to Shelekhov and nearby settlements until the circumstances surrounding this threat are clarified," the Baykalsk city administration said in a post at 8:28 a.m. local time.
The post was deleted at 10:21 a.m., according to Lyudi Baikala.
Pro-Kremlin broadcaster REN TV also deleted its Telegram posts reporting the number of people hospitalized. All five posts about the reported spread of plague were later removed.
The governor of Russia's far-eastern Buryatia Republic, which borders Irkutsk Oblast, appeared to confirm Shipilova's death from plague in a social media post on Oct. 2. While refuting rumors that Shipliova had visited Buryatia, Governor Alexei Tsydenov wrote that the woman had died of plague.
However, he later edited the post to add the word "possibly."
Irkutsk Oblast Governor Igor Kobzev has also been publicly quiet about the situation. On Oct. 2, he made a statement on the "particularly dangerous infection"while reporting on a special meeting of the regional commission on sanitation and epidemic prevention.
Kobzev made his first comments on Shipilova's death on Oct. 4, though he did not refer to her by name but only as "an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute."
"Preventive measures are being carried out in the region under the strict supervision of Rospotrebnadzor (Russia's national public health and consumer protection agency)," the governor said.
Kobzev did not directly discuss plague, saying instead that the employee contracted "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Rospotrebnadzor.
"No microorganisms linked to the employee's professional duties were detected in samples taken from the patient," Kobzev claimed.
"No reports of infectious diseases have been recorded among institute staff over the past 10 days. All individuals who had contact with the patient have been identified, examined, and placed under medical observation involving daily laboratory testing."
The Irkutsk plague scare is not the first time Russian officials have tried to suppress details about a potential health risk. In April, Russian authorities tried to downplay another outbreak — a cattle epidemic that had swept parts of Siberia since February, saying it was under control and caused by pasteurellosis, a relatively minor bacterial infection.
Veterinarians and independent journalists questioned that account, pointing to mass slaughter, village lockdowns, and secrecy more typical of a foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) outbreak.
Editor's Note: This story has been corrected to clarify the dates the mask mandate was introduced at the Irkutsk Aluminum Plant.

title: Ukraine war latest: Germany supplies Kyiv with interceptors, air defense missiles in $1.5 billion aid package
description:
Key developments on Oct. 3-4:

 * Germany announces $1.46 billion in aid for Ukraine, including interceptor drones, air defense missiles
 * Russian Su-35, Su-34 fighter jets hit by drones at airfield in Adygea, SBU says
 * Russia targets Kyiv bridges for fourth consecutive day, hits Northern Bridge
 * U.S. peace negotiations with Russia could now involve multi-billion dollar Lukoil deal, NYT reports
 * Moscow unveils 'new doctrine' targeting Ukrainian civilians, Zelensky vows to respond with mor
content:
Germany on Oct. 4 announced a new support package worth more than €1.3 billion ($1.46 billion) for Ukraine, including funding for interceptor drones and energy assistance.
The package was announced by President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at a joint press conference in Kyiv.
"The total value of today's agreements is more than €8.5 billion ($9.57 billion)," Zelensky said. "A special agreement was signed that creates more opportunities for our joint counter-drone efforts."
Zelensky said the package included weapons needed immediately, support for Ukraine's energy sector, and funding to produce new interceptors specifically designed to counter Russia's jet-powered attack drones.
"These are weapons that will help now, support for our energy sector — this is very important," Zelensky said.
The package includes €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid, including financing the production of interceptor drones capable of countering Russian jet-powered weapons, Merz said.
The defense package also includes "thousands" of missiles for the German-made IRIS-T air defense systems and the delivery of additional IRIS-T fire units.
Additionally, the chancellor announced around €350 million ($394 million) in energy assistance, including support for generators and repairs to infrastructure damaged by Russian attacks .
He added that the energy package was intended to mitigate the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine's power infrastructure ahead of winter.
The European drone manufacturer Quantum Systems will receive financing from Germany to produce tens of thousands of interceptors in Ukraine. The joint production program is designed to adapt to Russia's evolving threats, including the increased use of deadly high-speed jet drones in aerial attacks.
Quantum Systems also signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point on Oct. 4. The two companies have agreed to jointly develop new technologies for unmanned systems.
A number of other German and Ukrainian companies also signed MOUs during Merz's visit.
Ukraine's Culver Aerospace signed a letter of intent with the German company Helsing to cooperate on the mass production of long-range strike systems for Ukraine. The Lviv-based Roboneers also signed an MOU with Germany's ARX Robotics on the development of ground drones.
German and Ukrainian companies also reached a framework agreement regarding 25 and 40 mm air defense systems and 155 mm artillery systems.
Ukrainian drones struck two Russian fighter aircraft and an ammunition depot at the Khanskaya military airfield in Russia's Republic of Adygea, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said on Oct. 4, .
Drones operated by the SBU's Alpha special operations unit hit a Su-35 multirole fighter jet and a Su-34 fighter-bomber at the airfield, located around 500 kilometers (310 miles) from Ukrainian territory.
"Both aircraft are carriers of guided aerial bombs, which the enemy massively uses along the front line and against Ukrainian cities," the SBU said .
The agency estimated the export value of a Su-35 at around $100 million and a Su-34 at around $50 million.
An ammunition depot on the airfield was also struck, according to the SBU.
The extent of the damage could not be independently verified.
"The SBU systematically targets Russian military facilities, consistently reducing its ability to wage war against Ukraine," the agency said. "Enemy strikes on Ukrainian cities, civilian and critical infrastructure will not go unanswered."
The Su-34 is a multifunctional fighter-bomber used to deploy different types of guided bombs (KAB) and high-explosive bombs (FAB), as well as air-to-surface missiles. It can also be used for reconnaissance and electronic warfare missions.
The Su-35 is a multirole fighter designed primarily for air superiority but also capable of striking ground targets. It can carry air-to-air and air-to-surface missiles, as well as guided bombs, and is among the most advanced combat aircraft currently operated by Russia.
Russia struck the roadway of Kyiv's Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River with a drone on the morning of Oct. 4, injuring two people, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The attack marked the fourth consecutive day that Russian forces targeted bridges across the Dnipro River in the capital.
"This morning, the Russians once again struck Kyiv's Northern Bridge with a drone," Zelensky said . "Just this week, Russia has used more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 25 missiles against Ukraine. More than 800 of the drones were jet-powered."
Klitschko said emergency services were sent to the Northern Bridge after the roadway was hit. Two people were injured in the strike, with one hospitalized and the other treated at the scene.
He later said a heating main was also damaged in the Russian attack, temporarily cutting hot water to parts of Kyiv's Desnianskyi district.
The full extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
From Oct. 1 to Oct. 3, Kyiv's Southern and Northern bridges were targeted in multiple Russian drone strikes amid an intensifying campaign against infrastructure in the capital.
Kostiantyn Kryvolap, an aviation expert and former Antonov test engineer, told the Kyiv Independent that destroying the bridges was unlikely to be the primary objective of the attacks.
"Destroying a bridge with a 50-kilogram explosive charge, even with a highly effective warhead designed to destroy steel bridge structures, is a major exaggeration. It is practically impossible," Kryvolap said. "For a bridge like this, these strikes are more like mosquito bites."
Instead, the strikes may be intended to disrupt traffic and logistics and exert psychological pressure on Kyiv residents, according to Kryvolap.
Both the Northern and Southern bridges are among Kyiv's main transport arteries, carrying tens of thousands of residents across the Dnipro each day.
The repeated strikes have prompted preparations for pontoon crossings that could be used if key bridges across the Dnipro are damaged or become unusable. The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMDA) also announced new restrictions on movement across Kyiv's bridges during air raid alerts.
The Trump administration's peace negotiations with the Kremlin have come to include discussions of a multi-billion-dollar deal involving assets owned by Russian oil company Lukoil, the New York Times (NYT) reported on Oct. 3.
The newspaper reported that business executives with ties to U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are pursuing a potential deal involving Lukoil refineries, oil fields and gas stations around the world. The deal would require approval from both the U.S. government and the Kremlin, according to the NYT.
Russian President Vladimir Putin raised the potential deal with Kushner and Witkoff during their visit to Moscow on Sept. 5, proposing it as a way to demonstrate to Russians that they could still do business with the United States, NYT reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The two envoys responded that they would work on the proposal, as a way to build good will with the Russians, according to the NYT report. Another benefit for the Americans is that global oil prices, which have skyrocketed following the U.S. war with Iran, could go down as a result of the deal, following sanctions against Lukoil assets potentially being lifted.
Lukoil is Russia's second-largest oil producer and one of the country's largest companies, accounting for 2% of global oil output. The corporation has been under U.S. sanctions since 2025, with the American government freezing its U.S.-based assets and threatening secondary penalties for foreign entities engaging with them.
The sanctions, the first such measures imposed by the second Trump administration, were designed to pressure Moscow into peace talks in Ukraine, as fossil fuel revenues play a key role in sustaining Russia's war efforts. The U.S. government then proceeded to issue a limited sanctions waiver on some of Lukoil's foreign assets, which was extended earlier this year.
While the U.S. Senate recently passed a bill that would make it easier to impose sanctions on countries that subsidize Russia’s war economy, this new potential agreement could allow Lukoil's assets to be relieved of sanctions, potentially increasing their value, according to NYT
In response to a new airstrike policy targeting Ukrainian civilians by Moscow, President Zelensky said on Oct. 3 that Ukraine would increase attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky told Reuters that Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents revealing that Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a "new doctrine" allowing Russian forces to launch broader strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets this upcoming winter.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them [to] ‌attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelensky said. With this shift, Putin wants to appear strong even as Russian troops continue to l ose ground while suffering massive casualties , said Zelensky.
The president's comments come as Russian forces have increasingly battered Ukrainian civilian infrastructure in recent weeks, including attacks on key bridges and medical and educational facilities .
In response to Moscow's changing tactics, Zelensky vowed to increase strikes on Russian energy sites, though without indiscriminately targeting Russian civilians.
"We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refineries: what gives money to them for this war," Zelensky said. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."

title: 'Very dangerous moment' — Russia sharing jet-powered drone tech with North Korea, Zelensky says
description: The president's comments come a week after he warned that Moscow is preparing to recruit another 10,000 North Korean military personnel to fight alongside Russian troops against Ukraine.
content:
Russia has transferred jet-powered drone technology to North Korea as part of its intensifying defense partnership, President Volodymyr Zelensky said at a press conference on Oct. 4.
Zelensky's comments come a week after he warned that Moscow is preparing to recruit another 10,000 North Korean military personnel to fight alongside Russian troops against Ukraine.
When asked if Russia had also shared its new jet drone technology with Pyongyang, Zelensky's response to journalists was unequivocal: "Yes, of course."
Zelensky outlined Russia and North Korea's history of weapons cooperation throughout the full-scale war, including Pyongyang's supplies of artillery and missiles used to attack Ukraine.
"They're sharing with North Korea all the technologies," Zelensky said. He added that he was not certain if Russia was sharing its ballistic missile supplies as well, but he believed it to be likely.
"I think yes, because North Korea helped them with missiles. It's a very dangerous moment."
The president compared the situation to Russia's cooperation with Iran. Early in the war, Tehran gave Moscow the means to produce its own Shahed attack drones . Years later, when Iran came under attack by the U.S. and Israel, Russia came to its ally's aid with drone supplies, Zelensky said.
Russia has now upgraded its Shahed-type attack drones with high-speed, jet-powered versions that have relentlessly attacked Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities in recent weeks.
Moscow's jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 kamikaze drones can reach speeds of up to 500 and 600 kilometers per hour, respectively, making them much harder for FPV drones and mobile fire teams to intercept.
The increased use of these weapons in aerial attacks has further exhausted Ukraine's air defenses, already strained by Russia's frequent ballistic missile strikes. In some recent attacks on Kyiv, jet-powered drones have accounted for around two-thirds of all drones launched.
Zelensky said on Sept. 26 that Russia plans to spend $12 billion next year on the production of jet-powered drones and loitering munitions.

title: Latvia's pro-Ukraine party wins parliamentary election by wide margin
description: "I congratulate Andris Kulbergs on his convincing victory in the parliamentary elections in Latvia ... Ukraine deeply appreciates Latvia's unwavering friendship and support," President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 4.
content:
Latvia's ruling party, the centrist, pro-Ukrainian United List faction led by Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, has won the country's parliamentary election with over 35% of the vote.
Nearly 800,000 Latvians took to the polls on Oct. 3, representing a turnout of 51.8%, according to the Central Election Commission. United List won 35.3% of the vote, earning them 41 seats in the Saeima, Latvia's 100-member unicameral parliament.
"I congratulate Andris Kulbergs on his convincing victory in the parliamentary elections in Latvia," President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on X on Oct. 4.
"This strong result reflects the Latvian people's confidence in your leadership and your vision for the country's future. Ukraine deeply appreciates Latvia's unwavering friendship and support."
Latvians took to the polls on Oct. 3 to decide what their parliament will look like for the next four years. Affordability and security concerns have been top political issues in the Baltic country which shares a border with Russia and is home to a large Russian-speaking minority.
The election marked a test for Kulbergs, who has been prime minister since May, following a political crisis triggered by a Ukrainian drone incursion into Latvian airspace. Former Prim Minister Evika Silina was forced to resign, leading to a government collapse that paved the way for a four-party coalition led by Kulbergs.
Affordability and security concerns were the top political issues for Latvians going into the Oct. 3 vote. Warnings from Western officials over escalating hybrid threats from Russia are taken seriously by the Baltic nation, an EU and NATO member which shares a border with both Russia and Belarus.
The populist Latvia First party came second in the parliamentary election, winning about 13%, or 17 seats. The pro-Russian Sovereign Power party ranked third, with 11.7% (15 seats).
Sovereign Power is Latvia's only political party that opposes military aid to Ukraine.
Latvia's conservative National Alliance party came in fourth with 8.9% (10 seats). In fifth place, the Progressive party gained 7.9%, also earning 10 seats.
While pro-Russian parties increased their representation in Latvia's legislature, they still lack the necessary numbers to meaningfully influence policy.
Throughout his term, Kulbergs has expressed unwavering support for Ukraine throughout his term. Latvia has also sharply increased defense spending since 2022, reaching 5% of GDP — one of the highest levels in NATO.

title: Russian Su-35, Su-34 fighter jets hit by drones at airfield in Adygea, SBU says
description: Drones operated by the SBU's Alpha special operations unit hit a Su-35 multirole fighter and a Su-34 fighter-bomber at the airfield, located around 500 kilometers (310 miles) from Ukrainian territory.
content:
Ukrainian drones struck two Russian fighter aircraft and an ammunition depot at the Khanskaya military airfield in Russia's Republic of Adygea, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) said on Oct. 4, .
Drones operated by the SBU's Alpha special operations unit hit a Su-35 multirole fighter jet and a Su-34 fighter-bomber at the airfield, located around 500 kilometers (310 miles) from Ukrainian territory.
"Both aircraft are carriers of guided aerial bombs, which the enemy massively uses along the front line and against Ukrainian cities," the SBU said .
The agency estimated the export value of a Su-35 at around $100 million and a Su-34 at around $50 million.
An ammunition depot on the airfield was also struck, according to the SBU.
The extent of the damage could not be independently verified.
"The SBU systematically targets Russian military facilities, consistently reducing its ability to wage war against Ukraine," the agency said. "Enemy strikes on Ukrainian cities, civilian and critical infrastructure will not go unanswered."
The Su-34 is a multifunctional fighter-bomber used to deploy different types of guided bombs (KAB) and high-explosive bombs (FAB), as well as air-to-surface missiles. It can also be used for reconnaissance and electronic warfare missions.
The Su-35 is a multirole fighter designed primarily for air superiority but also capable of striking ground targets. It can carry air-to-air and air-to-surface missiles, as well as guided bombs, and is among the most advanced combat aircraft currently operated by Russia.
Russia's Defense Ministry separately claimed that its air defenses intercepted and destroyed 559 Ukrainian drones between 8 p.m. on Oct. 3 and 8 a.m. on Oct. 4.
Moscow said drones were detected over multiple Russian regions, including Adygea, as well as occupied Crimea and the Black and Azov seas. The Russian claim could not be independently verified.
The strike follows other recent Ukrainian attacks on Russian military aviation. Overnight on Sept. 16, Ukrainian forces hit a Russian Su-24 bomber at the Saky air base in occupied Crimea, the General Staff said .
Ukraine frequently targets Russian military airfields, ammunition depots, and other defense infrastructure with long-range drones in an effort to reduce Moscow's ability to launch attacks against Ukraine.

title: News from occupied Ukraine: Military delivers aid by drone to occupied Oleshky in second operation
description: The operation was the second large-scale drone delivery to the occupied city, where residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and medicine.
content:
This weekly update from the Kyiv Independent aims to shed light on the situation facing Ukrainians living under Russian occupation and the ever-tightening control of information imposed by the Kremlin.
Ukrainian forces delivered nearly four metric tons of humanitarian aid by drone to Russian-occupied Oleshky in Kherson Oblast overnight on Oct. 4, Ukraine's Interior Ministry said.
The operation was the second large-scale drone delivery to the occupied city, where residents have faced severe shortages of food, water, and medicine.
Oleshky in Kherson Oblast has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Mines, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make it impossible to evacuate safely.
Nearly 400 packages containing food, medical supplies, and kits for children were transported into Oleshky, according to the ministry. The National Guard said all of the packages successfully reached the city.
The operation involved troops from the National Guard's 11th Mykhailo Hrushevskyi Brigade and 34th Kherson Regiment, working alongside the 30th Marine Corps, the 34th Borysfen Marine Brigade, and the State Border Guard Service's 79th Detachment.
During the operation, a drone crew from the Perun unit also evacuated six animals from Russian-occupied territory, the Interior Ministry said.
The delivery follows a similar operation in late September, when Ukrainian forces transported around four metric tons of food into Oleshky by drone after conventional humanitarian deliveries became effectively impossible.
Russian forces have also confiscated some of the food delivered by Ukrainian drones, Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said earlier this week.
According to Hasanenko, residents found with non-Russian products have also been questioned over possible cooperation with the Ukrainian military.
Ukraine's Foreign Ministry said that around 2,000 people, including nearly 50 children, remained in the occupied town with severely limited access to food, drinking water, electricity, and other basic services.
The humanitarian situation in Oleshky has drawn growing international concern. On Sept. 25, Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights Michael O'Flaherty warned that civilians, including children, were struggling to access food, medicine, medical care, clean water, and electricity, and that some could face a serious risk to their lives.
O'Flaherty said international humanitarian law requires an occupying power to ensure civilians have access to food and medical supplies and to facilitate humanitarian assistance.
Ukraine's military struck several Russian military targets in occupied parts of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Luhansk oblasts on Oct. 3 and overnight on Oct. 4, the General Staff said .
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Buk-M3 air defense system.
In Donetsk Oblast, near the city of Dobetsk, the military hit a site used to store, prepare, and launch Russian attack drones. They also struck Russian military telecommunications hubs near Hirnyk, Yasynuvata, and Donetsk.
In Luhansk Oblast, Ukrainian forces struck Russian repair units near Vesela Tarasivka and Lysychansk.
The strikes are part of a series of attacks on Russian military infrastructure in occupied Ukrainian territories.
Forty-one Ukrainian citizens, including four children and five teenagers, returned from Russian-occupied territories through a Volyn border crossing in August and September, Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 2.
Among those returned was a family that had reunited after their father had been released from Russian captivity, Lubinets said . Their eldest son had also been held captive since April 17, 2022. The mother and youngest son, meanwhile, were earlier confined to a facility against their will and subjected to forced treatment under the pretext of receiving medical care by occupation authorities, Lubinets said.
A young medical worker had been returned to Ukraine shortly before she would have been mobilized into Russia's armed forces , Lubinets also said.
The fate of thousands of Ukrainians currently in captivity, as well as those living under occupation , remains uncertain. Ukrainian authorities say up to 16,000 Ukrainians are considered missing, while Russia is holding thousands of Ukrainian civilians in detention.
Located in Ukraine's northwestern Volyn Oblast, the Volyn humanitarian corridor is the only working checkpoint between Ukraine and Belarus and is almost exclusively used by people escaping the occupied territories.
The last direct route from Russia to Ukraine through a checkpoint in Sumy Oblast was closed in August 2024 amid escalating Russian attacks in the oblast.
Given that the territory of Belarus was used by Russia to launch its full-scale invasion, the area around the crossing is heavily fortified with mines and anti-tank hedgehogs.
Read more about the process of leaving the occupied territories through the Volyn corridor in the earlier reporting of the Kyiv Independent.
Fifty countries and four other organizations signed a pledge on Sept. 29 calling for the return of Ukrainian prisoners of war (POWs), unlawfully detained civilians, and children abducted by Russia.
The pledge condemned Russia's forced militarization of Ukrainian children living in Russian-occupied territory as Moscow continues to wage its war against Ukraine.
"We also express concern about the militarization of children in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine by the Russian Federation. These actions have serious negative consequences for their identity, well-being, family unity, human rights and fundamental freedoms," the Toronto Pledge says .
Austria, Denmark, Hungary, Japan, and the United Kingdom are among the signatories alongside organizations including the Council of Europe and the European Union.
Norwegian Foreign Ministry State Secretary Eivind Vad Petersson noted that Russia's treatment of Ukrainians is a systemic issue that must receive a systemic response.
Canadian Foreign Minister Anita Anand said that new technology and methods, including artificial intelligence and working with third countries as intermediaries, must be utilized as "gaps remain" in efforts to return Ukrainians home.
The U.K. sanctioned seven Russian individuals involved in the forced deportation and re-education of Ukrainian children from occupied territories on Oct. 1, the Ukrainian President's initiative, Bring Kids Back, said on Oct. 2.
Russia is militarizing Ukrainian children and youth in the occupied territories, removing their Ukrainian identity to "raise future soldiers" and involve them in the fight against their own people.
Russia has abducted tens of thousands of Ukrainian children since the start of the full-scale invasion. As of September 2026, Ukraine's Justice Ministry has officially confirmed 20,610 cases of deportation, though Ukrainian officials estimate the real total could number in the hundreds of thousands .
According to Bring Kids Back's press release, the sanctions target Artur Orlov, head of Russia's Movement of the First, a state-backed organization for children and young people, as well as five heads of its regional branches in occupied parts of Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, and Zaporizhzhia oblasts and Crimea .
The Movement of the First was established in 2022 at the initiative of Russian President Vladimir Putin and has more than 344,600 members in occupied Ukrainian territories, according to a report from an Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE) expert mission.
Russia's abduction of Ukrainian children could constitute an act of genocide, according to the U.N.'s Genocide Convention, which lists "forcibly transferring children of the group to another group" as one of the five acts that fall under the definition
In 2023, the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova , Russia's Commissioner for Children's Rights, for their role in state-sanctioned child abductions.
The U.K. announced the sanctions on Oct. 1 as part of a wider package targeting 31 individuals over Russia's war against Ukraine. The package also includes eight people accused of involvement in arbitrary detention, torture, and ill-treatment of civilians in Russian-occupied Ukrainian territories, including Kherson and Zaporizhzhia oblasts.
"We are targeting both the revenues that help sustain Russia's aggression and the perpetrators of horrendous crimes against Ukrainian civilians, including children. The UK will not flinch in our support for Ukraine," UK Minister for Europe Lord Wood of Anfield said.

title: Germany announces $1.46 billion in aid for Ukraine, including interceptor drones, air defense missiles
description: The package was announced by President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at a joint press conference in Kyiv.
content:
Editor's Note: This story has been updated with additional details.
Germany on Oct. 4 announced a new support package worth more than €1.3 billion ($1.46 billion) for Ukraine, including funding for interceptor drones and energy assistance.
The package was announced by President Volodymyr Zelensky and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz at a joint press conference in Kyiv.
Zelensky said on Oct. 5 that the broader value of agreements reached with Germany during the visit exceeded €8.5 billion ($9.57 billion), including a separate agreement aimed at expanding joint efforts to counter drones.
"The total value of today's agreements is more than €8.5 billion ($9.57 billion)," Zelensky said. "A special agreement was signed that creates more opportunities for our joint counter-drone efforts."
Zelensky said the package included weapons needed immediately, support for Ukraine's energy sector, and funding to produce new interceptors specifically designed to counter Russia's jet-powered attack drones.
"These are weapons that will help now, support for our energy sector — this is very important," Zelensky said.
The aid package includes €1 billion ($1.13 billion) in military aid, including financing the production of interceptor drones capable of countering Russian jet-powered weapons, Merz said.
"This will quickly and noticeably strengthen Ukraine's air defense, and this reinforcement is urgently needed," Merz said.
The defense package also includes "thousands" of missiles for the German-made IRIS-T air defense systems and the delivery of additional IRIS-T fire units.
Additionally, the chancellor announced around €350 million ($394 million) in energy assistance, including support for generators and repairs to infrastructure damaged by Russian attacks .
He added that the energy package was intended to mitigate the impact of Russian attacks on Ukraine's power infrastructure ahead of winter.
The European drone manufacturer Quantum Systems will receive financing from Germany to produce tens of thousands of interceptors in Ukraine.
"Ukraine needs interceptor drones at industrial scale," Sven Kruck, Quantum Systems Co-CEO, said in a press release announcing the agreement. "By expanding production in Ukraine, we can respond faster to the immediate threat while building an industrial capability that will also strengthen Germany and its allies."
The joint production program is designed to adapt to Russia's evolving threats, including the increased use of deadly high-speed jet drones in aerial attacks.
Quantum Systems also signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) with the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point on Oct. 4. The two companies have agreed to jointly develop new technologies for unmanned systems.
The company also signed an agreement directly with Ukraine's National Guard, which comprises a large portion of the ground force fighting in some of the hottest parts of the front line.
"It is strategically important for Ukraine to have an alternative to foreign systems developed by its own manufacturers," National Guard commander Oleksandr Pivnenko said about the deal.
"Expanding production in Germany gives us access to additional, critically needed production capacities, while maintaining Ukrainian technologies and combat experience at the core."
A number of other German and Ukrainian companies also signed MOUs during Merz's visit.
Ukraine's Culver Aerospace signed a letter of intent with the German company Helsing to cooperate on the mass production of long-range strike systems for Ukraine. The Lviv-based Roboneers also signed an MOU with Germany's ARX Robotics on the development of ground drones.
German and Ukrainian companies also reached a framework agreement regarding 25 and 40 mm air defense systems and 155 mm artillery systems.
The announcements build on Germany and Ukraine's expanded joint defense production. In May, Berlin and Kyiv launched "Brave Germany," a joint initiative backed by Ukraine's Brave1 defense-tech platform to support Ukrainian and German defense companies and accelerate development of new military technologies.
The much-needed weapons package comes as Russia continues to terrorize Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure with jet-powered attack drones. "Just this week, Russia has used more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 25 missiles against Ukraine. More than 800 of the drones were jet-powered," Zelensky said .
Earlier in the day, Merz visited the National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv, which was damaged in a Russian drone strike on Sept. 28.
"Mr. Putin, stop this senseless war," Merz said during the visit, according to dpa. "We are ready for talks, we are ready to speak with one another about ending this war. But these barbaric attacks on the civilian population of Ukraine must stop."
Zelensky described air defense as Ukraine's current "number one priority," saying he and Merz had discussed additional measures the two countries could take together.
The new package was announced during Merz's visit to Kyiv on Oct. 4, where he arrived with German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and executives from the country's defense and energy sectors.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 5, injure 30 across Ukraine
description: Overnight, Russia launched 135 attack drones of various types, including 52 jet-powered drones, the Air Force said.
content:
At least five people were killed and 30 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, as Russian forces targeted Sumy Oblast with drones and glide bombs, local authorities said on Oct. 4.
Overnight, Russia launched 135 attack drones of various types, including 52 jet-powered drones, Ukraine's Air Force said.
Ukrainian air defenses shot down 125 targets, including 123 Shahed-type, Gerbera, and other drones, as well as two Banderol loitering munitions, according to the Air Force. Strikes were recorded at five locations, while debris from downed targets fell at five others.
In Sumy Oblast , at least three people were killed and 16 others injured in a series of Russian attacks, according to local authorities. On Oct. 4, a Russian drone attack on a warehouse storing medical supplies in Sumy killed a 52-year-old employee and injured three others, local authorities said.
Russian glide bomb attacks on Sumy and the surrounding area also injured 13 people, including a child. Apartment buildings, homes, and vehicles were damaged.
In Kharkiv Oblast , two people were killed and five others injured as Russian forces attacked Kharkiv and nine other settlements over the past day, local authorities said. Russia used multiple weapons, including FPV drones, Molniya drones, a Lancet drone, and a multiple-launch rocket system.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , three people were injured as Russian forces carried out more than 50 attacks using drones, artillery, and a glide bomb, local authorities said. Two people were injured when a strike hit food warehouses in Pavlohrad and caused a fire, while a 34-year-old man was injured in the Nikopol district.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast , two people were injured in Russian attacks on the Zaporizhzhia district, Ivan Fedorov , co-head of the Zaporizhzhia Oblast Defense Council, said. Russian forces carried out 745 attacks against 47 settlements across the region over the past day.
In Kherson Oblast , two people were injured as Russian forces struck critical infrastructure and residential areas, regional authorities said.
In Donetsk Oblast , two people were injured in Sloviansk in Russian attacks over the past day, regional Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Kyiv , a Russian drone struck the Northern Bridge on the morning of Oct. 4, hitting the roadway, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said. The attack marked the fourth consecutive day that Russian forces targeted bridges across the Dnipro River in the capital.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had launched more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 glide bombs, and 25 missiles against Ukraine over the past week, including more than 800 jet-powered drones.

title: Russia targets Kyiv bridges for fourth consecutive day, hits Northern Bridge
description: From Oct. 1 to Oct. 3, Kyiv's Southern and Northern bridges were targeted in multiple Russian drone strikes amid an intensifying campaign against infrastructure in the capital.
content:
Russia struck the roadway of Kyiv's Northern Bridge across the Dnipro River with a drone on the morning of Oct. 4, injuring two people, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The attack marked the fourth consecutive day that Russian forces targeted bridges across the Dnipro River in the capital.
"This morning, the Russians once again struck Kyiv's Northern Bridge with a drone," President Volodymyr Zelensky said . "Just this week, Russia has used more than 1,900 attack drones, 1,700 aerial bombs, and 25 missiles against Ukraine. More than 800 of the drones were jet-powered."
Klitschko said emergency services were sent to the Northern Bridge after the roadway was hit. Two people were injured in the strike, with one hospitalized and the other treated at the scene.
He later said a heating main was also damaged in the Russian attack, temporarily cutting hot water to parts of Kyiv's Desnianskyi district.
The full extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
From Oct. 1 to Oct. 3, Kyiv's Southern and Northern bridges were targeted in multiple Russian drone strikes amid an intensifying campaign against infrastructure in the capital.
Kostiantyn Kryvolap, an aviation expert and former Antonov test engineer, told the Kyiv Independent that destroying the bridges was unlikely to be the primary objective of the attacks.
"Destroying a bridge with a 50-kilogram explosive charge, even with a highly effective warhead designed to destroy steel bridge structures, is a major exaggeration. It is practically impossible," Kryvolap said. "For a bridge like this, these strikes are more like mosquito bites."
Instead, the strikes may be intended to disrupt traffic and logistics and exert psychological pressure on Kyiv residents, according to Kryvolap.
Both the Northern and Southern bridges are among Kyiv's main transport arteries, carrying tens of thousands of residents across the Dnipro each day.
The repeated strikes have prompted preparations for pontoon crossings that could be used if key bridges across the Dnipro are damaged or become unusable. The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMDA) also announced new restrictions on movement across Kyiv's bridges during air raid alerts.

title: Kyiv now feels like a front-line city — but its resolve is holding, for now
description:
For much of Russia's full-scale war, massive attacks on Kyiv came mainly at night. Residents learned, as much as possible, to organize their lives around them. They would sleep in hallways or bathrooms, check Telegram channels for updates in the dark, then emerge in the morning and go to work, cafes, concerts, or dinner.

That fragile division between wartime nights and relatively normal days is now disappearing. In recent weeks, Russia has increasingly launched jet-powered attack drones toward
content:
Firefighters work after a Russian drone attack struck a residential building in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Sept. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Francisco Seco)
For much of Russia's full-scale war, massive attacks on Kyiv came mainly at night. Residents learned, as much as possible, to organize their lives around them. They would sleep in hallways or bathrooms, check Telegram channels for updates in the dark, then emerge in the morning and go to work, cafes, concerts, or dinner.
That fragile division between wartime nights and relatively normal days is now disappearing. In recent weeks, Russia has increasingly launched jet-powered attack drones toward the capital around the clock, bringing air raid alerts, air defense fire, and explosions into the middle of workdays, commutes, and afternoons in the city. The Russian campaign, started in late August, has changed the rhythm of life in the Ukrainian capital.
"In this sense, Kyiv can already, to some extent, be called a frontline region."
The last days of September and the first of October were particularly intense, and Kyiv has barely had time to come up for air.
On Sept. 25, a Russian drone tore into a high-rise apartment building in the central Pecherskyi district, killing a 14-year-old boy. The next morning, Sept. 26, residents had already heard the air raid siren five times by 10 a.m. On Sept. 27, another attack stretched into a nine-hour alert.
On Sept. 28, Russian drones struck central Kyiv in broad daylight, killing two people and injuring 26. A building of Ukraine's National Academy of Sciences, an institution behind many of the country's major scientific achievements, caught fire after a Russian attack. Videos showed people trying to escape through windows as smoke poured from inside.
The following night, Russian missiles and drones hit an educational facility, apartment buildings, a railway depot, data centers, and business centers.
By Sept. 30, Russia had struck again, this time targeting Kyiv's energy infrastructure, already weakened by repeated attacks during the previous cold season. In the afternoon, authorities announced emergency power shutdowns in the capital.
On Oct. 1, the attacks pushed further into Kyiv's daytime routine. A drone hit a school, and two others struck the Southern Bridge as cars and a metro train were crossing. The next day , bridge restrictions caused major traffic jams across the city, with some residents crossing the Dnipro on foot to get to work.
At least 16 people were killed and more than 100 others injured in Kyiv and the surrounding region between Sept. 25 and Oct. 2, according to a Kyiv Independent count based on official reports. The highest number of injuries came on Sept. 25, when at least 59 people were wounded as drones caught residents in the middle of the working day.
By the end of this intense stretch, the city had disappeared beneath a dense gray haze. It was not mere autumn fog, but smoke from the prior attacks that had accumulated over Kyiv in the still air. Authorities urged residents to keep their windows closed.
Buildings faded into the gray, as temperatures were falling. Parts of the city were without electricity. After more than a week of continuous strikes, the city looked as exhausted as it felt, and winter had not even begun.
A shift is visible not only in Russia's attack frequency. Sociologists are starting to see Kyiv move closer, on certain indicators, to Ukraine's eastern regions much closer to the front line.
Oleksii Antypovych, director of Rating Group, a Ukrainian polling and sociological research organization, said Kyiv residents increasingly resemble people in the east on several indicators, including worsening health, loss of income, and damage or destruction of property.
"In this sense, Kyiv can already, to some extent, be called a frontline region," he said.
Antypovych described the prevailing mood not as panic, but as anxiety and uncertainty about security, the city's protection, and what comes next.
"Before, at least you could expect the worst to happen at night and, if you wanted, prepare for it. Now it just feels like a lottery."
A survey conducted from Aug. 21 to Sept. 10 by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS) found that 83% of Kyiv residents believed Ukraine should continue armed resistance even if Russia tried to deprive people of electricity, heating, and water during the winter.
"Kyiv had the highest share of people (compared to other surveyed regions) who supported continuing armed resistance under any circumstances," Anton Hrushetskyi, KIIS executive director, told the Kyiv Independent.
A separate KIIS survey conducted in late July and early August found that the share of Kyiv residents ready to endure the war for as long as necessary had risen from 61% to 69% since April.
That people in Kyiv continue to stay, work, and build their lives in the city suggests that they are adapting, Antypovych said.
These latest polls suggest Kyiv residents are defiant in the face of Russia's effort to exhaust the country and weaken its will to resist. Yet, the polls were conducted prior to the continuous pressure Russia subjected the capital to in the last week.
Daria Lisich, a 28-year-old poet, had lived in Kyiv for only three months when Russia's attacks intensified in late August. She lives on the top floor of a five-story building. Staying in Kyiv is partly about conserving what little energy she has left, she said, because another move feels even harder.
"Moving is a huge effort and a major change. I just want this to end or at least to get easier," she said.
For four consecutive days, Russia struck the area close to where she lived. On the fourth day, a strike landed right next to her home, prompting her to leave the city for a while.
"All of the strikes were nearby, but the last one was the closest — right next to my home, in the neighboring building. I was at home during all of them," Lisich said. "I couldn't even take a shower. I constantly had my phone next to me, tracking where it was flying."
She left Kyiv for Lviv for three weeks. Back in the capital, the attacks continued.
Semen Krishtal, a 27-year-old creative marketer, has thought about leaving Kyiv for years, and the latest attacks have only intensified them.
"I want to move to Odesa, but the situation there is even worse in winter than in Kyiv," he said.
He felt the new reality set in clearly on Sept. 28, when a Russian drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv.
Krishtal was riding a trolleybus along Shevchenko Boulevard with his headphones on, listening to Sophie's "Immaterial" — a bright, euphoric pop song about freedom and becoming whoever you want to be. The city had already been filled with alerts and explosions that day, so he kept turning the music up to drown out the noise.
"At night, it's medication and deep sleep. During the day, it's music at full volume," he said. "Just so my brain can function at something other than a critical level of anxiety, at least at a moderate one."
But reality broke through anyway when the sound of another explosion cut through the music in his headphones. Minutes later, police cars and ambulances began speeding past his trolleybus.
Krishtal got off and walked toward the National Academy of Sciences. By the time he reached the attack site, emergency crews were already unfolding ladders to reach people trapped inside the burning building. He stopped and watched the scene unfold.
"Normal life has been a forgotten concept in Kyiv for a long time," Krishtal said. "Before, at least you could expect the worst to happen at night and, if you wanted, prepare for it. Now it just feels like a lottery."
Tania Myronyshena is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent. She has written for outlets such as United24 Media, Ukrainer, Wonderzine, as well as for PEN Ukraine, a Ukrainian non-governmental organization. Before joining the Kyiv Independent, she worked as a freelance journalist with a focus on cultural narratives and human stories. Tania holds a B.A. in publishing and editing from Borys Hrinchenko Kyiv University.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,540,700 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The number includes 1,750 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,540,700 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 4.
The number includes 1,750 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,391 tanks, 25,483 armored combat vehicles, 157,258 vehicles and fuel tanks, 50,686 artillery systems, 2,179 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,686 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,837 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy. Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1." A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA). While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action. The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: German Chancellor Merz arrives in Kyiv, pledges further support for Ukraine
description: Merz was accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and 10 executives from Germany's defense and energy sectors.
content:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Oct. 4 for a visit aimed at reaffirming Berlin's support for Ukraine, the German news agency dpa reported.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said he welcomed Merz to Kyiv on Sunday morning and that the chancellor would hold talks with President Volodymyr Zelensky on bilateral relations, European affairs, and international issues.
"A very substantive agenda lies ahead today, focused on strengthening Ukraine, our defense and resilience, and our shared European security," Sybiha wrote on X.
"If Russia is not stopped, its military machine will sooner or later turn against us," Merz said after arriving in the Ukrainian capital by train.
Merz was accompanied by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and 10 executives from Germany's defense and energy sectors.
According to German government sources cited by dpa, Merz is expected to make new commitments on financial and military assistance, including the delivery of thousands of interceptor drones and support for faster production of long-range weapons for Ukraine.
The visit comes as Ukraine faces an intensifying Russian missile and drone campaign and continues to press its partners for additional air-defense systems and interceptors.
Merz said in late September that Germany was working on ways to strengthen Ukraine's air defenses, which remain one of Kyiv's most urgent military needs.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 29 that Ukraine had received new air-defense support packages from several countries. European governments have also been discussing mechanisms that could allow Ukraine to obtain additional Patriot interceptor missiles, including through purchases financed by the EU's 90-billion-euro loan package.

title: U.S. peace negotiations with Russia could now involve multi-billion dollar Lukoil deal, NYT reports
description: The Trump administration’s peace negotiations with the Kremlin have come to include discussions of a multi-billion dollar deal involving assets owned by Russian oil company Lukoil, the New York Times (NYT) reported on Oct. 3.
content:
The Trump administration’s peace negotiations with the Kremlin have come to include discussions of a multi-billion dollar deal involving assets owned by Russian oil company Lukoil, the New York Times (NYT) reported on Oct. 3.
The newspaper reported that business executives with ties to U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are pursuing a potential deal involving Lukoil refineries, oil fields and gas stations around the world. The deal would require approval from both the U.S. government and the Kremlin, according to the report.
Russian President Vladimir Putin raised the potential deal with Kushner and Witkoff during their visit to Moscow on Sept. 5, proposing it as a way to demonstrate to Russians that they could still do business with the United States, NYT reported, citing people familiar with the matter.
The two envoys responded that they would work on the proposal, as a way to build good will with the Russians, according to the NYT report. Another benefit for the Americans is that global oil prices, which have skyrocketed following the U.S. war with Iran, could go down as a result of the deal, following sanctions against Lukoil assets potentially being lifted.
Lukoil is Russia's second-largest oil producer and one of the country's largest companies, accounting for 2% of global oil output. The corporation has been under U.S. sanctions since 2025, with the American government freezing its U.S.-based assets and threatening secondary penalties for foreign entities engaging with them.
“Given President Putin’s refusal to end this senseless war, Treasury is sanctioning Russia’s two largest oil companies that fund the Kremlin’s war machine,” U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in an October 2025 press release,
The sanctions, the first such measures imposed by the second Trump administration, were designed to pressure Moscow into peace talks in Ukraine, as fossil fuel revenues play a key role in sustaining Russia's war efforts. The U.S. government then proceeded to issue a limited sanctions waiver on some of Lukoil’s foreign assets, which was extended earlier this year.
While the U.S. Senate recently passed a bill that would make it easier to impose sanctions on countries that subsidize Russia’s war economy, this new potential agreement could allow Lukoil’s assets to be relieved of sanctions, potentially increasing their value, according to NYT
In January, the Russian energy giant agreed to sell most of its foreign assets to the American investment firm Carlyle, Lukoil's press service announced on Jan. 29. But the deal remains subject to U.S. government approval
Apart from stakes in oil fields in Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, the Middle East, Africa, and elsewhere, Lukoil also operates three oil refineries in Europe and hundreds of gas stations worldwide, including in the U.S.
Swiss-based oil trader Gunvor initially sought the purchase of the company's foreign assets, but withdrew its bid in November after the U.S. Treasury Department described the trader as the "Kremlin's puppet."

title: At least 15,000 civilian casualties documented in Ukraine in 2026, UN report finds
description: The UN Human Rights Office found that an average of more than 400 civilians were killed or injured every week in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, a 55% increase from the same period in 2025, High Commissioner Volker Turk told the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Oct. 2.
content:
The UN Human Rights Office found that an average of more than 400 civilians were killed or injured every week in Ukraine during the first eight months of 2026, a 55% increase from the same period in 2025, High Commissioner Volker Turk told the Human Rights Council in Geneva on Oct. 2.
Turk’s office documented 15,280 civilians killed or injured during the first eight months of the year, as Russia has intensified attacks on civilian infrastructure in recent months. On the frontlines, the office found that nearly 2,500 civilians were killed or injured by Russian aerial glide bombs in the span of eight months, which is 62% more than last year.
"The war in Ukraine is a human rights catastrophe that is growing and intensifying by the week, causing unfathomable pain to civilians, and threatening an even greater disaster across the entire region," Türk said .
Russian strikes on schools , medical centers , apartment buildings, railways and shops are leading to a growing number of civilian casualties, as people across Ukraine live in "constant dread ," the UN office said in a summary of his remarks.
His office also outlined how a "sharp increase" of Russian attacks on energy infrastructure and commercial properties like supermarkets and food companies will continue to cause pain to civilians, who are forced to grapple with temporary shortages of dairy and food items as the winter months approach.
In his Geneva remarks, Turk urged "states with influence" over Russia to push for peace now, before the “tragedy becomes even worse.” He also criticized Russia’s leadership, who he said had created a militarized economy "that puts death and destruction ahead of healthcare and education."
In a response to the UN office’s findings, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha echoed Turk’s call for accountability, saying that the High Commissioner’s call to states with influence over Russia "must be acted upon."
"While Russia cannot achieve any of its goals on the frontline, it is killing and injuring more Ukrainian civilians," Sybiha said. "The principles of the UN Charter cannot survive as words alone while a country that illegally occupies the seat of a permanent member of the Security Council violates them day after day."
The UN office had also found “shocking” levels of sexual violence against civilians and prisoners of war, he said. Turk accused the Russian Federation of using such “abhorrent acts to torture , intimidate and coerce individuals and communities.”
According to the report , out of the 1,004 verified cases of conflict-related sexual violence between February 2022 and July 2026 against civilians and prisoners of war (POWs), 89% were attributed to Russian forces. 11% of total verified cases were attributed to Ukrainian forces, with threats of sexual violence comprising almost half of these violations.
A summary of the report’s findings outlined that while the Ukrainian government has taken "concrete steps to prevent and address such violations," Russia has failed to do the same.
"This is just one terrible manifestation of the cruelty that has come to define this war,” Turk said, adding that “alongside peace, there must be accountability."
The High Commissioner elaborated that his office was also concerned about human rights violations against foreign nationals recruited by Russia to join the war effort. His office interviewed prisoners of war from 36 countries held by Ukraine, many of whom said they had been deceived into joining Russian forces.

title: Exit polls show pro-Ukraine United List party leading Latvian parliamentary elections as counting begins
description: Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ centrist United List party is projected to win the greatest number of seats in the Latvian parliament with 35% support, exit polling commissioned by public broadcaster LSM showed on Oct. 3.
content:
Editor's note: Read the latest on Latvia's parliamentary election results.
Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs’ centrist United List party is projected to win the greatest number of seats in the Latvian parliament with 35% support, exit polling commissioned by public broadcaster LSM showed on Oct. 3.
Votes are still being counted , with final results expected in the early hours of Oct. 4. The vote for the 100-member unicameral parliament — the Saeima — will be the second since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, a war in which Latvia threw its full support behind Kyiv.
Latvians took to the polls on Oct. 3 to decide what their parliament will look like for the next four years. Affordability and security concerns have been top political issues in the Baltic country which shares a border with Russia and is home to a large Russian-speaking minority.
The election marked a test for Kulbergs, who has been prime minister since May. His predecessor, Evika Silina, was forced to resign following a political crisis triggered by a Ukrainian drone incursion into Latvian airspace. This led to a government collapse and paved the way for a four-party coalition led by Kulbergs.
Throughout his term, Kulbergs has expressed unwavering support for Ukraine, and Latvia has sharply increased defense spending since 2022, reaching 5% of GDP.
"Ukraine’s security is linked to the security of Europe as a whole, including Latvia," he said in a state visit to Ukraine in August.
Warnings from Western officials over an escalating hybrid threat from Russia is of particular concern to Latvia, an EU and NATO member which shares a border with both Russia and Belarus. Latvia is a key part of NATO’s Baltic defense structure on its Eastern flank.
While Latvia has said it sees no sign of an imminent conventional Russian attack , the Russia-Ukraine war has already spilled over into Latvian airspace, with several stray drones shot down by NATO planes.
The majority of Latvia’s electoral parties are pro-Ukraine, despite a third of the country speaking Russian as their first language.
If, as the exit polls suggest, United List wins 35% support, the party would still have to form a coalition government to achieve a majority.
The exit polls suggest the populist Latvia First party is expected to come in second with 11.3% support, followed close by the social democrat Progressive party with 11.1% of the vote. The Russia-friendly Sovereign Power/Young Latvians alliance is projected to win 10.8% of the vote, making it the fourth biggest party in the legislature.
Sovereign Power is the only political party in Latvia which opposes military aid to Ukraine.
The Latvian State Security Service (VDD) said that it was employing enhanced security measures to get ahead of potential Russian election interference, according to LSM on Sept 28. But no significant systematic interference had been detected, the VDD said.

title: Russian strike on Liberian-flagged cargo ship in Black Sea kills 1, injures 3
description: The attack comes amid an international call for Russia to halt attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea and allow the passage of grain exports.
content:
Russian forces attacked a civilian cargo ship sailing under the Liberian flag at a port near Odesa in the Black Sea on Oct. 3, killing one.
The sailor killed was a motor engineer, and three other crew members were injured in the strike, according to the Ukrainian Sea Ports ​Authority. 13 other crew members were evacuated from the vessel.
"This is yet another deliberate attack by Russia on civilian shipping," said the Sea Ports Authority. "Russia continues to terrorize the peaceful merchant fleet and sailors who risk their lives every day to ensure the operation of Ukrainian maritime routes."
The attack comes amid an international call for Russia to halt attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea and allow the passage of grain exports .
While the Black Sea isn’t officially blocked , vessels are avoiding Ukraine for fear of being hit by missiles. Since June, Moscow has deliberately stepped up attacks on civilian ships as well as port facilities, as Ukraine puts pressure on Russia’s economy by increasingly striking oil refineries, the shadow fleet , and dual-use logistics hubs.
Ukraine established its own Black Sea maritime corridor in August 2023, after Russia withdrew from a U.N.- and Turkey-brokered grain deal. Since then, Russia has regularly targeted ports and civilian shipping.
On Sept. 17, a Russian drone attacked a Tanzania-flagged civilian vessel in the Black Sea en route to a Ukrainian port, killing the ship's captain and injuring three crew members, Ukraine's Infrastructure Ministry said.
A Ukrainian unmanned surface vessel destroyed a Russian naval drone in the Black Sea in what Ukraine's Navy described as the "first-ever naval battle" between unmanned boats, on Sept. 12.

title: Moscow unveils 'new doctrine' targeting Ukrainian civilians, Zelensky vows to respond with more energy strikes
description: Zelensky said that Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents revealing that Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a "new doctrine" allowing Russian forces to launch broader strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets this upcoming winter.
content:
In response to a new airstrike policy targeting Ukrainian civilians by Moscow, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Oct. 3 that Ukraine would increase attacks on Russian energy infrastructure.
Zelensky told Reuters that Ukrainian intelligence obtained documents revealing that Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a "new doctrine" allowing Russian forces to launch broader strikes against Ukrainian civilian targets this upcoming winter.
"We saw documents and we know that they allow them [to] ‌attack infrastructure ... logistics ... roads, schools, hospitals, to pressure people to leave the capital, leave different cities," Zelensky said. With this shift, Putin wants to appear strong even as Russian troops continue to lose ground while suffering massive casualties , said Zelensky.
The president's comments come as Russian forces have increasingly battered Ukrainian civilian infrastructure in recent weeks, including attacks on key bridges and medical and educational facilities .
In response to Moscow's changing tactics, Zelensky vowed to increase strikes on Russian energy sites, though without indiscriminately targeting Russian civilians.
"We have to respond in any way [we can]. With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refineries: what gives money to them for this war," Zelensky said. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."
For weeks, U.S. President Donald Trump has been pressing Ukraine and Russia to halt energy strikes in order to help lower high oil prices brought on by his war with Iran.
