The EU should rein in its ambitions for the Drone Wall to "do just about everything" and focus on the most successful national initiatives in Poland and the Baltics, Franke argues. The bloc, she writes, should also prod other frontier states to step up.
Both she and Borsari see interoperability among individual allies and industry players as a key obstacle to overcome.
And while Borsari lists other weaknesses — such as insufficient training, experimentation, and, in some cases, funding — he acknowledges progress.
The EU is opening the tap for drone investment, with its 150-billion-euro ($175-billion) SAFE loans helping fund air defense acquisitions in Poland and Romania.
The NATO summit in Ankara, in turn, saw allies pledge to invest $40 billion in counter-drone capabilities over the next five years.
Since spring 2026, the alliance has been holding regular LCI-X Crucible exercises focused on countering drones, with Ukrainian soldiers participating.
"I expect (counter-drone) capabilities across the alliance to improve significantly in the near future, though for some areas, especially training and full operational capability… may require time," Borsari predicts.
Barring physical constraints, countering drone incursions is still hitting political obstacles.
Only last May did Romania adopt a law authorizing its military to shoot down drones and aircraft that violate its airspace in peacetime.
Lithuania's parliament adopted similar legislation in September, a few weeks after the incursion into Poland.
And there is still the question of the readiness to pull the trigger.
The obstacles here are two-fold, says Iulian Chifu, a Romanian security analyst and president of the Center for Conflict Prevention & Early Warning, a research institute in Bucharest.
Firstly, the allies worry that the downing — or an attempt at it— may cause more collateral damage than if the intruding drone is allowed to leave the airspace or crash in an empty area.
Secondly, many fear that opening fire will bring Russia to view European countries as co-belligerents — an idea Moscow "succeeded in putting into the heads of European leaders," Chifu adds.
But the recent incidents seem to be changing the risk calculus for European nations.
In Romania, the breaking point was when the Russian drone hit the residential building, according to Chifu.
And in Latvia, a crash of stray Ukrainian drones at a local oil facility in May led to the fall of the Latvian government.
The political cost of letting the drones slip through may begin to outweigh the cost of shooting them down.
Editor's note: The article mistakenly said that a Russian drone killed civilians in Romania. The drone strike against a residential building in Galati injured two people, with no fatalities recorded. The mistake has been corrected.
I hope you enjoyed this article. In our team, we believe fact-based and truthful reporting should be available to all — that's why we don't use any paywall.
If you want to see more in-depth coverage of regional politics and how it shapes Ukraine's struggle against Russian aggression, please consider joining the Kyiv Independent community.
Martin Fornusek is an assistant editor at the Kyiv Independent. Until recently, Martin held the role of foreign affairs reporter specializing in international and regional politics, history, and disinformation. Based in Lviv, Martin often reports on international politics, focusing on developments related to Ukraine and Russia. His career in journalism began in 2021 after graduating from Masaryk University in Brno, Czechia, earning a Master's degree in Conflict and Democracy Studies. Martin has been invited to speak on Times Radio, France 24, Czech Television, and Radio Free Europe. He speaks English, Czech, and Ukrainian.

title: Former Pussy Riot member escapes Russia after 3 years of forced work for FSB
description: "They began recruiting me, threatening me in every possible way, humiliating me, saying some very unpleasant things, threatening to kill my family, and telling me that I would never in my life be able to prove who killed my mother," Rita Flores said.
content:
Editor's Note: This article was updated on Aug. 26, 2026, to include a statement by Pussy Riot co-founder Nadya Tolokonnikova . Former Pussy Riot member Rita Flores was forcibly recruited by Russia's Security Service (FSB) as an intelligence asset for three years before she was able to escape Russia, she said in an interview with Port Media on Aug. 24.
According to Flores, whose real name is Margarita Konovalova, the FSB recruited her in 2023 after conducting searches of her apartment.
"They began recruiting me, threatening me in every possible way, humiliating me, saying some very unpleasant things, threatening to kill my family and telling me that I would never in my life be able to prove who killed my mother," Flores said .
"They attacked me personally, telling me how disgusting and horrible I was, that they would turn me into the biggest Satan in all of Russia."
The FSB initially ordered Flores to provide information on artists and political activists both within and outside of Russia and took her passport so she couldn't leave the country, she said. According to Flores, they reportedly wanted her to help develop some into fellow "assets" and to help line up new targets for criminal cases.
In an Instagram post, Flores described those three years as being defined by "prolonged depression... complete, unrelenting derealization, PTSD from being followed and surveilled... several attempts at suicide, and so, so, so much more."
The pressure from the FSB ramped up when they tried to force her to help lure Mediazona co-founder and activist Pyotr Verzilov to Serbia so they could murder him.
According to Flores, she contacted lawyer Dmitry Zakhvatov afterward and managed to stall the FSB's demands until she was finally able to escape Russia.
The Kyiv Independent reached out to Verzilov after the revelation.
"The FSB has been trying to kill me for the last 10 years in various parts of the world," Verzilov said.
"Their repeated attempts in the last several years are a testament of the work we do, first of all of the work focused on the defense of Ukraine in the face of Russian aggression."
Pussy Riot co-founder Nadya Tolokonnikova wrote on X on Aug. 26 that she only learned about Flores being recruited by the FSB when the interview was published online.
"We never worked together as Pussy Riot activists, and she was not part of the circle of people I trusted. Luckily, this means she was not part of group chats, planning, or even casual discussion," Tolokonnikova said.
Although they weren't acquainted, Tolokonnikova said she reached out to Flores in 2023 after learning that police had searched her apartment in Moscow because she feels compelled to help others who are targeted by Russian authorities for their connections to Pussy Riot.
"In 2011, when we were forming Pussy Riot, there was a saying, 'anyone can be Pussy Riot.' Some things did not age so well. In 2026, in this fifth year of full-scale violence and aggression against Ukraine, there must be much stronger moral lines," Tolokonnikova added.
"Peter chose his side, and they wanted him dead. For my part, I have tried my best to be on the right side. Rita, for three years, chose hers. I will not be in contact with her in the future. I hope she and her lawyer work with local authorities to expose the spies and murderers that may still be operating within dissident circles."

title: 'It's war against the West' — Latvian PM on Russian provocations against European countries
description: "That's the war of Russia against the West, the EU, and NATO, as we've seen," Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said on Aug. 24.
content:
Russia poses a growing hybrid threat to Europe, using disinformation, migration, and other tactics to destabilize the continent, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs said on Aug. 24 during a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing in Kyiv.
"That's the war of Russia against the West, the EU, and NATO, as we've seen," Kulbergs said.
Russia has long used hybrid warfare tactics across Europe including sabotage cyberattacks, disinformation. Cases of each have escalated since the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with several drone incursions recorded in recent years.
Kulbergs said the EU was also seeing attacks on its border, highlighting how Russia is using Belarus to organize a migration crisis toward the bloc.
"We see that it is one of the highest threats, with a case that is well organized by the Kremlin through the hands of Belarus and through criminal organizations that are also making money from it as a service," Kulbergs said.
"This is testing our ability to fight back, our technical ability, our reaction times," he added.
Belarus has previously been accused by European countries of deliberately facilitating irregular migration to the EU's eastern borders as a form of hybrid warfare. Minsk helped channel migrants from the Middle East, Africa, and Asia toward Lithuania, Latvia and Poland after the EU imposed sanctions on Belarus in 2021. The Kremlin has also been accused of supporting the renewed campaign.
Kulbergs said migration was only one part of a broader campaign that also includes cyberattacks and attempts to disrupt elections and influence public opinion.
"We also see cyberattacks happening. We see potential disruptions of public aspects, as we've seen in many countries — attacking elections, trying to disrupt the mindset of the people," he said.
The Baltic states have faced a series of drone incidents in recent months. In May, Lithuania issued its first air raid alert over a suspected drone threat after an unidentified drone crossed into Lithuanian airspace from Belarus. Fighter jets operating as part of NATO's Baltic Air Policing mission shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace on Aug. 14, according to the Latvian military.
More recently, Lithuania said on Aug. 6 that it had intelligence suggesting Russia could use Ukrainian-made drones in false-flag attacks against critical infrastructure in the Baltic region. Lithuanian Defense Minister Robert Kaunas said Russia was considering "unconventional kinetic attacks" as tensions rose following repeated drone incursions across the region.
Kulbergs said Russia's actions had ultimately strengthened NATO rather than weakening it.
"Russia does not understand. They have actually made us stronger together. They have made NATO stronger. We now have Sweden and Finland joining in," he said.

title: ‘Everything except nukes’: As the world watches Wildberries, Russia unleashes war on Ukraine’s economy
description: As Ukraine captures global attention with dramatic strikes on Russia’s oil infrastructure and e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon, Russia has unleashed its most devastating campaign yet against Ukraine’s economic infrastructure.
content:
Firefighters put out a fire after Russian missiles hit a warehouse in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Aug. 5, 2026. (Dan Bashakov / AP)
Walk through a supermarket in Kyiv, and you will find rows of empty shelves. Drive your car to a gas station in Kharkiv, and a Russian drone may have gotten there first. Across Ukraine, packages are at risk of being turned to ash as Russian missiles pummel post offices. Once bustling ports sit empty, as ships stay clear of Ukraine.
As Ukraine captures global attention with dramatic strikes on Russia’s oil infrastructure and e-commerce giants Wildberries and Ozon , Russia has unleashed its most devastating campaign yet against Ukraine’s economic infrastructure.
Over the last few months, Moscow’s relentless bombardment has torn apart postal services, supermarkets, factories, warehouses, gas stations, ports, civilian vessels, and railway infrastructure.
As a result, ships are no longer docking in Black Sea ports, slashing Ukraine’s exports. Retailers are laying off staff, mining companies have shut operations, and there are growing fuel shortages in southern and eastern regions.
The short- and long-term consequences look bleak, with the National Bank estimating it could cost Ukraine 0.9% of gross domestic product (GDP) this year.
"Russia is using more and more drones and missiles to hurt Ukraine’s economy, to make it weaker, and psychologically push the population towards peace talks," Oleksandra Betliy, leading research fellow at the Institute for Economic Research and Policy Consulting, told the Kyiv Independent.
And Russia currently has more drones and missiles than in previous years, meaning attacks are likely to continue, Betliy said.
"The Russians have no other answer but to escalate even further. They are utilizing everything they have except nukes," Bogdan Kostetskyi, an operating partner at consulting service Barva Invest that provides insights into how the war is impacting Ukraine’s agricultural trade, told the Kyiv Independent.
"It’s like a fight without rules. Unfortunately, this is the new normal," he added.
As blows intensify, Ukraine is desperately seeking ways to keep its economy afloat. While Kyiv’s strikes are alarming the Kremlin and inhibiting its war machine, Russia’s multi-trillion-dollar economy is unlikely to collapse any time soon, Konstantin Sonin, an exiled Russian economist and professor at the University of Chicago Harris School of Public Policy, told the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine, with a much smaller and weaker economy, is reaching out to international partners for support, while expanding financial programs to support affected businesses . But many companies are still having to adapt to Russia’s attacks at their own expense.
Russia launched a record 389 missiles at Ukraine last month, taking advantage of Ukraine’s Patriot air defense shortage. For comparison, Russia fired 244 missiles in July 2025. In May this year, Moscow launched 8,150 drones, more than double the 4,003 drones launched in May last year.
The attacks are costing war-damaged cities. In Kyiv alone, which has suffered several major strikes and numerous smaller attacks over the summer, each ballistic missile strike costs the city Hr 300-500 million ($7-12 million) to repair shelters and homes, the head of the Kyiv City State Administration, Petro Panteleev, told Ukrainian media, Liga.​
"They want to intimidate and wear down the population."
Roughly 20 gas stations were hit every week in July, NaftoRynok, a consulting firm, told the Kyiv Independent. Stations in front-line regions have reduced fuel in storage tanks, imposed refueling limits, and closed during air alerts, which can last hours at a time.
Moscow is also honing in on the nerve centers of critical businesses for maximum effect, like the warehouses and distribution centers of supermarkets rather than individual stores.
"We believe that, in the enemy’s view, this tactic is intended to destabilize the situation among the population and create a shortage of goods," the press service for Ukraine’s largest supermarket chain, ATB, told the Kyiv Independent in a written statement.
"They want to intimidate and wear down the population," it said
One of the most aggressive attacks on Ukrainian businesses took place overnight on Aug. 4-5 in Kyiv Oblast. Russia targeted the logistics center of supermarket firm Novus, two distribution centers belonging to Fozzy Group, another supermarket chain, a sorting center owned by leading private postal service Nova Post, and a distribution warehouse complex owned by Rozetka, Ukraine’s biggest online retailer.
For weeks after the attack, supermarkets across Kyiv were left with empty shelves and signs warning of delays — a rare sight in Ukraine where stores are usually packed with food. To avoid a future crisis, Novus stopped storing goods in one large unit, instead diversifying storage and sending two-thirds of "essential" products directly from factory to store, Krystyna Ivchenko, head of Novus’ external communications, told the Kyiv Independent in a written statement.
The chain is also campaigning for the government to introduce financial programs to help companies repair damages and better war risk insurance instruments.
Rozetka publicly said that the damages to its complex were irreparable — costing them 70 million euros ($81 million), destroying billions of hryvnias of goods, and forcing the company to lay off staff. Co-founder Iryna Chechotkina pleaded with the government to defer taxes, stressing that Rozetka won’t be able to recover without help.
Nova Post, the country’s largest private courier firm, has remained tight-lipped, not revealing the extent of the damage nor how much it has paid to compensate customers — unusual for a company that is normally communicative.
However, from open-source information, Russia has recently moved from targeting the company’s individual branches to much bigger logistics centers, hitting at least four sorting centers in June and at least seven in July.
"If you're hitting big distribution centers, you're destroying huge investments, and you destroy a big number of parcels, some of which might be dual-use. It makes logistics much slower and causes delays," Betliy said.
Ukraine’s steelmakers have also come under fire, with precise strikes on their production sites. On Aug. 11, Russian ballistic missiles destroyed blast furnace equipment at Metinvest’s steel plant in Zaporizhzhia, shutting the factory down. A few days later, another ballistic missile tore apart energy and blast furnace equipment at ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih’s factory on Aug. 16.
The attacks were a shock for many in the industry, which hasn’t suffered direct missile strikes since 2024. Some in the embattled sector are bracing for factories to be targeted more intensely the longer Ukraine doesn’t have adequate air defense.
The attacks on gas stations, supermarkets, and postal services disrupt the general population, but are unlikely to have a significant knock-on effect for the economy at large as businesses are quickly adapting. Instead, the most devastating attacks are on Ukraine’s ports in the Black Sea, causing Ukraine’s biggest industries to hemorrhage cash.
In a bid to choke trade in the Black Sea, Russia struck ports 67 times and vessels 57 times last month. Despite Kyiv publicly backing a maritime truce, Moscow’s officials have shown no interest in de-escalation.
Unsurprisingly, vessels are avoiding the ports. When Russia began systematically targeting civilian vessels, the families of sailors begged shipping companies to stop sending vessels to Ukraine, Gennadiy Ivanov, director of shipping firm BPG, told the Kyiv Independent.
Grain exports collapsed in the first two weeks of August — the start of export season — with Ukraine only exporting 30% of its normal grain volumes, Agriculture Minister Taras Vysotsky told reporters on Aug. 14.
As a result, Ukraine could lose 10.8 billion euros ($12.6 billion) from blocked agri-exports, while food prices will jump globally — Vysotsky estimates by 30% — impacting countries in West Asia and Africa that rely on Ukrainian grain.
But richer EU nations will feel the cost too, particularly as European livestock farmers depend on millions of tons of Ukrainian corn annually for feed, Oleh Khomenko, CEO of the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB), told the Kyiv Independent.
The situation is especially worse this year because of a corn deficit in Europe, with European farmers planning to increase corn imports by nearly 6 million tons, he said. Without Ukrainian corn, prices will increase across the board, leaving European livestock farmers to foot the bill, he said.
Ukrainian agribusinesses are looking at alternative routes, such as the Danube River ports, road, and railway to export goods. But these options can only handle half the volume of the Black Sea ports, and some products, like corn, require deep-water ports, which the Danube doesn’t have — particularly as water levels are at a record low due to summer heatwaves.
Even if Ukraine does manage to open up the Black Sea, cargo prices will be sky-high, Serhii Vovk, director of the Center for Transportation Strategies, a consulting firm in Kyiv, told the Kyiv Independent. Ukrainian goods risk losing their competitiveness on the global market as a result, he added.
Insurance prices for Ukraine’s Black Sea ports are around 10 times greater than before the summer, reaching levels last seen in 2023 after Moscow pulled out of the short-lived grain corridor that helped food exports bypass Russia’s naval blockade, said Ivanov.
For metallurgy companies, which rely on the Black Sea for exports to countries like China and Turkey, the blockade has forced factories to suspend work. Disruptions to coking coal imports, used to fuel blast furnaces, have slowed steel production, while iron ore exports are effectively at zero.
In total, metal exports dropped by 15% month over month in July. It’s another heavy blow for metallurgy companies after the EU imposed trade restrictions on steel products earlier this year, slashing revenues for Ukraine’s metallurgy sector — a major economic driver that accounted for over 5% of GDP last year.
Now, with railway tariffs increasing by 30% as a result of the blockade, exports have become economically unviable, the press service for Metinvest, Ukraine’s largest steel company, told the Kyiv Independent. The more the blockade drags on, the greater the risk of industrial shutdowns, tax losses, and economic instability, they added.
With the decline of its two main economic drivers — agriculture and metallurgy — Ukraine’s economy could slide next year if the blockade continues, said Betliy.
"If everything is just as bad as it looks now, then Ukraine’s GDP will probably not grow next year," she said.
Dominic is the business reporter for the Kyiv Independent, reporting on Ukrainian companies, investment, energy, corruption, and reforms. Based in Kyiv, Dominic joined the Kyiv Independent team in 2023, having previously worked as a freelancer. He has written articles for a number of publications, including the Financial Times, bne IntelliNews, Radio Free Europe/Liberty, Euronews and New Eastern Europe. Previously, Dominic worked with StopFake as a disinformation expert, debunking Russian fake news in Europe.

title: 10 Ukrainian soldiers believed missing return home from Russian captivity in 'special exchange'
description: Two had been considered missing since 2024, while the other eight had been missing since 2025, Ukraine's Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said.
content:
Ukraine brought home 10 service members previously considered missing in action from Russian captivity in a "special exchange" via Belarus on Aug. 24, President Volodymyr Zelensky announced, as Ukraine marked its Independence Day.
The service members served in the Ukrainian Armed Forces and National Guard and fought on the Donetsk sector of the front line, Zelensky said.
Two had been considered missing since 2024, while the other eight had been missing since 2025, Ukraine's Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said. The group included sergeants, soldiers and sailors, Lubinets added.
"It is very important that we managed to bring them back," Zelensky said.
"We remember every man and woman who remains in captivity. We are searching for every name. And we will do everything to free them and bring them home," he added.
The status of missing Ukrainian service members can remain unresolved for months or years, in part because intense fighting, Russian occupation, and continued attacks can prevent Ukrainian forces from recovering bodies from the battlefield and conducting DNA identification. Some of those listed as missing can later found to be alive in Russian captivity.
The exchange comes five days after Ukraine brought home 103 prisoners of war from Russian captivity on Aug. 19. Those released included service members from the Armed Forces, State Border Guard Service, National Guard, Navy, and Territorial Defense Forces.
Ukraine and Russia have also continued repatriating the bodies of fallen soldiers despite a broader diplomatic process that has largely stalled.
Ukraine repatriated on Aug. 13 the bodies of 261 people that Russia claimed were Ukrainian service members. Ukrainian investigators and forensic experts were tasked with identifying the remains.

title: Drama, determination, and risk: Remembering how Ukraine's independence unfolded
description:
Editor's note: Because both authors were direct participants in the events described, they are referred to by their first names — Nadia and Robert — throughout, to distinguish their individual roles and recollections.

Neither the United States nor any other country recognized Ukrainian independence when, on Aug. 24, 1991, the Verkhovna Rada adopted its Act of the Declaration of the Independence of Ukraine.

That fact is worth remembering. Why? Because passage of the Declaration reflected a shar
content:
Ukrainians wave Ukrainian flags and celebrate Ukrainian independence in front of the Communist Party's central committee headquarters in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Aug. 25, 1991. (Anatoly Sapronenkov / AFP / Getty Images)
Co-founder of the U.S.-Ukraine Foundation
Editor's note: Because both authors were direct participants in the events described, they are referred to by their first names — Nadia and Robert — throughout, to distinguish their individual roles and recollections.
Neither the United States nor any other country recognized Ukrainian independence when, on Aug. 24, 1991, the Verkhovna Rada adopted its Act of the Declaration of the Independence of Ukraine.
That fact is worth remembering. Why? Because passage of the Declaration reflected a shared calculation between Rukh (the Ukrainian democratic movement, not the political party formed later) and the Communist members who made up the majority of the Rada: Rukh wanted the political legitimacy that a popular vote would provide, while the Communists wanted a way out if the political winds in Moscow shifted in the months ahead.
Since Dec. 1 had already been set as the date for Ukraine 's first presidential election, the two votes were merged onto the same day. Thus, the Rada conditioned actual independence on a vote of the people of Ukraine on Dec. 1, 1991.
On Wednesday, Nov. 27, five days before the referendum, President George H. W. Bush hosted a meeting in the Roosevelt Room of the White House with leaders of Ukrainian American organizations and Ukrainian churches; Robert, along with senior White House staff, was also in the room.
At one point, the President said, "If Ukraine votes for independence, there are things I will want before we recognize Ukraine's independence."
He then listed the conditions he would want from Ukraine: commitment to the principles of the Helsinki Final Act (CSCE); non-nuclear status and a commitment to nuclear nonproliferation — commitments already made in Ukraine's 1991 Declaration of Sovereignty, its Declaration of Independence, and the text of the December referendum itself; and Ukraine's adherence to the Conventional Forces in Europe Treaty and other military agreements.
At one point, as Robert was taking notes on the President's pre-conditions to recognition of Ukraine's independence, Bush — who knew Robert from their years together in the Reagan Administration — turned to him and asked, "Bob, are you getting all this?"
The President then turned to his National Security Advisor, Brent Scowcroft, and asked if anything else would be needed from Ukraine before the United States would recognize Ukraine's independence, to which Scowcroft replied, "No."
Robert was shocked — the President had said, "If Ukraine votes for independence?" He had doubts?
We certainly had no doubt that the referendum would pass overwhelmingly, as did many others who were following events on the ground in Ukraine.
Among the reasons for our certainty was that we had been privileged to be eyewitnesses to and engaged in several key moments in events preceding Ukraine's declaration of independence and setting the date for the referendum.
Nadia was in Ukraine on Jan. 21, 1990, and, along with the leadership of Rukh, participated in the incredibly successful, unbroken Human Chain that was an unbroken line of people standing together for 550 kilometers from Lviv to Kyiv.
At the time, the Ukrainian flag was still illegal, but supporters had managed to smuggle enough fabric into Ukraine to sew hundreds upon hundreds of Ukrainian flags to cover the full length of the chain.
When Nadia stepped out of the hotel Lebed in downtown Kyiv, she saw buses from Ivano-Frankivsk with people dressed in vyshyvanky and carrying the blue and yellow flags of Ukraine. They ensured Ukrainian flags were displayed along the entire Human Chain and throughout the city of Kyiv .
Rukh's leadership had negotiated with the local authorities and the KGB to hold this rally.
Several days after the Human Chain, Nadia met with Maria Drach, wife of Rukh's chairman, Ivan Drach, in their apartment.
When Ivan Drach arrived, Maria reported a message he had received from the authorities that, in summary, was something like, "You have had your rally, it was time to take down the Ukrainian flag," which hung in front of Rukh's building.
Drach's response was, "We'll think about it," and, eventually, the flag never came down.
Both of us were in Kyiv in March 1990 for the first Verkhovna Rada elections under Soviet rule, in which candidates from outside the Communist Party were permitted to run.
The day after the election, we were invited to take part in the meeting of the Executive Council of Rukh, comprised of Members of the Communist Party, like Rukh's chairman, Ivan Drach, and one of Rukh's founders, Dmytro Pavlychko, as well as Mykhailo Horyn, Head of the Secretariat, and a member of the Helsinki Group who endured years of imprisonment in the Soviet Gulag .
The Executive Council decided to issue a statement blaming the Communist Party for a litany of wrongs committed against the people of Ukraine, and to include the formal resignation from the Communist Party of all the Council's members who still belonged to it.
We watched as one by one they came forward to affix their signatures to the statement. Among the statement's concluding comments were "We can only serve the truth by leaving the Communist Party" and the claim that "imperialist chauvinism remains the soul of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union ."
Several days later, after members of the Executive Council who had been voting in distant oblasts returned and signed the statement, it was presented and read at a press conference.
This was dramatic — this was still the Soviet Union. As those signatures were placed on the document, no one knew what the consequences might be.
In 1990 and 1991, we both made multiple trips to Ukraine and attended meetings with several key organizations that helped secure the referendum vote, including Mothers of Children of Chornobyl, Mothers of Afghan Veterans, youth and Jewish organizations, and Church leaders.
However, the most important of these meetings was with the incredibly strategic Rukh leadership. During these travels, Robert gave a nationally televised keynote speech at the Second Conference of Rukh in September 1990.
Nadia participated in several meetings of the Rukh women from Kyiv who were gathering humanitarian supplies and traveling to villages across Ukraine to prepare for the changes that were coming, including the referendum vote.
Rukh ran a large, deliberate get-out-the-vote effort ahead of the December 1, 1991, referendum — mobilizing an estimated 10,000 to 20,000 activists, who went door-to-door and held town-hall-style meetings with those still skeptical.
Rukh strategically used the time between the Proclamation of Independence and the Referendum to travel across Ukraine, speaking with people and answering their questions, promoting the democracy and freedom that would come with such independence.
However, let us return to President Bush's doubts about the December referendum receiving majority support for independence.
We — the U.S.-Ukraine Foundation — had opened an office in Kyiv in 1990 and not only were we confident the referendum would pass overwhelmingly, but we were also in close communication with Irene Jarosevich — with whom Nadia had worked on the Commemoration of Millenium of Christianity in Ukraine in 1988, and who was then serving as Rukh's international media representative — and with Jon Gunderson, who had arrived to serve as Consul General for the United States in Kyiv (later Charge d'Affaires ad interim with Ukrainian independence).
Both saw things the same way we did. How could the President have doubts?
After 92% of the people of Ukraine voted for independence, Ukraine became independent.
After the Nov. 27 White House meeting, Robert immediately sent an email — the email system then was not what it is today; it was cumbersome and expensive — to Irene, who translated it and delivered it to Ivan Plyushch, chairman of the Verkhovna Rada.
The message included a report about the White House meeting and the conditions stated by President Bush, as well as the observation that it was important to understand the President's conditions and that the President would be the one making the final decision on the recognition of Ukraine's independence.
On Monday, Dec. 2, after 92% of the people of Ukraine voted for independence, Ukraine became independent.
At a press conference, the Chairman of the Verkhovna Rada, Ivan Plyushch, was asked by an American reporter when Ukraine would be able to meet the 18-20 conditions the United States State Department would require for Ukraine's independence to be recognized.
Plyushch responded that the previous Wednesday, President Bush had listed the conditions he wanted met, and that it was a much shorter list — and the President was the one who would make the final decision with regard to recognizing Ukraine's independence.
Robert learned of Plyushch's exchange with the reporter during a call from the White House.
The Presidential aide said they knew Robert had been in touch with Chairman Plyushch, as he had been the one writing down the President's list in Wednesday's meeting.
On Dec. 2, Poland and Canada recognized the independence of Ukraine, followed by the Russian SFSR. Quite a few other countries then recognized Ukraine before the United States did so on Christmas Day, Dec. 25.
We later understood why President Bush and Mr. Scowcroft did not view the referendum in Ukraine the same as Jon Gunderson.
Gunderson had no secure communications in Kyiv, therefore he, or his number two, John Stepechuk, had to travel to the U.S. Embassy in Moscow to file their reports.
However, the Embassy, convinced by the Kremlin that the referendum was in doubt, did not forward Gunderson's reports as written.
What is not understood about Ukraine to this day is the strength of its civil society.
The strategic leadership of Rukh — Ivan Drach, Mykhailo Horyn, and Dmytro Pavlychko — as well as civic leaders such as Maria Drach and Mykola Horbal, parliamentarians such as Volodymyr Yavorivsky and Levko Lukyanenko, and student activists such as Oles Donii, deserve recognition as founders of Ukraine's modern civil society and of its independence.
Every significant development in Ukraine has been led by its people: Ukrainians and many other ethnic groups who call Ukraine home.
Civil society voted 92% in favor of independence and made up the Orange Revolution, the Revolution of Dignity, and the first responders to the full-scale Russian invasion and to Ukraine's ongoing defense.
Civil society's activism grew from Rukh's momentum, and it remains the heart and soul of Ukrainian democracy.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

title: Anti-drone net appears in central Berlin to mark Ukraine's Independence Day
description: At the center of Berlin's Pariser Platz, home to the Brandenburg Gate and meters away from the German Parliament, stands a large anti-drone net, there to highlight just how fragile Ukraine's air defenses can be.
content:
An anti-drone protective net was installed in the very heart of Berlin on Aug. 24 to raise awareness of the fragile protections Ukrainians live under, and to call for Germany and Europe to deliver more in terms of air defense capabilities.
The installation was installed by the Berlin -based Ukrainian civil society organization Vitsche and the German-Ukrainian defense industry consortium New Age Defense (NAD), as part of a program of events to mark the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's independence.
The aim of the event is to "raise awareness of the lived experience of Ukrainians during Russia's war and to make clear the link between protecting Ukrainian civilians to wider European security," Vitsche said in its statement .
At the center of Berlin's Pariser Platz, home to the Brandenburg Gate and meters away from the German Parliament, a large anti-drone net stands as a stark reminder of the fragility of Ukraine's air defenses .
Vitsche and NAD have issued a joint demand to "protect Ukraine's skies," with increased deliveries of interception technologies: both drones and missiles , to Ukraine.
"Every intercepted missile or drone means a life saved," said Kateryna Mykhalko, Managing Director of NAD.
She went on to explain that Ukraine's use of interception technology is leading to innovation taking place in the field.
"These experiences are invaluable for the security of the whole of Europe," Mykhalko said.
In addition to defense support, Vitsche and NAD are calling on Germany to establish more joint defense ventures as a means to ensuring long-term security, and for the EU and NATO to find a way to integrate Ukraine's real-world experiences in their respective security strategies.
They also note that Ukrainian membership of both is "essential for a secure European future."
Other demands include doing more to bring back Ukrainian children that have been abducted by Russia, the use of Russian frozen assets to support Ukraine's reconstruction, and the closure of Berlin's Russian House cultural center.
On the evening of Aug. 24 Vitsche will also lead a march through Berlin from Pariser Platz, to Potsdamer Platz, from 6:30 p.m. local time.

title: Russian drone strikes residential building in central Chernihiv, injuring at least 20, including 3 children, on Ukraine's Independence Day
description: "Cynical strike by Russian terrorists on a residential building in Chernihiv. Right in the middle of the day — on Independence Day," Chernihiv Oblast Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
content:
A Russian drone struck an apartment building in central Chernihiv on Aug. 24, injuring at least 20 people, including three children, and sparking a fire, local authorities said.
The Chernihiv City Council said Russian forces launched three waves of attacks on the city, with a drone striking a residential building during the final wave around noon local time.
Police bomb disposal officers said the attack may have involved a jet-powered Geran-5 drone, according to Chernihiv Oblast Governor Viacheslav Chaus .
"Cynical strike by Russian terrorists on a residential building in Chernihiv. Right in the middle of the day — on Independence Day," Chaus said .
A fire broke out on the ground floor of a nine-story residential building, Ukraine's Emergency Service said.
Rescuers were working to extinguish the fire at the site of the strike, while medical teams were providing assistance to the injured, according to Chaus.
Authorities said the drone hit the central part of the city, while the full extent of the damage is still being assessed.
The strike came as Ukraine marked the 35th anniversary of its independence on Aug. 24.
Russian attacks across Ukraine killed at least eight people and injured at least 43 over the previous day, according to local authorities, while Russia launched missiles and 143 drones overnight.
July of 2026 saw the most civilians killed or injured in Ukraine since March 2022, according to the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU).
At least 437 civilians in Ukraine were killed and 2,610 injured in July alone, the monitoring group said on Aug. 13. This represents a 30% increase from June, which previously held the record for the deadliest month since April 2022.
Ukrainian civilian casualties in July 2026 were 70% higher than July the previous year, while casualties among children also rose to their highest level since April 2022, with 17 children killed and 166 injured.

title: Zelensky says anti-corruption agencies have 'no questions' for him amid latest corruption scandal
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky said he has no further details, and the information that was made public was sufficient to dismiss Iryna Mudra as deputy head of the President’s Office.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky addressed the recent corruption scandal involving a top official in his administration, saying that anti-corruption agencies "have no questions" for him.
National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU) said on Aug. 19 published recordings allegedly implicating Iryna Mudra , then-deputy head of the President's Office, as well as other officials, in money laundering. Separate recordings allegedly link Mudra to a group involved in the illegal seizure of real estate.
The suspects are accused of laundering Hr 150 million ($3.4 million) and transferring the funds through Sense Bank to post bail for former Justice and Energy Minister Herman Halushchenko . Halushchenko has been charged with money laundering and organized crime in a separate case centered around state nuclear power monopoly Energoatom — the largest corruption investigation of Zelensky's tenure.
According to Zelensky, he has no further details, and the information that was made public was sufficient to dismiss Mudra.
"Let the law enforcement and anti-corruption systems do their work, and do it independently — what is there for me to comment on? We have to react," Zelensky told journalists on Aug. 22.
"I have no questions from the heads of the anti-corruption agencies. They understand perfectly well that I'm not involved in anything like that. And that is important to me."
A sitting president is immune from prosecution under Ukrainian law.
On the tapes, Mudra said that someone told her that "corruption shouldn't be fought — it should be controlled." The person's name is partially beeped out, but you can hear the first letter — B. This prompted speculation that Kyrylo Budanov , the head of the President's Office and Mudra's ex-boss, may have been involved.
Speaking about the charges against Mudra on Aug. 23, Budanov said that "it’s all up to the court."
Zelensky has faced a string of corruption scandals since the fall, with the President's Office typically remaining tight-lipped on the topic.
In May, ex-President Office Head Andriy Yermak was charged with money laundering tied to the construction of a luxury cottage complex — four expensive houses outside Kyiv, each roughly 1,000 square meters in size.
Investigators said three houses were being built for three of the president's allies — Yermak, businessman Timur Mindich, and former Deputy Prime Minister Oleksii Chernyshov. Leaked tapes published by journalists suggest a fourth house may have been intended for "Vova," a short form of Volodymyr.
The President's Office declined to comment on the investigation.

title: Russia reacts to UK sharing Storm Shadow blueprints with Ukraine
description: U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to formally announce the decision during his visit to Kyiv on Ukraine's Independence Day, his first overseas trip since taking office.
content:
The Kremlin condemned Britain's decision to share classified technical information on Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles with Ukraine, calling the move "fuel on the fire," Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Aug. 24.
London has agreed to let European defense company MBDA share classified technical information on British-made components in SCALP cruise missiles with Ukraine, a move that could help Kyiv expand domestic production of the weapons.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to formally announce the decision during his first visit to Kyiv since taking office.
Peskov said Moscow views the decision "extremely negatively," accusing London of doing everything possible "to prevent any progress in the peace process."
Peskov also claimed Russian forces were already gathering information on potential production sites for the missiles and other military equipment in order to target them.
The recent move builds on the U.K.'s 2023 decision to become the first country to provide Ukraine with long-range strike weapons for defensive purposes. It will pave the way for French-Ukrainian assembly of the missiles in Ukraine, while access to the blueprints could bring Kyiv and Paris closer to establishing local production lines, the U.K. government said on Aug. 24.
British Defense Minister Luke Pollard described the development as a transfer of military blueprints intended to help Ukraine strengthen its ability to defend itself.
Douglas Barrie, senior fellow for military aerospace at the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), told the Kyiv Independent that the decision has both symbolic and practical significance.
"One is kind of symbolic, showing continued French and British support for Ukraine. The second is practical," Barrie said, explaining that the release of previously classified missile technology could enable Ukraine to assemble the weapon domestically and, over time, build up a significant stockpile.
SCALP is the French version of the British Storm Shadow air-launched cruise missile. The weapon weighs around 1,300 kilograms, measures about 5.1 meters (16.7 feet) in length, and has a range of up to 250 kilometers (155 miles).
The missile is designed to strike pre-planned, stationary targets and can operate during the day or at night and in adverse weather conditions, according to manufacturer MBDA . It uses advanced navigation systems to carry out precision strikes.
Barrie cautioned that establishing production would not happen immediately. Under normal circumstances, such a process would be expected to take "a number of years rather than a number of months," he said, though Ukraine could move faster depending on how much preparatory work has already been completed and whether production initially consists mainly of assembly rather than full manufacturing.
Ukraine's defense industry has demonstrated an unusual ability to rapidly absorb and develop new technologies, Barrie added, meaning the process "might happen quicker than you would normally expect."
Potential bottlenecks include shortages of particular components and the challenge of quickly understanding and implementing supporting software technologies, according to Barrie.
The analyst also pointed to the possibility of deeper integration of SCALP with Ukraine's Mirage 2000-5 fighter jets. Ukraine's earlier integration of Storm Shadow with its Soviet-designed Su-24 aircraft was carried out rapidly and was relatively rudimentary, essentially allowing the aircraft to carry and launch the missile, Barrie said.
More sophisticated integration with the Mirage 2000-5 could allow Ukraine to exploit a wider range of the missile's capabilities, he added.
Ukraine has previously used French-provided SCALP and British Storm Shadow missiles against Russian military targets and facilities in occupied Ukrainian territories.
In May, the General Staff said Storm Shadow missiles destroyed an "important" Russian command-and-control and communications post in occupied Luhansk Oblast.
In March, Ukraine's Air Force used Storm Shadow missiles to strike the Kremniy El microelectronics plant in Bryansk, a major Russian defense-industry supplier producing components used in missile guidance systems.
Ukraine also used Storm Shadows in a large-scale strike on the Bryansk Chemical Plant in October 2025, a facility that produces gunpowder, explosives, and rocket-fuel components for Russian ammunition and missiles.
The transfer of technical information comes after months of negotiations between Kyiv and Paris over licenses that could allow Ukraine to manufacture SCALP missiles itself.
Then-Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said in June that Ukraine had made "progress" in discussions with France over SCALP production licenses following talks between President Volodymyr Zelensky and French President Emmanuel Macron.
Fedorov cautioned that the process remained complicated because of intellectual property rights and the bureaucracy involved in opening production, but said discussions over SCALP had advanced further than talks over some other Western weapons.
Zelensky has repeatedly pushed Ukraine's partners to provide licenses allowing Western weapons to be manufactured in Ukraine, including U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems.
Ukraine has not yet received permission to manufacture Patriot systems domestically, though Zelensky said in June that U.S. President Donald Trump's administration planned to raise the possibility of licensing production with American defense companies.
The issue has become more pressing as demand for air defense and long-range weapons has increased globally. Pollard said there remained "huge demand" for Patriot systems amid the conflict in the Middle East, adding that Britain was also supporting Ukraine with other air-defense and counter-drone capabilities.
G7 leaders also said earlier this year that they were prepared to consider extending military-production licenses to Ukraine.

title: Russian attacks kill 8, injure 43 over past day as Ukrainians celebrate Independence Day
description: Russia launched two Oniks anti-ship missiles, six Kh-31P and Kh-59 guided air-launched missiles, as well as 143 drones and other aerial targets overnight on Aug. 24, according to Ukraine's Air Force.
content:
Russian attacks killed at least eight people and injured at least 43 across Ukraine over the past day, as the country marked the 35th anniversary of its independence on Aug. 24, local authorities said.
Russia launched two Oniks anti-ship missiles, six Kh-31P and Kh-59 guided air-launched missiles, as well as 143 drones overnight on Aug. 24, according to Ukraine's Air Force . Around a third of the drones were jet-powered, the Air Force said.
Air defenses downed one Oniks missile, two Kh-31P and Kh-59 missiles, two Banderol munitions, and 109 drones. Strikes were recorded at 22 locations, while debris from intercepted drones and missiles fell at five locations.
In Kharkiv Oblast , Russian drones struck railway infrastructure in the Lozova community overnight, killing two women and injuring six other people, including an 11-year-old girl, local authorities said.
The girl, whose mother was among those killed, was in serious condition with burns, while five other people suffered blast injuries.
Russian attacks killed five people and injured 17 others, including two children, in Kharkiv and 16 other settlements across the oblast over the past day, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Donetsk Oblast , Russian attacks killed two people and injured one in Kramatorsk, while six others were wounded elsewhere in the region over the past day, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Sumy Oblast , one person was killed and 12 others injured in Russian attacks, according to local authorities . Russian forces carried out more than 50 attacks against 25 settlements in the region.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast , three people were injured in attacks on Zaporizhzhia and the surrounding district, Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out 518 strikes against 38 settlements across the oblast over the past day.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , three people were injured as Russian forces attacked three districts nearly 30 times using drones, artillery, and a guided aerial bomb, local authorities said.
In Chernihiv Oblast , a 59-year-old gas station employee was injured after a Russian Geran drone struck a facility in Korop, according to local Governor Vyacheslav Chaus .

title: EU greenlights $7 billion in defense loans on Ukraine Independence Day
description: "On Ukraine's Independence Day, Europe shows our support is unfaltering and concrete," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in the press release.
content:
BRUSSELS, Belgium — Ukraine will receive 6.1 billion euros ($7.1 billion) in defense loans to be spent on air defenses, missiles, ammunition, and radars, according to an Aug. 24 press release from the European Commission.
All the money being disbursed comes from the 90 billion euro ($105 billion) Ukraine Support Loan , which the bloc finalized in April to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's defense and budgetary needs until the end of 2027.
"On Ukraine's Independence Day, Europe shows our support is unfaltering and concrete," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said in the press release .
"As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine, and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it."
The European bloc has emerged as Kyiv's leading military supplier and partner as the Trump administration ended nearly all U.S. defense aid to the war-torn country.
Ukraine has named air defenses as the most acute need amid Russia's ongoing strikes against Ukrainian cities and dwindling supplies of Patriot interceptors.
In his final days in office , former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov submitted nine product schedules — proposed shopping lists of defense equipment — for the European Commission's sign-off.
Of the nine product schedules submitted by Fedorov, seven have been approved, a senior EU official told the Kyiv Independent, taking the total of approved product schedules to 11.
The two remaining lists submitted by Fedorov include a request to use EU funds to purchase U.S.-sourced Patriot missiles , which requires an exemption from EU member states.
Some 60 billion euros ($70 billion) of the Ukraine Support Loan is allocated to defense products, with 28.3 billion euros ($33 billion) of that sum ringfenced for 2026.
Products bought using that defense component generally must source 65% of their total component value from the EU, Ukraine, or Norway.
If products do not meet that threshold, an exemption must be requested. Ukraine already made one such request — which was approved — for Chinese-manufactured drone components in April.
There is no confirmed date for when Kyiv will get the green light to buy anti-ballistic missile interceptors from non-European companies, but it is expected in the coming weeks.
However, the senior EU official noted that the approved packages already include some European anti-ballistic capabilities, possibly including the Franco-Italian SAMP/T system , which was also among the items previously requested by Kyiv.
They also noted that Ukraine has submitted "several" more product schedules for approval since Yevhen Khmara stepped into the defense minister post in July.
With the 6.1 billion euros ($7.1 billion) approved on Aug. 24, Ukraine has been allocated around 22 billion euros ($26 billion) of the 28.3 billion ($33.1 billion) in defense spending it is due to receive in 2026.

title: UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham among leaders in Kyiv as Ukraine marks Independence Day
description: "For Ukraine, independence is not an abstract idea. We defended it against all odds. In times like these, nations learn how important it is to have allies by your side," Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
content:
Editor's note: This story is being updated.
Western leaders and officials arrived in Kyiv on Aug. 24 to mark Ukraine's Independence Day, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
"For Ukraine, independence is not an abstract idea. We defended it against all odds. In times like these, nations learn how important it is to have allies by your side," Sybiha said on social media.
"And today, we know for sure who our true friends are."
Among the visiting leaders is U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham , who is making his first trip to Kyiv since taking office. He is expected to chair the meeting of the Coalition of the Willing later in the day established by London and Paris under his predecessor Keir Starmer.
Burnham also said the U.K. had agreed to allow defense company MBDA to share classified information on British components for the long-range SCALP missile , paving the way for Ukraine to produce its own missiles.
European Council President Antonio Costa, Moldovan President Maia Sandu, Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Estonian President Alar Karis and other Nordic and Baltic leaders also arrived in the Ukrainian capital.
This year's holiday marks Ukraine's fifth Independence Day since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022.
In his address, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that Ukraine today is "not a victim, but a fighter," adding that Moscow shouldn't be allowed to seize the initiative and "deceive Europe and the world."
"You are not giving up our Donbas . You are not giving up Ukraine. You are the best defenders. You are the best army in Europe," Zelensky said, addressing Ukrainian soldiers.
"In all his plans for Ukraine, (Russian President Vladimir) Putin got the most important thing wrong. The enemy counted our resources, stockpiles and equipment, but failed to take into account the key factor: our people — the greatest achievement of Ukraine's independence."
Earlier, Sybiha said Ukraine's partners were expected to announce additional aid packages on Independence Day.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,478,070 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The figure includes 1,490 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,478,070 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 24.
The figure includes 1,490 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,293 tanks, 25,211 armored combat vehicles, 138,773 vehicles and fuel tanks, 48,519 artillery systems, 2,056 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,586 air defense systems, 440 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 478,327 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,368 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Ukraine hits Ozon logistics centers, rocket fuel plant, MiG-29 fighter jet in Russia, military says
description: Three Ozon warehouses were hit in Dagestan, Stavropol Krai and Adygea, Russian independent media outlet Astra reported. Ozon shares fell 12% following the Ukrainian strikes, according to the report.
content:
Ukraine launched a large-scale overnight attack on Russia on Aug. 24, striking Ozon logistics centers, the Kombinat Kamenskiy defense-industrial facility, and a MiG-29 fighter jet, among other targets, the Ukrainian military said.
Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, confirmed that the Ukrainian overnight attack hit Ozon facilities, but did not specify their location or how many were struck.
Three Ozon warehouses were hit in Dagestan, Stavropol Krai and Adygea, Russian independent media outlet Astra reported. Ozon shares fell 12% following the Ukrainian strikes, according to the report.
Murat Kumpilov, head of Russia's Adygea republic, confirmed that the Ozon warehouse caught fire following the attack and that its employees were evacuated. No one was injured, Kumpilov said.
Acting head of Dagestan Fyodor Shchukin said debris from downed drones sparked a fire at a warehouse. He did not specify which company operates the facility. Two warehouse employees were injured in the attack, Shchukin added.
Stavropol Krai Governor Vladimir Vladimirov also confirmed that Ukrainian drones attacked the city of Nevinnomyssk's industrial area, without saying what sites were targeted.
"Our air defense forces are repelling an attack by enemy drones targeting the industrial zone of Nevinnomyssk. Some drones have been shot down," he said.
Ukraine's General Staff separately confirmed that Ukrainian forces struck the Kombinat Kamenskiy, a Russian defense-industrial facility in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov Oblast, overnight on Aug. 24.
A fire was recorded at the facility following the strike, while the extent of the damage is still being assessed, the General Staff said.
The Kombinat Kamenskiy is part of Russia’s military-industrial complex and produces solid rocket fuel for Uragan, Smerch and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as various missile systems and air-launched weapons, according to the General Staff.
Brovdi, commander of Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces, also said Ukrainian drones successfully struck 66 Russian targets overnight on Aug. 24
Brovdi said the targets included a MiG-29 fighter jet near Dolotinka in Russia’s Rostov Oblast and four radar systems: two Kasta-2E2s and a Nebo-SV in Rostov Oblast, and an ST-68 near Rozdolne in occupied Crimea .
Brovdi also claimed Ukrainian forces destroyed a base used by Russia's SOBR special police unit in occupied Strilkove, Kherson Oblast, struck energy facilities in occupied Ukrainian territories, and targeted two Russian "shadow fleet" vessels in the Black Sea , identified as a tanker and a bulk carrier.
The overnight strikes also caused a fire at a facility belonging to Russian home goods retailer Kuchenland in the southern city of Krasnodar, Astra reported.
Two children were killed, with seven other children and another two adults injured in a childcare center as a result of fallen drone debris, Krasnodar Krai Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said.
"Debris from drones fell on residential buildings and apartment buildings under construction. The impact of the drones caused a fire in warehouse facilities," he added.
Krasnodar, located near Russia's Black Sea coast, is situated about 250 kilometers (155 miles) from southeastern Ukraine near occupied Berdiansk and 365 kilometers (225 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory near Orikhiv.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.
The attacks come as Ukraine celebrates its Independence Day on Aug. 24, marking 35 years since Ukraine declared independence from the Soviet Union.
Strikes on Ozon logistics hubs in recent days follow a weeks-long campaign of attacks on Russia's largest online retailer, Wildberries.
Ozon logistics centers were struck in Russia's Samara Oblast on Aug. 22 , and in the city of Orenburg overnight on Aug. 23.
On Aug. 16, Ukrainian forces struck cities across Russia's Moscow Oblast in a major overnight drone attack on Aug. 16, damaging a warehouse belonging to major Russian online retailer Wildberries , Moscow Oblast Governor Andrey Vorobyov claimed.
Ukraine's Defense Ministry confirmed the attack on the Wildberries warehouse, noting that it is the company's largest such facility, at 250,000 square meters.

title: Russian strike damages US-owned Mondelez facility in Sumy Oblast
description: Russia struck a factory belonging to U.S. multinational food company Mondelez International in Sumy Oblast on Aug. 23, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
content:
Russia struck a factory belonging to U.S. multinational food company Mondelez International in Sumy Oblast on Aug. 23, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
Two Russian drones hit the facility located in the city Trostianets, damaging the premises and injuring several employees, according to Sybiha. No fatalities were reported.
"Today, Russia once again struck a civilian facility in the Sumy region belonging to Mondelez International, a world-renowned American multinational corporation," Sybiha wrote on X.
Mondelez International is a large food and snack company whose brands include Oreo, Cadbury, Ritz, and Toblerone.
The foreign minister described the attack as part of a pattern of Russian strikes against business endeavors in Ukraine, calling them a "direct blow to American economic interests in Europe."
Sybiha called for increased military support for Ukraine, particularly additional air defense capabilities. He also urged the passage of the Sanctioning Russia Act, as part of efforts to increase economic pressure on Russia to end the war.
The city of Sumy is located around 30 kilometers (18 miles) from the Russian border. The region faces daily assaults from nearby Russian forces, including artillery, drone, and guided bomb strikes.

title: Ukraine war latest: 'Hunting their launch sites' — Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
description:
Key developments on Aug. 22-23:

 * 'Hunting their launch sites' — Zelensky reveals new details about Ukraine's ballistic missile defense
 * Ukraine weighing 'radical' mobilization changes amid recruitment challenges, official says
 * Ukrainian drones reportedly strike Wildberries rival, Ozon, in Russia's Orenburg
 * Russia planning 'peripheral' mobilization of 300,000 men after elections, Zelensky says
 * Ukraine strikes 2 Russian fighters, air defense assets in Krasnodar Krai, drone commander
content:
Ukraine has launched a new operation targeting Russian ballistic missile launchers near its borders, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 22, as Kyiv faces a shortage of missiles capable of intercepting ballistic weapons.
Zelensky said that Ukrainian military struck an Iskander ballistic missile launcher near Ukraine's borders on Aug. 22, without providing further details.
The strike was part of a separate operation to hunt down Russian missile systems positioned near Ukraine, which Zelensky described as an alternative tactic amid the dire lack of of anti-ballistic missile interceptors.
The Iskander is Russia's main surface to surface tactical ballistic missile system , with a stated range of around 500 kilometers.
Complemented with North Korean KN-23 ballistic missiles and advanced Zircon cruise missiles, the Iskander has been the workhorse of combined mass attacks again Ukrainian targets in recent months.
When attacking Kyiv and other targets inside Ukraine, Iskanders are launched from mobile erector-launcher systems inside Russian territory, usually in border regions like Bryansk or Kursk oblasts.
With Ukraine's stocks of Patriot ballistic missile interceptor at or near empty, strikes against Iskander launchers have long been proposed as an alternative method of fighting the Iskander threat, but Ukraine has lacked options for quickly detecting and hitting launch sites.
"At one point (the Russians) were planning to launch an attack, but didn’t go through with it. This is no coincidence," Zelensky told journalists.
"In other words, we're working to prevent them from carrying out large-scale missile attacks. These are individual, complex operations, and we're now starting to see the first results."
Zelensky said Russia could potentially produce up to 1,300 ballistic missiles annually and currently has around 600–630 in stock. Moscow could eventually aim to produce around 100 ballistic missiles per month, he said, although it has not yet reached that rate.
Ukraine is also seeking more Patriot interceptors ahead of winter, Zelensky said, revealing that Ukraine had only received 264 missiles for the advanced surface-to-air system this year so far.
The Air Force has requested 360 missiles, up from an initial target of 300. According to the president, Kyiv hopes to secure 5–10% of U.S. stocks, with Ukraine prepared to pay for the missiles.
Zelensky also said Germany had agreed to provide 600 PAC-2 missiles for Patriot systems in 2027–2028, while negotiations with Washington over additional supplies continue.
Longer-term alternatives to the Patriot are also moving ahead, the president said, referring specifically to the Freyja project, a joint effort by European and Ukrainian defense companies to produce a new anti-ballistic missile system.
The project has moved from political discussions to the technical stage, with companies now beginning practical work, Zelensky said.
Ukraine is preparing changes to its mobilization system, including potential revisions to the country's draft age, secretary of the parliamentary defense committee Roman Kostenko said on Aug. 22.
Kostenko said that financial incentives offered to encourage Ukrainians to sign military contracts have failed to significantly increase recruitment, prompting officials to consider other measures.
"There are already talks and, as far as I know, some things are changing in the draft age," Kostenko said , adding that the Defense Ministry or General Staff would provide further details. He declined to say whether the draft age could be lowered or raised.
The lawmaker noted that Ukraine does not plan to move away from compulsory mobilization in favor of an exclusively voluntary system.
Kostenko also denied reports that authorities are considering eliminating mobilization exemptions for parents with three or more children, saying there are no such legislative initiatives currently under consideration.
No changes are planned regarding the mobilization of women, Kostenko said, adding that military service for women will remain voluntary.
As the fifth year of Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine goes on, mobilization has become among the most contentious domestic issues in the country.
Ukraine's military faces a growing need to replenish fighting units, build reserves, and allow existing soldiers to rotate off the front line. As Ukraine steps up its mobilization efforts , draft offices are often accused of forced conscription without compliance with fundamental civil rights and ill-treatment of conscripts.
Under martial law, Ukrainian men aged 25 to 60 are currently subject to conscription and are forbidden from leaving the country except under a certain number of specific circumstances.
Meanwhile, Russia reportedly plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, but will do so without touching the country's major cities in an effort to minimize backlash from society, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists on Aug. 23.
Ukraine's military reportedly launched a drone attack on the Russian city of Orenburg overnight on Aug. 23, striking an Ozon logistics center, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Photos and videos posted to social media purport to show smoke rising from the warehouse following a reported strike. Air raid alerts were active in the region ahead of the reported strike.
The attack on Ozon, Russia's second-largest online marketplace and main competitor to Wildberries, marked the second reported strike on the company's facilities. The first direct attack on the company's logistics centers occurred just one night earlier on Aug. 22 in a Ukrainian attack on Samara Oblast.
The Kyiv Independent cannot immediately verify the reports. Ukraine's military has not yet commented on the reported attack.
The full extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
After months of strikes on Wildberries facilities, Ukraine’s military appears to have shifted its focus to Ozon sites across Russia, with Ukrainian officials justifying the attacks on the grounds that the company sells goods to the Russian military.
"Systematic strikes on storage centers for dual-use goods are making it more difficult for the enemy to operate and are negatively impacting the overall economy of Russia," the Defense Ministry said after the Aug. 22 attack.
Orenburg is located in southwestern Russia near the border to Kazakhstan, approximately 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from the Russia-Ukraine border.
Elsewhere in Russia, a massive blaze erupted at a warehouse in St. Petersburg overnight on Aug. 22, officials reported.
Russia's Emergency Situations Ministry said the first spread to engulf an area of at least 82,000 square metres (approximately 882,000 square feet) in the Kolpino district, southeast of central St. Petersburg.
The fire, located in an industrial part of the city, reportedly burned adjacent to an Ozon logistics center, owned by Russia's second-largest online marketplace and the main competitor to Wildberries.
The cause of the blaze was not immediately clear. Air raid alerts had not been declared in the Leningrad Oblast, nor were explosions heard in the area.
Russia plans to mobilize around 300,000 people after State Duma elections in September, but will do so without touching the country's major cities in an effort to minimize backlash from society, Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists.
Russia's voluntary recruitment system has increasingly struggled to make up for losses on the battlefield, while diminishing returns in Russian offensives on the front line have fuelled talk of a new wave of mobilization in the country.
Although baring no resemblence to a real democratic process, the Duma Elections are nonetheless seen as a litmus test for support for president Vladimir Putin's regime, and the Kremlin will wait until after to announce a new draft, Zelensky said.
According to Zelensky , the 300,000 mobilized troops will complement existing inflows of recruits into the Russian army, and will either be used to boost Moscow's main offensive effort on the "fortress belt" cities of Donetsk Oblast , or to create new threats in other areas, including Ukraine's northern border.
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Moscow has only once turned to forced mobilization to fill the ranks of its military: in autumn 2022, when successive Ukrainian counteroffensive successes threatened a broader collapse of Russia's defense lines.
The move triggered an exodus of hundreds of thousands of Russians from the country, with long lines at border crossing points, particularly at the state border with Georgia.
Since then, Putin has famously gone to great lengths to avoid more large-scale forced mobilization, seeing it as a threat to his image as provider of strength and stability to ordinary Russians apathetic to questions of politics and war.
Instead, Moscow has relied on lucrative bonuses offered to those who sign a contract, with responsibility resting largely on regional authorities to meet tough recruitment quotas.
According to Zelensky, Putin plans to minimize perceived political consequences by focusing mobilization efforts away from the large population centers, especially Moscow and St Petersburg.
"They are planning for a kind of 'peripheral mobilization,'" the president said.
"As we understand, it won't happen in the central cities. But I don't think they will succeed in hiding it."
Ukrainian drones have struck two Russian fighter jets, a large missile-carrying drone, high-value radars, and other air defense assets, Unmanned Systems Forces commander Robert "Magyar" Brovdi said on Aug. 23.
The two jets, a Su-33 and a Mig-29, as well as a large Orion strike drone, were hit at the Vityazevo airfield in Russia's southern region of Krasnodar Krai, Brovdi said.
The Orion is a large Russian unmanned aerial vehicle developed by Russia before the full-scale invasion and similar in class to the Turkish-made Bayraktar TB-2 operated by Ukraine.
On a battlefield dense with enemy air defense assets and interceptor drones on both sides, drones the Orion and TB-2 have been largely rendered useless.
Over 2026, Russia adapted the Orion for a new role: launching the cheap Banderol cruise missile , now regularly used against Ukraine's Black Sea port infrastructure.
All three strikes, videos of which were shared on Brovdi's Telegram channel, were carried out by the 1st Center of the Unmanned Systems Forces, which specializes in long-range strikes.
Other targets included S-400, Pantsir, and Tor air defense systems, as well as eight high-value radars in Krasnodar Krai, Rostov Oblast, and Russian-occupied Crimea.
