content:
A tanker passes a border security vessel and the detained Smyrtos shadow fleet tanker outside the harbour in Portland, UK on June 15, 2026. (Finnbarr Webster / Getty Images)
Europe's campaign to choke off Russia's ability to finance its war in Ukraine through oil revenues began with sanctions, legislation, and price caps. But as hundreds of ships helped Moscow evade those restrictions, Western governments increasingly backed those measures with aggressive maritime enforcement — deploying naval power and pirate-like tactics to disrupt the shadow fleet.
As of May 2026, a Ukrainian government register has identified 1,404 vessels belonging to Russia's so-called shadow fleet . Those ships are almost always dangerously old, uninsured, and registered in third countries where there are fewer laws to follow, so-called flags of convenience.
Moscow coordinates them to carry mostly oil , but also other sanctioned products like grain illegally taken from occupied territory in southern Ukraine, in a way that allows Russia to evade sanctions .
After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the EU banned Russian ships from accessing the bloc's ports as early as April and introduced its first price cap on Russian oil in December 2022.
Those two moves together led Moscow to seek alternative means to keep selling oil and keep the money flowing into state coffers.
However, it was only in June 2024 that the EU first issued sanctions directly against the shadow fleet: 27 tankers, "part of Putin's dark fleet," read an EU press release at the time.
Since then, the EU has added new ship listings in every subsequent sanctions package and quickly shifted its language from "dark fleet" to "shadow fleet," the more commonly used term for ships that aim to deceive and disregard the law.
By the time the EU adopted its 21st sanctions package in July 2026, 692 ships were on the EU's list, along with a range of individuals and companies involved in servicing shadow fleet ships and enabling the deception.
Those listings have been complemented by separate lists of sanctioned ships drawn up elsewhere.
The U.K.'s latest sanctions package against the shadow fleet on Aug. 6 brought the total number of ships listed to 659. The U.S has sanctioned 453 vessels, while Canada and Australia have sanctioned 731 and 262, respectively.
"The community is more confident in their legal position when they act."
And there are moves to increase cross-border coordination in adding ships to sanctions lists.
For example, a draft Shadow Fleet Sanctions Act has been introduced in the U.S. Senate that includes a chapter intended to align U.S. listings with those of the EU and the U.K. at least twice per year.
But listings alone do not stop Russia's shadow fleet from sailing. Countries need to enforce those sanctions.
"Coordination among European countries that border the Baltic and North Seas has been intense on shadow fleet monitoring over the past two years," said Tom Keatinge, director of the Center for Finance and Security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank.
Several multilateral organizations, including the G7 , the Nordic-Baltic Eight, and the Joint Expeditionary Force, discussed the issue more often, but also shifted "from understanding the problem to action," Keatinge said.
"The result is that the community is more confident in their legal position when they act," he added.
Days before an October 2025 summit of European leaders in Denmark , Copenhagen was threatened with Russian drone incursions, suspected to have been launched from a shadow fleet vessel.
European countries dispatched naval and air support to Denmark, French President Emmanuel Macron called for the Coalition of the Willing to double down on restrictions against the shadow fleet, and Paris boarded the ship suspected of being used to dispatch drones into Danish airspace.
But it was only in 2026 that boarding suspect ships became a more regular occurrence.
In March, Sweden began intercepting Russian shadow fleet vessels, and had already intervened against five ships by the beginning of May.
The first ship to be seized, the Caffa , was carrying grain taken illegally from Russian-occupied territory in southern Ukraine.
Courts in Stockholm have since agreed that the vessel and its cargo should be given to Kyiv .
"Since March 1 2026, the Swedish Coast Guard has, through several different legislative amendments, been given increased opportunities to conduct effective intelligence work, which makes it easier to make decisions to intervene against vessels on Swedish territory," a coast guard spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent.
"If Swedish law is violated and the conditions for intervention in accordance with international regulations are met, we will intervene," they added.
Also in March, then-U.K. Prime Minister Keir Starmer gave the green light for the British military to board shadow fleet vessels entering the country's waters.
London intercepted its first shadow fleet vessel, the Smyrtos, in June.
France also stopped a shadow fleet boat in the Mediterranean in June.
And Belgian Defense Minister Theo Francken announced on March 1 that his country had seized a ship belonging to the Russian shadow fleet for the first time.
In addition to greater coordination among European countries, Keatinge highlights that the respective postures of Moscow and Washington have also facilitated the newly assertive approach.
The U.S seized a Russian-flagged oil tanker in the Atlantic Ocean on Jan. 7 for the first time in recent history, even after Moscow had reportedly dispatched a submarine to protect it.
"There is no doubt that this (the U.S. posture) has also encouraged European countries to act as they can anticipate non-objection from the U.S," Keatinge said.
Likewise, Keatinge noted that "Russia is not retaliating in any sort of meaningful way," leaving Europeans confident they can "take action without repercussions."
Russia threatened Europe in February, saying it would deploy its navy if Europe seized shadow fleet vessels, but that threat did not materialize.
Ukraine has also stepped up its campaign against the shadow fleet, announcing on July 1 that it would be treated as military targets , before carrying out attacks on at least seven different nights that month, striking no fewer than 78 ships in the Black Sea.
That same month, the EU agreed its Atalanta naval operation in the Indian Ocean could start intercepting ships suspected of belonging to Russia's shadow fleet. On Aug. 2, its operation IRINI boarded a sanctioned tanker in the Mediterranean.
On July 24, the bloc also agreed on its 21st sanctions package , which introduced a provision allowing member states to confiscate the assets of any shadow fleet vessels that they board.
"It sends a clear and unmistakable signal: the European Union is serious about countering the shadow fleet and closing every loophole Russia seeks to exploit to finance its war of aggression against Ukraine," a European Commission spokesperson told the Kyiv Independent.
"Shadow fleet vessels are a threat to the environment and neglect safety rules. We are showing now that such tactics will not go unanswered," they added.
But whether Europe's more assertive stance is having any effect on Russia remains to be seen.
Keatinge said the impact is "difficult to measure, particularly in an environment where the oil markets are highly volatile due to the U.S. war in the Middle East."
Instead, he pointed to the impact of Ukraine's attacks on Russia's energy production capacity, which have already led to sales restrictions and export curbs .
Chris Powers is the Brussels Correspondent with the Kyiv Independent. He reports on EU news and policy developments relevant to Ukraine, bridging the gap between Brussels and Kyiv. He was formerly the Defense and Tech Editor at the EU media outlet Euractiv. Chris holds a BA in History from the University of Cambridge and an MA in European Studies from the College of Europe.

title: Russia's Supreme Court bars only 'pro-peace' party from parliamentary elections
description: The case was brought by the nationalist, pro-Kremlin Rodina party, which is also running in the election.
content:
Russia's Supreme Court barred the Yabloko party from participating in September's parliamentary elections, citing alleged violations of election campaigning rules, according to a ruling published Aug. 10.
The decision comes just weeks after Russia's Central Election Commission registered Yabloko's candidate list, allowing the party to participate in the election . The case was brought by the nationalist, pro-Kremlin Rodina party, which is also running in the election.
Rodina leader Alexei Zhuravlev told state-owned media outlet TASS that his party had identified numerous violations, particularly those involving campaign financing.
Zhuravlev also told the pro-state outlet Kommersant that Yabloko had placed advertisements on social media platforms banned in Russia and violated copyright rules by using Soviet songs.
The decision removes Russia's only remaining liberal political group from an election in which Yabloko had campaigned on a platform calling for an end to the war against Ukraine .
"Excluding Yabloko from the election means refusing to engage in dialogue with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for those in power," Grigory Yavlinsky, the party's founder and head of its political council, said.
"We disagree with the decision and will appeal it."
After its registration, Yabloko published what it described as "the shortest in the party's history" campaign platform.
"For peace and freedom! For a life without fear! For a ceasefire agreement, diplomacy, and the achievement of peace!" the platform says.
Yabloko's registration had already prompted attacks from lawmakers, who accused the party of "betraying the motherland" and failing to support Russian troops fighting in Ukraine.
On Aug. 6, allies of late Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, including his widow, Yulia Navalnaya, and other opposition figures in exile, urged voters to support Yabloko.
"We must view the upcoming elections — no matter how unfair they may be — as the only legitimate and safe opportunity to express our disagreement with the government," Navalnaya said .
Yabloko members across Russia have also faced pressure that has prevented some candidates from participating in elections.
Regional party members have been fined under legislation targeting extremist symbols, with some cases triggered by photographs of Navalny posted on social media, whose organizations have been designated as "extremist" and "terrorist" by Russian authorities.
Yabloko is not a totally Kremlin-controlled party, but its ability to operate has been sharply constrained under Russian President Vladimir Putin's political system.
The party entered the State Duma in 1993, 1995, and 1999 but has failed to clear the 5% electoral threshold in federal elections since 2003.
Some independent pollsters had assessed that Yabloko had a small chance of crossing the threshold in September. The state-run Russian Public Opinion Research Center, known as VTsIOM, previously put the party's support at around 3%.

title: Ukraine strikes Russian petrochemical plant more than 2,000 kilometers from border, General Staff says
description: The depth of the strike marks "a very significant achievement" for Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in his evening address on Aug. 10.
content:
Ukrainian forces struck the Tobolskneftekhim petrochemical plant in Russia's Tyumen Oblast on Aug. 10, the General Staff said.
An air raid alert was issued in Tyumen Oblast at around 1 p.m. local time amid a drone attack. Regional Governor Alexander Moor said around 4:40 p.m. that falling drones caused a fire at an industrial facility, but did not specify where the incident occurred.
The damaged facility is located in the city of Tobolsk, about 2,200 kilometers (1,370 miles) from the Ukrainian-Russian border . The attack struck the plant's central gas fractionation unit, according to the General Staff .
The unit processes 6.6 million tons of feedstock annually and produces materials considered critical to Russia's military-industrial complex, including butadiene, isobutylene, maleic anhydride, and MTBE, a high-octane oxygenate additive.
These products are used to manufacture rocket fuel components, aviation fuel, composite materials for drones, and high-octane gasoline, the report read.
The extent of the damage caused by the attack is still being assessed, the General Staff added.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the depth of the strike represented "a very significant achievement" for Ukrainian forces.
"This region is now within range of our precision strikes. ... I thank everyone for their accuracy," he said in his evening address on Aug. 10.
"There will be more Ukrainian precision strikes to demonstrate to Russia and the Russian people that peace is necessary."
Earlier on Aug. 10, Ukrainian forces also struck another facility in Russia's oil industry, an oil refinery in Tatarstan, as Russian air defenses reportedly intercepted 456 drones overnight.
The Ukrainian General Staff later confirmed the strike on the Taneco refinery, saying a fire was reported at the facility in Nizhnekamsk. The extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
Ukraine regularly strikes military infrastructure deep inside Russia and in occupied territories as part of efforts to weaken Moscow's ability to continue waging its war .

title: 'Serious violation' — Moldova recalls ambassador from Moscow following drone crash
description: "This is a direct consequence of Russia's war, and it endangers us all," Moldovan President Maia Sandu said.
content:
Moldova recalled its ambassador to Russia, Lilian Darii, for "consultations" after a drone crashed and exploded on Moldovan territory, the country's Foreign Ministry said on Aug. 10.
The drone crashed on Aug. 9 in the border village of Crocmaz, roughly 70 kilometers (40 miles) from the Ukrainian port city of Odesa , which Russia targeted in a large-scale attack that day.
Moldovan media outlet NewsMaker reported that police found debris of the "missile-type drone" that caused a fire and damaged buildings in the Stefan Voda district.
"This accident represents a serious violation of the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Republic of Moldova and has endangered the safety of our citizens," the Foreign Ministry said.
Although Russian drones have previously violated Moldova's airspace since the beginning of the full-scale war, this marks the first time such aircraft have been identified on its territory.
"This is a direct consequence of Russia's war, and it endangers us all," Moldovan President Maia Sandu wrote on X. "The risk to human life in our region is real and growing. It must stop."
Similar instances have occurred in Ukraine's neighboring countries, Romania and Poland, where fragments of Shahed-type drones have been found.

title: Russia's version of Starlink deploying quicker than planned, Ukraine's military intelligence says
description: "Moscow is implementing Rassvet, effectively a Russian analogue of the Starlink system. And they have begun launching it significantly faster than was envisaged in their plans," Skibitskyi said in an interview with RBC-Ukraine.
content:
Russia is accelerating the deployment of its Rassvet satellite communications system, a domestic equivalent of Starlink, faster than previously planned, Ukraine's military intelligence deputy chief, Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, said on Aug. 10.
" Moscow is implementing Rassvet, effectively a Russian analogue of the Starlink system. And they have begun launching it significantly faster than was envisaged in their plans," Skibitskyi said in an interview with RBC-Ukraine.
Russia launched its first 16 Rassvet satellites into low Earth orbit in March 2026 and is continuing to expand the constellation, according to Skibitskyi. Earlier reports said a second batch of satellites was launched in July.
Skibitskyi added that Russia plans to build a constellation of 292 satellites by 2027 and expand it to 924 satellites by 2035.
"At the moment, they can operate only intermittently, when a satellite passes over our territory. When the Russians deploy a full constellation of satellites, this system will work like Starlink," Skibitskyi said.
Skibitskyi also said Ukrainian officials are already discussing how to counter the system, without providing details.
In an interview with AP published Aug. 10, Commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces Robert "Madyar" Brovdi described the development as a "risk for the entire planet."
"Because a dictatorship will gain access to information across the whole globe," he added.
Russia continues developing alternatives to Starlink , which has played a key role in Ukraine's military communications since the beginning of the full-scale war. In February, Ukraine said unauthorized Starlink terminals used by Russian forces had been deactivated following coordination between the Defense Ministry and SpaceX, an effort in which former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov played a key role.
The network has already suffered a setback — one of the 16 operational satellites launched in March was lost , leaving 15 in orbit, Russian state-controlled newspaper Kommersant reported in June.
Rassvet is being developed by Russia's Bureau 1440 as a low-Earth-orbit broadband satellite network intended to provide high-speed internet connectivity. Russia has said the system is intended to begin commercial operations in 2027, while Ukrainian officials have warned it could eventually have military applications, including communications and drone control.

title: Russia rules out freezing war in Ukraine ahead of US envoy visits to Kyiv, Moscow
description: "No 'freeze' is possible without addressing the root causes of this crisis," Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said.
content:
Russia will not agree to "freeze" its war against Ukraine without addressing what Moscow calls the "root causes," Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told state-owned TASS on Aug. 10.
The comments come as the United States considers reviving stalled peace efforts, including a possible agreement to halt air attacks between Russia and Ukraine.
"As Russian President Vladimir Putin has said on numerous occasions, no 'freeze' is possible without addressing the root causes of this crisis," Galuzin said. "It is clear that (President Volodymyr) Zelensky has lost all touch with reality and is trying to escalate the conflict."
Galuzin also criticized Washington's approach to the war, calling U.S. policy contradictory.
"The ongoing deliveries of U.S. weapons, the provision of intelligence , and other forms of assistance speak for themselves — they are incompatible with a commitment to peace," he said.
U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner are expected to travel to Kyiv and Moscow as Washington seeks to restart negotiations, people familiar with the plans previously told the Kyiv Independent. The U.S. side has developed new proposals that it is expected to present during the visits.
Kyiv has argued that freezing the current front line would provide the most realistic basis for a ceasefire. Russia , however, continues to demand that Ukrainian forces withdraw from parts of Donbas as a condition for an agreement, a proposal Ukraine has rejected.
Ukraine has intensified attacks on Russian military infrastructure, logistics hubs, and strategic targets deep inside Russia. Russia, meanwhile, has stepped up missile and drone attacks against Ukrainian cities, repeatedly striking Kyiv and other civilian population centers.
One U.S. official told the Kyiv Independent that the White House increasingly believes both Moscow and Kyiv may have reasons to consider an air ceasefire.
Russia has previously signaled that it sees battlefield developments as more important than negotiations. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said in June that the course of the war would depend on developments at the front.
"Everything depends not on talks, but on the actions of our heroes on the front lines," he said.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 4, injure 50 across Ukraine over past day as KAB strikes hit Sumy
description: Russia launched 126 Shahed-type and other attack drones, as well as one Kh-59/69 guided aerial missile and three Banderol loitering munitions, the Air Force said.
content:
Russian attacks killed at least four people and injured 50 others across Ukraine over the past day, as Sumy Oblast came under heavy strikes, including overnight guided aerial bomb attacks on the city of Sumy that injured 13 people, local authorities said on Aug. 10.
In Sumy Oblast , Russian attacks killed two people and injured 28 others over the past day, according to the local military administration . Thirteen people were injured in overnight guided aerial bomb strikes on the city of Sumy, while Russian attacks also damaged homes, non-residential buildings, and civilian infrastructure.
The overnight attack was part of a wider Russian strike on Ukraine, with Russia launching 126 Shahed-type and other attack drones, as well as one Kh-59/69 guided aerial missile and three Banderol loitering munitions, the Air Force said. Ukrainian air defenses shot down 92 drones and three Banderol munitions, while 31 attack drones hit 22 locations and debris from downed drones fell at two others.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast , one person was killed and four others were injured in attacks on the Zaporizhzhia and Polohy districts, Governor Ivan Fedorov said. Russian forces carried out 867 strikes against 47 settlements in the region over the past day.
In Dnipropetrovsk Oblast , one person was killed and five others were injured as Russian forces attacked four districts nearly 60 times with drones, artillery and guided aerial bombs, Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said.
In Kherson Oblast , two people were injured, as Russian forces struck residential areas and critical and social infrastructure, damaging eight apartment buildings, private vehicles, the local military administration said.
In Kharkiv Oblast , Russian attacks hit 24 settlements and injured seven people, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Donetsk Oblast , Russian attacks injured four residents, in the Dobropillia, Sloviansk and Kramatorsk areas, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,457,740 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The figure includes 1,470 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day, according to the General Staff.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,459,210 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces reported on Aug. 10.
The figure includes 1,470 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day, according to the General Staff.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,255 tanks, 25,116 armored combat vehicles, 132,236 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,669 artillery systems, 2,019 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,558 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 452,994 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,181 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Tatarstan oil refinery targeted as Russia claims 456 Ukrainian drones intercepted overnight
description: Ukrainian forces targeted a Russian oil refinery in Tatarstan as a blackout took place in occupied Simferopol and fires broke out in Donetsk Oblast amid overnight attacks on Aug. 10, monitoring channels reported.
content:
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian oil refinery in Tatarstan and hit military targets in occupied Ukrainian territories overnight on Aug. 10, while Russia claimed its air defenses intercepted 456 Ukrainian drones across the country.
Russia's Defense Ministry claimed that its air defenses intercepted 456 Ukrainian drones overnight across 16 Russian regions, Moscow , the occupied Crimean Peninsula, and the Krasnodar Krai, according to their statement.
Eyewitnesses posted footage of drones flying over the Russian city of Nizhnekamsk in the Republic of Tatarstan as an oil refinery was targeted by Ukrainian forces, according to Telegram channel Supernova Plus.
The drone attack on Nizhnekamsk reportedly killed 12 people and injured 39, according to the press service of Tatarstan's head Rustam Minnikhanov.
The Ukrainian General Staff later confirmed the strike on Taneco, saying a fire was recorded at the refinery in Nizhnekamsk. The extent of the damage was not immediately clear.
In Russia's Belgorod Oblast, a woman was reportedly killed in the village of Novaya Tavolzhanka in the Shebekino district after a drone struck the grounds of a private home, according to the regional operational headquarters.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the reported casualty figures.
In Crimea's Simferopol, parts of the city were temporarily left without power after explosions and gunfire were heard amid a drone attack, pro-Ukrainian Telegram channel Crimean Wind reported , citing local residents.
The Ukrainian General Staff also said Ukrainian forces struck a repair unit in the occupied city of Khrustalnyi in Luhansk Oblast, a Russian military logistics depot in Novoselidivka in Donetsk Oblast, and a field artillery depot in Boikove, also in Donetsk Oblast.
The extent of the damage is being assessed.
Ukraine regularly strikes military infrastructure deep within Russia and the occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
On the night of Aug. 8, Ukrainian forces struck an S-400 "Triumph" anti-aircraft missile launch pad in Russia's Krasnodar Krai, hours after it was used to fire missiles at Ukraine, Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert Brovdi "Madyar" announced.
Early on Aug. 8, Ukraine struck an oil refinery in Samara Oblast and another in southern Russia's Krasnodar Krai, monitoring channels reported.
A fire broke out at an oil refinery in Syzran in Russia's Samara Oblast after being struck by Ukrainian forces, according to Telegram channel Exilenova Plus.
Another oil refinery in the town of Ilsky, Krasnodar Krai , was struck and set ablaze amid a Ukrainian attack, Supernova Plus reported .
Ukraine's General Staff later confirmed that long-range Ukrainian drones hit two oil refineries in Russia's Krasnodar Krai and Samara Oblast.

title: Foreign Minister Sybiha condemns UNICEF after agency fails to hold Russia accountable for Ukrainian civilian deaths
description: Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Aug. 9 condemned the U.N. Humanitarian Aid Organization for Children (UNICEF) for failing to recognize Russia's responsibility for Ukrainian civilian casualties in a recent statement.
content:
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha on Aug. 9 condemned the U.N. Humanitarian Aid Organization for Children (UNICEF) for failing to recognize Russia's responsibility for Ukrainian civilian casualties in a recent statement.
"It is deeply deplorable that UNICEF missed the essential point in its (Aug. 4) statement: All these children's deaths are a direct result of Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine. By presenting these casualties without this essential context, UNICEF creates a false equivalence between the aggressor and the victim," Sybiha said in a post to X.
The UNICEF statement called for both parties to follow obligations under international humanitarian law, did not mention that Russia was behind deadly strikes that killed Ukrainian children in recent days, and did not recognize Russia's responsibility for starting its war against Ukraine.
"Moreover, UNICEF's statement lacks basic fact-checking. It failed to mention that the casualties in Russia's Krasnodar were caused by a drone reportedly intercepted by Russian air defense . It also failed to verify the information on casualties in Ukraine: seven, not three, children from one family were killed in the Dnipropetrovsk" Oblast, Sybiha said.
The original UNICEF statement refers to a reported Ukrainian attack that killed seven in Russia's Krasnodar Krai after a drone crashed onto a beach amid Ukraine's campaign against Russian military infrastructure.
Russia's attack on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast initially killed at least six members of one family when it destroyed their home, and comes as Ukrainian civilians are killed in Moscow's attacks day after day.
"These are Russia's war crimes. We call on UNICEF to condemn these heinous crimes and urge Russia to stop killing innocent Ukrainian children," Sybiha said, adding that another three-year-old boy was killed in Kyiv Oblast on Aug. 8.
Russia launched the attack against Ukraine's capital and Kyiv Oblast overnight on Aug. 8, killing four people , including a three-year-old child, and injuring eight others, President Volodymyr Zelensky and the local authorities reported.

title: Syria announces plans to convert Russian military bases into joint training centers
description: The Syrian Foreign Ministry says the agreement "opens the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations" following Moscow's support of deposed former President Bashar al-Assad.
content:
Syria announced plans to reorganize Russian military bases and establish new joint training centers for the two nations on Aug. 9.
A memorandum of understanding was reached after 18 months of negotiation, according to the Syrian state news agency SANA , outlining the future of Russian bases at Tartus and Khmeimim on the Syrian coast.
Established during the Soviet period, the sites remain Russia's only military bases outside the former Soviet Union.
Under the new agreement, Syria will take over civilian facilities at the bases including the Khmeimim ​airport and commercial docks at the Tartus port. Military facilities at the bases will be converted into joint training sites ​​and qualification centers "aimed at safeguarding the interests of both countries," SANA reported, citing the Syrian Foreign Ministry.
The Syrian Foreign Ministry says the agreement "opens the way for a new phase in Syrian-Russian relations" following Moscow's support of deposed Syrian President Bashar al-Assad in the nation’s devastating civil war. Al-Assad has been living in Russia since 2024, when rebels toppled his regime.
The Kremlin has not yet commented on the agreement.
Between 2015 and 2024, Russian forces killed up to 6,500 Syrian civilians through bombing campaigns and airstrikes, according to the civilian harm watchdog organization Airwars.
After a six-month pause following the ousting of al-Assad, Russia resumed military flights to Syria in October 2025 amid a push to bolster its military presence in the Mediterranean. In January 2026, Russian President Vladimir Putin met with Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa in Moscow to negotiate the future of the bases and the possible transfer of al-Assad to Syria.
The visit marked al-Sharaa's second trip to Moscow since the fall of Assad , as Putin sought to strengthen ties with Syria's new leadership in order to retain control over its military bases.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also traveled to Syria in April 2026 as part of a string of visits to the Middle East in the wake of the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran. Meeting with al-Sharaa, Zelensky said the two discussed regional developments linked to Iran, economic cooperation, and infrastructure and energy projects.
"Ukraine was among the first to support a new Syria after the fall of the Assad regime," Zelensky said after the visit.
"We are ready to continue supporting stability and development. We will work even more closely together so that our peoples and our countries become stronger, and so that our economies can grow stronger as well."

title: Poles take to streets in 22 cities to protest hate crimes against Ukrainians
description: The demonstrations come amid a surge in physical and verbal assaults against Ukrainians in Poland in recent months, fueled by a crisis in diplomatic relations between the neighboring countries.
content:
Demonstrators in over 20 cities across Poland rallied on Aug. 9 to oppose the growing violence against Ukrainians and other minorities, the Polish outlet RMF 24 reported.
The demonstrations come amid a surge in physical and verbal assaults against Ukrainians in Poland in recent months, fueled by a crisis in diplomatic relations between the neighboring countries.
Protesters gathered in the evening of Aug. 9 in 22 cities, including Warsaw, Krakow, Lublin, and Wroclaw, to show solidarity with victims of discrimination. The campaign was organized by Poland's Committee for the Defense of Democracy, an NGO promoting civil society and human rights.
The movement is part of a broader aim to oppose violence against minorities based on nationality, language, or appearance, the organizers said.
Participants in the Aug. 9 demonstrations received stickers with the slogan "Don't Be Indifferent," which they were encouraged to place on stores, businesses, or other establishments to signal that Ukranians would be safe and welcome.
The protests came shortly after a similar demonstration in Warsaw on Aug. 7. During that rally, titled "My Poland Doesn’t Hit, Insult, or Incite," organizers submitted a petition signed by over 11,000 people to the government. The petition demands action against discrimination, including attacks against Ukrainians.
One of the inciting incidents behind these demonstrations was a brutal assault against a Ukrainian couple in Wroclaw on July 26. Three assailants beat a 20-year-old Ukrainian woman and her partner, a 21-year-old Ukrainian man. Police said they believed the victims were targeted because of their nationality.
Polish police received 180 reports of hate crimes against Ukrainians in the first half of 2026, an increase of over 30% compared to the same period last year, according to the Rzeczpospolita newspaper . The statistic dovetails with polls showing that a majority of Poles hold increasingly negative views toward Ukraine and no longer support welcoming Ukrainian refugees.
Animosity towards Ukraine has risen due to deteriorating relations between Kyiv and Warsaw. The most recent crisis began when Ukraine named one of its military units after the World War II-era Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA).
While UPA is seen in Ukraine as an anti-Soviet movement, the controversial group is known in Poland for participating in the Volyn massacres — the mass killing of Poles in what is today western Ukraine.

title: 'Kosovo must be respected' — Ukrainian flag stripped from Kosovo building after Zelensky's Serbia visit inflames controversy
description: In Serbia, Zelensky confirmed that Kyiv does not officially recognize Kosovo's independence. Officials in Kosovo said his stance was "deeply disappointing" given the country's support for Ukraine.
content:
Officials in Kosovo expressed outrage on Aug. 9, following President Volodymyr Zelensky's first official visit to Serbia, where he reiterated Ukraine's position that Kosovo is not an independent state.
Zelensky met with Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic in Belgrade Aug. 7-9, in a visit largely seen as symbolic given Serbia's close ties with Russia. Despite Kosovo's support for Kyiv in the war against Moscow, Ukraine does not formally recognize Kosovo as a state — a stance Zelensky confirmed during talks with Vucic.
Kosovars responded by stripping a large Ukrainian flag from a building in Pristina, Kosovo's capital, on Aug. 9.
"The state of Kosovo must be respected," Pristina Mayor Perparim Rama said in a Facebook post showing a video of the flag being removed. "When Kosovo is not respected, Pristina answers!"
Behgjet Pacolli, former foreign minister of Kosovo, also called Zelensky and Vucic's remarks "deeply disappointing," noting Kosovo's continued support for Ukraine. "Mr. Zelensky, your statement that Ukraine's position on Kosovo remains unchanged is deeply disappointing," Pacolli said on X.
"Kosovo has stood with Ukraine and genuinely sympathized with the suffering of its people. If this is Ukraine’s response to that solidarity, it is truly regrettable."
Relations between Kosovo and Serbia have remained tense since the 1998–1999 Kosovo War following the breakup of Yugoslavia. Serbian forces committed widespread war crimes, including the massacre of thousands of ethnic Albanians in Kosovo.
The crisis spurred a 78-day NATO bombing campaign to push out Serbian forces in 1999. At least 10,000 Kosovar Albanians were killed by Serbian forces in ethnic cleansings, according to the U.S. State Department. Kosovo later declared its independence in 2008.
Ukraine's reluctance to recognize Kosovo as a state has been linked, among other factors, to doctrinal adherence to territorial integrity, stemming from Kyiv's experience with Moscow's aggression and occupation.
During Zelensky's visit to Serbia, the president and Vucic held discussions regarding mutual respect for territorial integrity, humanitarian aid, and bilateral cooperation. Vucic also backed Ukraine's bid for EU membership .
"We will do everything we can to help Ukraine on the European path," he said.
Kosovo Foreign Minister Glauk Konjufca said that his country would continue to support Kyiv's sovereignty, but rejected the framing of Serbian "territorial integrity" as a reason to deny Kosovo's independence.
"We would welcome Ukraine’s recognition of the Republic of Kosovo," he said on X. "Such a decision would strengthen the very principles of freedom, democracy and international law that Ukraine itself is defending today."
In his post about Ukraine on Aug. 9, Rama said the people of Kosovo would always support victims of war.
"Our empathy and solidarity will always be with peoples facing war, violence and persecution," he wrote.
"Because we, better than most, know what it means to fight for freedom, dignity, and the right to exist as a state. But no cause and no policy can be built undermining Kosovo's citizenship and the sacrifice of its people."
Editor's Note: A previous version of this article incorrectly referred to Behgjet Pacolli as Kosovo's foreign minister. He is the former foreign minister; the article has been updated to reflect this. Statements from the current foreign minister, Glauk Konjufca, have also been added.

title: Ukraine war latest: Ukrainian-made ballistic missiles could hit Russia in the fall, Zelensky says
description:
Key developments on Aug. 8-9:

 * Ukrainian-made ballistic missiles could hit Russia in the fall, Zelensky says
 * Another overnight Russian attack on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast kills 4, including 3-year-old child
 * Kyiv strikes Russian missile system used in attack the previous day, Madyar says
 * Ukraine buys 70 ATACMS missiles, other US weapons from Turkey in major defense package
 * Ukraine says it struck 12 Russian shadow fleet vessels in Black Sea and Sea of Azov

President Volodymyr Zelensky c
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed earlier reports that ballistic missiles being developed by Ukrainian company Fire Point could be combat-ready in the space of 2-3 months , in an interview with Ukraine's state-run telethon on the evening of Aug. 8.
Fire Point told Reuters on Aug. 4 that its FP7 ballistic missile is being certified by Ukraine's defense ministry, a process expected to be complete within the month. They also said they expect their larger FP9 missile, ostensibly capable of reaching Moscow, to be ready by late fall.
"As for their large-scale use, I can't say, because some things do not depend on Ukraine. It is the same with Russian ballistic missiles: they contain components from other countries. The same applies to our ballistic missiles — there are few such components, but some do come from other countries," Zelensky said.
Despite sanctions, EU materials and equipment continue to find their way into the production of Russian military hardware.
A variant of Fire Point's FP7 ballistic missile is being fashioned into an anti-ballistic missile akin to the U.S. Patriot system, in collaboration with nine European partner countries under the Freya program.
The company aims to carry out its first successful ballistic missile interception by mid-2027, its CEO Iryna Terekh told Reuters.
Fire Point is primarily known for its middle- and deep-strike drones FP-1 and FP-2, which have been described as crucial to Ukraine's war effort. Since last year, however, the company has become embroiled in several controversies , including Ukraine's largest wartime corruption scandal, prompting questions about possible preferential treatment in the awarding of state contracts.
Russia launched an attack against Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight on Aug. 8, killing four people, including a three-year-old child, and injuring eight others, President Volodymyr Zelensky and the local authorities reported.
Zelensky said that the three people killed in Kyiv Oblast's Brovary district on Aug. 8 were a grandmother, grandfather, and their three-year-old grandson. The child's parents and his 15-year-old brother were among the four wounded in the village of Pukhivka, as well as a neighbor who had come to help them, according to the president. The injured victims were hospitalized, he added.
"Europe, the U.S., and Ukraine have long wanted to end the war," Zelensky said in his Facebook post.
"Only (Russian President Vladimir) Putin doesn't want to, and is clinging to his ballistic missiles and drones to keep the war going."
The rest of the injury count came from Kyiv, where the city's military administration said a person was killed and four others were wounded in the overnight attack.
Kyiv's surrounding region has been battered by aerial assaults throughout spring and summer, as a critical air defense shortage leaves the capital exposed to Russian ballistic missiles .
The attack damaged a residential building, cars, and outbuildings in the Brovary district, and a fire also broke out at a non-residential building, according to Kyiv Oblast Governor Tymyr Tkachenko. Emergency crews are continuing to work at the affected sites.
The latest strike on Brovary, a suburb east of Kyiv, comes as the community is still reeling from a mass Russian attack that killed eight people on a train platform . The attack marked one of the most intense Russian bombardments in Brovary since the start of the war.
In Kyiv, fires broke out in two separate garages and a commercial building in the Holosiivskyi district, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported.
Another fire was extinguished "on the territory of an enterprise" in the Obolonskyi district, DSNS wrote .
Ukrainian drones struck an S-400 "Triumph" anti-aircraft missile launch pad in Russia's Krasnodar region on the night of Aug. 8, hours after it had fired missiles at Ukraine, the Unmanned Systems Forces announced on Telegram.
The system had launched six missiles on the morning of Aug. 8, according to USF Commander Robert Brovdi, known by the call sign "Madyar."
"The S-400 position in Gelendzhik ... was ablaze and sputtering for three hours," Madyar wrote.
Russia's S-400 system was originally designed for air defense. With Ukraine low on interceptor missiles for its own air defenses , Moscow is increasingly repurposing the technology for offensive operations.
Madyar also highlighted that his drone forces had recently destroyed several other air defense systems in Russia's Krasnodar Kra i and Rostov Oblast , as well as two radar stations in the Rostov region.
Systematically targeting Russian air defense systems helps reduce Moscow’s ability to control airspace, which allows Ukraine to successfully attack other military and logistics targets across the country.
Ukraine has purchased a significant package of U.S.-made defense equipment from Turkey, including 70 long-range Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS), according to U.S. congressional records.
The weapons transfer has been approved by the U.S. State Department and is expected to be initiated in late August, following mandatory congressional review.
The package includes 70 M39 ATACMS missiles, 12 M270 multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), over 2,000 cluster munitions , and 47,000 howitzer rounds, according to a notice from the State Department recorded in congressional minutes on Aug. 6.
ATACMS are long-range surface-to-surface ballistic missiles produced by U.S. manufacturer Lockheed Martin. The M39 version represents an earlier model, with a range of approximately 165 kilometers (103 miles).
The upcoming transfer will be facilitated through a number of private companies, including Turkey's MKE, ASFAT, and ARCA Savunma, Bulgaria's VTIC International, and the U.S. firms Pansophico and Patriot Defense Group.
According to the State Department, Turkey aims to "reduce its inventory of older defense articles to focus its financial resources on modernization and sustainment of existing systems."
Ukraine, meanwhile, is looking to "bolster its offensive and defense fire support capabilities as it resists the Russian invasion." The State Department also noted that the transaction is "consistent with U.S. security assistance objectives."
Ukraine received its first batch of the shorter-range M39 ATACMS in the fall of 2023 from former U.S. President Joe Biden, after a long lobbying campaign from Kyiv.
In the spring of 2024, the U.S. began supplying upgraded models that could fly up to 300 kilometers (186 miles). At the time, Kyiv was only permitted to deploy these missiles against targets in occupied Ukrainian territory. In November 2024, Ukraine was finally permitted to launch ATACMS at targets within Russia .
In the past year, Ukraine has only used ATACMS a handful of times , as its stocks are understood to be severely depleted.
Ukrainian long-range drones have hit 12 Russian shadow fleet vessels in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov over the past week, Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces said on Aug. 8.
The strikes come after Ukraine launched Operation Molochka in July, a campaign targeting Russia’s shadow fleet in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in an effort to tighten the noose around Russian-occupied Crimea peninsula.
Since the start of the operation on July 6, Ukrainian drones have struck 218 Russian shadow fleet vessels, including 134 in the Sea of Azov and 84 in the Black Sea, according to the Unmanned Systems Forces.
The attacks that struck 12 Russian shadow fleet vessels in August were conducted by the Madyar's Birds Brigade, led by Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Brovdi, K-2 Brigade, and Raid Regiment, according to the report.
The Kyiv Independent couldn't independently verify the claim. Moscow had not commented as of publication time. The Russian Defense Ministry claimed on Aug. 8 that it had downed 83 Ukrainian drones overnight, including over the Azov Sea.
"Molochka Operation continues," the Unmanned Systems Forces said in its Telegram post.
The report comes as Ukraine ramps up its long-range drone strikes on occupied Crimea and across the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov to isolate the peninsula and disrupt key military routes.

title: Russia destroys World Health Organization warehouse in Dnipro
description: "Even wars have rules. One of those is that health must be protected," World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.
content:
A World Health Organization (WHO) warehouse in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro was destroyed during a recent Russian attack, sending emergency health supplies up in smoke, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus confirmed on Aug. 9.
Russia struck the facility during an attack in Dnipro, Ukraine's fourth-largest city, on Aug. 7.
The warehouse contained humanitarian medical supplies bound for the front line, Ghebreyesus wrote on X. Staff from the UN's health agency managed to evacuate 130 of some 300 pallets' worth of aid before the strike.
"I cannot say loudly enough: attacks on health care MUST STOP," Ghebreyesus said.
"Even wars have rules. One of those is that health must be protected."
Ukraine's Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets condemned the strike, which he described as a "cynical" Russian attack on the most vulnerable people.
"This is a blow to essential medicines intended for hospitals and people closest to the front line," Lubinets wrote on Telegram. "I see a clear and cynical goal of the Russians — to deprive people of the means to save lives."
The attack on the WHO warehouse is not the first instance of Russia targeting UN actors in Ukraine.
In May, a UN convoy delivering supplies to civilians in Kherson Oblast was severely damaged in two Russian drone strikes. WHO has also documented the increased risk faced by ambulance drivers and health transport personnel throughout the full-scale war.
Despite this record, Ghebreyesus kept to the passive voice when condemning the attack and did not call out Russia by name, a trend observed across United Nations social media accounts.
One EU diplomat told the Kyiv Independent that colleagues in Brussels were wondering if that approach might change after the UN's Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs called out Russia for attacking Ukrainian civilian targets on July 30.
Russia has systematically flouted the rules of war in its attacks against Ukrainian civilian targets. Russian forces have also committed numerous war crimes in Ukraine.
A European Commission webpage on Russia's war crimes, last updated in May 2026, says that "Ukraine is investigating more than 200,000 incidents of alleged international crimes, and the actual number of such atrocities is suspected to be even higher."

title: Ukraine strikes Russian missile system used in attack the previous day, Madyar says
description: "The S-400 position in Gelendzhik ... was ablaze and sputtering for three hours," the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces, Robert "Madyar" Brovdi, announced.
content:
Ukrainian drones struck an S-400 "Triumph" anti-aircraft missile launch pad in Russia's Krasnodar region on the night of Aug. 8, hours after it had fired missiles at Ukraine, the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces announced on Telegram.
The system had launched six missiles on the morning of Aug. 8, according to Robert Brovdi, known by the call sign "Madyar."

Russia's S-400 system was originally designed for air defense. With Ukraine low on interceptor missiles for its own air defenses , Moscow is increasingly repurposing the technology for offensive operations.
"While less accurate and lethal, they still represent a threat to civilian infrastructure, particularly when launched against densely populated areas," writes missile expert Fabian Hoffmann.
Madyar also highlighted that his drone forces had recently destroyed several other air defense systems in Russia's Krasnodar Krai and Rostov region , as well as two radar stations in Rostov region.
Systematically targeting Russian air defense systems helps reduce Moscow’s ability to control airspace, which allows Ukraine to successfully attack other military and logistics targets across the country.
Madyar added that "three vessels of the Russian shadow fleet were hunted down in the Black Sea," listing one oil tanker and two cargo ships.
Ukraine has increased the frequency of its attacks and interceptions against shadow fleet vessels in the Black Sea since declaring them to be military targets on July 1.
That has been accompanied by more interceptions by the EU and specific European countries, and by new sanctions passed by the bloc and the U.K. against ships helping Russia evade sanctions.

title: Russian attacks kill at least 13 people, injure 90 across Ukraine over past day
description: Overnight, Ukrainian forces downed 174 Shahed-type drones and five Banderol missiles, the Air Force reported on Aug. 9.
content:
Russian attacks killed 13 people and injured at least 90 others across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Aug. 9.
Overnight, Ukrainian forces downed 174 Shahed-type drones and five Banderol missiles, the Air Force reported on Aug. 9. Russian missiles and drones struck 22 targets, according to the military. Debris from downed drones or missiles caused damage at six locations. Several missiles did not reach their targets due to electronic warfare countermeasures.
Russia’s overnight attacks mainly targeted Odesa Oblast in southern Ukraine, according to the Air Force.
Attacks on Odesa Oblast injured at least 12 and left part of the city of Odesa without electricity and water supply.
In Kyiv Oblast, Russia killed three people in the village of Pukhivka, a three-year-old boy and his grandparents, President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram. The strikes hospitalized a further four people, including the child's parents, the 15-year-old brother, and a neighbor who came to help them but was injured in a second strike.
Russian forces also launched six ballistic missiles targeting civilian infrastructure in Kyiv , according to Zelensky. One person was killed as a result of the attack on the capital.
"More pressure is needed — new sanctions that will prevent Russia from producing these ballistic missiles. And our people absolutely need more protection. Anti-ballistic systems, interceptor missiles for Patriot, SAMP/T, NASAMS, and HAWK systems, as well as our F-16s — all of these work and help protect lives when they are here in Ukraine, rather than sitting in warehouses thousands of kilometers away from Russia’s attacks on human life," Zelensky wrote.
Russia killed three people and injured 37 others in an attack on Kharkiv Oblast , Kharkiv Mayor Ihor Terekhov reported on Telegram.
Moscow struck a high-rise residential building in the Saltivskyi district, destroying the 7th to 10th floors, according to Oleh Syniehubov, head of the Kharkiv Oblast Military Administration. Amog the killed are two men aged 50 and 66.
In Donetsk Oblast, Russian attacks killed three people and injured five others, said Governor Vadym Filashkin . Kramatorsk, Druzhkivka, Dobropillia, and other areas across the region came under attack, according to the governor.
In Sumy Oblast, Russia killed three people and injured five others, the oblast's military administration said . Air raid alert had been on in the region for almost the entire day, for 23 hours and 49 minutes, according to the administration.
In Kherson Oblast, Russian forces injured 10 people, including two children, Oleksandr Prokudin, head of the Kherson Oblast Military Administration, reported . The attacks targeted residential building and other civilian infrastructure, according to Prokudin.
In Zhytomyr Oblast, three people were injured, of whom one was hospitalized with burns, said Vitalii Bunechko, head of the Zhytomyr Oblast Military Administration.
Eleven people were injured in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration. Among the injured are four children.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast , Russia carried out 974 attacks, injuring two, according to the local military administration.
Mykolaiv Oblast was under multiple drone attacks, with one person getting injured, according to local officials .

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,457,740 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The figure includes 1,130 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day, according to the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,457,740 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of Ukraine's Armed Forces reported on Aug. 9.
The figure includes 1,130 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day, according to the General Staff.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,253 tanks, 25,103 armored combat vehicles, 131,775 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,621 artillery systems, 2,013 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,556 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 451,248 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,171 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Russian missile attack damages residential buildings in Odesa, injures at least 14
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky said that 300,000 families in Odesa lost power due to the attacks.
content:
Russia carried out a missile attack on Odesa overnight on Aug. 9, damaging residential buildings and injuring at least 14 people in the city, officials said.
Eleven of the injured victims were hospitalized, with one in serious condition, Odesa Oblast Governor Oleh Kiper reported . Previously, the regional administration said that most of the injured had shrapnel wounds.
In two districts, several residential buildings were damaged or partially destroyed, with residents' cars destroyed and damaged by fire, according to the administration.
Photos and videos posted to social media show fires burning at several high-rise residential buildings and homes in the city.
Ukraine's largest private energy company DTEK said that energy infrastructure came under attack, triggering power cuts in the city, which have also interrupted the water supply. DTEK expects water to flow again through the course of the morning, and are working on repairs to the power grid.
"The damage is severe, and repairs will take time. Energy workers across the Odesa region are doing everything possible to restore the electricity supply as quickly as possible," DTEK posted on its Telegram channel.
In his evening address on Aug. 9, President Volodymyr Zelensky said that 300,000 families in Odesa were left without power the morning after the attack. Power has been restored to a third of those affected, he said.
Repair and recovery efforts in Odesa are ongoing.
Ukraine's Air Force warned of the attack beginning around 3:30 a.m. local time moments prior to explosions being heard in the city, with additional waves of missile attacks reported later into the night.
The Ukrainian Armed Forces later said that Russia deployed 11 missiles on "a ballistic trajectory" against Odesa, along with almost 100 drones, 72% of which were intercepted.
However, they only downed one of the 11 missiles.
Located in southern Ukraine off the Black Sea, the port city of Odesa has served as a regular target of Russian attacks given its proximity to Russian-occupied Crimea. Russian forces have intensified attacks on Odesa and the surrounding region this summer, coinciding with the peak tourist season, when thousands of visitors travel to the Black Sea coast.
The city has been targeted with both drones and missiles, including Banderol missiles, which Russia has used to strike port infrastructure in the region.
The attacks have also damaged dozens of civilian vessels passing through Odesa’s ports and caused casualties among crew members.

title: Fires seen in Russia's Belgorod amid reported Ukrainian drone attack
description: Ukraine's military reportedly launched a wide-ranging drone attack on the Russian city of Belgorod overnight on Aug. 9, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
content:
Ukraine's military reportedly launched a wide-ranging drone attack on the Russian city of Belgorod overnight on Aug. 9, Russian Telegram media channels reported.
Photos and videos posted to social media purport to show fires at residential buildings within the city. Substantial damage was reported at several buildings, including the Avtograd shopping center which independent Russian Telegram channel Astra reports is "partially destroyed."
While the target of the attack was not clear, Astra, citing OSINT analysis, reported that a regional FSB (Russia's Federal Security Service) headquarters was located between three damaged buildings. Another building struck was located approximately 600 meters away from the Belgorod Thermal Power Plant.
Acting Belgorod Oblast Governor Alexander Shuvaev claimed that the attack injured 13 people.
The Kyiv Independent could not verify the reports nor claims made by Russian officials. Ukraine's military has not commented on the reported attack.
The city of Belgorod has been a frequent target of Ukrainian attacks given its proximity to the front line. The city is located just 34 kilometers (21 miles) from Ukraine's northeastern border with Russia and lies approximately 70 kilometers (43 miles) from the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.
In recent weeks, Russian forces have intensified ballistic missile attacks against Ukrainian cities, amid Ukraine's critical air defense shortage.
Overnight on Aug. 8, Russia launched an attack against Kyiv and the surrounding region, killing four people, including a three-year-old child, and injuring eight others.

title: Turkey urges halt to Russian, Ukrainian attacks on vessels in Black Sea
description: Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Aug. 8 called on Russia and Ukraine to impose a moratorium on attacks on vessels in the Black Sea amid the increasing number of strikes on ships in the region.
content:
Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan on Aug. 8 called on Russia and Ukraine to impose a moratorium on attacks on vessels in the Black Sea amid the increasing number of strikes on ships in the region.
"At first, ports and warships were attacked. Now all commercial vessels are being attacked indiscriminately. We need to create a mechanism that would allow us to declare a moratorium," Fidan said in an interview with Anadolu.
"The Ukrainians already had a corresponding proposal. We passed it on to our Russian colleagues and are waiting for a response."
In recent weeks, Ukraine and Russia have increasingly traded blows on vessels in the Black Sea, directly impacting foreign-flagged ships, including those owned and operated in Turkey.
On July 6, Ukraine launched Operation Molochka, a campaign targeting Russia’s shadow fleet in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in an effort to tighten the noose around Russian-occupied Crimea peninsula.
Since the start of the operation on July 6, Ukrainian drones have struck 218 Russian shadow fleet vessels, including 134 in the Sea of Azov and 84 in the Black Sea, according to the Unmanned Systems Forces.
In response, Russia has launched attacks primarily targeting civilian cargo ships near the port city of Odesa. The attacks have targeted foreign-flagged ships carrying grain and fertilizers, including Turkish-flagged and Turkish-owned ships.
One attack struck a Turkish-flagged fishing vessels near occupied Crimea, killing one person and injuring four others.
Ukrainian attacks have also targeted vessels as far south in the Black Sea as around 50 miles (80 kilometers) off the coast of northern Turkey .
"The conflict has spread across the whole Black Sea," Fidan added.
Attempts at brokering a ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia in the Black Sea have thus far been unsuccessful.
In March 2025, during early rounds of peace negotiations, the United States claimed it had secured a ceasefire in the Black Sea. While Ukraine agreed to the ceasefire, Moscow said it would only agree to the ceasefire only after Western sanctions on Russian food producers and exporters, were lifted — leaving the ceasefire proposal to quickly whittle away.
President Volodymyr Zelensky hinted on Aug. 8 that Kyiv's forces will continue to strike Russian logistics following the now-concluded "40-day influence operation," which included the operation designed to cripple dozens of Russian tankers supplying occupied Crimea.
Turkey, a NATO member, has positioned itself as a mediator in the Russia-Ukraine war , maintaining a close economic and political partnership with Moscow while also providing arms to Kyiv.
According to U.S. congressional records made public on Aug. 8, Ukraine has purchased a significant package of U.S.-made defense equipment from Turkey, including 70 long-range Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS). The weapons transfer is expected to be initiated in late August.

title: 'We understand all their weak points' — Zelensky 'satisfied' with Ukraine's '40-day campaign,' suggests more strikes on Russian logistics planned
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 8 that he was "satisfied" with the result of a 40-day influence operation designed to compel Russia to "end the war," suggesting that Kyiv's forces will continue to strike Russian logistics beyond the limited timeline.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Aug. 8 that he was "satisfied" with the result of a 40-day influence operation designed to compel Russia to "end the war," suggesting that Kyiv's forces will continue to strike Russian logistics beyond the limited timeline.
Zelensky tasked Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) to launch the 40-day operation in late June, with the operation culminating with Ukraine's crippling of dozens of Russian tankers supplying occupied Crimea, as well as the destruction of numerous warehouses across the country belonging to online retailer Wildberries.
Details of what the campaign actually constituted remained sparse until it ended, when the SBU released a statement on Aug. 4 clarifying the actions that the agency claimed were part of it. According to the statement, the campaign "was aimed at simultaneously weakening key elements of the Russian military machine."
"I am satisfied, absolutely. In terms of our logistical responses, we understand how much they have lost; they have major problems," Zelensky said in a wide-ranging interview on Ukraine's marathon television program.
"After they began striking our logistics, we found another logistical operation and responded to them. The losses there are staggering — one trillion rubles ($12.2 billion). It was a very successful operation by Ukrainian forces," the president added.
Despite not achieving an end to Russia's full-scale war, Ukrainian officials familiar with the planning previously told the Kyiv Independent that one of the operation's central political objectives was looking further ahead than the stated 40 days — to force Russians to experience the consequences of the war more directly with a view to influencing elections in September.
In his interview comments, Zelensky alluded to the impact the war was having on the Russian population, issuing thinly veiled threats that strikes on Russian logistics will continue.
"They have for a long time allowed themselves to target non-military targets, and they must know that Ukraine strikes military targets. But if they continue, we understand all their weak points... We have not had a normal life or such habits since the beginning of Russia's aggression. Russia does not feel this. Obviously, goods that do not reach ordinary consumers in Russia because of a lack of logistics will, understandably, be felt by people in Russia," Zelensky said.
"I would not advise Russia to continue striking Ukrainian logistics, because we have clearly studied what Russia's logistics look like."
Amid Ukraine's efforts to target logistics facilities, Russia has intensified its efforts to launch large-scale attacks on Ukrainian cities — with Ukraine facing a shortage of air defense capabilities.
Another overnight attack on Kyiv on Aug. 8, killed four people, including a three-year-old child, and injured eight others, Zelensky and local officials reported.

title: Unidentified drone explodes near gas pipeline at Bulgarian-Romanian border, Kyiv to launch inquiry
description: The drone entered Bulgarian airspace from Romania and exploded approximately 1 kilometer away from a compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline. There were no casualties or damage.
content:
An unidentified drone exploded on Bulgarian territory near an international gas pipeline on Aug. 8, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said.
The drone entered Bulgarian airspace from Romania and exploded about 100 meters within Bulgaria , approximately 1 kilometer away from a compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, according to Radev. The UAV was not detected in either Romanian or Bulgarian airspace.
No casualties or damage to any buildings resulted from the explosion.
The Bulgarian Defense Ministry later said that its initial analysis of the wreckage suggests the drone is a "Maya" decoy drone , widely used by Ukrainian forces.
"At the moment, there is no reason to believe that the incident was intentional," the ministry said.
Kyiv responded to the report by saying it had not targeted Bulgaria and was open to a joint investigation to determine the cause of the incident.
"We are in close contact with the Bulgarian side to clarify the circumstances," Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi said. "We can say with certainty that the Ukrainian Armed Forces did not intentionally direct any assets toward Bulgaria."
Tykhyi added that the root cause of any drone incursion into countries bordering Ukraine is Russia's continued war.
The explosion in Bulgaria follows a series of drone incursions in Romania this summer. Romanian air defenses shot down three Russian UAVs in three days between July 24 and 26, prompting Bucharest to summon its Russian ambassador.
The country had also logged multiple other incursions throughout the full-scale war. Most dramatically, a Russian drone struck a residential building in the city of Galați on May 29, injuring two people.
Ukrainian drones have also strayed into other countries , including Latvia and Estonia.
Both Ukraine and Russia use complex networks of jamming and navigation spoofing devices to defend against mass drone and missile attacks on their territory, which can cause some of the drones to fly off course.

title: Ukraine buys 70 ATACMS missiles, other US weapons from Turkey in major defense package
description: The package includes 70 M39 ATACMS missiles, 12 M270 multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), over 2,000 cluster munitions, and 47,000 howitzer rounds, according to a notice from the U.S. State Department.
content:
Ukraine has purchased a significant package of U.S.-made defense equipment from Turkey, including 70 long-range Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS), according to U.S. congressional records.
The weapons transfer is expected to be initiated in late August.
The package includes 70 M39 ATACMS missiles, 12 M270 multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), over 2,000 cluster munitions , and 47,000 howitzer rounds, according to a notice from the U.S. State Department recorded in congressional minutes on Aug. 6.
ATACMS are long-range surface-to-surface ballistic missiles produced by U.S. manufacturer Lockheed Martin. The M39 version represents an earlier model, with a range of approximately 165 kilometers (103 miles).
The upcoming transfer will be facilitated through a number of private companies, including Turkey's MKE, ASFAT, and ARCA Savunma, Bulgaria's VTIC International, and the U.S. firms Pansophico and Patriot Defense Group.
According to the State Department, Turkey aims to "reduce its inventory of older defense articles to focus its financial resources on modernization and sustainment of existing systems."
Ukraine, meanwhile, is looking to "bolster its offensive and defense fire support capabilities as it resists the Russian invasion." The State Department also noted that the transaction is "consistent with U.S. security assistance objectives."
Under U.S. President Donald Trump, Washington ended large-scale defense funding and delivery of U.S. military aid to Ukraine, leaving Kyiv to rely on support from other partners to obtain key weapons systems.
Turkey, a NATO member, has positioned itself as a mediator in the Russia-Ukraine war , maintaining a close economic and political partnership with Moscow while also providing arms to Kyiv.
The U.S. Arms Export Control Act requires Congress to review transfers of American weapons to third countries if the initial cost of the materiel exceeds $14 million. The package Ukraine will receive from Turkey carries an original acquisition value of around $280 million.
As long as Congress does not pass a joint resolution banning the re-export of the weapons within the next two weeks, the transfer will automatically be authorized.
Ukraine received its first batch of the shorter-range M39 ATACMS in the fall of 2023 from former U.S. President Joe Biden, after a long lobbying campaign from Kyiv.
In the spring of 2024, the U.S. began supplying upgraded models that could fly up to 300 kilometers (186 miles). At the time, Kyiv was only permitted to deploy these missiles against targets in occupied Ukrainian territory. In November 2024, Ukraine was finally permitted to launch ATACMS at targets within Russia .
In the past year, Ukraine has only used ATACMS a handful of times , as its stocks are understood to be severely depleted.
The U.S. is also reportedly facing a serious shortage of ATACMS due to the war against Iran.

title: Serbia's Vucic backs Ukraine's EU membership on 2nd day of summit with Zelensky
description: Serbian President Alexander Vucic on Aug. 8 backed Ukraine's bid for EU membership on the second day of President Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to the country.
content:
Serbian President Alexander Vucic on Aug. 8 backed Ukraine's bid for EU membership on the second day of President Volodymyr Zelensky's visit to the country.
"We want Ukraine to open all clusters as soon as possible, to close them as soon as possible. We have already said that this is the wish of the Ukrainian people, the Ukrainian leadership, and as far as we are concerned, we have not had or will not have any problem with that in the future," Vucic said .
"On the contrary, we will do everything we can to help Ukraine on the European path," he added.
Zelensky first arrived in Belgrade on Aug. 7 in what is seen as a symbolic visit , as Serbia has traditionally maintained close relations with Moscow.
The two leaders held wide-ranging discussions, including mutual respect for territorial integrity, humanitarian aid, and bilateral cooperation, Zelensky said .
"The parties discussed measures that could strengthen infrastructure, ports, and railways, as well as the economies and security of both countries overall. In particular, Serbia is interested in Ukraine's experience in developing railway infrastructure to improve its transport network. The leaders discussed specific projects that could be implemented jointly, as well as cooperation in the area of food security."
At the meeting, Ukraine's State Service on Food Safety and Consumer Protection and Serbia's Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Water Management signed a Memorandum of Understanding in the presence of both leaders.
"The document provides for cooperation to control, prevent, and eradicate animal diseases, as well as to protect national territories from the cross-border introduction of such infectious diseases," the Presidential Office said.
Vucic also invited Zelensky to return to Serbia to attend the opening of a drone factory Belgrade built in cooperation with Israel.
"Ukrainians are very successful and have many of their own drone factories. We will invite you to the opening," Vucic said.

title: Belgian company seeks exception to keep operating in Russia's drone hub — as it does so anyway
description: A Belgian factory continues to operate in Russia's special economic zone known as a key defense production site despite EU requirements to leave the zone by late January 2026.
content:
A Belgian factory continues to operate in Russia's special economic zone known as a key defense production site despite EU requirements to leave the zone by late January 2026.
Belgium's Federal Public Service Economy (FPS Economy) has not yet granted a derogation to any Belgian company under the relevant EU regulation, according to a statement obtained by Belgian media and seen by the Kyiv Independent.
That includes Drylock Technologies, a Belgian company that came under scrutiny in a Kyiv Independent investigation into Western companies that have continued operating in Russia's Alabuga Special Economic Zone.
The zone is home to the country's largest factory producing Shahed attack drones — weapons that have terrorized Ukraine's civilians for nearly four years.
Drylock Technologies is a Belgian manufacturer of diapers and other hygiene products. It has factories across the world, including in Russia . The Kyiv Independent found that the manufacturer's Russian subsidiary has publicly voiced support for its Russian employees' participation in the war against Ukraine.
Under European Union restrictions, EU-linked companies were required to leave the Alabuga zone by Jan. 25, 2026. A number of companies failed to comply, Drylock Technologies among them.
Following the Kyiv Independent’s reporting , the Belgian newspaper De Tijd found that Drylock Technologies is in talks with the Belgian government over a possible exception that would allow its plant in the Alabuga Zone to continue operating — but has not yet been granted it.
"The derogation options included in this article are exceptions to a general prohibition and are therefore assessed strictly, exhaustively, and on a case-by-case basis," said Etienne Mignolet, an FPS Economy spokesperson.
The spokesperson added that applicants must demonstrate that the specific activities in question are strictly necessary for one of the purposes expressly listed in the regulation.
"It is not sufficient that the activities or products concerned have a civil, hygienic, or socially useful character," Mignolet said.
"Alabuga is well known as the center of manufacturing for the Shahed drones, which have been heavily used by Russia in its terror campaign against civilian infrastructure in Ukraine," EU Sanctions Envoy David O'Sullivan earlier told the Kyiv Independent, explaining the rationale behind the restrictions.
Sanctions circumvention is a crime, he added, and it falls to the national competent authorities of member states to ensure the measure is effectively enforced.
