Months after the Kyiv Independent investigation that highlighted that Drylock's Russian subsidiary publicly supports its employees who join the war against Ukraine, the company keeps on it.
Drylock's official page in VK, a Russian social network, continues to post messages supporting units of the Russian armed forces, De Tijd reported.
"Have a nice Airborne Forces Day," read a post in August, accompanying an image of a paratrooper. In July, the page marked the Russian Navy Day, saying its team "includes people connected to this holiday."

title: US intelligence believes explosives-equipped drone at German airport likely belongs to Moscow, WSJ reports
description: The details come a few days after a Ukrainian cargo plane loaded with ammunition was targeted by a drone carrying explosives at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport late on Aug. 4, German media reported.
content:
A drone carrying explosives found at the Leipzig airport in Germany likely belongs to Moscow, the Wall Street Journal reported on Aug. 7, citing U.S. intelligence.
The details come a few days after a Ukrainian cargo plane loaded with ammunition was targeted by a drone carrying explosives at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport late on Aug. 4, German media reported.
Flights at the airport were suspended overnight on Aug. 5 after a " modified drone " was sighted and later found next to a Ukrainian Antonov Airlines An-124 transport aircraft, and a second "unidentified flying object" collided with an incoming DHL cargo plane.
The authorities are still investigating the second drone that collided with the plane, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The news comes as U.S. intelligence reports raised renewed alarms that Russian President Vladimir Putin could provoke a NATO nation with a limited attack as early as this fall, the Wall Street Journal reported .
According to the Journal, officials in Washington previously believed that an attack on a NATO ally would not occur amid Russia's preoccupation with its war in Ukraine. The newfound belief by U.S. intelligence matches a chorus of similar warnings made by European officials in recent months.
Citing police reports, Suddeutsche Zeitung said the Antonov Airlines plane had been transporting an unspecified type of military ammunition from France to Leipzig, which was still onboard when the drone was found.
The outlet also said the drone was carrying Semtex, a military-grade explosive. Those behind the attempted attack are yet to be identified.
Speaking on Aug. 5, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the incident as a " hybrid attack scenario ." He did not name Russia, but the Kremlin has been waging a hybrid war aimed at destabilizing European countries for several years.
"Drone threats, including hybrid threats, are something we are familiar with from the past. However, the fact that a drone — armed with explosives — is on airport property is a new threat scenario," he said.
Suspected Russian-linked drone incidents have repeatedly disrupted airports across Europe, causing flight suspensions and diversions.
Leipzig/Halle Airport has served as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines since shortly after the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion. According to the German outlet Bild, four Ukrainian cargo aircraft were present during the suspected attack.
Suspicious drones have also been sighted near military bases in Europe, including an incident in Germany just two days after the drone was discovered at the Leipzig Airport.
Multiple drones were detected over a military base in the town of Mechernich in western Germany on Aug. 7, a Bundeswehr official confirmed. German media later reported that the site hosts specialists tasked with maintaining and repairing Patriot air defense systems.
The German military reportedly refers to the facility as the "Patriot Shipyard."
The U.S.-made Patriot system is a crucial component of Ukraine's defense against Russian aerial attacks. It remains the only weapon capable of reliably shooting down Russian ballistic missiles , which now strike Ukrainian cities multiple times a week.

title: Russian drone hits Sumy-Kyiv train, passengers evacuated on time
description: The attack occurred at around 8 a.m. local time, according to the local branch of public broadcaster Suspilne.
content:
A Russian drone struck a passenger train traveling in Sumy Oblast from Sumy to Kyiv on Aug. 8, state-owned Ukrainian Railways (Ukrzaliznytsia) said.
The drone hit the locomotive but a timely evacuation helped prevent casualties, the railway company said.
The latest attack comes as Russia increasingly targets Ukrainian trains in front-line regions, such as Sumy, Zaporizhzhia, Dnipropetrovsk, and Kharkiv oblasts. The intensified attacks have forced Ukrzaliznytsia to implement tight security protocols, which have helped prevent passenger casualties.
The attack occurred at around 8 a.m. local time, according to the local branch of public broadcaster Suspilne. It added, citing the police, that a fire had erupted following the attack.
Ukrzaliznytsia said the monitoring team detected the threat on time, allowing the train and locomotive crews to evacuate the passengers to a safe distance. It reported that one of the railcars had sustained damage.
Despite the heightened threat from drone strikes, particularly in front-line regions, Ukrainian Railways remains one of the key transport routes for civilians and soldiers traveling in and out of such areas.
Earlier this week, a Russian drone struck the Lozova railway station in Kharkiv Oblast on the morning of Aug. 6, killing two people and injuring eight others, regional authorities and Ukrainian Railways reported . A train carriage was struck at the station, and the two men killed were railway workers, Ukrainian Railways CEO Oleksandr Pertsovskyi confirmed .
In 2025, Russia has attacked Ukraine's railway infrastructure nearly 1,200 times, more than in 2024 and 2023 combined, Oleh Yakovenko, a top executive at Ukrainian Railways (Ukrzaliznytsia), said in April.

title: Ukraine says it struck 2 oil refineries in Russia
description: Ukraine's recent strikes have targeted some of the biggest oil refineries in Russia, seeking to further exacerbate the country's fuel crisis.
content:
Long-range Ukrainian drones have hit two oil refineries in Russia's Krasnodar Krai and Samara Oblast, the General Staff said on Aug. 8.
In Krasnodar Krai , in southern Russia, the Ilsky Oil Refinery sustained "a direct hit," sparking a fire on the plant's grounds, according to the General Staff. It added that the refinery has six processing units with a total capacity of about 6.6 million metric tons of crude oil per year and that its products are used to support the Russian military.
Over 1,000 kilometers northeast in Samara Oblast , the Syrzan Oil Refinery had also sustained "a direct hit," with the General Staff reporting a fire at the facility.
The refinery belongs to state-controlled oil company Rosneft and produces over 20 types of petroleum products, from motor fuels to road bitumen, according to the General Staff. It has a design capacity of about 8.5 million metric tons of crude oil annually, it added.
"The facility is one of the key sites in the Samara Region's oil refining industry and supplies fuel, in particular, to meet the needs of the Russian armed forces," the General Staff said in its Telegram statement.
The Russian Defense Ministry has not commented on the General Staff's claim. Moscow claimed it had downed 83 Ukrainian drones overnight, but did not name Krasnodar Krai or Samara Oblast among the regions over which the drones were intercepted.
The attacks come as Ukraine ramps up its long-range strikes on occupied Ukrainian territories and deep inside Russia, targeting oil refineries, airfields, vessels belonging to Russia's shadow fleet, energy infrastructure, and military-industrial facilities.
Outmanned and outgunned on the front, Ukraine is trying to slowly grind down Russia's combat capability from afar.
Ukraine's recent strikes have targeted some of the biggest oil refineries in Russia , seeking to further exacerbate the country's fuel crisis.
Russia has tapped into its fuel reserves, with stocks falling by about 4% compared to the previous year, Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed in late June at a meeting with leaders of the Russian energy industry.

title: Ukraine says it struck 12 Russian shadow fleet vessels in Black Sea and Sea of Azov
description: Since the start of the operation on July 6, Ukrainian drones have struck 218 Russian shadow fleet vessels, including 134 in the Sea of Azov and 84 in the Black Sea, according to the Unmanned Systems Forces.
content:
Ukrainian long-range drones have hit 12 Russian shadow fleet vessels in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov over the past week, Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces said on Aug. 8.
The strikes come after Ukraine launched Operation Molochka in July, a campaign targeting Russia’s shadow fleet in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov in an effort to tighten the noose around Russian-occupied Crimea peninsula.
Since the start of the operation on July 6, Ukrainian drones have struck 218 Russian shadow fleet vessels, including 134 in the Sea of Azov and 84 in the Black Sea, according to the Unmanned Systems Forces.
The attacks that struck 12 Russian shadow fleet vessels in August were conducted by the Magyar's Birds Brigade, led by Unmanned Systems Forces Commander Robert Brovdi, K-2 Brigade, and Raid Regiment, according to the report.
The Kyiv Independent couldn't independently verify the claim. Moscow had not commented as of publication time. The Russian Defense Ministry claimed on Aug. 8 that it had downed 83 Ukrainian drones overnight, including over the Azov Sea.
"Molochka Operation continues," the Unmanned Systems Forces said in its Telegram post.
The report comes as Ukraine ramps up its long-range drone strikes on occupied Crimea and across the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov to isolate the peninsula and disrupt key military routes.
"We will isolate Crimea in the near future," Brovdi, known by his callsign "Magyar," told Reuters in June.
Russia relies on a so-called shadow fleet, consisting largely of aging tankers sailing under flags of convenience, to export oil in circumvention of international sanctions, embargoes, and the G7-led price cap. The fleet enables the Kremlin to sustain oil revenues and continue financing its war against Ukraine.
Ukraine regularly strikes military infrastructure deep within Russia and the Russian-occupied territories in an effort to slowly diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war. The effect of the Ukrainian long-range strikes on Russia's military capability on the front is unclear.

title: Russian attacks across Ukraine kill at least 12, injure 81
description: The Air Force said Russia launched six Iskander-M ballistic missiles and S-400 surface-to-air missiles overnight. No missiles were shot down.
content:
Editor's note: The story was updated at 12:16 p.m. to reflect the latest report by the Kyiv City Military Administration and President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Russian attacks across Ukraine have killed at least 12 people and injured 82 others over the past day, local authorities said on Aug. 8, as yet another deadly overnight strike pounded Kyiv and its surrounding region.
The Air Force said Russia launched six Iskander-M ballistic missiles and S-400 surface-to-air missiles overnight. No missiles were shot down in the overnight strike, as Ukraine faces a critical shortage of Patriot interceptors, according to the Air Force.
The Air Force also said that 151 drones were used in the attack, and 135 drones were shot down or neutralized with electronic warfare.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said that the three people were killed in Kyiv Oblast's Brovary district on Aug. 8, including a grandmother, grandfather, and their three-year-old grandson. The child's parents and his 15-year-old brother were among the four wounded in the village of Pukhivka, as well as a neighbor who had come to help them, according to the president. The injured victims were hospitalized, he added.
The falling debris from Russian projectiles used in the attack damaged a house and cars, and a fire broke out in the territory of "a non-residential building," according to Kyiv Oblast Governor Tymur Tkachenko.
In Kyiv, a person was killed, and four others were wounded by the overnight strike, according to the city's military administration.
"Russia continues to terrorize the civilian population," Tkachenko said in his Telegram post.
In southeastern Zaporizhzhia Oblast, three people were killed, and four others were wounded by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Ivan Fedorov reported .
In northeastern Kharkiv Oblast, two people were killed, and seven others were wounded by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Oleh Syniehubov said . The two people killed were men aged around 60 in the front-line town of Izium, about 30 kilometers (19 miles) from the front.
In central Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, a person was wounded by Russian attacks over the past day, according to regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha. He said that Russia attacked six districts of the region over 10 times with drones.
In northeastern Sumy Oblast, 19 people were injured in Russian attacks over the past day, including 14 in the border community of Bilopillia, according to the regional military administration.
In eastern Donetsk Oblast, a person was killed in Sloviansk, and 15 others were injured by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Vadym Filashkin said .
In southern Kherson Oblast, two people were killed, and 26 others, including a child, were wounded by Russian attacks over the past day, regional governor Oleksandr Prokudin said .
In the southern city of Odesa, a Russian attack on one of Ukraine's largest football stadiums, home to FC Chornomorets, injured two people, according to regional governor Oleh Kiper.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,456,610 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The figure includes 1,190 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,456,610 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 8.
The figure includes 1,190 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,251 tanks, 25,099 armored combat vehicles, 131,417 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,580 artillery systems, 2,009 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,556 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine had likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers had been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: Ukraine reportedly strikes Russian oil refineries in Samara Oblast, Krasnodar Krai
description: Ukraine struck an oil refinery in Samara Oblast and another in southern Russia's Krasnodar Krai overnight on Aug. 8, monitoring channels reported.
content:
Ukraine struck an oil refinery in Samara Oblast and another in southern Russia's Krasnodar Krai overnight on Aug. 8, monitoring channels reported.
A fire broke out at an oil refinery in Syzran in Russia's Samara Oblast after being struck by Ukrainian forces, according to Telegram channel Exilenova Plus.
Another oil refinery in the town of Ilsky, Krasnodar Krai , was struck and set ablaze amid a Ukrainian attack, news channel Supernova Plus reported .
The reports could not be immediately verified by the Kyiv Independent.
Ukraine regularly strikes military infrastructure deep within Russia and the occupied territories in an effort to diminish Moscow's ability to continue waging its war.
On Aug. 7, Ukrainian forces struck a logistics center belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries in the city of Yekaterinburg, Russia, independent Russian outlet Astra reported.
Ukrainian drones targeted another warehouse belonging to major Russian online retailer Wildberries in Russia's Tula Oblast overnight on Aug. 5, authorities reported.

title: Another overnight Russian attack on Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast kills 4, including 3-year-old child
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky said that the three people killed in Kyiv Oblast's Brovary district on Aug. 8 were a grandmother, grandfather, and their three-year-old grandson.
content:
Russia launched an attack against Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight on Aug. 8, killing four people, including a three-year-old child, and injuring eight others, President Volodymyr Zelensky and the local authorities reported.
Zelensky said that the three people killed in Kyiv Oblast's Brovary district on Aug. 8 were a grandmother, grandfather, and their three-year-old grandson. The child's parents and his 15-year-old brother were among the four wounded in the village of Pukhivka, as well as a neighbor who had come to help them, according to the president. The injured victims were hospitalized, he added.
"Europe, the U.S., and Ukraine have long wanted to end the war," Zelensky said in his Facebook post.
"Only (Russian President Vladimir) Putin doesn't want to, and is clinging to his ballistic missiles and drones to keep the war going."
The rest of the injury count came from Kyiv, where the city's military administration said a person was killed and four others were wounded in the overnight attack.
Kyiv's surrounding region has been battered by aerial assaults throughout spring and summer, as a critical air defense shortage leaves the capital exposed to Russian ballistic missiles .
The attack damaged a residential building, cars, and outbuildings in the Brovary district, and a fire also broke out at a non-residential building, according to Kyiv Oblast Governor Tymyr Tkachenko. Emergency crews are continuing to work at the affected sites.
The latest strike on Brovary, a suburb east of Kyiv, comes as the community is still reeling from a mass Russian attack that killed eight people on a train platform . The attack marked one of the most intense Russian bombardments in Brovary since the start of the war.
In Kyiv, fires broke out in two separate garages and a commercial building in the Holosiivskyi district, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) reported.
Another fire was extinguished "on the territory of an enterprise" in the Obolonskyi district, DSNS wrote .
Shortly after midnight on Aug. 8, Ukraine's Air Force began alerting residents that waves of drones were approaching Kyiv and the surrounding region. Explosions were first heard in the city at around 12:45 a.m. local time, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground.
Less than 15 minutes later, another round of blasts rocked the city. At around 3 a.m., as rescue crews were putting out fires in Brovary, Kyiv Independent journalists reported more explosions and said ballistic missiles were attacking the capital.
The Air Force also warned that Russian drones and guided aerial bombs were bound for other areas of the country. Explosions have been reported in Dnipro, the fourth-largest city in Ukraine.
Attacks are ongoing, and the full extent of the damage and casualties is not yet known.
While Russia has terrorized Ukrainian cities with aerial attacks throughout the full-scale invasion, the intensified bombardments of 2026 exploit Ukraine's air defense crisis, leading to deadlier and more devastating strikes.
Russia has been launching barrages of ballistic missiles at Kyiv and other cities with increasing frequency, destroying apartment buildings, critical energy facilities , and civilian infrastructure . Without a sufficient supply of Patriot interceptors, these targets are nearly defenseless against Russian ballistic missiles.
The Defense Ministry reported on Aug. 7 that Ukraine managed to intercept only 29 of the 195 ballistic missiles Russia launched at the country in July.
Russia's most recent mass attack hit Kyiv and the surrounding region only 48 hours earlier, killing 17 people and injuring nearly 30 others overnight on Aug. 5. 24 None of the 24 ballistic and four hypersonic missiles Russia launched during the assault were intercepted, Ukraine's Air Force said.

title: Suspicious drones sighted over German military base days after Leipzig airport incident
description: Two drones were detected over a military base in the town of Mechernich in western Germany, authorities said. Police are investigating the incident, which comes mere days after a serious drone breach at Leipzig Airport.
content:
Editor's Note: German media later reported that the Mechernich military base is used to repair U.S.-made Patriot air defense systems. Read the latest update .
Two drones were detected over a military base in the town of Mechernich in western Germany, a Bundeswehr official said on Aug. 7.
The suspicious sighting comes two days after a serious security incident involving unknown drones at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport overnight on Aug. 5. One drone was found next to a Ukrainian transport plane while another collided with an incoming cargo plane, causing minor damage and temporary suspension of flight operations.
Two days later, at around 10:00 a.m. local time on Aug. 7, two drones were spotted over the Mechernich military base, located in Germany's Euskirchen district in the state of North Rhine-Westphalia. A spokesperson from the Bundeswehr Operational Command confirmed the sighting, according to the German media outlet Die Zeit.
Military police first investigated the incident, the spokesperson said. The investigation has now been handed over to local law enforcement in Euskirchen.
Suspected Russian-linked drone incidents have repeatedly disrupted airports across Europe, causing flight suspensions and diversions. Similar incidents have been reported at military bases in EU and NATO countries.
The Leipzig airport incident marks an escalation in the security threat posed by such incidents, with German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt calling it "very serious."
Authorities reported that a "modified drone" containing a detonator and an "unknown substance" was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov Airlines An-124 transport aircraft at the airport, which has served as a base for Antonov Airlines since shortly after the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion.
Another "unidentified flying object" collided with a DHL plane, forcing it to re-route to Hamburg Airport. No casualties resulted from either incident.
The drone breach triggered a meeting of Germany's National Security Council. Dobrindt did not rule out the possibility that "foreign powers" were behind the operation, which might represent a "hybrid attack."
The increase in drone sightings has raised alarm over Russia's potential military capabilities in Europe and NATO.
In June, German Army Chief Christian Freuding warned that Russia might be ready to strike NATO countries within the next three years.

title: Russian attacks on critical Ukrainian energy infrastructure destroy key facilities ahead of winter
description: Russia hit seven Naftogaz facilities in eastern Ukraine overnight, destroying critical equipment and forcing multiple sites to shut down.
content:
Russian attacks against Ukraine on Aug. 7 targeted critical energy sites operated by state oil and gas company Naftogaz, shutting down production at several facilities, the firm reported.
The targeted sites were owned by the oil and gas extraction company Ukrnafta , a subsidiary of Naftogaz . Seven Ukrnafta facilities in eastern Ukraine were hit overnight.
"Russia is systematically attacking Ukrainian oil and gas production in order to cause maximum damage to our infrastructure on the eve of winter," Serhii Fedorenko, acting Naftogaz Board Chairman, said following the strikes.
"Tonight, the most massive shelling of Ukrnafta facilities in recent times took place."
Russia targeted facilities that ensure the production of oil and gas in eastern Ukraine , Naftogaz reported. Critical equipment was destroyed in the attacks, forcing multiple facilities to shut down and causing significant production losses.
There were no casualties at any of the targeted sites, the company said.
During the day on Aug. 7, Russia continued assaulting Ukraine's energy infrastructure, hitting four Ukrnafta gas stations in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts.
Throughout summer 2026, Russia has been increasing attacks against gas stations across Ukraine, striking not only facilities in the east and south but also targets in central regions.
The attacks have made routine fueling stops dangerous for civilians and have disrupted supply deliveries to front-line areas.
Ukraine's growing air defense emergency makes it difficult to defend these facilities or slow the expansion of the Russian campaign. The situation could become more dire as summer draws to a close.
Since the first year of the full-scale invasion, Russia has hammered Ukraine's critical energy infrastructure during the fall and winter months, crippling the power grid and freezing civilians as temperatures plunge.
Officials have warned that this winter could be even harsher than the last, which saw daily blackouts and heating outages during subzero conditions.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said in July that Ukraine's energy sector was falling behind its winter preparedness goals and needed to accelerate operations.

title: Ukraine war latest: Ukraine intercepted 29 of 195 Russian ballistic missiles in July as air defense shortages deepen, ministry says
description:
Key developments on Aug. 7:

 * Ukraine intercepted 29 out of 195 Russian ballistic missiles in July as air defense shortages worsen, Defense Ministry says
 * 60% of Ukrainians oppose ceding Donbas to Russia, but same share back freezing war with security guarantees, poll shows
 * Ukraine attacks Wildberries logistics center in Russia located nearly 2,000 km from front line
 * One of Ukraine's largest football stadiums damaged in Russian strike on Odesa
 * Skelia Assault Regiment troops to be tr
content:
Ukraine intercepted only 29 of the 195 ballistic missiles Russia launched at the country in July as air defenses faced a critical shortage of interceptor missiles, the Defense Ministry said on Aug. 7.
"Ukrainian air defense operated in July under conditions of a critical shortage of interceptor missiles to counter ballistic terror," the ministry said .
The list of ballistic missiles included in the Defense Ministry's report covered Russian Iskander-M and 48N6DM missiles, as well as North Korean KN-23 missiles. The report also covered Zircon missiles , which Russia has presented as hypersonic cruise missiles, though recent analysis suggests they may be capable of a quasi-ballistic flight path.
In addition to the ballistic missiles intercepted by Ukraine, another 40 failed to reach their targets, the ministry added.
Russia also launched 265 cruise missiles, including Kalibr, Iskander-K, and Kh-101 missiles, of which 187 were intercepted by Ukrainian forces.
Sixty percent of Ukrainians are opposed to territorial concessions in the Donbas region to Russia, while the same share would be willing to accept a freeze of the war along the current front line in exchange for security guarantees, according to a poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KIIS).
According to the poll results , 33% of respondents said they would be willing to give up territory in eastern Ukraine, including Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts , though most viewed such a decision as a difficult concession. Another 7% were undecided.
The poll also showed that a majority of Ukrainians do not expect Russia's war against Ukraine to end in the near future.
Forty-five percent of respondents said they believe the war could end no earlier than the second half of 2027, while 21% expect it to end by the end of this year. Another 15% said they expect the war to conclude in the first half of 2027. Another 19% of respondents were undecided on the issue.
The share of Ukrainians willing to endure the war for as long as necessary has also risen to 61%, after falling to 48% in April 2026.
The poll, conducted from July 20 to Aug. 3 and published on Aug. 7, surveyed 974 respondents aged 18 and older living in Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Ukrainian forces struck a logistics center belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries in the city of Yekaterinburg, Russia, on Aug. 7, Russian independent outlet Astra reported.
The first photos and videos emerged on Russian social media around 5 a.m. local time, showing smoke rising from the Wildberries facility.
About an hour earlier, Sverdlovsk Oblast Governor Denis Pasler said the region was under attack by Ukrainian drones , while Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsiya, imposed temporary flight restrictions at Koltsovo Airport in Yekaterinburg.
The strike, located about 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles) from the front line, sparked a large fire, according to the Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ .
Artem Zhoga, the Russian presidential envoy to the Ural Federal District, said no one was injured in the attack and that about 800 people were evacuated from the facility.
Wildberries also confirmed the attack on its facility, saying the fire had been contained and that the processing of new deliveries was temporarily restricted and redirected to other sites.
Pasler said Russian forces had allegedly downed eight drones over the region during the attack, three of which crashed onto the roof of the logistics center. Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses had shot down a total of 203 Ukrainian drones overnight on Aug. 7.
A Russian strike on Odesa on Aug. 7 damaged one of Ukraine's largest football stadiums, home to FC Chornomorets, and injured at least two people, Governor Oleh Kiper said.
The attack occurred at around 3:30 p.m. local time, shortly after Ukraine's Air Force warned that jet-powered drones were approaching Odesa Oblast .
A 29-year-old woman who was at the stadium during the attack was injured. She received medical treatment at the scene, Kiper said.
Around 8 p.m. local time, Kiper said the number of injured had risen to two after a 31-year-old man sought medical treatment. He was hospitalized.
The venue, located in central Odesa near the city's port, suffered significant damage. The roof was partially destroyed, while the glazing and spectator stands were also damaged.
Chornomorets Stadium is one of Ukraine's largest football venues, with a capacity of 34,164 spectators. Before Russia's full-scale invasion, it hosted UEFA competition matches, as well as international fixtures involving Ukraine's national team.
The stadium is now home to the men's FC Chornomorets and the women's SeaSters football club. The facility hosts top-flight matches in both Ukraine's men's and women's football leagues.
It was scheduled to host the next Ukrainian Premier League men's match on Aug. 8. Organizers said the match would be postponed, but did not specify when or where it would be played.
As of July 20, Russian forces had damaged or destroyed 915 sports infrastructure facilities across Ukraine, according to Youth and Sports Ministry .
Russian forces have intensified attacks on Odesa and the surrounding region this summer, coinciding with the peak tourist season, when thousands of visitors travel to the Black Sea coast.
Soldiers from the 425th Separate Assault Regiment "Skelia" are being transferred to other formations following reports of alleged abuse within the unit, Ukrainska Pravda reported on Aug. 7, citing sources in the regiment and Ukraine's Defense Forces.
"Skelia" is one of Ukraine's largest assault formations, with more than 10,000 personnel. The unit expanded rapidly under former Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi , receiving a disproportionate share of newly mobilized recruits even as regular mechanized brigades struggled with severe personnel shortages.
The order to reassign "Skelia" personnel was issued roughly a week ago, with soldiers being transferred to around 10 other units, according to Ukrainska Pravda . The outlet did not specify the exact number of personnel affected but reported that some "Skelia" soldiers were dissatisfied with the decision.
An undisclosed source in Ukraine's Defense Forces told Ukrainska Pravda that the regiment was being restructured because it had been "artificially inflated," while the quality of its command remained low despite its large number of personnel.

title: Skelia Assault Regiment troops to be transferred to other units following abuse allegations, media reports
description: The order to reassign "Skelia" personnel was issued roughly a week ago, with soldiers being transferred to around 10 other units, according to Ukrainska Pravda.
content:
Soldiers from the 425th Separate Assault Regiment "Skelia" are being transferred to other formations following reports of alleged abuse within the unit, Ukrainska Pravda reported on Aug. 7, citing sources in the regiment and Ukraine's Defense Forces.
"Skelia" is one of Ukraine's largest assault formations, with more than 10,000 personnel. The unit expanded rapidly under former Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi , receiving a disproportionate share of newly mobilized recruits even as regular mechanized brigades struggled with severe personnel shortages.
The order to reassign "Skelia" personnel was issued roughly a week ago, with soldiers being transferred to around 10 other units, according to Ukrainska Pravda . The outlet did not specify the exact number of personnel affected but reported that some "Skelia" soldiers were dissatisfied with the decision.
An undisclosed source in Ukraine's Defense Forces told Ukrainska Pravda that the regiment was being restructured because it had been "artificially inflated," while the quality of its command remained low despite its large number of personnel.
The transfers follow broader changes affecting Ukraine's assault formations. On July 31, newly appointed Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi had ordered Ground Forces assault regiments to stop receiving additional personnel as of July 26 amid allegations of misconduct.
"Skelia" has become the most prominent example of controversy surrounding the assault-unit system. An investigation documented at least 26 reported noncombat deaths among its recruits between late 2025 and spring 2026, as well as allegations of abuse and denial of medical treatment.
Regiment commander Lieutenant Colonel Yurii Harkavyi was subsequently suspended pending an investigation into alleged violations of soldiers' rights, while two "Skelia" service members were charged in July with allegedly torturing fellow soldiers.
The General Staff also announced on July 29 that it had begun reviewing the staffing of military units and the fairness of personnel distribution across the Armed Forces. It did not specify whether the review concerned individual formations or the military as a whole.

title: Fedorov continues talks with Musk on using Starlink to help counter Russian ballistic missiles
description: "We're in touch with Musk; we last spoke a few days ago. And it's, let's just say, a difficult task right now to achieve the outcome we need through this communication," Mykhailo Fedorov said in an interview with his former adviser, Serhii Sternenko.
content:
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said on Aug. 6 that he remains in talks with Elon Musk over the potential use of Starlink terminals to counter ballistic missile systems deployed on Russian territory.
"We're in touch with Musk ; we last spoke a few days ago. And it's, let's just say, a difficult task right now to achieve the outcome we need through this communication," Fedorov said in an interview with his former adviser, Serhii Sternenko .
Starlink terminals are not officially sold or supported in Russia, as SpaceX does not provide services there. Despite this, Russian forces have obtained the terminals through third countries and are using them in occupied Ukrainian territories for communications and drone operations.
Fedorov added that restricting access to the terminals is crucial, warning that Starlink access could give Russia "the ability to control operations from Moscow, fly over roads, change flight paths beyond the reach of our radars and acoustic sensors, take out all the F-16s and Patriots, and strike all military targets."
Fedorov did not provide further details on the status of the negotiations.
Fedorov's statement comes as Ukraine faces a critical shortage of air defense capabilities to intercept Russian ballistic missiles. Patriot systems are currently the only weapons in Ukraine's arsenal capable of countering such targets, but Kyiv faces severe shortages of Patriot interceptors , also affected by U.S. military demands related to the war in Iran.
Fedorov, who was controversially dismissed from his post in mid-July, initiated talks with Musk over restricting Starlink access for Russian forces operating in Ukrainian territory. The move was credited with helping Ukraine regain the initiative in early 2026 by disrupting Russian communications and logistics.
Russian forces have since started developing a domestic alternative, the Rassvet ("Dawn" in English) satellite internet network, though the project's status and timeline remain unclear.

title: Zelensky begins first official visit to Serbia, says 'Ukraine is always ready to work constructively'
description: Zelensky held talks with Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic on the evening of Aug. 7.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky met with Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic in Belgrade on Aug. 7, marking his first official visit to the country.
The trip is seen as symbolic, as Serbia has traditionally maintained close ties with Russia.
"We will discuss expanding economic ties between our countries, relations with the European Union, other areas that can benefit our nations, and security issues," Zelensky wrote following his arrival.
"Ukraine is always ready to work constructively, for mutual benefit, and on the basis of mutual respect," the president added.
The two-day trip will include meetings with both Vucic and Serbian Prime Minister Duro Macut. Late in the evening on Aug. 7, Zelensky reported that his discussions with Vucic had begun.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Serbia has sought to strike a careful diplomatic balance between Moscow and the West. Russia has historically been one of Serbia's key diplomatic allies, and Serbia relied heavily on Russia for natural gas .
According to reports, Serbia has also indirectly supplied arms to Ukraine, although Vucic publicly denied it in May 2025.
At the time, Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, the SVR, accused Serbia's defense industry of "trying to shoot Russia in the back."
Vucic made his first official trip to Ukraine in June 2025 as part of the Ukraine-Southeast Europe summit in Odesa.
Unlike the other participants at the summit, Vucic did not sign a joint declaration that denounced Russia's illegal aggression, called for a full withdrawal of Russian forces from Ukraine, and reaffirmed support for Ukraine's territorial integrity.

title: Ukraine intercepted 29 out of 195 Russian ballistic missiles in July as air defense shortages worsen, Defense Ministry says
description: "Ukrainian air defense operated in July under conditions of a critical shortage of interceptor missiles to counter ballistic terror," the ministry said.
content:
Ukraine intercepted only 29 of the 195 ballistic missiles Russia launched at the country in July as air defenses faced a critical shortage of interceptor missiles, the Defense Ministry said on Aug. 7.
"Ukrainian air defense operated in July under conditions of a critical shortage of interceptor missiles to counter ballistic terror," the ministry said .
The latest attacks illustrate the growing challenge. Ukrainian forces failed to intercept any of the 24 ballistic missiles or four Zircon anti-ship missiles launched by Russia on Aug. 5, according to the Air Force. Days earlier, on Aug. 1, Ukraine shot down only one of 27 ballistic missiles, citing shortages of air defense interceptors, particularly U.S.-made Patriot systems .
The list of ballistic missiles included in the Defense Ministry's report covered Russian Iskander-M and 48N6DM missiles, as well as North Korean KN-23 missiles. The report also covered Zircon missiles , which Russia has presented as hypersonic cruise missiles, though recent analysis suggests they may be capable of a quasi-ballistic flight path.
In addition to the ballistic missiles intercepted by Ukraine, another 40 failed to reach their targets, the ministry added.
Russia also launched 265 cruise missiles, including Kalibr, Iskander-K, and Kh-101 missiles, of which 187 were intercepted by Ukrainian forces.
Ukrainian forces detected 8,653 Russian attack drones over the month and intercepted 5,142, including Shahed-, Gerbera-, and Italmas-type drones, according to the ministry.
In total, Russia launched more than 9,000 attack drones and missiles against Ukraine in July, excluding reconnaissance drones. Ukrainian forces intercepted more than 5,300 of them using aircraft, anti-aircraft missile systems, electronic warfare, unmanned systems, and mobile fire groups, the report read.
Ballistic missiles proved particularly difficult to intercept during July's largest combined attacks. Ukraine downed four of the 28 missiles flying along ballistic trajectories on July 2, none during the July 6 attack , and one during the July 30 attack, the ministry said.
The Defense Ministry said ballistic missiles remained the main challenge for Ukrainian air defenses and that it was working with international partners to obtain additional air defense systems and interceptor missiles.
Ukraine is also seeking Meteor missiles for its Gripen fighter jets to counter Russian aircraft launching guided aerial bombs, the ministry added.

title: What's missing from Ukraine's EU checklist?
description:
Ukraine has opened the sixth negotiation cluster, "External Relations," bringing the country one step closer to European Union membership. Although the cluster's description underscores the importance of aligning Ukraine's sanctions policy with that of the EU, the benchmarks make no mention of the reforms needed in this area – at least not yet.

That omission is deeply troubling.

Sanctions have become an increasingly contentious issue in Ukrainian society following yet another round of personal
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky (L), European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen (R) at an emergency EU leaders summit on Ukraine and defense in Brussels, Belgium, on March 6, 2025. (Nicolas Economou / NurPhoto / Getty Images)
Head of the Institute of Legislative Ideas
Ukraine has opened the sixth negotiation cluster, "External Relations," bringing the country one step closer to European Union membership. Although the cluster's description underscores the importance of aligning Ukraine's sanctions policy with that of the EU, the benchmarks make no mention of the reforms needed in this area – at least not yet.
Sanctions have become an increasingly contentious issue in Ukrainian society following yet another round of personal restrictions imposed on politicians without transparent justification, controversial judicial practices, and losses before the European Court of Human Rights.
A closer look at the principal flaws in Ukraine 's sanctions policy shows both the necessity and the value of making reform in this field a separate benchmark.
Recently, many people criticized Ukraine's imposition of sanctions on its own citizens, particularly on political figures and government opponents, including former President of Ukraine Petro Poroshenko , former Member of the Verkhovna Rada Boryslav Bereza, former Head of the Presidential Office Andriy Bohdan , and others.
One point should be clear from the outset: Ukraine has long had a legal framework for imposing sanctions on its own citizens, and the EU likewise imposes sanctions on its own citizens in exceptional cases where a demonstrable security threat exists.
The problem, though, is not the use of sanctions itself, but the procedure by which they are imposed, the reasons given for them, and the transparency of the process.
When resolutions of the National Security and Defense Council are based on classified reports, while the affected individual is denied access to the allegations and any meaningful opportunity to defend themselves, the process begins to look less like a means of countering an enemy and more like an instrument of domestic political pressure.
That, in turn, erodes trust in the sanctions system itself. Ukraine has already lost its first case before the European Court of Human Rights, and more such cases are likely to follow.
The inability to challenge sanctions effectively, either before the authority that imposed them, even when the grounds for extending them no longer exist, or in court, because the Supreme Court declines to assess the substance of those grounds, bears little resemblance to European practice and further undermines confidence in Ukraine's sanctions machinery.
EU membership requires compliance with sanctions regulations as directly applicable legal acts. Yet Ukraine still lacks several mechanisms needed to make its sanctions policy predictable, effective, and consistent with human rights.
One significant gap between Ukrainian and European sanctions law is the absence of a dedicated "authorization" mechanism.
As a result, sanctions can inflict "collateral damage" on business partners, employees, and family members who are not themselves sanctioned. In some cases, they can even harm the national economy when the operations of major enterprises are blocked.
One of such examples is the dispute over the division of property between the Poroshenko spouses.
The former president's wife, who was not subject to sanctions, succeeded on appeal in securing the right to use her share of the assets. In a similar but non-public case, courts at several levels rejected such an arrangement. The contrast exposes the need for uniform, clear, and transparent rules in Ukraine's sanctions policy.
Ukraine also lacks a sanctions-reporting system, an effective mechanism for monitoring assets and preventing sanctions evasion.
European countries hold sanctions violators accountable. Ukraine, by contrast, still imposes no penalties for circumventing sanctions. A solution was developed long ago, yet it has remained stalled in Parliament for more than a year.
The Institute for Legislative Ideas, together with more than 10 government agencies, developed a comprehensive bill to align Ukrainian sanctions legislation with European standards.
In January 2025, Volodymyr Zelensky submitted it to the Verkhovna Rada as urgent.
Yet there simply "are not enough votes" in the Verkhovna Rada. Political expediency on one side, and lawmakers' reluctance to impose liability before the problems described above are resolved on the other, appear to outweigh the state's strategic interests and the demands of the rule of law .
The need to reform sanctions policy has long been apparent, and there seems to be broad agreement on that point. Yet the political process has reached an impasse between two competing approaches.
The first is a simple and rapid political fix: exempt Ukrainian citizens from sanctions while leaving the current system intact — a system that remains largely opaque, unpredictable, and highly dependent on political expediency.
The second is more difficult but strategic: use this moment to pursue comprehensive reform by introducing clear rules, transparent procedures, and guarantees for the protection of human rights in line with European standards.
Without an external incentive, the Ukrainian authorities are unlikely to reach a political consensus on this choice in the near future.
The European Union can therefore play a decisive role by making the alignment of Ukraine's sanctions legislation with the EU acquis a specific benchmark in the accession negotiations, as it would provide Ukraine with the leverage needed to complete a long-overdue transformation.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.
Tetiana Khutor is the chairwoman of the Institute of Legislative Ideas, an independent Ukrainian think tank that provides anti-corruption policy analysis, and a non-resident fellow at the Centre for Defence Strategies. Khutor was a legislative director for the Ukrainian Anticorruption Parliament Committee head from 2015-2018. She is also a senior lecturer on anticorruption policy and asset recovery at the National University of "Kyiv-Mohyla Academy" and holds a Ph.D. in law focusing on civil confiscation of unjustified assets.

title: 'Time to act is now' — US Senate passes long-delayed Russia sanctions bill targeting energy buyers
description: The Senate vote clears the way for House consideration as early as next month.
content:
A majority of the U.S. Senate backed sweeping Russia sanctions legislation on Aug. 7 that would impose tariffs on countries purchasing Russian oil and gas, aiming to cut off a key source of funding for Moscow's war against Ukraine.
The bill had been stalled in Congress since April 2025 amid President Donald Trump's evolving approach to Russia's war against Ukraine. The Senate vote clears the way for House consideration as early as next month. The vote was 86-11.
The revised bill emerged from negotiations between the White House and the late Senator Lindsey Graham , who said shortly before his death on July 11 that he had secured the Trump administration's support for the proposal.
Lawmakers argue the measure would provide the Trump administration with another tool to pressure Moscow to end its war against Ukraine.
"Today, the Senate sent Vladimir Putin an unambiguous and bipartisan message in the only language he understands: pressure," Senator Jeanne Shaheen said.
"When the House returns, they must send this legislation to the President's desk without delay... Every day this legislation waits is another day Putin profits from energy sales to buy rockets, drones, and weapons to kill Ukrainians. The time to act is now."
President Volodymyr Zelensky thanked senators for supporting the bill and continuing to mount pressure against Russia.
"We are deeply grateful to the U.S. Senate and to everyone who supports Ukraine," he wrote on Aug. 7.
"The passage of Senator Lindsey Graham's bill regarding sanctions against Russia and Iran will undoubtedly help to increase pressure on the aggressor to end this insane Russian war against our independence and our people."
Unlike the original version, which proposed a blanket 500% tariff on imports from countries purchasing Russian oil or natural gas, the revised legislation would impose tariffs of up to 100% on the world's five largest buyers of Russian energy.
The same maximum tariff would apply to the five countries most involved in helping Russia evade oil sanctions.
Under the draft legislation, the list of the five largest purchasers would be reviewed every 180 days. Countries that import less than 15% of Russia's total natural gas exports and are actively reducing those imports would be exempt.
China, India, and Turkey are currently the largest buyers of Russian oil, while the EU, China , and Turkey are among the largest importers of Russian natural gas.
The legislation would also target Russian President Vladimir Putin and other senior Russian officials, as well as major Russian financial institutions, including the Central Bank, Sberbank, and Gazprombank.
It would further target Russian state-owned companies, foreign entities supporting Russia's defense-industrial base, and major Russian energy projects.
The bill also includes measures targeting Russia's shadow fleet , which Moscow uses to continue exporting oil despite Western sanctions, as well as China's support for Russia's defense industry.

title: 60% of Ukrainians oppose ceding Donbas to Russia, but same share back freezing war with security guarantees, poll shows
description: According to the poll results, 33% of respondents said they would be willing to give up territory in eastern Ukraine, including Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts.
content:
