The poll was conducted as peace talks involving Ukraine , Russia , and mediators including the U.S. remained deadlocked . At the same time, Russian forces have continued attacks across Ukraine, where a shortage of air defense missiles has contributed to mounting civilian casualties.
According to the poll results , 33% of respondents said they would be willing to give up territory in eastern Ukraine, including Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts , though most viewed such a decision as a difficult concession. Another 7% were undecided.
Under a scenario involving a freeze of the war along the current front line in exchange for security guarantees in the form of substantial funding and weapons supplies, 59% of respondents said they would be willing to support the arrangement, although most did so reluctantly. Thirty-one percent strongly opposed the idea.
The poll also showed that a majority of Ukrainians do not expect Russia's war against Ukraine to end in the near future.
Forty-five percent of respondents said they believe the war could end no earlier than the second half of 2027, while 21% expect it to end by the end of this year. Another 15% said they expect the war to conclude in the first half of 2027. Another 19% of respondents were undecided on the issue.
The share of Ukrainians willing to endure the war for as long as necessary has also risen to 61%, after falling to 48% in April 2026.
The poll, conducted from July 20 to Aug. 3 and published on Aug. 7, surveyed 974 respondents aged 18 and older living in Ukrainian-controlled territory.

title: One of Ukraine's largest football stadiums damaged in Russian strike on Odesa
description: The attack occurred at around 3:30 p.m. local time, shortly after Ukraine's Air Force warned that jet-powered drones were approaching Odesa Oblast.
content:
A Russian strike on Odesa on Aug. 7 damaged one of Ukraine's largest football stadiums, home to FC Chornomorets, and injured at least two people, Governor Oleh Kiper said.
The attack occurred at around 3:30 p.m. local time, shortly after Ukraine's Air Force warned that jet-powered drones were approaching Odesa Oblast .
A 29-year-old woman who was at the stadium during the attack was injured. She received medical treatment at the scene, Kiper said.
Around 8 p.m. local time, Kiper said the number of injured had risen to two after a 31-year-old man sought medical treatment. He was hospitalized.
The venue, located in central Odesa near the city's port, suffered significant damage. The roof was partially destroyed, while the glazing and spectator stands were also damaged.
Chornomorets Stadium is one of Ukraine's largest football venues, with a capacity of 34,164 spectators. Before Russia's full-scale invasion, it hosted UEFA competition matches, as well as international fixtures involving Ukraine's national team.
The stadium is now home to the men's FC Chornomorets and the women's SeaSters football club. The facility hosts top-flight matches in both Ukraine's men's and women's football leagues.
It was scheduled to host the next Ukrainian Premier League men's match on Aug. 8. Organizers said the match would be postponed, but did not specify when or where it would be played.
As of July 20, Russian forces had damaged or destroyed 915 sports infrastructure facilities across Ukraine, according to Youth and Sports Ministry .
Russian forces have intensified attacks on Odesa and the surrounding region this summer, coinciding with the peak tourist season, when thousands of visitors travel to the Black Sea coast.
The city has been targeted with both drones and missiles, including Banderol missiles, which Russia has used to strike port infrastructure in the region.
The attacks have also damaged dozens of civilian vessels passing through Odesa’s ports and caused casualties among crew members.
In July, Russian forces carried out 124 attacks on Ukraine's maritime infrastructure, targeting seaports, civilian vessels in ports, and ships operating within the Ukrainian maritime corridor, according to the Development of Communities and Territories Ministry.

title: Ukraine stalls on justice, anti-corruption reforms promised to EU
description:
Back in December, Ukraine agreed to a comprehensive package of rule-of-law reforms, as one of the steps needed to move forward with EU accession talks and secure necessary funding.

Soon after the agreement was signed, the government deprioritized the promised reforms.

"None of the crucial reforms related to the justice system, law enforcement, or anti-corruption have been implemented," Vitaly Shabunin, head of the Anti-Corruption Action Center's executive board, told the Kyiv Independent.

The
content:
Ukraine's then-Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration Taras Kachka (C) arrives for a press conference with Cyprus Deputy Minister for European Affairs Marilena Raouna (L) and EU Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos (R) in Brussels, Belgium, on March 17, 2026. (Nicolas Tucat / AFP / Getty Images)
Back in December, Ukraine agreed to a comprehensive package of rule-of-law reforms, as one of the steps needed to move forward with EU accession talks and secure necessary funding.
Soon after the agreement was signed, the government deprioritized the promised reforms.
" None of the crucial reforms related to the justice system, law enforcement, or anti-corruption have been implemented," Vitaly Shabunin , head of the Anti-Corruption Action Center's executive board, told the Kyiv Independent.
The roadmap was endorsed by EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos and Ukraine's then Deputy Prime Minister for European Integration Taras Kachka . Most of the clauses of the Kachka-Kos plan are included in the benchmarks for Ukraine's EU accession.
Several clauses of the initial 10-point plan were also included in July in the EU's Ukraine Facility lending program as requirements for loan disbursements.
Anti-corruption and judicial experts argue that President Volodymyr Zelensky 's administration has little appetite for implementing the promised reforms. They say Zelensky fears losing political control over law enforcement, and he is also wary of independent investigators taking on corruption in his inner circle.
"What is at stake is Ukraine's future in the EU," Shabunin said.
The President's Office did not respond to requests for comment.
Spokespeople for Vsevolod Chentsov, the new deputy prime minister for European integration, the Justice Ministry, and the Ukrainian parliament's law enforcement committee all declined to comment.
According to an EU assessment published in June, only 15% of the Kachka-Kos plan had been implemented despite the end-of-year deadline, with progress largely limited to the initial stages of the legislative process.
Mykhailo Zhernakov , head of judicial watchdog Dejure, said that, according to his information, Kachka "had been urging the authorities to at least start taking action" to implement the plan.
Kachka lost his job during the July government reshuffle and is set to be appointed as Ukraine's ambassador to the EU.
"It feels as though Kachka ended up paying the price for the bold commitments he made," Anastasia Radina, head of parliament's anti-corruption committee, told the Kyiv Independent.
At the same time, Kachka has also faced criticism for not pushing strongly enough for the plan's implementation.
Kachka did not respond to a request for comment.
According to the Kachka-Kos plan , Ukraine must adopt a law improving the mechanism of integrity declarations for judges — statements in which judges answer questions linked to integrity and ethics standards.
In June, parliament passed a law on integrity declarations.
However, the judicial watchdog Dejure said that "while presented as a measure to improve judicial integrity declarations, the bill would in fact make it easier for judges to evade accountability for false statements."
" Instead of reviving a weak but important mechanism for vetting judges' integrity, lawmakers have chosen to dismantle it altogether," the watchdog added.
The Ukrainian authorities denied the accusations.
It is not clear if the European Commission will accept the bill as complying with its Ukraine Facility lending program.
" The European Commission is assessing the law carefully in the context of the conditionality under the Ukraine Plan, and will finalize its assessment once Ukraine submits it as part of a payment request," the commission told the Kyiv Independent. "In carrying out this assessment, the (European) Commission will take into account any relevant opinions of the Venice Commission."
The next installment in the program is scheduled for September.
However, Kos, the EU commissioner for enlargement, allegedly persuaded lawmakers to support the bill, two sources familiar with the matter told the Kyiv Independent.
The plan also envisages auditing the integrity declarations of incumbent Supreme Court judges with the help of international experts. The EU has demanded a reform of the Supreme Court due to the corruption scandals that have engulfed the institution.
The bill on integrity declarations passed by parliament contains a clause instructing the Cabinet of Ministers to draft, within six months, a separate bill on Supreme Court declarations.
" It's unclear why they need six months to draft a bill that will contain just three provisions," Anton Zelinsky, an expert at Dejure, told the Kyiv Independent.
The European Commission told the Kyiv Independent that "while there is no specific deadline," the commission "encouraged Ukraine to prioritize this reform."
Another clause of the so-called Kachka-Kos plan stipulates passing a bill to reform the State Investigation Bureau "in line with best European practices."
Since its creation in 2016, the State Investigation Bureau has faced accusations of being a political tool of the President's Office. Oleksiy Sukhachov was appointed as the bureau's head in 2022 as a result of a non-transparent contest that anti-corruption activists described as fake and politicized.
Zelensky pledged in January to submit a bill to reform the bureau by the end of the month. So far, he has failed to do so.
Radina and opposition lawmaker Yaroslav Zheleznyak submitted an alternative bill on State Investigation Bureau reform in August 2025. But the Ukrainian parliament has so far failed to consider it.
" Unfortunately, nearly a year has passed since then, and there has been virtually no progress on it," Radina said .
The Kachka-Kos plan envisages "strengthening the independence of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau ( NABU ) and the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office ( SAPO ) and protecting their jurisdiction from circumvention and undue influence." It also calls for "expanding the jurisdiction of NABU and SAPO to cover all high-risk positions" — a reference to employees of the President's Office currently exempt from oversight — and ensuring that the NABU has access to impartial forensic examinations.
The demands followed a conflict between the Zelensky administration and the anti-corruption institutions.
The standoff culminated in July 2025, when Zelensky signed a law that subordinated the NABU to the prosecutor general, an official appointed by the president. The bureau's independence was later restored amid protests and Western pressure.
Radina said that she and her colleagues are working on a bill on independent forensic assessments for the NABU. The Anti-Corruption Bureau remains heavily reliant on external forensic procedures, limiting its ability to operate independently and raising concerns about potential leaks of sensitive information from the institution.
According to the reform roadmap, Ukraine should also "conduct a comprehensive review of the selection and dismissal procedure of the prosecutor general, with a view to aligning it with European best practice." The plan also envisages reinstating transparent contests for other top prosecutor jobs.
In June, Radina submitted to parliament a bill seeking to select the prosecutor general in a transparent contest with the participation of international experts.
Radina's opponents argue that the Kachka-Kos plan does not envisage a contest involving international experts.
Kachka himself has faced criticism for saying in a July 27 interview that there is no direct demand for a transparent contest and claiming that Ukraine's controversial prosecutor's office is "good."
"There may be different interpretations of the benchmark, but I'm not aware of anyone having proposed an alternative approach so far," Radina said.
Ukraine's prosecutor generals are appointed by the president with parliament's approval and have been seen as closely aligned to whoever is in power. Radina's bill seeks to depoliticize the prosecutor general's appointment.
Ruslan Kravchenko , the current prosecutor general, has faced scrutiny , partially due to his role in the crackdown on the Anti-Corruption Bureau in 2025.
"Revised selection and dismissal rules should improve objectivity, transparency, and merit-based procedures, and lead to the depoliticization of the position of the prosecutor general," the European Commission told the Kyiv Independent.
According to the plan, Ukraine must also extend "the involvement of international experts in the selection commission for the High Qualification Commission," a judicial governing body.
The international experts' mandate expired in June 2025. So far, the Ukrainian authorities have not extended it.
Another clause concerns canceling the controversial 2017 amendments that dealt a major blow to corruption cases by severely limiting the terms of investigations and setting strict deadlines for sending cases to trial. Some of the amendments were repealed in 2023, but the main ones remain.
The plan also stipulates appointing, without delay, internationally vetted Constitutional Court judges and members of the High Council of Justice, the judiciary's main governing body.
Zelensky has so far failed to appoint one of the Constitutional Court judges nominated in February 2025, while the Ukrainian parliament failed to appoint two Constitutional Court judges the same year.
Oleg Sukhov is a reporter at the Kyiv Independent. He is a former editor and reporter at the Moscow Times. He has a master's degree in history from the Moscow State University. He moved to Ukraine in 2014 due to the crackdown on independent media in Russia and covered war, corruption, reforms and law enforcement for the Kyiv Post.

title: EU adopts new sanctions in response to Russian airstrikes on Kyiv
description: "Each new attack on Ukraine is another reason for Europe to tighten the screws on Russia," Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, said.
content:
Editor's note: This article was updated to include the reaction of Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The EU voted through five new sanctions listings targeting Russia's military-industrial complex on Aug. 7, Kaja Kallas, the EU's top diplomat, said.
Russia has taken advantage of Ukraine's lack of adequate air defenses to bombard Kyiv and civilian areas across the country. Moscow dropped more glide bombs on Ukraine in July than in any month since the start of the full-scale invasion.
"Each new attack on Ukraine is another reason for Europe to tighten the screws on Russia," Kallas wrote.
Of the five new listings, an EU official highlighted to the Kyiv Independent Ramil Badgutdinov, General Director of JSC Serpukhov Plant Metallist, which produces precision electromechanical components, used in systems such as Russia's Iskander-M ballistic missile.
They also mentioned Aleksandr Dyukarev, who leads JSC "Krasnoyarsk Machine-Building Plant", a company producing ballistic missiles, including the RS-28 "Sarmat" missile system
Rounding out the five listings were the Directors of Irz-Svyaz, which produces navigation components for Russian missiles; drone software company Aeromaks; and the space and military company JSC Research Instrument of Precision Instruments NII TP.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha thanked Kallas for pushing through the latest EU sanctions, and reiterated that "every act of terror must be met with a resolute response."
The EU's External Action Service, which Kallas heads, is discussing a new package of listings with EU countries of as many as 1,600 to 2,000 separate entries, two EU officials told the Kyiv Independent.
"The EU must continue to intensify pressure on Russia until Moscow ends its war," Kallas wrote.

title: Russian attacks kill 9, injure 89 across Ukraine over past day as Dnipropetrovsk Oblast comes under nearly 80 attacks
description: Russia launched 147 Shahed-type drones against Ukraine overnight on Aug. 7, with air defenses shooting down 114 of them, the Air Force said.
content:
Russian attacks killed at least nine people and injured 89 others across Ukraine over the past day, while Dnipropetrovsk Oblast came under attack nearly 80 times, local authorities said on Aug. 7.
Russian forces killed five people and injured 16 others over the past day in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast in southeastern Ukraine , a region that remained deep behind the front lines until July last year.
In his evening and morning updates on Russian attacks on Aug. 6 and Aug. 7 , Governor Oleksandr Hanzha said Russian forces struck the region about 80 times using drones, artillery, guided aerial bombs, and missiles.
In addition, Russia launched 147 Shahed-type drones against Ukraine overnight on Aug. 7, with air defenses shooting down 114 of them, the Air Force said. The remaining 29 drones hit 15 locations, while debris from downed drones fell at four other sites.
In Kherson Oblast , Russian forces targeted 39 settlements, including the regional center of Kherson, killing one person and injuring 32 others, including a child, over the past day, the local military administration said.
In Kharkiv Oblast , Russian forces killed two men and injured 11 others in the city of Lozova, while seven more people were injured elsewhere across the region, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said.
In Donetsk Oblast , Russian attacks killed one person in Bilenke and injured five others elsewhere in the region, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast , 10 people were injured in Russian attacks, the local military administration said.
In Sumy Oblast , eight people suffered injuries in Russian strikes over the past day, according to the local military administration .

title: Ukraine attacks Wildberries logistics center in Russia located nearly 2,000 km from front line
description: The first photos and videos emerged on Russian social media around 5 a.m. local time, showing smoke rising from the Wildberries facility.
content:
Ukrainian forces struck a logistics center belonging to Russian e-commerce giant Wildberries in the city of Yekaterinburg, Russia, on Aug. 7, Russian independent outlet Astra reported.
The first photos and videos emerged on Russian social media around 5 a.m. local time, showing smoke rising from the Wildberries facility.
About an hour earlier, Sverdlovsk Oblast Governor Denis Pasler said the region was under attack by Ukrainian drones , while Russia's Federal Air Transport Agency, Rosaviatsiya, imposed temporary flight restrictions at Koltsovo Airport in Yekaterinburg.
The strike, located about 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles) from the front line, sparked a large fire, according to the Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ .
Artem Zhoga, the Russian presidential envoy to the Ural Federal District, said no one was injured in the attack and that about 800 people were evacuated from the facility.
Wildberries also confirmed the attack on its facility, saying the fire had been contained and that the processing of new deliveries was temporarily restricted and redirected to other sites.
Pasler said Russian forces had allegedly downed eight drones over the region during the attack, three of which crashed onto the roof of the logistics center. Meanwhile, Russia's Defense Ministry said its air defenses had shot down a total of 203 Ukrainian drones overnight on Aug. 7.
The attack on the Wildberries warehouse is part of a broader Ukrainian campaign targeting facilities linked to the Russian retailer, which, among other activities, distributes dual-use goods that can be used in the production of Russian weapons.
The first strikes on Wildberries logistics centers began in late July. Since then, Ukrainian forces have targeted about 20 such facilities across various Russian regions and in Russian-occupied Crimea.
Meanwhile, on Aug. 5, Russian forces carried out a large-scale missile and drone attack on Ukraine, with Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast among the main targets. The strikes hit critical infrastructure, residential buildings, and numerous warehouses containing goods from international and Ukrainian brands, causing substantial losses for businesses.
Companies affected included German brands Liqui Moly and Puma, Japanese automaker Toyota, Ukrainian postal operator Nova Post, online marketplace Rozetka, retailer Epicentr-K, and grocery chain Silpo, among others.

title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,455,420 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
description: The figure includes 1,210 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
content:
Russia has lost around 1,455,420 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 7.
The figure includes 1,210 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report , Russia has also lost 12,247 tanks, 25,098 armored combat vehicles, 131,068 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,522 artillery systems, 2,008 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,550 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 447,855 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,152 unmanned ground systems, 34 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

title: US intel warns Russia could test NATO as early as this fall, WSJ reports
description: U.S. intelligence reports raised new alarms that Russian President Vladimir Putin could provoke a NATO nation with a limited attack as early as this fall, the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on Aug. 6.
content:
U.S. intelligence reports raised new alarms that Russian President Vladimir Putin could provoke a NATO nation with a limited attack as early as this fall, the Wall Street Journal (WSJ) reported on Aug. 6.
According to WSJ, officials in Washington previously believed that an attack on a NATO ally would not occur amid Russia's preoccupation with its war in Ukraine. The new-found belief by U.S. intelligence matches a chorus of similar warnings made by European officials in recent months.
In June, the head of Germany's army, Lieutenant General Christian Freuding, cautioned that Russia might have the capabilities to strike NATO countries within the next three years. According to WSJ, U.S. officials believe that a large-scale hybrid-warfare attack, or even limited land incursion, may come between the fall of this year and 2029. The latest intelligence report comes amid warnings from European countries that Russia may also attempt to use false flag-style attacks using Ukrainian-made drones to strike critical infrastructure in the Baltic region.
"The Kremlin, Putin, needs a new escalation, some kind of new victory, and in this case the Baltic region and Poland are the closest targets," Lithuania Defense Minister Robert Kaunas told LRT Radio on Aug. 6, voicing new intelligence.
The statement came after drone incidents and incursions in all three Baltic states have raised tensions in the region in recent months. On Aug. 5, an unidentified drone was found near a Ukrainian aircraft while another collided with a DHL plane at Leipzig airport in Germany.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the incident as a "hybrid attack scenario." He did not name Russia but the Kremlin has been waging a hybrid war aimed at destabilizing European countries for several years.
Citing unnamed U.S. officials, WSJ reported that recent Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure and minimal gains on the battlefield could push Putin to attempt to secure a victory against NATO. The attack would likely target NATO’s eastern flank to test the alliance’s Article 5 commitments — the collective defense clause for member nations.
The warnings from the intelligence communities come amid reports that the U.S. now faces shortages for critical munitions amid its ongoing war with Iran. Certain long-range and short-range missile system stockpiles, such as Patriot systems and Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) interceptors, remain low, according to the WSJ. In response to the shortages, U.S. President Donald Trump said that the United States "needs missiles too" on Aug. 6 when President Volodymyr Zelensky renewed calls for military aid.
Allied supplies of air defense missiles to Ukraine fell by two-thirds in the first half of this year compared with the same period in 2025, Zelensky said on Aug. 5.
Taking advantage of defense shortfalls, Russian forces have increased strikes on Kyiv. On Aug. 5, ballistic missile and drone attacks killed 17 people near the capital and injured dozens more. Ukraine's Air Force said Russia launched 24 ballistic and four hypersonic missiles during the attack, as well as 115 Shahed-type drones. None of the missiles were intercepted.

title: Despite frustration over country's direction, majority of Ukrainians want future in NATO, EU, survey finds
description: Nearly 70% of Ukrainians support joining the EU, and over 60% of Ukrainians support joining NATO amid growing frustration with the government, according to a new survey by the Socis Center for Social Research released on Aug. 6.
content:
Nearly 70% of Ukrainians support joining the EU, and over 60% of Ukrainians support joining NATO amid growing frustration with the government, according to a new survey by the Socis Center for Social Research released on Aug. 6.
The survey , conducted between July 28 and Aug. 2, polled 2,000 Ukrainians about their views on the outlook of the war and attitudes towards the government.
If a referendum for Ukraine to join the EU was held in the near future, only 22.2% of those polled would vote against it, survey results show. If a similar vote was held to join NATO, 29.5% of respondents said they would vote it down.
This most recent polling was conducted days before Ukraine's Ambassador to the U.K. and former Commander-in-Chief Valerii Zaluzhnyi claimed that Ukraine would "never" become a member of NATO on Aug. 3. Ukraine's Foreign Ministry has since sought to clarify the statement, claiming that the remarks had been "taken out of context," noting that the ambassador's full answer referred primarily to the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF), not NATO.
Despite an optimistic views of Ukraine's potential future accessions, over half of the respondents, 55.6%, believe the embattled nation is moving in the wrong direction.
The survey found that a total of 35.1% of respondents believe the general situation in Ukraine is likely to worsen in the next year, compared to 23.3% who believe it will improve.
The biggest issues negatively impacting the country, respondents say, is governmental corruption, attacks on energy and civilian infrastructure, and declining living standards. 50.5% of those polled believe that corruption in the country is "very high"
When asked about their views on the nation’s political leaders, survey participants said they most trust former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov and Zaluzhnyi. The survey shows strong support for Fedorov following weeks of protests against his dismissal by President Zelensky. 62.5% of respondents said they had mostly negative attitudes regarding his removal.
Fedorov’s trust rating soared from 35% to 65% following his ouster, surpassing Zelensky, according to separate opinion poll published by Rating Group on July 22.
Fedorov, on Aug. 3, said that he still hopes to return to his previous post.

title: 'We want missiles too' — Trump responds to Zelensky's appeal for additional military aid
description: U.S. President Donald Trump said on Aug. 6 that the United States "needs missiles too" when asked about President Volodymyr Zelensky's latest appeal for long-range missiles and Patriot air defense systems.
content:
U.S. President Donald Trump said on Aug. 6 that the United States "needs missiles too" when asked about President Volodymyr Zelensky's renewed calls for long-range missiles and Patriot air defense systems.
Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump also commented on former President Joe Biden's military support for Ukraine, claiming Biden had provided "so much" military assistance.
"We want missiles too," Trump said. "Biden gave (Zelensky) $300 billion worth of ammunition."
Trump argued that the military aid had depleted U.S. stockpiles, saying the country is now rebuilding its arsenal and relying on munitions it otherwise may not have needed to use.
When asked about Russia's increased attacks on civilian targets, Trump said the U.S. was not directly involved in the war.
"Look, we're not involved. We're separated by an ocean," Trump stated.
He noted, however, that he was troubled by the war's casualty toll.
"I hate to see 25,000 young people a month get killed," Trump said, claiming that Russia and Ukraine are losing "on average 25,000 people each month, mostly soldiers."
As Russia continues to increase the number of ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine, Kyiv is seeking ways to strengthen its defenses.
Zelensky has appealed to Trump for a license to produce Patriot air defense missiles domestically, while the White House said it has not yet made a final decision on the request.

title: 'I have no moral right to engage in anything else' — Fedorov hopes for reinstatement as defense minister
description: Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said he still hopes to return to the post after being dismissed during the government's recent reshuffle, speaking on Serhii Sternenko's Aug. 6 YouTube show.
content:
Former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said he still hopes to return to the post after being dismissed during the government's recent reshuffle, speaking on Serhii Sternenko's Aug. 6 YouTube show.
"I currently have no moral right to engage in anything else," Fedorov said . "While people are fighting for tomorrow and my name is being mentioned... today there is no clear 'no,' I believe we always have a chance."
Fedorov noted that Ukraine currently has only an acting defense minister, Yevhenii Khmara, who cannot vote on Cabinet decisions.
"This may be a temporary situation, but it cannot go on for long," he said, adding that it would be "irresponsible" for the country to remain without a permanent defense minister after parliament returns from recess on Aug. 18, when lawmakers will again be able to approve a ministerial appointment.
Asked what he would do if he is not reinstated, Fedorov said he would wait until after parliament returns before discussing his future.
"Let's wait until we pass those dates, and then I will talk more about my path and what we will do. I have options B, C, D, and so on," he said.
Fedorov stressed that, regardless of whether he returns to the ministry, he intends to continue contributing to Ukraine's war effort.
"It is important to work towards our victory," he said, adding that Ukraine does not have "hundreds of teams with hundreds of people who understand the war and are ready to serve their country 24/7."
"We will find a format in which we will serve our country regardless," he added.
Fedorov also said he had already handed his action plan for the ministry to acting Defense Minister Khmara.
Asked whether President Volodymyr Zelensky had remained in contact with him since his dismissal, Fedorov replied: "We have had some communication," without further details.
During his tenure, Fedorov oversaw a series of high-profile reforms and initiatives aimed at strengthening Ukraine's military capabilities.
Fedorov, who was widely seen as highly effective, was removed as defense minister on July 16. Since then, thousands of people have taken to the streets to demand the reinstatement of the minister.
While a new government has since been approved, parliament has yet to appoint permanent defense and foreign ministers.
Zelensky said on July 21 that he had offered Fedorov "a prominent position in the government" focused on strengthening Ukraine's technological sector.
Fedorov has rejected alternative government roles, maintaining that he is prepared to serve only as defense minister.

title: The downfall of Ukraine’s ex-ambassador to US, explained
description:
Olha Stefanishyna, Ukraine's former ambassador to the U.S. and deputy prime minister for European integration, was widely regarded as an effective manager.

But her involvement in several corruption investigations cast a shadow over her career and likely contributed to her dismissal as ambassador on Aug. 3.

On Aug. 5, authorities charged Stefanishyna with illicit enrichment totaling Hr 13.9 million ($310,000) and filing false asset declarations. She denies the allegations.

For critics of Presi
content:
Olha Stefanishyna, former Ukrainian Ambassador to the United States, attends a hearing at the High Anti-Corruption Court of Ukraine in Kyiv, Ukraine, on Aug. 5, 2026. (Ivan Antypenko / Suspilne Ukraine / Global Images Ukraine / Getty Images)
Olha Stefanishyna, Ukraine's former ambassador to the U.S. and deputy prime minister for European integration, was widely regarded as an effective manager.
But her involvement in several corruption investigations cast a shadow over her career and likely contributed to her dismissal as ambassador on Aug. 3.
On Aug. 5, authorities charged Stefanishyna with illicit enrichment totaling Hr 13.9 million ($310,000) and filing false asset declarations. She denies the allegations.
For critics of President Volodymyr Zelensky, the timing of the case has reinforced broader concerns about how his administration handles senior officials accused of corruption.
Opposition lawmaker Yaroslav Yurchyshyn argued that Stefanishyna remained in high office despite longstanding allegations because loyalty, rather than integrity, is the president's overriding criterion for key appointments.
"The main issue is the Zelensky team's reluctance to bring in people from outside his inner circle," Yurchyshyn told the Kyiv Independent. "Loyalty takes precedence over common-sense logic."
He argued that the authorities also believe they can bring anti-corruption institutions under control and shield Zelensky's close allies from prosecution.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comments from Stefanishyna and the President's Office and will publish their responses once they are received.
Stefanishyna, 40, has degrees in international law, English translation, and finance.
She has been involved in European integration since she worked at the Justice Ministry under pro-Western President Viktor Yushchenko in the late 2000s.
When Yushchenko was voted out in favor of pro-Russian President Viktor Yanukovych , she kept her seat, being later promoted to deputy head and then head of the Justice Ministry's department for international law and European integration.
Yanukovych was ousted by the 2014 EuroMaidan Revolution .
Olena Lukash, justice minister from 2013 to 2014, and Stefanishyna were charged in 2019 with embezzlement allegedly carried out during Yanukovych's presidency.
Lukash and Stefanishyna allegedly embezzled Hr 2.52 million ($315,000 at the 2013 exchange rate) in government funds intended for bringing Ukrainian law in line with European legislation, according to the investigators.
Stefanishyna allegedly played a crucial role in the embezzlement scheme since she was responsible for signing the documents, a source familiar with the investigation told the Kyiv Independent.
In 2023, the case was sent to the High Anti-Corruption Court .
However, the trial has been delayed by the defense, and there are concerns that it may be closed due to the statute of limitations, Roman Verbovskyi, a lawyer at the Anti-Corruption Action Center, told the Kyiv Independent.
" In the positions she held (under Yanukovych), Stefanishyna was more of an implementer than a decision-maker," opposition lawmaker Yurchyshyn said in turn.
"But the real question is whether concerns should already have been raised when she joined Zelensky's team, given that she had already been charged in the Lukash case. Should that have given the authorities a sign?"
From 2017 to 2019, Stefanishyna also worked as the head of the government office responsible for European integration.
In the 2019 parliamentary election, Stefanishyna unsuccessfully ran on the list of then-Prime Minister Volodymyr Groysman's party.
Later, Stefanishyna served as deputy prime minister for European integration from 2020 to 2025 and as justice minister from 2024 to 2025.
Stefanishyna was likely put in charge of European integration because she already had vast experience in the area, according to Yurchyshyn.
"She was seen as fairly effective," political analyst Volodymyr Fesenko told the Kyiv Independent. "I've heard positive feedback from both European diplomats and Ukrainian journalists who cover European integration."
Yurchyshyn admitted that she had been effective but argued that she was involved in blocking some reforms in the interests of Zelensky's former Chief of Staff, Andriy Yermak.
"Loyalty takes precedence over common-sense logic."
" She consistently acted as an advocate for the positions of the President's Office and the government while maintaining strong working relations with the European Union," Yurchyshyn said. "She managed to do so far more skillfully than many of her predecessors."
Stefanishyna interfered in the contest for the selection of the National Agency for Corruption Prevention's (NACP) chief in 2024, an anti-corruption prosecutor said at a court hearing on Aug. 6.
She promoted some candidates and tried to kick out others, according to the prosecutor.
Stefanishyna has also been investigated by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau for alleged corruption at the Asset Recovery and Management Agency ( ARMA ), but has not been charged so far in that case. Ukrainian media reported in 2025 that companies linked to Stefanishyna's former husband had received contracts to manage assets seized by the ARMA.
In 2025, Stefanishyna was suddenly appointed as ambassador to the U.S.
"She was very active as ambassador," Fesenko said. "She worked closely with both members of Congress and senators, and was involved in a number of legislative initiatives. In other words, she did her job well."
Fesenko alleged, however, that "Yermak maintained exclusive control over the U.S. portfolio and contacts with the White House," and "her direct contacts with the White House were limited."
" When she first arrived in the U.S., it was clear that adapting wasn't easy for her," a senior government official told the Kyiv Independent. "At first, she struggled to settle into the new environment. By the end of her tenure, though, it felt like she had fully found her footing. She had built the right contacts, established working relationships with the Treasury Department and other institutions, and overall gave the impression of being completely comfortable in the role."
Zelensky dismissed Stefanishyna from her post on Aug. 3. The senior government official said she had resigned of her own accord.
Both Fesenko and Yurchyshyn argued that the most plausible reason for her dismissal is the illicit enrichment case.
Stefanishyna's decision to resign was perceived by analysts as the trigger for a government reshuffle in mid-July since Prime Minister Yuliia Svyrydenko was expected to replace Stefanishyna as Ukraine's ambassador to the U.S.
If a prime minister resigns, the entire cabinet is ousted.
However, a person with direct knowledge of the matter told the Kyiv Independent that Svyrydenko hasn't agreed to accept the post, hinting that the president has jumped the gun with the reshuffle.
The Ukrainian authorities still don't know whom to replace Stefanishyna with, a senior government official said.

title: Zelensky to make first-ever visit to Serbia on Aug. 8, source says
description: President Volodymyr Zelensky is set to make his first trip to Serbia on Aug. 8, a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
content:
President Volodymyr Zelensky is set to make his first trip to Serbia on Aug. 8, a senior Ukrainian official told the Kyiv Independent.
The trip is seen as symbolic, as Serbia has traditionally maintained close ties with Russia.
Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Serbia has sought to strike a careful diplomatic balance between Moscow and the West.
Russia has historically been one of Serbia's key diplomatic allies, and Serbia relied heavily on Russia for natural gas .
Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic attended Moscow's Victory Day Parade in 2025 but was notably absent this year.
According to reports, Serbia has indirectly supplied arms to Ukraine, although Vucic publicly denied it in May 2025.
At the time, Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service, the SVR, accused Serbia's defense industry of "trying to shoot Russia in the back."
Vucic made his first official trip to Ukraine in June 2025 as part of the Ukraine-Southeast Europe summit in Odesa.
Unlike the other participants at the summit, Vucic did not sign a joint declaration that denounced Russia's illegal aggression, called for a full withdrawal of Russian forces from Ukraine, and reaffirmed support for Ukraine's territorial integrity.
At the summit, Vucic claimed he wanted to go beyond political declarations and provide practical assistance to Kyiv.
Vucic was also among a recent delegation of European leaders who visited Kyiv on July 15, Ukraine's Statehood Day.

title: Ukraine war latest: Lithuania warns of Russian false flag drone threat to Baltic states
description:
Key developments on Aug. 6:

 * Russia could use Ukrainian drones in false-flag strike against Baltic infrastructure, Lithuania says
 * Drone targeted Ukrainian cargo plane carrying ammunition at German airport, media reports
 * Russian drone kills 2 railway workers at station in Kharkiv Oblast
 * Ukraine hits 2 Russian oil refineries in latest deep strike drone attack, Zelensky says
 * NATO fighter jet scrambles increase 250% as Russia tests border with military planes, Alliance says

Lithuania
content:
Lithuania has intelligence suggesting Russia could use Ukrainian-made drones to carry out false flag-style attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region, the country's Defense Minister Robert Kaunas told local media outlet 15min on Aug. 6.
The statement comes after drone incidents and incursions in all three Baltic states — both from Ukrainian deep-strike drones and suspicious drones likely to be Russian — have raised tensions in the region.
"We have data that Russia is considering unconventional kinetic attacks on critical infrastructure in the Baltic region. Russia is likely to use Ukrainian production drones to do so," said Kaunas.
Just a day earlier, an unidentified first-person view (FPV) drone reportedly attacked a Ukrainian cargo plane at Leipzig airport in Germany.
Over 2026, Ukrainian long-range drones targeting oil infrastructure in Russia's Leningrad Oblast have strayed into the airspace of Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia, and Finland.
Likely diverted off course by Russian GPS jamming and spoofing, they have, on several occasions, exploded, such as in March 2026, when Ukrainian drones landed in both Latvia and Estonia in a single night.
Meanwhile, Russia has on several occasions been found using drones to test NATO's response on the alliance's eastern flank, most notably in September 2025, when 21 drones without explosives flew into Polish airspace.
On July 30, Kaunas had warned that Russian President Vladimir Putin was considering escalatory attacks or provocations in the Baltics as advances on the front line in Ukraine were stalling.
According to the Lithuanian defense minister: " Russian society is already asking the regime" why it has thus far failed to achieve a victory in Ukraine while Russia itself faces strikes and fuel shortages.
"The Kremlin, (Russian President Vladimir) Putin, needs a new escalation, some kind of new victory, and in this case the Baltic region and Poland are the closest targets," Kaunas told LRT Radio .
Recent weeks saw leaders from both Poland and Lithuania — two NATO nations bordering Moscow's ally Belarus and the heavily armed Russian exclave of Kaliningrad — warn about potential Russian provocations against their countries.
A Ukrainian cargo plane targeted by a drone carrying explosives at Germany's Leipzig/Halle Airport was loaded with ammunition at the time of the incident, German media reported on Aug. 6.
Flights at the airport were suspended overnight on Aug. 5 after a " modified drone " was sighted and later found next to a Ukrainian Antonov Airlines An-124 transport aircraft, and a second "unidentified flying object" collided with an incoming DHL cargo plane.
Citing police reports, Suddeutsche Zeitung said the Antonov Airlines plane had been transporting an unspecified type of military ammunition from France to Leipzig, which was still onboard when the drone was found.
The outlet also said the drone was carrying Semtex, a military-grade explosive. Those behind the attempted attack are yet to be identified.
Speaking on Aug. 5, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described the incident as a " hybrid attack scenario ."
He did not name Russia but the Kremlin has been waging a hybrid war aimed at destabilizing European countries for several years.
"Drone threats, including hybrid threats, are something we are familiar with from the past. However, the fact that a drone — armed with explosives — is on airport property is a new threat scenario," he said.
Suspected Russian-linked drone incidents have repeatedly disrupted airports across Europe, causing flight suspensions and diversions.
Leipzig/Halle Airport has served as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines since shortly after the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion. According to the German outlet Bild, four Ukrainian cargo aircraft were present during the suspected attack.
A Russian drone struck the railway station of Lozova in Kharkiv Oblast on the morning of Aug. 6, killing two people and injuring eight others, regional authorities and Ukrainian Railways both reported.
A train carriage was struck while at the station, Ukrainian Railways President Oleksandr Pertsovskyi confirmed, adding that the two men killed were both railway workers.
According to Ukrainian Railways, the attack was preceded by an air raid alert that should have given people enough time to move to special shelters installed at the station.
Located near the border with front-line Donetsk Oblast, Lozova has become an important logistical hub for the defense of Ukraine's east.
After trains stopped running to Kramatorsk in Donetsk Oblast last year, Lozova is now the last stop on the line heading east, making the station a common meeting point for soldiers, volunteers, and residents evacuated from front-line areas.
Ukrainian drones struck two oil refineries deep inside Russian territory overnight on Aug. 6, including a large refinery in Yaroslavl Oblast hit for the second night in a row, President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed after reports first emerged in local media.
Videos emerging online the morning after showed a large-scale fire at the Slavneft-Yanos oil refinery in Yaroslavl, over 700 kilometers (435 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Footage shared by Yaroslavl residents on Aug. 6 showed plumes of smoke rising over the city during an overnight drone attack. The independent Russian Telegram news channel Astra analyzed the footage using geolocation and determined that the Slavneft-Yanos refinery was on fire.
Another smaller refinery was hit further east in Russia's Bashkortostan Republic, Zelensky reported , over 1,300 kilometers from the front line.
"Today, our long-range sanctions once again worked to limit Russia’s oil revenues, which it uses to finance the war and the killing of Ukrainians," the president wrote on Facebook.
NATO fighter jets were scrambled over twice as many times in July 2026 as they were during the same period last year, the NATO Allied Joint Force Command in Eastern and Central Europe reported on Aug. 5.
The report follows an uptick in unregistered Russian military flights near NATO's eastern border.
"Compare July 25 with July 26 and the picture is impossible to ignore: Alpha Scrambles along NATO'sEastern Flank increased by more than 250%," the Alliance said .
"The reason? Russian military aircraft repeatedly flew close to NATO airspace without a flight plan and transponder signal, leaving our fighters to launch, intercept, and identify them."
NATO countries regularly dispatch fighter jets in response to suspicious Russian military activity.
The latest report comes a week after Poland's Air Force launched fighter jets on July 31 to intercept a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft flying over the Baltic Sea without a flight plan. No violation of Poland's airplace occurred during the incident, authorities said.
The Russian Ilyushin Il-20, derived from the Soviet-era Il-18 transport plane, is used for electronic surveillance and reconnaissance operations. The aircraft is equipped with radar and signal intelligence systems designed to gather information on military infrastructure and communications networks.
Poland has described these incidents as "provocations" and acts of aggression meant to test the country's air defenses.
Multiple nations bordering the Baltic Sea have reported similar encounters this summer.
"Every scramble proves that we are alert," the Alliance said on Aug. 5. "Every interception proves that NATO airspace is protected."

title: What did Ukraine's '40-day campaign' against Russia deliver?

But 40 days later, Russia's
content:
A large plume of smoke rises over Wildberries logistics facilities in St. Petersburg, Russia on July 24, 2026. (Stringer / Anadolu / Getty Images)
In late June, President Volodymyr Zelensky tasked Ukraine's Security Service (SBU) with launching a "40-day influence operation" designed to compel Russia to "end the war."
In the weeks following, Ukraine's mid- and long-range drones scored some headline-grabbing successes — the crippling of dozens of Russian tankers supplying occupied Crimea and, perhaps most notably, the destruction of several warehouses across the country belonging to online retailer Wildberries.
But 40 days later, Russia's war in Ukraine still rages, and Russian President Vladimir Putin shows no signs that he intends to stop any time soon.
"I think the ultimate aim was not achievable given Putin's commitment to the war and Russian society's general apathy to and accommodation of the war," Dr. Jade McGlynn, head of the Ukraine and Russia Program at King's College London, told the Kyiv Independent.
But according to Ukrainian officials familiar with the planning, one of the operation's central political objectives was looking further ahead than the stated 40 days — to force Russians to experience the consequences of the war more directly with a view to influencing elections in September.
Details of what the campaign actually constituted remained sparse until it ended, when the SBU released a statement on Aug. 4 clarifying the actions that the agency claimed were part of it.
According to the statement, the campaign "was aimed at simultaneously weakening key elements of the Russian military machine."
One of the significant military developments in the timescale of the "40-day operation" was a series of strikes against Russian oil and cargo vessels by Ukraine's Unmanned Systems Forces in the Sea of Azov, a part of Ukraine's months-long campaign to isolate the Crimean peninsula with drone and missile strikes.
Other long-standing Ukrainian military campaigns continued during the period. Ukraine's systematic demolition of Russia's oil industry continued, leading to shortages of diesel, gasoline, and other refined petroleum products across Russia, and long queues at gas stations.
"These successful strikes significantly hampered the resupply of Russian units on the front line and disrupted logistics and the supply of ammunition and fuel," Nazarii Barchuk, an analyst at the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, told the Kyiv Independent.
The SBU statement claimed that the campaign included "systematic destruction of military aviation and air defense," "kinetic sanctions on the Russian fuel and energy sector," "defeat of the ' shadow fleet '," as well as strikes against targets on the battlefield.
Although Kyiv publicly argues that Wildberries was targeted because it facilitated the sale of dual-use goods , officials speaking privately acknowledged another objective.
While declining to confirm whether strikes on Wildberries facilities officially formed part of the campaign, one Ukrainian official said the attacks fit that broader strategy by disrupting Russia's strained wartime economy while affecting the daily lives of ordinary citizens.
Ukraine began striking warehouses of the Russian logistics giant " Wildberries " overnight on July 18. Frequently compared to the U.S. retail giant Amazon, Wildberries holds about 45-50% of the Russian e-commerce market, with a turnover of around $75 billion annually.
Wildberries also supplies significant amounts of explicitly military materiel, such as body armor, fiber-optic spools for military drones, and equipment that allows civilian drones to be converted to drop grenades, making the chain a potentially legitimate military target under international law.
As well as the direct financial impact on Wildberries itself, and the associated damage to the Russian economy of the loss of its e-commerce giant, the chain holds stock for tens of thousands of Russian small businesses.
As of Aug. 4, Ukraine claimed to have hit 15 Wildberries warehouses , damaging or destroying 13 of them. Reports of further strikes have emerged since then.
Russia also has more than 94,000 Wildberries pickup points, most of them operated by franchisees.
57% of Russians now report feeling anxious because of Ukrainian drone attacks.
In many smaller towns, those locations have become essential distribution hubs where residents collect everything from school supplies to household goods.
"When Russians prepare their children for school, they often order uniforms, notebooks, pencils, and other essentials through Wildberries," one Ukrainian official said.
Internal Ukrainian documents reviewed by the Kyiv Independent indicate that 57% of Russians now report feeling anxious because of Ukrainian drone attacks.
According to one Ukrainian official, exposure to strikes further increases those levels of anxiety.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the data, and officials declined to explain how it had been collected.
McGlynn told the Kyiv Independent she believed the operation had "clearly exacerbated existing strains and brought the war home to lots more people who wish to ignore it and its consequences."
Another factor shaping Kyiv's thinking is Russia's parliamentary election, scheduled for Sept. 18-20.
Ukrainian officials say they do not expect genuinely independent opposition parties to enter parliament.
Instead, they see the vote as an opportunity to weaken confidence in the Kremlin by showing the gap between public sentiment and official election results.
"If Russians go to the polls and vote against Putin's United Russia, then see the official results showing the party winning 60%, they'll understand the numbers were fabricated," one Ukrainian official said. "That changes how people perceive the legitimacy of the system."
Officials in Kyiv remain skeptical that any political party can gain parliamentary representation without Kremlin approval.
They pointed to nominal opposition groups, including Yabloko, which campaigns on a platform calling for peace, but argued that no meaningful parliamentary opposition can emerge without Moscow's consent.
One Ukrainian official said, citing internal documents, that Kyiv believes the rating of United Russia stands at around 30-33%, the lowest ever.
Officials also said that some top Ukrainian envoys remain in contact with several Russian business figures.
According to the officials, those conversations have become noticeably more pessimistic in recent months, particularly after Ukraine expanded strikes against economic targets such as Wildberries.
Several Russian businessmen have privately voiced frustration over the economic costs of the war, one Ukrainian official said.
Even as Kyiv continues to publicly promote proposals for an air ceasefire and a broader halt to hostilities, Ukrainian officials insist the decision ultimately depends on Putin.
The officials said Russian businessmen and oligarchs have repeatedly suggested that Putin might eventually be willing to compromise, only for the Kremlin to reject any such possibility.
In Kyiv's assessment, this shows that, despite frustration among parts of Russia's business elite, authority over decisions about the war remains concentrated in Putin's hands.
"This creates a dangerous precedent for him," the official said.

title: Draft officers searched in Zakarpattia amid allegations of over 1,000 illegal exemptions, media reports
description: According to local journalist Vitalii Hlahola, who cited sources in law enforcement, several current and former members of staff were searched in their homes.
content:
Staff of the Ukrainian military's draft offices and military medical commissions in the city of Mukachevo in Zakarpattia were allegedly searched on Aug. 6 by law enforcement in connection with over 1,000 alleged cases of men taken illegally off the draft register, Ukrainian media reported.
The alleged searches reflect persistent problems in Ukraine's strained mobilization system, where draft offices and medical commissions accept bribes from military-eligible men to provide exemption documents or remove them from the register entirely.
According to local journalist Vitalii Hlahola , who cited sources in law enforcement, several current and former members of staff were searched in their homes.
Two figures — former draft office head Yevhen Pilhui and his former deputy Ihor Hvozdynets — have already been charged, Hlahola said.
Other Ukrainian media, including Ukrainska Pravda and RBC-Ukraine, also reported the searches, citing their own sources.
The draft office of Zakarpattia Oblast denied reports of the searches in a post on Facebook, saying they "did not reflect reality."
According to the sources cited by Hlahola, around 500 of the military-eligible men involved in the scheme had left Ukraine, adding that the bribes paid for the "service" of being removed ran up to around $20,000.
Ukraine's State Bureau of Investigation , usually responsible for searches at draft offices nationwide, did not respond to the Kyiv Independent's request for comment.
Forced mobilization remains one of the greatest sources of social and political tension in Ukraine, as the military's need for the replenishment and rotation of combat units clashes with a reluctance to serve among much of the eligible male population not already in the armed forces' ranks.
While exemption letters are offered legally to those working in state structures, other essential roles or the defense industry, military-aged men looking to illegally avoid service have other options, including bribes paid for fake medical documents, removal from the register, or to leave Ukraine.
Bordering Romania, Hungary, Slovakia, and Poland, Zakarpattia Oblast has traditionally been a hub of illegal cross-border activity throughout the history of independent Ukraine, from flows of contraband in peacetime to illegal border crossing since Russia's full-scale invasion.

title: Germany arrests Ukrainian man suspected of spying on defense company for foreign intelligence
description: The Munich General Prosecutor's Office and the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office said that there are "strong grounds" to suspect the man was a "low-level agent" acting on behalf of the intelligence service of a foreign nation.
content:
A 33-year-old Ukrainian man has been arrested on suspicion of photographing the premises of a Bavarian defense company as part of a possible plot to carry out acts of sabotage, German authorities reported on Aug. 6.
The Munich General Prosecutor's Office and the Bavarian State Criminal Police Office said that there are "strong grounds" to suspect the man was a "low-level agent" acting on behalf of the intelligence service of a foreign nation.
While German authorities did not specify which foreign power the man is suspected of acting for, his arrest comes amid a string of previous detentions across Europe of individuals allegedly recruited by Russian security services as part of broader hybrid warfare efforts to sow discord.
Russian intelligence services offer easy money to so-called low-level agents to carry out sabotage operations on their behalf, according to Western authorities.
In early February, German authorities indicted a Ukrainian citizen in connection with an alleged Russian-orchestrated plot to send explosive packages across Europe.
Meanwhile, Polish prosecutors charged four Ukrainian citizens and one Russian citizen in early January with allegedly planning to deliver explosive devices to several Western countries.

title: Ukraine aids Hungary amid heatwave-induced energy crisis
description: High temperatures across Europe led Hungary to temporarily power down the country's only nuclear power plant on July 29 and increase electricity imports from its neighbors, including Ukraine.
content:
Kyiv exported 61 gigawatt hours in the last week of July to Budapest, reported the EU media Euractiv on Aug. 6, citing ENTSO-E, which represents European electricity grid operators.
High temperatures across Europe led Hungary to temporarily power down the country's only nuclear power plant on July 29 and increase electricity imports from its neighbors, including Ukraine.
Due to Russia's constant attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure , Ukraine has mostly been a net importer of electricity from Hungary.
But Ukraine's electricity grid has been synchronized with the wider EU grid since 2022, a process rushed through by the bloc to help Kyiv keep the lights on, but flows can move in both directions.
As much of Europe endures a record-breaking hot summer, nuclear power plants across the continent, which rely on water to cool their reactors, have had to wind down their operations because the water is either too hot or, in the case of Hungary, has nearly dried up altogether.
The Danube River's water level reached an all-time low in July, at only 30 centimeters in Budapest, which led Hungary to temporarily close its Paks Nuclear Plant for the first time ever.
The plant normally supplies half of the country's electricity.
Filling in that shortfall are the country's neighbors, with Ukraine second only to Poland in electricity exports to Hungary.
The Ukrainian and Hungarian governments did not respond to requests for comment by the time of publication.
However, Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar tweeted on Aug. 6 that the Paks Nuclear Plant is beginning to come back online, as the Danube's water level gradually recovers.
"Regardless of this, on today's hot day there will still be a strong need for voluntary reductions in electricity consumption," Magyar said.
A European Commission spokesperson said that in all countries experiencing production shortfalls due to the heatwave, neighboring countries can cover the gap.
"Our assessment at the moment is that the situation is stable and there are no immediate security or supply concerns," the spokesperson told journalists.

title: Russian drone kills 2 railway workers at station in Kharkiv Oblast as attacks kill at least 9, injure 84, across Ukraine over past day
description: A train carriage was struck while at the station, confirmed Ukrainian Railways President Oleksandr Pertsovskyi, who added that the two men killed were both railway workers.
content:
A Russian drone struck the railway station of Lozova in Kharkiv Oblast on the morning of Aug. 6, killing two people and injuring eight others, regional authorities and Ukrainian Railways both reported.
A train carriage was struck while at the station, Ukrainian Railways President Oleksandr Pertsovskyi confirmed, adding that the two men killed were both railway workers.
According to Ukrainian Railways, the attack was preceded by an air raid alert that should have given people enough time to move to special shelters installed at the station.
Located near the border with front-line Donetsk Oblast, Lozova has become an important logistical hub for the defense of Ukraine's east.
After trains stopped running to Kramatorsk in Donetsk Oblast last year, Lozova is now the last stop on the line heading east, making the station a common meeting point for soldiers, volunteers, and residents evacuated from front-line areas.
The attack came as at least nine civilians were killed and 84 more injured across Ukraine over the past 24 hours, regional authorities reported.
In Kharkiv Oblast itself, three people were killed and 14 more injured in the region over the previous day, oblast governor Oleh Syniehubov reported .
In neighboring Sumy Oblast, three people were killed, all by Russian drones, and a total of 24 injured as Russia continued attacks along both the front line and state border, the regional administration said.
One person was killed and nine more injured in Donetsk Oblast, according to regional authorities.
Russian attacks on 66 different settlements in front-line Zaporizhzhia Oblast killed one person and wounded four more, according to regional governor Ivan Fedorov.
In Odesa Oblast, a Russian attack on a civilian grain ship flying the flag of Guinea-Bissau left one person killed and three more injured, regional governor Oleh Kiper reported .
Over recent weeks, Russian forces have escalated a strike campaign against civilian shipping in the key Black Sea port.
A total of 20 people were injured in Kherson Oblast as Russia continued daily attacks with artillery, glide bombs, and drones on coastal communities on the Dnipro River, governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In neighboring Mykolaiv Oblast, a Russian Shahed-type drone attack injured six people, regional authorities said.
Two civilians were injured in attacks on Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, governor Oleksandr Hanzha said, after Russian drones attacked Nikopol district from the occupied side of the Dnipro River.
In northern Chernihiv Oblast, two women sought medical help after separate Russian attacks on settlements near the state border with Russia, governor Viacheslav Chaus said.

title: UK slaps fresh sanctions on Russian shadow fleet
description: "The U.K. will continue to step up our action against Russia and its shadow fleet activity to protect our national security, our economy, and global stability," said John Healey, the British economy minister.
content:
The U.K. government unveiled a new sanctions package against Russia on Aug. 6, which targets its banks, companies trading in rare metals, and six newly acquired shadow fleet tankers.
Russia works with a vast network of aging and often uninsured vessels , flying under the flags of other countries, to evade restrictive measures imposed by the U.K. and others against Russian fossil fuels .
New ships keep being identified as belonging to the Russian shadow fleet, presenting an ongoing challenge for countries wishing to enforce their sanctions have to continually update their listings to include these ships and the companies servicing them.
"The U.K. will continue to step up our action against Russia and its shadow fleet activity to protect our national security, our economy, and global stability," said British Economy Minister John Healey.
The latest shadow fleet listings come as European countries are adopting an increasingly assertive stance against suspect ships.
The U.K. , France , and Belgium have all boarded shadow fleet vessels in recent months, as has a joint EU naval mission .
Sweden not only intercepted a shadow fleet ship, but ruled that it and its cargo of grain, illegally taken from occupied territory in southern Ukraine, should be given back to Kyiv.
That development preceded EU countries agreeing in their latest 21st sanctions package to consider any shadow fleet ships they intercept, along with the cargo they carry, as income.
The British sanctions announcement also includes restrictions placed on six Russian banks and four Russian companies importing the rare earth metals tantalum and niobium, which the announcement says are "critical for producing military equipment used on the battlefield in Ukraine."
"Ukraine’s fight is our fight. Those that threaten Ukraine’s freedom and democracy are a threat to Britain’s security at home," said British Foreign Minister Ed Miliband.
"That’s why we will continue stepping up the pressure on Russia until a just and lasting peace has been reached."
